【中文】
第164章 一号实验场的红眼睛

地面以下一百米，翡冷翠郊外的荒野已经变成了另一个世界。

一号实验场不像工厂，更像一座教堂——没有窗户，没有装饰，只有粗粝的岩壁和密密麻麻的红水银蒸汽管道。那些管道从天花板上垂下来，像巨兽的血管，每隔几秒就脉动一次，发出沉闷的嘶嘶声。红水银蒸汽从管道的接缝处渗出来，凝成一层淡红色的雾气，永远笼罩着整个空间。空气是热的，带着金属的腥味，呼吸起来舌根发甜。

实验场的中央，站着两个人。

他们穿着黑色的机械甲胄，甲胄表面没有任何徽记，连编号都没有喷涂，只有暗哑的黑色金属在红雾中吸收着光线。他们的身高都超过三米，肩甲宽阔，手臂垂在身体两侧，姿态像两尊尚未启动的雕像。

但他们的眼睛是亮着的。

血红。像是有人在他们的瞳孔里灌入了融化的红水银，不是反射外界光线的亮，而是从内部燃烧出来的亮。那种红在红雾中几乎看不出来，只是偶尔转动头部的时候，虹膜边缘会闪过一丝金红色的光芒。

零号站在左边，一号站在右边。

他们已经在这里站了四个小时，一动不动。

---

脚步声从实验场的另一端传来。

不是靴子踩在金属地板上的声音，而是某种机械关节咬合时发出的咔嚓声，节奏稳定，像钟表内部的齿轮在转动。

原罪机关的主人走进红雾中。

他穿着一件白袍，在这座充斥着暗红与黑色的实验场里显得格外刺眼。白袍的下摆很长，几乎拖到地面，上面没有一粒灰尘，干净得不像是在这种地方行走的装束。他的脸上戴着白银面具，面具的造型是一只展开双翼的猫头鹰，遮住了整张脸，只露出下颌的一小片皮肤。

那下颌是金属的。

白色的精密金属，关节处有细小的铆钉，咬合时发出轻微的机械声。他的下颌是假的。

"时间到了。"

他开口说话。声音经过面具的过滤变得空洞，像是隔着一堵墙在说话。他走到两个骑士之间的位置停下，抬起右手。

右手也是机械的。

白金属的手指修长，每一节关节都露出精密的齿轮和弹簧，食指上套着一枚黑铁指环，指环上刻着与面具相同的猫头鹰徽记。他的机械手指在空气中按了一下——什么都没有发生，只是空气中多了一丝几不可闻的电磁嗡鸣。

大屏幕亮了。

屏幕嵌在实验场正面的岩壁上，足有十米宽、五米高，表面是磨砂玻璃的质感，放出的光却冷得像手术灯。大屏幕上先是一片雪花，然后画面逐渐清晰——

一条矿道。

宽度九米，层高不到十二米，岩壁上裸露着红水银矿脉的暗红色纹理。矿道从画面深处延伸过来，地面铺着废弃的铁轨，轨道上结着一层黑色的锈。尽头处是死路，但岩壁上被凿出了一个巨大的洞，洞口里透出暗红色的光，像是一头巨兽张开了嘴。

维苏威火山底部废弃矿道。

明天的战场。

"这就是你们明天的舞台。"原罪机关主人说。他的机械手指在空气中划了一下，大屏幕上的画面跟着放大，矿道的细节变得更加清晰——岩壁上加固用的钢梁、地面上的碎石堆、几处因塌方而变窄的瓶颈。

"记住每一个拐弯，每一个瓶颈，每一处可以藏身的凹壁。"他说，"明天的对抗战不在空旷的实验场进行，而是在这条矿道里。宽度九米，限制巨型傀儡的机动，但同时也限制了炽天使的闪避空间。你们要利用地形。"

零号骑士缓缓地抬起头。

她的脸被黑色的全覆式头盔遮住，只露出两枚血红的眼睛。当她开口时，声音是从头盔内部的机械合成器中传出的，没有音调，没有情感，只有均匀的电子振动。

"主人，我们准备好了。"

她停了一拍。

"一定会在明天的对抗战中杀死西泽尔，拿到不朽之王芯片。"

一号骑士没有立刻说话。他比零号高半个头，肩甲更宽，手臂上外挂着额外的蒸汽排管，像是随时准备释放超荷运转。他低着头盯着地面上某一块生锈的铁轨，沉默了三秒钟。

然后他抬起头。

"主人。"

他的声音是低沉的，经过了甲胄内部扩音器的放大，在红雾中产生轻微的回声。

"胡安已经没用了。"

他的血红色眼睛在红雾中亮了一下。

"我们可以随时处理掉他。"

原罪机关主人没有立刻回答。他缓缓地走到大屏幕前，白袍的下摆擦过金属地面，发出沙沙的声响。他站在那面巨大的冷光屏幕前，像一个站在祭坛前的主祭。

"胡安还有用。"

他说。

"他的试制机二号古洛诺斯是明天的诱饵。如果不让他上场，西泽尔就不会进入矿道。西泽尔不进入矿道，我们的计划就少了最关键的一环。"

他抬起机械手，食指点在大屏幕上矿道尽头那个透出暗红光的洞口上。

"你们要杀的不只是西泽尔。"

"那是西泽尔·博尔吉亚。密涅瓦机关的新型红龙。传说中百万分之一的适格者。他穿上甲胄的时候，神经系统会和机械完全耦合，那种耦合度是常人不可能达到的。"

他收回手指，转身面对两个骑士。白银面具上的猫头鹰在冷光中闪着银色的光。

"但他还有另一重身份。"

"他是锡兰星见的血脉后裔。紫瞳。"

这两个字在红雾中落下，像两块石头沉进深水。

"星见的紫瞳不只是颜色。它是意识通道的接口。百年前，锡兰末代星见残枝01号用自己的血和骨头封印了一个东西在红水银深处——世界树的根。根的意识需要一个载体才能被激活，需要一个和残枝01号拥有同源血脉的人来连接。"

他停顿了一拍。机械下颌的关节发出咔的一声。

"西泽尔是唯一能同时连接残枝意识与保留人性的人。"

零号骑士的血红色眼睛没有变化。一号骑士的红色瞳孔微微收缩了一下。

"只要抓住他，"原罪机关主人说，"就能重启机械神国。"

这六个字像一把刀劈开了实验场沉闷的空气。管道中的红水银蒸汽似乎脉动得更剧烈了，嘶嘶声变得更加急促。

大屏幕上的画面突然闪烁了一下。

矿道的画面消失了，取而代之的是另一幅图像——

一座巨大的黑铁门。

门高五米，宽三米，表面镌刻着密密麻麻的圣言和古老印记，六角形的铆钉排列成蜂窝状的图案。门是关着的，但门缝中透出一丝极淡的金色光芒，像是有什么东西在门的另一边燃烧。

黑铁巨门前的阴影里，站着一个人。

她穿着黑色的长袍，兜帽拉得很低，只露出下半张脸——嘴唇苍白，下颌线条锋利，嘴角微微下弯，像是永远在冷笑。她的一只手按在黑铁门上，手指间夹着一枚小小的五芒星印记。

达斯蒙德的姑姑。

她似乎感觉到了什么，缓缓地抬起头，兜帽下的眼睛看向了大屏幕的方向——像是隔着屏幕与画外的人对视。

画面消失。

大屏幕重新变回了雪花，然后又恢复了矿道的图像。

原罪机关主人站在屏幕前没有动。

"她也来了。"他低声说，声音里第一次出现了某种微妙的情绪——不是恐惧，是期待。

他转身走回两个骑士之间。白袍在红雾中划出一道弧线。他抬起机械右手，从袍袖中取出一个东西——

一个遥控器。

黑色的，巴掌大小，表面只有一个按钮。按钮旁边刻着一行极小的文字，需要凑近才能看清——

"世界树残枝激活开关"。

他用拇指按住那个按钮，但没有按下去。

"明天的对抗战不是测试普罗米修斯和炽天使孰强孰弱。"

他说。

"密涅瓦机关以为这是一场公开的武器对抗战，胜者会成为教皇国未来的主力武装。枢机会以为这是一场展示武力的表演，各方势力都会派人来观战。"

"他们都不知道矿道的尽头通往什么。"

"那条矿道在四十年前被前任密涅瓦总长封闭时，矿道尽头被凿通了一条岔路，岔路通向维苏威火山的更深层——"

"骷髅地。"

这两个字落下来的时候，零号骑士和一号骑士同时微微侧头。

骷髅地。

密涅瓦机关维苏威火山深处被前代总长封锁的禁区。传说里面存放着会自行活动的灵异炽天使甲胄残骸。那里是甲胄的坟场，也是甲胄的子宫。

"世界树残枝02号就在骷髅地的最深处。"

原罪机关主人说。

"残枝01号是锡兰末代星见，她用自己的血和骨头封印了世界树的根，意识沉入红水银深处，阻止根的意识苏醒。但01号不是唯一的残枝——02号是她的妹妹，在01号封印世界树之前就已经被原罪机关的前身找到了，一直封存在骷髅地中。"

"01号的封印是不完整的。因为02号还在。"

"世界树需要两片残枝合一才能完全苏醒。01号用她的命阻止了这件事，但她的意识已经随着西泽尔一起苏醒——西泽尔穿甲胄的时候，会触碰到红水银深处的封印层，他的血脉就是钥匙。"

他的机械手指在遥控器上轻轻敲了两下。

"明天，西泽尔穿上新型红龙进入矿道，战斗的余波会震碎矿道尽头的封印层。骷髅地会打开。残枝02号会被释放。"

"而当残枝01号的意识通过西泽尔与残枝02号接触的时候——"

他没有说完这句话。

他按下了按钮。

咔。

实验场中央的金属地面开始震动。零号骑士和一号骑士同时后退了一步。地面上的铁轨开始扭曲，螺丝从螺栓孔中弹射出来，发出清脆的金属声。地面中央出现了一条裂缝，裂缝以极快的速度扩展，伴随着蒸汽管爆裂的嘶嘶声，红水银蒸汽从裂缝中喷涌而出。

地面裂开了。

裂口的中央，缓缓升起一个平台。平台上是一具被铁链锁住的巨型机械甲胄。

那具甲胄的高度超过了五米，全身覆盖着暗金色的装甲板，装甲板上镌刻着密密麻麻的圣言和古老印记，每一道刻痕中都流淌着微弱的金色光芒。它没有头盔——头部是一个完整的球形面罩，面罩的表面光滑如镜，映出实验场中的红雾和三个人的身影。

它的胸前镶嵌着一块巨大的红水银核心。

核心是暗红色的，跳动着，像一颗心脏。

欧米茄。

不是密涅瓦机关封存的那一具。是原罪机关秘密制造的原型体。

铁链缠绕在它的四肢和躯干上，每一条铁链都有成人手臂那么粗，链环是黑铁铸造的，表面刻着和骷髅地黑铁巨门相同的古老印记。但那些铁链已经在铁链与甲胄的接缝处生出了锈迹——不是因为潮湿，而是因为甲胄内部溢出的能量在持续腐蚀着束缚。

原罪机关主人站在裂口的边缘，俯视着这具被铁链锁住的巨神。

"它已经饿了四十年了。"

他说。声音里的那种期待变得更浓了，像是火焰从灰烬中重新燃起。

零号骑士和一号骑士的血红色眼睛同时亮了一下。

而在大屏幕的角落里，一行几乎看不清的字符正在闪烁——

"残枝02号……同步率……上升中。"

九个小时后，维苏威火山底部废弃矿道。

五条龙和一头钢铁巨兽将在这里相遇。

而那具被铁链锁住的巨神，也将在那里醒来。

【English】
Chapter 164 — The Red Eyes of Site One

A hundred metres below the earth, the barren land beyond the walls of Florence had become another country.

Site One was no factory. It was a chapel cut from raw stone. No windows, no ornament, only the rough-hewn rock walls and a dense thicket of red-mercury steam pipes. The pipes descended from the ceiling in thick bundles, as if some enormous beast had threaded its veins through the stone, and every few seconds they pulsed — a slow, heavy throb that ran through the entire cavern, accompanied by a muffled hiss. Red mercury vapour leaked from the joints of the pipes, settling into a thin red mist that never quite lifted. The air was hot, tasted of metal, and lay on the tongue with a faint sweet burn.

In the centre of the experimental hall, two figures stood.

They were clad in black mechanical armour. The armour bore no insignia, no painted number, no maker's mark — only dull black metal that drank the light of the red mist. Both stood over three metres tall, broad at the shoulders, their arms hanging at their sides. They were posed like two statues that had not yet been told to move.

But their eyes were lit.

Blood red. As if someone had poured molten red mercury into their pupils. The glow was not a reflection of the surrounding mist; it came from inside, burning outward. In the red haze, the colour was almost invisible — except when one of them turned its head, and a thin ring of gold-red fire flashed at the edge of the iris.

Zero stood on the left. One stood on the right.

They had stood there, motionless, for four hours.

---

Footsteps sounded from the far end of the hall.

Not the sound of boots on metal flooring. Something else — a soft mechanical clicking, the steady rhythm of a clockwork joint engaging and releasing, engaging and releasing. The rhythm of a heartbeat that had been replaced by cogs.

The master of the Original Sin Bureau walked into the red mist.

He wore a white robe, and in that hall of dark red and dull black the white was unbearable. The hem of the robe nearly touched the floor. There was not a single speck of dust on the cloth. The garment did not belong in such a place, and yet it showed no sign of soiling. His face was covered by a silver mask — a mask shaped like an owl with its wings spread. The mask hid everything except a small triangle of skin beneath the jaw.

That jaw was metal.

White, precise metal, articulated with tiny rivets at the joints. When he spoke, the jaw clicked faintly, as if gears were grinding against each other. His jaw was false.

"Time," he said.

His voice, filtered through the mask, was hollow. As if a wall stood between his mouth and the room. He walked to a point between the two knights and stopped. He raised his right hand.

The right hand was mechanical, too.

The fingers were long, made of white metal, each joint revealing a small nest of gears and springs. On the index finger he wore a black iron ring, and the ring was engraved with the same owl emblem as the mask. His mechanical fingers pressed once in the air.

Nothing happened. Only the faintest hum of electricity drifted through the red mist.

The great screen lit up.

The screen was set into the rock wall at the far end of the hall — ten metres wide, five metres high, its surface the matte texture of frosted glass. The light it threw was cold, surgical. Snow filled the screen for a moment, then the picture steadied.

A mine tunnel.

Nine metres across, less than twelve high. The rock walls were striped with the dull red veins of raw red mercury. The tunnel ran from the depth of the picture toward the camera, its floor laid with old iron rails, the rails rusted black. At the end of the rails, the passage stopped — but the wall had been bored through, and in the bored-out darkness, a dim red light was leaking, as if some vast animal had opened its mouth.

The abandoned workings at the base of Mount Vesuvius.

Tomorrow's battlefield.

"This," the master of the Original Sin Bureau said, "is your stage for tomorrow."

His mechanical finger drew a line in the air, and the image on the screen expanded, the details of the tunnel sharpening — the steel buttresses that reinforced the walls, the piles of fallen stone on the floor, the places where the passage had narrowed from a cave-in.

"Memorise every turn, every choke-point, every alcove you can press yourselves into." His voice did not rise. "Tomorrow's engagement will not take place in the open yard. It will take place in this tunnel. Nine metres wide. Large enough to limit the mobility of a giant puppet, small enough to deny the Seraphim its full evasive arc. You will have to use the terrain."

The knight called Zero lifted her head, slowly.

Her face was hidden behind a full-visor black helm. Only the two red eyes were visible. When she spoke, the voice came from an internal mechanical sounder. No inflection, no emotion, only a flat electronic pulse.

"Master. We are ready."

A beat.

"We will kill Cesare in tomorrow's engagement. We will take the Immortal King's chip."

Knight One did not answer at once. He was half a head taller than Zero. His pauldrons were wider, and an extra set of steam exhausts hung from his arms, ready to vent into overcharge at any moment. He stood with his head lowered, staring at a single stretch of rusted rail at his feet. He was silent for three seconds.

Then he raised his head.

"Master."

His voice was low. The amplifier in his armour broadened it, and the red mist made the words echo.

"Juan has become a liability."

His red eyes flared a little brighter in the haze.

"We can dispose of him whenever you wish."

The master of the Original Sin Bureau did not answer at once. He walked, slowly, toward the great screen. The hem of his white robe hissed against the metal floor. He stopped in front of the cold-lit surface, and stood there, looking up at it, the way a high priest might stand before an altar.

"Juan still has his uses."

He said it without turning.

"His trial machine, the prototype Gurnos-II, is tomorrow's bait. If he does not enter the field, Cesare will not enter the tunnel. And if Cesare does not enter the tunnel, our design is missing its most critical piece."

He raised his mechanical hand and pressed one fingertip against the screen, against the bored-out mouth at the end of the mine where the red light bled through.

"Besides Cesare, there is something else you must take."

He drew back his hand. He turned to face the two knights. The owl of his silver mask caught the cold light of the screen.

"Cesare Borgia. The new Red Dragon of the Minerva Bureau. The so-called one-in-a-million Compatible. When he wears his armour, his nervous system couples completely with the machine — a coupling no ordinary pilot can ever achieve."

He paused. The joint of his mechanical jaw clicked once.

"But he has another identity."

"He is a blood descendant of the Seers of Ceylon. Purple Eyes."

The two words fell into the red mist like stones dropped into deep water.

"The Purple Eyes of the Seers are not a colour. They are the interface of a consciousness channel. A century ago, the last Seer of Ceylon — Remnant One — used her own blood and her own bones to seal something in the deep red mercury. The root of the World Tree. The root's consciousness requires a vessel to be roused. It requires a person of the same bloodline as Remnant One to form the connection."

He paused again, longer this time.

"Cesare is the only person alive who can both link to the Remnant's consciousness and remain human."

Zero's red eyes did not change. Knight One's red pupils contracted, a fraction.

"Capture him," the master said, "and we restart the Machine Kingdom."

The six words struck the stale air of the hall like an axe. The pulse of the red-mercury pipes seemed to quicken. The hiss grew sharper, more urgent.

The great screen flickered.

The picture of the mine tunnel was gone. In its place —

A black iron door.

Five metres tall, three metres wide. The surface was covered in the dense, careful engraving of Sacred Words and ancient seals. The rivets were hex-shaped, set in a honeycomb pattern across the whole of the door. The door was shut. But through the seam of the door, a thin line of gold light leaked out, as if something on the other side was burning.

In the shadow at the foot of the door, a figure stood.

She wore a black robe, the hood pulled low. Only the lower half of her face was visible — pale lips, a sharp jaw, the corner of her mouth turned down in a permanent cold smile. One of her hands rested flat against the iron door, and between her fingers she held a small pentagram seal.

Dasmund's aunt.

She seemed, somehow, to sense the watching. Slowly, she raised her head. Beneath the shadow of the hood, her eyes found the screen — found the watching eye behind the picture — and held it.

The image vanished.

The screen dissolved into snow, then settled back to the mine.

The master of the Original Sin Bureau had not moved. He stood in front of the screen as he had stood before, white robe still, silver mask still.

"So she has come as well," he said, quietly. And the first thing his voice had carried since the beginning of the meeting slipped into it — not fear. Anticipation.

He turned and walked back to stand between the two knights. The hem of his white robe drew a slow arc through the red mist. He raised his mechanical right hand, and from inside the sleeve of his robe he drew out —

A remote.

Black. Palm-sized. A single button on the face. Beside the button, an inscription in very small letters, the kind of letters you have to bring the object close to read.

World Tree Remnant Activation Switch.

He rested his thumb on the button. He did not press it.

"Tomorrow's engagement is not a test of Prometheus against the Seraphim," he said.

"Minerva believes it is a public weapons competition, that the victor will become the principal armament of the future Papacy. The Sacred Council believes it is a display of force, and every faction under it will send its observers."

"They do not know what waits at the end of the tunnel."

"The tunnel was sealed by the previous Commander of Minerva forty years ago. But before it was sealed, a side passage had been bored at its end, leading deeper into the body of Vesuvius."

"Golgotha."

The word fell into the red mist. At the sound of it, Zero and One both tilted their heads, a fraction of an inch to the side.

Golgotha.

The forbidden ground beneath Vesuvius, sealed off by the previous Minerva Commander. Rumoured to hold the remains of phantom Seraphim armours that moved of their own accord. A graveyard of armours. A womb of armours.

"Remnant Two lies in the deepest chamber of Golgotha."

"Remnant One was the last Seer of Ceylon. She used her own blood and her own bones to seal the root of the World Tree. Her consciousness sank into the deep red mercury, to keep the root from waking. But One was not the only Remnant. Two was her younger sister, taken by the predecessor of the Original Sin Bureau before One ever cast her seal, and kept in Golgotha ever since."

"One's seal is imperfect. Because Two is still there."

"The World Tree requires both Remnants to be reunited before it can fully rouse. One gave her life to prevent that. But her consciousness has woken, along with Cesare — when Cesare dons his armour, he brushes the sealed layer at the bottom of the red mercury. His bloodline is the key."

His mechanical fingers tapped the remote twice, lightly.

"Tomorrow, when Cesare dons the new Red Dragon and enters the tunnel, the shock of combat will shatter the seal at the end of the workings. Golgotha will open. Remnant Two will be released."

"And the moment Remnant One's consciousness, through Cesare, comes into contact with Remnant Two —"

He did not finish the sentence.

He pressed the button.

Click.

The metal floor of the hall began to shake. Zero and One stepped back, a single step, in unison. The rails beneath their feet began to warp. Screws popped from their bolts, ringing off the floor like small bells. A crack ran through the centre of the floor, and raced outward at speed, accompanied by the high-pitched scream of red-mercury pipes bursting, and from the crack a great gout of red-mercury vapour erupted into the air.

The floor split open.

From the split, a platform rose, slowly. On the platform, bound in iron chains, stood a massive mechanical armour.

The armour was more than five metres tall. Its body was sheathed in plates of a dark gold metal, and every plate was engraved in the dense script of Sacred Words and ancient seals. In the engraving, a thin gold light was running, as if the lines themselves were bleeding fire. It had no helm — its head was a single spherical visor, smooth as a mirror, and in the visor the hall and the red mist and the three figures were reflected, small and distant.

In its chest, a great red-mercury core was set.

The core was a dark red, and it was beating. Like a heart.

Omega.

Not the Omega that the Minerva Bureau had sealed away in its vaults. A prototype, made in secret, by the Original Sin Bureau.

Chains of black iron were wound around its limbs and its torso. Each chain was as thick as a man's arm, the links cast in the same ancient seals that covered the iron door in Golgotha. But the chains had rusted at the joints where they met the armour — not from moisture, but from the slow, constant erosion of the energy leaking from the thing they were trying to bind.

The master of the Original Sin Bureau stood at the edge of the split, looking down at the chained giant.

"It has been hungry," he said, "for forty years."

The anticipation in his voice was thicker now. Like a flame rekindling from its own ash.

Zero's and One's red eyes flared at the same time.

And in the corner of the great screen, a line of text was flickering, almost too small to read —

Remnant Two … synchronisation rate … rising.

---

Nine hours later, in the abandoned workings at the base of Vesuvius.

Five dragons, and one beast of iron, would meet in the dark.

And the chained giant would wake there, too.

第165章 骷髅地的召唤

【中文】
第165章 骷髅地的召唤

他又一次梦见了那座城。

莲花盛开的城，尖塔如林，街道上铺着白色的沙，妇女们穿着纱丽从井边走过，笑声和铃声混在一起。可今夜那座城在燃烧，火焰从每一条街巷里钻出来，像是大地张开了无数张嘴，吐出橘红色的舌头。圣女塔的轮廓在火光中若隐若现，塔顶的莲花形穹顶被烧得通红，穹顶上的金箔一片片剥落，飘进夜色里，像金色的蝴蝶。

他站在塔下，仰头望去。

塔的每一层都亮着灯，每一层的窗后都站着一个女人。她们都穿着白色的纱丽，长发垂到脚踝，面容模糊。他想喊"妈妈"，但嘴唇动不了。他想跑上台阶去，但脚步钉在原地。塔越来越高，从十层变成二十层，从二十层变成五十层，尖顶刺入星空，像是某种不甘心的存在在向天空索取一个回答。

然后他听见了哭声。

不是女人的哭声，是一种更低沉、更古老的悲鸣，像大地深处有什么东西在叹息。那声音穿过了塔的砖石，穿过了燃烧的街道，穿过他的胸腔，震得他整个人都在颤抖。

天空裂开了。

不是云层裂开，是天空本身像一块黑铁板一样从中分开，露出后面更深的黑暗。那黑暗的中央有一扇门——黑铁铸造的门，门上铸着圣言和古老印记，每一道刻痕都散发着冷光。门缝里透出金色的光，光芒脉动着，像心跳。

门在等他。

他知道只要推开那扇门，他就能看到所有的答案。可他的手刚抬起来，一个声音就在他耳边响起——

快去骷髅地。

声音苍老而遥远，像是隔着很深的水传来的。那不是任何一个活着的人的声音，那是某种被封印在红水银深处的、超越了时间的意识。

"……快去……"

声音变得更急促了，带着某种近乎哀求的急切。

"你姑姑……她遇到危险了……残枝02号……要被激活了……快……"

——！

西泽尔猛地睁开眼睛。

天花板是陌生的，灰白色钢板拼接而成，铆钉和焊缝在昏暗中像一张张沉默的脸。他躺在密涅瓦机关的临时休息舱里，枕头被冷汗浸透了，贴在后颈上冰凉一片。他大口地呼吸，胸口剧烈起伏，手掌无意识地攥紧了被单，指节发白。

残枝意识的声音还在耳边回响，像是余音在金属舱壁之间反复弹跳。

"残枝02号要被激活了"——这句话像是烧红的铁条，烙在他的意识里。

他抬手摸向后颈。

黄金套管烫得厉害。

不是体温的那种温热，是真正的烫，像是被一枚刚从炉膛里取出的硬币贴在皮肤上。他下意识地缩了一下手指，但手又按了回去——指腹下能感觉到黄金套管表面细微的震颤，那种震颤的频率和心跳一致，却又比心跳更深沉，更古老。

他把左手举到眼前。

昏暗的舱室里，他能清楚地看见自己的瞳孔——不再是那种深得近乎黑色的暗紫，而是被金色的纹路贯穿了的、灼热的亮紫。那些金纹像毛细血管一样分布在虹膜上，每一条都在微微发光，随着他心跳的节奏一闪一灭。

紫瞳金纹。

上次出现这个状态，还是在马斯顿教堂里，不朽之王模式被激活的那一刻。

西泽尔缓缓坐起身。舱室外传来密涅瓦机关深层管道里蒸汽循环的低沉嗡鸣，像巨兽的呼吸。他摸到床头的黑色作战服，一件一件地穿上。动作不快，但每一个动作都极其精确——贴身的防弹内衬，膝盖和肘部的硬金护片，外层黑色作战服的拉链拉到喉结下方。

他把那枚嵌着冰原寒玉的银戒指从床头柜上拿起来，套在右手中指上。戒指很凉，凉意从指尖传到掌心，像瓦莲京娜握着他的手。

最后是那个黑色锦盒。

他打开舱室角落的保险柜，从里面取出那只黑色锦盒。锦盒的表面蒙着一层细灰，是从维苏威火山改造室带来的。他没有打开它，但他知道里面是什么——Excalibur的碎片，那柄曾经劈开过普罗米修斯心脏的圣剑的残骸。

他关上保险柜，锦盒夹在腋下。

他看了一眼腕表。凌晨两点十七分。

走廊里很安静。密涅瓦机关的大多数工作人员都已经进入了战前休眠状态，只有几盏应急灯在走廊的尽头投下暗红色的光斑。他的脚步几乎没有声音——黑色作战靴的鞋底是软金材料制成的，踩在钢板上不会发出任何回响。

改装室的门虚掩着，里面透出一线微弱的光。

西泽尔停下脚步。

改装室是密涅瓦机关专门为五台新型炽天使试制版机体进行最终调试的区域，这个时间应该没有人。但那线光很稳定，不是照明灯的光，是某种设备待机时的指示光。

他轻轻推开了门。

改装室里空无一人。五台甲胄试制版的骨架排列在维修架上，像五具沉睡的巨兽。红龙的骨架最靠近门口，暗金色的硬金骨骼在昏暗中散发着微弱的光——那些光来自骨架上残留的神经接驳微电路，它们和西泽尔的神经系统保持着某种永恒的连接，即便没有通电也在低频震颤。

但西泽尔的目光没有停留在红龙上。

他看向了改装室角落里的行军床。阿方索、昆提良和唐璜的临时铺位就在那里，三张行军床并排，床头的柜子上放着各自的私人物品。昆提良的枕边放着一束干花——是艾莲从医院托人带来的，昆提良宝贝得不行。唐璜的枕边放着一只粉色的发卡，大概是宝儿·拉瑟的。

阿方索在最里面那张床上，睡得很沉。

他翻身的时候右手垂在床沿外面，那只精密的机械手在睡梦中仍然保持着微微张开的姿态，随时准备扣动扳机。但此刻他的呼吸很均匀，面容在昏暗中也柔和了下来，嘴角甚至带着一丝不易察觉的弧度——他在做一个好梦。

西泽尔在床边站了很久。

然后他从作战服内袋里抽出一张折叠好的信纸，展开，用放在床头柜上的铅笔写了几个字。

他的字迹很淡，力道很轻，像是在纸上落了一层薄薄的霜：

"如果我明天早上没回来，你们就继续参加对抗战——守护你们想守护的东西。"

他没有署名。

他不需要署名。他们会认出他的字迹的。

他把信纸折好，压在阿方索的枕头旁边——压在他垂下的机械手掌心下面，这样阿方索醒来时第一眼就会看到。

他在床边又站了两秒。

低头看了阿方索一眼。阿方索的面容安静，像个真正的少年——在他身边的时候他总是最放松的，因为他知道阿方索会替他挡掉所有的暗箭。

西泽尔转身走了。

改装室的门在他身后无声地合上。

密涅瓦机关的走廊在凌晨时分显得格外漫长。蒸汽管道在天花板上方交错，偶尔有一根管道的接缝处漏出白雾，飘过他的头顶。他沿着走廊向深处走，脚步不停，方向明确——向着叹息之墙的侧门走去。

那条路他在脑子里已经走过无数遍了。

叹息之墙是密涅瓦机关入口处的巨型黑色机械门，原本设计用来分隔机密区域和普通区域。墙的厚度超过三米，嵌满了硬金铆钉和红水银传感装置，正门由佛朗哥教授和薇若兰联合管理，权限最高。但侧门——

侧门在墙的东侧尽头，一扇不起眼的小门，铁皮蒙面，看起来像是维修通道的入口。正常情况下它由一道机械锁锁住，钥匙只有薇若兰和佛朗哥教授各一把。

但那扇门的锁是西泽尔真正在意的。

三天前他在查阅密涅瓦机关旧档案的时候，在B-07号卷宗的封底发现了一行手写的注释——字迹潦草，墨水已经褪色，但笔锋锐利得像是刻在纸上的：

"骷髅地入口在叹息之墙东侧侧门之后，经废弃矿道可达。该门钥匙由历代炽天骑士团团长保管，战时可由团长授权任何炽天铁骑开启。"

他姑姑留给他的字条上提到的骷髅地——就在这扇门后面。

走廊的尽头，叹息之墙的轮廓在应急灯的暗红色光线下隐约可辨。那面巨大的黑色机械门沉默地矗立着，像一头蹲伏的巨兽，表面的铆钉在昏暗中像无数只闭合的眼睛。

侧门就在巨兽的脚边。

西泽尔放慢脚步，靠近。

他伸手去摸门锁——

手指碰到了金属。

门锁的盖板是开着的，锁孔暴露在外面。而锁孔里，插着一枚铁戒指。

西泽尔的手指停在那枚戒指上，没有动。

那是一枚暗铁色的戒指，戒环上缠绕着精致的火焰花纹，戒圈内壁刻着一行小字。他不需要拿出来看也知道那行字写的是什么——

"李锡尼。"

炽天骑士团荣誉铁戒指。

佩戴者荣誉战死沙场后，戒指会被供奉在翡冷翠英灵殿，不会转给他人。但李锡尼还活着，他只是把戒指留在了这里——留在了这扇门的锁孔里。

西泽尔缓缓转过头。

侧门旁边的墙壁阴影里，一个人靠在墙上。

李锡尼穿着一身深灰色的便装，没有穿军服，也没有披那件标志性的猩红色披风。但他的右手握着一杆长枪，枪身细长，枪尖在暗光中泛着冷蓝色的光——

圣枪装具·Longinus。

密涅瓦机关的顶级武器之一，能够撕裂一切装甲的传说之枪，此刻被一个异端审判局的副局长像握拐杖一样随意地握着。

"我知道你要去骷髅地。"

李锡尼的声音从阴影里传出来，低沉，带着某种沉淀了很久的疲惫。

西泽尔看着他。

李锡尼从墙边站直了身子。他比西泽尔记忆中又瘦了一些，颧骨更高了，脸上的线条像是被刀削过。但他的眼睛仍然是那种冷灰色的，像是冬天结冰的湖面。

"我跟你一起去。"

他说，语气平淡得像是在说今天天气不错。

"当年的事，我也有责任。"

西泽尔没有立刻回答。

他的目光从李锡尼的脸上移到了他手中那杆Longinus上，又从枪尖移到了李锡尼灰白的鬓角上。

当年的事。

李锡尼没有说具体是哪件事。但西泽尔能猜到——那件事的范围太大了，大到可以指代过去十年里发生的任何一件。琳琅夫人的手术、普罗米修斯心脏的封存、西泽尔被投入马斯顿、炽天使适格者计划的黑暗面……每一件事的背后都站着不同的人，而李锡尼在其中的位置——

是旁观者。

是知情者。

是有能力阻止却没有阻止的人。

"你为什么在这里？"西泽尔问。声音很轻，几乎没有起伏。

"我值夜班。"李锡尼淡淡地说，"异端审判局副局长的职责是监视可能引发神圣灾难的一切动向。今晚翡冷翠有七个人在夜间活动异常，你是第六个。"

"第七个是谁？"

"教皇陛下。"

李锡尼把戒指从锁孔里转了出来，捏在指间。那枚暗铁色的戒指在暗光中看起来比它的实际重量要沉得多——不是因为材质，而是因为它承载的重量。

"这是我的钥匙。也是我的邀请函。"李锡尼把戒指递向西泽尔，"戴上它，叹息之墙的侧门就会为你打开。"

西泽尔接过了戒指。

戒指很凉，戴在手上之后却迅速被他的体温焐热了。戒圈内壁的刻字硌着他的皮肤，那两个字像是被烫进了他的指骨里。

"走吧。"李锡尼说。

他伸手在侧门上推了一下。门无声地向内滑开，露出后面一条向下延伸的通道。通道很窄，只够两人并肩而行，两侧的墙壁是粗糙的岩石，没有经过任何修饰，岩壁上还留着当年开凿时工具留下的痕迹。通道的深处一片漆黑，隐约能听到某种低沉的嗡鸣声——那是密涅瓦机关深层管道里蒸汽循环的声音，被岩石过滤后变成了一种像是来自地底的呼吸。

西泽尔走进了通道。

李锡尼跟在他身后，Longinus的枪尖在岩石上划出一道浅浅的白痕。

他们在黑暗中走了大约五分钟。通道开始向下倾斜，角度越来越大，有些地方甚至需要扶着岩壁才能保持平衡。空气变得潮湿了，带着一股矿物质和金属混合的气味——是红水银的味道。

西泽尔后颈的黄金套管越来越烫。

金纹已经不再只出现在他的眼睛里了——他低下头，能看到自己手背上的血管也在隐隐发光，呈现出一种诡异的淡紫色脉络。那是星见血脉在共振——残枝01号和残枝02号之间跨越时空的连接正在被激活。

"你知道那条路通向哪里吗？"西泽尔在黑暗中问。

"知道。"李锡尼的声音从后面传来，同样压得很低，"维苏威火山底部的废弃矿道。矿道的尽头是——"

他没有说完。

因为在他们前方大约二十米的地方，通道的尽头透出了一线暗红色的光。

那光不是应急灯的光，也不是蒸汽管道泄漏的光。那是一种有生命的光——它在脉动，像心跳一样有节奏地一亮一灭。

西泽尔停下了脚步。

李锡尼也停下了，Longinus的枪尖不自觉地抬起了几度。

暗红色的光芒越来越亮，脉动的频率越来越快。从光源的方向传来一个声音——不是残枝意识的声音，也不是任何人类的语言。那个声音像是金属在振动，像是蒸汽在尖叫，像是无数个齿轮同时咬合又脱开，发出一种刺耳的、超越了正常听觉范围的嘶鸣。

然后，在那嘶鸣声中，一个声音从光的深处传来。

苍老，遥远，但清晰得像是在他耳边说出的：

"西泽尔，你终于来了。"

【English】
Chapter 165 — The Summons of Golgotha

He dreamed again of that city.

The city of white sand and lotus towers, where women in pale veils walked from the wells with laughter and the bright thread of bells. Constantinople. The New Rome. He had never been there. He had never stood on its streets. Yet in the dream he knew it the way the body knows its own name, and tonight the city was on fire.

Flames came up through every street, from every crack in the white sand, as though the ground itself had opened a thousand mouths and put out orange tongues. The Saintess Tower rose above it all, its petal-shaped dome going red with heat, the gold leaf of it peeling off in slow curls that drifted up into the smoke like a flock of small golden birds.

He stood beneath it and looked up.

Every floor of the tower was lit. Behind every window a woman stood, veiled, hair falling to her ankles, her face not quite there. He tried to say mother. He could not move his lips. He tried to run up the steps. His feet were nailed to the ground. The tower climbed — ten floors, twenty, fifty — and the spire bit into the stars as if some indignant thing in the earth were demanding a reply from the sky.

Then he heard the weeping.

Not the women. Something lower. Older. A sound as though the deep of the world were sighing in its sleep. It passed through the brick, through the burning streets, through his chest, and set his whole body to trembling.

The sky cracked.

Not clouds. The sky itself, parting like a slab of black iron, and behind it a deeper black. And in the centre of that black, a door. Black iron, cast with Holy Words and older marks, every cut in the metal breathing cold light. Through the seam of the door a thin gold light came pulsing, the way a heart pulses.

The door was waiting for him.

He knew that if he pushed it open he would see all the answers. He raised his hand.

A voice spoke at his ear.

Go to Golgotha.

The voice was old, far off, as though it were coming up through deep water. It was not the voice of anyone living. It was something sealed into red mercury, something that had outlasted its own time.

"—go quickly—"

The voice grew more urgent, almost pleading.

"Your aunt—she is in danger—the Withered Branch Two—is being woken—go—"

—!

Cesare opened his eyes.

The ceiling above him was a stranger's ceiling. Plates of grey-white steel, the rivets and welts of them staring down at him in the dim like a row of small, silent faces. He was lying in one of the rest-bunks at the Minerva Bureau, and the pillow under his head was soaked through with cold sweat, the damp cloth pressed against the back of his neck.

He breathed. The breath came in, harsh, lifting his chest. His hand, somewhere beneath the blanket, had closed into a fist without his permission; the knuckles were white.

The Withered Branch's voice still hung in the air of his skull, ringing faintly off the metal walls.

"The Withered Branch Two is being woken."

The sentence sat in him like a heated iron rod laid along the back of his mind.

He raised his hand and felt the back of his neck.

The gold collar was hot.

Not the warmth of a body. Truly hot, the way a coin taken from a forge is hot. He pulled his fingers away, then pressed them back. Under the pad of his thumb he could feel a small fine tremor in the gold, a tremor that ran at the same rhythm as his own pulse, and yet lower, deeper, more ancient.

He lifted his left hand into what little light there was.

In the half-dark of the bunk he could see his own pupils clearly. They were no longer the near-black violet of his usual sight. They were threaded with gold, a web of fine bright lines that ran through the iris like the capillaries of a leaf. Each line glowed faintly, pulsing once for each beat of his heart, going dark, then bright again.

Purple eye, gold pattern.

The last time he had seen it on himself had been in the church at Marston, when the Immortal King mode had been brought up out of him.

Cesare sat up slowly. Beyond the wall of the bunk, somewhere deep in the Bureau, the steam mains gave out their long low hum — the breathing of some great animal asleep in the earth.

He found the black field-clothes folded on the shelf at the head of the bunk and began to put them on. The movements were slow and very precise. The close-woven ballistic undersuit first, the hard-gold plates at knee and elbow, and over them the black outer coat whose zip he drew up to the hollow of his throat.

From the small locker he took the silver ring with the chip of Polar Ice Jade set into its face and slipped it on the middle finger of his right hand. The metal was cold, and the cold ran from his fingertip down into the centre of his palm, and for a moment it was Valentina's hand he was holding.

The last thing was the black silk case.

He went to the strongbox in the corner of the bunk, opened it, and lifted out the case. A fine grey dust clung to it — ash from the modification chamber under Vesuvius, carried back with him on the train. He did not open it. He did not need to. He knew what lay inside. The fragment of Excalibur. The broken tooth of the holy sword that had once, in another age, been driven through the heart of Prometheus.

He closed the strongbox, the case under his arm.

He glanced at his wrist. Two-seventeen in the morning.

The corridor outside was quiet. Most of the Bureau's people were in the wartime sleep-cycle now, and only a few of the emergency lamps were lit, throwing small red shapes on the floor a long way off. His own boots made no sound on the steel — the soles were of soft gold, and the gold did not ring against metal.

The door of the modification chamber was ajar. A thin line of light came through it.

Cesare stopped.

The chamber was where the five prototype Seraph units were put through their last checks. At this hour it should have been empty. But the line of light was steady, and it was not the colour of the working lamps; it was the standby colour of some instrument that was simply on.

He pushed the door open.

The chamber was empty. The five great armoured skeletons stood on their maintenance frames like five sleeping beasts. The Red Dragon was nearest the door — its dark-gold skeleton gave out a faint light of its own, the light of the fine neural-link circuits that still ran along its bones, still tied to Cesare's own nervous system, still quivering at a frequency no power was feeding them.

But he did not look at the Red Dragon.

He looked at the camp-beds in the far corner. Three of them, set side by side, with the small lockers of their owners behind them. Alfonso. Quintilian. Don Juan.

On Quintilian's pillow there was a small bunch of dried flowers, brought over from the hospital by Aileen. He guarded them the way a man guards a relic. On Don Juan's pillow there was a pink hairclip — Bao'er Lasser, presumably. The thought flickered and was gone.

Alfonso was on the inside bed. He slept heavily. When he turned, his right hand slipped off the edge of the mattress, and the mechanical hand — the engineered one, the one that could draw and fire and never tire — hung in the air with the fingers a little open, even in sleep, as though waiting to pull a trigger. His breathing was slow. His face, in the dim red light, had gone soft, and the line of his mouth was almost a smile. He was having a good dream.

Cesare stood at the bedside for a long time.

Then he took from the inside of his coat a single sheet of paper, already folded. He unfolded it on the locker and, with the pencil that lay there, wrote a few words. The strokes were light, the pressure small, as if a thin frost had fallen on the page.

"If I am not back by morning, you are to go on with the Contest. Guard what you have chosen to guard."

He did not sign it.

He did not need to sign it. They would know the hand.

He folded the note and laid it under the loose mechanical hand, so that it rested in the open palm. When Alfonso woke, the first thing he would see would be the hand, and inside the hand, the note.

Cesare stood a moment longer.

He looked down at Alfonso's sleeping face. The face was open, untroubled, the face of a boy — the boy he could only be, Cesare understood, in the presence of another who had been willing, for years, to take every hidden arrow meant for him.

Cesare turned and went out.

The door of the chamber closed behind him without a sound.

The corridors of the Minerva Bureau at this hour seemed longer than during the day. The steam mains ran across the ceiling in a thicket, and here and there at a joint a small leak of white mist came drifting out, passing over his head like a slow ghost. He did not stop, did not hesitate. He knew the way. He had walked it in his head a hundred times.

The Wall of Sighs.

The great black mechanical gate that stood at the entrance of the Bureau's classified section. Three metres of solid plate, studded with hard-gold rivets and red-mercury sensors, its front door under the joint authority of Professor Franco and Verolan, with the highest clearance of any door in the building.

But the side door —

The side door was at the eastern end of the wall, a small, plain thing, sheet-iron over a frame, looking like the mouth of a maintenance shaft. It was held by a single mechanical lock, and the key to it was supposed to exist in two copies only, one on Franco's person, one on Verolan's.

That was the door Cesare wanted.

Three days ago, in the Bureau's archive, he had been reading the back cover of volume B-07. The ink of the file number was half faded, and below it, in a hand that was not the clerk's, someone had written a few lines, the strokes sharp as though cut with a chisel rather than put down with a pen.

"The Golgotha entrance lies behind the eastern side door of the Wall of Sighs, accessible through the disused mine-shaft. The key of that door is held, in each generation, by the Commander of the Order of the Seraph Knights; in time of war the Commander may depute any Seraph Knight to open it."

The place his aunt had written of, in her last note to him, lay on the far side of that door.

At the end of the corridor, the Wall of Sighs came up out of the dim, lit only by the small red of the emergency lamps. A vast black slab of a thing, crouched, the rivets along its face like the closed eyes of a sleeping animal.

The side door was at the foot of the animal.

Cesare slowed. He reached for the lock.

His fingers met metal.

The cover of the lock was already open. The keyhole was exposed. And in the keyhole, a ring of iron had been placed.

His fingers stopped on the ring. He did not move it.

It was a dark iron ring. The band was wrapped in fine flamework. On the inside of the band, in small letters, an inscription.

He did not need to draw the ring out to read it. He knew the name that would be there.

Lignini.

The honour ring of the Order of the Seraph Knights. By custom, when a knight fell honourably in the field, the ring was taken to the Hall of Heroes in Florence and was never given to another. But Lignini had not died. He had left the ring here — left it in this lock, as a man leaves a calling card.

Cesare turned his head slowly.

In the shadow of the wall beside the door, someone was standing, leaning.

Lignini was in a dark grey civilian coat. No uniform. No scarlet cloak. But in his right hand he held a long slender spear, and the point of the spear, in the dim light, gave off a thin cold blue.

The Holy Lance. Longinus. One of the Bureau's first-rank weapons — the lance that was said to unmake any armour, carried now by the Vice Director of the Heretical Inquisition as though it were a walking-stick.

"I know you mean to go to Golgotha," Lignini said. His voice came out of the shadow low, and tired, the way a stone sounds when it has been in a river for a long time.

Cesare looked at him.

Lignini pushed himself off the wall. He was thinner than Cesare remembered; the cheekbones stood out, the lines of his face were as though a knife had pared them. But his eyes were the same. Cold grey. The colour of a winter lake gone over with ice.

"I am going with you," Lignini said. The tone was that of a man remarking on the weather.

"What happened in those days — I had a part in it."

Cesare did not answer at once.

His gaze moved from Lignini's face down to the lance in his hand, then up to the greying hair at Lignini's temple, then back to the eyes.

What had happened in those days.

Lignini had not said which days. But Cesare could read the range. The range was wide enough to cover almost any one of the last ten years. Lady Linglang's operation. The sealing-away of the Prometheus heart. Cesare's being sent to Marston. The dark side of the Seraph-concord programme. Behind every one of those things a different name stood; and Lignini's name stood, in some way, beside each.

As a witness.

As a man who knew.

As a man who could have stopped it and did not.

"Why are you here?" Cesare asked. His voice was quiet. It had no real lift to it.

"I am on the night watch," Lignini said. "The duties of the Vice Director of the Heretical Inquisition include the surveillance of any movement that might bring on a holy catastrophe. Tonight there are seven people in Florence whose night movements are not what they should be. You are the sixth."

"And the seventh?"

"His Holiness the Pope."

Lignini turned the ring in the lock and drew it out. He held it between his fingers. The dark iron, in the dim light, looked heavier than its actual weight — heavier not in metal but in what it was made to carry.

"This is my key," he said. "It is also my invitation." He held the ring out toward Cesare. "Put it on, and the side door of the Wall of Sighs will open for you."

Cesare took the ring.

The iron was cold, but once it was on his hand the warmth of his skin worked into it quickly. The inscription on the inside of the band pressed into his flesh, and the two letters of the name felt as though they were being branded into the bone of the finger.

"Let us go," Lignini said.

He put his hand on the side door and pushed. The door slid inward, soundless, and behind it a passage opened and went down. The passage was narrow, only wide enough for two men to walk abreast, and the walls of it were rough-cut rock, unworked, still showing the tool-marks of whoever had first cut the way. Far down, the passage was black. From far down, too, came a low humming — the sound of the steam mains far below the Bureau, filtered through stone until it had become a kind of breathing, as of something asleep at the foot of the world.

Cesare stepped in.

Lignini followed. The point of Longinus, as he walked, drew a thin white line on the rock at his side.

For about five minutes they walked in the dark. The passage began to tilt downward; the slope grew, and in places Cesare had to put a hand to the wall to keep his balance. The air grew wet. A smell came into it — a mineral smell, a metal smell, the smell of red mercury.

The gold collar at the back of Cesare's neck was hotter now, distinctly hotter.

It was no longer only his eyes. He looked down at the back of his own hand and saw, in the dark, a faint purple pattern running along the lines of the veins, the lines themselves beginning to give out a low, unnatural light. The Star-Seeing blood, in him, was answering something. The link between Withered Branch One and Withered Branch Two, running across time, was being woken in his flesh.

"Do you know where this leads?" Cesare asked, in the dark.

"I do," Lignini said, from behind him, in the same low voice. "The disused mine-shafts under Mount Vesuvius. At the end of the shafts is —"

He did not finish.

Twenty metres ahead of them, at the end of the passage, a line of dark red light was showing.

It was not the colour of an emergency lamp. It was not the colour of a steam leak. It was the colour of a thing that was alive. It pulsed, the way a heart pulses — on, off, on, off — and the pulse was quickening as they came closer to it.

Cesare stopped.

Lignini stopped. The point of Longinus, without his willing it, came up a few degrees.

The dark red light grew brighter. The pulse grew faster. Out of the direction of the light there came a sound — not the voice of the Withered Branch, not any human tongue. A sound as of metal vibrating, of steam screaming at a pitch just past hearing, of a thousand gear-teeth all engaging and slipping at the same moment, a high thin shrieking that was almost beneath the ear.

And in the shrieking, a voice, from somewhere inside the light, spoke.

Old. Far off. But as clear as though it were being spoken into his ear.

"Cesare. You have come at last."

第166章 黑铁巨门前的真相

【中文】
第166章 黑铁巨门前的真相

光脉动的频率在加快。

那暗红色的光一明一灭，像一颗埋在岩石深处的心脏正在苏醒，从通道的尽头挤出来，照亮了前方的空间——那不是普通的洞穴，而是一座被人工开凿过的巨大空腔，岩壁上的凿痕早已被岁月磨平，边缘生满了暗红色的锈迹。

空腔的正中央矗立着一扇门。

黑铁巨门。

西泽尔停下了脚步。

那扇门高约十二尺，由整块黑铁铸成，表面布满了层层叠叠的铁质封条，每一条都有成年男人手臂那么宽，封条上刻着密密麻麻的圣徽和经文，大半已经被锈蚀侵蚀得模糊不清。最底层的封条已经和门板融为一体，边缘生出了铁锈的结晶，像凝固的血滴。

门缝间透出的暗红色光从封条的缝隙中渗出，在黑铁的表面投下忽明忽暗的影子，仿佛门后有什么东西正试图用光来呼吸。

巨门的正中央，刻着一个圣徽——卡巴拉之树，十一枚果实围绕着一棵枝繁叶茂的大树，树的根须深入门板的最底部。但那圣徽被一道深深的刀痕劈成了两半，刀痕的边缘锋利如新，不知道是什么人用什么武器留下的。

"这就是骷髅地的入口。"李锡尼站在西泽尔身后，声音压得很低，"前代总长封死这扇门的时候，我还没进炽天骑士团。"

西泽尔没有回答。他的目光被另一样东西吸引住了。

黑铁巨门前的岩石地面上站着一个人。

那人穿着一身黑色的长裙，裙摆一直拖到脚踝，头上披着黑色的纱巾，把脸遮得严严实实。她背对着西泽尔和李锡尼，一只手撑着一把红色的伞——就是那把伞，骨白伞柄，红得像是凝固的血。

她似乎已经在那里站了很久了。

岩石地面上的灰尘被伞尖划出了一道弧线，说明她在等人来的时候一直在画圈。

"你来了。"黑衣女人没有回头，声音苍老而平静，像是在说一件早已注定的事。

西泽尔的手无声地搭上了剑柄。

"你是谁？"

"你姑姑。"黑衣女人说。

李锡尼的Longinus枪尖微微抬起了一度。

"达斯蒙德的姑姑？"西泽尔问。

"达斯蒙德是我的侄子。"黑衣女人缓缓转过身来，"但我先是你母亲的妹妹。"

她伸出手，揭下了脸上的黑纱。

灯光从门缝中透出来，照亮了她的脸。

那是一张和琳琅夫人有七分相似的脸。同样的轮廓，同样的眉骨，同样的下颌线条。只是更瘦削，更苍老，眼角和唇边刻着深深的皱纹，丝绸般的黑发中夹杂着大片的白发。唯一和琳琅夫人不同的是眼睛——她的眼睛是紫色的，淡得像是将要褪色的紫藤花瓣。

西泽尔的手指在剑柄上僵住了。

"我叫琉璃。"她说，"琉璃·星见。你母亲的亲妹妹。你的亲姑姑。"

她顿了顿，目光落在西泽尔的眼睛上。

"你继承了你母亲的紫瞳。"

那双紫色和淡紫色对望了一眼，通道深处红水银的嗡鸣声像是安静了一瞬。

"你母亲……"琉璃的声音微微颤抖了一下，但她很快控制住了，"她还好吗？"

西泽尔没有立刻回答。

他看着那张和母亲相似的脸，脑海里浮起的是另一个画面——一个下午，窗外下着雨，母亲坐在窗边，丝绸般的长发垂在肩头，眼神空洞地望着窗外的雨幕。他走过去给她扎头发，她的头发是黑色的，带着淡淡的茉莉香气。

"她还活着。"西泽尔说，"在翡冷翠。教皇把她囚禁了。"

"我知道。"琉璃说，"我知道很多年前博尔吉亚就把她带走了。我知道她被做了脑白质手术，记忆被抹去了一部分。我也知道……"她的声音忽然哽了一下，"我知道她已经不记得我了。"

她低下头，枯瘦的手指攥紧了伞柄。

"但她还记得你。"西泽尔说，"她每天都会坐在窗边等你回去。虽然她不知道自己在等谁。"

琉璃的肩膀颤了一下。

她没有哭。

"琳琅……"她低声说，"姐姐……"

这个名字从她嘴里说出来的时候，西泽尔感觉到自己的心被什么东西轻轻攥了一下。不是疼，是一种很闷的感觉，像是被压在水底呼吸。

他按下了那点情绪。

"你说你是星见。"他的声音恢复了平静，"锡兰星见？"

琉璃抬起头看着他，紫色的眼睛在红光中显得格外深邃。

"你脖子上那枚项链坠，"她说，"拿下来给我看看。"

西泽尔犹豫了一秒，解开了领口的扣子。

银链垂下来，末端的银质吊坠在暗红色的光中晃动。吊坠的正面是一朵盛开的莲花，锡兰的国花，线条流畅做工精细。

"翻过来。"琉璃说。

西泽尔把吊坠翻了过来。

吊坠的背面刻着一个徽记——一朵莲花，花瓣中央嵌着一个齿轮，齿轮的每一颗齿都打磨得锋利如刀。莲花与齿轮的组合，是西泽尔从未见过的图案，但那种线条的风格让他想起了锡兰王宫的壁画。

"这是锡兰星见家族的徽记。"琉璃说，"齿轮代表观星——星见用齿轮仪来计算星辰的轨迹。莲花代表血脉——星见家族的女儿世世代代都是莲花之子。"

她的目光从吊坠移到西泽尔的脸上。

"这枚吊坠是星见家族传了十几代的东西。你外祖母传给你母亲，你母亲传给了你。你母亲让你带着它逃出翡冷翠的时候，大概是希望你将来能凭这枚吊坠找到自己的根。"

"我的根在锡兰？"西泽尔问。

"在锡兰。"琉璃说，"锡兰星见家族，莲花之子，世代守护世界树。"

世界树。

这两个字从她嘴里说出来的时候，西泽尔后颈的黄金套管忽然滚烫了一下，手背上的淡紫色脉络也亮了一瞬。

"你知道世界树？"他问。

"我知道的比这个世界上大多数人都多。"琉璃缓缓地说，"我知道锡兰战争不是新罗马帝国挑起的，是教皇国挑起的。我知道你们的教皇隆·博尔吉亚从一开始就不是为了传教才攻打锡兰，他要的是锡兰守护的东西——世界树的残枝01号。"

"你姐姐琳琅是星见家族最后的血脉之一，也是唯一知道残枝01号激活密钥的人。教皇把她带回翡冷翠囚禁起来，做了脑白质手术，反复审问她激活密钥是什么。她不说，他就反复做手术，反复抹去她的记忆，直到她连自己是谁都不记得了。"

西泽尔的呼吸停了半拍。

"你是说……"他的声音发紧，"我母亲被做手术……是教皇的命令？"

"是。"琉璃说，"但他不是在折磨她。他是在试图从她的大脑里挖出一个密钥。残枝01号只有拥有星见血脉的人才能激活，你母亲是当时仅存的几个星见之一。后来她怀了你。你是她的儿子，你继承了她全部的星见血脉，包括——"

她用手指了指西泽尔的眼睛。

"紫瞳。这是星见家族的标志。在西方被当作诅咒，但在锡兰，这是最高贵的血脉。教皇囚禁你母亲，真正的目标不是她本人，而是她肚子里的孩子——一个星见血脉更纯正的继承者。"

"残枝01号的激活密钥，就是你。"

西泽尔站在原地，握剑的手一点一点收紧。

他的脑海里闪过很多画面——母亲空洞的眼神，下午雨窗前的背影，脑白质切除手术的英文术语，博尔吉亚家族家长赫克托耳意味深长的目光，还有教皇隆·博尔吉亚在新年晚宴上和母亲跳舞时低沉的咳嗽声。

所有这些画面忽然被一根线串了起来。

"所以教皇从来不杀我。"西泽尔的声音很轻，像是在说一件与自己无关的事，"他需要我活着。"

"他需要你的血。"琉璃说，"也需要你的眼睛。残枝01号沉睡在红水银的深处已经几百年了，只有星见血脉的紫瞳才能让它重新苏醒。你母亲不肯配合，他就用更迂回的方式——把你培养成他的利剑，让你在不知情的情况下成为他的工具。"

"那个脑白质手术，"西泽尔的手指在剑柄上捏得发白，"是教皇让做的？"

"是他让做的。但执行手术的人，不是他安排的。"琉璃说，"当年做第一次手术的主使另有其人，你外祖母——星见家族的前代星见——在手术中被人趁机做了一些手脚，你母亲大脑里的一部分记忆被永久封存了。教皇后来才知道，他拿到的不是一个完整的星见，而是一个残缺的。"

"他知道以后并没有善罢甘休。后来异端审判局又来做了第二次补全手术。"

"第二次手术的幕后推手是谁？"

"我不知道。"琉璃摇了摇头，"我在翡冷翠潜伏了十几年，调查到的线索到这里就断了。但你母亲的大脑深处一定藏着什么，他们不想要她记起来。"

西泽尔沉默了几秒。

通道深处的红水银蒸汽发出低沉的嗡鸣声，像是大地深处某种古老生物的呼吸。

"你今晚来骷髅地，"他看着琉璃，"是为了放出残枝01号？"

琉璃的紫色眼睛闪了一下。

"放出残枝01号需要两样东西。"她说，"一是星见血脉的紫瞳——你有。二是打开这扇门的钥匙。"

她从黑色的长裙里取出一样东西。

那是一把钥匙。

钥匙长约一尺，由某种暗金色的金属铸成，表面布满了细密的裂纹。裂纹之间透出一种脉动的金色光芒，和西泽尔后颈黄金套管发出的光芒一模一样。

"这把钥匙是初代密涅瓦总长留下的最后一件遗物。"琉璃说，"是完美焊料。但它不是用来焊接的——它是欧米茄原型体的核心碎片。原罪机关的人从这扇门里偷走了残枝01号的残片，用来制造欧米茄原型体的核心。而这把钥匙，就是当年切割残枝01号时留下的边角料。"

"你从哪里得到的？"

"从你母亲那里。"琉璃说，"她被做手术之前，偷偷藏起来交给了一个信使。那个信使辗转了十几年，最后交到了我手上。"

她把钥匙递向西泽尔。

"这扇门后面封着的不只是残枝01号。"她说，"是整个锡兰星见家族用了几百年来守护的秘密。包括残枝01号本体的位置，包括你母亲大脑深处那段被封存的记忆的真相。"

"我来找你，就是要把这把钥匙交给你。让你自己打开这扇门，看到里面的一切。"

西泽尔的手伸向钥匙。

就在他的指尖即将碰到钥匙的瞬间——

通道的另一头传来了一阵整齐的脚步声。

金属靴底踩在岩石上的声音，沉闷，均匀，带着一种经过长期训练的节奏感。每一步都踏在同一拍上，像是战鼓。

那是圣堂装甲师的脚步声。

西泽尔的手缩了回来。

脚步声越来越近，夹杂着枪机上膛的金属摩擦声。从通道深处透出的红光中，一个身影出现了——一个穿着银白色军服的中年男人，军服的肩章上刻着双头鹰的纹章，那是圣堂装甲师最高指挥官的标志。

他身后跟着十二名全副武装的圣堂装甲师士兵，每人都端着一支新型连射铳。

"琉璃小姐。"中年男人停在二十步外，声音冰冷而克制，"把钥匙交出来。否则别怪我们不客气。"

"莱希特伯爵。"琉璃没有回头，"你来得比我想象的快。"

"你在这扇门前站了太久。"莱希特伯爵冷冷地说，"你的侄子达斯蒙德在马斯顿王立机械学院里当间谍的时候，我们就已经盯上你了。你以为你潜伏了十几年没人知道？"

"我知道。"琉璃说，"我从来就没指望过能瞒过你们。我只是需要有人比我更晚到。"

她说着忽然转过身，把钥匙塞进了西泽尔的手里。

钥匙冰冷的触感透过西泽尔的指尖传来，那种暗金色的脉动光芒和他后颈的黄金套管产生了某种共鸣，他的后颈像是被针扎了一下，一阵发麻。

"你——"西泽尔皱起眉。

"走！"琉璃一把推在他的肩膀上，把他推向巨门旁边的一处岩壁。她的力气大得出奇，和她那瘦削的身躯完全不成比例。

"那里有一条密道，是我前几年在岩石里凿出来的，通向矿道另一端的出口。"她急促地说，"走矿道，到维苏威火山的另一边。快！"

莱希特伯爵的脸色沉了下来。

"开枪。"他低声说。

十二支连射铳同时开火。

琉璃撑开了那把红色的伞。

伞面忽然展开，不是普通的布，而是一层暗金色的金属薄片，像花瓣一样层层展开。子弹打在上面发出密集的金属撞击声，火星四溅，但没有一发穿透。

"欧米茄的碎片……"李锡尼的瞳孔微缩，"那把伞是用欧米茄原型体的外壳做的！"

"李锡尼副局长。"莱希特伯爵冷冷地看着他，"我奉枢机会之命行事。你和西泽尔·博尔吉亚擅闯密涅瓦机关禁区，我现在给你最后一次机会——让开。"

李锡尼没有动。

"莱希特。"他平静地说，"我身上的这枚戒指，是炽天骑士团荣誉铁戒指。"

他伸出左手。

无名指上那枚铁戒指在红光中闪着暗淡的光泽，戒指的内圈刻着一个名字——李锡尼。

"我戴着这枚戒指的时候，做过的事就不会否认。"他说，"今天晚上我跟着西泽尔来到这里，是我自己的选择。枢机会要追究，我一人承担。"

"你承担得起吗？"莱希特伯爵冷笑了一声。

"砰——"

一颗子弹从斜上方射来，打在莱希特伯爵脚边的岩石上，溅起一片火星。

莱希特伯爵猛地抬头。

通道高处的岩石上站着一个人——穿着黑色斗篷，戴着白色的面具，手里端着一支带瞄准镜的长管连射铳，枪口还在冒着烟。

"少主！"那个人从高处跳下来，落在西泽尔面前，"跟我走！"

西泽尔认出了他——密涅瓦机关的工程师，塔拉夏。

"密涅瓦副总长薇若兰小姐让我来接应您。"塔拉夏急促地说，"密道在那边——"

琉璃还在撑着伞抵挡着密集的弹雨。那把红伞的伞面上已经布满了弹痕，但暗金色的金属薄片依然没有破损。

"快走！"琉璃冲西泽尔吼了一声，"我来挡住他们！"

"你——"

"记住！"琉璃的声音在枪声中显得格外清晰，"世界树的根在东方，叶在西方！只有两者合一，才能结束这一切！"

"你母亲大脑里藏着的那个秘密——就是打开这扇门的方法——"

一颗子弹擦过琉璃的肩膀，鲜血飞溅。

她咬了咬牙，把伞面又撑开了几分。

"走啊！"

西泽尔看着那张和母亲相似的脸，鲜血从她的肩膀上流下来，染红了黑色的长裙。

他的手指在剑柄上收紧，又松开。

"走！"李锡尼一把拉住他的胳膊。

西泽尔被拖着向岩壁那边冲去。塔拉夏已经在一处不起眼的岩缝前撬开了一块伪装成岩石的金属盖板，露出了一条向下延伸的狭窄密道。

"下去！"塔拉夏先跳了下去。

李锡尼跟着跳下。

西泽尔回头看了一眼。

琉璃还在撑着伞。伞面的金属薄片已经有一处开始碎裂了，子弹从那道裂口里钻进去，擦过她的脸颊，在她的脸上留下了一道血痕。

但她没有倒下。

她的紫色眼睛穿过弹雨的缝隙看着他，那双眼睛里没有恐惧，没有痛苦，只有一种说不清的东西——像是一个守护了几十年秘密的老人终于把担子交到了下一代的手上。

西泽尔纵身跳进了密道。

金属盖板在他身后合上，把红光、枪声、琉璃的喊声、莱希特伯爵的怒吼——所有的一切都隔绝在了头顶。

黑暗从四面八方涌来。

密道很窄，只能容一个人侧身通过，岩壁上长满了湿滑的苔藓，空气中弥漫着浓重的红水银气味。塔拉夏在前面开路，脚步声在密道里回荡。

"这条路通向哪里？"西泽尔在黑暗中问。

"通向维苏威火山底部的废弃矿道。"塔拉夏的声音从前面传来，"就是明天对抗战的战场。"

西泽尔的手指在黑暗中握紧了那把钥匙。

钥匙的暗金色脉动光芒照亮了他手背上的淡紫色脉络，那种光芒正沿着他的血管向上蔓延，一直蔓延到他的手腕。

他的后颈烫得像是要烧起来。

黄金套管在共鸣。

而密道的尽头，隐约传来了蒸汽嘶吼的声音——那是废弃矿道里某台巨大的机器正在启动的声响。

像是有什么钢铁的巨兽正在苏醒。

【English】
Chapter 166 — The Truth Before the Black Iron Gate

The pulse of the light was quickening.

A dull red gleam, on, off, on, off, like a heart buried in the deep rock stirring awake. It bled from the far end of the passage and laid open a great hollow ahead — not a natural cave, but a cavity hewn by human hands. The chisel-marks on the walls had long since been softened by centuries of mineral seep; their edges crusted over with a dark red rust that might have been iron, or might have been something older, something with a memory of blood.

At the centre of the hollow stood a door.

The Black Iron Gate.

Cesare stopped walking.

It rose about twelve feet from the rock floor, cast as a single slab of black iron, the surface layered over with sealing bands — each one as broad as a grown man's arm, each one incised from end to end with saints' marks and passages of scripture. Most of the lettering had rusted to illegibility. The lowest band had fused into the door itself, and at its edges the rust had crystallised into shapes that, in the unsteady light, looked like drops of congealed blood.

Through the seams between the bands, the red light seeped. It pulsed — dimming, rising, dimming — and on the black surface the shadows of the seals shifted as if something on the other side were trying to breathe itself out.

In the centre of the gate, an emblem had been cut deep — the Tree of Kabbalah, eleven fruits set around a great leafy trunk, the roots plunging down to the base of the slab. But the emblem had been slashed from crown to root by a single blade-stroke. The cut was sharp, as if made yesterday. Whatever had left it, whatever weapon had done it, had not dulled in all the time since.

"This," said Licinius, his voice carefully low, "is the entrance to Golgotha. When the last Commander-General sealed this gate, I had not yet been admitted to the Seraph Knights."

Cesare did not answer.

His eye had been taken by something else.

On the bare rock in front of the gate, a woman stood.

She wore a black gown whose hem brushed her ankles, and a black veil drawn down over her head, low enough to cover the whole of her face. Her back was to them. One hand rested on the handle of an umbrella — a red umbrella. The handle was bone-white. The cloth was the colour of clotted blood.

She appeared to have been standing there a long time.

In the dust of the rock, the point of the umbrella had traced a slow, meandering arc. A person marking time. A person waiting.

"You came," said the woman in black. She did not turn.

Cesare's hand, without his having willed it, had found the grip of his sword.

"Who are you?"

"Your aunt," she said.

Behind him, Licinius's Longinus shifted in its sling. The muzzle rose by a single degree.

"Desmond's aunt?" Cesare asked.

"Desmond is my nephew." She turned, slowly. "But first, I am your mother's sister."

She lifted a hand and drew the veil from her face.

The light from the door-seams fell across her.

It was a face that resembled Lady Linlang's by perhaps seven parts in ten. The same bones of the brow, the same set of the jaw, the same clean line of cheek. Only thinner. Only older. The wrinkles at the corners of eye and mouth were cut deep, and through the silk of her black hair ran broad skeins of white. The single difference, the one Cesare's eye caught and held, was the colour of her eyes. They were violet. A violet so pale it looked as if the dye were leaching out of the petals of a dying wisteria.

His fingers went still on the sword grip.

"My name is Liuli," she said. "Liuli of the Xingjian. Your mother's own sister. Your own aunt."

She paused, studying his face.

"You have your mother's violet."

The violet and the near-violet regarded one another across the dark. Somewhere down the passage, the deep hum of the red mercury dimmed for a moment, as if the air itself were holding its breath.

"Your mother—" Liuli began. Her voice faltered, almost imperceptibly, then steadied. "Is she well?"

Cesare did not answer at once.

He was looking at a face that was almost his mother's, and what came to him was another image entirely — a different afternoon, rain on the windows, his mother seated at the sill, her long black hair over one shoulder, her eyes fixed on the rain as if she were looking for someone in it. He had crossed the room and lifted her hair to tie it back for her. It had smelled of jasmine. He had not understood then why she did not turn to look at him, or why her hands, when she reached to take the ribbon, had not been quite steady.

"She is alive," he said. "In Florence. The Pope has her imprisoned."

"I know," said Liuli. "I have known for many years that Borgia took her from Ceylon. I have known that the white-matter surgery was performed on her, and that part of her memory was taken. And I have known—" Her voice caught, briefly, a thread breaking. "—I have known that she no longer remembers me."

She lowered her head. The thin fingers of one hand tightened on the umbrella's handle.

"But she still remembers you," said Cesare. "Every day she sits by the window and waits for you. She does not know who she is waiting for. But she waits."

Liuli's shoulders moved once, sharply, as if something had struck her across the back.

She did not cry.

"Linlang," she said, under her breath. "Sister."

When she said the name, Cesare felt something close around his chest. Not pain. A weight, like being held under water and made to breathe through a straw.

He closed the feeling down.

"You said you are Xingjian," he said, his voice level. "Ceylon Xingjian?"

Liuli looked up at him. In the red glow, her violet eyes seemed to deepen, like wells filling.

"The pendant you wear about your neck," she said. "Take it off. Show it to me."

He hesitated for the length of a heartbeat, then undid the clasp at his throat.

The silver chain swung down. At its end, a silver pendant turned slowly in the red light. The face of it was a lotus in full bloom, the national flower of Ceylon, the lines of it clean and finely wrought.

"Turn it over," Liuli said.

He turned it.

On the reverse, cut into the silver, was a device he had never seen before — a lotus, and in the heart of the flower a gear, the teeth of the gear sharpened to fine cutting edges. The combination was not one he recognised, but the style of the linework stirred some half-buried memory of the murals in the royal palace of Ceylon.

"This is the mark of the Xingjian family," said Liuli. "The gear is for the reading of stars — the Xingjian calculate the courses of the heavens with geared instruments. The lotus is for blood. The daughters of the Xingjian have been Children of the Lotus, generation upon generation."

She lifted her gaze from the pendant to his face.

"This pendant has passed down through the family for more than ten generations. Your grandmother gave it to your mother. Your mother gave it to you. When she made you flee Florence with it, she must have hoped that one day you would use it to find your own roots."

"My roots are in Ceylon," Cesare said.

"In Ceylon," she said. "The Ceylon Xingjian, Children of the Lotus, keepers, generation upon generation, of the World Tree."

The World Tree.

As the words left her mouth, the golden cannula at the back of Cesare's neck grew hot, and the pale violet tracery along the back of his hand flared for an instant.

"You know of the World Tree?" he said.

"I know more about it than almost anyone alive." Liuli spoke slowly, as if she were choosing each word for its weight. "I know that the Ceylon War was not begun by the Empire of New Rome. It was begun by the Papacy. I know that your Pope, Leo Borgia, never went to Ceylon to spread the faith. He went for what Ceylon was guarding. He went for a branch of the World Tree — Branch Zero-One."

He felt his jaw set.

"I know that your sister Linlang was one of the last bloodline of the Xingjian, and the only person alive who knew the activation key for Branch Zero-One. The Pope took her back to Florence and put her in a cell, and the surgeons opened her head, and he tried to prise the key out of her mind. She would not speak. So he had the surgery done again. And again. Until she could no longer remember who she was."

Cesare's breath stopped, halfway in.

"You are saying," he said, and his voice was tight in his throat, "that the surgery on my mother — the surgery that took her memory — was on the Pope's orders?"

"It was." Liuli's voice was flat. "But he was not trying to torment her. He was trying to dig a key out of a brain. Branch Zero-One can only be woken by a person of Xingjian blood. Your mother was one of the last Xingjian alive. And then she conceived you. You are her son. You have inherited the full measure of her Xingjian blood. Including—"

She lifted a finger and pointed at his eyes.

"The violet. It is the mark of the Xingjian. In the West they call it a curse. In Ceylon it is the highest blood. The Pope did not truly want your mother. He wanted the child she was carrying. A still purer inheritor of the Xingjian line."

"The activation key for Branch Zero-One," she said, "is you."

Cesare stood where he was. The hand on his sword tightened, very slowly, until the knuckles went white.

A number of images came at him then, unbidden — his mother's vacant eyes, her back to him at the rainy window, the Latinate clinical term for a white-matter excision, the considering look that the head of the Borgia family, Hector, had sometimes turned upon him across a table, the low deliberate cough of Pope Leo Borgia as he danced with his mother at the New Year's ball.

All of them, suddenly, hung on a single thread.

"So the Pope has never tried to kill me," Cesare said. His voice was quiet, as if he were remarking on the weather. "He needed me alive."

"He needed your blood," said Liuli. "And he needed your eyes. Branch Zero-One has slept in the deep red mercury for hundreds of years. Only the violet of a true Xingjian can wake it again. Your mother would not cooperate. So he took a longer way around. He raised you to be his blade. He made you, without your knowledge, into his instrument."

"The first surgery," he said, and his fingers on the sword grip had gone the colour of old bone, "the white-matter surgery — that was on the Pope's order?"

"It was on his order. But the surgeon who performed it was not one of his choosing." Liuli said. "At the time of the first operation, someone else was present in the theatre. Someone used the moment to do an extra piece of work. Your grandmother — the previous Xingjian — saw it done, and was not able to stop it. A portion of your mother's memory was sealed away forever. Later, the Pope learned what had happened. What he had was not a whole Xingjian. It was a broken one."

"He did not stop. The Inquisition came back to perform a second, completing operation."

"Who was behind the second?" Cesare said.

"I don't know." Liuli shook her head. "I have been inside Florence, moving quietly, for more than ten years. The trail I followed breaks at that point. But there is something sealed away in the deep of your mother's mind. Someone did not want her to remember it."

Cesare was quiet for a few seconds.

Somewhere down the passage, the red mercury hissed, low, like the breath of some very old animal turning in its sleep.

"You came to Golgotha tonight," he said, watching her. "To release Branch Zero-One?"

Liuli's violet eyes flickered.

"To release Branch Zero-One," she said, "you need two things. The first is the violet of a true Xingjian. You have it. The second is the key that opens this door."

She drew something from the folds of her black gown.

A key.

It was about a foot long, cast in some dark gold-coloured metal, the surface of it laced with fine cracks. Through the cracks, a slow pulse of gold leaked out, and the pulse was of exactly the same character as the pulse from the cannula at the back of his neck.

"This key," said Liuli, "is the last relic left by the first Commander-General of Minerva. It is a piece of perfect solder. But it is not for soldering. It is a fragment of the core of the Omega prototype. The people of the Original Sin Bureau stole a sliver of Branch Zero-One out of that door, and used it to forge the heart of the Omega. This key is the offcut that was left over, from the cutting of the Branch."

"Where did you get it?"

"From your mother." Liuli said. "Before the surgery, she hid it and gave it to a courier. That courier carried it for more than ten years, and at the end of the road gave it to me."

She held the key out toward him.

"What is sealed behind that door," she said, "is not just Branch Zero-One. It is the whole of the secret the Xingjian of Ceylon have spent centuries guarding. The location of the main body of the Branch. The truth of what is sealed in the deep of your mother's mind. I have come to find you, to put this key into your hand, so that you may open the door yourself, and see what is inside."

Cesare reached out.

The instant before his fingers touched the key —

From the other end of the passage came a sound. The measured, even tread of boots on stone. Metal on rock, in a rhythm that was the same on every step, the rhythm of soldiers who had been marched until the marching had become part of their bones.

The tread of the Holy Chapel Armored Division.

Cesare's hand drew back from the key.

The boots grew louder. Mixed in with them was the dry, vicious little sound of gun-bolts being thrown forward.

Out of the red glow, at the far end of the passage, a figure appeared — a man of middle age in a silver-white uniform. On his shoulders, the double-headed eagle of the supreme command of the Holy Chapel Armored Division.

Behind him, twelve soldiers in full kit, each with a new-model repeating rifle at the shoulder.

"Miss Liuli," said the man. He had stopped at twenty paces. His voice was the cold, controlled voice of a man who did not intend to repeat himself. "Hand over the key. Otherwise, do not blame us for what happens."

"Count Reicht," said Liuli, without turning. "You are quicker than I gave you credit for."

"You have been standing at that door a long time." Count Reicht's voice was as flat as a blade. "When your nephew Desmond was a spy at the Royal Maslov Mechanical Institute, we had already been watching you. Did you think your years of hiding had gone unmarked?"

"I knew they had not," Liuli said. "I never expected to fool you. I only needed you to arrive later than I did."

She turned, then, and in the same motion thrust the key into Cesare's hand.

The metal was cold, but the cold bit through him, and the gold pulse inside it answered something in the cannula at the back of his neck, and the base of his skull stung as if a needle had been driven into it.

"You—" he began.

"Go!" She shoved him, hard, in the shoulder, in the direction of a section of the rock wall beside the gate. The force of it was extraordinary, out of all proportion to the thinness of her. "There is a passage there. I cut it into the rock a few years ago. It leads to an exit on the far side of the mine. Take the mine. Come out on the other side of Vesuvius. Quickly."

Count Reicht's face darkened.

"Open fire," he said.

Twelve rifles spoke at once.

Liuli threw the red umbrella open.

It was not a canopy of cloth. It was a fan of dark-gold metal leaves, layered one over the other, like the petals of a great iron flower unfolding. The bullets struck it in a continuous bright hail of sparks. None of them came through.

"A fragment of the Omega—" Licinius's pupils tightened. "That umbrella is made from the hull of the Omega prototype."

"Deputy-Commander Licinius," said Count Reicht, his eyes on him now. "I act on the orders of the College of Cardinals. You and Cesare Borgia have trespassed into a forbidden zone of the Minerva Bureau. I am offering you, for the last time. Step aside."

Licinius did not move.

"Reicht," he said, mildly. "On the little finger of my left hand, I wear the iron honour-ring of the Seraph Knights."

He lifted his hand. On it, in the red light, the iron band sat dull and unadorned. On the inside of the band, a name had been engraved. Licinius.

"As long as I wear this ring," he said, "I will not deny what I have done. Tonight I came to this place of my own choice, with Cesare. If the College of Cardinals wants someone to answer for it, I will answer alone."

"Can you afford to?" said Reicht.

A single shot cracked from above.

The bullet bit into the rock at Reicht's foot, throwing up a fan of sparks. Reicht's head snapped up.

On a ledge of stone high in the passage, a figure stood — a black cloak, a white mask, a long-barrelled repeating rifle with a telescopic sight, the muzzle still smoking.

"Young master!" The figure dropped from the ledge and landed in front of Cesare, lightly, like a cat. "Come with me!"

Cesare knew him — Talasha, the engineer of the Minerva Bureau.

"Deputy-Commander Veronese sent me to fetch you," Talasha said, breathing hard. "The passage is over here —"

Liuli, in the storm of bullets, was still holding the umbrella up. The red canopy was pitted and torn now, the dark-gold leaves scarred by a hundred impacts, and in one place the metal had begun to splinter. A bullet had found a crack and worked its way through. The flat of her cheek had been opened to the bone. A red line ran from the corner of her eye to the corner of her jaw.

She did not fall.

"Go!" she shouted, over the guns. "I will hold them!"

"You —"

"Listen to me!" Her voice came clear, somehow, through the noise of the firing. "The roots of the World Tree are in the East! The leaves are in the West! Only when the two are joined will it end!"

"The secret your mother carries in her mind — the way to open this door —"

A bullet clipped her shoulder. Blood fanned out across the black of her gown. She bared her teeth, and pushed the canopy wider.

"Go!"

Cesare looked at her — at the face that was so nearly his mother's, the blood running down it, the violet eyes that, through the rain of lead, found his and held them. There was no fear in them. There was no pain. There was something else — the look of a person who has carried a thing for forty years and has, at last, set it down into younger hands.

His hand tightened on the sword. Loosened.

"Go!" Licinius caught his arm.

They ran. Talasha had already prized up a panel of stone that had been dressed to look like a part of the wall, and under it was a shaft, narrow, dropping steeply down into blackness.

"Down!" Talasha went first, sliding into the dark.

Licinius went after him.

Cesare looked back, once.

Liuli was still there, the umbrella over her head, the bullets still coming, the red of her gown darker now where the blood had soaked into it. In the cracks of the umbrella, more of the dark-gold was breaking loose.

He threw himself into the shaft.

The metal panel slammed shut above him, and the red light, the guns, Liuli's voice, Count Reicht's shouting — all of it was cut off, sealed away, on the other side of a few inches of iron.

Darkness came in from every side.

The passage was narrow. He had to turn sideways to fit. The walls were wet with a thin slime of moss, and the air was thick with the sharp, sweet, mineral reek of red mercury. Talasha's footsteps led him on, the sound of them going before him down the dark.

"Where does this come out?" he asked, into the black.

"At the foot of Vesuvius," Talasha's voice came back. "In the abandoned mine. The same mine that is to be tomorrow's battlefield of the confrontation."

Cesare's hand, in the dark, tightened on the key.

The gold pulse inside it threw a faint light over the violet tracery on the back of his hand, and the tracery was moving, creeping up his wrist as he watched, the way ivy creeps up a stone wall.

The back of his neck was hot. So hot it felt as if it were burning.

The cannula was answering the key.

And from the end of the passage, somewhere ahead, he could hear the first distant sound of it — the long rising scream of a steam boiler being fired up. Of a great engine being woken. Of a thing made of iron and brass and red mercury beginning, somewhere in the dark, to breathe.

第167章 红水银蒸汽的第一声嘶吼
