【中文】
第167章 红水银蒸汽的第一声嘶吼

密道尽头是一扇厚重的铁门，塔拉夏拧动阀门时铰链发出尖锐的呻吟，像是被惊醒的野兽的磨牙声。冷风从门缝里涌出来，带着红水银特有的金属腥味和灼热感。

西泽尔侧身挤出最后一段窄道，脚踏上硬金的地面时腿微微一软，扶住了岩壁。

"西泽尔少爷？"

一个声音从阴影中传来。

西泽尔抬起头，看见一个高大的身影从实验场深处快步走来——阿方索。他的机械臂在昏暗中泛着暗淡的铜光，脸上的表情先是一怔，继而是一种压抑许久的惊恐。

"老板！"阿方索冲上来，一把抱住了他，机械臂的关节处咔哒作响。他没有说话，只是用力地、紧紧地箍着西泽尔的肩膀，喉头哽住了。西泽尔感觉到他胸口剧烈地起伏，肩头的衣料很快就湿了一片。

"……我们都担心死了。"阿方索的声音闷在喉咙里，像是被砂纸磨过。

西泽尔的手抬起来，在他后背轻轻拍了一下。

"没事。"

就这两个字。

李锡尼从密道里最后出来，拍了拍身上的灰尘，扫了一眼四周。封闭实验场极其宽阔，穹顶高得看不清顶部，墙壁上嵌着熄灭的工业灯架，地面是整块的硬金板，中央区域的地板上还残留着高温灼烧的暗红色痕迹——那是不久前某台巨型设备运转时留下的。

空气中红水银的气味浓得呛人。

阿方索这才松开手，退后半步，抬手胡乱抹了一把脸。他看见李泽尔尼身上的制服和胸口的黑天使徽章，没有多问，只是低声说："跟我来，佛朗哥教授和薇若兰副总长都在。"

三人穿过实验场。两侧停放着几具未完工的甲胄框架，电火花从断裂的电缆中劈劈啪啪地跳出，在黑暗中如同萤火虫。实验场尽头的一扇铁门半掩着，里面透出明亮的灯光和人声。

阿方索推开门。

灯光里，一张宽大的作战地图铺在中央的长桌上，桌边围满了人。

佛朗哥教授站在桌首，老人的脸上带着深深的倦意，眼底有明显的青黑。他的白发在灯光下显得格外干燥，像是一蓬将熄的火焰。他一只手撑在桌面上，另一只手捏着一支炭笔，正在地图上勾画什么。薇若兰站在他右侧，一身黑色作战服，长发用银簪高高束起，露出修长的颈线。她的手指在地图上点着维苏威火山的位置，嘴唇抿成一条锋利的线。

瓦莲京娜坐在桌角，军服笔挺，金色长发编成一条粗辫搭在肩头，白靴翘在桌腿上。她手里握着一杯黑咖啡，目光冷冽如冰。

昆提良和唐璜站在另一侧，昆提良怀里还抱着昏迷的艾莲，女孩的头上缠着新的绷带，脸色苍白。唐璜靠在墙上，双手抱胸，嘴唇翕动着像在跟昆提良说什么，看见门开的一瞬间回过头来。

碧儿也在。她站在佛朗哥身后不远处，双手捧着一叠文件，眼圈红红的，看见西泽尔时嘴唇抖了一下。

所有人都转过了头。

"老板！"唐璜第一个冲上来，拳头砸在西泽尔的肩膀上，力道不轻，"你他妈跑哪去了？李锡尼那个老狐狸半夜把你带出去，我们以为你被异端审判局抓走了！"

昆提良也大步走过来，没有说话，只是伸出大掌在西泽尔的后脑勺上揉了一把，力气大得让他脑袋一偏。

"我没事。"西泽尔说。

他的声音很平，没有多余的情绪。苍白的面孔在灯光下显得近乎透明，嘴唇还有些干裂，但那双紫色的眼睛——此刻在灯光下仍然是沉静的深紫色，还没有金纹浮现——重新扫过在场的每一张脸。

最后他的目光落在佛朗哥身上。

"教授。"

佛朗哥放下炭笔，浑浊的老眼在西泽尔身上停留了三秒钟，然后从西泽尔的脸上移到他手里握着的东西——那把散发着暗金色脉动光芒的钥匙，和一块拳头大小的银白色金属碎片。

"那是什么？"佛朗哥的声音嘶哑，像是被砂纸磨过。

西泽尔走到长桌前，将钥匙和碎片放在作战地图上。钥匙的暗金色脉动照亮了地图的边缘，而那块银白色碎片在灯光下折射出冰冷的寒光。

"这是打开骷髅地黑铁巨门的钥匙。"西泽尔说，"这是圣剑装具·Excalibur的碎片。"

桌边安静了一瞬。

薇若兰的指尖在桌面上无声地收紧了。

"骷髅地？"佛朗哥的眼睛骤然亮了起来，像是烧到最后一丝余烬的火堆突然被人吹了一口气，"你说的是初代总长封锁的那个区域？"

"是的。"西泽尔的目光环视所有人，"我今晚去了那里。"

他停顿了一下，像是在组织语言。然后他平静地开口，语速不快，但每一个字都像是铁钉钉进木板里。

"明天对抗战的真实目的，不是测试。"

唐璜皱起了眉。

"原罪机关要用战斗的余波震碎骷髅地的封印，释放封存的世界树残枝02号。他们要借助我身上的星见血脉，同时连接两片残枝。"西泽尔的声音依然平静，"他们的最终目标是——重启机械神国。"

密闭的实验场里落针可闻。远处的某根管道发出细微的嘶嘶声，像是有什么东西在地下深处喘息。

佛朗哥的手撑在桌面上，指节发白。

"世界树残枝……"老人的嘴唇动了动，像是在回忆某个久远的、不愿触碰的词，"初代总长留下的记录里提到过这个词。传说锡兰的星见家族守护着什么东西……我还以为那只是神话。"

"不是神话。"西泽尔说，"我亲眼见过残枝01号。"

他抬手指了指自己的眼睛。

"我的紫瞳。"

佛朗哥的目光死死钉在他的瞳孔上，沉默了很久。

"所以原罪机关的真正计划是利用明天那个矿道作为战场，借你们交战时产生的能量冲击震碎封印。"薇若兰接过话，她的声音清冷如刀刃切冰，"可他们是怎么知道残枝02号在骷髅地的？"

"原罪机关的主人。"李锡尼开口了。他站在门边，声音粗哑，"我今晚在骷髅地入口处遇到了他。"

所有人的目光都转向他。

"那个人戴着银面具，身躯有多处机械修补的痕迹。"李锡尼的黑色十字纹蜂巢手铳在腰间发出一声轻响，"他不是泛泛之辈，他清楚密涅瓦机关的所有机密，包括初代总长封锁骷髅地的真正原因。"

佛朗哥的手开始发抖。

"琉璃小姐呢？"碧儿小声问。

"她挡住了圣堂装甲师。"西泽尔的声音微微低了一些，"她让我们先走。"

沉默像一块巨石压在所有人头顶。

"明天我们必须同时面对第三代普罗米修斯和欧米茄原型体。"佛朗哥终于打破了沉默，他的声音变得沙哑而果决，像是做出了某个艰难的决定，"原本我们的计划是五人驾驶新型炽天使试制版对抗古洛诺斯，现在多了一台欧米茄——"

"不是多了一台。"薇若兰打断了他，"是敌方在原罪机关的普罗米修斯之外，还藏着一张底牌。欧米茄原型体——那个东西如果被完全唤醒，它的战力不亚于我们任何一台试制机。"

她说完，转向西泽尔。

"你拿到了完美焊料和Excalibur碎片？"

"完美焊料就是这把钥匙。"西泽尔点头，"我把它带来了。"

薇若兰伸出手，将那块银白色的碎片从桌上拿起来，对着灯光转了转。碎片的表面镌刻着极其精密的圣言纹路，在灯光下折射出淡蓝色的光晕。

"这块碎片是Excalibur的核心部分。"薇若兰说，"如果重新熔铸，它可以成为不朽之王芯片的最后一块组件。"

她放下碎片，转身向实验场深处走去。

"跟我来。"

西泽尔跟上她。李锡尼犹豫了一瞬，也迈步走了。

实验场最深处，一具崭新的甲胄安静地伫立在金属支架上。它通体呈暗红色，线条流畅而凶悍，每一块装甲板的接缝处都泛着极淡的金色微光。头盔的左肩上刻着两个东方文字——"红龙"。

新型红龙试制版。

这是密涅瓦机关为西泽尔打造的最终决战兵器。

薇若兰走到甲胄前，攀上支架，将那块Excalibur碎片嵌入了头盔的侧面凹槽中。碎片与凹槽完美契合，咔哒一声轻响，碎片表面的圣言纹路亮起了淡蓝色的光，光芒沿着凹槽蔓延开来，与甲胄的暗红色装甲融为一体。

"这块碎片是用完美合金打造的。"薇若兰从支架上跳下来，拍了拍手上的灰尘，"它可以让你在不朽之王模式下维持更长时间。原本你的神经系统只能承受三分钟，融合了它之后，可以延长到八分钟左右。"

她转头看向西泽尔，目光里少有地带着一丝认真。

"但三分钟和八分钟的差别，可能是生和死的差别。"

西泽尔点了点头。

他伸手触碰甲胄的胸甲。硬金与影金属复合装甲的触感冰凉而坚实，表面的微光像是有生命一样在他指尖下跳动。

"作战服在哪里？"他问。

"这边。"佛朗哥已经跟了过来。

作战服挂在支架旁的衣架上，深红色的紧身衣料，银色的神经接驳导线从领口延伸出来。佛朗哥将作战服取下递给西泽尔。

"穿上它，然后我们需要讨论新的战术分工。"佛朗哥说，"原定的计划必须修改——我们现在不只是要打赢普罗米修斯，还要阻止原罪机关激活残枝02号。"

西泽尔接过作战服，走向实验场一侧的更衣室。

瓦莲京娜不知什么时候已经跟到了门口。她靠在门框上，金色长发在灯光下泛着冷冽的光泽，白靴的鞋跟在地上轻轻叩着。

"西泽尔。"她叫住他。

他停下脚步，转头看她。

瓦莲京娜从腰间取下一样东西，递到他面前——是一枚银色的戒指，内侧镶嵌着一粒米粒大小的冰原寒玉碎料。

"上次给你的那枚只是见面礼。"她的声音冷硬，但眼睛里有些什么柔软的东西在闪，"这枚是我请王宫的工匠重新打的，尺寸刚好适合你的右手中指。"

西泽尔沉默了一瞬，接过戒指，将它套在右手中指上。银环冰凉的触感贴着他的皮肤，那粒冰原寒玉的碎料散发着淡淡的凉意，像是握着一小片雪原。

"谢谢。"

"别谢我。"瓦莲京娜转过身，军靴的鞋跟在地上磕出清脆的声响，"打赢再说。"

西泽尔推门进了更衣室。

作战服紧贴着他的身体，神经接驳导线从领口延伸出来，轻轻搭在他的肩头。镜子里映出他苍白的面孔和紫色的眼睛，紫色的虹膜里还带着暗金色的光晕——是星见血脉被钥匙共鸣后留下的残余痕迹。

他伸手触碰自己的后颈。黄金套管滚烫。

钥匙的共鸣还没有完全消退。

他推开门走出来。

实验场中央已经聚集了所有人。新型红龙试制版、所罗门王、奥古斯都、蔷薇之鬼，四具试制甲胄并排矗立，像四尊等待出征的钢铁神像。瓦莲京娜的改装神怒Ⅲ型停在它们旁边，暗红色的涂装与新型红龙相呼应。

"最终的战术分工。"佛朗哥站在作战地图前，炭笔在矿道的布局图上划出几个标记，"西泽尔驾驶新型红龙，作为主攻力量，目标直指普罗米修斯。昆提良的奥古斯都作为前排肉盾，正面承受攻击为西泽尔创造机会。阿方索的所罗门王在后方提供远程火力支援和战场维修。唐璜的蔷薇之鬼作为刺客，寻找机会突袭骑士舱。"

"我呢？"瓦莲京娜问。

"公主殿下驾驶改装神怒Ⅲ型机动接应，随时支援最薄弱的位置。"佛朗哥看了她一眼，"您的冰原寒玉神经接驳技术可以大幅降低反噬，是我们在持久战中的关键。"

"明白。"瓦莲京娜点头。

"还有欧米茄原型体。"薇若兰开口了，她的目光落在西泽尔身上，"如果原罪机关唤醒它，谁来对付？"

佛朗哥沉默了一瞬。

"欧米茄原型体……"他低声说，"原罪机关封存了它四十年，他们没有我们的神经接驳技术，也没有适格者。它被唤醒后只能依靠预设的AI程序作战，战力应该会打折扣。"

"但它毕竟是欧米茄。"薇若兰说，"即便打折扣，也不是普通试制机能够对抗的。"

"所以我们必须速战速决。"西泽尔说，"在欧米茄被完全唤醒之前结束战斗。"

"说得好听。"唐璜嘟囔，"可普罗米修斯也不是吃素的。"

"欧米茄交给西泽尔。"瓦莲京娜突然说。

所有人看向她。

"普罗米修斯由我们四个牵制。"她的目光在西泽尔脸上停留了一瞬，"欧米茄只能由你来对付。"

她没有解释为什么。但西泽尔懂了。

欧米茄的核心是红水银。而红水银与星见血脉之间存在某种古老的共鸣。只有他才能与那台沉睡四十年的金色甲胄对抗。

"好。"他说。

佛朗哥深吸一口气，浑浊的老眼里重新燃起了光。

"明天日出时，维苏威火山底部废弃矿道。"他的声音苍老而坚定，"这场仗，不只是为了打赢测试。"

"是为了阻止机械神国的重启。"薇若兰接过话。

"是为了保护我们的国家。"佛朗哥说。

"是为了活下去。"阿方索低声加了一句。

唐璜耸了耸肩："为了明天还能吃上翡冷翠的烤鸡。"

昆提良重重地点了点头。

碧儿抱紧了手里的文件，眼眶里有泪光在打转。

远处的管道里，蒸汽的嘶吼声越来越近了。那声音低沉而绵长，像是一头沉睡在地底的巨兽正在被唤醒。

地面开始微微震动。

佛朗哥抬起头，看向实验场的穹顶。

"欧米茄原型体……"他的声音低了下去，"原罪机关开始激活它了。"

西泽尔转身，走向新型红龙。

暗红色的甲胄在灯光下泛着冷冽的光泽，左肩的"红龙"二字像是用鲜血写成。头盔的侧面，那块新嵌入的Excalibur碎片散发着淡蓝色的微光，像是一只沉睡的眼睛。

"穿上它。"薇若兰说。

西泽尔点头。

作战服紧贴着他的身体，神经接驳导线沿着脊椎延伸到后颈的黄金套管。他抬手触碰甲胄的胸甲，暗红色的装甲板自动向两侧分开，露出内部的骑乘舱。骑乘舱的设计符合人体工学，内衬是柔软的记忆合金，可以完美包裹骑士的身体。

他踏进骑乘舱，背部贴合上脊椎支撑架。黄金套管与甲胄的神经接驳系统自动连接，一连串数据流涌入他的脑海。

甲胄的装甲板在他周围合拢。咔哒。咔哒。咔哒。每一块装甲板都精准地扣合在他的四肢和躯干上，像是一件量身定做的钢铁外衣。

头盔降下，扣在他的脑袋上。面罩合拢的瞬间，他的视野变成了360度的全景模式——实验场的每一个人、每一具甲胄、每一盏灯都清晰地映在他的视网膜上。

左肩上，"红龙"二字透过面罩映入他的眼睛。

他的紫色瞳孔里，暗金色的纹路开始缓缓浮现。

紫瞳金纹。

星见血脉在共鸣。

他抬起右手，握紧，又松开。冰原寒玉银戒指的凉意从指尖传来，清醒而冷冽。

"准备好了吗？"

他的声音通过甲胄的扩音器传出，低沉而平静，在整个实验场里回荡。

唐璜第一个响应，他跳进蔷薇之鬼的骑乘舱，超轻型甲胄的关节处发出清脆的咔哒声："随时！"

昆提良闷哼一声，奥古斯都的重型装甲在他周围合拢，闭眼狮头纹章在灯光下闪着暗金色的光。

阿方索沉默地攀进所罗门王，机械臂与甲胄的接口完美连接，狙击镜在他眼前亮起。

瓦莲京娜最后一个登上改装神怒Ⅲ型。暗红色甲胄合拢的瞬间，她的声音冷冷地传来：

"走吧。"

四具甲胄齐步向实验场的出口走去。新型红龙走在最前面，暗红色的装甲在灯光下泛着冷冽的金属光泽，像是一头即将出征的钢铁巨龙。

地面在震动。

远处的红水银蒸汽嘶吼声越来越近，越来越响。维苏威火山开始微微颤抖，穹顶上有灰尘簌簌落下。

他们要去打一场改变世界的仗。

而在地底深处，某个被封存了四十年的金色巨人，正在缓缓睁开眼睛。

【English】
Chapter 167 — The First Roar of Red Mercury

The iron door at the end of the passage was older than anyone still living, and heavier than it had any right to be. Tarasha turned the wheel, and the hinges screamed — a thin, teeth-on-edge shriek that went on too long, the kind of sound that lived in the bones of the mountain and resented being woken.

Cold air came through the gap first, then the smell: red mercury. Metallic, hot, vaguely sweet, the way a fruit is sweet only just before it begins to rot. Cesare squeezed through the last narrow stretch of stone sideways, and when his boot met the floor his knee almost buckled. He caught himself against the wall. His palm found cold metal, and the surface felt, absurdly, alive.

"Young master Cesare?"

A voice, low and startled, from the dark of the testing hall.

He looked up.

A tall shape was coming toward him out of the shadows — Alfonso, his mechanical arm catching the dim light in dull copper. The man's face went through three things in two heartbeats: surprise, then the slack-mouthed relief of a man who has just seen the dead walk, and then something he tried to hide and failed.

"Chief." Alfonso closed the distance in three long strides. His arms went around Cesare, the joints of the left one clicking and whirring as it locked into place. He did not speak. He held on. Cesare could feel the man's chest heaving against him, the damp soaking quickly through the shoulder of his coat, the rough grind of a throat that had forgotten how to swallow.

"We thought — " Alfonso's voice broke. He tried again, muffled into Cesare's collar. "We thought you were dead. We thought the Inquisition had you. We sat here in the dark and waited for them to bring us the news."

Cesare lifted his hand and laid it, once, between Alfonso's shoulder blades.

"I'm here."

That was all.

Licinius came through last, dusting powder from his coat. He looked around the sealed testing hall with the practiced eye of a man who had once been paid to walk into worse places and come out again. The chamber was vast — high-domed, the ceiling lost in shadow, dead industrial lamp brackets bolted to the walls like iron thorns. The floor was one continuous sheet of hardened gold alloy, and at the center of it the plating was discolored, a long smear of dark red where something enormous had run hot only hours before. The air was so thick with mercury vapor it caught the back of the throat like smoke.

Alfonso let go. He stepped back, scrubbed his face with the heel of his hand, and only then looked at what Cesare was wearing — the unfamiliar uniform, the black angel insignia over the heart. He did not ask. He had learned, over the years, which questions a man answered by his silence.

"This way," he said quietly. "Professor Franco and Vice-Commander Verolan are inside."

They crossed the floor between ranks of half-built armor frames, silent sentinels whose cabling still spit pale sparks into the dark. The sparks drifted and died like fireflies that had given up. At the far end of the hall, a door stood half open, and through it spilled a wedge of yellow lamp-light and the low murmur of too many people trying not to shout.

Alfonso pushed it open.

The room beyond was small for what it contained. A campaign map the size of a dining table had been spread across the central workbench, and every inch of it was occupied — by hands, by pencils, by the bent heads of people who had not slept. The lamps overhead were turned up too high, the way lamps are when people are afraid of what the dark might let in.

Franco stood at the head of the table. He looked older than Cesare remembered. The skin beneath his eyes was the color of a bruise three days old, and his white hair, which had always had a kind of fierce, weather-worn nobility to it, lay against his skull now like the last flames on a dead hearth. He was marking something on the map with a stick of charcoal, his free hand planted flat on the table to keep himself upright. To his right, Verolan was in field black, her long hair pinned high with a silver pin that caught the lamplight when she moved. She was tapping a fingertip at the position of Mount Vesuvius. Her mouth was a thin, sharp line.

Valentina sat at the corner of the table, boots up on a leg of it, uniform crisp as if she had ironed it onto herself. A cup of black coffee steamed at her elbow, untouched. Her eyes were the color of a frozen lake and gave back nothing.

Quintilian and Don Juan stood across from her. Quintilian had Aileen in his arms — the girl's head freshly bandaged, her face the particular white of a person whose body has decided it is finished with being awake. Don Juan leaned against the wall, arms folded, lips moving as he muttered something to Quintilian. He turned at the sound of the door.

Biel was there too, behind Franco, clutching a stack of papers to her chest. Her eyes were red-rimmed. When she saw Cesare, her lower lip trembled once and she bit it still.

Every head in the room turned.

"Chief!" Don Juan crossed the room in four long strides and drove his fist into Cesare's shoulder hard enough to make his teeth click together. "Where in the name of God have you been? Licinius dragged you out in the middle of the night and we thought the Holy Office had you!"

Quintilian followed, slower. He did not say anything. He put one large hand on the back of Cesare's skull and squeezed, hard, the way a man handles a thing he was afraid he would not get to handle again. Cesare's head tilted sideways with the pressure.

"I'm all right," he said.

His voice came out level. No theater in it. His face, in the lamplight, was nearly translucent — the kind of pallor that has nothing to do with fear and everything to do with what the body has been made to do. His lips were cracked. But his eyes — those eyes, which the lamp-light still read as a deep, settled violet, the gold veins not yet stirred — moved across the room and touched each face there in turn, the way a man takes attendance of the living.

His gaze came to rest on the old professor.

"Professor."

Franco set the charcoal down. His clouded eyes held Cesare for a long three seconds, then traveled down to the things in his hands — to the key, which pulsed with a slow dark-gold heartbeat, and to a shard of silvery metal the size of a man's fist that seemed to drink the lamplight rather than reflect it.

"What is that?" Franco's voice was a ruin of itself.

Cesare walked to the table and laid both objects on the map. The key's pulse lit the paper's edge in a slow, living bronze. The shard sat there and did nothing at all, which was somehow worse.

"This is the key that opens the black iron gate of Golgotha," Cesare said. "And this is a fragment of the holy sword assembly — Excalibur."

The table went quiet in a way that has a sound of its own.

Verolan's fingers, which had been resting on the map, drew slowly closed.

"Golgotha," Franco said. The word came out of him like something dragged from the back of a chest that had been nailed shut. "You mean the place the first Grandmaster sealed off?"

"Yes."

Cesare looked around the table. He paused, the way a man pauses before stepping off a height, gathering the words into the right shape.

"The real purpose of tomorrow's trial is not a test."

Don Juan's mouth pulled to one side.

"The Order of Original Sin intends to use the shockwave of the battle to shatter Golgotha's seal, and to release the sealed World Tree Branch — Number Two. They intend to use the Seer blood in my veins to form a connection between the two branches at once." Cesare's voice was still level. Each word landed like a nail driven flush into oak. "Their ultimate objective is the reactivation of the Machine Kingdom."

In the sealed hall, a pipe somewhere in the wall gave a long, thin hiss. It sounded like something breathing underground.

Franco's hand on the table went the color of bone.

"The World Tree Branch," the old man murmured. "The first Grandmaster's records mentioned the phrase. There were stories, in Ceylon, that the Seer family kept something — I had always thought it was myth."

"It is not myth." Cesare lifted a finger to his own eye. "My violet sight."

Franco stared at his pupil in silence for a long time.

"So." Verolan spoke before anyone else. Her voice was a blade drawn across ice. "The Order's real plan is to use the mine at Vesuvius as their battlefield, to ride the energy of our clash into the seal."

"Yes."

"Then how do they know Number Two is in Golgotha at all?" Verolan asked.

"Because of the master of the Order," Licinius said, from the doorway. He had not moved from it. His black cross-sting honeycomb sidearm shifted against his hip with a small dry sound. "I met him tonight, at the Golgotha entrance. He wore a silver mask. The body under it had been repaired in too many places. He knew the Minerva Bureau's every secret — including the true reason the first Grandmaster sealed the place."

Franco's hand had begun to tremble.

"And Livia?" Biel asked, very quietly. "Where is Miss Livia?"

Cesare's voice, when it came, was half a tone lower than before.

"She held off the Cathedral Armored Division. She told us to go."

The silence that followed sat on the room like a stone.

"Tomorrow," Franco said, at last, "we must face the third-generation Prometheus and the original Omega prototype at the same time." He straightened. The decision he had been postponing settled into his shoulders. "Our original plan was five pilots in the new Serafim prototypes against Kronos. Now there is an Omega besides —"

"Not a beside," Verolan said. "A trump card. The Omega prototype, fully awakened, will outclass any one of our prototypes by itself."

She turned to Cesare.

"You have the perfect alloy, and the Excalibur fragment?"

"The key is the perfect alloy. I brought it."

Verolan reached out and took the silver shard from the map. She turned it slowly under the lamp. The Holy Word runes carved into its face were extraordinarily fine, and in the light they gave back a thin, cold bloom of pale blue.

"This fragment is the heart of Excalibur. If it is reforged, it becomes the last component of the Immortal King core."

She set it down and walked toward the far end of the testing hall.

"Follow me."

Cesare followed. Licinius hesitated a heartbeat, then followed too.

At the deepest part of the hall, on a metal cradle, a suit of armor stood in the lamplight as if it had been waiting there for years and had not been bored. The lines of it were clean and a little cruel, the color of old blood. Along the seams of every plate, a faint gold light ran like a vein under the skin. On the left shoulder of the helm, two characters had been etched — *Red Dragon*.

The new Red Dragon prototype.

The final weapon the Minerva Bureau had built for Cesare Borgia.

Verolan climbed the cradle and set the fragment into a recess cut for it on the side of the helmet. It seated itself with a small, decisive click, and the runes on the silver woke — a thin blue glow that ran along the recess and bled down into the dark-red plates of the armor, as if the suit had just drawn a breath.

"This fragment is forged of the perfect alloy," Verolan said, dropping back to the floor and brushing her palms on her coat. "It will let you hold the Immortal King mode far longer. Your nervous system could only bear three minutes before. With this, eight."

She looked at him. There was, for once, something careful in the look.

"The difference between three minutes and eight," she said, "is the difference between alive and not."

Cesare nodded.

He laid his palm against the breastplate. Beneath his fingers, the gold light moved.

"Where is the flight suit?"

"This way." Franco had followed. He took the suit down from its hook and held it out — deep red, close-cut, with silver nerve-interface cabling trailing from the collar like a fringe of thin wires.

"Put it on. Then we need a new plan of attack. We are not only fighting Prometheus tomorrow. We are stopping the Order from activating Branch Number Two."

Cesare took the suit and walked toward the changing room at the side of the hall.

Valentina, who had followed without anyone noticing, was leaning in the doorway. The lamplight picked out the cold gilt of her hair. The heel of her white boot tapped the floor, once, twice.

"Cesare."

He stopped.

She reached to her belt and held something out to him. It was a silver ring, and set on the inside of the band, so small it might have been a flaw, was a single grain of polar ice jade.

"The one I gave you before was a meeting gift." Her voice was hard. Something in her eyes was not. "This one was made for you, by the palace smiths. It will fit the middle finger of your right hand."

Cesare was still for a moment. He took the ring and slid it on. The silver was cold, and the tiny jade set into it carried the ghost of a colder place — a snowfield, somewhere, that had not seen sun.

"Thank you."

"Don't." She turned on her heel. The hard white sound of the boot against the floor was very final. "Win first. Thank me after."

She walked away.

He pushed the changing-room door shut and dressed. The suit pulled tight against him. The nerve-cables lay along his shoulders and ran down his spine to the gold cannula set into the back of his neck. In the mirror, his face was the color of old paper. His eyes, in the glass, were still violet — but the iris was ringed now with a thin dark-gold corona, the residual echo of the key's resonance. The gold cannula at the back of his neck was almost too hot to bear.

The resonance had not finished.

He pushed the door open and walked back out.

They had all gathered at the center of the hall. Four prototypes stood in a row on their cradles, like four iron gods waiting to be woken. Red Dragon. Solomon. Augustus. Rose Ghost. Beside them, Valentina's modified Wrath of God Mk. III waited, her dark-red paint a quiet match to the new Red Dragon.

"Final assignments." Franco stood over the map, the charcoal in his hand. "Cesare takes Red Dragon. He is the main strike — he goes for Prometheus. Quintilian in Augustus is the front line, absorbing the first blows to open the way. Alfonso in Solomon provides long-range fire and field repair. Don Juan in Rose Ghost is the assassin — he finds the cockpit."

"And me?" Valentina.

"Your Highness takes Wrath of God III as mobile support, reinforcing whichever position is weakest. Your polar-ice nerve interface gives us our best resistance to the backlash. We will need that, if the fight is long."

"Understood." Valentina nodded.

"And the Omega." Verolan looked at Cesare. "If the Order wakes it, who takes it?"

Franco was quiet for a moment.

"The Omega prototype," he said, at last. "The Order has had it sealed for forty years. They do not have our nerve-interface technology. They do not have a compatible pilot. It will have to run on its pre-set AI. That should blunt it."

"It is still an Omega," Verolan said.

"Then we must end the fight before it is fully awake," Cesare said.

Don Juan snorted. "Easy to say. Prometheus is not going to roll over and cooperate."

"The Omega is Cesare's," Valentina said.

Every head turned.

"Prometheus, the four of us will contain. The Omega is his to kill."

She did not explain why. She did not need to. Cesare understood.

The core of the Omega was red mercury. Between the mercury and the Seer blood in his veins there was an old, terrible sympathy. He was the only one of them who could face a forty-year-old gold giant and survive the meeting.

"Good," he said.

Franco drew a long breath. The light in his old, ruined eyes had come back — not the easy light of hope, but the harder light of a man who has decided what he is going to do.

"Tomorrow at sunrise," he said. "The abandoned mine at the foot of Vesuvius. This is not a test."

"It is to stop the Machine Kingdom from waking," Verolan said.

"It is to defend our country," Franco said.

"It is to live through it," Alfonso said, very quietly.

Don Juan shrugged. "It is so that I can still eat roast chicken in Florence tomorrow night."

Quintilian nodded once, like a hammer falling.

Biel pressed the stack of papers to her chest. The shine at the rims of her eyes was very bright and she did not blink.

Somewhere in the pipes behind the walls of the testing hall, something was beginning to roar. It was the sound of red mercury moving under pressure — a long, slow, living bellow, like the breath of an animal that had been asleep under the mountain for a very long time. The floor was trembling, almost imperceptibly, the way a table trembles when a heavy cart goes by outside.

Franco lifted his head and looked up at the unseen ceiling of the sealed hall.

"The Order has begun to wake it," he said softly. "The Omega prototype."

Cesare turned toward the Red Dragon.

Under the lamps, the dark-red plates of the new armor gave back a cold, clean light. The two characters etched into the left shoulder of the helmet — *Red Dragon* — looked, in that light, as though they had been written in fresh blood. In the recess on the side of the helmet, the Excalibur fragment pulsed faintly with its cold blue rune-light, like a single sleeping eye.

"Put it on," Verolan said.

He did.

The flight suit bit in against him. The nerve-cables ran down the channel of his spine and clicked, one by one, into the gold cannula at the back of his neck. He laid his palm against the breastplate. The plates parted for him with a long, oiled whisper, opening the way into the cockpit. The padding inside was a memory-metal weave that had been made to the shape of him. He stepped in. His back met the spine cradle. The gold cannula mated with the armor's interface. A long, cold stream of data slid into the back of his skull.

The plates closed around him. *Click. Click. Click.* Piece by piece, the suit folded itself onto his arms, his legs, his torso, until he was wearing a hundred and eighty kilos of red-gold steel like a second skeleton. The helmet came down last. The visor sealed itself. His vision went dark for a heartbeat, and then opened out into a perfect three-hundred-and-sixty-degree world — every face, every cradle, every lamp in the hall, sharp as a coin.

Through the visor, the two characters on his left shoulder looked back at him.

*Red Dragon.*

The gold threads in the violet of his eyes, far back in the part of him that was still only a man, began at last to stir.

He flexed his right hand. The cold of the silver ring on his middle finger reached him through the gauntlet, clean and bright, like a handful of snow.

"Ready?" he asked.

His own voice came back to him through the armor's speakers, low and level, and rolled out across the floor of the testing hall.

"Always," Don Juan said, from inside Rose Ghost. The light frame clicked sharply around him as he climbed in.

Quintilian grunted. The heavy plates of Augustus locked around him one by one. The closed-eyed lion on its chest caught the lamp-light and held it, a single dark-gold coin.

Alfonso climbed into Solomon in silence. His mechanical arm and the armor's port found each other and married with a low hum. The scope in front of his eye lit up.

Valentina was the last. The dark-red plates of Wrath of God III sealed around her.

"Move," she said.

The four prototypes stepped out from their cradles, in time, the sound of it heavy on the metal floor. Red Dragon went first, the red of its plates almost black under the lamps, the long shape of it cutting the air in front of the others like the head of something that had been promised a war and intended to collect.

The floor was shaking harder now.

The roar in the pipes was louder. The red mercury was moving, deep under the mountain, drawing in its long, slow breath for the day that was coming. Vesuvius was beginning, at its deepest foundations, to wake.

They were walking out to a fight that would change the world.

And far below, in a chamber no living man had entered in forty years, something gold was opening its eyes.

【中文】
第168章 命运决战的倒计时

车厢很长，铁壁上刷着暗绿色的防锈漆，每隔三米挂一盏防震油灯，灯光昏黄，把六具甲胄的剪影拉得老长。

五具新型炽天使依次固定在车厢两侧的支撑架上——新型红龙居中，暗红色装甲在油灯下泛着冷冽的金属光泽，左肩"红龙"二字若隐若现；蔷薇之鬼超轻型的骨架最纤细，像一柄被竖起来的窄刃；奥古斯都最重，闭眼狮头纹章的铁壁上沾着未擦净的机油；所罗门王的胸甲上嵌着维修工具箱的接口；最后一具是瓦莲京娜的改装神怒Ⅲ型，暗红涂装加忍冬花纹的纹章，临时改的肩甲上还留有焊接的痕迹。

它们静静地站着，像一群等待被唤醒的钢铁巨人。

西泽尔坐在车厢最里面的角落，背靠着装甲板，双腿微曲，右手摊开在膝盖上，掌心里躺着两样东西——一枚嵌着米粒大小冰原寒玉碎料的银戒指，和一片嵌在红龙剑柄凹槽里的圣剑Excalibur碎片。

银戒指的玉料在灯光下透着极淡的蓝，像一滴凝固的冰湖。

碎片的断口还泛着冷光。

他没有说话，目光落在车厢尽头那台老式蒸汽电视机上，屏幕闪着雪花，断断续续地播报着翡冷翠深夜的新闻。

"……万国盛典明天正式开幕！本届盛典的重头戏，是新型普罗米修斯与新型炽天使的公开对抗战，胜者将成为教皇国未来的主力武装……各国使节已陆续抵达翡冷翠，枢机会表示对抗战将全程向万国公开……"

画面切换，一架重型运输车载着蒙着帆布的巨型物体穿过翡冷翠的凯旋门，帆布下面是第三代普罗米修斯·古洛诺斯的模糊轮廓。

屏幕右下角的红色倒计时牌跳动着白色的数字——

距离对抗战开始：11:59:47。

11:59:46。

11:59:45。

车厢微微颠簸了一下，窗外是台伯河底隧道的石壁，昏黄的壁灯一盏接一盏地向后退去，节奏单调如心跳。

西泽尔的左手边，瓦莲京娜·罗曼诺夫端坐着，金色长发在脑后编成一条粗辫子，白靴交叠在甲胄固定架的横杠上，忍冬的清香从她的衣领间淡淡地透出来。她没有看他，目光落在自己暗红色甲胄的胸甲纹章上，嘴唇微微抿着，像是在心里默算什么。

再过去半米，阿方索坐在一张折叠维修凳上，机械臂搁在膝盖上，他的右手——那只布满电路纹路的金属手——正牵着塔拉夏。

塔拉夏靠着他的肩膀，年轻机械师的脸上还带着从鹰巢赶路时沾上的油污，眼底有深深的疲倦，但嘴角微微上翘着。

阿方索面无表情，只是那只机械手的拇指轻轻摩挲着塔拉夏的手背。

车厢中段，昆提良坐在靠窗的位置，背挺得笔直，闭眼狮头纹章的奥古斯都就在他身后。他的目光穿过防弹玻璃的缝隙看着外面——但外面只有台伯河底隧道的石壁，灰黑色的凝灰岩在灯光下泛着潮湿的光。

"看什么呢？全是石头。"唐璜的声音从车厢另一头传来。

唐璜斜靠在蔷薇之鬼的支撑架旁，右臂搂着宝儿·拉瑟的肩膀，宝儿缩在他怀里，金色的短发蹭着他的下巴，眼睛半睁半闭，像是困极了却又不肯睡。

"我在看这座城底下埋了多少年的石头。"昆提良闷声说，"台伯河底这条隧道是百年前修的，听说用的石料全是从东方运来的花岗岩。"

"你对石头很有感情啊。"

"我对历史有感情。"

"你对石头有感情。"唐璜纠正他。

昆提良不说话了，依旧看着窗外。

李锡尼副局长坐在车厢最后排的折叠椅上，一身黑色制服融进阴影里。他摘下军帽搁在膝盖上，露出的半边脸在油灯下显得格外苍老，那枚猩红死神徽章别在领口，黑色十字纹蜂巢手铳的枪柄露在腰间的枪套外面。

他闭着眼，像是在养神，但每一根神经都是绷紧的。

佛朗哥教授没有来车厢，他在驾驶室，亲自监督运输车的蒸汽动力系统。这位密涅瓦总长已经连续工作了三十六个小时，面颊凹陷下去，眼底的青黑色像是用炭笔画上去的。

薇若兰站在驾驶室和车厢之间的隔离门前，门开着一条缝，她能看见西泽尔，也能看见运输车前方那台蒸汽电视机的屏幕。

倒计时：11:58:12。

11:58:11。

11:58:10。

车厢里没有人说话。

马达的轰鸣声低沉而稳定，像是某种巨兽均匀的呼吸，震得铁壁嗡嗡响。西泽尔能感觉到身下甲胄固定架传上来的那种微弱颤动——新型红龙的骨架在共振。

他低头看了看掌心里的银戒指和圣剑碎片。

冰原寒玉的凉意从指尖传上来，清醒而冷冽。

Excalibur碎片的断口在他掌心里硌出一道浅浅的压痕。

他想起了龙德施泰特。

那个在马斯顿的雨夜里告诉他"穿上甲胄，骑在马上，握紧骑枪，冲锋"的男人的脸；那个在马斯顿事件中背叛了教皇国、投奔撒旦教团、却又在密涅瓦改装室门口提醒他"明天战场别冲动"的人的脸。

他想，黑龙现在在哪里？

他又想起了琳琅夫人。

母亲在博尔吉亚夏宫的房间里醒来又睡去，丝绸般的长发散在枕头上，碧蓝色的眼睛空空的，看他的时候像是在看一个陌生人。教皇的吻还留在她额头上，留下的那道淡红色印痕，像是一枚烙在雪地上的、永远擦不掉的火漆。

他攥紧了掌心的银戒指。

冰原寒玉碎料的凉意刺进了骨头。

他想起了琉璃·星见——母亲的亲妹妹，那个有着和他一样的紫色瞳孔、却在骷髅地的黑暗中独自守护了数十年的女人。

她用欧米茄外壳撑开红伞挡在圣堂装甲师的枪口前的那一刻，那道暗金色的光芒照亮了她苍白的脸，照亮了她嘴角渗出的血丝，照亮了她紫色的瞳孔里映出的他的倒影。

"去吧，西泽尔。"她说，"我守在这里。"

他还想起阿黛尔。

那个在马斯顿王立机械学院的钟楼下面，把哥哥从坍塌的废墟里拽出来的女孩。她放弃了翡冷翠的贵族生活，选择和他一起回到马斯顿，两个人约好了相依为命。

她的声音在记忆里还是那么清亮："哥哥，我们回家吧。"

回哪个家呢？他不知道。

他只知道现在他坐在一辆驶向维苏威火山底部的重型运输车里，身边是他的伙伴们、他的战友、他的盟友。

运输车驶出台伯河底隧道，翡冷翠的夜景在车窗外铺展开来。

西泽尔转过头，看着窗外。

深夜的翡冷翠笼罩在淡青色的月光里，圣母百花大教堂的穹顶闪着银白色的光，圣十字大殿的钟楼指向天空，美第奇宫的窗户零星亮着灯。台伯河在月光下泛着粼粼的银光，河面上倒映着两岸古老的建筑。

远处，维苏威火山的轮廓在夜空中隆起，像一头沉睡的巨兽。

他想起了圣伊里涅号沉船里打捞上来的那个齿轮吊坠——世界上第一台蒸汽机就装在那艘船上，那台蒸汽机改变了整个世界。

他想起了佛朗哥教授给他看的百年前炽天使的图纸，密涅瓦机关为重现那种技术花费了整整一个世纪。

他想起了骷髅地黑铁巨门上那张暗红色铁脸——他母亲的母亲、锡兰星见家族的祖先、用自己的血和骨头封印了世界树的女人。

他想起了原罪机关主人——米迦勒，那个隐藏在枢机会中的年轻枢机卿，银面具下带着笑意的声音："明天日出，我们维苏威火山见。"

他想起了欧米茄原型体——封存了四十年的金色巨人，正在维苏威火山深处缓缓睁开眼睛。

他想起了五台新型炽天使试制版——密涅瓦机关百年来心血的结晶，此刻就在他身边，在昏暗的车厢灯光下安静地等待。

他想，他们要去打一场改变世界的仗。

车窗外的翡冷翠夜景在移动，月光照着教堂的穹顶，照着钟楼的尖顶，照着维苏威火山黑沉沉的轮廓。

他忽然不想再看了。

他闭上眼睛，把头靠在身后的装甲板上。

瓦莲京娜伸出手，握住了他的左手。

她的手指很凉，指节分明，掌心有薄茧——那是常年握剑柄磨出来的。她没有说话，只是握着，力度不大不小，恰好让他感觉到她的存在。

西泽尔睁开眼，侧头看她。

瓦莲京娜没有看他，目光依旧落在自己甲胄的纹章上，但她的嘴角微微上翘了一点。

"别担心。"她用叶尼塞口音很重的通用语轻声说，"我们都会站在你这边的。"

西泽尔没有回答。

他只是微微收紧了手指，回握住了她的手。

对面，唐璜注意到了这个动作，吹了一声口哨，但声音很轻，轻到被马达的轰鸣声盖住了。

宝儿在他怀里动了动，抬起头来，金色的短发乱糟糟的，绿色的眼睛半睁着，看了看瓦莲京娜和西泽尔交握的手，又看了看唐璜。

"你握我的手。"她含混不清地说。

"我在握。"唐璜立刻回答，把她搂得更紧了一些。

宝儿又闭上眼睛，蹭了蹭他的肩膀。

昆提良终于从窗外收回了目光，转过身来看着车厢里的众人。他的目光扫过西泽尔和瓦莲京娜，扫过唐璜和宝儿，扫过阿方索和塔拉夏，扫过李锡尼，扫过车厢两侧那五具钢铁巨人。

他深吸了一口气。

"伙计们。"他说。

车厢里安静了一瞬。

"把手伸出来。"昆提良说。

唐璜挑了挑眉，宝儿从他怀里挣扎着坐起来。阿方索松开塔拉夏的手，抬起了机械臂。瓦莲京娜看向西泽尔，西泽尔微微点头。

他们一个一个把手伸到了车厢中央的空中——

西泽尔的左手握着瓦莲京娜，右手掌心里银戒指和圣剑碎片被收进了衣袋，摊开了空着的手掌。

瓦莲京娜的右手覆上他的手背。

阿方索的机械手从另一边伸来，金属指尖搭在瓦莲京娜的手腕上。

塔拉夏的手覆在阿方索的机械手背上，指尖还沾着油污。

昆提良的手从上方压下来，沉甸甸的，覆在塔拉夏的手上。

唐璜最后伸出了左手，宝儿迷迷糊糊地把右手叠在了最上面。

七只手叠在一起。

灯光昏暗，马达轰鸣，运输车穿行在翡冷翠的深夜里，车窗外是月光下的教堂穹顶和钟楼尖顶。

"我们四面受敌，"昆提良说，声音低沉，"却不被困住。"

唐璜接上去："绝了道路，却不绝希望。"

阿方索："遭逼迫，却不被丢弃。"

西泽尔看着那一叠手，看着那上面的每一张脸——阿方索没有表情，昆提良眼眶微红，塔拉夏在笑，唐璜在笑，宝儿在打哈欠，瓦莲京娜的嘴角微微上翘。

他开口，声音很轻：

"打倒了，却不至死亡。"

七个人沉默了一瞬。

"身上常带着神赐的死，"瓦莲京娜接过最后一句，叶尼塞口音让那几个字听起来格外冷硬，"使神赐的生，也显明在我们身上。"

炽天骑士团格言。

百年来每一任炽天骑士在战前都会说的话。

运输车猛地一震，车厢剧烈颠簸了一下，灯光闪烁，固定架上的甲胄发出金属碰撞的清脆响声。

他们到了。

蒸汽电视机的屏幕闪了两下，倒计时的数字跳了一下——

11:59:03。

11:59:02。

11:59:01。

车厢尾部的隔离门被从外面打开，翡冷翠郊外的冷风裹着维苏威火山口特有的硫磺气味灌了进来。

薇若兰从驾驶室走出来，黑色长发在夜风中飘扬，她站在隔离门的门框里，目光扫过车厢里的每一个人。

"到了。"她说。

车厢外面，维苏威火山底部的废弃矿道入口张着黑洞洞的大嘴，矿道口两侧的岩壁上钉着生锈的铁轨和蒸汽管道，红水银管道里流淌着淡红色的液体，在月光下发出幽幽的暗光。

矿道入口前的空地上，站着三个人。

最前面的是龙德施泰特。

他穿着一身朴素的黑色风衣，没有佩戴任何徽章，双手插在风衣口袋里，脸色苍白得近乎透明，但眼神很平静。他站在月光照不到的阴影里，黑色短发被山风吹得微微凌乱。

他身后站着两名炽天骑士——一男一女，穿着炽天骑士团制式铠甲，但甲胄上没有佩戴任何武器，像是无声的守卫。

旁边还站着莱希特伯爵和圣堂装甲师的十几名黑甲士兵，黑天使军徽别在胸口。

莱希特伯爵的脸色很难看，显然他没有预料到龙德施泰特会出现在这里。

西泽尔从车厢里探出身来，看见龙德施泰特的那一刻，手指无声地扣紧了车门的边缘。

龙德施泰特也看见了他。

两个人隔着十米的距离对视了一瞬。

龙德施泰特点了点头，没有说话。

西泽尔也没有说话。

有些话不需要说。

李锡尼从车厢最后排站起来，戴上军帽，把猩红死神徽章别正，提起那只黑色十字纹蜂巢手铳，走下车厢。

佛朗哥教授从驾驶室下来，面颊凹陷，眼底青黑，他走到薇若兰身边，薇若兰递给他一杯冷咖啡，他一口喝干了。

车厢里，伙伴们开始准备。

阿方索率先起身，把塔拉夏扶了起来，机械臂的指尖轻轻碰了碰她的脸。塔拉夏踮起脚在他额头上亲了一下，转身走向车厢尾部的工具箱。

昆提良闷哼一声站了起来，活动了一下脖子。

唐璜最后把宝儿抱起来，宝儿已经彻底睡着了，金色短发贴着他的胸口，绿色眼睛闭得紧紧的。他把她轻轻放在折叠维修凳上，脱下自己的外套盖在她身上。

"等我回来。"他低声说。

宝儿没有听见。

西泽尔是最后一个起身的。

他站在车厢中央，看了看身后的伙伴们，看了看面前的维苏威火山，看了看矿道入口前那些等待的人。

然后他弯腰，从衣袋里掏出那枚冰原寒玉银戒指，套在了右手的中指上。

冰原寒玉碎料的凉意从指尖传上来，渗进了骨头。

他推开车门。

夜风扑面而来，硫磺的气味灌进鼻腔，远处维苏威火山的山顶在月光下泛着暗红色的光。

他第一个跳下车。

靴子踏在矿道入口前的碎石地面上，发出清脆的一声响。

月光照在他的脸上。

苍白的、锋利的、眼神冷得像刀刃的脸。

但他的紫色瞳孔里，暗金色的纹路正在缓缓浮现。

紫瞳金纹。

星见血脉在共鸣。

他站在维苏威火山底部的废弃矿道入口前，面前是黑沉沉的矿道，身后是重型运输车里那五具钢铁巨人和他的伙伴们，再远一点是龙德施泰特、是李锡尼、是薇若兰、是佛朗哥、是莱希特伯爵、是黑甲士兵。

更远的地方是翡冷翠，是圣母百花大教堂的穹顶，是教皇的夏宫，是美第奇宫的窗户。

更更远的地方是马斯顿，是阿黛尔。

他张开嘴，声音很轻，被山风送出去，被维苏威火山的沉默吞没。

"我来了，命运。"

【English】
Chapter 168 — The Countdown to the Decisive Battle

The carriage was long. Its iron walls had been painted, long ago and badly, in a dark green anti-rust lacquer, and every three metres a shock-absorbing oil lamp hung from the riveted ceiling, throwing out a dim yellow light that stretched the silhouettes of six armours into long, wavering shadows against the floor.

Five new-model Seraphims stood in their cradles along either side of the carriage, lashed down for the run. The new Red Dragon took the centre. Its dark red plating caught the lamplight with a cold metallic gleam, and the two characters 红龙 — Red Dragon — were barely visible on its left pauldron, as though the painter had not quite committed. Beside it, the Rose Ghost, ultra-light, was the slenderest of the five, its frame a narrow blade stood on end. The Augustus was the heaviest, its iron chestplate stamped with a closed-eyed lion's-head crest still smeared with machine oil that no one had bothered to wipe clean. The breastplate of Solomon's King bore the recessed interface of a maintenance toolkit. And last, modified for Valentina — a Wrath of God Mark III, in dark red lacquer, with honeysuckle scrollwork as its device; on its shoulder plate, hastily welded on, the fresh seams still showed.

They stood in silence, five steel giants waiting to be woken.

Cesare sat in the corner at the far end of the carriage, his back against an armour plate, his legs slightly bent. His right hand lay open on his knee. In the palm sat two things: a silver ring set with a fragment of glacial jade no bigger than a grain of rice, and a sliver of the holy sword Excalibur still fitted into the socket of the Red Dragon's hilt.

The jade in the ring, under the lamplight, was the faintest blue, like a drop of lake water that had been frozen and never quite thawed.

The shard's broken edge still held a cold glint.

He did not speak. His eyes were on the old steam-television set at the far end of the carriage. Its screen fizzed with snow, and through the static a voice read out, in relays, the late-night news from Florence.

"— the Grand Festival of Nations opens officially tomorrow. The centrepiece of this year's festival will be a public duel between a new-model Prometheus and a new-model Seraphim. The victor will become the principal armament of the Papal States in the coming years. Envoys of every nation are already arriving in Florence. The Sacred College has announced that the duel will be broadcast in full to the assembled nations—"

The picture cut. A heavy transport lorry was rolling under an arch of triumph in Florence, a vast shape under canvas strapped to its flatbed. Beneath the canvas, the blurred outline of a third-generation Prometheus, Gurnossos, leaned against the sky.

In the corner of the screen a red countdown panel blinked white numerals.

Eleven hours, fifty-nine minutes, forty-seven seconds.

Eleven fifty-nine forty-six.

Eleven fifty-nine forty-five.

The carriage jolted. Outside the windows the stone walls of the Tiber's subterranean tunnel slipped past, the yellow wall-lamps going one after another, the rhythm of them as regular and indifferent as a heartbeat.

To Cesare's left, Valentina Romanov sat upright, her long golden hair plaited into a single thick braid down her back, her white boots crossed at the ankle over the crossbar of an armour cradle. The faint sweet smell of honeysuckle came off the collar of her coat. She was not looking at him. Her eyes were on the device stitched into the breastplate of her own dark-red armour, and her lips were pressed together as if she were running numbers behind them.

Half a metre further on, Alfonso sat on a folding maintenance stool, his mechanical arm laid across his knee. His right hand — that hand threaded all over with circuitry, the metal one — was holding Tarasya's.

Tarasya leaned against his shoulder. She was a young mechanist, and the smudges of oil from the haste of leaving the Eagle's Nest were still on her cheek. There was a deep tiredness under her eyes, but the corners of her mouth were turned up, just slightly.

Alfonso's face was unreadable. Only the thumb of his metal hand moved, stroking Tarasya's knuckles.

In the middle of the carriage, Quintilian sat by the window, his back very straight. The Augustus, with its closed-eyed lion's-head crest, stood in its cradle directly behind him. His eyes were on the gap in the bulletproof glass through which a thin line of outside could be seen — but outside there was only the tunnel's stone, the grey-black tuff of it shining wet in the lamps.

"You're looking at nothing," Don Juan's voice came from the other end of the carriage. "Just rock."

Don Juan was leaning against the cradle of the Rose Ghost, his right arm around the shoulders of Bao'er Laserre. Bao'er was tucked into him, her short gold hair brushing his chin, her eyes half-shut — too tired to sleep, too stubborn to give in.

"I'm looking at how many years of stone lie under this city," Quintilian said, in his low voice. "This Tiber tunnel was cut a hundred years ago. The granite came, by all accounts, from the East."

"You have feelings for stone, do you."

"I have feelings for history."

"You have feelings for stone," Don Juan corrected him.

Quintilian said nothing. He kept watching the window.

Deputy Director Lignini sat in the last row of folding seats at the rear of the carriage, his black uniform folding him into the shadows. He had set his military cap on his knee. The half of his face that the lamplight reached looked older than it had any right to. The Crimson Reaper badge was pinned to his collar. The grip of his black-cross-hivework pistol showed above the holster at his hip.

His eyes were closed, as though he were resting. None of his nerves were resting.

Professor Franco had not come into the carriage. He was up front, in the driver's cab, personally overseeing the lorry's steam-power plant. The head of Minerva had been working for thirty-six hours straight. His cheeks were hollowed, the bruise-coloured shadows under his eyes looked as though they had been drawn on with a stick of charcoal.

Vioran stood at the hatch between the cab and the carriage, the door opened just a crack. Through it she could see Cesare. She could also see, at the front of the lorry, the steam-television screen.

The countdown read: eleven fifty-eight twelve.

Eleven fifty-eight eleven.

Eleven fifty-eight ten.

No one in the carriage was speaking.

The motor's note was low and steady, like the breathing of some vast animal, and the iron walls hummed faintly with it. Under Cesare's hand, on the floor of the cradle, he could feel the smallest tremor rising from the new Red Dragon's frame — a sympathetic resonance, as if the armour were already listening.

He looked down at the silver ring and the Excalibur shard in his palm.

The chill of the glacial jade came up through his fingertips, clean and biting.

The broken edge of the shard pressed a faint line into the skin of his palm.

He thought of Longdesteed.

Of the man who had told him, in the rain at Marston, *Put the armour on. Sit the horse. Grip the lance. Charge.* Of the same man, the traitor to the Papal States who had gone over to the Sabbatarian Order, who had nevertheless stopped outside the door of the Minerva refit bay and said, *Don't do anything rash on the field tomorrow.*

He wondered where the Black Dragon was now.

He thought of his mother.

Of his mother, lying in the Borgia summer palace, sleeping and waking, sleeping and waking, her hair like silk spilled across the pillow, her eyes that pale, pale blue looking through him as if he were a stranger. The Pope's kiss was still on her brow, a faint red mark there, a wax seal pressed into snow that nothing would ever rub out.

He closed his fingers tighter on the ring.

The chill of the jade bit into the bone.

He thought of Liuli Stellavision, his mother's younger sister, the woman with the same purple irises as his, who had spent decades alone in the dark of Golgotha guarding — something. Who had taken the Omega's outer shell, opened up the red parasol, and stepped between herself and the guns of the Sanctus Panzer Corps. That dim gold light, the way it had lit her pale face, the blood at the corner of her mouth, the small reflection of himself caught in the purple of her eye.

*Go on, Cesare,* she had said. *I'll hold here.*

He thought of Adele.

The girl who, under the clock tower of the Royal Mechanist College at Marston, had dragged her brother out of the rubble of a collapsed building. Who had given up her life among the Florence aristocracy to come back with him to Marston. Who had said, in a voice that memory still kept clean and bright, *Let's go home, brother.*

Home. Where was that.

He did not know. He only knew that he was sitting in a heavy transport lorry rolling toward the base of Mount Vesuvius, and that the people beside him were his friends, his comrades, the ones he had chosen and the ones who had chosen him.

The lorry came out of the Tiber tunnel, and the night of Florence opened across the windows.

Cesare turned his head to look.

Florence under late moonlight was the colour of pale blue milk. The dome of Santa Maria del Fiore caught the light and threw it back as silver. The campanile of Santa Croce reached up into the sky. A few of the windows of the Palazzo Medici were still lit. The Tiber ran under the moon in a slow shiver of silver, and the old buildings along its banks were doubled in the water.

Far off, the bulk of Mount Vesuvius rose into the night sky, the dark shape of it like a sleeping beast.

He thought of the gear-pendant that had been raised from the wreck of the Saint Irenaeus — the first steam engine in the world, fitted to that ship, the engine that had changed everything.

He thought of the hundred-year-old plans for the first Seraphim that Professor Franco had shown him, the plans the Minerva Bureau had spent a full century trying to bring back to life.

He thought of the dark iron gate at Golgotha, and the dark-red iron face on it — the face of his mother's mother, of the ancestor of the Ceylan Stellavision line, the woman who had sealed the World Tree with her own blood and bone.

He thought of the master of the Original Sin Bureau — Michael, the young Cardinal hidden in the Sacred College, the silver mask, the smiling voice. *Tomorrow, at sunrise, on Vesuvius.*

He thought of the Omega prototype, sealed away for forty years, the golden giant deep in the mountain, slowly opening its eyes.

He thought of the five trial new-model Seraphims, the century-long labour of the Minerva Bureau made iron, waiting in this very carriage under the dim lamps.

He thought: they are going to fight a battle that will change the world.

The Florence night slid past the windows. The moonlight laid itself across the dome, across the bell tower, across the dark shoulder of the volcano.

He found, suddenly, that he did not want to look at it any more.

He closed his eyes and laid his head back against the armour plate.

Valentina put her hand out, and took his left hand in hers.

Her fingers were cool. The knuckles were clearly defined. The palm had the thin calluses of someone who had spent years on a sword grip. She did not speak. She only held, the pressure of her hand neither too much nor too little, just enough to let him know she was there.

Cesare opened his eyes and turned his head to look at her.

Valentina was not looking at him. Her eyes were still on the device on her own armour, but the corner of her mouth was turned up, just slightly.

"Don't worry," she said, in heavily accented Common, the vowels shaped by the Yenisei. "We will all stand with you."

Cesare said nothing.

He only tightened his fingers, slightly, and held her hand back.

Across the carriage, Don Juan noticed, and let out a soft whistle — so soft that the motor's hum swallowed it.

Bao'er stirred against him, lifting her head. Her short gold hair was a mess, her green eyes barely open. She looked at Valentina's and Cesare's joined hands, and then at Don Juan.

"You are holding my hand," she said, muzzily.

"I am holding," Don Juan said at once, and drew her closer.

Bao'er closed her eyes again and nuzzled into his shoulder.

Quintilian, at last, drew his gaze from the window, and turned to look at the others. His eyes moved over Cesare and Valentina, over Don Juan and Bao'er, over Alfonso and Tarasya, over Lignini, over the five steel giants on their cradles.

He drew a long breath.

"Friends," he said.

The carriage was quiet for a beat.

"Put your hands out," Quintilian said.

Don Juan raised an eyebrow. Bao'er struggled, half-asleep, into a sitting position. Alfonso let go of Tarasya's hand and lifted his mechanical arm. Valentina looked at Cesare. Cesare gave a small nod.

One by one, they reached their hands out into the air at the centre of the carriage.

Cesare's left hand held Valentina's. His right hand he turned palm-up, having slipped the ring and the Excalibur shard into his coat pocket, the palm empty now.

Valentina's right hand settled over the back of his.

Alfonso's mechanical hand reached from the other side, the metal fingertips resting against Valentina's wrist.

Tarasya laid her hand on the back of Alfonso's, the fingertips still faintly smeared with oil.

Quintilian's hand came down from above, heavy, settling on the back of Tarasya's.

Don Juan, last, reached out his left hand. Bao'er, muzzily, stacked her right on top.

Seven hands, one on the other.

The lamplight was dim. The motor was loud. The lorry was running through the late hours of Florence, and outside the windows there was moonlight on the cathedral dome and the bell tower's spire.

"We are pressed on every side," Quintilian said, his voice low, "but not crushed."

Don Juan took it up. "We are cut off, but not without hope."

Alfonso: "We are persecuted, but not abandoned."

Cesare looked at the stack of hands, at every face above it. Alfonso with no expression. Quintilian with reddened eyes. Tarasya smiling. Don Juan smiling. Bao'er yawning. Valentina with the corner of her mouth lifted, just slightly.

He spoke, his voice very quiet:

"Knocked down, but not destroyed."

The seven of them were quiet for a moment.

"We carry in our bodies," Valentina took the last line, the Yenisei accent making the words sound almost hard, "the death that God has given, that the life of God may be made visible in us."

The motto of the Order of the Seraphim.

The words that every Seraphim knight, for a hundred years, had spoken before a battle.

The lorry lurched, hard. The carriage jolted. The lamps swung on their hooks. The armours in their cradles clanged, iron on iron, a single clean note.

They had arrived.

On the steam-television screen, the numbers jumped.

Eleven fifty-nine oh-three.

Eleven fifty-nine oh-two.

Eleven fifty-nine oh-one.

The hatch at the rear of the carriage was thrown open from outside, and the cold wind of the Florentine countryside came pouring in, carrying with it the particular bitter reek of sulphur that rose out of the throat of Vesuvius.

Vioran came out of the cab. Her long black hair lifted in the night wind. She stood in the frame of the hatch, and her eyes moved over each of them in turn.

"We're here," she said.

Outside, the entrance to an abandoned mine shaft at the base of Mount Vesuvius gaped black in the rock face. Iron rails and steam pipes had been bolted into the cliff on either side, most of them rust-eaten. The pipes of red mercury, running with a thin pale red liquid, gave off a dim and strange light in the moonlight.

In the clearing before the shaft, three figures were waiting.

The first of them was Longdesteed.

He wore a plain black overcoat. No badge. No insignia. His hands were in his coat pockets. His face was so pale it was almost translucent, but his eyes were calm. He stood in the shadow the moon would not reach, his short black hair slightly stirred by the wind coming down the mountain.

Behind him stood two Seraphim knights, a man and a woman, in the standard armour of the Order. They had no weapons fitted to their suits. They were silent, and they were guarding him.

Beside Longdesteed, Count Reichter of the Sanctus Panzer Corps stood with a dozen men in black plate, the Black Angel badge at their chests.

Count Reichter's face was tight. He had not, evidently, expected Longdesteed to be here.

Cesare leaned out of the carriage. The moment he saw Longdesteed, his fingers, without his telling them, tightened on the edge of the door.

Longdesteed saw him too.

Across ten metres of ground, and across however many years of choices, the two of them looked at each other for one beat.

Longdesteed gave a small nod. He did not speak.

Cesare did not speak.

Some things did not need to be said.

Lignini stood up from the last row, put on his cap, pinned the Crimson Reaper straight, picked up the black-cross-hivework pistol, and stepped down from the carriage.

Professor Franco came down from the cab, his cheeks sunken, the bruise under his eyes almost black. Vioran put a cup of cold coffee in his hand. He drank it in one swallow.

In the carriage, the others began to make ready.

Alfonso was the first to move, easing Tarasya to her feet, the fingertips of his mechanical arm brushing, just once, against her cheek. Tarasya stood on her toes and kissed him, very lightly, on the forehead, then turned and walked back along the carriage to the toolbox.

Quintilian grunted and stood up, working the stiffness out of his neck.

Don Juan, last, gathered Bao'er up in his arms. She was fully asleep now, her short gold hair against his chest, her green eyes sealed shut. He set her down, very gently, on the folding maintenance stool, and took off his own coat and laid it over her.

"I'll be back," he said, very softly.

Bao'er did not hear.

Cesare was the last to stand.

He stood in the centre of the carriage. He looked at the people behind him. He looked at Vesuvius in front of him. He looked at the figures waiting in the clearing at the mouth of the shaft.

Then he bent, took the silver ring with its grain of glacial jade out of his coat pocket, and slid it onto the middle finger of his right hand.

The chill of the jade went up through his finger and into the bone.

He pushed open the door.

The night wind hit him. The reek of sulphur filled his lungs. The peak of Vesuvius, far above him, was a faint dark red against the sky.

He jumped down from the carriage.

His boot struck the loose stone in front of the shaft with a single clear sound.

The moonlight fell on his face.

A pale face. A sharp face. Eyes the colour of cold metal.

But in the purple of his irises, the dim gold traceries were beginning to surface, slow, like the first writing on a page.

Purple pupil, gold tracery.

The Stellavision blood, answering something.

He stood at the mouth of the abandoned shaft, the dark of the mine in front of him, the heavy lorry with its five steel giants and his friends behind him, and a little further off, Longdesteed, Lignini, Vioran, Franco, Count Reichter, the black-armoured soldiers.

Further still, Florence. The dome of Santa Maria del Fiore. The windows of the Pope's summer palace. The lit windows of the Palazzo Medici.

Further still still, Marston. Adele.

He opened his mouth. His voice was quiet. The wind off the mountain took it. The silence of Vesuvius took what the wind did not.

"I have come, Fate."
