【中文】
第171章 峡谷入口的巨影

矿道入口的风很冷，裹着硫磺和铁锈的味道，从那条九米宽的裂缝里涌出来，像是从地底深处呼出的长气。

第一台甲胄的脚掌踏上了碎石地面，沉闷的一声轰响传遍了整条矿道，像是有人在地壳上敲了一记。

那是一台赭红色的甲胄。

龙纹从肩甲蔓延到护臂，鳞片般的甲板层层叠压，在灰白的晨光下泛着暗沉的赤铜色泽。左肩刻着东方文字"红龙"，笔锋凌厉仿佛刀刻。甲胄的高度只有三米出头，比正常的炽天使试制版略矮，但它站在那里的姿态沉稳得不像是一台机械，而像一柄被竖在战场入口的、还没出鞘的刀。

驾驶舱密封前，西泽尔最后看了一眼身后的晨光。

维苏威火山的天空是铅灰色的，远处有几缕白烟从山腰升起，懒洋洋地被风吹散。他想起很久以前——克里特岛上校修理铺后面那扇斜窗，窗外也是这样的灰色天空，妈妈坐在窗下给他和阿黛尔缝校服。

他把面甲合上。

"红龙位置确认就位！"观测厅的解说员声音猛地拔高，像是憋了太久的弹簧终于弹开，"密涅瓦机关参赛甲胄——新型红龙试制版，驾驶者西泽尔·博尔吉亚，前炽天骑士团红龙！"

观测厅里响起一阵低沉的骚动，像蜂群被搅动。

"西泽尔·博尔吉亚——那个私生子？"
"就是他，异端罪被判的那个……后来被赦免了？"
"不是说神经损毁再也不能穿甲胄了吗？"

解说员没理会这些杂音，声音像一把利刃切开嗡鸣。

"第二台！密涅瓦机关参赛甲胄——奥古斯都！"

沉重的金属踏步声从运输车深处传来，一台灰黑色的甲胄缓缓走出。它比红龙高出半头有余，宽度几乎是红龙的两倍，厚重的装甲板层层堆叠，肩甲上铸着一枚闭眼狮头纹章，狮头张嘴怒吼，仿佛要将一切冲来的敌人都吞入腹中。右臂外挂着一面几乎和人等高的秘银重盾，盾面上密密麻麻的铆钉排列成棋盘格，每一个铆钉都闪烁着影金属特有的暗哑银光。

它的每一步都让碎石地面发出沉闷的呻吟。

"驾驶者昆提良！炽天骑士团旧部！密涅瓦的工程师们说这台甲胄是五台参战机体中最重的，强化了装甲和动力——"解说员顿了一下，"说白了就是拿来挡子弹的！"

"第三台！所罗门王！"

这台甲胄的画风突变。银蓝色的装甲板上布满了精密的电子元件，散热孔如鱼鳞般排列在躯干两侧，胸口的透明面板下能看到复杂的线路和红水银微晶的淡红色光脉。它背着一管比人还长的远程狙击武器，枪管上缠绕着冷却铜管，远看像一条盘在甲胄背上的银蛇。

"驾驶者阿方索！炽天骑士团旧部！天才机械师！负责远程火力支援！"

阿方索的所罗门王走得不快，但每一步都精准到厘米级，脚掌落点几乎没有偏差，碎石在它脚下被精确碾碎而非踩飞。

"第四台——"解说员的声音忽然变得有些困惑。

从运输车深处飘出来的这台甲胄让人一时间以为自己看错了。粉紫色的轻量装甲板，薄得像蝉翼，关节处裸露着精密的影金属骨架，整个机体轻到甚至没有常规甲胄的蒸汽排气口——它根本不需要高压蒸汽，动力系统藏在胸口的紫铜色核心里。

"蔷薇之鬼？驾驶者唐璜！炽天骑士团旧部！"解说员的声音里带着一种掩饰不住的困惑，"呃……造型很独特，工程师们说它采用了超轻量化设计，呃……"

"这是打仗还是选美啊？"
"粉的？教皇国的新型机密武器是粉紫色的？"
"我看是拿来当花瓶的吧。"

第三层包厢里，高文·美第奇端着酒杯差点没笑出声。路易吉·博尔吉亚的眉头皱了一下，目光在蔷薇之鬼的关节结构上停留了两秒——那裸露的影金属骨架太细太密，关节活动度远超常规甲胄，这不是花瓶，这是刺客。

运输车最后拖出来的是一台空舱。

深灰色的剑舞者甲胄被固定在拖车上，没有驾驶者，关节处微微泛着冷光。它的右肩甲上雕刻着一枚银白色的忍冬花纹章——叶尼塞王国的国花。

"替补参战机体——剑舞者！驾驶者——"解说员深吸了一口气，"叶尼塞王国公主，瓦莲京娜·罗曼诺夫！"

观测厅里瞬间炸了。

"叶尼塞公主？！"
"替补？不是真的上场吧？"
"疯了……叶尼塞公主参加教皇国的机密武装对抗战？这算什么？外交事件？"
"罗曼诺夫家族和博尔吉亚家族联手了？"

密涅瓦主观测厅的第二层包厢里，纯公主的手指在扶手上的敲击停顿了整整三秒。她慢慢偏过头看了叶素理一眼，叶素理面色如常地翻着笔记本，但翻页的速度慢了半拍。

"叶素理大人。"纯公主的声音很轻，混在周围各国的议论声里几乎听不见。

"公主殿下。"

"叶尼塞公主的甲胄……和新型红龙是同一批次的设计。"

"是。"叶素理翻过一页，"尺寸数据不一样，我记下来了。"

纯公主没再说话。密语传声筒被她轻轻推回袖中，那把暗藏微型相机的龙雀剑复制品此刻正安静地靠在她椅背后面。

夏国武官的座位在第一层最右侧的角落，他闭着眼睛，像是在打盹。但他的手指在膝盖上无声地画着什么——新型红龙三米出头、奥古斯都三米六左右、蔷薇之鬼两米八。他在用指尖丈量这些机体的尺寸差。三个数字已经刻进他的记忆里了，和红龙胸口那枚拳头大的嵌入物的位置一起。

矿道入口，新型炽天使小队在晨光中列成一线。

红龙居中，龙纹在铅灰色天光下显得格外暗沉。奥古斯都和所罗门王分列两侧，像是城墙的两座角楼。蔷薇之鬼没有走上前，它悄无声息地滑入了矿道入口侧壁的阴影中，粉紫色的装甲板和岩石的颜色几乎融为一体——本来就没打算让敌人看见它。

空舱的剑舞者被拖到了矿道入口最深处，等待启动的指令。

观测厅的球形屏幕切换到矿道深处——暗红色的红外镜头画面里，三台巨型机动傀儡的轮廓在热成像中像三座燃烧的铁塔。

"现在——原罪机关参赛甲胄入场！"

矿道深处传来一声沉闷的汽笛长鸣，声波沿着九米宽的矿道反复弹跳放大，到达入口的时候已经变成了一种让人牙根发酸的嗡鸣。

那是一艘利维坦级飞艇——漆黑的气囊长百余米，悄无声息地悬浮在矿道深处被人工拓宽的洞厅里。它的下方投下了一道垂直的白色光柱，像是某种宗教仪式中的圣光降临。

白光中，一个影子缓缓站起来。

古洛诺斯。

九米高的巨大轮廓在光柱中像一座移动的钟楼。它的全身覆盖着暗铁色装甲板，肩部宽度超过四米，每一块装甲板都厚得像是从战舰舰体上切割下来的。右臂握着一柄六米长的巨型反曲锯齿巨刃，刃口上锯齿的间距能塞进一个成人的拳头。左臂是一面三米高的塔盾，盾面上铸着原罪机关的纹章——一棵倒悬的枯树，根系朝天。

暴龙级动力核心在它胸腔里发出低沉的轰鸣，整个矿道都在随之震颤。

"第三代普罗米修斯·古洛诺斯！驾驶者——"解说员的声音被矿道的回音扭曲了，"胡安·博尔吉亚！教皇嫡次子！原罪机关试驾骑士！"

古洛诺斯的骑士舱里，胡安·博尔吉亚盯着面前的屏幕。屏幕被分割成十几个小格，矿道入口的五个光点清晰地排列在左下角——最近的那个是赭红色，带着龙纹。

他的嘴角向上扯了一下。

扩音器的电流声在矿道里噼啪作响，然后一个带着冷笑的年轻声音从古洛诺斯的胸腔里传出来，沿着矿道传到每一个角落——

"西泽尔——"

那声音在回音中变得狰狞，像是从地底深处爬出来的毒蛇。

"今天我要让你跪在我面前道歉！"

观测厅的解说员张了张嘴，想说什么圆场的话，但扩音器的电流声盖过了他。

矿道入口，红龙没有动。

西泽尔坐在驾驶舱里，神经接驳系统还没有启动，他只是透过面甲的缝隙看着矿道深处那道缓缓移动的暗影。古洛诺斯的脚步声像远处的雷暴，一下一下地敲在他的耳膜上。

胡安的声音还在矿道里回荡，被岩壁反射成重叠的回音。

"我亲爱的弟弟——你以为你回到翡冷翠就能翻身？你以为那个老头子把你放出来就能改变什么？"胡安的声音拔高了一度，尖锐得刺人，"你不过是个私生子！你妈妈不过是个——"

西泽尔抬起了右手。

红龙的右手在驾驶舱内同步抬起，指节轻轻落在龙纹肩甲上，拍了两下。

肩甲上"红龙"两个东方文字在触碰下微微发亮——不是炽天使的能量反应，只是晨光落在金属表面时的折射。

他的紫瞳在面甲内侧闪了一下。

很快，很短，像一道紫色的闪电划过黑色的天空，然后消失不见。

驾驶舱里很安静。西泽尔没有按下列车上的扩音器按钮，他甚至没有皱眉。他只是把右手从肩甲上收回来，搭在了操控杆上。

矿道深处，古洛诺斯身后，两道更小的影子从利维坦飞艇的阴影中走了出来。

零号和一号。

它们比古洛诺斯矮了近两米，体型更加紧凑，但四肢比例更接近人类，关节处的活动范围明显更大。暗铁色的装甲板在白光中闪着冷光，行走时几乎无声——它们的脚掌包裹着消音橡胶材质。

解说员的声音再次响起："原罪机关参赛机体——第三代普罗米修斯试制机零号、一号！驾驶者代号零号骑士、一号骑士！原罪机关王牌试驾骑士！"

"零号和一号没有公开的驾驶员身份……"
"机密？连名字都不让说？"
"原罪机关到底在搞什么？"

观测厅里议论声更大了。夏国武官睁开了眼睛，目光紧紧锁在零号和一号身上——他的指尖在膝盖上轻轻敲了两下，关节活动度，至少比古洛诺斯多出百分之三十。

零号和一号走过古洛诺斯身侧的时候，它们的动作让观测厅里不少人倒吸了一口气——

零号的头颅忽然偏转了。

不是随意的偏转，是一种精确到毫米的、用伺服电机驱动的、像猛禽侧首锁定猎物一样的偏转。它的头盔面甲上没有眼窝，只有一条狭长的水平视窗，此刻那道视窗正对着球形屏幕上矿道入口方向的红龙。

一号几乎在同一瞬间做出了同样的动作。两台甲胄的头颅同时转向同一个方向——红龙——像是在确认什么。

"它们……在看红龙？"有记者低声说。

零号的面甲视窗里闪过一线极淡的金色光芒——那不是视窗的反光，是从面甲内部透出来的，像是面甲后面有什么东西在发光。非常短暂，不到零点三秒，如果不是球形屏幕的高清镜头恰好捕捉到了这一帧，没有任何观众会注意到。

一号的面甲下似乎也有同样的微光，但被角度遮住了，只露出了一丝转瞬即逝的金色尾迹。

解说员愣了一下："呃……零号和一号的光学系统似乎在进行校准……"

没有人注意到那两线金光。

至少观测厅里没有人注意到。

纯公主注意到了。

但她没看到金光，她看到的是两台甲胄偏转头部时的动作——那种动作太精确了，精确得不像是一台机械在执行指令，更像是背后有一个活生生的人在用极其专注的目光打量着猎物。

她把密语传声筒悄悄推回袖中，在叶素理看不到的角度用指尖在椅子扶手上无声地写了一个字。

"猎。"

叶素理微微点头。他的笔记本上，"零号"和"一号"两个名字旁边多了三个小字——"非装饰"。

那两台甲胄关节处的某种东西——一种极细的丝状物，颜色近乎透明，在白光中偶尔闪一下——被他记下来了。他不知道那是什么，但他知道原罪机关不会给关节装装饰品。

球形屏幕突然切换了画面。

不再是矿道入口的特写镜头，而是采石场的全景——维苏威火山冒着淡淡的白烟，从半山腰蜿蜒向下的矿道像一条灰白色的巨蛇钻入山体。采石场是矿道前方的开阔地带，方圆五公里，遍布碎石堆、坍塌的旧矿井入口和被遗弃的采石器械。

白色的粉尘在晨光中浮沉，远看像一层薄薄的雾。

矿道入口在采石场的西侧，灰白色的岩壁上有被炸药和蒸汽钻凿出的巨大豁口，五台新型炽天使的影子正从豁口后方走出来。

采石场的东侧，更深的矿道入口处，古洛诺斯的九米高轮廓在黑暗中若隐若现，像一座蹲伏的钢铁巨兽。零号和一号站在它两侧，更小，更暗，更安静。

两支队伍隔着整个采石场对峙。

"战场已就绪！"解说员的声音终于恢复了沉稳，"密涅瓦机关五台新型炽天使试制版甲胄——红龙、奥古斯都、所罗门王、蔷薇之鬼，以及替补剑舞者！原罪机关三台第三代普罗米修斯——古洛诺斯、零号、一号！"

"对抗战规则再次确认！双方参战机体使用薄壳弹，禁止实弹及红水银填充弹头！一方全部机体倒地不起超过十秒者判负！战场范围——采石场方圆五公里！"

解说员深吸了一口气，观测厅里几百号人都跟着屏住了呼吸。

"本场对抗战——"

解说员举起信号枪。

银色的枪身在球形屏幕的反射中亮了一下，枪口指向天花板。

"开始！"

【English】
Chapter 171 — The Shadow at the Mine's Mouth

The wind at the mine's mouth was cold. It came rolling out of the nine-metre fracture in the rock face carrying the smell of sulphur and rust, like a long breath drawn up from somewhere far below the earth's skin.

The first machine set its foot on the gravel.

A single, heavy impact travelled the length of the tunnel — the kind of sound a man might make, were he enormous, and striking the ground with a closed fist. Dust lifted from the cut stone and drifted sideways through the pale morning light.

The machine was the colour of dried blood.

A dragon's scales ran from its shoulder plate down the length of its arm, layer upon layer of overlapping plate that caught the grey dawn in a dull, coppery undertone. The left pauldron bore two characters in an Eastern script — Hong Long, Red Dragon — cut with a knife-stroke severity that made the metal look scored rather than engraved. The machine stood a little over three metres at the crown, half a head shorter than a standard Seraph prototype, but it stood the way a weapon stands when it has been set down carefully at the threshold of a fight and not yet drawn.

Before the cockpit sealed, Cesare Borgia looked back, once, at the morning.

Above Vesuvius the sky was the colour of old lead. A few threads of white smoke rose from the mountain's flank and idled apart in the wind. He thought, for a moment, of the slanted window behind the repair shop on Crete — of the same grey light coming through it, and of his mother sitting beneath it with a needle in her hand, sewing school uniforms for him and Adèle.

He closed the visor.

"Red Dragon in position!" The announcer's voice in the observation gallery rose with a strange, pent-up energy, like a spring finally let go. "Minerva Engine entry machine — new-pattern Red Dragon prototype. Pilot: Cesare Borgia, former Knight of the Order of the Crimson Dragon!"

A low stirring went through the gallery. It sounded, Cesare thought, like a hive being disturbed.

"Cesare Borgia — the bastard?"
"Him, the one condemned for heresy. He was pardoned, wasn't he?"
"They said the nerve damage was permanent. That he'd never pilot again."

The announcer did not wait for the noise to settle. His voice came in like a blade parting a swarm.

"Second machine. Minerva Engine entry machine — Augustus!"

A second, slower tread rolled out from the deep of the transport wagon. A grey-black frame emerged, half a head taller than the Red Dragon and nearly twice its breadth. Layer upon layer of thick plate was stacked at the shoulders. A closed-eyed lion's head was cast into the right pauldron, the lion's mouth open, snarling as if it meant to swallow whatever came at it. The right arm carried, slung on the outside, a shield of secret-silver nearly the height of a man; the shield's face was studded with rivets set in a checkerboard, every one of them dulling the air around it with the particular non-light of shadow-metal.

Each step made the gravel at the mine's mouth groan.

"Pilot: Quintilian. Veteran of the Order of the Crimson Dragon! Minerva's engineers say this is the heaviest of the five entry machines, reinforced in armour and motive power—" the announcer paused, briefly, as if to let the gallery catch up, "—which is to say, it is built to take a bullet."

"Third machine! Solomon!"

The third frame was a different creature altogether. Silver-blue plate was studded with precision electronics, vents laid in fish-scale rows along the torso, and through a clear panel in the chest one could see the complicated arterial wiring of the machine's interior and the pale red pulse of the red-mercury micro-crystal at its heart. Across its back it carried a long-barrelled rifle taller than a man, the cooling coils wound around the barrel like a silver serpent asleep along the spine of a metal god.

"Pilot: Alfonso. Veteran of the Order of the Crimson Dragon! Genius mechanist! Responsible for long-range fire support!"

Alfonso's Solomon did not move quickly, but each step fell within a centimetre of where one would have drawn it with a ruler. The gravel beneath it was crushed, not kicked.

"Fourth machine—" The announcer's voice developed, for the first time, a small note of uncertainty.

Out of the interior of the transport wagon drifted a machine that several people, on first seeing it, took for a mistake. Thin shell of pink-purple armour, gossamer, the joints beneath showing the bare skeleton of shadow-metal. The frame was so light it had none of the usual steam-vents of a working armour — it did not need high-pressure steam, the engineers had hidden its motive system inside a copper-coloured heart in the chest.

"The Rose's Ghost?" The announcer struggled to keep his voice even. "Pilot: Don Juan. Veteran of the Order of the Crimson Dragon! The, ah, the silhouette is, ah, distinctive. The engineers describe a hyper-lightweight—"

"Is this a war or a beauty pageant?"
"Pink? The Holy See's new classified weapon is pink?"
"A vase, more like. They've made us a vase."

In the third-tier box, Gawain Medici nearly laughed into his wine. Luigi Borgia's brow moved a single fraction; his gaze stayed, a beat too long, on the joints of the Rose's Ghost. Those bare threads of shadow-metal were too fine, too densely packed. The range of motion they implied was well past anything a normal armour could manage. This was not a vase. This was an assassin.

The last thing the transport wagon dragged out was an empty cockpit.

A dark-grey sword-dancer frame, lashed to the trailer, joint-work glinting faintly cold. A single emblem was chased into its right pauldron — a silver-white honeysuckle, the national flower of the Kingdom of Yenisei.

"Reserve entry machine — Sword Dancer! Pilot—" The announcer drew a breath. "Princess of the Kingdom of Yenisei, Valentina Romanov!"

The gallery came apart.

"A Yenisei princess?"
"Reserve? She's not actually going to fight?"
"This is mad. A Yenisei princess fighting in a Holy See classified arms trial — what is this, a diplomatic incident?"
"The Romanovs and the Borgias have joined hands?"

In the second-tier box of the Minerva main observation gallery, Princess Chun's fingers, tapping softly on the arm of her chair, stopped. For a long three seconds they did not move. She turned her head, slowly, and looked at Ye Suli. Ye Suli was turning a page of his notebook, his face as unreadable as ever, but the page turned half a beat late.

"Master Ye Suli," Princess Chun said, very quietly, her voice lost almost entirely in the noise of the various delegations arguing around them.

"Your Highness."

"The Princess of Yenisei's armour. It is of the same design batch as the new-pattern Red Dragon."

"Yes." Ye Suli turned another page. "The sizing data is different. I have noted it down."

Princess Chun said nothing more. The silent speaking-tube was slid back into her sleeve. The copy of the Dragonfinch sword — the one with its tiny camera nested in the pommel — rested quietly against the back of her chair.

The Xia Kingdom's military attaché sat in the far right corner of the first tier, eyes closed, apparently dozing. But his fingers, on his knee, were drawing something soundlessly in the air. The new-pattern Red Dragon, a touch over three metres. Augustus, around three and a half. Rose's Ghost, two and a half. Three numbers. He had committed them to memory along with the position of a certain fist-sized inset in the Red Dragon's chest.

At the mine's mouth, the new-pattern Seraph team drew up in a single line in the thin morning light.

Red Dragon at the centre, the dragon-scales very dark under the lead-coloured sky. Augustus and Solomon on either flank like the corner towers of some small fortification. The Rose's Ghost did not step forward. It slid, soundlessly, into the shadow of the side wall of the tunnel mouth, and the pink-purple of its plates was so close to the colour of the rock that within a few metres it had nearly ceased to exist. It had never intended to be seen.

The empty Sword Dancer was towed to the deepest part of the tunnel mouth, and waited there for the order to be lit.

The spherical screen at the centre of the gallery switched view. Down the throat of the tunnel now, through the red of the infrared lens. Three vast silhouettes stood in the heat-imaging picture like three iron towers on fire.

"And now — the Original Sin Engine's entry machines, into the arena!"

From the depths of the tunnel came a long, low note of steam — a horn, perhaps, or a pressure-valve somewhere singing. The sound travelled the nine-metre bore of the rock and came back, again and again, multiplied, until what reached the gallery was a single sustained ache at the root of the teeth.

A Leviathan-class airship.

The gas envelope was a hundred metres of black silk, hovering without sound in a chamber the miners had widened by hand. From beneath it, a single column of white light fell vertically, like a thing out of some cathedral rite — the descent of the holy.

In the white column, a shadow stood up.

Gulonoth.

Nine metres of it, a moving bell-tower of dark iron. The shoulders alone were more than four metres across; every plate looked as though it had been cut from the side of a warship and bolted on. In its right hand it carried a six-metre recurve saw-toothed blade whose teeth were spaced wide enough to take a man's fist. In its left, a three-metre tower-shield, and on the shield's face the emblem of the Original Sin Engine — an inverted dead tree, roots reaching upward for a sky that was not there.

The thunder of its reactor, a Tyrannosaur-class core, sat in its chest like a second heart, and the rock of the tunnel beat faintly with it.

"Third-generation Prometheus, Gulonoth!" The announcer's voice came back along the tunnel strangely distorted, as if it had been dragged through the rock. "Pilot — Juan Borgia! Second legitimate son of His Holiness! Test pilot of the Original Sin Engine!"

Inside the cockpit of Gulonoth, Juan Borgia looked at the screen in front of him. The screen was split into a dozen small windows, and in the lower-left of the cluster, five points of light stood in a careful row. The nearest of them was the colour of dried blood, and had a dragon's scales.

The corner of his mouth went up.

The public-address system crackled. There was a spit of current, and then a young voice — smiling, but the smile wrong — came out of the chest of Gulonoth and rolled down the tunnel and reached every corner of it.

"Cesare."

The echo made the word uglier, as though it had been dragged against stone.

"Today I will make you kneel to me and apologise."

The announcer in the gallery opened his mouth to say something conciliatory. The crackle of the speaker swallowed him whole.

At the mine's mouth, the Red Dragon did not move.

Cesare sat in his cockpit, the nerve-link not yet engaged. Through the slit of his half-closed visor he watched the slow, dark movement far down the tunnel. The tread of Gulonoth was like a storm at a distance, beating at his eardrum in slow waves.

Juan's voice was still in the rock, folding back on itself.

"My dear brother. You think, because you have come back to Florence, that everything has changed? You think, because the old man has let you out, that something has changed? You are still a bastard. Your mother was a —"

Cesare raised his right hand.

Inside the cockpit, the Red Dragon's right hand rose in sympathy. The fingertips came to rest on the dragon-scaled pauldron, and tapped it, twice.

The two characters — Hong Long — caught the morning light where he had touched them, and brightened a fraction. It was not the light of any reaction in the Seraph's heart. It was only the sun, briefly, on metal.

His violet eyes flashed, once, behind the visor. Quick. Short. A single bolt of purple across a black sky, and then gone.

The cockpit was very quiet. Cesare did not reach for the speaker. He did not frown. He drew the hand back from the pauldron and set it on the control stick.

Far down the tunnel, behind the great shoulder of Gulonoth, two smaller shadows stepped out of the shadow of the Leviathan.

Zero and One.

They stood a full two metres shorter than the giant in front of them, and the lines of them were tighter, more compact; the proportions of the limbs were nearer to those of a man, and the range of motion at the joints was, to anyone who knew what to look for, markedly greater. The dark-iron of their plates caught the white light in cold glints. They walked nearly without sound — the soles of their feet were wrapped in a sound-dampening rubber.

"Original Sin Engine entry machines!" the announcer was saying, finding his voice again. "Third-generation Prometheus prototypes, Zero and One! Pilots designated Zero-Knight and One-Knight, ace test pilots of the Original Sin Engine!"

"Their pilots aren't even public?"
"Classified? They won't even give a name?"
"What in the world is the Original Sin Engine doing?"

The murmurs in the gallery grew. The Xia attaché opened his eyes, and his gaze fixed, very carefully, on Zero and One. His fingertip tapped, twice, on his knee. Range of motion: at least thirty per cent more than Gulonoth.

As Zero and One passed the flank of the great machine, a number of people in the gallery drew a breath at the same time.

Zero tilted its head.

It was not a casual tilt. It was a tilt driven by servo-motors to a tolerance of fractions of a millimetre, the kind of tilt a raptor makes when it turns its head sideways to fix a piece of prey. There were no eye-holes in its faceplate. Instead, a single long horizontal slit, a viewing window. That window, at that moment, was aimed, through the length of the tunnel, at the mine's mouth. At the Red Dragon.

One did the same, within the same heartbeat. Two helmets, turning, together, on the same axis. Towards the same point.

"They are — looking at the Red Dragon?" a reporter said, very quietly.

Inside the slit of Zero's faceplate there passed, for an instant, a thin line of gold. It was not a reflection. It came from within — as if, behind the plate, something was glowing. The line lasted less than a third of a second. The spherical screen's high-definition lens happened, by accident, to have caught that single frame; no one in the gallery would otherwise have noticed anything at all.

The faceplate of One had a similar glow, but the angle hid most of it; only the last, fading edge of the gold leaked out, and then was gone.

"Zero and One's optical systems appear," the announcer said, after a small pause, "to be calibrating."

No one in the gallery remarked on the gold.

No one in the gallery, that is.

Princess Chun had noticed it.

She had not, in fact, seen the gold. What she had seen was the manner in which the two helmets had turned. The motion was too precise. It was the motion of a thing executing a command, yes — but more than that. It was the motion of a thing being looked through, by someone very intent, at something he meant to kill.

She slid the silent speaking-tube back into her sleeve, and in the angle of the chair that Ye Suli could not see, she wrote, with one fingertip, a single character on the wood of the arm.

Hunt.

Ye Suli inclined his head, slightly. Beside the names Zero and One in his notebook, he wrote three small characters. Not ornamentation.

In the joints of the two machines, something — a thread-fine filament, almost transparent, occasionally catching the white light in a single glint — he had noted, and not understood. He did not need to understand it. He knew that the Original Sin Engine did not put ornamentation on its machines.

The spherical screen changed.

It was no longer a tight view of the mine's mouth. It lifted, drew back, and the whole of the quarry opened under the camera. Vesuvius drifted pale smoke from the middle of its flank; from the flank, the mine-cut wound in the mountain snaked downwards like a great grey-white serpent, disappearing into the body of the rock. The quarry itself lay in front of the mine, a five-kilometre disc of broken ground — old pits, the gaping mouths of abandoned shafts, rusting quarrying machinery left to lean in the dust.

A thin white powder hung in the morning light, and made a faint mist of the distance.

At the western edge of the quarry, the mine's mouth gaped in the pale rock. The five new-pattern Seraphs' shadows were moving, one by one, out from behind the gash.

At the eastern edge, deeper in, the nine-metre silhouette of Gulonoth sat in the shadow like a steel animal waiting to spring. Zero and One, on either side of it, were smaller, and darker, and quieter.

The two forces faced each other across the whole of the quarry.

"The field is set," said the announcer, and his voice had at last settled into a working steadiness. "Five new-pattern Seraph prototype machines of the Minerva Engine — Red Dragon, Augustus, Solomon, Rose's Ghost, and reserve Sword Dancer. Three third-generation Prometheus of the Original Sin Engine — Gulonoth, Zero, One."

"Rules, once more, for confirmation. Both sides to use thin-shell rounds. No live ammunition, no red-mercury-filled warheads. A side whose machines are all downed for more than ten seconds is the loser. Field of engagement: the quarry, five kilometres in radius."

The announcer drew a long breath. Several hundred people in the gallery, all of them, drew a long breath.

"This engagement of the trial of arms —"

He raised the signal pistol.

The silver of its barrel caught a flash off the spherical screen, and for an instant, only that, the room was full of small lights.

"Begin."

第172章 蝉翼之舞的第一刀

【中文】
第172章 蝉翼之舞的第一刀

采石场的白雾被撕开了。

不是被风吹散的，是被一发炮弹撕开的。信号枪的银光还悬在天花板的反射里，古洛诺斯胸甲上的六管转轮连射铳已经轰然旋转起来，第一批薄壳弹在零点三秒内泼洒出去，弹幕横扫整个采石场的西侧入口。

碎石崩飞，粉尘炸起，矿道入口的岩壁被连珠的薄壳弹凿出一片蜂窝状的弹坑。岩屑和砂尘形成的灰白色浪潮在晨光中翻涌，看起来像有人在采石场上空泼了一桶石灰。

"古洛诺斯率先开火！"解说员的声音拔高了半度，"它没有等待对峙——六管转轮连射铳全速射击，弹幕覆盖矿道入口整整三十米！密涅瓦的机体还没走出矿道！"

但弹幕扫过的烟尘中，什么都没有被击中的声响。没有人倒地，没有金属碰撞的回音，只有薄壳弹砸进岩壁的闷响和碎石滚落的杂音。

"蔷薇之鬼不在矿道里。"解说员的声音顿了一下。

古洛诺斯背后的驾驶舱里，胡安·博尔吉亚面甲下的脸沉了下来。他盯着的战术屏幕清楚地显示密涅瓦的机体还没有走出矿道——但他的弹幕本能地觉得该打。职业骑士的直觉告诉他，如果他是密涅瓦的指挥官，绝不会让所有机体从同一个入口走出来。

但他的弹幕打空了。

蔷薇之鬼根本没在矿道入口。

观测厅的球形屏幕上，一台超轻型甲胄的身影出现在古洛诺斯左后方约四十米的一处坍塌矿井入口边缘。它的装甲板薄得像蝉翼，灰白色的涂装和采石场的粉尘几乎融为一体，背部蒸汽管路喷出的蒸汽被调到了最低限度，连排气声都被压制在环境噪音以下。

唐璜早在矿道内部分兵时就脱离了主力编队，从侧面的废弃通风井迂回到了古洛诺斯的侧后方。

蔷薇之鬼是五台试制版甲胄中最轻的——只有两吨出头，结构强度按剑舞者的六成来做，牺牲装甲换来了超越所有参战机体的敏捷。它不像一台甲胄，更像一把被人握在手里的匕首。

"这是什么技术？！"解说员脱口而出。

蔷薇之鬼没有继续前进。它蹲在坍塌矿井的边缘，右手从腰后抽出了黑刃曲刃镰——那把专门用来切割管线和小口径钢缆的精密武器，刃长不到一米，弯如新月，刃口涂抹了消光涂层，连反光都没有。

古洛诺斯的六管转轮铳还在狂吼。胡安终于发现了蔷薇之鬼的方位，转轮铳的射击轴线猛地偏转——但蔷薇之鬼已经不在原来的位置了。

它跳下了矿井边缘，落入了采石场地面上一道被遗弃的排水沟槽。

"目标丢失！"古洛诺斯的战术系统发出干涩的提示音。

与此同时，采石场东侧另一道矿道入口的阴影中，传来了一阵极其轻微的金属摩擦声——蜘蛛的声音。

六只微型机械蜘蛛从所罗门王背部展开的腕表式发射舱里弹射出来，腹部嵌入的红水银微晶亮起暗红色的微光，腿节划动，沿着采石场地面的碎石缝隙向古洛诺斯的方向高速爬行。

"电子蛛巢启动。"阿方索坐在所罗门王的驾驶舱里，声音平稳得像在念实验报告，"信号干扰模式开启。"

六只蜘蛛在接近古洛诺斯约六十米时同时张开腹部的信号发射面，释放出密集的宽频电磁脉冲。这种脉冲不会损坏任何设备，但会在目标周围形成一个直径约八十米的雷达干扰幕——古洛诺斯的战术屏幕上瞬间爆出一片雪花般的噪点，雷达锁定功能几乎失效。

"雷达受干扰！无法稳定追踪小型目标！"古洛诺斯的系统发出警报。

"所罗门王释放了电子蛛巢！"解说员的声音带着一丝兴奋，"那是阿方索·罗德里格兹的独门改装——他在微型机械蜘蛛上加挂了红水银微晶作为动力源，有效控制距离一百二十米，持续活动八分钟！"

胡安的脸色更加阴沉。他切掉了雷达，改用目视搜索。古洛诺斯的头部射灯猛地打开，炽白色的光柱扫过采石场的碎石堆和坍塌的矿井入口，把一切都照得惨白。

光柱扫过蔷薇之鬼之前蹲伏的那处矿井边缘——空的。扫过排水沟槽——还是空的。

"唐璜！你在哪里？"胡安低声骂了一句。

唐璜没有回答。他正在排水沟槽里匍匐前进，蔷薇之鬼的膝关节和肘关节贴着沟壁，蒸汽管路的排气阀门被他手动调到了最低，整个机体像一只趴在水面下的鳄鱼。黑刃曲刃镰的刃尖在沟壁的阴影中偶尔闪一下，随即又消失。

采石场的中央，奥古斯都站住了。

昆提良让奥古斯都站在峡谷入口的最前方，举起了那面秘银重盾。盾面上的闭眼狮头纹章在晨光中沉默地注视着前方，狮眼紧闭，狮耳高竖。奥古斯都是五台试制版甲胄中最重的——将近七吨的钢铁巨人，正面装甲厚度可以和早期量产的重型甲胄掰手腕。

它站在那里，像一堵会移动的墙。

零号动了。

没有任何预兆，零号从古洛诺斯的右侧迈出了第一步。它的肩炮——那门和古洛诺斯同型号的单装龙吼炮——缓缓抬起，炮口对准了奥古斯都的方向。

"零号开始瞄准奥古斯都！"解说员的声音骤然紧绷。

零号没有射击。它在等。

昆提良也没有动。奥古斯都的蒸汽核心开始提升功率，硬金骨架内的传动机构发出低沉的嘎吱声，盾牌被它举到了胸甲正前方。

采石场上出现了一个诡异的瞬间——蔷薇之鬼在暗处匍匐，零号在明处举炮，奥古斯都在中间举盾，所罗门王在远处释放蜘蛛，古洛诺斯在疯狂搜索——五台甲胄在方圆不到两百米的范围内对峙着，谁也没有先开火。

然后零号开炮了。

龙吼炮的炮口喷出一团青白色的火焰，薄壳弹以肉眼难以追踪的速度划过采石场。昆提良在炮口闪光的瞬间就做出了反应——奥古斯都的重盾微微偏转角度，让弹着点落在盾面最厚的中央区域。

"砰！"

龙吼炮的冲击力透过秘银盾面传到奥古斯都的手臂关节，昆提良在驾驶舱里闷哼一声。奥古斯都后退了三步——不是一步两步，是三步，每一步都在碎石地面上踩出半尺深的坑印。

盾面上出现了一道划痕。

划痕从狮头纹章的左耳斜切到右眼，狮头的一只耳朵被打缺了，狮眼被裂缝切开。秘银重盾的表面被龙吼炮的薄壳弹犁出了一道清晰的弹道痕迹，弹头碎裂后嵌入盾面约两毫米深。

"龙吼炮命中！奥古斯都后退三步！"解说员的声音拔到了极限，"盾牌受损但没有击穿！"

昆提良把奥古斯都的脚重新扎稳在地面上，低头看了一眼盾面。闭眼狮头纹章的眼睛被裂缝切开了，裂缝的宽度刚好能塞进一根手指。

"还行。"他低声说。

奥古斯都没有后退。它站稳了，重盾重新举正，面对着零号的方向。

零号的肩炮缓缓复位，准备第二次射击。

但就在这个瞬间，排水沟槽里有什么东西动了。

唐璜等的就是这个。

零号开炮的震动通过地面的岩层传导到排水沟槽，蔷薇之鬼的足底传感器捕捉到了这个信号——零号的注意力完全被奥古斯都吸引了，雷达被蜘蛛干扰，射灯正对着奥古斯都的方向，古洛诺斯还在疯狂扫描着它自己的侧后方。

没有人看着古洛诺斯的腘窝。

腘窝——膝关节后方的弯曲处，平衡系统管线集中通过的位置。对于一台九米高的重型机动傀儡来说，腘窝的管线布置最为复杂：液压平衡管、蒸汽回收管、姿态校正气压管、还有连接膝关节陀螺仪的信号线缆。所有这些管线都暴露在膝关节外侧，没有装甲板覆盖——因为设计者认为，没有任何小型目标能突破到那个距离。

蔷薇之鬼从排水沟槽中跃出。

它跳得很高——两吨重的超轻型甲胄在蒸汽弹射器的助推下腾空而起，灰白色的涂装在晨光中像一只突然展开翅膀的巨大灰色蜻蜓。从古洛诺斯的腘窝方向看过去，它就是一个从地平线下方升起的不明物体。

"蔷薇之鬼——"解说员的声音在球形屏幕切换画面的瞬间卡住了。

黑刃曲刃镰在晨光中划出一道几乎没有反光的弧线。

唐璜的目标不是古洛诺斯的装甲，不是结构骨架，不是任何一块能挡住子弹的金属板。他的目标是那束从腘窝缝隙中暴露出来的管线——液压平衡管，外径四厘米，壁厚不到两毫米，材质是普通紫铜合金。

曲刃镰的刃尖精准地切入了液压管的表面。

蔷薇之鬼落地的同时，唐璜的手腕拧了一个极小的角度。曲刃镰的刃口沿着管壁横向拉扯了不到五厘米的长度——

高压液压油从切口喷涌而出。

古洛诺斯的膝关节瞬间失去了部分平衡支撑。九米高的钢铁巨兽在惯性的作用下微微晃了一下，陀螺仪发出刺耳的校正警报，姿态控制系统疯狂地输出补偿信号——但被切断的液压管让左腿膝关节的力量输出骤然下降了两成。

古洛诺斯晃了晃。

它没有倒。驾驶舱里的胡安在零点五秒内就做出了反应——古洛诺斯的左腿引擎强制点火，喷出的蒸汽把周围的碎石吹得四处飞溅，硬生生把倾斜的重心拉了回来。

但它确实晃了。

观测厅的球形屏幕上，几百号人清清楚楚地看到了这个画面：一台九米高的第三代普罗米修斯，被一台不到两吨的超轻型甲胄在背后切了一刀，晃了一下，差点摔倒。

"蔷薇之鬼得分！古洛诺斯平衡系统暂时受损！"解说员的声音带着压抑不住的激动，"左腿膝关节液压平衡管被切断！高压液压油正在泄漏！古洛诺斯的左腿出力下降！"

古洛诺斯的驾驶舱里，胡安的面甲下是铁青的脸。

他低头看了一眼左腿的状态面板——液压油压力从正常的每平方厘米一百四十公斤降到了不到九十公斤，左腿膝关节的输出功率限制在设计值的七成。装甲没有损伤，骨架没有断裂，但平衡系统出了大问题。

"卑鄙。"胡安从牙缝里挤出了一个字。

古洛诺斯猛地转身，巨大的身躯在碎石地面上划出两道深槽。六米长的反曲锯齿巨刃在转身的离心力加持下横扫而出，刃锋切开空气的声音像裂帛一样尖锐，扫过的轨迹覆盖了蔷薇之鬼可能撤退的全部方向。

唐璜不在那里。

蔷薇之鬼在古洛诺斯转身的零点三秒前就已经跳开了——它借着落地的反作用力弹向了侧面一处废弃矿井的通风口，一个两米见方的铁栅格洞口。蔷薇之鬼的体型刚好能钻进去。

六米长的巨刃切过通风口外的岩壁，锯齿在灰白色的石头上犁出一道半米深的沟痕，火星和碎石一起飞溅。通风口的铁栅格被巨刃的余波震得变了形，但没有碰到蔷薇之鬼的一片装甲板。

蔷薇之鬼蹲在通风口的深处，曲刃镰上的液压油还没干透，在黑暗中泛着微光。

"蔷薇之鬼消失在废弃矿井的通风口中！"解说员的声音追着古洛诺斯的巨刃跑，"古洛诺斯的反击落空！它砍了个空！"

观测厅里，各国使团的反应像油锅溅了水。

有人鼓掌——那是密涅瓦机关的技术人员，他们太清楚刚才那一切意味着什么。有人骂——拜占庭使团的一个武官拍着桌子站了起来，嘴里的词大意是"刺客"、"不讲骑士规矩"。叶素理坐在中山国使团的座位上，手里还在记录，脸上的表情没有任何变化。纯公主握着青丝古剑的剑柄，指节微微发白。

VIP包厢的第二层，冈扎罗·博尔吉亚的手捏碎了手里的酒杯。

高脚杯的碎片落在他手背上，玻璃割破了皮肤，血和酒混在一起滴在了白色的桌布上。他没有去擦。他的眼睛死死地盯着球形屏幕上蔷薇之鬼钻进通风口的那个画面，脸上的表情从震惊变成了——

他猛地站了起来，把椅子撞得向后滑了两米。

"那是刺客。"他的声音不大，但很冷，"不是骑士。"

没有人回应他。

球形屏幕上的画面在快速切换——解说员正试图同时追踪五个目标。

奥古斯都还站在采石场中央，盾牌上的弹痕清晰可见。零号的龙吼炮刚刚完成了复位，正准备第二次射击。所罗门王在远处的一座碎石堆后面稳稳定位，电子蛛巢的第二波蜘蛛正在装填。古洛诺斯在原地旋转着射灯搜索蔷薇之鬼的下落，但通风口的位置被岩壁的死角遮住了大半，射灯打不进去。

"蔷薇之鬼得分！古洛诺斯平衡系统暂时受损！"解说员再次确认了这个结果，"液压油正在泄漏！如果不能在短时间内修复，古洛诺斯的左腿战力将持续下降！"

然后，零号停止了瞄准奥古斯都。

它的肩炮炮口缓缓偏转，离开了昆提良的方向。龙吼炮的炮管在空中划过一道弧线，最终指向了——

蔷薇之鬼消失的那处废弃通风口。

零号迈出了脚步。它没有跑，也没有快步走，而是用一种极其稳定的步频向通风口的方向移动，每一步都像在丈量距离。它的头低垂着，肩炮的炮口始终对着通风口的方向，面甲内部透出极淡的金色微光。

它在走过去。

"零号……零号放弃了攻击奥古斯都！"解说员的声音带上了一丝困惑，"它正在向通风口移动！零号要和古洛诺斯汇合吗？它要去支援古洛诺斯吗？"

奥古斯都的驾驶舱里，昆提良愣了一下。

零号不理他了。它转身了。龙吼炮的炮口从他的盾面上移开，对准了另一个方向。他本能地想要追击——但所罗门王的通讯频道里传来了阿方索的声音。

"别追。"阿方索说，"让它走。"

昆提良咬了咬牙，把奥古斯都的脚步钉在了原地。

零号的脚步声在采石场的碎石地面上回响，沉稳而精确，像一台正在执行预设程序的机器。走到通风口外约二十米处时它停了下来，肩炮炮口微微下压，对准了通风口铁栅格的缝隙。

那里面蹲着蔷薇之鬼。

观测厅的VIP包厢里，博尔吉亚家族的家长们交换了一个眼神。教皇隆·博尔吉亚端坐在主位上，面前的绿色泡腾片水杯被他端起来又放下。他的脸色比昨天更差，但眼睛依然锐利。

"它知道蔷薇之鬼在里面。"一个家长低声说。

零号没有射击。它只是站在那里，肩炮对着通风口，像一尊沉默的雕像。

通风口里，唐璜能感觉到那个东西就在外面。蔷薇之鬼的被动传感器捕捉到了龙吼炮炮口散发的微量热量信号——一门大炮正对着他蹲着的这个洞口，距离不到二十米。

如果零号开炮，龙吼炮的薄壳弹会直接轰穿铁栅格和通风井的岩壁，把蔷薇之鬼埋在碎石里。

唐璜的手心出了汗，但握紧曲刃镰的手没有抖。

通讯频道里，西泽尔的声音忽然响了。

"都别动。"

红龙还没有走出矿道。但它的声音清晰地传进了每台甲胄的驾驶舱里。

"让它站在那里。"西泽尔说。

【English】
Chapter 172 — The First Cut of the Cicada-Wing Dance

The white haze over the quarry was torn open.

Not by the wind. Not by the pale sun climbing above the eastern rim. By a shell. The signal flare's silver smear was still drifting through the reflected light off the quarry's vaulted ceiling when the six barrels on Guloños' breastplate began their slow, terrible rotation.

"Guloños opens fire! No pause for the parley — the rotary cannon is cycling at full rate, the barrage is sweeping thirty metres of the western mine entrance! Minerva's machines have not yet cleared the tunnel mouth!"

Stone came apart. The far wall of the western approach flaked under the barrage in a clean sweep, the rock face opening into a honeycomb of fresh pits, each pit the size of a man's fist. The percussion of each thin-shell round rolled back from the stone in a steady, hungry drumbeat. The haze in the quarry turned the colour of bone-flour, the way the air looks above a lime-kiln at first light.

Empty. Every impact was empty.

No metal on metal. No body falling. Only the dry slap of shells into stone, and the small avalanche of loosened grit sliding down into the pit.

"The Rose-Phantom is not in the tunnel," the commentator said, after a beat.

Inside Guloños' cockpit, the face behind Juan Borgia's visor set. The tactical plate on his screen said clearly enough that Minerva's machines had not cleared the tunnel mouth. But his barrage had felt right. The professional instinct of a career knight had said: do it. If I were the opposing captain, I would not send every machine through the same mouth.

His barrage had been wasted.

The Rose-Phantom had never been in the mine mouth at all.

On the spherical screen in the observation hall, a shape resolved at the back of Guloños' left flank, forty metres out, balanced on the lip of a collapsed air-shaft. The armour plates on the shape were thin as a cicada's wing. The finish was a dusty off-white, so close to the powder of the quarry it almost disappeared into it. The steam venting from the back-bone piping had been throttled almost to nothing, the exhaust note pushed down under the level of the ambient noise.

Don Juan had peeled off from the main body inside the tunnel. He had come around through a disused ventilation shaft. He had been behind Guloños' left shoulder for some time.

The Rose-Phantom was the lightest of the five prototypes. Two tons, perhaps two and a little. The structural rating was six-tenths of a Sword Dancer's. They had spent armour to buy an agility no other machine on the field could match. It did not look like a knight at all. It looked like a dagger a man was holding in his hand.

"What is that construction?!" the commentator said, before he could help himself.

The Rose-Phantom did not advance. It crouched on the lip of the collapsed shaft, and the right hand came up from behind the small of the back with a black-bladed sickle. The weapon was built for cutting cable and small-bore steel line. The blade was under a metre long, curved like a young moon, its edge washed in a non-reflective coating that swallowed the light.

Guloños' six barrels were still screaming. Juan at last found the bearing. The line of fire slewed across the field. But the Rose-Phantom was no longer where it had been.

It had stepped off the lip of the shaft, and dropped into a disused drainage gutter at the quarry floor.

"Target lost," Guloños' tactical system said, in a dry, mechanical voice.

From the shadow of a different mine-mouth on the quarry's east side, at the same moment, came a sound so small it was almost not a sound at all. The chitter of small metal on stone.

The sound of spiders.

Six micro-mechanical spiders came out of a wrist-launched bay in the back of Solomon's carapace. In the belly of each, a small red-mercury micro-crystal began to glow a dim, dirty red. Their legs fanned. They set off at speed along the cracks in the quarry floor, scuttling in the direction of Guloños.

"Spider-nest is up," Alfonso Rodriguez said, from the pilot's cradle inside Solomon. His voice was as flat as a man reading from a laboratory ledger. "Signal-jam mode, active."

At sixty metres from Guloños the six spiders fanned open the small emitter vanes on their abdomens and loosed a dense, wide-band electromagnetic pulse. The pulse damaged nothing. It did not need to. It built a wall of radar noise eighty metres across, and the wall came down over Guloños' tactical screen in a single, bright, snowy crash. The lock-on function went blind.

"Radar jammed! Cannot hold a track on small targets!" Guloños' system told him, with the same dry insistence.

"Solomon has deployed the spider-nest!" the commentator's voice had picked up a thread of excitement it could not quite suppress. "Alfonso Rodriguez's private modification — red-mercury micro-crystal drive, effective control radius one hundred and twenty metres, sustained operation eight minutes!"

Juan's face, behind the visor, went another shade darker. He cut the radar. He took the system off-line with a hard mental switch and began to drive by eye. Guloños' headlamp flared, a hard, white bar of light raking across the quarry's rubble piles and the broken mouth of the collapsed shaft. Everything it touched went the colour of a freshly-washed corpse.

The light passed over the lip where the Rose-Phantom had been. Empty. It passed over the drainage gutter. Empty again.

"Don Juan. Where are you?" Juan Borgia said, very quietly, between his teeth.

Don Juan did not answer. He was belly-crawling in the gutter. The Rose-Phantom's knee- and elbow-joints were pressed against the trench wall. He had wound the exhaust valves down to their last detent by hand. The whole machine lay along the bottom of the drain like a crocodile at the surface of a quiet river. The tip of the black-bladed sickle, where it showed for a moment in the shadow of the wall, caught a flake of light. Then it didn't.

In the centre of the quarry, Augustus stopped where it was.

Quintilian had put Augustus at the very mouth of the canyon approach, with the mithril great-shield raised before its chest. The closed-eyed lion crest on the shield face watched, in silence, down the length of the quarry. The lion's eyes were shut. Its ears were cocked. Augustus was the heaviest of the five prototypes — close to seven tons of iron, its frontal plate thick enough to argue with the early production heavies and come away without an apology.

It stood there, and it looked like a wall that could move.

Zero moved.

There was no warning. Zero took a single step out of Guloños' right flank, and the shoulder-mounted piece — the same single-shot Dragon's Roar as Guloños carried — began to rise. The muzzle lifted, slow and patient, and settled on the line of Augustus' centre mass.

"Zero is taking aim on Augustus!" the commentator said. The line in his voice had gone taut.

Zero did not fire. It was waiting.

Quintilian did not move either. Augustus' steam core began to climb. The hard-gold skeleton inside the frame took the rising pressure with a low, grinding complaint, the kind a mill-wheel makes when the sluice is opened too far. The shield came up square to the breastplate.

For an odd, suspended instant, the quarry held still. The Rose-Phantom crouched in the dark. Zero stood in the light with its cannon up. Augustus stood between them with its shield. Solomon watched from behind a rubble mound, spiders still in the field. Guloños swung its headlamp in frantic arcs, hunting for what it could not see. Five machines, within a circle two hundred metres across, none of them willing to be the next to fire.

Then Zero fired.

The muzzle of the Dragon's Roar bloomed a hard cyan-white. The thin-shell round crossed the quarry faster than the eye could follow. Quintilian had read the muzzle-flash the instant it came. Augustus' shield tilted by the smallest possible degree, the angle of it pulling the impact onto the central boss of the plate — the thickest square inch of the whole shield.

The sound was a single hard syllable.

The impact of the Dragon's Roar came through the mithril face and into Augustus' arm-joint, and Quintilian, in the pilot's cradle, grunted, once, under his breath. Augustus took three steps back. Not one, not two — three. Each step ground a half-foot crater into the rubble floor.

A score was opened in the shield.

The line of it ran from the left ear of the lion's crest, down across the face, and out through the right eye. The lion's left ear had been bitten off. The closed eye was split open by the crack. The thin-shell round had done its work, and then it had died two millimetres into the mithril, the broken head of it seated in the metal like a spent tooth.

"Dragon's Roar — hit! Augustus three steps back!" The commentator's voice was climbing towards the gallery ceiling. "Shield damaged, not penetrated!"

Quintilian set Augustus' feet back into the rubble. He looked down, once, at the shield. The lion's eye had been opened. The crack was wide enough to take the tip of a finger.

"Still good," he said, under his breath.

Augustus did not retreat. It stood where it had been put down. The shield came back to square. The lion faced the line of Zero's gun, the closed eye cracked open now, and the open eye on the other side still shut.

Zero's shoulder-piece came back down to the ready, slowly, the long barrel cycling for the second shot.

But in that instant something moved in the drainage gutter.

Don Juan had been waiting for that instant.

The kick of the Dragon's Roar had gone through the bedrock and into the floor of the trench, and the sole-plates of the Rose-Phantom had felt it. He had been counting, the way a fencer counts a tempo. Zero's attention was on Augustus. The radar was blind with the spider noise. The headlamp was pointed at Augustus. Guloños was still swinging its lamp across its own back-quarter in long, useless arcs.

No one was watching the back of Guloños' knee.

The popliteal — the bend at the back of the knee, where the balance lines of the system were bundled. On a nine-metre heavy walker, the bundle there was the worst-protected part of the frame. The hydraulic balance line, the steam recovery line, the attitude-correction pneumatic, the signal cable to the knee-gyro — they were all routed through that single gap, and none of them were plated over, because the designers had been certain that nothing small enough to threaten them could ever get to that range.

The Rose-Phantom came up out of the drainage gutter.

It went up high. The two tons of the super-light frame came off the floor on the thrust of the steam-ejectors, and the dust-white finish caught the morning light for the first time like a great grey dragonfly opening its wings a long way above the ground. From the angle of Guloños' back-knee, it was simply an unknown shape coming up over the horizon.

"The Rose-Phantom —"

The commentator's voice caught on the cut, because the spherical screen was switching feeds at the same instant and the picture lost him a beat.

The black-bladed sickle drew an arc in the air that gave back almost no light at all.

Don Juan was not aiming at Guloños' plate. He was not aiming at the hard-gold skeleton. He was not aiming at any piece of metal that was designed to stop a bullet. He was aiming at the line that was visible in the gap of the popliteal — the hydraulic balance line, four centimetres across the outside, less than two millimetres of wall, common copper alloy, the kind of material that took a press-brake in any machine-shop in Florence.

The point of the sickle went into the line.

The Rose-Phantom landed. The instant the soles touched the rubble, Don Juan turned his wrist through the smallest possible angle. The edge of the blade drew along the line, laterally, for less than five centimetres.

The hydraulic oil came out of the cut in a sheet.

Guloños' left knee lost a measure of its balance support at once. The nine-metre iron beast, moving under all the inertia of its own mass, took a single hitch to port. The gyro threw out a correction so shrill it cut the inside of the cockpit. The attitude controller screamed for compensation, and the compensation was sent, but the cut line had pulled twenty per cent of the left knee's power off the floor in the same instant the order was being written.

Guloños hitched.

It did not fall. Juan Borgia's hand, inside the cockpit, made the correct decision in a half-second. Guloños' left leg engine was forced to fire on the limiter; the steam it blew out threw the loose stone around the foot in a flat ring. The iron beast, leaning, dragged its centre of mass back over its own feet by main strength.

But it had hitched.

On the spherical screen in the observation hall, several hundred people watched, very clearly, the picture that had just been made. A nine-metre third-generation Prometheus, and a two-ton super-light, and a single cut at the back of the knee, and the heavy staggered.

"Point to the Rose-Phantom! Guloños' balance system is compromised!" The commentator's voice was riding the edge of his own restraint. "Left knee hydraulic balance line cut! High-pressure oil in the open! Guloños' left leg output is down!"

Inside Guloños' cockpit, the face behind Juan Borgia's visor was the colour of old iron.

He looked once at the status panel for the left leg. The hydraulic pressure had fallen from its working one-forty kilos per square centimetre to under ninety. The left knee was running capped at seventy per cent of design output. The plate was undamaged. The skeleton was whole. The balance system was in pieces.

"Base cur," Juan said, between his teeth, very quietly.

Guloños wrenched itself around. The nine metres of iron cut two long, deep lines into the rubble as it turned. The six-metre reverse-curved serrated great-sword went around with it, the centrifugal mass of the swing putting the full weight of the blade out at the tip. The sound the cutting edge made through the air was the sound of strong silk being torn. The arc it traced covered every line along which the Rose-Phantom could have retreated.

Don Juan was not on any of those lines.

The Rose-Phantom had been gone three-tenths of a second before the turn. It had used the kick of its own landing to throw itself sideways, into the open mouth of a disused mine's ventilation shaft — a two-metre-square grid of rusted iron set in the rock. The Rose-Phantom's shoulder-span just fitted.

The six-metre blade took the rock face outside the shaft, and the serrations tore a half-metre trench out of the grey stone, the sparks and the grit thrown out together. The iron grid at the mouth of the shaft was bent by the wash of the swing, but it had not been there at the moment of the cut. Not a plate of the Rose-Phantom had been touched.

"The Rose-Phantom is gone into a disused ventilation shaft!" the commentator's voice was chasing the great-sword across the picture. "Guloños' counter-stroke — misses! The cut went home on empty air!"

In the observation hall, the national delegations reacted the way oil reacts to a hot pan.

Somewhere a man was clapping — the technical staff of the Minerva bureau, who knew very well what they had just been shown. Someone else was cursing. A Byzantine military attaché had got to his feet at his bench and was putting his hand down on the wood, hard, the gist of his words having to do with assassins and with the proper forms of the order of chivalry. Ye Suli, in the seat of the Zhongshan mission, kept on writing. The expression on his face did not change. The Princess of Chun had her hand on the wrapped grip of the Blue Silk old sword, and the knuckles under the silk were white.

In the second tier of the VIP box, Gonzalo Borgia's hand closed on the stem of his wine glass, and the glass did not survive it.

The shards came away from the back of his hand, and a thin line of blood followed the wine down on to the white cloth of the table. He did not wipe it. His eyes were fixed on the picture of the Rose-Phantom ducking into the shaft, and the look on his face, which had been a kind of surprise, finished its journey somewhere else.

He got to his feet. The chair he had been sitting on went back two full metres on the floor.

"That is an assassin," he said. His voice was not loud. It was very cold. "Not a knight."

No one in the box answered him.

The picture on the spherical screen was running, and the commentator was trying to follow five things at once.

Augustus still stood in the middle of the quarry, the score across the lion's crest easy to read. Zero's Dragon's Roar had finished its cycle and was setting up for the second shot. Solomon had taken a steady position behind a rubble mound in the distance, and the second wave of spiders was loading into the wrist bay. Guloños stood where it had stopped, the headlamp still swinging in slow arcs across its own back-quarter, looking for the shaft it could not quite get its light into.

"Point to the Rose-Phantom! Guloños' balance system is compromised!" the commentator confirmed again, as if the hall had not heard. "Hydraulic oil still in the open air. If the line is not repaired in the next few minutes, Guloños' left leg will keep on losing output."

Then Zero stopped aiming at Augustus.

The shoulder-piece began to slew, slowly, off the line on Quintilian. The long barrel of the Dragon's Roar drew an arc through the air above the quarry floor, and the line it ended on was not the line of Augustus at all.

The barrel came to rest, and pointed at the dark mouth of the disused ventilation shaft in which the Rose-Phantom had just disappeared.

Zero took a step. It was not running. It was not walking fast. It was using a step-length so measured that each pace seemed to be measuring something. The head was low, and the shoulder-piece stayed on the shaft mouth the whole time, and the visor threw out a very thin gold line of light from somewhere inside.

It was walking over.

"Zero — Zero has broken off from Augustus!" the commentator said, and there was a small bewildered note in his voice now. "It is moving on the ventilation shaft! Is Zero going to join Guloños? Is it going to support?"

In the cockpit of Augustus, Quintilian hesitated for the length of a breath.

Zero had stopped minding him. The gun had lifted off his shield, and the line had gone somewhere else. Every instinct he had said to follow, to press in, to take the free shot at the unprotected flank. And then the comm-channel to Solomon opened in his ear, and Alfonso's voice came through.

"Don't follow," Alfonso said. "Let it walk."

Quintilian set his teeth into the muscle at the side of his jaw, and he nailed Augustus' feet to the rubble where they were.

The sound of Zero's footfalls came back off the stone floor of the quarry, steady and exact, the way a clock sounds when it is not being wound. Twenty metres from the mouth of the shaft it stopped, and the muzzle of the shoulder-piece dropped a fraction, and the line of the bore came down to bear on the iron grid of the grate.

Inside the grate, in the dark, the Rose-Phantom was crouching.

In the VIP box, the heads of the Borgia family turned to one another, in the same half-second. Pope Leone Borgia sat in the central chair, and the green glass of the effervescent water in front of him was lifted, and put down again, and lifted, and put down again. His face was worse than the day before. His eyes were as sharp as they had ever been.

"It knows the Rose-Phantom is in there," one of the elders said, very quietly.

Zero did not fire. It stood where it had stopped, the shoulder-piece on the shaft, like a figure on a plinth that had been carved out of one piece of stone.

Inside the shaft, Don Juan could feel the thing on the other side of the grate. The Rose-Phantom's passive sensors had picked up the small heat-leak from the mouth of the Dragon's Roar — a single cannon, less than twenty metres, pointed at the hole he was sitting in.

If Zero fired, the thin-shell round would go through the iron grid and the rock of the shaft wall and bury the Rose-Phantom under its own ceiling.

Don Juan's palm was wet. The hand on the sickle did not shake.

And then a voice came on the comm-channel.

"None of you move."

The Red Dragon had not yet come out of the mine. But Cesare's voice came through, clean and even, into the cockpit of every machine on the field.

"Leave it standing where it is," Cesare said.

第173章 堡垒之盾的两次倒下

【中文】
第173章 堡垒之盾的两次倒下

零号站在通风口外二十米处，肩炮的炮口微微下压，面甲内部的金色微光一闪一灭，像某种正在计算什么的精密仪器。采石场里安静得能听见碎石从矿壁上滑落的声音。

"它不动了。"阿方索的声音在通讯频道里响起，压得很低。

"在等。"西泽尔说。

红龙站在矿道出口外的峡谷中央，超重武装的龙骑兵套装把它的身躯撑得比常规炽天使大了整整一圈，胸甲上嵌着的那枚圣剑碎片在暗处隐隐泛着光。它没有动，背后的屠龙巨刃也没有拔出。它只是站在那里。

而一号站在它的正前方八十米外。

两台甲胄隔着整座采石场的宽度对峙。零号在通风口前，一号在矿道出口前，三个原罪机体恰好将密涅瓦的五台试制甲胄分割成了三个互不相连的孤岛。

唐璜蹲在通风井的黑暗中，蔷薇之鬼的被动传感器捕捉着外面零号龙吼炮散发的微量热量信号。他能感觉到那个东西还没走。曲刃镰握在手中，关节上的弹簧锁已经松开，随时可以弹射出刀刃。

"再给我三十秒。"他压着声音说。

通讯频道里没有人回答他。所有人都在等。

然后阿方索说了两个字："动了。"

零号动了。

它转身。龙吼炮的炮口从通风口的方向偏转，肩部的液压机构发出沉闷的嘶响，炮管缓缓抬升——不是对准通风口，而是对准了奥古斯都。

"它要开炮了！"解说员的声音陡然拔高，"零号的龙吼炮正对准奥古斯都！"

昆提良咬了咬牙。奥古斯都的脚步重重地顿在碎石地面上，他没有后退。

"别送死！"阿方索的声音从通讯频道里炸开。

"它一开炮我背后就是唐璜。"昆提良说。

他没等阿方索回答，奥古斯都已经迈开了步子。五吨重的重型甲胄踏碎脚下的碎石，朝零号的方向正面冲了过去。秘银重盾从背上解下来，双臂端平，盾面上的闭眼狮头纹章正对着零号的炮口。

零号的龙吼炮开火了。

那门肩炮发射时没有传统火炮那种震耳欲聋的轰鸣，取而代之的是一种深沉的、仿佛来自地底的咆哮。薄壳弹拖着一道青蓝色的尾焰划过采石场，直直地撞上了奥古斯都的秘银重盾。

"轰——"

秘银重盾和龙吼炮弹的碰撞点在盾面正中央绽开一圈白色的冲击波。奥古斯都的双脚在碎石地面上犁出两道深深的沟槽，整台甲胄被巨大的推力向后推出十几米，最后撞上了一堆崩塌的碎石才停下来。盾面承受冲击的位置凹下去一块，闭眼狮头的左耳被冲击波震裂，碎片飞溅。

驾驶舱里，昆提良的背狠狠撞在靠背上，安全带勒进肩膀，肋骨传来一阵钝痛。驾驶舱内的红色警示灯亮了起来，三块仪表板同时跳出警告——左臂液压系统压力骤降，脊椎缓冲机构受力过载，盾面完整度百分之八十七。

"昆提良！状态报告！"阿方索的声音里带着一丝少见的急促。

昆提良吐掉嘴里的血沫。那是刚才冲击时咬破了舌头，满嘴都是铁锈味。他抬头看了一眼驾驶舱里的读数，笑了。

"还能打。"

他把奥古斯都从碎石堆里推起来。秘银重盾上凹进去的那块清晰可见，狮头左耳缺失，但整体结构没有破裂。零号没有追击，它仍然站在通风口外，龙吼炮的炮口微微下压，似乎在重新计算。

观测厅里，数百名各国使团的成员齐声倒吸了一口气。

"奥古斯都还站着！"解说员的声音带着难以置信的颤抖，"昆提良骑士用秘银重盾正面承受了一发龙吼炮！盾面只出现局部凹陷，机体结构完整！他还能战斗！"

密涅瓦主观测厅的VIP包厢里，薇若兰面前的茶杯被她无意识地攥紧了。她盯着屏幕上奥古斯都缓缓站起来的画面，指节发白。

佛朗哥教授坐在她旁边的轮椅上。老人今早的状态很差，薇若兰发现他连续咳了两次，第二次的时候用手帕捂住了嘴，手帕收起来时她瞥见了上面暗红色的痕迹。她没有说话。

现在屏幕上正在回放奥古斯都被龙吼炮击中的慢动作，秘银重盾承受冲击的瞬间，盾面的金属纹理在高速摄影下清晰可见——那是密涅瓦最新的多层锻造技术，每一层硬金的结晶方向都不同，用来分散冲击能量。

佛朗哥的眼睛亮了一下。

"盾面是五层交错锻造的，"他低声说，"外两层是影金属，中间三层是硬金，最后那层是……"他眯起眼，"冰原寒玉夹层。"

薇若兰愣了一瞬。

"冰原寒玉？叶尼塞的技术？"她低声问。

"不，不是叶尼塞的工艺。叶尼塞是把寒玉嵌在脊椎甲胄的内层，用来缓冲神经反噬。这个是反过来用的——把寒玉锻进盾面夹层，利用寒玉的低温特性在冲击瞬间让金属表面产生微收缩，形成第二层缓冲。"佛朗哥的眼睛里闪着技术人员特有的那种光芒，"这是……昆提良自己的改装？还是阿方索的手笔？"

薇若兰摇了摇头。她也不确定。但她知道这种改装不是凭空出现的，一定是奥古斯都制造过程中某个没写进报告的改动。

"昆提良那家伙，只是个扛盾的莽夫吧？"佛朗哥忽然说了一句。

"他是西泽尔最早选中的旧部之一。"薇若兰说。

"选他扛盾？"

"因为盾在他手里不会碎。"

佛朗哥沉默了一会儿，然后咳了一声。他用手帕捂住了嘴，白色的布面上洇出一小片暗红。薇若兰伸手去拿纸巾，他摆了摆手，把手帕折好塞进口袋里。

"没事。"老人说，"看比赛。"

采石场里，零号重新抬起了龙吼炮的炮口。

这一次它的目标不是奥古斯都的盾面——它把炮口偏了五度，对准了奥古斯都的左肩关节。

"它在瞄准关节！"解说员叫了起来，"零号调整了射击角度，它要打的是奥古斯都的肩部——如果左臂被废掉，秘银重盾就举不起来了！"

通讯频道里，阿方索的声音冷静得不像话。

"昆提良，左移三步。"

"收到。"

奥古斯都向左横移了三步，把重盾的盾缘对准了零号龙吼炮的新射角。盾面上凹进去的那块恰好挡住了炮口最集中的冲击区域。

零号开炮。

第二发龙吼炮。

青蓝色的尾焰再次划过采石场，薄壳弹准确地撞上了奥古斯都秘银重盾上那个先前被击凹的位置。冲击波比第一次更加猛烈，秘银重盾整个盾面都在颤抖，凹坑的底部出现了一条极细的裂纹。

奥古斯都再次被推飞。这一次它没能站稳，整台甲胄从碎石堆上翻了过去，在地面上滚了半圈，最后背撞在采石场东侧一面废弃矿井的井壁上。井壁的岩石在撞击中碎裂了一大块，碎石哗啦啦地落下来，有几块砸在奥古斯都的肩甲上，发出沉闷的响声。

"奥古斯都——倒地了！"解说员的声音里带着焦急。

驾驶舱里，昆提良被安全带勒得几乎喘不过气。第二次冲击让他的肋骨又疼了一层，嘴角溢出一缕血丝，顺着下巴流进了领口。他低头看了一眼仪表板——左臂液压系统彻底失压，盾面完整度百分之六十一，脊椎缓冲机构发出了第二级过载警告。

"昆提良！你怎么样？"阿方索的声音。

昆提良没回答。他解开安全带，双手撑着驾驶舱的边缘，把自己从座椅上撑起来。肋骨在动的时候像是被人拿锤子敲了一下，他没忍住，吐出一口血，溅在操作面板上。他用袖子擦了擦嘴，从破碎的驾驶舱舱门爬了出去。

奥古斯都的外部应急开关在左肩甲的侧面，他摸索着按了下去。肩甲弹开一条缝，露出了内部的骨架结构。外面是维苏威火山采石场的灰暗天光和飘浮的粉尘，空气中弥漫着红水银蒸汽特有的金属腥味。

他蹲在肩甲的缝隙边，往下吐了一口带血的唾沫，然后用袖子擦了擦嘴。

通讯频道里阿方索的声音第三次响起，这一次带了一点罕见的焦急。

"你出来干什么？回去！"

"手臂没压了，盾举不起来，得手动复位。"昆提良一边说一边钻回驾驶舱，"给我十秒。"

他在驾驶舱里摸索着找到了左臂液压系统的紧急复位阀。那是一个铜色的旋钮，藏在座椅左侧的检修面板后面。他用蛮力把面板撕开，旋了两圈，液压系统发出嘶嘶的泄压声，然后重新建立压力。指针缓缓爬回了安全区。

他又爬出去一次，从腰部的外挂武器架上取下了备用战斧。那是一柄沉重的单手战斧，斧刃上涂着暗红色的防锈漆，斧柄缠着粗麻绳——不是精密武器，是战场上拿来拼命的家伙。

他拎着战斧站在奥古斯都残破的肩甲上，低头看着八十米外的零号。零号也看着他，龙吼炮的炮口没有抬起来，面甲内部的金色微光沉默地亮着。

"来吧。"昆提良说。

然后他拎着战斧重新钻回驾驶舱，坐下来，系好安全带，把奥古斯都重新推了起来。

秘银重盾抬起来的时候，盾面上已经出现了第二条裂纹，从闭眼狮头的左眼斜切到右下角。闭眼狮头被裂缝切成了两半，一只狮眼已经被裂纹穿过。昆提良看了一眼那条裂纹，用力吐掉了嘴里的最后一点血腥味。

"还举得动。"他说。

观测厅里，数百人沉默了。

一分钟前还在窃窃私语的那些声音——"西泽尔的旧部不过是一群特洛伊酒店出身的侍者和鞋匠"、"那个扛盾的连骑士衔都没有"、"密涅瓦拿什么跟原罪机关打"——此刻全都消失了。VIP包厢里，拜占庭使团的武官放下了手中的记录本，叶尼塞使团的一名老将军缓缓点了一下头，中山国使团的座位上，叶素理正低头在笔记本上飞快地画着什么——那是奥古斯都秘银重盾的多层锻造结构剖面图，影金属、硬金、冰原寒玉夹层，每一层的厚度和位置他都标注得清清楚楚。

"奥古斯都坚持住了！"解说员的声音响彻观测厅，"昆提良骑士在承受两发龙吼炮后仍然站立！他正在重新举盾——盾面已经出现裂纹，但他还在继续牵制零号！这是何等的——"

解说员停顿了一下，像是在寻找合适的词。

"——这是何等的骑士精神。"

而在采石场的另一端，红龙和一号之间的八十米距离里，空气忽然变得沉重了。

西泽尔能感觉到自己的后颈在发烫。黄金套管的接口处传来一阵微弱的灼热感，不是疼痛，更像是某种共鸣——和他在不朽之王模式激活前感受到的那种共鸣相似，但微弱得多，像远处传来的回声。

他盯着前方八十米外的一号。一号也没有动。它站在碎石地面上，六米多高的巨型甲胄像一座沉默的铁塔，肩炮的炮口自然下垂，面甲后面透出的金色微光和零号一样，一闪一灭。

西泽尔紫瞳的瞳孔微微收缩了一下。

不是因为恐惧。是因为他在一号的面甲后面看到了什么东西。

那双眼睛。透过面甲的缝隙，一号的骑士在看着他。西泽尔看不清那个人的脸，但他能感觉到那双眼睛——冰冷的、计算性质的、像是在翻阅一本已经读完的书。对方的目光穿透八十米的距离，精准地落在他身上，像一根针。

然后那种感觉来了。

不是疼痛，不是眩晕，而是一种更深层的触动——像是有什么东西在他的意识深处翻了个身。红水银的共鸣信号在他后颈的黄金套管里嗡嗡作响，那声音太微弱了，微弱到几乎可以忽略，但它确实存在。

"锡兰的孩子们啊……"

西泽尔的手指无声地收紧了操纵杆。

那个声音不是他听到的，而是直接出现在他的意识里的，像从红水银的深处浮上来的一缕残响。模糊的、遥远的，像一个人在很深的井底说话。他听不清那句话的完整内容，只捕捉到了几个字的碎片。

……世界树……

然后那缕残响就消失了。后颈的灼热感退去，黄金套管恢复了正常的温度。视野重新变得清晰，一号仍然站在八十米外，纹丝不动。

西泽尔深吸了一口气。

"西泽尔？"通讯频道里，瓦莲京娜的声音忽然响起。她是替补，一直待在矿道入口外的备用机库里，通过通讯系统监听着战场。她的声音里带着一丝警觉——她听到了他呼吸节奏的变化。

"没事。"西泽尔说。

他的声音平静得和平时一样。但握操纵杆的右手手背上，有一条极细的淡紫色脉络亮了一瞬，然后熄灭了。没有被任何人看到。

阿方索的声音在通讯频道里响起来，冷硬如常。

"蜘蛛放完了。"

六只微型机械蜘蛛从所罗门王的腕表中释放出来，贴着地面向零号和古洛诺斯的方向高速爬行。它们的体型只有指甲盖大小，腹部的红水银微晶在黑暗中发出极微弱的红色光芒。六只蜘蛛分成两组——三只朝零号，三只朝古洛诺斯。

零号没有任何反应。它似乎没有注意到这些微型的机械造物，又或者它注意到了但并不在意。

与此同时，通风井深处，蔷薇之鬼正在黑暗中安静地工作着。唐璜把四枚微型炸弹一枚一枚地安装在通风井的关键承重结构上——井壁的支撑柱、通风管道的连接点、铁栅格的焊接处。每一枚炸弹都不大，只有拇指粗细，但里面装填的炸药足够炸断一根小腿粗的硬金支撑柱。

安装最后一枚的时候，他的手在通风井冰冷的铁壁上停了一瞬。外面就是零号。隔着铁栅格，他能感觉到龙吼炮炮口散发的热量信号，炙热、稳定、像一头正在呼吸的猛兽。

他把最后一枚炸弹拧紧，缩回了手。

"装好了。"他在通讯频道里说。

"别引爆。"西泽尔说。

"我知道。"

采石场里，时间仿佛凝固了。

零号站在通风口外，肩炮对着奥古斯都。奥古斯都举着裂开的秘银重盾，盾面上的闭眼狮头被裂纹切成了两半。昆提良坐在驾驶舱里，嘴角带着血，握着操纵杆，等着零号的第三次射击。

红龙站在峡谷中央，盯着前方的一号。一号一动不动，面甲后的金色微光沉默地闪烁着。

所罗门王站在采石场边缘的高地上，蜘蛛巢腕表上的六只微型蜘蛛正在接近各自的目标。蔷薇之鬼蹲在通风井深处，四枚微型炸弹安静地嵌在承重结构上。

所有的棋子都已经就位。

观测厅里，解说员的声音低沉而紧绷。

"双方陷入了对峙——密涅瓦方的奥古斯都仍在牵制零号，但盾面已经出现严重裂纹。第三次龙吼炮如果再命中同一个位置——"

他没有说完那句话。

因为一号动了。

那台六米多高的巨型甲胄像一头苏醒的猛兽，肩炮的炮口猛然抬起，青蓝色的光芒在炮口凝聚——但它没有开火。它的双足猛地踏碎了脚下的碎石地面，整台甲胄以与其体型完全不成比例的速度朝红龙的方向冲了过来。

不是肩炮。是冲锋。

"一号——一号直接朝红龙冲过去了！"解说员的声音在观测厅里炸响，"它放弃了肩炮射击！它要用近身战！一号要和红龙——"

西泽尔的手握紧了操纵杆。

红龙胸甲上的圣剑碎片忽然亮了。

【English】
Chapter 173 — The Shield Falls Twice

Twenty metres from the vent, Zero stood with the muzzle of its shoulder-cannon tipped a few degrees down. Behind the faceplate, a thin gold light pulsed — on, off, on, off — like a patient instrument at its calculations.

The quarry was quiet enough to hear pebbles sliding from the rock wall.

"It has stopped," Alfonso said on the channel, low.

"Waiting," Cesare said.

Red Dragon stood in the middle of the gorge outside the mine's mouth. The Dragoon configuration's super-heavy loadout had bulged the frame out a full ring larger than any standard Seraph, and the Holy Sword fragment set into its breastplate cast a faint, feverish gleam into the dark. It had not moved. The dragon-slayer greatblade across its back had not been drawn. It simply stood there.

And Number One stood eighty metres in front of it.

The two armours faced each other across the full width of the quarry. Zero at the vent. Number One at the mine mouth. The three Original Sin frames had neatly cut Minerva's five prototypes into three disconnected islands.

Don Juan crouched in the dark of the ventilation shaft. The Ghost of the Rose's passive sensors caught the faint thermal wash bleeding off Zero's Dragon Roar cannon. He could feel the thing had not left. The falx in his hand, joint-spring released, ready to flick the blade out in a single motion.

"Give me thirty seconds," he murmured.

No one answered him on the channel. Everyone was waiting.

Then Alfonso said two words: "It's moving."

Zero moved.

It turned. The Dragon Roar's muzzle swung away from the vent. Hydraulic actuators in its shoulder gave a muffled hiss, the barrel rising — not toward the shaft, but toward Augustus.

"It's going to fire!" the announcer's voice pitched sharp. "Zero's Dragon Roar is aimed directly at Augustus!"

Quintilian set his teeth. Augustus's foot came down hard on the gravel. He did not step back.

"Don't be a hero," Alfonso's voice cracked through the channel.

"If it fires, Don Juan is right behind me," Quintilian said.

He did not wait for an answer. Augustus was already moving. Five tons of heavy frame ground the rubble underfoot as it went straight at Zero, head-on. The mithril greatshield came off the back, both arms level, the closed-eyed lion of the heraldry square to the cannon's mouth.

Zero fired.

The shoulder-cannon had none of the customary bark of an artillery piece. What came out of it was something deeper, a snarl that seemed to rise from beneath the floor of the world. A thin-shell round trailed a line of cold blue flame across the quarry and struck the mithril shield dead centre.

The impact bloomed a white shock-ring across the face of the shield. Augustus's feet carved two deep furrows in the gravel. The whole frame was shoved back fifteen metres, rammed finally into a heap of fallen scree before it stopped. The struck point of the shield caved inward. The lion's left ear blew apart in the shock, fragments hissing away into the dust.

In the cockpit, Quintilian's back slammed into the seat. The harness bit into his shoulders. A blunt pain rolled along his ribs. Red warning lamps came on. Three panels at once threw up alarms — left arm hydraulics in pressure collapse, spinal buffer overload, shield integrity at eighty-seven percent.

"Quintilian! Report!" Alfonso, and for once, quickened.

Quintilian spat the blood from his mouth. He had bitten his tongue on the impact, and his mouth tasted of rust. He looked at the readouts. Smiled.

"Still in the fight."

He hauled Augustus up out of the scree. The inward dent in the mithril shield was plain to see, the lion's left ear gone, but the structure held. Zero had not pursued. It still stood outside the vent, muzzle tipped down, as if recalculating.

In the observation gallery, several hundred delegates from every nation drew a single breath.

"Augustus is still standing!" the announcer's voice shook with disbelief. "Knight Quintilian has taken a direct Dragon Roar hit on the mithril greatshield! Only local deformation — the frame is intact! He can still fight!"

In Minerva's VIP box, Verolan's fingers had whitened around her teacup. She stared at the slow-motion replay of Augustus rising. The knuckles of her hand had gone the colour of bone.

Professor Franco sat in his wheelchair beside her. The old man had been in poor shape that morning. Verolan had heard him cough twice. The second time he had covered his mouth with a handkerchief, and when he had folded it away, she had seen the dark red on the cloth. She had said nothing.

Now the screen was replaying the moment of impact in slow motion. The high-speed camera had caught the layered forging of the mithril shield in sharp detail — Minerva's newest multi-layer technique, each layer of hard-gold with a different grain orientation, set to scatter the shock energy.

Franco's eyes lit.

"Five layers, cross-forged," he murmured. "Outer two are shadow-metal, middle three are hard-gold, and the last one — " He squinted. "Cold-ice jade interleave."

Verolan blinked.

"Cold-ice jade? A Yenisei technique?"

"No. Not Yenisei. They embed the jade in the spine armour's inner layer to buffer neural backlash. This is the opposite — the jade has been forged into the shield's interleave. It uses the jade's low temperature to make the metal surface micro-contract at the moment of impact. A second buffer layer." Franco's eyes had taken on that particular gleam of a technician. "This is… Quintilian's own modification? Or Alfonso's hand?"

Verolan shook her head. She wasn't sure. But she knew a modification like that did not appear out of thin air. It must have been some undocumented change in Augustus's construction.

"Quintilian, surely, is just a brash man with a shield?" Franco said suddenly.

"He was one of Cesare's earliest choices from the old guard," Verolan said.

"Choice to carry a shield?"

"Because the shield will not break in his hands."

Franco was quiet a moment. Then he coughed. He covered his mouth with the handkerchief. A small dark red spread on the white cloth. Verolan reached for a napkin, but he waved her off, folded the cloth, and tucked it into his pocket.

"I'm fine," the old man said. "Watch the match."

In the quarry, Zero raised the muzzle of the Dragon Roar again.

This time the target was not the face of Augustus's shield — the muzzle shifted five degrees, fixed on the left shoulder joint.

"It's aiming at the joint!" the announcer cried. "Zero has adjusted! It is targeting Augustus's shoulder — if the left arm is disabled, the mithril shield cannot be raised!"

Alfonso's voice on the channel was cold as a blade.

"Quintilian. Three steps left."

"Understood."

Augustus slid three paces to the left, presenting the edge of the shield to the new firing angle. The earlier dent in the shield face was now exactly covering the densest part of the cannon's strike zone.

Zero fired.

The second Dragon Roar round.

The blue flame streaked across the quarry again, and the thin-shell round struck the same dent in the mithril shield that the first round had made. The shock was heavier than the first. The whole shield-face shuddered, and a hair-thin crack appeared at the bottom of the dent.

Augustus was thrown back again. This time the frame could not stay upright. The whole machine rolled off the scree and went over, half a turn on the ground, and came to rest with its back against the wall of an abandoned mine shaft on the east side of the quarry. The impact shattered a great slab of rock from the wall, and rubble cascaded down, several pieces striking Augustus's shoulder-plate with a heavy, hollow sound.

"Augustus — is down!" the announcer's voice pitched with alarm.

Inside the cockpit, the harness had pulled Quintilian half out of his breath. The second impact had cost him another layer of rib, and a thin thread of blood ran from the corner of his mouth down his chin into his collar. He glanced at the board — left-arm hydraulics at zero pressure, shield integrity at sixty-one percent, the spinal buffer now showing a second-level overload warning.

"Quintilian! Status?" Alfonso.

Quintilian did not answer. He unfastened the harness, braced his hands against the edge of the cockpit, and pushed himself up out of the seat. A rib felt like a hammer blow when he moved; he could not hold it, spat a mouthful of blood onto the console. Wiped his mouth with his sleeve. Pulled himself out through the broken cockpit hatch.

The emergency release for Augustus's exterior systems was on the side of the left shoulder-plate. He fumbled for it, found it, pressed it. The shoulder-plate cracked open a sliver, exposing the inner skeleton. Outside was the grey Vesuvius quarry light, the floating dust, the metallic tang of red-mercury vapour in the air.

He crouched in the gap of the shoulder-plate, spat out one more mouthful of blood-flecked saliva, wiped his mouth with his sleeve.

Alfonso's voice came a third time on the channel, this time with a rare edge of urgency.

"What are you doing out there? Get back in!"

"Arm's lost pressure. Can't lift the shield. Have to do a manual reset." Quintilian climbed back into the cockpit as he spoke. "Give me ten seconds."

He groped his way to the emergency reset valve for the left-arm hydraulics. A copper knob, hidden behind the maintenance panel on the left of the seat. He tore the panel off with brute force, turned the knob twice. The hydraulic system gave a long, slow hiss of venting pressure, then rebuilt. The needle climbed back into the safe band.

He climbed out once more, took a spare battle-axe from the waist rack. A heavy one-handed axe, blade coated in dark red anti-rust, the haft wrapped in rough hemp cord — not a precision weapon, something to fight with when all the careful options were gone.

He stood on the broken shoulder-plate of Augustus, axe in hand, looking down at Zero eighty metres away. Zero looked back at him, the Dragon Roar's muzzle still tipped down, the gold light behind the faceplate burning quiet.

"Come on, then," Quintilian said.

Then he took the axe, climbed back into the cockpit, sat down, fastened the harness, and stood Augustus up.

The mithril greatshield came up. A second crack had appeared on its face now, slicing from the closed-eyed lion's left eye down to the lower right corner. The closed-eyed lion was cut in two, one eye already crossed by the crack. Quintilian looked at the crack, spat the last of the iron taste out of his mouth.

"Still lifts," he said.

The gallery went silent.

A minute ago the murmuring voices — "Cesare's old guard is just a pack of barbers and boot-boys from the Hotel Troy," "That shield-carrier doesn't even hold a knighthood," "What does Minerva have to fight the Original Sin Bureau with?" — were all gone. In the VIP box, the Byzantine delegation's military attaché set down his notebook. A Yenisei veteran of some forgotten border war gave a single slow nod. And in the seats of the Zhongshan delegation, a young officer — Ye Suli — sat bent over a notebook, sketching rapidly. He was drawing the cross-section of Augustus's mithril greatshield, the shadow-metal, the hard-gold, the cold-ice jade interleave, with each layer's thickness and position marked in clear detail.

"Augustus is holding!" the announcer's voice rang out across the gallery. "Knight Quintilian has taken two Dragon Roar hits and is still standing! He is raising the shield again — there are visible cracks in the face, but he is still drawing Zero's fire! This is — "

The announcer paused, as if searching for the right word.

" — this is the very spirit of knighthood."

And at the other end of the quarry, in the eighty metres between Red Dragon and Number One, the air suddenly grew heavy.

Cesare could feel the heat at the back of his neck. The gold cuff at the joint of the spinal interface gave off a faint burning — not pain, but something close to resonance, the way a tuning fork feels when the same note is struck somewhere far off. The same feeling as before Immortal King mode engaged, but fainter. A distant echo.

He stared at Number One, eighty metres away. Number One had not moved. The frame stood on the gravel, more than six metres tall, a silent iron tower. The shoulder-cannon's muzzle hung at rest. The pale gold light behind the faceplate pulsed the same way Zero's did — on, off, on, off.

Cesare's violet pupils narrowed.

It was not fear. It was what he had seen, behind Number One's faceplate, through the slit of the visor.

Those eyes. He could not see the pilot's face, but he could feel those eyes — cold, calculating, like someone turning the last page of a book already read. The gaze came across eighty metres of air and found him like a needle.

Then the feeling came.

Not pain. Not vertigo. Something deeper — as if something inside his consciousness had turned over in its sleep. The red-mercury's resonance signal hummed in the gold cuff at the back of his neck. The sound was faint, almost negligible, but it was there.

"Children of Ceylon…"

Cesare's fingers tightened on the joystick, soundless.

The words were not something he had heard. They had risen up directly into his mind, like some leftover echo surfacing out of the deeps of the red-mercury. Distant, faint, like someone speaking from the bottom of a deep well. He could not catch the full shape of the sentence. He caught only a few broken syllables.

…World Tree…

Then the echo was gone. The burn at the back of his neck faded. The gold cuff returned to its normal temperature. The vision cleared. Number One still stood at eighty metres, motionless.

Cesare drew a long breath.

"Cesare?" Valentina's voice came on the channel. She was a reserve pilot, waiting at the auxiliary hangar outside the mine's entrance, listening to the battle through comm. There was a sharp alertness in her voice — she had heard the change in his breathing.

"I'm fine," Cesare said.

His voice was as even as ever. But on the back of his right hand, a thin thread of pale violet lit up for a moment, and went out. No one saw it.

Alfonso's voice on the channel, cold as usual.

"Spiders are out."

Six tiny mechanical spiders had been released from Solomon's wristwatch, scuttling along the ground toward Zero and Goronos at high speed. The size of a thumbnail. Pale red glints of red-mercury crystallite in their bellies, in the dark. Three toward Zero, three toward Goronos.

Zero gave no reaction. Whether it had not noticed the small machines, or had noticed and did not care, was unclear.

Meanwhile, deep in the ventilation shaft, the Ghost of the Rose was at work in the dark. Don Juan set four micro-bombs one by one into the shaft's key load-bearing structures — the support pillars of the shaft wall, the joints of the ventilation pipe, the welds of the iron grate. Each bomb was small — no thicker than a thumb — but the charge inside each was enough to snap a hard-gold strut the thickness of a calf.

Setting the last one, his hand paused a moment on the cold iron wall of the shaft. Right outside, Zero. Through the grate, he could feel the heat washing off the Dragon Roar's muzzle. Hot. Steady. Like the breath of some sleeping beast.

He tightened the last bomb. Drew his hand back.

"Set," he said on the channel.

"Don't detonate," Cesare said.

"I know."

In the quarry, time seemed to freeze.

Zero stood outside the vent, the shoulder-cannon aimed at Augustus. Augustus held up the cracked mithril greatshield, the closed-eyed lion on its face sliced in two. Quintilian sat in the cockpit, blood at the corner of his mouth, hands on the sticks, waiting for Zero's third shot.

Red Dragon stood in the middle of the gorge, watching Number One. Number One had not moved. The pale gold light behind the faceplate pulsed in silence.

Solomon stood on the high ground at the edge of the quarry, the six mechanical spiders of the Spider Nest approaching their targets. The Ghost of the Rose crouched deep in the ventilation shaft, four micro-bombs quietly set in the load-bearing.

Every piece was in place.

In the gallery, the announcer's voice was low, tight.

"The two sides have settled into a standoff — Minerva's Augustus is still drawing Zero's fire, but the shield-face is severely cracked. If a third Dragon Roar round strikes the same point — "

He did not finish the sentence.

Because Number One moved.

The giant frame, more than six metres tall, moved like something waking from a long sleep. The shoulder-cannon's muzzle snapped up. Pale blue light gathered at the muzzle — but it did not fire. The feet came down hard on the gravel and shattered it. The whole frame went charging at Red Dragon, at a speed that should not have been possible for its size.

Not the cannon. A charge.

"Number One — Number One is charging Red Dragon directly!" The announcer's voice exploded across the gallery. "It has abandoned cannon fire! It is going to engage in close combat! Number One and Red Dragon are about to — "

Cesare's hand tightened on the joystick.

On the breastplate of Red Dragon, the Holy Sword fragment flared to light.
