【中文】
第174章 蛛网上的电子风暴

一号朝红龙冲过来的瞬间，阿方索已经看清了。

不是它的速度——虽然那速度确实不可思议，六米高的巨型甲胄却跑出了轻骑的步频——而是它的肩关节。每一步踏下时，肩甲和胸甲之间有零点三秒的信号延迟，电流先到左侧、再传导到右侧，微不可察，但蛛巢腕表上的感应器亮了一下。

"塔拉夏教过我的。"阿方索低声说。

那是三个月前在鹰巢深处，塔拉夏指着第三代普罗米修斯试制机的假人模型给他看的一句话："再强的甲胄，关节处的信号传导都不可能完全同步，问题是延迟在哪一侧、多长时间。找到了，就是电子蛛爬进去的门。"

腕表上的六只微型机械蜘蛛已经接近了各自的目标。但阿方索没有让它们全部扑向古洛诺斯。他临时改了指令。

两只继续爬向古洛诺斯，四只转向一号。

通讯频道里，西泽尔什么都没说。但红龙微微侧身，闪开了一号的第一次冲撞。

一号的速度太快了。

它从红龙身侧擦过的风压让红龙甲胄表面的风金属装甲板发出尖锐的颤鸣，六米高的钢铁巨兽带着低沉的蒸汽轰鸣转向，青蓝色的光芒在肩炮炮口凝聚。它抬炮的动作流畅得不像巨型甲胄，倒像一头训练有素的猎豹在抬起前爪。

但它没有开火。

"近身战。"阿方索咬着牙说，"它想近身。"

一号将肩炮甩到背后，双手从腰部抽出了那柄反曲锯齿巨刃。刃长六米，灰黑色的锯齿在采石场的灯光下泛着冷光。

西泽尔拔剑。

龙牙剑从红龙腰侧的挂架弹出，入手的震动沿着神经接驳系统传入他的脊椎。他能感觉到剑的温度，金属的寒意，和自己后颈黄金套管微微发烫的热度。

"唐璜，堵住它退路。"西泽尔说。

通讯频道里传来一声极轻的"好"。

一号没有退路。它也没有打算退。

它挥刃。

那柄六米长的反曲巨刃划破空气时发出的声音不像金属碰撞，倒像一匹丝绸被猛地撕开。刃锋朝红龙的头部斜劈下来，带着巨型甲胄全部的重量和动能。

西泽尔侧闪。

红龙的身形比一号小了整整两号，但它的灵活性远非巨型甲胄可比。龙牙剑在闪避的同时向上格挡，剑脊擦过巨刃的侧面，金属摩擦迸出一串暗红色的火星。

那一剑的重量压得红龙的双足陷入碎石地面足足三厘米。

"好重。"西泽尔面无表情。

一号不给红龙喘息之机，巨刃回收，紧接着第二击横斩，从右向左，目标是红龙腰部最薄弱的关节连接处。反曲锯齿在这种角度下会像锯木头一样切进风金属装甲板。

红龙后退三步。碎石在它脚下炸开。

就在这时，四只电子蛛爬上了一号的右腿膝关节。

它们很小，比拇指甲还小，腹部嵌着米粒大的红水银微晶。阿方索没有急着释放干扰脉冲——他在等。

一号第三击劈下。

就在巨刃距离红龙头顶不到一米的时候，阿方索释放了干扰。

四只电子蛛同时炸开宽频电磁脉冲，密集的信号噪声像一盆冰水泼进了一号的电子系统。蛛网从右腿膝关节沿着液压管线的缝隙向上蔓延，干扰信号穿透管线连接处，直达电子元件的核心。

一号的巨刃停在了半空。

龙牙剑
连射铳的枪管卡死了，发出"咔咔"的空转声。肩炮的炮口青蓝色光芒忽然涣散，变成了微弱的闪烁。右腿膝关节的液压平衡管痉挛了一下，整台甲胄向右倾斜了五度。

"成了！"阿方索在通讯频道里低吼。

观测厅里，解说员的声音都变了调："一号的武器系统出现异常——龙吼炮没有击发！连射铳卡壳！它——它的巨刃举不起来了！"

各国使团的看台上响起一片惊呼。

西泽尔没有犹豫。

红龙踏前一步，龙牙剑前指，剑尖直指一号胸甲正中偏左的位置——骑士舱所在。

"胡安！"古洛诺斯的驾驶舱里，通讯频道里传来一声低吼。不是胡安的声音，是操控古洛诺斯的技术员。

胡安没空回话。

古洛诺斯的左腿膝关节液压平衡管被蔷薇之鬼切断了，整台六米高的巨型甲胄正在以每秒钟零点五度的速度向左倾倒。备用管线——他提前让人在左腿内部加装的第二条液压管线——终于被激活，古洛诺斯猛地顿住，像一棵被风吹弯的树又硬生生地直了回来。

"稳住。"胡安对自己说。

他操控着古洛诺斯转向红龙的方向。平衡系统在备用管线的支撑下恢复了七成功力，古洛诺斯的步态不再像先前那样稳健，但足以行动。

"一号！"他通过战频呼叫，"撑住！我来——"

他的声音被一声尖锐的金属嘶鸣淹没了。

一号关节处忽然亮起了光。

不是青蓝色的蒸汽光芒，也不是红水银的暗红色脉冲，而是一种纯粹的金色——像液态的太阳从甲胄内部溢出来，从一号右腿膝关节的缝隙里、从肘关节的铆钉间、从肩甲与胸甲的接缝处，涌出无数条极细极细的金色丝线。

那些丝线比蛛丝还细，却硬得像是红水银铸成的刀刃。

它们朝四只电子蛛缠绕过去。

丝线触到电子蛛的一瞬间，六只微型机械蜘蛛同时烧毁了。不是短路，不是过载，而是从内部被加热到红热状态，腹部的红水银微晶在高温下膨胀、炸裂，碎片从蛛壳里迸射出来，叮叮当当地落在碎石地面上。

"备用蛛巢！"阿方索咬着牙启动了腕表上的第二组微型机械蜘蛛。

六只新的蜘蛛从蛛巢中涌出，比第一批更小、更快，阿方索给它们镀了一层影金属外壳，可以多撑三秒。他把指令改成了自杀式突进——不是释放干扰脉冲，而是直接钻进一号的关节缝隙，引爆体内的红水银微晶。

三只扑向一号右腿膝关节。三只扑向一号左肘关节。

金色的丝线再次涌出。

这一次比上一次更多、更快，像是从甲胄内部长出来的金色藤蔓，迎着电子蛛的方向伸展。六只蜘蛛在半空中被逐一缠住、加热、烧毁，空气中弥漫着一股烧焦的金属和红水银蒸发的刺鼻气味。

观测厅里死寂了一秒钟。

然后各国使团的看台上爆发出比刚才更响的惊呼声。

"那是什么！"解说员的声音在颤，"一号关节处出现了——出现了某种金色的丝状物！我们的电子侦察设备无法识别！这是——这是什么物质！"

密涅瓦机关中央圣所的观战室里，佛朗哥教授猛地站了起来。

他的脸色在一秒之内变得像纸一样白。不是苍白，是那种大病初愈又遭重击的、血色全无的灰白。

"欧米茄的碎片。"他的声音很轻，像是在自言自语，又像是在对身旁的薇若兰说，"他们居然给骑士植入了欧米茄的碎片。"

薇若兰转过头看他。

佛朗哥教授的嘴唇在发抖。他的手按在控制台上，指节因为用力而泛白。咳嗽的冲动被他硬生生地压了下去，但喉头还是动了一下。

"欧米茄原型体的残片。"佛朗哥说，"第三代普罗米修斯和欧米茄原型体共享一条技术线……他们把欧米茄的自愈纤维植入了骑士的神经接驳系统。"

薇若兰的瞳孔在暗处微微收缩。

"自愈纤维。"

"那些金色的丝线不是武器。"佛朗哥的声音越来越低，"是神经。是欧米茄原型体在四十年封存中自行生长的、替代神经的人工纤维。他们把这种纤维接入了试制机骑士的脊髓。"

"所以一号才能做出那些不可能的动作。"薇若兰说。

"对。它的反应速度已经超越了蒸汽传动的极限。那些金色丝线在直接读取骑士的脊髓信号，跳过了机械传导的全部延迟。"佛朗哥剧烈地咳嗽了一声，嘴角有淡淡的铁锈味，"代价是——"

他没有说下去。

因为一号的关节处，金色的丝线忽然暴长。

那些细如蛛丝的金色纤维从甲胄的每一条缝隙里涌出，不再是缓慢的蔓延，而是狂暴的爆发，像金色的洪水从一座即将崩溃的大坝里倾泻而出。它们覆盖了一号的右臂、左腿、胸甲、头盔，把六米高的巨型甲胄裹成了一个金色的茧。

然后那些丝线开始收缩。

朝着甲胄内部收缩。

像是有什么东西在从外部被拉回去，又像是甲胄内部有什么东西在主动吞噬那些丝线。金色的光一寸一寸地黯淡，一号的轮廓重新显现出来——肩炮炮口的青蓝色光芒重新凝聚，连射铳的枪管恢复了正常转速。

"武器系统恢复正常！"解说员的声音带着一种难以置信的颤抖，"它——它自己修好了！"

佛朗哥的手在控制台上猛地一按。

"薇若兰。"

"我在。"

"联系瓦莲京娜。"佛朗哥说，"让她准备替补。情况不对。"

薇若兰没有问为什么。她伸手拉过通讯器，手指在频道旋钮上快速转动。叶尼塞的专用加密频段在耳机里发出细微的电流声。

"罗曼诺夫公主殿下。"

通讯器里传来风声和金属碰撞的声音——瓦莲京娜正站在矿道入口的替补甲胄旁。

"讲。"

"情况有变。"薇若兰的声音很稳，但语速比平时快了一倍，"一号试制机的骑士被植入了欧米茄原型体的自愈神经纤维。常规电子战已经失效。请你做好随时替补出战的准备。"

通讯器里沉默了两秒。

"替补出战需要密涅瓦总长授权。"瓦莲京娜说。

"授权我来拿。"薇若兰说，"你只需要确保剑舞者甲胄随时可以启动。"

"收到。"

薇若兰切断了通讯，转向佛朗哥。

佛朗哥已经重新坐回了控制台前。他的手指在键盘上飞速跳动，调出一号的实时数据流。屏幕上的数据在跳——一号的神经信号强度比五分钟前提升了三倍，而且还在攀升。

"它在失控的边缘。"佛朗哥说，"那些自愈纤维在无限制地增强骑士的神经信号。如果超出阈值——"

"会怎样？"

佛朗哥没有回答。

他不需要回答。薇若兰见过炽天使神经接驳系统过载的后果——圣痕之血从耳道和鼻腔里涌出来，骑士的身体被自己的神经系统烧成空壳。

采石场里，阿方索的脸色铁青。

备用蛛巢的六只蜘蛛全部报废了。腕表上的电子蛛巢指示灯一盏一盏地熄灭，从绿色变成暗红，最后彻底暗了下去。他低头看了一眼自己的机械臂——手指在微微颤抖，不是恐惧，是愤怒。

"阿方索？"西泽尔的声音从通讯频道里传来。

"蛛网被烧光了。"阿方索说，"我的电子战对一号已经无效。那东西——"他顿了一下，"那东西里面有欧米茄的碎片。"

通讯频道里沉默了一秒。

"我知道了。"西泽尔说。

红龙正面对着一号。

龙牙剑还指着一号胸甲的方向，但剑尖在距离目标不到半米的地方被一号的左臂格开了。一号的反应速度——在金色丝线暴长又收缩之后——又提升了一个层级。它格挡的动作不再像是巨型甲胄在挥动手臂，倒像是一个训练有素的剑手在用刀背磕开对手的刺剑。

古洛诺斯在后方已经稳住了身形，备用管线撑住了它的平衡。胡安操控着古洛诺斯举起了右臂上的焚城炮——炮口对准了红龙的后背。

两面包夹。

西泽尔在零点二秒之内做出了判断。

"唐璜！古洛诺斯！别让它开炮！"

通讯频道里传来一声极快的回应——蔷薇之鬼从通风井中弹射而出，超轻型甲胄的脚底喷出青蓝色蒸汽，整台机体像一把匕首直插古洛诺斯的右侧腰际。

但古洛诺斯已经开炮了。

焚城炮的炮口喷出一团暗红色的火光，炮弹划出弧线，朝红龙的后背落下。薄壳弹的威力不足以击穿红龙超重武装的龙骑兵套装，但冲击力足以让红龙失去平衡。

西泽尔侧身。

炮弹在红龙右侧三米处炸开，碎石和金属碎片打在龙骑兵套装的外挂装甲上，发出密集的叮当声。红龙被气浪推得向左踉跄了两步。

就在这一刻，一号动了。

它不是冲过来。它是在原地消失——不，是它的速度太快，快到红龙的光学传感器在一瞬间丢失了目标。六米高的巨型甲胄带着残影出现在红龙面前不到两米的位置，反曲锯齿巨刃高高举起。

金色的丝线从一号的关节处最后一次涌出，这一次不是防御，不是蔓延，而是集中在巨刃的刃锋上。灰黑色的锯齿被金色的光芒覆盖，巨刃的重量和锋利程度都翻了一倍。

"西泽尔——！"阿方索在通讯频道里喊。

西泽尔举剑格挡。

龙牙剑的脊背迎上了一号巨刃的刃锋。

金属碰撞的声音在采石场里炸开，像一口巨钟被重锤敲响。龙牙剑是密涅瓦机关用究极金属锻造的顶级武装，但一号的巨刃在金色丝线的加持下已经超越了常规材料的极限。龙牙剑的剑脊上出现了一道肉眼可见的裂纹。

西泽尔的双手死死地握着操纵杆。

红龙的双足在碎石地面上被巨刃的压力推出了两道深沟。背上的外挂装甲板发出不堪重负的金属呻吟。黄金套管在后颈灼烧，右手手背上淡紫色的脉络猛地亮了起来。

他挡不住。

"——后退！"西泽尔低吼了一声。

红龙在最后一刻放弃了格挡，向右侧滚翻。巨刃从它的左肩甲上擦过，龙骑兵套装的外挂装甲板被削掉了一整块，露出了下面暗红色的内层结构。

一号没有给红龙喘息的机会。

巨刃回收，再次劈下。这一次是从左上方到右下方的斜劈，目标是红龙暴露在外的左肩关节。

金色丝线在刃锋上疯狂地闪烁。

西泽尔来不及举剑。

他没有看那柄正在落下的巨刃。他的目光穿过一号的面甲——那两片透出深紫色光的观察镜——直直地盯着面甲后面的骑士。

后颈的黄金套管烫得像要烧穿皮肤。意识深处，红水银的残响在翻涌。

巨刃落下。

西泽尔举起了右臂。

不是格挡。是用龙牙剑的剑柄——连同他自己的手臂——挡在了刃锋的轨迹上。龙牙剑已经缺了口，但他把残破的剑身横在了左肩关节前方，用整条右臂的力量死死撑住。

金属碰撞的尖啸刺穿了采石场里所有的声音。

龙牙剑断了。

断成两截的究极金属残片在碎石地面上弹跳、翻滚，发出清脆的叮当声。上半截飞出了十几米远，插在一堆碎石里，刃口朝上，泛着暗红色的余光。

巨刃的刃锋在距离红龙左肩关节不到十厘米的地方停住了。

不是被挡住了。

是金色丝线在一号的关节处发出了一声尖锐的、类似金属断裂的脆响。那些丝线——那些从欧米茄原型体上长出来的、连接着试制机骑士脊髓的自愈神经纤维——忽然从内部断裂了。

金色的光从一号的全身每一处缝隙里同时涌出，像是被打碎的灯笼里流出的灯油。不是暴长，不是蔓延，而是失控的、无序的、像鲜血一样从伤口里涌出。

一号的巨刃停在了半空。

它的面甲后面，那两片深紫色的观察镜忽然熄灭了。

然后重新亮起。

然后又熄灭。

佛朗哥教授从控制台前站了起来。他的手按在胸口，嘴角有淡淡的血迹——他刚才把那口带血的咳嗽硬生生地吞了回去。

"神经信号——"他的声音沙哑得像砂纸，"一号的神经信号正在突破阈值。自愈纤维在失控。"

薇若兰的手指已经按在了通讯器上。

"瓦莲京娜。"

"我在。"

"现在。"

通讯器里传来一声利落的回应。金属碰撞声、蒸汽阀门开启声、甲胄关节锁定声，在三秒钟之内依次响起。

采石场里，一号的面甲后面传来了一声极其微弱的、金属扭曲的声响。

金色的丝线在它全身的关节处重新凝聚——但这一次不是暴长，而是收缩。急速地、猛烈地朝着甲胄的核心收缩，像是一个黑洞在吞噬周围的一切光线。

一号的声音系统忽然激活了。

不是通讯频道。是面甲的外部扬声器。金属扭曲的嗓音从扬声器里传出来，像是有两个人在同时说话——一个是训练有素的军人，另一个是某种不属于人类的、更古老的声音。

"——控制——不住——"

然后那柄六米长的反曲锯齿巨刃，以所有人都没有预料到的速度和角度，朝红龙的头顶劈了下来。

【English】
Chapter 174 — The Electronic Storm on the Web

As Number One came at the Red Dragon, Alfonso had already seen it.

Not its speed—though the speed was unbelievable, a six-meter war machine running at the cadence of a light cavalry horse—but its shoulder joints. With every footfall, there was a three-tenths-of-a-second signal lag between the pauldron and the cuirass. The current arrived at the left side first, then crossed to the right. Imperceptible. But the sensor on his Nestwatch had blinked.

"Old Tarashe taught me that," Alfonso murmured.

Three months ago, deep in the Eagle's Nest, the old engineer had stood him before the dummy frame of the third-generation Prometheus prototype and pointed. No matter how strong the armor, no joint ever synchronizes perfectly. The question is which side, and how long. Find that, and the electronic spider has a door.

Six micro-spiders were already crawling toward their targets. But Alfonso had revised the order on the fly.

Two continued toward Guronos. Four turned toward Number One.

The comm said nothing. The Red Dragon shifted a half-step and let Number One's first charge slide past its flank.

Number One was too fast.

The wind pressure of its passing made the aerometal plates on the Red Dragon's hide sing with a high, thin keening. The six-meter iron beast turned, steam snarling low in its chest, and a pale blue light began gathering in the bore of its shoulder cannon. It raised the gun with a fluency no war machine of that size should possess, like a cheetah lifting a paw.

It did not fire.

"Close combat," Alfonso said through his teeth. "It wants to come in close."

Number One flung the cannon behind its back and drew the recurved serrated greatblade from the magnetic rack at its waist. Six meters of grey-black sawtooth. Cold in the quarry's light.

Cesare drew his sword.

Dragon's Fang slid from the Red Dragon's hip mount into his hand, and the vibration ran up the neural interface and into the base of his spine. He could feel the temperature of the metal. The cold of it. The heat of the gold sleeve at the nape of his neck.

"Don Juan. Cut his retreat."

A soft acknowledgment in his ear.

Number One had no retreat. Nor did it want one.

It swung.

The sound the six-meter blade made cutting the air was not the sound of metal, but of silk being torn. The edge came down at the Red Dragon's head, carrying the full weight and momentum of a war machine.

Cesare stepped aside.

The Red Dragon was two full sizes smaller than Number One, but it was faster than any war machine had a right to be. Dragon's Fang came up as it turned, the spine of the sword scraping the flat of the greatblade. Sparks the color of dried blood spat from the contact.

The weight of that one blow drove the Red Dragon's feet three centimeters into the loose stone of the quarry floor.

"Heavy," Cesare said. His face was expressionless.

Number One gave it no breath. The blade came back and cut across, right to left, aimed at the thinnest joint in the Red Dragon's waist. The recurved serrations at that angle would bite into aerometal the way a saw bites into pine.

The Red Dragon stepped back three paces. Stonework exploded under its feet.

And that was the moment the four spiders reached the right knee of Number One.

They were smaller than a thumbnail, each one, a grain of red-mercury micro-crystal set into the belly. Alfonso did not release the jamming pulse. He was waiting.

Number One's third stroke came down.

A meter above the Red Dragon's helmet, Alfonso let go.

The four spiders detonated a broadband electromagnetic pulse in unison. The signal-noise hit Number One's electronics like a basin of iced water thrown into the face. The web spread from the right knee up through the gaps in the hydraulic lines. The interference signal punched through the line couplings and into the heart of the electronic core.

Number One's blade stopped in the air.

The Dragon's Roar cannon's bore flickered, blue light scattering. The chain-gun's barrel seized with a clicking whir. The hydraulic equalizer in the right knee spasmed. The whole machine tilted five degrees to starboard.

"It's working!" Alfonso hissed into the comm.

In the observation gallery, the commentator's voice had gone up half an octave. "Number One's weapons are showing anomalies—the Dragon's Roar has not fired—the chain-gun is jammed—its blade is not coming up—"

A wave of gasps rolled through the ambassadorial stands.

Cesare did not hesitate.

The Red Dragon stepped forward. Dragon's Fang pointed at Number One's chest plate, an inch to the left of center. The knight's cabin.

"Juan!"

Inside Guronos's cockpit, the shout over the comm was not Juan's voice. It was the technician driving Guronos.

Juan had no time to answer.

The hydraulic equalizer in Guronos's left knee had been cut by the Rose Wraith. The six-meter machine was tipping leftward at half a degree per second. The backup line—the second hydraulic line he had ordered threaded through the leg weeks ago—finally cut in. Guronos lurched upright like a tree bent by a wind that had suddenly decided, no, not yet.

"Hold," Juan said to himself.

He brought Guronos around toward the Red Dragon. The balance system, propped up by the backup line, was at maybe seventy percent. The gait was not what it had been. It would do.

"Number One!" he called over the battle-frequency. "Stay up. I'm coming—"

His voice was drowned under a thin shriek of metal.

Number One's joints lit up.

Not the pale blue of steam. Not the dull red pulse of red mercury. Something else. A pure gold, like liquid sun, pouring from inside the war machine. From the seams of the right knee. From the rivets of the elbow joint. From the gap between pauldron and cuirass. A thousand hair-fine threads of gold, welling out.

Thinner than spider-silk. Harder than blades cast of red mercury.

They reached for the four spiders.

The moment the threads touched the spiders, all six of Alfonso's micro-machines burned out. Not a short. Not an overload. Heat, from the inside, the red-mercury micro-crystals swelling and detonating inside their shells. Shrapnel spat across the loose stone with a musical clatter.

"Backup nest," Alfonso said through his teeth, and triggered the second swarm on his Nestwatch.

Six new spiders boiled out of the nest. Smaller than the first. Faster. Alfonso had plated them in a skin of umbrametal. Three more seconds of survival. He changed the order to a suicide run. No jamming pulse this time. Straight into the seams of Number One's joints. Detonate inside.

Three to the right knee. Three to the left elbow.

The gold threads came again.

More of them this time. Faster. Like a golden vine, springing up out of the armor to meet them. The six spiders were caught in midair, one by one. Heated. Burned. The smell of scorched metal and evaporating red mercury thickened the air of the quarry.

A second of silence in the observation gallery.

Then the ambassadorial stands erupted louder than before.

"What—" the commentator was shaking, "what is that—some kind of gold filament—we cannot identify it on our electronic survey—what material is that—"

In the central viewing chamber of the Minerva Order's sanctuary, Professor Franco was on his feet.

The color had gone out of his face in a single second. Not the pallor of illness. The grey-white of a man who has been struck a second blow before the first one has healed.

"Fragments of Omega," he said. Very quietly. Half to himself. Half to Virolan beside him. "They have put Omega fragments into the knight."

Virolan turned to him.

Franco's lips were trembling. His hand was flat on the console, the knuckles bloodless. The urge to cough, which he had forced down, was still working in his throat.

"Remnants of the Omega prototype," Franco said. "The third-generation Prometheus shares a technical lineage with the Omega prototype. They have grown the self-repair fibers of Omega into the knight's neural interface."

Virolan's pupils contracted in the dim light.

"Self-repair fibers."

"The gold threads are not a weapon," Franco said, lower. "They are nerves. Artificial nerve fibers the Omega prototype grew during its forty years of sealed storage, to replace its own. They have threaded these fibers into the prototype knight's spine."

"That is how Number One does what it does."

"Yes. Its reaction speed is past the limit of any steam-driven transmission. The gold threads are reading the knight's spinal signal directly. They have skipped the entire mechanical delay." Franco coughed once, hard, and tasted the faintest iron at the back of his mouth. "The cost is—"

He did not finish.

Because the gold threads at Number One's joints had begun, all at once, to grow.

Out of every seam in the armor, the hair-thin fibers of gold came boiling—not the slow creep of the last few minutes, but a violent outrush, a flood of gold pouring from a dam about to break. They covered Number One's right arm, left leg, cuirass, helmet. The six-meter war machine was being wrapped in a cocoon.

Then the threads began to contract.

Inward. Toward the core of the machine. As if something outside was pulling them back. Or as if something inside was drinking them down. The gold light dimmed by the inch. Number One's outline re-emerged. The pale blue of the shoulder cannon's bore gathered again. The chain-gun's barrel resumed its spin.

"Weapon systems are back online!" the commentator's voice was a kind of disbelieving croak. "It—it has repaired itself!"

Franco slammed his palm on the console.

"Virolan."

"Here."

"Get Valentina on the line. Tell her to stand by. Something is wrong."

Virolan did not ask why. She reached for the comm unit, fingers working the channel dial with quick, practiced turns. The Yenisei's dedicated encrypted band hissed faintly in her earpiece.

"Princess Romanov."

Wind and metal through the comm—the sound of a woman standing beside a backup suit at the mouth of a mine shaft.

"Speak."

"Situation has changed," Virolan said. Her voice was level, but the words came at twice her usual speed. "The pilot of Number One has been implanted with the self-repair nerve fibers of the Omega prototype. Conventional electronic warfare is ineffective. Please prepare for immediate substitution into combat."

Two seconds of silence on the comm.

"Substitution requires authorization from the Magister of Minerva."

"I will get the authorization," Virolan said. "You make certain the Sword Dancer is ready to fire."

"Understood."

Virolan cut the line. Turned to Franco.

Franco had already sat back down at his console. His fingers were moving across the keys, pulling up the live data feed from Number One. The numbers on the screen were dancing. Number One's neural signal strength had tripled in the last five minutes. And it was still climbing.

"It is approaching the edge of the threshold," Franco said. "The self-repair fibers are amplifying the knight's neural signal without limit. If it crosses—"

"What happens?"

Franco did not answer.

He did not need to. Virolan had seen the result of an overloaded Seraph neural interface. Stigmata blood pouring from the ear canals and the nose. The knight's body burned out from the inside by its own nervous system, left a hollow shell standing upright in its cockpit.

In the quarry, Alfonso's face was the color of iron.

The backup nest was spent. The indicator lamps on his Nestwatch were going out, one by one. Green to dark red to nothing. He looked down at his own mechanical hand. The fingers were trembling. Not with fear. With anger.

"Alfonso?" Cesare's voice, in his ear.

"The web is burned out," Alfonso said. "My electronic warfare is useless against Number One. That thing—" he paused. "That thing has fragments of Omega in it."

A second's silence on the comm.

"Understood," Cesare said.

The Red Dragon stood face to face with Number One.

Dragon's Fang was still pointed at Number One's chest, but the tip had been knocked half a meter off-line by Number One's left arm. Number One's reaction speed—after the gold threads had boiled out and drawn back in—had climbed another notch. The parry had not looked like a war machine's arm moving. It had looked like a trained swordsman knocking aside an opponent's foil with the back of his blade.

Guronos had stabilized behind them. The backup line was holding. Juan brought Guronos's right arm up. The muzzle of the Flaming City cannon came to bear on the Red Dragon's back.

Pincer.

Cesare made his call in two-tenths of a second.

"Don Juan! Guronos! Don't let it fire!"

A fast acknowledgment in his ear. The Rose Wraith blew out of the ventilation shaft, the soles of its ultra-light armor jetting pale blue steam, the whole machine a dagger thrust at Guronos's right flank.

But Guronos had already fired.

A ball of dull red fire bloomed at the muzzle of the Flaming City cannon. The shell drew an arc through the air and began to fall toward the Red Dragon's back. A thin-shell round. Not enough to pierce the Dragoon plate of the Red Dragon's over-armor. Enough to knock it off its feet.

Cesare turned.

The shell went off three meters to the Red Dragon's right. Shrapnel and stone chips spattered the outer plates of the Dragoon suit with a rapid patter. The blast wave shoved the Red Dragon two stumbling steps to the left.

In that instant, Number One moved.

It did not charge. It vanished on the spot. No—that was not it. It was too fast. The Red Dragon's optical sensor lost the target for a single frame. The six-meter war machine, with a smear of after-image behind it, was suddenly two meters in front of the Red Dragon. The recurved serrated greatblade was already up.

The gold threads in Number One's joints had come out for the last time. This time they were not defensive. Not creeping. They were gathered along the edge of the blade, packed into the sawteeth. The grey-black steel was under a skin of gold. The weight and the cutting edge of the greatblade had doubled.

"Cesare—" Alfonso shouted into the comm.

Cesare raised his sword to parry.

The spine of Dragon's Fang met the edge of Number One's greatblade.

The sound of metal on metal went off in the quarry like a hammer-blow to a great bronze bell, and did not stop ringing. Dragon's Fang was the Magister of Minerva's own make, forged of ultimum, the highest-grade alloy in the Order's vaults. Number One's greatblade, under the gold threads, had gone past the limit of any conventional material. A crack opened along the spine of Dragon's Fang that could be seen with the naked eye.

Cesare's hands locked white on the control sticks.

The Red Dragon's feet were pushed back through the loose stone, gouging two deep furrows. The outer plates on the suit's back gave out a long, strained, metallic groan. The gold sleeve at the nape of his neck began to burn. The faint violet tracery on the back of his right hand flared up.

He could not hold it.

"—back!" Cesare barked.

The Red Dragon let go of the parry in the last possible instant and threw itself into a sideways roll. The greatblade scraped along the left pauldron. The Dragoon plate on the outside was sheared off in one piece, exposing the dull red substructure underneath.

Number One did not let the Red Dragon breathe.

The greatblade came back and swung down. A left-to-right diagonal this time. Aimed at the left shoulder joint, now exposed.

The gold threads flickered along the edge, frantic.

Cesare did not have time to raise the sword.

He was not looking at the falling blade. His eyes had gone past it, through the slits of Number One's visor—the two dark violet lenses in the faceplate—and were fixed on the knight inside.

The gold sleeve at the nape of his neck was burning as if it would go through the skin. Deep in his mind, the leftover resonance of red mercury was rolling and turning.

The blade fell.

Cesare raised his right arm.

Not a parry. He put the hilt of Dragon's Fang—and his own arm—across the path of the edge. The sword was already chipped, but he jammed the broken blade across the front of his left shoulder joint and locked his whole right arm under it.

The shriek of metal on metal cut through every other sound in the quarry.

Dragon's Fang broke.

The two halves of the ultimum blade went tumbling across the loose stone, ringing against each other, ringing against the rock. The upper half flew a dozen meters, stuck point-down in a pile of rubble, the edge still glowing with a faint dull red.

The greatblade stopped. Ten centimeters from the Red Dragon's left shoulder joint.

It had not been stopped.

The gold threads at Number One's joints gave out a single, thin, sharp, metallic snap—like a wire breaking. The threads, the self-repair nerve fibers of the Omega prototype that had been threaded into the prototype knight's spine, had come apart, all at once, from the inside.

A gold light poured out of every seam of Number One at once. Not the boil of a moment ago. Not creeping. A wild, disordered outpouring. The light of a smashed lantern spilling its oil.

Number One's greatblade stopped in midair.

Behind the faceplate, the two dark violet lenses of the visor went out.

Then came back on.

Then went out again.

Professor Franco stood up from his console. His hand was at his chest. The corner of his mouth was flecked with a faint brown. He had forced the cough that wanted to come back down, swallowed it.

"Neural signal—" his voice was hoarse, "Number One's neural signal has broken the threshold. The self-repair fibers are out of control."

Virolan's fingers were already on the comm.

"Valentina."

"Here."

"Now."

A clean acknowledgment. The sound of metal. The hiss of a steam valve. The click of a joint lock. Three sounds in three seconds.

In the quarry, something very small and very wrong sounded from inside Number One's faceplate.

The gold threads in its joints began to gather again. Not a flood this time. A contraction. Fast, violent, in toward the core of the armor, like a black hole swallowing every photon in its neighborhood.

Number One's external speakers cut in.

Not the comm channel. The faceplate's outward voice projector. The sound that came out was metal being twisted. Two voices speaking at the same time. One, the voice of a trained soldier. The other, something older, something that had not been a man for a long time.

"—control—cannot—"

Then the six-meter recurved serrated greatblade, at an angle and a speed that no one in the quarry had predicted, came down at the Red Dragon's helmet.

第175章 龙牙剑断的瞬间

【中文】
第175章 龙牙剑断的瞬间

巨刃落下的速度比西泽尔预想的更快。

不是劈砍——是坠落。一号的整具甲胄像一块从绞刑架上松开的铁，那柄六米长的反曲锯齿巨刃裹挟着失控的神经电流，以近乎自由落体的速度斩向红龙的头顶。刃锋上反射着采石场顶灯的冷光，锯齿在空气中拉出尖锐的啸声。

西泽尔举起了龙牙剑。

密涅瓦用究极金属锻造的顶级长剑，剑刃泛着冷白色的光。佛朗哥把它交到他手里时说过，究极金属可以斩断已知的一切——可此刻西泽尔的手在剑柄上感受到了一股他从未接触过的力量。金属撞击金属的瞬间，一号的力量从刃锋传到了剑柄，再传到了他的双臂，再传到了他的脊椎。

那不是军人的力量，是欧米茄自愈神经纤维在失控的边缘爆发出的最后脉冲。

剑刃在半空中相遇。

一刹那间西泽尔听见了自己最害怕的声音——不是金属的撞击，是金属的碎裂。究极金属没有坚持住。龙牙剑的剑身从中央裂开，裂纹沿着金属的纹理蔓延，碎片飞溅出去，在采石场的碎石上弹跳。密涅瓦机关百年巅峰的武器，在一号的巨刃下像一根折断的骨头那样断成了两截。

剑断了。

紧接着是胸口的灼热。

嵌入红龙胸甲的圣剑装具·Excalibur碎片，那块他亲手从阿瓦隆之舟的残骸里捡回来、用自己的血喂过的残片，忽然亮了。不是之前那种若有若无的脉动，是真正的、炽烈的金色光芒，沿着胸甲的缝隙向全身蔓延。仿佛红龙的心脏里有什么东西被唤醒了。

西泽尔来不及细想那股光芒意味着什么。他被巨刃上残余的力道掀起，红龙像一具被踢飞的铁壳那样向后倒飞，肩甲在采石场的岩壁上擦出一长串刺耳的火花。

轰然一声，撞进了岩壁。

岩壁上出现了蜘蛛网般的裂缝，其中一道从红龙左肩的位置裂开，露出了一片黝黑的虚空——地下暗河。冰冷的河水气息从裂缝里涌出，带着铁锈和硫磺的味道，混合着深处的腥气。

红龙卡在了岩壁的裂缝里，左臂关节脱臼，胸甲变形，驾驶舱内的减震系统已经过载。西泽尔被震荡得耳中嗡鸣，视野里全是金色的光斑，脖颈处的黄金套管在发热，那股热度沿着他的脊椎向全身蔓延。

可那块碎片的光越来越亮。

亮得几乎要刺穿胸甲。

——

控制室里，佛朗哥教授从椅子上站了起来。

他的手按在胸口，嘴角有淡淡的血迹——他刚才把那口带血的咳嗽硬生生地吞了回去，可他的脸色比那块血迹更白。

"一号的神经信号——"他的声音沙哑得像砂纸，"它在突破阈值。自愈纤维已经……"

他没有说完。屏幕上，一号面甲后面的深紫色观察镜剧烈地闪烁，像是暴风雨中的灯塔。红色的警告信息一排排地跳出来，每一行都意味着新的损伤。

"瓦莲京娜。"薇若兰的手已经按在了通讯器上。

"我在。"

"现在。"

通讯器里传来一声利落的回应，金属碰撞声、蒸汽阀门开启声、甲胄关节锁定声，在三秒钟之内依次响起。可剑舞者甲胄的启动需要时间，从待机状态到全面出力至少还要三十秒。

三十秒太长。

因为一号的脚步声已经在逼近。

每一步都让采石场的碎石震颤。那柄折断了龙牙剑的巨刃被重新举起，刃尖对准了红龙骑士舱的方向——对准了卡在裂缝里的西泽尔。奥古斯都的狮头盾已经被龙吼炮轰裂，唐璜的炸弹已经在通风口布好，可这些都需要时间。

一号不会等。

——

三个方向同时传来了甲胄启动的声音。

奥古斯都从零号的方向冲来。

昆提良把那具最重的试制机开到了他能达到的极限速度，每一步都让地面颤抖。秘银重盾已经被龙吼炮轰得裂开，闭眼狮头纹章上狮头的一只耳朵不见了，一只狮眼被裂缝切开，可他还举着它。

"老板——！"

他看见了红龙卡在裂缝里，看见了一号举起的巨刃，看见了那刃尖对准的方向。

他没有减速。

奥古斯都整个人扑到了一号的侧面，举起残破的重盾，挡在了巨刃和红龙之间。

一号的巨刃砸了下来。

那柄六米长的反曲锯齿巨刃在欧米茄自愈神经纤维的驱动下以全功率落下，击在秘银重盾的中央。闭眼狮头纹章的第三层硬金直接被击穿，影金属夹层撕裂开来，五层交错锻造的盾面在那一瞬间被压成了麻花，碎裂的金属片飞溅出去。

奥古斯都被巨力掀翻，秘银重盾从中间断成两截，昆提良在驾驶舱里被震得七窍流血。他整个人像被巨人踩了一脚那样从甲胄里飞了出去，撞在了地下暗河入口旁边的岩壁上，岩壁上的裂缝又扩大了一寸。

他滑落下来，半个身体悬在暗河边缘，昏迷了过去。

——

唐璜是从一号的右后方冲过来的。

蔷薇之鬼是五台试制机中最轻的一具，专为突袭设计，没有配备任何重火力，双手各持一柄曲刃镰。他没有去救西泽尔——他知道奥古斯都已经冲过去了，他要做的是让一号分心，哪怕只是零点几秒。

曲刃镰的刃锋瞄准了一号的腘窝——那个机甲最脆弱的关节之一。只要切开那里的动力管线，一号的速度会瞬间降低一半，密涅瓦的胜算就会回来。

刃锋接触到了一号的关节。

然后他感觉到了阻力。

不是金属——是某种更柔软也更坚韧的东西。金色的丝线从一号的关节缝隙里涌出来，像有生命的藤蔓缠住了曲刃镰的刃身。那些丝线在接触到金属的瞬间开始收紧，发出了金属扭曲的尖锐声响。

唐璜想抽回曲刃镰。

他抽不回来。

金色的丝线在零点几秒内勒断了曲刃镰——那柄用究极金属锻造的武器在那些丝线面前像根面条那样被绞断，碎片飞溅出去。然后那些丝线顺势缠上了蔷薇之鬼的右臂，从手腕一直绞到肘关节。

唐璜被整个人甩了出去。

他撞在了采石场边缘的碎石堆上，碎石滚落下来把他半埋在下面。蔷薇之鬼的右臂从肘关节处断裂，驾驶舱里到处都是红色警告灯。他没有死，可他的视野在快速变暗。

他还来得及笑了一下。

"这下……真的亏了……"他喃喃地说。

然后他闭上了眼睛。

——

阿方索是最后一个。

所罗门王的距离最远，他没有奥古斯都那样的重盾，也没有蔷薇之鬼那样的速度。他有的只是腕表里那只更换过微型轴承的备用机械蜘蛛。

他把它释放了出去。

那只蜘蛛只有拇指大小，腹部嵌着的红水银微晶在采石场的灯光下泛着微弱的红光。它沿着地面快速爬行，从碎石之间穿过，朝一号的观察镜爬去。

一号没有注意到它。

那几乎是不可能的——一号的全身都布满了欧米茄自愈神经纤维，那些金色的丝线像有生命的传感器网，连空气中的振动都能感知。可阿方索的蜘蛛爬得太低、太平，贴着地面走，几乎是贴着碎石堆的缝隙钻过去的。

它爬上了一号的面甲。

它停在了观察镜的正中央。

阿方索的手指按下了释放键。

"嘭——"

微型的电磁脉冲在观察镜前爆炸，宽频干扰波瞬间淹没了面甲后面的所有电子信号。一号的视野瞬间一片模糊。它停顿了零点三秒，巨刃悬在半空，像是被按下了暂停键。

然后它的右手抬起来，伸到面甲前面，五指合拢。

"喀嚓。"

那只蜘蛛在它的指缝里被捏成了齑粉，金属碎屑和红水银微晶从指缝间洒落。

可电磁脉冲的余波还在扩散。冲击波沿着空气传到了所罗门王的位置，阿方索整个人在驾驶舱里被震得飞起，后脑撞在了座椅靠背上，眼前一黑。他昏迷前最后看到的画面是塔拉夏在通讯频道里惊慌失措地喊着什么。

三台试制机全部失去了战斗能力。

采石场里忽然安静了下来，只剩下一号脚步的沉重回响和地下暗河隐约的水声。

——

控制室里，佛朗哥教授的手从胸口滑落。

他刚才吞回去的那口血现在又涌了上来，从他的嘴角、鼻腔甚至眼角同时渗出来。塔拉夏扑过去扶住他的时候，他已经软得像根没有骨架的绳子。

"教授！教授！"塔拉夏扶着他在椅子上坐下，单手按下了急救通讯键，"医务组！密涅瓦机关圣所！佛朗哥总长咳血！立刻！立刻！"

他的声音在颤抖。

佛朗哥的眼睛半闭着，他伸手想去按控制台上的开关，可手指在距离开关一寸的地方停住了。

"一号……自愈纤维……"他的声音像风穿过裂缝，"已经……越过阈值……"

他没有说完。

他的手落在了控制台上，整个人软在了椅子里。塔拉夏手里的通讯器还开着，里面传来医务组惊慌的回应声："收到！三分钟内到！三分钟内到！"

可采石场里的战斗不会等三分钟。

——

红龙的驾驶舱卡在了岩壁的裂缝里，胸甲已经变形，左臂关节脱臼，外部通讯系统全部失效。西泽尔的身体被安全带勒得生疼，脖颈处的黄金套管在持续地发烫，热度从后颈传到了他的整条脊椎。

他没有停下来等。

他伸手抠住了胸甲缝隙里那块还在发光的圣剑碎片。

那块碎片很烫，几乎要把他的手指烧穿。可他没有松手，他用力往外一撬——

"咔。"

碎片从胸甲的卡扣里被撬了下来，握在了他的左手里。

那是一块不规则的金属片，边缘是断裂的痕迹，中心却泛着耀眼的金色光芒。光芒在他手心里跳动，仿佛有什么东西在碎片里呼吸。红龙胸口的圣痕之血检测试剂的瓶子在这时碎了，深琥珀色的液体洒在了他的手背上。

"圣痕之血……已检出。"红龙的AI系统在他耳中响了一声。

西泽尔没有听。

他在意的是另一件事——那块碎片的光芒正在和他手背上的血管产生共鸣。淡紫色的发光脉络在他皮肤下浮现，从手背一直蔓延到小臂。

紫瞳金纹。

他在这一刻明白了，那块碎片不是普通的金属。它和红龙体内的每一根神经接驳线路相连，和他后颈的黄金套管相连，和他的血液相连。

和他血脉深处的某种古老东西相连。

他把那块碎片握在左手里，右手则摸到了自己右手中指上的银戒指。

冰原寒玉的凉意从指尖传上来，让他发烫的神经稍微冷静了一分。

他抬起头，推开了变形的驾驶舱舱盖。

冰冷的空气涌进来，带着硫磺和河水的气味。他从半毁的驾驶舱里爬出来，胸口的衣服已经被汗水和血水浸透，脸色苍白得几乎没有血色。

他站在红龙残破的肩甲上。

手里的圣剑碎片还在发光，右手中指上的银戒指在裂缝里漏出的光线中泛着微弱的蓝光。

他低头看了一眼岩壁裂缝里的水——水面映出了他的倒影，苍白的脸，紫色的眼睛。

不，不对。

那紫色正在被某种更炽热的颜色替代。像是烧红的铁在冷却前的最后一刻，金色的纹路从瞳孔中心向外扩散，灼热的亮紫色正在向深处燃烧。

他抬起了头。

他看向了一号。

一号的巨刃正在缓慢地、不可阻挡地朝他的方向斩下来，欧米茄自愈神经纤维在失控中恢复了一部分功能，金色的丝线重新爬上了一号的关节，巨刃的锯齿在空气中拉出尖锐的啸声。

红龙已经不能动了。

可西泽尔还能动。

他想起了那个名字。

那个名字不属于他，不属于他认识的任何人。那个名字来自梦境的最深处，来自圣女塔的阴影里，来自一个十九岁就坠塔而死的王女。

苏伽罗。

他在那个梦里听见过一串字符。在梦境最底层的黑暗中，那个白色的身影把这串字符送进了他的意识，像是一把钥匙被塞进了他手里。

他从来不知道那串字符是做什么用的。

他从来不知道开启的是什么。

可此刻他知道。

"Rex Immortalis。"

他低声说出了那串字符。

声音很轻，几乎被采石场的风声和机械的轰鸣淹没。

可他后颈的黄金套管在这一瞬间剧烈地颤动起来，金色的光从皮肤下涌出，沿着他的脊椎向全身蔓延。不朽之王系统的芯片在他的神经深处醒来，像是沉睡了百年的心脏重新开始跳动。

一号的巨刃距离他的头顶还有三米。

两米。

一米。

红龙的眼睛重新亮了起来。

【English】
Chapter 175 — The Moment the Dragontooth Breaks

The great blade came down faster than Cesare had prepared for.

It was not a cut. It was a fall.

The whole frame of Number One, a collapsing iron scaffold the size of a gallows, had let go of itself above him. The six-meter recurve saw-tooth broadsword came down under its own weight, with the dying pulse of a hundred runaway omega nerve fibers feeding the last unregulated charge into its spine. Cold light off the quarry's overhead lamps ran along the edge. The saw-teeth screamed against the air.

Cesare raised the Dragontooth.

The blade of the sword — a masterwork of the Minerva Foundry — was a clean cold white in his grip. Franco had put it into his hands two days before with the words: *it will cut anything we know of.* The weapon had a name in some old register, and a maker's mark, and the particular pale hum of a metal that did not exist anywhere else on earth. None of that mattered now. The instant the two edges met, Cesare felt something he had never felt before on a sword's grip — a force that had no business being there.

It came up the blade and into the hilt and through the hilt into his hands and up through the wrists and into the bones of his shoulders and down through the cage of his ribs into the base of his spine. Not a soldier's force. A nerve's force. The final burst of an organic filament pushed past the limit of what any nervous system, even an artificial one, was built to survive.

The two blades met in the air above the quarry.

For one instant Cesare heard, above every other sound, the one sound he had always been afraid of. It was not the ring of metal on metal. It was the sound of metal giving up. A dry, almost polite crack, like a knuckle bent too far.

The ultimate metal did not hold.

The Dragontooth split at the middle. The fracture ran along the grain of the forging, threw off a small bright shower of splinters that bounced and rang against the rubble below. The finest weapon the Minerva Foundry had produced in a hundred years broke in two across Number One's broadsword, like a long bone across a paving stone.

The sword was gone.

Then came the heat in his chest.

The Holy Sword Apparatus — Excalibur fragment, the shard he had pulled with his own hands from the wreck of the Ship of Avalon, the shard he had fed with his own blood — woke up. Not the teasing, almost-there pulse he had learned to live with. A true ignition. Gold light spilled out of the shard's broken edges and ran along the seams of the chest plate and into the joints of the Red Dragon, bright as a forge mouth, bright as an opened wound.

Cesare did not have time to think about what the light meant.

The leftover force of Number One's stroke caught him under the broken crossguard of his own sword and threw him. The Red Dragon left the ground the way a kicked tin can leaves the ground. Its shoulder plate dragged along the quarry wall behind it for a long, shrieking yard, throwing up a tail of sparks that lit the dark like a string of cheap firecrackers.

Then it hit.

There was the sound of a very large thing being put where a very large thing does not belong. A section of the quarry wall caved inward in a web of cracks, one of them running straight up from the Red Dragon's left shoulder and out into nothing — into a thin black opening, out of which came a current of cold air. Underground river water. Iron, sulfur, the older smell beneath both, the smell of things that lived where the sun never went.

The Red Dragon was stuck. The cockpit's shock-dampers were already past their limits. Cesare's left shoulder joint was dislocated. The chest plate had folded around him like a crushed hat. The cockpit rang. He rang with it. The gold conduit at the back of his neck was running hot — not the gentle warmth he had grown used to in the last weeks, but a true heat, an animal heat, the heat of something inside him being dragged out of sleep.

And the fragment on his chest was getting brighter.

Brighter than the quartz lamps on the quarry ceiling. Brighter than the warning indicators on the inside of his visor.

— 

In the control room, Professor Franco stood up.

His hand was flat against the center of his chest. The blood on the corner of his mouth was the only color in his face, and his face had gone past the color of paper and arrived somewhere worse. He had swallowed the cough that had tried to come out of him. He had swallowed it the way a man swallows a coin he has promised not to spend.

"Number One's nerve signal —" His voice was the voice of a man dragging a file across a piece of wood. "It's crossed the threshold. The self-healing fibers have —"

He did not finish the sentence.

On the screen behind him, the deep violet of Number One's interior eye-lens was flickering, a slow sick strobe, like the lamp of a coast tower in a storm. The warning feed was rolling line after line of new damage, each line a small death.

"Valentina," Verolan said. Her hand was already on the comm.

"Here."

"Now."

There was a short, clean acknowledgment down the wire. Then, in order, over the next three seconds: the click of a release catch, the long sigh of a steam valve opening, the chunk of an armor's lumbar locks engaging. The Sword Dancer, in standby since before the morning, was coming up. From cold to full output was a measured thirty seconds.

Thirty seconds was a long time.

Because Number One's foot had just come down on the quarry floor.

The sound came up through the stone. The scree jumped a quarter inch and settled. The second foot came down, and the scree jumped again. The great blade — the same blade that had just broken the Dragontooth — was being lifted back up, slowly, with the unhurried patience of a thing that had no reason to be hurried. The tip was already pointed at the Red Dragon. Pointed at the crack in the wall. Pointed at Cesare.

Augustus could not be in two places at once. Don Juan's satchel charges were already set in the ventilation shaft. None of it mattered, because none of it was here.

— 

Three separate armor-start sequences went off in three separate directions at once.

Augustus came in from where Zero had been holding the line.

Quintilian had the heaviest of the prototypes wound up to the highest speed it would bear, and the floor shook under every step. The argentum-alloy great shield on his left arm had already taken a direct hit from the Dragon Roar cannon. The closed-eye lion of the crest was missing an ear. One of the eyes of the lion was a long crack. He was still holding it up.

"Boss —"

He saw the Red Dragon rammed into the wall. He saw the saw-tooth blade being raised. He saw where the tip of it was aimed.

He did not slow down.

Augustus threw the whole of the suit, and the man inside it, between Number One's descending blade and the broken Red Dragon. He set the ruined shield square to the stroke and held it with both hands and the waist actuator and the soles of his feet against the quarry floor.

The blade came down.

The third layer of hard gold on the lion's crest went through in a single stroke. The shadow-metal sandwich beneath it split. The five crossed forgings of the shield face were, in that instant, compressed into a single twisted fold that had once been a shield and was now the shape of a rag being wrung. Pieces of it went past Cesare's canopy on both sides.

Augustus was lifted clean off the ground. The shield broke in two across his chest. Quintilian, in the cockpit, took the deceleration through every soft tissue in his head; blood came out of his ears, his nose, the corners of his eyes, the corners of his mouth. The suit left the ground the way a man leaves the ground when a giant has stepped on him. It hit the quarry wall beside the crack where the underground river ran, and the wall opened another inch.

He slid down. Half his body hung out over the black water. He did not move again.

— 

Don Juan came in from Number One's right rear.

The Ghost of Roses was the lightest of the five prototypes, designed for the kill at close quarters. No heavy cannon. No shield. A scythe in each hand, the long curved blade good for slipping between joints and finding the thing underneath.

He did not try to save Cesare. He had seen Augustus go. He could not afford to be the second man between the sword and the boy. He had to make Number One look away, even if only for a fraction of a second.

Both scythes went for the joint at the back of Number One's knee. The popliteal. The oldest weak point in any armor, the place where the power lines have to run, the place where there is never quite enough room for them.

The edges of the scythes touched the joint.

Then the edges stopped.

What came out of the joint was not metal. It was softer than metal. It was also, in its way, stronger. Strands of gold — not light, not paint, actual gold-colored filaments, the thickness of a finger, alive in the way that a vine is alive — boiled out of the seam and wrapped themselves around the scythe blades. The instant they touched the steel, they began to draw tight, and the steel began to complain in a high wire voice.

Don Juan tried to pull the scythes back.

He could not.

In less than a second the gold threads had cut through the scythe blades the way a wire-cutter goes through a piece of soft twine. The ultimate metal — the same metal that had been promised to cut anything — came apart in two neat pieces and went spinning into the dark.

The threads kept coming. They climbed the Ghost of Roses' right arm from the wrist to the elbow and began to tighten.

Don Juan was thrown.

He hit the loose scree at the far edge of the quarry, and a small avalanche of it followed him down and half-buried him. The right arm of the Ghost of Roses was no longer attached below the elbow. The cockpit was a Christmas tree of red. He was not dead. His vision, however, was going.

He had time, before it went, to smile a little.

"Well," he said, to no one. "That's a real loss."

Then he closed his eyes.

— 

Alfonso was the last.

The King Solomon was the farthest of the three. He did not have Augustus's shield. He did not have the Ghost of Roses' reach. What he had, in the second spare pocket of his left wrist, was a mechanical spider the size of a thumb. He had replaced the micro-bearings that morning, because the bearings it had come with were not the bearings he trusted.

He let it go.

The spider went down the inside of the suit's left gauntlet and out through a service hatch and onto the quarry floor. The red-mercury micro-crystal in its belly threw a small red wink back at the lamps as it went. It kept low. It kept flat. It went through the gaps between the loose stones, the way a real spider goes through the gaps between the loose stones, with the patient wrong-minded cleverness of a thing that does not know it is supposed to be afraid.

It climbed up Number One's shin plate. It went on climbing. It passed the knee. It passed the hip. It went up the breastplate. It arrived at the deep violet lens of the observation eye.

Number One did not seem to notice it.

That should not have been possible. The whole surface of the suit was threaded with the same gold filaments that had just torn off Don Juan's arm. They were, in their way, a sense organ. They should have heard the tiny tick of the spider's feet against the plating from across the quarry. They did not, because Alfonso's spider walked too low, too close to the stone, through the cracks where the vibrations did not propagate.

It stopped. Center of the lens. Belly down.

Alfonso pressed the key on his wrist.

The sound it made was the smallest possible sound a small explosion can make. The micro-EMP blew out, and the broad-band interference rolled across the lens and into the suit. Number One's vision went white. The suit froze. The great blade, which had been halfway through its next stroke, hung in the air as if someone had pressed a finger against a turning wheel and held it still.

Number One's right hand came up.

The fingers came together at the center of the face.

The sound the spider made, when the fingers closed on it, was the sound a man makes when he steps on a small dry insect. When the fingers opened, what fell out of them was a thin rain of powdered metal and powdered red mercury, scattering down the front of the breastplate.

But the backwash of the EMP was still running. The shock front in the air reached the King Solomon at the back of the quarry and put a fist through Alfonso's spine. He left his seat. The back of his head met the inside of the headrest. The world went out.

The last thing he heard, before it went out, was Tarasha's voice in his ear, on a frequency he had not known she was listening to, saying his name, twice, in a tone he had never heard her use.

— 

All three prototypes were down.

The quarry was quiet. The only sounds were the slow, patient footfall of Number One coming forward, and, far below, the small unending commentary of the underground river on the stones at the bottom of the crack.

In the control room, Franco's hand came away from his chest.

The blood he had swallowed was finished waiting. It came up out of him through every opening it had. The corner of his mouth. The inside of his nose. The corners of his eyes. Tarasha caught him before he reached the floor and put him into the chair. Her hand found the medical comm. Her voice, when she spoke, was the voice of a person who has decided to be calm.

"Medical! Minerva Sanctuary! Professor Franco is coughing blood! Now! Now!"

The comm answered her, twice, in a panic she did not have time to be polite to.

Franco's eyes were half shut. His hand drifted toward a switch on the panel in front of him. His fingers got to within an inch of the switch and stopped.

"Number One," he said. "The fibers. Past the threshold."

He did not finish the sentence.

His hand came down on the panel. The rest of him followed his hand, the way a coat follows the hook it is hung on. Tarasha was still holding the comm, and the medical team's voices were still coming out of it, and the words *three minutes* were still in the air, and the fight in the quarry would still be the fight in the quarry in three minutes and in zero minutes, and there was no third number for it.

— 

In the Red Dragon's cockpit, the air was the temperature of a sickroom.

The chest plate had folded around Cesare. The left shoulder actuator was out of its socket. Every external comm was dead. The harness had cut two long lines into the skin of his chest, and the gold conduit at the back of his neck was running a heat he could feel at the base of his skull.

He did not wait for anything to repair itself.

He put the fingers of his right hand into the seam of the chest plate, found the edge of the Excalibur fragment where it sat in its cradle, and pried.

The metal was hot. Hotter than hot. The kind of hot that means the next thing is the kind of hot that takes skin off. He did not let go. He set his weight against it and levered.

The fragment came out of the cradle with a small, polite click. It sat in the palm of his left hand.

It was a small, ugly thing. A sliver of metal the size of a man's palm, broken at one edge where it had been broken a long time ago, and still warm from the cradle. The center of it was throwing a steady gold light, the color of the inside of a forge. The light was moving. The light was, in some sense Cesare did not have a word for, breathing.

The vial of the Holy Mark reagent in the diagnostic rack on the inside of the canopy chose that moment to break. The dark amber of the reagent ran out across the inside of the rack and down the side of Cesare's left hand and onto the back of his hand.

"Holy Mark blood reagent: positive," the Red Dragon's onboard said, in his ear, in the same flat voice it always used.

Cesare did not hear it.

What he was looking at was the back of his own hand. The light from the fragment in his palm was meeting the blood on the back of his hand and doing something to the blood. Faint violet lines were coming up through the skin, branching, running up the tendons of his hand and along the inside of his wrist and disappearing under the cuff of his uniform. The color was not the violet of a bruise. The color was the violet of an old, deep fire seen down a long corridor.

Purple pupils. Gold veins.

He understood it then. The fragment was not a piece of metal. It was a piece of him. It was threaded into the Red Dragon the way the gold conduit was threaded into the base of his skull. It was threaded into his blood. It was threaded into something older than his blood, and longer than his blood, and further back than anything that had a name yet.

He closed his left hand around the fragment. The gold of it came out between his fingers.

He put the fingers of his right hand onto the silver ring on the middle finger of his right hand.

The cold of the ice-plain jade was the first cold thing that had touched him in a long time. It ran up through the bone of his finger and into the bones of his hand and began, slowly, to put the inside of him back into some kind of order.

He reached up, found the catch of the canopy, and pushed.

The deformed hatch ground against the folded frame of the suit and gave. The air of the quarry came in. It was cold, and it carried sulfur, and it carried the iron of the underground river, and it carried the deeper smell that Cesare had no name for but had been smelling his whole life.

He pulled himself up out of the broken cockpit. The uniform on his chest was soaked through with sweat and with something darker. His face was the color of a clean sheet of paper. He got one boot onto the shoulder plate of the Red Dragon and then the other. He stood up.

The fragment was still in his left hand, throwing a slow gold light between his fingers. The silver ring on the middle finger of his right hand caught the thin strip of light coming up out of the crack in the wall and threw back a small, faint blue.

From where he stood, on the broken shoulder of his own suit, he could see the crack in the wall and a long thin strip of water at the bottom of it, and the strip of water was holding his reflection up to him.

A pale face. Purple eyes.

No.

Not purple. Not any longer.

The color was being eaten, from the center of the pupil outward, by something hotter. The way a piece of iron being taken out of a forge is eaten, in its last second at temperature, by the first color of cooling. Gold lines were running out of the dark center of his eyes and across the violet and out toward the edge of the iris. The violet was still there, underneath, but the violet was, for the first time in his life, no longer in charge.

He looked up.

He looked at Number One.

The great saw-tooth blade was being lifted, slowly, patiently, with the unhurried certainty of a thing that had been promised the next ten minutes of the world. The gold filaments on the suit had finished their work on the joint at the back of the knee and were beginning to reappear at the wrist and the elbow and the shoulder. The teeth of the blade were screaming against the air.

The Red Dragon could not move.

Cesare could.

He thought of a name.

It was not a name that belonged to him. It was not a name that belonged to anyone he had ever met. It was a name from the deepest part of a dream he had had once, in the shadow of the Saintess Tower, from a princess who had been nineteen when she had gone over the edge of the tower and not come back.

Sucaro.

He had heard a string of characters spoken to him, once, in that dream, by a figure in white, in the dark at the very bottom of the dark. The figure had pressed the string into his mind the way a person presses a key into the hand of another person.

He had never known what the string of characters was for.

He had never known what it was meant to open.

He knew now.

"Rex Immortalis."

He said it under his breath. The wind of the quarry and the long grind of the suit took the words almost as soon as they were out of his mouth.

But the gold conduit at the back of his neck heard them.

It shuddered. The shudder went down the length of his spine and into the soles of his feet and up into the bones of his skull. A light, gold-colored, hotter than the light in his hand, came up out of him through the skin of his neck and ran down the muscles of his back and along the insides of his arms. Something inside him, something that had been asleep for a hundred years, opened one eye.

The blade of Number One was three meters above his head.

Two meters.

One.

The eyes of the Red Dragon came on.

【中文】
第176章 红莲舞于紫瞳之上

红龙的眼睛重新亮了起来。

不是上一次那种失控的、吞噬一切的炽金色，而是一种更内敛、更锋利的光，仿佛一双被锁在深水底部的利刃终于出鞘。后颈的黄金套管在发热，热度沿着脊椎向全身蔓延，可那热度不像从前那样灼得他发疯，反而被什么东西精确地包裹住了，像是一条无形的缰绳套住了狂奔的野马。

芯片在工作。

他能感觉到那东西——一粒比他小指指甲还小的超微芯片嵌在颈椎深处，实时监控着他全身的神经电流。英雄人格在试图挣脱，那股力量正在冲击他的意识边界，像一头发了疯的犀牛横冲直撞，可芯片像是一道闸门，把那股力量精准地限制在可控的范围内。

他知道这很疼。

疼得他全身的肌肉都在颤抖，疼得他视野边缘泛起了血色的雾。可他还清醒。他第一次在这种状态下清醒着。

"Rex Immortalis。"

他低声重复了一次，那串字符在喉咙里像金属一样冰冷。

脚下的红龙已经半毁了，左臂从肘关节处断裂，胸甲裂开了一道长长的口子，暴露出里面暗金色的硬金骨架。驾驶舱勉强还能运作，蒸气管路有几处破裂，正在往外喷着高温白雾。

他踩着肩甲爬回了驾驶舱。

舱内的温度高得令人窒息，到处都是金属烧焦的气味。他把断裂的控制杆用备用零件临时固定，把脱离的神经接驳线一根根重新插回接口。紫瞳金纹在视野中闪烁，后颈的热度已经稳定下来——不是消失了，而是被芯片驯服了。

"老板！红龙还能动？"阿方索的声音从通讯频道里传来，带着他惯常的冷静，可底层藏着一丝颤抖。

"能动。"西泽尔说。

"昆提良和唐璜都失去了战斗力，我——"阿方索的声音停了一下，"我在路上。"

"不用来了。"西泽尔说，"帮我盯着古洛诺斯。"

他从残破的甲胄里翻出了一块备用的硬金连接件，勉强把龙牙剑的断茬卡进了凹槽里。剑刃只剩半截，断裂面的硬金呈锯齿状，参差不齐。

然后他从胸口拔出了那块发光的圣剑碎片。

碎片在他掌心里跳动，金色的光芒与后颈的黄金套管同频闪烁，像是某种古老的信号在呼唤他的血脉。紫瞳金纹又亮了一层，手背上的淡紫色脉络像是被点燃的引线，一路烧到指根。

他把碎片插进了龙牙剑断茬的位置。

硬金与圣剑碎片咬合的瞬间，整把剑都变了。断裂面上涌出了金色的焊光，仿佛两种金属在高温下被强行焊接到了一起。剑柄上残存的纹路亮了起来，那不是西泽尔在龙牙剑上见过的任何纹路，而是更加古老的花纹——莲花、齿轮、星辰。

Excalibur残刃。

它不是一把完整的圣剑，连残刃都算不上，只是一截断茬勉强续接着一块碎片。可它散发出的气场让西泽尔后颈的黄金套管都安静了下来，仿佛一把真正的剑被重新握在了它该被握住的人手中。

红龙甲胄的龙纹亮了。

那些雕刻在肩甲、护臂和胸口的红色龙纹一条条被点亮，仿佛有滚烫的血液在金属纹理中流淌。蒸气管路中喷出的白雾也染上了一层淡红，整台甲胄仿佛从沉睡中苏醒的巨龙。

采石场上响起了蒸汽笛的长鸣。

那是密涅瓦机关的警报系统——检测到了红水银级别的能量信号波动。各国使团的VIP包厢里传来此起彼伏的惊呼，有人以为是战斗出了意外，有人以为有新的神圣灾难正在酝酿。

可这一次那警报不是失控的前兆。

芯片在监控一切。

西泽尔握紧了Excalibur残刃，金色与红光在剑身上交织成一片，他的瞳孔里紫金色的纹路正在以稳定的频率跳动，像是心跳的节奏。

他闭上了眼睛。

一秒。

就一秒。

黑暗中他看见了莲花。

满池的莲花，粉的白的紫的，花瓣在风中微微颤动，每一朵都连着根茎，根茎在池底的淤泥中彼此相连，像一张巨大的网。那是锡兰王都的水池，在他出生前就已经存在了上千年的古莲池。

他听见了声音。

不是苏伽罗的声音，不是末代星见的声音，是一个男人的声音——苍老、温和、带着一种被苦难打磨过的尊严。

"孩子。"

那声音说。

"用我们的力量，保护你想保护的人。"

然后莲花消失了。

西泽尔睁开了眼。

一号就在三十米外，巨刃举在头顶，金色的自愈神经纤维正在失控中疯狂增殖，从关节处向外蔓延，像是一具正在被某种寄生物吞噬的傀儡。一号的眼睛——那本该是甲胄光学瞄准镜的位置——已经变成了两团不稳定的金红色光团，像是两团即将爆炸的恒星。

巨刃落下来了。

西泽尔动了。

红龙的双足在采石场的碎石上炸开两道深坑，引擎以最大功率喷发，整台甲胄像一枚炮弹一样弹射出去。他的速度——

快得不正常。

快得让所有人都来不及反应。

主观测厅的球形投影屏幕上，一道红光从屏幕的底部以不可思议的速度直冲画面中央，红龙甲胄的轮廓在高速运动中被拉成了一条模糊的残影，像一道红色的闪电劈开了矿道中弥漫的硝烟。

"什么——"解说员的声音卡在了嗓子里。

叶素理手中的茶杯停在了嘴唇前。

纯公主的手搭在了腰间的青丝古剑上。

高文少爷手中的美杜莎金币掉在了桌面上，发出了清脆的响声。

拜占庭大使卢瑟半站起身来，动作僵在了半空。

所有人都在看那道红色的光。

而那道光已经撞上了一号。

Excalibur残刃的尖端精准地刺入了一号右腿膝关节的内侧，那里是自愈神经纤维最密集的节点，金色丝线从缝隙中疯狂涌出试图缠住剑身。可那不是普通的剑——圣剑碎片的金色光芒在接触神经纤维的瞬间爆发了，像是被投入火堆的干燥丝线，金色的纤维一段段断裂、燃烧、化为灰烬。

一号发出了一声惨叫。

不是机械的嘎吱声，是从骑士舱里传出的人类的嘶吼。那声音里带着痛苦，带着恐惧，带着某种正在被撕碎的疯狂。

西泽尔没有停。

他旋转剑身，Excalibur残刃的锯齿状断茬在关节处切出了一道弧线，暴露出底下暗金色的硬金骨架和断裂的蒸汽管路。高温的润滑液从伤口中喷涌而出，溅在红龙的胸甲上，发出嗤嗤的声响。

然后他转向第二个目标。

一号的腘窝。

甲胄的腘窝是设计中最薄弱的关节，所有仿生学的设计都让这个弯曲点成为防护的死角。西泽尔的剑尖像手术刀一样精准地切入了那个缝隙，第二束自愈神经纤维在接触碎片的瞬间断裂，喷出的金红光粉在空气中画出一道诡异的弧线。

一号的右腿失去了支撑。

三米高的巨型傀儡向后踉跄，巨刃失控地劈在了采石场的岩壁上，炸开一片碎石。

西泽尔的第三击。

Excalibur残刃的尖端对上了一号的胸口——那是欧米茄自愈神经纤维汇聚的核心节点，也是骑士舱正下方的位置。残刃刺入的瞬间，整台一号甲胄都剧烈地颤抖起来，金色的纤维从胸口向外疯狂抽动，像是一颗正在被剖开的心脏。

骑士舱的玻璃出现了裂缝。

裂缝从撞击点向四周扩散，像蛛网一样爬满了整面防弹玻璃。透过裂缝，西泽尔能隐约看到里面那个失控的骑士——他全身插满了神经接驳的电极，金色的纤维从甲胄的接口处钻入他的脊椎，他的面部肌肉在不受控制地抽搐，口鼻中有液体流出。

"你——"一号骑士的嘴唇在动，可声音被破碎的电子信号扭曲成了噪音。

西泽尔抽出了剑。

他后退一步，红龙在碎石上重新站稳，Excalibur残刃上的金色光芒在空气中留下了短暂的尾迹。一号失去了右腿的支撑，整个身体向右侧倾斜，巨刃插在岩壁中勉强撑住，可那姿态已经不像是一台战斗兵器，更像一具正在倒塌的雕像。

主观测厅里爆发出一阵惊呼。

"红龙——红龙在压制一号！"解说员的声音从颤抖恢复到了亢奋，"不可思议！新型红龙的速度远超预期！它——它正在逐个击破一号的关节！"

"这是……"叶素理放下茶杯，目光钉在投影屏幕上。

"他赢了？"纯公主低声说。

"不，还差古洛诺斯。"叶素理说。

仿佛在回应他的判断，采石场的另一端传来沉重的脚步声。

古洛诺斯冲过来了。

胡安·博尔吉亚操控着第二代普罗米修斯从侧翼发起突袭，六米长的反曲锯齿巨刃在矿道的狭窄空间里几乎无法施展，可胡安没打算用刃——他直接用整台巨型傀儡的身体去撞红龙，像一头被激怒的犀牛。

三米对七米。

重量差距是压倒性的。

可西泽尔没有闪避。

红龙转身的速度比古洛诺斯冲击的速度更快——那是西泽尔近身狂化格斗术的精髓，完全放弃传统甲胄格斗的架势，用最短的路径改变重心。他不是正面对撞，而是侧身——红龙背部的超重武装龙骑兵套装的尾段，那个在设计中被嘲笑为"华而不实"的装饰性尾翼，像一根钢铁鞭子一样抽了出去。

尾翼抽在了古洛诺斯的膝关节外侧。

那是一个精妙到极致的角度——既不是正面的硬抗，也不是单纯的闪避，而是用最小的力在最关键的位置制造最大的失衡。古洛诺斯的膝关节本来就是腿部弱点，叶素理拍摄下的情报中已经记录了这一点，可胡安以为自己的冲击速度足以碾压任何反击。

他错了。

七米高的巨型傀儡在惯性中失去了平衡。

右膝向外侧偏转了十五度，古洛诺斯的上半身在惯性中继续前冲，下半身却已经支撑不住，三十吨的钢铁巨兽在采石场的碎石上轰然倒地，扬起的尘埃和碎屑形成了一道灰白色的浪潮。

巨刃从古洛诺斯的手中脱落，砸在红龙的脚边，嵌入碎石中。

胡安·博尔吉亚在驾驶舱里发出了一声嘶吼，可那声音被厚重的装甲隔绝在外，只有通讯频道里传来断断续续的骂声。

"西泽尔——你——"

西泽尔没有理他。

红龙转身，重新面对一号。

一号已经彻底失去平衡了，半跪在碎石中，巨刃撑在地上，胸口那个被Excalibur残刃切开的伤口还在冒着金色的光粉。骑士舱的裂缝已经扩展到了大半面玻璃，从外面可以清楚看到里面那个浑身抽搐的骑士。

"一号倒地不起！一号倒地不起！"解说员的声音已经近乎嘶吼，"一——"

一秒。

两秒。

三秒。

"西泽尔·博尔吉亚得分！"解说员几乎是在尖叫，"一号倒地不起！新型炽天使小队——获胜！"

主观测厅里炸了。

密涅瓦机关的工程师们从座位上跳起来，有人拥抱，有人拍桌，有人把手中的图纸抛向空中。各国使团的VIP包厢里掌声雷动，查理曼、叶尼塞、拜占庭的代表们纷纷起身，有人面带惊讶，有人若有所思。

"赢了……"阿方索靠在石壁上，缓缓坐了下去，"赢了。"

史宾赛在教廷核心的指挥位置上长长地吐出一口气，他的脊背已经被冷汗浸透，那只紧握权杖的手终于松开了。

"陛下，红龙获胜。"他转向身侧。

教皇隆·博尔吉亚站在指挥台前，脸色比平时更苍白了一些。他微微点头，嘴唇动了动，像是要说什么——

一阵剧烈的咳嗽打断了他。

绿色的泡腾片从他的袖口滑落，掉在地上滚了两圈，碎成了粉末。史宾赛立刻扶住了他的手臂，可教皇摆了摆手，另一只手捂住了嘴，指缝间有暗色的液体渗出。

"没事。"教皇低声说，声音沙哑，"我没事。"

史宾赛没有说话，只是把袖中的手帕递了过去。

采石场中，红龙缓缓转身。

Excalibur残刃上的光芒正在消退，后颈的热度也在芯片的监控下逐渐回归正常。紫瞳金纹没有消失，但跳动的频率已经从刚才的狂乱恢复了稳定的节律。

他的视野里，锡兰莲花池的画面残影还在。

根脉相连。

保护你想保护的人。

"老板！一号——"阿方索的声音从通讯频道里传来，带着一丝警觉。

西泽尔的目光落回一号身上。

那台半跪在碎石中的第三代普罗米修斯试制机没有动。骑士舱的裂缝布满玻璃，暗金色的光粉从胸口的伤口中不断飘出，像是某种正在燃尽的余烬。

一切都结束了。

可西泽尔的手指无声地收紧了剑柄。

因为骑士舱的门——正在打开。

【English】
Chapter 176 — Red Lotus Dances Above Purple Eyes

The Red Dragon's eyes came back on.

Not the devouring molten gold of the last fit — that light had eaten everything, world and self together — but something leaner, colder, a pair of blades lifted out of deep water. The gold sleeve at the back of his neck ran hot. The heat climbed his spine and should have maddened him as it had before; instead it rode him. He felt it harnessed, as a horseman feels a runaway stallion finally gathered between his knees.

The chip was working.

He could feel it — that sub-pinkie-nail speck of circuitry lodged at the third vertebra, drinking the current of every nerve in his body. The heroic personality was still trying to tear loose. It came at the walls of him like some maddened rhinoceros, blunt and absolute, and the chip was the gate: not killing the beast, only shaping the charge. Letting it through where it would not kill him.

It hurt. His muscles shook with it. The rim of his vision flushed red. But he was awake. He was, for the first time in any of these fits, fully, coldly awake.

Rex Immortalis.

He mouthed the words once, and the syllables tasted of cold metal in the back of his throat.

The Red Dragon beneath his feet was half a corpse. The left arm was sheared off at the elbow, the breastplate split along a single long seam that opened onto the dark gold of the alloy skeleton underneath. The cockpit still answered to him, but the steam lines had cracked in three places and were venting high white fog into the dust-thick air of the quarry.

He climbed back in by the shoulder plate.

Inside the cabin the heat was a small private hell. Metal and ozone, the iron-burn of scorched cabling. He strapped himself in, jammed the snapped control stick upright with a spare coupling, and re-seated the severed neural leads one by one into their sockets, feeling each plug bite home with a small bright jolt at the base of his skull. The violet-gold sigils in his vision steadied. The heat at his nape stopped climbing.

Alfonso's voice came down the line. The man was trying to sound the way he always sounded, which was bored, but the wires under the words were trembling.

Boss. The Red Dragon still runs?

It runs.

Quintain and Don Juan are both out. I'm — I'm on my way.

Don't. Watch Goulonoth for me.

He killed the channel.

From the wreckage of the cabin he fished a spare hard-gold connector and a length of locking pin. The Dragon Fang sword was a ruin. The blade had snapped somewhere above the hilt; the broken stub was ragged, the torn edge of the hard gold standing up in jagged teeth where the alloy had sheared. He jammed the stub into a fitting in the cabin wall and locked it there. It would have to do.

Then he reached into the breast of his armor.

The Holy Sword fragment had been sitting against his chest since the Medici courier had pressed it into his hand outside Florence, wrapped in a black cloth that smelled of incense and old iron. It had been cold then. It was not cold now. It pulsed against his palm in time with the gold sleeve at his neck, the two signals in conversation, the way two clocks in the same room will fall into step. The violet-gold sigils in his eyes climbed a shade brighter. The thin purple veins on the back of his hand lit up from wrist to knuckle, slow, like a fuse that had been waiting for him.

He fitted the fragment to the broken stub of the Dragon Fang.

The two metals met, and the sword changed.

Hard gold and relic. The join blazed. A welding light ran along the seam, too white to look at, and when it dimmed the broken edge of the blade had been fused into something else — a stub of a stub, a half-hand of metal, but a different metal now, and differently ancient. The patterns that woke along the hilt were not the ones he had learned on the Dragon Fang in the old fighting yards outside Constantinople. They were older. Lotus. Gear. Star. The kind of work that was being done somewhere before the Romanovs were a name, before the Medicis had any coin to lend.

Excalibur. Or the last broken inch of her that anyone still living had any right to.

The dragon carvings on the Red Dragon woke.

The veins of red worked down from the pauldrons through the vambraces and on into the breastplate, one after another, lighting in their order, as though hot blood were being poured into channels cut for it. The white steam from the cracked pipes took on a faint rose. The whole machine drew a long shuddering breath, like a sleeping animal that has been spoken to in its own language and has, at last, chosen to answer.

In the quarry, the long steam-whistle of a Minerva mechanism went up.

It was the alert system. It was reading the signature of red mercury, and the signature was climbing. In the VIP boxes above the pit the foreign delegations stood or craned, a rising murmur going from box to box. Some thought a fresh disaster was being born up out of the ground. Some thought it was only the new Seraph unit finally losing control of whatever was inside it.

It was neither. For the first time in any of their lives, it was a man in command of the thing that had been trying to kill him.

Cesare closed his hand tighter around the half-sword. Gold and red braided along the short blade and went on braiding beyond the metal, hanging in the air for a breath before they let go. The violet-and-gold tracery in his pupils was pulsing now at the steady rate of a healthy heart.

He closed his eyes.

He let himself have one second.

In the dark behind his lids he saw the lotuses.

The whole pool in the old capital of Ceylon, in the courtyard where he had been born — a thousand years of lotuses, his mother had said, before he was old enough to understand the number. Pink ones. White ones. A few bruised violets, the color of his own eyes in certain lights. The petals shifted in a wind that did not quite touch the rest of the world. Each flower ran on its own stem down into the black silt at the bottom, and the stems were joined, and the joined stems were joined again, a great net under the water that no one had ever drawn a picture of.

A voice came.

Not Sugero's voice. Not the voice of the last stargazer of his line, the one who had taught him to read the skies over Florence when he was too young to hold a sword. A man's voice. Old, and kind, and worn smooth by long suffering, the way a stone in a riverbed is worn smooth without ever being made smaller.

Child.

The voice said, in a tongue that was somehow both Latin and something older.

Use what we have given you, to keep safe the people you have chosen to keep safe.

Then the lotuses were gone.

Cesare opened his eyes.

Number One was thirty meters away.

The third-generation prototype Prometheus frame stood with the great curved cleaver raised above its head, the gold healing fibers of its Omega weave running wild out of every joint, sprouting in pale spider-tongues into the dust-thick air. A puppet already half-eaten by whatever was living inside it. Where the optical sights should have been, two unsteady orbs of gold-red light had kindled, looking out at the world with the dumb, furious patience of stars about to go nova.

The cleaver began to come down.

Cesare moved.

The Red Dragon's feet struck the quarry floor and the stone came apart under them, two small craters where the struts landed. The boilers vented at maximum. The machine left the ground the way a shell leaves a mortar — straight, sudden, a short hard arc, fast past anything the workshop had ever rated it for. Faster, certainly, than anything Lord Gawain's intelligence people had thought to put in the briefing book for the Byzantines.

The observation gallery's spherical screen showed it as a single red line. The line rose from the lower edge of the picture and crossed the entire image before the eye could follow. The Red Dragon's outline in the projection had been smeared by its own speed into a red smear, a kind of red lightning drawn through the smoke of the pit.

The commentator's mouth opened and nothing came out.

Ye Sulei's teacup stopped halfway to his lips.

Princess Jun's hand, very quietly, went to the old blue-silk sword at her hip.

Lord Gawain dropped the Medusa coin he had been turning between his fingers. It rang against the marble of the table.

Luther, the ambassador from Byzantium, half-rose from his seat, and stayed there, a man in two pieces.

The red line hit Number One.

The broken tip of the Excalibur remnant found the inside of Number One's right knee — the densest knot of healing fibers in the entire frame. The fibers, on contact with the relic, did what dry silk does in a fire. They flared. They burned. They came apart in little gold curls that drifted to the ground and were already ash before they landed.

The man inside the cockpit screamed.

It was not a mechanical noise. The armor was three meters tall and built to take a shell, and through all of it, a man was screaming — high, ragged, drowning. There was pain in it, and terror, and the particular shrillness of a mind being torn open from the inside.

Cesare did not stop.

He turned the blade in the joint. The serrated broken edge of the relic drew a small neat arc through the gap it had made, and underneath the fibers he could see the dark gold skeleton of the frame, and the severed steam lines drooling hot lubricant onto the Red Dragon's breastplate. The lubricant hissed and ran.

He took the second target.

The popliteal — the hollow behind the knee. The weak point in any biomimetic design, the place the engineers always protected least because the mathematics of the joint made any extra plating a liability. The tip of the relic went in the way a scalpel goes in. The second sheaf of healing fibers died the same screaming gold death, and the arc of bright dust they left hanging in the air was, for one quiet second, almost beautiful.

Number One's right leg gave.

The three-meter frame pitched backward and fetched up on the cleaver, the blade buried in the quarry wall at an angle, the body of the puppet slumped across it in a posture that had stopped being a fighting stance and had started to be a pose of a body that was about to fall.

The third strike was for the chest.

The relic found the convergence node of the Omega weave — the place every self-healing thread in the frame eventually ran to, the place directly above the cockpit where the pilot sat. The frame shuddered the way a heart shudders when the surgeon puts the knife in. Gold fibers burst out of the chest in every direction, lashing, whipping, dying. The cockpit's blast glass cracked from the impact point outward in a long slow web, and through the spreading web Cesare could see the man inside.

He was young. He was young the way the contents of a ruin are young when the ruin is old enough. Electrodes bristled out of his spine at every vertebra. The fibers of the weave had come up through the deck plates and into him; he wore them the way a man wears vines that have decided to climb him. The muscles of his face were moving without him. Something was running out of his nose. Something darker was running out of the corner of his mouth.

You — the man in the cockpit was trying to speak. The comm had broken. What came out was not a word.

Cesare drew the sword out.

He stepped back. The Red Dragon set itself on the broken stone and waited. The relic, in his hand, trailed a short afterimage of gold that hung in the air and then was gone. Number One hung on the cleaver, the right leg folded under it, the great frame canted to starboard, the chest wound still breathing out a slow weather of gold dust. From the outside, for the first time, the man inside was fully visible through the cracked glass, and he was a very small thing to be inside so much iron.

In the gallery, the commentator's voice finally came unstuck.

Red Dragon — Red Dragon is on top of Number One! He is — he is taking the joints apart one at a time, this is — I have not — in twenty years of commentating, I have not —

Ye Sulei set the teacup down. His eyes did not leave the screen.

He has won? Princess Jun said, very low.

No, Ye Sulei said. Not yet. Guronoth.

The quarry, as if in answer, began to shake.

Juan Borgia brought the second-generation Prometheus frame in from the flank, six meters of it, the long recurved saw-tooth cleaver almost too wide to fit the gallery it was being swung down. He did not try to swing the blade. He put the whole of the seventy-ton machine into the charge and tried to make the Red Dragon into a bruise.

Three meters against seven. The mass difference was a verdict in itself.

Cesare did not meet it.

The Red Dragon turned faster than a thing its size had any business turning — the essence of the Borgia close-in berserker school, no school at all, no posture, only the shortest line between where the weight was and where it needed to be. He was not in front of the charge. He was beside it. The tail of the superheavy Dragoon back-unit — the part the engineers in New Rome had laughed at, the decorative tail-fin, the part that served no tactical purpose any of them could name — scythed out sideways like an iron whip.

The fin caught Guronoth just above the outside of the right knee.

It was, in its small way, a perfect blow. Not a block. Not a parry. A strike made at the exact point where the forward motion of the charge had to become the forward motion of a fall. The Medici intelligence file on Guronoth's joints was already in Cesare's head, the weak point marked in red. Juan had been certain the speed of his charge would smother any answer. He had been wrong, the way a man is wrong who has never watched a fish.

Guronoth's right knee went fifteen degrees out of true. The upper body of the frame kept going where it had been going, and the lower body had stopped, and the disagreement between the two halves of seventy tons was settled, the only way it could be settled, by the floor of the quarry. The frame went down with a sound like a cathedral being laid on its side. The cleaver left Juan's hand and tumbled, point first, into the scree at the Red Dragon's feet.

Juan's voice, from inside the dead cabin, was a string of curses cut into short syllables by the loss of the comm.

Cesare Borgia — you —

Cesare did not answer.

The Red Dragon turned back to Number One.

Number One had not moved. He was on one knee among the broken stone, the cleaver still in the rock, the chest wound still coughing its slow weather of gold dust. The cracks in the cockpit glass had spread. Through them, the man inside was visible all the way down.

Number One is down! Number One is down! The commentator's voice had given up being a voice and was just sound. Number One is — he is — by every saint in the calendar — Number One is down! The new Seraph squad has won!

The gallery went up around them.

The Minerva engineers were on their feet. Some of them were hugging. Some of them were beating the table with the rolled drawings they had been working from two hours before. The foreign delegations, in their boxes, were on their feet as well — Charlemagne, the Yenisei, Byzantium — and the room was a forest of moving hands. Some of the faces were startled. Some of the faces were already going careful, working out what this would cost them.

We won, Alfonso said, from somewhere on a stone wall. He had sat down on it without meaning to. We won.

In the command platform at the heart of the Curia, Spencer let out a long breath. His shirt was wet through. The hand that had been locked on his crosier for the last six minutes opened, finger by finger, as if he had forgotten he had a body.

Your Holiness. The Red Dragon has won.

Pope Leon Borgia stood a little way in front of him, very still, paler than his office. He inclined his head. The small movement was supposed to be the beginning of a sentence.

A cough took him instead.

It went through him the way a wave goes through a thin wall. The green tablet he had been carrying in his sleeve slid out and fell, bounced twice on the marble, broke in two. Spencer's hand was on his arm at once. The Pope lifted the other hand to say he was all right, and the fingers came away from his mouth with a dark color between them.

I am well, the Pope said, in a voice that had been scraped out of him. I am well.

Spencer did not say anything. He put the folded square of linen into his hand, the way a man puts a coin into a hand he knows will not give it back.

In the quarry, the Red Dragon turned slowly.

The light on the Excalibur remnant was dimming. The heat at the back of his neck was settling back to its working temperature, the chip in his third vertebra keeping its quiet watch. The violet-gold sigils in his eyes had not gone away, but the pulse in them had slowed to the rate of a sleeping man's breath.

In his mind's eye, the lotuses were still there.

The roots in the silt, the petals in the wind, and the old voice laid over them, like a hand laid over a hand.

Use what we have given you, to keep safe the people you have chosen to keep safe.

Boss — Alfonso's voice came back on the channel, and there was a new note under it, the note of a man who has just remembered a thing he had managed to forget. Boss. Number One —

Cesare's eyes came back to the ruined frame.

The third-generation prototype Prometheus had not moved. It was on one knee in the broken stone, the great cleaver propping it up, the chest wound still breathing out its slow weather of gold. The cracked cockpit was a spider's web of white fracture lines. Through them, the man inside was quiet now, in the way a man is quiet when he has stopped fighting the thing that is killing him.

Everything, by every reasonable measure, was finished.

Cesare's fingers, very slowly, tightened on the hilt of the broken sword.

Because the door of the cockpit — the door of Number One's cockpit — was beginning to open.

第177章 黄金血液的失控
