【中文】
第177章 黄金血液的失控

骑士舱的舱门缓缓开启。

不是被撬开的，不是被撞开的，是从内部打开的。那些被红龙圣剑碎片劈出的裂缝扭曲了门框的形状，金属边缘向外翻卷，像是某种巨大的花。液压杆已经损坏，舱门只开了三分之一的宽度就卡住了，暗金色的光粉从缝隙中涌出。

然后一只手从里面伸了出来。

那只手比正常人大了将近一倍，灰白色，不是皮肤的颜色，而是某种金属与血肉混合后的质感。指节处长出了暗金色的鳞片状突起，关节处的皮肤裂开，露出底下流淌着金红色液体的组织。手指扣住舱门边缘，金属在指尖下被捏得变形。

各国使团的VIP包厢里有人倒吸了一口冷气。

"那是什么东西？"有人低声说。

一号骑士从骑士舱里爬了出来。

他的甲胄已经碎裂了大半，胸甲的右半边完全缺失，露出底下的驾驶服——不，那已经不能叫驾驶服了。驾驶服的布料被某种力量从内部撑破，金红色的液体浸透了残余的纤维，顺着他的躯干和四肢向下流淌。那液体不是红色，偏向黄金，带着一种灼热的荧光质感，在维苏威火山底部暗淡的光线中显得异常刺目。

他的脸暴露在空气中。

那张脸年轻得出奇，也许只有二十岁，五官端正，甚至算得上清秀。但此刻那张脸上的表情已经消失了，取而代之的是一种近乎空白的宁静。他浑身是血，金红色的液体从他的眼角、鼻腔、嘴角和耳道同时溢出，像是全身所有的黏膜都在渗出这种东西。

他的眼睛变了。

原本是什么颜色已经看不清了，虹膜和瞳孔都被一种翡翠般的绿色覆盖。那种绿不像是生物体应有的颜色，更接近某种矿石或宝石的色泽，深邃、冰冷、带着不属于人间的光泽。翡翠色的眼睛直直地望向正前方，没有焦距。

然后他开口了。

那不是人类的声音。喉咙里发出的音节低沉、浑浊，像是从地底深处传来的回响，断断续续，却带着某种可怕的韵律。不是任何一种已知的语言——不是拉丁语，不是希腊语，不是德语，不是法语，不是东方方言。那些音节古老得像是史前的遗物，每一声都像是在敲击教堂的丧钟。

主观测厅里瞬间死寂了半秒。

"异端！"

有人尖叫起来，来自叶尼塞使团的VIP包厢，一位穿着绣金礼服的老人跌坐在椅子上，手指颤抖地指向采石场中央的屏幕，"异端！那不是人类的语言！"

"怪物！"另一个声音从查理曼使团的包厢中炸开，一个年轻贵族把手中的高脚杯摔碎在地上，玻璃碎片溅了一地，"那是……那是红水银感染的症状！他在自燃！"

采石场中，一号骑士还在念着那些无人能懂的祷文。他已经彻底从驾驶舱中爬了出来，站在半跪的试制机肩甲上，金红色的液体从他的脚下开始蔓延，沿着暗金色的装甲板向下流淌，像是某种有生命的颜料。那些血液接触到甲胄表面的金属时，发出轻微的嘶嘶声，金属表面竟然被腐蚀出了细密的纹路。

叶素理站在密涅瓦机关高层技术人员的通道里。

他的手很稳。没有人注意到这位中山国外交大臣在什么时候从包厢里走了出来，混入了通向外围疏散区的走廊。他举着一只精巧的微型相机，镜头对准了采石场上方悬浮的实时投影屏幕。相机快门的声音被周围的喧哗完全掩盖。

咔嚓。

金红色血液从骑士眼角溢出的特写。

咔嚓。

翡翠色瞳孔放大到极致的特写。

咔嚓。

那张年轻却已经完全失去人类表情的脸。

叶素理的表情很平静，但他的瞳孔深处有什么东西在燃烧。他收起相机，将其塞入外套内袋的夹层中，动作熟练得像是做过无数次。

三楼的VIP包厢里，一个戴着银色猫头鹰面具的身影端坐在天鹅绒座椅上。面具遮挡了他的全部面容，只露出下颌和嘴唇，嘴角的弧度冰冷而精确。

"时机到了。"

他低声说，声音被面具的回音结构扭曲成一种金属质感的耳语。

在他身后两步远的地方，另一道身影——同样戴着面具，穿着深红色枢机袍服——伸出右手，手指落在座椅扶手侧面一个不起眼的凸起上，轻轻按下。

按钮沉入。

三楼的灯光闪烁了一下。

　　* * *

西泽尔站在碎石中，距离一号的残骸不过二十步。

他看到了一号骑士从舱中爬出来的全过程。他的手指还扣在Excalibur残刃的剑柄上，指节发白。

不对劲。

非常不对劲。

那个金红色的液体不是普通的血液。它在发光，在流淌，在腐蚀金属。那双翡翠色的眼睛也不对，那不是人类应有的瞳孔颜色。而那些祷文……

西泽尔的后颈忽然一热。

不是黄金套管发烫的那种热，而是一种从脊椎深处向外扩散的、带着酸涩感的灼烧。视线的边缘开始模糊，一帧帧画面在他的意识深处闪过——

莲花池。

残枝的意识。

"快走！"

那个声音不是西泽尔自己的。它从红水银深处涌来，带着一种古老的、颤抖的紧迫感。那个声音从未如此急切过——这个沉睡了不知多少年的意识在恐惧。

"他要引爆自己！"

西泽尔的瞳孔骤然收缩。

他刚要后退——

一号骑士动了。

没有预备动作，没有助跑，没有任何人类战士应有的战术准备。一号骑士从试制机肩甲上直接跳了下来，七米多高的距离，他像一块陨石一样砸向地面，碎石灰飞溅，落地的瞬间双脚踩出一个浅坑。

然后他扑向西泽尔。

速度极快。快到西泽尔的动态视觉几乎无法捕捉他的运动轨迹——那不是人体能爆发出的速度，是欧米茄自愈神经纤维将他的脊髓信号增幅到了某种极限后的产物。空气被他奔跑时卷起的气流撕裂，发出尖锐的呼啸。

西泽尔举剑。

Excalibur残刃横在胸前，剑身上残留的圣光还没有完全消退，金色的微光在刃口上跳动。一号骑士的拳头砸了下来，目标是西泽尔的头颅。

拳头撞击在剑身上。

轰！

那股力量从剑身传到西泽尔的手臂，再传到肩膀，再传到整个身体。红龙甲胄的脚跟在碎石地面上向后滑出半米，胸甲的共鸣腔发出刺耳的金属摩擦声。西泽尔的手指在剑柄上几乎要脱臼，关节被震得发麻。

一号骑士的力气太大了。

这不是正常骑士应该有的力量。即使植入了欧米茄的自愈神经纤维，即使神经信号被增幅到了极限，纯粹的力量输出也不可能达到这种程度。唯一的解释是那些金红色的血液——那些从全身黏膜渗出的、带有腐蚀性的黄金血液——在某种程度上强化了他所有的生理机能。

一号骑士没有停。

他的第二拳紧跟着砸下来，和第一拳之间只隔了零点几秒。西泽尔侧身闪避，拳头擦着红龙甲胄的头部掠过，拳风在面甲上刮出一道浅痕。

第三拳。

第四拳。

第五拳。

西泽尔连续后退，Excalibur残刃勉强招架。每一拳的力道都让他整条手臂发麻，剑柄上的皮革已经被汗水浸透。他的紫瞳金纹在跳动——不是之前激活不朽之王模式时那种狂乱的闪烁，而是快速的、警觉的脉动，像某种生物在感知到危险时的本能反应。

一号骑士的眼睛锁定了西泽尔。

那双翡翠色的瞳孔里没有任何情感——没有愤怒，没有恐惧，没有杀意，只有一种空洞的、被某种东西彻底占据了的专注。嘴唇还在开合，那些无人能懂的祷文没有中断过一秒。

他举起双拳，蓄力。

这一次西泽尔看清了。一号骑士的双拳表面已经被金红色的血液完全覆盖，那些血液在他出拳之前就开始发光，像是某种预热的燃料。

"让开！"

一个声音从侧面传来，伴随着沉重的蒸汽喷射声。

一道白色的人影从战场的边缘高速切入。她的身形比常规甲胄小了不止一号——那是神怒Ⅲ型改装甲胄的外骨骼版本，没有完整的全身装甲板，只有躯干和四肢的关键部位覆盖了加固的影金属板，甲胄的关节处裸露着银色的液压传动机构。她手中举着一柄巨大的破甲锤，锤头是实心硬金锻造的六角棱柱，重量超过两百磅。

瓦莲京娜·罗曼诺夫。

她从斜后方高速接近一号骑士，破甲锤在空中划出一道弧线，锤头带着撕裂空气的尖啸砸向一号骑士的后背。

正中。

沉闷的金属撞击声在采石场中回荡。破甲锤的六角棱柱实打实地撞上了一号骑士的脊椎——那是人体最脆弱的要害之一，即使穿着甲胄也足以让任何骑士当场失去行动能力。

一号骑士的身体只是向前踉跄了一步。

他甚至没有回头。

瓦莲京娜的瞳孔在面甲后面收缩。破甲锤击中目标的瞬间，她的双手感觉到了一种完全不对的触感——不是撞击人体的沉闷，而是撞上了某种密度远超金属的、带有弹性的硬物。那些金红色的血液似乎在冲击点凝聚成了某种保护层，将她全力一击的力量完全吸收了。

一号骑士转过身来。

翡翠色的瞳孔落在瓦莲京娜身上。

他没有说话。祷文还在继续，但那双眼睛已经不再看西泽尔了。他看着瓦莲京娜，视线像两把冰冷的手术刀，要把她从头到脚剖开。

然后他扑向了她。

瓦莲京娜收锤格挡，一号骑士的拳头砸在破甲锤的锤杆上，金属的嗡鸣声在空气中炸开。她的双臂在那一击下几乎失去了知觉，神怒Ⅲ型外骨骼的液压系统发出过载的嘶嘶声。紧接着第二拳又到了，她只能侧身闪避，拳风擦着她的肩膀掠过，把外骨骼上的一块影金属护板直接掀飞了出去。

第三拳直奔她的面甲。

瓦莲京娜的身体已经来不及做出任何反应。那只覆盖着金红色血液的拳头在她的视野中急剧放大，死亡的预感像冰水一样从她的头顶浇了下来——

一只手从侧面猛地推了她一把。

巨大的力量让瓦莲京娜整个人向侧面飞出了三米多，滚落在碎石中。她抬起头，看到红龙甲胄挡在了她原本站立的位置上。

一号骑士的拳头砸在了红龙的胸甲上。

这一拳没有打在Excalibur残刃上，而是直接命中了红龙甲胄正面的装甲板。圣剑碎片嵌入的位置传来一阵剧烈的高温震荡，碎片本身发出嗡鸣声，紫色的光从碎片与装甲板的缝隙中渗出。一号骑士的拳头在胸甲表面砸出一个清晰的凹痕，紧接着第二拳又到了，红龙向后踉跄。

第三拳。

第四拳。

红龙被逼得连续后退，每一步都在碎石地面上留下深深的脚印。瓦莲京娜想爬起来，但一号骑士的每一拳都带起的气浪让她无法站稳。

第五拳落下时，一号骑士的拳头和红龙胸甲的距离归零。

西泽尔被一号骑士扑倒在地。

巨大的身躯压在他身上，那双翡翠色的眼睛近在咫尺，嘴巴还在念着祷文。金红色的血液从一号的嘴角滴落，一滴，两滴，落在红龙的面甲上，顺着面甲的弧面向下流淌，最终滑进了面甲和颈部装甲的缝隙。

有一滴落进了西泽尔的眼睛。

灼热。

像是被熔化的金属溅到了一样灼热。西泽尔感到自己的左眼视野瞬间变成了一片金红色，那滴黄金血液沿着眼球表面扩散，接触到虹膜边缘时，他的紫瞳中金红色的纹路突然变得异常明亮——不是之前那种随心跳跳动的脉动，而是一种持续的、几乎要溢出的光。

后颈的黄金套管烫得像要烧穿皮肤。

视线的边缘，莲花池的画面残影在剧烈闪烁。

"走！离开他！他的红水银核心在共振！"

残枝的声音几乎是在尖叫了。

"他不是要杀你！他在变成炸弹！"

西泽尔拼尽全身力气推开了压在身上的躯体。红龙甲胄的液压系统全功率输出，他的双手扣住一号骑士的肩膀，腿部推进器同时点火——两个人从纠缠中分开，西泽尔借着推进器的反冲力向后滑出了十几米远。

一号骑士重新站了起来。

他站在碎石中，双臂垂在身侧，翡翠色的眼睛低垂着看向自己的胸口。

胸甲已经碎裂了大半。裸露出来的不是驾驶服，而是一团暗红色的、跳动的、像是心脏一样搏动着的球状结构。

那团球状结构在发光。

不是金色，不是暗金色——是红色。一种深沉的、浓郁的、像是浓稠的血液一样的暗红色。光的亮度在不断攀升，从暗红到正红，从正红到亮红。

红水银核心。

它在共振。在和那些金红色的血液共振。在和一号骑士体内被欧米茄自愈神经纤维改造过的每一个细胞共振。它在积蓄能量。

在准备引爆。

"不……"西泽尔的声音从面甲后面传出来，沙哑得像是砂纸摩擦，"不！所有人撤出——"

主观测厅的屏幕上，采石场的实时画面已经变成了以一号骑士为中心的红色警报。工程师们从座位上弹起来，有人按下了紧急疏散的按钮，警报声在密涅瓦机关的每一层走廊中炸响。

叶尼塞使团的包厢里，瓦伦京娜的父亲——叶尼塞特使——猛地站了起来，脸色铁青。

查理曼使团的包厢里，高文少爷端着酒杯的手顿住了，酒液从杯沿溢出。

"圣痕之血……"一个来自美第奇家族的老商人从座位上跌坐下来，声音发颤，"那是圣痕之血！红水银和生物体液混合后产生的特殊沉淀！只有炽天使甲胄神经接驳系统超载爆裂时才会产生！"

"每一滴都意味着一次致命的神经反噬……"另一个人接话，声音里带着不可遏制的恐惧，"他全身都是……他全身都是圣痕之血！"

三楼的VIP包厢里，戴着银色猫头鹰面具的身影缓缓站起身。

"退后。"他对手下说。

包厢的暗门在几秒钟内打开又关闭，那个身影消失在密道中。

同一时刻。

维苏威火山山腰的救护车里，佛朗哥教授从昏迷中猛地睁开了眼睛。

他的胸腔剧烈起伏，氧气面罩从脸上滑落。心电监护仪发出急促的蜂鸣声，医务人员立刻围了上来，但他一把推开了那个试图按住他肩膀的年轻护士。

"屏幕！"他的声音嘶哑得几乎听不清，"给我看屏幕！"

一个助手慌忙把便携式投影屏幕转到了他面前。

佛朗哥看到了那个画面。

站在碎石中的一号骑士，胸口的暗红色光球已经亮到了让周围十米内的碎石都在反射红光的地步。

"快走！"

佛朗哥的声音撕裂了整辆救护车里的空气，嘶哑、尖锐、带着一种绝望的力度。

"他要引爆红水银核心！所有人快走！核心的爆炸当量足以把整个矿道——"

他的话没有说完。

因为屏幕上的红光在这一刻达到了峰值。

一号骑士的胸口发出一道耀眼的红光——

红水银核心开始引爆。

【English】
Chapter 177 — The Runaway of the Golden Blood

The cockpit hatch began to open.

It was not forced, not struck loose. It opened from the inside. The seams cut into the frame by the broken blade of the Red Dragon's holy sword had warped the metal into something that resembled the petals of an enormous iron flower, curling outward. The hydraulic arm had failed, so the hatch lodged half-open, and through the gap a fine dust of dark gold poured like pollen in a slant of light.

Then a hand came through the gap.

The hand was nearly twice the size of a normal man's. Grey-white in color, the grey of ash rather than skin, the texture somewhere between flesh and forged metal. Along the knuckles, plates of dark gold had pushed up through the dermis like scales. The skin had split at the joints, and what lay beneath was a tissue that wept a gold-and-red liquid, almost luminous, almost molten.

The hand closed on the edge of the hatch. The metal of the frame dimpled inward under the fingers as though it were wet clay.

Somewhere in the VIP gallery a member of one of the visiting delegations drew a sharp breath.

"What in God's name—"

"Quiet."

The first knight pulled himself out of the cockpit.

Half his armor was gone. The right side of the cuirass had been sheared away, exposing what lay beneath—the driving suit. Only it could no longer be called a suit. Whatever had been done to him inside that coffin of steel had burst the fabric from within, and the shredded remnants of the liner hung from his torso and limbs like wet paper, soaked through with the gold-red fluid that ran from him in a slow, continuous curtain. The color was wrong for blood. It was closer to gold, with a hot fluorescence at its heart, and in the dim air of the quarry floor it looked almost like a flame that had learned to crawl.

His face was bare to the air.

The face was young—shockingly young. Twenty, perhaps. The features were even, almost handsome. But whatever expression had once lived there had been wiped clean, replaced by a kind of blank, ecclesiastical stillness. He was drenched in the gold-red liquid. It ran from the inner corners of his eyes, from the margins of his nostrils, from the corners of his mouth, from the canals of both ears, as though every mucous membrane in his skull were weeping the same substance.

His eyes were no longer human.

Whatever their original color, it could no longer be read. Iris and pupil had both been swallowed by an emerald, the green of certain gemstones, deep and cold, with a polish that belonged to no living thing. The eyes were fixed on a point in middle distance, or perhaps on nothing at all.

Then he began to speak.

It was not a human voice. The syllables that rose out of his throat were low, muddy, the way sound travels when it comes from the bottom of a well—broken, heavy, but patterned, as though they were the words of a liturgy no one present had ever been taught. Not Latin. Not Greek. Not Frankish. Not any of the eastern patois. The phonemes were older than any of them, older than the empire in the West, older perhaps than the Creed. Every syllable struck the listening air with the slow, funereal authority of a cathedral bell.

For half a heartbeat the observation deck above the quarry was perfectly silent.

"Heretic!"

The scream came from the Yenisei delegation's box. An old man in a gold-embroidered coat had half-fallen into his chair, one trembling finger leveled at the great projection screen above the pit. "Heretic! That is no human tongue!"

"Monster!" Another voice, sharper and younger, from the Charlemagne box. A young noble had hurled his wineglass to the floor; the crystal broke with the brittle sound of splintered ice. "That is quicksilver contamination! He is burning from within!"

In the pit itself, the first knight was still reciting. He had clambered fully out of the cockpit and was now standing, somehow upright, on the shoulder pauldron of the ruined trial mech, the gold-red blood pooling at his feet and beginning to creep down the dark gold of the armor plate. Where the blood touched the metal it made a faint, sibilant sound, the way fat hisses in a pan, and the surface beneath it began to pit and craze with delicate filigree marks, as though the metal were being eaten.

---

Yessuli stood in the high technicians' corridor of the Minerva Order.

His hand was steady. No one had noticed the foreign minister of Zhongshan slip from his box and into the passage that led out toward the emergency perimeter. He held a small, finely made microcamera at arm's length, its lens centered on the floating projection screen above the quarry. The sound of the shutter was swallowed whole by the shouting that filled the corridors.

Click. A close image of the gold-red fluid weeping from the knight's eye.

Click. A close image of the emerald pupil, blown wide.

Click. The young, emptied face.

Yessuli's expression was neutral. Something burned far back in his eyes. He slid the camera into a hidden inner pocket of his coat with the practiced ease of a man who had done so a thousand times before.

On the third floor, in one of the VIP boxes, a figure sat back in a velvet chair wearing a mask of silver shaped like an owl's face. The mask covered everything but the jaw and the mouth, and the mouth, where it could be seen, was set in a small, precise, bloodless curve.

"Now," the figure said, very softly. The mask's echo-chamber turned the word into a thin metallic whisper.

Two paces behind, a second figure, similarly masked, this one dressed in the deep red robes of a cardinal, reached out and laid two fingers against a small, inconspicuous boss on the side of the chair's armrest. He pressed.

The boss sank.

The lights on the third floor flickered once.

---

* * *

Cesare stood in the broken stone, twenty paces from the ruin of the trial mech. His fingers were still locked on the hilt of the broken Excalibur. The knuckles of his gauntlets had gone white.

Something was very wrong.

The gold-red liquid was not blood. It moved wrong; it had weight and a faint luminance of its own; it was eating the armor it touched. The emerald of the eyes was not a color he had ever seen on a living man, and the language—

Heat ran up the back of his neck.

Not the dry heat of the golden sleeve warming. A different heat, rising from somewhere in the base of his spine, spreading outward, and with it a sour, astringent burn that prickled along the inside of his skull. The edges of his sight began to blur, and in the blur, frames of memory began to flicker across his mind—

The lotus pool.

The voice of Canzhi.

"Go."

The voice was not his own. It came up from somewhere deep in the column of quicksilver that was his inheritance, ancient, unsteady, and now, for the first time in the years he had carried it, frightened.

"He is going to detonate himself."

Cesare's pupils contracted.

He was already beginning to step back when the first knight moved.

There was no preparation. No crouch, no gathering of the legs, no warning of any kind that a trained duelist would have read. The knight simply stepped off the seven-meter pauldron and fell. He struck the broken stone floor with a sound like a dropped anvil, the impact blowing a small crater of dust and gravel into the air, and was already running.

The speed was inhuman.

Cesare's eyes, augmented by every enhancement the Order had ever wired into him, could barely track the moving shape. The Omega self-healing nerve fibers had amplified the knight's spinal signals to a level no organic system was meant to carry, and the body answered with a velocity that simply should not have been possible. The displaced air cracked behind him, leaving a thin, white line of shock in the dust.

Cesare raised the broken sword.

He got it across his body in time. The first knight's fist came down like a dropped hammer, and the blow met the blade just above the crossguard.

The force of the impact ran up the steel and into his wrists, into his shoulders, into the arch of his back. The Red Dragon's feet slid backward through the gravel for half a meter. The resonance chamber in the breastplate let out a thin, shrieking howl of metal on metal. His fingers tried to come loose of the hilt. The joints of his hands went numb to the wrist.

The strength was not sane.

Even with Omega nerve augmentation, even with every enhancement the Empire had ever authorized, raw power at this level should not have existed inside a human frame. There was only one explanation: the gold-red blood itself, the strange fluid that wept from every membrane of the knight's body, was doing something to the muscles it touched. The tissue was not just being fed. It was being driven.

The second blow came a fraction of a second after the first.

Cesare twisted sideways. The fist passed a finger's width from the side of the Red Dragon's helm, and the wind of it scored a long, shallow scratch across the faceplate.

A third. A fourth. A fifth.

He gave ground, the broken Excalibur in a high guard, absorbing what he could, deflecting what he could not. Each impact deadened his arm from shoulder to fingertip. The leather of the hilt was soaked through with sweat. The violet sigils traced in gold across the lenses of his helm were pulsing—quickly, alertly, the way the heart of a cornered animal pulses when it knows there is nowhere else to go.

The emerald eyes found him.

There was nothing in them. No anger, no fear, no hatred, no pleasure in killing. Only a kind of absolute, occupied attention, the focus of a thing that has been wholly given over to something else. The lips of the knight were still moving, still shaping those untranslatable syllables without a pause. The liturgy did not stop.

The knight raised both fists. The gold-red blood that coated them began, in the half-second before the blow, to glow.

"Out of the way!"

The voice came from the flank, and with it the heavy, wet bark of a steam vent cycling. A white figure cut in at the edge of the pit at high speed, moving on the auxiliary thrust of a small steam engine. The frame was smaller than a standard suit, a stripped-down exoskeleton version of the Wrath-of-God Mark III—no full plating, only a fitted shell of shadow-metal over the vital areas of the torso and limbs, with the silver of the hydraulic lines exposed at every joint. The figure was carrying, in both hands, a sledgehammer the size of a man's torso, its head a solid six-sided prism of hard-gold, weighing in at over two hundred pounds.

Valentina Romanova.

She came in from the knight's rear quarter, the hammer rising in a high arc, and brought it down across the line of the first knight's spine.

A clean hit.

The sound of it rolled across the quarry like a struck drum. The prism of the head met the body in the exact center of the back, between the shoulder blades, where the spinal cord lay. Against any knight in any suit, the blow should have ended the fight in an instant.

The knight took a single half-step forward.

He did not even turn his head.

Behind the faceplate of her own helm, Valentina's pupils shrank to pinpoints. Her hands remembered something her eyes had not yet been able to name. The feeling of the impact had been wrong. She had not struck flesh, not even struck steel. She had struck a thing whose density was somewhere above that of metal and whose surface had a kind of elastic give, as though the gold-red blood had gathered at the moment of contact and built itself into a shell that simply took the force and gave none of it back.

The knight turned.

The emerald eyes found her.

He did not speak. The syllables continued, but the eyes had left Cesare. They were on her now, and they regarded her with the flat, clinical attention of a surgeon deciding where to make the first cut.

Then he moved toward her.

Valentina brought the hammer up into a guard. His first fist met the shaft of the hammer with a crack of metal on metal, the sound rolling out across the pit like a struck bell. The shock ran the length of the wooden handle and into her shoulders, and the hydraulic lines of her exoskeleton screamed as the system tried to bleed off the overload. The second fist she managed to twist out of the way, taking the edge of it across her left shoulder; the strike tore a plate of the shadow-metal clean off her frame and sent it spinning into the gravel.

The third fist was aimed at her face.

There was no time. Her body had nothing left to give. The fist came at her, growing in her vision, and the knowledge of what was about to happen reached her half a second before the fist did, cold and absolute—

A hand caught her by the shoulder and threw her.

The force of it lifted her clear of the gravel and put her down three meters away, rolling. When she raised her head, the Red Dragon was standing in the place she had been.

The first knight's fist met the Red Dragon's breastplate.

The blow did not land on the broken Excalibur. It landed on the main plate of the cuirass, square in the center of the chest. The setting that held the holy-sword fragment sang at the impact, a high thin note of tortured metal, and a wash of violet light leaked from the seam between the fragment and the plate. The metal dimpled inward, a clear, round depression the size of a fist. The second blow arrived almost before the first had finished. The Red Dragon stepped backward. The third. The fourth. Each step left a deep, sharp imprint in the broken stone.

Valentina tried to rise. The wind of each strike kept her down.

The fifth blow landed with the knight's fist flush against the Red Dragon's chest.

Cesare went over backward.

The weight of the other body came down on top of him. The emerald eyes were inches from his face. The lips were still moving, the syllables still rising, and the gold-red blood that was weeping from the knight's mouth fell, drop by drop, onto the faceplate of the Red Dragon. It traced the curve of the metal and began, slowly, to find its way toward the gap at the neck.

One drop, carried by gravity, fell through the slit of the visor and into Cesare's left eye.

The world became heat.

It was the heat of a single drop of molten metal. The drop spread across the surface of the eye, and where it touched the rim of the iris, the violet sigils in the lenses of the helm flared in a way he had not seen before—not the slow, heartbeat pulse of the immortal-king mode, but a continuous, almost overflowing radiance, as if something in his blood had recognized the intruder and were trying to answer it.

The golden sleeve at the back of his neck was no longer hot. It was trying to burn its way out through his skin.

At the edge of his sight, the lotus pool was strobing.

"Go," Canzhi's voice screamed, "get away from him. His core is in resonance. He is not trying to kill you. He is becoming a bomb."

Cesare planted both hands against the shoulders of the body on top of him. He opened the hydraulic system of the Red Dragon to full power. The leg thrusters fired at the same instant. The two of them came apart, and the recoil of the thrusters threw him backward across the broken stone, ten meters, fifteen, until he fetched up against the tilted flank of a fallen pillar.

The first knight rose.

He stood in the gravel, arms loose at his sides, and looked down at his own chest.

Most of his cuirass was gone. What was exposed was not the driving suit. It was a structure. A dark red, pulsing, almost spherical thing set in the center of his torso, beating with a rhythm that was not the rhythm of a human heart, but something slower, something with a tide of its own.

The thing was beginning to glow.

Not gold. Not the gold of the blood. A deeper red, the red of old wine, the red of coagulated blood held to a candle. The brightness climbed. Dark red to red. Red to a hot, almost living red.

The quicksilver core.

It was in resonance. It was resonating with the gold-red blood in the knight's veins. It was resonating with every cell in the knight's body that the Omega nerve fibers had rewritten. It was gathering itself. It was preparing to give back.

"No," Cesare heard himself say, and his voice through the helm sounded like sandpaper dragged across stone. "No. Everyone out—evacuate—"

On the great screen above the pit, the tactical display had become a single red field centered on the knight. Engineers were on their feet. Someone had thrown the master emergency. Klaxons began to wail in every corridor of the Minerva Order, their tone rising and falling in the rhythm of a fire alarm.

In the Yenisei box, Valentina's father was on his feet, the color gone from his face.

In the Charlemagne box, the young Lord Gawain had stopped in the middle of lifting his glass. The wine was running over the rim and falling unnoticed onto the floor.

"It is the blood of the holy stigmata," an old man in the Medici entourage had half-fallen back into his chair. His voice shook. "The precipitate that forms when quicksilver meets the body's own fluids. It is what the Seraph's neural interface produces when the connection is overloaded. It only ever appears when the wearer is dying."

"Every drop of it is a death in itself," said another voice, from somewhere behind him. The words were almost lost in the noise. "He is carrying it in every vein. He is the wound."

In the third-floor box, the figure in the silver owl mask rose slowly to his feet.

"Back," he said to the man behind him.

The hidden door of the box opened and closed again. The figure was gone.

At the same moment, on the middle slope of Vesuvius, in the rear cabin of a field ambulance, Professor Franco's eyes snapped open.

His chest heaved. The oxygen mask slid from his face. The monitor at his side began to scream, the green of the trace spiking into a series of jagged peaks. The medics around him lunged forward, and the youngest of them put a hand on his shoulder to press him back down.

He flung the hand off.

"The screen," he said. The words were barely a sound, more a tearing of the throat. "The screen. Turn it around."

An aide swung the portable projector on its mount until the image faced him.

Franco saw it.

The first knight, standing in the gravel. The dark red sphere in the center of his chest, now bright enough to throw a red wash across the broken stone for ten meters in every direction.

"Get them out," Franco screamed, and his voice tore the inside of the ambulance. "Get everyone out. The core is going to blow. The yield of that detonation will level the whole—"

He did not finish the sentence.

On the screen, the red reached its peak.

【中文】
第178章 炼狱之上的红莲之翼

红光达到了峰值。

维苏威火山底部废弃矿道里，碎石在红光中浮动起来，仿佛失重。一号骑士的胸口像是嵌了一颗正在坍缩的微型太阳，暗红色的光球骤然膨胀到了极限，裂纹从核心蔓延到胸甲，滚烫的红水银液顺着钢钉拼合的甲缝淌下来，滴在碎石上，碎石瞬间被烧成红热的玻璃珠。

西泽尔站在碎石堆中，距离一号骑士不到三十米。

他的龙牙剑断了，右手还握着那截断茬，断茬的断面在红光中反射着暗淡的银光。他的左手攥着从红龙胸甲中撬出的圣剑碎片，碎片发出灼热的金色脉动，温度高得几乎要烫穿手套。

瓦莲京娜被击飞后靠在一根断裂的石柱旁，嘴角挂着血痕，但还站着。她的改装神怒Ⅲ型甲胄右肩装甲被撕开了一大片，露出下面冒烟的关节结构。塔拉夏缩在她身后的碎石堆后，双手抱着脑袋，脸色惨白。

昆提良仰面倒在十米外，奥古斯都的秘银重盾碎成了三块，散落在他身侧。唐璜的蔷薇之鬼右臂被自愈神经纤维绞断，鲜血和润滑液混在一起从断口处不断涌出。阿方索倒在更远的地方，蜘蛛巢腕表碎裂，额头磕在石头上，血流进了眼睛。

三台试制机，全部失去了战力。

三个旧部，全部昏迷。

西泽尔看了一眼一号骑士胸口那颗膨胀到极限的红水银核心。

三秒。

也许只有两秒。

他的后颈黄金套管发烫了——不是计划二三五适配款那种温和的温度，而是仿佛有一根烧红的铁针沿着脊椎刺入颅腔。那是圣剑碎片与他锡兰星见血脉的共鸣，是世界树残枝01号沉入红水银深处的意识在回应他。

他的紫瞳亮了。

金色纹路从瞳孔中央向虹膜边缘蔓延，像是有人在紫色的琉璃里注入了熔化的金水。心跳声在他耳膜里轰鸣，每一跳都沉重如铁锤砸在铁砧上。

不朽之王系统。

安全阈值：三分钟。

超过三分钟，芯片过载。超过五分钟，永久失去身体控制权。超过八分钟，被英雄人格彻底吞噬。

三分钟。

他用三分钟护住所有人，然后他就会倒下去。

西泽尔握紧了左手的圣剑碎片，碎片上的金色光芒沿着他手背的血管向手臂蔓延，灼热的痛觉像是被滚水浇过。他没有犹豫。

"Rex Immortalis。"

他用那种平静到近乎空洞的声音念出了密码。

红龙甲胄的双眼重新亮起来。

不是之前那种清醒而克制的光——是金红色的、灼热的、仿佛把太阳塞进了眼眶的暴走之光。甲胄全身的铆钉同时发出金属膨胀的咯吱声，背部龙骑兵套装的六组排气阀全部弹开，蒸汽从每一条缝隙中喷涌而出，浓白色的蒸汽柱在红光中染成了金红色。

然后是翅膀。

那不是真正的翅膀——红龙甲胄没有翼装结构，没有飞行动力——那是蒸汽在极限压力下从甲胄肩部两组临时弹出的辅助喷射口中喷出，被圣剑碎片的金色光芒和红水银核心的暗红色光照亮，在半空中凝结成的两片扇形气幕。每一组喷射口各有十二个喷孔，排列成莲花花瓣的形状，喷出的蒸汽速度接近音速，凝结成一米多长的金红色光翼。

红莲之翼。

它不稳定，边缘不断地碎裂又重新凝结，像是随时会熄灭的火焰，又像是黎明前最浓重的夜色里挣扎着绽放的最后一朵花。

但它展开着。

西泽尔动了。

不朽之王模式下的速度已经超出了人类神经系统的正常反应极限——他不是"跑"过去的，他是以一种近乎瞬移的方式出现在了昆提良身边。他单手抓住奥古斯都的肩甲，把这个体重超过一百五十公斤的骑士连人带甲胄拎了起来，甩到自己背上；然后是唐璜——蔷薇之鬼的断臂还在流血，他把唐璜的腰带扣抓住，拖到右臂下方；最后是阿方索，他弯腰把这个混血数学家扛在左肩上，阿方索的碎裂的蜘蛛巢腕表磕在他的肩甲上，发出清脆的金属碎裂声。

三个昏迷的旧部，全部在他身上。

重量超过了三百公斤。

但此刻的西泽尔感觉不到重量——不朽之王系统把疼痛、疲劳和恐惧全部屏蔽了，他的身体变成了纯粹的机械。

"瓦莲京娜！"

他的声音穿透了矿道里隆隆的震动。

"带塔拉夏！暗河入口！跑！"

瓦莲京娜没有犹豫。她一把抓住塔拉夏的手腕，拖着这个吓坏了的年轻机械师向矿道深处的方向冲去。改装神怒Ⅲ型甲胄的右肩冒着白烟，但叶尼塞公主跑得比蒸汽驱动的机械还快，金色长发在身后飘成一面旗。

她信任他。

就像她把剑交给他的时候那样——没有废话，转身就走。

红莲之翼在头顶完全展开。

两片金红色的光翼向前合拢，把西泽尔和三个昏迷的旧部包裹在一层半透明的蒸汽茧中。蒸汽茧的厚度不到十厘米，但它以接近音速的速度在流动，形成了一道高温高压的气幕屏障。

一号骑士的红水银核心在这一刻引爆了。

没有声音。

或者说，声音太大了，大到超过了人类耳朵能接收的频率，变成了一种无声的、纯粹的暴力。一道纯白色的光柱从一号骑士的胸口冲天而起，直径超过三米，矿道的顶部被瞬间汽化，碎石、金属、蒸汽管道全部在白光中化为飞散的粒子。

冲击波紧随其后。

它以肉眼可见的速度——一道翻涌的灰白色气浪——向四面八方扩散，所过之处，矿道的石壁像饼干一样碎裂，支撑用的铁柱被扭成了麻花形状，碎石被卷上半空又被气浪压成齑粉。

冲击波撞上了红莲之翼。

西泽尔感觉到了——红莲之翼的左翼边缘在接触冲击波的一瞬间就碎裂了，金红色的光翼像玻璃一样从外向内层层剥落。但蒸汽茧的核心还在，十二组喷射口以最大功率喷出蒸汽，高温高压的气幕疯狂地修补着破损的部分。

一秒。

矿道塌了。

维苏威火山的山体发出了一声悠长的、仿佛来自地壳深处的呻吟，像是这头沉睡了千年的巨兽被人捅了一刀。整个采石场——方圆五公里的矿道网络——在冲击波的作用下开始连锁坍塌，碎石如雨般落下，灰尘遮蔽了一切。

两秒。

冲击波穿透了红莲之翼的右翼。

西泽尔的背甲被一块飞来的碎石击中，甲胄发出了金属变形的闷响。他嘴角溢出一丝血——不是外伤，是不朽之王系统强行榨取他神经系统能量造成的内伤。

但蒸汽茧还在。

三台试制机和他自己，都在蒸汽茧的保护下。

他感觉到了振动——不是冲击波的振动，是更深的、更大的、来自维苏威火山山体内部的振动。那是红水银核心爆炸当量撕裂了矿道最深处的一段岩壁，岩壁在自身重力和爆炸冲击力的双重作用下断裂、坍塌、向外倾倒。

三秒。

冲击波开始衰减。

红莲之翼的左翼已经彻底消失了，只剩下右侧残存的光翼在苟延残喘。但它撑过了最致命的那三秒。

蒸汽茧缓缓消散。

西泽尔看到了——

矿道西侧的岩壁塌了一大片，露出了一个巨大的、不规则的黑色空洞。空洞的形状像是一张被撕开的嘴，边缘参差不齐，碎裂的岩层中夹杂着扭曲的钢筋和断裂的蒸汽管道。

那个空洞的深处，隐约可见一条向下延伸的通道。

通道的入口处，钉着层层叠叠的铁质封条。

不是一条——是七条。

每一条都有成人手臂那么宽，半指厚，边缘被铆钉死死钉在岩壁上。铁条表面的锈迹和灰尘说明它们已经存在了很长时间——几十年，也许上百年。铁条上刻着不同的圣徽，有些已经模糊不清，但最近的两条还能辨认：一条刻着弥赛亚圣教的十字架与火焰，火焰缠绕的样式和密涅瓦机关军徽上的火焰几乎一致；另一条刻着一棵树——不是普通的树，是有着十一根枝杈、每根枝杈末端都结着果实的树。

卡巴拉之树。

生命之树。

那个传说中神创造宇宙的蓝图，被弥赛亚圣教从不对外展示的古老圣徽。

红莲之翼的残存光翼在这一刻终于耗尽了最后的能量，化作漫天的金红色蒸汽碎屑飘散在矿道的灰尘中。

不朽之王系统关闭了。

西泽尔感觉自己的意识像是被人从身体里猛地抽走，疼痛、疲劳、寒冷一齐涌上来，像是三天的酷刑压缩在了一瞬间。他的膝盖发软，手指失去了力气，但他的左手还攥着那枚嵌着冰原寒玉的银戒指——那枚瓦莲京娜送给他的见面礼，尺寸刚好适合他的右手中指——他的右手还握着那截拼接了圣剑碎片的龙牙剑断茬，Excalibur残刃的表面还残留着一丝金色的余温。

他倒下了。

膝盖先撞在碎石上，然后是肩膀，然后是侧脸。碎石硌着他的面颊，他闻到了铁锈和灰尘的味道。他听到自己胸甲里的维生系统在发出断断续续的蜂鸣声，那是甲胄在最后的能源耗尽前发出的告别。

他感觉到背上还压着三个人的重量——昆提良、唐璜、阿方索——他们都被他护住了。甲胄的重力感应告诉他，他们的心跳都还在，弱，但还在。

他还感觉到瓦莲京娜的脚步声越来越远——她跑得足够快，已经带着塔拉夏消失在了暗河入口的方向。

那就够了。

西泽尔闭上了眼睛。

意识沉入了黑暗。

在黑暗降临前的最后一瞬间，他看到了那个通道口层层叠叠的铁质封条，看到了卡巴拉之树圣徽上那些沉默的果实。铁条的缝隙中透出一丝几乎不可见的暗金色光芒，像是有什么东西在极深极远的地方呼吸。

然后黑暗吞没了一切。

---

同一时刻。

密涅瓦机关主观测厅。

球形大屏幕上的画面在一瞬间被白光吞没——不是普通的高光过曝，是信号源本身被摧毁后的彻底断流。屏幕闪了几下，然后黑了。

黑得彻底，像一只死去的眼睛。

"怎么回事？！"叶尼塞特使猛地站起来，椅子向后翻倒的声音在观测厅里炸开。

"信号中断！是信号中断！不是过曝！"密涅瓦机关的通讯工程师满头大汗，双手在控制台上疯狂地敲击着，"一号到五号信号源全部丢失！所有甲胈的通讯频道都——都断了！"

"那意味着什么？"查理曼使团的高文少爷缓缓地放下酒杯，声音冷得像冰，"意味着战场上的甲胈全部被摧毁？还是意味着……"

他没说完。

但在场的人都听懂了。

如果甲胈只是被摧毁，通讯中断前应该有剧烈的信号波动，会有损坏告警。但现在信号是"丢失"——像是被什么东西瞬间抹除了一样。

美第奇家族的老商人跌坐在座位上，嘴唇哆嗦着说不出话。刚才他还在数一号骑士身上的圣痕之血——他数到了二十七滴，还在数，就被白光吞没了。

叶素理站在中山国使团的角落里，竹制密语传声筒握在手中，指节发白。他的另一只手插在口袋里，口袋里是龙雀剑复制品剑柄里藏着的微型相机——刚才的画面已经被他拍了下来，但那些都不重要了。重要的是，一号骑士失控时那全身渗出的金红色圣痕之血，那种只有在炽天使甲胄神经接驳系统超载爆裂时才会产生的致命沉淀。

他拍到了。

但战场上的人……

"圣堂装甲师！"三楼VIP包厢里有人高声下令，"立刻进入矿道！清场！"

观测厅里一片混乱，各国使团有人站起来有人跌坐，吵嚷声和惊呼声搅成一团。在这片混乱中，没有人注意到那个戴着银色猫头鹰面具的身影早已消失在了包厢的暗门之后。

---

维苏威火山山腰。救护车。

佛朗哥教授看到了黑屏。

便携式投影屏幕上，那道白光把矿道里的一切吞没后，信号就断了。屏幕变成了一片死寂的黑色。

佛朗哥的瞳孔在那一刻放大了。

不是因为恐惧——是因为他瞬间明白了那道白光意味着什么。红水银核心引爆。维苏威火山底部矿道里此刻的温度可能已经超过了两千度，冲击波的范围覆盖了整个采石场——

所有人。

他的学生、他的骑士、他用一辈子心血制造出来的甲胄、他还没有来得及教给西泽尔的最后一项技术——

全完了。

"不……"

他从担架上挣扎着坐起来，氧气面罩掉在地上，连接的管子被扯断了。心电监护仪发出了刺耳的连续蜂鸣——心率超过了一百八十次每分钟。年轻的护士扑过来按住他的肩膀，但他一把推开了她。

他的嘴张开了，但什么声音都没发出来。

然后他开始咳血。

不是那种肺部感染引起的小口咳痰，是大口的、几乎是喷射状的鲜血从他的喉咙里涌出来，溅在白色的担架布上，溅在医务人员的手上，溅在便携式投影屏幕黑色的表面上。

血是鲜红色的，混着气泡。

医务人员尖叫着把他按回担架上。有人在喊"肾上腺素"，有人在喊"准备电除颤"，有人在喊"教授！教授你听到我说话吗？"

佛朗哥的眼睛翻了上去，露出了大半的眼白。他的身体剧烈地抽搐了两下，然后软了下去。

心电监护仪的蜂鸣声变成了一条直线。

"除颤！两百焦耳！充电！"

救护车在维苏威火山山腰的公路上颠簸着冲向了翡冷翠方向，车顶的蓝色警灯在夜色中疯狂旋转。

---

密涅瓦机关。观战室。

薇若兰坐在指挥席上，一动不动。

她穿着一身黑色的密涅瓦机关核心骑士制式军服，巧克力色的长腿交叠着，白色的长发披散在肩上。她的右手还搭在面前的通讯台面板上，手指按在紧急广播按钮上。

屏幕上什么都没有了。

黑色的。

她看着那片黑色看了整整五秒钟。

然后她按下了按钮。

"这里是密涅瓦机关副总长薇若兰。"她的声音不大，但在安静的观战室里每个人都听得清清楚楚，"从现在起，密涅瓦机关进入一级封锁状态。所有人员不许外出。所有通讯频道关闭，只保留与枢机会和圣堂装甲师的专用通道。擅离岗位者，以叛国罪论处。"

她松开了按钮。

她的手指在发抖。

很轻微的抖，如果有人注意看的话会看到她的指尖在微微地颤动。但没有人看——观战室里的工程师们已经在执行她的命令了，通讯频道一个接一个地关闭，只有几盏红色的指示灯还亮着。

薇若兰把那只发抖的手收回来，放在了膝盖上，用另一只手按住了它。

她的脸上没有表情。

但她的嘴唇是白的。

---

维苏威火山底部矿道。

圣堂装甲师的士兵们进入了矿道。

他们穿着深灰色的制式动力甲，手持军用连射铳和光束照明器，沿着坍塌的矿道向战场推进。碎石、扭曲的铁柱、断裂的蒸汽管道在他们的靴子下发出咯吱的碎裂声。空气中弥漫着浓重的灰尘和红水银燃烧后的金属腥味，温度高得让他们的甲胄散热系统满负荷运转。

"前方发现大型坍塌区域！"领队的军官通过对讲机报告，"矿道西侧岩壁完全断裂，露出了一个……长官，我不确定该怎么描述……一个通道？"

对讲机里传来一个沉稳的、经过变声器处理的声音。

"找到它了。"那个声音说，"那里是矿道最深处连接熔岩之心的通道入口。所有士兵听令——第一，找到那个通道的精确位置和入口状态，记录所有可见的圣徽和封条样式；第二，从现在起，关于这个通道的一切信息列为最高机密，泄露者就地正法；第三，对外宣称矿道坍塌是由红水银核心失控引爆造成的自然事故，与通道无关。"

"明白！"领队军官立正敬礼，尽管对方看不到。

"还有一件事。"那个声音停顿了一下，"找到西泽尔·博尔吉亚。活的最好。如果死了……"

"如果死了？"

"把他的甲胄带回来。"

"是！"

圣堂装甲师的士兵们继续向矿道深处推进。光束照明器的光柱穿透了灰尘，照亮了一地狼藉的战场——扭曲的试制机残骸、碎裂的秘银重盾碎片、被高温熔化成玻璃珠的碎石。

他们找到了密涅瓦方的三台试制机——奥古斯都、蔷薇之鬼、所罗门王——全部倒在地上，甲胄严重损坏但结构完整。骑士们都被护在甲胄里，生命体征微弱但还活着。

他们也找到了红龙。

红龙甲胄半跪在碎石中，背上扛着三个昏迷的骑士，全身的装甲板严重变形，背部的龙骑兵套装已经完全脱落。它的驾驶者——西泽尔·博尔吉亚——面朝下倒在地上，右手还紧紧攥着一截断剑，左手的手指勾着一枚银戒指。

他昏迷了。但还活着。

"长官！找到了密涅瓦方的骑士和试制机！四名骑士全部存活！"领队军官再次报告。

对讲机里沉默了两秒。

"很好。"那个声音说，"把他们全部带走，送到密涅瓦附属医院。走专用的密封运输车，不经过任何公开路线。"

"是！"

圣堂装甲师的士兵们开始搬运伤员。医疗兵展开便携式生命维持设备，给四个昏迷的骑士挂上了生理盐水。

搬运西泽尔的时候，一个士兵注意到了他右手握着的那截断剑。

断剑的剑身是一截断裂的龙牙剑断茬，但断茬的顶端嵌入了一块发着暗金色微光的碎片——圣剑装具·Excalibur的碎片。碎片已经不再发光了，但温度还没有完全冷却，握在手里有一丝残余的温热。

"这是什么？"那个士兵好奇地伸手想去碰那块碎片。

"别碰。"领队军官厉声制止，"所有缴获物品封存上交！不许私自触碰！"

士兵缩回了手。

西泽尔被抬上了担架。他的手指始终没有松开——右手握着Excalibur残刃，左手勾着冰原寒玉银戒指。即使在昏迷中，他的指节依然泛白，仿佛那两样东西是他最后的气脉。

"那边！通道入口！"另一个士兵喊道。

圣堂装甲师的小队向那个坍塌后露出的黑色空洞推进。

他们走到了通道入口前。

七条铁质封条层层叠叠地钉在岩壁上，每一条都锈迹斑斑，每一条都刻着不同的圣徽。弥赛亚圣教的十字架与火焰、卡巴拉之树、密涅瓦机关的六翼猫头鹰、还有一些已经模糊到无法辨认的古老纹样。铁条之间的缝隙里透出一丝几乎不可见的暗金色光芒，像是有什么东西在那极深极远的地方呼吸。

"长官，通道入口确认。铁质封条七条，保存完好，尚未有被破坏的痕迹。"领队军官举着光束照明器仔细查看，"圣徽样式初步辨认——弥赛亚圣教卡巴拉之树、密涅瓦军徽，以及……其他几种我需要查阅档案才能确认。"

对讲机里传来一声极轻的、近乎满意的呼吸。

"很好。不要碰那些封条。在入口处设置警戒线，等候后续指示。"

"是！"

一个士兵走到了最前面，举起光束照明器仔细查看那些铁质封条上的圣徽。他伸出手，准备撕掉最外面那层已经被爆炸冲击波震松的铁条——

突然。

通道深处，黑暗的最底层，亮起了一盏灯。

不——不是灯。是一双眼睛。

一双在铁面具的缝隙中闪烁的、暗淡而锐利的眼睛。

一个穿着黑袍的身影从通道深处的黑暗中缓缓走了出来。

那件黑袍很长，拖在地上，被灰尘覆盖着，看不出原来的材质。袍子的兜帽遮住了来人的头顶，只露出了一张铁制的面具——不是装饰性的面具，是实打实的、沉重的、似乎是用整块铁锻造出来的面具。面具的表面没有任何花纹，没有任何孔洞，只在眼睛的位置开了两条细长的缝隙，暗金色的光从缝隙中透出来。

那个身影在通道口站定了。

他——或者她——没有说话。

他只是站在那里，像是一尊被遗忘在黑暗中的铁像。

圣堂装甲师的士兵们同时举起了枪。

"不要动！"领队军官厉声喝道，枪口对准了那个黑袍身影，"报上身份！否则我们——"

黑袍身影没有回答。

他只是微微抬起了右手。

那只右手的食指上，戴着一枚戒指。

戒指的形状是一条蛇，蛇缠绕着一颗骷髅。

撒旦教团印记。

【English】
Chapter 178 — The Wings of the Red Lotus Above Purgatory

The red light crested.

In the abandoned mining tunnels beneath Vesuvius, loose stones lifted from the ground and hung, suspended, as if the air had forgotten which way was down. The chest of the First Knight blazed. A sphere of dark crimson had swollen to fill the cavity behind the breastplate, light cracking from its surface in vein-thin branches. Liquid red mercury ran in bright threads along the seams of the buckled armor, and where a single drop struck a piece of fallen stone the stone did not melt — it vitrified, a glass bead glowing at its heart.

Thirty meters from that impossible glow, Cesare Borgia stood in a drift of rubble.

His right hand still held what was left of the Dragon's Fang. Most of the blade lay somewhere in the dark behind him. What he gripped was a stub of broken metal, the cross-section catching the red light in a dull silver glint. His left hand held something worse: a shard of the Holy Sword torn from the First Knight's breastplate, the fragment pulsing a slow furious gold, the heat of it searing through his glove and into the bones of his fingers.

Behind him, against a fractured pillar of stone, Valentina braced herself on one knee. Blood traced the corner of her mouth. The right shoulder plate of her modified Wrath of God III was peeled open like a flower forced past its season, the joint beneath still hissing white vapor. Taras had curled himself into the smallest shape he could behind her, both hands over his head, his face the color of tallow.

Ten meters further on, Quintilian lay on his back. The three pieces of Augustus's mithril greatshield lay around him like the petals of a metallic flower. Don Juan's Rose Ghost had lost its right arm above the elbow — healing nerve-fiber and lubricant and arterial blood braiding together at the stump, the discharge endless, sickly. Alfonso was worse, the Spider's Nest wrist-console shattered against his temple, his forehead split where it had met stone, blood running freely into his open eyes.

Three prototype armors, all out of the fight.

Three old retainers, all unconscious.

Cesare looked at the heart of the First Knight. The core was at the limit. He could see it — the way a man can see when a rope is about to snap — not by counting the fibers, but by the sound it begins to make.

Two seconds. Maybe three.

The gold sleeve around the back of his neck went hot. Not the gentle warmth of the Type-235 adaptation — a needle of red iron pushed along the vertebrae, climbing the spine, prying at the base of the skull. The shard in his left hand was singing. The branch of the World Tree, number 01, sunk deep in red mercury at the bottom of an unmeasured ocean, had heard him and was answering.

His purple irises lit. Gold lines bled outward from the pupils across the iris, slow as poured honey, then faster, as if someone had tipped molten metal into glass. His heartbeat filled the inside of his head, each beat the weight of a hammer on an anvil.

Rex Immortalis.

Three minutes. Past three, the chip would burn out. Past five, his body would no longer answer to him. Past eight, the hero who lived in the machine would finish eating what was left of the man.

Three minutes. He had three minutes to keep everyone alive. Then he would fall.

Cesare tightened his fist around the Holy Sword shard. The gold light ran down the back of his hand along the line of his veins, and the pain was immediate, the kind of pain that begins to feel like weather. He did not hesitate.

"Rex Immortalis."

He said the words in a voice flat enough to pass for empty.

The eyes of the Red Dragon came on. The light in them was not the cool, contained light of a man still inside his own head — it was the light of something unchained. Gold-red, fevered, the kind of light a man would see if he had somehow wedged the sun into the eye sockets of a metal god. Every rivet on the armor cried out at once, a single metallic groan as the plates expanded against each other. The six exhaust valves of the dragoon pack across the Red Dragon's back blew open in a line, and from every seam of the suit, steam jetted into the red-lit air. The columns of vapor caught the color and turned — copper, brass, then gold-red, the cloud above him burning like a low fire.

And then the wings.

They were not real wings. The Red Dragon had no flight rig, no glider struts, no aileron arrays. What it had were two clusters of auxiliary jets that had been folded, unannounced, behind the shoulder plates — emergency fittings, each cluster twelve nozzles arranged in the geometry of a lotus flower. They opened now. Steam tore out of them at near-sonic speed, caught the gold of the shard and the dark red of the failing core, and condensed, in the half-second of its existence, into two curving fans of light.

The Wings of the Red Lotus.

Unstable. The edges kept breaking apart and re-forming, a burning paper at the edge of an updraft, a last blossom fighting its way open in the heaviest dark before the dawn. But they were there.

Cesare moved.

The speed of Rex Immortalis passed the upper limit of what a human nervous system is built to register. He did not run to Quintilian — he was simply there, beside him, between one blink and the next, the way a card turns up under the hand. One hand took Augustus by the pauldron. Quintilian, in full armor, weighed more than one hundred and fifty kilos. Cesare hauled him upright and slung the whole armored weight across his shoulders. Then Don Juan — he caught him by the belt-clasp, hooked the limp body under his right arm. Last, Alfonso. He bent and took the mathematician across his left shoulder. The broken watch on Alfonso's wrist ticked against Cesare's pauldron with a small bright sound, the sound of a small thing dying.

Three unconscious men on one body. More than three hundred kilos of metal and bone.

He could not feel it. Rex Immortalis had sealed the doors of pain, of fatigue, of fear. He was a mechanism now, and a mechanism does not feel what it carries.

"Valentina."

His voice went through the rumble of the tunnel as a clean line.

"The underground river. Take Taras. Go."

She did not hesitate. Her hand found the boy's wrist. She pulled him up out of the rubble, and the two of them ran. The Wrath of God III, smoking from its shattered shoulder, moved with a speed that had nothing to do with the steam in its joints. Valentina's gold hair streamed out behind her like a flag in a gale.

She trusted him. The way she had trusted him when she laid the sword in his hand and walked away without a word.

The Wings of the Red Lotus finished their opening. The two fans of gold-red light bent forward, folding across Cesare and the three unconscious men on him. They closed into a translucent cocoon of moving vapor, less than ten centimeters thick, but flowing at near-sonic speed, a high-temperature curtain of gas under pressure.

The First Knight's red mercury core chose that moment to die.

There was no sound. Or rather, the sound was so vast it had stepped over the threshold of what an ear can hold, and what was left on the other side was a silence so total it had its own weight. A column of pure white light punched upward out of the Knight's chest — three meters across, absolute. The roof of the tunnel did not fall. It ceased to exist. Stone, metal, steam pipe, all of it converted in the same instant into a bright cloud of scattering particles.

The shockwave came next. A wall of churning gray-white air, eating the tunnel walls as it went. Stone cracked like biscuit. The iron stanchions that had held the ceiling up for a century twisted on themselves like wet rope. Boulders lifted into the air, hung, then were pressed into powder by the same hand that had lifted them.

The shockwave struck the Wings of the Red Lotus.

The left wing shattered on contact. The light broke in sheets from the outside in, glass falling upward. But the heart of the cocoon held. Twelve jets at full output, the high-pressure vapor re-sealing itself, rebuilding the broken places as fast as they tore.

One second. The mine came down. The body of Vesuvius made the sound a sleeping animal makes when, at last, it has been cut. The whole quarry — every tunnel in a five-kilometer web — began to fall in on itself, a chain of collapses, stone after stone, the dust rising in such a curtain that the world disappeared.

Two seconds. The shockwave went through the right wing. A piece of flying stone struck Cesare's backplate and the metal dimpled inward with a flat, sick sound. A thread of blood appeared at the corner of his mouth. It was not a wound. It was Rex Immortalis pulling on the wiring of his nervous system, the first of the internal debts coming due.

The cocoon held.

Three seconds. The shockwave began to ebb. The left wing was gone. The right wing was a torn remnant, still trying to hold its shape. It had lasted the length of the worst of it.

The cocoon thinned and finally dissolved.

Cesare saw. The western wall of the tunnel had caved in a long way. Behind the fallen stone, a hole gaped, irregular, black, the shape of a mouth torn open by force. At the back of the mouth, a passage went down. At the entrance to the passage, iron seals had been nailed to the rock.

Not one. Seven.

Each one as wide as a man's arm, half a finger thick, the edges hammered flat against the stonework with iron pins. The rust on their surfaces was old, decades old, perhaps a century. Each one carried a different holy emblem, hammered into the iron. Some had been worn almost smooth by time. The two most recent ones were still legible. One carried the cross and flame of the Messiah Church, the flame wound around the cross in a way that was nearly identical to the flame on the Minerva military crest. The other carried a tree. Not an ordinary tree. A tree with eleven branches, and at the end of every branch, a fruit.

The Tree of Life.

The Kabbalistic Tree.

The ancient blueprint, the Church of the Messiah's most guarded emblem, the one it had never displayed in any public chapel.

The last of the right wing spent its final breath. The gold-red vapor broke into a slow rain of bright motes that drifted down through the dust of the collapsed mine like a funeral of small suns.

Rex Immortalis closed. The system stepped out of his nerves the way a man steps back from a window he has been gripping too long. Pain came in, all of it, at once, three days of torture compressed into the space between one breath and the next. His knees unlocked. His fingers lost their grip. But the left hand, even so, kept its hold on the silver ring set with the cold-jade stone of the northern ice-plain — the ring Valentina had given him the first day they had met, sized to his right middle finger. And the right hand, the hand that had not let go since the first moment, still held the broken stub of the Dragon's Fang, the Excalibur shard still warm at its tip.

He fell. Knees first into the rubble. Then shoulder. Then cheekbone. The stones cut his face. He smelled iron and dust. Inside the breastplate, the life-support system was making the sound a man makes when he is running out of everything — a thin broken bleep, a goodbye in the language of broken instruments.

The weight on his back had not shifted. Quintilian, Don Juan, Alfonso. The armor's pressure sensors told him what his own body no longer could: their hearts were still going. Weak, the way a small lamp is weak in a high wind. But going.

Valentina's footsteps were leaving him. The sound of her boots on stone grew smaller. She had made it to the underground river, and the dark had taken her and Taras into itself.

Cesare closed his eyes. The dark came up to meet him. In the last instant before it took him, he saw the iron seals at the mouth of the passage, the fruits of the Kabbalistic Tree, the narrow gap between the bands of iron where a thin line of dark gold was leaking out — a kind of light that did not behave like light, the way something very far down breathes out the last of its heat.

Then the dark had him.

---

In the Minerva Mechanism's observation hall, on the same instant, the great spherical screen died. It did not go to static. It went out the way a candle goes out — one frame, then nothing, black, the absolute black of a dead eye.

"What —" The Yenisei envoy was on his feet before he knew he had moved. The crash of his chair rang through the hall like a single struck bell.

"Signal loss! It is a signal loss, not overexposure!" the Minerva communications engineer had sweat running into his collar. His hands were a blur on the console. "Sources one through five are all gone. Every suit's comm channel is dark."

"What does that mean?" The young lord Gawain of the Charlemagne delegation set his wine glass down with a small, precise movement. His voice had the temperature of an ice-house. "That the armors on the field have been destroyed? Or that —"

He did not finish the sentence. He did not need to. If the suits had only been destroyed, the comm logs would have screamed first — a cascade of damage warnings, a great electronic howl. Instead the signal was simply gone. Not broken. Erased.

The old Medici factor dropped into his chair as if his legs had decided, on their own, to stop working. He had been counting. Twenty-seven drops of stigmata blood. Twenty-eight. The white light had reached him in the middle of the count and taken the count away.

In a corner of the hall, a man in the dress of the Zhongshan Kingdom's delegation stood with a bamboo speaking-tube in one hand, the knuckles white. The other hand was in his pocket. Inside the pocket, hidden in the hilt of a replica Dragon Sparrow sword, a small camera had done its work. Ye Suli had filmed the moment of the First Knight's rampage. He had filmed the gold-red bloom of stigmata blood that came only when a Seraphim's neural interface was overloaded past the point of no return. The film was safe in its tiny dark box.

None of it mattered.

"Sanctuary Armored Division!" a voice roared from the third-floor VIP box. "Into the mine! Clear the tunnel!"

The hall broke open into chaos. In the middle of it, no one saw the figure in the silver owl mask slip out through the side door of the box and disappear into the dark.

---

On the road that climbed the flank of Vesuvius, in the back of a swaying ambulance, Professor Franco saw the black.

The portable projection screen, no larger than a prayer-book, had shown him everything up to the white. The white had come, and the screen had become a black the size of a coffin.

His pupils blew open. It was not fear. It was the understanding of a man who knows exactly what the white meant. Red mercury, at full yield, in a confined space — the temperature inside the deepest tunnels at this moment was the temperature of a fired kiln. The shockwave would have eaten the entire quarry. The students, the knights, the machines he had spent his life teaching his hands to make, the last technique he had not yet had time to teach Cesare —

All of it.

"No."

He tried to sit up. The oxygen mask fell from his face. The tube trailing from it snapped against the rail of the stretcher. The cardiac monitor began to scream — a thin unbroken note. His heart was running at a hundred and eighty, a hundred and ninety, a small animal trying to claw its way out of a ribcage.

A young nurse lunged for his shoulders. He flung her off with a strength that surprised both of them.

He opened his mouth. Nothing came out.

Then the coughing began. A great heaving, the body bending in half, blood coming up out of him in a sheet, bright red and full of small bright bubbles. The blood struck the white sheet of the stretcher. It struck the nurse's hands. It struck the black face of the dead screen.

Somewhere in the ambulance, a voice shouted for adrenaline. Another shouted for the defibrillator. A third called his name, over and over, in the tone of a person who knows that the person they are calling is no longer in the room.

Franco's eyes rolled up. The whites showed. His body lifted once, twice, in two hard spasms, and then settled.

The cardiac monitor drew its line.

"Clear! Two hundred joules! Charging!"

The ambulance lurched along the mountain road, blue lights turning in the dark, on its way down toward Florence.

---

In the Minerva Mechanism's war room, Verolan sat at the command desk and did not move.

She wore the black uniform of the Mechanism's core knightly service. Her legs, the color of bitter chocolate, were crossed. Her white hair lay loose across her shoulders. Her right hand was on the comm panel, the index finger resting on the emergency broadcast key.

The screen in front of her was black.

She looked at the black for five full seconds. Then she pressed the key.

"This is Vice-Marshal Verolan of the Minerva Mechanism." Her voice was not loud. It did not need to be. "As of this moment, the Minerva Mechanism is in full lockdown. No personnel are to leave the compound. All comm channels are to be closed, with the exception of the dedicated lines to the College of Cardinals and the Sanctuary Armored Division. Anyone found off-station will be treated as a traitor to the state."

She took her finger off the key.

Her hand was shaking. It was a small shake. The tip of the index finger trembled, then the next finger, then the small muscles of the wrist, the way a single held string begins to shiver before it breaks.

Verolan brought the hand in. She laid it on her knee. She laid her other hand on top of it, and held it still.

Her face was the face she always wore in front of her staff. Unreadable. A closed door.

Her lips were white.

---

In the tunnels beneath Vesuvius, the soldiers of the Sanctuary Armored Division moved forward.

Their suits were the regulation gray of Church armor, heavy and unhandsome. They carried magazine rifles and beam-lanterns, and the beams cut cones of white light into the dust. The air tasted of dust and the strange metallic sweetness of burnt red mercury. The heat was high enough to keep the suit-cooling systems on their last notch.

"Large collapse ahead!" the officer in the lead called into his comm. "The western wall of the main tunnel has failed completely. We have what looks like — sir, I am not sure how to put this — a passage of some kind."

The comm clicked. A voice came back, processed through a vocoder until it had the temperature of a well and the patience of a stone.

"You have found it. The passage is the deep access to the lava heart of the mountain. Listen carefully. First — the exact location of the passage, and the state of the entrance. Record every visible holy emblem and every seal. Second — from this moment, all information regarding this passage is classified at the highest level. Anyone who leaks it dies where they are standing. Third — the public story is that the tunnel collapse was a natural accident caused by the uncontrolled detonation of a red mercury core. The passage is not to be mentioned. To anyone."

"Understood." The officer saluted, though the man on the other end could not see him.

"One more thing." The voice paused. The pause was the kind that costs a man a small piece of himself to maintain. "Find Cesare Borgia. Alive if possible. If he is dead —"

The officer waited.

"Bring back his armor."

"Yes, sir."

The Sanctuary soldiers went deeper. The beam-lanterns found, in the dust, the wreckage of the field — the twisted remains of prototypes, the broken pieces of a mithril greatshield, a scatter of stones that had been turned to glass marbles by the heat.

They found the three Minerva prototypes — Augustus, the Rose Ghost, the Wisdom of Solomon. They were down, every one of them, the armor plates buckled and split, the knights inside them alive in the barest sense of the word. Hearts going. Lungs going. The lights on the diagnostic panels flickering like fireflies at the end of summer.

They found the Red Dragon.

The Red Dragon knelt in the rubble, three unconscious knights across its back, every plate on the suit warped out of true, the dragoon pack on its back gone entirely. The driver was on the ground, face down, the broken stub of a sword still locked in his right hand, the fingers of his left hand hooked through a small silver ring.

He was unconscious. He was breathing.

"Command! We have the Minerva knights and the prototypes! All four knights alive!" the officer called in.

The comm was silent for two seconds.

"Very well." The voice said. "Take them all. Minerva auxiliary hospital. Use the sealed transport, the one that does not come in on any public route."

"Yes, sir."

The medics unfolded their portable life-support rigs. They laid the four unconscious knights on stretchers with the careful, deliberate hands of men who understood that what they carried could not be replaced.

When they came to lift Cesare, one of the soldiers saw the broken sword in his right hand. The sword was a stub of the Dragon's Fang. Into the broken end of the stub, a fragment of metal had been set — dark gold, faintly warm, the surface still holding a breath of heat. The soldier knew, without being told, that the fragment was not metal. The fragment was the Holy Sword's regalia, Excalibur, in the only shape it had left in the world.

"What is that?" The soldier's hand went out toward the fragment.

"Don't." The officer's voice was a single cut of a blade. "Every piece of recovered materiel is to be sealed and surrendered. Nobody touches anything."

The soldier pulled his hand back.

They put Cesare on the stretcher. His fingers did not uncurl. The right hand, the Excalibur stub. The left hand, the silver ring with the cold-jade stone. Even in unconsciousness, his knuckles were bloodless, the color of old bone, as if the two small objects were the last two ropes that held him to the world.

"This way! The passage entrance!" another soldier called from ahead.

The Sanctuary team moved toward the mouth of the opening the explosion had torn.

Seven iron seals, one on top of the other, nailed into the rock. The rust on them was old. The emblems on them were older. The cross and flame of the Messiah Church. The Kabbalistic Tree. The six-winged owl of the Minerva crest. Other emblems, rubbed nearly smooth by the years. Between the iron bands, through the narrow gaps, a thin line of dark gold breathed out, so faint it could have been imagined, except that several soldiers saw it at once.

"Command. Passage entrance confirmed. Seven iron seals, intact, no sign of breach." The officer held his beam-lantern close. "Emblems so far — Messiah Church, Kabbalistic Tree, Minerva military crest, and several others I will need to consult the archive to identify."

A sound came back through the vocoder. It might have been a breath. It might have been a laugh. It was the kind of sound a man makes when, after a long search, he has at last put his hand on the thing he was looking for.

"Good. Do not touch the seals. Mark a perimeter at the entrance. Await further orders."

"Yes, sir."

A soldier stepped to the front. He raised his beam-lantern and studied the outermost seal, the one the shockwave had loosened from the rock. He reached out, his hand going for the iron band —

And then.

At the bottom of the dark, deep in the passage, a light came on. Not a light. A pair of eyes. Two narrow slits of dim, sharp light, set in an iron mask.

A figure in a black robe walked out of the dark of the passage and into the dust of the collapsed mine.

The robe was long. It trailed on the ground, thick with dust, the original cloth hidden under a century of the mountain's breath. The hood was drawn up over the head, and beneath it, where a face should have been, there was only iron. A single piece, beaten, heavy, set with no ornament at all. Two slits, narrow, where the eyes of the mask were. Out of those slits, the dark gold light moved.

The figure stopped at the entrance of the passage.

He did not speak. He stood as a man might stand who has been forgotten in a dark place for a very long time, and who is only now remembering that he is allowed to leave it.

The Sanctuary soldiers raised their rifles as one.

"Hold!" the officer barked. "Identify yourself! If you do not —"

The black-robed figure did not answer.

He lifted his right hand, a small movement, almost a courtesy.

On the index finger of the right hand, a ring. The ring was a snake. The snake was wound around a skull.

The mark of the Satanist Order.

第179章 铁面具下的异端审判官

【中文】
第179章 铁面具下的异端审判官

"撒旦教团！"

不知道是谁先喊出来的，那声音在矿道里被回声拉得又尖又长，仿佛有人在空铁罐里尖叫。

领队军官的拇指扣上了击锤，眼睛死死盯着那只戴着蛇缠骷髅戒指的手。三十名士兵同时上膛，枪栓拉动的声音连成一片，清脆得像折断一排冰凌。

"开——"

"枪"字还没出口。

黑袍身影开口了。

只有一个字。

"停。"

那声音不大，却像一块铁砧从高处落下来，把矿道里所有杂音都砸得粉碎。三十个士兵的手指同时僵在了扳机上——不是服从命令，是身体本能地停下了，就好像一群猎犬忽然面对着一头抬起头来的、不可名状的猛兽。

黑袍人慢慢抬起了左手。

他没有做出任何攻击性的动作，只是用左手的指尖轻轻捏住黑袍的胸襟，向外拉开。

黑袍内侧露出了第二层衣料。

黑色。

纯粹的、没有一丝杂色的黑。

黑色底布上，一对被黑色火焰包裹的黑色羽翼在红水银照明灯的光线下泛着令人胆寒的金属冷光——那是用影金属丝一针一线绣出来的，羽毛的纹理纤毫毕现，仿佛真有两片黑翼贴在那人的胸口，随时要展翅飞去。

黑天使军徽。

异端审判局的身份徽章。

矿道里静得能听见每个人的心跳。

"黑……黑天使……"领队军官的喉结上下滚了一下，声音都变了调，连扣着击锤的拇指都松开了。

黑天使军徽意味着什么，在场每个人都清楚。那个部门是教廷手里最锋利也最隐秘的刀，人数从不超过二十人，权限却大到可以越过枢机会直接抹杀任何人，连十字禁卫军军部的将官见了都要退让三分。圣堂装甲师再精锐，也不是他们的管辖范围。

更重要的是，黑天使军徽的持有者，没有一个不是踩着尸体爬上来的。

"报上……你的代号和姓名。"领队压低声音说，这是他作为军官最后的倔强。

黑袍人用右手摘下了铁面具。

那是一张棱角分明的脸，颧骨高耸，下颌线条像用刀削出来。嘴角有一道斜斜的旧伤疤，从右侧嘴角一直延伸到下颌骨的转角处，仿佛被某种利器划过，再也没有愈合。他的眼睛是灰色的，没有温度，像两块被打磨过的铅。

"李锡尼。"

他说出了自己的名字。

"异端审判局第一副局长。"

矿道里更静了。连矿道深处偶尔滴落的水声都清晰可闻，像有人用指甲一下一下地敲着铁板。

对讲机里传来一声短促的、近乎尖锐的吸气声。

然后是那个变了调的声音。

"李锡尼！"

每个字都像是被牙齿咬碎了再吐出来的。

"你敢违抗枢机会的命令！"

李锡尼的灰色眼睛微微眯了一下。

他认得这个声音。米迦勒的替身——那个声音年轻，带着属于枢机卿的傲慢，又夹杂着掩饰不住的焦躁，就好像一个刚被揭穿了把戏的赌徒。

"违抗？"

他重复了一遍这个词，语调平得像一张白纸。

"枢机会的命令原文是'配合圣堂装甲师搜救幸存者并维持圣域秩序'，里面没有授权任何人撕毁封存四十年的铁质封条。"

对讲机里沉默了一拍。

"这些封条是原罪机关的——"

"错了。"

李锡尼打断了对方。

他用左手探入黑袍内侧，取出了一样东西。

那是一截断枪。

断枪只有成年男子小臂长短，断面参差不齐，像是被某种巨力生生折断的，边缘还残留着几道极细的裂纹。枪尖的位置是断口，断口处泛着淡淡的青蓝色冷光，仿佛里面封着一团永不熄灭的火焰。枪身上镌刻着极细极密的圣言和圣徽，在昏暗的矿道中依然清晰可辨——那些文字比米粒还小，排列得密密麻麻，像是一群被钉死在金属上的蚂蚁。

那是朗基努斯圣枪的碎片。

圣堂装甲师的士兵们几乎同时后退了一步。

他们不是普通士兵，他们隶属于圣堂装甲师，是教廷用来处理神圣灾难的核心力量。所以他们比任何人都清楚，朗基努斯圣枪的碎片意味着什么。

那是教廷最高等级的圣物之一。

《宗教秘密法》第四十七条明文规定：朗基努斯圣器的持有者，在涉及神圣灾难与异端事件时，拥有先斩后奏之权。任何部门、任何人，不得妨碍持有者执行职务。

"这是异端审判局的管辖范围。"

李锡尼举起断枪，青蓝色的冷光照亮了他半边脸，铅灰色的眼睛里终于有了一丝寒意。

"不是圣堂装甲师的。"

对讲机里又是几秒钟的沉默。

然后那个声音从牙缝里挤了出来，一字一顿。

"好。"

只一个字，但每个字都带着咬碎铁的恨意。

"李锡尼。你给我等着。"

对讲机里传来啪的一声——对方掐断了通讯。

矿道里重新安静下来。

圣堂装甲师的士兵们没有动，他们看着李锡尼手中那截泛着冷光的断枪，没有人敢上前一步。领队军官缓缓收起了左轮手枪，对李锡尼行了一个标准的军礼。

"长官。"

然后他转身，对士兵们一挥手。

"撤。"

士兵们列队退出矿道，皮靴踩在碎石上的声音渐渐远去，被黑暗一点一点地吞没。

李锡尼没有看他们。

他的灰色眼睛盯着熔岩之心通道入口处那七条铁质封条，盯着封条上那些古老到几乎无法辨认的纹样。

然后，矿道的另一端传来了脚步声。

不是圣堂装甲师整齐的军靴声，是急促的、带着水声的脚步。

李锡尼转过身。

维苏威火山底部的暗河出口处，一道身影从岩洞中跳了出来。

金色的长发湿漉漉地贴在她苍白的面颊上，军服湿了大半，贴身的剪裁勾勒出叶尼塞女人特有的修长线条。但她怀里还稳稳当当地抱着一个人——那是密涅瓦机关的年轻机械师塔拉夏，脸色惨白，嘴角挂着一丝血迹，已经昏迷了。

瓦莲京娜·罗曼诺夫。

叶尼塞王国公主，神怒骑士团副团长。

在她身后，两名密涅瓦机关的工兵正用临时担架抬着三个昏迷的身影。

昆提良。

唐璜。

阿方索。

西泽尔的三名旧部。三人一身焦黑的灰尘和润滑液混合物，炽天使试制版甲胄已经被卸下，只穿着内部的神经接驳紧身衣。昆提良的肩膀上还缠着染血的绷带，那是他护住塔拉夏时被碎石划伤的，绷带外面已经洇出了一片暗红。

瓦莲京娜在矿道里扫了一眼，目光落在了那个手持断枪的黑袍人身上。

她的脚步停住了。

"李锡尼……副局长？"

她认出了那张脸。

那张在马斯顿事件中曾指挥搜捕、又在密涅瓦机关的几次内部会议上见过一面的脸——异端审判局第一副局长，代号猩红死神。

李锡尼的灰色眼睛从瓦莲京娜怀里的塔拉夏扫到担架上的三人，又扫回她脸上。

他微微点了点头。

"公主殿下。"

他把断枪收回黑袍内侧，重新将铁面具戴回头上。暗金色的光再次从他眼睛的缝隙中透出。

"带他们走。"

他的声音没有任何起伏，平淡得像在说今天的天气。

"这里交给我。"

瓦莲京娜的下颌收紧了。

她的第一反应是质问——李锡尼为什么在这里，他是怎么找到这个入口的，他手边的朗基努斯碎片又是从哪里来的，他食指上那枚撒旦教团印记的戒指到底是什么意思。

但她看了一眼担架上三个昏迷的旧部，又看了一眼怀里面色惨白的塔拉夏，把这些话都咽了下去。

她是叶尼塞的公主，不是分不清轻重的人。

"……好。"

她对身后的两名密涅瓦工兵点了点头。

"走。"

工兵们抬起担架，跟着她往矿道出口走。

"等一下。"

李锡尼忽然开口。

瓦莲京娜停下脚步，回头。

"红龙。"李锡尼的声音从铁面具后面传出来，带着沉闷的金属质感，"西泽尔·博尔吉亚，现在在哪里？"

瓦莲京娜的目光微微一紧。

"……密涅瓦附属医院。"

"活着？"

"活着。"

李锡尼沉默了一拍。

"照顾好他。"

他的声音没有任何感情色彩，但那句话在矿道里回荡了几秒钟才消散。

"他活着，比什么都重要。"

瓦莲京娜没有再问。

她转身，带着人继续往外走。

矿道外，采石场的空地上，一辆酒红色礼车已经等在那里。礼车前挡风玻璃上插着叶尼塞王国的国旗——银白色的忍冬花纹在夜色中分外醒目，蒸汽引擎低低地轰鸣着，排气管冒出白色的水汽。

瓦莲京娜把塔拉夏小心地安置在后座上，又帮着工兵把三个担架固定在车厢的临时床位上。她自己坐进驾驶座，拧动钥匙，蒸汽引擎的轰鸣声大了起来。

礼车的车灯亮起，两道金色的光柱照亮了前方的石子路。

她踩下油门之前，回头看了一眼矿道口。

李锡尼还站在那里。

黑袍的下摆在夜风中轻轻飘动，铁面具上的两个缝隙透出暗金色的光。他没有看礼车，他转过了身，面对着那七条铁质封条，黑色的背影被矿道口的照明灯拉得很长。

"他真要一个人进去？"瓦莲京娜自言自语。

没有人回答她。

她踩下油门，礼车驶出了采石场。

矿道里又只剩李锡尼一个人了。

圣堂装甲师的士兵已经撤干净了，对讲机被留在了地上，米迦勒替身掐断通讯后再没有联系过——他会回去汇报，会向原罪机关的主人报告这里发生的一切，后面会有新的命令下来，会有更多的人来。

但他不在乎。

他缓步走到了熔岩之心通道入口的正前方，伸出了右手。

他的手指抚上了最外面那条铁质封条。

铁条冰凉，表面覆着一层细密的灰尘。灰尘之下，铁条上的纹样在红水银照明灯的光线下清晰可见——弥赛亚圣教的卡巴拉之树，密涅瓦机关的六翼猫头鹰，以及更多他需要查阅档案才能确认的古老圣徽。

他的手指顺着铁条的纹路慢慢向下滑动，停在了最下面那条封条靠近底部的一个位置。

那里有一枚极小的、几乎被灰尘完全覆盖的徽记。

不是卡巴拉之树，不是六翼猫头鹰。

蛇发女妖。

美杜莎。

美第奇家族的家徽。

李锡尼的灰色眼睛微微眯了起来。

"终于找到你了……"

他的声音在空旷的矿道里回荡，像一块石头落进深井。

"骷髅地。"

酒红色礼车在夜色中疾驰。

车窗外是翡冷翠郊区的秋夜景色，远处的城市灯火通明，隐约能看见万国盛典主会场正在搭建的巨大脚手架，蒸汽吊车的灯光像一串低垂的星星。蒸汽路灯的光芒被礼车抛在身后，连成一条金黄色的光带。

车厢里很安静。

昆提良、唐璜和阿方索都还昏迷着，呼吸平稳了些，但脸色仍然苍白。塔拉夏靠在后座上，脸色比刚才好了许多，眉头不再紧锁。瓦莲京娜没有说话，专注地开车。她的金色长发已经被夜风吹得半干，在车灯的反光中像一面飘扬的旗帜，发间隐约飘出一丝忍冬的清冷香气。

忽然，后座传来了一个极轻的声音。

"……妈妈……"

瓦莲京娜的目光从挡风玻璃外收回，落在了后视镜上。

是西泽尔。

他躺在车厢的临时担架上，眼睛还闭着，脸色苍白得像一张没有上墨的纸。爆炸的冲击波让他的神经接驳系统严重超载，虽然已经被卸下了甲胄，但他的意识还没有完全恢复。

"……姑姑……"

瓦莲京娜的手在方向盘上微微一紧。

姑姑？

她不知道西泽尔在说谁。但她知道西泽尔·博尔吉亚的母亲——琳琅夫人——已经去世多年了。

"……骷髅地……"

西泽尔的嘴唇还在动，但声音越来越轻，越来越模糊，最后变成了听不清的呓语。他的手指在担架的边缘无意识地抓了一下，指节泛白，又松开了。

瓦莲京娜收回了目光。

她没有叫醒他。

她只是把油门又踩深了一些，礼车的蒸汽引擎发出一声低沉的咆哮，驶过最后一个弯道。

前方，密涅瓦机关的灯火已经隐约可见了。

【English】
Chapter 179 — The Heretic Inquisitor Beneath the Iron Mask

"Satanist cult!"

Someone was the first to shout it. The sound was dragged thin and high by the echo of the mining tunnel, as though someone were screaming inside an empty iron drum.

The squad leader's thumb hooked the hammer of his sidearm. His eyes had found the hand — the ring on its finger, the serpent coiled about a skull. Thirty soldiers cocked their rifles in a single breath. The sound of bolts being drawn back ran together the way a row of icicles breaks, clean and brittle.

"Fire—"

The word had not left his mouth.

The black-robed figure spoke.

A single word.

"Hold."

It was not loud. It fell like an anvil dropped from a great height and shattered every other sound in the workings. Thirty fingers went still on thirty triggers — not from obedience, but from a reflex older than any training, the way a pack of hounds goes rigid when something they cannot name lifts its head from the grass.

The black-robed man slowly raised his left hand.

He made no aggressive motion. With the fingertips of his left hand he simply took hold of the front of his robe and drew it open.

Beneath the outer cloak, a second layer was revealed.

Black. Pure, unblemished black.

On that dark ground, worked in shadow-metal thread, a pair of wings enfolded in black flame caught the red-mercury lamp-light and threw back a metallic cold that tightened the gut. The plumage was rendered with the patience of a relic-maker — every barb and vein of every feather laid down needle-stroke by needle-stroke, as though two real wings had been pinned to the man's chest, waiting only for the moment they would unfurl.

The Black Angel insignia.

The badge of the Office of Heresy.

The workings went quiet enough to hear a man's heart.

"B-Black Angel..." The squad leader's Adam's apple worked. His voice had shifted keys. His thumb slipped, by itself, off the cocked hammer.

Every man present knew what the Black Angel meant. The Office of Heresy was the Pope's sharpest, most secret knife. Its roster had not numbered more than twenty in living memory; its writ ran past the Sacred College, and could unmake any man alive. Even generals of the Crusader Guard stepped out of its path. The Hallowed Order might be the Church's foremost armored fist, but it was not, and had never been, the Office's concern.

There was also, as the men in the tunnel knew, the small matter that no man who wore the Black Angel had ever come by it cheaply. They had all climbed to it on a ladder of bodies.

"State... your codename and your name." The officer dropped his voice. It was the last scrap of authority left to him.

The black-robed man reached up with his right hand and lifted the iron mask away.

The face beneath was all angles. Cheekbones high, the jaw as though it had been cut with a chisel. From the right corner of his mouth a diagonal old scar ran down to the turn of his jaw, as though something sharp had been drawn across it and the flesh had simply refused to close. His eyes were grey. They had no temperature in them. They looked like two pieces of lead that had been polished.

"Licinius."

He spoke his own name as though he were reading it from a tomb.

"First Deputy Director of the Office of Heresy."

The workings went quieter still. Somewhere deeper in, the slow drip of water became audible, each drop a small nail struck against an iron plate.

From the field-radio clipped at the squad leader's belt came a sharp, almost strangled breath.

Then a voice, pitched wrong with anger.

"Licinius!"

Every word was bitten through and spat out.

"You dare defy the Conclave's order!"

Licinius's grey eyes narrowed, a fraction.

He knew that voice. The stand-in for the Archangel Michael — a young one, who wore a cardinal's arrogance the way a small boy wears his father's coat, the brittle, cornered sound of a gambler whose trick has just been seen through.

"Defy?" Licinius repeated the word. The inflection was as flat as a sheet of paper.

"The Conclave's directive reads, in its entirety, 'cooperate with the Hallowed Order in the rescue of survivors and the preservation of the Holy Ground's order.' It contains no authorization for any party to break seals that have stood for forty years."

The radio was silent for a beat.

"Those seals belong to the Original Sin Bureau—"

"Wrong."

Licinius cut him off.

He slid his left hand into the inner lining of his robe and drew something out.

A broken spear.

It was no longer than a grown man's forearm, from elbow to fingertip. The break across the shaft was ragged, as though it had been torn apart by some immense force, and along the edge ran a constellation of hairline cracks. Where the spearhead had been, the cross-section gave off a faint cyan light, as though a flame that would never go out had been sealed inside the metal. Across the shaft, in script too fine for the eye to take in at a glance, were incised the holy words and the sacred emblems — characters smaller than grains of rice, packed shoulder to shoulder like a colony of ants nailed to the metal.

A fragment of the Longinus Spear.

The Hallowed Order's soldiers took one step back, all in the same breath.

They were not ordinary men. They were the core of the Church's response to holy disasters, and so they knew, better than almost any other body of men alive, what a fragment of the Longinus Spear meant.

It was among the highest-grade sacred relics the Church held.

Article Forty-Seven of the Religious Secrets Act was explicit. A bearer of a Longinus relic, in matters touching holy disaster and heresy, held the right of summary judgment. No department, no person, might obstruct him in the execution of his office.

"This falls under the Office of Heresy's jurisdiction," Licinius said, and raised the broken spear. The cyan light fell across half his face, and at last something moved in those leaden eyes — the first suggestion of cold.

"Not the Hallowed Order's."

The radio gave him several more seconds of silence.

Then the voice came through the teeth, a word at a time.

"Fine."

A single syllable, and each of its letters ground like iron filings.

"Licinius. I will remember this."

There was a click — cut off from the other end.

The workings settled.

None of the Hallowed Order's soldiers moved. They looked at the broken spear in Licinius's hand, at the cold light it bled, and no one stepped forward. The squad leader slowly holstered his revolver, brought his right fist up to his breastplate in the regulation salute.

"Sir."

He turned and signed to his men.

"Withdraw."

The soldiers filed out of the workings in good order. The sound of their boots on the loose stone died away by degrees, swallowed piece by piece into the dark.

Licinius did not watch them go.

His grey eyes had found the entrance to the Lava-Heart corridor, and the seven iron seals laid across it, and the markings on the seals — so old they had almost forgotten what they were.

From the other end of the workings came another sound of footfall.

Not the orderly stamp of Hallowed Order boots. A quicker tread, with the splash of water in it.

Licinius turned.

From the mouth of the subterranean river at the foot of Vesuvius, a figure vaulted out of the rock.

Her hair was gold, plastered wet to the pale planes of her face. Her uniform was soaked through, and the cut of it laid out, in the way only wet cloth can, the long Yenisei line of her. Cradled against her chest, held steady as though she had been carrying him all her life, was a young Minerva mechanic. The girl's face was the colour of tallow; a thread of blood at the corner of her mouth; her eyes closed.

Princess Valentina Romanovna.

Vice-commander of the Wrath-of-God Order.

Behind her, two Minerva engineers carried a stretcher between them, and on the stretcher three more unconscious figures.

Quintilian.

Don Juan.

Alfonso.

Three of Cesare's old officers. They were black from head to foot with a mixture of grit and lubricant, the prototype Seraph stripped from their bodies, only the neural-link under-suits they wore beneath remaining. Quintilian's shoulder had been hastily bandaged, and a dark rose of blood was already soaking through the cloth — the price of putting himself between a fall of stone and the mechanic in Valentina's arms.

Valentina's eyes swept the workings and came to rest on the black-robed man with the broken spear.

Her stride broke.

"Deputy Director Licinius?"

She knew that face.

The face that had, in the Marston affair, commanded the hunt for heretics; the face that had sat across from her, more than once, at closed-door meetings inside Minerva. The First Deputy Director of the Office of Heresy. Codename: the Scarlet Reaper.

Licinius's grey eyes moved from the mechanic in her arms, along the stretcher, and back to her face.

He gave a small nod.

"Your Highness."

He slid the broken spear back inside the inner lining of his robe and fitted the iron mask over his face once more. Through the eye-slits, the dim gold of his irises leaked out again.

"Take them and go."

His voice carried no inflection. He might have been remarking on the weather.

"This place is mine from here."

Valentina's jaw set.

Her first instinct was to interrogate him. Why was he here. How had he found this entrance. Where had the Longinus fragment come from. What the serpent-and-skull ring on his finger was meant to say.

But she looked at the three unconscious men on the stretcher, and at the mechanic in her arms, and swallowed every question.

She was a Romanovna. She knew how to choose which fight to take into the next minute.

"...Good."

She signed to the two Minerva engineers behind her.

"Move."

The engineers shouldered the stretcher and fell in behind her.

"One moment."

Licinius spoke again.

Valentina stopped. Half-turned.

"Red Dragon." His voice came from behind the iron mask, muffled to a metallic hush. "Where is Cesare Borgia, now?"

Something in Valentina's eyes tightened.

"...the Minerva annex hospital."

"Alive?"

"Alive."

Licinius was quiet for the length of a breath.

"Look after him."

There was no expression in the words. Yet the sentence went on echoing in the workings for several seconds before it died.

"His being alive is more important than anything else."

Valentina did not ask him what he meant.

She turned and walked her people out.

Outside the workings, on the open ground of the old quarry, a maroon ceremonial car was already waiting. From the staff on its front grille the flag of the Kingdom of Yenisei snapped in the night wind — silver honeysuckle on a dark field, sharp and pale in the lamplight. The steam engine idled low, a soft complaint; a thin plume of white water-vapor rose from the exhaust and was at once lost in the dark.

Valentina settled the mechanic in the back seat, then helped the engineers secure the three stretchers along the fold-down berths the cabin had been fitted with. She took the wheel herself, turned the brass ignition, and the engine's note deepened.

The headlights came on — two gold bars laid across the gravel road ahead.

Before she put the car in gear she looked back, once, at the mouth of the workings.

Licinius was still there.

The hem of the black robe moved in the night wind. Through the two eye-slits of the iron mask, that dim gold leaked. He was not looking at the car. He had already turned his back to it. He stood facing the seven iron seals, his shadow thrown long by the work-lamp at the tunnel's mouth.

"Is he really going in alone?" Valentina said, to no one.

The car gave no answer.

She let out the clutch. The maroon car pulled out of the quarry.

The workings were Licinius's again, and his alone.

The Hallowed Order's men were gone. The field-radio lay where its owner had dropped it in his retreat. The stand-in for Michael had not attempted to call back. He would be on his way to his masters at the Original Sin Bureau, to make his report, and from there new orders would be issued, and other men would come.

Licinius did not concern himself with that.

He walked the few steps to the mouth of the Lava-Heart corridor and lifted his right hand.

His fingers found the outermost iron seal.

The bar was cold. A fine dust had settled over it. Beneath the dust, in the red-mercury light, the bar's engravings stood plain: the Kabbalistic Tree of the Messianic Church, the six-winged owl of Minerva, and older things still — emblems he would have to take back to the archive before he could put a name to them.

His fingers traced the line of the engraving slowly downward, and stopped, near the foot of the lowest seal, at a point that had been almost entirely choked with dust.

A tiny device, almost lost in the corrosion.

Not the Kabbalistic Tree. Not the six-winged owl.

A Gorgon.

Medusa.

The coat of arms of the House of Medici.

Licinius's grey eyes narrowed a fraction of a fraction.

"At last," he said. "I have found you."

His voice went down the workings and came back to him, the way a stone comes back up from a deep well.

"Golgotha."

The maroon car was running hard through the autumn dark on the edge of Florence.

Through the windows the suburbs slid past — the long stone walls of the villas, the orange pools of gas-lamp, the distant skeleton of scaffolding going up around the United World Festival's main venue, strung with the small stars of steam-crane lights. The lamps of the road slid past and stitched themselves into a single yellow ribbon behind the car.

The cabin was quiet.

Quintilian, Don Juan, and Alfonso were still unconscious. Their breathing had steadied, but their faces were the colour of skimmed milk. The mechanic had been set upright against the rear seat and was breathing on her own; the blood at the corner of her mouth had dried to a brown line. Valentina drove. She said nothing. Her hair, drying in the warm air of the cabin, lifted and fell in the draft from the heater, and the faint cold sweetness of honeysuckle came off it.

Then, from one of the stretchers, a very small sound.

"...Mama..."

Valentina's eyes flicked from the road to the rear-view mirror.

It was Cesare.

He lay on the improvised berth with his eyes closed, his face the white of an uninked page. The blast had overloaded his neural-link; the Seraph had been stripped from him, but the damage to the system ran deeper than the suit. He had not yet come all the way back.

"...Aunt..."

Valentina's grip on the wheel tightened, by a single degree.

Aunt?

She did not know who Cesare meant. But she did know that his mother, Lucrezia, had been dead some years now.

"...Golgotha..."

Cesare's lips were still moving. The sound was thinning, growing soft at the edges, the way a radio signal thins at the horizon, until it was no longer a word at all. His fingers found the edge of the stretcher. They closed on the canvas, knuckles white. Then they let go.

Valentina looked back at the road.

She did not wake him.

She only pressed the pedal a little further down. The steam engine answered with a low, rough cough, and the maroon car took the last bend before the Minerva compound at speed.

Ahead of her, the lights of the bureau were already in the sky.

第180章 密涅瓦机关的血色清晨
