【中文】
第182章 格里高利家的钢铁防线

叹息之墙前，莱希特伯爵的声音还在回荡。

"开门吧，密涅瓦。"他说，声音不大，但每个字都像是钢钉钉进木板里，"枢机会给你们的时间，已经到了。"

中央圣所的屏幕把这一切忠实地传回来。巴别塔平台上，薇若兰站在原地一动不动，工程师们屏息凝神地等她的命令。

屏幕上的莱希特伯爵抬起手腕，看了一眼表。

"十，"他开始倒计时，"九，八……"

就在他数到"七"的时候，翡冷翠郊外公路的尽头又亮起了车灯。

不是一辆。

是一整队。

重型履带车的引擎声从远方传来，低沉、绵密，像是远方滚来的雷。莱希特伯爵的手停在了半空，他微微侧头，望向声音的来源。

那队车的速度不快，甚至可以说是慢条斯理地在逼近。但车身上喷涂的徽记让他的面色变了。

那不是枢机会的标志，也不是教廷任何一支部队的徽记。

那是双头狮鹫。

"格里高利。"莱希特伯爵低声说出了那个名字。

格里高利家族，掌控着西方世界红水银命脉的顶级豪门，双头狮鹫家徽。翡冷翠的每一台机动甲胄、每一座蒸汽工厂都流着他们的血。

"停。"莱希特伯爵抬手，示意自己的车队不要轻举妄动。

那队车在距离圣堂装甲师大约三百米的地方停下了。领头的不是重型履带车，而是一辆通体银灰的礼车，车门上镌刻着精致的狮鹫浮雕。

车门打开。

一个年轻男人走了下来。

他穿着一身剪裁考究的灰色西装，肩线笔直，胸口别着一枚双头狮鹫胸针。右手套着白色手套，左手提着一把金色的手枪——不是军用制式，是私人定做的收藏品，枪管上刻着繁复的狮鹫纹饰。

亚历山大·格里高利。

薇若兰的未婚夫。

格里高利家族年轻一代的佼佼者，被追随者称为"少君"的男人。

他下车后没有立刻说话，而是慢慢地环视了一圈圣堂装甲师的车队，目光从铅灰色的装甲车顶扫过架设的探照灯、蒸汽驱动的机枪塔，最后落在了莱希特伯爵身上。

"亚历山大·格里高利！"莱希特伯爵的嗓音陡然拔高，带着压抑不住的怒意，"你敢违抗枢机会的命令！"

亚历山大·格里高利笑了。

那是一种礼貌的、得体的、却带着冷意的笑容，嘴角微微上扬，像是翡冷翠社交场上最标准的笑法——只是眼底没有半分温度。

"违抗？"他缓步向前，白手套在枪柄上轻轻敲了两下，"我只是来接我未婚妻回家。枢机会的命令管得了密涅瓦机关，管不了我格里高利家的家事。"

"你——"

"薇若兰是我的未婚妻。"亚历山大打断了他，声音依旧平静，却像一块铁板砸在地面上，"密涅瓦机关是格里高利家投资的——你们用的每一滴红水银，有四成是从我家的矿井里流出来的。"

他顿了顿，环视着莱希特伯爵身后那些面面相觑的圣堂装甲师士兵。

"我看谁敢动。"

叹息之墙内侧的监控室里，工程师们发出了一阵低低的惊叹声。屏幕上的对峙还在继续，但密涅瓦这一方所有人都看出来了——圣堂装甲师的阵脚乱了。

莱希特伯爵的面色铁青，他显然没有料到这个变数。格里高利家族不是普通的贵族，他们是教廷的财脉，是西方机械文明的血管。动格里高利，等于拿刀捅自己的心脏。

"亚历山大，你不要自误。"莱希特伯爵压低了声音，"枢机会的命令不是儿戏——"

"我知道不是儿戏。"亚历山大举起那把金色手枪，枪口朝天。

"开枪。"他对自己的车队说。

"警告射击。"

格里高利家车队最前排的三辆装甲车同时开火，枪口喷出灼热的火舌，子弹打在了圣堂装甲师车队前方的地面上，泥土飞溅，石屑迸射，几发子弹甚至擦着莱希特伯爵脚下那辆装甲车的车头铁皮飞过去，在钢板上犁出几道深深的弹痕。

警告射击。

不是要杀人，而是要告诉你——我有能力杀你。

莱希特伯爵身边的人下意识地往后退了一步。圣堂装甲师是精锐不假，但格里高利家带来的不只有礼车。在那三辆开火的装甲车后面，更多的车辆正在展开——全副武装的格里高利家私人卫队，士兵们清一色穿着灰蓝色军服，手持军用级连射铳。

更后面，还有两台机动甲胄。

不是炽天使，只是普通的军用甲胄，但已经足够在数量上对圣堂装甲师形成压制。

莱希特伯爵沉默了。

他是个老军人，不是不懂战场的傻子。格里高利家的红水银供应如果真的切断，不只是密涅瓦机关瘫痪——整个翡冷翠的军工体系都会出问题。这个代价，枢机会承受不起。

"指挥官。"身边的副官低声说，"我们的人还没到齐，如果格里高利家真的要动手——"

"我知道。"莱希特伯爵抬起手，示意他不必再说。

他深深地看了亚历山大一眼，那双深陷的眼睛里闪过复杂的情绪——愤怒、忌惮、权衡。最后，他把目光移向了叹息之墙上方那面巨大的黑色机械门。

"撤退。"他说。

副官一愣："指挥官？"

"撤退。"莱希特伯爵重复了一遍，声音沙哑，"回去向枢机会汇报。"

圣堂装甲师的士兵们如释重负地松了口气。铅灰色的装甲车缓缓启动，蒸汽引擎重新轰鸣，履带从地面上碾压过去，碾碎了之前犁出的弹痕。

莱希特伯爵最后回头望了一眼叹息之墙，目光在监控探头的位置停了一瞬——他知道薇若兰在看。

"告诉你们的副总长，"他的声音通过车载扩音器传出来，"今天的事还没完。"

然后车队调头，缓缓驶回翡冷翠的方向，浓黑的煤烟在秋日的阳光里拉出一条长长的尾巴。

叹息之墙前安静了下来。

亚历山大·格里高利收起了那把金色手枪，把枪别回腰间，抬手正了正领口的狮鹫胸针。

他转向叹息之墙的方向，微微颔首，像是在隔着无数吨钢铁对薇若兰点头。

"开门。"他说。

密涅瓦机关的观战室里，瓦莲京娜把双脚从扶手上放了下来。

她今天穿了一件深蓝色的叶尼塞军裙，裙摆下露出一双修长笔直的腿，套着锃亮的黑色长靴。金色的长发盘在脑后，一根银色的忍冬发簪穿过发髻，整个人靠在观战室的软椅上，手里端着一杯已经凉透的红茶。

屏幕上，亚历山大·格里高利正站在圣堂装甲师撤退后的空地上，灰色西装的衣摆被风吹得微微翻起。

"终于来了一个靠谱的盟友。"瓦莲京娜笑了，把茶杯放下，声音清亮如碎冰。

她转头看了一眼身旁同样盯着屏幕的塔拉夏："你那个总长呢？还躺着？"

"佛朗哥教授还在重症监护室，"塔拉夏低声说，"刚才醒了一次，问了西泽尔的情况，又昏过去了。"

瓦莲京娜沉默了一瞬，点了点头，没有再说什么。

叹息之墙的第三重锁开始解除。

层层叠叠的机械咬合发出沉闷的咔嗒声，巨大的黑铁门缓缓向两侧分开。亚历山大·格里高利带着两名贴身护卫走了进来，格里高利家的私人卫队则留在叹息之墙外警戒。

他没有多看密涅瓦机关内部的那些机械——虽然这里每一台设备都流着格里高利家的红水银——他径直走向中央圣所的方向。

薇若兰就站在那里。

巴别塔平台上，她还维持着刚才的站姿，一只手搭在黄铜栏杆上，脊背挺得笔直。工程师们已经散了大半，只剩塔拉夏和几个核心成员在控制台前待命。

亚历山大走上平台，脚步不急不缓，皮鞋踩在金属地板上发出清脆的声响。

他在薇若兰面前站定。

薇若兰转过头来看他。她的脸上依旧没什么表情，但眼底的那层冰似乎薄了一点。

"你来了。"她说。

"我说过会来。"亚历山大说。

他伸出手，握住了她的手。薇若兰的手指冰凉，带着金属的触感——长年在密涅瓦机关里摆弄机械，她的指尖总是凉的。

"你没事吧？"他问。

"我没事。"薇若兰说，把手从他掌心里轻轻抽出来，低头看了一眼自己发白的指节，"佛朗哥老师和西泽尔有事。"

亚历山大点了点头，没有追问。佛朗哥教授的病情他在来的路上已经听说了——那位疯疯癫癫的老枢机卿撑不了多久了，这是公开的秘密。而西泽尔·博尔吉亚，那个在马斯顿掀起腥风血雨的年轻人，此刻正躺在密涅瓦的病房里，生死未卜。

"枢机会不会善罢甘休。"亚历山大说出了在场所有人都在想的话，"今天他们退了，是因为没准备好。莱希特回去汇报之后，枢机会会重新评估局势——他们会考虑是不是要把格里高利家也一起收拾。"

薇若兰没有说话。

"不过那是以后的事。"亚历山大环视了一圈中央圣所，"现在最重要的是争取时间。"

脚步声从平台下方传来。

碧儿·丹缇端着一个银质托盘走上平台，托盘上放着一杯热气腾腾的咖啡，咖啡杯是纯白瓷的，杯沿镶着一道金线——那是密涅瓦机关接待最高规格来宾时才会用的杯子。

"亚历山大少爷。"碧儿微微欠身，把托盘递过去，"咖啡，不加糖。"

亚历山大看了她一眼，接过杯子。他认得这个姑娘——西泽尔从克里特岛带出来的女侍长，平民出身，却有一种不卑不亢的沉稳。

"谢谢。"他喝了一口，皱了皱眉——太烫了——但没有放下杯子。

"别担心。"他对薇若兰说，"我已经派人去联系其他顶级家族了。美第奇家在银行业有根基，他们未必会公开站队，但暗地里帮忙调些资金周转不是问题。"

他顿了顿，又补了一句："高文少爷那边也递了话，他在翡冷翠的人脉比想象中广。"

薇若兰的眉头微微动了一下。

美第奇家。美杜莎家族。和格里高利家同为西方三大顶级豪门之一，掌控金融命脉。如果美第奇家愿意暗中援手，密涅瓦机关短期内不会因为经费问题停摆。

"还有一件事。"亚历山大把咖啡杯放回托盘上，声音放低了，"枢机会这次动用的理由是'密涅瓦私藏失控炽天使'，他们需要把所有罪名推到西泽尔和你们身上。如果能找到证据证明那具欧米茄原型体并非密涅瓦的——"

"它不是密涅瓦的。"薇若兰说，"是原罪机关的。"

亚历山大沉默了一瞬。"你能证明吗？"

"能。"薇若兰的声音冷硬如铁，"我花了两年的时间在原罪机关里安插眼线，证据链是完整的。"

亚历山大的眼睛亮了一下。

正当他准备继续追问的时候，平台下方的通道里又传来了脚步声——这次更急促，带着金属碰撞的声响。

贝隆快步走上平台。

他今天没穿军服，套了一件深灰色的便装外套，但腰间别着武器——那把他从不离身的黑色十字纹蜂巢手铳。他的脸色不太好，眼窝底下有明显的青黑，显然也没怎么睡。

"副局长也来了。"贝隆对薇若兰和亚历山大点了点头，然后说，"李锡尼在密涅瓦外围的地下通道入口布了人，骷髅地那边暂时安全。"

"暂时？"亚历山大皱眉。

"欧米茄原型体的信号源虽然停止了移动，但没有消失。"贝隆压低声音，"它还在那里，在维苏威火山深处，安静地待着。"

薇若兰的手指在栏杆上无声地收紧了。

"还有一件事。"贝隆从口袋里摸出一张折叠的纸条，"李锡尼让我转交给你。"

薇若兰接过来，展开看了一眼。那是一串地址和几个名字。

"他说，异端审判局里还有愿意帮我们的人。"贝隆说，"不多，但关键时刻能用。"

薇若兰把纸条折好，收进了袖口。

平台上方忽然安静下来。工程师们各自回到了自己的工位上，低声交谈着处理善后事宜。巴别塔的黄铜圆台在灯光下泛着暗沉的光泽，像一座沉默了千年的祭坛。

亚历山大看着薇若兰的侧脸——她的面容依旧平静，但眼底的疲惫掩饰不住。密涅瓦机关的副总长，教皇国最顶尖的技术天才，此刻看起来也只是一个在重压下支撑着的年轻女人。

"你应该休息一下。"他说。

"西泽尔还没醒。"薇若兰说，"佛朗哥老师还在抢救。我没有休息的时间。"

她转身走向控制台的方向。

"让人去把美第奇家和高文家的联络人约来。"她的声音恢复了往日的冷硬和果断，"还有——继续监测欧米茄的信号源，一有异动立刻报告。"

"是。"塔拉夏应道。

亚历山大看着她的背影，嘴角微微动了动，没有再劝。

碧儿端着空了的托盘走下平台，经过贝隆身边时低声问了一句："西泽尔少爷那边……有人守着吗？"

"碧儿小姐一直在。"贝隆说，"薇若兰副总长派了两个护士轮流值班。"

碧儿点了点头，加快脚步往病房的方向走去。

维苏威火山的深处，欧米茄的信号源依旧沉默着。

它像一头蜷缩在巢穴中的远古巨兽，闭着眼睛，安静地呼吸。

但所有人都知道——它还活着。

而骷髅地的秘密，还没有被打开。

在密涅瓦机关深处的某间病房里，西泽尔躺在床上。

他的面色依旧苍白得近乎透明，嘴唇毫无血色，胸口裹着厚厚一层纱布，心电监护仪上的绿色波形缓慢地起伏着。碧儿给他换了三次额头上的冷毛巾，每一次他都毫无反应。

但就在亚历山大的车队进入密涅瓦机关的那一刻——就在所有人的注意力都集中在叹息之墙的那一刻——

西泽尔的手指动了一下。

极其轻微的一下。

像是水面下有什么东西正在苏醒。

【English】
Chapter 182 — The Gregori Steel Wall

Lechite's voice was still ringing against the Wailing Wall when the first headlight appeared.

"Open the gates, Minerva." The count spoke quietly. Each word fell like a steel nail driven into oak. "The time the Curia gave you is finished."

Inside the central sanctuary, the screens relayed every syllable back to the Babel Platform. Veronika stood where she had stood for the last two hours, one hand resting on the brass railing, her spine a plumb line. The engineers around her had stopped breathing.

On the screen, Count Lechite raised his wrist and glanced at his watch.

"Ten," he began. "Nine. Eight."

He had reached seven when a second set of lights came on at the far end of the Florence arterial road. Then a third. Then a fourth — a long, slow constellation rolling out of the dark.

Not one vehicle. A convoy.

The engines were the low, patient rumble of heavy treads, the sound of distant thunder that had decided where to land. Lechite's hand, still raised for the count, paused in mid-air. He turned his head a fraction toward the noise.

The column moved at a walking pace. Almost leisurely. But the moment the headlights caught the insignia painted on the lead vehicle's flank, something left the count's face and did not come back.

Not the crossed keys of the Curia. Not the seal of any Vatican regiment.

A double-headed griffin, gold on a field of slate grey.

"Gregori," Lechite said, under his breath.

The Gregori. The family with their fingers on the red mercury pipelines of the Western world. Whose mines bled into every steamworks, every walking engine, every Seraph-class chassis forged inside the walls of Florence. To move against the Gregori was to take a knife to the heart of one's own army.

"Hold," Lechite said, lifting a hand to his own drivers. "Nobody moves."

The convoy stopped at three hundred meters from the Cathedral Armored Division's line. The lead vehicle was not a treaded troop carrier at all. It was a town car, silver-grey, long as a hearse, the doors chased with a relief of griffins so fine the headlights caught each feather.

The door opened.

The man who stepped out wore a grey suit cut with a precision that bordered on the theological. The shoulder line was a straight edge. On his left breast, a single griffin brooch in oxidized gold. His right hand was sheathed in a white kid glove. In his left he carried a pistol — not a service weapon, but a private commission, the barrel chased with the same griffin motif repeated like a prayer.

Alexander Gregori.

The young master. The Minor Prince, as the house organs called him. Veronika's betrothed.

He did not speak at once. He let the silence do the work. His gaze travelled the Cathedral Armored Division's line — over the slate-grey hulls, the searchlight rigs, the steam-driven gun turrets that were only idling now — and came at last to rest on Lechite.

"Alexander Gregori!" The count's voice jumped half an octave, anger shearing through his control like a blade through silk. "You dare flout the Curia's order?"

Alexander Gregori smiled.

It was a Florentine smile. The corners of the mouth lifted exactly the correct distance. The teeth were not shown. The eyes were not warmed. The whole thing was a perfect little piece of social engineering, the sort of expression that opens doors in palaces and closes them in alleyways.

"Flout?" He stepped forward, white glove tapping the pistol grip twice, very lightly. "I've come to fetch my fiancée home. The Curia's writ runs on Minerva. It does not run in my family."

"You—"

"Veronika is my betrothed." He cut Lechite off the way one cuts a card. His voice had not risen. It fell on the gravel like an iron plate. "And Minerva is a Gregori investment. Four-tenths of every drop of red mercury running through your walking engines came out of our mines. You are standing on my family's blood."

He let that land. Then he turned his head, slowly, and looked along the row of Cathedral Armored Division soldiers who had begun, very quietly, to look at one another.

"I'd like to see who wants to try me."

Inside the Wailing Wall's monitoring room, a low murmur ran through the engineers. On the screen the standoff held, but the geometry of it had shifted, the way a beam shifts a moment before it gives. Everyone in the room could see it: the Curia's line was no longer steady.

Lechite's face had gone the color of a tarnished blade. He had not expected this variable. The Gregori were not nobility in the ornamental sense. They were the blood in the Western war machine. To cut them out was to cut out one's own.

"Alexander." He lowered his voice. The anger was still in it, but now it had a leash. "Don't mistake yourself. The Curia's order is not a piece of theatre—"

"I know what it is."

Alexander raised the gold pistol. The barrel pointed up at the pale autumn sky.

"Open fire," he said to his own convoy. "Warning shots."

The first three Gregori armored cars spoke at once. The muzzles spat a clean white flame. The rounds cracked into the dirt at the Cathedral Division's feet, threw up clods and pebbles, and one of them — a single, almost idle round — stitched a bright furrow down the lead plate of Lechite's command car, sparks flying in a long, hissing line.

Warning fire.

The grammar of it was older than the Curia. It said: I have the power to kill you. I am choosing, for the moment, not to.

The men at Lechite's shoulder stepped back, almost in unison. The Cathedral Armored Division was elite, yes, but what the Gregori had brought was not a parade. Behind the three lead cars the column was unfolding: grey-blue uniforms, military-grade repeaters, the disciplined silence of men who were paid to be dangerous. And at the rear, two walking engines took their first heavy steps out of the transporters — not Seraphs, only common military chassis, but common in the way a sledgehammer is common.

Lechite said nothing for a long moment.

He was an old campaigner. He had been in enough rooms where the wrong word cost a province. He could read the math: if the Gregori chose to cut the red mercury, it would not be Minerva that went dark. It would be the whole Florentine military-industrial complex. The Curia could not pay that bill, not this quarter, perhaps not this year.

"Commander." His aide spoke low, at his elbow. "We are not at full strength. If they mean it—"

"I know."

Lechite raised a hand. He looked at Alexander Gregori for a long, measuring moment. Anger. Calculation. The small, cold math of who could afford to bleed. Something behind his eyes settled, the way a dog settles when it has decided not to bite.

"Fall back," he said.

"Commander?"

"Fall back. Report to the Curia."

The relief on the faces of the Cathedral Division men was almost indecent. The slate-grey armor began, one vehicle at a time, to move. The steam plants coughed back to life. The treads ground over the dirt and the fresh furrows of the warning fire, smoothing them out as if the morning had not happened.

Lechite turned once, in his command car, and looked up at the Wailing Wall. He knew where the camera was. He knew Veronika was watching.

"Tell your deputy director," he said, into the vehicle's amplifier, "this is not finished."

Then the column turned, and the long black coal smoke from its funnels dragged a tail across the autumn sun.

In the observation room above the central sanctuary, Valentina put her feet down from the arm of the chair.

She was wearing the dark blue of the Yenisey military dress — a long skirt, a fitted jacket, her gold hair pinned up at the back of her head with a silver honeysuckle pin. Black boots, polished to a depth that swallowed the room's light. She had been holding a cup of red tea for the better part of an hour. It was cold now. She set it aside.

On the screen, Alexander Gregori stood alone on the empty road in the leftover dust, the tail of his grey coat lifting slightly in the wind.

"Finally," she said, "a sensible ally."

She glanced at Talasha beside her. "Where is your Director-General? Still flat on his back?"

"Professor Franco woke once," Talasha said quietly. "He asked about Caesar. Then he was gone again."

Valentina did not reply for a moment. She nodded, once, and said nothing else.

The third of the Wailing Wall's three locks began to come undone.

The sound was enormous and unhurried — a deep, mechanical chuck-chuck-chunk as gear engaged gear, as if the wall itself were clearing its throat. The great black iron gate, thicker than a cathedral's nave, began to drift apart, a hand's width at a time. Alexander Gregori walked in with two of his personal guards at his shoulders. The rest of the column stayed outside, deployed in a quiet ring, watching the road back to Florence.

He did not look at the machinery as he passed through it, though every joint, every cable, every steam gland in the place was paid for in his family's red mercury. He was not here to admire the décor. He walked straight to the central sanctuary, and then up, to the Babel Platform.

Veronika was waiting for him.

She had not moved. One hand on the brass rail, the line of her back like a drawn blade. The engineers had thinned out. Talasha remained at the console with two of the core staff. That was all.

Alexander's heels rang on the metal floor. He stopped two paces from her.

Veronika turned her head. Her face was unreadable, the way a closed book is unreadable. But somewhere behind the eyes, the ice had thinned a fraction.

"You came," she said.

"I said I would."

He held out his hand. She took it. Her fingers were cold, as they always were — the coldness of long years spent among cold metal. The contact lasted a moment, then she drew her hand back, glanced at her own pale knuckles, and looked away.

"I'm all right," she said. "It is Franco and Caesar who are not."

Alexander nodded. He did not press. He had heard, on the drive in, about the old cardinal-engineer slipping toward the end, and about the young Borgia bastard lying somewhere below them in a sickbed with a hole in his chest. Both stories were public secrets by now, the kind of news that travels under doors.

"The Curia will not let this rest," he said, which was the sentence every person in the room had been thinking. "They withdrew because they were not ready. When Lechite reports, the College will sit down and decide whether they can afford to take us on at the same time. They will decide they cannot. But they will try something else."

Veronika said nothing.

"For now," Alexander said, looking around the central sanctuary, "we buy time."

Footsteps on the metal stair. Belle Dante came up onto the platform carrying a silver tray. On the tray, a single cup of coffee in the white china with the gold rim that Minerva kept for heads of state. Steam curled off it like a small white flag.

"Lord Alexander." She inclined her head and offered the tray. "Coffee. No sugar."

He looked at her. He knew who she was — Caesar's housekeeper, pulled out of Crete, common-born, the sort of woman who should have been invisible in a room like this. She was not invisible.

"Thank you." He took the cup. It was too hot. He drank anyway, and the corner of his mouth tightened.

"Don't worry," he said to Veronika. "I have already sent word to the other great houses. The Medici are bankers. They will not stand in the open with us, but they will move money in the dark. They can keep Minerva solvent through the winter."

He paused, as if choosing his next sentence from a small rack of them.

"Gawain's people have reached out as well. He has wider reach in Florence than anyone gives him credit for."

A small movement at the corner of Veronika's mouth. The Medici. The Medusa. The Gregori. The three great pillars of the Western financial spine, and two of them, at least, were willing to keep the lights on in this particular basement.

"There is one more thing," Alexander said, setting the cup back on Belle's tray. He lowered his voice. "The Curia's pretext for this morning is that Minerva has been concealing an out-of-control Seraph. They mean to pin the whole affair on Caesar and on you. If we can produce evidence that the Omega prototype was never ours—"

"It wasn't ours." Veronika's voice went iron-hard. "It was the Original Sin Bureau's."

Alexander was quiet for a beat. "Can you prove it?"

"Yes." Veronika's chin did not move. "I have spent two years placing eyes inside that office. The evidence chain is complete."

Something lit behind Alexander's eyes.

He started to say something else. He did not get the chance. From the stairwell below the platform there came the sound of faster footsteps — a stride that meant business, with the faint metallic jingle of a sidearm.

Byron came up onto the platform.

He was out of uniform today, in a dark grey civilian coat, but the weapon at his hip was the same — the black crosshatch hive-pattern pistol he never let more than a foot from his body. He had not slept. The bruise-coloured hollows under his eyes said so as eloquently as a signed confession.

"Deputy Director." He nodded to Veronika, then to Alexander. "Licinius has people at the underground approach outside Minerva. Golgotha is quiet for the moment."

"For the moment," Alexander repeated.

"The Omega signal has stopped moving." Byron kept his voice down. "But it hasn't gone dark. It's still down there, in the guts of Vesuvius. Waiting."

Veronika's fingers tightened on the brass rail. The metal gave a small, unwilling creak.

"One more thing." Byron reached into his coat and produced a folded slip of paper. "Licinius asked me to give you this."

Veronika took it. Unfolded it. A string of names, and a single address in old-town Florence.

"He says there are still people inside the Office of the Inquisitor-General who will help us," Byron said. "Not many. Enough."

Veronika refolded the paper. It disappeared into her sleeve as if the sleeve had been waiting for it.

A hush settled over the platform. The engineers drifted back to their consoles. The great brass disc of the Babel turned slowly in its housing, catching the overhead lamps and giving back a dull, sacrificial gold.

Alexander looked at Veronika's profile. The composure was still there, but he could see, beneath it, the architecture of a woman holding up a ceiling. The deputy director of Minerva. The most brilliant technician in the Papal States. Also, at this precise hour, a young woman running on reserves she did not have.

"You should rest," he said.

"Caesar hasn't woken up," she said. "Professor Franco is still in surgery. I don't have time to rest."

She turned toward the console.

"Get the Medici and Gawain contacts into one room by tonight," she said. Her voice was the old Veronika voice, the one that cut clean. "And keep eyes on the Omega signal. Anything — anything — at all, I want to know before it finishes moving."

"Yes, Deputy Director," Talasha said.

Alexander watched her go. The corner of his mouth moved a fraction. He said nothing further.

Belle took the empty tray down the platform stairs. As she passed Byron she lowered her voice.

"Caesar's room — is someone with him?"

"Mistress Belle has been there since last night," Byron said. "The Deputy Director posted two nurses. They're rotating."

Belle nodded, and went on, faster, toward the ward.

In the depths of Vesuvius, the Omega signal held its silence.

It crouched in its hollow the way a great old thing crouches — eyes closed, breathing slow, patience older than the men who were watching for it. It had not moved. It had not spoken. It had only, in the small hours, very slightly, exhaled.

But everyone in the room above the world knew it was still there.

And the secret of Golgotha was still sealed.

In a ward somewhere deep in the Minerva complex, Caesar Borgia lay on a clean white bed.

His face was the colour of paper. His lips had no colour at all. The bandages across his chest rose and fell in the small, mechanical rhythm of a body that had not been consulted. The green line of the heart monitor crawled across the screen in its long, patient, indecisive hum.

Belle had changed the cold cloth on his forehead three times. Each time, nothing.

But at the moment the Gregori column rolled through the Wailing Wall — at the moment every eye in Minerva turned toward the gate and the savior it had brought —

Caesar's right hand, lying palm-up on the sheet, had moved.

A single finger. A twitch. A fraction of an inch.

As if, somewhere far below the green line of the monitor, something was beginning, very quietly, to wake.

第183章 紫瞳里的两个灵魂

【中文】
第183章 紫瞳里的两个灵魂

心电监护仪上的绿色波形忽然加速。

不是平稳的起伏，而是被什么东西从内部拨弄了节奏，频率陡升，像一湖死水被投进了滚烫的铁。守在床边的护士抬起头，看了一眼屏幕，又看了一眼床上那张苍白得近乎透明的脸——西泽尔的睫毛在颤动。

极其轻微的，像蝴蝶翅膀被风吹拂。

然后他睁开了眼睛。

那双眼睛是紫色的，澄澈得像锡兰山上融化的雪水。但雪水之下有什么东西正在游动——金红色的纹路从瞳孔深处浮现出来，像岩浆在冰层下流淌，同时另一种翡翠色的纹路交织其中，两种光芒交替闪烁，紫色被金红与翡翠撕扯成明暗不定的碎片，仿佛他的虹膜里住着两个互不相让的灵魂。

护士呆住了，手里的托盘险些脱手。

金红与翡翠的纹路闪烁了三次，然后缓缓消隐，像潮水退去了。最后他的瞳孔恢复了那种独特的深紫，只在后颈的黄金套管处，隐约透出一丝暗红色的微光——像是某种余烬尚未彻底冷却。

西泽尔慢慢坐了起来。

他的动作很慢，像是一台沉睡太久的机器在重新校准每一个关节。胸口的纱布还裹着厚厚一层，心电监护仪发出短促的报警声，他伸手按掉了那个声音，然后低头看自己的手。

右手攥着一样东西——一枚银戒指，内嵌米粒大小的冰原寒玉碎料，泛着清冷的光。左手攥着另一样东西——一片暗金色的金属碎片，边缘锋利如刃，那是圣剑装具·Excalibur的碎片。

他都没有松手。

"……"

西泽尔沉默着，目光从手心移到周围。洁白的病房，消毒水的气味，窗帘被拉得严实，只透进一线苍白的灯光。他的身体还很虚弱，但意识已经清晰得像一柄擦亮的刀。

他翻转右手中的银戒指。

戒指的内侧是光滑的，而外侧——靠近指根的那一面——有一行极细的刻字，小到几乎要用放大镜才能看清。那字不是现代西方的通用文字，而是某种古老的东方篆体，笔画繁复，被岁月磨得发暗。

他用拇指摩挲着那些笔画，辨认了很久。

"吾乃博尔吉亚·艾琳娜……"

他的声音很轻，像是自言自语，又像是在确认什么。

"……机械神教左使。"

他把戒指翻到背面，凑近眼前，眯起眼睛想看清剩余的刻字。后面似乎还有更小的字，但光线太暗了，他只能辨认出"左使"与"艾琳娜"两个词组，其余的笔画连在一起，像一条被拧断的锁链，意义不明。

他没有把戒指放下，而是用拇指反复摩擦着那行字，指节微微发白。

脑海里有一幅画面浮现出来——那是他在意识深处遇见的叩门者说过的几句话，当时他听不清，现在字迹落在银戒指上，才终于和他记忆深处的某个片段对上了。叩门者留下过线索，他当时没有留意。

走廊上传来急促的脚步声。

门被推开了。

第一个进来的是碧儿·丹缇，手里还端着一盆刚换过的冷水。她看到西泽尔睁着眼睛坐在床上，盆子险些脱手，水洒了一地。

"少爷！您醒了！"碧儿的声音里带着颤抖。

紧接着是昆提良，他那颗铁塔一样的身体挤在门框里，一只手按着门框，大步冲进来，跪在了床边。他不会说什么漂亮话，只是一把攥住了西泽尔的肩膀，上下打量，确认他还活着。"老板。"他的声音沙哑得几乎听不出原来的样子。

唐璜紧跟其后，眼底有明显的红血丝，显然已经很多天没有好好睡过了。但那张嘴还是不肯闲着："得，总算醒了。我还以为您要睡到万国盛典开幕那天。"

阿方索最后一个走进来，没有说话，只是站在唐璜身后，机械右手的手指无声地动了动——那是他在确认自己的微型机械蜘蛛储能状态的习惯动作，紧张时就会做。

然后是瓦莲京娜·罗曼诺夫。

叶尼塞公主站在门口，没有立刻走进来。她的金色长发用一根素色发带束在脑后，忍冬的清香和病房里的消毒水味混在一起。她穿着一件简单的白衬衫，袖口卷到小臂，双手交叉抱在胸前，目光落在西泽尔的右手上——那枚银戒指。

"你醒了。"她说，语气平得像叶尼塞冰原上的冻湖。

最后进来的是三个人——薇若兰、亚历山大·格里高利和李锡尼。薇若兰的面容依旧清冷，但眼底的血丝出卖了她——这位密涅瓦机关的副总长显然已经连续工作了很久。亚历山大站在她身侧，那张年轻的面孔上罕见地出现了如释重负的表情，但随即被压了下去。李锡尼则靠在门框上，黑色制服的领口敞着，朗基努斯圣枪碎片的握柄从腰间露出一角。

病房不大，一下子挤进来这么多人，连空气都变得稀薄了几分。

西泽尔环顾四周。

他看到了碧儿端着空盆的手在发抖，看到了昆提良攥着他肩膀的手指关节发白，看到了唐璜眼角的红血丝和阿方索无声跳动的机械指节，看到了瓦莲京娜抱着双臂靠在门框上的姿态，看到了薇若兰眼底的血丝和亚历山大刻意维持的平静，看到了李锡尼袖口沾着的一小块暗红色痕迹——那是血，不是他的血。

他看了很久。

然后他低声开口。

"我知道了。"

声音平静，像是在陈述一个已经确认过的事实。

"妈妈的秘密。"

他的目光落在那枚银戒指上，拇指又一次摩挲过那行小字。

"姑姑的秘密。"

"机械神教的秘密。"

"骷髅地的秘密。"

每说一个词，他的声音就更低一些，但没有任何人觉得他是在胡言乱语——他太清醒了，那双紫色瞳孔在苍白的脸上像两盏冷灯，映着在场每一个人的脸。

"但我还不能全部说。"

他抬起了右手，让银戒指的内侧朝向薇若兰。"你看这个。"

薇若兰走近一步，俯身接过那枚银戒指，凑到眼前。她转动戒指，目光扫过那行细小的东方篆体刻字。起初她的表情没有变化——只是技术人员面对一组需要辨认的符号。

但当她的目光扫到"艾琳娜"三个字时，她的手停住了。

"艾琳娜……"她重复了一遍这个名字，眉心拧成了一道纹。

她抬起头，看向西泽尔。"你说这上面刻的是'博尔吉亚·艾琳娜，机械神教左使'？"

"嗯。"西泽尔说。"只看清了这些，后面的字太密，光线不够。"

薇若兰把戒指还给了他，但脸上的表情没有恢复。她垂下目光，沉默了几秒，然后说："艾琳娜……我父亲的日记里提到过这个名字。"

所有人的目光都集中到了她身上。

"佛朗哥老师年轻时候并不是枢机卿，他只是一个痴迷机械的年轻工程师。"薇若兰的声音很轻，像在回忆很久以前的事。"他有一个小圈子，都是对机械文明狂热追求的同好，他们自称'蒸汽机械神教'，相信机械终有一天能取代血肉之躯，成为通向神的阶梯。"

她顿了一下。

"那个圈子里有一个人——叫艾琳娜·博尔吉亚。"

唐璜吹了一声口哨。"博尔吉亚？"

"初代教皇的妹妹。"薇若兰说。"她的全名是艾琳娜·博尔吉亚。教廷的官方记载说她在'净化异端'的火刑中被烧死了，但佛朗哥老师的日记里写过——'艾琳娜不是异端，她是最纯粹的机械信徒，她看到了我们所有人都没看到的东西。'"

"然后她消失了。教廷宣布她死于火刑，但佛朗哥老师说他从来不信。"薇若兰抬起头，"他在日记里写：'她的脑子比在场所有人都清醒，她不会被烧死的。'"

"她是机械神教的创始人之一。代号左使。"

病房里安静了下来。

西泽尔没有说话，他只是把银戒指重新套回了右手中指，指节刚好贴合——那是瓦莲京娜送的见面礼，内嵌的冰原寒玉碎料在接触皮肤的瞬间传来一阵凉意，像是冰原上吹来的风。

"没错。"另一个声音从门口传来。

李锡尼。

异端审判局第一副局长靠在门框上，双手抱胸，黑色制服上的血渍还没来得及换掉。他那双锐利得像鹰的眼睛盯着西泽尔手中的银戒指，喉头动了动。

"我在异端审判局的档案里也看到过这个名字。"

他的声音粗粝如砾石，和他这身血迹斑斑的制服很配。"艾琳娜·博尔吉亚——初代教皇的亲妹妹，机械神教创始人之一，代号左使。教廷把她列为头号异端。"

"公元星历六百四十二年，翡冷翠大教堂广场上举行了盛大的火刑仪式，宣判她为'亵渎神明的机械魔女'，公开焚毁。"

"但火刑之后，她的尸体从未被找到。"

李锡尼松开抱着的双臂，往前走了一步。

"异端审判局的绝密档案里有一句话——'火刑之夜，广场上起了一场无名之火，烧毁了半座广场的帐篷，但目击者说他们看到了一个黑影从火焰中走出，消失在夜色里。'"

"档案的批注是：'疑为幸存，已下令全球搜捕，未果。'"

他看着西泽尔。"另一份档案里写着——她最后出现的地点，是东方。"

"东方？"瓦莲京娜皱眉。"她从火刑柱上活了下来，然后逃到了东方？"

"据说。"李锡尼点头。"但异端审判局的人追到东方边境就失去了她的踪迹。那里是夏国的地盘，我们的触手伸不了那么深。"

"之后再也没有人见过她。"

他顿了一下。"但她的名字——艾琳娜·博尔吉亚——在异端审判局的通缉名册上挂了六百年。六百年了，还没有人敢把她从名册上划掉。"

西泽尔没有接话。

他低下头，摸了摸自己的后颈——黄金套管的位置。那块嵌入脊椎的金属片此刻微微发烫，像是有什么东西在里面脉动。他能感觉到后颈的皮肤下有电流在跳动，细密而急促，像被什么东西从内部叩响。

"我还知道……"他开口了，声音比刚才更低。

"熔岩之心的通道……可以通往骷髅地。"

薇若兰的身体僵了一瞬。

"那里有……"他顿了顿，像是在整理那些从意识深处浮上来的画面。"炽天使的残骸。"

"还有……"

他的手无意识地攥紧了那枚银戒指。

"世界树的残枝。"

这三个字落下去的时候，病房里的温度仿佛骤降了几度。

薇若兰的脸色彻底变了——不是惊讶，而是一种技术人员面对最危险的核心机密被意外暴露时的那种紧绷。"你怎么知道这些？"她的声音很冷，但语速比平时快了一倍。"这些信息在密涅瓦机关的档案库里都属于绝密，你不可能在任何公开资料里看到。"

"我在……"西泽尔的目光有些恍惚，像是在努力抓住某些正在消散的画面。"在醒过来之前，意识深处有人告诉我的。"

"或者不是'告诉'。"他皱眉。"是……灌进来的。像红水银灌进管道，强制注入。"

"红水银？"

"红水银深处。"西泽尔的声音变得很慢，每一个字都像是从极深的地方打捞上来。"锡兰的末代星见……残枝01号……她的意识就在那里。"

"她告诉我……世界树的根在东方，叶在西方。只有两者合一，才能结束这一切。"

没有人接话。

就在这个时候——

控制台方向传来一声尖锐的警报。

"副总长！主屏幕出现异常信号！"塔拉夏的声音从对讲机里传出来，带着明显的紧张。"不是欧米茄的信号源——是另一个！它从外部入侵了我们的通讯频道！"

薇若兰猛地转身，冲出了病房。

亚历山大紧跟其后，李锡尼最后一个离开，他走之前看了西泽尔一眼，那双鹰眼里有某种说不清的复杂。

西泽尔也下了床。

他的身体还很虚弱，双腿像是灌了铅，但他还是站了起来。碧儿想扶他，被他摇头拒绝了。昆提良伸手过来，他接住了那只粗糙的大手，借力站稳。

"走。"他说。

"去主控室。"

一行人穿过密涅瓦机关深处的走廊，脚步声在金属地板上回响。灯光昏暗，空气中弥漫着机油和金属的气味——那是维苏威火山特有的味道，几百度的地热从地底升起，被循环冷却系统勉强压制，但总有一丝热度逃逸出来，让空气带着一种沉闷的暖。

主控室的大门前已经被工程师们围得水泄不通。

西泽尔拨开人群，走到最前面。

那块三米直径的球形实时投影屏幕上，原本显示的是密涅瓦机关内部各区域的监控画面——鹰巢车间、巴别塔圆台、叹息之墙外围、维苏威火山深处的信号追踪界面。

现在，所有画面都消失了。

取而代之的是一片纯黑。

然后，纯黑的画面中央，缓缓浮现出一个人影。

那是一个女人。

她穿着一件拖地的黑袍，兜帽压得很低，只露出下半张脸——苍白的皮肤，薄薄的嘴唇，嘴角挂着一丝意味不明的弧度。她的右手撑着一把伞。

那把伞是红色的。

鲜艳的红，像凝固的血。

"红伞……"李锡尼的声音从身后传来，压得极低。"红伞级能量信号——S级危险等级。这把伞本身就是一件武器。"

屏幕上的黑衣女子缓缓抬起头。

兜帽下露出了一双眼睛。

那双眼瞳是深紫色的——和西泽尔一模一样的深紫。

"锡兰星见的紫瞳。"薇若兰的声音从牙缝里挤出来。

西泽尔盯着那双眼睛，指节无声地收紧了右手中的银戒指。

屏幕上的女子对着镜头——对着密涅瓦机关里所有正在观看的人——笑了笑。

那个笑容很淡，但带着一种让人脊背发凉的笃定。

"西泽尔。"

她开口了。声音通过加密频道传出来，带着一点杂音，像是从很深很深的地方传上来的回声。

"我在骷髅地等你。"

她把手中的红伞轻轻转了半圈。

"带着你的伙伴们一起来。"

她的紫色瞳孔在屏幕的微光中闪了闪，像两口深不见底的井。

"——两个人一起到，才能打开那扇门。"

然后屏幕恢复了正常。

监控画面重新跳出来，欧米茄信号追踪界面恢复运转，但那个黑衣女子的影像已经被彻底清除了——像从未出现过一样。只有主控室记录仪上的时间戳还留着，证明刚才的一切不是幻觉。

主控室里安静得能听到冷却管里蒸汽流动的声音。

西泽尔站在人群最前面，苍白的脸上没有任何多余的表情，但后颈的黄金套管正在发烫——烫得像一块烧红的铁，烙在他的脊椎上。

他低头看着右手中的银戒指。

"博尔吉亚·艾琳娜……"

他的声音极轻，像是在对自己说。

"左使……"

他把目光投向维苏威火山深处的方向——那里，欧米茄的信号源依旧沉默着，骷髅地的秘密依旧封着，而那扇门后面等着的，已经不只是一个秘密了。

是两个。

"两个人一起到，才能打开那扇门。"

他把银戒指从右手中指上取下来，翻到背面。灯光太暗，那些更小的字他依然看不清。

但他知道——

很快他就会看清的。

【English】
Chapter 183 — Two Souls in Violet

The green trace on the heart monitor quickened.

Not the steady rise and fall of a body mending itself, but something else, a thing tugged out of rhythm from within, as if a stone had been dropped into still water and the rings of it were racing outward. The nurse on duty looked up from her book, glanced at the screen, and then at the bed.

Cesare's lashes were trembling.

It was the smallest possible movement, the brush of a moth's wing against the air.

Then he opened his eyes.

They were violet. The clear, washed violet of meltwater running off the high Ceylonese peaks, the kind of color you could almost drink. But beneath the violet something was moving. Threads of molten gold and crimson rose out of the pupils, and through them wove something cooler, something like green jade lit from within. The two colors took turns. The violet was torn between them, and for a moment the iris looked as though two people were trying to speak out of the same mouth and neither would yield.

The nurse stood frozen. The enamel tray in her hands tilted, and only the clatter as it righted itself on the side table brought her back.

The threads flickered three times, and then they receded. The violet settled back into itself, deeper now, and only at the back of his neck, where the golden cannula sat flush against the spine, was there a faint ember-glow, as though something there had not finished cooling.

Cesare sat up.

Slowly. As if some long-dormant mechanism were finding each joint in turn. The bandages across his chest were thick, white, still faintly pink at the centre. The monitor began to bleat. He reached out and pressed the silence, and then looked down at his own hands.

In his right fist, something small and cold. A silver ring set with a sliver of polar ice-jade the size of a grain of rice.

In his left fist, something hot and sharp. A fragment of dark-gold metal, the edges still honed, a piece of the broken regalia the world had called Excalibur.

He did not let go of either.

For a long time he was silent. His gaze moved from hand to hand, and from his hands to the room. A white ward. The smell of carbolic. The curtains drawn so tight that only one pale band of light came in. His body was still badly broken, but his mind had come back sharp, the way a knife does when you draw it across a strop.

He turned the ring in his right hand.

The inside of the band was smooth. The outside, near the root of the finger, was engraved. The letters were very small, almost too small to read without a glass. They were not the common Western script of any modern nation. They were some older Eastern seal-script, the strokes dense, age-darkened.

He worked his thumb across them for a long time.

"I am Borgia . . . Elena . . ."

His voice was very low. Half to himself. Half to make sure.

". . . Left Emissary of the Church of the Machine."

He turned the band over. The remaining characters were smaller still, packed so close together they ran into one another like a chain whose links had been wrenched apart. He could make out only two phrases — *Left Emissary* and *Elena*. The rest of the inscription was dark, and the light in the ward was poor.

He did not put the ring down. He kept rubbing the engraved line with his thumb, and the knuckle of his thumb had gone white.

Some image surfaced in him. Words spoken by the knocker at the door of his mind, in that place between unconsciousness and waking, words he had not been able to hear at the time. The knocker had left a sign. He had not seen it then. He saw it now, letter by letter, on the silver band of a ring.

Down the corridor, footsteps. Quick ones.

The door was pushed open.

The first one in was Beryl Danti, who was still carrying the basin of cold water she had just changed. When she saw Cesare sitting up in bed with his eyes open, the basin nearly went out of her hands. Water splashed over the linoleum.

"Young master." Beryl's voice was shaking. "You're awake."

Then Quintilian. His great iron-tower of a body filled the doorframe. He had one hand on the lintel as he came through, and he dropped to his knees at the bedside in a single motion. He was not a man given to speeches. He simply took Cesare by the shoulders and looked him up and down, checking that he was still in one piece.

"Boss." His voice was a ruin. There was almost nothing of the man they had known in it.

Don Juan came in a step behind. The whites of his eyes were netted with red. He had not slept in days; it was there in every line of his face. But the mouth had not changed.

"Well," he said. "At last. I'd begun to think you meant to sleep through the opening of the Universal Gala."

Alfonso was the last of them. He did not speak. He stood just behind Don Juan, and the fingers of his mechanical right hand moved in their quiet, habitual way, that small dance he did when he was testing the charge of the micro-spiders he carried in the knuckles. He did it when he was worried. He did it now.

Then Valentina Romanovna.

The Princess of the Yenisei stood in the doorway, and she did not come in at once. Her gold hair was tied back with a plain band, and the small scent of honeysuckle that always followed her was fighting the carbolic in the ward. She wore a white shirt, sleeves rolled to the elbows, arms folded across her chest. Her eyes went at once to the silver ring in Cesare's right hand.

"So," she said, in a voice as level as a frozen lake. "You're awake."

Last in were three. Verolan, Alexander Gregory, and Licinius. Verolan's face was the same careful mask it always was, but the bloodshot whites of her eyes betrayed her — the Deputy-Director of the Minerva Bureau had clearly been working without pause for days. Alexander stood at her shoulder, and on that young face, for once, the relief was visible before it was forced down. Licinius leaned in the doorframe, his black uniform half-undone at the collar, and the grip of the broken Longinus lance showed at his hip.

The ward was not a large room, and with this many people in it the air had begun to feel thinner.

Cesare looked around.

He saw Beryl's hand on the empty basin, shaking. He saw the white of Quintilian's knuckles where he gripped his shoulder. He saw the red veins in Don Juan's eyes, and the small mechanical dance of Alfonso's fingers. He saw Valentina folded against the doorframe. He saw the sleepless red in Verolan's, and the calm Alexander was trying to keep on his face. He saw, on the cuff of Licinius's black coat, a small dark smear. Blood. Not his.

He looked at all of them for a long time.

Then he spoke.

"I know."

The words were even. As though he were stating a fact he had already confirmed.

"About my mother."

His gaze dropped to the silver ring. The thumb passed once more over the engraving.

"About my aunt."

"About the Church of the Machine."

"About Golgotha."

With each phrase his voice fell lower, but no one in the room thought he was raving. He was too awake. Those violet eyes, in that white face, were like two cold lamps throwing light on every other face there.

"But I cannot tell you all of it. Not yet."

He raised his right hand and turned the ring so that the inside faced Verolan. "Look at this."

Verolan took a step forward, took the ring, and lifted it close to her eyes. She turned it. Her gaze moved over the tiny characters in the old Eastern seal. At first her face was unreadable — a technician confronted with a string of symbols that needed deciphering.

But when her eyes crossed the name *Elena*, her hand stopped.

"Elena," she said. She said the name again, as if to be sure of the shape of it. A line drew itself between her brows.

She looked up at him. "You are saying the inscription reads 'Borgia Elena, Left Emissary of the Church of the Machine'?"

"Yes," said Cesare. "That is all I could make out. The rest is too dense, and the light here is no good."

Verolan gave the ring back, but the look on her face did not go with it. She was quiet for a few seconds, her eyes on the floor, and then she said, "Elena. My father's journal mentions that name."

Every eye in the room was on her.

"Franco was not always a Cardinal," she said, and her voice was quiet, the way it gets when one is remembering a thing that is far away. "He was once a young engineer, obsessed with mechanism. He had a small circle of friends, all of them bitten by the same obsession. They called themselves the Church of the Machine. They believed that mechanism would, in the end, replace the flesh, and that it was a stairway to God."

She paused.

"There was a woman in that circle. Her name was Elena Borgia."

Don Juan whistled, low through his teeth. "Borgia?"

"The first Pope's sister," said Verolan. "Her full name was Elena Borgia. The Vatican's official records say she was burned at the stake in the purification of the heretics. But my father wrote, in his journal — 'Elena was not a heretic. She was the purest of the Machine-faithful. She saw what none of the rest of us had eyes for.'"

She stopped again. "Then she disappeared. The Vatican announced her death at the stake, but Franco wrote that he had never believed it. He wrote: 'Her mind was clearer than any other mind in that square. She was not the kind of woman who gets burned.'"

"She was one of the founders of the Church of the Machine. Her code-name was Left Emissary."

The ward went quiet.

Cesare said nothing. He slid the ring back onto the middle finger of his right hand. It fitted exactly. The sliver of polar jade touched his skin, and a small coldness passed through him, as though a wind from the Yenisei had found its way into the room.

"That is correct."

Another voice, from the doorway.

Licinius.

The First Deputy-Director of the Holy Office of the Inquisition was leaning against the frame, arms folded, the dark blood on his coat not yet changed out of. His eyes were sharp, the sharp of an eagle. They were on the ring.

"I have also seen that name," he said, "in the archives of the Office."

His voice was rough, the way gravel sounds underfoot. "Elena Borgia. Sister of the first Pope. Co-founder of the Church of the Machine. Code-name: Left Emissary. The Vatican listed her as the first heretic of the new age."

"In the year of the star-calendar 642, a great burning was held in the square of the Cathedral of Florence. She was condemned as the 'mechanical witch who had profaned the Lord,' and was burned in public."

"But after the burning, her body was never found."

Licinius dropped his arms and took a step forward.

"In the top-secret files of the Office, there is one line. 'On the night of the burning, an unexplained fire broke out in the square, consuming half the pavilions. Witnesses say they saw a black figure walk out of the flames and vanish into the dark.'"

"The file is annotated: 'Survival suspected. Order issued for worldwide search. No result.'"

He looked at Cesare. "Another file says that the last place she was seen was in the East."

"In the East?" Valentina's brow drew together. "She walked off the pyre and fled east?"

"So the file has it," Licinius said. "But the agents of the Office lost her trail at the eastern frontier. That was the land of the Summer Empire. Our reach did not extend that far."

"No one has seen her since."

He paused. "But her name — Elena Borgia — has remained on the Wanted List of the Holy Office for six hundred years. Six hundred. No one has dared to strike it off."

Cesare did not answer.

He lifted a hand and touched the back of his neck, where the golden cannula sat in the bone. The metal there was faintly warm, faintly alive, as if something inside it were pulsing. He could feel a current running under the skin, small and quick, like a knocking from within.

"There is something else I know," he said, and his voice was lower than before.

"The passage under the Lava Heart . . . leads to Golgotha."

Verolan's body went still for a moment.

"There is," he said, and he paused as though he were pulling the words up from a great depth, "the wreckage of a Seraph."

"And . . ."

His hand closed, of its own, around the silver ring.

"A branch of the World Tree."

When the last three words fell, the temperature in the ward seemed to drop several degrees.

Verolan's face changed. Not to surprise. To the tension of a technician who has just heard the most dangerous piece of core information spoken aloud in the wrong room. "How do you know this?" Her voice was cold, and twice as fast as usual. "That information is classified at the top level in the Minerva Bureau. You could not have read it in any public source."

"I was told," Cesare said. His eyes were slightly unfocused, as though he were trying to hold on to a thing that was moving away. "Before I woke. Someone spoke to me in the deep place."

"Or it was not 'spoken,'" he said, frowning. "It was . . . poured in. The way red mercury is poured into a pipe. Forced in."

"Red mercury?"

"In the deep of the red mercury," Cesare said, and each word came up slowly, as if it were being dredged. "The last Stargazer of Ceylon . . . Branch Fragment One . . . her consciousness is there."

"She told me . . . the root of the World Tree is in the East, and the leaf is in the West. Only the two together can end this."

No one answered.

Then —

A sharp alarm from the console at the far end of the ward.

"Deputy-Director! The main screen is receiving an anomalous signal!" Tarasha's voice came through the speaking-tube, tight with tension. "It is not the Omega source. It is another. It has intruded on our comms channel from outside!"

Verolan turned on her heel and went out of the ward.

Alexander followed. Licinius was the last to leave. Before he stepped through, he looked back at Cesare, and there was something in that eagle's eye that was not easy to read.

Cesare got out of bed.

His body was still very weak. His legs were heavy, as if lead had been poured into them while he slept, but he stood. Beryl reached for his arm; he shook his head. Quintilian's great hand came forward, and Cesare took it, and used it to find his balance.

"Walk," he said.

"To the main hall."

They went through the corridors of the deep Minerva Bureau. Their footsteps rang on the iron floor. The light was poor, and the air carried the smell of oil and hot metal — the breath of Vesuvius, far below, where the geothermal heat was piped up through a hundred radiators and never quite cooled. There was a weight to the air. A warmth that did not want to leave.

The doors of the main control hall were already ringed with engineers.

Cesare pushed through them and came to the front.

The spherical three-metre display in the centre of the room had been showing the standard feeds: the Eagle's Nest workshop, the round table of Babel, the perimeter of the Wall of Sighs, the signal-trace interface at the bottom of Vesuvius.

All of those were gone.

The sphere was black.

Then, in the centre of the black, a figure resolved itself out of the dark.

A woman.

She wore a black robe that dragged the floor. The hood was pulled low, and only the lower part of her face was visible. The skin was very pale. The lips were thin, and at the corner of the mouth there was a small curve, as if she knew something none of the rest of them knew. In her right hand she held an umbrella.

The umbrella was red. The bright red of curdled blood.

"Red umbrella," Licinius's voice said from behind him, very low. "Red-umbrella-grade energy signal. Threat-level S. The umbrella itself is a weapon."

The woman on the screen slowly raised her head.

Out of the hood, two eyes.

They were deep violet. The same deep violet as Cesare's.

"The violet of the Ceylonese Stargazers," Verolan said between her teeth.

Cesare stared at the eyes. The knuckles of his right hand, around the ring, were white.

The woman on the screen smiled at the camera. At everyone in the Minerva Bureau who was watching.

The smile was small. It was also, somehow, certain. The certainty of a thing that has been waiting a long time and has at last been paid.

"Cesare."

Her voice came through on the encrypted channel with a small hiss, as if from a long way down.

"I will be waiting for you at Golgotha."

She turned the red umbrella a half-rotation in her hand.

"Bring your companions with you."

Her violet eyes, in the small light of the screen, glittered like two wells with no bottom.

"It takes two to open the door."

Then the screen was normal.

The feeds came back. The Omega signal-trace interface resumed its quiet blinking. The woman's image was gone, cleared from every buffer, as if it had never been. Only the timestamp on the recorder in the corner of the room still showed the seconds she had been there, and proved that the rest of them had not dreamed it.

The control hall was so quiet you could hear the steam moving in the cooling pipes.

Cesare stood at the front of them. There was nothing on his white face that needed to be read. But at the back of his neck, the golden cannula was hot — hot as a piece of iron that has been left in the fire too long, and is now being pressed to the spine.

He looked down at the silver ring in his right hand.

"Borgia . . . Elena . . ."

The words were very soft. Almost to himself.

"Left Emissary . . ."

He raised his eyes to the deep direction of Vesuvius. The Omega source was still silent. The secret of Golgotha was still sealed. And what waited behind the door was no longer one secret.

It was two.

"Two to open the door," he said.

He slid the ring off his right middle finger, and turned it over, to the side where the smallest characters were. The light in the hall was no better than the light in the ward. The characters he had not yet read still ran together like a chain whose links had been wrenched apart.

He knew, though.

He would read them soon.

【中文】
第184章 红伞下的约定

监控画面恢复成死寂的灰白色，那个黑衣女子的影像像从水面上蒸发的雾一样消失了，只留下时间戳的微弱蓝光在记录仪上闪烁。

主控室里的空气依然凝滞。

西泽尔转过身来，苍白的脸上没有多余的表情，但他的目光从每一个伙伴脸上扫过时，像一道冰凉的刀锋划过，所有人都感觉到了那股不容质疑的决意。

"我要去骷髅地。"

他的声音很平，平得像秋天无风的翡冷翠。

沉默了两秒。

"我们一起去。"

三个声音几乎同时响起——阿方索在西泽尔右侧半步，唐璜靠着主控台，昆提良从军医身边站直了身体。三个男人，三种语气，说出的话却一模一样。

"老板您先别急着感动，"唐璜第一个补充，嘴上的笑容比他眼里的认真更先到，"说实话您要真打算一个人去我可能还得拦您——您一个人往那种鬼地方跑我们这群兄弟怎么办？天天在翡冷翠等您死讯？太惨了。"

"不是感动。"西泽尔说。

"我知道，"唐璜说，"您感动也不承认，这事儿我熟。"

"闭嘴。"阿方索冷冷地看了他一眼。

"瓦莲京娜公主那边有外交豁免权通道，她的车明天还能进密涅瓦机关外围。"阿方索转头看向西泽尔，"如果需要人接应，公主是最合适的。"

西泽尔没有立刻回答。

"我也去。"

人群之外传来一个清冽如冰原寒风的声音。

瓦莲京娜·罗曼诺夫不知何时从走廊里走了进来，金色长发束成简洁的马尾，深蓝色军服外套披在肩上，露出里面贴身的神怒骑士团制式衬衫。她的白靴在金属地板上敲出清脆的节奏，每一步都走得稳当有力，像踩在战场上。

"我是叶尼塞公主，也是神怒骑士团副团长，"她走到西泽尔面前，与他平视，那双深灰色的瞳孔里没有女儿家的柔波，只有刀刃般的清醒，"我可以帮你们。"

西泽尔看着她。

"公主殿下，叶尼塞的外交豁免权是用来保护您安全的，不是让您去送命。"他说。

"那是我的事。"瓦莲京娜回答，"而且——"她停顿了一下，嘴角微微勾起一个几乎看不出来的弧度，"我不记得答应过只做你名义上的未婚妻。我答应过要嫁的是盖世英雄，盖世英雄去的地方，我没有理由不去。"

唐璜轻轻吹了声口哨。

"老板，我越来越觉得您不娶她简直是对神的亵渎。"他低声说。

西泽尔没有理他。

"我也去。"

另一个声音从主控室另一侧传来，沉而硬，像铁块砸在铁砧上。

李锡尼副局长站在阴影里，黑天使军徽在他胸口反射出冷冷的黑光。他的右手自然下垂，那只手里曾经握着那枚让整个翡冷翠颤抖的Longinus圣枪碎片——现在碎片还在不在，没有人能看清。

"我手里有Longinus的碎片，"李锡尼的声音没有起伏，"骷髅地封存了几百年的东西，没有比这更合适的钥匙。"

"李锡尼副局长，异端审判局在枢机会里被压着打，您此刻去骷髅地，等于把把柄送到对手手里。"薇若兰皱着眉说。

"副局长亲自去开一道被初代教皇亲妹妹下了禁令的封门——这个罪名够异端审判局把我烧十次。"李锡尼说，"但枢机会既然敢动密涅瓦机关，就别怪我不按他们的规矩来。"

他的目光扫过在场所有人，最后停在了西泽尔脸上。

"你母亲琳琅夫人——"他开口，又停住了，仿佛有什么话卡在喉咙里，吞不下去也说不出来。

沉默持续了三秒。

"我去。"李锡尼最后只说了这两个字。

"我也去。"

贝隆从角落走了出来。这位十字禁卫军军部少校今早还押着那列装载炽天使的火车穿过翡冷翠郊区，此刻他的脸上没有了伪装时的油滑，取而代之的是一种老兵特有的沉稳。

"我知道密涅瓦机关的秘密通道，可以避开圣堂装甲师的封锁。"贝隆说，"从叹息之墙东侧第七号竖井下去，穿过旧时代排水渠，能直接通到鹰巢的地下第七层，那里有一条维修通道可以绕过叹息之墙的所有锁。"

"你什么时候摸清这条路的？"薇若兰问。

"三年前，"贝隆回答，"密涅瓦机关刚启用我设计的易容系统时，我替前任总长走了一遍所有紧急撤离通道，那条路在那之后就被封了，但封门的锁芯型号我记得。"

阿方索看了西泽尔一眼。

"现在不是问贝隆少校怎么摸清密涅瓦机关秘密的时候，"阿方索说，"老板，您看——"

"我听到了。"西泽尔说。

他抬起手，示意所有人都安静。

"我们明天晚上出发。"

他的声音不大，但主控室里所有人都闭上了嘴。

"今天先养好身体，准备好甲胄和武器。"他看了看自己的右手——紫瞳金纹已经退去，只剩下手背上淡得几乎看不见的紫色脉络，"今晚所有人留在密涅瓦机关。塔拉夏，准备五间客房。"

"是。"塔拉夏在角落里应声。

"还有一件事。"西泽尔说。

他从军服内侧的口袋里取出一个锡封匣。

那匣子大约有成年男人拳头大小，表面是黯淡的锡灰色，边缘处镌刻着复杂的咬合齿轮纹路，每一个齿轮都和相邻的齿轮精密啮合。匣子的两端各有一个小小的钥匙孔，但钥匙孔的形状不是常见的齿形——而是一片极细的莲花瓣。

西泽尔把匣子放在主控台冰凉的金属台面上。

"这是三个月前我在君士坦丁堡郊外，利维坦级飞艇残骸里找到的东西。"他说。

主控室里安静得能听到冷却管里蒸汽流动的声音。

"打不开。"阿方索走上前，仔细看了看那两个钥匙孔，"这种咬合齿轮结构是旧时代的机械锁，钥匙孔里必须同时插入两片形状完全互补的金属薄片才能解锁。"

"我知道钥匙是什么。"西泽尔说。

他从脖子上取下那条银色项链，链坠是一枚小小的莲花齿轮。

莲花齿轮嵌入了左边的钥匙孔。

他从右手取下冰原寒玉银戒指——瓦莲京娜送的那枚——戒面朝下嵌入了右边的钥匙孔。

咔哒。

锡封匣发出一声轻响。

西泽尔双手合住匣盖两侧，按照齿轮纹路的反向旋转了半圈。咬合的齿轮松开，匣盖缓缓弹开。

匣子里躺着两样东西。

一张折叠得很仔细的羊皮纸。

一本薄薄的、没有任何封面标识的纸册。

西泽尔先拿起羊皮纸。

羊皮纸泛黄，边缘有被火燎过的焦痕，但折痕依然工整。他小心地展开，露出来的是一张精密的地下通道图——不是密涅瓦机关的现行布局，而是另一个时代的、规模更庞大的地下工程网络。图纸上用红墨水标注着几条粗实线，旁边写满了密涅瓦机关从未见过的古代机楲文字。

西泽尔只认出了其中几个字——"熔岩之心"、"第七号冰封室"、"王座之厅"。

"这是一张通往骷髅地的秘密通道地图。"他说。

阿方索凑近来看，眉头越皱越紧："这些通道大部分已经塌了，但还有两条是通的。"

"另一条通过维苏威火山底部废弃矿道，就是明天对抗战的预定战场。"西泽尔说。

"还有一条呢？"唐璜问。

"还有一条从旧时代排水渠系统绕过去，"贝隆上前一步，"就是我刚才说的那条。"

图纸上的两条红线在维苏威火山最深处交汇，汇合点被画了一个圆圈，圈里写着一个词——"黑铁之门前厅"。

西泽尔放下图纸，拿起那本纸册。

纸册很薄，封面已经被撕掉了，但内页保存完好，每一页都印着竖排的繁体字。西泽尔翻开第一页，念出了开头几句——

"'我们自火中行走，于无声处听见轰鸣……'"

他的声音忽然顿住了。

"怎么了？"昆提良紧张地问。

西泽尔把纸册递给薇若兰。

薇若兰接过纸册，目光落在那些竖排的繁体字上。她的手指在某一页停住了，停了很久。

"这是我父亲那本无封面书册里的祷文。"她的声音很轻。

主控室里所有人的目光都集中到她脸上。

薇若兰慢慢从自己军服的内侧口袋里取出一本同样薄、同样没有封面的纸册。

她把两本纸册并排放在主控台上。

字迹一致。纸张一致。断句方式一致。

"完全一致。"薇若兰说。

她抬头看着西泽尔，眼神里的震惊被她自己压了下去，但握着纸册的指节却微微发白。

"西泽尔，这本祷文——机械神教的祷文——是我父亲佛朗哥从密涅瓦机关最深层档案库编号B-07里取出来的。我从小看到大，我敢用命担保，这世上没有第二本。"薇若兰说，"你这本是从哪里来的？"

"三个月前君士坦丁堡郊外，利维坦级飞艇残骸里。"西泽尔重复了一遍，"那架飞艇是四十年前原罪机关秘密运输炽天使原型体的专机，爆炸坠毁后残骸被封存在当地的旧矿区。"

"四十年前……"阿方索低声说，"那正是原罪机关总长封存欧米茄原型体的时间节点。"

西泽尔点了点头。

"也就是说，在封存欧米茄的同一架运输机上，还装着一本机械神教的祷文——一本我母亲家族信奉的祷文。"他说。

"你母亲家族？"瓦莲京娜轻声重复。

"锡兰星见家族。"西泽尔说。

主控室里的空气再次凝固。

"那本祷文是谁放在飞艇上的？是机械神教的左使艾琳娜·博尔吉亚本人，还是别的什么人？"李锡尼问。

"我不知道。"西泽尔回答，"但这本祷文现在在我们手里。"

他合上纸册，把纸册和羊皮纸都放回锡封匣，重新锁好。

"先休息。明天我们还要打一场对抗战。"

他顿了顿。

"后天，骷髅地。"

主控室里没有人再说话。

亚历山大·格里高利站在人群最后方，这位格里高利家族的年轻佼佼者从薇若兰拒绝打开叹息之墙那一刻起就站到了密涅瓦机关这一边，他的身后站着三百名格里高利家族的私人卫队，那些穿着双头狮鹫纹章军服的老兵在叹息之墙外排成了三道钢铁防线。

"我会继续率格里高利家的私人军队守在密涅瓦机关。"亚历山大说，"莱希特伯爵的圣堂装甲师虽然被暂时逼退，但枢机会不会善罢甘休，他们会卷土重来。"

他看向西泽尔。

"我去联络美第奇家族和高文少爷。"亚历山大说，"高文家族和我们格里高利家有三代联姻的交情，美第奇家族虽然墙头草，但只要让他们知道枢机会的人已经把手伸到密涅瓦机关——他们会明白下一个就是自己。"

"亚历山大，"薇若兰低声说，"枢机会不会把你也列入异端名单。"

"我父亲是格里高利家的掌门人，"亚历山大微微一笑，那个笑容里有一种属于未来君主的从容，"枢机会敢动格里高利家的人，整个西方世界的红水银供应就断了。莱希特伯爵带的那几千人，吃什么喝什么？烧红水银矿吗？"

薇若兰没有再说话。

"所以你守在这里。"西泽尔对亚历山大说。

"我会守住。"亚历山大说，"你去做你该做的事。"

西泽尔点了点头。

人群渐渐散去。阿方索拉着唐璜去检查五台试制甲胄的能源储备，昆提良去了密涅瓦机关附属医院拿神经接驳缓冲剂。贝隆被塔拉夏领着去确认东侧第七号竖井的通道状态。

李锡尼走到西泽尔身边，沉默了几秒。

"我替我兄弟照顾你母亲。"李锡尼最后只说了这一句，便转身离开了。

西泽尔看着他的背影消失在主控室的金属门后。

主控室里只剩下他和薇若兰。

"你今天差点就死在这里。"薇若兰说。

"我死不了。"西泽尔说。

"别学你父亲。"薇若兰说，"咳血都要瞒着别人。"

西泽尔愣了一下，然后微微低下了头。

"薇若兰，"他说，"谢谢你。"

"谢什么，"薇若兰转身走向主控台，背影笔直得像一杆枪，"你要真死了，我去哪儿找第二个能让密涅瓦机关不被枢机会拆了的人？"

她顿了一下，又回过头来。

"明天对抗战，你打算让谁上？"

"我上。"西泽尔说。

"你确定你的身体撑得住？"

西泽尔抬起自己的右手，看着手背上那几道淡得几乎看不见的紫色脉络。

"撑得住。"

……

夜幕降临了。

翡冷翠城外的郊区，那座挂着木制牌匾的使馆建筑在月光下显得安静而神秘——牌匾上用东方文字写着"中山国使馆"四个烫金大字。

二楼的书房里还亮着灯。

叶素理坐在红木书桌后面，桌上摆着一套茶具，茶香袅袅。他的面前站着一个穿着灰色外套的中年男人，那是他安插在翡冷翠城里的密探。

"你确定？"叶素理把茶杯放下。

"确定。"密探压低声音，"西泽尔一行明天晚上要去维苏威火山深处的骷髅地。"

叶素理的嘴角缓缓勾起。

"机会来了。"他说。

他从椅子上站起来，走到窗边。窗外的翡冷翠城在夜色中闪着点点灯火，远处的维苏威火山像一头沉睡的巨兽，火山的轮廓在月光下显得格外清晰。

"跟着他们，"叶素理对密探说，"找到世界树的残枝。"

"大人，我们的人手不够，"密探迟疑着说，"格里高利家的私人卫队把密涅瓦机关围得水泄不通，圣堂装甲师虽然退了但还在叹息之墙外扎营，我们根本无法靠近。"

"不需要靠近。"叶素理转过身来，烛光在他脸上投下明暗分明的影子，"西泽尔他们既然要进维苏威火山，就一定要从矿道走。矿道入口在火山北麓，那里的地形我三年前就摸清了。"

他从书桌的抽屉里取出一张地图，地图上用红墨水标注了维苏威火山北麓的每一条小路。

"带上三十个人，"叶素理说，"在矿道入口东侧两公里处的废弃伐木场等他们。他们进矿道的时候，就是我们跟进去的时候。"

"如果被发现了呢？"

"那就不是被发现的问题，"叶素理的眼中闪过一丝冷酷的光，"我们中山国想要的东西，从来没有拿不到的。"

密探点了点头，无声地退出了书房。

叶素理独自站在窗前，端起那杯已经凉了的茶。

"世界树的残枝……"他喃喃自语，"有了它，中山国就能重启史前文明的技术……"

他一饮而尽。

"我中山国等这一天，等了四百年。"

……

深夜的密涅瓦机关终于安静了下来。

叹息之墙外，格里高利家族三百名私人卫队的篝火在夜色中明明灭灭。圣堂装甲师的营地在一公里外，和格里高利家的卫队遥遥相对。

主控室下方的临时宿舍区，西泽尔的房间里亮着一盏小灯。

他坐在床沿，身上还穿着那套密涅瓦机关核心骑士的制式军服。军服胸口绣着六翼猫头鹰的密涅瓦徽记，徽记上方的金色细线勾勒出炽天骑士团军徽的火焰轮廓。

他面前的床头柜上，锡封匣安静地躺在那里。

他的右手从军服口袋里取出了那枚银戒指。

银戒指的正面——瓦莲京娜的冰原寒玉银戒指。

他把它翻过来，露出背面的那些小字。

灯光下，那些字终于看清了。

最内圈的一行极小的字，和旁边那行"博尔吉亚·艾琳娜，机械神教左使"排列在一起：

"琉璃，照顾好自己。"

西泽尔的手指在那行字上停了很久。

他把银戒指重新戴回右手中指——现在那枚戒指的背面紧贴着他的皮肤，那行小字被他的体温焐热。

"姑姑。"他低声说。

房间里没有别人。冷却管里蒸汽流动的声音很轻，像远处的潮汐。

"我来了。"

【English】
Chapter 184 — The Promise Under the Red Parasol

The monitor screen returned to the dead grey-white of static. The image of the black-clad woman had dissolved like mist lifting from a river's surface, leaving nothing behind but the pale blue blink of a timestamp on the recording apparatus.

The air in the main control room had not moved.

Cesare turned from the screen. His face was pale in the monitor's afterglow, and there was nothing on it—not anger, not relief, not even the particular exhaustion of a man who had just stared down an armed assassination. When his gaze passed across the faces of his companions it moved the way a cold blade moves across a cutting board, slow and sure, and every man in the room felt the edge of what was being asked of him.

"I'm going to Calvary."

His voice was level. Level as autumn in Florence with no wind in it.

Two seconds of silence.

"We are coming with you."

Three voices rose almost in unison—Alfonso half a step to Cesare's right, Don Juan leaning against the main console, Quintilian straightening from beside the field surgeon. Three men, three different temperaments, the same words.

"Don't get teary on us, boss," Don Juan added first, his grin arriving a heartbeat before the seriousness did. "Honestly, if you were planning to go alone, I'd have had to talk you out of it. You off to that hellhole by yourself—what do the rest of us do? Sit in Florence waiting for news of your death? Too grim a way to make a living."

"It isn't that," Cesare said.

"I know," Don Juan said. "You wouldn't admit it even if it were. I'm familiar with the breed."

"Shut up," Alfonso said, throwing him a cold look.

"Princess Valentina still has diplomatic immunity on the roads," Alfonso went on, turning to Cesare. "Her carriage can reach the outer perimeter of the Minerva Bureau tomorrow. If we need a clean contact, she is our best option."

Cesare did not answer at once.

"I am coming too."

The voice came from beyond the cluster of men. Clear as a wind off the steppe.

Valentina Romanov had entered from the corridor at some point no one had marked. Her gold hair was pulled back in a plain horsetail, the deep-blue uniform coat slung over her shoulders, the standard-issue shirt of the Divine Wrath Knights buttoned tight at the throat. Her white boots struck clean rhythms against the metal floor—each step planted, each step deliberate, as though she were crossing a battlefield rather than a corridor.

"I am the Princess of Yenisei, and second captain of the Divine Wrath Knights," she said, drawing level with Cesare, meeting his eyes at the same height. The grey of her pupils held no softness; it was the grey of a blade that has just been honed. "I can help you."

Cesare looked at her.

"Your Highness. The diplomatic immunity of Yenisei exists to keep you alive, not to send you to your death," he said.

"That is my concern." Valentina's mouth moved a fraction—an almost imperceptible curve at one corner. "And—" she paused, "I do not recall promising to be your bride in name alone. The man I promised to marry was a hero. Where the hero goes, I have no reason not to go."

Don Juan whistled, very softly.

"Boss," he murmured, "I am beginning to think not marrying her would be a kind of sacrilege."

Cesare ignored him.

"I am coming too."

Another voice, this one from the far side of the room—low, hard, the sound of an ingot set on an anvil.

Deputy Director Licinius stood in the shadow. The black angel insignia on his chest caught the light and gave back only the cold black of itself. His right hand hung at his side. That hand, once, had held the fragment of the Longinus Spear that had made all of Florence shudder. Whether the fragment was still in his grip, no one in the room could tell.

"I hold the Longinus fragment," Licinius said, his voice uninflected. "Calvary has been sealed for centuries. There is no better key."

"Deputy Director, the Inquisition is being crushed underfoot inside the Conclave already," Veronika said, frowning. "If you go to Calvary now, you are handing your enemies the excuse they have been waiting for."

"A deputy director personally unsealing a door that the first Pope's own sister put under interdict—that is a charge the Inquisition could burn me on ten times over," Licinius said. "But if the Conclave dares to lay hands on the Minerva Bureau, they cannot expect me to keep playing by their rules."

His gaze swept the room and finally settled on Cesare's face.

"Your mother—Lady Linlang—" he began, and stopped. Something had caught in his throat. He could neither swallow it nor set it free.

The silence lasted three seconds.

"I am going," Licinius said at last. Only those two words.

"I am coming too."

Belon stepped out from the corner. The major of the Cross Imperial Guard's headquarters staff had, that very morning, shepherded the trainload of Seraphim armor through the Florentine suburbs. Now the oiled obsequiousness was gone from his face, replaced by the particular steadiness of a soldier who has outlived a great many things.

"I know the secret passages through the Minerva Bureau," Belon said. "We can avoid the Cathedral Armored Division's blockade. From the seventh vertical shaft on the eastern side of the Wall of Sighs, down through the old-era drainage system—we come out under the Eagle's Nest at the seventh sublevel. There is a maintenance tunnel that bypasses every lock on the Wall."

"When did you map that route?" Veronika asked.

"Three years ago," Belon said. "When the Minerva Bureau first came online, I designed the Bureau's disguise protocols. I was made to walk the entire emergency-evacuation network for the previous director. That passage was sealed afterward, but I remember the lock cylinder."

Alfonso glanced at Cesare.

"This is not the moment to ask Major Belon how he came to know the Minerva Bureau's secrets," Alfonso said. "Boss, if I may—"

"I heard him," Cesare said.

He raised his hand. Everyone in the room closed their mouths.

"We leave tomorrow night."

His voice was not loud. The room obeyed.

"Rest today. Prepare the armor and the weapons." He looked at his own right hand. The violet sigil with its gold traceries had faded; what remained were thin purple veins, so pale they were almost imaginary. "Tonight, everyone stays inside the Minerva Bureau. Talaxia—prepare five guest rooms."

"Yes." Talaxia answered from his corner.

"One more thing," Cesare said.

From the inside pocket of his uniform he drew out a tin-sealed case.

The case was about the size of a grown man's fist. Its surface was the dull pewter of unpolished tin, and along its edge ran a chain of interlocking gear-teeth, each one meshing with the next in a precision that looked almost biological. At each end of the case was a small keyhole—but the shape of the keyhole was not the usual tooth-and-bit. It was a single, very narrow lotus petal.

Cesare set the case down on the cold metal of the main console.

"I found this three months ago, in the suburbs of Constantinople, in the wreckage of a Leviathan-class airship," he said.

The room went so quiet that the steam moving through the cooling pipes could be heard.

"It will not open." Alfonso stepped closer, examining the twin keyholes. "This kind of interlocking gear-work is Old Era mechanical lockwork. You would need two complementary metal wafers inserted at the same time to release it."

"I know what the keys are," Cesare said.

From his neck he drew the thin silver chain. The pendant was a small lotus-gear.

The lotus-gear seated itself in the left-hand keyhole.

From his right hand he drew the silver ring set with ice-plain jade—the one Valentina had given him. The face of the ring, turned down, seated itself in the right-hand keyhole.

Click.

The tin case gave a small, precise report.

Cesare brought both hands to either side of the lid and turned it half a rotation against the grain of the gears. The teeth released one another. The lid lifted of its own weight.

Inside the case lay two things.

A piece of parchment, folded with care.

A thin booklet, without a cover, without a title.

Cesare took up the parchment first.

The parchment had yellowed with age. Its edges were singed where some long-ago fire had licked at them. But the creases of the original folding were still sharp, still regular. He unfolded it with care, and what was revealed was a precise diagram of an underground passage network—not the present-day layout of the Minerva Bureau, but a vaster scheme, from another age, of which the Bureau was only the smallest, latest fragment. In red ink, several thick lines were drawn across the diagram, and along those lines were annotated in a script of ancient machine-letters that the Minerva Bureau had never catalogued.

Cesare could make out only a few of the words: Heart of Magma. Cryo-Chamber Seven. Hall of the Throne.

"This is a map to Calvary," he said.

Alfonso bent closer, his frown deepening. "Most of these passages have collapsed. But two are still clear."

"The second runs through the abandoned mine tunnels beneath Mount Vesuvius," Cesare said. "That is the field of battle we have set for the engagement exercise tomorrow."

"And the other?" Don Juan asked.

"The other runs through the old-era drainage system," Belon said, stepping forward. "The route I just described."

The two red lines on the diagram converged at the deepest point under Mount Vesuvius. The point of convergence was marked with a circle, and inside the circle a single word had been written: Forecourt of the Black Iron Gate.

Cesare set the diagram down and took up the booklet.

The booklet was thin. The cover had been torn away long ago, but the inner pages had survived, each one set in vertical columns of dense type. Cesare opened the first page and read aloud the opening lines.

"We walk through fire, and from the silence we hear the thunder—"

His voice stopped.

"What is it?" Quintilian asked, his shoulders tight.

Cesare handed the booklet to Veronika.

Veronika took it. Her eyes fell on the vertical columns of type, and her finger, traveling down a page, came to rest at a particular point. She stayed there a long time.

"This is a prayer from my father's own coverless booklet," she said, quietly.

Every eye in the room found her face.

Veronika slowly drew from the inside pocket of her own uniform a booklet, identical in size, identical in its absence of a cover.

She laid the two booklets side by side on the console.

The type matched. The paper matched. The punctuation matched.

"Identical," Veronika said.

She looked up at Cesare. The shock in her eyes was being held down by force of will, but the knuckles of the hand holding the booklet had gone white.

"Cesare—this prayer, this prayer of the Mechanical Church—my father Franke took it out of the deepest archive of the Minerva Bureau, file B-07. I have read it since I was a child. I would stake my life on it: there is no other copy in the world." She said. "Where did yours come from?"

"Three months ago. Suburbs of Constantinople. The wreckage of a Leviathan-class airship." Cesare repeated. "That airship was the prototype transport the Original Sin Bureau used, forty years ago, to ship the Seraphim prototypes. After the crash, the wreckage was sealed inside the local old mine."

"Forty years," Alfonso said, low. "That is exactly the time the Original Sin Bureau's director sealed away the Omega prototype."

Cesare nodded.

"In other words, on the same transport that carried the Omega, there was a prayer of the Mechanical Church," he said. "A prayer that my mother's family keeps."

"Your mother's family?" Valentina repeated, softly.

"The Star-seers of Ceylan," Cesare said.

The air in the room solidified again.

"Who placed the prayer on that airship? Was it the Left Envoy of the Mechanical Church, Erinice Borgia herself, or someone else?" Licinius asked.

"I do not know," Cesare said. "But the prayer is in our hands now."

He closed the booklet. He placed the booklet and the parchment back into the tin case and relocked it.

"Rest now. Tomorrow we still have an engagement exercise to win."

He paused.

"The day after, Calvary."

No one in the room said anything more.

Alexander Grigori stood at the back of the crowd. The young scion of the Grigori family had been on the Minerva Bureau's side from the moment Veronika refused to open the Wall of Sighs. Behind him, three hundred of the Grigori family's private guards—their uniforms bearing the double-headed griffin—had drawn up in three steel lines outside the Wall.

"I will continue to hold the Bureau with the Grigori private army," Alexander said. "Count Reicher's Cathedral Armored Division has been pushed back for now, but the Conclave will not let this rest. They will return."

He looked at Cesare.

"I will reach out to the Medici and to young Lord Gawain," he said. "The Gawain family and the Grigori family have been intermarrying for three generations. The Medici are weather-vanes, true—but the moment they understand the Conclave has reached into the Minerva Bureau, they will realize they are next."

"Alexander," Veronika said, low, "the Conclave will put your name on an Inquisition list."

"My father is head of the Grigori house," Alexander said, with a small smile. The smile had the particular composure of a man who already knows he will one day be called king. "If the Conclave dares to touch a Grigori, the entire Western world's red mercury supply is cut off. What are Count Reicher's few thousand men supposed to eat? Smelt red mercury ore?"

Veronika said nothing more.

"Then you hold this place," Cesare said to Alexander.

"I will hold it," Alexander said. "Go do what you must do."

Cesare nodded.

The room began to empty. Alfonso pulled Don Juan off to check the power reserves of the five trial suits of armor. Quintilian went to the Bureau's attached infirmary for the neural-coupling buffer solution. Talaxia led Belon off to confirm the state of the seventh vertical shaft on the eastern side.

Licinius came to stand beside Cesare. He was silent for several seconds.

"I looked after your mother for my brother's sake," he said at last. Then he turned and walked out through the metal door.

Cesare watched his back disappear.

The control room had only himself and Veronika in it now.

"You almost died here today," Veronika said.

"I do not die," Cesare said.

"Do not be your father." Veronika said. "Coughing blood and hiding it from everyone."

Cesare was quiet for a moment. Then he lowered his head a fraction.

"Veronika," he said. "Thank you."

"Thank me for what," Veronika said, turning back toward the console, her spine as straight as a pike. "If you really died, where would I find a second man who can keep the Conclave from dismantling the Minerva Bureau?"

She paused. Then she turned her head.

"Tomorrow's engagement exercise. Who do you plan to send in?"

"I will go," Cesare said.

"Are you certain your body can hold?"

Cesare raised his right hand and looked at the thin purple veins, now almost invisible on the back of his hand.

"It will hold."

...

Night fell.

In the Florentine suburbs, the embassy building with the wooden nameplate stood quiet and strange under the moon. The characters on the nameplate were Eastern script, four gilt characters: Embassy of Zhongshan.

On the second floor, the study lamp was still burning.

Ye Suli sat behind the red-wood desk. A tea set had been laid out on it. The fragrance of the tea curled upward in the cool air. Standing in front of him was a middle-aged man in a grey coat—one of his agents, planted deep in the city of Florence.

"You are certain?" Ye Suli set the teacup down.

"Certain," the agent said, low. "Cesare and his people go tomorrow night, into the deep of Mount Vesuvius, to Calvary."

Ye Suli's mouth lifted, slowly, at one corner.

"Then the chance has come," he said.

He rose from his chair and walked to the window. The lights of Florence were scattered in the night like so many seeds. Far off, the bulk of Mount Vesuvius made a great sleeping shape against the moon, and the line of its rim was unusually clear.

"Follow them," Ye Suli said to the agent. "Find the branch of the World Tree."

"My lord, we are short of men," the agent said, hesitating. "The Grigori private army has the Minerva Bureau ringed. The Cathedral Armored Division has pulled back but is still camped outside the Wall of Sighs. We cannot get close."

"We do not need to get close." Ye Suli turned. The candlelight on his face threw the planes of it into sharp divisions of light and dark. "Cesare and his men, if they mean to enter Mount Vesuvius, must go by way of the mine tunnels. The entrance to those tunnels is on the northern flank of the volcano. I have known that ground for three years."

He drew a map from a drawer of the desk. In red ink, every little track on the north side of the volcano had been marked.

"Take thirty men. Wait for them at the abandoned lumber camp two kilometers east of the mine-tunnel entrance. The moment they go into the tunnels—that is the moment we follow them in."

"And if we are seen?"

"That will no longer be a question of being seen." A cold light moved in Ye Suli's eye. "What Zhongshan wants, Zhongshan has always taken."

The agent nodded. He retreated from the study without a sound.

Ye Suli stood alone by the window. He lifted the teacup. The tea had gone cold.

"The branch of the World Tree," he murmured to himself. "With it, Zhongshan can restart the technology of the pre-historic age—"

He drank it down in one swallow.

"Zhongshan has been waiting for this day for four hundred years."

...

Deep in the night, the Minerva Bureau at last went quiet.

Outside the Wall of Sighs, the Grigori family's three hundred private guards had their campfires burning in the dark, glowing and fading in the wind. The Cathedral Armored Division's camp lay a kilometer out, opposite them across the dark plain.

In the temporary quarters below the main control room, a small lamp still burned in Cesare's room.

He sat on the edge of the bed, still in the regulation uniform of the core knights of the Minerva Bureau. Across the chest of the uniform was embroidered the six-winged owl of Minerva; above the owl, fine gold lines traced the flame-outline of the Seraphim Knights' insignia.

On the bedside table, the tin-sealed case lay quiet.

From the pocket of his uniform his right hand drew out the silver ring.

The face of the silver ring—the silver ring set with ice-plain jade that Valentina had given him.

He turned it over. The small characters on the inside of the band came at last into the light.

The innermost line, in very small type, sat beside the line that read: Erinice Borgia, Left Envoy of the Mechanical Church.

"Erinice. Take care of yourself."

Cesare's finger rested on the line a long time.

He slid the silver ring back onto the middle finger of his right hand. The inside of the band, with its small characters, lay now against his skin. The line of type was warming with the heat of his hand.

"Aunt," he said, under his breath.

There was no one else in the room. The steam in the cooling pipes moved softly, like a distant tide.

"I have come," he said.
