【中文】
第185章 出发前的最后准备

坎特伯雷堡的管家在凌晨两点接到了电话。

电话那头是西泽尔。管家听出少主的声音一如既往地平静，甚至比平时还要平淡些，像是翡冷翠秋夜里刮过石板路的风。

"有几件事拜托你。"西泽尔说。

管家立刻打起精神，握紧了听筒。他知道少主从来不在深夜打电话，更不会在凌晨两点用这种语气说话。上一次少主用这种语气说话，是两年前他独自离开翡冷翠去马斯顿的那晚。

"如果我不能回来，"西泽尔说，"把阿黛尔留在堡里的东西寄往亚琛。她住的那间卧室里有一只锡盒子，盒子里是母亲的梳子，还有几张旧照片。一起寄。"

管家沉默了一秒。他是个老仆人了，跟过西泽尔的外祖母，跟着琳琅夫人，跟着西泽尔。他比任何人都清楚少主说"如果我不能回来"意味着什么。

"少主……"

"还有，告诉她我爱她。"西泽尔说，"就说哥哥说的。"

电话挂断了。

管家握着听筒站在电话机前，听筒里传来断线后嘟嘟嘟的忙音。他站了很久，直到电话机上的铜铃被震得轻轻响了一下才回过神来。

他走到窗边，看着翡冷翠深夜漆黑的天际线。叹息之墙的方向，密涅瓦机关的铜质烟囱吐着暗红色的火光，把半边天都映得绯红。

"圣母保佑。"老人低声说。

密涅瓦机关的地下三层，临时改装的车间里灯火通明。

这里原本是密涅瓦存放退役甲胄零件的仓库，现在被临时清理出来当作战前整备场。到处堆着拆开的甲胄零部件，空气中弥漫着润滑油和金属摩擦产生的焦味。

西泽尔坐在车间的检查台上，薇若兰站在他身后。

她手里拿着一柄极细的黄铜螺丝刀，螺丝刀的尖端是特制的，能伸入黄金套管与皮肤之间那不到半毫米的缝隙。黄金套管已经完成了最后的焊接，外壳上看不出接缝，但薇若兰还在反复检查每一颗微型固定螺栓。

"扭矩正常。"薇若兰的声音冷硬，像是精密仪器在报告数据，"接驳触点的电阻值稳定在0.003欧姆以下，神经信号的传导损耗可以忽略不计。"

她放下螺丝刀，用酒精棉片擦了擦手，然后从旁边的工具盒里取出一只小小的黑色盒子。盒子里躺着一枚比指甲还小的芯片，芯片表面有金色的线路在灯光下若隐若现。

"不朽之王系统的控制芯片。"薇若兰说，"上次在矿道里你用过一次，芯片的过载保护程序已经更新过了，安全阈值从三分钟延长到了五分钟。"

她抬起头，灯光照着她那被白色长发遮住半边的脸。巧克力色的眼睛里没有平时的飒爽，只有一种被压在冷静下的凝重。

"但五分钟是极限。"薇若兰说，"超过五分钟，芯片会烧毁，你的神经系统会失去最后一道闸门。超过八分钟，英雄人格会彻底吞噬你，你就不再是西泽尔了，只是一具穿着甲胄的活武器。"

西泽尔微微点头。

"这次去骷髅地，可能会遇到很多危险。"薇若兰把芯片放回盒子，递给旁边的助手，"不朽之王系统最多用五分钟，否则你会彻底失去自我。"

她的语气平淡得好像在说今天天气不错，但递盒子的手指比平时慢了半拍。

西泽尔接过来，放在贴身的口袋里。

"我知道。"

车间的另一侧，阿方索坐在工作台前。塔拉夏站在他对面，把一只已经拆开的手腕装备放在工作台上。

那是一只蜘蛛巢腕表。

阿方索把它从手腕上取下来，露出了表带下方密密麻麻的微型机械接口。表壳已经磨损了，边缘有几道细小的划痕，那是在矿道里释放蜘蛛时被碎石弹片刮出来的。

"旧款只有六只蜘蛛，干扰半径八十米，持续八分钟。"塔拉夏一边检查内部线路一边说，"对付普通甲胄够用了，但如果你们要去骷髅地……"

他抬起头，湛蓝色的眼睛里映着工作灯的白光。

"维罗妮卡给我看了密涅瓦最深层档案库的资料，欧米茄自愈神经纤维会产生持续的高频电磁场，常规的宽频脉冲根本近不了身。旧款的功率不够。"

阿方索拿起桌上的一只新蜘蛛。这只蜘蛛比旧款大了一圈，腹部嵌着的红水银微晶在灯光下发出暗红色的微光，像是某种昆虫的眼睛。

"新款，"塔拉夏说，"八只蜘蛛，每只都加装了一组高频聚焦天线。单独释放的时候是常规的宽频干扰幕，但如果八只同时定位到同一目标，可以把脉冲能量汇聚到一点。"

他拿起另一只蜘蛛，和第一只并排放在桌上。

"汇聚后的功率是旧款的四倍。"塔拉夏说，"足够烧穿欧米茄自愈神经纤维外层的绝缘鞘。"

阿方索沉默了一秒。

"但这八只里面只有六只是新的。"他说，"还有两只是从旧款里回收改装的，稳定性会差一点。"

"我知道。"塔拉夏说，"没有时间做更多了。"

阿方索点了点头，把新款蜘蛛巢腕表戴回手腕。表壳和他手腕的弧度完美贴合，锁扣咔哒一声扣上。

同一时间，隔壁的整备间里传来金属碰撞的沉闷声响。

那是昆提良。

奥古斯都试制型甲胄已经被竖直固定在整备架上，甲胄的左臂上原本挂载着旧款秘银重盾。现在旧盾已经被取下来了，昆提良正蹲在地上，用一只蒸汽驱动的铆钉枪把新的盾面固定到盾架上。

新盾的盾面是一种他从未见过的合金。

那是一种近乎纯银的颜色，但银中带着一丝极淡的蓝。盾面打磨得如镜面般光滑，在整备灯下反射出冷冽的金属光泽。盾面中央压印着闭眼狮头纹章，狮头的耳朵微微翘起，线条刚硬如刀刻。

昆提良用指节敲了敲盾面。

盾面发出一声极低沉的嗡鸣，像是大钟被极远处敲响，余音在金属内部震荡了很久才消散。

"完美合金。"他低声说。

密涅瓦机关的最高级合金，整个密涅瓦的库存只有不到三吨。完美合金的冶炼工艺是密涅瓦初代总长留下的遗产，一百年来无人能完全复现，它不是简单的金属混合，而是经过特殊电磁场处理的原子级合金，强度是普通秘银的三倍，韧性是影金属的两倍。

佛朗哥教授亲自从封存仓库里取出了这批合金，亲手切割成盾面交给了昆提良。

"五层交错锻造，"昆提良身旁的技术员翻着图纸说，"外两层影金属，中间三层硬金，最内层夹层嵌入冰原寒玉。和旧盾一样的结构，但材料的等级完全不同。"

昆提良没有说话。他把盾面举起来，单手握住盾架内侧的把手，试着挥动了一下。

完美合金比普通秘银重了将近一倍，但昆提良的手臂纹丝不动。

"好盾。"他说，声音里有一种只有老兵才有的满足。

他用粗大的手指摸了摸盾面上闭眼狮头的纹章。狮头的眼睛是闭着的，像是在沉睡，又像是在忍耐。

"老伙计，"他对盾说，"明天就靠你了。"

隔壁的整备间里，唐璜正坐在一张高脚凳上，双腿交叉，手里端着一杯从不知哪里弄来的红酒。他的面前，蔷薇之鬼的右臂甲被固定在台钳上，甲胄手腕处的曲刃镰卡扣已经拆了下来。

新的曲刃镰放在台面上。

那是一把弧度极大的弯刀，刀身和旧款一样轻薄如纸，但刀刃的材质完全不同。完美合金的刀刃呈现出一种近乎半透明的银色，刃口处细如发丝，灯光照上去会在刀刃上折射出一条极细的彩虹线。

唐璜放下酒杯，拿起新曲刃镰，拇指轻轻在刀刃上蹭了一下。

一滴血珠从拇指指腹冒了出来。

"好快。"唐璜面不改色地吮掉那滴血，"密涅瓦的老家伙们总算干了件漂亮事。"

他把曲刃镰装回蔷薇之鬼的卡扣上，咔哒一声锁死。曲刃镰和甲胈手臂浑然一体，像是手臂自然延伸出的利爪。

"漂亮。"唐璜满意地点了点头，转头看向站在门口的阿方索，"阿方索，帮我拍张照，我要发给我那些小情人看看我的新刀。"

"滚。"阿方索面无表情地走过。

整备车间的最深处，瓦莲京娜蹲在一台拆开了胸甲的神怒Ⅲ型甲胄前。

改装后的神怒Ⅲ型比原版高了一截，这是因为她在甲胄的胸腔内部嵌入了一颗新的红水银核心。新的红水银核心不是密涅瓦或格里高利家的标准产品，而是她从叶尼塞皇宫的私人收藏里带来的——那是她母亲生前最后一次实验的遗物，一颗纯度极高的红水银晶块，蕴含的能量是普通红水银核心的1.5倍。

瓦莲京娜用一方白色的丝绸手帕擦去核心表面的指纹。

忍冬的香气从她身上淡淡地飘散开来，和金属的冷腥味混合在一起。

"神经接驳系统的回路测试正常。"她用叶尼塞语低声念着检测数据，切换回了通用语，"脊椎接口的冰原寒玉嵌入位置准确，缓冲效率达到百分之四十三。"

她站起来，拍了拍膝盖上沾上的铁屑。

神怒Ⅲ型的胸甲在她面前竖直站立，灯光照在甲胄的冰蓝色涂装上，反射出冷峻的金属光泽。那是一台为冰原上的战斗而生的甲胄，每一个关节都被设计成能在零下四十度的严寒中灵活运转。

瓦莲京娜伸手抚过甲胈的面罩，面罩的造型是一头张着嘴的冰原狼，冰蓝色的眼睛在灯光下闪烁着冷光。

"走吧。"她对手甲说，声音很轻，"去杀龙。"

李锡尼独自坐在整备间角落的一张桌前。

桌上铺着一方黑丝绒布，丝绒布上躺着两样东西。

一样是朗基努斯圣枪的碎片，碎片只有小指长，断面参差不齐，像是从一整块神圣的金属上生生撕下来的。另一样是一只极小的手持式打磨机，打磨机的砂轮是密涅瓦特制的，砂轮表面镀着一层极薄的红水银。

李锡尼用戴着黑手套的手指捏起圣枪碎片，凑到灯光下。碎片在灯光中不反射任何光线，像是一个吞噬光线的微型黑洞。

他打开打磨机的开关，砂轮发出极轻的嗡鸣声。

然后他开始打磨。

打磨圣枪碎片是一件极其精细的活。碎片的材质不属于任何已知的金属分类，它的硬度远超完美合金，但同时又具有一种诡异的脆性——稍微用力过猛，碎片就会碎成粉末。李锡尼必须用最轻的力道、最精准的角度，一点一点地把碎片断面的毛刺磨平，让它能够完美地嵌入卡槽。

他打磨了很久。

等他终于放下打磨机的时候，碎片的断面已经平滑如镜。他用一方黑丝绒把碎片重新包好，放回贴身的口袋里。

"这次一定能打开骷髅地的门。"他低声说，像是在对自己发誓。

隔壁的房间里，贝隆把那张从锡封匣里取出的秘密通道图铺在桌上。

通道图是一张用极细的黑色墨水在羊皮纸上绘制的立体图，线条精密复杂，像是某种古老机械的内部构造图。图上标注着三条不同的路线，每条路线都用了不同颜色的墨水。

贝隆用手指沿着红色的路线慢慢滑动。

"这条通道，"他指着图上起点处的一个标记说，"从密涅瓦机关地下七层的废弃通风井开始，进入维苏威火山北麓的矿道。矿道走大约两公里后，会接入一条地下暗河。"

他的手指滑动到图上一个蓝色的标记。

"暗河的水温很低，常年保持在四度左右。河水来自火山深处的地下水系，水流方向是从东向西，最终汇入维苏威火山底部的熔岩之心。"

他的手指停在图上一个红色的标记——那是整个通道图上最大的一个标记，标记旁边用古老的花体字写着两个字："熔岩之心"。

"从熔岩之心到骷髅地，还有一段路要走。"贝隆说，"这段路是最危险的，因为熔岩之心的温度极高，普通甲胈的隔热层撑不了太久。"

他抬起头，看向站在桌边的西泽尔。

"这条通道通往维苏威火山的地下暗河，然后从地下暗河通往熔岩之心，最后从熔岩之心通往骷髅地。"贝隆说，"全程大约十二公里。按正常行军速度，需要四个小时。但如果遇到阻击，时间可能要翻倍。"

西泽尔看着那张图，目光在每一个标记上停留片刻。

就在这个时候，车间外传来一阵急促的脚步声。

脚步声在金属地板上敲出轻快的节奏，伴随而来的是一阵若有若无的花香——不是忍冬的清冷，也不是兰花的浓烈，而是一种更温暖、更甜润的香气，像是翡冷翠仲夏夜花园里盛放的金合欢。

车间门被推开了。

宝儿·拉瑟站在门口。

她穿着一身翡冷翠流行的深红色骑马装，剪裁得体，把她纤细的腰肢和修长的双腿勾勒得恰到好处。她的头发挽成一个简单的发髻，露出一张在车间冷光下依然明艳的脸。

"我也去。"

她的声音在车间的金属回音中显得格外清亮。

所有人同时抬头。

"宝儿？"唐璜第一个反应过来，"你怎么进来的？密涅瓦机关的叹息之墙——"

"我和塔拉夏有旧交情，他帮我进来的。"宝儿走进来，高跟马靴在金属地板上敲出清脆的声响，"我是炽天骑士团的旧部，也是隐形下属。"

她停在西泽尔面前，抬起下巴。

"我熟悉翡冷翠的每一条暗道、每一家地下酒吧、每一个愿意用金币买消息的人。我可以帮你们打探消息。"

西泽尔没有立刻回答。

宝儿·拉瑟，前炽天骑士团S级评价见习甲胄骑士，出身寒门，后脱离军籍成为翡冷翠知名歌舞剧女演员。西泽尔在马斯顿的时候就认识她，在斗兽场的那段日子里她是他隐藏的隐形下属。

她曾经请西泽尔帮忙消除她的军籍，换一个普通人的身份。西泽尔做到了。但她没有隐姓埋名，她把新的人生过得比原来更精彩。

"我不要报酬。"宝儿说，"上次你帮我消除了军籍，我还欠你一个人情。"

"不欠。"西泽尔说，"那是交易。"

"那就让我再做一笔交易。"宝儿说，"我帮你们打探消息，你们活着回来。"

西泽尔看了她很久。

宝儿的眼神很直，那种曾经在斗兽场里当过见习骑士的人才有的直。她不是那种会在危险面前退缩的人。

"好吧，你跟着我们。"西泽尔说，"但要注意安全。"

宝儿露出了一个笑容，那个笑容在车间冷硬的灯光下显得格外温暖。

"放心，我命硬。"

碧儿·丹缇推着餐车从车间后门走进来。

餐车上堆满了用油纸包好的干粮和装满清水的皮囊，还有几瓶密涅瓦附属医院特制的营养液。

她把干粮一份份地分到每个人手里，动作利落得像是她在特洛伊酒店当女侍长时养成的习惯。

"这是黑面包，密涅瓦食堂今天烤的，能放三天不坏。这是腌肉，盐放得很重，也是为了防腐。这是水，维苏威火山附近的地下水，我尝过了，没有硫磺味。"

她把一份干粮塞到西泽尔手里。

"你们一定要活着回来。"

碧儿的声音很平，但西泽尔注意到她在分干粮的时候手指一直在抖。

碧儿·丹缇，平民鞋匠的女儿，毕业于都灵圣教院初等院文秘专业，是西泽尔的女侍长。出身平民却勇敢坚定，是她主动接应了被释放后的西泽尔。

"碧儿。"西泽尔说。

"嗯？"

"谢谢你。"

碧儿低下头，整理了一下餐车上已经空出来的位置。

"不用谢我。"她说，"您和三位骑士一定要平安回来。我还等着给您烫明天早上穿的白衬衫。"

西泽尔没有说话。他低头看着手里那份干粮，油纸包上还留着碧儿手指的温度。

午夜。

密涅瓦机关地下七层的废弃通风井前，集合完毕。

西泽尔换上了密涅瓦核心骑士的制式军服，军服胸口绣着六翼猫头鹰的密涅瓦徽记。徽记上方的金色细线勾勒出炽天骑士团军徽的火焰轮廓。

他的腰间挂着指挥剑，右手中指上戴着一枚银戒指——冰原寒玉银戒指。他把那枚戒指的背面贴着皮肤，让那行刻字紧贴着他的体温。

阿方索、昆提良、唐璜三人站在他身后，分别穿着所罗门王、奥古斯都和蔷薇之鬼的甲胈。三台试制版甲胈在走廊的灯光下反射出冷硬的金属光泽。

瓦莲京娜站在一侧，神怒Ⅲ型甲胈已经完成了着装调试，冰蓝色的涂装在灯光下闪着冷光。

李锡尼站在另一侧，黑色长风衣的下摆几乎拖到地面。他的左胸口袋里，朗基努斯圣枪的碎片安静地躺着。

贝隆的怀里抱着那张秘密通道图。

宝儿·拉瑟站在最外围，深红色骑马装在金属走廊里显得格外醒目。

薇若兰站在西泽尔正对面。

她没有穿甲胈，只穿着一身工程师的白大褂，白色长发用一根发带随意地扎在脑后。巧克力色的眼睛在灯光下闪着冷冽的光。

"从你们踏出这道门开始，"薇若兰说，"密涅瓦机关的通讯系统会全程保持开放。但维苏威火山内部的地形复杂，信号可能会中断。"

她看着西泽尔。

"如果信号中断超过一个小时，我会认定你们遇到了无法解决的危险。届时我会启动应急方案，亲自带人进去接应。"

"不用。"西泽尔说。

"这不是在跟你商量。"薇若兰说。

她伸出手，把西泽尔衣领上一个微微翻起的角摁平了。动作很轻，但手指停留了一秒钟才收回。

"去吧。"

西泽尔点了点头。

他转身走向废弃通风井的入口。入口是一扇已经被锈蚀得不成样子的铁栅门，铁栅门后是一道向下的金属梯，金属梯延伸进一片漆黑。

昆提良第一个迈步。他的奥古斯都甲胈在金属地板上踩出沉重的声响，每一步都让走廊的灯光微微摇晃。

阿方索跟在他后面。所罗门王甲胈的脚步声更轻一些，但每一步都精准得像是机械钟表。

唐璜走第三个。蔷薇之鬼的曲刃镰在他手臂上微微晃动，反射出一线冷光。

瓦莲京娜走在队伍中间偏后的位置，神怒Ⅲ型甲胈的冰蓝色涂装在黑暗中像是一团冷焰。

李锡尼走在队伍的最后，黑色长风衣的下摆几乎拖在地面上。

宝儿·拉瑟紧跟在西泽尔身侧，骑马装的下摆随风微微摆动。

贝隆抱着秘密通道图走在队伍中段。

西泽尔走到铁栅门前。

他回头看了最后一眼。

薇若兰还站在走廊的灯光下，白大褂在灯光中白得耀眼。她的双手垂在身侧，没有挥动，也没有做出任何告别的手势。

但她的眼睛在看着他。

那种目光，西泽尔见过。

在马斯顿斗兽场外的暴雨中，在密涅瓦机关的维苏威火山熔炉前，在每一次他走上战场的时刻——她都会用这种目光看着他。

不是担忧，不是害怕。

是信任。

西泽尔转过头，钻进了铁栅门后的黑暗中。

午夜十二点，密涅瓦机关的秘密通道打开了。

【English】
Chapter 185 — The Last Preparations Before Departure

The butler at Canterbury Keep took the call at two in the morning.

He had been asleep — or something near asleep, that shallow dozing of old men whose bodies no longer commit fully to the business of rest. The bell of the speaking-tube beside his bed cut once through the dark, low and discreet, and he was on his feet before the second ring, his nightshirt still tucked at the throat, his slippers finding the cold flagstones by memory.

The voice at the other end belonged to the young lord. The butler recognised it the way a man recognises the sound of a particular door closing in a house he has lived in for forty years — not by any single quality, but by the weight of it.

Young Cesare Borgia sounded the way he always sounded. That was the trouble. There was the same unhurried diction, the same slight hush of vowels, the same habit of treating each sentence as if it had been set down on paper first and was now only being read aloud. If anything, he was calmer than usual. Calmer than calm. The steadiness of a man who has already done the arithmetic and knows what the numbers say.

"Three things," Cesare said. "If you would."

The butler tightened his grip on the receiver. He did not interrupt. He had been young Cesare's grandmother's man, and then Lady Liniang's man, and now he was Cesare's man, and he knew the register in which the boy spoke when he meant to be obeyed without discussion. The last time he had heard that exact register was the night Cesare had left Florence alone for the college at Marston. Two winters ago. The butler had stood at the same window afterward and watched the same dark line of the rooftops, and had not been sure, even then, which of the two of them had been the more frightened.

"If I do not come back," Cesare said, "you will send what Miss Adele left in the keep on to Aachen. Everything that was in her room. There is a tin box on the dresser. Inside it is a comb that belonged to our mother, and some photographs. Send those with the rest."

A pause. The speaking-tube made the small wet sound of an open line held in a closed hand.

"And tell her I love her," Cesare said. "Tell her her brother says so."

The line went dead. The butler stood in the dark, the receiver still pressed to his ear, listening to the empty hiss where his lord's breathing had been. The speaking-tube rattled faintly against its hook, once, as if someone at the exchange had bumped a table in a faraway room. He did not move for a long time.

When he did, he crossed to the window and looked out over Florence. The city was a black wash of roofs and chimneys. To the east, beyond the river, the Wall of Sighs rose against the lower sky, and behind it the copper stacks of the Minerva Institute were breathing out their slow red exhalations. The glow turned the underbellies of the clouds the colour of dried blood, and from where he stood the man could almost have believed a small private fire was burning somewhere in the world, a thing that belonged to him.

"Mother of God," he said, very softly, to no one.

---

Beneath the Minerva Institute, three floors down, the converted workshop burned with light.

The room had been a long-term store for retired armour parts before the engineers had dragged the racks aside and laid down fresh canvas on the floor. Now it smelled of linseed oil, of iron filings, of the sharp scorched note that brass makes when it has been worked too long against leather. The lamps had been turned up to their highest setting. Under that merciless white wash, every gear and cable on the benches looked like a thing drawn with a needle.

Cesare sat on the inspection slab, his back to the room, his tunic cut away at the spine. Behind him, Verolan stood on a low platform, a brass screwdriver the thickness of a needle in her right hand. The tip of it was her own design; she had had it ground down at the Institute's own workshop to fit into the gap, no wider than half a millimetre, between the gold tubing and the skin.

The tubing had been welded shut that afternoon. From the outside you could not see the seam. Verolan was checking each of the tiny retaining bolts in turn, her thumb feeling the torque the way a watchmaker feels the seat of a screw.

"Torque nominal," she said. Her voice was the voice she always used in here, flat and almost mechanical, the voice of an instrument reporting its own readings. "Contact resistance steady under three-thousandths of an ohm. Neural conduction loss is negligible."

She set the screwdriver down. She wiped her hands on a square of alcohol-soaked cotton, then reached for a small black case on the bench beside her. Inside the case, on a bed of grey velvet, lay a chip no bigger than a fingernail. Its surface was traced with lines of gold that caught the overhead light and threw it back in fine, broken threads.

"The control chip for the Immortal King system," Verolan said. "The overload safeguard was rewritten after the mine. We have raised the safety threshold from three minutes to five."

She raised her eyes to his. The lamp put a hard white line across the bridge of her nose and left her chocolate-coloured irises in shadow. There was none of the bright, teasing sharpness that usually lived in her face. What lived there instead was something held very carefully down, like a foot pressed firmly on the throat of a sound she would not allow herself to make.

"Five minutes is the ceiling," she said. "Past five, the chip will burn out, and the last gate in your nervous system will be gone. Past eight, the hero pattern will have eaten what is left of you, and you will not be Cesare Borgia any longer. You will be a weapon in a suit, that is all."

Cesare inclined his head a fraction.

"You are going to Golgotha," Verolan said. She put the chip back into its case and passed it to an assistant at her elbow. "You may use the Immortal King system for up to five minutes. If you use it for more than that, you will lose yourself."

She said it the way a person might say it has been a fine day for walking. Her hand, when she let the case go, was a half-beat slower than usual.

Cesare took the case and slipped it into the inside pocket of his coat, against his ribs.

"I know," he said.

---

Across the workshop, Alfonso sat on a stool with his wrist laid flat on the bench. Tarasha stood opposite him, an opened Spider Nest watch on the cloth between them. The watch was old. The case was scuffed along one edge, and the strap was marked with pale scratches where, in the mine below the Institute, flying grit had struck it.

"The old design carries six spiders," Tarasha said. She had the back of the case tilted toward the light, and was tracing a circuit with a pair of tweezers as she spoke. "Eighty-metre interference radius. Eight minutes of operation. Against a common suit that is enough. But for where you are going—"

She looked up. The workshop lamp caught the blue of her irises and held it.

"Veronica has pulled the deep files for me. The Omega self-healing nerve fibres put out a continuous high-frequency field. A standard wide-band pulse will not get close. The old spiders do not have the power."

Alfonso reached across the bench and lifted the new spider from where it sat in its cradle. It was a little larger than the old one, the size of a good grape, and a small red-mercury crystal set into its belly glowed with a dull arterial light, the colour of an insect's eye in a dark room.

"This one has a focused high-frequency array," Tarasha said. "Released singly, it acts as a normal wide-band disruptor. But if you release all eight at once and lock them onto a single target, the pulses will combine. You can focus the energy to a point."

She laid a second spider beside the first.

"Combined output is four times the old model. That is enough to burn through the insulation sheath on the Omega fibres."

Alfonso considered this. "Six of these eight are new."

"Yes."

"The other two are rebuilt from the old stock. Their tolerances are not as good."

"There was no time to do more," Tarasha said.

Alfonso put the watch back on. The case seated itself against the bone of his wrist with the clean click of a thing that has been worn a long time. The lock caught.

---

Next door, in the second preparation bay, the air had a different weight to it. It was the weight of a man working alone with iron.

The Augustus prototype had been racked upright against the wall. Quintilian crouched at its left arm, the old mithril shield already off, a new one strapped to the frame under a steam-driven rivet gun. The shield face was a metal he had never seen before. It was almost the colour of silver, but there was a faint, cold blue buried in it, like a vein of ice under clean water. It had been polished to a mirror finish, and the workshop lamp threw a clean, hard rectangle of light back out of it. In the centre of the face, stamped deep into the metal, was a lion's head with its eyes closed. The ears were tipped slightly forward. The lines of the jaw and the brow were cut like knife work.

Quintilian tapped the face with the knuckle of his forefinger.

The metal answered with a low, distant hum, the way a great bell answers a far-off bell. The note lived inside the shield for a long time before it was gone.

"Perfect alloy," he said, to no one in particular.

There were, in the entire subterranean store of the Minerva Institute, less than three tonnes of it. The recipe had been left behind by the Institute's first Director-General, a hundred years dead, and no one since had been able to reproduce it cleanly. It was not, in the strict sense, a metal at all; it was a structure. The ingots had been re-melted in a precise electromagnetic field, atom by atom, until the resulting lattice was something the old metallurgists had been willing to call, with proper reverence, *perfect*. Three times the tensile strength of common mithril. Twice the toughness of orichalcum. Professor Franco himself had carried the bars down from the sealed vault and cut them, by his own hand, into the shape of a shield.

"Five-layer cross-forging," the technician beside Quintilian said, his finger running down the spec sheet. "Outer two, orichalcum. Middle three, hard gold. Innermost, a sheet of glacier jade sandwiched in."

Quintilian did not answer. He lifted the shield, took the inside grip in his right hand, and swung it once, in a slow controlled arc that ended in front of his chest. The new alloy was nearly twice the weight of the old. His arm did not move.

"Good shield," he said. There was a satisfaction in his voice that only a soldier who has held many shields recognises. He set his thumb against the closed-eyed lion.

"Old friend," he said, to the shield. "Tomorrow, then."

---

Across the corridor, in the third bay, Don Juan sat on a high stool with one long leg crossed over the other. He held a glass of red wine that had appeared from no identifiable source. In front of him, the right arm of the Ghost of the Rose was held in a bench vice. The old scythe-blade had been unhooked from the wrist and set aside. The new one lay on the bench, catching the lamp.

The new blade was curved in a deeper arc than the old. It was thin as paper at the spine and at the edge. The metal was the same pale, almost-translucent silver as Quintilian's shield face. At the cutting edge, where the light fell, a hair-thin line of colour ran the length of it, a faint broken rainbow, as if the metal refused to behave as a single substance.

Don Juan set down his glass. He picked up the blade. He pressed his thumb against the edge, lightly, as a man might test a new razor.

A bead of blood came up at once.

"Very fast," he said, and sucked the bead off his thumb without changing his expression. "The old men at Minerva have at last done one thing well."

He slotted the blade back into the wrist of the Ghost of the Rose. The lock engaged with a clean click. The scythe and the arm looked, after that, as if they had always been a single thing — a hand grown into a claw.

"Beautiful," he said, with real satisfaction. He turned his head toward the doorway, where Alfonso was passing. "Alfonso. Take a portrait of me. I want to send it to my little friends."

"Go to hell," Alfonso said, and walked on.

---

At the far end of the workshop, Valentina knelt on a square of clean canvas in front of an opened Wrath of God III. The breastplate had been lifted off. Inside the chest cavity, where the original red-mercury core should have been, there was now a crystal block the size of a man's fist. It had not come out of Minerva's stores. It had not come out of the Gregorian works. It had come out of the private collection of the Yenisei palace, in a small cedar box that had been carried, for nineteen years, in the bottom of a trunk.

It was the last thing her mother had ever made.

Valentina drew a square of white silk across the surface of the crystal. The silk came away clean. The faint smell of honeysuckle came up from her wrists and from the inside of her sleeves and lay over the iron-smell of the workshop like a hand laid over a wound.

"Neural interface loop test, nominal," she said, in Yenisei, more to herself than to anyone. She switched, in the same breath, to the common tongue. "Spinal coupling is seated in the glacier jade at the prescribed depth. Buffering efficiency, forty-three per cent."

She got to her feet. She brushed a few flecks of iron off her knee.

The Wrath of God III stood on its own frame before her, breastplate re-fitted. The lacquer of the suit was the cold blue of deep glacial ice. Under the lamps it looked like a piece of the far north, wheeled in on a trolley and stood upright to wait. The faceplate was modelled on a snow-wolf's head, the jaws open, the eyes lit with a thin pale blue that did not flicker.

Valentina reached up and laid her palm against the faceplate. The metal was cold. She held it there a moment.

"Come on, then," she said, to the suit, in a voice that was almost a whisper. "We are going to kill a dragon."

---

In a corner of the preparation bay, alone at a small table, Licinius sat with a black velvet cloth spread out before him. On the cloth lay two things.

The first was a fragment of the Lance of Longinus, no longer than the last joint of his little finger. The break at either end was ragged, the way a thing looks when it has been wrenched, not cut, from a larger whole. Under the lamp the metal did not reflect the light. It swallowed it. The fragment had the look of a small, polite hole in the air.

The second was a hand-held grinding tool. The wheel on it was a Minerva special, plated with an almost imperceptible skin of red mercury.

Licinius, in his black gloves, picked up the fragment. He brought it close to the lamp and turned it once between thumb and forefinger, the way a jeweller turns a suspect stone.

He pressed the switch. The wheel made a very small, very private hum.

Then he began.

To grind a fragment of the Lance was one of the most difficult small tasks in the world. The metal did not belong to any category the metallurgists had agreed to recognise. It was harder than perfect alloy, and far more brittle. Too much pressure and the fragment would shatter into a powder that was worse than useless, because the powder could not be reassembled. He had to work with the lightest possible hand, at the most accurate possible angle, taking off the burrs one at a time, leaving a face that would, in the end, sit in a slot as a key sits in a lock.

He worked for a long time. When at last he set the tool down, the broken face of the fragment was as smooth as a mirror. He wrapped the fragment in its square of black velvet and put it back into the inside pocket of his coat, against his heart.

"This time," he said, in a low voice, as if swearing to himself, "this time the door will open."

---

In the room beside his, Byron had spread the secret-route map out on a trestle. It was drawn on sheepskin in a black ink so fine that the lines looked, at first glance, like the lines on a fairy's handwriting. The map was a three-dimensional schematic of an underground way. Three routes had been inked in three colours. Each ended in a place marked by a small cipher.

Byron's finger moved slowly along the red line.

"This route," he said, "begins at the abandoned ventilator shaft on Sublevel Seven of the Institute. It enters the old mine workings on the north slope of Vesuvius. After roughly two kilometres of mine, it joins an underground river."

His finger came to a blue mark.

"The water of the river is cold," he said. "It holds at about four degrees, year-round. It comes up from the deep aquifers of the mountain and runs from east to west, eventually to the chamber that is marked here."

He rested the tip of his finger on the largest mark on the whole map. Beside it, in a tall florid hand, two words had been written: *Cuore di Lava*. The Heart of Lava.

"From the Heart to Golgotha there is still a stretch to go," Byron said. "It is the most dangerous part. The temperature at the Heart is very high. The insulation layer of a common suit will not last."

He raised his eyes to Cesare, who stood on the other side of the table.

"The route is twelve kilometres end to end. At a normal march, four hours. If we are engaged, possibly double that."

Cesare looked down at the map. He let his gaze rest on each of the marks in turn.

The sound of quick footsteps in the corridor cut the silence.

The steps were light, and they fell on the iron floor in a way that was almost musical. With them came a faint scent, not the cold clean scent of honeysuckle, not the heavy scent of an orchid, but something warmer and a little sweeter — the scent, perhaps, of the acacia trees in the Florentine gardens at midsummer.

The door opened.

Bauer Lasser stood in the doorway.

She was in a dark-red riding habit, cut close to the body in the Florentine fashion, that set off the line of her waist and the long line of her legs. Her hair was drawn up in a simple knot that left her face bare. The harsh white of the workshop lamp could not take the colour from her.

"I am coming with you," she said. Her voice rang off the metal walls.

Every head in the bay lifted at once.

"Bauer?" Don Juan was the first to find words. "How did you get in? The Wall of Sighs—"

"Tarasha and I have been friends for some time. She let me in." Bauer walked forward. The heels of her riding boots struck the floor in a small, definite rhythm. "I am a former member of the Seraphim Order. I am also, more pertinently, one of Mr Borgia's silent assets."

She stopped in front of Cesare and lifted her chin.

"I know every back lane in Florence, every underground bar, every person in the city who will sell you a piece of information for a coin. I can be useful to you for intelligence."

Cesare said nothing.

"I was a rated trainee pilot," she said, "in the Seraphim Order, before I was de-listed. I can hold my own."

He did not answer at once. He looked at her for a long time.

Cesare knew Bauer Lasser. He had known her in the years at Marston. In the fighting pits of the lower yards, where he had been sent to be sharpened, she had been the cleanest of his secret hands; she had moved messages for him, passed him warning, brought him out of pits he ought not to have come out of. She had once asked him, in a small bare room above a wine shop, to help her erase her military record and give her a quiet life. He had done it. He had been faintly surprised, afterward, to find that she had not gone quiet at all. She had simply gone and lived her new life at a higher volume than her old one.

"I do not pay you for this," she said. "For the record business, you are still owed nothing. We are even."

"We were even when I gave you the record," Cesare said. "It was a transaction."

"Then let us have another transaction." She held his gaze. "I gather your intelligence. You come back alive."

Cesare studied her. There was in the set of her jaw, in the line of her shoulders, the same look he had seen in the pits — the look of a person who, in the moment when the gate is lifted, does not step back.

"Very well," he said. "You will come with us. Keep yourself out of the way of the suits."

A small, warm smile came over her face. It looked, under the cold light of the workshop, like the single lit window of a house at the edge of a snowfield.

"Don't worry about me," she said. "I am hard to kill."

---

A little before the hour, Beryl Danti came through the service door at the back of the bay, pushing a trolley.

The trolley was piled with rations wrapped in oiled paper, with water in heavy leather flasks, and with a small row of bottles of the concentrated recovery broth that the Institute's medical annex made for its pilots. She handed out a packet to each man at the benches with the briskness of a head of service who has done the same thing, more or less, in finer dining rooms.

"This is black bread," she said. "Baked this morning in the Institute kitchens. It will keep for three days. This is salt pork, heavy with the salt for the same reason. This is water, from the wells under Vesuvius. I have tasted it. There is no sulphur in it."

She put a packet into Cesare's hand.

"You must come back," she said. Her voice was even. He noticed, without looking directly at her, that her fingers, as she passed the rest of the packets around, were trembling very slightly.

Beryl Danti. Daughter of a cobbler in the lower town. Trained, against the odds, at the elementary scriptorium of the Holy See school in Turin. Cesare's head of household. A commoner by birth, and braver, in her own quiet way, than half the people in this room.

"Beryl," Cesare said.

"Sir?"

"Thank you."

She looked down and rearranged the emptier corner of the trolley.

"Do not thank me, sir," she said. "You and the three knights must come home safe. I still have a white shirt to press for you in the morning."

Cesare said nothing. He stood for a moment looking down at the packet in his hand. The oiled paper was still warm from her fingers.

---

At the stroke of midnight, the party gathered at the abandoned ventilator shaft on Sublevel Seven.

Cesare had changed into the field uniform of a rated Knight of Minerva, the owl of six wings stitched in thread of gold at the breast, and above the owl, in a fine line of red, the flame of the Seraphim Order. His command sword hung at his left hip. On the middle finger of his right hand he wore a ring of silver and glacier jade. The inside of the band was engraved. He had turned the ring so that the engraving sat against his skin, against the warmth of him, and he had not moved it.

Alfonso, Quintilian and Don Juan stood behind him in the suits — Solomon King, Augustus, and the Ghost of the Rose. The three trial-pattern suits threw back the corridor lamps in cold sheets of light.

Valentina stood to one side, the Wrath of God III fully sealed now, the blue lacquer drinking the light from the lamps.

Licinius stood to the other side, the hem of his long black coat almost touching the floor. In the inside pocket of the coat, the fragment of the Lance lay against his chest and did not move.

Byron stood with the secret-route map folded against his body.

Bauer Lasser stood at the outside of the group, her dark-red riding habit very bright in the grey of the corridor.

Verolan stood across from Cesare, in the path he would have to take.

She was not in a suit. She was in a white engineer's coat, her long white hair caught up at the back of her neck with a plain tie. Her eyes, in the lamp, were the colour of good dark chocolate, and they were very steady.

"From the moment you pass the door," she said, "the Institute's communication line will remain open. The interior of Vesuvius is irregular. We may lose you."

She looked at him.

"If the line is broken for an hour, I will assume the worst. I will start the contingency. I will come in after you with a recovery party."

"That will not be necessary," Cesare said.

"This is not a discussion," she said.

She reached forward and pressed down, with two fingers, a small corner of his collar that had begun to turn up at the edge. The gesture was very light. Her fingers stayed there for the length of a second before she drew them back.

"Go," she said.

Cesare nodded once.

He turned toward the ventilator shaft. The hatch was an old iron grate, rusted to a dark orange, the kind of grate that belongs in the back of an unused building and is not meant to be looked at. Beyond the grate, a metal stair dropped down into a darkness that the corridor lamps could not reach.

Quintilian took the first step. The feet of the Augustus suit struck the floor of the shaft with a heavy, slow rhythm that made the corridor lamps swing faintly in their housings.

Alfonso followed. The steps of Solomon King were quieter, and more precise, and fell in the manner of a clock.

Don Juan went third. The scythe-blade at the wrist of the Ghost of the Rose moved as he moved, and threw a single fine thread of light back along the wall.

Valentina, in the Wrath of God III, walked in the middle of the column, a little behind the front rank. The blue of the suit, in the half-dark, looked like a flame that had been frozen where it stood.

Licinius walked at the rear, the hem of his black coat nearly brushing the floor.

Bauer Lasser fell in at Cesare's right, the hem of her riding habit swinging slightly as she walked.

Byron walked in the middle of the column with the map.

Cesare stopped at the grate. He looked back once.

Verolan was still standing in the lamp. The white of her coat was very white against the iron walls. Her hands were at her sides. She had not raised one of them. She had not made a sign.

But her eyes were on him.

He knew that look. He had seen it in the rain outside the pits at Marston. He had seen it at the smelter of Vesuvius, in the Minerva works. He had seen it at the foot of every field on which he had ever been asked to go and perhaps not come back.

It was not fear. It was not worry. It was the look of a person who has chosen, with full knowledge of the cost, to put her weight on a particular beam, and to leave it there.

Cesare turned his head away. He ducked through the grate, and the dark of the shaft took him in.

At midnight, the secret way of the Minerva Institute opened.

第186章 地下暗河的幽灵船

【中文】
第186章 地下暗河的幽灵船

金属梯向下延伸了大约二十米，铁栅门在身后沉重地合上，回声在狭窄的竖井中来回弹了很久。昆提良的奥古斯都甲胄每踩一级，金属梯就发出一声闷响，像是巨人在敲击一口空棺材。

西泽尔走在最前面，手电筒的光柱切开黑暗。

竖井的墙壁是粗粝的黑色玄武岩，上面留着百年前凿岩的痕迹，有些地方还能看到生锈的铁钉和断裂的电缆。空气很冷，带着一股潮气和铁锈的味道，越往下走潮气越重。

"这条路是百年前密涅瓦初代总长修的。"贝隆走在队伍中段，低声说，"矿工们从这里往山体深处运红水银矿石，后来矿脉枯竭，矿道就废弃了。"

"密涅瓦初代总长。"西泽尔说，"就是留下完美焊料的那个人。"

"是。"贝隆说，"传说他把所有的秘密都封在了骷髅地，连后来的总长都不知道里面到底有什么。"

队伍在竖井底部转入一条更宽的矿道。矿道的高度足够奥古斯都甲胄直立行走，宽度大约能容三台甲胄并排。地面铺着锈蚀的铁轨，铁轨上长满了白色的矿盐结晶。

阿方索打开蜘蛛巢腕表，八只微型机械蜘蛛从腕表中爬出来，沿着矿道顶部散开，红水银微晶的微光在黑暗中闪了几下就消失了。

"前方五公里没有异常。"阿方索说，"但……我感觉到了一些奇怪的东西。"

"什么东西？"唐璜问。

"不确定。"阿方索皱了皱眉，"是电磁信号，很微弱，像是……水在流动。"

队伍继续前行。

矿道开始向下倾斜，空气越来越潮湿，温度也在缓慢上升。走了大约四十分钟后，西泽尔听到了声音。

水声。

不是滴水声，而是大面积的水流声，像是有一条暗河在矿道深处奔涌。

"到了。"贝隆停住脚步，指着前方的一道铁门，"穿过这道门就是暗河。"

铁门上刻着密涅瓦机关的六翼猫头鹰徽记，徽记已经被锈蚀得只剩下一道模糊的轮廓。铁门的铰链发出刺耳的尖叫声，缓缓向内打开。

门后是一片出乎所有人意料的广阔空间。

矿道在这里突然变大了，仿佛地底张开了一张巨嘴。穹顶高达三十米以上，挂着密密麻麻的钟乳石，钟乳石上滴落的水珠在黑暗中闪着微光。空间的最底部是一条宽约二十米的暗河，河水无声地流淌，散发着一层薄薄的红雾。

河水是红色的。

不是血的那种深红，而是一种近乎透明的绯红，像是红葡萄酒被兑了十倍的水。河面上飘着一层若有若无的白雾，白雾的边缘泛着微弱的金色光晕。

空气中弥漫着一股淡淡的香气。

西泽尔站在河岸边，怔了一下。

这股香气他闻到过。

在马斯顿的密涅瓦仓库里，当欧米茄的黑铁冰封棺被打开的瞬间，在密涅瓦机关的深层实验室里，当佛朗哥教授用神经电流读出器检测他的后颈黄金套管时——都是这股香气。清冽、微苦，像是被碾碎的草药，又像是某种金属被加热到临界点时散发出的气息。

"红水银。"李锡尼从队伍后面走上来，黑色的长风衣下摆几乎拖在潮湿的地面上。他蹲下身，用戴着黑手套的手指沾了一点河水，放到鼻端嗅了嗅，"浓度不低。暗河的上游应该有一处被封闭的红水银矿脉，河水长年冲刷矿脉，溶解了微量的红水银。"

"这水有毒吗？"宝儿·拉瑟问。

"对普通人有微毒。"李锡尼说，"但对甲胄骑士来说，短时间内不会有太大影响。"

"那香味呢？"瓦莲京娜走到河岸边，改装神怒Ⅲ型甲胈的冰蓝色涂装在红色水雾的映衬下显得格外冷冽，"这香味不像红水银的味道。"

"是不像。"李锡尼沉默了一瞬，"这股香气……和欧米茄核心的能量溢出信号一致。"

所有人都安静了。

"也就是说，"昆提良慢慢地说，"这条河的水里有欧米茄的成分？"

"不是欧米茄本身。"李锡尼站起身，拂去手套上的水珠，"而是红水银被某种特殊能量场浸泡过后产生的副产物。欧米茄原型体的红水银核心在封存期间，会持续向外辐射微量的能量脉冲，这些脉冲和周围的红水银发生反应，就产生了这种香气。"

"换句话说，"唐璜吹了声口哨，"我们离欧米茄越来越近了。"

"或者，"阿方索看了一眼腕表上的读数，"离骷髅地越来越近了。"

西泽尔没有说话。他注视着暗河的对岸，紫色瞳孔在黑暗中微微发亮。暗河在前方大约五十米处拐了一个弯，拐弯处的岩壁上似乎刻着什么图案，但距离太远看不清。

"贝隆。"西泽尔说，"通道图上标的是这条路吗？"

贝隆展开秘密通道图，红色微光照亮了泛黄的纸面。

"标的是。"贝隆说，"沿暗河向下游走大约六公里，经过一处地下瀑布，就能到达熔岩之心的外围通道。"

"那我们走吧。"西泽尔说。

"等一下。"李锡尼忽然说。

他从怀中取出朗基努斯圣枪碎片，碎片在黑暗中散发着一丝微弱的金色光芒。他把碎片举高，金色光芒向暗河深处投射出去。

在光芒照亮的范围内，西泽尔看到了河面上的东西。

一艘船。

它停在暗河中央，距离河岸大约十米。船身是黑色的，狭长而低矮，像是一条沉睡在水中的巨蛇。船头雕刻着一个齿轮形状的徽记，徽记中心是一只闭合的眼睛，眼缝中镶嵌着一颗已经失去光泽的红色宝石。

"那是什么？"宝儿的声音压得很低。

没有人回答。

因为船上有人在动。

一个身影坐在船尾，背对着他们。那身影穿着一件黑色的长袍，袍子的边缘已经磨损得不成样子，露出里面灰白色的布衬。身影的手中握着一支黑色的船桨，船桨正在缓慢地、一下一下地划动。

但暗河的水流几乎是静止的，根本不需要划船。

"机械神教的齿轮徽记。"李锡尼低声说，"那不是密涅瓦的标记，是更早的东西。"

"机械神教？"唐璜压低声音。

"蒸汽机械神教。"李锡尼说，"密涅瓦机关的前身，初代总长创立的组织。"

黑色的船缓缓转向。划船的人似乎终于察觉到了河岸上的这群不速之客，停止了划桨。船身在红色水面上轻轻打了个转，船头对准了西泽尔他们所在的方向。

然后那人站了起来。

他确实很老了。灰白色的头发稀疏地贴在头皮上，面容枯瘦，颧骨高耸，皮肤上布满了像是被酸液腐蚀过的疤痕。他穿的黑袍拖在甲板上，袍角浸在红色的河水中，被染成了更深的暗红。

他看着西泽尔他们。

然后他笑了。

那笑容很平静，平静得不像是一个在地下暗河中独处了几百年的老人，更像是一位在自家花园里迎接远方来客的主人。

"你们终于来了。"

他的声音很轻，但在空旷的地下空间中却传得很远，带着一种奇异的回响。

"机械神教的使者……"他的目光在每个人身上扫过，最后停在了西泽尔的脸上，停在了那双紫色的瞳孔上。"……锡兰星见的后裔。"

西泽尔的手指无声地扣紧了手电筒。

"你是谁？"

老人没有立刻回答。他弯下腰，重新拾起船桨，把桨叶插入红色的河水中，轻轻一推。黑色的船无声地滑向了河岸。

"我是机械神教的右使。"他说，"我在这里等了你们三百年。"

"三百年？"昆提良的眉头拧了起来。

"三百年。"老人点了点头，"自从姐姐被烧死在火刑柱上之后，我就一直在这里划船。"

船靠在了河岸。老人把船桨横在船舷上，向西泽尔伸出了一只手。那只手枯瘦如柴，皮肤下面的骨骼和青筋清晰可见。

"上船吧。"他说，"从这里到熔岩之心还有六公里的水路，走路太慢了。"

所有人面面相觑。

"你怎么知道我们要去熔岩之心？"唐璜问。

老人看了他一眼，笑了笑："因为来这里的人，都只有一个目的地。"

"你是人还是鬼？"宝儿直截了当地问。

"这个问题，"老人说，"等你们从骷髅地回来之后再回答吧。"

他再次向西泽尔伸出手。

西泽尔没有动。他站在那里，手电筒的光柱打在老人身上，照亮了老人黑袍上的齿轮徽记。徽记是银色的，被磨损得只剩下一层薄薄的金属膜，但齿轮的齿牙和中心的闭眼图案依然清晰可辨。

"三百年。"西泽尔重复了一遍，"你是说，你在这条暗河上划了三百年？"

"三百年是很长的时间。"老人说，"长到足够一个人忘记自己是谁，也长到足够一个人记住自己为什么还在这里。"

"你为什么还在这里？"

老人没有回答。他的目光从西泽尔脸上移开，落在了西泽尔的右手上。那只手的无名指上戴着一枚银戒指，银戒指的内侧在灯光下隐约反射出一行小字。

老人的眼睛亮了一下。

"那是姐姐的东西。"他说。

西泽尔的指尖下意识地触碰了戒指表面。银戒指的凉意透过指腹传来，那种凉不像是金属本身的冷，而像是某种更深层的东西——像是在触摸一段被封存的记忆。

"你是说艾琳娜·博尔吉亚？"西泽尔问。

"艾琳娜。"老人轻轻念出这个名字，像是在念一首很古老的诗。"她是我的姐姐。她被教廷定为头号异端，烧死在火刑柱上，但她的灵魂还在骷髅地……等着你们。"

西泽尔沉默了。

他想问更多。他想问艾琳娜为什么把戒指留给了琉璃，想问机械神教到底是什么组织，想问骷髅地的黑铁巨门后面究竟藏着什么。但老人已经转过身去，重新拿起了船桨。

"上不上船？"老人问，"暗河的水位会在日出前上涨，到时候河岸就会被淹没，你们就只能在齐腰深的红水银溶液里涉水前进了。"

李锡尼走到西泽尔身边，压低声音："他可能不是敌人。但如果他不是人，我们也未必是对手。"

"我同意。"贝隆说。

"你们是来骷髅地探秘的，还是来考古的？"唐璜翻了个白眼。

西泽尔看了一眼队伍。昆提良握紧了他那只备用单手战斧的柄；阿方索沉默着，手腕上的蜘蛛巢腕表微微闪烁；瓦莲京娜的右手搭在改装神怒Ⅲ型的剑柄上，冰蓝色的涂装在红色水雾中显得格外冷冽；宝儿·拉瑟紧紧跟在西泽尔身侧，她的眼睛在黑暗中像两颗琥珀色的宝石。

"上船。"西泽尔说。

昆提良第一个跳上了船。奥古斯都甲胈的重量让黑色的船身猛地一沉，河面上泛起一圈绯红色的涟漪。他站在船头，战斧横在胸前，像是石像。

阿方索第二个上船。所罗门王甲胈的脚步很轻，他在船舷上找了个位置坐下，腕表上的微型机械蜘蛛沿着船身散开，悄无声息地爬进了暗河的水中。

唐璜第三个上船。蔷薇之鬼的曲刃镰在他手臂上微微晃动。他跳上船时故意踩得很重，船身又晃了一下。

"喂，老头。"唐璜说，"这船结实吗？别划到一半散架了。"

老人看了他一眼："这船比你爷爷的爷爷还结实。"

"那可够老的。"唐璜嘿嘿一笑。

瓦莲京娜和宝儿跟着上了船。瓦莲京娜的改装神怒Ⅲ型在船的中央稳稳地落下，溅起的水花打湿了宝儿·拉瑟的骑马装下摆。

李锡尼最后一个上船。他的黑色长风衣在红色水面的映衬下显得格外诡异。他没有坐下，而是站在船尾，朗基努斯圣枪碎片被他握在手中，金色光芒微弱但稳定。

西泽尔最后上船。

他在船舷上停了一下，回头看了一眼他们刚才站立的河岸。河岸的黑色玄武岩上覆盖着一层红色的水渍，水渍正在缓慢地蒸发，升起一缕缕红色的丝状雾气。

丝状物。

白色的，纤细如发丝的丝状物。

它们从暗河的水面下浮起来，像是某种活着的生物一样缓缓飘动，在红色水雾中扭动、伸展、缠绕。

西泽尔的手指无声地收紧了。

他见过这种东西。

在马斯顿的斗兽场地下，在密涅瓦机关的深层实验室里，在维苏威火山的熔岩之心通道前——欧米茄原型体的黑铁冰封棺被打开后，那些丝状物就从棺盖的缝隙中涌出来，像是沉睡了几十年的菌丝突然苏醒。

"开船。"西泽尔说。

老人划动船桨，黑色的船缓缓离开河岸，驶入了暗河中央。

河水很静，静到船桨划动的声音显得格外清晰。暗河两侧的岩壁在灯光中缓缓后退，岩壁上布满了被水流侵蚀的沟壑，沟壑的形状像是一张张人脸。

"那是什么？"宝儿指着岩壁。

"矿工们留下的。"老人说，"他们在岩壁上刻人脸，是为了记住死去的同伴。"

"死了多少？"

"够多的。"

船继续向前。红色水雾越来越浓，视线缩短到不足二十米。西泽尔发现水中的白色丝状物也越来越多，它们不再只是偶尔浮出水面，而是成片成片地从船底经过，像是水底有另一片白色的草原在风中摇曳。

"这些是什么东西？"阿方索问。

"欧米茄的残留物。"李锡尼说，"丝状神经纤维，欧米茄自愈系统的副产物。它们会附着在金属表面，腐蚀金属，但不会攻击活体。"

"你怎么知道？"阿方索问。

"我是异端审判局的人。"李锡尼说，"我们的工作就是和这些东西打交道。"

船在红色的河面上无声地滑行。灯光照不透浓雾，周围的黑暗像是有了质量，压在所有人的肩膀上。昆提良不自觉地握紧了战斧，唐璜的手也搭上了曲刃镰。

"你在暗河里待了三百年，"西泽尔忽然开口，"你吃什么东西？"

老人回头看了他一眼，笑了。

"吃东西？"他说，"你以为我是活人吗？"

船上的空气瞬间凝固。

"别吓人。"唐璜说。

"我没有吓人。"老人说，"三百年前我的身体就已经死了，是姐姐的红水银秘药让我的意识没有消散。我不需要吃东西，也不需要呼吸。我只是一缕被锁在这条暗河里的残念。"

"残念也能划船？"昆提良说。

"划船不需要力气。"老人说，"只需要方向。"

西泽尔低下头，看着自己右手无名指上的银戒指。戒指内壁刻着的小字在灯光下若隐若现——"博尔吉亚·艾琳娜，机械神教左使"。那行小字旁边还有另一行字，是更早的手工刻上去的，笔画纤细而有力：

"等弟弟来。"

西泽尔的手指摩挲着那行字。

"你认识琉璃吗？"他问。

老人停止了划桨。

他转过身来，看着西泽尔，枯瘦的面容上浮现出一种极其复杂的表情——像是惊讶，像是痛苦，又像是某种被压抑了三百年的东西终于找到了出口。

"琉璃……"他说，"你见到她了？"

"见到了。"

"她还好吗？"

"她很好。"西泽尔说，"她把戒指给了我，让我来骷髅地。"

老人沉默了很久。

河水无声地流过船底。白色丝状物在船底扭动，红色水雾在船上升腾。

"那就好。"老人最终说，"那就好。"

他重新转回身去，划动船桨。船桨切入红色的水面，溅起的水珠在灯光中像是绯红色的宝石。

"琉璃是我姐姐的女儿。"老人说，"姐姐被烧死的时候，她还是个婴儿。"

"你是说……"瓦莲京娜的声音微微变了。

"是的。"老人说，"琉璃是艾琳娜·博尔吉亚的女儿。也是锡兰星见家族的后裔。她的紫瞳不是后天获得的，是从娘胎里带来的。"

"所以艾琳娜·博尔吉亚也是紫瞳。"西泽尔说。

"姐姐的紫瞳是天生的。"老人说，"她是初代教皇的亲妹妹，但她和教皇长得一点也不像。教皇有一双灰蓝色的眼睛，姐姐有一双紫色的眼睛。在那个年代，紫瞳被西方视为不祥的征兆，教皇家族把姐姐视为耻辱。"

"但她创立了蒸汽机械神教。"李锡尼说。

"是的。"老人说，"她比任何人都聪明，比任何人都疯狂。她用红水银制造出了第一台机动甲胄的原型，教会了西方世界如何驾驭蒸汽的力量。但她不愿意把这种力量交给教廷去发动战争，所以教廷把她烧死了。"

"红水银……"西泽尔喃喃地说。

"红水银的秘密不在西方。"老人说，"在东方。在你们锡兰星见家族世代守护的世界树里。姐姐一辈子都在寻找世界树的秘密，但她在找到之前就被烧死了。我接替了她的遗志，在这条暗河里等了三百年。"

"等什么？"

"等一个锡兰星见的后裔。"老人说，"等一个紫瞳的人，带着艾琳娜的戒指，走进这条暗河，来到我面前。"

"为什么必须是锡兰星见？"

"因为打开黑铁巨门需要两把钥匙。"老人说，"一把是艾琳娜的戒指，另一把是锡兰星见血脉。"

"两把钥匙……"西泽尔低声重复。

"是的。"老人说，"黑铁巨门的锁是双重的。一重锁在艾琳娜的设计里，一重锁在世界树的根里。只有同时拥有艾琳娜的遗产和锡兰的血脉，才能打开那扇门。"

船继续向前。

暗河在这里变宽了，河道至少有五十米。红色水雾变薄了，但灯光照出去的距离反而更远了，因为前方的黑暗不是浓雾造成的，而是某种更深层的、连光线都无法穿透的黑暗。

"前面就是地下瀑布。"老人说。

西泽尔抬起头。

前方大约一百米处，暗河的水流突然消失在一道巨大的裂缝中。裂缝的宽度至少有三十米，水流从裂缝的边缘倾泻而下，发出震耳欲聋的轰鸣声。瀑布的下方是看不见底的深渊，瀑布的水落入深渊后，会在深渊中激起大量的水雾，水雾在灯光中呈现出一种诡异的玫红色。

瀑布的岩壁上刻着巨大的齿轮徽记。齿轮的齿牙比船头那个大了十倍不止，齿轮的中心不再是闭眼的图案，而是一只睁开的眼睛，眼睛的瞳孔是空的，像是在等待什么东西被安装进去。

"那只眼睛……"宝儿的声音有些发抖。

"是的。"老人说，"在很久以前，那里镶嵌着一颗红水银宝石。是姐姐从世界树上摘下来的。"

"现在呢？"

"被人取走了。"老人说，"四十年前。"

所有人都沉默了一瞬。

四十年前，正是原罪机关秘密运输欧米茄原型体的时间。

"是你放的丝状物吗？"西泽尔忽然问。

老人回头看了他一眼。

"你很敏锐。"老人说，"欧米茄原型体的能量脉冲让红水银发生了变异，水中的丝状物是变异后的产物。它们不是活的，但也不是完全死的。它们像是被冻住的时间，悬浮在水中，不会生长也不会死亡。"

"那为什么越来越多了？"

"因为我们在靠近它。"老人说，"靠近欧米茄原型体的封存地。"

船驶到地下瀑布前。瀑布的水雾扑面而来，打湿了所有人的面甲。老人把船桨插入水底，让船停在了瀑布的边缘。

"从这里开始就要走路了。"老人说，"瀑布后面的岩壁上有一条裂缝，裂缝通往熔岩之心的外围通道。"

他站起身，黑色的长袍在瀑布的水雾中飘动。他向裂缝走去，脚步踩在湿滑的岩石上，却没有发出任何声音。

西泽尔跟在老人身后。当他走到裂缝入口的时候，忽然停下了脚步。

因为他看到了远处的东西。

裂缝的另一端，远远地，岩壁的尽头，有一团光。

不是灯光，不是红水银的光，不是任何他见过的光。

那团光是红色的，炽热的，浓烈得像是凝固的火焰。它从岩壁的深处透出来，把周围的岩壁映成了一片暗红。那光太浓了，浓到让人无法直视，但西泽尔还是看了。

因为那团光里面有影子。

一个巨大的、模糊的、像是山岳一样的影子，矗立在红色的光芒之中。

影子在动。

很慢很慢地，像是一头沉睡了四十年的巨兽终于苏醒，正在缓慢地舒展它的四肢。

"那是什么？"宝儿的声音从身后传来，带着明显的颤抖。

老人回过头，看了西泽尔一眼。

他的枯瘦面容上，那抹笑容消失了。取而代之的，是一种西泽尔从未在任何人脸上见过的表情——

敬畏。

"那是熔岩之心。"老人说，"欧米茄原型体……醒了。"

红色的光芒在岩壁尽头持续脉动，像是有什么东西正在呼吸。

【English】
Chapter 186 — The Ghost Ship of the Underriver

The metal ladder ran downward for the better part of twenty metres. The iron grate clanged shut behind them, and the echo took its time dying in the narrow shaft, bouncing off wet stone the way a coin would bounce inside a well. Quintilian's Augustus frame clanged against every rung, a slow iron heartbeat in the dark — boom, boom, boom — like some great sarcophagus being hammered shut.

Cesare went first. The cone of his lantern cut the blackness in half.

The shaft walls were rough black basalt, marked with the chisel-strokes of men a century dead. Rusted nails jutted out at intervals. Cables, severed and forgotten, hung in loops from bolts. The air was cold, and tasted of damp iron; and as they went lower, of something sweeter and more dangerous — the faintest mineral sweetness of mercury.

"This shaft was cut by the first Director-General of Minerva," Byron said from the middle of the line, his voice low. "Miners used to carry red mercury ore down it, deep into the mountain. The vein went dry. The road was abandoned."

"The first Director-General," Cesare said. "The one who left behind the perfect solder."

"Yes. By all accounts he sealed all his secrets inside Golgotha. None of the later directors ever knew what was in there."

They stepped off the ladder into a wider gallery. The ceiling was high enough for an Augustus to stand without ducking; the width held three armours abreast. Rusty iron rails ran down the centre of the floor, crusted with a white bloom of mineral salt.

Alfonso lifted the lid of his spider-nest watch. Eight tiny mechanical spiders spilled out and scuttled up the walls, fanning across the roof of the tunnel, the dull red gleam of their micro-cores blinking once, twice, and then gone into the dark.

"Five kilometres ahead — nothing." Alfonso said. Then his face changed. "But I'm picking up something odd."

"What odd?" Don Juan asked, from the rear.

"Uncertain. An electromagnetic signature. Very weak. Like — like water. Running."

They kept going.

The gallery began to slope downward. The air grew damp. The temperature climbed, degree by slow degree. Forty minutes in, Cesare heard it.

Not drip. Not trickle. A long, full-bodied sigh of moving water, like a river running somewhere just past the next bend.

"Here," Byron said, and stopped.

A metal door stood in the face of the tunnel. On it, eaten half away by a hundred winters of rust, the six-winged owl of Minerva.

The hinges screamed. The door swung inward.

The chamber beyond was not a chamber. It was a mouth.

The ceiling vaulted upward thirty metres or more, hung with a forest of stalactites whose dripping points caught the lantern-light in cold points of white. And at the bottom of the vault ran a river — twenty metres across, silent, slow, breathing a thin red mist at its surface.

The water was the colour of pale wine. A watery claret, almost translucent, and above it hung a low white fog whose edges were lit with a faint sick gold.

There was a smell.

Cesare stood at the bank and felt the world go small.

He had smelt that smell before.

In the Minerva warehouse at Marston, the moment the black iron cryocoffin of the Omega prototype had cracked its seal. In the deep laboratory of the Bureau, when Professor Franco had run the neural current reader along the back of his neck and touched the gold cannula buried in his spine. That clear, slightly bitter scent — of crushed herbs, or of some metal brought to the edge of melting.

"Red mercury," Licinius said. He had come up from the back of the line. The hem of his black coat nearly trailed in the wet stone. He knelt, dipped a gloved finger into the river, raised it to his face, sniffed. "Not weak. There's a sealed vein of the ore somewhere upstream. The water has been washing through it for a very long time."

"Is it poisonous?" Paula Lasher asked.

"To a normal man, mildly. To a knight in frame, not for a short immersion."

"And the smell?" Valentina had walked to the water's edge. The ice-blue lacquer of her modified Wrath III caught the red mist and threw it back, cold and strange. "That isn't the smell of red mercury."

"No." Licinius was quiet a moment. "It isn't. The signature of this scent — it matches the bleed-off signature of the Omega core."

The chamber went silent.

"Then," Quintilian said, slowly, "this river has Omega in it."

"Not Omega itself." Licinius stood, shook a droplet from his glove. "A by-product. When the Omega prototype's red-mercury core is in stasis, it puts out a constant trickle of energy pulses. They react with any red mercury nearby. The result is — this."

"In other words," Don Juan said, with a small whistle, "we're getting warmer."

"Or," Alfonso said, glancing at his dial, "we're getting closer to Golgotha."

Cesare did not speak. He was looking at the far bank of the river. Some fifty metres on, the water bent around a corner of rock, and on the rock face at the corner there seemed to be carving. Too far to read.

"Byron," he said. "Is this the route on the map?"

Byron unfolded the secret passage-map. Red light from a hidden lamp spilled across the yellowed paper.

"It is. Six kilometres downstream, past an underground waterfall, into the outer ring of the Lava Heart."

"Then we go."

"Wait," Licinius said.

He drew from inside his coat the fragment of the Longinus Spear. The sliver of relic-metal gave off a thin gold light, steady as a pulse. He held it high. The gold cast itself out across the red water, and at the edge of its reach Cesare saw something on the surface of the river.

A ship.

It sat in the middle of the current, ten metres from the bank. Black. Long and low, like a sleeping eel. At the prow a gear was carved, and at the centre of the gear a closed eye, the lid of the eye set with a single red stone whose polish had long since gone out of it.

"What is that?" Paula asked, very low.

No one answered.

Because there was someone on the ship.

A figure sat at the stern, his back to them. He wore a long black robe whose hem had rotted away to reveal a lining of grey-white cloth. In his hands he held a black oar, and with it he was rowing, slowly, slowly, in long even pulls.

The river, as far as Cesare could see, was almost still.

"The gear sigil," Licinius murmured. "That is not the mark of Minerva. It is older."

"The Mechanical Theocracy?" Don Juan's voice dropped.

"The Theocracy of Steam and Mechanism. Yes. The body that existed before Minerva. Founded by the first Director-General."

The black ship began to turn. The rower, at last, seemed to have noticed the uninvited guests standing on his bank. He stopped rowing. The hull swung, lazy, in a slow half-arc, the prow coming round to face Cesare and his company.

Then the figure stood up.

He was very old. White hair lay flat and thin on a scalp that the same mottled, acid-etched scars covered from neck to hairline. His cheekbones stood out like blades. The robe trailed in the red water, and the water had dyed the cloth a deeper, fouler red.

He looked at them.

Then he smiled.

The smile was calm. Too calm — the calm of a man who has waited, who has been waiting so long that the waiting itself has worn smooth all the angles of his face. It was the smile of someone welcoming guests to a garden he had been tending in the dark for three hundred years.

"You have come at last."

His voice was thin, but it carried in the chamber with an odd bell-like resonance, as if the cavern were built to ring at the right pitch.

"Envoys of the Theocracy." His gaze moved across the line, face by face, and stopped on Cesare. Stopped on the eyes. "A scion of the Ceylan star-seers."

Cesare's fingers, of their own accord, tightened on the lantern.

"Who are you?"

The old man did not answer at once. He bent, picked up the oar, dipped the blade into the red water, and pushed. The black ship slid, soundless, toward the bank.

"I am the Right Emissary of the Theocracy of Steam," he said. "I have been waiting for you on this river for three hundred years."

"Three hundred?" Quintilian's brow folded.

"Three hundred." The old man nodded. "Ever since my sister was burned at the stake."

The ship kissed the bank. He laid the oar across the gunwale and held out a hand toward Cesare. The hand was a thing of bone and tendon under yellowed skin, the veins standing up like cords.

"Step aboard. It is six kilometres by water from here to the Lava Heart. Walking is slow."

Every face looked at every other face.

"How do you know we mean to go to the Lava Heart?" Don Juan asked.

The old man glanced at him, still smiling. "Because no one comes down this river meaning to go anywhere else."

"Are you a man, or a ghost?" Paula asked, without ceremony.

"That," the old man said, "is a question to be answered on the way back from Golgotha."

He held out his hand again.

Cesare did not move. He stood, the lantern-beam cutting across the old man's robe and lighting, in silver, the gear-and-eyelid sigil — almost worn through, the metal only a thin skin on the cloth, but still readable, the gear-teeth and the closed eye and the empty red setting.

"Three hundred years," Cesare said. "You are telling me you have been rowing this river for three hundred years."

"Three hundred years is a long time." The old man. "Long enough for a man to forget who he is. Long enough, also, for a man to remember why he is still here."

"Why are you still here?"

The old man did not answer. His eyes left Cesare's face and travelled down to Cesare's right hand. The ring on the fourth finger. Silver. The inside of the band caught the lantern-light and threw out a thin line of shadow, and in the shadow there seemed to be letters.

Something moved in the old man's face.

"That," he said, very softly, "is my sister's."

Cesare's fingertip, of itself, brushed the silver.

The chill of the metal passed through the skin of his finger. But it was not a metal chill. It was a deeper cold — the cold of touching a thing that has been shut away.

"Elina Borgia," Cesare said.

"Elina." The old man said the name as a man says a poem he has not been allowed to speak for a long time. "She is my sister. The Holy See named her the first of heretics and burned her at the stake. But her soul is still in Golgotha. Waiting for you."

Cesare was quiet.

He wanted to ask more. Why Elina had left the ring with Liuli. What the Theocracy had really been. What lay behind the black iron door of Golgotha. But the old man had already turned away, and was reaching for the oar again.

"Will you come aboard?" he said. "The water in this river rises before sunrise. When it does, the bank will be drowned. You will have to wade the rest of the way in red-mercury solution to the hip."

Licinius came to Cesare's side. His voice was low. "He may not be an enemy. If he is not a man, he may be more than we can match."

"I agree," Byron said.

"Are we here to find out what is in Golgotha," Don Juan said, "or to make conversation about it?"

Cesare looked at the company. Quintilian's hand was on the haft of his spare hand-axe. Alfonso sat with his wristwatch dimly ticking. Valentina's right hand rested on the grip of her Wrath III sword, the ice-blue lacquer bleeding cold into the red air. Paula Lasher was at Cesare's shoulder, her eyes two pieces of amber in the dark.

"Aboard," Cesare said.

Quintilian went first. The weight of the Augustus frame sank the black hull with a low groan, and a claret-coloured ring went out from the ship across the water. He took the prow, planted the axe across his chest, and stood like a statue.

Alfonso was second. The King Solomon frame stepped light as a cat. He found a seat on the gunwale; the little spiders of his watch ran down the side of the ship and disappeared into the river.

Don Juan was third. The curve-bladed scythe of the Rose Ghost swung on his arm as he stepped down hard, on purpose, and made the ship pitch.

"Hey, old man," he said, "is this tub going to hold? I'd hate to break apart in the middle of the river."

The old man looked at him. "This boat was old before your great-grandfather's grandfather was a thought."

"That old?"

"Older."

Valentina and Paula came aboard. The Wrath III settled in the middle of the hull, sending a low splash up over Paula's riding-coat skirt. Licinius stepped down last of all, his long black coat striking a strange note against the red reflection of the water. He did not sit. He stood at the stern, the Longinus fragment in his hand, its gold a thin unwavering thread.

Cesare was the last to step down.

He stopped at the gunwale, and looked back at the bank.

The basalt of the bank was sheeted in red water, and the water was already drying, sending up thin threads of red vapour into the air.

Threads.

White. Hair-fine.

They were rising from under the surface of the river, drifting up like living things, twisting, stretching, knotting in the red mist.

Cesare's hand, unseen, closed into a fist.

He had seen these before.

In the pit under the Marston arena. In the deep laboratory of the Bureau. Outside the corridor of the Lava Heart of Vesuvius. Each time the cryocoffin of the Omega prototype had cracked, these filaments had poured out of the gap of the lid, like a sleeping mycelium that had waked from a forty-year sleep.

"Cast off," Cesare said.

The old man pulled the oar. The black ship left the bank and slid, silent, into the middle of the river.

The water was so still that the sound of the oar was obscene in its clearness. The walls of the cave began to drift past on either side, and on the walls the water had carved a thousand small troughs, each trough shaped, by some trick of erosion, like a human face.

"What are those?" Paula pointed.

"Left by the miners." The old man did not turn his head. "They carved faces into the rock, so they would not forget their dead."

"How many dead?"

"Enough."

The ship went on. The red mist thickened. Vision shrank to twenty metres. Cesare noticed that the white filaments were growing thicker too — no longer a stray hair on the surface, but sheets of them passing under the keel, a white meadow under the water, swaying as if in a wind no one could feel.

"What are they?" Alfonso asked.

"Omega residue," Licinius said. "Filament neural fibre. A by-product of the Omega's self-repair system. They will corrode metal. They will not attack the living."

"How do you know?"

"I am a man of the Heretic Inquisition. It is my trade to know."

The ship slid on. The lantern could not punch through the mist. The dark pressed on them now, a dark with weight to it, leaning on the shoulder of every man. Quintilian's hand tightened on his axe. Don Juan's hand found the scythe.

"You have been on this river for three hundred years," Cesare said, into the dark. "What have you been eating?"

The old man turned his head. Smiled.

"Eating." He said. "You think I am alive?"

The air on the ship went out of the air.

"Steady on," Don Juan said.

"I have not been trying to frighten you." The old man. "My body died three hundred years ago. My sister kept my mind from scattering with a preparation of red mercury. I do not eat. I do not breathe. I am a thought that was chained to this river."

"A thought can row a boat?" Quintilian said.

"To row," the old man said, "you need only a direction."

Cesare looked down at the silver ring on the fourth finger of his right hand. The lettering on the inside of the band was almost too small to read. *Borgia, Elina. Left Emissary of the Theocracy of Steam.* Beside that line, in older, finer hand — almost like a child's careful cutting — there ran another:

*Wait for little brother.*

Cesare's thumb moved across the letters.

"Do you know Liuli?" he asked.

The old man stopped rowing.

He turned, and looked at Cesare. The old face was a knot of muscle and scar, and across it passed, like a slow storm, a thing Cesare had not yet seen on any face: surprise, and grief, and the long-creased expression of a thing that has been held shut for a long time and has at last been allowed to come open.

"Liuli," he said. "You have seen her?"

"Yes."

"Is she well?"

"She is well." Cesare said. "She gave me the ring. She sent me to Golgotha."

The old man was quiet for a long time.

The river passed under the keel. The white filaments turned below them. The red mist climbed around them.

"That is well," the old man said, at last. "That is well."

He turned back to his oar. The blade bit the red water. The drops that flew up hung for a moment in the lantern-light like claret stones.

"Liuli is my sister's daughter." The old man, over his shoulder. "When my sister was burned, Liuli was an infant."

"You mean —" Valentina's voice changed.

"Yes." The old man. "Liuli is the daughter of Elina Borgia. And a scion of the house of Ceylan. Her purple eyes are not a gift. They are an inheritance."

"So Elina Borgia also had purple eyes."

"My sister's purple eyes were born in her." The old man. "She was the blood-sister of the first Pontiff. But they did not look alike. The Pontiff had eyes of pale grey-blue. My sister had eyes of purple. In that age, purple eyes in the West were a sign of ill omen. The Pontiff's house considered my sister a disgrace."

"But she founded the Theocracy of Steam and Mechanism," Licinius said.

"Yes." The old man. "She was cleverer than anyone, and madder than anyone. With red mercury she made the first prototype of a mobile frame. She taught the West how to harness steam. But she would not give that power to the Holy See for the waging of war, and so the Holy See burned her."

"Red mercury," Cesare said, under his breath.

"The secret of red mercury is not in the West." The old man. "It is in the East. It is in the World-Tree, which the Ceylan family has guarded for generations. My sister spent her whole life searching for the secret of the Tree. She was killed before she found it. I inherited the task. I have been on this river three hundred years, waiting."

"Waiting for what?"

"For a scion of Ceylan." The old man. "For a purple-eyed man, with my sister's ring, walking onto this river and standing before me."

"Why must it be a Ceylan?"

"Because the black iron door has two locks." The old man. "The first lock is Elina's design. The second is the root of the World-Tree. You need both Elina's legacy and the blood of Ceylan to open the door."

"Two locks," Cesare said.

"Yes."

The ship went on.

The river had widened. It must have been fifty metres across. The red mist had thinned, but the darkness ahead was not mist. It was a deeper dark, a dark that the lantern could not even dent.

"Ahead," the old man said, "is the underground waterfall."

Cesare looked up.

A hundred metres ahead, the river simply disappeared. The water fell off the edge of a great crack in the rock — a crack thirty metres wide — and poured down into a depth the lantern could not reach. The sound of the fall was a low continuous thunder, felt as much in the chest as heard. The spray came up, and where the lantern-light touched it, it was the colour of old roses.

On the rock wall above the fall, a gear was carved. It was ten times the size of the gear on the ship's prow. At the centre of the gear, the closed eye was no longer closed. The eye was open. The pupil of the eye was an empty socket, as if waiting for something to be put into it.

"That eye," Paula said, and her voice shook a little.

"Yes." The old man. "A long time ago, a red mercury stone was set there. My sister took it from the World-Tree and put it into that eye with her own hands."

"Where is it now?"

"It was taken." The old man. "Forty years ago."

The ship was quiet for a long time.

Forty years. Forty years ago was the year the Bureau of Original Sin had smuggled the Omega prototype into the mountain in secret.

"Were these filaments yours, before?" Cesare said.

The old man looked at him.

"You have a quick eye." He said. "The energy pulse of the Omega prototype causes a mutation in red mercury. The filaments in the water are the by-product. They are not alive. They are not dead. They are a kind of frozen time, suspended in the water. They will not grow, and they will not die."

"Why are there more of them now?"

"Because we are getting closer." The old man. "Closer to the place where the Omega prototype is sealed."

The ship reached the lip of the fall. The spray came into every face-plate. The old man shipped the oar, let the ship drift against the wet stone at the edge.

"From here we walk." He said. "There is a crack in the rock behind the fall. The crack leads into the outer ring of the Lava Heart."

He stood. The black robe swung in the spray. He stepped out onto the wet stone as if it were dry, and not a footfall came back from under him.

Cesare followed.

When he came to the mouth of the crack, he stopped.

Because at the far end of the crack, far away, a long way down, there was a light.

Not the lantern's light. Not the red light of the water. Not any light he had ever seen.

The light was red. Hot red. Dense red, like a flame that had been poured into a mould and set. It came up out of the rock ahead, and the rock around it was stained the colour of dried blood. The light was so thick it hurt to look at, and Cesare looked at it.

Because in the light there was a shape.

A shape the size of a hill. A blurred, mountain-shouldered shape, rising in the red glow.

The shape was moving.

Slowly. Very slowly. The way a beast moves when it has been asleep for forty years and at last, at last, has begun to stir. A shoulder coming up. A limb unfolding.

"What is that?" Paula's voice came from behind, and was shaking.

The old man looked at Cesare.

The smile was gone from his face. In its place was an expression Cesare had never seen on any living face.

It was awe.

"That," the old man said, "is the Lava Heart. The Omega prototype — has woken."

The red light pulsed at the end of the rock. Slow. Patient. As if something enormous were breathing.

第187章 熔岩之心中的黑铁巨门
