【中文】
第190章 灰烬中的日记残片

通道里的空气像被烧过一遍。

灰色的炭灰覆盖了地面和墙壁，脚踩上去发出细碎的沙沙声，像是踩在烧透的骨灰上。岩壁上残留着大片焦黑的灼痕，有些地方挂着冷却的熔岩流，暗红色，表面结着一层灰扑扑的硬壳，仿佛凝固的血管。空气中弥漫着硫磺和铁锈混在一起的气味，吸进喉咙里带着灼热感。

碧儿·丹缇送来的A级防火防爆服裹在身上，内衬缝着的影金属丝线贴在皮肤上，凉丝丝的。西泽尔走在最前面，肩灯的光在前方十几米的岩壁上投下一个晃动的光圈。

"我说，"唐璜在后面开口，嗓音因为硫磺气味变得沙哑，"这地方真有人来过？我怎么觉得像走进了一条龙的嗓子眼？"

"闭嘴，保留体力。"昆提良闷声说。

"我就随便说说嘛。"唐璜耸耸肩。

瓦莲京娜走在西泽尔身侧半步的位置，金色长发用发带束在脑后，白靴踩在炭灰上留下清晰的印痕。她从防火服的内袋里抽出一卷折叠的羊皮纸，展开，边缘用铜夹固定。

"维苏威火山地下通道示意图。"她说，"我母亲生前绘制的。"

西泽尔侧目看过去。羊皮纸上的墨线已经泛黄，但标注仍然清晰——螺旋形的下降通道，标注着深度和温度，旁边有密密麻麻的注释，字迹纤细工整，是叶尼塞王妃的手迹。

"我们现在在这里。"瓦莲京娜的手指点在通道的某个分叉口上，"这条支路一直往下，通向维苏威火山底部。"

"底部？"阿方索皱眉。

"不是熔岩之心。"瓦莲京娜摇头，"是一条旧矿道。四十年前被封死的那个。"

她从防火服口袋里取出一支短铅笔，在羊皮纸的某处画了个圈："密涅瓦初代总长在世时，矿道尽头连接着叹息之墙的备份通道。"

"备份通道？"昆提良问。

"叹息之墙是密涅瓦机关入口的屏障，但屏障不是唯一的。"瓦莲京娜的铅笔沿着羊皮纸上的墨线滑动，"初代总长在修建叹息之墙的时候，同时在维苏威火山底部开凿了一条备用通道——用于紧急撤离或秘密运输重型设备。这条通道四十年没人用过了。"

"也就是说，我们不需要从正门穿过叹息之墙。"阿方索说。

"绕过它。"瓦莲京娜收起羊皮纸，"但这条路会经过叹息之墙的地下基座。"

唐璜把肩灯往左边墙壁上照了照，灯光只够映出一小片灰扑扑的岩面。他从口袋里掏出手机，打开手电筒功能，白光比肩灯弱了不少，照出去两三米就散成一团模糊的光晕。

"这破手机还能撑二十分钟。"唐璜嘟囔着，"照个屁，墙上连个虫子的轮廓都看不清。"

他骂骂咧咧地把手机塞回口袋，伸手去解背包外侧的一盏肩灯——那是从炽天骑士团配发装备中拆下来的备用照明器，铜质外壳，玻璃罩上刻着火焰纹章，原本是绑在甲胄肩甲上的配件。

"我拆一盏用。"唐璜把肩灯扣在自己肩甲上，按下开关，暖黄色的光猛地亮起来，把前方十几米的通道照得通透。

"好家伙，这可比手机强多了。"唐璜满意地拍了拍肩灯。

然后他的脚步停了。

灯光扫过左侧岩壁，映出一片不该出现在那里的东西。

墙壁上密密麻麻地刻着字。

不是自然裂纹，不是弥赛亚圣教的祷文，也不是施工时的工程标记——是被人用尖锐的金属工具一笔一划凿进石壁里的文字。笔迹工整而有力，每个字母都有小指宽，深陷进岩壁约半寸，有些地方的凿痕已经被岁月磨圆了边缘，有些地方还保留着新鲜的金属光泽。

"这是什么？"昆提良走上前，举起另一盏肩灯，光线汇聚在一处，映出了第一段完整的文字。

西泽尔走近了几步。

"1884年。锡兰王都之战。"

第一行字的开头用了那个年份。西泽尔的手指无声地收紧了——1884年，锡兰王都被攻破的那一年，弥赛亚圣教东征军踏平莲花之国的那一年。

"我第一次摸到世界树的残根。那根须比我的腰还粗，盘踞在地下数百米深处，像一条沉睡的巨蟒。我把耳朵贴上去，还能听到它的心跳——极慢的、跨越百年的心跳。"

阿方索蹲下身，从装备包里取出一台微型摄影机，对准岩壁开始逐字拍摄。

"那一刻我知道了。弥赛亚圣教教导的'神创论'是谎言。世界不是神创造的，神从来没有降临过这片土地。所谓的神迹，不过是史前文明的余烬。"

"史前文明……"昆提良喃喃重复。

"嘘。"阿方索低声说，示意他别打断拍摄。

西泽尔继续往前走。肩灯的光在岩壁上移动，照出第二段文字——笔迹和第一段略有不同，字体更紧凑，凿痕更深，像是在不同的时间、更急迫的心情下刻上去的。

"我建立了密涅瓦机关。但不是为了教皇国的权力。"

"我需要这个地方。我需要这里的熔炉和工程师。因为我知道——神国是可以被重启的。"

"只要找到完美的神使载体。"

瓦莲京娜停下了脚步。她盯着"神使载体"四个字，眉头微微皱起。

"这段文字的作者……"她低声说。

"初代教皇。"西泽尔说。

所有人都看向他。

"签名在下面。"西泽尔用肩灯照了照文字末尾。那里有一个潦草的签名，墨线已经模糊了，但依稀能辨认出几个拉丁字母的轮廓。

"初代教皇……在维苏威火山的地下矿道里刻日记？"唐璜挠了挠头。

"他来过这里。"阿方索放下摄影机，"不只是来过——他在叹息之墙的备份通道里，刻下了这些。"

"继续往前。"西泽尔说。

他们继续前进。通道在脚下缓缓下降，每走几十米就能在墙壁上发现新的文字段落。有些段落保存完好，有些段落被岁月侵蚀得只剩下几个残缺的字母，西泽尔用手指拂去覆盖在凿痕上的炭灰，辨认着每一个字。

"叹息之墙是分隔人间与机械神国的第一层屏障。"

读到这一行时，西泽尔的脚步顿了一下。

他记得叹息之墙。

七岁那年，他第一次被带进密涅瓦机关。从克里特岛到翡冷翠，颠簸了三天三夜。他被教廷军人交给一个穿白大褂的工程师，那人用注射器往他后颈推了一管金色液体，然后把他推进一个装满蒸汽和金属的房间里。

房间的尽头就是那面黑色的巨门——叹息之墙。

他站在门前，仰头看着那扇比他高十倍的铁门，门面上雕刻着天使与恶魔交战的浮雕。工程师推开了门，他走了进去。

然后他看到了那个东西。

房间的正中央，站着一个人形的甲胄——炽天使。

但不是完整的炽天使。甲胄的胸甲被撕裂了，露出里面焦黑的内骨骼和纠缠在一起的神经电缆。骑士的躯体已经和甲胄融为了一体——或者说，甲胄的金属已经长进了骑士的肉里。他的半边脸还保持着人类的轮廓，另外半边被银色的金属覆盖，露出的眼窝里没有眼球，只有一颗缓缓旋转的红水银核心。

他还在动。

手指在抽搐，胸腔在起伏，嘴里发出一种不像人类也不像机械的嗡鸣声。工程师告诉年幼的西泽尔——那是一个实验体。一次失败的神经耦合实验，骑士的神经系统与甲胄的电路无法同步，产生了不可逆的融合。

那是西泽尔第一次看到人变成非人的样子。

七年过去了，他依然记得那具实验体空洞的眼窝里旋转的红水银核心，和那声像金属摩擦一样的嗡鸣。他站在密涅瓦机关的走廊里，后颈传来金色液体推入时的微凉感。

现在他站在维苏威火山底部的废弃矿道里，肩灯照亮初代教皇百年前刻下的文字："叹息之墙是分隔人间与机械神国的第一层屏障。"

原来那面墙不只是密涅瓦机关的大门。它是第一层屏障。他七岁时看到的那具实验体，就站在屏障的另一侧。

"老板？"唐璜的声音从身后传来，带着一丝不确定，"你脸色不太好。"

"没事。"西泽尔说。

他伸手摸了摸后颈的黄金套管。指尖传来金属的微凉，还有脉搏的跳动——黄金套管接口处的神经在搏动。

继续往前走。墙壁上的文字又出现了。

"神国不是虚无缥缈的天堂。它是真实的，是可以被触摸的。"

"在维苏威火山的深处，在世界树的根须之间，沉睡着旧时代的遗产。"

"我将它们封存在叹息之墙的后面，因为人类的双手还没有准备好触碰它们。"

最后一行字，在通道拐角处的墙壁上——凿痕最深最深，几乎要把整块岩壁凿穿。

"神使需要紫瞳的眼睛。"

西泽尔的手指停在这行字上。

他的手指停了。

"紫瞳……"阿方索放下摄影机，看向西泽尔。

西泽尔没说话。通道里很安静，只有远处偶尔传来的岩石开裂声。他把手从岩壁上收回来，手指上沾着灰色的炭灰。他又摸了摸后颈的黄金套管——那颗金属圆片正贴在皮肤上，和他的后颈体温一样。

神使需要紫瞳的眼睛。

他就是紫瞳。

日记残片上每一个字都像是写给他的。

"初代教皇……在百年前就知道会有紫瞳的人出现？"瓦莲京娜低声说，语气里罕见地带上了一丝动摇。

"或者他在找。"阿方索说，"一直在找。"

"密涅瓦机关……就是为了这个目的建立的？"昆提良问。

西泽尔没有回答。他站在通道中央，肩灯的光把他的影子拉得很长，投在对面那面刻满文字的岩壁上。

初代教皇。

建立密涅瓦机关的教皇。密涅瓦机关的工程师们崇拜的"初代总长"。他在维苏威火山底部的废弃矿道里刻下了自己的秘密——弥赛亚圣教的神创论是谎言，神国可以被重启，而重启神国需要一位"紫瞳的神使"。

然后他建立了密涅瓦机关，建造了叹息之墙，把通往世界树深处的道路封存在屏障之后。

他一直在等。

等那个紫瞳的人出现。

"继续走。"西泽尔说。

他们继续前进。通道越来越窄，天花板也越来越低，昆提良不得不微微弯腰才能避免头撞到突出的岩石。墙壁上的文字渐渐消失了，取而代之的是大片大片的焦黑灼痕——这里曾经被极高温灼烧过，岩石表面甚至出现了玻璃化的光泽。

"温度在升高。"阿方索看了一眼防火服内衬的温度计，"再往下走，防火服能撑的时间会变短。"

"快到了。"瓦莲京娜说。

就在这时，通道的深处传来一阵低沉的金属摩擦声。

那声音像是两块巨大的铁板在缓慢地挤压，尖锐而刺耳，在狭窄的矿道里反复回响，震得墙壁上的炭灰簌簌落下。

所有人同时停下了脚步。

"那是什么？"昆提良的手已经按上了腰间备用单手战斧的柄。

唐璜关掉了肩灯。

通道瞬间陷入黑暗，只有远处矿道尽头透出的一丝微光——不是火光的暖色，是一种暗沉的、带着金属质感的冷光。

金属摩擦声越来越近。

然后他们看到了。

矿道的尽头，一个巨大的轮廓从黑暗中缓缓显现。

那是一台机动甲胄——不，不只是机动甲胄。那是西泽尔见过的最庞大的人形机械体。高度超过五米，通体覆盖着暗金色的装甲板，肩甲的线条像是展开的巨翼，胸甲的中央嵌着一块比人头还大的红水银核心，正散发出暗沉的脉动光芒。六片翼状散热片从背部展开，金属边缘反射着微弱的光——像是传说中的六翼天使。

屠龙者圣乔治。

密涅瓦机关封存了四十年的初代炽天使原型机。历代炽天骑士团团长的专用武装。被前代总长锁在熔岩之心最深处的禁忌兵器。

它就站在矿道的尽头，六翼微微展开，红水银核心的脉动像心跳一样缓慢而沉重。

"别动。"西泽尔低声说。

没有人动。

但屠龙者圣乔治也没有动。

那台古老的甲胄就那样静静地站在矿道尽头，六翼半展，暗金色的装甲板上映着矿道壁上的焦痕和炭灰。它没有举起武器，没有启动推进器，甚至没有调整站姿。

它只是站着。

金属摩擦声停了。矿道里恢复了死寂，只有红水银核心脉动时发出的低沉嗡鸣。

然后，屠龙者圣乔治动了。

不是攻击。它的右臂缓缓抬起，金属关节发出沉重的"咔咔"声。那只巨大的机械手伸向自己的胸甲——准确地伸向胸甲中央的骑士舱。

机械手扣住了舱门边缘。

"咔嚓。"

舱门从里面被打开了。

一股陈旧的气味从舱内涌出——金属、机油、陈年的皮革，还有一个淡淡的花香。像是有什么花被封存在这个密闭空间里很多很多年。

舱内亮着微弱的暖光。

一个身影坐在骑士舱里。

那是一个年轻的男人。看年纪不过二十出头，肤色微深，五官轮廓带着一种异域的柔和感——既不像纯种的西方人，也不像西泽尔见过的任何一种东方长相。他穿着一身西泽尔从未见过的服饰：白色的长袍，料子薄如蝉翼，领口和袖口绣着精致的金色莲花纹样，腰间系着一条深红色的腰带，带扣是一朵镂空的银莲花。

那是锡兰的传统服饰。

男人坐在骑士舱的座椅上，姿态闲适，仿佛他不是坐在一台被封存了四十年的禁忌兵器里，而是坐在某座宫殿的花园中。

他的手里拿着一朵纸莲花。

白色的纸，折工精细，花瓣层层叠叠，在昏暗的舱内灯光下泛着柔和的光。

他看着西泽尔。

然后他笑了。

那笑容温和而熟悉，仿佛他们不是第一次见面，仿佛他们已经认识了很久很久，仿佛他在某个遥远的、属于另一个时代的地方见过西泽尔，并且一直在等他走到这里。

"西泽尔·琳琅。"

他开口了，声音清澈如流水，咬字带着一种古老的、属于莲花之国的韵律。

"我等你很久了。"

矿道里静得能听见自己的心跳。

唐璜的肩灯不知什么时候又亮了，暖黄色的光打在那台古老的甲胄上，映出暗金色装甲板上的岁月痕迹——划痕、凹坑、被修补过的焊缝。四十年封存留下的印记。

年轻男人手中的纸莲花在灯光下微微晃动。

他看着西泽尔，紫色的眼睛里映着红水银核心的脉动光芒。

【English】
Chapter 190 — Fragments of a Journal in the Ash

The air in the passage had been burned once already.

Grey cinder lay thick on floor and wall. Underfoot it whispered — a fine, dry sound, like stepping through calcined bone. The rock on either side was scarred with long black scabs of old flame, and in places a slow tongue of cooled lava still clung to the stone, dark red beneath a powdery crust, veined and ridged as if something had bled there and dried. Sulphur and rust hung in the breath, and every inhalation came back tasting of hot iron.

Cesare walked at the head of the column. The A-grade fire-and-blast suit Bel Danti had sent cinched tight at the wrists and throat, its inner lining threaded with shadow-metal filaments that lay cool and slick against his skin. The shoulder lamp threw a wobbling coin of yellow light some ten paces ahead.

"I have to ask," said Don Juan from behind him, his voice thinned to gravel by the sulphur, "has anyone actually been this way before? Because it feels like I've just walked down a dragon's throat."

"Save your breath," Quintilian said, low and flat.

"I'm only saying."

Don Juan shrugged. His shoulders bumped the rock.

Valentina walked half a pace off Cesare's right shoulder. Her hair, gold and very long, was bound back with a leather thong; her white boots left clean prints in the grey ash. From inside the inner pocket of the fire-suit she drew a roll of folded parchment, shook it open, and clipped the edges to copper spreader-bars.

"Diagram of the Vesuvius sub-tunnels," she said. "Drawn by my mother, in her own hand."

Cesare glanced at it. The ink had yellowed, but the lines were clean — a long spiral of descent with the depths and the temperatures marked in a fine neat hand, and the margins crowded with notes in the slanted, fastidious script of Princess Yenisei.

"We are here." Valentina's fingertip settled on a junction. "This branch continues down, all the way to the base of the mountain."

"The base," Alfonso said.

"Not the lava-heart." She shook her head. "An old mining gallery. The one that was sealed forty years ago."

She took a stub of pencil from her breast pocket and drew a small circle on the parchment. "In the time of the first Director of the Minerva Bureau, the far end of that gallery connected to a maintenance passage behind the Wall of Sighs."

"Maintenance passage," Quintilian repeated.

"The Wall of Sighs is the barrier over the main entrance to the Bureau's inner vaults. It is not the only one." Her pencil traced the yellow line. "When the first Director built the Wall, he also cut a backup route through the floor of Vesuvius — for emergency evacuation of personnel, and for the secret transport of heavy equipment. The route has been closed for forty years."

"So we don't need to go through the Wall head-on," Alfonso said.

"We go around it." She rolled the parchment and slid it back. "But the route passes under the Wall's foundation. There is no avoiding that."

Don Juan swung his shoulder lamp against the left wall. The light reached two, three metres before the dark ate it. He fished his phone from his coat, thumbed on the torch; the white LED was a poor, anaemic thing, scattering into a fuzzy halo after a couple of paces.

"Phone says twenty minutes of charge left." He shoved it away, muttering. "Useless. Can't even pick out a beetle's outline on the rock with it."

He was already reaching for the spare lamp clipped to the outside of his pack — a copper-cased unit he'd cannibalised from a Seraph Knight's pauldron, the glass etched with the flame-and-sword device of the Order, meant to be bolted to a suit of plate.

"Stealing from the Order again, Don Juan," Quintilian observed.

"It's redistribution of resources." Don Juan clipped the lamp to his own shoulder plate, thumbed the switch, and a thick warm yellow beam lashed forward, throwing the next dozen metres of the passage into clean relief. "Now we're talking."

He took a step. Took another.

Then he stopped.

The lamp had swung across the left-hand wall, and on the rock was something that should not have been there.

Not natural fracture. Not a votive verse of the Messiah's Holy Church. Not the engineer's marks of a mining crew. It was text — carved into the stone, one letter at a time, with a sharp metal point. The strokes were even and deliberate. Each letter was the breadth of a little finger, driven a half-inch into the rock; in places the edges had been worn round by decades of damp, but elsewhere the cut still showed the dull shine of recent metal.

"What the hell is that," Quintilian said, and stepped forward, lifting his own lamp. The two beams converged, and a stretch of wall came clear.

Cesare moved closer.

The first line began with a year.

1884. The Fall of the Royal City of Lanka.

His hand closed at his side without his telling it to. 1884 — the year the Holy Church's eastern crusade had trampled the Lotus Kingdom, had put the white-and-gold palaces to the torch and salted the lotus gardens.

He read.

*My first touch of the World-Tree's root. The root was thicker than my waist, coiled hundreds of metres beneath the earth, sleeping like a great python. I pressed my ear to it. I could hear its heartbeat — so slow, a beat that took a century.*

Alfonso crouched, drew a micro-photographic plate from the equipment case, and began to record the wall, letter by letter, his breath held.

*I understood in that moment that the Church's doctrine of divine creation is a lie. The world was not made by God. God has never set foot on this land. What we call miracles are no more than the embers of an older civilisation.*

"Older civilisation," Quintilian murmured.

"Shh." Alfonso did not look up.

Cesare went forward. The beam of his lamp moved on along the wall and found a second passage. The hand was different — the letters tighter, the cuts deeper, as if they had been carved in a different mood, a different season, with a different urgency in the writer's chest.

*I founded the Minerva Bureau. Not for the power of the Papal States.*

*I needed this place. I needed its forges and its engineers. Because I knew — the Kingdom of God can be restarted.*

*If only the perfect vessel for a divine messenger can be found.*

Valentina had stopped. She was looking at the last two words of that paragraph. The lamplight gave the carved letters a small moving shadow.

"The author of this," she said, very quietly.

"The first Pope," said Cesare.

They all looked at him.

"The signature is at the foot of the wall."

He tilted the lamp. There, in a corner, a hurried signature, the ink or the carbon long since rubbed to a smudge, but the Latin letters of the name were still recognisable in the chisel-marks.

"The first Pope … kept a diary in the tunnels under Vesuvius," Don Juan said, scratching his head. "Of all the places."

"He came down here," Alfonso said, lowering the camera. "More than came. He carved his secrets into the wall of the maintenance passage behind the Wall of Sighs."

"Keep going," said Cesare.

They kept going.

The passage dipped a few degrees with every hundred metres. The air grew warmer, drier, the sulphur heavier. And every few paces, the wall offered up another fragment — sometimes whole, sometimes gnawed half away by time, so that only a few broken letters remained. Cesare brushed the cinder from each cut with his fingertips, and read.

*The Wall of Sighs is the first barrier between the world of men and the Kingdom of the Machine-God.*

He stopped.

He knew the Wall.

He was seven the first time they brought him to the Minerva Bureau. Three days and three nights by coach and rail from Crete to Florence. The Papal guard had handed him over to an engineer in a white coat, and the engineer had pressed a tube of gold-coloured fluid into the nape of his neck, and then pushed him, alone, into a chamber full of steam and iron.

At the far end of the chamber, the black door.

The Wall of Sighs.

He remembered standing before it, a child in a coat too large for him, looking up. The gate was ten times his height, cast in some dark alloy, and on its face were carved the writhing relief of an angel at war with a demon. The engineer had cranked it open. Cesare had walked through.

And there, in the middle of the chamber on the far side, a suit of armour had been standing.

A Seraph. But not a whole one. The breastplate had been torn open from within, and what showed through was a charred inner skeleton and a knot of nerve-cables. The knight's body had grown into the armour, or the armour into the knight — it was no longer possible to say which. Half his face was still a man's; the other half was plated in a dull silver metal. Where an eye should have been there was only the socket, and in the socket something turned, slowly — a red-mercury core.

The thing had still been moving.

Fingers twitching. The chest rising, falling. A sound from the throat that was neither breath nor the whine of a machine. The engineer had told the boy, quietly, that this was a test subject. A failed neural-coupling. The knight's nervous system and the suit's circuitry had failed to synchronise, and the failure had been total.

Cesare had been seven years old. He had not slept, that night, in the Bureau dormitory. He had lain on his back and stared at the iron ceiling and seen, every time he closed his eyes, the slow rotation of that red core in its empty socket, and heard the thin, scraping hum of it.

Seven years ago. He could still see it.

And now he stood in a sealed mining gallery at the floor of Vesuvius, lamp in hand, reading the words the first Pope had carved into the rock a century before he was born.

*The Wall of Sighs is the first barrier between the world of men and the Kingdom of the Machine-God.*

So the Wall was not the door to the Bureau.

It was the first barrier. And the thing he had seen as a child, the half-man, half-machine, had been standing on the far side of that barrier.

"Boss?" Don Juan's voice came from behind him, careful. "You've gone the colour of old parchment."

"I'm fine."

Cesare's hand went, of its own accord, to the back of his neck. The gold collar-piece was warm against his skin. Under it, the nerves that met it pulsed in time with his heart.

He kept his hand there a moment, then let it drop.

They went on. The walls spoke again.

*The Kingdom of God is not a vague heaven. It is real. It can be touched.*

*Deep in Vesuvius, among the roots of the World-Tree, the legacy of the old world lies sleeping.*

*I have sealed it away behind the Wall of Sighs. Mankind's hands are not yet ready to touch it.*

And then, at a turning of the passage, a final line. The cut of it was the deepest of all, as if the writer had driven the chisel into the stone with the whole of his weight and all of his arm. The letters were almost torn through the rock.

*The Messenger will need eyes of purple.*

Cesare's hand stopped on the wall.

His fingers had been brushing the cinder from the letters as he read. Now they lay still, resting on the carved P of *purple*.

"Purple eyes," said Alfonso, and lowered the camera, and looked at Cesare.

Cesare said nothing. The passage was very quiet. From somewhere far off came the small, sour sound of rock cooling — a tick, a crack, another tick.

He drew his fingers back. The pads were dusted with grey ash. He lifted the same hand to the back of his neck, and felt the gold plate lying flat against the skin, blood-warm.

The Messenger will need eyes of purple.

He had been born with purple eyes.

It might have been a coincidence. Almost certainly it was not.

"Could the first Pope," Valentina said at last, and her voice for the first time held something that was not certainty, "have known, a hundred years ago, that a man with purple eyes would come?"

"Or he was looking for one," Alfonso said. "Always."

"The Minerva Bureau," Quintilian said. "It was founded for this?"

Cesare did not answer. He stood in the middle of the passage with the lamplight throwing his shadow a long black lance against the carved wall opposite.

The first Pope.

The man who had built the Minerva Bureau. The man the Bureau's engineers worshipped, still, as the First Director. He had come down into the floor of a volcano and chiselled his secret into the wall: the Church's creation story was a lie; the Kingdom of God could be restarted; the restart required a messenger with purple eyes.

Then he had founded the Bureau. He had built the Wall. He had sealed the deeper road, the road to the roots of the World-Tree, behind the Wall of Sighs.

He had waited.

A hundred years he had waited, for the purple-eyed man to be born.

"Move," Cesare said.

They moved.

The passage narrowed. The ceiling lowered; Quintilian began to duck under the worst of the spurs of rock. The carved letters on the walls thinned, and then stopped. What replaced them was worse — long, broad stains of black char, sheets of vitrified stone where the heat had been so intense the rock itself had half-melted and resolidified into a dull, glassy skin.

"The temperature's climbing," Alfonso said, reading the gauge tucked into the suit's inner lining. "At this rate, the suit's rated life gets shorter with every step."

"Almost there," said Valentina.

And then, from deeper in the tunnel, came the sound.

A long, slow grinding of metal on metal — the sound of two enormous iron plates being forced against each other. It rose, held, fell, rose again, and the walls of the narrow gallery shook with it. A fine rain of ash sifted from the ceiling.

Quintilian's hand dropped to the haft of the spare single-handed war-axe at his belt.

Don Juan killed his shoulder lamp.

Darkness, sudden and total. A breath away, at the very end of the gallery, a faint light — not the warm orange of fire, not the white of a service lamp, but a low, sullen glow with the cool wet sheen of polished metal.

The grinding grew louder.

Then, at the end of the tunnel, a shape came out of the dark.

It was a suit of plate. That was the first impression. A standing suit of plate. Then the eye, struggling against the gloom, took the dimensions of it and refused them, and took them again. The thing was over five metres tall. Its plates were a dark old gold, dulled by decades of stillness; the shoulder pieces were shaped like the spread pinions of a great bird; in the centre of the breastplate a red-mercury core the size of a man's head turned over and over, giving out that low, slow, throb of light.

Six wing-plates fanned out from the back. Six. The wings of a seraph.

Saint George the Dragon-Slayer.

The first-generation Seraph. The original prototype. The private weapon of every Grand Master of the Order. The forbidden engine that the previous Director had locked away in the deepest vault of the lava-heart.

Forty years sealed. And now, here, standing at the end of an old mining gallery, wings half-spread, the red core beating in its chest like a heart that had refused to stop.

"Don't move," Cesare said.

No one moved.

Saint George did not move.

The great machine stood in the dying light of the gallery, wings half-spread, the old gold of its plates scarred with the years — nicks, gouges, weld-marks where someone had repaired it, long ago, in haste. The grinding sound had stopped. The only sound now was the low hum of the core, a note felt as much in the teeth as heard.

And then the machine moved.

Not an attack. The right arm came up, slow, the joints grinding in their ancient grease. The vast metal hand reached across its own chest, found the edge of the cockpit hatch set in the centre of the breastplate, and took hold.

*Click.*

The hatch cracked open from the inside.

A smell came out. Old metal. Old oil. Old leather. And beneath those, very faint, a smell of flowers — of something floral that had been locked in that small space for a very long time, and had not quite given up.

A dim warm light was on within the cockpit.

Someone was sitting inside.

A young man. Twenty, perhaps twenty-two. His skin was a warm brown. The bones of his face had a soft, foreign cast — neither the pure Occidental line Cesare knew, nor any Eastern face he could put a name to. He was dressed in a way Cesare had never seen outside an illustration in a Book of Hours: a long robe of a white so fine the cloth looked like the skin of an insect, the collar and the cuffs picked out in a gold thread worked into the tight pattern of a lotus, and at the waist a sash of deep red fastened with a clasp of openworked silver in the shape of a lotus blossom.

The dress of the old Kingdom of Lanka.

The man sat in the pilot's cradle as if he were sitting in a garden. His posture was easy, his hands in his lap. In his right hand he held a flower.

A paper lotus. White. Folded tight and neat, the petals laid petal upon petal, and even in the dim warm light of the cockpit it gave back a small soft glow, like something newly made.

He looked at Cesare.

And he smiled.

The smile was warm, and was familiar, in the way that a face you have seen in a dream is familiar — the kind of recognition that has no name for itself, and no memory attached. It was the smile of a man who had met Cesare before, somewhere a long way off, in a different age, and had been waiting, all this time, for Cesare to find his way to him.

"Cesare Rinrangi," he said.

His voice was clear, like water over stones, and the vowels had an old, lotus-country music in them.

"I have been waiting a long time for you."

The gallery was silent. The only sound was the slow, slow pulse of the red-mercury core.

Don Juan's lamp had come on again, without his seeming to have touched it. The warm yellow beam lit the ancient plates of the Seraph, picked out every nick and scar of its forty years of sleep, and threw the figure in the cockpit into sharp relief.

The paper lotus in the young man's hand trembled, very slightly, in the moving light.

He looked at Cesare.

His eyes were purple.

第191章 锡兰纸莲花

【中文】
第191章 锡兰纸莲花

矿道里很静。

那台被封存了四十年的古老甲胄蹲在矿道尽头，暗金色的装甲板上映着众人肩灯的微光，像一尊沉睡了太久忽然被惊醒的远古神像。骑士舱敞开着，暖黄色的灯光从里面溢出来，照亮了那个年轻男人和他手中的白色纸莲花。

西泽尔没有说话。

他看着那朵纸莲花。花瓣层层叠叠，折工精细得不像是匆忙间的产物，倒像是用了很多很多年来折叠的，每一道折痕都带着某种仪式般的神圣感。纸莲花在灯光下微微晃动，影子投在矿道壁上，像一只振翅欲飞的白蝶。

唐璜的肩灯扫过那台甲胄的肩甲，肩甲上镌刻着六翼炽天使的纹章——那是历代炽天骑士团团长才配拥有的印记。暗金色装甲板上的划痕和凹坑讲述着这台甲胄曾经经历过的惨烈战斗，四十年的封存只是让那些伤疤变得更深了。

年轻男人从骑士舱里站了起来，动作很轻，像是一阵风从莲花池上吹过。他从甲胄的肩部纵身跳下，长袍在矿道的穿堂风中微微飘动，那一瞬间西泽尔看清了他脖子上挂着的东西——半块青铜色的圆镜，边缘残缺，镜面朝外，背面刻着繁复的纹路，正中是一枚倒置的五芒星。

五芒星。

西泽尔的手指无意识地碰了碰自己胸口的银色项链坠。

"东方贵族怎么驾驶西方古式甲胄？"唐璜的声音里带着他惯有的调侃，"我在翡冷翠的地下斗兽场见过不少花活儿，但穿着锡兰长袍开炽天使的还是头一遭。"

年轻男人没有理会他的调侃。

"我叫莲生。"

他站在矿道中央，手中仍然举着那朵纸莲花。他的紫色眼睛平静得像莲花池里的水，看着西泽尔微笑：

"叶素理的师兄。锡兰末代星见座下最后一位见习星使。"

西泽尔的手指停在了胸口。

叶素理的师兄。

这个信息像一颗石子投入了平静的湖面，在场的每个人脸上都掠过了不同的神色。唐璜的嘴微微张开又合上，昆提良的手臂下意识地垂到了腰间，阿方索的机械臂发出轻微的咔咔声。

只有瓦莲京娜没有动。

她站在西泽尔身侧半步远的地方，金色的长发在风中微微飘动，那双浅色的眼睛钉在莲生手中那朵纸莲花上。

纸莲花在昏暗的矿道里发着光。

不是反射的光，是从纸莲花内部透出来的淡淡金色光芒，像是有人在花瓣之间藏了一颗小小的萤火虫。那光芒很微弱，却在这条充斥着蒸汽和铁锈味的矿道里显得格外不真实。

然后瓦莲京娜闻到了那股香气。

很淡，淡得几乎捕捉不到，但她的鼻翼还是微微动了动——那是她从小就熟悉的味道，是母亲叶尼塞王妃的书房里常年萦绕的味道。母亲说那是"阿瓦隆残片"的味道，是从她随身携带的一块破碎金属片上散发出来的，母亲从不让人碰那块碎片，只是偶尔会把它拿出来放在鼻尖闻很久很久。

"那朵花……"瓦莲京娜的声音微微压低，"是什么？"

"锡兰的纸莲花。"莲生说，"用星见家族传承了三百年的折法折成，每一道折痕里都封着一句祷词。这是星见在观星之前用来静心的信物。"

他顿了顿，目光移向西泽尔的胸口。

"你的项链，"莲生说，"可以让我看看么？"

西泽尔没有动。

他低头看着自己胸口的银色项链坠，那是他母亲琳琅夫人留给他的唯一遗物，小时候他和阿黛尔都曾经把它当作护身符贴着胸口入睡。项链坠的正面是一个小小的圣母像，背面……

西泽尔把项链翻了过来。

项链坠的背面刻着一枚五芒星，但不是正常的五芒星，而是倒置的——五个角朝下，尖端朝上，像是有人故意把这枚五芒星翻转过来钉在金属上。

"项链坠背面的刻字并非如你所知。"

那是叩门者告诉他的话，就在他打开骷髅地黑铁巨门之前。

他一直以为那枚五芒星只是母亲留给他的某种装饰，但此刻他盯着它看，盯得时间久了，竟然发现五芒星中央似乎还有更细小的刻痕，只是被岁月磨得几乎看不清了。

"给我看。"莲生说，语气很平静，但那双紫色的眼睛里映着的光变了。

西泽尔犹豫了一瞬。

他看了瓦莲京娜一眼，瓦莲京娜微微点头。

然后他走上前去，把项链坠翻过来递到莲生面前。

莲生举起脖子上那半块青铜镜，镜面朝外，背面对上了项链坠背面那枚倒置的五芒星。

两枚五芒星重合在一起。

一枚刻在青铜镜上，一枚刻在银质项链坠上，线条竟然严丝合缝，像是同一把刻刀在不同的金属上留下了同样的印记——不，不只是印记。西泽尔看得分明，青铜镜上的五芒星和项链坠上的五芒星各是完整图案的一半，合在一起之后才是一枚完整的倒置五芒星，而在五芒星正中央，原本各自独立的两条纹路合拢成了一个完整的图案——

一颗心脏。

不，不是心脏，是世界树的根。

纹路在金属表面上蜿蜒，分出无数细小的须根，每一条须根的末端都刻着细如发丝的梵文。西泽尔看不懂那些梵文，但他忽然感到后颈的黄金套管微微发烫——

紫瞳金纹在他后颈蔓延开来。

那不是疼痛，是一种极其熟悉的感觉，像是某段被封印了很久的记忆在他血管深处苏醒。他的手指微微颤抖了一下，但脸上没有任何表情。

"我认识这个纹路。"

瓦莲京娜的声音从身后传来。

她走上前两步，浅色的眼睛在两枚合拢的五芒星上来回扫视，然后从长靴侧袋里取出一本泛黄的小册子——那是她母亲叶尼塞王妃的日记，她一直随身带着。

她翻到某一页，把日记举到肩灯下。

"这里。"她的指尖点在日记页边的一幅铅笔素描上，"母亲把它叫做'世界树残根守护符'。她说这是锡兰星见家族代代相传的东西，象征着星见守护世界树根部的职责。"

莲生看了瓦莲京娜一眼，点了点头。

"叶尼塞王妃说得对。"

他把青铜镜收了回来，脖颈上的细链在灯光下晃了晃。

"这是世界树残根守护符。三百年前，我的老师——锡兰末代星见亲手把它一分为二，一半交给了她最信任的人，让她带着它去西方寻找星见的血脉；另一半留在了东方，留在了世界树身边。"

他指了指西泽尔的项链坠。

"你母亲带着的那一半，在某个时间点被交给了我的老师的盟友——初代教皇的妹妹，艾琳娜·博尔吉亚。"

艾琳娜。

西泽尔在心里重复了一遍这个名字。

蒸汽机械神教的左使。

琉璃——他母亲的亲妹妹——告诉过他这个名字。

"那另一半呢？"唐璜插嘴问。

"一直留在世界树最深处。"莲生说，"直到四十年前，有人闯入了那里，把它和屠龙者圣乔治一起封存在了这台甲胄的骑士舱里。"

"是你？"阿方索问。

"是。"

莲生点头，声音很平静。

"我来这里，不是为了伤害任何人。"

他轻轻拍了拍屠龙者圣乔治的胫甲，那一掌在寂静的矿道里发出沉闷的回响。

"屠龙者圣乔治被封存在这里四十年，我花了十年时间才找到它的控制权，又花了十年时间才解开它的封印。"

他环视了一圈矿道，目光最后落回西泽尔身上。

"我要做的只是让世界树的低语被你听到。"

"世界树的低语？"阿方索沉声问。

"你的甲胄曾经是密涅瓦机关最强的武器，但它真正的主人不是密涅瓦机关，不是原罪机关，也不是任何一任炽天骑士团团长。"莲生说，"它真正的主人是锡兰星见家族，是我的老师。"

他的目光再次落在西泽尔胸口那枚倒置的五芒星项链坠上。

"而你，"莲生说，"是老师留给这个世界的最后一份礼物。"

矿道里又静了下来。

唐璜张了张嘴，显然有一肚子话想问，但阿方索在旁边轻轻碰了碰他的手肘，示意他不要打断这个节奏。昆提良沉默地站在最后方，一双大手垂在身侧，随时准备应对任何突发状况。

瓦莲京娜依然没有说话，她的目光在莲生和西泽尔之间来回移动，似乎在评估这个人话语中的真伪。

远处忽然传来一声低沉的长鸣。

那是蒸汽喇叭的声音，从矿道的另一端传来，带着金属共振特有的颤抖。在密涅瓦机关待过的人都听过这种声音——那是圣堂装甲师的重型运输车启动时才会发出的声音。

莲生的脸色变了。

他侧耳听了片刻，紫色的眼睛微微眯起。

"他们来得比我预想的快。"莲生说，"跟上我。"

他转身向屠龙者圣乔治旁边的一处岩壁走去，矿道的尽头看似是封死的，但他伸手按在了某处凸起的岩石上，岩石发出一声低沉的"咔嗒"声，然后向内缩了进去。

一条仅容一人通过的裂缝出现在众人面前。

裂缝的入口很窄，但内部却出乎意料地深，借着肩灯的光照进去，只能看见粗糙的岩壁向内延伸，消失在黑暗中。

"从这里走可以绕过圣堂装甲师正在搜查的那一段矿道。"莲生说，"但里面的路很窄，炽天使进不去，你们得步行。"

蒸汽喇叭的声音又响了一次，比刚才更近了。

西泽尔回头看了一眼那台屠龙者圣乔治。

暗金色的古老甲胄蹲在矿道尽头，骑士舱的灯光还亮着，像一盏四十年来从未熄灭的灯。那朵纸莲花留下的淡淡金色光芒还残留在装甲板上，像是一个温柔的吻。

然后他转身，跟着莲生钻进了裂缝。

裂缝里很暗，岩壁从两侧贴过来，肩灯的光只能照亮前方一两米的距离。瓦莲京娜走在他身后，呼吸声很轻，忍冬的香气混着矿道里的金属味在狭窄的空间里弥漫。

唐璜和阿方索在后面跟着，昆提良殿后，脚步声在岩壁间回荡。

走了大约二十步，前方传来莲生的声音：

"小心脚下。"

西泽尔低下头，借着莲生袖口透出的微光，他看见脚下的岩壁上出现了一道道细密的纹路——不是天然的岩石纹路，而是某种机械的痕迹，像是无数细小的齿轮嵌在了岩层之中。

然后他听到了那个声音。

"沙沙沙。"

那声音极轻，像是有无数细小的金属齿轮在岩壁深处转动，从四面八方向他们包围过来。不是蒸汽泄漏的嘶嘶声，不是机械运转的轰鸣，是齿轮——大量细小的、黄铜色的精密齿轮在岩层内部咬合转动的声音，带着一种几乎算得上优雅的节奏。

不是圣堂装甲师。

不是原罪机关的自律炽天使。

是别的什么东西。

莲生的脚步停住了。

前方大约十步远的地方，岩壁上出现了一道更深的裂缝，裂缝的边缘镶嵌着和脚下一样的齿轮纹路，"沙沙沙"的声音就是从那里传来的。

"那是什么？"昆提良在后面低声问。

莲生没有回答。

他回过头，纸莲花袖口里透出的金色微光照亮了他半张脸，那双紫色的眼睛里映着某种复杂的情绪。

"是世界树。"莲生轻声说，"它在呼吸。"

矿道深处，齿轮转动的声音越来越响。

【English】
Chapter 191 — The Ceylon Paper Lotus

The mining tunnel was quiet.

The ancient suit of armor, sealed away for forty years, squatted at the far end of the passage. The dark-gold of its plating caught the faint glow of their shoulder-lamps, a sleeping god-stone roused at last. The knight's cockpit stood open, the warm yellow light from inside spilling out across the young man and the white paper lotus he held in his hand.

Cesare said nothing.

He studied the lotus. Petal upon petal, the folds so precise they could not have been made in haste. They looked as though they had been folded for many, many years, every crease carrying something of the ritual. In the lamplight the flower trembled, and its shadow on the tunnel wall moved like a white butterfly gathering its wings for flight.

Don Juan's shoulder-lamp swept the shoulder-plate of the suit, where the device of the six-winged Seraph was engraved — the mark borne only by the successive commanders of the Seraphic Order. The scratches and pits in the dark-gold armor spoke of battles no archive had recorded. Forty years of sealed quiet had only deepened the scars.

The young man rose from the cockpit with the lightness of a wind crossing a lotus pond. He stepped down from the shoulder of the machine, his long robe stirring in the draft that ran the length of the tunnel, and for an instant Cesare made out what hung at his throat — half a round bronze mirror, the edge chipped, the polished face turned outward; on the back, a complex web of engravings, and at the center, an inverted five-pointed star.

The pentagram.

Cesare's fingers moved, unbidden, to the silver pendant at his own breast.

"What manner of Eastern noble drives a Western antique?" Don Juan's voice carried the drawl he liked to affect. "I have seen every kind of trick in the underground pits of Florence, but a man in Ceylonese robes at the stick of a Seraph — that is new to me."

The young man did not trouble himself with the jest.

"I am called Liansheng," he said.

He stood in the center of the tunnel, the paper lotus still held before him. His eyes were the color of purple, and as calm as the water of a lotus pond. He looked at Cesare and smiled.

"The senior brother of Yasuri. The last apprentice of the last Star-Seer of Ceylon."

Cesare's fingers stilled at his breast.

Yasuri's senior brother.

The information dropped into the silence the way a single stone drops into a still pool, and across every face there passed a different shadow. Don Juan's mouth opened and closed. Quintilio's hand fell, of its own, to his hip. Alfonso's mechanical arm gave a faint, dry click.

Only Valentina did not move.

She stood half a step behind Cesare, her fair hair stirring in the draft, and her pale eyes were fixed on the paper lotus in Liansheng's hand.

The paper lotus was glowing in the dim tunnel.

Not reflected light. From inside the folds a faint gold was leaking out, as though a small firefly had been laid between the petals. It was a very small light, and yet in that tunnel, which stank of steam and rust, it was unlike anything real.

Then Valentina smelled it.

Faint. So faint she almost missed it. But the muscles of her nose moved — the scent she had known since childhood, the scent that lived year-round in her mother Princess Yenisei's study. Her mother had called it the smell of the Avalon Fragment, rising from a piece of broken metal she always carried and would never let anyone touch. Sometimes, her mother would take the fragment out and hold it beneath her nose for a long, long time.

"That flower," Valentina said, her voice dropped low, "what is it?"

"The paper lotus of Ceylon," Liansheng said. "Folded according to a method passed down through three hundred years of the Star-Seer line. Every crease contains a sealed prayer. It is the object the Star-Seers use to quiet their minds before they look upon the heavens."

He paused. His gaze moved to Cesare's breast.

"Your pendant," Liansheng said. "Will you let me see it?"

Cesare did not move.

He looked down at the silver pendant — the only thing his mother Lady Linlang had left him. As a child, he and Adèle had fallen asleep with it pressed against their hearts as a charm. The face of the pendant was a small image of the Virgin; the back...

Cesare turned the pendant over.

On the back was engraved a five-pointed star, but not the kind drawn upright. The five points were down, the single tip upward — as though someone had taken a proper pentagram and nailed it to the metal upside-down.

*The inscription on the back of the pendant is not as you have been told.*

That was what the Knocker had said to him, just before he had opened the great black iron gate of Skull Hill.

He had always taken the inverted star for some kind of decoration his mother had worn for reasons of her own. But now, looking at it long enough, he saw that at the center of the star there were smaller marks, hairline, almost erased by time.

"Let me see it," Liansheng said. His voice was even, but the light in those purple eyes had changed.

Cesare hesitated a moment.

He glanced at Valentina. She gave a small nod.

Then he stepped forward and held the pendant, face-down, before Liansheng.

Liansheng lifted the bronze mirror from his own throat. The polished side faced outward; the back of the mirror met the back of the pendant, the two inverted stars coming together.

Two pentagrams, meeting.

One cut into bronze, the other into silver, and the lines met with a precision that said the same hand, the same knife, had made both — and not only that. As Cesare watched, the half-pattern on the mirror and the half-pattern on the pendant joined to form, at last, a single whole — and at the very center of that whole, where the lines of each half had stopped alone, a new figure now appeared.

A heart.

No — not a heart. The root of the World Tree.

The lines wandered across the surface of the metal, throwing out a thousand fine rootlets, and at the end of each rootlet was etched a Sanskrit character so thin it was a wonder it had not been lost. Cesare could not read the characters. He felt, suddenly, the gold tubing at the back of his neck grow warm —

The purple iris with the gold veins spread at the nape of his neck.

It was not pain. It was a feeling almost of recognition, as though some memory long sealed away had begun, somewhere deep in his blood, to stir. His hand trembled, just a little. His face did not change.

"I know this device."

Valentina's voice, from behind him.

She came two steps forward, her pale eyes traveling back and forth across the joined pentagrams, and from the side pocket of her long boot she drew out a small, yellowed booklet — the diary of her mother Princess Yenisei, which she had carried with her always.

She turned to a page and held the diary up under the lamp.

"Here." The tip of her finger rested on a pencil sketch in the margin. "My mother called it the Sigil of the World Tree's Last Root. She said it had been passed down through the Star-Seer line of Ceylon for generations — a mark of the Star-Seer's duty to guard the root of the World Tree."

Liansheng looked at Valentina, and inclined his head.

"Princess Yenisei spoke truly."

He drew the bronze mirror back; the thin chain at his throat caught the light.

"This is the Sigil of the World Tree's Last Root. Three hundred years ago my teacher, the last Star-Seer of Ceylon, split it in two with her own hand. One half she gave to the person she trusted most in all the world, that she might carry it west and seek out the Star-Seer's blood. The other half remained in the east, beside the World Tree."

He pointed to the pendant at Cesare's breast.

"The half carried by your mother was, in time, given to my teacher's ally — the sister of the first Pope. Eléna Borgia."

Eléna.

Cesare repeated the name, in his mind.

The Left Hand of the Church of Steam and Mechanism.

Livia — his mother's own sister — had spoken that name to him, once.

"And the other half?" Don Juan put in.

"Stayed at the deepest place of the World Tree," Liansheng said. "Until, forty years ago, someone broke in there and sealed it away, together with Saint George the Dragon-Slayer, in the cockpit of this machine."

"You?" Alfonso asked.

"Yes."

Liansheng nodded, his voice still even.

"I did not come here to harm any of you."

He laid his palm, very lightly, against the greave of Saint George the Dragon-Slayer, and the sound of that small pat rang dull down the quiet tunnel.

"Saint George the Dragon-Slayer was sealed here for forty years. I spent ten of those years finding the right of control over it, and another ten undoing that seal."

He let his gaze travel around the tunnel, and at last returned it to Cesare.

"All that I have done is so that the whisper of the World Tree might at last be heard by you."

"The whisper of the World Tree?" Alfonso asked, low.

"Your machine was, in its time, the most powerful weapon ever made by the Minerva Bureau. But its true master was never the Minerva Bureau, nor the Original Sin Bureau, nor any commander of the Seraphic Order." Liansheng said. "Its true master was the Star-Seer line of Ceylon. My teacher."

His eyes went again to the inverted star on Cesare's breast.

"And you," Liansheng said, "are the last gift my teacher left to this world."

The tunnel fell quiet again.

Don Juan opened his mouth. He plainly had a hundred questions. Alfonso touched him, very lightly, on the elbow — a sign to let the rhythm hold. Quintilio stood at the back, his great hands at his sides, ready for anything. Valentina, still silent, moved her eyes between Liansheng and Cesare, weighing the truth of what the man had said.

Then from far away there came a long, low note.

It was the sound of a steam horn, traveling down the tunnel from the other end, with the metallic shiver proper to that instrument. Anyone who had ever served at the Minerva Bureau had heard that note before — the note a heavy transport of the Sanctum Armored Division made at the moment of starting up.

Liansheng's face changed.

He turned his head, listening. His purple eyes narrowed a fraction.

"They have come faster than I had thought," Liansheng said. "Follow me."

He turned toward the rock beside Saint George the Dragon-Slayer. At the far end of the tunnel the stone looked, to the eye, to be sealed shut, but he laid his hand upon a certain outcropping; the rock gave a low click and slid inward.

A crack appeared in the wall, just wide enough to take a single body.

The mouth of the crack was narrow, but the space inside was, surprisingly, deep. The shoulder-lamps could only light the rough rock walls for a pace or two ahead before it fell off into dark.

"Through here you can get around the stretch of tunnel the Sanctum is now searching," Liansheng said. "But the passage is narrow. The Seraph will not fit. You must go on foot."

The steam horn sounded again, nearer than before.

Cesare looked back, once, at Saint George the Dragon-Slayer.

The dark-gold machine squatted at the end of the tunnel. The cockpit light was still on, a lamp that had not gone out in forty years. The faint gold of the paper lotus still lay, like the memory of a kiss, across the plates of the armor.

Then he turned, and followed Liansheng into the crack.

The crack was dark. The rock pressed in from both sides; the shoulder-lamp could only light a pace or two ahead. Valentina walked behind him, her breathing light, and the scent of honeysuckle rose from her and mingled with the metal-tang of the tunnel.

Don Juan and Alfonso followed, and Quintilio brought up the rear, his footfalls echoing between the walls.

After perhaps twenty paces, Liansheng's voice came from ahead:

"Watch your step."

Cesare lowered his gaze, and by what little light came from the cuff of Liansheng's sleeve he saw that the rock underfoot was no longer plain. A tracery of fine lines ran through the stone — not the lines of natural rock, but the marks of mechanism, as though a thousand small cogs had been set into the living rock.

Then he heard the sound.

*Shhh-shhh-shhh.*

Very soft, like a great number of small metal cogs, somewhere in the deep of the walls, turning against each other — coming at them, now, from every side. Not the hiss of leaking steam. Not the grind of a single machine. It was cogs — countless, fine, brassy cogs, meshing and turning with a rhythm that was, in its way, elegant.

Not the Sanctum Armored Division.

Not the autonomous Seraph of the Original Sin Bureau.

Something else.

Liansheng's steps came to a stop.

A few paces ahead, a deeper cleft opened in the rock. The edges of the cleft were set with the same cog-work as the floor; the *shhh-shhh-shhh* came from there.

"What is that?" Quintilio asked, low, from behind.

Liansheng did not answer.

He turned his head. The paper lotus at his cuff gave out its small gold light across half of his face, and in the purple of his eyes there was something the others could not quite read.

"It is the World Tree," Liansheng said, softly. "It is breathing."

Down in the deep of the tunnel, the sound of the cogs turning grew louder.

第192章 齿轮隧道

【中文】
第192章 齿轮隧道

裂缝尽头不是死路。

西泽尔侧身挤过最后一段窄得几乎要把他肩胛骨夹碎的岩缝，脚下忽然一空，落在一片相对开阔的空间里。瓦莲京娜紧跟在他身后，防火服的衣摆刮过粗糙的岩壁发出细碎的声响，再后面是阿方索、唐璜、昆提良，一个接一个地从裂缝里钻出来。

莲生走在最前面，袖口里透出的金色微光在黑暗中勾勒出他消瘦的背影。

"沙沙沙"的声音变得更响了。

不是从远处传来的，而是从四面八方——头顶、脚下、左右两侧的岩壁里——那些黄铜色的微型齿轮正在以某种精确的节奏咬合转动，仿佛整座山体本身就是一台巨大的机械。

西泽尔举起肩灯。

灯光扫过岩壁的瞬间，所有人都沉默了。

那条隧道不像是被人开凿出来的。岩壁上密密麻麻地镶嵌着数以万计的微型齿轮，每一个只有指甲盖大小，黄铜质地，边缘刻着极其精密的锯齿纹。它们排列得整整齐齐，从地面一直延伸到头顶看不见的黑暗里，组成了一组又一组复杂的几何图案——莲花的形状、星轨的弧线、还有无数个倒置的五芒星。

每一个齿轮的表面都刻着细如发丝的文字。

"那是锡兰星见的祷文。"莲生的声音在隧道里回荡，"三百年前，我的老师——锡兰末代星见亲手刻上去的。"

阿方索走到最近的一面岩壁前，伸出手想要触碰那些齿轮，手指停在距离齿轮不到一寸的地方。

"别碰。"莲生没有回头，"它们还在休眠状态，但不接受陌生人的触碰。"

唐璜靠在另一侧岩壁上喘了口气，防火服的兜帽蹭过齿轮排列的边缘。他的肩膀微微侧了一下，肩甲的金属扣碰到了岩壁上一个突出的齿轮边缘。

只是一声极轻的"叮"。

然后整个隧道亮了。

所有微型齿轮同时开始转动，方向一致，速度惊人，从休眠到全速运转之间没有任何过渡。数以万计的黄铜齿轮咬合在一起发出的声音不再是"沙沙沙"的低语，而是变成了一种尖锐的、持续的蜂鸣——像是有千万只金属蜂同时振翅。

"唐璜你干的好事！"昆提良在后面低吼。

"我又不是故意的！"唐璜往后退了半步，后背贴上了岩壁上更多的齿轮，那些齿轮在他的肩胛骨两侧疯狂旋转，发出灼热的红光。

从齿轮的中心射出了光。

不是金色，而是暗红色。

一道又一道暗红色的光束从隧道两侧的岩壁中射出，交叉、汇合、编织成一张密不透风的光网，将所有人都笼罩在内。那光束的温度不高，但带有某种令人本能恐惧的压迫感，仿佛是被什么东西从黑暗中惊醒的野兽在用目光打量闯入者。

"该死……"阿方索抬起左臂挡在脸前，机械手指攥成拳头，臂甲上的微型机械蜘蛛感知到危险开始自动收缩进甲缝里。

莲生猛地转过身。

"西泽尔！站到隧道中央去！"

"什么？"

"站到中间！现在！快！"

莲生的声音里带着一种从未有过的急迫，那双紫色眼睛里的金色光芒骤然变亮，几乎像是在燃烧。他一把抓住西泽尔的手腕，把他推向隧道的正中央。

西泽尔踉跄了一步，脚下踩到了一排嵌在地面的齿轮。那些齿轮在他的靴底下疯狂旋转，发出刺耳的金属摩擦声。他的脚踝被齿轮边缘的锯齿划开了一道口子，鲜血渗出来，被齿轮的旋转带成了细小的红色弧线。

暗红色的光束立刻改变了方向。

所有的光束——从岩壁两侧、从头顶、从脚下——全部对准了西泽尔。

不是攻击，更像是……扫描。

光束的温度骤然变化，从暗红转为橙黄，又从橙黄变为一种柔和的、温暖的、仿佛被稀释了无数倍的金色。那金色的光不是照射在西泽尔身上，而是涌入他的眼睛。

西泽尔的紫瞳猛地亮了起来。

不是普通的亮——金红色的纹路从他瞳孔深处浮现出来，像是有谁用烧红的铁笔在他的虹膜上书写梵文。金纹随着心跳的节奏一明一灭，从瞳孔扩散到巩膜，再沿着泪腺的纹路蔓延到眼角。灼热的感觉从眼眶蔓延到后颈——后颈那个黄金套管猛地发烫，仿佛被人用烧红的烙铁按在了脊椎上。

他右手手背上的淡紫色脉络也亮了起来，从指缝间向手腕方向扩散，脉络中流淌着的光芒带着淡金色的脉动。

齿轮停了。

数以万计的微型齿轮在同一瞬间停止了转动，那种尖锐的蜂鸣骤然消失，隧道里重新陷入了死一般的寂静。金色光束从西泽尔的瞳孔中缓缓消散，那些齿轮表面的祷文文字一个接一个地暗了下去，恢复了之前那种沉默的、黄铜色的暗淡光泽。

唐璜最先开口："……所以它认他？"

莲生长长地吐出一口气。

"不。"莲生说，"不是认他。是确认他。"

隧道里恢复了安静。暗红色光束消失后，空气里还残留着一股极淡的金属焦糊味，那是被齿轮高速旋转摩擦岩壁时产生的高温灼烧出来的。

"这条隧道是世界树残枝的根系延伸通道。"莲生转过身来面对众人，那双紫色眼睛里映着肩灯的光，"你们看到的每一个微型齿轮，都是残枝的'神经末梢'。它们通过红水银驱动，已经在这座火山里沉睡了三百年。"

"三百年？"阿方索皱着眉头，"那时候还没有密涅瓦机关。"

"密涅瓦机关是百年前建立的。但世界树……比密涅瓦早了两百年。"莲生说，"初代教皇博尔吉亚一世找到它的时候，它已经在这里了。"

"初代教皇……就是那个把日记刻在矿道岩壁上的疯子？"昆提良在后面低声嘀咕。

"不是疯子。"莲生的语气平静得近乎冷淡，"他是一个比任何人都清醒的人。他知道弥赛亚圣教的神创论是谎言，所以他倾尽毕生之力去寻找能重启机械神国的'神使'——也就是拥有紫瞳星见血脉的人。"

他看向西泽尔。

"但他失败了。不是因为找不到紫瞳，而是因为紫瞳的'筛选'远比任何人类的检测手段都严苛。"

"筛选？"西泽尔的声音很轻。

莲生没有直接回答。他伸手按在岩壁上一组倒置五芒星图案的正中央——那组齿轮仍然保持静止，但在他手指触碰的瞬间，表面的祷文文字重新亮了起来，发出微弱的金色光芒。

"世界树残枝有自己的意志。"莲生说，"它只接受'紫瞳星见遗传者'的指令，标准极其严苛——不是有紫瞳就可以，必须是锡兰末代星见直系血裔，且在胚胎期就被残枝的意识碎片'记住'的个体。三百年来，通过筛选的人……"

他停顿了一下。

"只有锡兰末代星见本人。"

"还有她的妹妹——残枝02号。"莲生补了一句，"而末代星见用自己封印了世界树的根之后，再也没有第三个通过筛选的人了。"

"直到我。"西泽尔说。

"直到你。"莲生点头，"你不只是'有紫瞳'。你的后颈黄金套管、你的神经接驳系统、你体内的红水银——它们全部源自三百年前末代星见用自身血肉封印世界树时留下的碎片。世界树认得你，因为它认得它自己的一部分。"

"所以刚才那些暗红色光束……"阿方索开口了，机械手指敲着自己的大腿，"是某种检测程序？"

"是警告。"莲生说，"对于没有通过筛选的闯入者，它会直接发动攻击。刚才那些暗红色光束的功率只释放了不到一成——如果它判定我们是敌人，射出来的就不是光束，而是高能红水银粒子束。"

"高能红水银粒子束？"唐璜的脸色有点发白，"这山洞里有那玩意儿？"

"整个维苏威火山的岩层里都是。"莲生平静地说，"这就是为什么叹息之墙要建在这里。"

瓦莲京娜一直沉默地站在西泽尔身后，忍冬的香气混着空气中残留的金属焦味。她的金发被防火服的兜帽压得有些凌乱，但那双灰蓝色的眼睛极其冷静。

"叹息之墙的失控实验体。"她忽然开口，声音低沉，"你说的筛选——和那些失控实验体有什么关系？"

莲生看了她一眼，眼神里闪过一丝难以辨别的复杂情绪。

"你很聪明，叶尼塞公主。"他说，"叹息之墙里封存的那具'自行活动的甲胄残骸'——以及那些不断侵蚀防线、不断被打回去的失控实验体——它们不是'意外'。"

"它们是博尔吉亚家族在三百年前强行从东方抓来的孤儿。"

隧道里的空气仿佛凝了一下。

"孤儿？"西泽尔的声音很轻。

"初代教皇建立密涅瓦机关的真正目的，是寻找'神使'重启机械神国。但紫瞳星见的血脉极为罕见，三百年才出了一个末代星见。初代教皇等不了那么久。"莲生的声音变得极冷，"所以他派人去东方，去锡兰，去所有可能存在星见血脉遗存的地方——强行抓来有微弱紫瞳特征的幼童，把他们接驳上半成品甲胄，强行让他们'通过筛选'。"

"结果呢？"阿方索低声问。

"结果就是残枝拒绝了他们。半成品甲胄的神经接驳系统在没有通过筛选的孩子体内失控，红水银反噬侵蚀了他们的神经系统——他们变成了既不是人也不是机械的怪物，被初代教皇封存在叹息之墙的深层。"

"封存了三百年？"昆提良的声音有些发紧。

"叹息之墙每隔一段时间就会传出异动——那是那些失控实验体在岩层里挣扎。"莲生说，"密涅瓦机关历任总长都以为是前代封印不稳，只有我知道真正的原因——它们还活着。"

"它们在试图回到世界树残枝面前。"莲生看向隧道深处无尽的黑暗，"因为它们在死前最后一刻的意识里，仍然残留着'未被残枝接受'的痛苦。三百年来，那种痛苦一直在驱动着它们。"

隧道里沉默了很长时间。

"所以……"唐璜吞了口唾沫，"我们现在走的是一条只有西泽尔能走的路？"

"是的。"莲生说，"从现在起，所有遇到微型齿轮的地方，都必须由西泽尔走在最前面。只有他的紫瞳能让这些'神经末梢'保持安静。"

西泽尔低头看了一眼自己的右手。手背上的淡紫色脉络已经暗了下去，但后颈的黄金套管仍然微微发烫，仿佛有什么东西正在他的脊椎深处低声吟唱。

"走。"他说，"继续。"

众人重新列成纵队，由西泽尔走在最前面，莲生紧跟其后提供指引。每经过一组倒置五芒星图案的齿轮阵，齿轮表面的祷文文字就会短暂地亮起，释放出微弱的金色光芒——那是一种确认，是残枝在"问候"自己遗落在外的碎片。

走了大约十分钟。

"停。"莲生忽然伸手拦住西泽尔。

西泽尔停下脚步。

前方的隧道出现了一个分叉口——左右两条通道的岩壁上同样镶嵌着密密麻麻的微型齿轮，但形态不同：左侧通道的齿轮排列成莲花状，右侧通道的齿轮排列成齿轮状。

"该选哪条？"阿方索凑过来。

"右侧。"莲生说，"莲花的通道通往世界树残枝01号——也就是末代星见封印世界树根部的圣所。我们要去的是黑铁巨门，必须走齿轮通道。"

"你们听到什么了？"瓦莲京娜突然压低声音。

所有人屏住呼吸。

从身后——从他们来时的方向——传来了另一种声音。

不是齿轮转动的"沙沙沙"。

是脚步声。

密集的、沉重的、带着金属碰撞声的脚步声。

"沙沙沙"的齿轮声再次响起。

西泽尔猛地回头。

身后的岩壁上，那些刚才还安静下来的微型齿轮突然再次转动起来——但这次的方向不对。不是朝向他，而是全部转向了来时的方向。

从齿轮中心射出的光也不再是暗红色的警告光束。

而是金色的——和刚才扫描他时一模一样的柔和金色光芒。

那些光束全部射向来时方向的那条隧道深处，仿佛是在为某种东西照亮前路。

或者……是在引导什么东西过来。

莲生的脸色骤变。

"圣堂装甲师。"他低声说，"他们找到了裂缝入口——微型齿轮在给它们指路。"

"什么？！"昆提良猛地转身，"给敌人指路？"

"不是给敌人指路。"莲生的声音变得极快，"是世界树残枝在'召唤'！它感知到了大量带有红水银能量的外来者进入它的根系——它以为是来觐见的神使候选者！"

"那些齿轮……"阿方索的脸色也变了。

"它们在用光束标记来者的位置。"莲生说，"不是给圣堂装甲师指路——是在标记它们自己的'猎物'。"

来时的隧道深处，金属碰撞声越来越近。伴随着那声音的，是一种沉重的机械液压驱动声——那是重型机动甲胄的标志性声响。

"多久？"西泽尔的声音极其平静。

"按他们的速度——"莲生侧耳听了一下，"七分钟。"

"太慢了。"西泽尔转身看向右侧那条齿轮通道，"我们走。"

"等等！"莲生一把抓住他的手臂。

西泽尔停下脚步。

莲生从长袍的内层掏出了一个锡封的卷轴。

卷轴不大，大约一尺长，外面包着泛黄的锡封纸，锡封上刻着七个烫金的锡兰文字——西泽尔虽然不认识那些古老的梵文字符，但他后颈的黄金套管在看到那卷轴的瞬间猛地发烫，仿佛有什么东西在共鸣。

"'世界树残枝预言书'。"莲生把卷轴塞进西泽尔手里，"这是末代星见留下的最后一份手稿。里面记录了世界树残枝02号的封印位置——也就是黑铁巨门后面真正藏着的东西。"

"你为什么现在给我？"西泽尔问。

莲生转过身面向来时的方向，那双紫色眼睛里的金色光芒正在以某种节奏明灭。

"因为你们必须先去黑铁巨门。"他说，"而我——"

他从长袍里抽出了一把短剑。剑身极窄，刃口泛着暗金色的光泽，剑柄上缠绕着锡兰传统样式的纸莲花纹饰。

"我来挡住他们。"

"你疯了？"唐璜第一个叫出来，"你一个人怎么挡圣堂装甲师？"

"不需要挡住。"莲生轻声说，那把短剑在他手中转了一个圈，"只需要拖住七分钟。"

他回头看了西泽尔一眼。

"黑铁巨门就在齿轮通道尽头。两把钥匙——你的紫瞳，琉璃姑姑给你的冰原寒玉银戒指。两把钥匙一起用，门才会开。"

"门后面是什么？"西泽尔问。

莲生没有回答。

他只是微微一笑，那张年轻的脸上浮现出某种古老的、属于三百年前星见家族的沉静。

"你进去就知道了。"

他的身影消失在来时的隧道转角处。

"沙沙沙"的齿轮声越来越响，金色的光束在他身后的岩壁上投射出一片流动的光河。

然后，金属碰撞声在转角处炸响。

"走！"西泽尔转身冲向右侧的齿轮通道，卷轴被他死死攥在手里，锡封纸的边缘嵌进了他的掌心。

齿轮在他面前依次亮起，金色的光为他照亮了前路。

【English】
Chapter 192 — The Tunnel of Gears

The crack did not end in a wall.

Cesare turned sideways for the last squeeze and felt the stone try to take the meat off his shoulder blades. He came through with a scrape and a half-step, and his boot found nothing. He dropped half a foot, caught himself, and stood in a space that was almost a room. The air was different here. Older. It tasted of brass and very old dust, and of a heat that had been banked in the rock for a very long time.

Valentina came through behind him, the hem of her fireproof coat whispering against the stone. Then Alfonso. Then Don Juan. Then Quintilian, each one extracted from the crack with the gracelessness of a man being born into a world that had not been built for him.

Liansheng waited for them at the far end of the new space.

He was thinner than he had any right to be after three days underground. The pale gold glow that leaked from the cuff of his sleeve marked him in the dark — a small, steady light that was not a lamp and not a flame, just the light of a man who was made, in part, of something that had no business being alive.

The rustling had been growing louder for ten minutes. Now Cesare understood why.

It came from everywhere.

Above them. Below them. The walls on either side. The ceiling they could not see, and the floor they were about to put their weight on. A thin, dry, mechanical whisper, like ten thousand small pages turning at once, or like a sleeve of dried seedpods held up to a wind. The rhythm of it was exact. The rhythm of it was, in some way Cesare could not have said, wrong.

Cesare lifted his shoulder lamp.

The beam crossed the wall. Nobody spoke for a long time.

The tunnel had not been carved out of the rock. It had been grown into it, or seeded into it, or assembled into it — a long bore through the living stone, and every inch of its surface had been set, one by one, with little brass wheels.

Thousands of them. Tens of thousands.

Each no bigger than a thumbnail. The metal was a dull honey-gold, the colour of an old coin, and the edges of each wheel were cut into teeth so fine they looked like the lines on a fingerprint. The gears were laid out in pattern after pattern, marching up the walls in geometries that no engineer would have chosen for ornament — lotuses in full bloom, arcs of star-tracks through a sky no one alive had seen, and, over and over again, the five-pointed star turned upside down.

On the face of every wheel, in letters no thicker than a hair, was cut a prayer.

"These are the invocations of the Ceylon seer," Liansheng said. His voice went down the tunnel and came back from a long way off. "My teacher cut them. The last seer of Ceylon. Three hundred years ago."

Alfonso stepped closer to the wall. He lifted his right hand. He stopped, an inch out.

"Don't," Liansheng said, without turning.

"What happens?"

"They sleep. They do not like strangers."

Don Juan had his back against the opposite wall, breathing hard. The hood of his fireproof coat was pushed up; one of the metal catches on his pauldron had dragged, just slightly, against the rows of gears.

A small sound. A single clear *tink*, like a spoon on a wineglass.

Then the tunnel was lit.

Every gear, in the same instant, began to turn. There was no warm-up. There was no acceleration. They were still, and then they were running at a speed that should have torn them off the wall, and the whisper of them rose to a single sustained high note — a keen, like a swarm of metal bees coming up out of a hive.

"Don Juan, you absolute —"

"That wasn't me!"

Don Juan stepped back. His shoulders hit the wall behind him. The gears at his back spun hotter, the brass going from gold to a dull red, the way iron does on a forge before the colour has decided what it wants to be. He pressed himself into them without meaning to. The metal of his pauldron was black against the red, and the red ate at the black, and the air around his shoulders began to smell of scorched lacquer.

Light came out of the centre of the gears.

Not gold. Dark red.

Beam after beam, all of them the colour of old blood, lanced from the wall and crossed the tunnel in a lattice. They did not burn. They were not hot to the touch. But they laid themselves on the skin of everyone in the corridor with a pressure that was not a pressure — the feeling of being seen by something that had been asleep for a very long time and was deciding, very slowly, what to do about the fact that it was not asleep any more. We are hard pressed on every side, Cesare thought, and was not sure why he thought it, and yet not crushed.

Alfonso put his left arm up across his face. The little mechanical spiders that lived in the joints of his vambrace had already pulled themselves in, retreating into the seams of the metal. Even the spiders knew.

"Cesare." Liansheng's voice had something in it that Cesare had not heard from him before. Something that was not fear, exactly, but the shape that fear leaves in a man's throat when he is too busy to be afraid. "The centre of the tunnel. Now."

"What?"

"Move. Centre. Now."

Liansheng's hand closed on Cesare's wrist. His grip was stronger than a man his size had any right to have. He hauled Cesare off his feet, set him down three paces further on, and let go.

Cesare stumbled. His boot came down on a row of gears set into the floor.

They spun under his heel. The teeth of them caught at the leather, and then at the leather's wearer. Something bit him across the ankle, a thin bright line of pain, and the blood that came out was taken up by the rotation and pulled into red arcs, like ink in a turning well.

The dark-red beams changed direction.

All of them.

The beams that had been crossing at random now swung as one, like the barrels of a hundred guns being re-aimed in a single motion, and they found Cesare in the centre of the tunnel. They passed through him. They didn't. They hung on him, sweeping him up and down, the way a clerk's finger runs down a page to make sure the page is the right one.

The colour of the beams warmed. Dark red. Orange. Then a gold that was almost friendly — the colour of late afternoon in a country Cesare had never been to, falling on a window he had never opened.

The gold went into his eyes.

Cesare's vision went out for a moment, and what came back was not his own.

His irises lit.

Not the way a lamp lights. From the inside. From the back of the eye outward, in a slow bloom of writing, as if a brand had been heated in a fire and was being used, very carefully, to mark him. The marks were not letters he could read. They pulsed with his heartbeat, opening and closing, opening and closing, and they spread from the pupil to the white of the eye, then down the tear-line to the corner. The heat ran down the back of his neck and found the gold cuff that had lived in his spine since he was a child. The cuff woke. It felt, for one clear second, like someone had pressed a hot iron to the back of his neck and held it there, and Cesare was a bastard by birth, and bastards learned early not to flinch, and he did not flinch.

On the back of his right hand, the faint violet tracery of the conduits under his skin brightened. The light in the lines was no longer violet. It was violet and gold, and the gold was winning.

The gears stopped.

Every one of them, in the same instant, in the same breath, in the same fraction of the breath. The keen of them cut off as if a throat had been closed, and the tunnel dropped into a silence so complete that Cesare could hear the blood in his own ears.

The gold went out of his eyes, slowly, the way a hand lifts off a page it has been reading.

The letters on the gears dimmed, one by one, the way the lights of a city go out street by street before dawn.

Don Juan cleared his throat.

"So," he said, very carefully, "it knows him."

Liansheng let out a breath that he had been holding for a long time.

"No," he said. "It confirmed him."

The tunnel settled. The air still smelled of hot brass — that thin, acrid note of metal that has been worked too fast and too hot — but the light was gone, and the walls were just walls again, except that they were not just walls.

"This is the root channel of a branch of the World Tree." Liansheng turned to face them. The gold in his eyes was dim, but it was there, and in the dim of it Cesare could see that Liansheng was afraid. "Every one of those little wheels is a nerve-ending of the branch. They run on red mercury. They have been asleep in this mountain for three hundred years."

"Three hundred," Alfonso said. "There was no Minerva Bureau three hundred years ago."

"No. The Bureau was founded a century ago. The World Tree is older than the Bureau by two centuries. When Pope Borgia the First found it, it was already here."

"Borgia the First," Quintilian said from the back. "The madman who carved his diary into the gallery walls."

"He was not mad," Liansheng said. "He was the most awake man of his age. He knew the creation myth of the Messianic Church was a lie, and he spent his life looking for the emissary who could wake the Machine Kingdom — a person of the purple-eyed seer blood."

He looked at Cesare.

"He failed. Not because the blood was rare, although the blood was rare. Because the World Tree's test is harder than any test a man can design."

"Test," Cesare said.

Liansheng did not answer him directly. He turned and laid his palm against the wall, against a wheel set in the centre of a ring of inverted stars. The wheel did not move. The letters on its face, in their hair-thin lines, lit up under his hand, gold, briefly, like a coal that has been breathed on.

"The branch has a will of its own," Liansheng said. "It will only take orders from a true heir of the Ceylon seers. And a true heir does not mean a pair of purple eyes. It means a direct descendant of the last seer of Ceylon, in the mother's line, in the father's line, or in some combination the branch can read, and the heir must have been remembered by the branch — in the womb, in the blood, in whatever the branch uses for thought — before he was born. In three hundred years, the branch has accepted only two people."

He paused.

"The last seer of Ceylon," he said. "And her sister. The Second Branch."

"After the last seer sealed the root of the World Tree in her own body, no third person passed the test."

"Until me," Cesare said.

"Until you," Liansheng said. "You are not only a carrier of the blood. The cuff in your neck, the nerve-link in your spine, the red mercury that lives in your marrow — they are all fragments of the body the last seer used to seal the root, three hundred years ago. The branch knows you, because the branch knows a part of itself."

"The red beams," Alfonso said. "Before. The scan."

"Warning," Liansheng said. "For an intruder, the branch attacks. What you saw a moment ago was the branch at less than a tenth of what it can do. If it had judged us enemies, the beams would not have been light. They would have been focused red mercury."

"Focused red mercury?" Don Juan said, very quietly. "In this mountain?"

"The whole rock of Vesuvius is soaked in it. That is why the Sighing Wall is built where it is built."

Valentina had been standing just behind Cesare's shoulder, silent, her grey-blue eyes taking the measure of the walls. The honeysuckle of her perfume was almost lost in the burnt-brass smell of the air. Her hair was a mess under the hood of her coat. Her face was not.

"The experiments at the Sighing Wall," she said. "The ones that went wrong. You said the branch tests people. What does that have to do with them?"

Liansheng looked at her. For a moment something moved behind his eyes, something that did not have a name Cesare could have used, and then it was gone.

"You are quick, Princess of the Yenisei," he said. "The armoured remains that walk in the deep of the Wall, and the failed experiments that the Wall keeps throwing back at itself — they are not accidents."

"They are children," Liansheng said. "Orphans. The first Borgia pope had them brought from the East, from Ceylon, from every place a trace of the seer blood might still be found. He had them bound into half-built suits of armour, and he had the suits joined to their nerves, and he forced them to the test."

The tunnel was very quiet.

"They failed," Liansheng said. "The branch rejected them. The half-built suits broke loose in their bodies. The red mercury ate the children's nervous systems, and what was left was not a man and not a machine, and Borgia the First sealed them in the deep of the Sighing Wall."

"For three hundred years?" Quintilian said.

"The Wall moves," Liansheng said. "Every Director of the Minerva Bureau since has called it instability in the old seal. I am the only one who knows what it actually is. They are still alive in there. They have been alive in there, in the rock, for three hundred years."

He looked into the dark ahead of them.

"Because in the last moment of their lives, the last thing they felt was the pain of having been refused. That pain has not gone out. It is what is moving the Wall."

For a long time, nobody spoke.

"So," Don Juan said at last, "we are on a road that only Cesare can walk."

"From here," Liansheng said, "every wheel we pass must see Cesare first. The branch will be quiet while he is in front. Anyone else goes first, the branch wakes, and the branch does not ask twice."

Cesare looked at the back of his right hand. The violet in the lines had gone back to violet. The gold cuff at the back of his neck was still warm. There was something in it, low down, almost under the hearing, like a voice singing one note very far away.

"Move," he said. "Keep moving."

They went forward in single file. Cesare at the head. Liansheng a step behind, to tell him where to put his feet. The rest of them in the order they had come in through the crack, which was to say, no order at all.

Every time they passed a ring of inverted stars, the letters on the wheels lit. Just for a moment. Just a single breath of gold. A greeting, Liansheng said. The branch greeting a piece of itself that had wandered out into the world and had wandered home.

Ten minutes.

Then Liansheng held up a hand.

"Stop."

Cesare stopped.

The tunnel forked.

Left and right, two corridors going forward, the walls of each one set with wheels the way this one was, but the wheels in the left-hand corridor were laid out in lotuses, full and open, the petals of them opening into the dark, and the wheels in the right-hand corridor were laid out in wheels — gear inside gear inside gear, the geometry of them turning in on itself until the eye lost the place where it had started.

"Which way?" Alfonso said, from behind Cesare's shoulder.

"Right," Liansheng said. "The lotus corridor leads to the First Branch — the sanctuary where the last seer of Ceylon sealed the root of the World Tree. We are not going to the sanctuary. We are going to the Black Iron Gate."

"Shh," Valentina said. "Listen."

They listened.

From behind them. From the way they had come.

Not the rustle of the wheels.

Footsteps.

Many of them. Heavy, regular, the slow crunch of boots on stone, and under the boots, the deeper, oilier note of a hydraulic drive — the unmistakable working sound of a heavy suit of armour on the march, cable and piston and the slow whistle of steam venting from a knee-joint that had been worked too long.

And the rustle of the wheels was back.

Cesare turned his head.

The wheels on the walls behind them were turning again. But not the way they had been turning a moment ago. They were all turning the same way — away from Cesare, towards the dark they had come out of, towards the crack, towards the sound of the boots.

The light that came out of them was not red this time.

It was gold.

The same gold that had poured into Cesare's eyes ten minutes ago. Soft, warm, the colour of late afternoon. It fell in long bars down the tunnel behind them, as far as Cesare could see, and where it fell on the rock it stayed, painting the walls a colour that was not stone.

It was lighting the way.

Or — Cesare thought, and the thought was a cold one, and his face, when he set it, was the cold austere face of his father, who had never once in his life acknowledged him — it was lighting the way for something.

Liansheng's face changed.

"Holy See Armoured Division," he said. "They have found the crack. The wheels are showing them the path."

"Showing —" Quintilian turned. "Showing them the path?"

"Not the path." Liansheng's voice was very fast now. "The branch is calling. It has felt a great deal of red-mercury energy entering its root system, and it is doing what the branch does when it feels energy that is not its own — it is summoning the candidates. It thinks the men coming up the tunnel are supplicants. It thinks they have come to be tested."

"So the wheels are —"

"Marking them," Liansheng said. "Tagging them. The branch is not guiding them. The branch is making a list."

The footsteps were louder now. And under the footsteps, the unmistakable clank of a heavy suit taking a corner at speed, and the crunch of a knee that had been hit in a fight not long ago, and was not going to take the corner cleanly.

"How long?" Cesare said.

"At their pace," Liansheng said, after a second of listening, his head tilted the way a dog's head tilts, "seven minutes."

"Seven minutes is too long," Cesare said. "Right corridor. Now."

He turned to go. Liansheng caught his arm.

Cesare stopped.

Liansheng had already taken a small tin-sealed scroll from the inner pocket of his robe. The scroll was about a foot long. The tin was yellow with age. On the seal, seven characters of Sinhalese script were struck in tarnished gold, and as Cesare looked at them the cuff at the back of his neck went hot, then hotter, as if a wire inside him had been plucked and was now ringing, low and clear, somewhere down in the bone.

"The Prophecy of the Branch," Liansheng said, and he put the scroll into Cesare's hand. "The last writing of the last seer of Ceylon. It has the location of the Second Branch's seal. The Black Iron Gate is the door. The thing behind the door is what the seal is for."

"Why are you giving this to me now?"

"Because you must reach the gate," Liansheng said. "And I —"

He drew a short sword from the inside of the robe.

The blade was narrow. It was the colour of dark gold, and the edge of it caught the gold light of the wheels on the wall in a way that the walls themselves did not. The grip was wound with a strip of paper cut into the shape of a Ceylon lotus, the kind that is offered at a shrine. The whole of the sword, blade and grip and the strip of paper, was not much longer than a man's forearm. It was a thing for close work.

"You are out of your mind," Don Juan said, before anyone else could. "You cannot hold a corridor against the Armoured Division by yourself."

"I don't have to hold it," Liansheng said. "I only have to hold it for seven minutes."

He looked back at Cesare. The gold in his eyes was pulsing now, in time with something Cesare could not hear.

"The Black Iron Gate is at the end of the right-hand corridor. Two keys open it. Your purple eyes. And the silver ring of cold jade that Aunt Liuli gave you, from the ice-plain. The two keys together, or the gate does not open."

"What is behind the gate?"

Liansheng did not answer.

He smiled. It was a small smile, and it sat on his face the way an old coin sits in a closed fist — something kept for a long time, and not yet spent.

"You'll know when you see it."

He turned. He went back down the tunnel, in the direction they had come, and his shadow stretched out long in front of him, the wheels on either side of him going gold as he passed them, lighting his way for him the way a road lights for a king.

At the turn of the corridor he did not look back.

The sound of the wheels rose. The gold light ran along the walls behind him in a moving river. Then, from the turn, a clatter of metal — and a voice, a voice that was not Liansheng's, raised in a language Cesare did not speak, and a heavier voice answering it, and a third, and the clatter of the clatter as a hydraulic knee hit the stone and went down and the suit behind it did not stop in time. And over it all, very clear, the small bright voice of Liansheng's narrow sword meeting the first suit of armour, and the second sound after that, which was the sound of a man in armour discovering that the small bright thing in the hand of the man in the robe was sharper than the joint of his suit.

"Go," Cesare said.

He turned. He ran.

The scroll was in his hand. The tin seal of it was cutting into his palm, and the pain of the cut, the warm bright line of blood on his skin, was the only thing he was sure of in the dark.

The wheels on the walls of the right-hand corridor woke as he came to them, one ring of inverted stars after another, gold after gold, a path of small fires laid out ahead of him as if a hand were lighting candles in a long room. The blood on his palm felt cold against the tin. The cuff at the back of his neck was ringing, low and clear, the way a bell rings in a city you have not been to in a long time, and the city is glad to see you, and the bell will not stop.

He did not look back.

Behind him, in the dark, a sword met armour again, and the sound of it rang down the corridor, and the gold light of the wheels ran with him, and the footsteps behind him were heavier than the footsteps of one man, and the tunnel was very long, and the door, when he came to it, was black, and the door was iron, and the door was waiting.
