【中文】
第193章 圣堂的脚步声

金属碰撞声在身后此起彼伏。

西泽尔跑在最前面，齿轮隧道里的微型黄铜齿轮在他经过时依次亮起，金红光束照亮他苍白的面孔。他的右手攥着莲生塞来的锡封卷轴，锡封纸的边缘已经嵌进掌心，渗出一线细血。他没擦，也没停。

"右转！"

阿方索在后面喊。

齿轮通道在前方裂开一条岔路，比主通道窄得多，岩壁上没有任何齿轮雕饰。莲生在分岔口停了半秒，用那把暗金色短剑在岩壁上划了一道痕——那是给西泽尔他们指的退路。下一秒他转身跳回屠龙者圣乔治的骑士舱，舱门轰然合拢，那台百年前封存的初代炽天使发出沉重的蒸汽轰鸣。

西泽尔没有回头。

他听见圣堂装甲师重型蒸汽靴踏在齿轮上的声音了——"轰、轰、轰"，节奏沉稳如巨人的心跳。莲生一个人挡在那里，要拖七分钟。

"快走！"西泽尔说。

唐璜从后面冲上来，蔷薇之鬼的轻甲在岩壁上投下拉长的影子。瓦莲京娜最后一个进入岔路，落地时无声无息，改装神怒Ⅲ型的膝关节轻微弯折，金色面甲朝后方扫了一眼。

"关上了。"她说。

那扇通往主通道的隔断岩门是莲生用短剑触发的某个机关——准确地说，是齿轮隧道三百年前就埋好的黑铁板。厚重的门扇落下时发出一声沉闷的金属撞击，之后莲生那边的所有声音都被隔绝在外。

只剩下西泽尔他们的脚步声和呼吸声。

岔路越走越窄，岩壁潮湿，缝隙里长着不知名的白色苔藓。偶尔有什么小东西被惊起，扑棱着翅膀消失在黑暗中。阿方索一边走一边用机械手敲击岩壁，听回声。

"这后面有空腔。"他说。

裂隙尽头是一扇锈迹斑斑的铁门，门上没有任何锁，但铰链已经几乎锈死。阿方索伸出机械臂，用力一推，铰链发出刺耳的金属尖叫，铁门向内开启，露出一片昏黄的光芒——是透进来的金色齿轮余光，反射在岩壁上。

那是一间大约三十平米的地下休息室。

穹顶低矮，由整块岩石凿成，墙壁上挂着一盏早已燃尽瓦斯的旧灯。房间中央是一张长方形的木桌，桌面覆着厚厚一层灰，灰里有几个清晰的手指印，印在某个位置很久了，几乎成了桌面的一部分。

桌子中央放着一只玻璃杯，杯子里残留着小半杯干涸的液体。液体已经从鲜红变成了暗褐色，像凝固的旧血，边缘析出细小的金属晶体。

"红水银。"阿方索走到桌边，用机械手指敲了敲玻璃杯壁，"纯度不低。"

他皱起眉。

"这杯东西放了至少三五年了。"

西泽尔扫了一眼那杯红水银。他见过这种东西——在密涅瓦机关的鹰巢里，在枢机会的地下室里，在他母亲琳琅夫人的病床边。这是这个世界最危险的物质之一，碰一下都嫌多，但这里曾经有人喝下半杯。

桌子另一端摊开着一卷图纸草稿，纸质发黄，墨线细如蛛丝。阿方索展开来看了一眼，神色微变。

"这是密涅瓦初代总工程师的图纸。"他压低声音，"看落款。"

图纸右下角有一个潦草的签名——"A. M."。字母下方还有一行更小的字，写着"星历117年·维苏威火山内部结构勘测第三版"。

"星历一百一十七年。"唐璜走过来瞅了一眼，"密涅瓦机关建立的头三年。"

"这里……曾经是初代总工程师的临时驻点。"阿方索把图纸小心地放回桌上，"他在这座火山里勘测了至少三年。"

西泽尔没有接话。他走到休息室唯一的铁门前，拨动了门闩。铁门沉重地合上，将外面潮湿的裂隙隔绝。

"先休息两分钟。"他转过身，从怀里抽出莲生塞给他的锡封卷轴，"然后我们继续找路。"

唐璜已经一屁股坐在了墙角的石凳上，长长地吐了口气。昆提良站在门边，替大家把风。瓦莲京娜站在桌边，安静地打量着那只红水银杯子，金色面甲掀起一道缝，露出她冰蓝色的眼睛。

休息室陷入短暂的沉默。

---

锡封纸在指尖下沙沙作响。

西泽尔把卷轴平放在桌上，用小刀轻轻挑开锡封。卷轴里裹着一本薄薄的手稿，手稿装订简陋，封面和封底都是粗糙的锡兰草纸，纸面上刻着一个倒置的五芒星——五芒星中央是一个复杂的齿轮图样，齿轮的齿牙上缠绕着极细的梵文。

手稿的纸张已经发黄发脆，有些页面甚至有被火烧过的焦痕。

他翻开了第一页。

第一行文字用暗红色的墨水写成，墨水已经褪色，但字迹依然清晰可辨——是古老的锡兰文，字体方正如刀刻。瓦莲京娜凑近看了一眼，轻声念了出来。

"'紫瞳不是诅咒。'"

"'紫瞳是锡兰星见与世界树残枝沟通的钥匙。'"

"'初代教皇偷走了世界树残枝的西方分支，还把紫瞳污为诅咒，就是为了独占钥匙。'"

瓦莲京娜的声音在地下休息室里回响，带着一种不真实的轻，像风穿过空旷的教堂。

西泽尔的手指停在纸页上。

他想起了克里特岛。

那年他六岁，被继父家的孩子们用麻袋套住脑袋，推进了诺丁山修道院后院的枯井里。麻袋里漆黑一片，井水冰冷，肺里的空气一点一点被挤出。他想喊，但麻袋堵住了嘴。他想挣扎，但井水已经淹到了下巴。

就在他几乎要放弃的时候，他听见母亲的声音——不，那不是真的声音，那是他自己的想象。

井水淹过他的鼻子，他的眼睛在麻袋里挣开。黑暗中什么都看不见，但他感觉到一种奇异的"回声"，仿佛整个克里特岛的山脉、海洋、教堂、修道院都在向他传递某种信息。

然后麻袋被人从井里拉了上来。

"看看这孩子的眼睛。"有人举着火把靠近，"紫色的……和圣女塔里那幅画上的女人一样。"

他被火把的余温烫伤了左眼，眼角到现在都有一道浅浅的疤。

从那之后，他就再也不是"普通孩子"了。

他被送到了诺丁山初等学校读书。学校里的孩子叫他"紫眼睛的怪物"，教师们则有意无意地避开他，连他的继父都开始用奇怪的眼光看他，仿佛他身上带着某种不洁的印记。

直到莉诺雅修女把他带到翡冷翠的圣教院，他在那里才第一次被当作普通孩子对待。

他一直以为自己的紫瞳只是体质问题，是母亲遗传给他的某种"缺陷"。他从未想过——

"初代教皇知道紫瞳的意义。"西泽尔的声音很轻，"所以他把它污名化。克里特岛人把紫瞳当作诅咒，杀了不知道多少紫瞳的孩子。博尔吉亚家族……害怕我母亲，害怕我。"

他顿了顿。

"因为我母亲是锡兰星见。我是她的儿子。"

休息室里没有人说话。

"你从来没有怀疑过？"阿方索轻声问。

"我怀疑过。"西泽尔说，"但我不敢确认。因为如果是真的，那就意味着——"

他没有说下去。

意味着他不是真正的"博尔吉亚"。

意味着他真正的家族，是三百年前被西方世界灭族的那个家族。

意味着整个西方对"紫瞳"的所有恐惧、所有驱逐、所有杀害——都建立在一个弥天大谎之上。

唐璜在墙角吹了声口哨，没说话。昆提良低下了头。瓦莲京娜静静地站在桌边，视线落在西泽尔翻动预言书的指尖上。

西泽尔继续往后翻。

第二页、第三页、第四页——预言书的内容大多以锡兰古文写成，瓦莲京娜一页一页地翻译过来。

"'世界树残枝02号封存在维苏威火山最深处，封印分为三层。'"

"'第一层是叹息之墙后的物理隔绝——三百年前由星见亲手刻下的微型齿轮，会自动筛选来者是否携带锡兰星见直系血裔的气息。'"

"'第二层是黑铁巨门的双重锁——一把钥匙是艾琳娜·博尔吉亚的冰原寒玉银戒指，另一把钥匙是紫瞳。'"

"'第三层是世界树残枝自身的意志——只有被残枝意识碎片记住的紫瞳星见才能通过。'"

"'三百年来，除我与我妹妹外，唯有一人通过筛选。'"

"'他的名字叫西泽尔·琳琅。'"

"西泽尔·琳琅？"唐璜皱了皱眉，"这不是你的全名吗？西泽尔·博尔吉亚。"

"琳琅是我母亲的姓。"西泽尔说，"莲生在屠龙者圣乔治里等我的那个男人……他自称'西泽尔·琳琅'。"

"所以他就是……"阿方索停了一下，"末代星见预言中的第三个通过筛选的人？"

"或者更早。"瓦莲京娜继续翻译着，"'第三个人，他的血统已经超越了我。他母亲的血是红的，他父亲的血是黑的，红与黑的混合产生了新的紫瞳。'"

"'新的紫瞳可以打开新的锁。'"

"什么意思？"昆提良忍不住问。

"我也不完全懂。"瓦莲京娜摇了摇头，"但如果这个'西泽尔·琳琅'就是屠龙者圣乔治里的那个男人，那他应该和西泽尔有某种血缘关系——但他又姓'琳琅'，是西泽尔母亲的姓。"

她停顿了一秒。

"他是西泽尔母亲的……"唐璜欲言又止。

"继续翻。"西泽尔打断他。

手稿翻到了最后一页。

最后一页是空白的。

"没了？"唐璜凑过来。

"应该有结尾预言。"阿方索也凑过来，"这种手稿一般都有一段结尾预言——"

话音未落，空白页面上忽然浮现出一行字。

那行字像从纸面下透出来的金色光芒，缓缓地、一个字一个字地显现出来——字体极古老，是锡兰文的方块字，笔画像刀刻的痕迹，边缘泛着烫金般的微光。那光不是反射的，而是纸面本身在发光，像血液在皮肤下流动。

瓦莲京娜的嘴唇微微动了动，没有出声。她把页面凑近看，片刻后念了出来。

"'龙战于野，其血玄黄。'"

"'见群龙无首，吉。'"

"什么意思？"西泽尔问。

"前半句……是一种战争的预兆。"瓦莲京娜说，"龙战于野——两条龙在旷野上战斗，流出玄黄之血。玄黄是天地混沌之色，意思是这场战争将改变天地。"

"后半句……"

她停顿了一下。

"'见群龙无首，吉'——在东方占卜里，这是一句爻辞。群龙无首，意味着所有龙都失去了首领，没有人能统帅他们，各方势力混战。卦象说这是吉利的。"

"吉利？"唐璜嗤了一声，"各方混战还叫吉利？"

"在东方占卜里，'吉利'不代表正义。"瓦莲京娜摇头，"它只代表'事态将按照它应有的方向发展'。群龙无首——没有谁能一手遮天，所有潜龙都会浮出水面。对有些人来说，这是灾难的开始。对另一些人来说……"

"是机会。"阿方索低声说。

西泽尔没有接话。

他盯着那行金色的字，总觉得它在告诉他什么。

"龙战于野"——哪两条龙？

"群龙无首"——这个"首"，是谁？是教皇？是枢机会？还是——

"咣当——"

门外突然传来沉重的金属撞击声。

"搜！给我搜遍每一个角落！"

是一个男人的声音，沙哑、凶狠，带着钢铁般的冷意。

"一定要找到西泽尔·博尔吉亚和那个锡兰异端！"

所有人都安静下来。

西泽尔把预言书一把塞进怀里，贴着心口的位置。锡封纸隔着内衬仍能感觉到一丝微弱的温热，仿佛那颗金色的字还在燃烧。

他看向门的方向——铁门关着，但那种"咣当"声是从隔壁传来的，隔壁还有别的房间。

脚步声越来越近，整齐划一，是训练有素的士兵。

"这里有扇门！"另一个声音说。

"试试能不能打开！"

门外传来枪栓拉动的咔哒声，金属与金属摩擦的声音尖锐刺耳。

"老板——"唐璜压低声音，眼神示意大家退到阴影里。

西泽尔没有动。

他突然注意到阿方索还站在桌边，机械手按在那张图纸草稿上，脸色发白，眼神死死钉在图纸的某一处。

"阿方索？"

"老板。"阿方索抬起头，指向图纸上的一条细线。

那条线非常细，几乎和纸面融在一起，但颜色不同于其他墨线——是银色的。银线从图纸的左下角蜿蜒到右下角，绕过复杂的矿道结构图，旁边标注着一行细小的文字。

阿方索的机械手指落在那行字上，指尖微微颤抖。

"'黑铁巨门的第三层封印解除通道'。"他念道。

"终点……"

他的声音哑了一瞬。

"就在这里。"

阿方索猛地抬起头，目光越过西泽尔的肩膀，指向休息室角落那张积满灰尘的、看起来像是普通行军床的木床。

"床底下。"

门外，金属铰链发出尖锐的惨叫。

【English】
Chapter 193 — Footsteps in the Sanctuary

The metal sounds chased them down the corridor like dogs.

Cesare ran first. The little brass gears set into the tunnel walls woke in sequence as he passed, throwing a gold-red glow across the sharp bones of his face. In his right hand he held the tin-sealed scroll Liansheng had pressed into his palm; the edge of the tin had bitten into his flesh, and a thin line of blood ran down into his sleeve. He did not wipe it. He did not slow.

"Turn right!"

Alfonso's voice came from behind.

The gear tunnel split ahead, one branch narrower than the rest, the bare rock untouched by brasswork. Liansheng halted at the fork for half a breath. He drew the short dark-gold sword across the wall, leaving a single mark — that for Cesare, that for the way back. Then he turned and dropped back into the knight-chamber of Saint George the Dragonslayer, and the hatch of the machine crashed shut behind him, and a hundred-year-old Seraph woke with the slow, heavy thunder of pressurised steam.

Cesare did not look back.

He could hear them now. The Holy See Armored Division marched in cadence, the heavy steam-boots striking the gears in a rhythm like a giant's pulse — boom, boom, boom. Liansheng, alone, to hold that corridor for seven minutes.

"Move," Cesare said.

Don Juan came up from behind, the light plate of the Spectre casting a long, twitching shadow along the wall. Valentina entered the narrow branch last, her modified Wrath III kneeling a fraction on impact, the golden faceplate of her helm turning once to the rear.

"It's sealed," she said.

The rock-cut door between them and the main tunnel had been a mechanism built into the mountain three centuries before any of them were born — a black iron plate that Liansheng's sword had only to touch. It had fallen with a single, muffled impact, and now Liansheng's war was on the other side of it, sealed away with all its sound.

There was nothing left but their own breathing and the rasp of boots on wet stone.

The branch narrowed as they went. Moisture beaded the rock. White moss, nameless, grew in the seams. Small things fled the light of their lamps into the dark with a soft clatter of wings. Alfonso walked with his mechanical hand pressed to the wall, listening to the echoes it gave back.

"There's a hollow behind this," he said.

At the end of the cleft, set into the rock without ceremony, a door of rusted iron. There was no lock upon it; the hinges had simply rusted into place. Alfonso pushed with the mechanical arm. The hinges screamed, and the door swung inward, and a dim yellow light fell across them — not a lamp, but the reflected glare of distant gearwork washing the far wall of the room.

It was a chamber perhaps thirty feet across, hewn out of living stone. The ceiling was low. On one wall hung a lamp whose gas had burned out long ago. In the middle of the floor stood a long wooden table, thick with dust, and in the dust were several clear finger-prints pressed into the same spot so many times that they had almost become part of the wood.

In the centre of the table sat a single glass. Inside the glass, a small residue of liquid had dried to the colour of old blood; around its rim, tiny metallic crystals had precipitated out of the solution.

"Red mercury," Alfonso said, tapping the glass with one metal finger. "Not a low grade, either."

He frowned.

"This cup has been sitting here three, maybe five years."

Cesare gave the glass a look. He had seen this substance before — in the eyrie of the Minerva Engine, in the vault beneath the College of Cardinals, at his mother Linlang's bedside, where it had dripped, drop by drop, into the veins of a dying woman. One of the most dangerous things in the world. And here, somebody had once drunk half a glass of it and walked away.

At the other end of the table lay a yellowed draft, the paper gone the colour of weak tea, the ink lines on it as fine as a spider's web. Alfonso unrolled it a hand's width and his face changed.

"These are the working drawings of Minerva's first chief engineer," he said, low. "Look at the signature."

A scrawl in the lower right corner. Two initials.

A. M.

And beneath them, in smaller writing — *Star Calendar, Year 117. Third edition. Survey of the internal structure of Vesuvius.*

"Year one-seventeen," Don Juan said, leaning in. "Third year after Minerva was founded."

"Then this," Alfonso said, and laid the draft back with the care one uses for a sleeping child, "was the chief engineer's field camp. He was surveying this volcano for three years before anyone in Florence had even heard of him."

Cesare said nothing. He walked to the iron door of the chamber, threw the bolt. The door closed on the wet cleft behind them with a weight that was almost comforting.

"Two minutes," he said, turning back. He drew the tin-sealed scroll from inside his coat. "Then we keep going."

Don Juan had already dropped onto the stone bench against the wall and let out a breath he had been holding for a quarter of an hour. Quintilian took the door. Valentina stood by the table, the gold visor of her helm tipped up just enough to show the cold blue of her eyes, watching the red mercury as if she expected it to move.

For a time nobody spoke.

---

The tin crinkled under his thumb.

Cesare laid the scroll flat on the dusty table and worked the seal loose with the point of his knife. Inside, a thin manuscript. The binding was rough — both covers were a coarse Ceylonese straw paper, and on the front was stamped, in dry impression, an inverted pentagram, and inside the pentagram a complex arrangement of gears, and around the gears a fine ring of Pali script no thicker than a hair.

The pages had gone the colour of bone. Some were brittle. Some were scorched at the edges, as if the book had once been pulled from a fire.

He opened the first page.

The first line was written in a dark red ink, faded now but still legible. The script was square, sharp — old Ceylonese, the kind a stone-cutter would use. Valentina bent close, and read it aloud, and her voice in the underground room was a thin, light thing, like wind through an empty basilica.

"*The Purple Eyes are not a curse.*"

"*The Purple Eyes are the key by which the Star-Reader of Ceylon speaks with the remnant of the World Tree.*"

"*The first Pope stole the western branch of the World Tree, and called the Purple Eyes a curse, that he might keep the key to himself.*"

Valentina's voice went on echoing after the words had ended.

Cesare's hand had stopped on the page.

He remembered Crete.

He was six. The sons of his stepfather had put a sack over his head and thrown him down the dry well at the back of the Notting Hill priory. Inside the sack, dark. Cold water rose to his chin. The air in his lungs thinned, and thinned, and thinned. He tried to scream, but the sack was in his mouth. He tried to thrash, and the water was at his jaw.

Just as he was about to stop trying, he heard his mother's voice.

It was not her voice. It was the shape of her voice, the way a memory puts a hand on a child's shoulder in the dark.

The water went over his nose. He opened his eyes inside the sack. There was nothing to see. But something else was there — a kind of echo, not a sound, as if the whole island of Crete, its mountains, its sea, its churches, its priories, were saying something to him at once.

Then someone dragged the sack out of the well.

"Look at the child's eyes," a man said, holding a torch close. "Purple. Like the woman in the painting in the tower of the saint."

The torch burned the corner of his left eye. The scar was still there, a pale crescent, when he was thirty and a cardinal's son and not yet a heretic.

After that he was no longer an ordinary boy. They sent him to a primary school in Notting Hill. The other children called him the purple-eyed monster. The masters avoided him, not out of cruelty but out of a small, careful fear. Even his stepfather began to look at him the way a man looks at a horse that has just spoken — as if some contract between them had been broken without warning.

It had been Sister Linora who took him, in the end, to the catechetical school in Florence, where for the first time he was a child and nothing more.

He had always assumed his eyes were a small inherited flaw — his mother's small flaw, passed to him. He had never thought to ask —

"The first Pope knew what the eyes were for," Cesare said, very quietly. "So he slandered them. The Cretans grew up burning purple-eyed children in their beds. The Borgias feared my mother. The Borgias feared me."

He paused.

"Because my mother was a Star-Reader of Ceylon. And I am her son."

The chamber was quiet.

"Did you never suspect?" Alfonso said, softly.

"I suspected." Cesare said. "I would not confirm it. Because if it was true, then—"

He did not finish the sentence.

If it was true, then he was not a Borgia by blood.

If it was true, then his true family was the family the Western world had, three hundred years before, hunted to the last child.

If it was true, then every execution, every expulsion, every whispered fear of the Purple Eyes in the West had been built on a single, very old lie.

Don Juan whistled, low, at the wall. Quintilian looked down. Valentina did not move; her eyes rested on the fingers with which Cesare held the page, as if she were reading him, not the book.

Cesare turned the leaves.

The second, the third, the fourth — the manuscript was written almost entirely in old Ceylonese, and Valentina translated it aloud, page by page, her voice falling now and then into the sing-song cadence of a child reciting scripture.

"*The second branch of the World Tree is sealed at the deepest point of Vesuvius. The seal has three layers.*"

"*The first is the physical barrier behind the Wall of Sighs — set, three hundred years ago, by a Star-Reader's own hand, in the form of micro-gears which will, of their own logic, sort the breath of any direct blood-descendant of the Ceylon line from the breath of a stranger.*"

"*The second is the double lock of the black iron gate — one key is the silver ring of cold jade from Elena Borgia's ice-plain, the other key is the Purple Eyes themselves.*"

"*The third is the will of the remnant of the World Tree itself. Only a Purple-Eyed Star-Reader whose fragment the Tree has already remembered may pass.*"

"*In three hundred years, only three have passed the sorting.*"

"*Myself, and my sister, and one other.*"

"*His name was Cesare Linlang.*"

"Cesare Linlang?" Don Juan frowned. "But that is your full name. You are Cesare Borgia."

"Lìn is my mother's name," Cesare said. "The man waiting for us in Saint George — the man who calls himself *Cesare Linlang* —"

"Then he is—" Alfonso stopped.

"The third," Valentina said. She was still reading. "*'The third, whose blood has passed beyond my own. His mother's blood is red. His father's blood is black. The mixing of the two has bred a new kind of Purple.*'"

"*'The new Purple can open the new lock.*'"

"What does that mean?" Quintilian asked.

"It means," Valentina said, slowly, "that the man in Saint George is bound to Cesare by blood. He bears our mother's surname. He bears *your* name."

She stopped, and was silent for a beat.

"He must be—" Don Juan began.

"Turn the page," Cesare said.

He turned it.

The last page of the manuscript was blank.

"That's it?" Don Juan leaned in. "There's meant to be a closing prophecy. These old Ceylon codices always—"

He stopped.

On the blank page, a line of writing was appearing.

It came up out of the paper, slowly, one character after another, the way a vein of light rises in dark water. The script was the old square Ceylonese. The strokes looked cut with a knife. Around the edges of each character there was a faint metallic sheen, the colour of gilt that has been left too long in a fire. It was not reflected light. The page was producing it, as if a slow warm current was running under the skin of the paper.

Valentina held the page closer. She did not speak for a long moment. Then she read.

"*Dragons war in the wild, and their blood is the colour of heaven darkened.*"

"*Seeing a flight of dragons without a head — auspicious.*"

"What does it mean?" Cesare asked.

"The first half is a war-sign." Valentina said. "Two dragons fight in the open, and the blood they spill is the colour of the world's first chaos. It means the war will change the shape of heaven and earth."

"The second half—"

She paused.

"*'A flight of dragons without a head'* is a line from the Eastern Book of Changes. It is an image of many dragons, none of them led. Every power fighting every other power. No single hand upon the reins. The Book of Changes marks the omen as auspicious."

"Auspicious?" Don Juan gave a short, dry sound. "All-out war is auspicious?"

"In the Eastern reading," Valentina said, "auspicious does not mean *righteous*. It means *the thing will, at last, take the shape it has always been trying to take.* No dragon is at the head. No single throne can hold the sky. The hidden dragons of the world must come up out of their holes."

"For some," Alfonso said, low, "that is the beginning of the end. For others—"

"—it is the opening," Cesare finished.

He did not say the word. He was looking at the gilt characters, and he felt, with a small cold certainty, that the page was looking back at him, and that it was not asking a question.

*Dragons war in the wild* — which two dragons?

*No head* — which head? The Pope's? The College of Cardinals'? His own?

"Crack —"

A heavy metallic strike came from the other side of the iron door.

"Search me every inch of this level!"

A man's voice, hoarse and merciless, with the clean cold of a steel edge drawn across stone.

"Find Cesare Borgia and the Ceylonese heretic! Search!"

Everyone went still.

Cesare thrust the manuscript inside his coat, against his chest. Through the lining he could still feel the faint warmth of the last page, as if the gilt characters were still working their way up out of the paper, one by one.

He looked towards the door. It was shut. The strikes were coming from the chamber on the other side of the cleft, not from this one.

Boots, now, and a great many of them. Trained men. The rhythm of an outfit on the move.

"There's a door here!" another voice called, from very close.

"Try it!"

The sound of a rifle-bolt being worked, the bright, obscene little chatter of metal on metal.

"Chief —" Don Juan said, very low, and gestured towards the shadows at the back of the room with his chin.

Cesare did not move.

He had noticed that Alfonso was still standing by the table, the mechanical hand pressed flat on the yellowed draft, his face the colour of candle wax, his eyes fixed on one particular line of the drawing.

"Alfonso?"

"Chief." Alfonso looked up. He pointed to a single thin line on the draft.

The line was almost lost against the paper. The ink was not black, like the rest — it was silver. From the lower left of the page it ran to the lower right, threading its way past the workings of the mine-survey, and beside it was a single line of small neat text.

Alfonso's metal finger came to rest on the words. The tip of the finger trembled, just once.

"*Bypass of the third seal of the black iron gate.*" he read.

He swallowed.

"The end of the road," he said. "It's under this room."

He looked up, across Cesare's shoulder, towards the far corner of the chamber, where a low wooden cot sat against the rock wall, heaped with a coverlet of undisturbed dust, the kind of camp-bed a surveyor might use for a decade and never mention.

"Under the bed," he said.

From the other side of the iron door, the hinges began to scream.

第194章 床底的机关

【中文】
第194章 床底的机关

"咣当——"

隔壁的门被暴力撞开，金属铰链发出尖厉的惨叫。

"搜！一个角落都不许放过！"那个沙哑凶狠的声音再次响起，靴底踩在石板上的声音整齐划一，像是一台精密的杀人机器在运转。

西泽尔看向阿方索。

阿方索已经动了。

这个前天才机械师的手掌稳得惊人，机械指节和人类指节交替发力，扣住行军床的床板边缘，轻轻往上一掀。灰尘簌簌落下，扑了阿方索半边脸，他连眼睛都没眨一下。床板被无声翻起，靠在墙上，露出下面的木框架。

木框架也是伪装。

阿方索用机械手敲了敲框架底部的木板，听声音判断了厚度，然后沿着木纹方向用力一推。整块木板滑出去，露出一层积满灰尘的铁板。铁板正中嵌着一个直径约半米的金属圆盘，表面发黑，像是被时间氧化了不知多少年。

"你们过来。"阿方索压低声音。

西泽尔、瓦莲京娜、昆提良和唐璜围拢过来。

圆盘上刻着一个完整的倒置五芒星，线条深嵌入金属表层，边缘锋利得能割破手指。五芒星周围环绕着一圈又一圈的微型齿轮纹饰，齿轮与齿轮之间用极其纤细的连线相连，仿佛一张精密的机械蛛网。灰尘下面隐约透出暗银色的金属光泽——那不是普通的铁，是某种更高级的合金。

"这是什么？"昆提良皱着眉，伸出一根粗壮的手指想戳，被阿方索一巴掌拍开。

"别碰！你手上有汗，盐分会腐蚀合金表面。"

西泽尔蹲下来，目光沿着倒置五芒星的线条走了一遍。五芒星的五个角分别指向五个方向，每个角的顶端都嵌着一颗极小的红水银微晶，早已失去光泽变成暗红色，但内部结构仍然完好。这个图案他见过——在锡封匣的祷文纸册封面上，在世界树残根守护符的背面，在莲生交给他的预言书扉页上。

都是倒置五芒星加齿轮。

锡兰星见家族的印记。

"这是机关的启动盘。"西泽尔说。

"我认得这些纹路。"瓦莲京娜忽然开口。

她从制服内袋里取出一样东西，摊在掌心。

那是一块银饰，拇指盖大小，边缘不规则，像是被人用力掰断的。银饰的断面上刻着半朵莲花，花瓣的线条纤细流畅，每一道弧度都精确到毫厘不差。银饰背面则刻着密密麻麻的微型纹路，和金属圆盘上的齿轮纹饰一脉相承。

"我母亲留下的。"瓦莲京娜说，"她叫它'世界树残枝启动符'。叶尼塞皇宫的私人收藏室里只此一块，我走的时候偷了出来。"

她将银饰放在金属圆盘的中央。

凹槽的形状和银饰严丝合缝。

"咔哒。"

一声极轻的机括声从圆盘深处传出，像是沉睡了几十年的钟表忽然被拨动了第一下。

所有人屏住呼吸。

圆盘没有完全打开，只是微微震动了一下，表面的灰尘被震落，露出下面原本的暗银色光泽。倒置五芒星五个角上的红水银微晶同时亮起微弱的暗红色光芒，光芒沿着齿轮纹饰的连线流动，像五条细细的暗红色溪流汇入中央的银饰。

银饰上的半朵莲花缓缓旋转了半圈，然后停住。

"咔哒。"

第二声机括声比第一声更重，圆盘开始以银饰为轴心缓慢旋转。五芒星的五个角依次亮起，每亮一个就伴随着一声沉重的金属撞击，像是某扇尘封已久的门正在被一点一点打开。

"后退。"阿方索说。

西泽尔站起来，退后两步。

圆盘完全打开了。

它不是一扇门，而是一面盖板。盖板翻起九十度靠在旁边的铁板支架上，露出下面一个直径约半米的圆形洞口。洞口内壁上镶嵌着一根根细长的金色灯柱，灯柱表面刻着极其精密的花纹，从上到下一直延伸到视线无法抵达的深处。

"这是一条通道。"唐璜低声说，"通往更深的地方。"

"等等。"阿方索突然抬手，指着洞口边缘的一根金色灯柱。

灯柱的底座上刻着一行小字。

字迹是用机械刻刀一笔一划刻上去的，笔画锋利，带着机械师特有的精确。字很小，如果不是阿方索的机械眼能够放大十倍观察，普通人根本看不清。

阿方索念了出来，声音在颤。

"'达·芬奇·博·吉·亚。'"

整个房间安静得能听见隔壁士兵翻箱倒柜的声音。

"达芬奇·波吉亚？"昆提良挠了挠头，"这名字……听着耳熟。"

"密涅瓦机关初代总工程师。"阿方索的声音干涩，"星历117年的维苏威火山内部结构勘测图纸上签的就是这个名字。密涅瓦机关的所有建造蓝图都出自他之手。传说他在密涅瓦机关建成之后就消失了，没有人知道他去了哪里。"

"他就藏在维苏威火山底下。"唐璜说，"他建了这条通道，从初代教皇的眼皮底下。"

西泽尔没有说话。他盯着那行签名，脑子里飞速转动。

达芬奇·波吉亚。

这个姓氏——波吉亚。

和教皇国博尔吉亚家族同源。

这不可能是巧合。

阿方索已经从桌上拿起那张图纸草稿，蹲在洞口旁边，将图纸摊在地板上。图纸的纸张已经发黄发脆，边角卷曲，但上面的墨线和标注依然清晰。这是密涅瓦初代总工程师亲手绘制的维苏威火山内部蓝图，比后来所有版本都更详细，因为它是勘测者本人在火山内部实地测绘的第一手资料。

阿方索的机械手指沿着图纸上标注的路线滑动，最终停在一处被红墨线圈出的区域。

"黑铁巨门的三层封印。"他指着图纸上密密麻麻的标注文字，"第一层是圣徽封印——就是我们在外面看到的那扇卡巴拉之树圣徽，需要朗基努斯圣枪碎片和锡兰星见血脉才能打开。第二层是机械封印——黑铁巨门本身，由一整套机械锁机构成，这部分由密涅瓦初代总工程师设计，需要通过特殊的启动程序解除。"

他的手指继续往下滑。

"第三层是精神封印。"

图纸上关于第三层封印的标注极少，只有一行字——"非血亲不可解"。

"精神封印需要什么来解除？"瓦莲京娜问。

"不知道。"阿方索摇头，"图纸上没有写。也许初代总工程师故意没有写，怕这个信息落入错误的人手中。"

昆提良蹲下来，用粗壮的手指沿着图纸上的路线走了一遍，然后抬头看了看那个洞口，又低头看了看图纸，眉头皱得更紧了。

"这图纸上的路线……和这个洞口连得上吗？"

"连得上。"阿方索说，"这个洞口就是图纸上标注的'第三层封印解除通道入口'。初代总工程师在设计密涅瓦机关的时候，就已经预留了这条秘密通道，从维苏威火山底部的一个废弃休息室直通黑铁巨门的第三层封印。"

"他为什么要建这条通道？"唐璜问。

阿方索没有立刻回答。他的机械手按在图纸草稿的空白处，指尖微微发白。

图纸草稿的空白处写着字。

不是印刷的，是手写的，笔迹和金色灯柱上的签名一模一样——达芬奇·波吉亚的亲笔。

字迹潦草而急切，像是在极短的时间内匆匆写下的，某些笔画因为用力过猛而穿透纸背。墨水的颜色已经褪成了深褐色，但每一笔每一划都清晰可辨。

阿方索念了出来，声音压得极低，但每个字都像铁锤砸在石板上。

"'初代教皇波吉亚一世偷走了世界树残枝的西方分支，创造了欧米茄原型体——那不是神的使者，是毁灭世界的怪物！'"

他停了一下，手指移到下一行。

"'我建立密涅瓦机关的真实目的，就是阻止他重启机械神国，销毁所有欧米茄原型体！'"

死寂。

隔壁的士兵还在翻箱倒柜，靴底踩在石板上的声音、枪托撞击墙壁的声音、金属铰链的尖叫声混成一片嘈杂的背景噪音。但在这个房间里，安静得能听见自己的心跳。

西泽尔盯着那几行字，喉头动了动，却没出声。

"初代教皇……波吉亚一世？"昆提良的声音发干，"那是几百年前的人了吧？"

"星历元年到星历一百五十年间的人物。"阿方索说，"弥赛亚圣教官方记载他是一位伟大的圣徒，统一西方世界，建造了维苏威火山和密涅瓦机关的雏形。但按照这份文件……"

"弥赛亚圣教的神创论是假的。"瓦莲京娜接过了他的话，声音冷而硬，"密涅瓦机关的真实目的不是发展机械文明，而是阻止初代教皇重启机械神国。"

"欧米茄原型体也不是什么神的使者。"唐璜的声音里带着一丝不易察觉的颤抖，"是初代教皇造出来的武器。用世界树残枝的西方分支造出来的。"

"难怪佛朗哥教授总说密涅瓦机关是天才的乐园也是地狱。"阿方索低声说。

他抬起头，目光落在洞口内那根刻着签名的金色灯柱上。灯柱上的花纹在微弱的光芒中若隐若现，像是某种古老的密语。

"他一直在初代教皇的控制和初代总工程师的遗愿之间挣扎。密涅瓦机关表面上是教廷的技术心脏，实际上是初代总工程师埋下的一颗钉子。佛朗哥教授继承了初代总工程师的遗志，却也被绑在教廷的战车上不能脱身。"

"难怪他让我们去骷髅地。"瓦莲京娜低声说，"他大概早就知道初代总工程师的这些安排，只是没办法明说。"

西泽尔一直沉默着。

他的手按在胸口，隔着内衬按住那本预言书。锡封纸透出的温热仍然在，像是某种沉默的回应。

初代教皇波吉亚一世偷走了世界树残枝的西方分支。

创造了欧米茄原型体。

初代总工程师达芬奇·波吉亚——

他也姓波吉亚。

"老板？"唐璜注意到西泽尔的沉默，凑过来低声问。

西泽尔摇了摇头，没有解释。

他的目光落在金色灯柱底座的那行签名上，脑子里有太多碎片还没有拼到一起。但他知道有一条线正在浮出水面——一条从初代教皇到初代总工程师、从密涅瓦机关到世界树残枝、从博尔吉亚家族到锡兰星见家族的隐秘连线。

这条线的尽头，就是维苏威火山最深处的黑铁巨门。

"时间不多了。"阿方索率先打破沉默，"隔壁那些人的搜索范围越来越近了，最多还有三四分钟就会搜到这间休息室。我们必须现在就走。"

他将图纸草稿折好塞进怀里，机械手抓住洞口边缘的金属框架，率先翻身钻了进去。他的身体消失在圆形的黑暗入口中，靴底踩在金属阶梯上发出沉闷的回响，一层一层往下。

"我先下。"昆提良拍了拍唐璜的肩膀，"你殿后。"

"凭什么你殿后？我比你灵活。"唐璜瞪眼。

"你腿比我长，殿后跑得快。"昆提良一把将唐璜推到自己身后，自己翻身进了洞口。

唐璜翻了个白眼，骂了句脏话，跟在后面。

瓦莲京娜没有犹豫，她把那块世界树残枝启动符从圆盘凹槽中取出来收好，最后看了一眼隔壁的方向——金属铰链的尖叫声更近了——然后利落地翻进洞口，金色的长发在消失前最后飘了一下。

只剩下西泽尔。

他还站在原地，看着那个圆形的洞口，看着洞口边缘金色灯柱上那行小小的签名。

达·芬奇·波·吉·亚。

他忽然伸出手，用食指轻轻触碰了那个签名。

签名上没有灰尘。像是有人在他来之前就已经把灰尘擦掉了。

或者说——这条通道里的时间，和外面的时间不一样。

西泽尔没有深想。他收回手，翻身钻进了洞口。

"咣当！"

几乎在他落入通道的同一瞬间，休息室的铁门被撞开了。几个穿着军服的士兵冲了进来，枪口对准了空无一人的房间。

"长官！这里有——"

士兵的话没有说完。

他看到了那张被翻起的行军床，看到了床底的黑色铁板，看到了铁板正中那个完全打开的金属圆盘和深不见底的洞口。

还有洞口边缘金色灯柱上，正在一盏一盏亮起来的灯光。

金色光芒沿着通道一路延伸下去，像是有人在黑暗中点燃了一串金色的火种。光从洞口溢出来，照亮了士兵们惊愕的脸。

"报……报告！"士兵转身冲出门外，声音都在发抖，"发现地下通道！密涅瓦机关的地下有——有——"

他的话被一声低沉的"嗡嗡"声打断了。

那声音从通道深处传来，穿过金色灯柱的缝隙，穿过金属圆盘的边缘，震动着每一个人的耳膜。不是机械运转的噪音，而是某种更古老、更沉重的声响——像是一颗沉睡了三百年的心脏，终于重新开始了跳动。

黑铁巨门的封印在颤抖。

西泽尔站在通道的第一个台阶上，感受到脚下金属地板传来细微的震动。震动越来越强，金色灯柱上的光芒也随之越来越亮，整个通道被染成了一片温暖的金色。

他抬头向上看。洞口外，士兵们的身影被金色光芒勾勒出黑色的轮廓，像是舞台上的剪影。

他转身向下看。

通道很长，一眼望不到底。灯光沿着通道延伸下去，在最远处汇聚成一个小小的光点，像是黑暗大海尽头的灯塔。

唐璜的声音从下方传来，带着回音："老板！快下来！前面还有很长一段路！"

阿方索的声音紧随其后，更冷静也更急促："灯柱的亮度在增加。通道正在被激活。初代总工程师在这里设置了某种自动唤醒程序——有人打开了第一道锁，后面的门就会逐级解除。"

昆提良的声音闷闷的："所以我们现在是在和一个三百年前的老头子设计的自动机关赛跑？"

"不是赛跑。"阿方索说，"是他在替我们开门。"

瓦莲京娜的声音从更远的地方传来，已经带上了回声的尾巴："我看到通道尽头了！那里有一扇门——不是黑铁巨门，是另一扇门！门上刻着——"

她的声音突然断了。

"刻着什么？"西泽尔快步往下走。

瓦莲京娜的回答被一阵尖锐的蜂鸣声淹没了。

西泽尔下意识摸向腰间——蜘蛛巢腕表。腕表的通讯模块正在疯狂震动，指示灯由绿转红，发出密集的"滴滴"声。这是薇若兰设置的紧急密报信号，只有在最危急的情况下才会触发。

他按下接收键。

薇若兰的声音从通讯模块中传出，夹杂着电流的杂音和金属碰撞的背景声，但每一个字都清晰得像是刻在玻璃上。

"西泽尔，佛朗哥教授醒了。"

通讯模块里传来一声沉重的撞击，像是有什么东西被推倒了。

"他说他有话要立刻告诉我们。"薇若兰的声音急促而克制，"他说他藏了四十年的东西——'初代总工程师留下的最后一件遗物'——必须亲手交给你。"

"他在哪里？"西泽尔问。

"在密涅瓦机关的叹息之墙前。"

又是一声撞击，比上一次更近。

"他身后是圣堂装甲师。"薇若兰的声音里终于出现了一丝裂痕，"他们已经到了。莱希特伯爵亲自带队。他们要——"

通讯中断了。

西泽尔站在金色灯柱之间，感受到脚下的震动越来越强，黑铁巨门的封印在远方发出沉闷的"嗡嗡"声。

他面前是一条通往未知深处的通道，通道尽头是瓦莲京娜没有说完的那扇门。

他身后是蜂拥而至的圣堂装甲师，是佛朗哥教授，是薇若兰中断的紧急密报。

他脚下的金属地板还在颤抖。

而这个通道的深处，有什么东西正在苏醒。

【English】
Chapter 194 — The Mechanism Under the Bed

The bang came from the next room. Not a knock — a kick. The metal hinges screamed.

"Search it! Not a single corner!" The same hoarse, vicious voice, and beneath it the crunch of boots on stone in perfect military cadence, like a piece of killing machinery wound up and set loose.

Cesare looked at Alfonso.

Alfonso was already moving.

The former mecha-engineer's hands were steady in a way that was almost obscene given the noise. Mechanical fingers and flesh fingers alternating, he hooked the edge of the camp cot and lifted. Dust poured off it onto his face; he did not blink. The cot-board swung up against the wall without a sound and revealed a wooden frame beneath.

The frame was a fake.

Alfonso rapped the bottom panel of the frame with his metal knuckles, judged the thickness by the sound, and pushed along the grain. The whole board slid out. A second skin of dust, older and grayer, fumed upward. Beneath it lay an iron plate. And at the center of the plate, set flush, a metal disc about half a meter across, blackened with what must have been centuries of oxidation.

"Over here," Alfonso said, low.

Cesare, Valentina, Quintilian, and Don Juan closed in.

The disc was engraved with a complete inverted pentacle, the lines sunk deep into the metal, the edges sharp enough to slice a finger. Around the pentacle, a labyrinth of micro-gears, one feeding the next, connected by filaments of metal so fine they caught the light like spider silk. Beneath the dust the metal had the dull silver of something far better than iron — an alloy Cesare did not recognize.

"What is that?" Quintilian reached out a thick finger to poke it. Alfonso slapped his hand away without looking up.

"Don't. Salt from your skin will eat the alloy."

Cesare crouched. He traced the lines of the pentacle with his eyes. At each of the five points sat a tiny red-mercury crystal, lost-luster red, the structure still intact inside even after however many decades or centuries the disc had lain there in the dark. He had seen this pattern before. On the cover of the prayer booklet sealed in the tin casket. On the back of the world-tree root talisman. On the flyleaf of the prophecy book Lian Sheng had pressed into his hands on a night he did not want to remember.

Always the same. Inverted pentacle, micro-gears, red-mercury crystals.

The mark of the Silan Stargazer line.

"It's a starter plate," Cesare said.

"I know these engravings."

Valentina's voice. Quiet, certain.

She drew something from the inside pocket of her uniform and laid it in her palm.

A silver ornament, no bigger than a thumbnail, the edges irregular, as though it had been wrenched apart from something larger. The broken face was engraved with half a lotus blossom, each petal traced with a precision that admitted no imprecision. The reverse was covered in micro-grooves that matched the gear-pattern on the disc beneath them like a key matched its lock.

"My mother left it to me," she said. "She called it the World-Tree Branch Starter. There was only one, in the private collection of the Yenisei Palace. I stole it when I left."

She set the silver half-lotus into the center of the disc.

The groove was made for it. The fit was absolute.

Click.

A sound so small it was almost imagined, somewhere deep in the iron, like a watch that had been asleep for eighty years and had just been given its first nudge.

No one breathed.

The disc did not open. It only shuddered. The dust on its surface lifted off and fell in a slow curtain, and underneath, the dull silver of the alloy came up to meet the light. The five red-mercury crystals at the points of the inverted pentacle woke one after another in their dark, dried-blood glow. The light ran along the gear-filaments, five thin red rivulets meeting at the silver in the middle.

The half-lotus turned. Half a rotation. Then it stopped.

Click.

This second click was heavier. The whole disc began to turn on the silver as a pivot, slow, grinding, and the five points of the pentacle lit in turn, each with a deep metallic thump, like a succession of heavy doors being opened from the inside.

"Back," Alfonso said.

Cesare stood. Stepped back. Two steps.

The disc opened all the way.

It was not a door. It was a hatch. The plate swung up on a hidden iron arm to a full ninety degrees and rested against a bracket set in the iron, and beneath it gaped a round shaft a half-meter across. Down the inside wall of the shaft ran a ladder of thin gold-painted lamp posts, each one chased with extremely fine patterns, descending beyond the reach of the eye into a darkness that looked almost solid.

"A passage," Don Juan said, half to himself. "Deeper in."

"Wait." Alfonso lifted a hand. He was pointing at one of the gold posts at the rim of the shaft. "There. The base."

A line of small letters was cut into the base. Cut with a mechanical graver, the strokes clean and exact, a hand that knew what it was doing. The letters were tiny; it took Alfonso's mechanic's eye at ten-times magnification to read them.

He read them aloud, and his voice shook.

"da Vinci B-o-r-g-i-a."

The room went quiet enough to hear the soldiers next door tearing the place apart, boot-heels, rifle butts against the wall, the slow patient howl of the hinges.

"da Vinci Borgia?" Quintilian scratched his head. "That name—"

"First chief engineer of the Minerva Mechanism," Alfonso said, dry. "He signed the Vesuvius internal-survey plans of Stardate 117. Every construction blueprint of the Mechanism came from his hand. After the Mechanism was built, the story goes, he disappeared. Nobody knew where he went."

"He came down here," Don Juan said. "He built this passage under the first Pope's nose."

Cesare said nothing. He was staring at the signature and his mind was working very fast.

da Vinci Borgia.

The name. Borgia.

The same name as the Pope's own family.

It could not be a coincidence.

Alfonso had crossed to the table and picked up the draft blueprint. He crouched at the lip of the shaft and spread the paper on the floor. The paper was yellow, brittle at the edges, the ink faded but still legible. It was the first chief engineer's own hand-surveyed map of the inside of Vesuvius — more detailed than any later copy, because it had been drawn by the man who had walked the tunnels himself.

Alfonso's metal fingers walked the routes marked on the paper and stopped at a circle drawn in red.

"The three seals of the Black Iron Gate." He pointed to the dense block of annotation around it. "First seal: the Holy Emblem — the Kabbalah-tree sigil we saw outside, which only opens for a fragment of the Lance of Longinus and the blood of the Silan Stargazers. Second seal: the Mechanical — the Black Iron Gate itself, an arrangement of mechanical locks designed by the first chief engineer, requiring a particular starting sequence to release."

His finger moved down.

"Third seal: the Spiritual."

The annotations on the third seal were sparse. A single line.

Not to be released by any but kin.

"What does it take to release the third seal?" Valentina asked.

"Unknown." Alfonso shook his head. "The blueprint does not say. Perhaps the first chief engineer did not write it down for fear the knowledge would fall into the wrong hands."

Quintilian crouched. He walked his thick finger along the route on the paper, looked up at the shaft, looked back down, and frowned harder.

"Does the route on the paper line up with this opening?"

"It does," Alfonso said. "This opening is the entrance to the release passage for the third seal. When the first chief engineer designed the Minerva Mechanism, he left a hidden route: from an abandoned rest chamber at the foot of Vesuvius, straight through to the third seal of the Black Iron Gate."

"Why did he build it?" Don Juan asked.

Alfonso did not answer at once. His metal hand rested on a blank margin of the paper, the fingertips whitening where the pressure was.

There was writing on the margin.

Not printed. Handwritten. The same hand as the gold post, the same exactness, the same long-tailed g's — da Vinci Borgia, in his own hand.

The writing was hurried. The strokes were cut fast. Some of them had bitten through the paper. The ink had faded to the color of old blood, but every letter of it was still readable.

Alfonso read it out, his voice pressed low, each word a hammer on stone.

"The first Pope, Borgia the First, stole the western branch of the World Tree. With it he made the Omega prototype — not a messenger of God, but a monster for the ending of the world."

He paused. His finger moved to the next line.

"The true purpose for which I built the Minerva Mechanism was to stop him from restarting the Mechanical Kingdom — and to destroy every Omega prototype."

Silence.

Next door the soldiers went on with their work, a steady background noise of boots, of rifle butts, of hinges. But in this room the air had stopped moving.

Cesare stared at the lines of writing. His throat worked. He did not speak.

"The first Pope — Borgia the First?" Quintilian's voice was dry. "That is what, six, seven hundred years ago?"

"Stardate 0 to Stardate 150," Alfonso said. "The official record of the Holy Church of the Messiah calls him a great saint. The unifier of the Western lands, the one who laid the foundations of Vesuvius and the first shape of the Minerva Mechanism. But according to this—"

"The Church's Creation doctrine is a lie," Valentina finished him. Her voice was cold and hard. "The Minerva Mechanism was not built to develop the mechanical civilization. It was built to keep the first Pope from restarting the Mechanical Kingdom."

"The Omega prototype was never a messenger of God," Don Juan said, and there was a faintest tremor in it. "It was a weapon. Built from the western branch of the World Tree."

"No wonder Professor Franco always said the Minerva Mechanism was a paradise for geniuses and a hell for them too," Alfonso said, half under his breath.

He lifted his head. His eyes went to the gold post at the rim of the shaft. The patterns chased into it shifted in the dim light, like an old language being half-heard.

"He spent his whole life caught between the first Pope's leash and the first chief engineer's last wish. The Minerva Mechanism looks like the technological heart of the Church. In fact it is a nail the first chief engineer drove into the heart of it. Franco inherited the engineer's will, but he was harnessed to the Church's war-chariot and could not slip the harness."

"He sent us to Golgotha for a reason," Valentina said, low. "He must have known, all along, what the first chief engineer had arranged. He had no way to say so outright."

Cesare was silent.

His hand was pressed flat against his chest, against the inner lining, against the book of prophecy. The tin-sealed paper was still warm. As if something on the other side of it was answering in a voice too low to be heard.

The first Pope, Borgia the First, stole the western branch of the World Tree.

Made the Omega prototype.

The first chief engineer, da Vinci Borgia —

He too was a Borgia.

"Boss?" Don Juan had come up to him, pitched low. "Boss, you've gone somewhere."

Cesare shook his head. He did not explain.

His eye went back to the small signature on the gold post, and his mind was full of fragments that had not yet fit together. But he could feel a line drawing itself up out of the dark — a line that ran from the first Pope to the first chief engineer, from the Minerva Mechanism to the World Tree, from the Borgia family to the Silan Stargazer line.

That line ended, somewhere beneath them, at the Black Iron Gate.

"We are out of time," Alfonso said.

He broke the silence first, because that was his job.

"The search pattern next door is tightening. We have three minutes, perhaps four, before they reach this room. We go. Now."

He folded the draft blueprint and tucked it into his coat. His metal hand caught the rim of the shaft and he went through head-first, dropping out of sight. The sound of his boots on the metal rungs came back up, dull and far, one step under the last.

"I will go first." Quintilian clapped Don Juan on the shoulder. "You bring up the rear."

"Why me? I am the quicker of us."

"You are the longer-legged. Longer legs run faster at the back." Quintilian pushed Don Juan behind him with one arm and dropped into the shaft.

Don Juan rolled his eyes, swore under his breath, and followed.

Valentina did not hesitate. She lifted the World-Tree Branch Starter out of its groove in the disc, pocketed it, glanced once at the wall they shared with the next room — the hinges were screaming louder now — and dropped cleanly through. Her hair of pale gold caught the light for one instant as she went, and then she was gone.

Only Cesare was left.

He stood a moment longer, looking at the round mouth of the shaft, at the row of gold posts, at the small signature at the foot of the first one.

da Vinci B-o-r-g-i-a.

He reached out, without deciding to, and let the tip of his index finger touch the signature.

There was no dust on it. None. As if someone had wiped the dust off before he came. As if —

Or as if the time inside the shaft did not run at the same speed as the time outside.

Cesare did not think about it for long. He pulled his hand back, turned, and dropped feet-first into the shaft.

CRASH.

Almost in the same instant he cleared the rim, the rest-room door came off its hinges. A squad in the uniform of the Hallowed Armored Corps came in, rifles up, swinging on the empty room.

"Sir! Here —"

The soldier did not finish.

He saw the tipped cot, the iron plate, the open disc, the round black mouth beneath it, and the gold posts at its rim — and he saw the gold posts beginning, one after another, to come on.

The light ran down the shaft like a lit fuse. Gold on gold on gold, each post taking up the brightness from the one above and passing it on, until the eye could not follow it to the bottom. The light came flooding up out of the shaft and laid itself across the faces of the soldiers, who stood with their rifles half-raised, and made them look, for one unguarded moment, like men caught in a stage-light.

"Report!" one of them turned and ran back through the door, voice cracking. "Underground passage found! The Minerva Mechanism has a — has a—"

The word he was looking for was swallowed by a sound.

A low, deep humming from the bottom of the shaft, working up through the metal rungs, through the gold posts, into the bones of everyone standing near it. Not the noise of a machine winding up. Something older than that. Heavier than that. As if a heart that had been sleeping for three hundred years had, at last, remembered how to beat.

The seals of the Black Iron Gate were trembling.

Cesare stood on the first rung of the ladder. He felt the metal floor humming under his boots. The hum got stronger. The gold posts got brighter. The shaft was a long warm tube of yellow light falling away beneath him.

He looked up. Through the round mouth of the shaft, the soldiers stood outlined in the gold. Cut-out shapes against the brightness, black on gold.

He looked down.

The shaft was very long. The light ran on down it, rung by rung, and at the far end it gathered itself into a single small bright dot, like a lantern hung at the bottom of a dark sea.

"Boss!" Don Juan's voice came up from somewhere down the shaft, with the bounce of an echo. "Hurry up! There is a long way still to go!"

Alfonso's voice, after, calmer and quicker: "The brightness of the posts is increasing. The passage is waking up. The first chief engineer built a kind of automatic unlocking sequence into it — the moment the first lock was opened, the rest of the doors will open in order."

Quintilian's voice, muffled: "So what you are telling me is that we are now in a foot-race with an automatic system designed by a man who has been dead three hundred years."

"Not a race," Alfonso said. "He is opening the doors for us."

Valentina's voice, further off now, the echo already lengthening behind it: "I can see the bottom of the shaft! There is a door there — not the Black Iron Gate, a different door — the door has—"

Her voice cut off.

"What is on the door?" Cesare was already moving, rung over rung.

Valentina's answer was drowned in a sharp stuttering buzz.

Cesare's hand went to his wrist without thinking. The Spider's Nest watch. The communication module was vibrating so hard he could see the casing blur. The indicator light had gone from green to red, and was giving off a rapid staccato pip. It was the emergency cipher that Verolan had set, the one she had told him, very seriously, to use only in the worst extremity.

He pressed receive.

Verolan's voice came through, layered over the hiss of static and a deep metallic clanging in the background, but each word was cut clean, as though typed on glass.

"Cesare. Professor Franco is awake."

Another heavy crash, this one closer.

"He says there is something he must tell you, immediately, with his own mouth. He says he has been sitting on it for forty years — 'the last relic left behind by the first chief engineer' — and he must put it into your hands in person."

"Where is he?"

"In front of the Wall of Sighs, in the Minerva Mechanism."

Another crash, nearer still.

"The Hallowed Armored Corps is already on him. Count Reichert at the head. They intend to—"

The line cut.

Cesare stood between the gold posts. The hum under his feet was stronger. From somewhere far below, the seals of the Black Iron Gate gave their deep, slow answer.

In front of him, the shaft dropped away into the dark, and at the bottom of it was a door he had not yet seen, with something carved into it he had not yet been told.

Behind him, somewhere above, the Hallowed Armored Corps was moving on the Wall of Sighs, on Professor Franco, on Verolan, on whatever the first chief engineer had been careful to leave for him to find.

The metal floor under his feet was still trembling.

And somewhere in the deep of the passage, something that had not moved in three hundred years was, at last, beginning to wake.

【中文】
第195章 达芬奇的日记（上）

维苏威火山底部的金色灯柱还在延伸，但这一刻，故事暂时离开了那条矿道。

镜头向北，越过层层叠叠的岩层和蒸汽管道，落回到翡冷翠城下的密涅瓦机关。

叹息之墙前方的临时医疗室，灯光白得刺眼。

三天三夜。

薇若兰站在病床边，丝绸般的长发用一根黑色发带随意地束在脑后，白大褂的袖口沾着碘酒的颜色。她已经连续工作超过七十二个小时，眼底是淡青色的倦意，但那双眼睛本身仍旧亮得像是淬了火的金刚石。

病床上躺着的老人面色灰白。密涅瓦机关的总长，枢机卿，机械文明活着的传奇——佛朗哥教授，此刻看起来不过是个形容枯槁的老人。监测仪上跳动着几条绿色的波形线，心率六十二，血压正常，神经电流读出器的读数却一直在怪异地波动。

李锡尼靠在门边，黑色长风衣的下摆沾着矿渣，朗基努斯圣枪碎片别在腰间，蜂巢手铳装满了实弹。这位异端审判局第一副局长一反常态地没有戴帽子，露出的面容冷峻而疲惫，下颌的线条绷得像是要切开空气。

"第三天了。"薇若兰的声音很低，"他的神经系统几乎没有恢复的迹象。神学那边的人说，他的脑白质在三十年前就做过切除手术，剩余的髓鞘承受不了这种强度的消耗。"

李锡尼没有回答。

"枢机会已经发了第四道命令。"薇若兰低头看着病床上那张苍老的脸，"莱希特伯爵带着圣堂装甲师，明天正午之前必须进入叹息之墙后方。莱希特本人已经在会议室等了六个小时了，他要求立刻提审你。"

李锡尼这才开口，声音沙哑："让他等。"

"你知道这意味着什么。枢机会如果认定你抗命——"

"我说让他等。"李锡尼的拇指摸过腰间那块打磨完成的圣枪碎片，"佛朗哥活着一天，密涅瓦机关就还有总长。佛朗哥死了，这里就是圣域，圣域里枢机会的命令才生效。"

薇若兰的嘴角微微抽动了一下，像是想笑又没笑出来。

她认识李锡尼太久了。从她还是密涅瓦机关那个最年轻的天才学徒开始，李锡尼就已经是异端审判局最冷血的执行官。他们之间的关系谈不上朋友，更谈不上敌意，只是一种长年累月并肩作战后磨出来的默契——这个人从不会在关键时刻说废话，也不会在压力下后退半步。

"我进去看看他。"薇若兰说。

她转身走向病床。监测仪上的波形线仍然在规律地起伏，佛朗哥教授的呼吸很浅，胸口几乎看不出起伏。

薇若兰伸出手，想要调整一下监测仪的角度。

她的手指刚碰到仪器的边缘，那只手突然被攥住了。

力道不大，但精准得出奇——攥住的恰好是她的腕骨，正是腕部最薄弱的位置。

薇若兰低头。

佛朗哥教授睁开了眼睛。

那双眼睛浑浊，瞳孔收缩得很慢，像是一台报废的蒸汽机被重新点燃。但那双眼睛里确实有光，一种疲惫的、几乎要熄灭却还在挣扎的光。

"教授！"薇若兰压低声音，但她没有抽手，因为她知道佛朗哥教授需要这个接触点来确认自己回到了现实。

佛朗哥教授没看她，而是用那只攥住她手腕的手，缓慢而坚定地撑着床沿坐了起来。输液管被扯得紧绷，针头险些从血管里脱出。薇若兰伸手想要按住他，佛朗哥教授只是摇了摇头，伸出另一只手，猛地拽下了手背上的针头。

鲜血从针孔里涌出来，顺着他干瘦的手背流下去，滴在白色的床单上。

李锡尼快步走过来，左手按住了他的肩膀："教授，您不能——"

"让开。"佛朗哥教授的声音像是生锈的齿轮被强行转动，嘶哑、刺耳、却每个字都咬得极重，"都让开。"

他的目光扫过薇若兰，扫过李锡尼，最后落在医疗室角落那张小小的床头柜上。

他伸出手，把手伸进枕头底下。

薇若兰和李锡尼对视一眼。

佛朗哥教授从枕头底下摸出了一个用旧报纸包裹着的东西。报纸已经泛黄，卷了好几层，看起来放了很久。他用颤抖的手指一层一层地剥开，报纸发出沙沙的声响。

最后露出来的，是半块青铜镜。

镜子大约掌心大小，断面整齐，边缘有被暴力折断的痕迹。镜面早已失去了光泽，只剩下暗沉的铜绿。但镜面正中，刻着一个完整的五芒星，五芒星的每一个角都嵌着细如发丝的齿轮纹路。

薇若兰的呼吸停了一拍。

那五芒星她认得。

在维苏威火山底部，莲生交给西泽尔那半块信物的时候，她从通讯视频里看到过完整的样子。两块镜子拼合，齿轮纹路咬合，组成的是一个倒置五芒星加齿轮的徽记——锡兰星见家族的印记。

但莲生手里的那半块，五芒星并不完整。

这一块，五芒星是完整的。

"教授……"薇若兰的声音变了调，"这块镜子，您从哪里——"

"我知道你认识。"佛朗哥教授抬起头，浑浊的眼睛里忽然浮出一丝苦笑，"认识就好。"

他低头看着手中那半块青铜镜，拇指摩挲过镜面上冰冷的五芒星纹路。

"我藏了四十年。"他说，"四十年，每一天都怕被人翻出来。但我没想到，最后还是要亲手交出去。"

"交给谁？"李锡尼问。

"西泽尔·博尔吉亚。"佛朗哥教授说，"或者说，交给那个有资格拿着它的人。"

他停顿了一下，像是在鼓起某种勇气。

"薇若兰，李锡尼。"他抬起头，环顾两人，"你们跟我共事多少年了？"

薇若兰轻声说："十八年。"

"十六年。"李锡尼说。

"十八年，十六年。"佛朗哥教授苦笑一声，"可你们从来不知道我是谁。"

"您是密涅瓦机关的总长。"薇若兰说。

"那是官职。"佛朗哥教授摇头，"我问的是，我是谁。"

他没有等他们回答，而是把那块青铜镜小心地放在床单上，靠着枕头坐直了身子。监测仪上的心率数字在稳步上升，从六十二变成七十，又变成七十八。

"我是达·芬奇·博尔吉亚的直系后裔。"他说，"也就是初代教皇博尔吉亚一世的旁系后裔。"

医疗室里安静了几秒钟。

薇若兰的手指收紧了。她没有惊呼，也没有后退，只是那双亮得像是金刚石的眼睛里，终于出现了真正的震动。

"初代……"她重复了一遍，声音极轻。

"三百年前那位。"佛朗哥教授点头，"教会史书里不会写，但事实是，博尔吉亚一世并不只有一个儿子。他有嫡系，也有旁系。嫡系继承了教皇的位置，旁系被打散，隐姓埋名。达·芬奇·博尔吉亚——密涅瓦机关的初代总工程师——也是博尔吉亚一世的孩子，但不是那位嫡系。"

"等等。"李锡尼的声音沉了下来，"您的意思是——"

"密涅瓦机关的初代创立者，不是别人，正是初代教皇博尔吉亚一世自己。"佛朗哥教授说，"达·芬奇·博尔吉亚只是他的化名。"

这句话像是一块石头投进了静止的深水。

薇若兰的嘴唇微微张开，想要说什么，又咽了回去。

"您是说……"她斟酌着用词，"三百年前那位在维苏威火山深处留下'初代教皇日记'的初代教皇，和创建密涅瓦机关的初代总工程师，是同一个人？"

"是。"佛朗哥教授点头。

"那个人……在三百年前背叛了自己。"

"准确地说，"佛朗哥教授的声音变得异常平静，"初代教皇博尔吉亚一世在位时，曾经有过一个疯狂的计划——用紫瞳星见的血脉打开世界树残枝的锁，重启机械神国，把整个西方世界变成神的机械王国。但这个计划在执行到一半时，被他自己——'达·芬奇·博尔吉亚'——亲自阻止了。"

他低下头，看着自己那只苍老的手。

"达·芬奇·博尔吉亚是初代教皇用过的化名。当他意识到自己的计划会毁灭世界的时候，他以另一个身份重新建立了密涅瓦机关，把紫瞳星见从初代教皇的追捕中救出来，把世界树残枝封入维苏威火山深处。叹息之墙是分隔人间与机械神国的第一层屏障，但那道墙的建造者，不是要打开那扇门的人，而是要永远关上它的人。"

"所以……"薇若兰的声音发涩，"密涅瓦机关成立的真正目的——"

"是阻止初代教皇自己。"佛朗哥教授说，"或者说，阻止三百年前那个疯狂的他。"

医疗室的灯光照在他灰白的脸上，那张脸上浮着一种奇异的表情——不是骄傲，也不是痛苦，更像是一个背负了太久秘密的人，在终于把秘密交出去的那一刻，感到一种奇异的轻松。

"而我，"佛朗哥教授说，"是达·芬奇这一脉的后裔。我的家族世世代代守护着这个秘密，也世世代代做着和初代总工程师同样的事——研究如何永久封印世界树残枝，研究如何让红水银不再为这个世界带来灾祸。"

他伸手拿起那块青铜镜。

"这块镜子，是初代教皇留给达·芬奇的信物。也是初代教皇用来标记'有资格打开黑铁巨门的人'的钥匙。三百年前被一分为二，一半在紫瞳星见手里，一半在达·芬奇手里。我这一脉世世代代守护着这一半。"

"另一半……"薇若兰低声说。

"另一半在莲生手里。"佛朗哥教授说，"她是锡兰末代星见最后的传承者。"

他把青铜镜放回床单上，抬起眼睛，目光比任何时候都清醒。

"我之所以拼命研究新型炽天使，就是因为我知道，三百年前那个疯狂的他——那个用'达·芬奇'这个化名改头换面却从未真正消失的他——还有后手。他用初代教皇血脉创造了一个代行者，那个代行者今天还活着。他用红水银制造了机械傀儡普罗米修斯，他用紫瞳星见的血做引子，制造了欧米茄原型体。"

"他要的是用炽天使的力量，对抗初代教皇即将创造的普罗米修斯大军。"

他停顿了一下。

"但我没想到，这一切会来得这么快。"

佛朗哥教授把那块青铜镜推到了薇若兰面前。

"拿去。"他说，"交给西泽尔。他有资格持有它。"

薇若兰伸手，指尖刚刚碰到那冰凉的铜面——

李锡尼突然从怀里掏出了手机。

那是一部改装过的军用通讯器，外壳是厚重的硬金合金，屏幕只有邮票大小，但加密等级是异端审判局最高级。他盯着屏幕，眉头猛地拧紧。

"塔拉夏的密报。"他说。

屏幕上是一段简短的文字，薇若兰凑过去看，只看到几行字——

"西泽尔一行已进入金色灯柱通道，莲生留下断后。"
"达·芬奇通道已启动，地下深度正在增加。"
"圣堂装甲师第二分队正向维苏威火山北麓矿道入口移动。"

薇若兰的脸色瞬间变了。

"第二分队？"她的声音尖锐了起来，"莱希特伯爵明明只带了一个分队！第二分队从哪里来的？"

"调动命令来自枢机会。"李锡尼的声音压得很低，"半小时前下达的。格拉古大主教亲自签发。"

"格拉古……"薇若兰的指节抵着床沿慢慢收拢，"他绕过莱希特伯爵，又调了一支分队？"

"不只是绕过他。"李锡尼说，"调动令上写的是'接管叹息之墙以西全部作战区域'——这意味着莱希特伯爵的命令在矿道入口处失效了。"

"那不是莱希特的人。"薇若兰抬头，"那是格拉古自己的人。"

"是。"李锡尼点头。

佛朗哥教授的脸色在这一刻变得煞白。

他挣扎着想要从病床上站起来，第一次没有成功。监测仪上的心率数字从七十八飙升到九十二，薇若兰伸手想要按住他。

"不好。"佛朗哥教授的声音突然变得急促，"不好！初代教皇的代行者——那个戴着银色猫头鹰面具的人——他知道。他一定已经察觉到了。"

"您怎么知道？"李锡尼问。

"因为我能感觉到。"佛朗哥教授把输液管一把扯断，扶着床沿勉强站直，"三百年前达·芬奇在叹息之墙里留下的封印正在松动——那种震动是有节奏的，是有人在从里面敲那扇门。我这一脉的血液能感应到那个节奏。"

他抬起头，看着薇若兰和李锡尼。

"初代教皇用'达·芬奇'这个名字活了四十多年，建造密涅瓦，研究封印。但在那四十年里，他也秘密建造了另一个组织——一个和密涅瓦对立的、专门破坏封印的组织。那个组织就是今天的原罪机关。"

"原罪机关的主人，"佛朗哥教授说，"就是初代教皇的嫡系后裔。是三百年前那个疯狂的他，亲手选定的继承者。"

薇若兰的嘴唇动了一下，没有发出声音。

"他们带着欧米茄原型体。"佛朗哥教授说，"他们等这一天等了四十年。"

他看向密涅瓦机关最深处的方向——那里是叹息之墙的更深处，是密涅瓦机关的最高机密区，是连薇若兰都只去过一次的"初代总工程师密室"。

"他会派更多圣堂装甲师去追杀西泽尔。"佛朗哥教授说，"他会让一切挡在路中间的人全部消失。"

他扶着床沿的手收紧，指节发白。

"薇若兰。"

"在。"

"你去初代总工程师密室。"佛朗哥教授说，"那里有达·芬奇·博尔吉亚留下的完整日记。三百年来我的家族世世代代守护着那个房间，从未有人打开过。那里面记录了阻止初代教皇重启机械神国的所有方法。"

薇若兰的瞳孔微微放大。

"李锡尼。"佛朗哥教授转向猩红死神。

"在。"李锡尼的声音没有一丝犹豫。

"你带一队炽天骑士团旧部去维苏威火山支援西泽尔。"佛朗哥教授说，"用你的圣枪碎片和你的权限，给那些圣堂装甲师开路——谁敢挡在前面，就执行《宗教秘密法》第四十七条。"

李锡尼右手按在腰间的圣枪碎片上，那枚打磨完成的金属碎片在医疗室的灯光下反射出冷冽的光芒。

"我会的。"他说。

佛朗哥教授看了一眼那块躺在床单上的青铜镜。

"带上它。"他说，"一起带去维苏威火山。"

薇若兰伸手拿起了那半块青铜镜，冰凉的铜面压在她温热的掌心里。镜面上那完整的五芒星，在医疗室惨白的灯光下像是一只沉睡的眼睛。

而密涅瓦机关更深处的叹息之墙，那道分隔人间与机械神国的屏障，正在发出一种低沉的、规律性的震动。

"嗡——嗡——嗡——"

像是有什么东西，正在从里面敲那扇门。

【English】
Chapter 195 — Leonardo's Diary (Part One)

The golden lamp-pillar beneath Vesuvius was still extending, sinking its roots deeper into the black rock, but the story, for this moment, turned its back on that mine-shaft.

The lens, as it were, swung north. Through strata of pale stone, through bundled steam-pipes and the ribbed iron veins of the earth, until it came to rest in a place far older than the lamp-light: the Minerva Bureau, buried under Florence. The temporary medical room they had set up before the Wall of Sighs. The light there was not golden. It was the white, eye-stabbing white of a surgical lamp turned too high.

Three days. Three nights.

Veronika stood at the bedside. Her silken hair had been pulled back at the nape of her neck with a single black ribbon — the kind of carelessness a woman permits herself only when no one important is watching. The cuffs of her white coat were stained the colour of iodine. Seventy-two hours without sleep. The bruise-coloured shadows under her eyes had deepened to a tired, pale blue, but the eyes themselves — those famous eyes, the ones the youngest apprentices in the Bureau whispered about — were still bright. Diamond-bright. Lit from some furnace inside her that had not, despite everything, gone out.

The old man on the bed was grey. Franco. Director-General of the Minerva Bureau, Cardinal of the Conclave, living legend of the mechanical civilisation. In that white light, with that white sheet pulled up to his chest, he looked like nothing more than a very old man whose body had given up. The monitors beside him traced three green lines in steady, patient loops. Heart rate: sixty-two. Blood pressure: acceptable. The third line — the neural current readout — wavered and twitched, as if it could not quite decide what it was reading.

Licinius leaned against the doorframe.

The Deputy Director of the Inquisition, first of the two, looked wrong without his hat. The brim had been a part of his face for so long that seeing the bare architecture of his skull felt like seeing a fortress with its battlements removed. The black riding-coat he wore was dusted with mine-sludge to the knee. The shard of the Lance of Longinus hung at his hip, newly polished, catching the surgical light in a thin, cold line. The hive-pistol in his belt was loaded with real rounds.

He did not look at Veronika. He did not look at Franco. He looked at the door behind him, as if measuring the distance to the corridor in strides.

"Day three," Veronika said. Her voice was very low. "There has been no real recovery in his nervous system. The Theologians tell me his cerebral white matter was excised thirty years ago. The remaining myelin cannot sustain this kind of strain."

Licinius said nothing.

"The Conclave has issued its fourth order." Veronika did not look up from the grey face on the pillow. "Count Reichert is here with the Cathedral Armoured Division. He must pass behind the Wall of Sighs before noon tomorrow. He has been waiting in the conference chamber for six hours. He is demanding that we bring you to him for formal questioning."

Now Licinius spoke. His voice was rough, as if he had been shouting in the mine-tunnels and had not yet remembered how to pitch it for an indoor space.

"Let him wait."

"You know what that means. If the Conclave rules you are in defiance—"

"I said let him wait."

His thumb moved across the polished surface of the lance-shard at his hip. "Franco is alive. As long as Franco is alive, the Minerva Bureau has a Director-General. As long as the Bureau has a Director-General, the Bureau is not the Holy See, and the Conclave's writ does not run here."

A small movement passed over Veronika's mouth. Not quite a smile. The kind of expression that an old soldier permits herself in the company of a younger soldier, when the younger one has just said the only correct thing in an impossible situation.

She had known Licinius for a long time. Since she had been the youngest prodigy-apprentice in the Bureau, since he had been the coldest executioner in the Inquisition. The word friend had never been used between them. Nor enemy. What existed between them was something more useful and less comfortable: the long, friction-smoothed understanding of two people who had fought side by side often enough that words like hesitation and retreat had been worn out of their vocabulary.

"I'm going in," she said. "I'm going to look at him."

She turned back to the bed.

The monitor lines still rose and fell in their patient rhythm. Franco's chest barely moved. The shallowest possible rise. The shallowest possible fall. As if the body were only pretending to breathe.

Veronika reached out to adjust the angle of the monitor.

Her fingers had barely touched the edge of the instrument when her wrist was seized.

The grip was not strong. It was, however, exact. It closed precisely on the carpal bone, on the softest part of the wrist — the place where a slight turn of the captor's thumb would have made her cry out.

Veronika looked down.

Franco had opened his eyes.

They were the colour of bad brass. The pupils contracted slowly, with the painful slowness of a steam-engine being coaxed back to life after a winter of disuse. But there was light in them. Tired, nearly drowned, but still fighting. Still alight.

"Professor." Veronika kept her voice low. She did not pull her hand back, because she knew that Franco needed the pressure of another human being to be sure he had returned to the waking world.

Franco did not look at her. He used the hand that held her wrist to lever himself up on the bed, slowly, with the terrible deliberation of a man reassembling his own skeleton. The drip-line pulled taut. The needle in the back of his hand began to slip from the vein. Veronika reached to steady him. Franco only shook his head. He lifted his other hand, gripped the needle, and wrenched it out.

Blood welled from the puncture. It ran down the back of his hand, gathered at the knuckle, fell in a single dark drop onto the white sheet.

Licinius came forward in two strides and put his left hand on the old man's shoulder.

"Professor. You cannot—"

"Out of the way." Franco's voice sounded like a rusted gear being forced to turn. Hoarse. Grinding. Each word bitten off as if he were chewing it out of the air. "Both of you. Out of the way."

His gaze passed over Veronika. It passed over Licinius. It came to rest on the small bedside cabinet in the corner of the room.

He reached out. He slid his hand beneath the pillow.

Veronika and Licinius exchanged a glance.

From beneath the pillow, Franco drew out something wrapped in old newspaper. The paper had gone yellow. It had been folded many times. It looked as if it had been there for a long, long time. With trembling fingers, Franco peeled back the layers one by one, the paper giving off a faint dry whisper as it unfolded.

What was left, in his palm, was half a bronze mirror.

The mirror was about the size of a spread hand. The break was clean, the edge ragged in the way that only violent force can make metal ragged. The face of the mirror had long since lost its sheen. It was dark, dull, the colour of verdigris. But in the centre of the bronze, a complete five-pointed star had been cut. At each point of the star, a gear-tooth pattern no thicker than a hair had been engraved.

Veronika's breath stopped for a beat.

She knew that five-pointed star. She had seen its twin, three days ago, on the communication-screen, when Lien-sheng had handed her half of the token to Cesare in the tunnel beneath Vesuvius. The two halves of the mirror, fitted together, would complete an inverted pentagram-and-cog — the crest of the Star-Reader House of Ceylon.

But the half in Lien-sheng's hand had not been a complete star. This half was.

"Professor." Veronika's voice changed register. "Where did you—"

"I know you recognise it," Franco said. He raised his head. The brass-coloured eyes were full of a tired, bitter amusement. "Good. That saves time."

He looked down at the bronze half-mirror in his hand. His thumb traced the cold lines of the pentagram, as if reading a sentence he had read ten thousand times.

"I have been hiding it for forty years," he said. "Forty years. Every day I lived in fear that someone would find it. I never thought I would have to give it away with my own hand."

"To whom?" Licinius asked.

"To Cesare Borgia." Franco said. "Or, if you prefer, to the man who has the right to hold it."

He paused, as if gathering some last reserve of courage.

"Veronika. Licinius. How long have you served with me?"

"Eighteen years," Veronika said.

"Sixteen," Licinius said.

"Eighteen years. Sixteen years." Franco's mouth twisted. "And in all that time, you have never known who I am."

"You are the Director-General of the Minerva Bureau," Veronika said.

"That is a title." Franco shook his head. "I asked you who I am."

He did not wait for an answer. He set the half-mirror down carefully on the sheet. He levered himself up against the pillow. The monitor beside the bed began to register a change: sixty-two, sixty-seven, seventy, seventy-eight. The green line climbed in small, cautious steps, as if the old heart were remembering what it was for.

"I am a direct descendant of Leonardo Borgia," Franco said. "A cadet branch of the bloodline of Pope Borgia the First."

The medical room went quiet.

Veronika's fingers tightened. She did not gasp. She did not step back. But the diamond-brightness in her eyes, for the first time in three days, gave way to something that looked very much like shock.

"The First," she said, in a voice that was almost a whisper.

"The First," Franco agreed. "The Church histories will not tell you this, but it is a fact all the same. Pope Borgia the First did not have only one son. He had a legitimate line and a cadet line. The legitimate line inherited the papacy. The cadet line was scattered, names changed, memories buried. Leonardo Borgia — the founding Chief Engineer of the Minerva Bureau — was also a child of Borgia the First. Not the legitimate one."

"Wait." Licinius's voice had dropped half a register. "You are saying—"

"The first founder of the Minerva Bureau was none other than Pope Borgia the First himself. Leonardo Borgia was the name he used when he did not wish to be the Pope."

The words fell into the room like a stone into a still well.

Veronika's lips parted. She began to say something, swallowed it, began again.

"You mean," she said carefully, "that the Pope who, three hundred years ago, left behind the so-called First Pope's Diary in the deep chambers beneath Vesuvius, and the founding Chief Engineer who created the Minerva Bureau, are the same man."

"Yes," Franco said.

"That man," Veronika said, and her voice had gone rough at the edges, "three hundred years ago, betrayed himself."

"More precisely," Franco said, and his voice had become very quiet, very even — the way a voice becomes when it is carrying a thing that has been carried for too long — "during the reign of Pope Borgia the First, he conceived a madness. A project. To use the bloodline of the Purple-Eyed Seers to open the lock on the branch of the World Tree, to restart the Machine Kingdom of God, to turn the entire Western world into a clockwork theocracy under his own hand. He carried this project halfway to completion. And then he — Leonardo Borgia — stopped himself."

He looked down at the back of his own hand. The blood from the pulled-out needle had dried to a dark crust.

"Leonardo Borgia was the alias the First Pope used when he no longer wished to be the Pope. When he understood that the project would destroy the world, he assumed, for the second time in his life, a different name, and built the Minerva Bureau. He smuggled the Purple-Eyed Seers out of the First Pope's own hunters. He sealed the branch of the World Tree in the deep stone beneath Vesuvius. The Wall of Sighs is the first barrier between the human world and the Machine Kingdom — and the man who built that wall was not the man who wanted to open the gate. He was the man who wanted to keep it shut forever."

"So," Veronika said, and her voice had gone dry, "the real purpose of the Minerva Bureau—"

"Was to stop the First Pope himself," Franco said. "Or, if you prefer, to stop the version of him that had been mad three hundred years ago."

The surgical light fell on his grey face. The expression there was strange. Not pride. Not grief. The expression of a man who has carried a weight for a very long time and is, in this moment, for the first time, allowed to set it down.

"And I," Franco said, "am a descendant of the Leonardo line. My family has kept this secret for generations. My family has done, in every generation, the same work the first Chief Engineer did. We have studied how to seal the branch of the World Tree forever. We have studied how to ensure that the red mercury no longer brings disaster upon this world."

He picked up the half-mirror.

"This mirror is the token the First Pope left for Leonardo. It is also the key the First Pope used to mark 'the man who has the right to open the Great Black Iron Gate.' Three hundred years ago it was broken in two. One half was kept by the Leonardo line. One half was kept by the Purple-Eyed Seers."

"The other half," Veronika said.

"Is in Lien-sheng's keeping," Franco said. "She is the last inheritor of the Star-Reader House of Ceylon."

He set the mirror back down on the sheet. He raised his eyes. They were, now, clearer than they had been in three days.

"The reason I have driven myself, these last years, to build a new kind of Seraphim, is that I knew — I have always known — that the mad version of him, the one who used the name Leonardo as a disguise and never truly disappeared, had a contingency. He used the First Pope's bloodline to create a single Executor. That Executor is alive today. He used red mercury to build the mechanical puppet Prometheus. He used the blood of the Purple-Eyed Seers as a primer, and built the prototype Omega."

"He meant," Franco said, "to use the power of the Seraphim to stand against the Prometheus army that the First Pope was about to create."

He paused.

"What I did not expect," he said, "was that all of it would come so soon."

Franco pushed the half-mirror across the sheet, until it lay in front of Veronika.

"Take it," he said. "Give it to Cesare. He has the right to hold it."

Veronika's fingers reached out. They had barely touched the cold bronze when—

Licinius pulled a phone from inside his coat.

It was a modified military communicator, cased in heavy hard-gold alloy, the screen no larger than a postage stamp, its encryption at the highest level of the Inquisition. He looked at the screen. The muscles of his jaw went tight, as if a wire beneath the skin had been pulled one notch too far.

"Dispatch from Tarasha," he said.

The screen held a few lines of text. Veronika leaned in.

Cesare's group has entered the Golden Lamp-Pillar passage. Lien-sheng has stayed behind to cover the retreat.
The Leonardo Tunnel has been activated. The subterranean depth is increasing.
The Second Detachment of the Cathedral Armoured Division is moving toward the northern foot of Vesuvius, the mine entrance.

Veronika's face changed.

"Second Detachment?" Her voice went sharp. "Reichert only brought one. Where has the second come from?"

"The order came from the Conclave," Licinius said, his voice very low. "Issued half an hour ago. Personally signed by Archbishop Gracchus."

"Gracchus." Veronika's knuckles, where they rested on the bed's edge, went pale. "He went around Reichert. He detached a second division."

"He did not go around him," Licinius said. "The order reads: 'Assume full command of all operational zones west of the Wall of Sighs.' It means Reichert's authority will become void the moment that order reaches the mine entrance."

"That is not Reichert's force," Veronika said. "That is Gracchus's own."

"Yes," Licinius said.

Franco's face, in the surgical light, had gone the colour of ash.

He tried, for the first time, to stand. He did not succeed. The heart-rate monitor climbed: seventy-eight, eighty-five, ninety-two. Veronika reached for him. He pushed her hand aside.

"No," Franco said, and his voice was suddenly urgent. "No. The First Pope's Executor — the man in the silver owl-mask — he knows. He must already know."

"How do you know?" Licinius asked.

"Because I can feel it." Franco tore the drip-line from his arm with a single motion. He got his feet under him, gripped the edge of the bed, and hauled himself upright. "The seal that Leonardo laid in the Wall of Sighs three hundred years ago is loosening. The vibration has a rhythm. Someone is knocking, from the inside, on the door. The blood of my line is attuned to that rhythm."

He looked up, first at Veronika, then at Licinius.

"During the forty-odd years the First Pope lived under the name Leonardo — while he built the Bureau, while he studied the seal — he also built, in secret, a second institution. An institution opposed to the Bureau, dedicated to breaking the seal. That institution is, today, the Bureau of Original Sin."

Veronika's lips moved. No sound came out.

"And the master of the Bureau of Original Sin," Franco said, "is a descendant of the legitimate line of the First Pope. The inheritor chosen, three hundred years ago, by the mad version of himself."

"The Bureau of Original Sin has the Omega prototype in its possession," Franco said. "They have been waiting for this day for forty years."

He looked, then, toward the deeper parts of the Minerva Bureau. Toward the place where the Wall of Sighs ran, in its ancient stone, beneath the city. Toward the most classified level of all — the room Veronika had been allowed to enter only once in her life: the First Chief Engineer's Chamber.

"He will send more Cathedral Armoured Divisions to hunt Cesare," Franco said. "He will erase everyone who stands in the way."

His fingers, on the edge of the bed, were bloodless. The knuckles showed white through the skin, sharp as the gear-teeth on the mirror.

"Veronika."

"Here."

"Go to the First Chief Engineer's Chamber. The complete diary of Leonardo Borgia is there. My family has guarded that room for three hundred years. No one has ever opened it. It contains, recorded in his own hand, every method by which the First Pope's plan to restart the Machine Kingdom of God may be stopped."

Veronika's pupils widened.

"Licinius," Franco said, and turned to the Scarlet Reaper.

"Here," Licinius said, without a moment's hesitation.

"Take a squad of our old Seraphic Knights and go to Vesuvius, to reinforce Cesare. Use the lance-shard and your authority to clear a path through the Cathedral Armoured Division. If anyone stands in the way, invoke Article Forty-Seven of the Religious Secrets Act."

Licinius's right hand dropped to the lance-shard at his hip. The polished metal caught the white light and threw a sliver of cold brightness across the floor, sharp as a drawn blade.

"I will," he said.

Franco looked, for a long moment, at the half-mirror lying on the sheet.

"Take it with you," he said. "Take it to Vesuvius."

Veronika picked up the bronze half. The cold metal pressed into the warmth of her palm. The complete five-pointed star on its face, in that white, surgical light, looked like an eye that had been closed for three hundred years and was, perhaps, on the verge of opening.

And in the deep places of the Minerva Bureau — beyond the curtained doors, beyond the lines of apothecary jars and clean white sheets, beyond the last of the brass lanterns — the Wall of Sighs let out a low, rhythmic sound.

A vibration. Patient. Measured. As if something, on the other side, had at last found the door.

Hmmmm. Hmmmm. Hmmmm.

第196章 达芬奇的日记（中）
