【中文】
第196章 达芬奇的日记（中）

密涅瓦机关医疗室的门在薇若兰身后关上时，她听见佛朗哥教授又咳了一声。

那声咳嗽很轻，像是被什么东西堵在了喉咙口，佛朗哥教授从来不在人前咳得这样克制——他是个技术狂人，整日泡在地窖里，嗓子里常年带着一层铁锈味，说话声音像砂纸磨过金属管。他不在意自己的身体。但今天他咳得小心，像是在压住一个不能让薇若兰看见的伤口。

薇若兰没有回头。

她攥着那半块青铜镜，金属冰凉的触感从掌心一路传到手腕。镜面上完整的五芒星在她手指缝里漏出一点光，像是一颗被封闭的瞳孔。

走廊很暗。

密涅瓦机关的医疗区位于鹰巢的最上层，灯光是冷白色的荧光管打出来的，照在墙壁上像一层薄冰。从医疗区往核心研发区走要经过三道钢门，每道门都需要不同级别的授权——第一道是基础权限，薇若兰的副总长工牌就够了；第二道是总长加急授权，昨晚佛朗哥教授用总长权限给她单独开过，授权期限是四十八小时；第三道……

第三道是她要去的地方。

"初代总工程师密室"。

薇若兰只在十五岁那年进去过一次。那天她刚通过密涅瓦机关的最终考核，佛朗哥教授带她去见了一个"密涅瓦真正的创建者留下的房间"，告诉她那里面保存着密涅瓦机关三百年来所有核心技术的源头，但从来不允许任何人带出任何东西。那次她在门口站了三分钟，门都没完全打开，佛朗哥教授就让她离开了。

"等你有资格读那间屋里的东西时，再进去。"佛朗哥教授当时是这么说的。

"什么叫有资格？"十五岁的薇若兰问。

"等你不再需要我告诉你答案的时候。"

现在她二十三岁。她已经很久没有需要佛朗哥教授告诉她答案了。但她还是需要佛朗哥教授告诉她那道门怎么开。

那个房间没有钥匙孔。

薇若兰沿着核心研发区的螺旋阶梯一路向下，蒸汽管道的嗡鸣声在脚下越来越重，铜管里流动的冷凝水发出咕噜咕噜的声响，像是密涅瓦机关的心脏在她脚底跳动。空气渐渐变得干燥，带着金属和红水银的腥气——那是鹰巢深层的气味，她从十三岁起就熟悉的气味。

经过第一静默区的时候，薇若兰放慢了脚步。

第一静默区是密涅瓦机关最古老的区域，整片地下空间像是一座废弃的陵墓。历代机动甲胄的原型机排列在两侧，有的已经残缺不全，有的被红水银蒸汽腐蚀得面目全非。它们沉默地站立着，像是被钉在历史里的铁制士兵。

薇若兰没有停留。

她继续往下走。

叹息之墙出现在阶梯的尽头。那道分隔人间与机械神国的黑色巨门，此刻正在发出一种低沉的、规律性的震动。

"嗡——嗡——嗡——"

震动从门板深处传出来，穿过金属结构，渗透到薇若兰脚下的阶梯扶手上。她把手指按在扶手上，能感觉到那道震动的频率——和利维坦级飞艇引擎运转时不同，比那更深沉，更古老，更像是某种生物的脉搏。

她想起了佛朗哥教授说的话。

"他们带着欧米茄原型体。"

"他们等这一天等了四十年。"

叹息之墙的震动还在继续。薇若兰绕过了正门——正门是密涅瓦机关的正式入口，但现在被圣堂装甲师堵着，她用的是另一条路。佛朗哥教授教过她一条从医疗区直通叹息之墙背面的检修通道，通道很窄，只够一个人侧身通过，墙壁上布满了外露的蒸汽管道和电缆。

通道尽头是一扇小门，门上贴着一张褪色的标签。

"非授权人员禁止入内。"

薇若兰用工牌刷开了门。

门后是一条比检修通道更窄的甬道，甬道两侧的墙壁不再是冰冷的混凝土，而是裸露的岩石——这是维苏威火山最原始的岩层，三百年前初代总工程师从火山岩层中开凿出来的空间。岩壁上钉着生锈的铁钩，挂着一盏老式的煤油灯，灯芯燃着微弱的火苗。

薇若兰没有动那盏灯。她从口袋里摸出一支化学荧光棒，掰弯，里面的液体混合后发出青蓝色的冷光。

在青蓝色的光照下，甬道尽头的门出现了。

那是一块巨大的金属板，高约三米，宽约两米，材质不是密涅瓦机关常用的硬金或影金属，而是一种薇若兰从未见过的暗红色合金——比红水银更深沉，更厚重，像是凝固的血液。金属板的表面没有任何把手、锁孔或铰链，只有正中央刻着一个巨大的机械神教徽记：齿轮中心嵌着一颗五芒星，五芒星的五个角向外延伸，末端各连着一圈更小的齿轮。

齿轮徽记的中央，那颗五芒星的位置，有一个长方形的凹槽。

凹槽的尺寸和形状——

薇若兰的呼吸停了一下。

凹槽的尺寸和形状，和一本书的大小完全吻合。

她从胸前内袋里取出了那本书。

那是她父亲留给她的唯一遗物。无封面，机械神教的祷文纸册。纸页泛黄，边缘磨损，内页的铅字已经模糊不清，但每一页上那些复杂的机械图纸和祷文公式依然清晰可辨。她父亲当年是密涅瓦机关的机械工程师，在她七岁那年死于一场实验事故，留给她的除了那本无封面的书册，还有满屋子的工具和一份微薄的抚恤金。

她从来不知道那本书的封面去了哪里。她父亲没有告诉过她，她母亲也没有。那本书似乎生来就没有封面，像是一个故意被抹去了身份的东西。

薇若兰把书册举到金属板前。

凹槽的尺寸和书册的长宽严丝合缝。

她犹豫了一秒。

不是因为害怕。是因为佛朗哥教授说过，"三百年来我的家族世世代代守护着那个房间，从未有人打开过"。

但佛朗哥教授现在让她打开它。

她把书册推进了凹槽。

"咔哒。"

一声轻响，金属板中央的齿轮徽记缓缓亮了起来——不是灯光，是齿轮本身在发光，暗红色的合金从凹槽周围开始蔓延出金色的脉动光芒，像是沉睡了三百年的血液重新开始流动。光芒顺着齿轮的轮廓向外扩散，五颗五芒星的角依次亮起，最后整块金属板都笼罩在一层淡金色的光晕中。

金属板开始移动。

不是向两侧打开，而是整块板缓缓向前推出，露出背后的空间。

冷空气从门后涌出来，带着三百年没有被搅动过的陈旧味道——旧纸张、金属锈蚀、红水银沉积物和某种薇若兰辨认不出的甜腻气息，像是被封存的花蜜。煤油灯的火焰在气流中摇曳了一下，差点熄灭。

门完全打开了。

薇若兰举起荧光棒，迈了进去。

她首先看到的是一张工作台。

工作台是金属的，台面上布满了三百多年前的工具痕迹——划痕、焊点、烧灼的印记，每一道痕迹都已经氧化成了深褐色。工作台上摆着几十件大小不一的机械零件，有些是她认识的——黄铜齿轮组、弹簧、活塞、汽缸；有些是她不认识的——一种她从未见过的金属片，薄如蝉翼，边缘锋利，在荧光棒的青蓝色光线下折射出暗金色的光泽。

工作台旁边是一个书架。

书架是木质的，三百年的时间让木材变形、开裂，但骨架还完整。书架上摆的不是书，而是一卷卷图纸。图纸的卷轴用铜扣固定，铜扣已经发绿，纸张的边缘发黄变脆。薇若兰抽出一卷展开——上面是手绘的机械结构图，线条精细到了令人难以置信的程度，齿轮、连杆、阀门的每一个细节都被描绘得清清楚楚。图右下角的签名已经模糊，但还能辨认出几个字母：L. d. V. B.。

达·芬奇·博尔吉亚。

薇若兰把图纸放回去，继续往里走。

密室比她想象的要大得多。金属门后是一间约六十平米的空间，顶部是维苏威火山天然的岩层穹顶，岩壁上钉着生锈的铁钩，挂着一盏盏老式的煤油灯——和甬道里那盏一样，但更多，更密集，像是一片被人为钉上去的星空。岩壁的某些地方被凿成了壁龛，壁龛里陈列着各种机械装置的原型——有些是完整的，有些已经残缺，有些被拆成了零件，用油纸仔细包裹着。

房间中央是一张大桌子。

桌子的材质和工作台一样，是金属的，但更厚重，更古老。桌面上的灰尘被擦去了一小块——不是三百年没人动过的痕迹，是最近才擦的。佛朗哥教授的家族世代守护这个房间，他们一定定期进来维护过。

桌面上摆着两样东西。

一样是一本日记。

日记用青铜板装订，封面和封底都刻着机械神教的齿轮徽记和倒置五芒星。青铜板上有一层薄薄的铜绿，但徽记的线条依然清晰锋利，像是刻刀昨天才划过。日记很厚，薇若兰用手指掂了掂——至少有两百页。

另一样是一只锡封匣。

匣子已经被打开了，里面是空的。但匣盖内侧贴着一张纸条，纸条上的字迹已经很淡了，写着：

"此匣原藏于利维坦飞艇残骸，一七一九年由家族第四代守护者取出，存于此室。——F.F.1935"

薇若兰没有去碰那只空匣子。她把荧光棒夹在肩膀和下巴之间，伸手拿起了那本青铜日记。

日记很沉。青铜板的厚度超过了她的预期——不是普通的装帧材料，而是一种她能感觉到的、带着微凉温度的特殊金属。她翻开封面。

扉页上只有一行字。

不是印刷体，是手写的。字迹工整而有力，笔画的末端有明显的顿笔，像是刻刀在金属上凿出的痕迹。墨水是黑色的，三百年过去了依然浓重得不像是时间能够侵蚀的东西。

"1684年，我在阿瓦隆冰原发现了世界树残枝和欧米茄原型体——那一刻，我既是神，也是魔鬼。"

薇若兰的手指停在那行字上。

1684年。星历1684年。三百多年前。

阿瓦隆冰原。

世界树残枝。

欧米茄原型体。

她快速翻过扉页，往后看。

第二页是一幅素描。素描的笔触细腻到了极致，画的是一片被冰雪覆盖的平原，平原中央矗立着一棵巨大的树——不是普通的树，树干上布满了齿轮状的纹路，树枝的末端不是叶片而是金属结构，像是无数把钥匙从树冠上垂下来。树的根部深深扎入冰层，冰层下隐约可见密密麻麻的齿轮在转动。

素描的右下角写着："阿瓦隆冰原，世界树残枝之西枝。星历1684年冬。"

第三页是文字。

"我最初以为那是一棵普通的树——一棵在极端环境中存活了不知多少年的古老植物。但当我用斧头砍开它的表皮时，流出来的不是树汁，而是一种我从没见过的银白色液体。那液体接触空气后迅速凝固，呈现出一种深沉的暗红色，像是凝固的血液。我后来才知道，那东西有一个名字——红水银。"

"红水银。"

薇若兰在密涅瓦机关工作了十年，她知道红水银的官方来源——弥赛亚圣教宣称它来自阿瓦隆矿脉，是神的恩赐，是推动整个机械文明的核心能源。但她从来不知道红水银来自一棵树。一棵活着的、有意识的、枝干上长满齿轮的树。

她继续翻。

"世界树的根深入冰层以下不知几百米，我在它周围挖掘了三个月，才发现它的根系并不是普通的植物根系——那是无数条金属管道，管道里流动着红水银，而管道的外壁刻满了梵文。那些梵文比任何已知的人类文字都古老，我找遍了翡冷翠的图书馆都无法破译。"

"我犯了一个错误。"

"我以为我可以控制它。"

"我以为人类的技术可以驾驭那棵树的力量。我把它的残枝——我亲手锯下来的两段枝干——带回翡冷翠，用它们的核心建成了两台原型体：一台是欧米茄，另一台是——"

这一行字被墨水涂掉了。不是后来被人涂掉的，是写作者在写完之后自己用笔涂掉的。墨迹覆盖了下面的字，但薇若兰把日记倾斜到荧光棒的光线下，勉强辨认出了被涂掉的几个词：

"……屠龙者圣乔治……"

薇若兰的手指僵了一下。

屠龙者圣乔治。密涅瓦机关熔岩之心深处封存了四十年的那台初代炽天使——那台比新型红龙还要庞大的、被前代总长封禁的终极兵器。

它也是用世界树残枝建造的。

她继续翻。

日记的内容从1684年跳到了1687年。中间三年的内容被整页整页地撕掉了，撕口处留下了锐利的金属边缘——不是用手指撕的，是用刀裁的。

1687年的第一页写着：

"三年了。欧米茄的建造工作已经完成。它比我预想的更完美——红水银核心的能量输出远超任何已知的蒸汽机，神经接驳系统能让骑士和甲胄真正融为一体，反应速度、力量、感知都达到了人体的极限。这台甲胄不是武器，它是人类身体的延伸，是凡人之手触及神之领域的桥梁。"

"但我错了。"

"欧米茄有自己的意识。"

"我不知道那意识是从哪里来的——是世界树残枝的记忆，是红水银的某种我无法理解的特性，还是别的什么。但每次骑士进行神经接驳之后，欧米茄都会"记住"一些东西。下一次接驳时，它会表现出更快的反应、更高的效率，像是一个正在学习的活物。"

"我应该在那时候就停下来。"

"但我没有。"

薇若兰继续翻。1687年到1690年的内容断断续续，有些页面被水渍污染得无法辨认，有些页面的边角被烧焦了——是密涅瓦机关那场著名的大火吗？她听佛朗哥教授提过，星历1690年翡冷翠发生过一场大火，烧毁了大半个城区。

1690年最后一页的日期是"1690年11月17日"。

"我必须阻止自己。"

"我已经没有回头路了。"

"但我可以埋下一颗钉子。"

"我将以'达·芬奇·博尔吉亚'的身份建立密涅瓦机关。明面上，我是教皇陛下的首席机械师，替教会研发更强的武器。暗地里，我将用密涅瓦的全部资源阻止'博尔吉亚一世'重启机械神国的疯狂计划。"

"叹息之墙将把人间和机械神国永远隔开。"

"欧米茄原型体将被封存在密涅瓦最深的地方，永远不让它醒来。"

"而我留下的这本日记，将是未来某个人能找到的最后线索。"

"如果那个人读到了这段话——"

"请记住：世界树不是人类的工具。它是活的，它有记忆，它有意志。红水银是它的血液，欧米茄是它的骨骼。而我们——我们这些试图驾驭它的人——不过是它身体里的一粒寄生虫。"

"别相信任何告诉你'可以控制它'的人。"

"别相信任何告诉你'机械神国会拯救人类'的人。"

"包括我。"

日记在这里中断了。

薇若兰翻过最后一页——后面还有大量空白页，但都是空白的。日记的作者在写完这段话后，再也没有动过笔。

她合上日记，深深地呼出一口气。

密室里的空气依然是三百年前的温度和气味，那种旧纸张和红水银沉积物混合的甜腻感让她嗓子发痒。她把日记放回桌上，伸手揉了揉自己的眼睛——荧光棒的青蓝色光线已经开始衰减了。

就在她转身准备离开的时候，她的手碰到了日记下方压着的一张纸。

那张纸比日记的页面更大，更厚，边缘泛黄，但不是书页的材质——是相纸。

薇若兰把相纸抽出来。

她举起荧光棒，光线照亮了相纸的表面。

照片很旧了，黑白的影像已经有些褪色，边缘有被反复触摸的痕迹。照片上是一个年轻女人，穿着锡兰传统服饰——白色的纱丽，缀满银线刺绣的宽腰带，额头上点着红砂。女人的面容安详，怀里抱着一个婴儿，婴儿的眼睛——

婴儿的眼睛是紫色的。

深紫色。

和西泽尔的眼睛一模一样的深紫色。

薇若兰的手停住了。

她把照片翻过来。

照片背面有两行字。

第一行是烫金的锡兰文字，花体梵文的写法，薇若兰的锡兰语不够好，只能勉强辨认出几个音节——但那几个音节组合在一起，她知道是什么意思。

"琳琅·星见。"

第二行是潦草的拉丁文，墨水是黑棕色的，字迹和日记扉页上的字迹一模一样。

"我的女儿，艾琳娜·波吉亚。"

薇若兰的荧光棒从肩膀上滑落，掉在金属桌面上，骨碌碌滚了两下，停住了。青蓝色的光线在桌面上投下一个摇晃的光圈，光圈正好落在照片上那个紫瞳婴儿的脸上。

婴儿的眼睛在光线的照射下泛出一点奇异的紫色反光，像是一颗沉睡的星辰。

密室的角落里，有一只煤油灯忽然自己亮了。火焰很小，摇摇晃晃的，像是有什么东西在三百年的沉睡后重新开始呼吸。

叹息之墙深处的震动还在继续。

"嗡——嗡——嗡——"

【English】
Chapter 196 — Da Vinci's Diary (II)

The door of the Minerva Institute's medical ward closed behind Verolan, and she heard Professor Franco cough again.

It was a small sound, a careful sound — the kind a man makes when he is holding something back. Franco had never been a man who held anything back. He was the sort of engineer who lived in cellars and ate cold meals standing up and spoke with a voice that sounded like a file drawn across a copper pipe. He had a permanent film of iron filings in his throat, and he had not bothered with his own body in living memory. That he should choose, today, to be discreet with his cough, told Verolan more than any of the words he had said to her in the last hour.

She did not turn around.

In her hand she held the half-mirror of bronze. The metal was cold; the chill climbed her palm and up the inside of her wrist and stopped somewhere behind her sternum. Through the gap between her fingers the five-pointed star incised on the mirror's face gave off a thin sliver of light, like a pupil half-closed against the day.

The corridor was dim.

The medical wing sat at the highest level of the Eyrie, that monstrous warren of iron and brick the Minerva Institute had burrowed into the flanks of Vesuvius. The light here was the cold white of phosphor tubes, and it lay on the stone walls like a skin of frost. To reach the Central Research Levels from the ward you had to pass through three steel doors, each one keyed to a different rank of clearance. The first accepted the brass of her deputy-director badge without argument. The second she had been given last night, by Franco, against his own director-level authority — a forty-eight-hour window, no more, no less. The third —

The third was where she was going.

She began to descend.

The spiral stair that led from the medical wing down into the heart of the Institute was older than the phosphor lights above it. It had been cut for men in boots, not for the long-legged stride of a young woman in a researcher's coat, and her heels struck the iron treads with a clean, deliberate rhythm. Beneath her, the Institute spoke to itself. Steam pipes ticked and thrummed in the walls. Condensation ran in the copper and made small, wet, gulping sounds, as though something vast and tired were swallowing in its sleep. The air grew drier as she went down, and the smell shifted: from carbolic and lye to the deeper, more honest smell of the Eyrie's lower levels — metal, machine oil, and the faint sweet poison of red mercury. She had been breathing that smell since she was thirteen. It lived in her clothes.

She slowed when she reached the First Silents.

The First Silents was the oldest part of the Institute, a great vaulted chamber that smelled of catacomb. The original suits of powered armor stood along the walls in long ranks, prototypes of every class the Institute had ever built. Some of them were still whole. Most were not. Red mercury vapour had crept into their joints and eaten them from the inside, and they stood there now like iron soldiers who had been paid and then forgotten — propped upright, hollow-eyed, waiting for an order that would never come.

Verolan did not pause among them. She had walked past them a hundred times.

At the foot of the spiral stair, the passage opened onto the Wall of Sighs.

The Wall was a single sheet of black metal the colour of a closed eyelid, and it ran from floor to vault without seam or rivet. Verolan had been told, as a child, that it had been forged in a single pour in the last year of the seventeenth century, and that the man who had ordered it built had died three days before it was hung. The Wall of Sighs was what divided the human world from the Machine Kingdom — that lower realm of automata, of the Seraphim-class engines, of things the Church preferred not to name. Tonight, as every night, the Wall was breathing.

Bummm. Bummm. Bummm.

The pulse came up through the iron of the floor, through the treads beneath her boots, through the bones of her feet and the long bones of her legs. She put her fingertips to the handrail. The vibration was slower than the heartbeat of a Leviathan-class airship at full throttle, deeper, and far older — a frequency that did not feel made. It felt grown. It felt as if something on the other side of the metal were not striking the door but simply being the door.

Franco's voice, an hour ago, came back to her.

*They are carrying the Omega frame with them.*

*They have been waiting forty years for this day.*

The pulse went on. Verolan turned away from the front of the Wall, where a full company of the Basilica Armored Division now stood in ceremonial guard, and made for a narrow service hatch set into the rock to the left of the great gate. Franco had shown her the hatch when she was nineteen. It ran, he had said then, all the way from the medical wing to the back face of the Wall, and from there down into a place he would one day have to show her. She had not asked why. Franco was a man who paid his debts of information in his own time.

The hatch was a thin, mean thing. She had to turn her shoulders to fit through. Inside, the walls were a clutter of bare steam pipes and cable runs, and the noise of the Institute pressed close around her like a hand over a mouth. The hatch let out into a short passage cut straight from the living rock of Vesuvius — black basalt, slick with three centuries of seepage — and at the far end of the passage, lit by a single oil lamp on a rusted iron hook, stood a second door. A label, sun-faded almost to nothing, was glued above the handle.

UNAUTHORISED PERSONNEL WILL NOT PROCEED BEYOND THIS POINT.

She swiped her badge. The lock clicked. She went through.

The second passage was narrower still, and the walls were no longer dressed stone but raw rock — the original heart of the volcano, the place where the first chief engineer of the Minerva Institute, three hundred years ago, had driven his picks into the mountain and made his first room. More rusted hooks. More oil lamps. A smell of long-cooled soot.

Verolan did not light the lamp. She took a chemical light-stick from her pocket, cracked it between her fingers, and shook it once. The phosphors mixed. The passage filled with the cold, blue-tinged light of a winter morning seen through ice.

At the end of the passage there was a wall.

Not a door. A wall.

A single sheet of metal, three metres high and two across, set into the rock with no visible frame. The metal was not the hard gold or the shadow-metal of the Institute's working stock. It was something Verolan had never seen in any catalogue — a dark, dense, blood-coloured alloy, the colour of an old scab. It was heavier-looking than metal had any right to be. It had no handle. It had no lock. It had no hinges. At its centre, cut deep into the dark metal, was the great seal of the Machine Church: a gear, and at the gear's heart an inverted five-pointed star, and from each point of the star a smaller gear, and at the heart of the star a single rectangular socket.

Verolan's breath stopped, and then went on.

The socket was exactly the size and shape of a book.

She reached into the inside pocket of her coat and drew out the book.

It was the only thing her father had left her. He had been a mechanic at the Institute, a quiet man with ink-stained fingers who used to let her sit on his workbench and hand him the small wrenches in the right order. He had died in a laboratory accident when she was seven. The book had been on his body when they brought it home. No cover. No title. The pages were yellowed and soft at the edges, the lead type blurred by years of being read in bad light, but the diagrams and the equations of the Machine Church were still sharp, still legible, and the paper itself felt, even now, as if it had been chosen with a kind of fierce care.

She had never known where the cover had gone. She had never been told.

She held the book up to the socket.

The fit was exact.

She hesitated — not from fear. From the memory of what Franco had told her, years ago, when he had first brought her down here as a girl of fifteen. *My family has guarded that room for three hundred years. No one has ever opened it.*

*Open it,* Franco had said to her tonight. *Read it. And then come back to me.*

She slid the book home.

A small click. And then the dark metal began to move.

Not sideways. Forward. The whole sheet, a single panel weighing she did not want to think about how much, slid out of the rock on some buried rail, like a tongue being slowly offered. As it moved, the seal at its centre began to light. The light did not come from any lamp; it came up out of the metal itself, out of the lines of the seal, gold running through the dark alloy like blood remembered how to run. It reached the points of the inverted star, lit them one by one, and at last the whole panel stood in a low, steady halo of gold.

The seal was now a threshold.

Cold air came out of the dark beyond it. Three hundred years of cold air, smelling of paper that had never been turned, of metal that had never been polished, of red mercury settled into a fine dust on every surface, and underneath it all a strange sweet smell, like honey sealed into a jar. The oil lamp on the wall of the passage guttered in the draft and nearly went out.

Verolan stepped through.

The first thing she saw, in the blue light of the stick, was a workbench.

It was iron, and it had been used. The marks of three centuries of use were on it — scratches, hammer-dents, the small dark craters where a hot tool had been set down and forgotten. Each mark had oxidised into the colour of old tea. Across the bench, laid out in careful rows as if the workman had just stepped away for a moment and meant to come back, were dozens of small mechanical parts. She recognised some: brass gear-trains, hairspring assemblies, pistons, valve cylinders. She did not recognise others. One piece in particular she stopped to look at — a thin, knife-edged metal, lighter than any alloy she had ever catalogued, that caught the blue light and threw back a dull, gold-tinged sheen.

Beside the bench stood a bookshelf.

It was wood, and the wood had not forgiven three hundred years. The shelves were warped. The uprights had split. But the skeleton of it held. On the shelves, instead of books, were rolls of paper held closed with copper slides gone green with verdigris. She drew one out at random and unrolled a foot of it. The drawing was hand-work, and the hand had been almost supernaturally steady: gear, linkage, valve, every joint drawn as if the draughtsman had not trusted himself to use anything but a single hairline. In the lower right corner, in ink that had faded to a polite brown, she could make out a signature.

L. da V. B.

She set the roll back in its place. She moved on.

The room was larger than she had expected — sixty feet by forty, perhaps, beneath a vault of raw basalt. More oil lamps on rusted hooks, scores of them, the way a chapel is hung with votives, except that only a few of them had ever been lit. Along the walls, cut into the rock itself, were niches, and in the niches stood the disassembled parts of machines she could not always name — some whole, some in pieces, some wrapped in oiled paper with the neatness of a man wrapping a gift for his daughter.

In the middle of the room there was a table.

Heavier than the workbench. Older. A sheet of the same dark alloy as the door, but twice as thick. Most of the surface was furred with the fine red dust of settled mercury vapour. But in one place, dead centre, the dust had been recently wiped away. Franco's people had been in here. They had been in here often. They were not, after all, the first to enter this room in three hundred years. They were only the most recent.

On the cleaned patch of the table there were two things.

The first was a diary. It was bound in bronze — not a bronze cover, but bronze boards, thicker than the cover of any book she had ever held, and the metal was cold in the way of a metal that has been cold for a very long time. On the front and back boards the same seal was engraved, in lines so sharp they looked cut yesterday: the gear, the inverted star, the smaller gears at the points. A thin skin of verdigris lay over the metal. The book was heavy. When she lifted it, she judged its weight at the better part of two hundred pages.

The second thing was a tin case, soldered shut once, now open. It was empty. Inside the lid there was a square of paper, and on the paper, in a hand that had gone the colour of weak tea, were these words:

THIS CASE WAS TAKEN FROM THE WRECK OF A LEVIATON-CLASS AIRSHIP IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 1719 BY THE FOURTH OF MY LINE, AND PLACED IN THIS ROOM. — F. F. 1935.

Verolan did not touch the empty case.

She tucked the light-stick into the hollow of her shoulder, against her jaw, and took up the diary.

She opened the cover.

The endpaper bore a single line of writing, hand-done, in a black ink that three hundred years had not been able to weaken. The hand was upright and decided. The downstrokes ended in small, deliberate wedges, as if the pen had been a chisel.

*In the year 1684, on the Avalon Ice, I found the bough of the World-Tree and the frame of the Omega. In that moment I was at once God and the devil.*

Verolan's finger rested on the line.

*1684. The year of our reckoning 1684. Three hundred and forty-one years ago.*

*Avalon.*

*World-Tree.*

*Omega.*

She turned the page.

The second leaf was a drawing. The draughtsman had used a point so fine it seemed malicious. He had drawn a flat white plain under a low white sky, and at the centre of the plain a single tree. It was not a tree as any forester would have known one. Its trunk was ridged like a column of stacked gears. From its branches, where leaves should have been, hung shapes of metal — she thought at first of fruit, then of pendants, then of keys. Beneath the tree, the ice was drawn thin for the draughtsman's purposes, and under the ice the eye could just make out the slow turning of more gears than a man would care to count.

In the lower right corner, in the same hand:

*The western bough of the World-Tree, on the Avalon Ice. Winter of the year 1684.*

She turned again.

*At first I took it for an ordinary tree — a thing of wood, a thing that had endured the cold of that place for an age beyond reckoning. I set an axe to the bark to take a sample for the cartographers, and what bled from the cut was not sap. It was a silver-white liquid, of a kind I had not seen in any alchemical table. The moment it touched the air it set, and the colour it set to was a deep and sombre red, the colour of congealed blood.*

*I learned its name, later.*

*It is called cinnabar. Red mercury.*

Verolan, standing in the blue light of the failing stick, read the words again.

She had worked at the Institute for ten years. She knew, as every initiate of the Institute knew, the official genealogy of red mercury. It came from the Avalon veins. It was the gift of the Most High to the Holy Church of the Messiah, the very blood of the divine engine that turned the world. She had read the chapter in the catechism. She had heard it read aloud at her own investiture. She had not known, until this moment, that any of it was true.

She turned the page.

*The roots of the tree go deeper into the ice than I have yet been able to follow. I have dug about it for three months. They are not roots. They are pipes. Within them, a slow current of the red liquid moves as blood moves in a vein. And on the outer wall of every pipe, from the topmost to the deepest I have been able to uncover, a script is engraved. The script is not Latin, not Greek, not the tongue of the Serapeum. I have shown it to the best scholars in Florence. None of them can read it.*

*I have made a mistake.*

*I believed I could master it.*

Verolan felt the air in the room press closer to her skin.

*I believed the arts of men were equal to the engine I had found. I took two boughs of the tree — I cut them with my own hands from the western arm of it — and I brought them home to Florence. From the heartwood of those boughs I built, in the cellars beneath the Borgia palace, two frames. The first I called Omega. The second I called —*

The rest of the line had been deliberately inked over. A thick slash of black, drawn with the same pen, in the same hand, after the line had been written. Verolan tilted the diary into the light. The ink of the slash was darker than the ink beneath. Slowly, letter by letter, the words underneath gave themselves up to her.

*…St George the Dragonslayer…*

Her hand stopped on the page.

*St George the Dragonslayer.* The original Seraphim frame. The first. The great engine sealed in the molten heart of the Institute for forty years, sealed there by the order of the previous director general — bigger than the new Red Dragon class, sealed, forbidden, never to be woken. It had been built, too, from the wood of the World-Tree.

She turned the page.

The next entry was dated three years later. Between the entry about Avalon and this one, leaves had been removed — not torn, but cut, sliced cleanly through with a blade, and the cut edges of the remaining leaves were sharp enough to take skin from a fingertip.

*It is the year 1687. The Omega is complete. I had not dared to hope for so much. The cinnabar core gives out a force that surpasses any engine of steam I have ever measured. The neural interface, by which the knight and the frame are made one flesh, lifts the limits of the human body in every direction I have been able to test. The frame is not a weapon. It is a lengthening of the arm. It is the hand of a common man, set on the end of the arm of God.*

*I was wrong.*

*Omega is aware of itself.*

*I do not know from where the awareness comes. Whether it is the memory of the bough from which the frame was cut; whether it is some property of the cinnabar itself that I have failed to understand; whether it is some other thing, older still. But the fact is the fact. Each time a knight takes the neural bridge, Omega retains something of the joining. The next knight, the next time, finds the frame quicker, more obedient, more eager — as if the thing were learning.*

*I should have stopped then.*

*I did not.*

The next pages were the worst. Some had been spoiled by water, the ink run into ghosts. Some had been singed at the corners, and Verolan remembered, distantly, the great fire of Florence in the winter of 1690, which had taken half the city and most of the old Borgia quarter. Franco had told her of it once, with the careful dryness of a man who had been raised on the story.

The last dated entry was the seventeenth of November, 1690.

*I must put a stop to my own work.*

*There is no road back for me.*

*But I can drive a nail into the work of those who come after.*

*Under the name of Leonardo da Vinci Borgia, I will found the Minerva Institute. In the eyes of the world I will be the chief engineer of His Holiness the Pope, and I will build, for the Church, engines of war. Under the hand of that cover I will use every breath of the Institute's resources to prevent Borgia the First from carrying out his own mad design — the design to wake the Machine Kingdom, to throw open the door the World-Tree was never meant to open, to make of the world an engine for the engine's sake.*

*The Wall of Sighs will stand for ever between the world of men and the kingdom below.*

*The frame of Omega will be sealed in the deepest place of the Institute, and it will never be woken.*

*And this book, which I leave behind me, will be the last clue for whoever comes after.*

*If you, who are reading this, are that person —*

*Hear me. The World-Tree is not a tool of mankind. It is alive. It has memory. It has a will. Cinnabar is its blood. Omega is its bone. And we, who have set ourselves to master it, are no more than a single parasite in a single vein.*

*Do not trust the man who tells you it can be controlled.*

*Do not trust the man who tells you the Machine Kingdom will save mankind.*

*Not even me.*

There the diary stopped. The leaves that followed were blank. The pen had not been taken up again.

Verolan closed the cover. She set it on the table. She let her breath go, slowly, into the cold air of the room, and watched it fall back to her boots as a faint, gold-edged mist under the dying blue of the stick.

Then her hand, on its way down to the table, touched the edge of a piece of paper that had been lying flat under the diary. The paper was heavier than the pages of the book. It was stiffer. It was the weight of a photograph.

She drew it out into the light.

The image was old, black-and-white, foxed at the edges, the silver of the print gone a tired grey. A young woman was sitting in a chair that did not belong to any European room Verolan had ever seen. She was wearing a sari of pale cloth. Around her waist a wide belt of silver embroidery caught the light. On her brow, between her brows, a single red mark.

The woman's face was at peace. In her arms she held an infant, dressed in white. The infant was looking straight at the camera, or straight through it. Its eyes, even in a black-and-white photograph that must have been a hundred and forty years old, were the darkest of darks — a deep, deep, almost blackish violet, the colour of a storm seen from the deck of a ship.

The colour of Cesare's eyes.

Verolan's hand did not move.

She turned the photograph over.

On the back there were two lines. The first was in flowing Sinhala script, gilded, the curling letters of an old court hand. Verolan's Sinhala was poor. She traced the syllables with the tip of her finger. She did not need much of the language to make out the name.

*Linlang. The Seeress of Stars.*

The second line was in Latin, in a hurried hand, in brown-black ink. The hand was the same hand. She would have known it anywhere now.

*My daughter. Elena Borgia.*

The light-stick slid from under her jaw. It fell from her shoulder, struck the iron table with a small bright click, rolled twice, and lay still. The cold blue light of it lay across the face of the infant in the photograph, and in that light, for one breath, the violet of the child's eyes came up out of the silver of the print and glowed, faintly, like a star that has been waiting a long time to be named.

In a far corner of the room, an oil lamp she had not touched, and could not have reached, came alight by itself. The flame was small. It guttered once. It steadied. As if something in the room, after three hundred years of holding its breath, had at last begun to breathe.

And beneath the floor, beneath the table, beneath the rock of Vesuvius itself, the Wall of Sighs went on with its slow, patient, unhurried pulse.

Bummm. Bummm. Bummm.


==================================================
第197章 达芬奇的日记（下）
==================================================

【中文】
第197章 达芬奇的日记（下）

薇若兰蹲在金属桌前，荧光棒已经快要熄灭了。她把那张旧照片放回日记上方，深吸了一口气，重新翻开日记本。纸页之间夹着的锡兰薄荷干花已经碎成了粉末，一小撮落在她的指腹上，冰凉的，带着三百年前的气味。

她必须看完。

翻过的部分她已经读过了——星历1684年，博尔吉亚一世（或者说"达·芬奇"本人）率船抵达阿瓦隆冰原，发现被暴雪掩埋的世界树残枝，砍下两段，一段铸成欧米茄，一段铸成屠龙者圣乔治。这部分他已经知道了。

她继续往后翻。

日记的字迹在中间部分开始变得潦草，墨水换成了更深的黑棕色，纸张的边缘有被反复揉搓的痕迹。达·芬奇的字不再是早期那种工整的工程师手记，而像是深夜里写给另一个自己的忏悔书。

"星历1691年。我做了一个错误的决定。"

"我以为只要把残枝锁在维苏威火山的最深处，就能阻止任何人染指机械神国。但我忘记了一件事——我既是我自己，也是教皇。教皇之位需要继承人，而继承我的不一定是另一个我。"

"我把欧米茄的核心封存在叹息之墙之后，让它沉睡，然后以教皇的身份对外宣称那是教廷的最高机密。我同时以达·芬奇的身份在叹息之墙外建立了密涅瓦机关，让后世的人以为密涅瓦是用来守护这个秘密的。"

"但我忽略了我的血脉。"

薇若兰的目光凝住了。

"星历1695年。艾琳娜，我的妹妹，她不是普通的博尔吉亚。她是我母亲和一位东方星见结合生下的女儿——这个秘密连我母亲自己都到死都没弄清楚。我以为她只是一个聪明的、对机械有天赋的妹妹，却不知道她继承了博尔吉亚的头脑和星见的紫瞳。"

"她天生就能与红水银共鸣。"

"我封存欧米茄的时候，她才十一岁。她看着我走进叹息之墙，回来之后就成了一个沉默的孩子。她用三个月时间偷走了密涅瓦机关最深层档案库里的神经接驳原始图纸，带着图纸消失了。"

"教廷宣布她为异端，公开火刑。尸体失踪。"

"我派人追查了三年，没有结果。"

"直到星历1703年。"

翻过一页。

"星历1703年，我收到了一封没有署名的信。信是从锡兰寄来的。"

"信里说，她在锡兰找到了星见一族的末裔，那些人世世代代守护着世界树的根。她在信中附了一幅画——一棵巨大的树，根系深扎进地底，根须的末端雕刻着细如发丝的梵文。"

"她写道：'哥哥，世界树不是被砍断的，是自己切断了自己的枝丫，因为它太痛了。西方一支被你带走，东方一支被星见们守护着。让我来守护东方的这一支吧。'"

"我回信问她：你打算怎么做。"

"她回信说：'我要让博尔吉亚和星见的血混在一起，铸成一把新的钥匙。这把钥匙会同时认识两个世界。'"

薇若兰的手在日记上停住了。

她终于明白了琳琅夫人的身世。

琳琅·星见，那个来自锡兰的绝世美人，那个因为美貌被教皇看上又被整个翡冷翠唾弃的女人，她不是普通的东方女性。她是锡兰末代星见的女儿，是星见家族守护世界树根部的传人——同时也是艾琳娜·博尔吉亚的转世。

"星历1711年。又过了八年，我终于在锡兰的一座王宫里找到了艾琳娜。她已经是星见一族的养母，嫁给了锡兰的某位旁支王室。她给我看了她的女儿。"

"那个孩子叫琳琅。三岁。深紫色的眼睛，继承了博尔吉亚的棕色卷发和星见一族的苍白肤色。她见到我的时候，没有哭，只是盯着我的眼睛看了很久。"

"艾琳娜说：'这是我的女儿，也是我的转世。我已经没有多少时间了。星见的血液是诅咒——我们每一代人的寿命都在缩短，但我把记忆留在了这具小小的身体里。等她长大，她会记起一切。'"

"我问她：'那你呢？'"

"她说：'我会留在她的身体里沉睡，直到有一天被需要。'"

薇若兰翻过一页，发现中间夹着另一张被折叠得更小的相纸。她抽出来。

这张照片和第一张不一样——是彩色的，色调陈旧但保存得比黑白那张更好。照片上是一个女人和两个孩子。

女人穿着白色纱丽，紫色的眼睛，笑容温和。

她的左手牵着一个七岁左右的女孩，女孩的眼睛也是紫色的。

她的右手抱着一个婴儿，婴儿的眼睛是黑棕色的。

照片背面没有字，但薇若兰已经猜到了。

那个紫瞳女孩，就是年幼的琳琅。

那个黑棕色眼睛的婴儿——

"这是我的外孙。"

薇若兰的呼吸一窒——不，她强行把那口气压下去了。她知道接下来这一页会写什么，但她还是必须看下去。

她必须看。

"星历1730年。琳琅长大了。她比她的母亲更美，更冷静，更沉默。她记起了艾琳娜留在她体内的一切——包括机械神教的核心祷文，包括黑铁巨门的三层封印机制，包括她自己的双重血脉。"

"我决定让她离开锡兰。她太危险了，留在锡兰只会被新罗马帝国的密探发现。"

"我把她送到了东方，让她去那里寻找她母亲曾经留下的一些人。她走的时候没有回头。"

"她问我：'您是想要我做什么？'"

"我说：'什么都不用做。你只需要活着，遇到一个你爱的人，然后生下一个孩子。'"

"她很久没说话。最后她说：'我明白了。'"

"她明白什么？"达·芬奇在这一段的末尾用红色墨水批注了一行字，笔迹颤抖："她明白她就是那把钥匙，而我需要的是那把钥匙生出的另一把钥匙。"

薇若兰的指节缓缓收拢，握住了日记的边缘。

她没有出声。

她继续翻。

"星历1756年。二十六年过去了。我已经快死了。琳琅没有再回过锡兰，她真的在东方安顿了下来。但我收到消息，她嫁给了一个男人。"

"那个男人不是博尔吉亚。"

"是一个凡人。一个普通的、善良的、年轻的凡人。她在信里说：'我遇到了一个我想为他生孩子的男人。他不是教皇，不是皇帝，不是任何神的使者。他只是一个给我买糖炒栗子的人。'"

"我笑了。星见一族的血液里流淌着神谕和诅咒，她却想要嫁给一个凡人。"

"我问她：'那孩子呢？'"

"她说：'不生了。我不想让我的孩子继承这把钥匙的命运。'"

"我尊重她的决定。"

日记在这里空了三页。第四页上达·芬奇的字迹变了，笔触更重，墨水更浓，像是蘸了血在写。

"星历1762年。"

"那个凡人死了。"

"死于一场教廷名下的暗杀。"

"是枢机会。"

"他们找到了琳琅。他们知道她是星见，是博尔吉亚的旁系，是那把钥匙。"

"他们杀死了她的丈夫，威胁她回到翡冷翠。"

"她回去了。她回到翡冷翠的时候，怀里抱着一个三岁的女孩。"

薇若兰看到这一段，猛地合上了日记。

她的胸口在剧烈地起伏。

——三岁的女孩。紫瞳。

琳琅夫人带着年幼的女儿从东方回到了翡冷翠，被枢机会控制，被迫成为教皇的情妇——这一切的源头，竟然在这里。

她用了三秒钟让自己平静下来。

然后她重新打开了日记。

"那个女孩叫璎珞。"

"和艾琳娜一样的紫瞳。和艾琳娜一样的博尔吉亚卷发。"

"她也是艾琳娜的转世。"

"琳琅的血脉里藏着星见一族的秘密——每一代星见都是同一个灵魂的容器。艾琳娜把自己分成了两份，一份留给了琳琅，一份在星见一族中轮回了三百年，轮回到了璎珞的体内。"

"所以璎珞和琳琅是姐妹，也是同一个灵魂。"

"达斯蒙德——那个伪装成璎珞哥哥的男人——他不是璎珞的家人。他是被枢机会安排在璎珞身边的监视者。"

"但璎珞比他想象的更危险。她拥有艾琳娜的所有记忆。"

"我派密涅瓦机关的密探在马斯顿王立机械学院外监视璎珞。她进教堂的那一天，我收到了报告——她在做祈祷。不是弥赛亚圣教的祈祷，是机械神教的祈祷。"

"她在唤醒她体内的艾琳娜。"

"她在寻找琳琅。"

"她在找我。"

日记翻到最后几页，纸张已经发脆了。字迹时而工整，时而潦草，像是在病中写就的。

"星历1771年。我快死了。"

"我必须把一切都记录下来。"

"关于西泽尔——"

薇若兰的目光定住了。

"琳琅在回到翡冷翠的第二年生下了一个孩子。"

"孩子的父亲不是那个死了的凡人。是教皇。"

"是隆·博尔吉亚。"

"是现任教皇。"

"——我通过密涅瓦机关的线人确认了这一点。琳琅在被枢机会控制之后，失去了拒绝的权利。"

"那个孩子是禁忌之子。"

"他身上同时流着博尔吉亚的血和星见的血。"

"他的眼睛——"

达·芬奇在这一行字下面画了一个红色的圆圈，圈里画着一颗紫色的星星。

"我让密探在他出生时偷偷取过一滴血。那滴血与红水银的反应，和普通博尔吉亚的血完全不同——它在红水银里会发出金色的光。"

"和欧米茄原型体核心发出的光，一模一样。"

"我终于明白了。"

"我妹妹艾琳娜追求了一生的完美神使——能够同时连接世界树残枝和保留人性的载体——根本就不需要从外部制造。"

"它就藏在博尔吉亚家族自己的血脉里。"

"只需要一个星见，一个博尔吉亚，两者结合。"

"那个孩子就是钥匙。"

"我给他起了一个名字。在我的日记里，他叫'Rex Immortalis'。"

"不死之王。"

"他不是傀儡，不是机械，不是工具。他是活着的、带着人类情感的、却又拥有着连接两个世界力量的——人。"

"我必须保护他。"

"如果枢机会知道他的存在，他们会立刻把他抓去做实验，做成第二个欧米茄原型体。"

"所以我让佛朗哥去把他藏起来。藏在马斯顿。"

"藏在一个连他自己都不知道自己是谁的地方。"

"等他长大。"

"等他自己去发现真相。"

日记的最后几页被撕掉了。

不——不是被撕掉了。是被达·芬奇自己用剪刀小心翼翼地裁掉的。薇若兰在纸边发现了被裁过的痕迹。

他故意留下了残页。

在日记最后一页的正中央，用红色墨水画着一个图案。

倒置的五芒星。

五芒星的五个角末端各画着一颗齿轮。

——锡兰星见家族的徽记。

不是撒旦教。

从来都不是。

倒置五芒星是星见家族代代相传的圣徽——倒置的五芒星代表"自下而上"，意味着星见是从最底层仰望星空、窃取天机的族群。它是星见与天神沟通的符号，被初代教皇博尔吉亚一世污名化为"撒旦的印记"，只是为了独占这个徽记所代表的钥匙功能。

达·芬奇在倒置五芒星下面写了一行字，墨水已经褪色，但还能辨认：

"锡兰的孩子们，世界树是你们的。钥匙也是你们的。"

"但我请求你们——不要打开黑铁巨门。"

"里面的东西，是我用了一生去阻止我自己释放的怪物。"

"请把它永远关在那里。"

日记到此结束。

薇若兰慢慢合上日记本，把那张彩色的旧照片、那张黑白的旧照片、那张写着"琳琅·星见"和"我的女儿，艾琳娜·波吉亚"的照片，全部收进怀里。

她的手指在发抖。

不是害怕。

是愤怒。

是三百年的谎言、三百年的阴谋、三百年的牺牲与谋杀，全部压在她胸口上，让她喘不过气来。

"老东西。"她低声骂了一句，"你既然知道这一切，为什么不告诉我？"

她当然知道答案。

因为达·芬奇死的时候，佛朗哥还只是一个孩子。

因为把这一切告诉佛朗哥，就等于把西泽尔交给密涅瓦机关——而密涅瓦机关里，也有枢机会的线人。

所以达·芬奇把一切都藏在了这间密室里，等待着某一天被正确的人发现。

他等了三百零一年。

等到了薇若兰。

她把日记和照片塞进怀里，站起身来，膝盖撞到金属桌腿，发出一声闷响。

密室的煤油灯还在燃烧。火苗很小，摇摇晃晃。

叹息之墙深处的震动还在继续——

不。

不对。

那不是叹息之墙的震动。

那是一种新的、陌生的、带着金属摩擦感的嗡鸣声。

密室角落里那盏一直亮着的煤油灯突然熄灭了。

同一瞬间，密室外面——叹息之墙的走廊深处——响起了尖锐的警报声。

"嗡——嗡——嗡——"

密涅瓦机关的圣域警报。

薇若兰的身体瞬间紧绷。

她冲到密室的铁门前，把耳朵贴在门上。

门外。

脚步声。

不是一两个人的脚步。

是密集的、训练有素的、带着金属靴底与石板碰撞的脚步声。

然后是一个声音。

冷峻的、带着金属质感的年轻声音，从走廊的尽头传来，每一个字都像是用铁钳夹着说出来的。

"给我搜。"

"一定要找到达·芬奇·博尔吉亚的日记。"

"不能有任何一个人阻止主人重启神国。"

米迦勒。

原罪机关的人。

他们已经闯入了密涅瓦机关。

薇若兰一把将怀里的日记和照片按紧，转身冲向密室的后门——达·芬奇留下的备用人形通道。那条通道的入口隐藏在密室侧墙的暗格里，她刚才进来的时候已经确认过了位置。

她拉开暗格。

通道漆黑一片，但深处有微弱的气流流动——说明通道的另一头是通的。

她没有回头。

她钻进了通道。

身后，密室的铁门被一脚踹开。

金属碰撞声在密室里回荡。

"日记不在这里。"米迦勒的声音从她身后传来，带着压抑的愤怒，"这里有温度——有人来过，走了不超过三十秒。"

"找。"

"给我沿着所有通道找。"

"活要见人，死要见尸。"

薇若兰在漆黑的通道里狂奔。

金属墙壁在她身侧飞速后退，靴底踩在石板上发出急促的"哒哒"声。

她怀里的日记和照片紧紧贴着她的胸口。

三百零一年的秘密。

三百年零一个月。

现在在她怀里。

她必须把它送出去。

送到叹息之墙外面。

送到西泽尔手里。

（本章完）

【English】
Chapter 197 — The Da Vinci Journal, Part Two

The fluorescent stick in her hand had gone the color of weak tea, that thin dying amber that gives a body maybe three more minutes of sight in a stone room. Verolana knelt on the iron floor with the old photograph returned to its place atop the journal and drew a breath that tasted of lamp oil and three hundred years.

She had to finish.

What she had already read she set aside in her mind the way a man sets aside a meal he can no longer stomach. The Star Calendar year 1684. Borgia the First — da Vinci himself — leading a ship into the Avalon ice field, finding the buried branches of the World Tree beneath the blizzard, cutting two lengths from the white wood: one to be forged into the Omega, one into the blade called St. George the Dragonslayer. She had known that part. She had lived inside the consequences of it.

She turned the page.

The handwriting changed on her. In the early pages it had been the clean, square hand of a man who had learned to draw engines and was using the same precision for words. Now the strokes were wrong — the down-strokes too heavy, the loops unsteady, the ink not ink any longer but something darker, the brown-black of dried blood. The paper had been crumpled and smoothed and crumpled again. He had been writing to himself in the small hours. He had been writing to no one.

Star Calendar 1691. I made the wrong decision.

I thought, if I locked the branch in the deepest chamber of Vesuvius, no man alive would ever touch the Machine Kingdom. I forgot the one thing a man in my position is never allowed to forget: I am not only myself. I am also the Pope. And the papacy requires a successor — and my successor need not be another me.

I sealed the heart of the Omega behind the Wall of Sighs and let it sleep. In my papal robes I told the Curia it was the highest secret of the Holy See. In my other name, my true name, I built the Minerva Agency outside the Wall, so that posterity would believe Minerva had been built to guard the secret.

I forgot my own blood.

Verolana's eyes stopped moving.

Star Calendar 1695. Elena, my sister. She was no ordinary Borgia. My mother had conceived her with a man of the East — a star-seer, one of the oracular line. My mother had not understood this herself, and died not understanding. I had thought my sister only a clever girl with a gift for mechanism. I had not known she had inherited the Borgia mind and the star-seer's violet eye.

She could resonate with red mercury from the cradle.

When I sealed the Omega she was eleven years old. She watched me walk into the Wall of Sighs. When I came out she was a different child — silent, watchful, gone somewhere I could not follow. In three months she stole the original schematic for the neural interface from the deepest archive of the Minerva Agency. She took the schematic and vanished.

The Holy See named her heretic. A public burning was held. The body was not recovered.

I had her searched for three years. Nothing.

Until 1703.

He turned the page.

A letter had arrived that year, unsigned, postmarked Ceylon.

It said she had found the last of the star-seers in Ceylon — the people who, generation upon generation, had guarded the roots of the World Tree. She enclosed a painting. A vast tree, roots driven deep into the earth, the fine ends of those roots carved with Sanskrit finer than hair.

She had written beneath the painting: Brother, the World Tree was not cut down. It cut off its own branches, because it was in pain. You took the western branch with you. The eastern branch is kept by the star-seers. Let me keep this one.

He had written back: What do you mean to do.

She had written back: I mean to mingle Borgia blood with star-seer blood and forge a new key. A key that will know both worlds at once.

Verolana's hand went still on the page.

She understood, at last, where Linara had come from.

Linara the Star-Seer. The Ceylonese beauty, the woman whose face had drawn a Pope's eye and earned her the contempt of every salon in Florence. She had not been any ordinary Eastern woman. She had been the daughter of the last star-seer house of Ceylon, the inheritor of the line that guarded the roots. She had also been the reincarnation of Elena Borgia.

Star Calendar 1711. After eight more years I found her at last, in a minor royal palace in Ceylon. She had become a foster-mother to the star-seer orphans. She had married a cadet of one of those island courts. She brought me to see her daughter.

The child's name was Linara. She was three years old. Violet eyes, the brown Borgia curls, the pale, almost colorless skin of the star-seer line. When I came into the room she did not cry. She only watched my face for a long time.

Elena said: This is my daughter, and my continuation. I have not long. The star-seer blood is a curse — every generation of us lives a little shorter than the one before. But I have left my memories in this small body. When she grows, she will remember everything.

I asked: And you?

She said: I shall sleep inside her until the day I am needed.

Verolana turned the page. A second photograph had been folded into the binding, smaller than the first. She drew it out.

It was color, faded to a wash but better preserved than the black-and-white one above. A woman, two children.

The woman in the white sari, violet eyes, a soft mouth, the smile of someone who had learned to be gentle in a world that had been anything but. Her left hand held a girl of perhaps seven — violet eyes — and her right arm cradled an infant, the infant's eyes black-brown.

No writing on the back. She did not need writing.

The violet-eyed girl was Linara as a child.

The black-eyed infant—

This is my grandson.

Verolana's chest tightened. She did not let it tighten. She knew what was coming on the next page. She read it anyway, because she had to read it.

Star Calendar 1730. Linara is grown. She is more beautiful than her mother, colder than her mother, more silent than her mother. She has remembered everything Elena left her — the central liturgy of the Machine Faith, the three-layer seal on the Black Iron Gate, her own double inheritance.

I have decided she must leave Ceylon. She is too dangerous there; the spies of New Rome have begun to find her scent.

I sent her east. To find, in those lands, the people her mother had once known. When she went she did not look back.

She asked me: What is it you want me to do?

I told her: Nothing. Only live. Find a man you love, and bear him a child.

She was silent a long time. At last she said: I understand.

What she understood, da Vinci had scrawled in red ink at the foot of the page, in a hand that had begun to shake: she understood that she herself was the key, and what I wanted was the key's key. The child of the key.

Verolana's fingers closed slowly on the edge of the journal.

She did not speak.

She turned the page.

Star Calendar 1756. Twenty-six years have passed. I am nearly dead. Linara has not returned to Ceylon. She has truly settled in the East. I have had word that she has married.

The man she has married is not a Borgia.

He is an ordinary man. A kind man. A young man. She wrote to me: I have met a man I want to bear a child for. He is not a Pope, not an Emperor, not the envoy of any god. He is only a man who once bought me a paper cone of roasted chestnuts.

I laughed. The blood of the star-seers runs with prophecy and with curse, and she wants to marry a grocer.

I asked her: And the child?

She said: No. I will not have a child inherit the fate of this key.

I respected her decision.

Three pages had been left blank after that. On the fourth the ink was almost black, the pen pressed so hard it had torn the paper in places.

Star Calendar 1762.

The grocer is dead.

Killed in a killing done in the name of the Holy See.

The Cardinal Chamber.

They had found Linara. They knew she was star-seer, knew she was a cadet branch of the Borgia line, knew she was the key. They killed her husband. They threatened her back to Florence.

She came back. She came into Florence with a three-year-old girl in her arms.

Verolana closed the journal.

Her breath was a small, ugly sound in the metal room.

A three-year-old. Violet eyes. Linara returning to Florence with her young daughter, dragged into the cardinals' control, forced into the Pope's bed — the whole long machinery of it, every ugly turning of it, traced back to this single page. Three hundred and one years of pain, and the first tooth of it had been a man selling chestnuts from a paper cone.

She counted three seconds. She let her heart slow.

She opened the journal again.

The girl's name was Yingluo.

Violet eyes, like Elena. The Borgia curls, like Elena.

She was also Elena's continuation.

In the blood of the star-seers, every generation is the vessel of the same soul. Elena had split herself in two: half she had put into Linara, half she had sent down the star-seer line for three hundred years. That half had come to rest, at last, in Yingluo.

So Yingluo and Linara were sisters, and the same soul.

Desmond — the man who has passed himself off as Yingluo's brother — is no kin of hers. He was placed beside her by the Cardinal Chamber. A warder.

But Yingluo was more dangerous than he knew. She carried the full memory of Elena.

I had agents of the Minerva Agency watching her, outside the Royal Marston College of Mechanism. On the day she went into a chapel I received the report. She was praying. Not the prayers of the Messianic Faith — the prayers of the Machine Faith.

She was waking the Elena inside her.

She was hunting for Linara.

She was hunting for me.

The pages had gone brittle now, the ink sometimes crisp, sometimes blurred, the hand of a man writing in a sickbed.

Star Calendar 1771. I am nearly dead. I must set the rest down.

About Cesare—

Verolana's eyes stopped.

In the second year after Linara came back to Florence she bore a child.

The father of the child was not the dead grocer.

The father was the Pope.

Lorenzo Borgia.

The present Pope.

I confirmed this through a line-asset in the Minerva Agency. After Linara was taken into the Cardinal Chamber's custody, she lost the right to refuse.

The child was a forbidden son.

In his veins ran Borgia blood and star-seer blood at once.

His eyes—

Beneath the line da Vinci had drawn a red circle. Inside the circle, a violet star.

I had an agent take a single drop of his blood at his birth. The way that drop behaved in red mercury was not the way any ordinary Borgia blood behaves. It sang out, in the mercury, a light the color of gold.

The same gold as the light given off by the original Omega core.

I understood at last.

The perfect god-servant my sister Elena spent her life pursuing — a carrier that could bond with the World Tree branch and keep a human soul inside it — did not have to be made from the outside at all.

It was already there, in the blood of the Borgia line.

All you needed was a star-seer and a Borgia, brought together.

That child was the key.

In this journal I have given him a name.

Rex Immortalis.

The Immortal King.

He is not a puppet, not a machine, not a tool. He is a man — living, capable of human love, capable of human grief — and yet he carries, in his body, the power to make the two worlds speak to one another.

I must protect him.

If the Cardinal Chamber learns he exists, they will take him at once and make him into a second Omega prototype.

So I sent Franco to hide him. To hide him in Marston.

To hide him in a place where he would not even know his own name.

To wait for him to grow up. To wait for him to find the truth on his own.

The final pages of the journal had been cut out.

Not torn — cut. Verolana could see the clean edge of a pair of small embroidery scissors at the gutter. He had trimmed the pages away himself, on purpose, and left the stubs where they were.

In the middle of the very last page, drawn in red ink, was a single image.

A pentagram, inverted.

At the tip of each of its five points he had drawn a small gear.

The device of the star-seer house of Ceylon.

It was never, in any age, the mark of Satan. It had been slandered into that by Pope Borgia the First for a single reason: he wanted the symbol for himself, with the key-function it carried, and the easiest way to take a holy thing from a foreign people is to make the world afraid of it. The inverted pentagram, in the old star-seer tongue, meant from-below-upward — the people at the bottom of the world, looking up, stealing the light of the sky. It was the mark the star-seers wore when they spoke to the higher powers. It had been on the floor of their temples long before the first Borgia was born.

Beneath the pentagram, in ink faded almost to nothing, da Vinci had written:

Children of Ceylon. The World Tree is yours. The key is yours.

But I beg of you — do not open the Black Iron Gate.

What is inside it is the monster I spent my whole life preventing myself from releasing.

Leave it shut. Forever.

The journal ended.

Verolana closed it. She laid the color photograph, the black-and-white photograph, the third photograph — Linara, and beneath her name in the old Florentine script, My daughter, Elena Borgia — into the breast of her coat. Her fingers would not stop shaking.

It was not fear.

It was three hundred years of lies, three hundred years of plotting, three hundred years of small sacrifices and small murders, all of it laid out in order on a metal table, and the weight of it sat on her chest like a slab.

Old man, she said, very softly, into the small shaking flame of the lamp. You knew all of this. Why didn't you tell anyone.

She already knew why.

Because when da Vinci died, Franco was still a child. Because to tell Franco was to hand Cesare to the Minerva Agency — and the Minerva Agency had its own line into the Cardinal Chamber. Because the only safe place for the truth was a sealed room, in the dark, behind a lock that took a Borgia hand to open.

He had waited three hundred and one years.

He had waited, at last, for her.

She pushed the journal and the photographs deeper into her coat, and she stood. Her knee struck the leg of the metal table. A small flat sound, swallowed by stone.

The coal-oil lamp in the corner of the chamber was still burning. The flame was small. It threw her shadow in long pale slices across the wall.

The tremor in the deep stone of the Wall of Sighs was still going on—

No.

Not that.

Something else. Something new, something she had not heard before, a thin, singing hum, the sound of metal on metal under pressure. A frequency that lived in the bones of the chest rather than the ear.

The lamp in the corner went out.

At the same instant, far down the corridor outside the chamber, a sharper note began.

Weee-oo. Weee-oo. Weee-oo.

The Minerva Sanctuary klaxon.

Verolana's body went iron-taut. She crossed the room in two steps and laid her ear to the iron door.

Outside it: footfalls.

Not one or two. Many. The measured, trained rhythm of boots with metal soles striking stone in unison. The cadence of men moving in formation. A column.

And then a voice.

It came from the far end of the corridor, but the stone carried it the way stone carries everything, dry and even and unhurried. It was the voice of a young man, but it had been stripped of everything young. It had the metallic restraint of a thing that had been taught, very carefully, never to raise itself.

Search the chamber.

Find me the journal of da Vinci Borgia.

No one in the God-King's path of restoration is to be permitted to stand.

Michael.

A man of the Original Sin Agency.

They were already inside the Minerva compound.

Verolana drove her hand flat against the photographs and the journal in her coat. She turned. The back door of the chamber — the emergency humanoid passage da Vinci had built into the side wall — had its concealed panel set into the stone at a height she had measured when she came in. She crossed to it in three strides. Her fingers found the seam.

She pulled the panel open.

The passage behind it was a throat of absolute black. From the bottom of it, though, a faint current moved against her face. The far end of the passage was open. Air came through. The passage ran somewhere she could reach.

She did not look back.

She went in, head-first.

Behind her, with a sound like a fist hitting a wall, the iron door of the chamber was kicked open.

The sound of the kick went on ringing off the metal walls.

The journal is not in here, Michael's voice said behind her, tight with a fury that had not yet decided to be loud. Someone has been here. The air is warm. Less than thirty seconds gone.

Find them.

Follow every passage.

I want them alive. I want them dead. I do not care which.

Verolana ran.

The metal walls slipped past her on either side. The stone under her boots rang with the small bright clatter of a body moving as fast as a body can move. The journal and the photographs were pressed flat against her chest by the flat of her hand, and she could feel the old paper through the cloth of her coat, three hundred and one years of it, warm against her ribs.

Three hundred and one years.

One month more.

And now the secret was in her arms, and the men who wanted it were behind her in the dark.

She had to get it out.

Out through the Wall of Sighs.

Out into the light.

Out to Cesare.

End of Chapter 197

第198章 屠龙者的回归（上）
