【中文】
第198章 屠龙者的回归（上）

维苏威火山深处，金色灯柱沿着通道两侧依次亮起，照亮了三百年来从未有人走过的路。

达·芬奇·博尔吉亚在三百年前开凿的秘密通道沿着维苏威火山北麓的岩层蜿蜒向下。通道内壁镶嵌着数以万计的黄铜微型齿轮，每个齿轮表面都刻着古老的梵文，齿缝中透出金色的光，光芒随着某种看不见的脉动微微明灭。

瓦莲京娜走在最前面。

她左手握着那枚拇指盖大小的银饰——母亲叶尼塞王妃留下的世界树残枝启动符。银饰断面上刻的半朵莲花在金光中隐隐泛着微光，像活的一样脉动。

"按照母亲的图示，"她低声说，"从这里到黑铁巨门的前厅还有不到五百米。"

"五百米？"唐璜抹了把脸，"早说啊，我还以为要走断腿呢。"

"你不是说后背发凉吗？"昆提良瓮声瓮气地说。

"凉和断腿是两回事。"

"都安静。"阿方索压低声音，目光扫过通道两侧的齿轮，"这里每一个齿轮都连着红水银网络。我们现在在维苏威火山的心脏里，说话音量控制在能听见就行。"

阿方索是这支队伍里最冷静的人。当年炽天骑士团里的机械师和数学家，后来在翡冷翠贫民区开修理店时那种工程师式的理性到现在也没丢。

西泽尔走在瓦莲京娜身后，安静地听着他们拌嘴。

他的手指无意识地按在后颈——黄金套管的位置。

套管在升温。

不是他熟悉的微温，而是真正的发烫，温度高到让他的皮肤感觉到刺痛。这是世界树残枝共鸣的征兆，而且比以往任何一次都要强烈。

他停下脚步。

"怎么了？"瓦莲京娜回头。

西泽尔没回答。他盯着通道两侧的墙壁。

墙壁上那些原本刻着梵文的黄铜齿轮开始转动。

"咔咔咔咔——"

细微的机械声在通道里回荡，像是某种古老的乐器被唤醒。齿轮的齿缝中透出光线——不是金色，而是一种更冷的颜色。

青蓝色。

光线交织、汇聚，在通道两面墙壁上形成了清晰的投影。

投影里，是维苏威火山北麓的矿道入口。

莲生。

他穿着屠龙者圣乔治的甲胄，站在被炸成废墟的矿道入口前。

那台甲胄比西泽尔见过的新型红龙还要大得多。肩高超过五米，全身覆盖着暗金色的装甲板，胸前镶嵌着一颗巨大的红水银核心——核心跳动得像是心脏。

不，不止一颗。

西泽尔数了数。

四颗。

四颗红水银核心分别嵌在甲胄的胸腔、左肩、右肩和背后，四颗核心同时运转，发出隆隆的轰鸣声，震得整个矿道的岩壁都在颤抖。

而莲生面前，是五台普罗米修斯。

圣堂装甲师的制式巨型机动傀儡。每台身高都在七米以上，配备重型火炮和近战武器。五台普罗米修斯排成弧形包围了莲生，蒸汽从它们的关节处喷出，金属摩擦声在矿道里回荡。

"他疯了吗？"唐璜失声说，"一个人对五台普罗米修斯？"

没有人回答。

因为投影里的莲生已经动了。

屠龙者圣乔治的四颗核心同时过载，喷射出上千度的红水银火焰——不是普通的蒸汽，而是液态的、燃烧着的红水银，温度高到空气都被扭曲。火焰形成四道扇形的喷射口，从四个方向同时扫过战场。

第一台普罗米修斯举起盾牌格挡。

红水银火焰的温度超过了影金属的熔点。盾牌在接触的瞬间就开始发红、软化、最终被烧穿了一个大洞。火焰穿透缺口，灌进了普罗米修斯的骑士舱。

沉闷的爆响。

第一台普罗米修斯倒下了，蒸汽从它破碎的关节处喷出。

"一台。"阿方索低声说。

莲生没有停顿。屠龙者圣乔治向前跨出一步——那一步的速度比西泽尔预想的快得多。五米高的巨型甲胄却有着不属于这个体型的灵活，像一头暴怒的犀牛冲进了羊群。

火焰再次喷射，吞噬了第二台普罗米修斯的腿部关节。

第二台轰然倒地。

"两台。"

然后是第三台。

这台普罗米修斯的骑士显然更有经验。他没有试图格挡，而是操控甲胄向后急退。但屠龙者圣乔治的速度更快——它的左臂抬起，手掌中凝聚出一团高密度的红水银火球，投射出去。

火球精准地命中了第三台普罗米修斯的胸腔。

爆炸。

红水银的火焰像是活物一样沿着装甲板的缝隙蔓延、侵蚀、燃烧。

"三台。"

三台普罗米修斯在不到两分钟的时间里被全部摧毁。

西泽尔的手指不自觉地按紧了后颈的黄金套管。

套管烫得发疼。

他意识到有什么不对。

屠龙者圣乔治的运作方式不对。

他见过这台甲胄。几年前它闯入密涅瓦机关时——那时候它确实可怕，每一个动作都精确而高效——但那种"精确"里带着明显的"操作"痕迹。每一个动作都像是从驾驶舱里通过神经接驳下达的指令，精确但生硬，像是一个技术高超的棋手在下棋。

但现在不一样了。

现在屠龙者圣乔治的每一个动作都像是有自己的意志。

它闪避普罗米修斯攻击的方式不是"看到攻击然后做出反应"，而是"预判攻击然后提前回避"。它选择攻击目标的顺序不是随机或按照骑士的指令，而是按照最有效率的方式——先烧毁腿部让普罗米修斯失去机动能力，再攻击胸腔摧毁骑士舱。

它知道自己在做什么。

不，它知道自己想做什么。

"这台甲胄……"阿方索的声音变得很轻，"它有自主行动模块吗？"

"不可能。"唐璜摇头，"原罪机关再疯狂也不会给一台巨型机动傀儡装这种模块。"

"那它现在的行为怎么解释？"昆提良皱着眉，"你看它闪避第三台普罗米修斯炮击的方式——那是提前了至少半秒预判出来的。神经接驳的信号传导做不到这个延迟，除非……"

"除非它自己看到了攻击。"阿方索接话，"自己做出了判断。"

通道里一阵沉默。

西泽尔后颈的黄金套管又烫了几分。

他觉得自己能"听到"什么。

那是一种节奏感——一种来自很远很远的、却又近在咫尺的节奏感。

咚。咚。咚。

屠龙者圣乔治的心跳。

不，不只是屠龙者圣乔治。

是世界树残枝的心跳。

西泽尔的紫瞳在通道的黑暗里亮了起来。金红色的纹路在瞳孔中浮现，沿着虹膜蔓延，像是有人用烧红的细针在他的眼睛里绣花纹。这是星见血脉共鸣时的表现——他曾经在激活不朽之王模式时出现过同样的状态。

"你怎么了？"瓦莲京娜立刻注意到了他。

"它在跳动。"西泽尔说，声音很轻。

"什么？"

"屠龙者圣乔治。"西泽尔说，"它不是一台甲胄。"

他顿了顿。

"它是世界树残枝的一部分。"

瓦莲京娜的表情微微变化。她从怀里取出母亲留下的示意图——一张泛黄的纸，上面用精密的线条画着黑铁巨门周围的结构。图纸的角落里标注着几行小字，是叶尼塞王妃的笔迹。

"按照这个图示，"瓦莲京娜指着图上的一条红线，"我们现在走的这条通道通向黑铁巨门的前厅。前厅距离我们还有不到五百米。"

"五百米。"阿方索重复了一遍，"不远。"

"但是……"瓦莲京娜皱起眉头，"图上这里没有标注其他的出口。如果投影里显示的是真的，那莲生现在是在维苏威火山北麓的矿道入口。从那里到黑铁巨门……"

"至少要穿过大半个火山。"西泽尔说。

通道里一阵沉默。

投影里，战斗还在继续。

两台普罗米修斯幸存了下来——它们是五台中体型最大的两台，肩高都超过了七米，装备着重型护甲和大口径火炮。它们学聪明了，不再试图近战，而是拉开距离，同时举起了炮管。

"龙吼炮。"阿方索的眼睛眯了起来。

那是普罗米修斯系列最强的远程武器——一门大口径火炮，炮弹内灌满了高纯度红水银。发射后炮弹划弧线下落，爆炸时可以把大片区域化为火海。

两台普罗米修斯同时开火。

两道红光划破矿道的黑暗，拖着长长的尾焰，精准地击中了屠龙者圣乔治。

第一发命中左肩。

第二发命中左胸。

爆炸。

红水银的火焰在屠龙者圣乔治的左半身炸开。装甲板在高温下变形、剥落，露出下面的骑士之骨。左胸的一颗红水银核心——四颗中的一颗——被直接命中。

核心爆裂。

那是一声沉闷的、带着金属碎裂声的爆炸。核心爆裂的瞬间，红水银的液体像是喷泉一样从缺口处喷涌而出，灌进了甲胄的内部，在地上汇成一片发光的红色池塘。

"莲生！"阿方索失声喊道。

投影里，屠龙者圣乔治的动作明显迟缓了下来。三颗核心还在运转，但左半身已经失去了大部分功能。它的左臂垂了下去，左肩的装甲板还在冒烟，破碎的核心里漏出的红水银在地面上蜿蜒流淌，像一条发光的血河。

但驾驶舱里，莲生没有倒下。

画面太远，看不清他的表情，但西泽尔能看到——驾驶舱的视窗玻璃上，有一抹红色。

血。

莲生吐出的血溅在了视窗上。

但他在笑。

即使隔着这么远的距离，西泽尔也能感觉到那笑容的存在。那不是恐惧、不是绝望、也不是疯狂，而是某种平静的、甚至是愉悦的笑。

像是期待已久的事情终于发生了。

"这个疯子……"昆提良低声说。

瓦莲京娜看着投影里莲生的脸，指节慢慢收紧，握住了腰间青丝古剑的剑柄。

西泽尔闭上了眼睛。

他双手合十。

紫瞳金纹在黑暗中亮得刺眼。金红色的纹路从瞳孔中蔓延到整个虹膜，再沿着他的眼角向太阳穴延伸。后颈的黄金套管发出了肉眼可见的暗红色光芒，温度高到让他的皮肤发红，像是有东西在他的血管里燃烧。

他在祈祷。

不，不是祈祷。

他在共鸣。

通过世界树残枝的共鸣，他将自己的意识延伸出去——延伸过五百米的岩层，延伸过数不清的黄铜齿轮，延伸过那三颗还在艰难运转的红水银核心——

他在寻找莲生。

"老板！"阿方索注意到了他的异常，伸手想要拉住他。

"别碰他！"瓦莲京娜拦住了阿方索，"他在使用世界树残枝的共鸣——"

西泽尔的声音在矿道里回荡，平静，清晰，带着一种奇异的穿透力：

"莲生！"

"带屠龙者圣乔治过来！"

"我能帮你修复它的机械心脏！"

【English】
Chapter 198 — The Dragon-Slayer Returns (Part 1)

The light found them first.

A column of gold woke in the rock. Then another. Then a third, a fourth, a long chain of them strung down the throat of the corridor, each one snapping on with the small click of an old brass latch. They had not been lit in three hundred years. They lit now because the party had entered, and the mechanism had been waiting — patient, mechanical, indifferent to politics and war and the long forgetting of men — for someone to enter.

Valentina walked in front.

The tunnel ran deep into the north flank of Mount Vesuvius, a wound in the rock carved three centuries ago by the engineer-philosopher Leonardo Borgia and sealed behind it on the day he walked out. The walls sweated brass. Tens of thousands of miniature gears were set into the stone — a fitted mosaic of toothed metal, each one no larger than a thumbnail, each one etched on its face with a syllable of old Sanskrit. The light bled up out of the gaps between the teeth, and the light pulsed, and the pulse was not the pulse of any flame Valentina had ever seen. It was slower. Wet. Like the throb of a vein.

She held her left hand closed around the silver charm her mother had left her. The size of her thumbnail, broken across the middle, the fracture running through a half-carved lotus. Yenisei, Princess of the Frozen Mouth, had pressed it into her daughter's palm the morning the convoy rode out, and the charm had been warm then, and it was warm now, and the half-lotus glowed faintly as if it were remembering how to bloom.

"According to my mother's diagram," Valentina said, her voice pitched low, "we are less than five hundred metres from the antechamber of the Black Iron Gate."

"Five hundred." Don Juan dragged the back of his glove across his cheek. "You could have said so. I was bracing myself for a three-day crawl."

"You were the one complaining your spine was cold," said Quintilian from the rear.

"Cold and broken are different provinces of suffering."

"Both of you, hush." Alfonso did not raise his voice. He never had to. He spoke the way a man tightens a bolt — one firm turn and the thing stopped moving. His eyes went along the corridor walls, lingering on the brass. "Every one of these gears is wired into the crimson mercury lattice. We are standing inside the heart of Vesuvius. Speak only as loud as you need to be heard."

Alfonso had been the calmest man in the room his entire life. He had been a mechanist and a mathematician under the Seraphim Order in his youth, and later, when the Order had stopped being a thing he could stand inside of, he had opened a small repair shop in the poor quarter of Florence and gone on being precise. Some men, stripped of rank, become smaller. Alfonso had simply continued.

Cesare walked two paces behind Valentina, listening to the others argue without joining.

His right hand had risen, almost of its own accord, and was resting against the back of his neck — the place where the golden cannula lay buried under the skin, the small bright tube the surgeons at the Minerva Mechanism had seated against his spine when he was a child. He had grown so used to it that most days he forgot it was there.

Today it was not letting him forget.

It was warming. Not the small, almost-tender heat he knew, the gentle ember of the thing, but a real heat, a heat that pricked the skin above it and made the fine hairs on the back of his hand lie flat. He let his fingers rest there. The cannula was answering something. Something at the other end of the mountain, or inside it, was calling down the same line.

He slowed.

Valentina turned. "Cesare?"

He did not answer her. He was watching the walls.

The little gears had begun to turn.

The sound was a small, dry music — tick, tick, tick — like a hundred pocket watches laid on a wooden floor. The teeth carried the light with them as they moved, and the light, as it shifted, was no longer gold. It was something colder, something with a name of its own — the colour of a vein seen through the thin skin of a temple, the colour of a sky just before it cuts loose. Cyan. The cyan light braided itself along the corridor, gathered, focused, and on the two walls of the passage, in parallel, a picture began to draw itself out of nothing.

A mine entrance. The north slope of Vesuvius. Rock and timber and the soft black mouths of a dozen shafts going down into the mountain. Smoke — or steam — rising in slow columns. The wooden frames of the head-gear were torn. The ground was broken. The night was very dark behind it.

And in front of the entrance, on legs like the trunks of small trees, stood a single figure in armour.

Liansheng.

The St. George the Dragon-Slayer.

Cesare had seen this machine once before, three years ago, when it had come clawing into the upper galleries of the Minerva Mechanism and the world had nearly ended. He had never forgotten the size of it. He had never forgotten the sound of its stride. Standing there now, in the cyan light, the armour was larger than he remembered. Five metres to the shoulder. A hunched and brutal silhouette, plated in dark gold, with a single great core of crimson mercury set into its breast — no, not a single core. Cesare counted. Four. Four cores, one in the chest, one over each shoulder, one set into the spine at the small of the back, and all four of them running at once, so that the machine seemed to breathe the way a horse breathes after a long hard gallop — in, out, in, out — and the air around it shimmered with the heat that bled off a thing burning that hot.

Across from Liansheng, arrayed in a half-circle at the mouth of the mine, stood five Prometheus battle-mechs of the Holy Chapel Armoury.

Seven metres apiece. The standard heavy configuration, with the long-barrelled deck guns folded up across their shoulders and the close-combat blades half-sheathed at their hips. They were the colour of dull iron. Steam hissed from the knuckle joints of their hands, and the metal of their masks gave back the cyan light of the projection in long, empty stares.

"He's lost his mind," Don Juan said. "One man against five Prometheuses?"

No one answered him. Inside the picture, Liansheng had already moved.

The St. George took one stride forward and opened its mouth. There was no mouth. There was an array of four nozzles set into the collar of the armour, and from those four nozzles, in the same instant, it vomited. Not steam. Liquid. A bright arterial flood of molten crimson mercury at a temperature the air could not survive — a thousand degrees, perhaps more — fanning out in four overlapping arcs that swept the half-circle of Prometheuses the way a scythe sweeps a field of wheat.

The first Prometheus tried to block. It swung up the heavy shield strapped across its left arm and held the shield in front of its breast and prayed to whatever mech-pilots pray to.

The shield went the colour of a cherry in a second. In two seconds it was soft. In three seconds there was a hole in the middle of it the size of a man, ragged, the edges still running like hot wax, and through the hole the flood of liquid mercury poured into the cockpit and met a man inside it. There was a sound — a deep, wet, percussive sound, like a barrel of apples dropped from a roof — and the first Prometheus went over backwards, its arms still raised, steam screaming from every broken joint.

Alfonso, very quietly, said, "One."

Liansheng did not stop. The St. George took a second stride and that stride was too fast. Five metres tall, half a tonne of crimson mercury in its heart, and yet the step had the easy, heavy grace of a charging rhinoceros. It came into the second Prometheus and the nozzles sang again, this time lower, at the legs, and the legs of the Prometheus came apart at the knee as if they had been designed to do so. The mech sat down in the rubble. It did not fall. It sat.

"Two."

The third pilot knew his trade. He was already walking his machine backwards, arms in, head down, trying to put distance between himself and the thing in gold. The St. George's left hand came up. The palm opened. Something was gathering in the palm — a tight, dense, white-hot bead of mercury, the size of a fist, the size of a heart, the size of a thing that has been told to remember it is a star. The St. George threw it.

The bead met the third Prometheus square in the chest and went through the breastplate as if the breastplate had been a suggestion, and the inside of the cockpit bloomed into a private sun, and the bloom of the sun reached up out of the collar and the shoulders and ate the head of the mech away to a stub of slag.

"Three."

Three Prometheuses, in less time than it takes to boil an egg.

Cesare's fingers, on the back of his neck, had gone white at the tips.

Something was wrong.

He had seen the St. George before, in the upper galleries of the Minerva Mechanism, and the St. George he had seen then had been — yes — terrible, but it had been terrible in the way a very good chess player is terrible. Every motion had been a decision. Every decision had a tell, the small, mechanical lag between the pilot's nerve and the machine's limb, the half-second of translation between a thought in a man's skull and the obedient act of a hand of forged gold. The St. George had moved, three years ago, like a man inside a man.

This St. George was not moving like that.

This St. George was moving like a man.

The way it had stepped around the second Prometheus's dying countermove — the casual, almost leisurely sidestep, the weight already transferred before the gun had finished its arc — that was not reaction. That was anticipation. Half a second, at least, ahead of the attack, the machine had already chosen where it would be standing when the attack arrived. And the order in which it had destroyed the mechs — legs first, mobility first, then the chest, then the cockpit — was the order any engineer in Florence would have prescribed, if the engineer had been asked to design the most efficient possible way to take a Prometheus apart.

It knew what it was doing. More than that. It knew what it wanted to do.

"Alfonso," Cesare said. His voice was very even. "Does the St. George have an autonomous action module?"

"No." Alfonso did not even hesitate. "Not even the original-sin engineers were mad enough to mount one in a heavy combat platform."

"Then how do you explain what we are watching?"

Quintilian leaned closer to the wall. "Look at the way it dodged the third mech's parting shot. That read came at least half a second before the gun fired. A pilot on a neural link cannot transmit intent that fast. The signal has to travel from eye, to brain, to spine, to jack, to actuator. It cannot be done."

"Unless," said Alfonso, slowly, "there is no pilot making the read."

The corridor was quiet for a long time. Only the small click of the gears.

Cesare's cannula was burning him now. Not gently. He could feel the heat travel down the small of his back, the warmth branching into the shoulder blades, the warmth settling into the soft place at the base of the skull. And with the heat came a sound. Not a sound his ears were hearing. A sound his spine was hearing. A rhythm, low and far and close at the same time, the way a great bell is both in the tower that holds it and in the ground that holds the tower.

Thud. Thud. Thud.

The heart of the St. George. No — more than that.

The heart of the World Tree Remnant.

He closed his eyes without meaning to. Behind his eyelids, in the dark, his purple irises began to glow. The glow was not purple. It was a thread of gold-red, fine as a hair, brighter than a hair, drawn through the iris the way a wire is drawn through a bead. The thread branched. It branched again. It wrote itself, line by line, across the coloured skin of his eye and out, in a slow hot tracery, along the corners of his lids and the soft skin at his temples. He had seen this happen to himself only once before, in the chamber beneath the Minerva Mechanism, when the Immortal King protocol had first woken in his blood and the floor had tried to eat the world.

He was not doing this. The blood was.

"What is it?" Valentina. Close. The word on her breath.

"It is beating," Cesare said.

"What is?"

"The St. George."

He opened his eyes. The gold-red threads did not leave them.

"It is not a mech."

He paused. The world, in that pause, was the small click of ten thousand brass gears and the slow wet pulse of a thing that was older than any of them.

"It is a piece of the World Tree."

Valentina did not answer at once. She drew the folded paper from inside her coat — the diagram her mother had drawn, on a sheet so old the ink had gone the colour of weak tea, the lines still fine, still exact, drawn by a hand that had loved precision more than it had loved most people. In the lower right corner, in her mother's small neat hand, were four lines of script. Valentina had read them a hundred times. She had never entirely understood them.

"According to this," she said, and her finger rested on a red line that ran the length of the page, "this corridor opens onto the antechamber of the Black Iron Gate. We are perhaps five hundred metres from it."

"Five hundred," said Alfonso. "Close."

"But." Valentina's finger moved. "The diagram marks no other exit. The projection is showing the north slope mine entrance, where Liansheng is now standing. From the mine to the Black Iron Gate —"

"You would have to go through the better part of the mountain," Cesare said.

The cyan light went on flickering on the wall. The battle was not finished.

Two Prometheuses were left. They were the largest of the five, both of them over seven metres, both plated in the heavy chapel-issue laminate, both carrying, mounted across the shoulder yoke, the long grey barrel of a weapon that needed no introduction. The Dragon Roar. The chapel's answer to anything that walked and breathed and was not, itself, a Prometheus. A high-calibre shell packed with refined crimson mercury, fired in a flat arc, detonating into a pool of fire the size of a town square.

Both barrels lifted together. The muzzles were aimed at the heart of the St. George.

They fired.

The first shell hit the left shoulder. The second hit the left breast. The detonations came a half-second apart, but the eye refused to register them separately. They were a single white event. The left side of the St. George vanished into a flower of red fire. The dark gold plating ran like tallow, slid down the arm in long bright strips, exposed the knight-skeleton beneath, the clean pale bone of the warframe, the rivet heads popping one after the other like a string of small detonations travelling down a fuse. The left shoulder core — one of the four, one of the four hearts — took a piece of shrapnel through its housing, and the core went. The sound it made going was not loud. It was the sound of a great glass bell struck once, very hard, in a quiet room.

The molten mercury from the broken core ran out of the wound in a bright slow river. It ran down the flank of the armour, down the thigh, and pooled on the ground of the projection, glowing, throwing back the cyan light in long wavering red lines, as if the machine were bleeding.

Cesare saw the cockpit.

The image was not close enough for detail, but it was close enough for the smear. A long, deliberate red smear on the inside of the vision slit. Liansheng's mouth had been open when the shell hit. He had bitten the inside of his cheek, or his tongue, or something deeper, and what came out had been thrown forward against the glass by the deceleration, and the glass had held it there.

And Liansheng was smiling.

Cesare could not have explained how he knew this. The image was a flat, grainy, blue-tinged thing. The cockpit was a black slot in a black mask. But he knew. The posture of the shoulders. The way the head was held. The almost devotional angle of the chin. The smile of a man for whom the worst thing that could happen had finally happened, and the worst thing was the thing he had been waiting for.

"He's mad," Quintilian said, very softly. "He is smiling."

Valentina's hand, without her having told it to, had closed on the wrapped grip of the ancient blade at her waist. The cord of the binding creaked.

Cesare folded his hands together.

The gold-red threads in his eyes had reached his temples. The cannula in the back of his neck was throwing off a visible heat, a shimmer in the cold air of the tunnel, a small red glow that he could feel against his own hair. Something was running in him. Not blood. Not quite. The Star-Sight line in his marrow had woken — the line of his blood that was older than the Borgias, older than the Order, older than the names they had given themselves — and it was answering, now, to the rhythm it had heard through the rock.

He was not praying. He was reaching.

Down the corridor. Through the brass. Through the toothed mosaic of ten thousand small wheels. Through the lattice of crimson mercury that Leonardo Borgia had strung, three hundred years ago, like a nervous system through the body of a sleeping mountain. Through the three wounded hearts of the St. George, still beating, still dragging their weight around the broken shoulder, refusing the order to stop. Through the wet red smear on the inside of the cockpit glass.

"Alfonso." He heard his own voice as if it belonged to someone further down the tunnel. "Don't."

Alfonso's hand had been reaching for his shoulder. The hand stopped. Alfonso looked at Valentina. Valentina shook her head, once.

"It is the resonance of the Remnant," she said. "Don't break it. He is out on the line."

Cesare spoke. His voice, in the brass throat of the corridor, was not loud. It did not need to be loud. It had the carrying quality of a thing that is being heard in a different place by a different ear.

"Liansheng."

The name went out of him.

"Bring the St. George to me."

A breath. The cannula flared once at the back of his neck, bright enough to throw a small coin of red light on the wall behind him.

"I can mend the machine's heart."


==================================================
第199章 屠龙者的回归（中）
==================================================

【中文】
第199章 屠龙者的回归（中）

投影里，屠龙者圣乔治缓缓后退。

那动作让所有人都屏住了半口气——一台重达二十吨的百年前顶级炽天使，正拖着被击穿左胸的身躯，笨拙地、如同一头受伤的巨兽般向后退缩。左臂彻底垂落，肩甲还在冒着青灰色的烟，被龙吼炮烧蚀的边缘泛着暗红色。

莲生在驾驶舱里笑了一下。

他吐出的血溅在视窗上，触目惊心，但他似乎毫不在意。投影太远，看不清他的脸，可西泽尔能感觉到那笑容的存在——平静的，甚至带着某种如释重负的欢愉。

投影里，五台普罗米修斯重新调整了阵型。

"他要跑了！"某台普罗米修斯的骑士在通讯频道里高喊，"别让他退进矿道！两翼包抄！"

"压住左翼！龙吼炮装填需要四十秒！四十秒内他跑不了多远！"

"零号机正面牵制，二号从右翼绕后！"

矿道入口外，蒸汽喇叭再次拉响。隆隆的回声传过五百米的岩层，在西泽尔他们所在的灯柱通道里嗡嗡作响。

"他听到我们了。"阿方索盯着投影，声音有些干涩，"他在朝我们这边退。"

"不是朝我们。"瓦莲京娜说。

西泽尔睁开了眼。

紫瞳金纹还在跳动，像烧红的铁丝被埋进冰里，正在缓慢熄灭。后颈的黄金套管已经不再灼热，但他的额头布满了汗珠，顺着苍白的颧骨滑下来。

"不是朝我们，"他重复瓦莲京娜的话，声音比平时更轻，"是朝那个维修站。"

"什么维修站？"昆提良问。

"三百年前达·芬奇留下的。"西泽尔抬手指向通道左侧岩壁，"那道门。"

众人顺着他的手指看去。

金色的灯柱照亮了两侧粗粝的岩壁，看不出任何门的痕迹。灰黑色的火山岩表面布满了凿痕和锈迹，和维苏威火山内部任何一段岩壁没有区别。

但西泽尔盯着那面墙看了一秒钟后，后颈的黄金套管再次发出了微弱的暗红色光。

岩壁上，一道发丝般细的红色线条浮现出来。

紧接着是第二条，第三条，第四条——那些线条像血管一样在岩壁表面蔓延，勾勒出一道高约四米、宽约三米的拱形轮廓。轮廓线的交汇处，嵌着一枚暗金色的齿轮徽记。

机械神教徽记。

齿轮中心嵌着五芒星，五芒星的每个角末端连接着一圈更小的齿轮。

"原来在那里……"阿方索喃喃道。

西泽尔抬起右手，将掌心按在那枚暗金色徽记上。

徽记的齿轮缓缓转动。

没有蒸汽喷发，没有机械轰鸣，只有齿轮与齿轮咬合时发出的细微咔嗒声，像心跳一样有节奏。那声音在安静的灯柱通道里格外清晰，一声接一声地传出去。

岩壁无声地裂开。

门后是一条短而窄的甬道，尽头透出暗淡的金色光。当那道门完全打开的时候，一股陈旧的气味扑面而来——不是腐烂，而是金属、机油、棉布和火药混合后被封存了几百年的干燥气息。

甬道尽头是一间宽阔的地下室。

"我的天……"唐璜的声音里带着不自觉的敬畏。

那是一间巨大的维修车间。

天花板上悬垂着数十条蒸汽管道和电缆，虽然已经锈蚀大半，铜管表面生出了绿色的铜锈，但依然保持着完好的结构。地面铺着厚实的铁板，被几百年的灰尘覆盖，踩上去发出沉闷的嘎吱声。

最引人注目的是车间两侧的货架。

那些货架从地面一直延伸到天花板，像图书馆里整齐排列的书架。每一层都摆满了形状各异的金属零件——有弯曲的脊椎骨架，有断裂的肩甲，有烧蚀过半的头盔，有内部线路裸露的胸腔模块，还有数不清的齿轮、轴承、铆钉、电缆和蒸汽导管。

全是炽天使的零件。

全是三百多年前的款式。

每一件都覆盖着厚厚的灰尘，但金属表面依然泛着暗光——那些零件的材质远超现代甲胄，保存了三个世纪也没有被腐蚀。

"这些全是……"阿方索走近最近的一个货架，伸手拂去一块肩甲上的灰尘。灰尘落下的瞬间，肩甲表面露出了一行烫金的小字：

"密涅瓦·原型·B-12·左肩组件·星历134年。"

"全是初代原型机的备件。"阿方索的声音微微发颤，"达·芬奇总长给屠龙者圣乔治准备的备件库。"

唐璜走到车间最里面，吹了一声口哨。

"你们看这个。"

那里是一面巨大的岩壁，上面用铜钉固定着一张展开的工程图纸。图纸高约五米、宽约三米，虽然纸张已经发黄变脆，但线条依然清晰。图纸上画着一台完整的人形甲胄，标注了每一个部件的名称、材质和加工工艺。

图的下方，用端正的拉丁文写着一行字：

"Dux Bellorum Georgius · 屠龙者圣乔治 · 达·芬奇·博尔吉亚·总工程师监制 · 星历1684年。"

就是屠龙者圣乔治的设计图。

三百年前的那张原图。

投影里，屠龙者圣乔治的身影出现在了矿道入口的边缘。

它跌跌撞撞地后退，残存的右臂撑着岩壁，每一步都踩出一个深深的脚印。三颗红水银核心在胸腔和双肩的位置透出暗红色的光，像三颗垂死的星辰。左胸那个巨大的空洞里，还残留着断裂的线路和烧焦的金属边缘。

它的身后，两台普罗米修斯正紧追不舍。

"他快到了。"瓦莲京娜说。

西泽尔已经走进了维修车间深处。

他在车间的尽头看到了他要找的东西——两条粗壮的机械臂从天花板上垂下来，末端是精密的金属手指。那些机械臂被锈蚀得几乎和周围的管道融为一体，但当西泽尔踏入车间时，它们开始发出微弱的嗡鸣声。

齿轮在转动。

整间维修车间都在缓缓苏醒。

那些锈蚀的管道里，蒸汽开始流动。铜锈从管壁上剥落，露出里面仍然完好的铜管内壁。天花板上的灯依次亮起，昏黄的光芒照亮了车间里每一件沉睡三百年的零件。

西泽尔站在两条机械臂的正下方。

他再次闭上了眼睛。

紫瞳金纹亮起。

这一次比之前更亮、更持久。金红色的纹路从瞳孔向外扩散，覆盖了整个虹膜，又从眼角向太阳穴延伸，像某种古老的文字被铭刻在他的皮肤表面。后颈的黄金套管发出强烈的暗红色光，温度高到他颈部的皮肤都泛起了潮红。

他在共鸣。

不是祈祷。不是呼唤。

是命令。

世界树残枝——这个沉睡在维苏威火山深处三百年的古老意志——通过他的血脉向外延伸，触达了这间维修车间里的每一条管道、每一个齿轮、每一台机械。

机械臂动了。

先是右手那条。

它缓缓升起，金属手指一张一合，像一个沉睡了很久的人伸了个懒腰。然后它转向了车间左侧的货架，从第二层取下了一个被油布包裹的方形物体。油布被剥落，里面是一颗拳头大小的暗金色球体。

机械心脏。

备用机械心脏。

三百年前达·芬奇为屠龙者圣乔治预制的第四颗备用核心。

右手机械臂托着那颗核心，转身朝车间入口的方向移动。左手机械臂则去取修复用的工具——焊枪、扳手、线路校准仪、固定夹具——一件件地送到了工作台上。

"他……"阿方索看着这一切，嘴唇动了动。

"他在用世界树残枝的权限。"瓦莲京娜替他说完了。她的声音很轻，但手已经按在了青丝古剑的剑柄上，指节微微泛白。

"机械臂认的不是他，是这间车间的初代管理权限。"她顿了一下，"但他正在夺取那个权限。"

车间外面，蒸汽喇叭的嘶鸣声越来越近。

投影里，屠龙者圣乔治终于退到了矿道入口边缘。它的动作越来越迟缓，每后退一步都伴随着金属关节的刺耳摩擦声。身后那两台普罗米修斯已经追到了不足五十米的距离，龙吼炮正在装填，炮口对准了它残存的背部。

"莲生！"投影里传来通讯频道中某个人的声音，"最后警告！交出屠龙者圣乔治，饶你不死！"

驾驶舱里，莲生抬起头，视窗上的血迹让他的脸看起来格外苍白。但他的嘴唇动了——

他说了什么。

投影没有声音，看不到他说的话。但西泽尔看到了他的口型。

西泽尔的身体微微一震。

"怎么了？"唐璜问。

"他说了两个字。"西泽尔没有睁眼，紫瞳金纹在他的眼睑下跳动，像两条被烧红的蛇，"'来了'。"

矿道入口处，屠龙者圣乔治忽然转身。

它残存的右臂猛地砸向身旁的岩壁，整台甲胄借力旋转，三颗红水银核心同时爆发出超负荷的光芒——一道暗红色的红水银火柱从它的胸腔中央喷涌而出，直扑追击的两台普罗米修斯。

那是屠龙者圣乔治的核心武器——液态红水银火焰。

温度足以熔化影金属。

那两台普罗米修斯的骑士被这突如其来的反击打了个措手不及，前冲的惯性让它们无法闪避，只能举盾硬扛。影金属的装甲板在红水银火焰中迅速软化、发红，边缘开始卷曲。

但屠龙者圣乔治已经转身了。

它没有继续战斗，而是朝矿道深处猛冲。三颗核心全功率运转，每一步都让整个矿道的岩壁震颤。它像一个浑身着火、但义无反顾奔向火葬场的巨人，一头扎进了矿道入口。

三步。

两步。

一步。

它冲进了金色灯柱通道。

"关门！"西泽尔说。

机械臂没有手来做这件事。

但车间的墙壁替他做了。门框两侧的岩壁在齿轮的驱动下缓缓合拢，将那条短甬道封闭得严严实实。合拢的瞬间，外面传来了金属碰撞的巨响——那两台普罗米修斯追到了门口，一头撞在了刚刚合上的岩壁上。

"咚咚咚！"

沉闷的撞击声从岩壁另一侧传来，每一下都让车间的天花板落下细碎的灰尘。那些蒸汽管道和电缆在震动中摇晃，铜锈像雪花一样纷纷坠落。

西泽尔睁开了眼。

他走向车间入口。

屠龙者圣乔治就站在甬道尽头，那道刚刚合拢的岩壁前面。它的三颗核心还在发出暗红色的光，但亮度比刚才又暗了一些。驾驶舱的盖板被从内部推开，莲生的脸出现在光线下。

他的左肩上有一道触目惊心的伤口。

那不是甲胄的伤口——是驾驶舱内部的管线断裂后，刺穿了他的肩膀。血顺着他浅色实验服的手臂流下来，滴在甲胄的胸甲上，被残留的余温蒸发成淡淡的血雾。

但他在笑。

和投影里一模一样的笑容。

"你真的……能修它？"他看向西泽尔，紫瞳里带着一种奇异的光芒。

"能。"西泽尔说。

他走向了工作台。左手机械臂已经把备用的机械心脏稳稳地放在了固定夹具上，焊枪和校准仪已经就位。右手机械臂悬停在一旁，等待指令。

"让它躺下。"西泽尔说。

莲生看了他一眼，没再多说什么。他的右手在驾驶舱内壁按下了某个按钮，屠龙者圣乔治发出一阵沉重的机械声响，膝盖弯曲，整个身躯缓缓跪倒，最终完全趴伏在了铁板地面上。

它倒下时的震动让整个车间都抖了一下。

西泽尔走到了屠龙者圣乔治的左胸。

那个被龙吼炮击穿的洞就在他面前。洞的边缘参差不齐，被高温烧蚀的金属向外翻卷，像一朵盛开的铁花。里面原本的四颗核心只剩下三颗还在运转，第四颗的卡槽空空如也，线路断裂，冷却液管道崩裂，蒸汽从裂缝中嘶嘶泄出。

他抬起右手。

机械臂立刻响应，将备用核心送到了他面前。

暗金色的球体在他掌心中发出微弱的光——那种光和他后颈的黄金套管所发出的暗红色光遥相呼应，频率完全一致。

"帮我装进去。"西泽尔对莲生说，"你来对准卡槽，我来接线路。"

莲生没有犹豫。他从驾驶舱里探出半个身子，带着血的右手伸进了那个洞里，摸索着找到了核心的卡槽位置。备用核心被放了进去，稳稳地嵌入了那个为它预留的空间。

西泽尔闭上眼睛。

再次共鸣。

紫瞳金纹亮起的瞬间，机械臂动了。它的金属手指精准地拨开断裂的线路，将备用核心的数据接口与甲胄主系统逐条对接。焊枪在另一只手的操控下自动点燃，蓝色的火焰舔舐着断裂的管路，熔化的金属像水银一样流淌，填满了每一道裂缝。

"校准仪。"西泽尔说。

左手机械臂将校准仪递到了他面前。他睁开一只眼，读取了校准仪上的数据。

"数据偏差零点三。"他说，"可以接受。"

机械臂继续工作。

焊接、接线、校准、紧固——每一步都精准到毫米级别。三百年前的机械臂被达·芬奇调校到了极致，即使沉睡了三百年，再次启动时依然保持着完美的精度。

三分钟后，备用核心完全就位。

屠龙者圣乔治的左胸深处，那颗沉寂了几百年的心脏重新跳动起来。暗红色的光芒从核心表面向外扩散，沿着线路和管道蔓延到了甲胄的每一条血管。

但它还不够强。

"四成。"莲生看着驾驶舱内的读数，说，"核心功率只有四成。要完全恢复需要……"

"半小时。"西泽尔替他说了，"核心需要预热。半小时后能到九成。"

"半小时……"莲生低声重复。

车间的岩壁外面，撞击声还在持续。

而且越来越重。

"他们在拆门。"阿方索说。他把耳朵贴在岩壁上听了三秒钟，然后退开，"三台普罗米修斯在轮流撞击岩壁。按照这个力度，五分钟内能破开。"

"三台？"瓦莲京娜皱眉，"刚才追踪的只有两台。"

"另一台从另一侧绕过来的。"阿方索说，"它们判断出莲生不是退却，而是要进某个地方。"

车间的岩壁发出了一声沉闷的嘎吱。

那条缝隙比之前更宽了。

西泽尔看着还在预热的核心，说："不够。半小时太久了。"

"那就不等了。"莲生说。

他从驾驶舱里站了起来。

血还在从肩膀上流，但他似乎完全不在意。他从驾驶舱后方的内置武器架上取下了什么东西——那是一把剑。

一把被油布裹了好几层的剑。

莲生把油布一层层剥开。油布落下的瞬间，露出了里面的东西——一柄断剑。

剑身从中间断裂，只剩下靠近剑柄的半截。断口处参差不齐，像是被某种巨大的力量硬生生折断的。剑柄是暗银色的，缠着已经褪色的皮革握柄。

但那不是让所有人注意的焦点。

焦点是剑柄尾端刻着的一行烫金拉丁文。

西泽尔看清了那行字。

"冈扎罗·博尔吉亚"。

莲生把断剑举到面前，看着那行字沉默了一秒钟。

"三百年前，第一任'断剑'骑士的佩剑。"他说，声音很轻，"冈扎罗·博尔吉亚，初代教皇博尔吉亚一世的旁系后裔。达·芬奇的远房侄子。"

他把断剑递向西泽尔。

"初代教皇造了屠龙者圣乔治，同时也造了欧米茄。两台原型体，两种完全不同的设计思路——欧米茄是完美的战争兵器，屠龙者圣乔治是完美的屠龙兵器。后来达·芬奇反悔了，决定封印世界树残枝，但他在封印之前，把初代教皇设计时用的几把原型武器封存在了屠龙者圣乔治的武器库里。"

"这是其中之一。"

"初代教皇留给完美神使载体的礼物。"

莲生把断剑塞进了西泽尔的手里。

那剑比看起来轻得多。剑柄上的皮革虽然褪色，但握上去温润如故。断口处的金属纹理在灯光下泛着暗银色的光泽，和现代任何一种合金都不同。

"它能斩断所有机械神国的造物。"莲生说，"初代教皇亲口说的。包括欧米茄。"

"包括……一号？"阿方索问。

"包括一号。"莲生点头。

岩壁又发出一声巨响。

裂缝已经有手指宽了。外面的普罗米修斯似乎找到了岩壁的薄弱点，撞击声开始集中在同一个位置。每一次撞击都让裂缝扩大一分，灰尘从缝隙中扑簌簌地落下来。

"三分钟。"阿方索说，"最多三分钟。"

"老板。"莲生从驾驶舱里看着西泽尔，紫瞳里倒映着甲胄胸腔中暗红色的光，"你带他们先走。"

西泽尔看着他。

"黑铁巨门就在前面，对吧？"莲生笑了笑，笑容里带着血，"从这里往前三百米就到门厅了。你们去开门。"

"那你呢？"

"我留在这里拖住它们。"莲生拍了拍屠龙者圣乔治残破的左臂，"这台大家伙的武器库还没清空。我在里面藏了不少好东西，够那三台普罗米修斯喝一壶的。"

"你受了伤。"瓦莲京娜说。

"叶尼塞公主，我知道你。"莲生看了她一眼，"你母亲设计的神经接驳技术救了我很多年。如果今天之后我还活着，我请你喝酒。"

瓦莲京娜没有说话。

她的手指在青丝古剑的剑柄上收紧了一下，又松开了。

"西泽尔。"莲生叫了他的名字。

西泽尔握着那把断剑，看着莲生。

三百年。

这个人在维苏威火山深处等了三百年，等的是今天。

"核心预热到四成够用吗？"西泽尔问。

"我不需要十成。"莲生说，"三成我就敢拆了那些铁棺材。"

"半小时后你来找我们。"西泽尔说，"不是'如果还活着'。是'来找我'。"

莲生愣了一下。

然后他笑了。

和之前不一样的笑。是那种被人从泥沼里拽了一把、踩到了实地的笑。

"好。"他说，"半小时。"

岩壁上的裂缝已经有一个拳头宽了。外面透进来的光被普罗米修斯庞大的身躯遮挡，只留下一道道暗红色的缝隙。

西泽尔转身，朝车间后方的备用通道走去。

"走。"他说。

阿方索、昆提良、唐璜、瓦莲京娜——四个人鱼贯跟上。西泽尔走在最前面，右手握着那把断剑，左手按在后颈发烫的黄金套管上。断剑的剑柄上，"冈扎罗·博尔吉亚"七个烫金拉丁文在昏黄的灯光下一明一暗。

他们身后，莲生从驾驶舱里取出了第二件武器——一柄比他整个人还高的骑枪。骑枪的枪身刻满了梵文，枪头是一枚六翼天使的浮雕。

他单手握住骑枪，朝西泽尔他们离开的方向看了一眼。

然后他转身面对岩壁。

岩壁的另一侧，普罗米修斯的龙吼炮已经对准了裂缝。

莲生把骑枪扛在肩上，靠在驾驶舱的椅背上，闭上了眼睛。

"来吧。"他说。

【English】
Chapter 199 — The Return of the Dragon-Slayer (II)

On the projection, the Saint George took one step back.

That single movement cost the room a held breath. A war-engine of twenty tons — the finest seraph of a century ago, named for a saint who had never in his life stood inside anything heavier than a horse — was dragging its broken body backward like a wounded bull. The left arm hung dead at its side. The shoulder plate was still smoking, a pale grey plume drifting off the scorched rim, the metal at the seam glowing the deep red of cooling iron.

Inside the cockpit, Liansheng smiled.

He had spat blood against the inner window. From a distance the projection couldn't show his face, but Cesare felt the smile there — a stillness, and something beneath the stillness that looked almost like relief.

Five Prometheuses reshuffled into a hunting formation.

"He's breaking off!" a rider's voice cracked over the open channel. "Don't let him reach the gallery — sweep the flanks!"

"Hold the left, the Dragon Roar reloads in forty seconds, forty seconds is all we need—"

"Zero holds center, Two swings right and gets behind him!"

Outside the gallery mouth a steam horn sounded again, the brass note rolling through five hundred meters of stone until it came to Cesare and the others as a low vibration in the bones of the lamppost corridor.

"He heard us." Alfonso's mouth had gone dry. "He's running toward us."

"Not toward us," said Valentina.

Cesare opened his eyes.

The violet iris with its thin gold tracery was still pulsing, like a red-hot wire buried in ice, slowly going dark. The gold collar at the back of his neck had stopped burning, but sweat was running freely down his temples, tracing the pale architecture of his cheekbones.

"Not toward us," he said, repeating her. Quieter than his usual voice. "Toward the maintenance bay."

"What maintenance bay?" asked Quintilian.

"Da Vinci's. From three hundred years ago." Cesare lifted one hand and pointed at the left wall of the corridor. "That door."

They all looked.

The golden lampposts threw their light on rough volcanic rock on either side. There was nothing to see — no seam, no hinge, no machine-mark. The grey-black stone was pitted and scarred with three centuries of chisel and rust, no different from any other stretch of wall in the bowels of Vesuvius.

Cesare looked at the wall for one full second. The gold collar at his nape woke again, a dim ember-red.

A hair-thin red line appeared in the rock.

Then a second. A third. A fourth. The lines ran across the face of the stone the way veins run beneath skin, sketching a tall arched outline roughly four meters high and three across. Where the lines met, a dark-gold cog sat flush with the surface.

The sigil of the Church of the Machine.

A five-pointed star set into the wheel, and around each point of the star a smaller wheel turning inside the larger one.

"So that was where he put it," Alfonso murmured.

Cesare raised his right hand and laid the flat of his palm against the cog.

The wheel began to turn.

There was no venting of steam, no mechanical thunder, only a soft click-and-tooth, click-and-tooth, like a heartbeat. In the silence of the corridor the sound carried cleanly, beat after beat, out and away.

The wall opened without a sound.

Behind the door was a short narrow passage, and at its far end a dim gold light. As the door finished opening, a smell came out — not rot, but the dry sealed-in ghost of metal, machine-oil, cotton and gunpowder preserved for three hundred years.

At the passage's end was a wide underground chamber.

"My God," Don Juan said, with an awe he had not asked permission to feel.

It was a maintenance hall the size of a small cathedral.

From the ceiling hung dozens of steam pipes and cables, most of them rusted, the copper gone green in places, but the bones of the installation were still sound. The floor was heavy plate iron, ankle-deep in three centuries of grey dust, and it complained under their boots in long low groans.

What held the eye, though, was the shelving.

The racks ran from floor to ceiling on both walls, as long and orderly as library stacks. Every level was crowded with metal parts of different shapes — curved spinal sections, snapped shoulder plates, helmets half burned through, chest modules with their wiring laid bare, and countless gears, bearings, rivets, cables and steam conduits.

All seraph parts.

All three hundred years old.

Every piece was thick with dust, but the metal still held a faint dark sheen — the alloy was far beyond anything the modern forges could lay down. Three centuries had not touched it.

"These are…" Alfonso stepped to the nearest shelf and swept the dust from a shoulder plate. Where the powder fell away, gilt lettering was visible underneath:

"Minerva · Prototype B-12 · Left Shoulder Assembly · Year of the Star 134."

"First-generation spare parts," Alfonso said, and his voice was not quite steady. "Da Vinci's reserve for the Saint George."

Don Juan had gone on to the back of the hall. He whistled once, low.

"You'll want to see this."

There, fixed to the rock wall with copper nails, hung a great engineering drawing, fully unfolded. Five meters tall, three wide. The paper had yellowed and gone brittle, but the lines were still clean. The drawing showed a complete humanoid seraph in elevation, every part named, every material noted, every machining step called out.

Beneath the drawing, in the careful upright hand of a Renaissance master, a line of Latin:

Dux Bellorum Georgius · Saint George the Dragon-Slayer · Supervised by Leonardo da Vinci Borgia, Chief Engineer · Year of the Star 1684.

The original design drawing of the Saint George.

The original, three hundred years old.

On the projection, the silhouette of the Saint George appeared at the edge of the gallery mouth.

It was walking backward. Its remaining right hand dragged against the rock for balance. Each step left a deep print in the slag floor. The three red-mercury cores at chest and shoulders threw a dim red glow, like three dying stars. The ruin of its left chest was open to the air — severed cabling, the blackened lip of a metal flower.

Two Prometheuses were fifty paces behind it and closing.

"He's almost here," Valentina said.

Cesare was already walking to the back of the chamber.

What he had been looking for stood at the far end. Two thick mechanical arms descended from the ceiling, ending in a fine spread of metal fingers. They were rusted nearly to the colour of the pipes around them, but the moment Cesare stepped under them they gave a thin working hum.

The gears began to turn.

The whole hall woke, slowly, around him.

Steam began to move in the rusted lines. Green copper scale flaked off the inside of the pipes and fell, exposing copper still sound. The ceiling lamps came on one by one, the yellow sodium light pooling across every sleeping part on every shelf.

Cesare stood under the two arms.

He closed his eyes again.

The violet-and-gold light in his eyes came on.

This time it was brighter, and it held. Gold-red lines ran outward from the pupil, covering the whole iris, then out past the canthus toward the temples, like an ancient script being inscribed into his skin as they watched. The collar at the back of his neck lit up a deep dull red, hot enough that the skin of his neck flushed underneath it.

He was not praying. He was not calling.

He was giving an order.

The Yggdrasil branch — that old will which had lain sleeping under Vesuvius for three hundred years — ran out through his blood and touched every pipe, every gear, every mechanism in the chamber.

The right arm moved first.

It lifted, the metal fingers spreading and closing again, like a man who has slept a long time and is working the stiffness out of his hand. Then it turned toward the left-hand rack, and from the second shelf took down a square bundle wrapped in oilcloth. The cloth fell away. Inside was a fist-sized orb of dark gold.

A mechanical heart.

A spare mechanical heart.

The fourth reserve core Da Vinci had pre-built for the Saint George.

The right arm carried the core and turned back toward the chamber entrance. The left arm meanwhile went for tools — a welding torch, a wrench, a line calibrator, a set of fixing clamps — and laid them, one after another, on the workbench.

"He…" Alfonso's mouth worked.

"He is using the Yggdrasil branch's authority," Valentina finished for him, very quietly. Her hand had come to rest on the grip of the Greenwire ancient sword, and her knuckles were white.

"The arms don't answer to him," she added. "They answer to the chamber's first-generation management key. He's taking that key from them."

Outside the hall, the steam horns were drawing closer.

On the projection, the Saint George reached the lip of the gallery. Each step was slower than the last, the joints screaming a dry metallic complaint. The two pursuing Prometheuses were inside fifty meters and still closing, the Dragon Roar barrel on the lead machine swinging onto the Saint George's back.

"Liansheng! Final warning! Stand down the seraph and you live!"

Inside the cockpit Liansheng lifted his head. The blood on the inner window made his face very pale. His lips moved.

The projection had no sound. They could not hear what he had said.

Cesare saw the shape his mouth made.

Cesare's body gave one small involuntary jerk.

"What is it?" Don Juan asked.

"He said two words." Cesare had not opened his eyes. Under his lids the violet-and-gold moved like two red-hot snakes. "He said 'It's here.'"

At the gallery mouth, the Saint George turned.

Its remaining right hand slammed down on the rock beside it. The whole engine pivoted on the point of impact. All three red-mercury cores spiked at once into overdrive — and a column of dark red liquid fire erupted from the center of its chest, straight at the two pursuing Prometheuses.

The Saint George's core weapon. Liquid red mercury flame.

Hot enough to melt dark metal.

The two pursuing riders had built up too much forward momentum to dodge. They raised shields and tried to absorb it. The dark-metal plating went soft, then red, then the edges began to curl.

The Saint George had already turned away.

It did not press the fight. It ran, full bore, into the gallery. All three cores at full power, every step shaking the gallery walls, the whole machine a burning thing that walked into its own pyre.

Three strides.

Two.

One.

It came through the corridor of golden lampposts.

"Close it," Cesare said.

The mechanical arms had no hands free for that.

The walls of the chamber did it for them. Under the slow turn of hidden gears, the rock on either side of the door-frame slid shut, sealing the short passage tight. The instant the seam closed there was a great metal crash from the other side — the two Prometheuses had hit the wall at full charge.

Boom. Boom. Boom.

The blows came heavy and methodical, the dust falling from the ceiling in a fine rain. The pipes and cables of the hall swung with each impact, copper scale coming off in little flakes.

Cesare opened his eyes.

He walked to the chamber entrance.

The Saint George stood at the end of the sealed passage, in front of the wall that had just closed. The three cores were still throwing a dim red light, but dimmer than a minute ago. The cockpit cover was pushed open from inside, and Liansheng's face was in the lamplight.

The wound on his left shoulder was terrible to look at.

It was not a wound in the seraph. A line inside the cockpit had snapped under load and punched through his shoulder. Blood ran down the arm of his pale work-coat and dripped onto the chest plate of the seraph, where the residual heat of the metal turned it, on contact, into a thin haze of red mist.

He was smiling.

The same smile as on the projection.

"You can really… fix it?" he said to Cesare. The violet of his eyes was strange, lit from somewhere.

"Yes," said Cesare.

He went to the workbench. The left arm had set the spare core carefully into the fixing clamp; the welding torch and the calibrator were already laid out. The right arm hovered, waiting.

"Lay it down," Cesare said.

Liansheng looked at him for a moment. Then he reached into the cockpit wall and pressed something. The Saint George made a long low mechanical sound. The knees bent. The whole engine went slowly down onto its knees, then forward onto its chest, and at last came to rest, prone, on the iron-plated floor.

The vibration when it came down made the whole chamber shake.

Cesare went to its left breast.

The hole the Dragon Roar had punched was in front of him. The rim was ragged; the metal at the edge had been turned back by the heat into a blackened iron flower. Of the four core slots inside, three were still turning, faintly. The fourth was empty. Cables hung loose. Coolant lines had cracked open and were venting steam in a thin, steady hiss.

He raised his right hand.

The right arm answered, the spare core in its grip.

The dark gold orb in the metal fingers threw a dim light of its own — a light that was already in sympathy with the dull red of Cesare's collar, the frequencies matching exactly.

"Hold it in for me," Cesare said. "You align the slot, I take the cables."

Liansheng did not hesitate. He leaned half out of the cockpit, his bloody right hand going up into the hole, feeling along the core housing until his fingers found the empty slot. The spare core was placed in, and settled home into the space that had been waiting three centuries for it.

Cesare closed his eyes.

He was in resonance again. The moment the violet-and-gold lit up, the arm moved. The metal fingers lifted the snapped cables out of the way one by one, set the spare core's data port against the seraph's main bus, and seated it. The welding torch in the other hand struck, a small blue flame, and ran along the broken lines; the melted metal flowed like mercury and filled every gap.

"Calibrator," Cesare said.

The left arm set the calibrator into his hand. He opened one eye, read the screen.

"Point-three deviation. Acceptable."

The arm kept working.

Weld, cable, calibrate, fasten. Each motion was precise to the millimeter. Da Vinci had tuned these arms to the limit of what mechanism could do, and three centuries of sleep had not cost them their accuracy.

Three minutes later, the spare core was fully in.

Deep inside the Saint George's left chest, a heart that had been dead for three hundred years began to beat again. The dark red light spread out from the core, down the cables, along the pipes, out into every limb of the seraph.

It was not enough.

"Forty percent," Liansheng said, reading the cockpit gauges. "Output is forty. To come up to full—"

"Half an hour," Cesare said. "The core has to warm. In half an hour it will be at ninety."

"Half an hour," Liansheng repeated, under his breath.

The blows on the wall outside had not stopped.

They were getting heavier.

"They're taking the wall apart," Alfonso said. He put his ear to the rock for three seconds, then stepped back. "Three Prometheuses, taking turns. At this rate, five minutes to break through."

"Three?" Valentina frowned. "There were only two in pursuit."

"The third came around the other side." Alfonso laid his hand back on the wall. "They worked out that Liansheng wasn't retreating. He was going somewhere."

The wall of the chamber made a long, low groan.

The crack was wider than it had been a minute ago.

Cesare looked at the warming core.

"Not enough," he said. "Half an hour is too long."

"Then we don't wait," said Liansheng.

He stood up in the cockpit.

The blood was still running from the shoulder, but he did not appear to notice. He reached behind the seat to the built-in weapon rack and took something down.

It was a sword.

Wrapped in oilcloth, several layers thick.

Liansheng peeled the oilcloth off. As the last layer fell, the thing inside was a broken sword.

The blade had snapped near the middle. What was left was the hilt half — a ragged, irregular break. The hilt itself was dark silver, wrapped in leather that had been black once and was now the color of old tea.

That was not the part everyone looked at.

The part everyone looked at was the line of gilt Latin letters stamped into the pommel.

Cesare read them.

"Gonzalo Borgia."

Liansheng held the broken sword up in front of his face and looked at the letters for a long second.

"The first Broken-Sword Knight's blade," he said, very quietly. "Gonzalo Borgia. A cadet of Pope Borgia the First. Da Vinci's second cousin, twice removed."

He held the broken sword out toward Cesare.

"Pope the First built the Saint George, and he also built the Omega. Two prototypes, two different design philosophies — the Omega was a perfect war engine, the Saint George a perfect dragon-killer. Later Da Vinci changed his mind and decided to seal the Yggdrasil branch. But before he sealed it, he locked away inside the Saint George's own weapon bay a few of the prototype weapons the first Pope had designed with."

"This is one of them."

"The first Pope's gift to the vessel of the Perfect Divine Messenger."

Liansheng pushed the hilt into Cesare's hand.

The sword was much lighter than it looked. The leather of the grip, faded as it was, sat warm in the palm. The grain of the metal at the break caught the lamplight in a dark silver the modern smelters could not have matched.

"It will cut through any work of the Machine Theocracy," Liansheng said. "The first Pope said so himself. Including the Omega."

"Including Number One?" Alfonso asked.

"Including Number One," Liansheng said.

The wall made another great sound.

The crack was now a fist wide. The light from the other side came in thin red slats where the bodies of the Prometheuses were blocking the gallery.

"Three minutes," Alfonso said. "Three minutes at the outside."

"Chief." Liansheng looked at Cesare from the cockpit. The violet of his eyes was lit from below by the dim red of the core in his chest. "You take the others and go."

Cesare looked at him.

"The Black Iron Gate is just ahead, isn't it?" Liansheng smiled, and the smile was bloody. "Three hundred meters from here to the door hall. You go open it."

"And you?"

"I'll stay here and hold them." Liansheng laid his hand on the ruined left arm of the Saint George. "This big fellow's weapon bay isn't empty. I have a few things stashed away. Enough to give those three tin coffins a headache."

"You're wounded," said Valentina.

"Princess Yenisei," Liansheng said, looking at her, "I know who you are. The neural-interface design your mother built has kept me alive for more years than I can count. If I'm still standing after tonight, I'll buy you a drink."

Valentina said nothing.

Her fingers tightened on the grip of the Greenwire sword, and then relaxed.

"Cesare," said Liansheng.

Cesare stood with the broken sword in his hand and looked at him.

Three hundred years.

The man in the cockpit had been waiting in the dark under Vesuvius for three hundred years. He had been waiting for this.

"Will forty percent be enough?" Cesare asked.

"I don't need a hundred," Liansheng said. "At thirty I'd take those iron boxes apart."

"Half an hour, then come and find us," Cesare said. "Not 'if I'm still standing.' Come and find us."

Liansheng blinked.

Then he laughed.

It was a different laugh from the one before. It was the laugh of a man who had been pulled out of a bog, suddenly, and had found his boots on solid ground.

"All right," he said. "Half an hour."

The crack in the wall was now the width of a fist. Beyond it, the shadow of the Prometheuses bulked against the lamplight, and the small red eye of a Dragon Roar barrel was already sighting through the gap.

Cesare turned toward the back passage of the hall.

"Move," he said.

Alfonso, Quintilian, Don Juan, Valentina — they fell in behind him, one after the other. Cesare walked at the front, the broken sword in his right hand, his left hand pressed to the gold collar at the back of his neck, where the heat was still pouring out. On the hilt of the broken sword, the seven gilt letters of GONZALO BORGIA went on and off in the lamplight, on and off, on and off.

Behind them, Liansheng took down a second weapon from the rack.

It was a lance.

A war-lance taller than a man. The shaft was covered in carved Sanskrit. The head was a relief of a six-winged angel.

He took it on his shoulder with one hand and looked once, briefly, in the direction the others had gone.

Then he turned to face the wall.

On the other side, the Dragon Roar fired.

Liansheng settled the lance against his shoulder, leaned back against the seat of the cockpit, and closed his eyes.

"Come on, then," he said.

【中文】
第200章 屠龙者的回归（下）

维修车间那扇沉重的铁门在西泽尔身后合上的时候，他听见了锁扣咬合的声响。

莲生从里面锁了门。

"那把锁撑不了多久。"阿方索回头看了一眼，声音很低。

"他不需要撑很久。"西泽尔说。

备用通道的岩壁呈暗红色，像是被高温烧过又冷却后的颜色。通道不宽，堪堪容两人并行，地面粗糙，靴底踩上去发出沙沙的声响。通道上方每隔十五米嵌着一根金色灯柱，灯柱是三百年前达·芬奇·博尔吉亚留下的，如今依然亮着，柔和的光在岩壁上投下长长的影子。

西泽尔走在最前面。

他右手握着那把断剑，左手按在后颈发烫的黄金套管上。断剑的剑柄上"冈扎罗·博尔吉亚"七个烫金拉丁文在灯光下一明一暗，像是某种古老的脉搏。

阿方索紧跟在他身后，手腕上的蜘蛛巢腕表微微闪烁，他习惯性地监测着周围的红水银浓度。昆提良和唐璜走在最后面，昆提良的手搭在腰间备用战斧的柄上，沉默如山。唐璜难得没有说话，只是偶尔抬眼看一下通道顶部的齿轮装饰。

瓦莲京娜走在西泽尔左侧半步之后的位置。

青丝古剑的剑柄上缠着新的皮绳，那是她在出发前从背包里翻出来替换的，旧的已经磨断了。她的目光一直盯着前方，金色的长发扎成利落的马尾，发梢在行走时轻轻摆动。

"这条路通向哪里？"唐璜终于忍不住开口了。

"黑铁巨门。"阿方索说，"达·芬奇留下的图纸上标注得很清楚。"

"黑铁巨门后面呢？"

"不知道。"阿方索顿了顿，"图纸只到那扇门。"

唐璜耸耸肩，不再问了。通道里重新安静下来，只剩下五个人的脚步声和偶尔的呼吸声。

走了大约五分钟，通道开始缓缓下倾。空气变得潮湿起来，能闻到淡淡的硫磺味和金属锈蚀的气息。岩壁上的金色灯柱依然亮着，但灯光的颜色从纯金变成了暗金，像是周围的红水银蒸汽在干扰光源。

"你们听到了吗？"昆提良突然停下脚步。

所有人同时停住。

通道里很安静，安静得能听到灯柱里红水银流动的细微嘶嘶声。除此之外，什么都没有。

"没有。"唐璜侧耳听了几秒，"昆提良，你——"

"继续走。"西泽尔平静地打断了他。

他不是在否定昆提良的判断。他知道昆提良听到了什么。

那是脚底传来的极轻微的震动，频率很低，不像爆炸，更像是某种巨大的机械正在启动。三百年前达·芬奇留下的维修车间里，那台屠龙者圣乔治的机械心脏正在被莲生唤醒。

莲生说过，三成就够。

他们继续前行。通道越来越窄，两侧岩壁上的裂缝也越来越多，有些裂缝里渗出暗红色的液体——不是血，是高浓度的红水银溶液，在空气中缓慢氧化成了铁锈色。瓦莲京娜伸手触碰了一下岩壁，指尖沾上了暗红色的粉末。

"三百年的氧化层。"她低声说。

"这里曾经被当作世界树残枝的根系延伸通道。"阿方索说，"达·芬奇的日记里提到过，残枝的根须渗透了整个维苏威火山山体。"

"那这些根须呢？"

"死了。"阿方索的声音很轻，"日记里说，世界树在三百年前就停止了生长。这些根须是最后枯死的那一批。"

昆提良回头看了一眼来时的方向，通道的灯光在远处汇聚成一个亮点。

"那个叫莲生的人，"他忽然说，"他真能一个人挡住三台普罗米修斯？"

没有人回答他。

走了大约十分钟，通道突然变宽了。不，不是变宽——是通道在这里分岔了。左侧的岔道通向更深的地方，右侧的岔道继续向前延伸，岩壁上刻着达·芬奇留下的箭头标记。

"右转。"阿方索看了一眼手表上的微型地图投影，"黑铁巨门在东北方向三百米。"

他们右转。

然后他们听到了爆炸。

不是听到。是感觉到。

先是脚底猛烈的震动，震得岩壁上的碎石簌簌落下，金色灯柱剧烈摇晃，灯光忽明忽暗。然后是声音——一种从地壳深处传来的、仿佛天穹被撕裂的巨响，震得耳膜生疼，通道里的空气被冲击波压缩成灼热的气浪，从他们身后呼啸而来。

西泽尔本能地伸手护住了脸。气浪卷着碎石和灰尘扑过来，呛得人无法呼吸。

然后是第二声爆炸，比第一声更沉闷，更持久，像是某样东西在持续燃烧。岩壁上的裂缝在扩大，有几根金色灯柱被震落，玻璃碎裂的声音被更大的轰鸣淹没。

第三声。

第四声。

每一声都像有人在用铁锤敲打大地的心脏。

瓦莲京娜单膝跪地，一手撑着岩壁，一手按着青丝古剑。唐璜被气浪推得后退了两步，后背撞在岩壁上，疼得呲牙咧嘴。昆提良张开双臂挡在唐璜前面，像一面人形盾牌，用身体替他挡住了飞溅的碎石。

阿方索趴在地面上，手腕上的蜘蛛巢腕表闪烁着红色警报——红水银浓度正在急剧攀升。

震动持续了大约四十秒。

然后一切归于寂静。

通道里弥漫着呛人的灰尘和金属灼烧的气味。金色灯柱大部分还亮着，但有些已经歪斜了，灯光照在升腾的灰尘中，像是水底的月光。

西泽尔站在原地，背对着来时的方向。

他的左手还按在后颈的黄金套管上，指节微微泛白。

刚才那四声爆炸间隔很均匀——第一声和第二声之间大约三秒，第二声和第三声之间也是三秒，第四声和第三声之间只有一秒。

四颗机械心脏。

包括那颗刚换上的。

他慢慢转过身来，面对着来时的方向。通道的尽头已经被坍塌的岩壁彻底堵死了，数以吨计的碎石和泥土堆积在那里，有些石块上还残留着暗红色的高温痕迹。坍塌的范围很广，从通道尽头一直延伸到他们目力所及的地方。

莲生和屠龙者圣乔治，被埋在了那下面。

和那三台普罗米修斯一起。

"……三百年。"西泽尔的声音很轻，轻到几乎听不见。

他低下头，看着自己右手握着的那把断剑。"冈扎罗·博尔吉亚"七个烫金拉丁文在昏暗的灯光下闪着微光。

他又低头看着自己的左手。

左手按在胸口，隔着衣料能摸到两样东西的轮廓——一样是世界树残枝预言书，锡兰星见家族代代相传的手稿，封面刻着倒置五芒星加齿轮的印记；另一样是刚刚放进胸口的完美焊料，密涅瓦初代总长留下的最后一块纯银色特殊金属，能修复任何断裂，能与后颈的黄金套管共鸣。

两样东西贴着他的心跳，一下一下。

他想起莲生的脸。那张被红水银蒸汽灼伤过的脸，在提到"锡兰的孩子们"时，瞳孔深处有什么东西在燃烧。

他想起安妮。马斯顿王立机械学院的高个子女孩，教他跳第一支舞的姑娘，被欧米茄的火焰烧成灰烬的时候甚至没来得及叫出声。

他想起锡兰王女苏伽罗。传说中从圣女塔坠落的少女，十九岁，骨骼断裂后被钢钉续接，像一具被强行拼凑起来的瓷器。

她们都死在了他还来不及做什么的时候。

莲生也死了。

死在三百年前就注定要死的那个位置上。

西泽尔的眼眶微微发酸。他以为自己不会哭的——他以为自己已经不会为任何人的死流泪了，从母亲离开的那一刻起，他就学会把所有东西压在心底，用苍白的脸和冷峻的眼神挡住一切。

但这一次不同。

这一次不是为了某一个人的死而流的泪。

是为了——

他终于明白了。

他之前想的"毁灭教皇国、夺回阿黛尔"，太狭隘了。太小了。小到像是一个孩子赌气的口号。

莲生等了三百年的不是复仇。

达·芬奇用一生阻止的不是某个敌人。

琳琅夫人被封存的记忆、艾琳娜被火刑后失踪的真相、贝尔纳黛特那张和苏伽罗一模一样的脸——所有的一切都指向同一个东西：世界树。

世界树不能被重启。

机械神国不能回来。

如果那些东西回来，会有更多的人像安妮一样被烧成灰烬，会有更多的苏伽罗从塔上坠落，会有更多的人被当作实验品、被植入自主行动模块、变成不需要灵魂的钢铁傀儡。

莲生用三百年的等待和四颗心脏的爆炸，只为给他买一张通往黑铁巨门的单程票。

西泽尔的手指收紧了。

有什么东西从他的眼角滑落。

不是一滴，是两滴。顺着苍白的脸颊流下来，滴在断剑的剑柄上，滴在"冈扎罗·博尔吉亚"那行烫金拉丁文上面，字母在泪水的浸润下变得更亮了一瞬。

他哭了。

没有声音，没有抽泣，甚至连表情都没有太大的变化。只是泪水从那双紫瞳里无声地溢出来，浸湿了睫毛，滑过颧骨，落在下颌。

像是冰在融化。

瓦莲京娜是第一个看到的。

她没有说话，只是从外套口袋里掏出一张手帕，递到西泽尔面前。手帕是白色的，边角绣着叶尼塞王国的国徽——一株盛开的忍冬花。

"西泽尔。"她说，声音和平时一样冷峻，但语速比平时慢了一点，"我和叶尼塞王国都会支持你的。"

西泽尔抬起头，看着她。

他接过那张手帕，粗糙的布料擦过眼睛，有些刺疼。

"谢谢。"他说。

他的声音有些哑。

昆提良走上前一步，沉默地把手搭在西泽尔的肩膀上。他没有说话，但他的手很稳，很重，像是一块锚。

唐璜站在昆提良后面，难得地没有贫嘴。他只是看着西泽尔，那双平时总是带着玩世不恭笑意的眼睛里，此刻是认真的。

"我跟你干到底。"唐璜说。

"我也是。"昆提良低声说。

阿方索走到西泽尔左边，看了一眼坍塌的方向，然后转回来。

"爆炸没有波及到黑铁巨门方向。"他说，"灯柱的线路是独立的，达·芬奇三百年前就考虑过这种可能性。"

他的意思很明确：莲生的牺牲没有白费。

西泽尔用那张绣着忍冬花的手帕擦干了眼泪，把手帕叠好，放进了自己的口袋里。

他的眼眶还有些红，但眼神已经恢复了平静。

不是之前那种空洞的平静。

是一种更深的、像是大火烧过之后留下灰烬的平静。

"走吧。"他说。

他转过身，右手握着断剑，左手按着胸口那两样东西的轮廓，朝着通道前方走去。

"黑铁巨门就在前面。"

"我们要阻止初代教皇重启机械神国。"

身后，四个人跟了上来。

阿方索走在他的左后方，手腕上的蜘蛛巢腕表持续监测着周围的红水银浓度，数据稳定。昆提良走在最后面，宽阔的后背挡住了来时的方向。唐璜走在阿方索旁边，难得安静，只有靴底踩在碎石上的声响。瓦莲京娜走在西泽尔的右侧，青丝古剑竖在背后，金色的马尾在行走中轻轻摆动。

通道越来越宽，岩壁上的金色灯柱越来越密。

空气里的硫磺味变淡了，取而代之的是一种干燥的、带着金属粉末气息的味道。岩壁的颜色从暗红变成了灰黑，上面密布着细如发丝的裂缝，有些裂缝里透出极微弱的光——不是灯光，是岩石本身在发光。

他们走过了最后一个弯道。

然后所有人都停住了。

通道在这里到达了尽头。尽头没有门，没有墙，只有一片巨大的、仿佛被刀切开的空旷空间。空间呈圆形，直径至少有五十米，穹顶高得看不见顶。

而在那片空间的正中央——

矗立着一扇门。

黑铁巨门。

十二尺高，至少六尺宽，厚得看不出具体的尺寸。门扇上布满了层层叠叠的铁质封条，每一道封条都刻满了密密麻麻的梵文和圣徽。最醒目的是门扇正中央的暗红色卡巴拉之树圣徽，十一枚果实排列成三个三角形，中心最小果实的位置是一个碗口大的凹槽。

凹槽是空的。

门扇的下方刻着一行梵文铭文，笔法苍老，和达·芬奇图纸上标注的完全一致。

门的两侧各立着一尊石像，石像是人形，但头部是机械构造，齿轮和弹簧取代了眼睛和嘴巴。它们的手中各持一柄已经锈蚀的长戟，戟尖指着门的方向。

这扇门已经在这里等待了三百五十年。

等待一个同时流淌博尔吉亚血脉和星见血脉的人。

等待一把能斩断所有机械神国造物的断剑。

等待一个在紫瞳深处藏着金色纹路的孩子。

等待西泽尔·博尔吉亚。

他站在通道的出口，握着断剑，看着那扇门。

门扇的表面泛着一层极淡的暗红色光芒，和他后颈的黄金套管同频共振。

那光芒正在变得越来越亮。

【English】
Chapter 200 — The Return of the Dragon-Slayer (II)

The heavy iron door of the maintenance shop closed behind Cesare, and he heard the bolt drop home.

Liansheng had locked it from the inside.

"That lock will not hold long," Alfonso said, glancing back.

"It doesn't need to," said Cesare.

The rock of the backup passage was a dull, scorched red — the colour of something that had been seared by a great heat and then left to cool. The passage was not wide: barely enough for two men abreast. The floor was rough, and the boots scraped against it, a dry and furtive sound. Every fifteen paces along the ceiling, a slender gold lamp-post was set into the stone, left there by Leonardo Borgia three hundred years before, and still it burned, throwing long, soft shadows against the rock.

Cesare walked at the front.

In his right hand he carried the broken sword. His left rested against the back of his neck, where the gold cannula sat under the skin, warm even through the collar. The seven gilded letters of the hilt — GONZALO BORGIA — caught the lamp-light and gave it back in faint pulses, as if some old heartbeat still lived under the gold leaf.

Alfonso followed close behind. The Spider's Nest on his wrist glimmered faintly as it took its constant, quiet readings of the red mercury in the air. Quintilian and Don Juan brought up the rear. Quintilian's hand rested on the haft of his spare battle-axe, silent as a stone wall. Don Juan, for once, said nothing, though every now and then he glanced up at the gear-shaped ornaments running along the ceiling.

Valentina walked half a pace behind Cesare's left shoulder.

The hilt of her old blade, Bluesilk, had been re-wrapped that morning with a length of fresh leather cord she had found at the bottom of her pack; the old one had finally worn through. Her gaze was fixed on the passage ahead. Her golden hair was tied back in a tight, practical tail, the ends swaying in time with her stride.

"Where does this lead?" Don Juan asked, at last, when the silence had begun to press on him.

"To the Black Iron Gate," said Alfonso. "Leonardo's diagrams mark it clearly."

"And beyond?"

"Nothing." A pause. "The diagrams stop at the door."

Don Juan shrugged and stopped asking. The passage fell quiet again, save for five sets of footsteps and the occasional breath.

After perhaps five minutes the floor began to slope gently downward. The air grew damp, and a thin smell of sulfur and old metal drifted up from somewhere ahead. The gold lamp-posts still burned, but their light had shifted from clean gold to a duller, tarnished gold, as though the surrounding red mercury vapour were clouding the source.

"Do you hear that?" Quintilian stopped.

Everyone stopped with him.

The passage was very still. So still one could hear the faint hiss of red mercury moving through the columns of the lamps. Nothing else.

"I don't—" Don Juan began, head tilted.

"Keep moving," Cesare said quietly.

He was not contradicting Quintilian. He knew what Quintilian had heard.

It was a tremor in the floor — so faint it was felt in the soles of the boots before it was heard at all. Low in frequency. Not an explosion. More like some vast mechanism drawing breath. Three hundred years old, and somewhere in the mountain, the mechanical heart of the Dragon-Slayer Saint George was being woken by Liansheng.

Liansheng had said three-tenths would be enough.

They went on. The passage grew narrower. The cracks in the walls grew more numerous. From some of them seeped a dark red liquid — not blood, but a high-concentration solution of red mercury, slowly oxidising in the air to the colour of rust. Valentina reached out and laid a fingertip against the rock. When she drew it back, the tip was dusted in dark red powder.

"Three hundred years of oxidation," she said, low.

"This was once a channel for the World Tree's root system," said Alfonso. "Leonardo's journals mention it. The roots permeated the whole body of Vesuvius."

"And the roots?"

"Dead." Alfonso's voice was light. "The journal says the Tree stopped growing three centuries ago. These were among the last to die."

Quintilian glanced back the way they had come. The lamp-light had gathered, far down the passage, into a single bright point.

"That man Liansheng," he said, suddenly. "Can he really hold off three Prometheuses alone?"

No one answered.

After perhaps ten minutes the passage widened. No — not widened. It forked. The left branch led deeper into the mountain. The right continued forward, its walls marked with arrows cut into the stone in Leonardo's careful hand.

"Right," said Alfonso, glancing at the micro-map projected from his watch. "The Black Iron Gate is three hundred metres to the northeast."

They turned right.

Then the explosion came.

Not heard. Felt.

The floor jumped under their feet hard enough to send chips of stone rattling down from the ceiling. The gold lamp-posts swayed, their light flaring and dying, flaring and dying. Then the sound came — a great tearing roar, as though the vault of heaven itself had been ripped open, so deep it pressed against the inner ear. The air of the passage was compressed by the shockwave into a wall of hot wind that came roaring at their backs.

Cesare threw his arm up to shield his face. The wind was thick with grit and dust; it stole the breath.

Then the second explosion, deeper than the first, more sustained, as if something were burning and would not stop. The cracks in the wall were widening. Several of the gold lamp-posts were shaken loose; the sound of their glass shattering was drowned by the greater noise.

The third.

The fourth.

Each one was like a hammer striking the heart of the earth.

Valentina dropped to one knee, one hand braced on the wall, the other on the hilt of Bluesilk. Don Juan was thrown two paces back by the blast and slammed against the stone, hissing with the pain. Quintilian threw his arms wide and stepped in front of Don Juan, a wall of flesh and bone, taking the flying rubble on his own back.

Alfonso lay flat against the floor, the Spider's Nest flickering red — the red mercury concentration was climbing fast.

The trembling went on for perhaps forty seconds.

Then there was silence.

The passage was thick with choking dust and the smell of burning metal. Most of the lamp-posts were still burning, though some leaned drunkenly, their light falling through the rising dust like moonlight seen from the bottom of a well.

Cesare stood where he was, his back to the way they had come.

His left hand was still pressed against the gold cannula at the back of his neck. The knuckles were white.

The four explosions had come at measured intervals. The first and the second — three seconds apart. The second and the third — three seconds apart. The third and the fourth — only one second.

Four mechanical hearts.

Including the one that had just been installed.

He turned, slowly, to face the way they had come. The far end of the passage had been utterly sealed by the collapse. Tons of rubble and earth were piled there, some of the stones still glowing with a dark, residual heat. The collapse stretched from the sealed end of the passage as far as the eye could follow.

Liansheng and the Dragon-Slayer Saint George lay under all of it.

Together with the three Prometheuses.

"Three hundred years," Cesare said.

The words were so soft that no one heard them.

He looked down at the broken sword in his right hand. The seven gilded Latin letters of GONZALO BORGIA caught the dim lamp-light and gave it back.

He looked down at his left hand.

His left hand was pressed against his chest. Through the cloth he could feel the shape of two things. One was the World Tree prophecy book, the manuscript handed down through the Star-Seer line of Ceylon, its cover stamped with the inverted pentacle and the gear. The other was the perfect solder, placed there only minutes ago — the last piece of pure silver alloy left behind by the first-generation Minister of Minerva, capable of mending any fracture, capable of resonating with the gold cannula at the back of the neck.

Both things lay against his heart, and beat in time with it.

He thought of Liansheng's face. That face, scarred by red mercury vapour, with something burning deep in the pupils when he said the children of Ceylon.

He thought of Anne. The tall girl from Marston Royal Mechanics Academy, who had taught him his first dance, who had not even had time to cry out when the Omega's flame turned her to ash.

He thought of Princess Sugarlo of Ceylon. The girl said to have fallen from the Holy Maiden Tower at nineteen, whose broken bones had been pinned back together with steel rods, like a piece of porcelain forcibly reassembled.

They had all died before he could do anything.

Liansheng too had died.

In a position he had been meant to die in, three hundred years before.

Cesare's eyes stung. He had thought he would not weep. He had thought, since the night his mother left, that he had learned to press everything down, to hold it all back with a pale face and a cold eye.

But this was different.

This was not grief for one death.

It was —

He understood at last.

The thing he had thought before — destroy the Papal States, take back Adele — had been too small. Too petty. The size of a child's sulking oath.

Liansheng had not waited three hundred years for revenge.

Leonardo had not spent his life holding back some single enemy.

Lady Linlang's sealed memories. The truth of Elena's disappearance after the burning. Bernadette's face that was the face of Sugarlo. All of it pointed to the same thing: the World Tree.

The World Tree must not be restarted.

The Mechanical God-Kingdom must not return.

If those things came back, more would burn like Anne. More would fall from towers like Sugarlo. More would be made into experimental subjects, fitted with autonomous action modules, turned into steel puppets that did not need souls.

Liansheng's three hundred years of waiting, and the explosion of four hearts, had bought one thing only: a one-way ticket to the Black Iron Gate.

Cesare's fingers tightened on the hilt.

Something fell from the corner of his eye.

Not one drop. Two. They ran down his pale cheeks and fell on the broken sword's hilt, falling on the gilded letters of GONZALO BORGIA, and where the tears touched, the letters seemed for an instant to shine the brighter.

He was weeping.

Without sound, without a sob, without any great change of expression. The tears simply spilled from those purple eyes, soaked the lashes, ran along the cheekbones, and fell from the line of the jaw.

Like ice melting.

Valentina saw it first.

She said nothing. She reached into her coat and drew out a handkerchief — white, with the royal emblem of Yenisei embroidered in one corner, a spray of honeysuckle in bloom.

"Cesare," she said. Her voice was as cold and level as ever, but she spoke more slowly than she usually did. "The Yenisei Kingdom and I are both behind you."

Cesare looked up at her.

He took the handkerchief. The rough cloth dragged a little at his eyes.

"Thank you," he said.

His voice was rough at the edges.

Quintilian stepped forward and laid his hand, silently, on Cesare's shoulder. He said nothing. But his hand was steady, and heavy, like an anchor.

Don Juan stood behind Quintilian and, for once in his life, said nothing clever. He looked at Cesare, and the look in those usually mocking eyes was, for the first time in a long while, serious.

"I'm with you to the end," Don Juan said.

"So am I," Quintilian said quietly.

Alfonso moved to Cesare's left, glanced once at the sealed end of the passage, then looked back.

"The blast did not reach the Black Iron Gate," he said. "The lamp-post circuit is independent. Leonardo considered this possibility three hundred years ago."

His meaning was plain: Liansheng's death had not been wasted.

Cesare dried his eyes with the honeysuckle handkerchief, folded it neatly, and put it into his pocket.

His eyes were still a little red. But the look in them had settled.

Not the empty calm of before.

A deeper calm. The kind left at the bottom of a great fire, in the ash.

"Let's go," he said.

He turned. In his right hand, the broken sword. His left hand pressed against the two shapes in his chest. He began to walk toward the front of the passage.

"The Black Iron Gate is just ahead."

"We have to stop the first Pope from restarting the Mechanical God-Kingdom."

Behind him, the four fell in.

Alfonso took his place at Cesare's left rear, his Spider's Nest still monitoring the red mercury in the air, the readings steady. Quintilian took the rear, his broad back to the way they had come. Don Juan walked beside Alfonso, uncharacteristically quiet, only the sound of his boots on the loose stone. Valentina walked on Cesare's right, Bluesilk upright against her back, the golden tail of her hair swaying as she walked.

The passage grew wider as they advanced. The gold lamp-posts grew denser.

The smell of sulfur faded, replaced by a dry, metallic smell, like powdered iron. The colour of the rock shifted from dark red to grey-black, laced with hairline cracks, some of which gave out a faint light of their own — not lamp-light, but a light that seemed to come from the stone itself.

They came around the last curve.

And stopped.

The passage ended there. There was no door, no wall — only a great open space, as though something had cut it cleanly out of the mountain. The space was circular, perhaps fifty metres across. The dome of the ceiling was so high its top was lost in shadow.

And in the very centre of that space —

Stood a door.

The Black Iron Gate.

Twelve feet high, six feet across at least, and so thick its exact thickness could not be made out. Its surface was layered with seal upon seal of iron strips, every strip engraved from end to end with Sanskrit and holy sigils. The most striking thing of all was the dark red Tree of Life sigil set at the centre of the door, eleven fruits arranged in three triangles, and in the place of the smallest central fruit, a bowl-shaped hollow.

The hollow was empty.

Along the bottom of the door was carved a line of Sanskrit in an old, tired hand, the lettering a perfect match for what Leonardo's diagrams had marked.

On either side of the door stood a stone figure — humanoid in body, but with mechanical heads, gears and springs in place of eyes and mouth. Each held a long, rusted halberd, the points aimed at the door itself.

This door had been waiting here for three hundred and fifty years.

Waiting for one in whose veins the blood of Borgia and the blood of the Star-Seers both ran.

Waiting for a broken sword that could sever any construct of the Mechanical God-Kingdom.

Waiting for a child with a thread of gold buried deep in the purple of his eyes.

Waiting for Cesare Borgia.

He stood at the mouth of the passage, broken sword in hand, and looked at the door.

The surface of the door had begun to glow, very faintly, a deep red, and the glow pulsed in the same rhythm as the gold cannula at the back of his neck.

The glow was growing brighter.

第201章 黑铁巨门
