【中文】
第201章 黑铁巨门

那扇门在等待。

西泽尔缓步走上前去，每一步都像踩在绷紧的琴弦上。阿方索跟在他身后半步的位置，蜘蛛巢腕表的微型机械蜘蛛已经释放出来，在圆形空间的边缘游弋，但那些精密的小东西刚进入门的正前方就急速调头，像遇到了某种令它们本能畏惧的气场。

门扇的暗红色光芒随着西泽尔的靠近变得越来越亮。

不是突然的变亮，而是一种缓慢的、有节奏的脉动，仿佛门后面有一个沉睡的心脏正在被唤醒。

西泽尔停下脚步，距门扇约三米。他能清晰地看到门扇表面每一道铁质封条上的铭文，那些梵文比密涅瓦机关档案库中保存的任何一份手稿都要古老，笔法苍劲而扭曲，像是刻写者并非用手而是用某种力量直接在铁面上烧灼出来的。

门扇正中央的暗红色卡巴拉之树圣徽格外醒目。十一枚果实排列成三个三角形，最上方的三枚、中间的四枚、下方的四枚，中心位置是一枚最小的果实。果实的位置是一道碗口大的凹槽，凹槽的边缘呈不规则的多边形，金属表面被打磨得极为光滑，像是被某种工具精确切割过。

凹槽是空的。

但它的形状——

西泽尔下意识地伸手摸向自己的胸口，那里藏着一枚从密涅瓦机关深处带出的坠饰，是琉璃交给他的完美焊料钥匙。他把坠饰从领口拉出来，链子在空中轻轻晃动。

坠饰是暗金色的，只有拇指盖大小，边缘呈不规则的多边形。

和门扇上那个凹槽的轮廓——

完全一致。

"……一样。"西泽尔低声说。

"什么一样？"阿方索在他身后问。

"这个凹槽的形状。"西泽尔把坠饰翻过来，坠饰的正面泛着暗金色的金属光泽，背面刻着清晰的梵文和一道复杂的纹章。纹章的图案是一个倒置的五芒星，五个角末端各嵌着一枚微型的齿轮。"和这个坠饰的边缘完全一致。"

他走到门扇正前方，与那道凹槽相距不到一臂。暗红色的光芒从门扇表面渗透出来，照在他苍白的面孔上，让他的皮肤看起来像是被一层薄薄的血膜覆盖。

他缓缓抬起手，手指触到了门扇的表面。

金属冰凉，却不像是普通钢铁的冷。那种冷意从指尖传入，顺着手臂一路向上蔓延，经过手腕、前臂、肘关节，最后抵达后颈的黄金套管。套管开始发烫，发出一阵微弱的嗡鸣，和门扇传来的脉动逐渐同步。

然后他看见了。

不是用眼睛看见，而是某种更深层的感知。后颈的黄金套管仿佛变成了一只沉睡的眼睛，被这扇门唤醒，透过这只眼睛，他看到了一些画面。

——

他站在一片冰原上。

天空是灰色的，低得仿佛伸手就能触到云层。风很大，吹得他的衣袍猎猎作响，但他感觉不到寒冷。

他低头看向自己的手。

那不是他的手。那双手比他自己的小一些，皮肤更白，骨节更纤细，手腕上戴着一枚古朴的青铜手镯，手镯上刻着莲花和齿轮交织的纹章。

他穿着锡兰的传统服饰，宽大的袖口，绣着金色莲花的领口，长发披散在肩头，发间缀着几枚细小的银质发饰。

冰原上矗立着一扇门。

一模一样的黑铁巨门。门扇上布满了层层叠叠的铁质封条，正中央是暗红色的卡巴拉之树圣徽。只是这扇门看起来比眼前这扇要新一些，封条上的铭文更清晰，圣徽的颜色也更加鲜艳。

而在门前站着一个年轻女子。

她穿着和西泽尔此刻所穿一模一样的锡兰传统服饰，面容和门扇凹槽中那枚旧照片上的女子极为相似——或者说，那就是照片上的女子本人。黑色的长发垂至腰际，面孔精致而苍白，眼眸是深邃的紫色，紫色之中隐约泛着一丝金色的纹路。

她就是琳琅夫人。

或者说，是三百年前的艾琳娜·博尔吉亚。

艾琳娜抬起右手，右手的掌心朝下，对准了门扇中央那道碗口大的凹槽。她的掌心也透出暗红色的光芒，和门扇的脉动完美同步。

她把掌心的纹路贴上了凹槽。

不，不是掌心的纹路——是掌心中隐藏的一道印痕。那道印痕是一个倒置的五芒星，五个角末端各嵌着一枚微型的齿轮，和坠饰背面的纹章完全一致。

倒置五芒星嵌入凹槽的瞬间，门扇上的暗红色光芒骤然变成了金色。

刺目的金色从门扇的每一条缝隙中喷涌而出，像是有无数条金蛇从铁门的背后挣脱出来，向着天空疯狂地舞动。光芒太强了，强到西泽尔不得不闭上眼睛。

但他依然能看见。

透过闭上的眼皮，他看见门扇正在打开。缓慢的，沉重地，伴随着铁链摩擦和齿轮咬合的声响。门缝越来越大，金色的光芒从缝隙中倾泻而出，铺满了整个冰原。

在门扇即将完全打开的那一刻，他看到了门后面的东西。

那是一片——

——

西泽尔猛地睁开眼。

他仍然站在维苏威火山深处的圆形空间中，面前是那扇黑铁巨门，手指还贴在门扇冰凉的金属表面上。黄金套管的热度已经退去，门扇的暗红色光芒也恢复了之前的脉动，仿佛刚才的一切都没有发生过。

但他知道发生了什么。

"你看见什么了？"阿方索走上前一步，目光紧盯着西泽尔的脸。"你刚才的表情——你看见什么了？"

"……一扇一样的门。"西泽尔说。他的声音很轻，带着一丝连他自己都没有察觉的沙哑。"还有一个穿着锡兰传统服饰的女人，用倒置五芒星打开了那扇门。"

"穿着锡兰传统服饰的女人？"阿方索皱眉。

"看起来……像琳琅夫人。"西泽尔停顿了一下，"但不是她。是她——或者更早的某个人。我分不清楚。"

唐璜吹了声口哨，很轻，立刻又压下去了。

昆提良一直沉默地站在稍远的位置，此刻走上前，用那面强化版秘银重盾轻轻碰了碰门扇的边缘。金属碰撞发出沉闷的响声，回荡在圆形空间里。

"这门后面是什么东西？"他问。

没有人回答。

"让我看看。"瓦莲京娜走上前。

她从腰间的暗格中取出一卷薄如蝉翼的银灰色丝绢，展开后足有半米见方。丝绢上绘制着密密麻麻的线条和标注，那是叶尼塞王妃留下的维苏威火山内部结构示意图。

瓦莲京娜把丝绢举到门扇正前方，对着暗红色光芒仔细比对。

"这扇门——"她的手指沿着丝绢上的某条线移动，最终停在一个被红墨水圈出的区域。"和密涅瓦机关的叹息之墙一样，是双重锁设计。但比叹息之墙更复杂。"

她抬起头，目光扫过门扇的每一条封条、每一道铭文。

"三层。"瓦莲京娜说，"这扇门有三层封印。"

"三层？"唐璜的声音微微发紧。

"第一层是圣徽封印。"瓦莲京娜的手指指向门扇正中央的暗红色卡巴拉之树圣徽。"你们看那枚最小的果实。那个位置就是圣徽封印的锁眼。达·芬奇在图纸上标注过——它需要锡兰星见家族的特定印痕才能打开。"

"特定印痕？"阿方索看向西泽尔。

"倒置五芒星。"西泽尔说。他的手无意识地摸向胸口的那枚坠饰。"刚才我看见的那个女人用的就是它。"

"倒置五芒星是锡兰星见家族的身份圣徽。"瓦莲京娜点了点头。"那不是撒旦教团的标记——初代教皇把它污名化了。它真正的含义是星见家族代代相传的圣徽，代表星见是从最底层自下而上仰望星空、窃取天机的族群。"

她的手指向下滑动，指向门扇下方的另一组铭文。

"第二层是机械封印。在圣徽封印的下面。达·芬奇的图纸上标注了它的位置——门扇内部有一套独立的机械系统，和圣徽封印完全分开。这套机械系统需要……"她停顿了一下，目光变得有些复杂。

"需要什么？"昆提良问。

"需要一种特殊的驱动方式。"瓦莲京娜说，"一种和密涅瓦机关现有技术完全不同的驱动方式。图纸上标注的关键词是——"她再次低头看向丝绢，仿佛在确认自己没有看错，"——'不朽之王'。"

西泽尔的身体微微一僵。

不朽之王系统。

那枚他后颈黄金套管中嵌着的芯片。

"你是说……"阿方索的声音也变了。

"第二层封印需要不朽之王系统的驱动才能打开。"瓦莲京娜看向西泽尔，眼神平静，但其中蕴含的份量让空气都变得沉重起来。"达·芬奇在三百年前就预留了这个机制。他知道只有一个人能同时打开圣徽封印和机械封印——一个同时拥有锡兰星见血脉和博尔吉亚血脉的完美载体。"

"西泽尔，你就是那个人。"她说，"只有你的倒置五芒星能打开第一层，只有你的不朽之王系统能驱动第二层。"

"那第三层呢？"唐璜问。

瓦莲京娜的手指继续向下滑动，最终停在了门扇最下方的一行铭文上。铭文极为古老，笔法比其他封条上的更加潦草，像是刻写者在极度匆忙中完成的。

"第三层是精神封印。"她轻声说。"达·芬奇的图纸上只标注了一个词——'意识'。"

"意识？"昆提良皱眉。

"需要完美神使载体的意识才能打开。"瓦莲京娜合上丝绢，重新卷好放回腰间的暗格中。"达·芬奇没有留下更多的信息。但从措辞来看，第三层不是任何物理手段能够触及的——它直接作用于意识层面。"

她转头看向西泽尔。

"西泽尔。"她的声音很平静，平静得像叶尼塞冰原上终年不化的冻土。"第一层需要倒置五芒星——你脖子上那枚坠饰的背面就有。第二层需要不朽之王系统——你后颈的黄金套管里就有。第三层需要完美神使载体的意识——"

"你就是那个完美神使载体。"她一个字一个字地说，"你同时流淌博尔吉亚血脉和星见血脉，你的身体里既有人类的心跳，也有红水银深处的灵魂。达·芬奇在三百年前就预见了你的存在。他把你命名为——"

她停顿了一下。

"Rex Immortalis。"

不死之王。

圆形空间里安静得能听见岩壁裂缝中岩石轻轻开裂的声响。

阿方索沉默地看着西泽尔，唐璜也收敛了所有的玩世不恭，昆提良把秘银重盾从门扇上收回来，转身面向西泽尔。

三个旧部，三双眼睛，都看着他。

没有恐惧，没有犹豫，只有信任。

西泽尔站在黑铁巨门正前方，手指还贴在门扇冰凉的金属表面上。暗红色的光芒继续脉动，和他后颈的黄金套管同频共振，每一次脉动都像是在催促他做出决定。

他把坠饰从领口取下。

链子在空中轻轻晃动，坠饰的正面泛着暗金色的光泽，背面的倒置五芒星和五枚微型齿轮清晰可见。

他又摸了摸怀里的断剑。初代断剑的剑柄冰凉，触感像是触摸一条沉睡的蛇。旁边是琉璃交给他的世界树残枝预言书，书页中透出极微弱的金色光芒。

他深吸一口气。

"我准备好了。"他说。

他的声音很轻，很平静，像是翡冷翠秋日里一缕落向地面的枯叶。没有壮志凌云的宣誓，没有慷慨激昂的陈词，只有这五个字。

但这五个字已经足够了。

他摘下脖子上的坠饰，托在掌心。坠饰背面的倒置五芒星正对着黑铁巨门中央那道碗口大的凹槽。

他抬起手。

坠饰的边缘一点一点地接近凹槽的轮廓。

暗红色的光芒在门扇表面急速脉动，频率越来越快，像是沉睡了几百年的心脏正在加速跳动。

凹槽的金属边缘和坠饰的边缘距离只剩一寸。

半寸。

——

他把坠饰按进了凹槽。

倒置五芒星嵌入凹槽的那一瞬间，整个维苏威火山仿佛都颤抖了一下。

黑铁巨门发出了一声沉闷的、来自深处的轰鸣，那声音不像是金属摩擦，而是一头沉睡了三百五十年的巨兽在黑暗中发出的第一声呼吸。

紧接着——

金色的光芒。

刺目的、几乎能把视网膜烧穿的金色光芒从门扇的每一条缝隙中喷涌而出，那些密密麻麻的梵文铭文在金光中仿佛活了过来，每一个字符都在门扇表面流动、旋转、重新排列。暗红色的卡巴拉之树圣徽变成了纯金色，十一枚果实依次亮起，从最上方到最下方，像是有人在逐一点燃十一盏灯。

圆形空间的穹顶被金光照亮，西泽尔这才发现穹顶上竟然绘着一幅巨大的壁画——壁画的内容是金色的齿轮、莲花、倒置五芒星和一只巨大的眼睛，眼睛的瞳孔是燃烧的紫色火焰。

而门扇正在移动。

缓慢地，沉重地，伴随着铁链绷断的声响和无数微型齿轮疯狂咬合的尖叫声，门扇向左滑动了半寸。

只有半寸。

但那半寸的缝隙中涌出的东西，让所有人的血液都在一瞬间凝固了。

那不是光。

那是一只手。

一只由纯粹的金色光芒构成的手，纤细而修长，手指上戴着一枚古朴的青铜手镯，手镯上刻着莲花和齿轮交织的纹章。

那只手从门缝中伸出来，五指张开，像是在等待什么人来握住它。

那枚青铜手镯上的纹章——

和西泽尔刚才在记忆中所看见的艾琳娜手腕上的那枚——

一模一样。

【English】
Chapter 201 — The Black Iron Gate

The door was waiting.

Cesare moved toward it step by step, each footfall set down on the stone as if the floor were a wire drawn to the point of breaking. Alfonso held his position half a pace behind. From the spider's-nest watch at his wrist a thread of micro-mechanicals had already been loosed, scuttling along the curved lip of the chamber, but the moment any of them crossed the threshold of the door's influence they wheeled about as if scalded and bolted for the dark behind them.

The dark crimson glow of the iron strengthened as Cesare drew closer.

It was not a sudden brightening. The light came on in a slow rhythm, the steady pulse of a sleeper's heart being coaxed into waking.

Cesare stopped at three paces. From there he could read the door clearly—every iron sealing-strip, every line of inscription cut into the metal. The Sanskrit was older than anything kept in the Minerva archive, older than any manuscript the Order had been built to keep. The strokes were sharp and crooked, as if the writer had not used a chisel at all but some force that had burned the letters straight into the iron, leaving a smell of hot metal that had not gone out in three centuries.

At the center of the door the crimson Tree of Kabbalah was unmistakable. Eleven fruits arranged in three triangles—three above, four in the middle, four below—and at the heart of the figure a single smaller fruit, set into a depression the size of a cupped palm. The edges of that depression were a precise irregular polygon, the metal polished to a glass-smooth finish, as if a tool had done work there that left no toolmarks at all.

The depression was empty.

But its shape—

Cesare's hand went to his chest without his meaning it to. Hanging against his sternum on a fine chain was a pendant he had brought up from the deep vaults of the Minerva, the perfect-solder key that Lia had given him. He drew it out by the chain. The pendant swung once in the dead air and went still.

It was the color of darkened gold, the size of his thumbnail, and its edge was an irregular polygon.

The exact outline of the depression in the door.

"The same," Cesare said, very quietly.

"What's the same?" Alfonso asked, from behind.

"The shape of the depression." Cesare turned the pendant over. The face was a dull metallic gleam; the back was engraved in a clean hand of Sanskrit, and beneath the letters a single complex device—an inverted pentagram, and at each of its five points a minute gear sunk flush into the metal. "It matches the edge of this pendant exactly."

He stepped up to the door. He was an arm's length from the central depression. The dark crimson of the seal bled out through the metal and lay across his face, and in that light his pale skin looked as if a thin film of blood had been drawn over it.

He lifted his hand. He set his fingers against the door.

The metal was cold, but it was not the cold of ordinary iron. The chill came up through his fingertips and ran the length of his arm—wrist, forearm, the joint of the elbow—and climbed into the base of his skull, into the gold socket set at the nape of his neck. The socket grew warm. It began to hum, a faint sound at the edge of hearing, and the door's pulse answered it, and the two rhythms locked together as if they had been made to.

Then he saw.

Not with his eyes. With something older, set deeper. Some hidden nerve in the gold socket, some long-dormant channel in the cabling, had been prised open, and through it he was shown.

—

He stood on a plain of ice.

The sky was a low gray, so close he felt he could put up his hand and touch the under-side of the clouds. The wind was hard, and it pulled at the wide sleeves of the robe he was wearing, but he could not feel the cold.

He looked down at his hand.

It was not his hand. The hand was smaller than his, the skin paler, the bones finer; on the wrist was a plain bronze bracelet worked with lotus and gear, the device of a guild that had once been great and was now broken.

He was dressed in the costume of Ceylon. Wide sleeves, the collar embroidered with gold lotus, his long hair loose on his shoulders and worked through with small silver pins.

On the ice stood a door.

The same door. The black iron, the layers of sealing-strips, the crimson Tree at the center. But this one was newer, the inscriptions sharper, the seal's red brighter, and in the way of things that have not yet been used it looked almost proud.

And before the door stood a young woman.

She wore the Ceylon costume he was wearing, and her face was very like the face in the old photograph that the pendant had once covered—a face that was narrow, beautiful, and colorless, the eyes a deep violet shot through with threads of gold.

It was the Lady Eleonora.

Or the woman who had been Eleonora three hundred years before. Elena Borgia.

Elena raised her right hand. Her palm faced the door. The crimson of the seal moved under her palm, and her palm answered it. The two pulses came into the same beat.

She set the print of her hand into the depression.

Not the whole print—only the mark at its heart. A mark in the shape of an inverted pentagram, and at each of its five points a minute gear. The same device that was engraved on the back of Cesare's pendant.

The moment the inverted pentagram seated itself in the depression, the crimson of the seal turned gold.

A hard, scalding gold poured out of every seam in the iron. The light moved like a thousand gold serpents writhing up out of the dark behind the door, throwing themselves at the sky. The light was so bright that Cesare had to shut his eyes.

He could still see.

Through his closed lids he watched the door begin to open. Slowly, heavily, with the long grinding sound of chains being paid out and gears being made to mesh that had not meshed in centuries. The gap widened. Gold light spilled through the gap and lay across the whole of the ice plain.

In the moment before the door was fully open, he saw what was on the other side of it.

It was—

—

Cesare's eyes came open.

He was still in the round chamber under Vesuvius. The black iron door was still before him, and his fingers were still laid against the cold metal. The heat had gone out of the gold socket at the nape of his neck, and the door's pulse had gone back to the slow rhythm of before, as if nothing had happened.

He knew what had happened.

"What did you see?" Alfonso stepped in a half-pace. He was watching Cesare's face. "Just now, your expression—what did you see?"

"A door." Cesare's voice was low and had a roughness in it that he had not put there. "The same door. And a woman in Ceylon dress, opening it with the inverted pentagram."

"A woman in Ceylon dress?" Alfonso's mouth drew in.

"It looked like the Lady Eleonora." Cesare paused. "But it wasn't her. It was her—or someone earlier. I cannot tell."

Don Juan, behind them, let out a low whistle and cut it off short.

Quintilian, who had been standing a little apart in silence, came forward and set the edge of his reinforced mithril greatshield against the door. The metal gave out a dead, ringing note, and the chamber took it up and rolled it round and round the curve of the walls.

"What is behind this door?" he asked.

No one answered.

"Here." Valentina stepped past them.

She drew from a hidden pocket at her belt a roll of silk the color of pale ash, thin as a spider's web, and shook it out square. The silk was a plan, lines and annotations drawn in fine ink, the internal map of Vesuvius that the Princess of Enisei had left behind.

Valentina held the silk up before the door and matched it against the seal, working by the crimson light.

"This door—" her finger moved along one of the lines and stopped in a region circled in red. "—is the same as the Wall of Sighs in the Minerva. A double lock. But this is more complicated."

She lifted her gaze and ran it down the sealing-strips, the inscriptions, the lines of the seal, with the cold, patient eye of a woman who had grown up on the permafrost of the Yenisei.

"Three locks," she said. "This door has three."

"Three?" Don Juan's voice was a half-tone higher than it had been.

"The first is the seal of the device." Valentina pointed at the crimson Tree of Kabbalah at the center. "Look at the smallest fruit, there. That is the keyhole of the holy lock. da Vinci marked the position in his drawings—it needs a specific imprint of the Star-seer house of Ceylon to open."

"A specific imprint?" Alfonso looked at Cesare.

"The inverted pentagram," Cesare said. His hand was on the pendant at his chest. "The woman I just saw used it."

"The inverted pentagram is the device of the Star-seer house of Ceylon." Valentina nodded once. "It is not, despite what the first Pope said, the mark of the Sabbatical. The Church blackened its meaning to suit its own hand. Its true reading is the house of those who have always looked up from the lowest ground and stolen the secrets of the stars."

Her finger moved down. It came to rest on a second band of inscription set below the seal.

"The second lock is mechanical. Below the holy lock. da Vinci's drawing shows its position—inside the door there is an independent system, kept wholly separate from the seal above it. That system needs—"

She stopped. The look on her face grew a degree more complicated.

"Needs what?" Quintilian asked.

"It needs a kind of drive that does not exist in the current architecture of the Minerva." Valentina's voice did not change. "The keyword da Vinci wrote on the drawing is—"

She looked down at the silk, as if to make sure she had read it right.

"—'Rex Immortalis.'"

Cesare went still.

The Rex Immortalis system.

The chip that sat in the gold socket at the nape of his neck.

"You mean—" Alfonso's voice had changed too.

"The second lock needs the Rex Immortalis system to turn it." Valentina looked at Cesare. Her eyes were calm, and what was in them was heavier than the air in the chamber. "Three hundred and fifty years ago, da Vinci built the mechanism with this in mind. He knew that only one person would be able to open both the holy lock and the mechanical lock at the same time—a perfect vessel carrying the blood of the Star-seers and the blood of the Borgias."

"Cesare. That is you." She said it without emphasis. "Only your inverted pentagram can open the first. Only your Rex Immortalis system can turn the second."

"And the third?" Don Juan asked.

Valentina's finger moved down a final time, to the lowest band of inscription on the door. The script was older than the rest, the strokes hurried, the work of a man who had run out of time and had not been allowed any more.

"The third lock is a lock of the mind." Her voice had gone quieter. "da Vinci wrote one word on the drawing. 'Consciousness.'"

"Consciousness?" Quintilian's brows drew together.

"It needs the consciousness of the perfect divine vessel to turn it." Valentina rolled the silk up and slid it back into the hidden pocket. "da Vinci left no more. But from the wording, the third lock is not something that can be reached by any physical means. It acts directly on the level of the mind itself."

She turned to Cesare.

"Cesare." Her voice had the same flat calm as the permafrost on the Yenisei. "The first lock needs the inverted pentagram—on the back of the pendant at your throat. The second lock needs the Rex Immortalis system—at the nape of your neck. The third lock needs the consciousness of the perfect divine vessel—"

"You are the perfect divine vessel." She said it one word at a time. "The blood of the Borgias and the blood of the Star-seers run together in you, and under your ribs a human heart beats, and in the deep places of the red mercury a soul. Three hundred and fifty years ago, da Vinci foresaw that you would be born. He gave you a name."

She stopped.

"Rex Immortalis."

The round chamber was quiet enough to hear the small sounds of the rock walls cracking under their own weight, the slow complaint of stone that had been asked to bear more than it was built for.

Alfonso was looking at Cesare in silence. Don Juan had put away every shade of his old impudence. Quintilian had lifted the edge of his mithril shield off the door and turned to face Cesare.

Three old comrades. Three pairs of eyes. All on him.

No fear. No hesitation. Only trust.

Alfonso's lips moved once, soundless, the way a man mouths a line he has carried since boyhood. We are hard pressed on every side, but not crushed. He did not speak it aloud. He did not need to. It was written in the set of his shoulders, the way he held his ground.

Cesare stood before the black iron gate, his fingers still laid against the cold metal. The crimson of the seal kept its slow pulse, and the gold socket at the nape of his neck kept the same pulse, and at every beat the door seemed to be asking him for a decision.

He took the pendant from his throat.

The chain swung in the still air. The face of the pendant was a dull gold, and on the back, in the half-light, the inverted pentagram and its five sunk gears were clear.

His other hand went to the broken sword at his hip. The hilt of the first Pope's broken sword was cold under his fingers, the cold of a sleeping snake. Beside it, in the inner pocket of his coat, was Lia's copy of the world-tree prophecy, and a very faint gold came off its pages, as if the book was breathing in its sleep.

He drew a long breath.

"I am ready."

His voice was quiet. It had the calm of a single yellow leaf coming off a tree in an autumn in Florence, drifting down through still air to the ground. There was no oath in it, no swelling of the breast, no brave word. Only those three words.

But the three words were enough.

He took the pendant off the chain and laid it in the flat of his hand. The inverted pentagram on its back was turned toward the depression at the center of the black iron gate.

He raised his hand.

The edge of the pendant came closer to the edge of the depression.

The crimson on the door's face was quickening. The pulse was running faster and faster, the heart under the iron was beating faster, the sleeper was nearer to waking.

An inch between them.

Half an inch.

—

He pressed the pendant home.

The instant the inverted pentagram seated itself in the depression, the whole of Vesuvius seemed to flinch.

A sound came out of the door—a deep, interior sound, not the sound of metal on metal but the sound a creature the size of a cathedral would make if it drew its first breath after three hundred and fifty years of sleep. A thunderous, grinding exhalation, the like of which had not been heard in the mountain since the day the door was closed.

Then—

Gold.

A gold so hard and so bright that it seemed to be aimed at the back of the eye. It poured out of every seam in the iron, and the Sanskrit characters drawn into the metal began to move, every letter loosening from its place, sliding, turning, taking up new positions. The crimson Tree of Kabbalah was beaten to a pure white-gold; the eleven fruits lit in order from the top of the figure down, as if someone were going round a dark room lighting eleven small lamps in turn.

The gold climbed the dome. It was only now, when the light reached the ceiling of the chamber, that Cesare saw the painting there—a vast work in gold leaf, a forest of gears and lotuses, of inverted pentagrams, and at the center of it a single eye whose pupil was a violet fire.

And the door was moving.

Slowly. Heavily. With the sound of chains breaking, and the scream of a thousand small gears being forced to mesh for the first time in centuries, the door slid to the left.

Half an inch.

Only half an inch.

But out of that half-inch gap there came something that froze the blood of every man and woman in the chamber.

It was not light.

It was a hand.

A hand made of pure gold light. Long and fine. On its wrist a plain bronze bracelet, worked with lotus and gear, the same device he had seen in his vision on Elena's wrist.

The hand came out of the gap, the fingers open, as if waiting for someone to take it.

The device on the bronze bracelet—

And the device on the bracelet Elena had worn in the memory Cesare had just been shown—

The same.

【中文】
第202章 第一层封印

那只手悬在门缝里，没有再往前伸。

五指张开，掌心向上，像是等了三百多年，等到手臂都僵了，等到光芒都快要熄灭。青铜手镯上的莲花和齿轮纹章在金色光芒中旋转，速度越来越慢，仿佛一个钟表的发条终于走到了尽头。

西泽尔没有动。

他的紫瞳里映着那只由纯粹光芒构成的手，那枚青铜手镯上细密的纹路他看得一清二楚——莲花的花瓣是六瓣的，齿轮是二十一个齿的，这和他之前在记忆中所看到的艾琳娜腕上那枚完全一致。但他也清楚地感觉到，那不是血肉的手，那是某种更深层的东西在向门外投射它的形态。

门缝里涌出的金色光芒开始减弱。

不是熄灭了，是稳定下来，从喷涌变成流淌，像是岩浆凝固成河道，光芒贴着门扇表面缓缓退去。那只手也跟着变淡，指尖率先失去了轮廓，然后是指节、手掌，最后只剩手镯的形状还悬浮在半空中，发出一声极轻的嗡鸣。

手镯也散了。

化作一片金色的尘雾，从门缝里退回门后。

西泽尔伸出手，掌心贴上了黑铁巨门的表面。

铁是冰的。不是普通的冰冷，而是一种能把热量从骨髓里抽走的寒意，仿佛这扇门从未被维苏威火山的岩浆温暖过，它在三百五十年的黑暗里把自己冻成了一块比铁还冷的铁。

但门不再抗拒了。

黑铁巨门表面的暗红色卡巴拉之树圣徽已经完全变成了纯金色，十一枚果实按照从大到小的顺序排列，金光从最上方的王冠果实开始，沿着一根根枝桠向下蔓延。圣徽下方的梵文铭文也在发光，每一枚齿轮和每一道圆弧都清晰地浮现在铁面上，像是一幅被覆盖了三百五十年的画终于重见天日。

然后他感觉到了门在动。

不是门缝里伸出的手带来的那种戏剧性的移动，是一种沉稳的、不可阻挡的滑动。黑铁巨门正在向左缓缓开启，厚重的门扇碾过地面上的碎石，发出一种远古巨兽翻身时才有的低沉闷响。

第一层铁质封条脱落了。

那张封条足有三指宽，上面铸着机械神教的齿轮徽记和一行谁也读不懂的梵文，它从门扇的右上方翘起一角，金属疲劳般地发出一声脆响，然后整张封条脱离门扇，掉落在地上，碎成十几片暗红色的铁片。紧接着是第二张，第三张，第四张——

每张封条脱落的间隔不到两秒，仿佛多米诺骨牌，一张触发一张。重叠的铁质封条从黑铁巨门表面纷纷弹开，像秋天的枯叶从枝头坠落，叮叮当当地砸在碎石地面上，在圆形空间里激起一连串空旷的回声。

"后退。"西泽尔低声说。

他不是在对自己的同伴说，而是本能地伸出手臂挡在瓦莲京娜和昆提良身前。黑铁巨门虽然已经不再抗拒，但三百五十年来第一次开启的机械结构谁也说不准会不会出问题——齿轮崩断，钢缆反弹，铁门倒下来砸死一两个人都是极有可能的事。

昆提良一手按在奥古斯都的重盾上，唐璜无声地闪到了门的侧面，阿方索蹲下来用微型摄影机对准门缝——他的镜头从不放过任何可能有价值的画面，这是刻进他骨子里的机械师本能。

最后一张铁质封条脱落了。

它从黑铁巨门的正中央裂成两半，暗红色的铁片在碎石地面上弹跳了几下，发出清脆的金属声，然后安静下来。

黑铁巨门的铁质外壳剥落了。

露出来的不是铁。

是纯金。

一扇由整块黄金铸成的巨门出现在众人面前，表面的纹路在维苏威火山深处的微光中熠熠生辉。巨门的上半部分密密麻麻地刻着锡兰星见祷文，那些古老的字符是西泽尔从未在任何西方典籍中见过的文字，但它们在他的紫瞳里却像水一样自然地流动；巨门的下半部分雕刻着机械神教的齿轮徽记，齿轮咬合齿轮，大齿轮带动小齿轮，一直延伸到门的最底部，和地面融为一体。

纯金巨门的中央，嵌着一枚倒置的五芒星。

那枚五芒星不是雕刻的，而是凸出的，像是从门的内部生长出来的金属骨骼。五个角末端各嵌着一颗微小的齿轮，此刻正缓缓转动，发出蚊子般细微的嗡鸣声。

倒置五芒星的正中央，是艾琳娜·博尔吉亚的手镯纹章。

莲花与齿轮。

和刚才那只金色光芒之手腕上的纹章分毫不差。

西泽尔后颈的黄金套管猛地发烫了。

不是那种缓慢升温的热，而是一瞬间从冰点跳到沸点的灼热，仿佛有人把一块烧红的铁贴在了他的后颈上。疼痛尖锐而短暂，从套管沿脊椎向下扩散，掠过每一节椎骨，在腰椎处炸开成一团热浪。热浪涌进了他的双腿，他的紫瞳在这一瞬间亮了——瞳孔里浮现出金红色的纹路，纹路沿着虹膜的边缘旋转，像是一圈正在燃烧的日冕。

那种感觉不是疼痛，是某种更古老的东西在试图和他的身体建立连接。

他认得这种感觉。

是不朽之王系统启动前的共振。但不完全一样——这一次更沉，更深，更像是有什么东西在从很远很远的地方呼唤他。

"门要开了。"唐璜低声说。

纯金巨门动了。

这一次没有铁链绷断的声响，没有齿轮疯狂咬合的尖叫，只有一种几乎听不到的、丝绸滑过丝绸般的细微摩擦声。纯金巨门沿着门框的轨道向左滑动，速度极慢，每一寸都像是在用黄金的重量碾碎三百五十年的黑暗。

门缝从半寸变成了一寸。

从一寸变成了三寸。

金色的光芒从门缝中涌出，这次不是刺目的白光，而是一种柔和的、带着暖意的淡金色，像是黄昏时分最后一缕阳光照在金箔上。光芒沿着圆形空间的地面流淌，漫过碎石，漫过他们的靴子，把每个人的影子都拉得很长很长。

门缝变成了一尺。

然后是一尺半。

然后是——

一扇足以让人侧身通过的宽度。

门停下了。

不是卡住了，而是恰到好处地停在了一个位置，仿佛这扇门已经被设定好了程序，只打开这么多。从门缝中涌出的金色光芒已经稳定，不再脉动，不再喷涌，只是静静地照亮着圆形空间。

门后是一条通道。

所有人都没有说话。

通道的地面上铺满了花瓣。

金色的莲花花瓣，一片叠着一片，从门槛一直铺到视野的尽头，密密匝匝，连地面的黑色岩石都看不见了。每一片花瓣都有巴掌大小，六瓣，边缘微微卷曲，像是真的从某棵不存在的莲花上落下来的。但它们不是花瓣——花瓣太厚了，厚到边缘处可以看到截面上暗金色的金属光泽，在纯金巨门涌出的光芒照射下，整条通道像是一条流淌着液态黄金的河。

通道两侧的墙壁上镶嵌着无数微型齿轮。

那些齿轮只有指甲盖大小，用某种暗红色的金属铸成，一个咬着一个，沿着墙壁一直延伸到通道深处。每一个齿轮的表面都刻着细如发丝的梵文，它们在红水银的驱动下缓缓转动，发出极其轻微的沙沙声，像是一千把极细的刷子同时扫过丝绸。红水银的淡红色光芒从齿轮的缝隙中透出来，和通道里金色的莲花花瓣交相辉映，把整条通道染成了一种奇异的、温暖而庄严的暗金色。

通道的尽头，是一片更亮的金色光芒。

那片光芒太亮了，亮到看不清后面到底是什么，只能隐约看到光芒中有某种巨大的、轮廓模糊的东西。像是建筑，又像是树木，又像是一尊雕像。具体是什么，站在门口的人谁也说不清。

西泽尔抬起脚，靴尖堪堪碰到门槛上第一片金色莲花花瓣的边缘。

他没有踩下去。

"你闻到了吗？"瓦莲京娜忽然问。

她站在西泽尔身后半步的位置，金色的长发在淡金色的光芒中泛着柔和的光泽，改装神怒Ⅲ型甲胄的肩部喷射口微微张开，冷凝系统的蒸汽正在缓缓排出，白雾在甲胄表面凝结成细密的水珠。

"什么？"西泽尔回头看她。

"香气。"瓦莲京娜的声音很轻，"莲花花瓣的香气。"

她弯下腰，伸出戴着白色手套的手指，从门槛上拈起了一片金色莲花花瓣。

花瓣在她指尖散发着淡淡的光泽，金属的质感和莲花的柔美奇异地统一在一起。花瓣的厚度大约有两毫米，边缘切割得极为精细，截面处可以看到暗金色的合金纹理。

瓦莲京娜把花瓣凑到鼻尖。

她的动作顿了一下。

"不对……"她低声说。

"什么不对？"昆提良紧张地问。

瓦莲京娜没有立刻回答。她把那片金色莲花花瓣翻了个面，用拇指轻轻摩挲花瓣的背面，然后再次凑到鼻尖，深深地吸了一口气。

"这个香气——"她的声音里有一丝不确定，这在叶尼塞公主身上极为罕见，"我母亲的房间里也有一模一样的香气。"

"叶尼塞王妃？"阿方索推了推眼镜。

"不是日常的熏香。"瓦莲京娜直起身，手指仍然捏着那片金色莲花花瓣，"是一块很小的金属碎片，母亲称它为'阿瓦隆残片'。她把那块残片保存在一个水晶匣子里，锁在她的私人收藏室最深处，说那是叶尼塞皇室代代相传的圣物。我小时候偷偷打开过那个匣子，残片本身没有任何特殊的地方，只是一片暗金色的金属片，但它的香气——"

她停了一下。

"和这片花瓣的香气完全一致。"

圆形空间里没有人说话。

阿方索的微型摄影机还在忠实地运转着，他把镜头对准了瓦莲京娜手中的金色莲花花瓣，红水银微晶的测光元件在花瓣表面投下一圈淡蓝色的光晕。

"不只是阿瓦隆残片。"唐璜忽然开口了。

所有人看向他。

唐璜从腰间的暗袋里取出了一样东西。

一朵纸莲花。

纸莲花被折得极为精细，每一片纸花瓣都按照严格的折痕层层叠压，整体只有拇指肚大小，但因为折叠了太多层，看起来有一种厚重的分量感。纸莲花在金色光芒中泛着淡淡的暖白色，半透明的纸面上可以看到隐约的金色纹路。

"莲生给我的。"唐璜说，"三百年前机械神教右使给我的。"

他把纸莲花凑到瓦莲京娜手中的金色莲花花瓣旁边。

两种"莲花"并排。一个是暗金色的金属，一个是泛金的纸张。它们的形状、大小、折法完全不同，但唐璜把纸莲花靠近花瓣的那一刻——

香气混合了。

纸莲花的香气是干燥的、清冽的，像冬天第一场雪落在松针上的味道；金色莲花花瓣的香气是湿润的、温暖的，像春天融化的雪水渗进泥土。两种香气在圆形空间的空气中交融，意外地和谐，像是同一首曲子的两个声部终于同时响了起来。

"一样吗？"西泽尔问。

"完全一样。"瓦莲京娜说，"底调是同一种东西。"

她把纸莲花和金属花瓣同时举到西泽尔面前。

西泽尔低头闻了一下。

紫瞳里的金红色纹路在这一瞬间又跳动了一下。那种香气很淡，淡到如果不用心去闻就会错过，但一旦捕捉到，它就像一根极细的银针，从鼻腔刺入，沿着神经一路滑到后脑——滑到黄金套管的位置。

套管又烫了一下。

这一次不是灼痛，是一种温暖的、带着亲昵意味的热度，像是有人从很远的地方向他伸出了手，碰到了他的后颈。

他认得这个温度。

在他很小很小的时候，在克里特岛的诺丁山，在那间永远飘着忍冬花香的旧屋子里，琳琅夫人从身后走过来，弯下腰，把一条毛毯盖在他肩上。毯子落在他后颈上的那一刻，暖意就是这样的。

一模一样。

西泽尔垂下眼睛，看着门槛上那片金色莲花花瓣。

"进去。"他说。

阿方索收起了微型摄影机，从背上的工具包里取出了备用的红水银测光仪，对准通道深处那片看不清的金色光芒扫了一遍。测光仪的表盘指针从淡红色区域直直弹到了最右端的深红色刻度。

"高能红水银反应。"阿方索说，"通道深处的红水银浓度至少是地面的四十倍。"

"甲胄的辐射屏蔽够用吗？"西泽尔问。

"勉强够。"阿方索说，"但不能待太久。"

昆提良一言不发地从奥古斯都甲胄背后抽出了他的骑士剑。

那把剑是密涅瓦机关为昆提良专门锻造的制式武器，剑身狭长，刃口处锻打出了极细的锯齿纹，专用于对付机动甲胄的关节缝隙。剑身中央锻有圣峰狮子会的狮头纹章和昆提良的家族徽记。昆提良把剑从鞘中抽出来，剑刃在金色光芒中反射出一道冷厉的银线。

他没有说话，只是用右手把剑握在身前，左手空出来——左手在三百年的密涅瓦历史中有一种不成文的含义：骑士的左手是留给需要保护的同伴的。

唐璜同时动了。

他的动作和昆提良完全不同，安静得像一只猫。唐璜从腰后抽出了一柄极细的曲刃短剑——那是他被密涅瓦机关特批的近身武器，剑身弯曲如新月，通体用完美合金锻造，刃口薄到可以在空气中切割出微弱的嘶嘶声。这把剑是蔷薇之鬼的专属武装，唐璜握着剑柄，把剑身藏在右臂的内侧。

他朝西泽尔看了一眼，眼神里没有紧张，只有一如既往的吊儿郎当。

但他的脚尖已经转到了通道入口的侧面，身体压得极低，重心落在后脚跟上，随时可以弹射出去。

瓦莲京娜把手中的金色莲花花瓣和纸莲花一起放进了腰间的密封金属盒里，然后从改装神怒Ⅲ型甲胄的腿部武器挂载点抽出了一柄短剑。

那是神怒骑士团的特制短剑，剑身比昆提良的骑士剑短了一截，但宽了将近一倍。剑柄上缠着冰原寒玉丝线，可以缓冲持剑者手腕承受的反震力。叶尼塞的公主握剑的姿势和翡冷翠的贵族小姐截然不同——她的手腕微微内翻，剑身与前臂成一条直线，这是叶尼塞剑术的起手式，冷冽，精准，不留余地。

"通道宽度大约六米。"阿方索最后说，他已经在心里计算好了队形，"昆提良居中举盾推进，我在他左后方负责中距离支援和探测，唐璜右翼游走，瓦莲京娜和老板在中间。我在通道入口释放两只微型机械蜘蛛先行侦查——"

"不用。"西泽尔说。

阿方索愣了一下。

"蜘蛛进去会被烧掉。"西泽尔说。他的后颈还在发烫，套管的热度稳定在一个微妙的温度上，不高不低，像是通道深处有什么东西正在替他探路，"前面有齿轮在转。"

"齿轮？"昆提良低声说。

"我能听到。"西泽尔说。

他说的是真话。从他后颈的黄金套管开始发烫的那一刻起，他就听到了一种极其轻微的声音——不是从耳朵里听到的，而是从脊椎里，从黄金套管与神经的接驳处，沿着神经纤维传入大脑的声音。

齿轮在转。

数以万计的齿轮在通道深处同时转动着，发出沙沙的、如同潮水般的声响。

西泽尔从怀里摸出了那本世界树残枝预言书。

那本手稿的封面是暗红色的皮革，倒置五芒星和齿轮的锡兰星见家族印记用金箔压印在正中央。他翻开手稿，翻到最后一页——那页一直空白的纸。

金色发光的字迹正在浮现。

不是一个字一个字的，是整句话同时从纸面深处涌出来，像是有谁把手指蘸了金粉，在纸上一笔写完。

"莲花通道，通往神国；踏入此门，再无退路。"

字迹在纸面上停留了三秒，然后缓缓渗入纸张内部，消失在纤维的纹路中。纸面重新变成了空白的，但纸的质地发生了细微的变化——原本粗糙的纸面变得光滑了，像是被人用指尖轻轻摩挲过几百遍。

西泽尔把手稿合上，塞回怀里。

他回头看了同伴们一眼。

昆提良举着重盾，盾面在金色光芒中反射出沉稳的银色反光，闭眼狮头纹章的眼睛虽然闭着，但那种沉默的坚毅比睁着眼更让人安心。

唐璜站在侧面，曲刃短剑藏在右臂后，嘴角挂着一丝似有若无的笑，但眼睛里没有半分笑意。

阿方索的手指悬在蜘蛛巢腕表的上方，没有按下释放键，镜片后面的目光冷静而专注。

瓦莲京娜握着叶尼塞短剑，金色的长发在淡金色的光芒中飘动，白靴踩在门槛上，冰原寒玉的微弱寒气从靴底渗出，在她脚下凝结出一圈薄薄的白霜。

西泽尔深吸一口气。

火山的空气带着硫磺和金属的腥味，从鼻腔一路灌到肺里，又被缓缓呼出。他的心跳稳定而有力，紫瞳里的金红色纹路在每一次心跳时都会亮一下，像是一盏由脉搏控制的灯。

他抬起了右脚。

靴底踩上了第一片金色莲花花瓣。

金属的花瓣在他的重量下微微弯曲，发出一声清脆的、像是风铃被弹了一下的轻响。那声响从脚底传上来，沿腿骨传到脊椎，再传到后颈的黄金套管。

套管猛地震了一下。

不是发烫。

是震动。整根套管像是被什么东西从远处猛击了一下，金色光芒从套管和他的皮肤接触的缝隙中溢了出来，极细，像是一根金线从后颈沿着脊椎向下飞快地抽去。

西泽尔的紫瞳变了。

瞳孔在一瞬间被金红色的纹路贯穿，灼热的亮紫色从虹膜深处翻涌上来，把原本的深紫色彻底吞没。金纹沿着虹膜的边缘旋转，每一道金纹都在随着他的心跳闪烁。手背上的血管浮起了淡紫色的发光脉络，像是有什么液态的光在他的皮肤下面流动。

然后是记忆。

不请自来的记忆。

碎片。

无数的记忆碎片像暴风雪一样涌入他的脑海——锡兰的莲花池，池水是紫色的，一个女孩坐在池边的石头上，赤着脚，脚下是倒置的五芒星；翡冷翠的地下教堂，一个女人站在祭坛前，手腕上戴着青铜手镯，祭坛上燃着紫色的火焰；维苏威火山的岩浆，岩浆中浮着一具被钢钉续接的骸骨，骸骨的胸口有一颗跳动的心脏——红水银的心脏；马斯顿的雨夜，一个少年站在斗兽场的铁栅栏后面，紫瞳里映着血和火，嘴里念着"我们四面受敌，却不被困住……"

碎片太快了，多到他的意识无法逐帧辨认。它们像刀片一样在他的脑海里搅动，把过去和现在搅成一团模糊的光影。

但他认出了一些东西。

那些碎片不属于他。

它们属于这扇门，属于通道深处的那些齿轮，属于这棵他从未见过但血脉深处却无比熟悉的世界树。

世界树在把它的记忆灌进他的脑子里。

西泽尔的身体晃了一下。

他右手猛然抬起，扣住了门框的边缘，五指陷进纯金的门框里，指节发白。他的膝盖弯了一瞬，但下一秒又绷直了，靴底牢牢地踩在那片金色莲花花瓣上。

"老板！"昆提良一步冲上来，左手抓住了西泽尔的肩膀。

"别碰我。"西泽尔低声说。

他的声音很平，平到像是在说今天天气不错。但昆提良的手感觉到了——西泽尔被他碰到的肩膀在剧烈地颤抖，肌肉不受控制地抽搐着，骨骼深处传出一阵嗡嗡的共鸣声。

唐璜的手按在了曲刃短剑上，他不确定接下来要面对的是敌人还是门本身。

阿方索的镜片后面目光一凝，手指在蜘蛛巢腕表上方悬停——他没有按下释放键，因为他的直觉告诉他，那些记忆碎片不是攻击。

瓦莲京娜上前一步，叶尼塞短剑横在身前，白靴踩上了门槛。

她看到了西泽尔的紫瞳。

那已经不是她认识的那个西泽尔的紫瞳了。

金色的纹路在他的虹膜上疯狂地旋转，像是有什么东西正在试图从他的眼睛里钻出来。他的瞳孔不再是深紫色，而是一种被金红色光芒烧透的、灼热的亮紫。后颈的黄金套管在发烫的同时发出了一声极低的嗡鸣，频率和通道深处那些转动的齿轮完全一致。

西泽尔的手指慢慢松开了门框。

他站稳了。

那些记忆碎片还在涌入，但速度变慢了，从暴风雪变成了涓涓细流。它们不再试图碾碎他的意识，而是沿着他的神经通路一条一条地沉淀下去，像雨后的水渗进干裂的土地。

他的紫瞳里映出了通道深处的金色光芒。

那片他之前看不清的金色光芒，此刻在他的视网膜上变得清晰了一些。

不是建筑。

不是树木。

是一棵巨大到占据了整片视野的——

他的意识在最后一瞬间被一道突如其来的金红色脉冲击穿。

视野一片空白。

【English】
Chapter 202 — The First Seal

The hand hung in the gap of the door, no longer reaching forward.

Five fingers spread, palm upturned, as though it had waited three hundred years, until the arm had stiffened, until the light had almost guttered. The bronze bracelet's lotus-and-gear emblem turned in the gold radiance, slower and slower, like a clockwork spring at last reaching the end of its run.

Cesare did not move.

His violet eyes caught the hand — a thing wrought of pure light — and through them he could trace every line of the bronze. Six petals to the lotus. Twenty-one teeth to the gear. Identical, in every particular, to the bracelet he remembered on Elena's wrist. But he felt, with the same clarity, that the hand was not flesh. It was something deeper projecting its likeness through the door.

The gold light pouring from the seam began to ebb.

Not snuffing out. Settling. Shifting from surge to stream, the way lava cools into channels, the radiance flattening against the door's surface and creeping back. The hand paled with it. The fingertip lost its edge first, then the knuckles, then the palm — until only the shape of the bracelet remained, suspended in the air, letting out a thin, high hum.

Then the bracelet too dissolved.

A drift of golden dust. It eddied back through the gap and was gone.

Cesare raised his hand and laid his palm against the black iron of the door.

The iron was cold. Not the ordinary cold of stone in a cellar, but a chill that leeched the warmth out of bone — as though the door had never been warmed by Vesuvius's lava, as though it had spent three hundred and fifty years in the dark learning to be colder than iron should be.

But the door was no longer resisting.

The dark-red sigil of the Kabbalistic Tree, set into the black iron, had gone entirely gold. Eleven fruits, ranged largest to smallest, and from the crown-fruit at the top the gold was spreading down through every branch. Beneath the sigil, the Sanskrit inscription glowed: every cog and every arc distinct now, a drawing that had been buried for three centuries at last uncovered to the light.

Then he felt the door move.

Not the theatrical gesture of the hand that had reached through. A slow, inevitable glide. The black iron shifted leftward, the great door's weight grinding over the rubble of the floor with a low, throaty sound — the kind of sound a sleeping beast makes when it turns in its den.

The first iron seal gave way.

A band of metal three fingers wide, stamped with the cog-and-wreath of the Mechanical Church and a line of Sanskrit no living scholar could read, sprang loose at its upper right corner. The metal gave out a brittle crack, the whole band broke from the door, and fell. It hit the floor and shattered into a dozen dark-red fragments. Then the second. The third. The fourth.

Less than two seconds between each, the seals giving way in sequence, like a line of dominoes. Iron bands peeled from the black surface and clattered to the ground, ringing against the rubble, the echoes running round and round the cylindrical chamber.

"Back," Cesare said quietly.

He was not addressing his companions so much as obeying his own instinct, lifting his arm to shield Valentina and Quintilian. The black door had ceased to resist, but no one could say what a mechanism that had not been opened in three hundred and fifty years would do next. A snapped cable. A sheared cog. A door that had stood for centuries toppling forward onto the men who had just unsealed it.

Quintilian set his hand against the face of Augustus's tower-shield. Don Juan drifted soundlessly to the door's flank. Alfonso dropped to one knee and swung the eyepiece of his miniature camera toward the widening gap — a machinist to the bone, the man never missed a frame.

The last iron seal fell.

It split clean in two at the door's middle, the two halves bounding off the loose stone with bright, brittle notes, and then was still.

The iron skin of the door peeled away.

What it left was not iron.

Gold.

A single slab of it, set into the wall of the chamber, every line of the carving catching the dim light from the deeper galleries of the volcano. The upper half of the gold door was closely inscribed with the prayers of the Ceylon Star-Seers — characters Cesare had never encountered in any Western text, and yet which, in his violet eyes, moved like water. The lower half was carved with the cogwork arms of the Mechanical Church: cog into cog, the great wheel driving the lesser, all the way down to the floor where the gold fused with the rock.

At the centre of the gold door, set proud of the surface as though it had grown there from within, was an inverted five-pointed star.

It was not carved. It had pushed itself out of the metal, the way bone pushes through skin. At each of the five points sat a single tiny gear, turning now, the five of them letting out a hum like a mosquito in a jar.

In the very centre of the inverted star, the Borgia device: lotus and gear.

Identical, in every line and curve, to the bracelet on the wrist of the hand that had just dissolved in the air.

The gold casing at the back of Cesare's neck flared hot.

Not the slow warmth of metal left in the sun. A leap from ice to boiling in a single beat, as though a red-hot iron had been pressed to the nape of his neck. The pain was sharp and brief; it ran down his spine, vertebra by vertebra, and burst against the small of his back in a wash of heat. The heat plunged into his legs. His violet eyes lit.

In his irises, gold-and-red lines surfaced, traced the edge of the pupil, and turned, slowly, like a corona in the act of burning.

It was not pain. It was something older, attempting a connection with his body.

He knew the feeling.

It was the resonance that came before the Immortal King system woke. But not quite. This was heavier. Deeper. As though something very far away were calling him by a name he had never been told.

"The door is opening," Don Juan said, low.

The gold door moved.

This time there was no sound of chains parting, no scream of cogs thrown against cogs. Only the almost inaudible friction of silk drawn across silk. The gold door slid in its frame to the left, slowly, every inch of it seeming to crush three centuries of darkness under its weight.

The gap grew from half an inch to one.

From one to three.

Gold light poured through. Not the searing white of before, but a soft, warm pale-gold, the colour of the last sliver of sun on a sheet of beaten gold leaf at the end of a long day. It ran along the floor of the chamber, over the rubble, over the men's boots, drawing out every shadow to an impossible length.

A foot.

Eighteen inches.

Then — a width that a man could pass through sideways.

The door stopped.

Not because it had jammed. It had stopped in the place it had been set to stop, as if it had been told to open only so far. The gold light from the gap steadied, no longer pulsing, no longer pouring — only shining, quietly, into the cylindrical chamber.

Beyond the door was a passage.

For a long moment no one spoke.

The floor of the passage was covered in petals.

Gold lotus petals. One laid upon another, packed so close that the dark rock beneath was nowhere to be seen. Each one was the span of an open hand, six-petalled, the edges a little curled, the way a real lotus petal curls when the morning has come. But they were not petals. They were too thick. The cut edge of one, catching the light from the door, showed a dark-gold metallic grain, and the whole corridor ran like a river of molten gold.

The walls on either side were studded with gears.

Tiny ones, no larger than a fingernail, of some dark-red alloy, each one meshed into the next, the train of them running on into the distance. Every face of every gear was inscribed with Sanskrit script so fine it was barely visible, and the gears turned under the drive of red mercury, whispering — a sound like a thousand very fine brushes drawn at once across silk. The pale-red light of the red mercury bled out through the gaps in the gear-train, and mingled with the gold of the petals, and the whole corridor was dyed a strange, warm, ceremonial dark-gold.

At the far end of the passage there was a brighter gold.

A brightness so strong it hid whatever lay behind it. The eye could catch, dimly, the shape of something enormous — indistinct, but suggesting, in turn, a building, a tree, a statue. None of the men at the threshold could say which.

Cesare lifted his foot. The toe of his boot came to rest against the edge of the first gold petal at the threshold.

He did not step on it.

"Can you smell it?" Valentina said, from half a step behind him.

Her long fair hair, in the pale-gold light, had the sheen of old honey. The shoulder vents of her modified Mark III Divine Wrath armour were cracked open, the cooling system venting a slow ribbon of steam; the steam beaded on the metal of the armour and ran down in fine drops.

"What?" Cesare glanced back at her.

"The scent," she said. "Lotus."

She bent and, in a white-gloved hand, picked up one of the gold petals from the threshold.

It lay across her fingers, faintly luminous, the metallic weight and the soft curve of a flower's petal somehow reconciled. The thickness of it was a couple of millimetres. The cut edge showed the grain of a dark-gold alloy.

She brought it to her nose.

Her hand paused in the air.

"That's not right," she said, under her breath.

"Not right how?" Quintilian asked, a tightness in his voice.

She did not answer at once. She turned the petal over, ran her thumb along the back, brought it again to her face, and drew a long breath.

"The scent — " Her voice held a note of uncertainty, which was not a thing one often heard in the Princess of Yenisei. "My mother's chambers smelled exactly like this."

"The Queen of Yenisei?" Alfonso pushed his spectacles up the bridge of his nose.

"Not her daily incense. Something else. A small piece of metal — she called it the Avalon Shard. She kept it in a crystal casket, locked away in the deepest part of her private collection. She said it was the holy relic of the Yenisei royal house, passed down through the generations. When I was a child I opened the casket once, when no one was looking. The shard itself was nothing to look at — a piece of dark-gold metal, no special feature — but the scent — "

She stopped.

" — and the scent of this petal is the same."

No one in the chamber spoke.

Alfonso's camera was still running, dutifully. He turned the lens on the petal between Valentina's fingers, and the photometer cell of the red-mercury crystal cast a pale blue halo across the gold.

"It is not only the Avalon Shard," Don Juan said.

Every head turned to him.

From a hidden pouch at his hip, Don Juan drew a thing.

A paper lotus.

Folded very fine. Every petal laid against the next along a strict crease, the whole thing no bigger than the ball of his thumb, but the layers were so many it had a kind of dense weight in the hand. In the gold light the paper glowed a faint warm white, and faint gold traceries could be seen through the thin sheet.

"Lien-sheng gave it to me," Don Juan said. "Three hundred years ago. The right hand of the Mechanical Church."

He brought the paper lotus close to the gold petal in Valentina's fingers.

Two lotuses, side by side. One dark-gold, of metal. One warm-white, of paper. Their shapes, their sizes, their ways of folding were utterly different. But as soon as Don Juan brought the paper near the gold —

The scents met.

The paper's scent was dry and clear, the way the first snow of winter smells on pine needles. The gold petal's was damp and warm, the way melting snow sinks into earth in early spring. They mingled in the air of the chamber, and the mingling was not strange — it was harmonious, like two parts of a single piece of music beginning, at last, to play together.

"The same?" Cesare asked.

"Exactly," Valentina said. "The base note is the same thing."

She held the paper lotus and the gold petal together in front of Cesare's face.

Cesare leaned down and smelled.

The gold-and-red lines in his violet eyes jumped a fraction.

The scent was faint. So faint that if a man were not paying attention he would miss it altogether. But once you had caught it, it was like a very fine silver needle, slipping from the nostrils along the nerves, up to the back of the skull —

— to the gold casing at the nape of his neck.

The casing warmed again.

This time it was not a burn. It was a warmth, with something almost tender in it, as though a hand from a great distance had reached out and laid itself against the back of his neck.

He knew that warmth.

When he was very small — so small he could not now remember the size of his own hands — in Notting Hill on the island of Crete, in the old house that always smelled of honeysuckle, Lady Linlang had come up behind him, bent down, and laid a woollen blanket over his shoulders. The weight of the blanket on the back of his neck had felt like this.

Exactly this.

Cesare lowered his eyes to the gold petal on the threshold.

"Inside," he said.

Alfonso closed the camera and took out his spare red-mercury photometer, holding it toward the brightness at the far end of the passage. The needle on the dial leapt from the pale-red band straight to the deep-red marking at the far right.

"High red-mercury reaction," he said. "Concentration at the end of the passage is at least forty times ambient."

"Will the armour's radiation shield hold?" Cesare asked.

"Just," Alfonso said. "We cannot stay long."

Quintilian, without a word, drew his knight's sword from the back of the Augustus harness.

The blade was a Minerva-forged weapon, long and narrow, the edge struck into a fine saw-tooth for the joints of mechanised armour. The centre of the blade was stamped with the lion's head of the Holy Peak Lions and Quintilian's own device. He drew the sword from its scabbard. In the gold light the edge ran with a hard, cold line of silver.

He did not speak. He held the blade in his right hand. His left hand was open.

In three centuries of Minerva history, an unwritten rule: the left hand of the knight is kept free for the one beside him who needs to be protected.

Don Juan moved at the same time.

He moved nothing like Quintilian. He moved the way a cat moves — soundless. From the small of his back he drew a slim, curved short-sword: a weapon the Minerva Bureau had specially cleared for him, the blade a new-moon arc, forged of perfect alloy, the edge so thin it hissed faintly in the air. The sword of the Ghost of the Rose. He took the grip and laid the blade flat against the inside of his right arm, out of sight.

He glanced at Cesare. The glance held no tension, only his usual faintly insolent half-smile.

But the toe of his boot was already turned sideways to the passage mouth. His body was low. The weight was on the rear heel. He was ready to spring.

Valentina set the gold petal and the paper lotus into the sealed metal case at her belt, and from the leg-mount of her modified Mark III Divine Wrath drew a short sword.

It was a Divine Wrath standard-issue blade — a hand shorter than Quintilian's knight's sword, and almost twice the width. The grip was bound in threads of ice-ridge jade to absorb the shock of a deflected blow. The Princess of Yenisei held the sword in a way no Florence lady of good family would have recognised: the wrist turned slightly in, the blade and the forearm a single line. It was the opening stance of Yenisei swordwork — clean, exact, and offering nothing back.

"The passage is about six metres wide," Alfonso said. He had already worked out the formation. "Quintilian in the centre with the shield, advancing. I will be on his left rear for mid-range support and survey. Don Juan on the right flank, working. The princess and the boss in the middle. I will release a pair of micro-spiders at the threshold for reconnaissance — "

"No," Cesare said.

Alfonso blinked.

"The spiders will be burned," Cesare said. The back of his neck was still warm, the casing settled at a particular temperature, neither high nor low, as though something far down the passage were scouting the way for him. "There are gears turning ahead."

"Gears?" Quintilian said, low.

"I can hear them."

He was not lying. From the moment the gold casing had begun to warm, he had been hearing a sound. Not through his ears. Through the casing, through the nerve junction at his nape, through the nerve fibres — into the brain. A sound of gears.

Tens of thousands of them, turning together, far down the passage, the sound of a slow tide of sand.

Cesare took the World Tree Splinter manuscript from inside his coat.

The cover was dark-red leather; the inverted star and the gear device of the Ceylon Star-Seers were tooled in gold leaf at the centre. He opened the manuscript, and turned to the last page — the page that had always been blank.

Letters of gold were rising out of the paper.

Not one by one. The whole sentence at once, as though a hand had been dipped in gold powder and written it in a single stroke.

"Lotus passage to the kingdom of god.
Set foot within this door, and there is no return."

The letters held on the page for three seconds. Then they sank into the paper, down through the fibres, and were gone. The page was blank again, but the paper itself had changed. The surface, which had been rough to the touch, was now smooth — as though a hand had stroked it, many times, over many years.

Cesare closed the manuscript. He put it back inside his coat.

He looked back at the others.

Quintilian, the great shield up, the silver of its face answering the gold of the door with a sober light, the lion's head on it with its eyes closed — and that closed-eye stillness, somehow, a more dependable thing than any open-eyed ferocity.

Don Juan, on the flank, the curved short-sword hidden along his right arm, the half-smile on his mouth, and not a trace of smile in his eyes.

Alfonso, the lens of his spectacles a cold, attentive stare, the finger of his right hand poised over the spider-nest of his wrist-watch — the key untouched.

Valentina, the Yenisei short-sword in her hand, fair hair moving in the pale-gold light, the white boot set on the threshold, the faint cold of the ice-ridge jade bleeding through the sole and laying a thin ring of frost at her foot.

Cesare drew a long breath.

The air of the volcano came into his lungs with a taste of sulphur and hot metal. He let it out again, slow. His heart was steady. The gold-and-red lines in his violet eyes brightened with every beat, a lamp that ran on his pulse.

He lifted his right foot.

The sole of the boot came down on the first gold petal.

The metal petal bent a little under his weight and rang — a clear, single note, like a wind-chime that has been struck once. The note ran up through the bones of the leg, up the spine, to the casing at the nape of his neck.

The casing shuddered.

Not heat this time. A shudder. The whole length of it, as though it had been struck from a great distance, and a line of gold light squeezed out of the seam where metal met skin — a single thread, racing down the spine from the nape toward the base.

Cesare's violet eyes changed.

The pupil was crossed in a single beat by the gold-and-red line. A hot bright violet boiled up from the depths of the iris and ate the dark violet whole. The gold lines traced the edge of the iris and turned, each one pulsing to his heart. Along the backs of his hands the veins rose as glowing pale-violet traceries, as though a liquid light were flowing under his skin.

And then the memories.

Uninvited.

Fragments of memory fell into him like a snowstorm — the lotus pool of Ceylon, the water a deep purple, a girl sitting barefoot on a stone at the water's edge, an inverted star drawn in the stone under her feet; an underground church in Florence, a woman standing at the altar, a bronze bracelet on her wrist, a violet flame burning on the altar-stone; the lava of Vesuvius, and in the lava a skeleton held together with steel pins, and at the chest of the skeleton a beating heart — a heart of red mercury; a rainy night in Maston, a boy standing behind the iron bars of an arena, his violet eyes full of blood and fire, his lips moving over the words, *We are hard pressed on every side, yet not crushed* —

Too fast. Too many. He could not sort one from the next. They turned through his mind like blades, stirring the past and the present into a single blurred light.

But he recognised some of them.

These fragments were not his.

They were the door's. They were the gear-trains' down the passage. They were the World Tree's — the tree he had never seen but had always, in some place deeper than blood, known.

The World Tree was pouring its memory into him.

Cesare's body swayed.

His right hand flew up and gripped the edge of the gold door-frame. His fingers sank into the gold, the knuckles white. His knee buckled for a heartbeat — then he set it, and the boot held its ground on the gold petal.

"Boss!" Quintilian lunged forward, his left hand catching Cesare by the shoulder.

"Don't touch me," Cesare said, low.

His voice was even. Even, the way a man sounds when he is remarking on the weather. But Quintilian's hand could feel it — the shoulder under his palm was shaking, the muscles twitching beyond his control, and a deep, almost musical hum rising out of the bone.

【中文】
第203章 记忆碎片（上）

视野里那片空白持续了很久。

久到瓦莲京娜的呼吸声在耳膜里变得清晰，久到通道深处那些黄铜齿轮转动时咬合的细微咔嗒声能够被分辨出来。昆提良扶着西泽尔左肩的手感觉到了——那些不受控制的肌肉抽搐正在一点一点地消退，取而代之的是一种更深层的、来自骨骼内部的静默。

像是什么东西正在他体内安顿下来。

西泽尔睁开了眼睛。

紫瞳里金红色的纹路还在，但不再疯狂地旋转，而是缓缓地、一下一下地脉动，与他心跳的频率完全一致。

"我没事。"他说。

他没有看任何人，目光直直地穿过敞开的纯金内门，投向通道深处那片他终于看清了的金色光芒。

那不是建筑。

不是光源。

是一棵树。

一棵庞大到他的视网膜都无法容纳的机械之树。

他重新迈步，靴底踩上第二片金色莲花花瓣。

金红色的脉冲击穿了他的意识。

视野再次碎裂，但这一次不再是空白——是无数锋利的画面碎片，像是被暴风撕碎的旗帜，从四面八方朝他涌来。

他看到了一片冰原。

那是三百多年前的阿瓦隆。

冰原一望无际，白得刺目，天空中悬挂着三个太阳，空气中弥漫着淡红色的雾气——那不是雾，是极低浓度的红水银蒸汽，是世界树残枝辐射出的能量在大气中凝结的痕迹。冰面在红雾的映照下泛着病态的粉色，仿佛整片大陆都在缓慢地流血。

一队人走在冰原上。

大约二十人，穿着厚重的毛皮大衣，踩着铁钉绑在脚底的防滑靴。领头的是一个年轻人——不，不算年轻了，三十岁出头，棕色短发，下颌线条硬朗，眼睛是一种深得近乎黑色的灰蓝。他穿着一件深红色的教会长袍，袍角被冰原的风吹得猎猎作响，但他的步伐极其稳定，每一步都踩在铁钉靴该落的位置上。

他的左手握着一本黑色封皮的经书，右手握着一根铸铁手杖。手杖的末端不是尖锐的铁头，而是一个精心铸造的齿轮造型——那个齿轮的造型和西泽尔在齿轮隧道里看到的黄铜齿轮如出一辙。

波吉亚一世。

三百多年前的初代教皇。

彼时他还只是教廷派往北方寻找圣物的年轻主教，被同僚讥笑为疯子，因为他坚信北方冰原之下埋藏着神创世时遗留的痕迹。

画面跳转。

探险队已经深入冰原三天。补给快耗尽了，队里的人开始低声抱怨，有人甚至在夜里偷偷讨论是否要杀掉主教分了他的干粮。但波吉亚一世没有休息，他站在冰原的裂缝前，蹲下来，把手杖末端的齿轮贴在了冰面上。

齿轮开始发光。

极淡的、几乎不可见的金红色光芒，沿着冰面下某种不可见的纹路向远方蔓延，像是一根被点燃的引线。波吉亚一世的灰蓝色眼睛里映出那道光，他猛地站起身，转头对身后那些冻得瑟瑟发抖的同伴说了一个字。

"来。"

他带头跳进了裂缝。

画面再转。

他们站在一片地下空间里。

那空间大到让人失去距离感。穹顶高得看不到尽头，四壁是光滑的深灰色岩石，表面镶嵌着数以万计的金色纹路——不是雕刻的，是天然生长在岩石中的金属脉络，像血管一样延伸到空间的中央，汇聚在同一个焦点上。

焦点是一棵树。

西泽尔的意识在看到那棵树的瞬间剧烈地震颤了一下。

那是一棵真正的树。

有树干，有树枝，有树叶，有果实。但每一寸都是金属的。树干是暗金色的合金，高达上百米，表面布满复杂的机械纹路，随着某种不可见的节奏微微起伏，仿佛在呼吸。树枝从主干上分出无数根，向上向外伸展，末梢挂着一颗一颗跳动着红色光芒的核心——那些核心有大有小，大的如人头，小的如拳头，全都散发着暗红色的脉动光芒，频率和人类的心跳极其相似。

红水银核心。

数以百计的红水银核心，挂在那棵机械之树上，像是一串串成熟的果实。

而树叶——

树叶是用红水银合金打造的金色齿轮。

成千上万的微型齿轮，大小不一，有的如手掌，有的如指甲，层层叠叠地镶嵌在树枝的末梢。它们全都在一起缓缓转动，发出一种低沉的、令人心悸的嗡鸣，像是整棵树都在用一种古老的语言喃喃自语。

世界树残枝。

西泽尔曾在达·芬奇的图纸上看过它的剖面图，在密涅瓦机关最深层的档案库里读过关于它的一切文献。但图纸和文字都无法传达那种站在它面前时灵魂深处被攥紧的感觉。

他——或者说三百多年前站在这里的波吉亚一世——在那棵树下站了很久。

然后他看到了树下的东西。

一个金色的身影。

那东西靠坐在世界树的根部，双腿盘曲，双手放在膝上，姿态像是一个正在冥想的人。它的身高和成年人类相仿，全身覆盖着暗金色的装甲板，装甲板的边缘雕刻着繁复的齿轮花纹。它的头部是圆润的，没有毛发，没有五官——只有两只眼睛。

翡翠色的眼睛。

那双眼睛闭着，但它身上散发着柔和的金色光芒，像是一盏被蒙了纱罩的灯。光芒随着它的呼吸——如果那能叫呼吸——缓慢地明灭，从胸腔中央某个位置透出来，频率比红水银核心更慢，更深沉。

欧米茄原型体。

西泽尔的意识在这一刻被一阵猛烈的金红色脉冲贯穿。他感觉到了自己的心脏在胸腔里疯狂地跳动，后颈的黄金套管烫得像一块烧红的铁，紫瞳里的金纹像是被风暴搅动，重新开始旋转。

画面加速了。

波吉亚一世走向那棵树下。他蹲下来，伸出手，手指颤抖着，几乎是虔诚地，触碰了欧米茄原型体胸腔中央那颗缓慢跳动的核心。

指尖接触核心的瞬间——

整个地下空间亮了。

所有的红水银核心同时爆发出一阵刺目的暗红色光芒，那些金色齿轮叶片同时加速转动，嗡鸣声变成了一种庄严的、仿佛来自天穹深处的和声。波吉亚一世的同伴们捂住了耳朵，有人跪倒在冰面上，不是因为恐惧，而是因为某种更原始的、铭刻在人类基因深处的东西迫使他们弯下了膝盖。

欧米茄原型体睁开了眼睛。

翡翠色的瞳孔里没有恶意，没有情感，只有一片比人类历史更古老的、深不见底的平静。它看着面前这个穿着深红色长袍的人类，沉默了很久。

然后它说了一句话。

西泽尔没有听清那句话。他只感觉到了那句话经过他的神经通路时留下的一阵灼热的、像是被烧红的细针刺穿后脑的痛楚。

但波吉亚一世听清了。

那个三十岁出头的主教慢慢地站起身来。他把手从欧米茄原型体的核心上收回来，握紧了手中的黑色经书。灰蓝色的眼睛里映着满树的红光，像是被什么东西彻底改变了。

他转身对身后的同伴们说："我们找到了。"

画面再次跳转。

回到地表。回到西方。回到翡冷翠——彼时的翡冷翠还只是一个被群山环抱的小城，教廷不过是一座朴素的石砌教堂。

波吉亚一世带回去了一颗红水银核心。

只有一颗。他把那颗核心藏在黑色经书的夹层里，用铁链锁住书箱，独自骑着一匹瘦马走了三个月。

回到翡冷翠的那天是个雨天。

他站在教堂的祭坛前，雨水从他的棕色头发上滴落，教会长袍的袍角满是泥浆。几位主教围上来问他这三个月的去向，他只是沉默地打开书箱，取出那颗红水银核心，举在烛光前。

暗红色的光芒照亮了整座教堂。

那几位主教的表情在光芒中变得复杂——恐惧、贪婪、敬畏、狂热——每一种情绪都混杂在一起，像是油和水被强行搅拌。

波吉亚一世开口了。

他的声音不大，但每个字都像铁钉一样钉进了在场每一个人的脑子里。

"这是上帝的血液。"

他顿了顿，让那颗核心缓慢地在众人面前旋转，暗红色的光影在穹顶的壁画上流转。

"北方冰原下埋藏的，是伊甸园的遗址。"

他闭上眼睛，声音变得庄严而低沉，仿佛不是在说话，而是在替某种更古老的东西发声："神创造了这棵树，用自己的血浇灌它，然后离开了。神走了，但他留下了自己的血，等待有资格的人来取回。"

他睁开眼。灰蓝色的瞳孔在红光中变成了一种灼热的暗金。

"我是有资格的人。"

画面加速。

弥赛亚圣教在那颗红水银核心的光芒中诞生。教廷从一座朴素的石砌教堂变成了庞大的白石宫殿。波吉亚一世从主教变成了教皇，他的深红色长袍换成了纯白的教皇法衣，头顶加冕了金质三重冠。

第一代普罗米修斯机动甲胄的蓝图被秘密绘制出来。

密涅瓦机关——彼时还不叫这个名字，只是一间藏在维苏威火山深处的工坊——开始秘密研究红水银的应用。

而那颗被带回来的红水银核心，变成了整个西方世界机械文明的种子。

画面继续推进，但西泽尔已经感觉到了——记忆碎片的流速在变快，密度在增加，不再是断续的画面，而是一整段被压缩过的历史。

他看到了波吉亚一世独坐在王座上，面前是跪满了一地的红衣主教。他的灰蓝色眼睛里已经没有了任何温度，只有一种冰冷的、属于计算者的光芒。

他听到了自己的声音——三百多年前那个人的声音，从记忆的深处传来，带着一种让人脊背发凉的平静：

"神已经死了。"

"我杀死了他。"

"他留在这世上的最后一样东西，现在在我手中。"

"我要用它建一个新的神国。"

"一个只有我的意志才能运转的、完美的机械神国。"

"在那个神国里，没有瘟疫，没有饥荒，没有战争。"

"也没有第二个神。"

画面猛地一黑。

西泽尔的身体剧烈地晃了一下。

这一次他没有抓住门框。他的膝盖直直地弯了下去，单膝跪在了金色莲花花瓣上，右手撑住地面，额头上的汗珠顺着鼻梁滴落在金属花瓣上，发出极轻的嗒嗒声。

"老板！"

昆提良已经蹲在了他身边，双手扣住他的肩膀，这一次他没有被推开。

阿方索单膝跪在另一侧，左手已经从腰间的急救包里摸出了一支琥珀色的注射器——神经接驳缓冲剂，五分钟起效，可强制降低神经系统的过载状态。

"打一针。"阿方索说，语气是陈述句，不是请求。

瓦莲京娜蹲在西泽尔面前，一只手扣住了他的手腕。她的指腹精准地压在脉搏上，感受着那种远超正常值的急促跳动——每分钟至少一百四十下，每一下都重得像是在用拳头砸她的指腹。

她没有说话，只是把身体挡在了西泽尔和通道深处之间，仿佛那些记忆碎片是一道刺骨的寒风，而她要用自己的身体替他挡一挡。

唐璜站在最后面，蔷薇之鬼的曲刃短剑已经出鞘。他不是在防备什么具体的威胁，他只是觉得手里没有东西会让他发疯。

"让开。"西泽尔说。

他的声音像是从喉咙深处挤出来的，沙哑，破碎，但每个字都稳。

阿方索没有动，注射器的针尖悬在西泽尔的颈动脉鞘旁，只差一寸。

"阿方索。"西泽尔抬起头，汗水模糊了他的视线，但他紫瞳里的金红色脉动依然在，一下一下，和通道深处那些齿轮的转动完全同步。

"我必须看完这些记忆。"他说，"这些是阻止初代教皇重启机械神国的关键。"

他伸出左手，缓慢但不容拒绝地按住了阿方索持针的手腕，把那支注射器推了回去。

"我们来这里不是为了活着回去。"他的目光从阿方索的脸上移开，扫过瓦莲京娜、昆提良、唐璜，最后停在通道深处那片金色光芒上，"是为了关上那扇门。"

他撑着地面站起来。

膝盖还在发抖，但他的脊背挺得笔直。

"而且，"他松开了阿方索的手腕，嘴角极轻地动了一下——那不是笑，是某种更复杂的、只有他们这些从翡冷翠贫民区一路爬过来的人才能读懂的东西，"如果我现在停下来，那些记忆会断掉。我不想再等三百年。"

阿方索盯着他看了两秒，然后把注射器收回了急救包，拉上了拉链。

"你的心率超过一百八十的时候我会把你打晕。"阿方索说。

"随你。"西泽尔说。

瓦莲京娜松开了他的手腕，但她的身体没有让开。她依然蹲在那里，仰头看着西泽尔，翡翠色的眼睛里映着他紫瞳中金红色的脉动。

"我跟着你走。"她说，语气和在西泽尔办公室门口等他开会时一模一样——平静、公事公办，但底下是一整条不会松手的锁链。

西泽尔低头看了她一眼。

他没有说谢谢。他说的是："鞋脏了。"

瓦莲京娜低头看了一眼自己白靴上沾到的金色莲花花瓣粉末，愣了一瞬，然后哼了一声站起来，把那些粉末用靴底蹭掉。

"穿白靴来探险是我的错？"她说。

西泽尔没有接话。

他深吸了一口气。通道里的空气带着一种让人头脑清醒的冷冽，混着极淡的金属腥味和某种他说不出名字的花香——那种香气和阿瓦隆残片、锡兰纸莲花的底调完全一致，像是同一棵树上飘落的不同季节的花瓣。

他重新迈步，靴底踩上第三片金色莲花花瓣。

金红色的脉冲击穿了他的意识。

但这一次他没有闭眼。

他睁着那双被金纹贯穿的灼热紫瞳，一步步向前走去，任凭新一轮的记忆碎片像刀片一样切入他的脑海。

这一次涌入的画面不再是冰原和初代教皇。

是一张女人的脸。

白色长发，翡翠色瞳孔，嘴唇的弧度和瓦莲京娜有七分相似。

她的背后是一棵开满金色莲花的树，树下的阴影里站着一个穿着东方服饰的年轻男人。

艾琳娜·波吉亚。

和锡兰。

【English】
Chapter 203 — Memory Fragments (I)

The white in his vision had lasted a long time.

Long enough that Valentina's breathing became a separate thing in his ears, close as a whisper pressed flat to the drum. Long enough that the small precise teeth of the brass gears turning in the corridor's throat resolved into discrete clicks, one after another, a slow mechanical pulse. Quintilian's hand on Cesare's left shoulder felt the change before anyone spoke: those involuntary muscle-flinches were quieting, draining out of him by degrees, replaced by something deeper, a hush that seemed to start in the bone.

As if something in him was settling into place.

Cesare opened his eyes.

The gold-red traceries in the violet of his irises were still there, but they were no longer spinning wild. They pulsed now — slowly, deliberately, once with each beat of his heart, a synchrony that had not been there a minute before.

"I'm fine," he said.

He did not look at any of them. His gaze went past the open inner door of pure gold, down the throat of the corridor, into the gold light he had at last been able to see.

It was not architecture.

It was not a light source.

It was a tree.

A tree so large that his retinas could not take it in.

He took the next step. His boot found the second gold lotus petal set into the floor.

The gold-red pulse went through him like a current.

And the world broke apart — but this time it broke into pieces with edges.

Ice. White as a wound. A sky with three suns, low and wrong-coloured, hanging at angles that ought not to have been possible. A thin bloody haze over the plain — not fog, not weather, but red mercury vapour at the lowest tolerable dilution, the exhalation of something buried under the ice, a continent slowly bleeding into its own air. The ice under that haze had turned a sick, impossible pink.

Three hundred and sixty years ago. Avalon. The northern waste.

A column of figures moved across the ice. Twenty of them, perhaps, in heavy fur, their boots studded with iron nails. At their head, a man in a deep crimson ecclesiastical cassock, cassock-hem snapping in the polar wind. Not young. Early thirties. Brown hair cut short, jaw like a cut of stone, eyes the deep grey-blue of a winter sea. He walked as if he had walked this way before, although he had not.

In his left hand, a black-bound book. In his right, an iron-shod staff whose ferrule was not a spike but a casting of interlocking gears, brass-bright, accurate to the tooth.

Borgia the First. Pope-Alexander-who-was-not-yet-Pope. Rodrigo, then, a bishop sent north by a Curia that mostly wanted him not to come back. They had called him mad. They had said: there is nothing under that ice but more ice.

He had come anyway.

The pictures jumped.

Three days into the deep field. Supplies thinning. The men no longer speaking to one another except in mutters. In the night tents, the soft, ugly arithmetic of mutiny. The bishop did not sleep. He stood at the lip of a crevasse that had not been on any map, and he knelt, and he pressed the geared ferrule of his staff against the ice.

Light.

So faint it was almost imaginary, a gold-red thread running outward under the surface along some pattern no human cartographer had ever charted, a fuse lit at the centre of the world. The grey-blue eyes caught it, and widened, and he rose to his feet, and turned, and said one word to the men behind him.

"Follow."

And he jumped.

The pictures jumped again.

They stood in a chamber so vast the eye refused to give it scale. The ceiling was lost in a black that might have been two hundred feet up, or two thousand. The walls were dark grey, polished by time, veined through and through with gold — not carved, not set in, but grown, native to the rock, like ore, like capillaries. The veins converged as he watched, drew inward from every direction, ran together toward a single centre.

A tree.

A real tree.

Trunk. Branches. Leaves. Fruit. And every inch of it metal.

The trunk was a dark-gold alloy, a hundred metres tall at least, the surface of it etched with mechanical tracery that pulsed faintly with a rhythm Cesare's body understood before his mind did — like breathing, like a tide. The branches fountained outward and upward, and at the end of every branch hung a core. Some the size of a fist. Some the size of a man's head. All of them dark red, all of them pulsing, all of them ticking at a frequency that almost — almost — matched a human heart.

Red mercury cores. Hundreds of them. Ripe fruit on an alloy tree.

And the leaves —

The leaves were gears. Gold alloy, every one, a thousand sizes nested, hand-sized, nail-sized, layered thick at the branch-tips, turning all of them, slowly, all of them together, producing a low sustained almost sub-auditory hum that one felt less in the ears than in the chest, in the back of the teeth, in the soft tissue behind the eyes. As if the tree were reciting something in a language older than speech.

The Remnant of the World Tree.

Cesare had seen its cross-section in da Vinci's plates, had read every word the Minerva Order kept in its deepest vaults. Plates and words had not prepared him. Standing at the foot of it — standing where Borgia the First had stood, three centuries and a half ago — one understood, in the marrow, why men had built cathedrals. Because this was what cathedrals were trying to be.

Then he saw what was under it.

A figure, gold, seated at the root of the tree in the lotus posture of a man at meditation. Its size was human. Its body was sheathed in dark-gold plate, the edges of the plate worked with gear-fret ornament so fine it looked like script. Its head was a smooth ovoid, hairless, featureless, save for two eyes, closed, set deep in the face it did not quite have.

Emerald eyes.

Even shut, the figure gave off a soft gold light, as if a lamp were burning inside it behind a silk screen. The light rose and fell with something that might have been breath — slower than the cores, slower than the tree, deeper, as if it were the tempo to which the rest of the machine was tuned.

The Omega prototype.

The pulse hit him again — gold-red, savage — and Cesare's body in the corridor jerked once, hard, his hand going briefly to the back of his neck where the gold coupling burned against the skin. In the memory, Borgia the First crossed the chamber floor with a slow, deliberate stride. He knelt. He reached out.

His fingers were shaking. He did not seem to mind.

He touched the core at the centre of the Omega's chest.

The chamber ignited.

Every core on the tree flared at once — a dark red so intense it was almost black, a haemorrhage of light. Every gear-leaf accelerated, and the hum became a chord, a chord that seemed to descend from the vault of some higher sky, pressing the men flat. Some of them fell to their knees on the ice, not in fear but in something more primitive, something written into the spine before language, something that said: this is not for you to stand under.

The Omega opened its eyes.

Emerald. Unblinking. No malice in them. No pity, no curiosity, no human weather at all. Only a calm so old that the hills were an amusement to it. It looked at the man in the red cassock for a long moment.

It said a word.

Cesare did not hear the word. He felt it pass through his nerve-paths like a hot needle drawn clean through the back of his skull, and the pain of it wiped the sound clean away. But Borgia the First had heard it. He withdrew his hand from the core. He closed his fingers on the black book at his chest. The grey-blue of his eyes had gone, replaced entirely by the red-lit dark gold of the tree above him, and he was not the same man who had knelt.

He turned to the men at his back.

"We have found it," he said.

The pictures jumped.

Florence. The Florence of the time, ringed by hills, a single stone church, no white marble, no golden dome, no name yet that the rest of the world would bother to learn. Rain. The bishop standing at the altar in his muddied cassock, brown hair plastered flat, water running off him onto the flagstones. Half a dozen senior clergy around him, asking where he had been. He did not answer. He opened the iron-bound travelling chest at his feet, and from between the false leaves of his black-bound breviary, he took a core.

He held it up in the candlelight.

The dark red light filled the church.

He watched their faces in it — the slow, ugly chemistry of fear and greed and awe and zeal mixing in each of them, oil and water churned. He gave them time to feel it. Then he spoke.

His voice was not loud. Each word arrived with the small finality of a nail being driven home.

"This," he said, "is the blood of God."

He let the core turn in his hand, slowly, so the shadows of it walked the painted ceiling.

"Under the ice of the north lies the site of Eden."

He closed his eyes. When he spoke again, the voice had left him; something older and colder was speaking through him, using his throat the way a man uses a key.

"He made this tree. He watered it with His own blood. Then He left. He left His blood behind, and He waited — for the man who would be worthy to take it back."

He opened his eyes. The grey-blue of them had gone dark gold in the red light.

"I am the worthy man."

The pictures quickened.

The Messianic Church took root in that red light, grew, threw out buttresses. The single stone church became a complex of white stone, columned, lifted, gold-domed. The cassock became white, and over it the gold triregnum was set on his head. The first blueprints for the Prometheus Armour were drawn up in rooms no outsider was permitted to enter. The workshop that would one day be called the Minerva Order began, in a chamber carved from the living rock of Vesuvius, its first cautious experiments with the blood of the world.

The core Borgia had carried home became the seed of an entire civilisation of machines.

The pictures came faster. Cesare felt them compress, the gaps between them closing until the fragments had fused into a continuous run of film, centuries of it, scrolling past him at a speed his mind could not quite catch.

Borgia the First alone on the throne. The hall below him filled with cardinals in scarlet, kneeling, all of them, in the prescribed posture. The grey-blue eyes, the only warmth left in that face, had gone. What was there now was a colder thing, the look of a man running sums in his head while the rest of the world slept.

And his own voice — Borgia's voice, the voice of three centuries and a half ago — rising out of the memory with a quiet that made the bones ache:

"God is dead."

"I killed Him."

"The last thing He left in the world is in my hand."

"I will use it to build a new Kingdom. A perfect mechanical Kingdom, in which nothing moves except by my will."

"In that Kingdom there will be no plague."

"No famine."

"No war."

"And no second god."

Black.

Cesare's body listed sideways.

This time he did not catch the doorframe. His knee folded cleanly under him and he went down on one gold lotus petal, his right hand flat on the metal, sweat falling in slow drops from the bridge of his nose onto the petal with a small, stupid sound, tick, tick, tick.

"Boss —"

Quintilian was down beside him, both hands on his shoulders, and this time Cesare did not push him off.

Alfonso was on his other side, already on one knee, a syringe of amber fluid already in his left hand out of the field-kit at his hip. A neural-coupling buffer, five minutes to take effect, enough to force the overloaded nervous system back down out of the red.

"Take it," Alfonso said. It was not a request.

Valentina was crouched in front of him. One of her hands had closed on his wrist with a precision that was not gentle; her fingertips were on his pulse, and she could feel it — over one hundred and forty beats a minute, each one heavy, each one slamming up against her fingers as if his heart were trying to break out through the heel of his hand. She did not say anything. She simply put herself between Cesare and the rest of the corridor, as if the stream of memory coming out of that gold light were a wind, and she could stand in it for him.

Don Juan was last. The curved blade of Rosa Fantasma was out. He was not defending against anything in particular; it was only that having nothing in his hand made him want to put his fist through a wall.

"Move," Cesare said.

His voice came from somewhere low in his chest, scraped and broken, but each word was planted.

Alfonso did not move. The needle hovered at the side of Cesare's neck, an inch from the carotid sheath.

"Alfonso." Cesare looked up. The sweat was in his eyes, but the gold-red pulse in the violet of his irises had not stopped, and it was in lockstep — perfect, mechanical — with the slow rotation of the brass gears somewhere down the corridor, as if some part of him were now being timed by that older, slower clock.

"I have to see the rest of the memory," he said. "It is the only way to stop the first Pope from restarting the Machine Kingdom."

He put his left hand on Alfonso's wrist, slowly, with the careful, irresistible pressure of a man who knew exactly how much force he was allowed, and pushed the syringe back.

"We did not come here to go home alive," he said. His gaze moved — Alfonso, Valentina, Quintilian, Don Juan — and settled at last on the gold light at the corridor's far end. "We came here to shut that door."

He braced his hand against the floor and stood. His knees were not entirely his own, but the line of his back was. It was very straight.

"And," he said, "if I stop now, the memory breaks. I have no intention of waiting another three hundred years."

Alfonso looked at him for two seconds. Then he returned the syringe to the kit, drew the zip shut, and said, flatly, "If your heart rate goes above one-eighty, I will put you down."

"Do as you like," Cesare said.

Valentina let go of his wrist. She did not, however, move from in front of him. She stayed where she was, crouching, looking up at him, her emerald eyes lit through with the gold-red pulse in his.

"I will go where you go," she said. The tone of voice was the same one she used when she was waiting for him outside the office before a meeting — level, businesslike, a chain at the bottom of it that did not come loose.

Cesare looked down at her.

He did not say thank you. He said, "Your shoes are dirty."

Valentina glanced down at the pale powder of the gold lotus petal that had come off on the white of her boot. She stared at it for a moment. Then she huffed, got to her feet, and scuffed the powder off on the sole.

"My mistake for wearing white shoes to an expedition?" she said.

Cesare did not answer.

He drew a breath. The air in the corridor was cold in a way that woke the brain, and under the cold there was a thin mineral tang, and under that a scent he could not quite name — a flower-scent, warm, soft, exactly the base-note of the Avalon fragments and of the paper-lotus of Ceylon, as if all these flowers had fallen, at different seasons, from the same tree.

He took the next step.

The third gold lotus petal.

The pulse went through him.

This time he did not close his eyes.

He walked forward with the gold-red pulse burning in his irises, the brass tick of the gears in his teeth, the memory pouring into him like broken glass — and what came to him now was not ice, was not the first Pope, was not the founding of any church.

It was a woman's face.

White hair. Emerald eyes. The line of her mouth, the slight set of it, was a thing Valentina had inherited by seven-tenths.

Behind her, a tree in full bloom with gold lotuses, and in the shadow of that tree, a young man in Eastern dress.

Elena Borgia.

And Ceylon.


==================================================
第204章 记忆碎片（下）
