【中文】
第204章 记忆碎片（下）

　　那双翡翠色的眼睛直直地看着他，瞳孔里没有映出西泽尔的脸，只映出莲花瓣上流转的暗金色纹路。

　　金红色的脉冲击穿了西泽尔的意识。

　　他的身体还在往前走，靴底踩在暗金色金属莲花瓣上发出清脆而细碎的声响，但他的目光已经空了，瞳孔里金纹剧烈闪烁，像是什么东西正在灼烧他的神经。

　　唐璜下意识地伸手要扶他。

　　"别碰他。"阿方索低声说。

　　"为什么？"

　　"他的心率已经过了一百七。"阿方索盯着腕表上的读数，咬了咬嘴唇，"让他自己走。记忆碎片中断比继续灌入更危险。"

　　唐璜缩回手。

　　昆提良默默地把奥古斯都的重盾从左手换到了背上，腾出右手护在西泽尔身侧，一言不发地跟着。

　　瓦莲京娜走在西泽尔身后半步的位置，右手按在改装神怒Ⅲ型甲胄腰间短剑的剑柄上，翡翠色的眼睛扫视着通道两侧缓缓转动的黄铜齿轮。

　　没人说话。

　　只有西泽尔的靴底踩在莲花瓣上的声音，一步，又一步，清晰得像节拍器。

　　画面来了。

　　———

　　这是一间密室。

　　翡冷翠的某个地下密室，空气里弥漫着烛油和古老羊皮纸的霉味。四面墙壁上没有挂任何装饰，只有密密麻麻的图纸和星图，钉得像是某种偏执狂的巢穴。

　　密室中央是一张巨大的橡木桌，桌面上铺着一张比桌面还大的照片——不是普通银版照片，而是用某种红水银显影技术制成的特殊照片，照片上是一棵树。

　　一棵树干由暗金色合金铸成的机械巨树。

　　树枝末梢挂着的不是叶子，而是一颗颗拳头大小的红水银核心，核心内部缓慢地跳动着，像是心脏。树冠最深处，无数金色齿轮以不同的速度缓缓旋转，发出极其细微的嗡鸣，像是远方的蜂群。

　　照片的一角被烧焦了，但烧焦的边缘能看见雪原和冰山——那是阿瓦隆。

　　照片前站着一个女孩。

　　白色长发，翡翠色瞳孔，十六七岁的样子，身上的长裙是翡冷翠最时兴的款式，腰间系着一条绣着齿轮和倒置五芒星的缎带。她的脸还没有长开，但已经能看出将来的绝世轮廓——那种冷峻而精致的美，和瓦莲京娜有七分相似，却多了几分东方女子才有的温润。

　　她的对面坐着一个男人。

　　看不清他的脸。记忆碎片里这个男人的面容始终模糊，像是被某种力量刻意遮蔽了。西泽尔只能看见他穿着一件裁剪考究的深红色长袍，袖口绣着卡巴拉之树的金色纹章。他的右手搁在桌面上，手指修长而苍白，食指上戴着一枚巨大的红宝石戒指，宝石里似乎有什么东西在缓缓流动。

　　——初代教皇。波吉亚一世。

　　西泽尔的神经猛然抽紧。

　　"艾琳娜。"那个看不清脸的男人开口了，声音低沉而平稳，像是在谈论天气，"你知道你是谁吗？"

　　"博尔吉亚家族旁系。"白色长发的女孩回答，声音比她的年龄更沉稳，"您的远房侄女。"

　　"不。"男人说，"你是我为这个时代准备的种子。"

　　他伸手点了点照片上那棵机械巨树："你看到它了吗？它叫做世界树。它是神留在人间的最后一件作品——也是我这一生唯一想要完成的作品。三百年来，我的每一代继承者都在为它努力，但没有人成功。"

　　艾琳娜·波尔吉亚的翡翠色瞳孔微微收缩，但她没有后退。

　　"要让它重新运转，需要一把钥匙。"男人的手指在照片上划过，停在树冠最深处那些缓慢旋转的金色齿轮上，"而那把钥匙不在西方。"

　　"在东方？"艾琳娜问。

　　"在世界的另一端。"男人说，"在东方一个叫做锡兰的国度。它的王都中央生长着世界树残枝的东方分支——一棵巨大的机械莲花，开满金色的花，每一片花瓣都是一扇门。"

　　他转身面向艾琳娜，红宝石戒指在烛光下闪了一下："我要你去那里。嫁给那个守护机械莲花的星见家族末裔——锡兰的末代星见。然后，为我生下一个孩子。"

　　艾琳娜沉默了很久。

　　"什么孩子？"她终于问。

　　"一个完美的容器。"男人的声音依然平稳，但那种平稳里藏着某种让西泽尔脊背发寒的东西，"能够同时承接博尔吉亚的血和星见的血的孩子。他将是连接世界树东西两支残枝的桥梁，是让机械神国重新运转的神使。"

　　"如果我生下的不是神使呢？"艾琳娜问。

　　"那就是死。"男人平静地说。

　　画面碎裂。

　　———

　　金红色的脉冲在西泽尔脑海里炸开，他的身体猛地一晃，膝盖撞上了通道的墙壁，肩甲在暗金色莲花瓣上擦出一声刺耳的金属摩擦声。

　　"西泽尔！"瓦莲京娜第一个冲上去，伸手扶住他的肩。

　　西泽尔摆手，没有让她碰，只是靠着墙壁喘了几口气。他的手指在微微颤抖，瞳孔里的金纹跳动得比刚才更剧烈了。

　　"继续走。"他说。

　　"你的心率已经——"阿方索的声音很紧。

　　"我说继续走。"西泽尔推开墙壁，重新站稳。

　　他的脑海里还残留着刚才那张照片的残影——暗金色的机械巨树，挂满红水银核心的树枝，旋转的金色齿轮，以及那棵他从未见过的机械莲花。

　　锡兰。

　　那个被新罗马帝国灭亡的东方小国。

　　不是贫穷的。

　　画面再次涌入，这次来得更猛烈。

　　———

　　这是一个完全不同的世界。

　　天空是深紫色的，不是夜晚的深紫，而是黄昏时分日落前最后那一抹深紫，像是天空的伤口正在愈合。空气里弥漫着某种清冽而微甜的花香，混着极淡的金属和红水银的腥味。

　　这里是锡兰。

　　不是后世那些帝国主义者笔下的贫穷东方小国。

　　街道宽阔而整洁，用某种暗金色的金属砖铺成，每一块砖上都刻着极其精细的齿轮纹路。街两侧的房屋是纯白色大理石和红木构建，屋顶装着机械驱动的旋转天线，接收着来自天空中某处看不见的信号。

　　机械鸟在街道上空盘旋。

　　不是装饰品，是真正的机械鸟——黄铜羽毛、红水银心脏，翼展不超过三十厘米，却能以极快的速度在楼宇之间穿梭，发出清脆的金属啁啾声。它们是锡兰的邮差、信使和天气预报员。

　　机械狗在街角小跑。

　　比猫大不了多少，铜腿银爪，背部有一个可以翻开的小舱，装着信件和小型包裹。它们摇着尾巴，看见行人经过就会蹲下来等一等，像是在说"请摸摸我的头"。

　　街上没有马车。

　　取而代之的是一种悬浮在地面上方半尺的金属平台，平台四角各有一个微型红水银核心提供升力，缓缓地在街道上滑动，无声无息。

　　一个穿着浅金色长袍的老人站在街角，对着一只机械鸟伸出手。机械鸟落在他指尖上，叽叽喳喳地叫了几声，然后从嘴里吐出一张叠好的纸条。老人看完纸条点了点头，机械鸟又扑棱着翅膀飞走了。

　　这就是锡兰。

　　世界树残枝东方分支的生根地。

　　一棵巨大的机械莲花矗立在王都的正中央，高达百米，底座由暗金色合金铸造，莲花瓣是镂空的齿轮和发条结构，每一片莲花瓣都在以不同的速度缓缓旋转。莲花的花心是一颗比屠龙者圣乔治的机械心脏还要大三倍的红水银核心，跳动时发出低沉的嗡鸣声，传遍整个王都。

　　而围绕着机械莲花的，是一座繁华的城。

　　不是废墟，不是贫穷的乡村，是一座比翡冷翠还要先进得多的城。锡兰人把红水银技术发展到了极致——他们没有走重型甲胄和巨型战舰的路，而是把红水银微型化，做成了精密的机械心脏，驱动那些可爱的机械鸟和机械狗，让整座城市活了过来。

　　但这一切都是世界树残枝东方分支的馈赠。

　　机械莲花是根，街道上的机械鸟是叶，锡兰人是花匠，守护这棵三百年前就在这里生根的树。

　　而在机械莲花的最高处，有一座塔。

　　圣女塔。

　　绯红色大理石，绿色琉璃顶，纯白石英岩地基——和君士坦丁堡的圣女塔一模一样。

　　画面再次碎裂。

　　———

　　"他妈的……"唐璜在通道里低声骂了一句。

　　他没有说更多，但所有人都听懂了那个词里的意思。

　　西泽尔刚才在通道里忽然停下了脚步，瞳孔里的金纹疯狂跳动，整个人像被电击了一样僵了将近十秒。阿方索的腕表上心率读数已经跳到了一百八十五。

　　"锡兰……"昆提良低声道，"原来是这样的地方。"

　　他想起了什么。昆提良不是贵族出身，但他在南部岛屿长大，南部岛屿的渔民们口口相传着一个关于东方的故事——那个故事里东方是一个遍地黄金、街道上跑着铁马铁狗的奇幻国度。

　　原来那不是故事。

　　是曾经真实存在过的世界。

　　西泽尔靠着通道的墙壁，手指在墙面的黄铜齿轮上留下了一道道汗印。他闭着眼，呼吸急促而粗重，后颈的黄金套管发烫得几乎要烧穿皮肤。

　　"老板——"阿方索上前一步。

　　"别管我。"西泽尔的声音很低，带着一种让阿方索后退一步的沙哑，"让我……让我缓一缓。"

　　瓦莲京娜站在他身后，没有说话，只是把手中改装神怒Ⅲ型甲胄的备用急救包打开，取出一支神经接驳缓冲剂，拔掉保险帽，递到他手边。

　　西泽尔没有接。

　　他睁开眼。

　　瞳孔里的金纹依然在跳动，但比刚才慢了一些。他推开瓦莲京娜递过来的缓冲剂，自己扶着墙壁站稳。

　　"继续走。"他说。

　　"你刚才看到了什么？"阿方索问。

　　"锡兰。"西泽尔说，"不是教科书上写的那个锡兰。"

　　他深吸了一口气。

　　"它是被毁灭的。"

　　画面第三次涌入。

　　———

　　圣女塔。

　　和君士坦丁堡那座一模一样的绯红色大理石塔身，绿色琉璃顶在深紫色的天空中泛着冷冷的光。

　　塔内的一间寝室里，烛光昏黄。

　　艾琳娜·波尔吉亚躺在床上。

　　她老了。白色长发里夹杂着几缕银丝，翡翠色瞳孔的焦点有些涣散，脸颊凹陷下去，但那双手依然修长而美，指尖还残留着红水银显影液的淡红色痕迹。

　　她的怀里抱着一个婴儿。

　　那个婴儿刚刚出生不到三天，皮肤皱巴巴的，眼睛闭着，小拳头攥得紧紧的。她的眼睛——

　　是紫色的。

　　不是瓦莲京娜那种翡翠色，也不是西泽尔平时那种深紫。

　　是被金色纹路贯穿的灼热亮紫。

　　和西泽尔在莲花通道里被记忆灌输时一模一样的紫瞳金纹。

　　门口站着一个男人。

　　依然是看不清面容的模糊影子，但能看见他穿着的那件深红色长袍，袖口的卡巴拉之树金色纹章，以及那枚红宝石戒指。

　　"是女孩。"男人的声音从门口传来，平静得像是在验收货物，"不是男孩。"

　　艾琳娜的手在婴儿身上收紧了。

　　"我说过。"男人的声音没有波动，"我要的是男孩。男人的意志更坚定，神经接驳的耐受力更强，更适合当神使载体。女孩……太软了。"

　　"她也是你的血脉。"艾琳娜低声说。

　　"血脉不够。"男人说，"我需要完美的容器。博尔吉亚的血，星见的血，紫瞳，而且必须是男性。你知道的。"

　　"那如果我再生呢？"艾琳娜问。

　　"你没有时间了。"男人说，"锡兰星见已经察觉到我的计划，末代星见在准备封印世界树残枝的东方分支。如果他在封印完成前还活着，你和这个女孩都会死在他的诅咒里。"

　　艾琳娜沉默了很久。

　　"如果我生不出男孩呢？"她问。

　　"那就让她成为转世的候选。"男人说，"候选不是容器，但候选可以不断转世。总有一天，某个转世的灵魂会恰好分裂出一半落进男性身体里。到那时，容器就完成了。"

　　"那要等多久？"艾琳娜的声音第一次有了裂痕。

　　"不知道。"男人说，"也许一百年，也许三百年。但只要她的血脉不断，候选就不断。"

　　他转身走向门口。

　　"你继续留在这里。保护好她。锡兰的末代星见很快就会被处理掉，但他身边还有一些死忠。如果他们发现你，就说你只是一个翡冷翠来的外乡人。"

　　"我什么时候能回翡冷翠？"艾琳娜问。

　　男人没有回答。

　　门关上了。

　　艾琳娜低下头，看着怀里那个紫瞳金纹的女婴。她的眼泪一滴一滴地落在婴儿的脸上。

　　"对不起。"她用一种极低极低的声音说，"妈妈……妈妈没办法保护你。"

　　画面再次碎裂。

　　———

　　西泽尔的手猛地攥紧了。

　　攥得太紧，指节发出咔咔的声响，鲜血从他的指缝里渗出来，顺着手套的内壁流下去。不是外伤，是他的指甲刺进了自己的掌心。

　　他的嘴唇在发抖。

　　不是冷的，是某种从骨头深处涌上来的、无法压制的愤怒。

　　"西泽尔。"瓦莲京娜的声音在耳边响起，平静而坚定，"你看到了什么？"

　　西泽尔没有回答。

　　他抬起左手，缓慢而用力地擦了一下眼角。

　　不是眼泪。

　　是汗水混着金红色脉冲的残光。

　　"锡兰战争。"他开口了，声音低得几乎听不见，"不是新罗马帝国挑起的。"

　　阿方索的手指在腕表上僵住了。

　　"是初代教皇。"西泽尔说，"是那个男人。三百多年前他就开始了。他要抢走世界树残枝的东方分支，他要清除所有锡兰星见的后裔，只留下琳琅夫人的前世——一个女婴——作为转世的候选。"

　　他的声音在最后几个字上变得沙哑。

　　"锡兰的毁灭不是新罗马帝国的侵略。"他重复了一遍，像是说给自己听，"是一个疯子为了重启机械神国，亲手点燃的战火。"

　　唐璜的拳头在蔷薇之鬼的曲刃镰柄上攥紧，指节发白。

　　"那新罗马帝国呢？"他问，"查士丁尼七世呢？"

　　"工具。"西泽尔说，"查士丁尼七世不过是被初代教皇推到台前的傀儡。他以为自己在开疆拓土，其实只是在替那个疯子清除世界树残枝东支的守护者。"

　　"那锡兰王呢？锡兰王女苏伽罗呢？"昆提良低声问。

　　"都是。"西泽尔说，"都是被那个疯子利用然后被丢弃的棋子。锡兰王到死都不知道自己为什么被灭国。"

　　昆提良的牙齿咬得格格响。

　　"锡兰末代星见呢？"阿方索问，"那个用自己的血给世界树最后的果实施咒、用自己的骨头做圣女塔地基的人呢？"

　　"他知道。"西泽尔说，"他知道初代教皇要做什么，所以他提前封印了世界树残枝的东支。但他还是晚了一步——艾琳娜已经被送到了锡兰，琳琅夫人的前世已经出生。"

　　他顿了顿。

　　"初代教皇拿到了他要的候选。剩下的锡兰星见后裔，全部清除。"

　　唐璜张嘴想说什么，但什么都没说出来。

　　通道里很安静。

　　只有黄铜齿轮转动的细微嗡鸣和西泽尔略微粗重的呼吸声。

　　画面第四次涌入。

　　———

　　这一次不是密室，不是圣女塔，不是翡冷翠的地下。

　　这是一片战场。

　　天空是血红色的，空气中弥漫着硝烟、鲜血和红水银燃烧的刺鼻气味。远处，新罗马帝国的攻城塔正在向锡兰王都的城墙推进，每一根撞木落下都溅起漫天的碎砖。

　　初代教皇站在一座山丘上。

　　他依然看不清脸，但他的身体已经和三百年前在密室里完全不一样了。他的右臂从肘部以下变成了精密的机械假肢，假肢表面刻着齿轮和梵文纹路，指尖能伸出红水银细线。他的下颌也是金属的，一侧脸颊的皮肉下隐约可见机械关节的轮廓。

　　——机械改造。

　　他把自己改造成了半个机器。

　　但画面在西泽尔的脑海里只停留了一瞬。

　　然后一切都碎了。

　　不是画面碎裂，是西泽尔自己强行掐断了这段记忆。

　　他不想看到那个男人的脸。

　　不想看到那个把自己改造成机械怪物、把自己的后代当作容器、把整个锡兰当作踏脚石的男人。

　　他不能再看了。

　　———

　　"西泽尔！"

　　瓦莲京娜的声音在耳边炸开。

　　他发现自己已经跪在了通道地面上，膝盖重重地撞在暗金色莲花瓣上，右手撑着地板，左手按在后颈的黄金套管上。套管滚烫得几乎要烧穿他的皮肤。

　　"心率两百零三！"阿方索的声音带着一丝他从未有过的紧张，"他再这样下去——"

　　"闭嘴。"西泽尔说。

　　他的声音很轻，但所有人都闭上了嘴。

　　他慢慢站起来。

　　膝盖上沾着金色莲花瓣的粉末，混着汗水和极淡的血迹。他低头看了一眼自己染血的掌心。

　　他记得琳琅夫人。

　　记得她抱着他读故事书的样子。

　　记得她在他发烧时用凉毛巾给他擦额头的样子。

　　记得她在那个阴暗的旧卧室里，给他扎头发时的手指的温度。

　　她是那个女婴。

　　被当作转世候选的女婴。

　　她从小就知道自己是被选中的容器吗？她知道自己的母亲是谁吗？她知道自己的前世死在哪个战场上吗？

　　她知道吗？

　　"西泽尔。"瓦莲京娜的手扶住了他的手肘。

　　他下意识地要抽开，但这一次他没有。

　　他只是抬起左手，用袖口极其快速地擦了一下眼角。

　　动作快得几乎看不见，但瓦莲京娜看见了。

　　她什么都没说。

　　她只是把手从他的手肘移到了他的肩膀上，轻轻地扶了一下。

　　"我们走吧。"西泽尔说，声音恢复了平静，"我要看看黑铁巨门后面到底是什么。"

　　他迈开步子。

　　瓦莲京娜、阿方索、昆提良、唐璜紧紧跟在他身后。

　　通道两旁的黄铜齿轮依然在缓缓转动，投射在暗金色莲花瓣上的光影明灭不定。那种和锡兰纸莲花底调完全一致的花香越来越浓，浓到几乎要把人淹没。

　　他们走了大约三百步。

　　然后通道到了尽头。

　　前方是一扇巨大的黑铁门——和叹息之墙一样沉重、一样古老、一样镌刻着密密麻麻的卡巴拉之树纹章。但这一扇比叹息之墙更大，更高，嵌在一整面黑色的岩壁里。

　　黑铁巨门。

　　半开着。

　　西泽尔之前打开的那半寸缝隙，在他们走过莲花通道的这段时间里，已经被某种力量从内部缓缓推开到了将近两米宽。门缝里透出的光不是烛光，不是红水银的光，不是任何他们见过的光。

　　是金色的。

　　像早晨第一缕穿透云层的阳光，又像是最纯的红水银核心燃烧时发出的光——温暖的、明亮的、带着某种让人无法移开视线的美。

　　唐璜的脚步停在了门缝前。

　　他的眼睛瞪得很大，蔷薇之鬼的曲刃镰从他松弛的手指间滑落，砸在莲花瓣上发出一声清脆的金属声。

　　"我的天……"他喃喃地说。

　　昆提良也停了。

　　阿方索的腕表上的心率读数开始疯狂跳动——但这次不是西泽尔的心率。

　　是阿方索自己的。

　　瓦莲京娜的手从西泽尔的肩膀上滑落。

　　她站在那里，翡翠色的眼睛映着门缝里透出的金色光芒，嘴唇微微张开，一个字都说不出来。

　　西泽尔站在最前面。

　　他透过那两米宽的门缝，看见了门后的世界。

　　他看见了——

　　所有人呆住了。

【English】
Chapter 204 — Memory Fragments (Part Two)

The emerald eyes looked straight at him. In those pupils he could see no reflection of his own face — only the slow dark-gold script running across the surface of the lotus petal.

The gold-red pulse broke Cesare's mind open.

His body kept walking. Boot-soles struck the dark-gold metal of the lotus floor and rang out in a brittle, ticking rhythm, but his gaze had emptied. The gold script blazed in his pupils, flicker on flicker, as if something were burning its way down the bundled nerve-channels of his spine.

Don Juan's hand started up to catch him.

"Don't touch him." Alfonso's voice was low.

"Why?"

"His heart rate's past one-seventy." Alfonso's eyes were on the dial of his wristwatch. He caught his lower lip between his teeth. "Let him walk it out. If you sever the fragment mid-flow, the shock could kill him."

Don Juan pulled his hand back.

Quintilian, without a word, shifted the great shield of Augustus from his left arm to his back and freed his right hand to hover an inch from Cesare's elbow as they moved.

Valentina walked half a pace behind him, the gloved fingers of her right hand resting on the short sword at the hip of her modified Wrath-of-God III. Her emerald eyes swept the corridor — the slow brass pinions turning in their housings on either wall, the glints of dark gold beneath their feet.

No one spoke.

Only the tick of Cesare's boots on the lotus floor. One step. Then another. As regular as a metronome.

The picture came.

—

A sealed room.

Somewhere beneath Florence. The air sat heavy in it, tasting of tallow and the slow rot of old vellum. No tapestries, no hangings on the four walls — only drawings pinned over drawings, and star-charts pinned over those, layer upon layer, as though some single-minded lunatic had been nesting here for a century.

In the middle of the floor stood a heavy oak table, and spread across that table was a photograph larger than the table itself. Not a daguerreotype. A red-mercury print — that forbidden process whose every plate had to be developed in a sealed chamber, the long-decayed secret of a vanished art.

The photograph showed a tree.

A tree whose trunk was cast in dark-gold alloy. From its branches, where leaves should have been, hung great bulbs of red mercury the size of a man's fist, and inside each bulb a slow beat pulsed, like a heart. At the deep heart of the canopy, a host of tiny gold gears turned at their separate speeds and gave off a thin, almost inaudible hum — like bees heard from a great distance.

One corner of the photograph was burned away. Through the char he could make out snowfield, ice cliffs. Avalon.

Standing before the photograph was a girl.

White hair. Emerald pupils. Sixteen, perhaps seventeen. The long dress she wore was of the cut then fashionable in Florence, and at her waist a ribbon was embroidered with cogs and an inverted five-pointed star. Her face had not yet settled into its final line, but one could see what it would become — a cold, precise beauty, seven parts Valentina, with the remaining three drawn from some softer, easterner well.

Across the table from her, a man sat.

The man's face Cesare could not see. Some force in the fragment itself had blotted the features into a smear, a deliberate smudge of memory. What he could see was a robe of deep crimson, beautifully cut, with the gold sigil of the Kabbalistic Tree embroidered at the cuffs. The right hand lay on the table. Long, white fingers. A single great ruby on the forefinger, and inside the ruby something seemed to turn, slow and slow.

The first Pope. Alexander Borgia the First.

Cesare's nerves drew taut.

"Elena." The faceless man's voice was low, measured — the voice of a man discussing the weather. "Do you know who you are?"

"A cadet branch of the Borgia." The white-haired girl's answer was more composed than her years. "Your distant niece."

"No." The man said. "You are the seed I have prepared for this age."

He lifted a finger and laid it on the photograph of the great metal tree. "Do you see it? It is called the World Tree. The last work God left in the world — and the only work I, in this life, mean to finish. For three hundred years, every heir I have raised has striven toward it. None has succeeded."

The emerald pupils of Elena Borgia contracted by a fraction. She did not step back.

"To set it turning again," the man went on, "one needs a key." His finger slid across the print, and stopped among the slow-turning gears at the deep heart of the canopy. "And that key is not in the West."

"In the East?" Elena asked.

"On the other side of the world." The man said. "In a kingdom called Ceylon. At the heart of its capital city there grows the eastern branch of the broken World Tree — a great mechanical lotus, open in a thousand golden flowers, and every petal of it a door."

He turned to face her. The ruby on his finger caught the candle and gave a single, dull flare.

"I mean for you to go there. To marry the last surviving scion of the Astromancer line — the last star-reader who still keeps the mechanical lotus. And to bear me a child."

Elena was silent for a long while.

"What child?" she asked at last.

"A perfect vessel." The man's voice stayed level, but in the steadiness of it there was something that raised the small hairs at the back of Cesare's neck. "A child who can carry both the blood of Borgia and the blood of the Astromancers. He will be the bridge between the eastern branch and the western branch of the Tree. The envoy who makes the mechanical kingdom turn again."

"And if I do not bear a god-envoy?"

"Then a corpse." The man said it pleasantly.

The picture shattered.

—

The gold-red pulse detonated inside Cesare's skull. His body lurched. His knee cracked against the wall of the corridor, and the joint of his pauldron screamed a long metallic note as it scraped across a dark-gold petal.

"Cesare!" Valentina was the first to him, her hand catching his shoulder.

He waved her off. Leaned his back against the wall and stood there, breathing. The gold script in his pupils was jumping faster than before. His fingers were trembling.

"Keep moving," he said.

"Your heart rate —" Alfonso began.

"I said keep moving."

Cesare pushed off from the wall and set his boot down on the lotus floor again. Behind his eyes the print of the photograph lingered — the dark-gold metal tree, the red-mercury hearts pulsing on its branches, the slow-spinning gold gears, and the great mechanical lotus he had never seen with his own eyes.

Ceylon.

That small eastern kingdom the New Roman Empire had, in its histories, prided itself on swallowing.

It had not been poor.

The picture came again. This time it crashed into him like a wave.

—

A different world.

The sky was a deep bruise of violet — not the violet of nightfall, but the last stain of sunset as the day's wound closed. The air carried some cool, faintly sweet floral scent, and beneath it the thin metallic bite of red mercury.

This was Ceylon.

Not the miserable eastern backwater the imperialists in their schoolbooks had later described.

The streets were wide and clean, paved in dark-gold metal bricks, every one of them incised with a fine pattern of cogs. On either side, houses of white marble and red heartwood rose into the air, and on every rooftop a mechanical receiving-antenna turned, catching signals from something somewhere in the sky.

Mechanical birds wheeled above the streets.

Not ornaments. Real birds — brass feathers, red-mercury hearts, wingspans no greater than a foot, swift as swallows through the gaps between buildings, calling to one another in a bright metallic chatter. They were Ceylon's postmen, its messengers, its weather-forecasters.

Mechanical dogs trotted at the corners.

No larger than a cat. Copper legs. Silver paws. A small hatch on the back opened to reveal letters, tiny parcels. They wagged their tails and sat down politely when a passerby came near, as if asking to be stroked.

There were no carriages.

In their place glided low metal platforms, suspended a hand's breadth above the street, each lifted at its four corners by a miniature red-mercury core. They drifted in silence.

At one corner an old man in a pale gold robe held out his hand. A mechanical bird alighted on his fingertip, twittered, and from its beak produced a folded slip. The man read it, nodded, and the bird launched itself into the air again.

This was Ceylon.

The place where the eastern branch of the broken World Tree had taken root.

And at the heart of the capital stood the tree itself.

A mechanical lotus a hundred metres tall, its calyx of dark-gold alloy, every one of its petals cut through into a delicate filigree of cogs and springs, each petal turning at its own unhurried speed. At the flower's heart a red-mercury core the size of three of St George the Dragonslayer's hearts pulsed with a low, slow thrum that travelled through the whole city.

Around the lotus, a city.

Not a ruin. Not a poor village. A city that outpaced Florence by a generation. The Ceylonese had taken red mercury where the West had taken it and miniaturised it — not into war-engines and vast leviathans of the air, but into a hundred thousand little mechanical hearts, all beating, all working, until the city itself seemed alive.

But all of it was the gift of the eastern branch.

The mechanical lotus was the root. The mechanical birds along the streets were the leaves. The Ceylonese were the gardeners, tending a tree that had been putting down roots here for three hundred years.

And at the top of the lotus, a tower.

The Tower of the Holy Maiden.

Crimson marble. A roof of green glazed tile. A plinth of pure white quartz. Identical, in every line, to the Tower of the Holy Maiden in Constantinople.

The picture shattered.

—

"Christ…" Don Juan said, very softly, in the corridor.

He did not finish the sentence. He did not need to.

Cesare had stopped mid-stride. The gold script in his pupils jumped and jumped. For nearly ten seconds he had stood stock-still, as if the air around him were a current that had frozen him where he stood. On Alfonso's wrist the needle had climbed to one hundred and eighty-five.

"Ceylon," Quintilian said under his breath. "So that is what it was."

He thought of a thing. Quintilian was no noble. He had grown up on the southern islands, where the fishermen still told a children's tale of the East — a country paved in gold, where iron dogs ran through the streets and iron horses flew. He had always taken it for a fairy story.

It had not been a fairy story.

It had been a world.

Cesare leaned his back against the wall of the corridor. His fingers, dragging across the brass pinion beside him, left four wet trails of sweat. He closed his eyes. His breath was short, hard, ragged. The gold coupling at the back of his neck was hot enough to feel through his collar.

"Boss —" Alfonso took a step forward.

"Leave me." Cesare's voice was rough. There was something in it that made Alfonso retreat. "Give me a moment. Just a moment."

Valentina said nothing. She unhooked the field kit from her belt, popped the seal, drew out a single dose of neural-coupling buffer, thumbed the safety cap and held it out to him at arm's length.

Cesare did not take it.

He opened his eyes.

The gold script in his pupils was still turning, but slower than before. He pushed Valentina's hand gently away, steadied himself against the wall, stood.

"Keep moving," he said.

"What did you see?" Alfonso asked.

"Ceylon," Cesare said. "Not the Ceylon in the textbooks."

He drew a long breath.

"It was destroyed."

The picture came a third time.

—

The Tower of the Holy Maiden.

The same crimson marble. The same green-glazed roof, cold against a violet sky.

A bedchamber inside. Candles burned low.

Elena Borgia lay on the bed.

She had aged. Strands of silver ran through her white hair. The focus of her emerald eyes had softened, gone vague. Her cheeks had hollowed. But her hands were still long, still beautiful, the fingertips still stained a faint red from the developing fluids of her forbidden art.

In her arms, she held an infant.

Three days old at most. Skin creased. Eyes shut. Tiny fists curled tight. The infant's eyes —

Were violet.

Not the jade of Valentina. Not the deep violet of Cesare's ordinary gaze.

A hot, searing violet, shot through with veins of gold.

Exactly the violet Cesare's own eyes had become in the lotus corridor.

In the doorway stood a man.

His face was still only a smear. But the crimson robe was there, and the gold embroidery of the Kabbalistic Tree, and the great ruby on the finger.

"It is a girl." The man's voice, from the doorway, was the voice of a clerk confirming a shipment. "Not a boy."

Elena's arm tightened around the child.

"I told you," the man said, "I need a boy. A man's will holds firmer. A man tolerates neural coupling more readily. A man is a fitter vessel for the envoy. A girl… is too soft."

"She is your blood as well," Elena said.

"Blood is not enough." The man said. "I need the perfect vessel. Borgia blood. Astromancer blood. Violet eyes. And male. You know this."

"And if I conceive again?"

"You have no more time." The man said. "The Ceylon Astromancers have begun to suspect what I am about. The last of their line is preparing to seal the eastern branch. If he finishes the seal while he is still alive, you and this child will both die under his curse."

Elena was quiet for a long while.

"And if I do not give you a boy?"

"Then she becomes a candidate." The man said. "A candidate is not a vessel. But a candidate can be reborn. Sooner or later, the soul of her, on some reincarnation, will split — and one half of the split will fall into a male body. When that happens, the vessel is finished."

"How long must I wait?"

"I do not know." The man said. "A hundred years. Perhaps three hundred. But if her line is not broken, the candidate is not broken."

He turned toward the door.

"You will stay here. Guard the child. The last of the Ceylon Astromancers will be dealt with shortly, but he has a few loyalists at his back. If they find you, you are a Florentine traveller. Nothing more."

"When may I return to Florence?"

The man did not answer.

The door closed.

Elena lowered her head. The tears fell from her eyes, one by one, onto the infant's face.

"Forgive me," she said, in a voice that was almost nothing. "Mama… mama cannot keep you safe."

The picture shattered.

—

Cesare's hand closed into a fist.

He closed it too hard. The knuckles ground against one another. He felt the hot wet trickle of blood running from his palm down the inside of his glove — not from any wound, but from his own nails driven into his own flesh.

His lips were trembling.

Not from cold. From a heat, deep in the bone, that no muscle could contain.

"Cesare." Valentina's voice came at his ear, level and steady. "What did you see?"

He did not answer.

He lifted his left hand and drew the heel of it, once, very deliberately, across the corner of his eye.

It was not tears.

It was sweat, and the dying red-gold flare of a spent pulse.

"The War of Ceylon," he said. His voice was almost inaudible. "It was not started by the New Roman Empire."

Alfonso's finger went still on the dial of his watch.

"It was the first Pope," Cesare said. "That man. Three hundred years ago, he began it. He meant to take the eastern branch of the World Tree. He meant to wipe out every Astromancer in Ceylon. He meant to leave nothing but Madame Linlang's previous life — that infant — as a candidate for rebirth."

His voice roughened on the last words.

"The destruction of Ceylon was not an invasion by the New Romans." He said it again, as if to himself. "It was a madman, single-handed, lighting the fuse of a war so that he might one day restart his machine god."

Don Juan's fist tightened on the haft of the Rose Ghost. The knuckles went white.

"And the New Roman Empire?" he asked. "And Justinian the Seventh?"

"Tools," Cesare said. "Justinian was the puppet the first Pope put on a throne. He thought he was making conquests. He was clearing the guardians of the eastern branch out of the way for that madman."

"And the King of Ceylon?" Quintilian asked, his voice low. "Princess Sugala of Ceylon?"

"Pawns." Cesare said. "Pawns used and then swept off the board. The King of Ceylon died not knowing why his country had been destroyed."

Quintilian's teeth ground together audibly.

"And the last of the Ceylon Astromancers?" Alfonso asked. "The man who cursed the last fruit of the World Tree with his own blood, and made the bones of his body the foundation of the Holy Maiden's Tower?"

"He knew." Cesare said. "He knew what the first Pope intended. That is why he sealed the eastern branch before he died. But he was still too late. Elena had already been sent to Ceylon. Madame Linlang's previous life had already been born."

He paused.

"The first Pope took the candidate he wanted. Every other Astromancer scion was put to the sword."

Don Juan opened his mouth, found he had nothing to say, and closed it.

The corridor was quiet.

Only the thin hum of the turning brass pinions. Only the rough edge of Cesare's breath.

The picture came a fourth time.

—

This time it was not a sealed room. Not the Holy Maiden's Tower. Not anywhere beneath Florence.

It was a battlefield.

The sky was the colour of blood. The air was thick with the reek of powder, of offal, and of red mercury burning. In the distance, the New Roman siege-towers lumbered toward the walls of the Ceylon capital; every ram-stroke flung a great fan of broken brick up into the smoke.

The first Pope stood on a low hill.

His face was still blurred. But the body that wore the crimson robe was no longer the body that had sat in the sealed room three centuries before. His right arm, from the elbow down, had been replaced by a mechanism — intricate, gear-toothed, inscribed with a fine tracery of Sanskrit. From the metal fingertips he could extrude threads of liquid red mercury. The jaw, too, was metal. Along one cheek, the skin had parted over a moving joint.

Augmetics.

He had rebuilt himself into half a machine.

The picture stayed in Cesare's mind for a single beat.

Then he crushed it.

He crushed it himself, on purpose, with the full force of a will that had been trained since childhood to resist whatever was poured into it. He did not want to see that man's face. He did not want to see the man who had rebuilt his own body into a mechanism, who had treated his own descendants as vessels, who had spent a whole kingdom as a footstool.

He would not look.

—

"Cesare!"

Valentina's voice exploded at his ear.

He found that he was on his knees on the lotus floor, his right hand flat on the metal, his left hand clamped to the gold coupling at the back of his neck. The coupling was so hot he could feel the skin underneath it trying to blister.

"Two hundred and three!" Alfonso's voice had a pitch Cesare had never heard in it. "If he keeps on like this —"

"Quiet." Cesare said.

Quietly. But everyone stopped talking.

He got to his feet.

Powder from the dark-gold petal clung to his knees, mixed with sweat and a thin smear of blood. He looked down at his own stained palm.

He thought of Madame Linlang.

He remembered the way she sat him on her lap and read him stories. He remembered the cool cloth she laid across his brow when his fever rose. He remembered the warmth of her fingers as she tied back his hair in the dim bedroom where he had grown up.

She was that infant.

The candidate.

Had she known, from the time she was small, what she had been chosen for? Had she known the name of the mother who had borne her? Had she known where her previous life had died, and on which field?

Had she known?

"Cesare." Valentina's hand came to rest on his elbow.

He almost pulled away. This time he did not.

He lifted his left hand, and with the cuff of his sleeve, very quickly, once, brushed the corner of his eye.

The movement was so brief it was almost invisible. Valentina saw it.

She said nothing.

She moved her hand from his elbow to his shoulder, and steadied him.

"Let's go," Cesare said. His voice had gone level again. "I want to see what is behind the Black Iron Door."

He set his boot on the lotus floor.

Valentina, Alfonso, Quintilian and Don Juan closed in tight behind him.

The brass pinions on either side of the corridor kept their slow, unhurried turning. The light they cast on the dark-gold petals came and went in a long, even breath. The scent of the lotus — the very same scent as the paper-lotus base in Ceylon — thickened, until it seemed to press against the skin.

They walked perhaps three hundred paces.

Then the corridor ended.

Before them stood a great black iron door — as heavy, as old, as thickly engraved with the sigils of the Kabbalistic Tree as the Wall of Sighs. But this door was larger, and taller, and set into a wall of black stone that ran from floor to ceiling.

The Black Iron Door.

Half open.

The crack Cesare had forced when he first came through had, in the time they had spent in the lotus corridor, been pushed wider from within — almost two metres now. And through that gap the light that fell was no light any of them had ever seen. It was not candlelight. It was not the glow of red mercury. It was not any daylight.

It was gold.

Like the first beam of the sun to break through the morning cloud. Like the cleanest flame of a pure red-mercury core. A warm, bright, living gold, the kind of gold that did not let you look away.

Don Juan's feet stopped at the edge of the gap.

His eyes went wide. The Rose Ghost slipped from his loosening fingers and clattered onto a lotus petal.

"God above…" he whispered.

Quintilian stopped.

Alfonso's watch began to run away with itself — but this time, it was not Cesare's heart on the dial.

It was his own.

Valentina's hand slid from Cesare's shoulder.

She stood very still, her emerald eyes lit through with that gold radiance falling across her face, her lips parted, no word in her throat.

Cesare stood at the front.

Through the two-metre gap, he looked in upon the world on the far side of the door.

He saw —

Everyone went still.


==================================================
第205章 莲花状的欧米茄
==================================================

【中文】
第205章 莲花状的欧米茄

他们就这样站在门缝前，很久没有人说话。

西泽尔的眼睛已经完全适应了门缝里透出的金色光芒，那光芒照在暗金色的莲花瓣上，又被莲花瓣反射回空气中，整条莲花通道都被染成了一种温暖的、蜂蜜般的颜色。香气在金色中流淌，浓烈得近乎粘稠，像是有人把整个锡兰王都的莲花池压缩进了这条隧道。

他深吸一口气，率先迈过了那道两米宽的门缝。

"老板！"阿方索在后面喊了一声。

西泽尔没有回答。他的脚步平稳，一步步踏上门后平整的黑色石板地面。他的影子被金色光芒拉得很长，投射在身后的莲花通道里，像一条瘦长的黑色裂缝。

门后是一个圆形的空间。

非常巨大。

巨大到西泽尔一时间无法估量它的直径和高度——穹顶在视线无法触及的远方合拢成一个完美的弧形，弧形之上镶嵌着数以万计的微小齿轮，每一个齿轮都缓慢转动，发出细微的嗡鸣声，汇合成一种恒定的、如同心跳般的低频震动。穹顶的最高处有一道光柱直直落下来，落在圆形大厅的正中央，亮度远超周围其他光源，刺眼得几乎要灼伤视网膜。

西泽尔抬手遮在眉骨前，透过指缝看向那道光柱的底部。

他的手指微微僵住了。

那是一棵树。

不是活的树——没有树皮，没有树叶，没有年轮。但它分明就是树的形状。树干是暗金色的，表面布满了细密的梵文纹路，每一笔每一划都在微微发光，像是镌刻在黄金上的经文。树干笔直向上，在大约十五米的高度开始分出枝丫，枝丫向四面八方伸展，末梢悬挂着一颗颗拳头大小的红色晶块——那些晶块散发着柔和的暗红色光芒，随着穹顶齿轮的转动一明一暗，仿佛在呼吸。

树枝的末梢没有树叶。取代树叶的是一片片薄如蝉翼的金色齿轮，每一片都在缓缓旋转，边缘刻着比树干上更细的梵文，旋转时发出叮叮当当的轻响。

那就是西方世界苦苦寻找了两百年的东西。

世界树残枝。

缩小版的。

西泽尔的目光缓缓从世界树残枝上移开，落到圆形大厅的四周。

他的呼吸停了一瞬——不是恐惧，而是因为眼前的景象太过庞大、太过密集、太过超出人类认知的范畴，大脑需要时间去处理那数以百计的、整齐排列的金属巨人。

圆形大厅的地面是深黑色的抛光岩石，从世界树残枝的位置向外延伸，呈完美的同心圆展开。在每一个同心圆上，都有一架金色的机动甲胄矗立。

不。不是一架。

是很多架。

非常多架。

西泽尔的目光从最近的一架扫向更远的一架，从更远的一架扫向更更远的一架，他数了第一圈——三十六架。再远一圈——七十二架。再远一圈——一百零八架。每一圈的数量都在增加，排列的方式呈现出花瓣般的弧度，整座圆形大厅的甲胄加在一起，像是一朵由金属巨人构成的、正在缓缓绽放的莲花。

那些甲胄全都是同一种颜色——暗金色。装甲板的表面镌刻着密密麻麻的微型齿轮纹路，和世界树残枝上的齿轮风格完全一致。胸腔的位置镶嵌着跳动的红水银核心，光芒一明一暗，和悬挂在大厅穹顶的那棵世界树残枝上的红色晶块保持着完全同步的频率。

它们的眼睛全是翡翠色的。

此刻那些翡翠色的眼睛是暗的，但表面仍然折射着微弱的金色光芒，让每一架欧米茄原型体都像是一尊沉睡的黄金神像。

西泽尔盯着最近那架欧米茄原型体胸前的铭牌。

铭牌上刻着一个小小的数字。

001。

他的目光向后跳了一架。

002。

再后面是003、004、005……数字一路延伸到他视野的尽头，消失在远处金色光芒的雾气中。

"这些……"唐璜的声音从身后传来，沙哑得像是喉咙里塞了砂纸，"这些全都是欧米茄？"

没有人回答他。

因为答案太明显了。

阿方索抬起左手腕，腕表内侧弹出一只微型机械蜘蛛，蜘蛛的腹部亮起一颗极小的红点，那是它自带的摄像头的指示灯。他把蜘蛛轻轻放在地面，蜘蛛立刻沿着黑色石板飞速向外围爬去。

"我去拍。"阿方索说，声音压得很低，"给我三分钟。"

西泽尔点了点头。

阿方索转身跟上蜘蛛，机械臂的关节在走动中发出细微的咔嚓声，他的身影很快就被金色的雾气吞没，只剩下腕表上跳动的信号灯表明他还在移动。

昆提良和唐璜几乎同时拔出了武器。昆提良手中是那柄跟了他多年的备用单手战斧，唐璜则把蔷薇之鬼的曲刃镰从腰间解下来，单手握住镰柄的末端，镰刀在金色光芒中映出一道冷冽的弧光。

两人没有说话，只是默契地背靠背站着，一左一右，面朝不同的方向，目光警惕地扫过最近的几架欧米茄原型体。

那些甲胈一动不动。

像一尊尊金身的佛像，沉默地矗立在自己的位置上，翡翠色的眼睛里没有光，也没有任何即将苏醒的征兆。但它们存在本身就带着一种让人无法忽视的压迫感——那是一百台、二百台、五百台、九百九十九台拥有自我修复神经纤维的恐怖决战兵器同时处于待机状态时产生的、纯粹的物理意义上的压力。

"西泽尔。"

瓦莲京娜的声音从他右侧传来，平静而克制。

西泽尔转过头，看见她正看着圆形大厅的地面。地面是黑色的抛光岩石，但在世界树残枝光柱的照射下，反光中浮现出一圈圈极淡的纹路——那些纹路是圆形的，从世界树残枝的位置向外扩散，每一圈都比上一圈更大、更复杂，一直延伸到大厅最外围的墙壁。

"你看那些纹路。"瓦莲京娜蹲下身，伸出一根手指轻轻碰了碰地面，指尖顺着最近的那道圆弧滑动，"是梵文。和大厅穹顶上的齿轮上刻的是同一种字体。"

西泽尔也蹲下来，目光落在她手指滑动过的地方。

确实是一行行极细的梵文，刻痕只有发丝那么细，如果不是光柱恰好以某个角度照射下来，根本看不出来。那些梵文从世界树残枝的基座开始，沿同心圆的弧度向外延伸，绕大厅整整一圈才回到起点，像是给整个空间画了一道经文构成的结界。

"这是初代教皇刻的。"西泽尔说。

"你觉得？"

"他既然要用这里来制造欧米茄原型体，就一定会留下某种……"西泽尔想了想措辞，"说明书。"

瓦莲京娜抬头看了他一眼，嘴角微微弯了一下，但很快又抿直了。

"你要过去看看那棵树吗？"她问。

西泽尔站起身，目光投向大厅正中央的世界树残枝。

那棵暗金色的金属树在光柱中静静矗立，树干上镌刻的梵文随着光柱的明暗变化而明明灭灭。悬挂着红水银晶块的枝丫向四周伸展，每一根枝条的弧度都像是有意计算过，让整棵树的形状呈现出完美的对称。空气中那种和莲花通道一脉相承的香气在这里更加浓郁，已经不是"闻到"的程度，而是整个人都浸泡在其中的感觉。

西泽尔迈开步子，朝世界树残枝走去。

"我跟你一起。"瓦莲京娜说。

她没有等西泽尔回答，径直走到了他左侧半步远的位置，既不靠得太近也不落得太远，刚好是并肩行走又不妨碍对方拔剑的距离。

他们向大厅中央走去。

每走过一架欧米茄原型体，西泽尔都能感觉到那架甲胈散发出的微弱热量——红水银核心在运转时会散发热量，哪怕只是在待机状态，温度也比周围的空气高出一两度。999架甲胈同时散发出的热量汇聚在一起，让整个大厅的温度比莲花通道高了至少十度。

"原来安妮说的是真的。"

瓦莲京娜的声音很低，像是在自言自语。

西泽尔没有接话。安妮的脸在他脑海中一闪而过——那个在马斯顿的广场上拉着他袖子、告诉他自己看见了金色甲胄的女孩。她的尸体后来被装在铁皮箱里运走，他连见她最后一面都没有赶上。

"我们当时所有人都以为她疯了。"瓦莲京娜继续说，"金色甲胄，翡翠色的眼睛，会自己走路……一个十三岁的小女孩告诉大人她看见了这种东西，谁会信？"

"我信了。"西泽尔说。

瓦莲京娜侧头看了他一眼。

"我信了。"西泽尔重复了一遍，语气没有变化，"但我没能保护她。"

瓦莲京娜沉默了几秒钟。

"现在你可以保护其他人了。"她说，"如果你能把这里的事情解决掉的话。"

西泽尔没有回答。他们继续向前走。

三分钟后，他们站在了世界树残枝的面前。

从这个距离看，那棵金属树比远处看起来更加庞大。树干的直径至少有两人合抱那么粗，表面的暗金色金属泛着一种温润的光泽，不是冷冰冰的金属反光，而是更接近于活体皮肤被太阳晒过后的那种柔和的光。树干上的梵文在近距离更加清晰，每一笔都像是用极细的刻刀一笔一划手工镌刻上去的，笔画的起承转合带着某种说不清的人情味。

西泽尔抬起手。

他的手指在距离树干大约一寸的地方停住了。

他能感觉到热量。

从树干表面辐射出来的、稳定的、均匀的热量。不是红水银核心运转时那种带着金属腥味的燥热，而是更接近于……

人体体温。

西泽尔的手指终于触碰到了树干的表面。

温热。

不是金属应有的温度。金属要么冰冷要么滚烫，没有中间状态。但这棵世界树残枝的树干是温热的，温度大约和人的体温相当，手指触碰上去的感觉就像握住了一个睡着的人的手臂。

西泽尔的手指停在树干上，没有移开。

然后他感觉到了别的东西。

树干在他掌心下微微震动。那种震动的频率非常低、非常稳，和他在莲花通道里听到的那种心跳般的低频嗡鸣完全一致，但当他的手掌贴上去之后，那个频率明显加快了——从每分钟大约六十次变成了每分钟大约七十次。

像是有什么东西察觉到了他的触碰。

西泽尔的瞳孔忽然刺痛了一下。

那不是普通的疼痛，而是像有一根烧红的细针从眼球后方刺入，沿着视神经一路烧到后脑。他的视野瞬间变成了一片灼热的亮紫色——紫瞳被激活了。暗金色的莲花通道、黑色的岩石地面、周围沉默的欧米茄原型体，所有的东西都蒙上了一层紫色的薄雾。

而他手掌下的树干开始发光。

不是之前那种微弱的、随着齿轮转动一明一暗的光，而是突然爆发出的、刺眼的、仿佛正午阳光直射眼睛的金色光芒。光从树干内部透出来，穿过梵文的刻痕向外喷涌，把整个圆形大厅都照得通明——那些原本暗淡的欧米茄原型体表面的暗金色装甲板被金光照亮，999架甲胈同时反射出耀眼的金属光泽。

"西泽尔！"瓦莲京娜的声音从旁边传来，带着一丝紧张。

西泽尔没有回答。

他能看见自己手背上的血管正在浮现淡紫色的发光脉络——和上一次在维苏威火山北麓矿道里看到的一模一样。紫色的光从手掌蔓延到手腕、从手腕蔓延到小臂、再从小臂一路向上。紫色的纹路像藤蔓一样在他的皮肤下生长，每一条都和他的心跳同步搏动。

后颈的黄金套管也在发烫。

那种烫不是普通的发烫，而是从骨头里透出来的、深入脊髓的热度，仿佛有一只看不见的手在黄金套管上拧动发条，要把什么东西从他的神经系统里强行拧出来。

"你的眼睛……"瓦莲京娜盯着他的脸，翡翠色的瞳孔微微收缩。

西泽尔知道自己现在是什么样子——紫瞳激活、金纹浮现。他看过镜子。上一次在维苏威火山北麓矿道里，他激活不朽之王模式时就是这个模样，瞳孔变成了被金色纹路贯穿的灼热亮紫，金纹会随心跳闪烁。

但这一次他没有激活不朽之王模式。

他只是碰了一下树干。

"我知道。"西泽尔说，声音比他自己预想的要平静，"别担心，还没到那一步。"

瓦莲京娜抿了抿嘴唇，没有再说什么。她上前一步，伸出右手，和西泽尔一样把手掌贴在了世界树残枝的树干上。

她的手指刚触碰到树干表面，眉毛就微微抬了一下。

"温的。"她说，语气里带着一丝意外，"真的是温的。像是有生命一样。"

她闭上眼睛，掌心紧紧贴着树干，似乎在感受那种温度。几秒钟后她睁开眼，翡翠色的瞳孔里映着树干内部透出的金色光芒。

"西泽尔，"她收回手，转过头看着他，"你知道这意味着什么吗？"

"你是说这棵树是欧米茄原型体的母体？"

瓦莲京娜点了点头。

"初代教皇不可能凭空造出999架完全相同的欧米茄原型体。"她说，"即使有达·芬奇的图纸、有最高级的红水银核心、有一百年的时间和整个教皇国的资源——他也无法手工制造999件一模一样的决战兵器。"

她的目光从世界树残枝上移开，扫过大厅四周那些呈莲花状排列的欧米茄原型体。

"所以他造了一棵树。"瓦莲京娜的声音很轻，但每个字都清晰无比，"一棵会生长、会复制、会自行制造欧米茄原型体的世界树残枝。他把欧米茄的制造工艺写进了这棵树的基因里，让它像真正的树一样结出果实——每一架欧米茄原型体就是这棵树结出的一颗果实。"

她顿了顿。

"莲花状的欧米茄。"她说，"999颗果实，围绕着母体，排列成莲花的形状。初代教皇的终极遗产。"

西泽尔听着她的话，目光再次落回到世界树残枝上。

温热的树干。自行加快的震动频率。触碰后爆发出的金色光芒。

这棵树确实像是有生命的。

或者说，它本来就是有生命的。

"老板！"阿方索的声音从远处传来，被大厅穹顶的嗡鸣声模糊了一些，但仍然听得清楚，"我已经绕着大厅转了一圈！蜘蛛把整个画面都拍下来了！"

西泽尔朝声音传来的方向看了一眼。阿方索的身影正从大厅外围的欧米茄原型体群中走出来，机械臂的关节还在咔嚓作响，腕表上的信号灯已经不再闪烁——说明蜘蛛的摄像任务已经完成。

"那边情况怎么样？"西泽尔问。

"和这边一模一样。"阿方索走到他们面前停下，呼吸有些急促，"999架。我数了三遍，每一圈的甲胈数量我都数过，第一圈36、第二圈72、第三圈108，每一圈数量递增36，全部加起来正好999。全部是暗金色、翡翠眼睛、胸前有红水银核心。"

他用机械手指了指自己腕表上新出现的一个图标——一只蜘蛛的剪影，下面有一行细小的数字"999/999"。

"全都拍下来了。"阿方索说，"包括那棵树。"

西泽尔点了点头。

他的手掌还贴在树干上，金色光芒已经从刚才那种刺眼的爆发状态缓和下来，变成了一种稳定的、持续的、从树干内部透出的暖光。紫瞳金纹也慢慢消退了——他手背上的淡紫色脉络从手腕向手指方向褪去，像退潮的海水从沙滩上撤回。

但树干仍然温热。

西泽尔没有把手收回来。

"阿方索，"他说，"让蜘蛛把数据全部上传到你的备用芯片里。"

"已经做了。"阿方索说，"双份备份。就算我现在死了，数据也不会丢。"

"那张照片呢？"西泽尔问，"达·芬奇留给薇若兰那张照片——艾琳娜和两个孩子的合影——你带着？"

"在密涅瓦机关。"阿方索说，"我出发前锁进了鹰巢的保险柜里，密码只有我知道。"

西泽尔沉默了一秒钟。

"那张照片里，琳琅夫人就是艾琳娜的后代。"他说，"艾琳娜是我祖母。达·芬奇三百年前就把一切都准备好了。他知道迟早会有人来这扇门后面，他需要那个人知道自己在做什么。"

阿方索没有说话。他只是轻轻推了推眼镜，镜片反射着世界树残枝的金色光芒。

"老板，"他说，"那张照片你也需要看一下。不过不是现在。"

"我知道。"西泽尔说。

他把视线从世界树残枝上移开，最后看了一眼树干上那些正在缓缓发光的梵文。

莲花状的欧米茄。

999架。

初代教皇用一百年的时间培育出来的终极遗产。

如果原罪机关把这999架欧米茄原型体全部唤醒……

西泽尔没有继续想下去。

"走吧。"他把手从树干上收回来，转身朝大厅外围走去，"我们需要在原罪机关的人赶到之前弄清楚这里的所有情况。"

他刚迈出两步。

一声尖锐的、刺耳的金属摩擦声突然从大厅穹顶最高处传来。

那个声音穿透了所有嗡鸣、所有心跳般的低频震动，像一根烧红的铁针直直刺入每个人的耳膜。昆提良和唐璜几乎是本能地举起了武器，背靠背站立的姿势瞬间绷紧，肩胛骨下面的肌肉隆起。

西泽尔停下脚步。

他的紫瞳再次亮了一下——不是他主动激活的，而是某种更强烈的刺激直接从他的神经通路深处把他的紫瞳硬生生点燃。

然后他看见了。

最近那架欧米茄原型体的翡翠色眼睛亮了。

不是一明一暗的待机状态，而是突然迸发出的、刺目的、像两颗压缩的翡翠炸弹同时引爆的绿光。绿光从001号的眼睛里射出来，穿过金色雾气，直直打在圆形大厅的穹顶上。

紧接着是002号。

003号。

004号。

一台接一台，像多米诺骨牌一样，翡翠色的眼睛一排排、一列列地亮起来。光从大厅最内圈开始，沿着同心圆的弧度向外扩散——内圈三十六台同时亮起、中圈七十二台跟上、外圈一百零八台补上——999架欧米茄原型体的眼睛在不到五秒钟的时间内全部点亮。

整个圆形大厅被翡翠色的光和暗金色的反光交织笼罩。

"它们醒了！"唐璜大喊，曲刃镰已经横在身前，"全部醒了！"

"别动！"西泽尔抬起左手制止了所有人，"它们还没有动！"

确实，999架欧米茄原型体的眼睛虽然全部亮了，但它们的肢体仍然保持着原来的姿态——矗立不动，沉默如山。没有一台迈出脚步，没有一台抬起手臂。

但它们在看。

999双翡翠色的眼睛全部转向了同一个方向。

西泽尔的方向。

就在这个凝固的瞬间，大厅入口的方向传来了一个声音。

那个声音很年轻，带着一种从容的、近乎优雅的节奏，像是在赴一场约好的茶会。

"西泽尔·博尔吉亚。"

声音从黑铁巨门的门缝里传进来，被金色雾气染上了几分失真，但每个字都清晰可辨。

"主人让我来请你去见他。"

"他说你既然都已经打开了门，不进来坐坐就太失礼了。"

大厅里的空气仿佛被抽走了一半。

唐璜的手在曲刃镰的镰柄上攥得发白，昆提良的战斧已经举过了头顶，阿方索的机械臂咔嚓一声弹出了隐藏的随身枪。

只有西泽尔站在原地。

他站在999双翡翠色眼睛的注视下，站在世界树残枝金色光芒的笼罩中，背对着大厅入口的方向，声音平静得像是赴一场早就约好的棋局。

"米迦勒。"他说。

"你来得正好。"

【English】
Chapter 205 — A Lotus of Omegas

They stood at the seam of the door for a long time, no one willing to speak.

Cesare let his eyes finish their slow surrender. The gold pouring from the crack had been painful at first — a white-hot wire laid across the retina — but the pain had dulled, then dissolved, until the light was simply part of the air. It caught on the lotus petals of dark gold ahead of them and was folded back into the corridor, dyeing everything the colour of warm honey. The scent ran in the light. It was thick. It was the smell of a hundred ponds in the Ceylon capital, pressed down into a single tunnel and left to ferment.

He took a breath, then a step. Two metres of door. He crossed them in three paces.

"Capo!" Alfonso's voice, behind him, sharp.

Cesare did not answer. His footfall came down on black stone, level as a billiard table, and the sound of it died in the gold before it could echo. His shadow stretched away behind him, very long, very thin, a black crack laid across the honey-coloured floor of the lotus corridor.

The space beyond the door was round.

It was, in fact, monstrous in its roundness. Cesare could not for a moment tell where its walls began or how high its ceiling rose. The dome above him closed in a perfect arc somewhere at the edge of sight, and across that arc, in a pattern so dense it might have been a sky made by a watchmaker, tens of thousands of tiny gears turned at their own unhurried pace. They gave a faint, collective hum — a low, almost subsonic throb that Cesare felt first in his teeth, then in the soft floor of his stomach, then in the bones of his wrist. It was the sound a heart makes when listened to from the inside of the chest.

At the apex of the dome a single shaft of light came down. It fell perfectly vertical, perfectly centred, and it was the brightest thing in the room — bright enough to make Cesare lift a hand to the ridge of his brow and peer through the gap of his fingers.

His fingers stopped.

There was a tree.

It was not, in the strict sense, a living tree. It had no bark, no leaves, no rings. But the shape of it was the shape of a tree, and the shape was unmistakable — the way the branches spread, the way they curved, the way they held the air above them as if they meant to give it shade. The trunk was a deep, dark gold. Across its surface, dense as embroidery, ran lines of Sanskrit script, every stroke faintly luminous, as though the metal had been carved full of candlewax and someone had lit every wick. The trunk rose straight, and at about fifteen metres it began to throw out branches, and the branches reached out in every direction with the patient geometry of things that had all the time in the world. From the ends of those branches hung, by gold chains no thicker than thread, clusters of red crystals the size of a man's fist. They gave off a soft, dull crimson glow that pulsed in time with the slow turning of the gears above.

There were no leaves on the branches. Instead, at the end of every twig, there turned a sheet of gold so thin it was nearly transparent — a disc cut into a gear, the edge of it inscribed with Sanskrit smaller and finer than any on the trunk, and as it turned it made a small, clean, glassy sound, like a fingernail against a wineglass.

A fragment of the World Tree.

A small one.

Cesare's gaze climbed down from the branches, down the long gold trunk, and went outward, into the round.

His breath stopped.

Not from fear. From the need to think. What he was seeing was too large, too regular, too far outside the small box the human mind keeps such things in, and the mind must, before it can be afraid, take a full breath and name what it sees.

The floor of the round was a black polished stone, and from where the tree stood the stone spread outward in perfect concentric rings, each one further out than the last, each one wider than the last. On every ring stood a suit of mobile armour, gold as the tree.

Not one suit.

Many.

Cesare's eye moved from the nearest to the next, from the next to the next, from the next to the next. He counted the first ring — thirty-six. The next ring out — seventy-two. The next — one hundred and eight. Each ring held more. The suits were not set in straight lines; they were set on curves, ring on ring on ring, and the curves bloomed outward from the tree the way a lotus blooms outward from its seed-pod. The whole of the great round hall was a flower of metal giants, mid-bloom.

All of them were the same colour. A deep, dark gold, like the trunk of the tree. Across every plate of every suit, etched fine as frost, ran the same dense pattern of micro-gears that the tree wore, the same patient clockwork. In the chest of every suit, set in a socket, beat a core of red mercury, and each core pulsed, dim, brighter, dim, brighter, in perfect synchrony with the crystals that hung from the tree.

Their eyes were jade.

All nine hundred and ninety-nine pairs of them, jade, and all of them dark. But the dark of jade is never quite dark; it throws back, even in shadow, a faint cold green, and the suits looked, in the gold light, like so many sleeping idols of a god Cesare did not yet know the name of.

He looked at the nameplate of the nearest suit.

A number, small, cleanly stamped.

001.

He looked at the next.

002.

The next: 003. 004. 005. The numerals walked away from him across the floor in their quiet, ordered file, and went on, and on, until they vanished into the haze of gold at the edge of sight.

"These—" Don Juan's voice, from behind. It had gone to sandpaper. "These are all Omegas?"

No one answered him. The answer was not the kind that needed voice.

Alfonso raised his left wrist. From inside the watch, with the soft click of a beetle unfolding, came a mechanical spider, no bigger than a thumbnail, and on its belly a red point of light came on — the indicator of its own eye. He set it on the floor. The spider ran off into the gold at a low, neat, busy pace.

"Three minutes," Alfonso said. "I'm going to shoot the whole room."

Cesare nodded.

Alfonso turned and followed the spider out, the joints of his mechanical arm ticking faintly as he went, and the gold ate him within a few paces. Only the small winking of his wrist-light, far out among the suits, marked that he was still moving.

Quintilian and Don Juan drew their weapons at almost the same breath. Quintilian's old spare hand-axe came up in his right hand, the kind of weapon a man carries because he has carried it since he was a boy. Don Juan unhooked the curved sickle of his Hellrose from his belt and took the grip one-handed, and the blade wrote a single cold arc through the gold. They did not speak. They turned and set their backs to each other, one looking left, one looking right, watching the nearest suits.

The suits did not move.

They stood where they stood, gold and silent, like so many gilt Buddhas in a temple that had not yet been opened. The jade in their eyes was dim, and there was no sign in the shoulders, in the hands, in the slight inward-tilted angle of the heads, that anything was about to change. But they were there. Five hundred, then nine hundred, then nine hundred and ninety-nine suits of self-healing nerve-fibre war machines in standby, and the pressure of that number in the air was a physical thing — a thing one felt in the eardrums, in the back of the teeth, in the place behind the sternum where a man keeps his sense of the room.

"Cesare."

Valentina's voice, from his right. Calm. Restrained.

Cesare turned. She was crouching, looking at the floor.

He looked at the floor too. The black stone, where the shaft of light fell, was throwing a faint reflection, and in that reflection were rings — rings within rings within rings — and the rings were not just shapes, they were inscriptions. Sanskrit, written so fine it was less than a hair's breadth deep, and it was only because the light came down at a certain angle that the scratches caught the eye at all. The script began at the foot of the tree and went outward, ring by ring, around the whole great hall and back to where it had started, so that the entire room was ringed in a kind of written ward.

"See the lines," Valentina said, and she put one fingertip to the stone, lightly, and ran it along the nearest arc. "Same script as on the gears of the dome. Same hand."

Cesare crouched beside her.

He saw what she meant. The lines were a continuous text, a vast single sentence that looped the room.

"The first Pope wrote it," Cesare said.

"You think so."

"He was going to build a factory here. He'd have left instructions."

Valentina looked at him a moment. The corner of her mouth moved, then was set again.

"Do you want to go to the tree?" she asked.

Cesare stood. He looked out across the rings of suits, across the gold and the dim jade, to the tree where the light was brightest.

The metal tree stood quietly in the pillar of its own light. The Sanskrit on its trunk flickered as the gears turned above. The crystal clusters in the branches pulsed in their slow red breath. The scent in the air was no longer a scent but an element — a thing one was standing inside, the way one stands inside warm water.

Cesare took a step toward it.

"I'll come with you," Valentina said.

She did not wait for his answer. She took her place at his left, half a pace behind, the exact distance that a woman walks with a man who might, in the next instant, have to draw a sword.

They walked.

Each time they passed a suit, Cesare felt the faint heat of it — the working of the red mercury core, even in standby, a degree or two above the air. Five hundred, six hundred, eight hundred such small warm bodies, and the sum of them was a heat, by the time they reached the inner ring, that was something. The air of the round was ten degrees warmer than the air of the lotus corridor, and the warmth was alive, and it sat on the skin like the warmth of a body asleep beside you in a bed.

"So Anne was right," Valentina said, very low, half to herself.

Cesare did not answer. A face came up in him — Anne's face, at the square in Marston, her hand on his sleeve, telling him she had seen the gold suits. The iron box they had put her in afterwards. The door of the carriage closed. He had not been there.

"We all thought she was mad," Valentina said. "A girl of thirteen. Telling her elders she had seen gold armour that walked, with eyes of jade. Who would believe that?"

"I did," Cesare said.

Valentina turned her head a fraction.

"I did," he said again. His voice did not change. "I couldn't save her."

Valentina was quiet for a few paces.

"You can save the others," she said, "if you can settle what is in this room."

Cesare said nothing. They walked.

Three minutes later they stood at the foot of the tree.

From this distance the tree was larger than the eye had taken it for. The trunk, at its base, was as wide as two men standing with their arms out, and the metal of it had a finish that was not the finish of metal. It was softer than that. Warmer than that. The way the gold caught the light was the way skin catches the light, the way a forearm does when the sun has been on it all morning. The Sanskrit was very clear up close, and every stroke of it had the small, careful, human imperfection of a thing carved by a hand, slowly, with a very fine tool, by someone who had meant every cut.

Cesare raised his hand.

His fingers stopped a finger's-breadth from the trunk.

He could feel heat.

It came off the gold in a slow, even wash. Not the dry, metallic, almost mineral heat of a working core of red mercury. Something else. Something closer to—

He let his fingertips touch the trunk.

Warm.

Not the temperature of metal. Metal is either cold or it is hot; it has no middle. But this gold had a middle, and the middle was the temperature of a person's skin, the temperature of a sleeping arm, the temperature of a hand held by a friend.

Cesare's hand stayed where it was.

Then, under his palm, he felt something more.

A tremor. Very low. Very even. The same tremor he had heard, in the corridor, as the slow throb of a heart. The same frequency. He let his attention rest on it, and the tremor was there, and it was steady, and then, as he kept his hand there, it quickened. Sixty beats to the minute. Sixty-five. Seventy. As if something, behind the gold, had become aware of him.

A needle of heat went in at the back of Cesare's left eye.

It was not pain in the ordinary sense. It was the feeling of a thin red wire being pushed along the optic nerve, from the back of the eyeball to the back of the skull, and the back of his vision went white, and then went violet, and then went bright. The Purple Eye was on.

The lotus corridor, the black floor, the suits, the haze of gold — all of it was now seen through a sheet of pale violet, and the violet had a pulse, and the pulse was his own. He watched the veins of his own hand come alive on the back of his hand, faint threads of violet, throbbing, and the threads walked up his wrist, and from his wrist up his forearm, like ivy on a wall.

The gold cuff at the nape of his neck was running hot.

Not the heat of weather. The heat of a thing being turned. The heat of a key being wound. The heat of something being drawn out of him along the wires of his own nerves.

"Your eyes," Valentina said, looking at his face.

He knew what he looked like. He had looked in a glass before. The last time had been in the northern mines of Vesuvius, and the same look had been on him then — the violet of the eye lit through with thin lines of gold, the gold blinking in time with the heart.

But he had not called the Immortal King this time.

He had only touched the trunk.

"I know," he said. His voice was calmer than he had expected it to be. "It hasn't gone that far. Don't worry."

Valentina set her mouth. She did not say anything more. She took one step forward, raised her right hand, and laid the flat of her palm against the trunk, as his was.

Her eyebrows went up a fraction.

"Warm," she said, and there was, in spite of herself, a small surprise in the word. "Truly warm. As if it were alive."

She closed her eyes. She held her hand there a moment, feeling the temperature. Then she opened her eyes, and her jade irises were full of the gold light coming through the trunk.

"Cesare," she said, and she took her hand away, and turned her head to him, "you know what this means."

"The tree is the mother of the Omegas."

Valentina nodded.

"The first Pope could not, by hand, have built nine hundred and ninety-nine Omegas that were all the same," she said. "Not with da Vinci's drawings, not with the highest grade of red mercury core, not with a hundred years and the wealth of the whole of the Papal States. He could not have done it by hand. He could not have done it by nine hundred and ninety-nine hands."

She looked out, past the trunk, at the lotus of suits.

"So he built a tree," she said. "A tree that grows, and copies, and builds its own Omegas. He wrote the making of the Omega into the tree's own nature, the way nature is written into a real tree, and the suits are the fruit of it. Each suit a fruit. Each fruit the same."

She paused.

"A lotus of Omegas," she said. "Nine hundred and ninety-nine fruits, set around the mother, in the shape of a flower. The first Pope's last inheritance."

Cesare listened. He looked back at the trunk.

The warm gold under his hand. The quickening tremor. The light that had come on at his touch.

Yes. It was alive.

Or it was the next thing to alive.

"Capo!" Alfonso's voice, from far out, blurred a little by the hum of the dome. "I've gone the whole way round! The spider's got the whole room!"

Cesare glanced in the direction of the voice. Alfonso was coming out from among the outer suits, ticking faintly at the joints, and the wrist-light was steady now — the spider's work was done.

"How is it out there?" Cesare asked.

"The same as in here," Alfonso said, when he came up. He was a little short of breath. "Nine hundred and ninety-nine. I counted three times. Thirty-six, seventy-two, a hundred and eight, every ring thirty-six more. Total, nine hundred and ninety-nine. All dark gold. All jade eyes. All red mercury in the chest."

He pointed with one mechanical finger at the new icon on his watch — a small silhouette of a spider, and under it, in a small line of type, the numbers 999 / 999.

"Got it all," he said. "The tree, too."

Cesare nodded.

His palm was still on the trunk. The gold light that had flared at his touch had calmed now to a steady, low, warm shine, pouring out of the trunk as if from a heart. The violet in his own veins was retreating — drawing back from his fingers toward his wrist, from his wrist toward his elbow, the way the tide draws back from a beach.

The trunk was still warm.

He did not take his hand off it.

"Alfonso," he said, "have the spider upload everything to your spare chip."

"Already done," Alfonso said. "Double backup. Even if I die here, the data is not lost."

"The photograph," Cesare said. "The one da Vinci left with Violante — Elena and the two children. Do you have it?"

"In the Minerva," Alfonso said. "Locked in the safe at the Eyrie before I left. The cipher is mine."

Cesare was quiet for a second.

"Lady Linara, in that photograph, is a descendant of Elena. Elena was my grandmother. Da Vinci, three hundred years ago, set the whole thing up. He knew that someone would come through this door eventually. He needed that person to know what he was doing."

Alfonso said nothing. He pushed his spectacles up the bridge of his nose, and the lenses caught the gold of the tree.

"Capo," he said, "you will need to look at that photograph yourself. Not now."

"I know," Cesare said.

He took his hand off the trunk at last. The warmth of it left his palm with a small, almost regretful slowness, as if the gold had not wished to let him go. He looked at the Sanskrit on the trunk, the slow breath of the crystals, the still suits in their rings.

A lotus of Omegas.

Nine hundred and ninety-nine.

A hundred years of work, by a man with a title of pope, raised into a single room.

If the Order of Original Sin woke all nine hundred and ninety-nine of them—

Cesare did not finish the thought.

"We go," he said. "We have to know the whole of this place before the Order gets here."

He took two steps toward the outer ring.

A sound came from the dome.

It was a thin, bright, ugly sound — the sound of metal being dragged along metal under a great weight, a sound with an edge to it like a razor being drawn across a strop. It passed through the hum, through the slow throb of the tree, and went into the ear of every person in the room like a heated pin.

Quintilian and Don Juan, in a single motion, lifted their weapons, and the two of them turned, hard, into one another, and the muscles along their shoulder-blades stood up like cords under the skin.

Cesare stopped walking.

The Purple Eye came on again. He had not called it. Something deeper than he had was calling it — something in the nerve-paths, something in the gold cuff, something that was being spoken to by the sound in the dome and was answering.

He looked.

The jade eyes of the nearest suit were lit.

Not the dim pulse of standby. A full green — hard, sudden, dense, as if two small bombs of compressed emerald had gone off behind the eye-sockets of the suit. The light came out of 001, crossed the gold haze, and struck the dome above.

002.

003.

004.

One after another, ring after ring, domino after domino. The jade came on at the inner ring, all thirty-six suits at once, and then the next ring, all seventy-two, and then the outer ring, all one hundred and eight, and in less than five seconds the nine hundred and ninety-nine pairs of eyes of the lotus were lit, and the round was full of a web of green and gold, and the shadows of the suits lay on the polished floor in nine hundred and ninety-nine long, sharp, complicated lines.

"They're awake!" Don Juan said. The sickle was up across his chest. "All of them!"

"Hold," Cesare said, and his left hand went up, palm out. "They haven't moved."

They hadn't.

The nine hundred and ninety-nine suits stood where they had stood. The jade in their eyes burned, but the limbs of them were still, the shoulders level, the heads straight, the great hands of metal at their sides, closed or open as the design of each one had it, but closed or open without intent. The lotus had opened its eyes, that was all. It had not yet moved its hands.

But they were looking.

All nine hundred and ninety-nine pairs of jade eyes were turned to the same point.

To Cesare.

The air in the round seemed to lose half its substance.

Then, from the direction of the door — from the seam they had come through, from the gold haze of the lotus corridor — a voice came in.

The voice was young. It was even. It had the cadence of a man arriving at a tea he had been invited to.

"Cesare Borgia."

The words came in through the crack of the door, and the gold haze took a little of the edge off them, and the dome put a little of its own edge on. Each word was still clear.

"My master sends me to ask you to come to him."

"He says that, having opened the door, it would be impolite of you not to come in."

Don Juan's hand went white at the wrist where it held the sickle. Quintilian had the axe above his head. The small gun hidden in Alfonso's mechanical arm clicked out, one quiet sound, and was held against his thigh.

Cesare stood where he stood.

He stood in the look of nine hundred and ninety-nine pairs of jade eyes, in the gold light of the tree, his back to the door, his voice as even as a man who has been invited, finally, to a game he has been expecting all his life.

"Michael," he said.

"You are right on time."

【中文】
第206章 白银面具的主人（上）

维苏威火山的夜是血红色的。

不是比喻。从山腰以上的位置望出去，浓密的火山灰云遮住了整片天空，云层底部被下方翻涌的岩浆映成一种浓烈的、仿佛随时要滴落下来的殷红，像是有人用一支巨大的画笔把整座山涂成了一颗正在腐烂的心脏。

李锡尼站在崩塌的矿道入口前，身后五架古式炽天铁骑一字排开。排气口喷出的白色蒸汽在红光中染上了淡淡的粉色，像是五条被夕阳染色的蛇。每一架甲胄都有近三十年的机龄，铁灰色的装甲上满是修补焊接的痕迹，关节处甚至能看到不同年代产出的金属拼合在一起，像被反复缝补的老兵身上的伤疤。但它们的胸腔里都换装了密涅瓦机关最新的红水银晶块核心，红水银的光芒从装甲缝隙中泄出，像是五颗正在燃烧的心脏。

"都到了？"李锡尼问。

"都到了。"身后传来一个低哑的声音。

说话的是老戈特，炽天骑士团退役上士，当年莲花作战时负责给龙德施泰特的中军传令。锡兰城破那天他就在最前线，亲眼看见过那个紫瞳男孩登上城头。三十年前的那场战争结束后他申请退役，回老家开了间铁匠铺，佛朗哥教授一封信他就来了，连铺子都顾上关。

他身后的四个人年纪都和他差不多。最年轻的也有四十五岁，最年长的一个头发全白了，名叫赫尔曼，是当年断剑骑士冈扎罗的副官。莲花作战时他是负责在城外埋设诡雷的工兵，锡兰王城地下那些致命的红水银地雷有不少是经他手安装的。

他们都曾是炽天骑士团最优秀的士兵。

他们都参加过那场本不该发生的战争。

他们都还活着。

"暗门入口在哪？"赫尔曼问。

李锡尼抬手指向前方。

矿道入口已经被炸塌了大半，几吨重的岩块和扭曲的金属梁堆积如山，断裂的蒸汽管道仍在碎石间嘶嘶作响，喷出残余的高压气体。但在这片废墟的左侧，一个被炸开的黑色豁口清晰可见——那是人为的爆破痕迹，岩壁上的焦黑纹路呈放射状向外扩散，豁口内部隐约透出昏暗的微光。

西泽尔他们从这里进去的。

李锡尼弯腰走进豁口，靴底踩在什么东西上发出金属碎裂的脆响。他低头看了一眼，鞋底碾碎的是一块普罗米修斯外部装甲板的碎片，边缘有一道被高温烧融后又凝固的痕迹，熔渣凝成了黑色的玻璃质地表。

"五台普罗米修斯堵在这个入口，全部被打成了废铁。"老戈特走到豁口前，用枪管拨开另一块碎铁，皱起眉头，"看这个厚度，至少是量产型。"

"不只是普罗米修斯。"李锡尼蹲下身，从废墟中捡起一块更小的金属片。那块金属片呈暗金色，材质远超现代工艺，边缘还残留着几道类似血管的纤细纹路，纹路中有微弱的红水银光在缓慢地明灭，像是某种死去很久却依然不肯彻底熄灭的东西。

屠龙者圣乔治的碎片。

"前面还躺着一个三百年前的东西。"李锡尼站起身，声音平淡，"四颗红水银核心全部自爆，换来五台普罗米修斯和通道里所有的圣堂装甲师残骸。"

"是那个叫莲生的姑娘？"老戈特问。

李锡尼没有接话。

他想起了佛朗哥教授交给他那张地图时说的话。佛朗哥教授说，这个世界上有些人活着是为了自己，有些人活着是为了别人。莲生等了三百年，等的是一个她从未见过的锡兰星见后裔。但她从未迟疑过，从未抱怨过，从未问过那个后裔是否值得她等。她说"我来开路"，就真的用命来开了。

"炸开它。"李锡尼下令。

老戈特点头，五架古式炽天铁骑同时举起右臂，五门小口径蒸汽炮对准了堵在豁口处的最后一块残片。轰然一声闷响，残片被炸飞，豁口扩大到了足以让重型甲胄通过的宽度。烟尘还没散尽，李锡尼就迈步走了进去。

暗门内部是一条倾斜向下的石质通道，宽约九米，高不到十二米——正好是密涅瓦初代总长设计时为了限制巨型机动傀儡活动而留下的尺寸。通道的墙壁上每隔十米嵌着一盏铜灯，但大部分已经熄灭了，只剩下零星几盏还在发出昏黄的微光，像是垂死之人最后的呼吸。空气里弥漫着一股混合了硫磺、铁锈和焦糊的气味，越往深处走温度越高。

"前面看到的不只是圣堂装甲师的残骸。"老戈特一边走一边说，外置扬声器把他的话压缩成沙哑的电音，"三百年前的初代炽天使原型机，居然还存在于这个世界上。我一直以为那只是传说。"

"传说总有变成现实的那一天。"赫尔曼闷声说，"你忘了锡兰城里的那个紫瞳男孩？当年我们都觉得，一个十五六岁的小孩不可能指挥攻破一座王城。"

老戈特沉默了。

"别说话。"李锡尼忽然停下脚步。

身后的五架炽天铁骑同时急停，蒸汽炮口自动转向了前方的黑暗。

老戈特想说什么，被赫尔曼一个眼神制止了。他是老兵，他立刻听出了李锡尼语气中那一丝异样的锐利——那不是命令，而是警告。

有人。

前方的黑暗中，有某种不属于这个地下空间的东西存在。不是机械运转的嗡鸣，不是蒸汽泄漏的嘶响，而是一种更微妙的、像是有人刻意控制了自己呼吸声后留下的……空白。

那种空白比任何声音都更危险。

"出来吧。"李锡尼说，声音平淡。

沉默了大概三秒。

然后前方的黑暗中亮起了一盏灯。

不是火，不是蒸汽灯，而是一种冷冽的、像月光一样的银白色光芒。光芒从一个人影的手中发出，驱散了周围十米范围内的黑暗，铜灯的昏黄微光在这道银白面前黯然失色。

那人穿着圣堂装甲师的白色军装。

军装剪裁考究，肩章上的银线在灯光下闪烁，胸口别着圣堂装甲师的徽章——但那枚徽章是倒过来的，五芒星的尖端朝下，和教廷公开使用的徽章完全相反。

他的脸上戴着一张白银面具。

面具造型是一张年轻的脸，线条优美，嘴角微微上扬，带着一种从容的、近乎优雅的微笑。面具的眼眶处没有开口，露出了一双湛蓝色的眼睛。

他的右手里握着一样东西。

一杆长枪。

长枪的枪身通体银色，长度接近两米，枪头雕刻着六翼天使的浮雕，在银白色光芒中闪烁着冷冽的金属光泽。枪身表面有细密的铭文在流动，像是某种被封印在金属内部的能量。

圣剑装具·朗基努斯的复制品。

"李锡尼·博尔吉亚。"白银面具开口了，声音年轻，带着一种从容的节奏，像是在赴一场约好的茶会，"没想到你也来了。"

他偏了偏头，湛蓝色的眼睛扫过李锡尼身后那五架锈迹斑斑的古式炽天铁骑，嘴角的弧度似乎更大了些。

"炽天骑士团的老人？好眼熟。锡兰那时候你们就跟在龙德施泰特后面跑吧？"

老戈特的炮口立刻锁定了他。但李锡尼抬手制止了。

"你是谁？"李锡尼问。

"米迦勒。"白银面具回答，仿佛这是世界上最理所当然的事情，"原罪机关的米迦勒。"

"那不是你的真名。"

"李锡尼副局长果然厉害。"白银面具举了举手中的银色长枪，枪尖指向通道深处更深的黑暗，"不过，你确定想知道答案吗？"

"说。"

"好。"

白银面具用空着的左手缓缓摘下了脸上的面具。

面具下面是一张年轻的脸。五官端正，肤色苍白，颧骨高耸，嘴角自然地微微向下——这是一张和他刚才戴着的那张优雅面具完全不同的脸，更冷硬，更疲惫，也更普通。像是摘掉了一张精心制作的面具后，露出了面具下面那具真实的、带着长期磨损痕迹的容器。

但最让人不安的是他的眼睛。

他的眼睛和面具上的眼睛一样，也是湛蓝色的。同样的颜色，同样的形状，甚至连眨眼的频率都完全一致。

"三百年前，我的祖先接到了一个任务。"他说，声音不再是刚才那种从容的节奏，变得平缓、单调，像是在背诵一段被重复了无数次的台词。"为教皇打造一个完美的替身。替身需要有一张永远不会老去的脸，需要有和本人完全相同的声线和体态，需要能够在任何场合替代本人而不被识破。"

"初代密涅瓦总长达·芬奇·博尔吉亚完成了这个任务。"

"但他自己也没有想到，这个替身的技术后来被用在了别的方面。"

"比如——制造更多的替身。"

他停了一下，像是在给听众留出消化的时间。

"我就是其中一个。"

"我们一共有十三个。"

"我们都是原罪机关主人。"

赫尔曼的甲胄在原地晃了一下。金属关节发出一声刺耳的摩擦声，像是整具机体都被什么东西击中了。老戈特的手在操纵杆上攥得发白，甲胄外置扬声器发出一阵无意义的电流杂音。

"你说什么？"赫尔曼的声音从扬声器里传出来，带着明显的失真，"十三个原罪机关主人？"

"不是十三个主人。"白银面具——不，那个摘下面具的年轻人——平静地纠正他，"是主人的十三个替身。"

"真正的原罪机关主人只有一个。"

"他活了三百多年。"

"他用机械改造了自己的身体。他现在百分之八十以上的躯体都是机械。他用白银面具和米迦勒替身来隐藏自己的真实身份，因为没有任何一个活人能接受——"

他停顿了一下，湛蓝色的眼睛直视李锡尼。

"他们的神在人间的代言人，是个怪物。"

"他是初代教皇。"

"波吉亚一世。"

李锡尼没有说话。

他脸上没有任何表情。他的呼吸甚至没有变化。但他的右手已经从枪套里抽出了那把黑色的十字纹蜂巢手铳，拇指无声地搭在了击锤上。

"三百年来，"那个自称是替身的年轻人继续说，声音依然平淡，"教廷对外宣称初代教皇在星历元年安详离世，留下遗训要后代继承他的遗志。教廷还追封他为圣人，在翡冷翠的英灵殿里给他塑了金身像，每个弥撒日都有红衣主教去给他献花。"

"但初代教皇并没有死。"

"他只是把自己藏了起来。藏在暗处，藏在历史背后，藏在一代又一代的替身和傀儡后面。"

"他用三百年的时间做了三件事。"

"第一，改造自己的身体，让自己不会老，不会死。"

"第二，渗透教廷，让每一任继任的教皇都成为他的棋子。"

"第三——"

年轻人抬手指向通道更深处那个看不见的方向。西泽尔所在的方向。

"培育一个完美的神使容器。"

"重启机械神国。"

老戈特手里的枪掉了。

金属碰撞地面的声音在通道里回荡了很久，像是一记被敲响的丧钟。

赫尔曼在原地一动不动，但他的呼吸频率已经明显紊乱了，甲胄外置的生理监测仪开始发出急促的嘟嘟声。这些都是参加过莲花作战的老兵。他们都曾在炽天骑士团的军旗下宣誓效忠教皇。他们都曾在心底深处相信，弥赛亚圣教的神圣和教廷的权威是不容置疑的。

而现在，有人告诉他们，这一切的基础——初代教皇，神在人间的代言人，上帝的意志在凡间的执行者——是一个已经活了三百多年的半机械怪物。

"不可能。"赫尔曼喃喃地说，"初代教皇三百年前就已经……"

"就已经什么？"年轻人平静地看着他，"死在历史里？被教廷追封为圣人？留下遗训要后代继承他的遗志？"

"他确实留下了遗训。"年轻人说，"但那不是他死前的遗言，而是他活了三百年后仍在执行的计划。"

"初代教皇的遗训只有一条。"

"重启机械神国。"

"为此他不惜毁灭锡兰，不惜让整个教廷变成他的工具，不惜让一代又一代的教皇成为他的傀儡。"

"包括你们效忠过的每一任教皇。"

李锡尼终于开口了。

"隆·博尔吉亚。"他说，"现任教皇。"

"也是他的替身之一。"年轻人的回答干脆利落，"只不过比我们要特殊一些。隆是初代教皇选定的继承人，也是他最成功的作品。他对'重启机械神国'这个目标同样虔诚，甚至可能比初代教皇本人更虔诚。"

"西泽尔呢？"老戈特忽然开口，声音沙哑，"西泽尔·博尔吉亚知道这些吗？"

"他正在知道。"年轻人说，"他比我们所有人都走得更深。他已经看到了世界树残枝，他已经打开了黑铁巨门，他已经唤醒了九百九十九架欧米茄原型体。"

"他现在正站在机械神国的门口。"

"而主人——"

年轻人重新戴上了那张白银面具。

优雅的微笑重新覆盖了他的脸，湛蓝色的眼睛在面具的眼眶后面闪了一下。

"主人让我来请你们。"

他举起了手中的银色长枪。

枪身表面的铭文忽然亮了起来，银白色的光芒沿着枪身向上攀升，最终在六翼天使浮雕的枪头处凝聚成一团刺目的光球。光球周围有微型的闪电在跳动，照亮了整个通道。

"李锡尼·博尔吉亚。"

"你们要么跟我一起去见主人。"

"要么——"

银色的枪尖直指李锡尼的眉心。

"就死在这里。"

【English】
Chapter 206 — The Master of the Silver Mask (I)

The night over Vesuvius was the color of blood.

Not as metaphor. From the lava line upward, dense ash clouds had sealed off the sky, and the underside of that vast lid was lit from below by the slow churn of the magma chamber — a thick, sick, almost liquid red, the way a heart might look through the ribs of something already dying. Above the treeline, the ash turned the moon into a rumor. The only honest light in the world was the false red of the mountain.

Licinius Borgia stood before the caved-in mouth of the mine. Behind him, in a single line, five old-pattern Seraphim Iron Knights idled in formation. Their exhausts vented a thin, white plume, and the plume caught the red light and bled into a pale, embarrassed pink, the way a wound weeps. Each machine was nearly thirty years old. Their armor was a flat gunmetal grey, sutured with welds of three different vintages; at the joints you could see the seams between metal that had been rolled in different decades, like the scar tissue of a soldier who had been opened and closed too many times. But inside each chest cavity, the engineers had fitted a new Minerva-red mercury crystal core, and the light leaked from the gaps in the plating like five small hearts still beating.

"Everyone here?" Licinius asked.

"Everyone." The voice behind him was low, hoarse, used to giving orders across battlefields and now mostly used to giving orders across a forge floor.

The speaker was Old Gott, retired sergeant of the Seraphim Order, who in the Lotus Campaign had carried dispatches to Rundstedt's central column. He had been in the front line the day Ceylon fell. He had watched, from a hundred meters away, the violet-eyed boy climb the broken city wall. When the war ended, he had asked out, walked home, opened a smithy. When Professor Franco's letter came, he had not even locked the door behind him.

The four men behind him were of an age with Gott. The youngest was forty-five. The oldest, his hair gone the color of iron filings, was Hermann — once the adjutant of the broken-sword knight Gonzalo. In the Lotus Campaign, Hermann had been the engineer who laid the city's subterranean mercury charges. Many of the red-mercury mines that had torn the Ceylonese royal quarter apart in the second hour of the assault had been planted by his own hands.

They had all been the Order's best.

They had all fought in a war that should never have been fought.

They had all survived it.

"Where's the hidden door?" Hermann asked.

Licinius lifted a hand and pointed.

The mouth of the mine had been half-buried by a deliberate collapse. Tons of rock and buckled I-beams lay piled in a choking slope; severed steam pipes still hissed in the rubble, releasing their last stored pressure with a wet, dying whisper. But on the left side of the ruin, a blackened gap was unmistakable — the radial scorch of shaped charges, the kind of break you only get when someone means to come through and does not care what it costs to do so.

Cesare and his people had gone in here.

Licinius ducked through the breach. Underfoot, something cracked with a brittle metallic report. He glanced down. His boot had crushed a fragment of a Prometheus-grade outer plate. Its edge bore a glazed seam where extreme heat had run the metal half to slag and then let it set again, black and glassy, like a frozen tear.

"Five Prometheuses blocked this entry," Old Gott said, joining him. He nudged another scrap of iron with the barrel of his rifle and frowned. "Look at the thickness. Production models, all of them."

"Not only Prometheuses."

Licinius crouched and picked something smaller from the debris. It was the color of tarnished gold, of a metallurgy no current workshop would recognize. Along its edges, fine, vein-like lines still ran; and inside those lines, a dim red light pulsed — the lazy, reluctant pulse of something that should have been dead and was not quite done dying.

A shard of the St. George's dragon-slayer.

"Three hundred years old and still warm," Licinius said, and stood. His voice was level. "Four mercury cores, all of them self-detonated. Took five Prometheuses with them, and every Cathedral Armored Lancer in the tunnel."

"The girl called Liansheng?" Gott asked.

Licinius did not answer.

He thought, instead, of what Professor Franco had said when he had handed over the map. *There are people in this world who live for themselves. And there are people who live for others.* Liansheng had waited three hundred years for a descendant of the Ceylonese stargazers whom she had never laid eyes on. She had not hesitated. She had not complained. She had not asked whether the descendant was worth the wait. She had said, *I'll open the path*, and she had opened it with her life.

"Blow it," Licinius ordered.

Gott nodded. The five old-pattern Seraphims raised their right arms in unison; five small-bore steam cannon came to bear on the last slab of wreckage blocking the breach. There was a flat, ugly thud, and the slab lurched sideways and fell. Smoke billowed. Before it had cleared, Licinius had already stepped through.

The hidden door opened into a long, sloping stone corridor, roughly nine meters wide, just under twelve high — the deliberate ceiling of the first Minerva Chief Architect, designed to keep any oversized mobile puppet from being maneuvered underground. Brass lamps were set into the wall every ten paces. Most of them had gone out. The few that still burned gave off a sullen, jaundiced yellow, the last breath of men who had stopped hoping to be rescued. The air, as they descended, thickened with sulfur and rust and something else — the dry, black smell of old burning.

"What we saw up there wasn't only the Cathedral remnants," Gott said, walking. His voice was compressed by the external speaker into a rasping, mechanical whisper. "A first-generation Seraphim prototype, three hundred years old, still functioning. I had always assumed that was legend."

"Legends have a way of becoming real," Hermann muttered. "You forget the violet-eyed boy in Ceylon? We all agreed, back then. A child of fifteen cannot take a royal city."

Gott said nothing.

"Quiet." Licinius stopped.

The five Seraphims braked hard behind him. The steam cannon turrets swung, in unison, to face the dark ahead.

Gott opened his mouth. Hermann caught his eye and killed the word before it left his lips. He was an old soldier, and he had heard, in the flat of Licinius's voice, a single extra half-degree of cold. Not a command. A warning.

Someone was there.

Ahead, in the dark, was something that did not belong to this underground place. Not the hum of a machine. Not the hiss of a venting pipe. Something more careful. The particular silence of a body that has learned to keep its own breathing quiet — the silence a man leaves when he is choosing to be silent, which is louder than any shout.

That kind of silence is more dangerous than any sound.

"Step out," Licinius said, in the same level voice. "I know you're there."

Three seconds. Maybe four.

Then a light came on in the dark ahead of him.

Not fire. Not a steam lamp. Something cooler, more spectral — a silver-white, the color of a winter moon, that fell from a single figure's hand and drove the shadows back ten meters in every direction. The brass lamps along the wall, in that light, looked like the last dying of a candle in a window where no one lived.

The man wore the white uniform of the Cathedral Armored Lancers.

It was well cut. The silver braid of his shoulder boards caught the moonlight from his own hand. Pinned to his breast was the Cathedral insignia — but mounted upside down, the five-pointed star inverted, the opposite of the version the Holy See displayed to its faithful.

His face was hidden behind a mask of silver.

The mask was a young man's face, beautifully made, the lines of it graceful, the mouth turned up at the corners in a small, composed, almost courteous smile. There were no openings at the eyes. Through the silver, two blue eyes looked out at Licinius — a true, vivid, unkind blue, the color of ice over deep water.

In his right hand he held a spear.

The shaft was silver, the length of a tall man. The blade, where the head met the haft, was carved with a relief of a six-winged angel; in the silver light, the carving seemed to move. Along the shaft, fine inscriptions crawled like slow water, as if some energy had been sealed into the metal and was trying to find its way out.

A replica of the Holy Lance. Longinus.

"Licinius Borgia," said the silver mask. His voice was young, unhurried, the tone of a man arriving at a tea he had been invited to and decided to enjoy. "I did not expect you personally."

He tilted his head. The blue eyes, behind the silver, traveled across the five old, scarred Seraphims behind Licinius. The smile in the mask seemed, by a small degree, to widen.

"The Order's old men. How familiar. In Ceylon, you ran behind Rundstedt, didn't you?"

Gott's cannon locked on him at once. Licinius raised a hand and stopped it.

"Who are you?" Licinius asked.

"Michael," the silver mask said, as if it were the only name in the world that mattered. "Michael of the Primal Sin Office."

"That is not your real name."

"Deputy Director Licinius, you are quick." The silver mask lifted the spear a little, and the silver point swung toward the deeper dark behind him. "But are you certain you want the real one?"

"Say it."

"As you wish."

The young man, with his free hand, slowly took the mask from his face.

Under the mask was another face. Younger than the first had pretended to be, and far less kind. The bones were sharp; the skin was the color of old paper. The mouth, by nature, turned down at the corners. It was an ordinary face, in the end — the face a man might have before he was chosen to wear another. A face that had done a long tour of duty inside its own skull.

But it was the eyes that were wrong.

They were the same blue as the ones in the mask. The same blue, the same shape, the same rhythm of blink. As if the silver face had been made, in every particular, to match what was already behind it.

"Three hundred years ago," the young man said, "my ancestor was given a commission. To build, for the Pope, a perfect double. The double was to have a face that would never age, a voice and a build identical to the Pope's own, the ability to take his place at any function without detection."

"The first Chief of Minerva, Leonardo Borgia, completed the commission."

"He did not foresee that the technique would be put to other uses."

"For instance," the young man said, "the making of more doubles."

He let the silence settle.

"I am one of them."

"There are thirteen of us, in all."

"We are, each of us, the master of the Primal Sin Office."

Behind Licinius, Hermann's Seraphim swayed. Metal at the joints screamed, as if the whole frame had been struck. Gott's hand on his control bar had gone bone-white. Through his external speaker came a sound that was not yet a word, only static.

"What did you say?" Hermann's voice, when it came, was badly distorted. "Thirteen masters?"

"Not thirteen masters." The young man — the unmasked one — corrected him, without heat. "Thirteen doubles of the master."

"There is only one true master of the Primal Sin Office."

"He has been alive for more than three hundred years."

"He rebuilt his body, piece by piece, with machinery. Eighty percent of him is no longer flesh. He wears the silver mask and sends out the Michael doubles to hide his own face, because no living person can stand to be in the same room with—"

He paused. The blue eyes fixed on Licinius.

"—with the fact that God's representative on earth is a thing."

"He is the first Pope."

"Borgia the First."

Licinius said nothing.

His face did not move. His breathing did not change. But his right hand had come out of the holster, and the black cross-patterned Hive revolver rested in his palm, the thumb laid, very softly, against the hammer.

"Three hundred years," the young man went on, in the same flat recitation. "The See announced that the first Pope passed in peace in the first year of the Star Calendar. The See made him a saint. They cast a gold statue of him in the Hall of Heroes in Florence. Every Mass day a cardinal lays flowers at its feet."

"But the first Pope did not die."

"He simply hid. In the dark. Behind history. Behind a long succession of doubles and puppets."

"In those three hundred years he did three things."

"First, he rebuilt his body so that it would not age, and could not die."

"Second, he seeded the See with his own people, until every Pope who followed him was his creature."

"Third—"

The young man lifted a hand and pointed, into the dark behind him, in the direction that Licinius and his men could not see.

"He cultivated a perfect vessel for the divine envoy."

"He began the reboot of the Machine Kingdom."

The rifle in Gott's hands slipped. The metal hit the stone floor. The sound of it rang a long time down the corridor, like a bell struck for a service no one wanted to attend.

Hermann did not move. But the rhythm of his breath, inside the suit, had become ragged; the external biomonitor started a thin, urgent beeping. These were veterans of the Lotus Campaign. They had all sworn the Seraphim oath. They had all, somewhere in the long sediment at the bottom of themselves, believed that the sanctity of the Messiah and the authority of the See were not things a man was entitled to doubt.

Now someone had told them the foundation under all of it — the first Pope, God's voice on earth, the executor of Heaven's will on the lower world — was a half-machine thing that had been alive for three hundred and fifty years.

"It is not possible," Hermann whispered. "The first Pope, three centuries ago, he—"

"He what?" The young man regarded him. "Died in his bed? Was made a saint? Left behind instructions for his successors to carry out his work?"

"He did leave instructions. But they were not the dying words of a dying man. They are the plan of a man who is still, three hundred years later, executing them."

"The first Pope's instructions are one sentence long."

"*Reboot the Machine Kingdom.*"

"He has been willing, for that, to destroy Ceylon. To make the entire See his instrument. To make Pope after Pope his puppet."

"Including every Pope you ever served."

At last Licinius spoke.

"Lorenzo Borgia," he said. "The present Pope."

"One of his doubles, yes." The young man answered at once, the way a student answers a question he was expecting. "But a special one. Lorenzo is the heir the first Pope has chosen, and the most successful of his works. Lorenzo is as devoted to the reboot as the first Pope himself. Perhaps more so."

"And Cesare?" Old Gott's voice came out of his speaker raw, scraping. "Does Cesare Borgia know any of this?"

"He is knowing it now." The young man said. "He has gone deeper into the mountain than any of us. He has already seen the World Tree fragment. He has already opened the Black Iron Gate. He has already woken nine hundred and ninety-nine of the Omega prototypes."

"He is standing, at this moment, on the threshold of the Machine Kingdom."

"And the master—"

The young man put the silver mask back on.

The composed, courteous smile settled over his face again. The blue eyes blinked once, behind the silver.

"The master has sent me to invite you in."

He raised the silver spear.

The inscriptions on the shaft woke. The silver-white light ran up the metal in a slow, deliberate wave, gathered at the head of the six-winged angel, and there condensed into a small, hard sun. Tiny forks of lightning crawled around it. The light of it filled the corridor, and every scar and weld on the old Seraphims was thrown into sharp relief, like a map of an old war.

"Licinius Borgia."

"You may come with me, and meet the master."

"Or—"

The silver point came to rest, unwavering, an inch from the bridge of Licinius's nose.

"—you may die here."

第207章 白银面具的主人（中）
