【中文】
第207章 白银面具的主人（中）

薇若兰从来不是个会哭的人。

密涅瓦机关的老技师们都知道这一点——副总长年轻的时候在鹰巢里被蒸汽管道崩出的热水烫伤了半条胳膊，咬着牙自己拧上螺栓，疼得额头全是汗也没哼一声。后来塔拉夏私下问她为什么不喊人，她说喊什么？喊了热水就不烫了？还不如多拧两圈。

但此刻她靠在改装蒸汽汽车颠簸的后座上，把那张泛黄的照片翻过来扣在膝盖上，另一只手按着胸口，肩膀在轻微地抖。

达·芬奇·波吉亚的日记本摊在腿上，最后几页的字迹歪斜潦草，显然是在极度仓促的情况下写的。有些墨水被什么液体洇开了，字迹模糊成一片。但核心内容她已经看了三遍，一个字都忘不了。

"用完美神使载体的意识，结合不朽之王系统，引爆紫瞳，发出世界毁灭之光——"

"——彻底摧毁所有世界树残枝和欧米茄原型体——"

"——代价是载体将永远消亡——"

窗外的翡冷翠郊野飞速后退，黄昏的余晖把废弃矿道入口方向的丘陵染成暗金色。蒸汽汽车的引擎发出低沉的轰鸣，履带碾过碎石路面时整个车厢都在震。

薇若兰把日记本合上，闭了一下眼睛。

"完美神使载体"这几个字在她脑子里反复轰鸣。达·芬奇·博吉亚用了极其冷静的笔触来描述这个过程，仿佛只是在写一份机械拆解报告——拆卸对象，拆解步骤，注意事项，以及最终结果。唯一带有感情的字是最后一行，写得很小，歪歪斜斜地缩在纸张的右下角：

"我穷尽一生都在阻止自己释放它，却在最后为它准备好了死亡。"

——"它"。

不是"他"。

不是"她"。

是"它"。

三百年前那个同时拥有教皇身份和密涅瓦初代总工程师身份的老人，把自己创造出的完美载体叫做"它"。

薇若兰睁开眼，低头看着自己的手。修长的手指，指甲剪得很短，掌心还有鹰巢车间里常年操作精密仪器磨出的薄茧。这双手曾经组装过密涅瓦最复杂的红水银核心，曾经在千分之一秒的误差范围内校准过炽天使甲胄的神经接驳接口，曾经把西泽尔从红龙试制版的驾驶舱里拖出来时稳稳地托住他的后颈——那个当时连接着黄金套管、还在微微发烫的后颈。

她把日记本最后几页撕下来，折好，塞进贴身的衬衣里面。纸张边缘有点扎人，硬邦邦地抵着她的心口。

引擎声在耳边轰鸣，窗外的光越来越暗。

改装蒸汽汽车在密涅瓦机关的备用通道出口处撞开了两道铁栅栏——那扇门上原本有原罪机关守卫，四个穿着灰黑色制服的枪手，还没来得及举枪就被塔拉夏从车窗探出去的手枪依次撂倒。塔拉夏的枪法比他的长相还漂亮，每一枪都打在膝盖上，干净利落，不致命但让对方站不起来。

"走！"塔拉夏吼了一声。

改装蒸汽汽车冲出密涅瓦机关的备用通道入口时，身后传来密集的脚步声和枪响，但改装后的蒸汽汽车加了六层影金属护板，普通弹头打上去只留下浅浅的白点。履带碾碎了一段栏杆，整辆车带着金属的尖啸冲上了郊区的土路。

三分钟后，骑警的路障出现在前方。

两辆骑警的重型蒸汽摩托横在路中央，六个骑警持枪站在路障后面，蒸汽摩托上的探照灯已经亮了起来，刺眼的白光扫过改装蒸汽汽车的车窗。

"停车！接受检查！"骑警长官的扩音器里传来严厉的声音。

塔拉夏从副驾驶座上直起身，手里已经多了一张金色的通行证——密涅瓦机关的A级通行证，六翼猫头鹰徽记在黄昏的光线里闪着暗金色的微光。他把通行证举出车窗，骑警长官愣了一下，接过通行证仔细查验。

"密涅瓦机关……"骑警长官抬头看了塔拉夏一眼。

"紧急公务。"塔拉夏说，语气里没有半分商量的余地，"让开。"

骑警长官犹豫了两秒钟，最终把通行证递了回来。密涅瓦机关的A级通行证意味着最高的通行权限，即便是在翡冷翠宵禁期间也能畅行无阻。他挥了挥手，路障被推开，改装蒸汽汽车再次轰鸣着冲了过去。

"你脸色不好。"塔拉夏从后视镜里看了薇若兰一眼。

"有点晕车。"薇若兰说。

她确实是晕车——但不是改装蒸汽汽车的颠簸让她晕的。

塔拉夏没再问。他是个聪明人，知道什么时候该沉默。

薇若兰把视线转向窗外，窗外的丘陵起伏着，黄昏的最后一抹光线从地平线上消失了，取而代之的是深蓝色的暮色。她想起了一些很久以前的事。

西泽尔刚来密涅瓦机关报到的时候，还不到十五岁，瘦得像是被翡冷翠的雨水淋了一个冬天。苍白的手指，苍白的嘴唇，苍白的脸，唯独一双紫瞳在密涅瓦的灯火里亮得刺眼。

彼时薇若兰也才十八岁，作为密涅瓦最年轻的技术员，被佛朗哥教授派去给这个新来的适格者做神经接驳前的全面体检。她记得西泽尔在体检台上一声不吭，任凭那些冰冷的仪器贴上他的太阳穴、后颈和脊椎，紫瞳始终平静地望着天花板。

"疼吗？"她当时问。

"还好。"他说。

语气和此刻一样，平静得仿佛在说今天天气不错。

后来她在密涅瓦的鹰巢里教他操控红龙试制版，纠正他的每一个微小动作，调校他与甲胄的神经耦合参数。她记得西泽尔第一次穿戴上红龙甲胄时，仪表盘上的耦合度曲线像是被什么力量猛地拉高，从正常值的六十直接跳到了九十七。

整个鹰巢的技术员都惊叫了起来。

西泽尔从驾驶舱里走出来时脸色惨白，汗湿透了衬衣，但紫瞳里没有半分恐惧。他只是站在原地，看着自己的手，微微动了动手指，仿佛在确认什么。

"很顺手。"他说。

薇若兰那时候就明白——这孩子不是驾驭甲胄，而是甲胄在迎接他。

那以后她把西泽尔当成了弟弟，或者说，当成了密涅瓦最重要的财产。

后来她成了密涅瓦的副总长，签了无数份文件，在无数个深夜里校对过红龙试制版的每一颗螺栓、每一道焊缝、每一根神经接驳线路。她从来没想过有一天，自己会拿着一本三百年前的日记，看着最后几页写着那个孩子必须死去的字句。

改装蒸汽汽车驶过一段颠簸的碎石路，车身猛地晃了一下。薇若兰的肩膀撞在车门上，疼得她皱了皱眉。

"副总长，要不要减速？"驾驶座上的密涅瓦旧部回头问。

"不用。"薇若兰说，"快点。"

她需要快点到达维苏威火山。

不是为了把日记交给西泽尔——日记最后几页的内容她绝不能让他看到。

而是为了亲眼看到他还活着。

哪怕只活一天。

改装蒸汽汽车在维苏威火山的山脚下停了下来。引擎熄火后，四周突然安静得让人耳朵发胀，只有远处火山深处传来低沉的隆隆声，仿佛地底有什么东西在呼吸。

薇若兰推开车门，冷冽的山风灌了进来。她裹紧了深色的大衣，把日记本贴身收好，朝被炸开的暗门入口方向走去。

塔拉夏和三个密涅瓦旧部跟在后面，每个人腰间都别着手枪和近战短刀。

走了大约十分钟，薇若兰的脚步慢了下来。

前方就是暗门入口——但入口已经被堵死了。巨大的金属残片堆叠在一起，有半截断掉的普罗米修斯巨刃，有碎裂的影金属装甲板，还有被拧成麻花状的机械关节。那些残片上还残留着高温灼烧的痕迹，边缘泛着暗红色的余温。

显然是刚刚经历过一场极其惨烈的战斗。

"被堵住了……"塔拉夏快步走上前，伸手摸了摸残片的边缘，缩回手时指尖已经被烫红了一块。

"原罪机关？还是圣堂装甲师？"薇若兰问。

"看这个断口，是圣堂装甲师的普罗米修斯。"塔拉夏指向残片堆里一块带着圣堂装甲师军徽的碎片，皱眉，"可是他们怎么会在这里？"

"不重要。"薇若兰说，"找别的入口。"

她的话音刚落，一个声音从残片堆的侧面传来。

"不用找了。"

薇若兰猛地转头。

残片堆的右侧——大约五米开外——岩壁上有一个新炸开的洞。洞口不大，勉强能容两人并肩通过，边缘还残留着刚刚爆炸的硝烟味。洞口旁边的岩壁上，有人用匕首刻了几行字，刀工锋利而潦草：

"李锡尼等六人已进入。通道通往废弃矿道深处，可直达黑铁巨门。后续人员跟随后注意地下高温。"

落款是一个简单的符号——一枚没有火焰的十字架。

异端审判局的徽记。

"猩红死神……"塔拉夏低声念了一句，神色复杂。

薇若兰盯着那几行字，沉默了两秒钟。

她想起密涅瓦机关里曾经流传过的一个玩笑——说如果有一天整个世界都崩塌了，猩红死神李锡尼大概会站在废墟上对废墟说一声"抱歉"，然后继续去逮捕下一个异端。

没想到玩笑成真了。

"进去。"薇若兰说。

她第一个钻进了那个新炸开的洞口。

洞口内部是一条狭窄的通道，岩壁上还残留着爆炸造成的焦痕。通道向下倾斜，越往里走温度越高，空气中开始弥漫着一股金属被高温炙烤后特有的腥味。

走了大约二十米，通道豁然开朗。

薇若兰的脚步停住了。

通道的尽头是一片巨大的地下空间——维苏威火山底部的废弃矿道。矿道的岩壁上镶嵌着数以万计的黄铜微型齿轮，齿轮表面刻着她看不懂的文字，所有的齿轮都在缓缓转动，发出低沉的嗡鸣声。

而在矿道的正中央，西泽尔正站在那座纯金巨门的门口。

他背对着薇若兰，身上穿的不是新型红龙试制版甲胄，而是一身深色军服。身形瘦削，肩胛骨在军服下微微凸起，仿佛随时会被维苏威火山深处的热风吹散。

但他的后颈——薇若兰看到了——后颈的黄金套管正在发出微弱的金红色光芒。

西泽尔似乎察觉到了什么，转过头来。

他的紫瞳在矿道深处齿轮的转光中闪了一下，被金色纹路贯穿的亮紫色在昏暗里灼热得刺眼。

"薇若兰。"他说，语气里没有惊讶，只有平静的确认。

薇若兰站在通道的入口处，手指无意识地按在了胸口那个硬邦邦的位置——日记最后几页叠成的纸块正抵着她的心口。

她看着西泽尔的紫瞳，喉咙动了一下，最终只说了一句：

"我来了。"

矿道深处的齿轮依然在缓缓转动，嗡鸣声越来越响。

而在西泽尔身后的纯金巨门后面，某种沉重的、仿佛来自大地最深处的震动正在加剧。

像是有什么东西……正在醒来。

【English】
Chapter 207 — The Silver Mask's Master (Part Two)

Verolan was not a woman who wept.

The old artificers at Minerva knew this as certainly as they knew the smell of red mercury and the small, dry click of a properly seated coupling. When she was twenty, a steam main had burst inside the Eagle's Nest and drenched half her arm in scalding condensate. She had bitten through her own lip, tightened the offending bolt herself, sweat running into her eyes, and refused to call for help. Tarashka, who had found her afterward, asked her why. Because shouting, she had said, does not undo the burn. Better to turn the wrench twice.

She was, by every account anyone inside Minerva could give, the kind of woman who turned the wrench twice.

Which is why the three of them — Verolan, Tarashka, and the single remaining veteran driver she had kept on the rolls long past the Bureau's official disbandment — were not expecting the sound that came from the back seat of the lurching steam car as it clattered down the long switchbacks above the old Vesuvian quarries.

It was not crying. Verolan did not cry. It was, more precisely, a single short breath, bitten off at the root, the way a man catches himself on a high ledge.

Then silence.

Tarashka kept his eyes forward. He was a long man with a long face and the look of someone who had spent a career being told he was decorative, and had made a quiet career out of proving otherwise. He did not turn around.

The photograph — the one that had been folded inside the back cover of the journal, dog-eared, the ink along one edge eaten by some old liquid she did not want to guess at — lay face-down on Verolan's knee. She did not need to look at it. She had already memorized the line of the jaw, the set of the shoulders, the way the photographer had caught the subject mid-turn, as if called by something off-frame. The face was young. The eyes, even in monochrome, were not.

On her lap, the leather cover of da Vinci Borgia's journal had fallen open to the last few pages. The handwriting there was no longer the steady, clinical script of the early folios. The strokes leaned. The letters crowded one another. Whoever had been writing had been writing against a clock that was already running down, and the ink had been smeared in places by something that was not water.

She had read the final pages three times. The words had not changed.

*To bind the consciousness of a perfect Divine Vessel to the system of the Undying King, and to ignite the Violet Eye — to release the Light that Unmakes —*

*— to consume utterly every surviving root of the World Tree and every prototype body of the Omega line —*

*— the cost is the permanent dissolution of the vessel.*

Outside, the Tuscan hills were sliding backward, the long grass gone the color of old brass in the last of the daylight. Somewhere ahead, the abandoned mine workings of Mount Vesuvius had swallowed the road. The steam car's engine hammered at the cracked air, and the whole cabin shuddered as the treads took each rut like a small, individual blow.

Verolan closed the journal.

She pressed her eyes shut, very briefly, very hard.

*Perfect Divine Vessel.*

da Vinci Borgia had written the phrase as he might have written a part number in a disassembly schematic. Subject to be opened. Steps to be followed. Final result. Even the punctuation was calm. He had, in three hundred years, never lost the engineer's habit of treating catastrophe as procedure. The only phrase in the entire section that carried any human temperature at all was the last line, written small and crooked in the lower right corner of the page, as if the hand that had set it down had already begun to forget what it was doing:

*I have spent my whole life preventing myself from releasing it, and in the end I have prepared its death for it.*

It.

Not *he.*

Not *she.*

*It.*

Three hundred years ago an old man had been both Pope and Minerva's first Chief Engineer, and he had referred to the thing he had made in the neuter.

Verolan opened her eyes and looked down at her own hands. They were long-fingered, the nails kept short, the pads callused where decades of miniature work had pressed the same small tools into the same small places. These hands had assembled the most complex red-mercury cores Minerva had ever produced. They had calibrated the neural-coupling interface on a Seraph-grade cuirass to within a thousandth of a second. They had once, very carefully, very steadily, slid behind the neck of a boy in a hot cockpit and lifted him clear of a Red Dragon prototype while the gold coupling still burned against his skin.

She tore the last few pages out of the journal. She folded them twice, into a small thick square, and tucked the square inside her shirt, against the place where her sternum rose and fell.

The paper's edge was sharp. It pressed in, with each breath, like a small accusation.

The steam car's engine note changed. Tarashka leaned, drew his sidearm, and rested it on the sill of his window without raising it. Ahead, the auxiliary gate of the Minerva compound was lit by a single swinging oil lamp, and four men in the gray-black of the Original Sin Bureau were stepping out of the guardhouse, lifting long-barreled pistols in a manner that was professional and unhurried.

"Brace," Tarashka said.

He did not fire immediately. He leaned out the window, took the nearest man's kneecap with his first shot, pivoted, and took the second man's kneecap with his second, the report of the pistol lost in the larger thunder of the engine. The other two went down on their own — the first, scrambling for his dropped weapon, took a third round through the meat of his thigh; the second, wiser, threw himself behind a stone pier and stayed there.

"Go," Tarashka said, conversationally, to the driver, and the modified car went.

It took the auxiliary gate at speed, shearing the ironwork aside in a long shriek of torn metal. Six layers of shadow-metal plating along the car's flanks caught the answering volley from the guardhouse in a spray of pale pock-marks. The treads ground a low stone balustrade to powder, and the car came out onto the southern road with the engine screaming and the smell of burnt powder hanging in the cabin like incense.

Three minutes later, the roadblock.

Two heavy steam-bikes of the mounted constabulary sat across the lane, their headlamps already lit, throwing white bars of light across the dust. Six constables stood in a line behind them, rifles up.

"Halt! Submit to inspection!" The command came through a brass-voiced megaphone and bounced off the hills.

Tarashka reached into his coat without looking down, and produced a small square of stamped gilt — Minerva's A-grade pass, the six-winged owl picking up the last of the dusk in its enameled eye. He held it out the window, in two fingers, the way a duelist holds a card.

The constable captain hesitated. He took the pass, turned it, read the seal, and looked up at Tarashka's face as if he were looking for a joke there and did not find one.

"Minerva Bureau —" he began.

"Urgent Crown business," Tarashka said. "Open the road."

Two seconds. The captain gave the pass back. He did not salute. He stepped aside, and his men followed, and the steam car went through with a sound like a held breath finally let out.

"You are pale," Tarashka said, to the rearview mirror.

"The road is bad," Verolan said.

It was, in fact, the road. It was also not the road. Tarashka was, however, a clever man, and clever men know the difference between an answer and a request.

He said nothing further. He did not look into the mirror again.

The hills rolled on outside the window, darkening, the last copper line along the horizon going out like a snuffed lamp. Verolan watched it go. She let herself remember.

Cesare had come to Minerva not yet fifteen, a thin boy who looked as though a Florentine winter had been slowly wringing him out. Pale at the fingertips. Pale at the mouth. Pale under the eyes, where the bruised-looking skin of an adolescent ought not yet to have settled. Only the irises had any color in them at all, and that color — that impossible, mineral violet — had been, on the first day, almost unbearable to look at in a workshop lit by red-mercury lamps.

She had been eighteen then. Franco, the Professor, had put her in charge of the new eligible's pre-coupling physical, mostly, she suspected, because he wanted to see whether she would lose her nerve on the boy with the strange eyes. She had not lost her nerve. She had stuck the cold contacts to his temples, his nape, the small of his back, and watched the readouts settle, and asked him, in the neutral voice of a technician, whether the procedure hurt.

"Not especially," he had said, in the tone of a man describing the weather.

The same tone he had used, years later, when he stepped out of the Red Dragon prototype after his first full coupling and stood in the middle of the Eagle's Nest, white as paper, his shirt dark with sweat, his pupils blown wide, and said, *It responds well.*

She had not forgotten the curve the coupling meter had made that day. The needle had lifted, in a single clean stroke, from the expected baseline at sixty all the way to ninety-seven, and held there, as if it had always been meant to. The other artificers in the bay had made sounds. Verolan had not. She had watched the boy look down at his own hand, open and close the fingers once, as though confirming that the hand was still his, and she had understood — in the same instant, and with the same small chill — that this was not a child learning to drive an armor. This was an armor recognizing the one it had been waiting for.

She had, after that, treated him as a younger brother. Or, in the colder light of her own position, as Minerva's single most irreplaceable asset.

She had risen, in time, to Deputy Chief. She had countersigned the drawings for the new Red Dragon, line by line. She had personally checked, in the small hours of more nights than she cared to count, every bolt, every weld-seam, every filament of the neural interface, in the way a mother checks the corners of a room her child will sleep in. It had never crossed her mind that one day she would be reading a three-hundred-year-old journal that ended, in a steady engineer's hand, with the conclusion that the child must die.

The steam car hit a length of broken road and jumped. Verolan's shoulder struck the door frame. Pain, bright and unhelpful.

"Deputy Chief — slow down?" the driver called over his shoulder.

"No," she said. "Faster."

She needed to reach Vesuvius. Not to deliver the journal to Cesare — never that, never the last pages, never that single crooked line in the lower right corner. She needed to see him standing. She needed to see him upright and breathing and wearing that thin, faintly amused expression he wore when he was already three moves ahead of the room. Even if it was for one more day. Even if the day was all that was left.

The steam car stopped at the foot of the mountain. When the engine cut, the silence rushed in like water, swelling the ears. From somewhere far below the rock, a low, slow grinding — the sound of something vast shifting in its sleep, or of something vast beginning, at last, to wake.

Verolan opened her door. The cold Vesuvian air came in like a blade. She drew her dark coat tight, felt the folded square of pages press once more against her breastbone, and started up the slope toward the ruined mouth of the sealed gate.

Tarashka and three of Minerva's old guard fell in behind her. Pistols on the hips. Short blades at the small of the back. None of them spoke.

After perhaps ten minutes of climbing, Verolan slowed.

The entrance to the old gate was gone. A heap of torn metal filled it from wall to wall — a half-sliced Prometheus blade, plates of shadow-metal buckled inward, joints of some war-engine twisted into shapes that did not belong to any blueprint. The edges of the wreckage were still faintly red, as though whatever had happened here had happened minutes ago.

"Blocked," Tarashka said, and put his hand to a shard of plating, and drew it back, and looked at the blister already rising on his fingertip.

"Original Sin, or the Sanctum armored division?" Verolan asked.

Tarashka pointed to a fragment near the top of the heap. The piece still carried, near its broken edge, the stamped sigil of the Sanctum.

"The Sanctum." His mouth compressed. "Here. That is — wrong."

"It is what it is," Verolan said. "Find another way in."

She had not finished the sentence.

"Here," said a voice, from the side of the heap.

Verolan turned, fast. Her hand found the butt of her sidearm before she had finished the turn.

A new opening had been blown into the rock five meters to the right of the sealed gate. The hole was narrow — two men abreast, no more — and the air that came out of it still smelled of burnt powder. Beside the opening, someone had taken a fighting knife and cut a few lines into the stone, in a hand that was quick and careless and entirely legible:

*Licinius, with six, has entered. Passage descends to the deeper workings and on to the Black Iron Gate. Followers, mind the heat below.*

The signature was a single small mark — a cross with no flame beneath it.

The sigil of the Heresy Tribunal.

"Scarlet Reaper," Tarashka said, very quietly, in the tone of a man mentioning a particularly persistent weather system.

Verolan stared at the scratched lines. There had been, in Minerva's mess hall, an old joke that if the whole world were to come down around their ears, Licinius would be the man left standing on the rubble, apologizing to the rubble for the inconvenience, and then going to arrest the next heretic. She had laughed at it, once, in another life.

"Through," she said.

She went in first.

The passage dropped steeply. The walls were still hot from the blasting. As they went down, the air thickened, and a smell crept into it — the dry, mineral, almost meaty reek of stone that has been cooked from within.

After perhaps twenty meters, the passage opened out, and Verolan's boots stopped where the floor did.

The Vesuvian mine had been, at some earlier century, a place of work. It was no longer. The walls of the vast chamber were set, edge to edge, with tens of thousands of tiny brass gears, each no larger than a thumbnail, each turning at its own small, slow rate. The gears' faces were inscribed with a script that Verolan did not read. The sound they made, together, was a low sustained hum, like a single held note in a cathedral, and the note was not quite at rest.

At the far end of the chamber, the Black Iron Gate had been replaced. What stood there now was a door of pure gold, untarnished, featureless, taller than the chamber's ceiling ought to have allowed, and in front of it —

Cesare.

He stood with his back to the passage. He was not wearing the new Red Dragon. He was wearing a dark field uniform, and the uniform hung on him as though there were less of him in it than there used to be. The shoulder blades pressed against the cloth, faintly, like the bones of a bird.

But the gold coupling at the nape of his neck was lit. A dim ember of red-gold, very faint, very steady, as if something at the end of a long wire had finally found its circuit and was, at last, beginning to flow.

Cesare turned his head, as if he had heard her breathing, or as if he had simply known.

His eyes, in the turning brass light of the chamber, were not the violet she remembered. They were violet, and they were lit through with gold, and the gold was not decorative. It moved. It was moving. It was, she understood, in the way one understands such things, awake.

"Verolan," he said. Not surprised. Confirmed.

She stood at the mouth of the passage, one hand pressed, without deciding to press it, against the small hard square of folded paper over her heart. Her throat worked.

"I have come," she said.

The brass continued its slow turning. The hum deepened, almost imperceptibly, into a lower register.

And behind Cesare, behind the golden door, something vast and slow-shifting pressed, once, against the far side of the gold — and the gold answered, with the smallest of low, patient sounds, as though it had been waiting a very long time, and was content, at last, to be asked.

第208章 维苏威阴影下的暂歇

【中文】
第208章 维苏威阴影下的暂歇

坎特伯雷堡的钟塔投下长长的阴影。

从维苏威火山侧门的密道撤离时还是黎明，队伍乘着塔拉夏安排的蒸汽履带车穿过翡冷翠郊外的松林，等马车驶入堡后的石板路，太阳已经升到了松树梢头，把整座古堡照得发白。薇若兰走在最前面，脚步比平时快，黑色军靴踏在石板上的声音清脆而急促，像一串打不匀的鼓点。她怀里紧抱着那本从达·芬奇密室里抢出的日记本，日记本的硬壳封皮已经被她的体温捂热了，可她仍把它夹在腋下，像是生怕它会自己飞走。

塔拉夏在堡门外的石阶前停下，抬手整了整领口。他看上去比昨夜在叹息之墙时更疲惫，眼睛里布满红色的血丝，但脊背依然挺得笔直。

"副总长，我就不进去了。"他低声说，"堡外三百米范围我布了三组旧部，都是当年密涅瓦机关最可靠的钳工和铸匠，佩枪，没穿制服。"

薇若兰点了点头，欲言又止。塔拉夏看出了她的心思，往前走了一步，压低了声音：

"机关最高层已经被渗透了。我不确定是谁，但昨夜叹息之墙外出现的那批圣堂装甲师，他们对密涅瓦机关备用通道的熟悉程度不正常——不是外人能有的熟悉。"他的目光沉了下去，"您和西泽尔少爷暂时不要回机关。在枢机会搞清楚谁在背后捅刀子之前，堡里比机关里安全。"

薇若兰沉默了几秒，嘴角动了一下，似乎想笑，最终只是轻声说："知道了。"

塔拉夏敬了个礼，转身走向停在松林里的蒸汽履带车，履带车碾过落叶，发出咔嚓咔嚓的声音，渐渐消失在松林的尽头。碧儿·丹缇站在堡门后，看见那辆车开走，才把一直攥在手里的那块教皇厅档案员制服的袖口碎片塞回了裙子口袋里。碎片是半个月前她从洗衣房偷出来的——她当时就预感到有一天用得上。密涅瓦机关的档案库进不去，教皇厅的也未必安全，可如果有一天她必须去查一份被封存的旧档案，这份碎片至少能让她在门口多走三步路。

她没有告诉任何人这件事。

西泽尔最后一个走进堡门。

他赤着脚，军靴被瓦莲京娜在密道里强制脱掉了——脚底有两道被滚烫的岩浆碎石烫出的水泡，走路会磨破。黑色制服的下摆有几处被岩浆溅出的焦痕，袖口被某种酸性的蒸汽腐蚀出几个细小的洞。他走过门廊时，碧儿发现他的右手一直插在裤袋里，握成拳头的形状，指节发白。

他没有和任何人说话，径直走向二楼西侧的那间旧卧室——琳琅夫人当年住过的那间。

门在他身后合上了。

* * *

薇若兰站在一楼门厅里，把日记本压在胸口，盯着那扇合上的门看了很久。她知道那扇门后面是什么：一间铺着褪色波斯地毯的小卧室，窗台上还摆着琳琅夫人年轻时养过的天竺葵盆栽——早已干枯，可碧儿每周都会换一次清水，仿佛那盆花还活着。

她也很清楚西泽尔关上门后要做什么——他会躺在床上，盯着天花板的石膏浮雕发呆，然后闭上眼睛，让昨夜那场世界树记忆灌输的余波在脑海里一遍又一遍地冲刷。

她本该叫住他，把日记里关于"完美神使"的那一页给他看。她已经把那一页撕下来了，叠成一个很小的方块，塞在军靴的鞋垫下面。可她的嘴唇动了动，最终没有开口。

不是时候。现在不是时候。

她转身走向厨房，把日记本锁进了堡里那台已经废弃多年的保险柜，转盘拧了三圈。保险柜的锁发出一声干涩的咔哒声，像某种老旧机械的最后一次呼吸。

* * *

厨房里，昆提良正在和唐璜争夺一口铸铁锅的归属权。

"我来煮。"昆提良坚持说，一边把可可粉罐子从架子上取下来。

"你上次煮可可把锅底烧穿了。"唐璜毫不客气地说，伸手去抢那口锅。

"那是煤气管堵了！"

"煤气管堵了你就往里面倒了一整瓶白兰地？"

"那是因为碧儿说白兰地配可可味道更好。"

碧儿从门边探进头来："我没说过。"

昆提良和唐璜同时转过头看她，昆提良的表情有些委屈，唐璜则是早知如此的样子。碧儿耸了耸肩，走进来坐到灶台边的高脚凳上，开始削苹果。

炉子上的铜壶开始发出轻微的咕嘟声，可可粉在热水里慢慢散开，浓郁的香气填满了整间厨房。这是翡冷翠最古老的平民饮品之一，也是这帮人在军营时养成的习惯——每次出完任务回来，不管几点，昆提良都会煮一锅热可可。唐璜骂他浪费煤气管，骂了三年，骂到最后自己也喝上了。

"老板怎么了？"唐璜压低声音问碧儿。

碧儿削苹果的手停了一下。"没怎么。就是累了吧。"

"累到连靴子都不脱就往床上躺的那种累？"唐璜撇了撇嘴，"他从来都是自己脱靴子的。"

"是瓦莲京娜公主给他脱的。"碧儿说。

唐璜愣了一下，张了张嘴想说什么，最终只是摇了摇头。昆提良在旁边发出一声意味不明的鼻音，往铜壶里又加了两勺可可粉。

"你说老板和这位公主殿下，到底算什么关系？"唐璜凑到昆提良耳边，声音压得更低。

"我要是知道，我还在这里煮可可？"昆提良闷声说。

"我赌一百金币，老板还没想清楚。"

"不跟你赌。碧儿会生气。"

唐璜看了碧儿一眼。碧儿没抬头，只是把削好的苹果切成薄片，一圈一圈摆在盘子里。她听到了他们的对话，但假装没听到。

* * *

二楼西侧的旧卧室里，光线从百叶窗的缝隙里漏进来，在褪色的波斯地毯上投下一道道细长的金纹。

西泽尔躺在床上，没有盖被子。

他睁着眼睛，左手举在半空，盯着自己的瞳孔看。晨光从百叶窗的缝隙里穿过虹膜，瞳孔深处那道金红色的纹路在光线下显得格外清晰——它没有消退，从昨夜红伞把能量注入他体内开始，它就一直盘踞在紫瞳最深处，像是某种被烙进虹膜里的烫金印记。

他想起莲生临终前那场对话。想起达·芬奇在三百年前的图纸上留下的字。想起初代教皇把艾琳娜送往锡兰之前，她回眸时眼角那一滴不知是泪还是血水的液体。

然后他想起了昨夜在熔岩之心深处，红伞的伞尖抵住他胸口的那一瞬——

滚烫的，灼热的，仿佛有某种液态的金属顺着伞尖注入他的血液，灌入他的脊椎，在他的神经网络里炸开了一片金红色的光海。光海退去之后，他看见了一扇门。一扇巨大的、纯黑色的、门楣上雕刻着卡巴拉生命之树纹样的铁门。门缝里透出奇异的金色光芒，门的两侧站着两列背对着他的身影——那些身影的肩甲上生着六片钢铁铸造的翅膀，翅膀上嵌满了红水银核心。

他当时还不知道那扇门叫什么。后来他知道了。

那是黑铁巨门。

门后藏着的，是初代教皇用三百年时间培育的果实——九百九十九架欧米茄原型体。

西泽尔把手放下来，搭在胸口。指尖碰到制服内袋里那枚冰原寒玉银戒指的边缘——瓦莲京娜在他昏迷时替他戴上的，尺寸刚好合适他的右手中指，仿佛那枚戒指本来就是为他而铸造的。

他闭上眼睛，试着让自己不再去想黑铁巨门后面那些眼睛——九百九十九双眼睛，每一双都镶嵌着跳动的红水银核心，在他踏入门厅的瞬间同时亮起，仿佛九百九十九盏金色的灯。

它们看向他的那一刻，他感觉到血脉深处的某种东西在回应它们。

他觉得很累。

* * *

楼下，瓦莲京娜坐在花园的石凳上。

坎特伯雷堡的花园在盛夏时节本该是最美的，紫藤爬满了铁艺凉亭的骨架，忍冬花的香气浓得化不开。可现在刚入秋，紫藤的叶子开始发黄，忍冬花也败了大半，凉亭的骨架在月光下投出嶙峋的影子。

她把右手搭在石凳的扶手上，左手则下意识地抚过自己的手腕。手腕内侧的皮肤很白，月光下几乎透明，静脉的青蓝色隐约可见。而在那层皮肤下面，藏着一枚她从出生起就一直戴着的小首饰——不是项链坠，不是耳环，是一枚被缝进腕带内侧的、拇指盖大小的银色五芒星。

五芒星的五个角末端各嵌着微型齿轮，背面刻着一行极细的梵文。

这是她母亲叶尼塞王妃的遗物。王妃去世时把它留在了襁褓里的瓦莲京娜手腕上，嘱咐贴身侍女永远不要取下来。瓦莲京娜小时候问过母亲那是什么，母亲只说"等你长大了自然会知道"。

她现在长大了。可她还是不知道那枚五芒星究竟意味着什么。

母亲在难产中去世后，叶尼塞皇宫里的老仆人私下议论过，说那是王妃从娘家带来的东西，王妃的娘家在叶尼塞最北端的冻土带，是一个已经消亡了三百年的古老家族。没人知道那个家族的名字。

瓦莲京娜把袖口往下拉了拉，盖住了那枚五芒星。

* * *

一楼的工具间里，阿方索坐在工作台前，面前摊着蜘蛛巢腕表的全部零件。

腕表的外壳在昨夜和圣堂装甲师的混战中被一颗流弹擦过，留下一道浅浅的沟痕，但机芯没有受损。真正出问题的是通讯模块——里面的微型红水银晶块被爆炸的冲击波震偏了位置，导致发射频率漂移，原本能接收三十公里范围内的信号，现在只能勉强听到两公里内的噪音。

他用镊子把晶块重新归位，又在固定卡扣上加了一层薄锡箔。通电测试的时候，腕表表面那圈微型齿轮开始缓缓转动，发出细密的咔哒声，绿色的指示灯亮了。

"成了。"他自言自语。

他把腕表戴回手腕，调试接收频道。信号开始稳定下来，杂音一点点退去。可就在他准备关掉测试模式的时候，纸带打印口突然吐出了一小段纸。

那是一段加密密文。

密文的编码方式很古老，是密涅瓦机关三十年前的退役制式——所有密涅瓦内部的加密电报，五年前就被统一更换为新制式了。能把旧制式密文发到他的私人频道上的人，要么是机关里的老前辈，要么是……拿到了密涅瓦旧制式密码本的人。

他皱着眉头，把纸带凑到台灯下。

密文大部分是乱码，只有前五个字符是明文——是发送者故意留下的、确保接收者能第一时间辨认出特定含义的明文锚点。

那五个字符是：

锡兰星见

阿方索的手指僵在纸带上。

锡兰星见。

他认识这四个字。三个月前西泽尔第一次在密涅瓦机关的密室里向他解释自己血脉来源的时候，就说过这四个字。可那之后，"锡兰星见"这四个字就再也没有在任何密文、任何档案、任何情报里出现过——锡兰已经灭国十七年了，末代星见早已死绝，"星见"这个词在西方世界的通用语里几乎已经成了古语的化石。

他把纸带从打印机里完全抽出来，仔仔细细地看了三遍。密文后半段是乱码，但前五个明文字符之后紧跟着还有三个字符被发送者刻意保住了——他不懂密文解码，可那三个字符的形状他认得。

是某种东方占卜用的赤金色钱币符号。

不，不是符号。是……名字？

他猛地站起来，把纸带攥在手里，几乎是冲出了工具间。

* * *

西泽尔卧室的门被敲响了。

三声。很急。

他没有立刻去开门。窗外的光线已经从晨光变成了午后的斜照，房间里飘着淡淡的忍冬香——那是碧儿换过花瓶里的水之后留下的味道。

敲门声又响了三下。这次伴随着阿方索压低却压不住急切的声音：

"老板，你得看看这个。"

西泽尔坐起来，披上搭在椅背上的黑色外套，走过去打开了门。

阿方索站在门口，工作服上还沾着机油，额头上有细密的汗珠。他把那条纸带拍在西泽尔面前的工作台上，纸带展开，前五个明文字符在台灯下泛着淡淡的墨绿色。

"前五个字是——锡兰星见，救，苏，伽，罗。"

他停顿了一下，喉头滚动了一下，仿佛那两个字要了他的命。

"苏伽罗。"阿方索盯着西泽尔的脸，"那不是锡兰末代王女的名字吗？"

西泽尔没有回答。

他看着那条纸带，瞳孔深处那道金红色的纹路在台灯的光线下微微跳了一下——仿佛那里面的某种东西认出了那五个字。

房间里很静。楼下厨房里昆提良和唐璜的笑声远远地传上来，衬得这份安静更加不真实。

西泽尔伸手，指尖慢慢触上那条纸带。指腹碰到墨迹的那一刻，他的指尖微微一凉。

纸带上那五个明文字符开始发出极淡的、几乎看不见的金色微光。

而那张工作台的另一端，从维苏威火山里带回来的、齿轮徽记模糊的锡封匣子安静地躺在桌角，无人触碰，匣盖上的暗红色卡巴拉圣徽在灯光下泛着幽冷的光泽。

【English】
Chapter 208 — A Rest in the Shadow of Vesuvius

The bell tower of Canterbury Keep threw its long shadow across the gravel.

It had still been dark when the company filed out of Mount Vesuvius's side gate and down the old escape tunnel to the lava shelf where Tarasius had the steam-crawler waiting. The crawler ground its way through the pine woods on the outskirts of Florence, and by the time its treads bit into the flagstones behind the keep, the sun had climbed above the treetops and the old walls were bleaching white with the heat of it.

Violante walked at the head of the column. Her black boots struck the paving in a quick, irregular beat, like a drummer who could not keep her own time. She carried the leather-bound journal they had taken from da Vinci's hidden chamber clamped under her arm, the cover already gone warm against her ribs, and she held it the closer as though she feared it might, of its own accord, fly.

Tarasius stopped at the foot of the stone steps outside the keep's gate. He straightened his collar with a small, habitual motion. He looked more worn than he had the night before, at the Wall of Sighs — the whites of his eyes laced with red, the skin under his jaw gone slack with sleeplessness — but his back was held straight as a surveyor's line.

"Vice-Commander," he said, low, "I will not go in. Within three hundred meters of the walls I have posted three squads of my old men — riggers and foundry-men from the Minerva Bureau in their better days. They are armed and out of uniform."

Violante nodded. She opened her mouth and closed it again.

Tarasius read the unsaid thing. He stepped closer, and dropped his voice.

"The upper levels of the Bureau have been turned. I do not know by whom. But the Cathedral Armored Division that appeared outside the Wall of Sighs last night knew our reserve passages too well — not the knowledge of an outsider." His gaze dropped to the flagstones. "You and young Cesare should not return to the Bureau. Until the College of Cardinals has worked out who is stabbing us in the back, the keep is safer than the Bureau is."

Violante was quiet for a few seconds. The corner of her mouth moved, as though she meant to smile, and gave it up.

"Understood," she said.

Tarasius saluted, turned on his heel, and walked back down the steps toward the steam-crawler waiting in the pines. The treads bit the carpet of dry needles as the machine turned, and the crackling of them grew fainter and fainter, and then there was nothing.

Beryl Danti had been standing just inside the gate. She watched the crawler go. Only when the last of its noise had been swallowed by the trees did she take the scrap of cloth she had been gripping in her hand — a torn cuff from a Papal Hall archivist's uniform — and slip it back into the pocket of her skirt.

She had stolen the scrap two weeks before, out of the laundry. Even then she had known she might have a use for it someday. The Minerva Bureau's archives were closed to her, and the Papal Hall's were not necessarily any safer, but if the day ever came when she had to look up some sealed old file, that scrap might at least buy her three steps past a doorway.

She had not told anyone.

Cesare was the last to come through the gate.

He was barefoot. Valentina had made him take his boots off in the escape tunnel — the soles of his feet were blistered where the hot lava grit had bitten through, and walking would have torn them open. The hem of his black uniform was pitted with flecks of burnt rock, and the cuff of his left sleeve was peppered with small holes where some acidic vent had spat at him. As he passed under the porch, Beryl noticed his right hand stayed in his trouser pocket, curled into a fist, the knuckles gone bloodless.

He said nothing to anyone. He went straight to the foot of the stairs and up them, and down the west corridor, and into the old bedroom that had been Lady Linlang's, years before. The door closed behind him.

* * *

Violante stood in the entrance hall, the journal pressed to her chest, and looked at that closed door for a long time.

She knew what was behind it: a small bedroom with a faded Persian carpet, a window seat where Lady Linlang had once kept a pot of geraniums — long since dried out, but Beryl changed the water in the saucer every week, as though the plant were still alive.

She knew, too, what Cesare would do once the door was shut. He would lie down on the bed without pulling a cover over him, and stare at the plaster rosettes on the ceiling, and then close his eyes, and let the afterwash of last night's world-tree memory pour through him again and again until it had scoured him hollow.

She ought to have called out to him. She ought to have shown him the page in the journal about the Perfect Divine Messenger. She had already torn that page out, folded it into a small square, and tucked it under the insole of her left boot. But her lips moved, and she said nothing.

Not yet. It was not the moment.

She turned on her heel and walked to the kitchen, and locked the journal in the keep's old wall-safe — a thing that had not been turned in years. The dial went around three times and the bolt fell with a dry click, like the last breath of some tired piece of machinery.

* * *

In the kitchen, Quintilian and Don Juan were at war over a cast-iron pot.

"I am cooking," Quintilian said, and reached for the cocoa tin on the shelf.

"You burned a hole through the bottom of the last pot you made cocoa in," Don Juan said, and reached for the same pot.

"That was the gas line was blocked."

"The gas line was blocked, and your solution was to pour in a whole bottle of brandy?"

"Beryl said brandy goes well with cocoa."

Beryl put her head in at the door. "I never said that."

Quintilian and Don Juan turned to look at her. Quintilian's expression was wounded. Don Juan's said he had known it all along. Beryl shrugged, came in, and perched on a high stool by the range, and began to peel an apple.

The copper kettle on the hob began to murmur. The cocoa loosened in the hot water, and the smell of it — heavy, almost burnt, the smell of long barracks nights — went through the kitchen. It was one of the oldest common drinks in Florence, and the habit of it had been bred into them in the camps: after a job, whatever the hour, Quintilian would put a pot on. Don Juan had been calling him a waster of gas for three years, and somewhere in the second year he had begun to drink it too.

"What is the matter with the boss?" Don Juan asked, sotto voce.

Beryl's hand paused on the apple for a beat. "Nothing. He is tired, that is all."

"Tired enough to fall into bed without taking his own boots off?" Don Juan tilted his head. "He always takes his own boots off."

"Princess Valentina took them off for him," Beryl said.

Don Juan blinked. He opened his mouth, and thought better of whatever had been about to come out of it, and shook his head. Quintilian, at the range, made a non-committal noise through his nose and tipped two more spoonfuls of cocoa into the kettle.

"Tell me," Don Juan said, leaning close to Quintilian's ear, "what is the actual situation between the boss and her Highness?"

"If I knew the answer to that, do you think I would be standing here cooking cocoa?"

"I will wager you a hundred gold pieces the boss has not yet worked it out for himself."

"I am not taking that bet. Beryl would be annoyed."

Don Juan glanced at Beryl. She did not look up. She sliced the peeled apple into thin rounds, and laid them in a ring on a plate, and pretended she had heard none of it.

* * *

In the old bedroom on the west side of the second floor, the light came through the slats of the shutter in long thin bars of gold, and lay down across the faded Persian carpet.

Cesare lay on the bed with no coverlet over him. His eyes were open.

He held his left hand up in the air, and stared at his own pupil. The morning light came through the slats and into the iris, and the gold-red mark at the back of it showed very clearly — a thread of molten colour, like a brand pressed into the wet clay of the eye, that had not faded since the red umbrella had poured itself into him in the night. It sat at the deepest part of the violet, and it did not move, and it did not dim.

He thought of Lien-sheng, and the conversation before the end. He thought of the diagrams da Vinci had left on his parchment three hundred years ago, and the words at the foot of the last page. He thought of the first Pope, and of Elena being sent away to Ceylon, and the single drop — of tears, or of blood, he had never been sure which — that had stood at the corner of her eye as she turned for a last look at the harbour.

And he thought of the moment, in the deepest chamber of the molten heart, when the point of the red umbrella had come to rest against his breastbone.

Hot. Scorching hot. As if some liquid metal were being poured through the tip of it, into his blood, down the length of his spine, and bursting in his nerve-web into a sea of gold-red light. When the light drew back, he had seen a door. A great door, black from top to bottom, with the Tree of Life carved across its lintel, and from the crack along its seam a strange gold radiance came. On either side of the door stood a long rank of figures with their backs to him — figures in shoulder-plates from which six steel wings had been forged, every feather set with a red-mercury core.

He had not known, then, what the door was called. He knew, now.

The Black Iron Gate. And what lay behind it, the fruit the first Pope had spent three hundred years cultivating: nine hundred and ninety-nine prototype Omegas, ranked in their alcoves like bottles in a wine cellar, waiting.

He lowered his hand and laid it across his chest. The tip of his finger touched the rim of something in the breast pocket of his uniform — a ring of pale jade-frost silver, set on a band so cold it burned. Valentina had put it on him while he was unconscious, and it had fitted his right hand as if it had been sized for no one else.

He closed his eyes, and tried not to think of the eyes behind the Black Iron Gate. Nine hundred and ninety-nine pairs of them, each one set with a beating red-mercury core, all of them lighting at the same instant he had stepped into the threshold, as though nine hundred and ninety-nine golden lamps had been turned on at once. They had looked at him, and something in his own blood had answered them.

He was very tired.

* * *

Downstairs, in the garden, Valentina sat on the stone bench.

The Canterbury Keep garden would have been at its best in the height of summer — the wisteria thick along the iron bones of the arbour, the honeysuckle so sweet it was almost a weight. But the season had barely tipped into autumn, and the wisteria leaves were going yellow at the edges, and the honeysuckle was half gone, and the iron ribs of the arbour threw a gaunt lattice of shadow across the path in the moonlight.

She rested her right hand on the arm of the bench, and with her left, almost without thinking, she drew a finger along the inside of her own wrist. The skin there was very pale, almost translucent in the moon, and the blue of the veins showed under it. And under the skin, sewn into the lining of the silk wristband she had worn since she was a baby, there was a thumbprint-sized silver five-pointed star.

The five points of the star each ended in a tiny gear, and on the back of it, in a script so fine it was almost invisible, a line of Sanskrit had been engraved.

It had been her mother's. The Princess of Yenisei had died in childbed, and the small silver star had been found in the swaddling of the baby girl on her breast, with a word in the old woman's ear that the nurse was to take it off her living body and on no account before. As a child Valentina had asked her mother what it was. Her mother had said only: when you are grown, you will know.

She was grown now. She did not know.

After the Princess of Yenisei died, the old servants of the palace had whispered among themselves that the star had come to the princess from her own family — a family that had lived at the very top of the Yenisei watershed, on the tundra, and had died out three hundred years before. No one in the household could remember the name of the family.

Valentina tugged the cuff of her sleeve down over the star.

* * *

In the tool room on the ground floor, Alfonso sat at the workbench, with the spider's-nest watch spread out before him in its full hundred and seven pieces.

The case had been clipped in last night's running fight with the Cathedral Armored Division — a spent ball had kissed the side of the casing and left a shallow furrow — but the movement was sound. The trouble was in the communications module. The micro red-mercury crystal inside had been jolted half a millimetre out of true by the blast wave, and the transmission frequency had drifted; the watch that had once been able to pick up signals over thirty kilometres could now barely hear the noise of the courtyard two streets away.

He set the crystal back in its cradle with a pair of tweezers, and laid a thin foil of tin over the retaining clip. He switched the watch on, and the ring of micro-gears on the dial began to turn, ticking, and the green telltale lit.

"It lives," he said to himself.

He buckled the watch back on his wrist, and began to run the receiver through its bands. The signal cleaned up; the static thinned. He was about to switch the test mode off, when the paper-tape slot spat out a small length of paper.

A piece of encrypted traffic.

The cipher was old — Minerva Bureau standard-issue, retired thirty years ago, every internal Bureau cipher replaced by the new standard five years back. Whoever had sent this on his private channel was either a greybeard of the old Bureau, or someone who had got their hands on a Bureau codebook of the previous generation.

He bent the paper to the lamp.

Most of the tape was garble, but the sender had left a plaintext anchor at the head of it — five characters set down on purpose, so the receiver would know in a single glance what the message was about.

The five characters were:

CEYLON STARGAZER

Alfonso's fingers stopped on the paper.

Ceylon Stargazer.

He knew the phrase. Three months ago, in the underground chamber of the Minerva Bureau, Cesare had first told him where his blood came from, and he had said those exact four words. Since then, neither in any cipher, nor in any file, nor in any report, had the words appeared again. Ceylon had been a dead kingdom for seventeen years. The last of its Stargazers had been hunted down and gone to the bonfire. The word *stargazer* itself had gone the way of old words, gone grey in the dictionaries of the West, fossil.

He drew the full length of tape out of the slot, and read it through three times. The second half of the tape was unreadable, but after the five plaintext characters the sender had deliberately preserved three more. He could not read cipher, but he could read the shape of the letters.

They were the shape of certain Eastern augur-coins, struck in a red-gold alloy, used in a kind of divination that had no name in the West.

No. Not a coin. A name.

He stood up so suddenly the stool rocked back against the wall. He had the tape crumpled in his fist, and he was out of the tool room before he knew it.

* * *

The door of the old bedroom on the second floor was knocked on.

Three knocks. Hurried.

Cesare did not get up at once. The light through the shutter had moved on past noon, and was slanting the other way now, and the room smelled faintly of honeysuckle — the ghost of the water Beryl had changed in the vase.

The knocks came again, three more, and with them Alfonso's voice, low but unable to keep the edge off:

"Boss. You have to see this."

Cesare sat up. He pulled on the black coat that was hanging over the back of the chair, and went to the door, and opened it.

Alfonso stood in the corridor, smears of machine oil still on his coverall, a fine sweat on his brow. He slapped the paper tape down on the worktable inside the door and smoothed it flat under the lamp. The first five plaintext characters gave back a faint greenish ink.

"The first five read: Ceylon Stargazer. Then, save. Then Su. Ga. Ra."

He stopped. The word in his mouth seemed to cost him something.

"Sukara," he said, watching Cesare's face. "That is the name of the last princess of Ceylon, is it not?"

Cesare said nothing.

He stood looking at the tape. And in the lamplight, at the back of his violet eye, the gold-red thread that Lien-sheng had set burning in him gave a single small jump — as though something deep in it had heard, and recognised, those five characters.

The room was very still. Far below, in the kitchen, the faint sound of Quintilian and Don Juan laughing at something drifted up the stairwell, and made the silence the more unreal.

Cesare reached out, and laid the tip of one finger on the tape. The pad of the finger came away with the faintest coolness from the ink.

And on the tape, the five plaintext characters began, very slowly, to give off a gold so dim it was almost not there at all.

At the other end of the worktable, untouched by any hand, the tin-sealed casket they had brought back out of the heart of Vesuvius lay where it had been left, the Borgia cog blurred on its lid, the dark-red Kabbalistic sigil at its centre giving back the lamplight in a cold, slow gleam.

【中文】
第209章 尘封的预言书（上）

纸带在台灯下安静地躺着，前五个明文字符的淡金色已经彻底消退，像从未出现过一样。

阿方索站在工作台前，双手撑着台沿，指节泛白。他不是容易被吓到的人——在翡冷翠贫民区开修理铺的这些年，见过比这更令人不安的暗号密文。可这条纸带不一样。

那三个被他保住的字符，赤金色的，形状像东方占卜用的铜钱……他其实认不全。可最末一个字符的轮廓他见过。

在翡冷翠英灵殿最深处的某只旧匣子里。

"老板。"阿方索压低声音，"这三个字符不是密涅瓦的编码，也不是枢机会的格式，是机械神教祷文里出现过的……"

"我知道。"

西泽尔的声音很轻，没有看阿方索，目光落在纸带上。

楼下传来轻缓的脚步声，沿着旋转楼梯上来，停在门外。

三下敲门声。很轻。

"进来。"

门被推开一条缝，碧儿·丹缇侧身挤了进来。

她穿着深色女侍长制服，头发别得整齐，双手捧着一只老旧的木盒。盒子的木纹模糊，铜皮边角磨得发亮——像一件被主人贴身带了几十年的东西。

"少爷。"碧儿的声音很低，"我有些东西……一直想给你看。"

她看了一眼阿方索，又看了一眼桌上那条纸带，喉头轻轻滚动了一下。

"这是夫人从克里特岛带过来的。"

阿方索皱眉。琳琅夫人当年从克里特岛被押送到翡冷翠时，什么也没带——至少所有人都是这么认为的。一具被神经接驳后遗症掏空的身体，一个女婴，一个还在襁褓中的婴儿。

碧儿把木盒放在工作台上，掀开盖子。

盒内是几片深棕色的叶子，边缘卷曲发脆，像风干了的蝴蝶翅膀。叶面上密密麻麻地写满文字，笔画繁复，一层叠着一层，像莲花瓣层层展开。

和纸带上的字形如出一辙。

"我……我不认识这些字。"碧儿的声音更低了，"从克里特岛到翡冷翠，夫人一直带着这只木盒。我是十年前才从她手上接过来的，她什么都没说，只说让我收好，等该来取的人。"

她抬头看向西泽尔，嘴唇微微颤抖。

"我……早该给你的。"

西泽尔没有立刻回答。他伸手拈起一片棕榈叶，指腹触上那些细密的笔划。

指尖微微一凉。

那种凉意不是来自叶面的温度，而是来自文字本身——仿佛笔划里封存着某种极古老的东西，正隔着三百年的时光与他对视。

"锡兰文。"他低声说，"古锡兰文。"

阿方索一步跨到台前。

"能翻译？"

"不能。"

阿方索愣了半秒，随即反应过来。西泽尔能认字，但不代表他能翻译。古锡兰文和现代锡兰语已经是两种完全不同的语言体系，需要专门的工具。

"城堡里应该有密涅瓦的旧翻译器。"阿方索说，"坎特伯雷堡曾经是密涅瓦的备用仓库，佛朗哥教授说过这里封存着他三十年前的东西……"

他没说完，已经转身冲出了房间，脚步声咚咚咚地下了楼梯。

碧儿站在原地，双手绞在身前。

"少爷，夫人她……知道这些字的意思吗？"

西泽尔把棕榈叶放回木盒。

"她知道。"

他合上盒盖，声音平静得像在陈述天气。

"她只是不想说。"

楼下传来阿方索和唐璜说话的声音，夹杂着金属碰撞的响动。碧儿低着头，目光落在工作台角落那个齿轮徽记模糊的锡封匣上。匣盖上的暗红色卡巴拉圣徽在台灯下泛着幽冷的光泽——她认得这个标记。

"少爷，那只匣子也是夫人的吗？"

"不。"西泽尔说，"那是达·芬奇留下的。"

碧儿没再问。她向来知道什么时候该闭嘴。

……

七分钟后，阿方索抱着一只沉重的铁皮箱子回来了。

箱子很旧，漆面剥落，箱角包着已经发黑的铜皮。他砰地一声把它放在工作台上，掀起箱盖。

里面是一台老式翻译器。

机体是黄铜的，结构复杂，看起来像一台缩小版的蒸汽机。各种齿轮、连杆、皮带轮挤在狭小的空间里，顶部有一只可以翻转的入料口，侧面是密密麻麻的字母按键——拉丁文、希腊文、阿拉伯文、梵文……唯独没有锡兰文。

可机体正面正中央，却用红水银漆画着一个徽记。

齿轮中心嵌着一颗五芒星。

阿方索的手停住了。

"机械神教的徽记。"他低声说，"这是三百年前的型号。"

他抬头看向西泽尔。

"佛朗哥教授怎么会……"

"他不只有一台。"西泽尔平静地说，"继续。"

阿方索深吸一口气，从木盒里取出一片棕榈叶，小心翼翼地送进入料口。

齿轮开始转动，发出低沉的咔哒声。皮带轮吱呀作响，带动整台机器震颤起来——像是沉睡了三十年的机械被重新唤醒，筋骨里发出咯吱咯吱的响。

翻译器的指针在刻度盘上缓缓移动，跳过一行又一行的符号。

"锡兰古文变体……"阿方索读着刻度盘上的数字，"匹配度……百分之七十三。"

他按下翻译键。

机体的输出口吐出一张泛黄的纸条，纸条上是用拉丁文打印的译文——

【倒置五芒星，锡兰星见家族之圣徽】
【星见继承人将回归，执掌遗失之冠】
【紫瞳之子，承载命运之力】

阿方索的手停住了。

他回头看向西泽尔。

"紫瞳之子。"他念出这几个字，声音干涩得像是喉咙里塞了砂纸。

西泽尔的眼睛是紫色的。

门外传来轻轻的敲门声。昆提良探进半个脑袋。

"老板，瓦莲京娜小姐来了。"

他身后，金发的叶尼塞公主站在走廊里，神情冷峻。白靴踩在地板上发出轻微的响声，像踩在冰面上。

"我听见了。"她直接走进房间，目光扫过工作台上的木盒、翻译器和那条纸带，"让我看看。"

她没有等任何人回答，已经走到翻译器前，伸手拿起了那张译文。

她的眼睛扫过那些文字。

脸色变了。

不是普通的惊讶，是一种从骨子里透出来的凝重——仿佛那些字印证了她心中某个隐秘的猜测，又仿佛撕开了她一直不敢正视的某层纱。

"倒置五芒星。"她低声念，"星见继承人。"

她放下纸条，缓缓卷起右手的袖口。

手腕内侧露出一只拇指盖大小的银饰。银饰正面是半朵莲花，背面刻着微型齿轮纹路——和棕榈叶碎片上某些图案的轮廓，分毫不差。

"这是我母亲留给我的。"她说，声音很平，"她说这是叶尼塞王室代代相传的东西，从她嫁入皇宫之前就一直戴着。"

她抬头，目光与西泽尔相碰。

"我从来不知道它是什么意思。"

房间里极静。

翻译器还在咔哒咔哒地响着，齿轮缓慢地转动。

阿方索伸手按下了停机键。

"瓦莲京娜小姐。"他沉声说，"这台翻译器能匹配古锡兰文百分之七十三的准确率，是因为它内置了某种专门的古语词库——这种词库，全世界不超过三台。"

他指了指机体正面的徽记。

"机械神教的东西，佛朗哥教授为什么要留一台在这里？"

没人能回答这个问题。

楼下的走廊里忽然响起急促的脚步声。

是唐璜。

他几乎是冲进来的，脸色发白，压着嗓子说：

"老板——骑警。街口。"

所有人都僵住了。

昆提良一个箭步冲到窗边，从帘缝里往下看。街道尽头，三名骑警骑着马缓缓走来，马蹄在石板路上敲出清脆的响声。领头那位穿着深蓝色的制服，腰间别着短枪，胸口佩着翡冷翠骑警的银色徽记。

他们正朝着城堡的方向而来。

"还有多少时间？"西泽尔问。

"五分钟。"昆提良低声说，"最多。"

阿方索已经在工作台上飞快地翻找着什么——他从铁皮箱子的夹层里抽出一只小型蒸汽机，外形像一只放大的怀表。他拧开发条，蒸汽机开始发出低沉的嗡嗡声。

"佛朗哥教授留的不只是翻译器。"他一边操作一边说，"这里还有一只……"

蒸汽机的输出端弹出一根细铜管，铜管的末端连着一个小喇叭。

阿方索把铜管对准窗外，按下蒸汽机顶部的一个按钮。

喇叭里传出悠远的管风琴声。

是《慈悲经》的旋律，低沉庄严，像从某个遥远的中世纪教堂里飘出来，在午后的斜阳里缓缓铺开。

"街对面那个废弃教堂。"阿方索压低声音说，"我们放管风琴的声音，骑警会以为里面在做弥撒——比这座城堡更值得他们检查的地方。"

管风琴声穿过街道，在空气里飘散。

骑警的马蹄声停了。

领头那位抬头望向街对面的废弃教堂，皱了皱眉，似乎在犹豫——可那庄严的《慈悲经》仿佛在提醒他什么不应当打扰的神圣。他挥了挥手，示意同伴转向。

马蹄声渐渐远去，朝着废弃教堂的方向。

房间里所有人都松了一口气。昆提良擦了擦额头的汗，唐璜靠在门框上，双腿一软差点滑坐下去。

瓦莲京娜缓缓卷下袖口，重新盖住手腕上的银饰。

"我母亲……她一定知道些什么。"她低声说，"否则她不会把这个东西留给我。"

"之后再说。"西泽尔的声音平静，"先翻译。"

阿方索点头，重新启动翻译器。可这次他注意到机体底部有一只被漆面盖住的小按钮。佛朗哥教授在按钮旁边用极小的字刻着一行拉丁文："Premere pro occulto"——按下以开启隐藏。

阿方索犹豫了一下。

"老板，我不知道这是什么意思，但……"

"按。"

阿方索按下了那只按钮。

翻译器发出一声沉闷的咔哒响。机体的侧面弹出一只小抽屉，可抽屉没有立刻打开——它上面还有一只小型数字键盘，红灯闪烁。

"需要激活码。"阿方索皱眉。

碧儿忽然抬起头。

"七月二十三。"

所有人看向她。

"那是……那是夫人的生日。"碧儿的声音有些发颤，"七月……七月二十三日。"

阿方索输入数字。

机体的红灯变成绿灯。

小抽屉无声滑开。

抽屉里躺着一本深蓝色的小册子。

册子的封面是锡兰棕榈叶编成，叶脉的纹路在灯光下清晰可见。叶面上用红水银墨水画着一个图案——

倒置的五芒星。

五芒星的中心，嵌着一朵白色莲花。

阿方索的呼吸在喉头卡了一下。

"锡兰星见……"他低声说。

西泽尔伸手拈起那本小册子。册子很轻，叶片干燥而脆，可他拿在手中却仿佛有某种温度透过来——不是来自册子本身，而是来自那朵白莲花图案。

红水银墨水在灯光下闪着幽冷的光泽。

"锡兰星见预言书。"西泽尔低声说。

他翻开封面。

扉页上只有一行字。

红水银写就，鎏金小字，笔画纤细如同发丝，在灯光下泛着幽幽的金色微光——仿佛在等待着某个紫瞳之人来读。

阿方索凑过去，目光落在那行字上，脸上的血色在瞬间褪尽。

"老板……"

西泽尔的目光也停在那一行字上，瞳孔深处那道金红色的纹路开始微微闪烁。

阿方索颤抖着把那几个字念出来，声音像是被什么东西掐住了喉咙——

"紫瞳之子诞生于圣女塔，将继承锡兰星见的意志，打碎枷锁，摧毁世界树。"

房间里静得能听见翻译器齿轮最后的转动声。

窗外管风琴的余韵还在回荡，可那悠远的旋律此刻听来却像是丧钟。

唐璜靠在门框上，喉结滚动了一下，没说出话来。昆提良的手从战斧柄上慢慢松开，又慢慢握紧。瓦莲京娜的目光钉在那行字上，脸色白得像纸。

西泽尔的手指按在那行鎏金小字上，指腹触到红水银墨水的瞬间——

册子上的白莲花图案突然亮起一道极淡的金色微光。

像是有什么东西在册子的深处苏醒了。

而那道光，正沿着西泽尔的指骨向上攀爬。

【English】
Chapter 209 — The Dust-Sealed Prophecy Book (Part I)

The paper tape lay quiet under the desk lamp. The pale-gold of the first five plaintext characters had vanished entirely, as though no hand had ever traced them there.

Alfonso stood at the workbench, both palms braced against the edge, his knuckles bloodless. He was not a man given to fright. In the years he had kept a repair shop in the Florentine slums he had read stranger codes and darker ciphers. But this strip of paper was something else.

The three characters he had managed to salvage still burned in a dull copper-red, their shapes rounded and strange, like the divination-coins of the Eastern markets. He could not actually read them. But the outline of the last one—he had seen that outline before.

Inside a certain old casket, in the deepest part of the Florentine Hall of Heroes.

"Chief." Alfonso dropped his voice. "These three characters are not Minerva's cipher, and they are not in the College of Cardinals' format. They appear in the prayer-texts of the Cult of the Machine."

"I know."

Cesare's voice was very quiet. He did not look at Alfonso. His gaze stayed on the paper tape.

From below, the sound of a light tread began to mount the spiral stair, and stopped outside the door.

Three knocks. Soft.

"Come in."

The door opened a crack, and Bel Danti slipped through sideways.

She wore the dark uniform of a senior lady-in-waiting, her hair pinned with a severe neatness, and both hands cradled an old wooden box. The grain of the wood had gone soft and indistinct with the years; the brass corners had been burnished to a dull shine by long handling—a thing its owner had carried against her body for decades.

"Young master." Bel's voice was low. "There is something I have… long wished to show you."

She glanced at Alfonso, then at the paper strip on the workbench, and her throat moved once.

"This was brought from Crete by the Lady Linlang."

Alfonso's brow furrowed. When the Lady Linlang had been brought under escort from Crete to Florence, she had carried nothing with her—at least, that was what all the records said. A body emptied out by the after-effects of nerve-coupling, a daughter, an infant boy still in swaddling clothes.

Bel set the wooden box on the workbench and lifted the lid.

Inside lay a few leaves of deep brown, their edges curled and brittle, like the dried wings of a butterfly. The surfaces were covered in a dense thicket of writing—brushwork elaborate, layer upon layer, opening outward like the petals of a lotus.

The shapes were identical to those on the paper tape.

"I… I cannot read these characters." Bel's voice dropped still lower. "From Crete to Florence, the Lady carried this box with her always. I only took it from her hands ten years ago. She said nothing. She only told me to keep it safe, and wait for the one who would come to claim it."

She raised her head toward Cesare. Her lips trembled.

"I should have given it to you long ago."

Cesare did not answer at once. He reached out and lifted a single palm-leaf between thumb and forefinger, the pads of his fingers settling against the fine lines of script.

A faint coolness.

Not the coolness of the leaf's surface. It came from the writing itself—as though the strokes had sealed away something very old, and it were peering back at him across three centuries.

"Ceylonese," he said, very softly. "Old Ceylonese."

Alfonso stepped to the bench in a single stride.

"Can you translate it?"

"No."

Alfonso stared for half a second, then caught himself. Cesare could recognize the script, but that did not mean he could read it. Old Ceylonese and the modern Sinhala tongue were two wholly different systems. He would need proper tools.

"There should be an old Minerva translator somewhere in the keep," Alfonso said as he moved. "Canterbury Keep used to serve as Minerva's reserve warehouse. Professor Franco said he had things stored here that he had set aside thirty years ago—"

He did not finish. He was already out the door, his boots thundering down the stair.

Bel remained where she stood, hands knotted together at her waist.

"Young master… did the Lady know what these characters meant?"

Cesare set the palm-leaf back in its box.

"She knew."

He closed the lid. His voice was as level as if he were remarking on the weather.

"She simply did not wish to say."

Below, Alfonso's voice rose to meet Don Juan's, a sharp clatter of metal between them. Bel lowered her gaze to the corner of the workbench, where a tin-sealed casket sat with its cogwheel insignia half-obliterated. The dark-red emblem of the Kabbalah on its lid caught the lamplight with a cool, quiet gleam—she knew that mark.

"Young master… is that casket also the Lady's?"

"No." Cesare said. "That one was left by da Vinci."

Bel asked nothing more. She had always known when to be silent.

…..

Seven minutes later, Alfonso returned carrying a heavy iron case.

The case was old. Its paint was flaking. Its corners were bound in blackened brass. He set it on the workbench with a thump, and threw back the lid.

Inside sat an old-style translator.

The body was brass, the construction complex, like a steam-engine shrunk down to something a man could carry under one arm. Gears, linkages and belt-pulleys were crammed into the narrow space. A feed-chute at the top folded outward. Along one side, a dense grid of letter-keys—Latin, Greek, Arabic, Sanskrit—but no Ceylonese.

And on the front of the housing, dead center, a sigil had been painted in red-mercury lacquer.

A pentagram set in the heart of a cogwheel.

Alfonso's hand stopped in midair.

"The Cult of the Machine's mark," he said, very quietly. "This is a three-hundred-year-old model."

He looked up at Cesare.

"Why would Professor Franco have—"

"He had more than one." Cesare's voice was calm. "Continue."

Alfonso drew a slow breath. From the wooden box he took a single palm-leaf, and with great care fed it into the chute.

The gears began to turn. A low clatter rose from inside the housing. The belt-pulleys whined, and the whole machine shuddered into life—as though some mechanism that had slept for thirty years had been roused at last, and was groaning in every joint.

The translator's needle drifted slowly across the dial, ticking past row after row of symbols.

"Old Ceylonese variant…" Alfonso read off the numbers. "Match percentage… seventy-three percent."

He pressed the translate key.

A strip of yellowed paper slid from the output slot, the translation set in crisp Latin type:

[Inverted pentacle — sacred emblem of the Star-Reader house of Ceylon]
[The Star-Reader heir shall return, to wield the Lost Crown]
[Son of the violet eye, bearing the power of fate]

Alfonso's hand stopped.

He turned to look at Cesare.

"Son of the violet eye." He spoke the words aloud, and his voice had gone dry, as though his throat had been packed with sand.

Cesare's eyes were violet.

A soft knock at the door. Quintilian poked half his head in.

"Chief. Miss Valentina is here."

Behind him, in the corridor, the golden-haired Princess of the Yenisei stood very still. Her white boots struck the floorboards with a faint sound, like footsteps on ice.

"I heard," she said, and walked into the room without waiting for an answer. Her gaze swept across the workbench—the wooden box, the translator, the paper tape. "Let me see it."

She did not wait for anyone's permission. She stepped up to the translator and picked up the printed strip.

Her eyes moved over the text.

The color left her face.

Not the surprise of an unexpected discovery. A stillness that seemed to rise from the bone, as though the words had confirmed some secret suspicion she had carried for years—or torn aside a veil she had never dared to lift.

"Inverted pentacle," she read softly. "Star-Reader heir."

She set the strip down, and slowly rolled back the cuff of her right sleeve.

On the inside of her wrist, a piece of silver no larger than a thumb-tip caught the lamplight. On its face, half a lotus. On its back, a pattern of micro-cogwheels—an outline that matched, in every particular, certain figures on the palm-leaf fragments.

"This was left me by my mother," she said, in an even voice. "She told me it was something the Yenisei royal house had passed down for generations, from before she ever came to the palace."

She raised her eyes. They met Cesare's.

"I never knew what it meant."

The room went very quiet.

The translator was still ticking, the gears turning slowly in the brass housing.

Alfonso reached out and pressed the stop key.

"Miss Valentina." His voice was heavy. "This translator can match Old Ceylonese at seventy-three percent accuracy because it carries a specialized archaic lexicon—and there are no more than three such lexicons in the world."

He pointed at the sigil on the machine's face.

"Why would Professor Franco leave a thing of the Cult of the Machine here?"

No one could answer him.

Then, in the corridor below, the sound of hurrying footsteps.

Don Juan.

He came through the door half-running, his face bloodless, his voice compressed to a hiss.

"Chief—mounted police. The street corner."

Everyone went still.

Quintilian darted to the window and peered through a gap in the curtain. At the end of the street, three riders were walking their horses forward, the hooves striking sharp and clear against the cobblestones. The man at their head wore a deep-blue uniform, a short pistol at his hip, the silver badge of the Florentine mounted police on his chest.

They were riding toward the keep.

"How long?" Cesare asked.

"Five minutes." Quintilian said it low. "No more."

Alfonso was already at the workbench, hands moving with practiced speed. From a hidden compartment in the iron case he drew out a small steam-engine, the shape of an oversized pocket-watch. He wound the spring, and the engine began to hum, deep and low.

"Professor Franco left more than a translator," he said as he worked. "There's also a—"

A thin copper tube sprang from the engine's output, ending in a small flared horn.

Alfonso aimed the tube at the window, and pressed a button on the engine's top.

From the horn came the sound of a distant pipe-organ.

The melody of the Miserere, low and solemn, drifting out of some imagined medieval cathedral, settling slowly across the slanting afternoon like a hand laid on the shoulder of the street.

"The abandoned church across the way." Alfonso's voice was barely a breath. "We play the organ, the riders will think there's a Mass in progress. An abandoned church is a far more interesting thing to inspect than this keep."

The Miserere floated out across the cobblestones and dispersed into the air.

The hoofbeats stopped.

The lead rider looked up at the derelict church, frowned, hesitating—but the solemn Miserere seemed to remind him of some sanctity he ought not to disturb. He raised a hand, and signaled his companions to turn.

The hoofbeats grew quieter, and faded away toward the church.

Everyone in the room exhaled at once. Quintilian wiped the sweat from his brow. Don Juan sagged against the door-frame, his knees nearly giving way beneath him.

Valentina slowly rolled her sleeve back down, and let the silver piece disappear beneath the cuff.

"My mother…" she said, very quietly. "She must have known something. Otherwise she would not have left me this."

"Later," Cesare said, his voice level. "Translate first."

Alfonso nodded, and reached for the restart key. Then he noticed a small button at the base of the housing, hidden under the paint. Beside it, in letters so small they were nearly invisible, Professor Franco had scratched a single line of Latin: Premere pro occulto—press, to reveal what is hidden.

Alfonso hesitated.

"Chief. I don't know what it means, but—"

"Press it."

Alfonso pressed the button.

A muffled clack came from inside the housing. A small drawer sprang out from the side of the translator, but it did not slide all the way open—a miniature keypad was set into its face, and a red light was blinking.

"It wants an activation code." Alfonso frowned.

Bel raised her head.

"July the twenty-third."

Everyone looked at her.

"That is… that is the Lady's birthday." Bel's voice was unsteady. "July. The twenty-third of July."

Alforno punched in the numbers.

The red light turned green.

The small drawer slid open in silence.

Inside lay a booklet bound in deep blue.

The cover was woven from Ceylonese palm-leaf, the veins of the leaves showing clearly under the lamplight. Across it, in red-mercury ink, a pattern had been drawn—

An inverted pentacle.

And at the pentacle's center, a white lotus.

Alfonso's breath caught in his throat.

"The Star-Reader of Ceylon," he said, very softly.

Cesare reached out and lifted the booklet between two fingers. It was light. The leaves were dry and brittle. But in his hand it seemed to carry some kind of warmth; not a warmth from the booklet itself, but from the white-lotus pattern.

The red-mercury ink glimmered with a cool, distant sheen under the lamp, as though something very old were watching from inside it.

"The Ceylon Star-Reader Prophecy Book," Cesare said.

He opened the cover.

On the inner page, a single line of text.

Rendered in red-mercury ink, in fine gilded script, the strokes thin as a hair, and glimmering under the lamplight with a faint gold—as though the words had been waiting there, in the dark, for a violet-eyed reader to come.

Alfonso leaned in. His gaze fell on the line, and the blood drained from his face in a single instant.

"Chief…"

Cesare's gaze rested on the line, and the gold-red thread at the back of his pupil began to pulse, faintly, like a living thing.

Alfonso's voice shook as he read the words aloud, as though something had him by the throat—

"The son of the violet eye shall be born in the Tower of the Holy Maiden. He shall inherit the will of the Star-Reader of Ceylon. He shall break the shackles, and destroy the World Tree."

The room was silent enough to hear the translator's gears turn, one last time, in the brass housing.

Outside, the dying echoes of the Miserere still hung in the air, but the solemn melody now sounded, to every ear, like a slow bell.

Don Juan swallowed, hard, against the door-frame, but no words came. Quintilian's hand loosened on the haft of his axe, then slowly tightened again. Valentina's gaze was nailed to that single line; the blood had gone from her face entirely, leaving her pale as paper.

Cesare's fingertip rested on the gilded script. At the moment his skin touched the red-mercury ink—

The white-lotus pattern on the booklet's cover lit up.

A very faint thread of gold.

As though something at the heart of the booklet had woken.

And the light, beginning at his fingertip, began to climb, slowly, up the bone of his finger.

第210章 尘封的预言书（中）
