【中文】
第212章 觐见教皇的闹剧（上）

清晨六点的翡冷翠还笼在淡薄的雾里，阿方索已经蹲在梵蒂冈对面那家面包店的阁楼窗前，手里捏着新款蜘蛛巢腕表，拇指在旋钮上缓缓转动。窗台上搁着半杯冷掉的咖啡和两块没吃完的烤面包，烤面包的边缘已经发硬了。

"信号稳了。"他压低声音说。

楼下厨房里传来面包师摔面团的闷响，混着远处教堂钟楼敲响的六声钟鸣。西泽尔站在他身后，披着密涅瓦机关核心骑士的制式军服外套，没系领口，露出里面深色衬衫的领口线条。他的脸色很白，眼底有淡青色的痕迹，显然一夜没睡好。

阿方索没有回头："你该眯一会儿。"

"睡不着。"

"那也坐着歇会儿，站了一夜了。"

西泽尔没接话，目光穿过雾蒙蒙的玻璃窗，落在对面梵蒂冈白石城墙的轮廓上。城墙在晨光中泛着冷白的微光，像一头蛰伏的巨兽的脊背。

"叶尼塞特使的礼车什么时候到？"阿方索问。

"七点整。"西泽尔说，"瓦莲京娜会先到教廷递交觐见文书，按流程，教皇会在七点半接见。"

"碧儿姐姐六点三刻从档案员通道进，跟早班交接的人混进去。"

"嗯。"

面包店楼下的门铃响了，碧儿走了进来。她穿着借来的档案员制服，深蓝色的长裙剪裁利落，袖口别着铜质档案员徽章，怀里抱着一个文件夹。她的头发梳得很紧，盘在脑后，露出线条干净的下颌和苍白纤细的脖颈。看上去和梵蒂冈档案室里那些年轻的女性档案员没有任何区别。

"鞋跟暗格里的东西检查过了吗？"西泽尔问。

"检查过了。"碧儿说，"通行证、虹膜贴膜、您给的倒置五芒星坠子，都在。"

"还有这个。"西泽尔从口袋里取出一枚银莲花别针，放在碧儿手心里，"我妈给你的。"

碧儿低头看了一眼别针背面的古锡兰文，手指微微收紧。

"愿莲花指引迷途之人。"她轻声念出那几个字，然后把别针别在自己制服的领口内侧。

"我会在面包店监控梵蒂冈内部的通讯频道。"阿方索说，"如果出了问题，我会通过蜘蛛巢的备用频段给你发信号。三声短促的嗡嗡声是危险，两声长一声短是撤离。"

"记住了。"碧儿说。

她转身要走，西泽尔忽然叫住了她。

"碧儿。"

"在。"

"你不用逞强。"西泽尔的声音很轻，像是在说一件无关紧要的事，"如果实在拿不到，就回来。"

碧儿回过头，微微一笑。那笑容很淡，但眼睛里有种沉静的光。

"您放心。我跟了夫人三年，夫人教会我一件事——翡冷翠的女孩出门，不带点防身的东西不行。"

她推门走了出去，深蓝色的裙摆消失在清晨的雾气里。

---

七点整，教廷广场上响起马蹄声和金属车轮碾过石板路的声响。

三辆酒红色的礼车在晨光中缓缓驶入广场。头车的车头上插着叶尼塞王国的忍冬花国旗，金色的花徽在阳光下闪着柔和的光。中间一辆礼车的车门打开，先跳下来四名穿着银白色甲胄的神怒骑士团随从，金属靴底踩在石板上发出清脆的"咔咔"声，整齐划一。

最后那辆礼车的门打开了。

瓦莲京娜·罗曼诺夫从车里走出来。

她穿着叶尼塞王室的正式礼服——深红色的长裙上绣着银色的忍冬花纹，裙摆拖地约半米，腰间束着镶嵌冰原寒玉的银色腰带。她的金发梳成叶尼塞王室的高髻，发顶戴着那顶小小的冰蓝色王冠。王冠的底座是纯银的，上面镶嵌的冰原寒玉在晨光中散发着冷冽的蓝色微光。

她的脸在阳光下白得近乎透明，冰蓝色的眼睛里没有任何多余的表情，冷峻得仿佛一尊冰雕。

广场上执勤的十字禁卫军士兵们不自觉地让开了一条路。

"叶尼塞特使瓦莲京娜·罗曼诺夫公主殿下，觐见教皇陛下。"一名神怒骑士团的随从用洪亮的声音宣布，声音在广场上空回荡。

教廷正门缓缓打开。

---

广场东侧的花坛后面，一个穿着围裙的年轻花贩正蹲在地上整理竹篮里的玫瑰。他生了一张讨人喜欢的脸，笑容温暖，浅棕色的卷发从歪戴的草帽下漏出来。竹篮里铺着湿布，摆着各色鲜切花，意大利白玫瑰、香石竹、蓝色飞燕草，色彩缤纷。

他抬头看了一眼瓦莲京娜走下礼车的背影，嘴角的弧度微微变了变。

唐璜从围裙口袋里摸出一只巴掌大的杉木盒子，掂了掂重量。盒子里传出"嗡嗡"的振翅声，密集而恼人，是上百只意蜂挤在狭小空间里躁动不安的声音。

"兄弟们，委屈你们了。"他用翡冷翠方言低声咕哝。

他把杉木盒子塞进玫瑰花束最底层，拿一朵开得最盛的白玫瑰盖住了盒盖。然后他站起身，挎着竹篮，不紧不慢地朝教廷正门旁侧的花园走去。

花园里已经聚了不少等候觐见结果的贵妇人，她们穿着五颜六色的丝绸裙，撑着蕾丝阳伞，叽叽喳喳地聊着昨夜的沙龙趣事。

"先生，买枝花送太太吧？"唐璜凑上去，露出最职业的笑容。

---

七点二十分，觐见厅。

觐见厅是一座穹顶高耸的大厅，穹顶上绘着弥赛亚圣教创世纪的壁画，金色的阳光从彩色玻璃窗里射进来，在大理石地面上投下斑斓的光斑。两侧站满了红衣枢机卿，他们穿着猩红色的法衣，胸前挂着白金十字架，面容严肃。

大厅尽头，教皇宝座前的红毯一直延伸到门口。

脚步声响起。

教皇隆·博尔吉亚从侧门走出来。

他穿着纯白的教皇法衣，头上戴着三重冠，面容依然是那张被无数画家描绘过的、充满威严与慈悲的脸。但他的步伐比平时慢了半拍，脚下似乎有些虚浮，猩红色法衣的袖口下，左手不易察觉地按了按胸口。

"叶尼塞特使觐见。"史宾赛厅长站在宝座侧前方，声音清朗。

瓦莲京娜走上前，在教皇面前三步的位置停下，按照叶尼塞王室的礼节行了一个屈膝礼。动作标准，干净利落，裙摆在她膝盖前铺成深红色的扇形。

"叶尼塞沙皇陛下向教皇陛下致以最诚挚的问候。"瓦莲京娜的声音清冷如水，"我奉沙皇陛下之命，前来与教皇陛下商讨两国关系事宜。"

教皇微微颓首，声音沉稳而温和："叶尼塞与教皇国是多年的盟友，公主殿下远道而来辛苦了。"

他伸手示意瓦莲京娜起身。就在他抬手的瞬间，喉头不受控制地滚动了一下。

史宾赛的目光从他的袖口下方掠过。教皇左手的手背上，指节微微泛白，像是在死死攥住什么。

瓦莲京娜起身后，目光平静地扫过两侧的枢机卿们，最后落回教皇脸上。

"教皇陛下，"她说，"我此次前来，除了例行的外交礼节，还有一件重要的事情需要当面与您商议。"

"请讲。"

"我代表叶尼塞沙皇陛下，正式向教皇国提出一项历史遗留问题的交涉。"瓦莲京娜的冰蓝色眼睛直直地看着教皇，"四十年前，锡兰王国覆灭之际，教皇国的十字军从锡兰王宫中掠夺了大量珍贵文物，其中有一件被称为'世界树残枝样本'的圣物，是锡兰国代代守护的神器。"

她的声音不大，但每一个字都清晰地落在觐见厅的穹顶下。

"根据《万国文物归还公约》，教廷应当将掠夺来的他国文物归还其合法所有者。锡兰虽已灭国，但锡兰王室的后裔仍然在世——"

"荒谬！"

一个苍老而尖锐的声音从枢机卿的队列中炸开。

格拉古大主教——枢机会中资历最老的红衣主教，拄着权杖走了出来，脸上的皱纹因为愤怒而扭曲成一团。

"锡兰是异端之国！当年教皇国出兵锡兰，是奉神之命铲除异端！那些从锡兰带回来的圣物是教廷的合法战利品，不存在什么'归还'之说！"格拉古大主教的声音在觐见厅里回荡，"公主殿下，叶尼塞虽然是大国，但也不该为已经灭亡的异端之国说话！"

觐见厅里的空气骤然凝滞。

神怒骑士团的四名随从手不约而同地按上了腰间佩剑的剑柄，发出轻微的金属声响。对面站岗的十字禁卫军士兵们立刻绷紧了身体，手里的长矛微微倾斜了一个角度。

瓦莲京娜的眼睛微微眯起，瞳孔里映着格拉古大主教扭曲的面容。

"格拉古大主教，"她的声音没有任何波动，"您是在说，叶尼塞王国为已经灭亡的异端之国说话？"

"我是在说——"

"我是在问您，"瓦莲京娜打断了他，"叶尼塞王国是西方联盟的核心成员，是教皇国在北方最重要的盟友。但您刚才的话，让我怀疑教皇国对叶尼塞的态度。"

她转向教皇，语气依然平静："教皇陛下，我带着叶尼塞王国的诚意而来，提出的不过是合理的历史遗留问题。如果教廷的态度是这样，那么我恐怕需要向沙皇陛下如实汇报此次觐见的结果。"

教皇没有立刻回答。

他的目光从瓦莲京娜身上移开，扫过格拉古大主教愤怒的脸，再扫过其他枢机卿们各异的表情。沉默了大约五秒。

"格拉古，"教皇的声音很轻，但在大厅里每个人都听得清清楚楚，"退下。"

"教皇陛下！"

"退下。"

格拉古大主教的脸涨成了猪肝色，但在教皇的目光下，他最终还是咬着牙退回了队列中，权杖在地面上重重地顿了一下。

教皇的左手在袖口下又按了按胸口，指节收紧又松开。

瓦莲京娜将这个细微的动作收入眼底，但脸上没有流露任何表情。

"公主殿下，"教皇转向瓦莲京娜，声音重新变得平稳，"您提到的《万国文物归还公约》是六十年前签订的，适用范围有限。锡兰一案的情况比较复杂，我们可以进一步商讨。"

"那么，"瓦莲京娜说，"我是否可以参观教廷的'历史文物展'？我听说那里收藏了从各地收集来的珍贵文物，或许我能在那里找到一些答案。"

教皇的手指在宝座扶手上微微一收。

历史文物展就在核心档案室的隔壁。那里陈列着从各地运回的战利品，锡兰的文物就在其中。

"陛下！"格拉古大主教再次忍不住出声。

"公主殿下的要求并不过分。"史宾赛厅长从一旁走出来，适时地插话，"历史文物展本就对外开放，让公主殿下参观并无不妥。"

教皇看了史恩赛一眼。

史宾赛微微点头。

教皇沉默了三秒，然后缓缓开口："好。"

就在"好"字落地的瞬间，觐见厅侧门外的花园里传来一声尖锐的惊叫。

"啊——！"

紧接着是第二声，第三声，尖叫声像被点燃的引线一样迅速蔓延开来，汇成一片刺耳的混乱。贵妇人们叽叽喳喳的闲聊声瞬间被压下去，取而代之的是拍打声、奔跑声、裙摆刮过花坛的沙沙声，还有某种高频的"嗡嗡"声——像一百只蜂同时振翅。

"什么东西！"一个贵妇人捂着被蜇的手腕尖叫。

花园里，上百只意蜂从一只摔碎的杉木盒子里炸了出来，像一团黑色的旋风席卷了整片花坛。意蜂并不致命，但被蜇一下足以让一个养尊处优的贵妇人大哭大叫。花园里顿时乱作一团，蕾丝阳伞被丢在地上，丝绸裙摆上沾满了花粉和碎叶，十几位贵妇人哭喊着朝觐见厅的大门涌来。

"蜜蜂！花园里有蜜蜂！"

"我的手！我的脸！快叫医生！"

"是哪家的混蛋把蜂箱带进教廷的！"

骚动的声音穿过侧门传进了觐见厅。格拉古大主教的脸色更加难看，权杖在地面上连连顿地，呵斥着让卫兵去查看。

十字禁卫军的几名士兵冲了出去，然后立刻被蜂群逼得退了回来。一个士兵被蜇了脖子，捂着伤处龇牙咧嘴。

瓦莲京娜的嘴角几不可察地动了动，但她的脸上维持着完美的冷峻，仿佛对花园里的骚乱毫不在意。她只是安静地站在那里，等待混乱自行平息。

广场东侧的花坛后面，那个挎着竹篮的花贩已经不见了。空竹篮被随手丢在玫瑰花丛里，里面只剩几片被踩碎的蓝色飞燕草花瓣。

---

七点三十五分。梵蒂冈档案室侧门。

碧儿混在一群刚下夜班的档案员中间，低着头快步走过走廊。走廊里的煤气灯还亮着，昏黄的光线让每个人的面容都模糊不清。她怀里抱着文件夹，深蓝色的制服裙摆在脚踝处轻轻摆动。

觐见厅方向的骚动声隐约传来，走廊里的几个档案员忍不住停下脚步张望。

"花园里怎么了？"一个年纪稍长的档案员皱眉问。

"好像是有蜜蜂。"年轻的档案员说，"听说是有个卖花的混进去了。"

"这种时候还出这种事……"年长的档案员摇了摇头，继续往前走。

碧儿低下头，跟着人流快步走过走廊。所有人都被花园那边的骚动吸引了注意力，没有人注意到队伍里多了一个陌生的面孔。

走廊尽头是一道铁门，门上嵌着三个黄铜圆盘——指纹识别器、通行证扫描仪和虹膜扫描仪。一个档案员刷了证，碧儿紧跟在她身后，在前一个人通过虹膜扫描的间隙里，她从鞋跟暗格里取出了那枚修改过的特别通行证。

通行证的绿灯亮了。

前一个人通过了，碧儿跟上。虹膜扫描仪的红光扫过她的眼睛，贴膜的纹路在这一瞬间与数据库中的记录完全吻合——五秒钟，足够了。

门"咔哒"一声打开。

碧儿走进了档案室。

她的心跳终于在胸腔里猛烈地撞击起来。

走廊深处，核心档案室C区的门就在前方。深灰色的金属门面上没有任何标识，只有一个小小的"VIP"铜牌。门旁边的墙壁上嵌着一台老式的密码锁和一台虹膜扫描仪。

碧儿深吸一口气，从鞋跟暗格里取出特别通行证。通行证在她手心里微微发凉，绿灯亮着，稳定而明亮。

她把通行证贴上扫描仪。

三秒。

五秒。

门锁内部传来一声轻微的"嗒"。

门，缓缓打开了。

---

面包店阁楼里，阿方索的蜘蛛巢腕表忽然亮起一串红色信号灯。

"老板。"他压低声音，眉头拧了起来，"有加密密文正在从梵蒂冈内部发出去。"

西泽尔没有说话。

"方向……"阿方索的手指在腕表的微型键盘上飞速跳动，读取信号源，"是朝着翡冷翠东郊去的。"

原罪机关的行刑地实验场，就在翡冷翠东郊。

"来不及拦截。"阿方索放下手，声音很轻，"密文已经发出去了。"

西泽尔的目光仍然落在窗外。晨雾已经散尽，梵蒂冈白石城墙在阳光下亮得刺眼。

他的表情没有任何变化，只是站在窗前，看着对面那座庞大的白色建筑。

像是看着一头正在苏醒的巨兽。

【English】
Chapter 212 — The Farce of the Audience (I)

Six o'clock in Florence, and the city was still a sketch of itself, drawn in pale chalk. Alfonso crouched at the attic window of the bakery opposite the Vatican wall, his new Spider's Nest watch pinched between thumb and forefinger, turning the dial in slow quarter-rotations. A cup of coffee gone cold sat on the sill beside two halves of a toasted roll whose edges had stiffened into something closer to kindling.

"Signal's steady," he murmured.

Below, the baker was throwing dough against marble with a sound like a man beating a carpet. Six tolls drifted across from the bell tower of the church of San Lorenzo. Standing behind Alfonso, Cesare wore the regulation greatcoat of a Minerva Order core knight over a dark shirt he had not bothered to button at the throat. The skin of his face was the colour of skimmed milk, and a faint bruise of sleeplessness sat beneath his eyes.

"You should have closed your eyes for an hour," Alfonso said, not turning.

"Couldn't."

"Then at least sit. You've been on your feet all night."

Cesare did not answer. He was looking past the dirty pane of glass, across the piazza, at the white wall of the Vatican. In the early light it had a kind of cold phosphorescence, the long spine of some great creature lying low.

"When does the Yenisei embassy arrive?" Alfonso asked.

"Seven sharp. Valentina will present the petition to the Holy See first, and the Pope receives her at half past."

"Beryl goes in at quarter to, through the archivist's corridor, mixed in with the morning shift change."

"Yes."

The bell of the bakery door rang downstairs. Beryl came in.

She wore a borrowed archivist's uniform — a deep blue wool dress cut plain and close, a small brass archivist's badge pinned at the cuff, and a manila folder held against her chest like a shield. Her hair was pulled back so tightly the bones of her face seemed to stand in higher relief — the clean line of the jaw, the white column of her neck. In that dim room she might have been any one of the young women who filed and carried in the Vatican archives.

"You checked the compartment in the heel?" Cesare asked.

"I did." Her voice was low and even. "Pass, iris film, the inverted pentacle pendant you gave me. All there."

"And this."

Cesare reached into his coat and set a small brooch in her open palm. A silver anemone, the petals worked in thin beaten silver, the back engraved in old Ceylonese script.

Beryl looked down at it. The fingers of her other hand closed slowly.

"May the lotus guide the lost," she said, very softly, in the old tongue. Then she pinned it to the inside of her collar, where no one would see.

"I'll hold the Vatican's internal communication lines from here," Alfonso said. "If something goes wrong, I'll signal you on the Spider's Nest reserve band. Three short buzzes for danger, two long and one short for pull-out."

"Understood."

Beryl turned to go. Cesare's voice stopped her at the door.

"Beryl."

"Yes."

"You don't have to be brave about it." His voice was light, as though he were remarking on the weather. "If you can't get it, come back."

Beryl looked over her shoulder. She smiled — a small, quiet thing, the kind that lives mostly in the eyes.

"Don't worry, my lord. I served your mother for three years, and she taught me one thing — a Florence girl never leaves the house without something to defend herself with."

She pushed the door open. The blue hem of her dress went out into the mist and was swallowed by it.

---

Seven o'clock. Hooves and the slow grind of iron-shod wheels on stone.

Three carriages of dark wine-red rolled into the piazza under the morning light. The lead carriage bore the standard of the Kingdom of Yenisei — a golden honeysuckle blazon, soft and slow-shining in the sun. From the middle carriage stepped four attendants of the Order of Divine Wrath in silver-white cuirasses; the click of their metal heels on the flagstones came in perfect time, like a single animal with many feet.

The door of the last carriage opened.

Princess Valentina Romanov descended.

She wore the formal court dress of the Yenisei royal house: a long gown of deep red brocade, silver honeysuckle embroidery running from hem to throat, the skirt trailing half a metre behind her in a dark river of fabric. At her waist, a silver belt set with slabs of glacial jade, the stones so cold-looking they seemed to throw a faint blue light against the cloth. Her hair was dressed in the high Yenisei court knot, and on her brow sat the small ice-blue crown — a base of pure silver, the blue stones set like chips of winter sky.

Her face, in the new sun, was almost translucent. Her eyes were the colour of glacial water, and held no expression a stranger could read. She looked, in that moment, less like a woman than like an ice sculpture of one, in a glass case.

The Cross Guard sentries on duty, without being told to, stepped aside and made a path.

"Her Highness Princess Valentina Romanov, Envoy of the Crown of Yenisei, requesting audience with His Holiness the Pope," one of the Divine Wrath attendants intoned, his voice ringing out across the empty piazza.

The main doors of the Vatican began to open.

---

Behind the eastern parterre, a young flower-seller in a stained apron was crouched over a wicker basket, sorting roses. He had a pleasant face, the sort that inspired confidence; warm brown curls escaped from beneath a straw hat tipped at a careless angle. The basket was lined with damp cloth, the colours of the flowers as bright as a parrot's wing — Italian white roses, carnations, sprigs of blue delphinium.

He glanced up at the back of Valentina's head as she stepped down from the carriage, and the curve of his mouth changed, just a little, into something less like a smile and more like a small private thought.

Don Juan drew from his apron pocket a small cedar box, the size of a prayer book, and weighed it in his hand. From inside the box came a sound: a tight, irritated buzzing, the trapped wing-chorus of a hundred Italian honeybees crushed into a space meant for prayers.

"Patience, brothers," he murmured, in Florentine so colloquial it would have made a schoolmaster wince.

He slid the cedar box into the bottom of the rose basket, under the biggest, most open-faced white rose in the bunch, the bloom's broad petals covering the lid from above. Then he stood, hoisted the basket onto his hip, and walked, unhurried, towards the small garden that flanked the Vatican's main door.

A number of noble ladies were already gathered there, waiting for word of who had been received and who had not. They stood in a soft murmuration of pastel silks and lace parasols, chattering to one another about the salon of the previous evening.

"Sir, a flower for your wife?" Don Juan said, with his most professional smile.

---

7:20. The Hall of Audience.

It was a vaulted hall of great height, the dome painted with the Creation scenes of the Holy Church in the Messianic style. Coloured light came through tall windows and lay on the marble floor in irregular bright patches — gold, red, a startling blue. The two long walls were lined with cardinals in scarlet, pectoral crosses of white gold at their chests, faces arranged in the careful blankness of men who have learned to betray nothing.

The crimson carpet ran from the door of the hall to the foot of the papal throne at the far end.

Footsteps.

Pope Leon Borgia came through the side door.

He wore the white of the papacy, and on his head the three-tiered tiara. His face was the same face that had been painted and re-painted by a hundred artists of the Renaissance — a face of great authority, and a face of great compassion. But his step was half a beat slower than the careful choreography of the occasion, as though the floor were uncertain beneath him. Under the long white sleeve of his left arm, his hand, unseen by the hall, pressed briefly against his chest.

"Her Highness the Yenisei Envoy," announced Director Spencer from his station at the side of the throne, in a voice trained to carry. "Princess Valentina Romanov."

Valentina stepped forward and stopped at the precise distance of three paces from the foot of the throne. She dropped into the court curtsy of the Yenisei house — knees together, head inclined — with the clean, dry precision of a clockwork figure. Her brocaded skirt pooled about her knees in a dark red fan.

"The Tsar of Yenisei sends his most sincere greetings to Your Holiness. I come, by his command, to confer with you on matters touching the relations of our two realms."

The Pope inclined his head, very slightly. His voice was steady, almost warm.

"Yenisei and the Papal States have been allies these many years. The Princess has had a long journey. We are grateful."

He lifted his hand to bid her rise. As the gesture passed his shoulder, his throat moved — a single, involuntary swallow.

Spencer's eyes flicked down. Beneath the white sleeve, on the back of the Pope's left hand, the knuckles had gone the colour of old bone. He was gripping something — or gripping against something — hard.

Valentina rose. Her gaze passed calmly along the row of cardinals to either side, then returned to the Pope's face.

"Your Holiness," she said, "beyond the customary courtesies of an envoy, I have one matter of substance that must be raised with you in person."

"Please."

"I come in the name of the Tsar of Yenisei to lodge a formal petition on a question left over from history." Valentina's glacial eyes held the Pope's without wavering. "Forty years ago, at the fall of the Kingdom of Ceylon, the crusading forces of the Holy See carried off a great quantity of precious objects from the royal palace of Ceylon. Among them was a relic called the Sample of the World Tree's Branch — an object held sacred by the Ceylonese crown from generation to generation."

Her voice was not loud. The vaulted ceiling took each word and laid it, distinct, against the silence.

"Under the Universal Convention on the Return of Cultural Property, the Vatican is bound to return objects of this kind to their rightful owners. Ceylon is fallen, yes, but the bloodline of its royal house is not extinct —"

"Absurd."

The old, sharp voice came down the line of cardinals like a stone dropped into still water.

Archbishop Gracchus — the senior cardinal of the College, white as a parchment, white as a sheet — stepped out from the row, his crosier in his hand. The wrinkles of his face had been rearranged by anger into a single ugly knot.

"Ceylon was a heretic kingdom! When the Holy See marched on Ceylon, it did so under divine warrant to extirpate heresy! The relics we brought back from Ceylon are the lawful spoils of a holy war! There is nothing to be 'returned,' Princess — and the Kingdom of Yenisei, however great, has no business speaking on behalf of a dead heretic state!"

The air in the hall seemed to thicken.

The four Divine Wrath attendants, at the same instant, let their hands drop to the pommels of their swords. The faint rasp of gauntleted fingers on steel sounded very loud in the stillness. Across the hall, the Cross Guards shifted; the angle of their pikes changed by a degree, which was enough.

Valentina's eyes narrowed. The Archbishop's contorted face swam small in the blue of her pupils.

"Archbishop Gracchus," she said, in a voice as level as a sheet of ice, "are you saying that the Kingdom of Yenisei has spoken on behalf of a dead heretic state?"

"I am saying —"

"I am asking you, Archbishop." She did not let him finish. "Yenisei is a core member of the Western Alliance, the Holy See's most important ally in the North. What you have just said makes me wonder, frankly, what the Holy See's present disposition towards Yenisei might be."

She turned back to the Pope, and her voice was the same — perfectly controlled, perfectly cool.

"Your Holiness, I came in good faith, with a reasonable historical petition. If the Holy See's answer is to be that one, then I am afraid I will have to report the outcome of this audience to the Tsar in those very terms."

The Pope did not reply at once.

His eyes went from Valentina's face, to the livid face of Gracchus, along the line of cardinals, catching the small differences in their expressions — the agreement, the discomfort, the careful blankness. He let the silence run for perhaps five seconds.

"Gracchus," he said, in a voice that was soft and that everyone in the hall heard. "Step back."

"Your Holiness —"

"Step back."

Archbishop Gracchus's face went the colour of liver. Under the Pope's gaze he bit down on whatever he had been about to say, swung his crosier once, hard, against the marble, and withdrew to his place in the line.

Under the long white sleeve, the Pope's left hand pressed once more against his chest, and the knuckles tightened and eased.

Valentina saw the movement. She did not let her face change by a hair.

"Your Highness," the Pope said, and his voice had its steadiness back, "the Convention you cite was signed sixty years ago. Its terms are limited. The matter of Ceylon, as you appreciate, is a complicated one. We can discuss it further."

"Then, Your Holiness," Valentina said, "may I be permitted to visit the Vatican's Historical Exhibition? I am told it contains the collection of objects brought back from various campaigns. Perhaps there I will find some of my answers."

The Pope's fingers, on the arm of the throne, drew in a fraction of an inch.

The Historical Exhibition was next door to the central archive. Among the items on display were the Ceylonese pieces.

"Your Holiness —" Gracchus could not help himself; the words came out like a cough.

"The Princess's request is not improper," Director Spencer put in, stepping forward at the right moment, in the right tone. "The Exhibition is open to the public. There is no reason to refuse her the visit."

The Pope looked at Spencer. Spencer inclined his head, the smallest possible inclination.

Three seconds of silence. Then the Pope said, slowly:

"Very well."

The moment the word left his mouth, a sharp cry came in through the open side door of the hall, from the garden.

"Ahh —"

And then a second, and a third, and the screams began to spread along a fuse of its own making, the sounds running together into a single ugly noise. The ladies' chatter in the garden was drowned under it. There was a clatter of dropped things, a clatter of running feet, the soft scrape of silk on box-hedge, and over it all a high, dense, furious buzzing — the sound of a hundred bees in flight at once.

"What —"

An elderly lady in lavender silk was clutching her wrist and weeping. Another had her parasol on the ground and was beating at her own sleeve. A third was running for the hall's side door with both hands over her face.

"Bees! There are bees in the garden!"

"My hand! My face! Fetch a physician!"

"Who on God's earth has brought a beehive into the Vatican!"

The noise came in through the side door and into the hall. Gracchus's face darkened further; he struck the floor with his crosier and shouted for the guards to see to it.

Two Cross Guardsmen ran out. A second later they were running back in again, with a bee each at the collar and an expression of outraged astonishment on their faces. One of them had been stung on the neck and was holding the place with a look of dignified, incredulous suffering.

Valentina's mouth, at one corner, made the smallest possible movement. The cold expression on her face did not change at all. She stood, hands folded, as if none of it concerned her in the slightest, and waited for the disorder to spend itself.

Behind the parterre to the east of the piazza, the flower-seller in the stained apron was no longer there. His wicker basket lay abandoned in the rose bed, and all that was left inside it were a few crushed petals of blue delphinium.

---

7:35. Side door of the Vatican Archive.

Beryl walked in among a small stream of archivists coming off the night shift, eyes down, the manila folder held to her chest. The gas lamps along the corridor were still lit, the yellow light making every face the colour of weak tea, features running into features. The hem of her deep blue dress brushed at her ankles with every step.

The noise of the disturbance in the garden reached them, faint and confused. A few of the archivists slowed.

"What's happening out there?" asked an older one, frowning.

"Something about bees," said a younger. "A flower-seller got in, it seems."

"At a time like this," the older one muttered, and walked on.

Beryl kept her head down, and let the current of bodies carry her with it. No one looked twice at the unfamiliar face in the line.

At the end of the corridor was an iron door with three brass discs set into it: a fingerprint reader, a pass scanner, and an iris scanner. The archivist in front of her put her pass to the brass. In the small window in which the woman's face was being read, Beryl slipped her hand down into the hidden compartment in the heel of her shoe and drew out the forged pass.

The pass light went green. The first archivist stepped through.

Beryl stepped after her. The red light of the iris scanner swept across her own eyes. The thin film of the false iris read, in that half-second, exactly as the database expected a certain pair of eyes to read. Five seconds was enough.

The lock clicked.

Beryl stepped into the archive.

Her heart, which until then had been merely present, now began to strike the inside of her ribs in earnest.

At the far end of the corridor was the door of Archive Section C. A featureless panel of dark grey metal, no marking on it but a small brass plate: VIP. In the wall beside the door, an old-fashioned cipher lock and a single iris scanner.

Beryl took a slow breath. She drew the forged pass out of the heel of her shoe. It lay in her palm, faintly cool, its small green light steady as a held note.

She pressed it to the scanner.

Three seconds. Five seconds.

From inside the lock, a small dry click.

The door began to open.

---

In the attic of the bakery, Alfonso's Spider's Nest watch lit up with a string of red signals.

"Sir," he said, his voice dropping a register. "There's an encrypted cipher leaving the Vatican. Right now."

Cesare said nothing.

"The direction —" Alfonso's fingers were running over the tiny keys of the watch, working out the origin. "It's heading east out of the city. To the eastern edge of Florence."

The execution grounds of the Original Sin Order were on the eastern edge of Florence.

"Can't intercept it," Alfonso said quietly. "It's gone."

Cesare's eyes were still on the window. The morning mist had lifted, and the white wall of the Vatican stood in the new sun, very bright, very still, and very much awake.

He did not move, and he did not speak, and his face, in the light from the window, was the same as it had been all morning — a still, cold thing, the face of a young man watching a great white animal open one eye.
