【中文】
第219章 叹息之墙的潜入（下）

又一声闷响。

铁门被撞得向内弹出一块凸痕，门轴处发出尖锐的金属摩擦声。门缝里漏进来的光闪烁不定——外面的人正在用某种重型器械反复撞击门板，每一次撞击都让整个囚室震颤，灰尘从天花板的裂缝中簌簌落下。

"不是人。"阿方索的耳朵贴近门板，半秒后退回来，脸色铁青，"是斯泰因重机的撞锤。圣堂装甲师从外层直接调了攻城设备过来，这扇门撑不了两分钟。"

"米迦勒故意的。"唐璜咬着牙，"他让我们进来，救到人，门一关——他要在密涅瓦机关里把我们和佛朗哥一起炸成碎片，对外说是西泽尔劫狱时被圣堂装甲师击毙。干净利落。"

西泽尔没有说话。

他蹲在佛朗哥面前，手指已经摸到了脚踝铁链的锁扣。这条铁链比手腕上的更粗，锁芯是三重拨轮——阿方索的工具片伸进去，只拨动了半圈就卡住了。

"三分钟内开不了。"阿方索摇头。

又一声撞击，比前两次更重。门板中央被撞出了一个拳头大的凹陷，铁屑飞溅到西泽尔肩上。紧接着是液压驱动的嘶嘶声——撞锤正在后退蓄力，下一击会比这更狠。

佛朗哥忽然开口了。

"墙壁。"他的声音沙哑，但出人意料地镇定，"西泽尔，后面那面墙。"

所有人转头看向囚室的最后面——那里只有一片灰黑色的岩壁，看上去和叹息之墙其他的原始岩层没有区别。没有任何缝隙，没有任何标记。

"第三块石砖，从地面往上数。"佛朗哥说，他的手腕还在微微颤抖，但目光已经清醒过来了，"用掌根推。"

"教授，"昆提良瞪着那面墙，"这看起来就是实心岩——"

"我修的。"

佛朗哥的声音带着一丝几乎不可察觉的苦笑。

"三十年前，叹息之墙刚刚封顶。我在这里做适配实验，每次从正门走都要经过三重安检，浪费时间。我在主控室隔壁的囚室里偷偷开了一条通风管道，直通外面——那面墙后面是我自己挖的，密涅瓦机关的建造图纸上根本没有这条通道。"

唐璜张了张嘴，硬生生把一句"教授你疯了"咽了回去。

"钥匙是什么？"西泽尔已经站起来，走向那面墙。

"我当年用的是声控锁。密涅瓦的声纹识别技术是我写的，但留了个后门给自己——"佛朗哥咳了一声，喉咙里像有砂纸在刮，"密码是'密涅瓦'。对，六个字。对着第三块石砖说。"

轰！

第三次撞击。门板终于承受不住了，从中央裂开了一条两指宽的缝隙，白色蒸汽从裂口里喷涌进来，带着重机机械臂特有的机油味。透过缝隙可以看到外面影影绰绰的重装机甲剪影——至少三台斯泰因重机。

西泽尔走到那面墙前，手指沿着岩壁表面摸过去，找到了第三块石砖——比旁边的石砖略新一些，边缘有极细的接缝线，肉眼几乎不可见。

他抬起掌根，贴上去，用力一推。

石砖向内滑了三寸，咔哒一声，弹出了一个巴掌大的金属面板。面板上只有一个拾音孔，周围环绕着六枚微型红水银指示灯——全是暗的。

"密码。"西泽尔回头看了佛朗哥一眼。

佛朗哥微微点头。

西泽尔俯身凑近拾音孔，声音压得很低，但每个字都咬得极清楚：

"密涅瓦。"

一秒。两秒。

金属面板上六枚红水银指示灯同时亮了起来，颜色从暗红变成亮金，像六只小小的眼睛。面板中央无声地裂开一条线，整块石砖向内凹陷，露出了一个勉强容一人侧身通过的黑色洞口。冷风从洞口里涌出来，带着地下深处特有的潮湿金属味。

"快。"西泽尔侧身让开洞口。

"佛朗哥教授先走。"阿方索二话不说弯腰背起了佛朗哥。老人比他想象中还轻——被关押了这些天，体重至少掉了二十磅。

阿方索第一个钻进了洞口，佛朗哥伏在他背上，头几乎垂到了他的肩膀。

然后是昆提良——他那条宽阔的肩膀勉强挤过洞口，蹭掉了一层岩壁上的苔藓。唐璜跟在后面，动作灵活得像一条蛇。

塔拉夏在洞口犹豫了半秒，回头看了一眼正在被撞得哐哐作响的铁门，一咬牙也钻了进去。

西泽尔最后一个。

他的手已经搭上了洞口的边缘，身后传来一声比之前所有撞击都更沉重的巨响——不是撞锤的声音，是某种爆炸。铁门在那种力量面前终于屈服了，整块门板从铰链上飞脱，砸在囚室地面上发出震耳欲聋的金属碰撞声。碎裂的铁片飞溅过来，有一片划过了西泽尔的后背，割开了一道浅浅的口子——他甚至没感觉到痛。

白光从炸开的门口涌进来，伴随着沉重的机甲脚步声和枪机拉动的咔咔声。

"——目标在囚室内！全——"

西泽尔侧身钻入了洞口。

他落地的瞬间，掌根拍在洞口内壁的某个凸起上——那是佛朗哥设计的自动关门机关。石砖面板在他身后轰然合拢，把那些枪口、火光和怒吼全部封在了外面。

密道里一片漆黑。

只听到六个人粗重的呼吸声，和远处密涅瓦机关深处传来的闷响——圣堂装甲师冲进囚室后发现人去楼空，正在砸墙。

"走。"西泽尔说。

密道很窄，只够两人并排通过，高度不到一米八——昆提良和唐璜不得不微微弯腰。地面是粗糙的岩石，没有铺设任何轨道或照明设施。佛朗哥当年开凿这条密道显然只是为了自己使用，没有考虑过舒适性。

阿方索启动了蜘蛛巢腕表上的微弱照明功能，腕表表盘弹出一束红色光线，只能照亮前方三米左右的距离。在这束红光中，他们看到了佛朗哥三十年前留下的痕迹——岩壁上每隔五米就有一道浅浅的凿痕，那是标记路程用的。某些凿痕旁边还刻着极小的数字和缩写。

"这是什么？"昆提良指着一处刻痕旁边的符号。

"距离标记。"佛朗哥趴在阿方索背上，声音微弱但清晰，"我当年每天走这条路去主控室……到第三百二十七号标记的时候，管道开始向上倾斜。"

他顿了顿。

"上面是我藏东西的地方。"

果然，密道在第三百二十七号标记处开始上坡。坡度不大，但在这种逼仄的空间里攀爬仍然困难。瓦莲京娜走在前面——她没有跟在密涅瓦机关外等候，而是从备用入口绕进来接应，在密道中途和他们汇合。金属靴底踩在岩石上发出沉稳的笃笃声。

"前面就是了。"佛朗哥说。

坡道尽头是一个稍宽敞的空间——大约三米见方，高度足够站直身体。密道在这里突然变宽了，四面岩壁上钉着铁钩和木架，上面摆满了大大小小的金属箱、卷轴和油布包裹。三十年的灰尘厚厚地积在所有物品表面，但保存状态出奇地好——这条密道深入叹息之墙的岩层内部，温度恒定，湿度极低。

"天哪。"唐璜吹掉一个金属箱表面的灰尘，箱盖上的密涅瓦六翼猫头鹰徽记露了出来，"这是密涅瓦机关的初代零件箱？"

"不止。"阿方索放下佛朗哥，走向最近的一面岩壁。他伸手揭开一块油布，底下是一排整齐码放的金属构件——每个都用防锈纸单独包裹，纸上用佛朗哥的字迹标注着编号和名称。

"红龙改型·左肩关节轴承组。"阿方索念出其中一个标签上的字，手指微微发抖，"这是……这是新型红龙试制版的原型零件。我在生产线上见过它们的量产版，但这些——"他翻过防锈纸查看背面的日期标记，"这些是三年前的设计版本。比我们手上的还要早两代。"

佛朗哥靠在岩壁上，看着阿方索翻动那些零件。

"我每次做完适配实验的零件替换，都会把淘汰下来的旧版藏到这里。"他的声音平静，但眼神里有一丝复杂的情绪，"最初只是为了留作纪念。后来……后来发生的事越来越多，我就明白了——总有一天会需要这些东西。"

西泽尔走到另一面岩壁前。

这里的木架上放着的不只是零件，还有几卷装订整齐的图纸册和金属文件夹。他随手拿起一个文件夹翻开——第一页是红龙改型的骨架应力分析图，图上的笔迹潦草而专注，每一处修改都用红色墨水标注了批注。

他继续翻，翻到第七页时手指停住了。

那一页画的是一个他非常熟悉的结构——新型红龙试制版胸腔与脊椎接驳区的核心组件。一组十二枚的金色微针排列成扇形，插入骑士的脊椎神经节后读取神经信号，实现人机合一。

这是神经接驳系统的核心组件。

西泽尔此前从未见过这个组件的设计图纸——佛朗哥在组装新型红龙时，把这个最关键的部件藏在了自己的记忆里，从不留下任何书面记录。密涅瓦机关的生产线上，制造这一组件的工人全部蒙眼操作，成品立即密封，不允许任何人长时间端详。

但此刻，那组十二枚金色微针的完整设计图就摊在西泽尔面前。每一枚微针的直径、弧度、镀层材质、针尖研磨角度，全部标注得清清楚楚。

"这——"西泽尔翻过一页，后面还有更多的细节图，包括微针与骑士神经末梢接触面的微观结构示意。

"你以前没让我看过这个。"他说。

"因为你以前还没准备好。"佛朗哥靠在岩壁上，闭了闭眼，"神经接驳系统的设计图是密涅瓦机关的最高机密，我只把它存放在两个地方——我的脑子里，和这里。"

他看着西泽尔。

"现在你准备好了。"

西泽尔把文件夹合上，夹在臂下。他又扫了一眼木架上的其他物品——更多的零件箱、几卷机械神教祷文纸册、一台便携式神经电流读出器，以及一个他没有见过的金属圆筒，圆筒表面刻着密涅瓦初代总长徽记。

"都带走。"西泽尔说。

阿方索和昆提良立刻动手。唐璜打开那些金属箱快速分拣——能用的零件装进背包，过大的无法携带的重新封好藏回原处。瓦莲京娜在一旁帮忙，她对机械零件的熟悉程度不亚于阿方索，哪些是关键件、哪些是辅助件，一眼就能分辨。

塔拉夏把几卷图纸和那台神经电流读出器小心翼翼地收进了她随身的防水文件袋。

整个过程不到五分钟。

"走。"西泽尔说。

密道继续向上延伸，比之前的路段更陡。有些地方甚至需要手脚并用攀爬——佛朗哥当年显然没考虑过会有一天需要带着一个昏迷的人通过这里。幸运的是佛朗哥此刻是清醒的，虽然体力极度虚弱，但阿方索背着他爬坡仍然比预想中轻松。

密道的出口在叹息之墙北侧的一处岩壁缝隙中，外面是一片低矮的灌木丛。缝隙太小，灌木的枝叶完全遮蔽了洞口，从外面看只是一个普通的山体褶皱。

西泽尔第一个钻出来。

秋夜的冷风灌进肺里，带着树林特有的腐叶和松针气味。他深深吸了一口气，瞳孔在黑暗中迅速放大，扫视四周——树林，岩石，远处叹息之墙的轮廓在星光下像一头沉睡的巨兽。叹息之墙的方向还能看到零星的光点在移动，那是圣堂装甲师的搜索队正在扩大范围。

"安全。"西泽尔低声说。

阿方索背着佛朗哥钻出来，昆提良和唐璜随后跟上。塔拉夏最后一个出来，她回身把灌木枝条重新拨拢，遮住洞口。

"瓦莲京娜，你留在外面等我们？"昆提良忽然想起来。

"我等了一个半小时。"瓦莲京娜的声音从树影里传来。

他们转头看去——树林边缘的一棵老橡树下，停着一辆酒红色的敞篷礼车。车头插着叶尼塞王国的忍冬花旗帜，在夜风中轻轻摇摆。瓦莲京娜靠在车门旁，双手抱在胸前，金色长发用一根粉色发带束在脑后，白靴踩在落叶上。

她看到西泽尔从灌木丛里钻出来时，紧绷了将近两个小时的肩膀终于松了下来。

"都出来了？"她问。

"都出来了。"西泽尔说。

瓦莲京娜的目光在人群中扫了一遍——西泽尔、阿方索、昆提良、唐璜、塔拉夏，最后停在阿方索背上的佛朗哥身上。她的眉头微微动了一下。

"教授。"她走过去，伸手探了探佛朗哥的额头，"你在里面关了多久？"

"四天。"佛朗哥的声音沙哑得像在磨砂纸，"可能五天。我记不太清了。"

瓦莲京娜的脸色沉了一瞬，但很快恢复了平静。她从腰间的急救包里摸出一管神经接驳缓冲剂——那种深琥珀色的药剂，本来是给甲胄骑士用的，但对极度虚弱的普通老人同样能起到稳定生命体征的作用。

"先注射一管。"她把针管递给阿方索，"颈动脉鞘，两侧各半管。注射后他会头晕三十秒，然后生命体征会稳定下来。"

阿方索照做了。佛朗哥在眩晕中闭上了眼睛，但呼吸明显比刚才平稳了许多。

"上车。"瓦莲京娜打开了礼车的后座，"回坎特伯雷堡。"

西泽尔站在原地没有动。

"怎么了？"瓦莲京娜回头看他。

"先等等。"

西泽尔走回灌木丛前。他蹲下来，把钻出密道时被枝条扯乱的衣服整理好，然后从口袋里摸出那块倒置五芒星圣徽——离开囚室前，他从佛朗哥的铁椅上找到了这个。佛朗哥在被俘时一直攥在手心里，直到被绑得太紧才松脱。

他用袖口擦去圣徽表面的灰尘，紫色的倒五芒星在星光下闪着冷光。

"西泽尔。"佛朗哥在车里叫他。

西泽尔转身走过去。

佛朗哥靠在座椅上，缓冲剂让他的脸色从灰白变成了一种虚弱的淡粉色。他看着西泽尔手里那块圣徽，嘴唇动了动，像是想说什么。

但最终他什么都没说。

"教授？"西泽尔等着。

佛朗哥移开了目光。

"……先回去。"他说，声音比刚才更轻了，"你手上那些图纸，回去再看。有些东西……需要时间来说。"

西泽尔看了他几秒钟，没有追问。

他把圣徽收回口袋，走向礼车副驾驶座。瓦莲京娜已经发动了引擎，蒸汽机的低吼在树林里回荡。

"回坎特伯雷堡。"西泽尔坐进车里，扣上安全带，"所有人都先休整，检查装备。薇若兰还在维苏威火山等我们——但不是今晚。今晚先理清楚手上有什么，明天再走。"

没有人反对。

酒红色礼车在星光下的山路上疾驰，车尾扬起一片落叶。瓦莲京娜开车的风格一如既往地又快又稳，转弯时的侧倾被她控制在一个几乎让人感觉不到的程度。

昆提良在后面打起了盹——今天消耗的体力太多了，即便坐在行驶的车里他也撑不住。唐璜靠在车窗上闭目养神，手里还攥着一把备用的薄刃匕首。阿方索坐在佛朗哥旁边，一只手搭在老人的手腕上监测脉搏，另一只手在翻看从密道里带出来的那台神经电流读出器的使用说明书。

塔拉夏抱着那袋文件，缩在座位角落里。她的伤还没好全，但精神看起来比几个小时前好多了。

"密道里那些零件，"瓦莲京娜一边开车一边问，"够用吗？"

"关键件够。"阿方索头也不抬，"红龙改型的左肩关节轴承组、神经接驳核心微针的设计图——这些是量产线上被替换掉的旧版，但加工精度比新版还高。佛朗哥教授三十年前的手工比现在的流水线强。"

"那台读出器呢？"

"便携式神经电流读出器。"阿方索翻了一页说明书，"能放大微弱神经电信号一万倍——我原本以为这东西只存在于密涅瓦的传说里。它能实时显示骑士的神经接驳状态，精度比密涅瓦机关总控台上的固定式设备还高。"

他顿了顿，语气里多了一丝困惑。

"但这台读出器的出厂编号是B-07-0001。"

"B-07？"瓦莲京娜从后视镜里看了他一眼。

"密涅瓦机关最深层档案库的编号。"阿方索说，"理论上那个档案库里存放的都是初代总长留下的遗物——不应该出现在佛朗哥教授的私人密道里。"

"佛朗哥教授自己就是初代总长的后裔。"西泽尔说。

"……是。"阿方索沉默了几秒，"但他从来没跟我提过B-07档案库的事。"

车里安静了片刻。

礼车驶出山路，汇入通往翡冷翠郊区的公路。坎特伯雷堡的轮廓在前方地平线上隐约可见——深灰色的石墙在星光下像一块沉默的棋盘。

瓦莲京娜把车速降下来。

"还有一件事。"她说，"我从备用入口绕进去接应你们的时候，在密道入口附近看到了一些脚印。"

西泽尔转头看她。

"不是圣堂装甲师的——军靴的纹路不对。也不是我们的——鞋底更窄，像是……"瓦莲京娜皱了下眉，"像是软底布鞋。"

"密涅瓦机关里穿软底鞋的人不多。"阿方索说。

"一个都没有。"瓦莲京娜说。

车里又安静了。

西泽尔没有说话。他把手伸进口袋，指尖碰了碰那块倒置五芒星圣徽冰凉的边缘。

礼车在坎特伯雷堡的铸铁大门前停了下来。

瓦莲京娜熄灭引擎，车灯熄灭，四周陷入黑暗。城堡的窗口没有灯光——碧儿在她们出发前接到通知，让所有仆人提前休息，整座城堡现在是空的。

昆提良第一个跳下车，打着哈欠走向大门。他的手刚搭上门环——

动作停住了。

"老板。"他的声音忽然清醒了，"门口有人。"

所有人同时绷紧了身体。

西泽尔推开车门，无声地走下礼车。秋夜的风把他黑色的头发吹得微微偏斜，紫瞳在星光下收缩成两个极细的点。

他看到了。

坎特伯雷堡的正门台阶上，站着一个人。

那人穿着一件黑色的长袍——不是西方的款式，衣襟交叠在胸前，腰间系着一根素色布带。袍子的剪裁和西方任何裁缝的手艺都不同，每一道衣褶都带着一种异域的、精确的肃穆感。

那是一个东方人。

他大约四十岁上下，面容清瘦，颧骨很高，下颌线条硬朗。黑发束在脑后用一根乌木簪子固定，没有任何多余的装饰。他的眼睛是深褐色的，在黑暗中反射着星光，目光平静地看着西泽尔一行人，像在看一群意料之中的访客。

他的双手交叠在身前。

左手里握着一封信——素白色的信封，封口处用火漆压着一枚印记。信封表面没有写收信人的名字。

右手里握着一样东西。

一块白色莲花形状的圣徽。

花瓣是半透明的乳白色玉石质地，花芯处嵌着一颗极小的暗金色齿轮。整块圣徽比西泽尔那块倒置五芒星圣徽略大一圈，做工精致到几乎不像是人手能完成的。

那个人看着西泽尔。

然后他微微低下头，用一种带着明显东方口音的西方通用语，缓慢而清晰地说：

"西泽尔·博尔吉亚殿下。"

他把手里的信和圣徽同时向前递出半步。

"我奉我主之命，从东方来。"

风从树林方向吹过来，把那人黑色长袍的下摆微微掀起。在长袍内侧的衣襟上，西泽尔看到了一个极小的刺绣图案——

一朵倒置的五芒星，五个角末端各嵌着一枚齿轮。

西泽尔的脚步停在了台阶前三步的位置。

【English】
Chapter 219 — The Wall of Sighs: Infiltration (Part Two)

Another thud. Deeper this time.

The iron door buckled inward at its center, a bulge of dented metal where the plating had been hammered past its yield point. The hinges screamed — a long, ratcheting note that seemed to come from the throat of the door itself. Dust sifted down from the ceiling cracks in fine grey streams.

"Not men," Alfonso said. He had his ear pressed flat to the plate; he pulled back half a second later, the color gone from his face. "A Stein siege ram. The Chapel Armored Division has pulled a war engine off the outer perimeter and aimed it at this door. We've got under two minutes before the whole thing comes off its frame."

"Michael planned it." Don Juan's jaw was set. "He let us in. Let us find Franco. The moment the door shut behind us, he was going to collapse the whole Minerva complex on top of us, dress it up as Cesare dying in a botched rescue. Clean. Nothing for the family to avenge."

Cesare said nothing.

He was crouched in front of Franco, fingers working the ankle chain. The lock was heavier than the wrist manacles — a triple pin-dial, the sort that took a trained locksmith in good light half an hour. Alfonso's picks had managed to nudge the first wheel a quarter turn before the mechanism refused to give.

"Three minutes and we can't open it," Alfonso said.

Another blow. Heavier. The center of the door dimpled inward like a struck drumhead, a fist-sized crater punched through the iron, splinters of hot metal hissing across the cell. A piece caught Cesare on the shoulder. He did not look up.

Then Franco spoke.

"The wall."

His voice was raw, scraped thin by days of thirst, but calm in a way that silenced the rest of them. "Cesare. The back wall."

Every head turned. The rear of the cell was nothing but grey-black stone — the same ancient bedrock as the rest of the Wall of Sighs, featureless, seamless, indistinguishable from the mountain itself.

"Third stone from the floor," Franco said. His wrists were still shaking; his eyes were not. "Push with the heel of your hand."

"Professor," Quintilian began, staring at the rock face, "this is solid granite, I can see the grain —"

"I built it."

There was a shadow of something that might have been a smile. Or a grimace.

"Thirty years ago, when they finished sealing the Wall. I was running adaptation trials in the complex, and every time I came in through the main entrance I had to clear three security checkpoints. A waste of an hour. So I cut a ventilation shaft out of the cell next to the master console — a hidden passage to the surface. The blueprints for Minerva don't show it. There is no record. There never was."

Don Juan opened his mouth. Closed it. The words he'd been about to say — Professor, are you mad — he swallowed back.

"What's the key?" Cesare was already on his feet, moving toward the back wall.

"Voice. I built it on a vocal lock. I wrote Minerva's voiceprint recognition system myself, and I left myself a back door." Franco coughed, the sound like sand dragged across glass. "The pass phrase is six syllables. The name of the system itself. Say it into the third stone."

Boom.

The third impact. The iron at last gave way along its center seam — a fissure two fingers wide cracked open from top to bottom. White steam jetted in, carrying the unmistakable petroleum reek of a hydraulic war engine. Through the gap, shapes: three of them at least, the angular silhouettes of Stein-class siege walkers shifting into firing stance.

Cesare ran his hand across the back wall. His fingers found the seam almost by instinct — a line so fine that you had to know it was there to feel it. The third stone from the floor was fractionally newer than the others. The mortar around it had a different texture.

He set the heel of his palm against the stone and pushed.

It slid inward three inches with a soft click. A panel of dark metal — palm-sized, machined to a mirror finish — emerged from the rock face. At its center was a single small aperture, a microphone the size of a pea. Around it, set into the metal in a perfect ring, six indicator lights of red mercury. All dark.

"The phrase," Cesare said, glancing back.

Franco nodded, once.

Cesare leaned close to the aperture. He pitched his voice low — barely louder than a breath — and spoke each syllable with the precision of a man laying down a charge.

"Minerva."

One second. Two.

The six red-mercury lights came on in unison. The color shifted — dark red bleeding to molten gold, six small eyes opening in the dark. Down the center of the panel a hairline split appeared, and the entire stone block sank into the wall like a sinking coffin lid. A black opening gaped where it had been: a shaft barely wide enough for a man to pass through sideways, exhaling the cold mineral breath of deep stone.

"Move," Cesare said, and stepped aside.

Alfonso did not hesitate. He had the old man on his back in one motion — Franco lighter than expected, hollowed out by days of captivity, a good twenty pounds gone from the body Cesare remembered from the lecture halls. He ducked into the shaft and was swallowed by the dark.

Franco lay across his shoulders, head almost touching his own ear.

Quintilian followed, his wide shoulders scraping the stone on either side, peeling a stripe of lichen from the wall as he squeezed through. Don Juan slipped in after him, sinuous as a snake, his breathing already measured. Tarashya glanced once at the cell door — the iron screaming now, the ram's hydraulic arm drawing back for the final blow — and dropped into the shaft after them.

Cesare was the last.

His hand found the lip of the opening. Behind him came a sound that was not the ram — a deeper concussion, a bloom of heat against his back. The cell door had come off its hinges entirely. The entire plate hit the floor with a sound like a cathedral bell, and iron shrapnel whined across the cell. One piece kissed the back of Cesare's neck as he pulled himself into the shaft; a thin hot line, no more. He did not feel it until later.

White light flooded the cell. Through the gap he was leaving he glimpsed a half-second of the world he was abandoning: the barrel-snouts of three siege walkers pivoting toward him, the flash of muzzle crowns catching light, a voice shouting something broken and official about targets and containment —

His palm hit the hidden catch on the inside of the shaft.

The stone panel slammed shut behind him. The noise of the world — the guns, the shouting, the boots, the searchlights — died as though someone had closed a hand around it.

Darkness. Complete.

Six sets of breath, ragged and close, in a space that smelled of wet rock and old iron. Somewhere far below, muffled by a hundred feet of stone, the Chapel Armored Division had reached the empty cell and was beginning, with great professionalism, to tear the walls apart.

"Walk," Cesare said.

The shaft was narrow. Two abreast at most, and the roof hung low enough that Quintilian and Don Juan had to duck their heads. The floor was unworked stone — Franco's hand thirty years ago had cut only what was necessary, and what was necessary had been a passage for one. There were no tracks, no rails, no lighting. Just the rock.

Alfonso turned on the smallest lamp his Spider Nest wristpiece could manage. A thin red beam lanced out from the dial, throwing a cone of dull light perhaps three meters long. In its wash they could see the marks of the man who had cut this place: a shallow chisel nick every five meters along the wall, some of them annotated in tiny numerals and the cramped shorthand of a working engineer.

"What's that?" Quintilian asked, pointing at a glyph beside one of the marks.

"Distance markers." Franco's voice was thin against Alfonso's shoulder, but distinct. "I walked this route to the master console every day for two years. At the three-hundred-and-twenty-seventh marker, the shaft begins to climb."

A pause.

"Up there is where I keep things."

The shaft tilted. The grade was gentle, but in a space this tight, climbing was climbing. Valentina met them at the bend — she had come in through the secondary access point, waited, and then fallen in at the rear without a word. Her metal-soled boots struck the stone in steady beats, the sound oddly reassuring.

"Almost there," Franco said.

The passage ended at a chamber — three meters on a side, ceiling high enough to stand upright. The shaft opened into a space the old engineer had carved out for himself, with iron pegs driven into the walls and wooden shelves cantilevered from the rock. On the shelves: metal cases of varying sizes, rolls of paper, oilcloth bundles. Thirty years of dust lay over everything, undisturbed, undisturbedable. The temperature in this deep pocket of the Wall of Sighs had not varied by more than a degree since the stone had been cut.

"God above," Don Juan breathed, brushing the dust from a metal case. The lid came up; the six-winged owl of Minerva, cast in brass, gleamed up at them. "These are the first-generation parts crates?"

"And more." Alfonso had set Franco down against the wall and was working his way along the nearest shelf, lifting oilcloth. Underneath, ranked in careful rows, lay component parts wrapped individually in rustproof paper, each bundle tagged in Franco's small, slanting hand.

He read the nearest tag aloud.

"Red Dragon Mark II — left shoulder bearing assembly." His hand was not entirely steady. "These are the prototype components for the new Red Dragon. I've seen the production-line versions — the ones they're fitting to the operational units. But these —" He turned the rustproof paper over. A date in the corner. "These are from three years ago. Two full design generations earlier than what we have in the field."

Franco, leaning against the wall, watched him lift the parts and turn them in the red light.

"When I ran the adaptation trials," he said, "every component I removed from the test articles I brought here. At first it was sentiment. I told myself I was keeping a record. Then the years changed, and I understood — I was keeping a reserve."

Cesare had moved to the opposite wall.

The shelving there was different. Not parts but papers — bound folios in metal clasps, a clutch of leather document tubes, and a portable neural-current reader, the kind that did not officially exist outside the Minerva archives. He drew one of the folios down and opened it.

The first page was a stress-analysis schematic of the Red Dragon's skeleton frame, every modification flagged in red ink, the handwriting the same cramped slant as the tags on the shelves. He turned the page. Turned again.

On the seventh page, his hand stopped.

He knew that geometry. He had lived inside it.

The neural interface core. The set of twelve gold micro-needles, arranged in a fan, designed to seat against a knight's spinal ganglia and read the electrical signature of intent. The heart of the man-machine merger. The component every Red Dragon pilot lived or died by.

Cesare had never seen the engineering drawings for it. Franco had kept that one design out of every file, out of every workshop, out of every conversation. The production-line workers who machined the needles were blindfolded; the finished assemblies were sealed before they cooled. No one had been permitted to study them at length.

Now, spread across the folio in Franco's meticulous hand, was the complete geometry of the device. The diameter of each needle. The arc. The plating alloy. The grind angle of the tip. The microscopic structure of the contact surface where the needle met the nerve.

"There are more," Cesare said, turning pages. "The contact-layer schematics. The full assembly sequence. This is —"

"You weren't ready for it before." Franco's eyes were closed, his breathing shallow. "The neural interface drawings are Minerva's highest classification. I keep them in two places. My memory, and here."

He opened his eyes and looked at Cesare.

"You are ready now."

Cesare closed the folio and tucked it under his arm. He scanned the rest of the shelves — more cases, several rolls of mechanical-ecclesiastical psalters, the neural reader, and a metal cylinder he did not recognize, its surface stamped with the seal of Minerva's first Director-General.

"Take everything," Cesare said.

They worked in silence. Alfonso and Quintilian bore the bulk of the heavier cases; Don Juan sorted the parts with the brisk instinct of a man who had been pricing salvage since he was twelve, separating the portable from the immovable. Valentina moved among them with an engineer's economy, distinguishing critical components from auxiliary ones in a glance, her hands sure.

Tarasya slipped the folios and the neural reader into her waterproof document case and held it against her chest.

Five minutes. They were done.

"Move," Cesare said.

The shaft continued to climb, the grade steeper now. There were stretches where they had to go on hands and knees. Franco had cut this passage for a man in a hurry, not a man carrying a prisoner, and the geometry of his foresight had not accounted for tonight.

But Franco was conscious, and conscious Franco was a man who could be reasoned with about angles, and after a few muttered corrections to their path they were through the worst of it.

The exit was a crack in the northern face of the Wall of Sighs, half-hidden by scrub oak. The opening was narrow enough that the brush had grown across it undisturbed, the way brush grows over a scar. From the outside, the rock face was only a rock face.

Cesare came through first.

Autumn cold. The smell of pine needles and rotting leaves filled his lungs. He breathed it in — once, deeply — and let his pupils widen in the dark. Trees. Stone. The bulk of the Wall of Sighs behind him, its silhouette a sleeping animal against the stars. Out across the tree line, pinpricks of light moved in patterns: the Chapel Armored Division's search teams, fanning out in widening arcs.

"Clear," he said.

Alfonso came through with Franco on his back, then Quintilian, then Don Juan. Tarasya came last, pausing at the mouth of the crack to pull the branches back into place behind her.

"Valentina?" Quintilian said suddenly. "Were you waiting outside?"

"Since before you went in."

They turned.

At the edge of the trees, beneath an old oak, a burgundy open-topped touring car sat in its own pool of shadow. A small flag mounted on the radiator cap — the white honeysuckle blazon of the Yenisei Kingdom — stirred in the night wind. Valentina stood at the driver's door, arms folded across her chest, her pale hair tied back with a pink ribbon, her white boots on a carpet of fallen leaves.

When she saw Cesare step out of the scrub oak, something in her shoulders — something she had been holding for the better part of two hours — let go.

"Everyone out?" she asked.

"Everyone out," Cesare said.

Her gaze ran the lineup. Cesare. Alfonso. Quintilian. Don Juan. Tarasya. Then Franco, still slung over Alfonso's shoulder. A small movement at the corner of her mouth. Not a smile. Something less public.

"Professor." She stepped forward, laid two fingers against Franco's temple. "How long have they had you?"

"Four days. Maybe five." Franco's voice was ground glass. "I stopped keeping count."

For a moment, Valentina's expression did something Cesare had rarely seen it do. Then it was gone, and she was unsnapping the medical pouch at her hip. From it she drew a slim glass ampoule of dark amber fluid — neural-interface buffer, the same compound she would have used to stabilize an armored knight coming out of full combat interface. On a man Franco's age, near death from dehydration and stress, the dose was small, but its effect on the vital signs was immediate.

"Carotid sheath," she told Alfonso. "Half a dose each side. He'll be dizzy for thirty seconds. After that his vitals will hold."

Alfonso administered the injection. Franco's color shifted from grey to a faint, feverish pink. His breathing evened out.

"In the car," Valentina said. "Canterbury Keep."

Cesare did not move.

"What is it?" she asked, turning back.

"A moment."

He walked to the scrub oak. He crouched at the base of the crack where they had come out, working loose the tangle of brambles that Tarasya had pulled across the entrance, and spent a few seconds straightening the threads of his coat where the branches had caught. Then he reached into the inner pocket of his jacket and drew out a small object.

The inverted pentagram.

He had found it on the floor of Franco's cell, beneath the iron chair, where the old man had been gripping it when they bound him — the small purple five-pointed star he had refused to surrender until they had wrenched his fingers open. Cesare had picked it up as he had lifted Franco onto Alfonso's back. Now he held it in the starlight, turned it once in his fingers, and wiped the dust from its surface with the cuff of his sleeve.

"Cesare." Franco's voice, from inside the car.

Cesare went to him.

The buffer was doing its work. Franco's face had settled into something that was not yet rest but was no longer distress. He looked at the pentagram in Cesare's hand. His lips moved. He seemed about to speak.

He did not speak.

"Professor?" Cesare waited.

Franco looked away.

"Go home," he said, very quietly. "Look at those drawings when you are home. Some things need time to be said. Not here."

Cesare studied him for a long moment. He did not press.

He put the pentagram back in his pocket, walked around the front of the car, and climbed into the passenger seat. Valentina already had the engine turning over; the steam plant's low, busy growl spread out under the trees.

"Canterbury Keep," Cesare said, fastening the restraint. "Everyone rest. Equipment checks. Verolan is waiting for us at Vesuvius, but not tonight. Tonight we sort what we have. We leave tomorrow."

No one argued.

The burgundy car cut through the starlit road, the tires hissing on the gravel, the wake of leaves streaming behind them. Valentina drove as she always drove — fast, level, the corners taken with a precision that made the car feel like a held breath. The body leaned into the turns by a degree or two, no more.

In the back, Quintilian had fallen asleep where he sat, the day's labor finally collecting its debt. Don Juan leaned against the doorframe with his eyes closed, a slim spare blade loose in his hand. Alfonso sat beside Franco, one hand on the old man's wrist taking his pulse, the other turning the pages of the neural-current reader's manual.

Tarasya held the document case against her chest and stared out at the passing trees.

"Will the parts be enough?" Valentina asked, eyes on the road.

"For the critical assemblies, yes." Alfonso did not look up. "The left shoulder bearings. The neural interface needle geometry, in the drawings. These were the design generations that were retired from the production line — the newer ones are cheaper to manufacture, but Franco's hand-machined tolerances were tighter than anything the current line produces. Two generations back, but better than what we have now."

"And the reader?"

"Portable neural-current amplifier. Magnification factor of ten thousand. I thought these were a Minerva myth." He turned a page. "Real-time display of a knight's interface state. Resolution higher than the fixed consoles in the master control room."

He paused.

"But the unit's serial number is B-07-0001."

Valentina's eyes flicked to the rearview mirror.

"B-07," she said.

"Deep-archive designation. The vault that is supposed to hold only the relics of the first Director-General." Alfonso's brow was furrowed. "It should not have been in Franco's private shaft. It should not have been anywhere outside the sealed basement under the Minerva complex."

"Franco is a descendant of the first Director-General," Cesare said.

"Yes." Alfonso was quiet for a moment. "He never mentioned the B-07 archive to me. Not once. In twenty years of working beside the man."

The car was quiet for a time.

They came down off the mountain road and joined the highway that wound through the outer Florence countryside. Canterbury Keep's silhouette was already visible against the eastern horizon — dark stone, square towers, a chessboard of walls in the starlight.

Valentina eased off the throttle.

"One more thing." Her voice was level, but Cesare had known her long enough to hear the texture under the levelness. "When I came in through the secondary access to meet you in the shaft, I saw footprints near the entrance."

Cesare turned his head.

"Not the Chapel Armored Division," she said. "Wrong boot pattern. Not ours, either. The prints were narrower. The soles were —" She frowned. "Soft. Cloth, or something like it. Indoor shoes."

"There is no one in the Minerva complex who wears soft-soled shoes," Alfonso said.

"No one I know of," Valentina said.

The car was quiet again. Cesare did not speak. His hand went to his pocket. His fingertips found the cool edge of the inverted pentagram through the fabric.

The car rolled to a stop in front of Canterbury Keep's wrought-iron gate. Valentina killed the engine. The headlights went out. The world went dark. There was no light in any of the Keep's windows — Beryl, at Cesare's instruction before they had left, had dismissed the household for the night. The whole castle was asleep, or pretending to be.

Quintilian yawned, pushed open his door, and stepped out. His hand went to the gate's iron ring.

It stopped.

"Boss." The yawn was gone from his voice. "There's someone at the door."

Every muscle in the car tensed at once.

Cesare opened his door and stepped out without a sound. The autumn wind caught his hair, tugged it sideways. The violet of his eyes, in the starlight, had contracted to two hard points.

He saw the figure.

A man was standing on the top step of the Keep's front entrance, halfway between the gate and the door. He was dressed in a long black robe — not a Western cut. The front of the robe crossed left over right at the breast, the way an Eastern scholar's gown crossed. A plain cloth belt was tied at the waist. The cut of the fabric was unlike anything Cesare had ever seen fitted by a Western tailor: each fold sat where it had been designed to sit, exact, deliberate, the way a stone sits in a wall.

He was an Eastern man. Somewhere north of forty. High cheekbones, a long hard jaw. His black hair was bound at the back of his skull with a single ebony pin. There was nothing decorative about him. Nothing decorative had ever touched him.

His eyes were dark brown. They reflected the starlight in steady points as he looked at Cesare's party. The look of a man regarding a delivery he had been told to expect.

His hands were folded at the front of his robe.

In the left hand, a letter. Plain white envelope, the seal unbroken, the wax stamped with an emblem Cesare could not make out at this distance. The envelope was otherwise unmarked. No name on the front.

In the right hand, a second object.

A holy sigil. White. The shape of a lotus blossom, the petals of a milky semi-translucent stone, a tiny gear of dark gold set at the heart of the flower. The sigil was fractionally larger than Cesare's inverted pentagram, and the craftsmanship was the kind of craftsmanship that makes you look twice because you do not believe the hand that made it.

The man looked at Cesare.

Then, with a small formal inclination of the head, he spoke. His Western Common was accented — heavily, unmistakably, in a way Cesare had not heard spoken aloud since his childhood tutor had left the household.

"Cesare Borgia. Your Highness."

He held the letter and the sigil half a step forward.

"I have come to you from the East, in the name of my lord."

The wind came down off the trees. The hem of the man's black robe lifted a finger's width. Cesare saw, in that brief flash, the inside of the lapel.

Embroidered there. Tiny. A single thread's width across.

An inverted pentagram. With a gear set into each of the five points.

Cesare's feet stopped, three steps from the bottom of the staircase.

【中文】
第220章 大夏的密使（上）

坎特伯雷堡的铁门在西泽尔身后合拢，秋夜的寒意被石灰岩的厚墙隔在外面。

风林被唐璜和阿方索一左一右夹着走进大厅的时候，脚步沉稳得像踩在自己的国土上。他环顾四周，目光在那些烛台和旧壁画上掠过，既不惊慌也不谄媚，只是平静地确认了这是座西方贵族的旧宅，仅此而已。

西泽尔让佛朗哥教授坐在壁炉旁的扶手椅上。教授刚被从密涅瓦机关的囚室里救出来，面色蜡黄，但精神还撑得住。瓦莲京娜把一条毯子搭在他膝上，昆提良去厨房烧水。碧儿站在走廊拐角处，默默注视着大厅里的动静。

风林在西泽尔对面站定。

壁炉的火焰把两人的影子投在石壁上，一长一短。

"我主楚舜华，"风林重新开口，措辞比刚才在门口时更正式，每一个音节都咬得极准，像是在替远在万里之外的人传达旨意，"命我前来拜见西泽尔·博尔吉亚殿下。"

他将手中的素白信封递出。

西泽尔接过信封。

火漆上压着一枚印记，不是西方的鹰也不是博尔吉亚家族的牛，而是两条交缠的龙，龙身鳞片清晰可辨，龙首相对，额间各嵌一颗极小的红水银珠。西泽尔从未见过这种纹章，但那两颗红水银珠在烛光下微微发亮，散发出一种他再熟悉不过的能量波动——和梵蒂冈档案室里那些S级封存文件相同的波动。

他用指甲挑开火漆，抽出信纸。

信纸是特制的桑皮纸，质地坚韧如绢，颜色泛着淡黄。上面写满了密密麻麻的文字，不是拉丁文，不是希腊文，更不是翡冷翠通行的任何一种西方文字。

那些字横平竖直，笔锋内敛，像是某种古老的东方篆体，又不完全相同。字的形状仿佛是被风吹过的竹叶，每一笔都藏着一种奇异的节奏。

西泽尔盯着那些字看了三秒。

然后他的手停住了。

不是因为他看不懂。恰恰相反——那些字在他眼中变得清晰无比，仿佛它们本就是他的母语，仿佛他曾无数次握着毛笔，一笔一画地临摹过这些字形。

"皇兄殿下台鉴——"

他在心里默念着。

不是拉丁文的直译，而是夏国文字本身在他脑海中发声。他看得懂。

他记得。

克里特岛诺丁山初等学校后面有一片小花园，花园的尽头是莉诺雅修女种的橄榄树。夏天的午后，橄榄树投下的阴影刚好能遮住一张石桌。

一个年轻女人坐在石桌旁。她穿着素色的东方长裙，黑发披散在肩上，额间画着一朵白色莲花。她握着一支毛笔，教一个七八岁的男孩写夏国文字。

"横要平，竖要直，"她说，"写字和做人一样，骨架先要正。"

男孩咬着笔杆，额头上全是汗，写出来的字歪歪扭扭。

女人笑了一下，伸手帮他把歪掉的笔画擦掉。她的手指修长而凉，指甲修剪得很整齐，腕上戴着一只银莲花别针。

"不着急，"她说，"等你长大了就写好了。"

那是苏伽罗。

他的母亲教他夏国文字的画面，在西泽尔以为早已遗忘了的某个角落里，此刻像被火焰烘烤的蜡封一样，缓缓融化开来。

他垂着眼看信，手指轻轻按住信纸的边角。

信上写着——

"我乃楚舜华，世人或称我大夏龙雀。今修书一封寄与素未谋面之皇弟，非为攀附血脉之亲，实为共谋天下之大事。"

"三百年前，东西方各持世界树残枝之一。东方持其根，西方持其叶。我楚氏一族代代守护东方之根，兄长一脉则远嫁锡兰，星见血脉辗转流落西方，直至落在你母亲苏伽罗与你的身上。"

"你我皆是星见之子，皆是世界树残枝选定的容器。区别只在于，你是根与叶的完美结合体，而我只是一个被残枝意识碎片记住的半成品。"

"如今楚昭华——我那位坐在龙椅上的弟弟——已暗中联合中山国的叶素理，试图夺回我对北方军团的控制权。他们不知道我们守护的究竟是什么，但他们的贪婪足以让世界树残枝落入不配持有它的人手中。"

"我无意与你争夺什么，但世界树的东西两支残枝必须在同一阵营，否则四分五裂之下，任何一人都将成为它复苏时的祭品。"

"此信抵达之日，恳请殿下容我派遣之人暂留翡冷翠，待殿下权衡利弊后，再议结盟之细节。"

"另：随信附赠我之圣徽一枚，以为信物。若殿下愿意见我，可令来使传话，我必亲赴西方，以龙雀之礼相迎。"

落款是一枚手绘的倒置五芒星，五角末端各嵌一枚齿轮。旁边盖着一方朱红私印，印文是夏国篆字。

西泽尔看完了。

他的面色始终没有变化。

"老板？"唐璜的声音从侧面传来，带着一丝小心翼翼的试探。

"我没事。"西泽尔把信纸折好，放回信封。

风林从长袍内侧取出另一样东西。

那是一块白色莲花形状的圣徽。

花瓣是半透明的乳白色玉石质地，花芯处嵌着一颗极小的暗金色齿轮，整块圣徽比西泽尔那块倒置五芒星圣徽略大一圈。

圣徽表面刻着精细的梵文纹路，但西泽尔第一眼看的不是梵文。他看到的是莲花本身——五片花瓣，花瓣的弧度和锡兰星见家族传统中额间装饰的莲花如出一辙。

他忽然想起了碧儿从梵蒂冈档案室带出来的那张银版照片。

照片里的苏伽罗额间画着一朵白色莲花。

莲花的花瓣数——五片。

和眼前这块圣徽一模一样。

"风林。"西泽尔的声音很平，"这块圣徽的背面——"

风林没有说话。他翻过圣徽。

圣徽背面的右下角刻着一行小字，字体是夏国篆字。西泽尔辨认出那六个字——

"楚舜华·星见之子"。

六个字。

西泽尔盯着这六个字，脑子里嗡嗡地响了一下。

楚舜华是星见之子。

风林开口了，声音依然是那种平静到近乎寡淡的语调："我主楚舜华，先皇楚昭华与末代星见所生之子。星见娘娘难产薨逝后，先皇对外宣称舜华殿下是自己的幼弟，以皇子之礼教养。"

"先皇对舜华殿下的感情极为复杂——一方面他是星见之子，是巫教认定的天命之人；另一方面他又手握北方军团，是大夏军功最盛的将领。"

"如今先皇……"

风林顿了一下。

"先皇近期与中山国叶素理过从甚密，试图以'削减军权'为名夺回北方军团的指挥权。中山国在翡冷翠的使团——尤其是叶素理本人——近期活动频繁，目的不明。"

"我主此番派我前来，"风林的目光落在西泽尔脸上，语速放缓，"是想与殿下结盟，共同守护东西方的世界树残枝。"

大厅里安静了片刻。

昆提良端着热水从厨房走出来，愣了一下，把水杯放在旁边的矮几上，没有出声。碧儿从走廊拐角走近了几步，停在烛光照不到的地方。

佛朗哥教授轻轻咳了一声。

"楚舜华，"教授低声说，"这个名字我在密涅瓦的旧档案里见过。三百年前东西方分裂时，东方那支残枝确实由楚氏家族守护。"

"我一直以为那是传说。"教授看向西泽尔，"没想到它竟然是真的。"

西泽尔没有接话。

他低下头，看着手中那块白色莲花圣徽。

五片花瓣。乳白色玉石。暗金色齿轮。

和他记忆中苏伽罗额间的莲花，他母亲留给他的银莲花别针，锡兰星见家族代代相传的倒置五芒星坠子——所有这些信物，在那朵莲花面前都像是从同一棵树上生长出来的枝叶。

他忽然把圣徽放在了矮几上。

不是放下——是松手。手指没有犹豫，也没有用力。

他转头看向瓦莲京娜。

"瓦莲京娜。"

"在。"瓦莲京娜站在壁炉另一侧，金发被火光照得发亮。

"你的手腕上——"

瓦莲京娜微微一怔。

她抬起右手，缓缓褪下腕上那枚五芒星首饰。

那是她从叶尼塞皇宫带来的家传之物——银质五芒星，五个角末端各嵌着一枚微缩的蓝宝石齿轮。据她母亲说，这枚首饰来自锡兰末代宰相的女儿，世代相传，从未离身。

风林看到那枚五芒星首饰的瞬间，眼神变了。

不是惊讶——是一种意料之外、情理之中的确认。

西泽尔伸手拿起矮几上的白色莲花圣徽，又看向瓦莲京娜手中的五芒星首饰。

"放在一起。"

瓦莲京娜没有迟疑，将五芒星首饰靠近那块白色莲花圣徽。

两件信物相距三寸——

光芒从两件信物之间同时迸发出来。

那不是反射的烛光，也不是红水银的能量波动。

是一道纯白色的、从信物内部透出的光。

白色莲花圣徽上那枚暗金色齿轮开始旋转，五芒星首饰上五枚蓝宝石齿轮同时亮起，两道白光在半空中交织成一片柔和的光幕。光幕中隐约浮现出某种极其复杂的几何纹路——像是树根，又像是星图——但只持续了不到两秒，便如晨雾般消散。

大厅里所有人都怔住了。

唐璜手里的水杯差点打翻。

"这……"昆提良瞪大了眼睛。

白光消失后，两件信物恢复了原本的模样。但西泽尔清楚地看到——白色莲花圣徽花芯处的暗金色齿轮上多了一道极细的白色纹路，瓦莲京娜五芒星首饰的中央也浮现出一枚微小的暗金色莲花印记。

像两枚锁和钥匙的齿痕刚刚咬合过一次。

"锡兰星见与楚氏皇族的信物本就同源，"风林的声音从旁边传来，依旧平静，但语气中多了一丝不易察觉的释然，"它们认出彼此了。"

瓦莲京娜低头看着自己手腕上那枚多出莲花印记的五芒星首饰，沉默了几秒。

"我母亲生前说，"她忽然开口，声音比平时轻，"这枚首饰来自她的外祖母——锡兰末代宰相的女儿。她生前从未告诉过我它的全部来历，只说有一天它会找到它的主人。"

她抬起头看向西泽尔。

"看来它的主人不只是我。"

西泽尔没有回答。

他把白色莲花圣徽握在掌心，感受着玉石传来的微温。

那温度不是火炉的余热，而是圣徽本身散发的——像是有生命的东西在掌心里轻轻呼吸。

"风林，"他再次开口，语气平淡如常，"你刚才说，中山国的叶素理近期在翡冷翠活动频繁。"

"是。"

"你知道他的具体目的吗？"

"不完全清楚。"风林微微摇头，"但根据我主截获的中山国密文，叶素理此行携带了至少三十名经过严格训练的密探，全部以商人或仆从的身份混入翡冷翠各处。他的目标似乎与三个月后举行的万国盛典有关。"

三个月后。万国盛典。

密涅瓦机关与原罪机关联合举办的机动甲胄公开对抗战，将在万国盛典上举行。胜者将成为教皇国未来的主力武装。

叶素理在这个时候潜入翡冷翠，携带三十名密探——

"他在找机动甲胄的技术。"佛朗哥教授低声说，"中山国是东西方之间的缓冲国，他们没有自己的甲胄制造工业，一直靠进口。如果他们能在万国盛典上获取新技术或新装备……"

"中原崛起。"瓦莲京娜接了一句。

风林点了点头："我主的判断也是如此。叶素理此人城府极深，手段老辣，绝非寻常外交大臣。他背后站着的中山国主原诚，野心更是不小。"

"他们不只是要崛起，"风林看着西泽尔，"他们想的是在东西方全面战争爆发时，能够左右逢源，甚至借机一统中原。"

大厅里又安静了一瞬。

壁炉里的木柴发出一声轻响，一颗火星飞出来，落在石板上熄灭了。

西泽尔把白色莲花圣徽收入胸前的内袋里。

"风林，"他说，"你的主上想与我结盟，共同守护世界树的东西两支残枝。"

"是。"

"这个提议很重要。"西泽尔的语速很慢，"我需要考虑。"

他看向佛朗哥教授，又看向瓦莲京娜，再看向唐璜、阿方索、昆提良、碧儿。

"明天给你答复。"

风林微微颔首。

"殿下慎重，是应有之义。"

他行了一个东方式的拱手礼——右手握拳，左手包住右拳，微微前倾。动作标准而自然，像是做过无数次。

"我在翡冷翠东郊的'金莲花'客栈等候殿下的消息。客栈是我主三年前秘密购置的产业，外人不知。"

"殿下若要见我，可让碧儿姑娘持这块圣徽的任意一角前往东郊，客栈掌柜自会通报。"

风林再次拱手。

然后他转身，走向大门。

他的脚步仍然沉稳如故，黑色长袍的下摆在石板上擦过，发出轻微的沙沙声。在跨出门槛之前，他停了一下，没有回头。

"我主让我转告殿下一句话。"

"说。"

"他说——'你我都是被命运选中的人，但被选中不等于被命运控制。西泽尔·博尔吉亚，你母亲苏伽罗当年拒绝成为世界树的祭品，你也一定可以。'"

门合上了。

脚步声沿着石阶向下走去，渐渐远去。

大厅里只剩下壁炉里木柴燃烧的噼啪声。

西泽尔站在原地，左手无意识地按在胸前内袋的位置。白色莲花圣徽的微温透过衣料传到他的掌心。

"老板，"唐璜凑过来，"那个楚舜华——他真的和你一样是星见之子？"

"风林说的应该不假。"阿方索在旁边开口，语气谨慎，"那块圣徽和梵蒂冈档案室里苏伽罗照片上的莲花图案一致，而且刚才和瓦莲京娜公主的五芒星首饰产生了共鸣——这不是能伪造的。"

"两件信物共鸣的时候，"昆提良挠了挠后脑勺，"那道白光是什么？"

"世界树残枝的东西两支之间存在某种深层联系，"佛朗哥教授缓缓说，"三百年前初代总长留下的笔记里提到过类似的现象。锡兰星见家族与东方楚氏皇族的信物同源同根，所以能产生共鸣。"

教授停了一下。

"但这意味着——西泽尔你身上同时流淌着这两支血脉的传承。"

西泽尔没有说话。

他走到壁炉前，蹲下来，用火钳拨了拨快要熄灭的木柴。火星飞溅起来，映亮了他苍白的面孔。

"信上写得很清楚，"他开口，声音被木柴的噼啪声衬得格外平静，"楚舜华是星见之子，被残枝意识碎片记住的半成品。而我是根与叶的完美结合体。"

"他需要我。"

"但我还没想清楚——他为什么需要我。"

瓦莲京娜走到他身边，把那条从佛朗哥教授膝上取下的毯子搭在他肩上。

"先别想了，"她说，"你刚把佛朗哥教授从密涅瓦机关救出来，又开了一整天的车。你需要休息。"

"瓦莲京娜公主说得对。"碧儿从阴影中走出来，手里端着一杯热水，"少爷，您喝点热水暖暖身子，我去准备宵夜。"

西泽尔没有动。

他蹲在壁炉前，看着火焰在木柴上跳动。火光映在他紫色的瞳孔里，明明灭灭。

"妈妈……"他低低地说了一声。

声音很轻，轻到只有他自己能听见。

唐璜想说什么，被阿方索拉住了。

昆提良默默地走到壁炉旁，往里面添了两根新木柴。火焰重新旺起来，温暖的光线照亮了整个大厅。

佛朗哥教授一直在看着西泽尔。

老人的目光在年轻人苍白的面孔上停留了很久。壁炉的光在他脸上投下深深的阴影，让他看起来比实际年龄更老。

等大厅里的气氛稍微缓和了一些，等唐璜去帮碧儿端宵夜、昆提良去检查城堡的防御设施、阿方索守在门口之后，教授才开口。

"西泽尔。"

西泽尔转过头。

佛朗哥教授的手伸进旧袍子的内袋里，摸索了一下，取出一个巴掌大小的黄铜圆筒。圆筒表面刻着精细的齿轮纹路，一端有一个可以拧开的盖子。

"在你去维苏威火山之前，"教授说，"我有一样东西要给你看。"

"是薇若兰临走前留给我的。"

"一段录音。"

西泽尔的目光落在那个黄铜圆筒上。

教授拧开盖子。

从圆筒里传出一个女孩的声音。

声音很轻，带着某种压抑的急切，像是在极短的时间内尽可能多地说出每一句话。

"西泽尔——如果你听到这段话，说明我已经被困在维苏威火山北麓的旧矿洞里了——米迦勒带人追上了我——我逃进了矿道但他紧追不舍——"

"听好——我拿到了达·芬奇的日记——日记最后一页写着一个达·芬奇用尽一生保守的秘密——"

"关于黑铁巨门——关于世界树——关于——"

录音忽然出现了一段刺耳的杂音，像是金属摩擦的声音。

"——西泽尔，你听我说完——摧毁世界树需要——"

又一段杂音。

这一次更长。

然后是最后一句话——

"——不要去——求你不要去——"

"——我会在矿道入口等你——你来了就一起走——"

"——我等你——"

杂音消失了。

圆筒里只剩下细微的电流声。

壁炉里的木柴发出一声爆裂。

西泽尔盯着那个黄铜圆筒，手指无声地扣紧了膝盖上的毯子边角。

【English】
Chapter 220 — The Envoy of the Great Xia (I)

The iron gate of Canterbury Castle closed behind Cesare. The autumn night pressed against the limestone walls and was beaten back, as it had been beaten back for four centuries.

Inside, the great hall smelled of cold stone and woodsmoke. Don Juan and Alfonso brought Fenglin forward between them, one at each shoulder. The envoy walked as if he were crossing a courtyard of his own. He did not look at the vaulted ceiling or the rows of dark portraits. He looked at the floor, the candles, the faded frescoes along the eastern wall. He took the measure of the place the way a man takes the measure of a room he intends to leave again — calmly, and only once.

Cesare had Professor Franco settled in a wing chair by the hearth. The old man was the color of tallow where the firelight did not reach him, but his eyes were steady. Valentina laid a wool blanket across his knees. Quintilian went off toward the kitchens to put water on. Biel stood in the angle of the corridor, half a step back from the light, and watched the room without seeming to.

Fenglin stopped across the flagstones from Cesare. The fire threw their shadows against the far wall — one long, one short.

"My lord Chu Shunhua," Fenglin said, and his voice was different from the voice he had used at the gate. Each syllable was set down like a coin on a counting board. "bids me come before Your Highness Cesare Borgia."

He held out a plain white envelope.

Cesare took it.

The seal was neither the Western eagle nor the Borgia bull. Two dragons were worked into the wax, scaled and unmistakable, jaws meeting, and between their brows sat two beads the size of peppercorns — red mercury, plainly, though the color was deeper than any he had seen. The little beads caught the candle flame and pulsed with a faint rhythm. Cesare knew that rhythm. He had stood among the S-class sealed files in the Vatican archive and felt that pulse through the iron racks.

He broke the seal with his thumbnail and drew out the letter.

The paper was a tough, silken thing, the color of weak tea, and it had been made from the inner bark of some tree he could not name. It was covered in writing. Not Latin. Not Greek. Not any of the Western hands that passed through Florence every day and were copied by clerks and cut into print.

These were the marks of another alphabet. Vertical strokes. Horizontal strokes. Each one squared off and held in, the way a man holds in a breath. They were not unlike the carved seals he had once seen set into a tomb in Crete — the same economy of line, the same sense that someone had decided exactly how much force a written character needed and would permit no more.

Cesare looked at them for three seconds.

Then his hand stopped.

Not because he could not read them. Because he could.

The shapes sorted themselves in his mind the way loose cards sort themselves when a player knows the deck. He had held a brush. He had pressed ink to paper with that same small pressure of the wrist. He knew the order in which the strokes had to come. He knew where the writer's hand had hesitated, and where it had sped up, and where — twice, near the bottom of the page — it had paused to let a drop of ink dry before the next character was laid down beside it.

Imperial Brother —

The words did not translate into his head. They spoke in the language they were written in, and he heard them.

He remembered a garden behind the primary school on Notting Hill, at the western end of Crete. A row of olive trees that Sister Linnoa had planted, and at the end of the row a stone table in the exact shape of the shadow those trees threw in summer.

A young woman had been sitting at the stone table. She had worn a plain gown of an Eastern cut, her black hair loose over her shoulders, and on her forehead she had painted a white lotus. She had held a brush between two fingers, very lightly, and she was teaching a boy of seven or eight to write.

The horizontal stroke must be level, she had said. The vertical stroke must be true. A character is built the way a person is built. The bones must be set first.

The boy had bitten the brush handle. His forehead had been wet with effort. The characters he produced were uneven and embarrassed.

She had laughed, quietly, and reached across to wipe the slanting strokes off with her thumb. Her fingers had been long and cool. Her nails were kept even. On her wrist she wore a silver pin shaped like a closed lotus.

There is no hurry, she had told him. When you are older, you will write well.

That was Sujala.

The image had been sealed somewhere he had believed was sealed forever. Now the fire in the hearth warmed it, and the seal gave, and it rose up into him the way a drowned thing rises to the surface of a still pond.

He stood looking down at the letter, his finger pressed to the corner of the page, and he read.

I am Chu Shunhua. To the world I am also called the Dragon-Sparrow of the Great Xia. I set down these words for an imperial brother I have never met, not to claim the kinship of our blood, but to speak of a matter that concerns the world.

Three hundred years ago the East and the West were each given a bough of the World Tree. The East took its root. The West took its leaf. My house, the house of Chu, has guarded the root in unbroken line. The elder branch, by an older arrangement, was sent to Ceylon in marriage, and the line of Star-Readers moved westward through the generations, until at last it came to rest in your mother, Sujala, and in you.

You and I are both children of the Star-Readers. We are both the chosen vessels of the World Tree's severed bough. The difference is this: you are the perfect joining of root and leaf, and I am the half-made thing the root's shard-consciousness has chosen to remember.

Now Chu Zhaohua — the brother of mine who sits on the dragon throne — has secretly allied himself with Ye Suli of the Zhongshan Kingdom, and is moving to take the Northern Army from my command. They do not know what it is we guard. Their greed is enough, however, to put the bough into hands that have no right to hold it.

I do not want to quarrel with you. But the two halves of the bough, Eastern and Western, must stand in one camp. If they are divided, then any one of us may become the sacrifice the World Tree requires when it wakes.

On the day this letter reaches you, I beg Your Highness to permit my man to remain in Florence until you have weighed the matter, and only then shall we discuss the terms of an alliance.

I send with this letter my own holy sigil, that you may know the words are mine. If you will see me, send word by this man, and I will come to the West in person, and greet you in the manner of the Dragon-Sparrow.

Beneath the closing, an inverted five-pointed star had been drawn by hand, each arm ending in a small gear. A square vermilion seal had been pressed beside it, cut in the same Eastern script as the letter.

Cesare finished reading. The color of his face did not change.

"Chief?" Don Juan's voice came from the side, careful as a foot on a frozen pond.

"I am well." Cesare folded the letter along its old creases and slid it back into the envelope.

Fenglin reached into the inner fold of his robe and brought out a second object.

It was a sigil, the size of a man's palm, in the shape of a lotus flower. The petals were a milky, almost translucent stone. The heart of the flower held a tiny gear of dark gold. The whole piece was a shade larger than Cesare's own inverted-pentagram sigil.

The surface was chased with fine lines of a script Cesare did not at first take in. He was not looking at the script. He was looking at the lotus itself. The five petals. The curve of each one, the way they met at the heart. It was the same curve he had seen painted on the foreheads of the Star-Reader women in Ceylon, in the only photograph of his mother that the Vatican had ever permitted out of its archive.

Biel had taken that photograph from the archive. Cesare remembered it now in perfect clarity. Sujala stood on a balcony of pale stone, dressed for some ceremony, her black hair drawn up. On her forehead a white lotus had been painted. Five petals.

Five.

He looked at the sigil. He looked at the shape in his mind.

"Fenglin," he said, evenly. "The back of this sigil —"

Fenglin said nothing. He turned the sigil over.

In the lower right corner of the reverse, six small characters had been engraved, in the seal-script of the Great Xia. Cesare did not need to study them. He knew them as he knew his own name.

Chu Shunhua, Son of the Star-Reader.

Six characters. The inside of his head made a sound like a struck bell.

Chu Shunhua was a Son of the Star-Reader.

Fenglin spoke, in that flat, almost colorless voice of his. "My lord Chu Shunhua is the son of the late Emperor Chu Zhaohua and the last of the Star-Reader women. The Star-Reader mother died of the birth. The late Emperor told the court that Shunhua was his younger brother, and raised him as a prince of the blood."

"The late Emperor's feelings toward the boy were not simple. On one hand he was a Son of the Star-Reader, marked by the shaman-priests as a child of heaven. On the other he commanded the Northern Army, and was the most successful general in the Xia."

"Now the late Emperor —" Fenglin paused, almost imperceptibly. " — has been spending a great deal of time in the company of Ye Suli of the Zhongshan Kingdom, and is moving, under the pretext of trimming the army's strength, to strip Shunhua of his command. The Zhongshan embassy in Florence — Ye Suli himself, in particular — has been unusually active of late. Their purpose is not yet clear to us."

"My lord sent me here," Fenglin said, slowing his words, and let his eyes rest on Cesare, "to ask for an alliance. To guard, together, the two halves of the World Tree."

The hall was quiet for a moment.

Quintilian came out of the kitchen with a pot of hot water, saw the room, and put the pot down on the side table without a word. Biel took two more steps forward from the shadows, and stopped where the candlelight could not quite find her.

Professor Franco cleared his throat, softly.

"Chu Shunhua," he said. "I have seen that name in the old files of the Minerva Bureau. Three hundred years ago, when the bough of the World Tree was divided between East and West, the Eastern half was indeed entrusted to the house of Chu."

He looked at Cesare. "I had always taken it for legend."

Cesare did not answer.

He was looking down at the lotus sigil in his hand. Five petals. Milky stone. A dark-gold gear at the heart.

It was the same curve as the lotus painted on Sujala's forehead. The same as the silver pin she had worn on her wrist when she taught a small boy to write at a stone table in Crete. The same as the inverted-pentagram pendant the women of the Star-Reader line in Ceylon had passed down from mother to daughter for generations. All of those tokens, in the presence of this one, looked the way leaves look at the foot of a tree.

He set the sigil down on the side table. He did not place it. He let it go. His fingers did not linger, and they did not hesitate.

"Valentina."

"Yes." Valentina stood on the other side of the hearth. The fire had turned her hair the color of beaten copper.

"Your wrist."

Valentina stilled.

She raised her right arm. Slowly, she unfastened the pentagram she had been wearing there since she was a child. A five-pointed star of silver, with a micro-gear of sapphire set into each of its arms. A piece that had come out of the Yenisay Palace with her. A piece her mother had told her came from the last chancellor's daughter of Ceylon, and had been passed from mother to daughter for as long as anyone remembered. A piece that had never left the arm on which it was clasped.

Fenglin's face changed, the moment he saw it. Not to surprise. To a kind of recognition that had been waiting to be confirmed.

Cesare picked the lotus sigil up from the table. He looked at the pentagram in Valentina's hand.

"Set them beside each other," he said.

Valentina did not hesitate. She brought the two pieces together, slowly, until they were three inches apart.

Light came out of the gap between them.

Not the candle's light. Not the red-mercury pulse. A clean, white light, thrown from inside the two objects, as if a small sun had been lit between the lotus and the star.

The dark-gold gear at the heart of the lotus began to turn. The five sapphire gears at the arms of the pentagram brightened, all at once. Two beams of white light wove together in the air above the table, and for a moment a pattern appeared there — a pattern that was at once the branching of roots and the lines of some star-chart, intricate past the point of following. It hung in the air for less than two seconds. Then it was gone, the way mist is gone when a door is opened in a warm room.

The hall stood still.

Don Juan's cup tilted in his hand. He caught it by instinct and a great deal of luck.

"Christ," Quintilian said, very quietly, to no one in particular.

The two sigils lay where they had been set down. The lotus was unchanged, except that the dark-gold gear at its heart now carried a single, very fine white line that had not been there before. The pentagram, too, was unchanged, except that at its center, between the five sapphire gears, a tiny mark had appeared — a dark-gold lotus, no bigger than a pin's head.

The mark of a key that has been fitted once into its lock.

"The sigils of the Ceylon Star-Readers and the Chu emperors are of the same root," Fenglin said, from the side of the room. His voice was still level, but the levelness had shifted; there was something in it now that Cesare, listening, could not have called relief, but could have called the first breath after a long dive. "They have known each other."

Valentina looked at the new mark on her pentagram for several seconds.

"My mother told me, before she died," she said, "that the piece had come down to her from her grandmother, the chancellor's daughter. She said she had never been told the whole of its history. She said only that one day it would find its master."

She looked up at Cesare.

"It seems its master is not only me."

Cesare did not answer her. He held the lotus sigil in the flat of his hand. The stone was warm. Not with the warmth of the room. With a warmth of its own, a faint and even heat, the way a sleeping animal is warm.

"Fenglin," he said, after a while. "You said Ye Suli of the Zhongshan Kingdom has been active in Florence of late."

"Yes."

"Do you know what he is here for?"

"Not in full." Fenglin shook his head, by a fraction. "But from dispatches my lord has intercepted, Ye Suli has brought at least thirty trained agents into the city. They are traveling as merchants and as household staff. The object of his attention, as far as we can determine, is the Pan-Grand Tournament three months from now."

Three months. The Pan-Grand Tournament.

The joint exhibition of the Mobile Armors, hosted by the Minerva Bureau and the Bureau of Original Sin, to be held in Florence during the Universal Festival. The victor would become the principal armored force of the Papal States for the next generation.

Thirty trained agents in the city, at such a time.

"He is here for the Armor technology," Franco said, from his chair. "The Zhongshan Kingdom sits between East and West, and has no industry of its own for the building of Mobile Armors. It buys what it uses. If Ye Suli can carry new schematics or new units out of the tournament —"

"A rising power," Valentina said.

Fenglin inclined his head. "My lord thinks the same. Ye Suli is not a common sort of diplomat. He is old, and he is patient, and his methods are not the methods of amateurs. The king he serves, Yuan Cheng, has an ambition to match his patience."

"It is not only a rising power they want," Fenglin said, looking at Cesare. "It is the position of the kingdom that decides who wins the next war between East and West. They mean to be that position."

The hall was quiet for another beat. A log shifted in the hearth and a single spark walked out of the fire and died on the stone.

Cesare slipped the lotus sigil into the inner pocket of his coat.

"Fenglin. Your lord wants an alliance with me, to guard the two halves of the World Tree."

"Yes."

"The proposal is not a small one. I will need to think on it."

He looked once at Franco, once at Valentina, once at Don Juan, Alfonso, Quintilian, and Biel.

"You will have my answer tomorrow."

Fenglin bowed his head, a fraction of an inch.

"A prudent lord is what my lord hoped for."

He brought his right fist up into the hollow of his left hand and inclined his body forward in the formal salute of the Great Xia. The motion was so practiced that it had no thought in it. It had been done a thousand times.

"I will wait at the Golden Lotus inn on the eastern edge of Florence. It is an establishment my lord acquired three years ago, in secret. It is not known to the city."

"If Your Highness wishes to speak with me, send Miss Biel with any corner of the sigil. The innkeeper will know what to do."

Fenglin bowed again.

He turned and walked toward the door. The hem of his black robe made a small dry sound against the stone, the sound a leaf makes when it is dragged over a paved path. At the threshold he paused. He did not look back.

"My lord asked me to give Your Highness one more thing."

"Speak."

"He said: we are both of us chosen, Cesare Borgia, but to be chosen is not the same as to be controlled. Sujala, your mother, refused to be the World Tree's sacrifice. You will be able to refuse it too."

The door closed.

The footsteps went down the stone stair, and were lost.

The hall was left with the fire, and the breathing of the people in it.

Cesare stood where he was, his left hand resting, without his noticing it, against the place in his coat where the sigil lay. Through the cloth he could feel its faint pulse against his ribs.

"Chief," Don Juan said, and came a step closer. "This Chu Shunhua. He's really one of the Star-Reader's children, like you?"

"What Fenglin said rings true," Alfonso said, from the door. His voice was measured. "The sigil matches the lotus on Sujala's photograph in the Vatican archive, and the resonance with the princess's pentagram could not be forged. I have seen forgeries of red mercury, and I know what they look like. This was not one of them."

"What was that light, when the two pieces touched?" Quintilian asked. He had given up trying to look as if he had understood.

"The two halves of the severed bough have some deep correspondence between them," Franco said, slowly. "The first Grand Master of the Bureau left notes in which he described a phenomenon of that kind. The sigils of the Ceylon Star-Reader line and the Chu imperial line are of one root, and they have recognized one another."

The old man stopped.

"It also means," he said, "that the two lines run in you together, Cesare. Root and leaf, in the same blood."

Cesare did not answer.

He walked to the hearth. He crouched. He took the iron poker and pushed at a log that was nearly burned through. Sparks went up into the chimney and were gone.

"The letter is clear," he said. His voice was held in by the sound of the fire. "Chu Shunhua is a Son of the Star-Reader, a half-made thing the shard-consciousness of the root remembers. I am the perfect joining of root and leaf."

"He needs me."

"I have not yet understood why he needs me."

Valentina came and stood beside him. She took the blanket that had been across Franco's knees and set it on Cesare's shoulders.

"Stop thinking for the moment," she said. "You have just pulled the professor out of the Minerva Bureau, and you have been driving since dawn. You need to rest."

"Her Highness is right," Biel said. She had come out of the shadow of the corridor, and was holding a cup of warm water. "Drink something. I will see to a small supper."

Cesare did not move.

He stayed at the hearth, watching the way the fire moved along the wood. The flames wrote shapes on his face and unwrote them, and wrote them again.

"Mother," he said.

It was a small sound. It was meant for no one but himself.

Don Juan opened his mouth. Alfonso put a hand on his arm. Quintilian crossed the room quietly and put two fresh logs on the fire. The flames came up again, and threw the room into a warmer light.

Franco had been watching him. The old man's eyes had not left the younger man's face, from the moment the letter had been broken open. The light of the fire put deep shadows in the hollows of his cheeks, and made him look older than his years.

When the room had emptied a little, when Don Juan had gone to help Biel, Quintilian to check the gate, and Alfonso to his post by the door, the professor spoke.

"Cesare."

Cesare turned his head.

The old man reached into the inner pocket of his coat. He drew out a brass cylinder the length of his palm, chased with the lines of small gears, with a screw-cap at one end.

"Before you go to Vesuvius," the professor said, "there is something I must let you hear."

"It is a recording."

"Violan left it with me, before she went."

Cesare looked at the brass cylinder.

The professor unscrewed the cap.

Out of it came a girl's voice, low, urgent, the words being set down in a hurry the way a woman sets down a basket of eggs when the floor is not steady.

"Cesare — if you are hearing this, then I am cornered in the old mine tunnels on the north slope of Vesuvius — Michael caught up with me — I got into the workings but he is right behind me —"

"Listen. I have the da Vinci journal. The last page of it. There is a thing in it that Leonardo kept to himself his whole life —"

"A thing about the Black Iron Gate — about the World Tree — about —"

A harsh noise, like metal dragged across metal, ate the middle of the sentence.

"— Cesare, listen to me — to destroy the World Tree you have to —"

Another scrape of metal, longer this time.

And then, the last line, almost whispered, as if the breath for it had to be stolen from somewhere.

"— don't come — please don't come —"

"— I will wait for you at the entrance to the workings — come and we will go together —"

"— I will wait for you —"

The voice was gone. What was left in the brass cylinder was only the small, even hiss of a current passing through a coil.

A log broke in the hearth with a sharp sound.

Cesare sat looking at the cylinder. His fingers had closed, without his noticing, around the edge of the blanket on his shoulder, and were holding it the way a man holds the rail of a ship in a rough sea.

第221章 大夏的密使（下）
