【中文】
第221章 大夏的密使（下）

佛朗哥教授把黄铜圆筒拧紧了盖子，重新塞回袍子的内袋里。

壁炉里的木柴又爆了一声，火星溅落在铁栅栏上，噼啪作响。壁炉光照着坎特伯雷堡大厅里几个人的脸，每一张都沉默着。

"她说完了？"唐璜问，声音难得没有开玩笑的意思。

"说完了。"佛朗哥教授说，"就这些。"

唐璜看着那个黄铜圆筒被教授塞回内袋的动作，嘴唇动了一下，但最终没有说话。昆提良抱着胳膊站在门边，他的目光从教授身上移到西泽尔身上，又移开。阿方索靠在窗台边，机械手指无意识地敲着膝盖，发出极轻微的嗒嗒声。

西泽尔没动。

他的手指还扣在膝盖上毯子的边角，那个动作和录音开始前一模一样。毯子的边角已经被他捏出了一道深深的褶皱。

他听见了。

那段杂音。

杂音出现在两个地方——"摧毁世界树需要"之后，以及"不要去"之前。薇若兰在极短的时间内尽可能多地说话，声音被压得很低很急，但杂音并不是外部环境造成的，那是铜质圆筒磁头转动时人为制造出来的噪音。有人——薇若兰自己——用手指按住了磁头。

她在删东西。

她删掉了什么？

"教授。"西泽尔说，"这个录音器，能倒回去重听吗？"

佛朗哥教授看了他一眼。老人浑浊的眼球里有什么东西闪了一下，但很快沉了下去。

"不能。"教授说，"铜质圆筒的磁带只够录这么长，她录完之后就已经没有余量了。而且这枚圆筒是一次性的，磁头不可逆。"

"杂音呢？"西泽尔问，"最后那段杂音。"

佛朗哥教授沉默了一瞬。

"杂音就是杂音。"教授说，"铜质磁头老化，录制时手指碰到了表面。"

西泽尔点了点头，没有再问。

他记在心里了。

壁炉光在他苍白的面孔上投下一层暖色，但他的眼神依旧冷得像是刀刃。佛朗哥教授说得对，铜质磁头老化、手指碰到表面，都会产生杂音。但薇若兰是密涅瓦机关的副总长，她经手过的精密仪器比这间大厅里所有人加起来都多。她不会犯这种低级的错误。

她删掉了什么内容，而那个内容比她说出来的更重要。

"再放一遍。"西泽尔说。

佛朗哥教授没有犹豫，重新取出黄铜圆筒，拧开盖子。

薇若兰的声音再次从铜管里传出来，焦急的、被压抑的，像是溺水的人在拼命伸手。

"西泽尔——如果你听到这段话，说明我已经被困在维苏威火山北麓的旧矿洞里了——米迦勒带人追上了我——我逃进了矿道但他紧追不舍——"

"听好——我拿到了达·芬奇的日记——日记最后一页写着一个达·芬奇用尽一生保守的秘密——"

"关于黑铁巨门——关于世界树——关于——"

杂音。

西泽尔的目光落在那个黄铜圆筒上，手指无声地微微收紧。

"——西泽尔，你听我说完——摧毁世界树需要——"

第二段杂音。

"——不要去——求你不要去——"

"——我会在矿道入口等你——你来了就一起走——"

"——我等你——"

电流声消失。

大厅里安静了几秒。

"重来。"西泽尔说，"从'日记最后一页'开始。"

佛朗哥教授照做了。

这一次所有人都听清了。

薇若兰说：日记里写着，原罪机关主人是初代教皇的后裔，他想要重启机械神国。他需要两样东西——一个完美适配者作为载体，以及东西方的世界树残枝和主根节点作为能量源。两者缺一不可。

她还说：唯一能阻止原罪机关主人的方法，就是让完美适配者结合东西方星见的意志，摧毁所有世界树残枝和主根节点，斩草除根。

"就这些？"昆提良皱着眉问。

"就这些。"佛朗哥教授说。

唐璜忽然开口："她说'摧毁世界树需要'，然后杂音就来了。后面那句没说完。"

大厅里又一次安静了。

"也许是信号干扰。"阿方索说。

"也许是磁头老化。"唐璜瞥了西泽尔一眼，语气里带着某种试探。

"也许是薇若兰删掉了什么。"昆提良闷声说。

没有人接话。壁炉里的木柴塌下去一块，火星飞溅。

西泽尔没有讨论这个话题。

"整理一下。"他开口了，声音平静得仿佛在念一份采购清单，"原罪机关的主人——米迦勒，或者他背后真正的操控者——是初代教皇的后裔，目的是重启机械神国。要做到这一点，他需要一个完美适配者，以及东西方世界树残枝和主根节点。我们现在知道了楚舜华是东方星见的守护者，手里握着世界树残枝东方主根节点。"

"所以原罪机关想要的"载体"，"瓦莲京娜的声音从大厅另一侧传来，她一直靠在书架边听，没有插话，"必须同时连接东西方的节点。"

"楚舜华的信使风林也说过，"西泽尔说，"他称我为'东西方世界树残枝血脉的完美结合体'。"

"也就是说——"唐璜的眼睛微微眯起来。

"原罪机关主人想要的载体，"佛朗哥教授缓慢地说，"很可能就是西泽尔本人。"

这句话落下来的时候，大厅里没有任何人说话。

壁炉光照着每个人的脸。瓦莲京娜的嘴唇微微抿紧，碧儿端着一盘宵夜从侧门走进来，停在门框边，脸色发白。昆提良下意识地往前走了一步，挡在西泽尔身前，然后意识到自己做了什么，又退回去。

"那薇若兰说的唯一阻止方法，"阿方索从窗台边直起身，机械手指停止了敲击，"就是让西泽尔——让完美适配者——去摧毁所有世界树残枝和主根节点。"

"对。"西泽尔说。

"那他要怎么做？"唐璜问。

"她没说。"西泽尔回答。

这是今天第二次有人注意到薇若兰没说完那句话。唐璜张了张嘴，最终还是没有追问。

西泽尔的目光在众人脸上掠过。

"现在讨论另一件事。"他说，"和楚舜华结盟。"

没有人反对先讨论正事。跟随西泽尔这么久，他们早就习惯了他处理问题的顺序——先把生死攸关的问题搁在心里，再处理眼前必须做的选择。

"风林是楚舜华的密使，"西泽尔说，"他带来楚舜华的亲笔信、白色莲花圣徽，并且当着我们所有人的面展示了楚舜华也是星见之子。风林说楚氏家族世代守护世界树残枝东方主根节点，而我的母亲苏伽罗是楚氏一族远嫁锡兰的星见后裔。他请求结盟。"

"看起来很合理。"阿方索说。

"看起来。"西泽尔重复了这两个字。

他低头看着自己手掌。苍白的手掌，骨节分明，后颈的黄金套管隐隐发出温热。他想起了风林站在坎特伯雷堡正门口的样子——黑色长袍，衣领绣着倒置五芒星，手里捧着那枚和碧儿从档案室带出来的圣徽一模一样的白色莲花圣徽。

风林说，楚舜华在翡冷翠东郊金莲花客栈等他答复。

"老板。"昆提良开口了，他叫西泽尔的方式还是当年在炽天骑士团训练营里的叫法，"我不懂政治，我只知道一件事——我们现在四面受敌。枢机会要逮捕你，圣堂装甲师堵在密涅瓦机关门口，原罪机关的米迦勒追着薇若兰跑，东方又有夏国大军压境。我们手里有什么？五台试制甲胄，六个随时可能死的人。"

"六台。"唐璜说，"把所罗门王、奥古斯都、蔷薇之鬼都算上，是六台。"

"六台。"昆提良点头，"和整个世界为敌。"

他看了西泽尔一眼。

"如果楚舜华真的和我们站在一起，至少东方那条战线不用我们同时去扛。他有北方军团，有鬼武者甲胄，有夔龙马骑兵。我们有密涅瓦机关的技术，有炽天使甲胄。互相补位，活下来的概率大得多。"

"而且，"唐璜接过话头，"如果原罪机关主人需要的载体必须同时连接东西方节点，那楚舜华和老板就是同一条绳上的蚂蚱。他保老板，等于保他自己。"

"结盟对双方都有利，"阿方索平静地说，"利益一致，关系才稳。"

佛朗哥教授没有说话。

老人从旧袍子的内袋里摸出一根烟斗，又摸了摸口袋，发现没有烟丝。他把空烟斗叼在嘴角，沉默了很久才开口：

"西泽尔，你信他？"

西泽尔没有立刻回答。

壁炉里的火势小了，光线暗下来一些。远处隐约传来翡冷翠城午夜钟声，沉闷而悠长。

"我不信他。"西泽尔说，"但我信利益。"

他转向瓦莲京娜。

瓦莲京娜一直靠在书架边，双手交叉抱在胸前，金色长发垂落在肩头。她是叶尼塞公主，神怒骑士团副团长，十五岁就能穿机动甲胄，在场所有人里除了佛朗哥教授就数她最了解世界局势。

"瓦莲京娜。"西泽尔说，"你怎么看？"

瓦莲京娜看了他一眼。

"楚舜华不是善人。"她说，声音清冷如她甲胄上镶嵌的冰原寒玉，"他在夏国架空了自己的亲弟弟楚昭华，独揽北方军团大权。这种人跟你谈结盟，不是因为他喜欢你，是因为你有他需要的东西。"

"什么东西？"唐璜问。

"你。"瓦莲京娜看着西泽尔，"或者说，你血管里流的东西。西泽尔，你同时拥有锡兰星见和博尔吉亚两个家族的血脉，你是唯一能连接东西方世界树残枝的人。如果楚舜华想要保住他手里的东方主根节点不被原罪机关夺走，他就需要你。反过来说，如果你想毁掉所有节点，你也需要他手里的那一半。"

她顿了一下。

"结盟对你们两个都有好处。但你要清楚——他不是来帮你的，他是来找合作伙伴的。合作伙伴之间没有忠诚，只有合约。"

"那就签合约。"西泽尔说。

瓦莲京娜嘴角微微翘了一下。

"我没意见。"她说，"叶尼塞的立场和你们一致——阻止任何人重启机械神国。"

碧儿站在门框边，端着宵夜的盘子，手指因为用力而微微发白。

"西泽尔少爷。"她开口了，声音不大但很稳，"我能说句话吗？"

"说。"

碧儿把宵夜放在旁边的矮桌上，走到大厅中间。她穿着梵蒂冈档案员的制服还没换，袖口的碎片还在领口上沾着，脸色因为这些天的奔波和惊吓有些苍白。但她的眼睛是亮的，盯着西泽尔。

"我不是军事家，也不是机械师，我只是一个文书出身的侍从。"碧儿说，"但我在梵蒂冈档案室待了几年，见过很多文件，知道一个道理——越是看起来完美的提议，背后藏的东西越多。"

"你在说楚舜华可能是在利用我。"西泽尔说。

"我在说，"碧儿斟酌着措辞，"风林来的时候太巧了。刚好是您最需要盟友的时候，刚好带来了您最需要的东西——结盟请求、亲笔信、星见圣徽。如果换做我是楚舜华，我不会在这个时间点派出信使。除非——"

"除非他确实很急。"西泽尔说。

"或者他确实很需要您。"碧儿说。

"这不是一回事吗？"唐璜说。

"不一样。"碧儿摇头，"需要一个人，可以是爱才，可以是互利。但太急切的'需要'，往往意味着对方也面临着同样的绝境。楚舜华也许不是在帮少爷您，也许是在找一根救命稻草。"

她说完之后似乎觉得自己说得太多了，低下了头。

"老板。"昆提良拍了拍碧儿的肩膀以示安抚，转向西泽尔，"碧儿说的有道理。但我的意思没变——现在不是挑盟友的时候。楚舜华是敌是友以后再说，先把眼前的坎过了。"

阿方索点了点头。

佛朗哥教授叼着空烟斗，嗯了一声，算是表态。

所有人的目光都落在西泽尔身上。

壁炉的最后一块木柴烧尽了，火光微弱下去，映在每个人的脸上忽明忽暗。

"明天。"西泽尔说，"我给风林答复。同意结盟。"

他顿了一下。

"但不是无条件结盟。"

"条件是什么？"唐璜问。

"我还没想好。"西泽尔说，"但至少有一条——楚舜华必须把他手里关于世界树残枝东方主根节点的完整情报交出来。位置、规模、防御力量、历史沿革。他来找我结盟，就要拿出诚意。"

大厅里没有人反对。

昆提良松了一口气。唐璜靠在墙上，脸上那点紧绷的神色也松开了。瓦莲京娜没有说话，但她微微点了一下头。

"那薇若兰呢？"碧儿问。

所有人的目光又聚到西泽尔身上。

"明天去维苏威火山。"西泽尔说，"先找到她。"

壁炉里最后一点火光也灭了，大厅陷入短暂的黑暗。有人摸索着去找新的木柴，黑暗中传来火石敲击的清脆声响，迸出几点橘红色的火星。

就在这一刻——

西泽尔的口袋里，有什么东西在发烫。

不是后颈的黄金套管，是另一个位置。他伸手进去，摸到了两枚硬物——一枚是今天风林交给他的白色莲花圣徽，楚舜华的星见信物；另一枚是碧儿从梵蒂冈档案室带出来的倒置五芒星坠子，西泽尔外祖母传下的锡兰星见家族身份信物。

两枚圣徽都在发烫。

不是普通的发热，是一种有节律的、像心跳一样的脉动。

西泽尔把两枚圣徽同时取出来，托在掌心。

白色莲花圣徽和倒置五芒星坠子，挨在一起的瞬间——

"嗤——"

一道白光从两枚圣徽的接缝处迸射出来，刺得人睁不开眼。大厅里所有人都下意识地举手遮眼，白光穿过指缝，把所有人的影子投在墙壁上。

光芒持续了大约三秒。

然后，光线稳定下来，柔和的白光从两枚圣徽的缝隙中向四周扩散，照亮了整面墙壁。

墙上出现了画面。

不是文字，是一幅地图。

一幅用白色光线绘成的、半透明的、悬浮在空气中的地图。线条精细如蛛丝，山川河流的轮廓清晰可辨。地图覆盖了整面墙壁——左边是西方，右边是东方，中间是无尽的大海。

唐璜"啊"了一声。

昆提良往前迈了一步。

阿方索的机械手攥紧了窗台。

瓦莲京娜从书架边走过来，金色长发被白光映成银灰色。

两枚圣徽持续发出脉动，每脉动一次，地图上的线条就亮一分。地图上标注着文字——不是拉丁文，不是希腊文，是一种古老得像是在骨头和龟甲上刻出来的文字。但西泽尔能读懂，他不知道自己为什么能读懂，也许是紫瞳在发光，也许是世界树残枝的血脉在他血管里流。

地图上，标注着两处。

一处标记在地图东方——一座巨大的城市的轮廓，城市的正中央是一座宏伟的宫殿群，宫殿群下方画着一个倒置的五芒星，五芒星中央是一颗心脏的图案。心脏图案旁边，用那种古老的文字写着一行字——

通天宫。

世界树·根。

东。

另一处标记在地图西方——一座火山，火山被剖开了一个截面，截面深处画着一朵盛开的莲花，莲花中央是一颗跳动的核。莲花旁边，用同样的文字写着——

熔岩之心。

世界树·叶。

西。

两处标记之间，用一条虚线连接，虚线穿越了整个欧亚大陆。

"这是……"碧儿捂住了嘴。

"世界树残枝和主根节点的位置。"佛朗哥教授的声音从角落里传来，带着一种压抑的颤抖，"两枚星见圣徽同源同根，当两件信物靠近时会迸发白光，投射出世界树残枝的位置。这不是魔法，这是星见家族代代相传的……技术。"

"技术？"唐璜瞪大了眼睛。

"我说过，"教授走向前，浑浊的眼睛盯着墙上的地图，"星见不是神棍，星见是用齿轮计算星辰轨迹的观测者。倒置五芒星不是诅咒符号，是星见与天神沟通的通道。这两枚圣徽——楚舜华的白色莲花圣徽和你外祖母的倒置五芒星坠子——它们是同一套系统的两个终端，当两个终端靠近，系统就会自动启动，投射出世界树残枝的全景图。"

"三百年前的设计者，"教授说，"把整套星见圣徽系统分散保管，东方一支，西方一支，防止任何一方单独启动。现在——"

他看着西泽尔。

"东西两支，第一次同时出现在一个人手里。"

西泽尔看着墙上的地图。

左边的标记——东方的世界树主根节点，在夏国洛阳，通天宫下面。

右边的标记——西方的世界树残枝样本，在维苏威火山的熔岩之心里。

明天，他必须去维苏威火山。

找到薇若兰。

然后——

他的目光落在那条贯穿东西方的虚线上，虚线的尽头，标注着一个他看不清的符号，像是一朵花，又像是一颗心脏。

"明天。"西泽尔握紧了拳头。

"先去维苏威火山找薇若兰。"

"然后再考虑去洛阳的事。"

他抬起头，苍白的面孔被白光映得近乎透明，紫色的瞳孔里有什么东西在翻涌。

"不管那边藏着什么，"他说，"我都要亲眼看一遍。"

壁炉里新添的木柴被点燃了，橘红色的火光重新照亮了大厅。但墙上那幅由两枚圣徽投射出的地图，依然悬浮着，白色的光线在火光中清晰可辨。

唐璜盯着地图看了很久，嘟囔了一句："老板，你有没有发现——这条虚线的终点，画的不是任何一方。"

西泽尔当然发现了。

虚线的终点在地图的正中央，位置不属于东方，也不属于西方。

它画在一个没有标注任何名字的空白区域里，只有一个符号。

一朵倒置的莲花。

碧儿忽然抓住了西泽尔的袖子。

"少爷。"她的声音有些发抖，"我刚才在档案室的时候……看到过这个符号。"

"在哪里？"

"在一份被封存的梵蒂冈绝密档案里。"碧儿说，"档案的标题——"

她犹豫了一下。

"《阿瓦隆冰原深处报告·星历纪元前》。"

大厅里安静得能听见木柴燃烧的噼啪声。

西泽尔看着墙上那朵倒置的莲花。

他不知道的是——

此刻。

距离翡冷翠八千公里之外。

夏国洛阳。

通天宫的地下三百米。

一群穿着黑色长袍的人影，正站在一扇用黑铁铸成的巨门前面。巨门紧闭，门上刻着倒置的五芒星，五芒星中央是一颗心脏的图案。心脏图案和西泽尔此刻在墙上看到的，一模一样。

黑袍人为首的一个人缓缓摘下了兜帽。

他有一双翡翠色的瞳孔。

"开门。"叶素理说。

身后三十名中山国密探同时拔出了刀。

黑铁巨门后面，传来了沉重的震动。

像是有什么东西，正在苏醒。

【English】
Chapter 221 — The Xia Envoy (II)

Franco finished tightening the cap on the brass cylinder and slid it back into the inner pocket of his robe.

A log in the hearth split with a soft crack. Sparks spat against the iron grate, and the sound filled the silence of Canterbury Hall the way rain fills an empty cistern. Firelight touched the faces of the six people standing around the long oak table, and none of them spoke.

"Is that all of it?" Don Juan asked. There was no joke in his voice, which was the first warning that the room had shifted.

"That's all of it," Franco said. "Word for word."

Don Juan watched the cylinder disappear into the robe. His mouth opened. It closed again. Quintilian stood with his arms folded by the door, his gaze moving from Franco to Cesare, and then away. Alfonso leaned against the windowsill, mechanical fingers drumming a quiet, absent tattoo against his knee. Tap. Tap. Tap.

Cesare did not move.

His fingers were still hooked around the edge of the wool blanket across his lap, the same grip he had held before the recording began. The fabric was creased now, deeply, the way cloth is creased when it has been squeezed for a long time by a hand that has forgotten it is squeezing.

He had heard it.

The static.

It came in two places—once after "to destroy the World Tree requires—," and once before "do not go." Verolan had been speaking fast, in a voice pressed down almost to a whisper, but the static was not from the room she was in. It was the sound of a copper cylinder's magnetic head being deliberately thumbed against the moving tape. Someone—Verolan herself—had put her finger on the recording surface and dragged.

She had cut something out.

The question was what.

"Professor." Cesare's voice was level. "Can the cylinder be rewound?"

Franco looked at him. Something moved in the old man's clouded eyes, a flicker, and then it was gone, sunk back under the surface.

"No," Franco said. "The tape is the length it is. She used the full spool, and the cylinder is single-use. The magnetic head is non-reversible."

"The static, then. At the end."

Franco was quiet for a moment.

"The static is static," he said. "An old copper head. Her finger may have brushed the surface during the recording."

Cesare nodded. He did not ask again.

He filed it.

The firelight threw a warm wash across his pale face, but his eyes, beneath it, were as cold as the inside of a blade. Franco was not wrong. An aged head, a careless brush, would both produce that sound. But Verolan was Deputy Director of the Minerva Agency, and she had handled more precision instruments in a single morning than everyone in this hall had touched in a year. She did not make that kind of mistake. She had made a deliberate cut. And what she had cut was more important than what she had kept.

"Play it again," Cesare said.

Franco did not hesitate. He drew the cylinder out, unscrewed the cap, and set it on the table.

Verolan's voice came back into the room. It was the voice of a drowning woman reaching upward, hoarse, half-strangled, the words crowding against one another.

"Cesare—if you are hearing this, it means I am already trapped in the old mine tunnels on the north slope of Vesuvius—Michael's men caught up with me—I made it into the shafts but he is right behind me—"

"Listen—I have da Vinci's journal—the last page contains a secret he guarded his whole life—"

"About the Black Iron Gate—about the World Tree—about—"

Static.

Cesare's eyes dropped to the brass cylinder. His fingers tightened, very slightly, in his lap.

"—Cesare, listen to me—to destroy the World Tree requires—"

A second burst of static.

"—do not go—please, please do not go—"

"—I will wait for you at the mouth of the shaft—when you come, we leave together—"

"—I am waiting—"

The current died. The hall was quiet for a few seconds.

"Again," Cesare said. "From 'the last page of the journal.'"

Franco obliged.

This time, every one of them caught the rest of it.

The journal, Verolan said, named the master of the Original Sin Agency as a blood descendant of the first Pope, a man who meant to restart the Mechanical God-Kingdom. To do so, he needed two things: a perfect adapter to serve as his vessel, and the World Tree's eastern and western main-root nodes as his power source. Neither would do without the other. And the only way to stop him was for the perfect adapter, joining the wills of the eastern and western Stargazers, to cut down every World Tree branch and every main-root node in existence. Root and branch. Nothing left to grow back.

"That's it?" Quintilian frowned.

"That's it," Franco said.

Don Juan spoke, very quietly. "She said, 'to destroy the World Tree requires—,' and then the static came. The sentence never finished."

The hall went silent a second time.

"Signal interference," Alfonso offered.

"An aged head," Don Juan said, and glanced at Cesare, the way a man tests a closed door with his shoulder.

"Or she cut it out," Quintilian said, low.

No one answered. A log in the fire settled, and a small fountain of sparks sprayed up against the grate.

Cesare did not pursue the thread.

"Let me lay this out," he said, and his voice had the flat clarity of a man reading a quartermaster's list. "The master of the Original Sin Agency—Michael, or whoever is behind Michael—is a blood descendant of the first Pope, and his aim is to restart the Mechanical God-Kingdom. To do that, he needs a perfect adapter, and he needs the eastern and western main-root nodes of the World Tree. We now know that Chu Shunhua is the eastern guardian of the Stargazers and holds the eastern main-root node in his own hands."

"So the vessel the Agency wants," Valentina's voice came from the far side of the room. She had been leaning against the bookshelf, arms crossed, listening, not speaking until now, "has to be able to address both nodes at once."

"Chu Shunhua's envoy, Feng Lin, said as much," Cesare replied. "He called me the perfect union of the eastern and western World Tree bloodlines."

"Then—" A long stillness settled on Don Juan's face.

"Then the vessel the master of the Original Sin Agency wants," Franco said slowly, "is almost certainly Cesare himself."

The sentence fell into the room, and the room did not move.

The firelight touched them all. Valentina's mouth drew to a hair-thin line. Beryl appeared in the side doorway with a tray of supper in her hands, saw the room, and stopped. Her face went the color of plaster. Quintilian took a half-step forward, putting himself between Cesare and the door, then realized what he had done, and stepped back again.

"Then the only way to stop him," Alfonso said, straightening up from the windowsill, his mechanical fingers gone still, "is for Cesare—for the perfect adapter—to go out and cut down every World Tree branch and every main-root node."

"Yes," Cesare said.

"And how is he meant to do that?"

"She didn't say."

That was the second time tonight someone had noted the missing verb. Don Juan opened his mouth. He closed it again.

Cesare let his gaze travel from one face to the next.

"Other business," he said. "The alliance with Chu Shunhua."

No one objected to the order of things. They had been following Cesare long enough to know how he sorted a crisis: the matter of life and death went into the cold-room at the back of the mind, the matter in front of him got handled first.

"Feng Lin is Chu Shunhua's envoy," Cesare said. "He brought us Chu Shunhua's signed letter, a White Lotus holy emblem, and, before all of us, he revealed that Chu Shunhua is himself a son of the Stargazers. He told us that the House of Chu has guarded the eastern main-root node for generations, and that my mother, Sugalo, was a Stargazer descendant of the Chu line, married off to Ceylon. He asked for an alliance."

"It sounds reasonable," Alfonso said.

"It sounds," Cesare repeated. The word sat in his mouth like a coin tested between the teeth.

He looked down at his own hands. Pale. The knuckles sharp. The gold cannula at the back of his neck faintly warm. He thought of Feng Lin, standing in the front gate of Canterbury, in the long black robe, the inverted pentagram embroidered at his collar, holding out the White Lotus emblem—the same emblem that Beryl had pulled, by chance, out of a Vatican archive.

Feng Lin had said that Chu Shunhua was waiting for an answer at the Golden Lotus Inn, on the eastern edge of Florence.

"Captain." Quintilian spoke. He still used the address he had picked up in the Seraphim cadet corps, years ago. "I'm no politician, and I know only one thing. We are surrounded on all sides, and we are not yet crushed—" He did not finish the line; the words were too well known. "The College of Cardinals wants you arrested. The Cathedral Armored Division is parked at the gates of the Minerva Agency. Michael is chasing Verolan up and down the Italian coast. To the east, the Xia Empire has a hundred thousand men on the border. We have five working suits of prototype armor, and six people who may be dead before the month is out."

"Six," Don Juan said. "Count Solomon, Augustus, and the Rose Ghost, and it's six."

"Six," Quintilian said. "Six, against the world."

He looked at Cesare.

"If Chu Shunhua stands with us in fact, at least we don't have to hold the eastern line with our own bodies. He has the Northern Army. He has the Ghost Warrior armor. He has the Kui Dragon cavalry. We have Minerva's technology, and the Seraphim suits. We cover each other's gaps. We live longer."

"And," Don Juan added, "if the master's vessel has to be able to touch both nodes, then Chu Shunhua and the captain are tied to the same rope. He protects the captain, he protects himself."

"Interest aligns," Alfonso said, evenly. "Aligned interest is the only kind of alliance that holds."

Franco said nothing. He had produced, from somewhere in the ancient robe, a pipe. He felt in his pocket, found no tobacco, and put the empty pipe between his teeth. He was quiet for a long time before he spoke.

"Cesare. Do you trust him?"

Cesare did not answer at once.

The fire had burned low, and the light in the hall had thinned. Somewhere out over Florence, the midnight bell of a church began to toll—low, slow, the kind of toll that goes on for a hundred counts and never quite reaches the end.

"I don't trust him," Cesare said. "I trust his interest."

He turned to Valentina.

She was still against the bookshelf, arms crossed over the breastplate of her dress uniform, the gold of her hair falling over her shoulders. She was a princess of Yenisei. She was second-in-command of the Divine Wrath Knights. She had been wearing mobile armor at fifteen, and, of everyone in this room, only Franco knew the shape of the world better than she did.

"Valentina."

She lifted her eyes to his.

"Chu Shunhua is not a good man," she said. Her voice was clear, and as cold as the ice-plain jade set into the collar of her armor. "In the Xia court, he has stripped his own younger brother, Chu Zhaohua, of every real office and kept the Northern Army under his own hand. When a man like that proposes an alliance, it is not because he likes you. It is because you have something he needs."

"Which is?" Don Juan asked.

"You." Valentina did not take her eyes off Cesare. "Or, more precisely, what moves in your blood. Cesare, you carry both the Ceylon Stargazer line and the Borgia line, and you are the only living person who can address both the eastern and the western World Tree nodes. If Chu Shunhua wants to keep the eastern node out of the hands of the Original Sin Agency, he needs you. And if you want to cut down every node, you need the half of it he is holding."

She paused.

"The alliance is good for both of you. But understand what it is. He is not coming to help you. He is coming to find a partner. There is no loyalty between partners. There is only the contract."

"Then we sign a contract," Cesare said.

A small movement at the corner of Valentina's mouth. It might have been a smile.

"I have no objection," she said. "The position of Yenisei is the same as yours—no one restarts the Mechanical God-Kingdom."

Beryl was still in the doorway, the tray of supper in her white-knuckled hands.

"Master Cesare," she said. Her voice was small but very steady. "May I say something?"

"Say it."

Beryl set the tray down on the low table by the wall. She walked to the middle of the room. She was still in the uniform of the Vatican archives—she had not had time to change—and there was a fragment of paper stuck to her collar. Her face, after the days of running and fright, was the same pale as Cesare's own, but her eyes were very awake, and they were on him.

"I am not a soldier, and I am not a mechanist," she said. "I am a clerk by training, and a maid by service. But I worked in the Vatican archives for years, and I have seen a great many documents, and there is one thing I have learned. The cleaner a proposal looks, the more it is hiding."

"You are saying that Chu Shunhua may be using me," Cesare said.

"I am saying," Beryl said, choosing her words carefully, "that Feng Lin arrived at a very convenient time. Precisely when you most needed a friend. Precisely with the things you most needed to be offered—the alliance, the signed letter, the Stargazer emblem. If I were Chu Shunhua, I would not have sent an envoy at that exact moment. Unless—"

"Unless he was in a hurry," Cesare said.

"Or unless he was in need of you."

"That is the same thing," Don Juan said.

"It is not," Beryl said, and shook her head. "Needing a man can be many things. It can be admiration. It can be convenience. But a need that is too urgent, too well-timed, usually means the other man is in the same kind of trap. Chu Shunhua may not be coming to help you, master. He may be coming to find a plank in the water."

She stopped, as if she had heard herself, and lowered her eyes.

Quintilian put a hand on her shoulder, briefly, and turned to Cesare. "Beryl has a point. But my point stands. We are not in a position to be choosers about allies. Chu Shunhua is enemy or friend for later. The ditch in front of us is for now."

Alfonso nodded.

Franco, with the empty pipe in his teeth, made a small sound that might have been agreement.

Every eye in the room went to Cesare.

The last log in the fireplace had burned through. The light in the hall flickered, guttering, and for a moment each face was lit and then unlit, lit and then unlit, as if they were being shown to the room one at a time and then taken away again.

"Tomorrow," Cesare said. "I will give Feng Lin my answer. The alliance is accepted."

He paused.

"But it is not an unconditional acceptance."

"What is the condition?" Don Juan asked.

"I haven't decided," Cesare said. "But this much is certain. Chu Shunhua must hand over the full intelligence on the eastern main-root node of the World Tree. Its location. Its scale. Its garrison. Its history. If he wants an alliance with me, he brings his cards to the table face-up."

No one in the hall objected.

Quintilian let out a breath he had been holding. Don Juan's shoulders, which had been a little too high, came down. Valentina did not speak, but she gave a single small nod.

"What about Verolan?" Beryl asked.

Every eye in the room went back to Cesare.

"Tomorrow, we go to Vesuvius," he said. "We find her first."

The last of the fire died. The hall went black for a moment, and in the blackness someone felt along the wall for the woodpile, and someone else struck a flint, and a small rain of orange sparks fell to the hearthstones.

It was at that exact moment—

that something in Cesare's coat began to grow warm.

Not the gold cannula at the back of his neck. A different place. He slipped his hand into the pocket and his fingers found two hard shapes: one, the White Lotus holy emblem that Feng Lin had given him that morning, the Stargazer sign of Chu Shunhua; the other, the inverted-pentagram pendant that Beryl had brought out of the Vatican archive, the sign of his own grandmother, the Ceylon Stargazer line.

Both of them were warming.

Not the warmth of a body in a pocket. A different warmth. A pulsing warmth, in rhythm, like a heartbeat.

He drew them out together and laid them, side by side, in the open palm of his hand.

The instant the White Lotus and the inverted pentagram touched—

A hiss of white light leapt from the seam where they met, bright enough to make everyone in the room throw up a hand against their eyes. The light lanced between the fingers, throwing their shadows, sharp and long, across the wall of the hall behind them.

The brightness held for about three seconds.

Then the glare steadied. A soft white radiance began to pour out from the crack between the two emblems, and it spread, slowly, across the wall, until the entire western wall of Canterbury Hall was lit up with it.

What was on the wall was not a sentence. It was a map.

A map drawn in white light, half-translucent, suspended in the air in front of the stonework. The lines were fine as a spider's web. The shape of mountains and rivers was unmistakable. The map covered the wall from end to end—on the left, the West; on the right, the East; in the middle, an unbroken sea.

Don Juan said, "Ah."

Quintilian took a step forward.

Alfonso's mechanical hand closed tight on the edge of the windowsill.

Valentina came away from the bookshelf. The white light turned her gold hair to a tarnished silver.

The two emblems kept pulsing in Cesare's palm. With every pulse, the lines on the map grew a little brighter. There were words written across the map—not Latin, not Greek, but something older, the kind of script you see scratched into bone and tortoise shell. Cesare could read it, though he did not know how he could read it. Perhaps the violet of his eyes had begun, on its own, to glow. Perhaps the blood of the World Tree was running in his veins, and the blood remembered.

Two places on the map were marked.

The first mark was in the East. A great city, and at its heart a vast palace complex, and beneath the palace an inverted five-pointed star, and inside the star a heart. Beside the heart, in that old script, a single line:

Tongtian Palace.
World Tree · Root.
East.

The second mark was in the West. A volcano, cut open in cross-section, deep in the cut a lotus in full bloom, and in the center of the lotus a beating core. Beside the lotus, in the same script:

Heart of the Lava.
World Tree · Leaf.
West.

A dotted line ran between the two marks, straight through the body of Eurasia, the spine of the world.

"This is—" Beryl put her hand over her mouth.

"The position of the World Tree branches and main-root nodes," Franco said, from the corner, and there was a tremor in his voice he was trying to keep down. "When two Stargazer emblems of common origin are brought together, they emit a white light, and they project a full view of the World Tree's positions. This is not magic. This is a technique."

"Technique?" Don Juan's eyes were wide.

"I told you," Franco said, and stepped forward, his clouded eyes fixed on the wall. "The Stargazers are not fortune-tellers. The Stargazers are observers. They observe the courses of the stars with gears. The inverted five-pointed star is not a curse mark. It is the channel through which a Stargazer speaks with the heavens. These two emblems—Chu Shunhua's White Lotus, and your grandmother's inverted pentagram—are two terminals of one system. When the two terminals are brought close to each other, the system starts up, and the panoramic view of the World Tree is projected."

He looked at Cesare.

"The original designers, three hundred years ago, broke the Stargazer emblem-system into two parts—an eastern line and a western line—so that no one side could start it on its own. Now—"

"—the two lines are, for the first time, in the same hand."

Cesare looked at the map.

【中文】
第222章 通天宫的叛乱（上）

黑铁巨门后面传来的震动还在持续，一下，又一下，仿佛某种巨大心脏的搏动，穿透三百米厚的岩层，沿着矿道的石壁传上来。

叶素理没有回头。

他手下的密探足够处理地下那扇门——二十人留在巨门两侧，以撬棍和炸药并行，按他事先测算好的方案，应该能在两炷香内把门后的第一层封印撕开。他今夜要处理的事在地面上。在通天宫的寝殿里。在那个十八岁的小皇帝身上。

"走。"叶素理压低声音说。

他沿着来时的矿道向上走去。靴底裹着软布，踩在湿滑的石阶上几乎不发出声响。身后跟着一队穿着黑色夜行衣的人影，每一个人的腰间都别着短刀，肩后的褡裢里塞着更长的兵刃。他们是中山国花了二十年培养出来的死士，个个精通暗杀和爆破，在西域的沙漠里执行过比今夜更艰难的任务。

从地下三百米到通天宫的地面，整整走了一炷香。

最后一层石阶被推开，露出后花园假山石间一道狭窄的缝隙。洛阳深秋的夜风裹着邙山上的松脂气息灌进来，叶素理眯起眼睛，翡翠色的瞳孔在月色下泛出冷光。

一个穿着深灰色太监服饰的老人已经等在那里了。

老人佝偻着背，颌下三缕稀疏的白须在夜风中微微颤动，乍看像是宫里随处可见的普通老阉人，但叶素理知道这个人在通天宫的权力核心盘踞了四十年——从楚昭华的父亲在位时他就是内侍监总管，如今楚昭华登基，他依然是内侍监总管。楚氏皇族两代帝王的起居饮食、密折私函，甚至后宫妃嫔的床帏之事，都曾经过这双枯瘦的手。

"高公公。"叶素理微微颔首。

"叶大人。"高德海躬身行礼，声音尖细如针，"陛下已经睡下了。寝殿外的侍卫，半个时辰前已照吩咐换成了金吾卫中咱家的人。"

"楚舜华呢？"

"监国公爵今夜在前朝值宿，处理北方军团的粮饷文书。"高德海压低了声音，"他的亲卫队驻扎在宫城以北的演武场。整座后宫，此刻没有任何人能从楚舜华手中接到调兵令。"

叶素理点了点头。

他侧过头，越过假山石，看向不远处的寝殿。

通天宫的寝殿修在整座宫殿的最高处，飞檐翘角，黑瓦如鳞。月光照在琉璃瓦上，泛出冷冷的青蓝色。殿前的石阶上积着薄薄一层落叶，踩上去会发出轻微的碎裂声——高德海已经提前派人扫过一遍，又洒了细沙。

今夜的风向也合适。从北面邙山吹下来的风会把寝殿里的声响朝南方送去，送进花园深处的池塘里。不会惊动任何人。

"开门吧。"叶素理说。

高德海犹豫了一下。

那张布满皱纹的老脸上有什么东西一闪而过，像是水面上的一道涟漪，转眼就消失了。他弯下腰，从袖中取出一把铜钥匙。钥匙的齿口被磨得发亮，握在他枯瘦的手里，像一根干枯的树枝。

"叶大人，"他低声道，"事成之后——"

"中山国会记得你的功劳。"叶素理打断他，语气平淡得像在谈一笔再普通不过的生意，"你在宫外的那几个干儿子，一个不少。事成之后，中山国会安排他们去南洋做正经的买卖，远离这是非之地。"

高德海不再说话。

他转身走向寝殿的侧门，佝偻的背影在月光下像一只被风干的虾米。叶素理跟在后面，十二名密探分成三组贴着墙根无声地散开，在寝殿的另外两个侧门各布了四人。高德海在前面领路，铜钥匙插进侧门的锁孔，咔哒一声轻响。

门轴没有发出任何声音——高德海提前上过油。

寝殿里很暗。

只有床头一盏小小的琉璃灯还亮着，发出橘红色的微光，光芒被层层纱帐滤过，到地面上时已经变成一片模糊的昏黄。空气中弥漫着沉香和丝绸特有的气味——那种只属于帝王寝殿的、过分精致的气味。透过纱帐，能隐约看到一个人形侧卧在锦被中，呼吸均匀，睡得很沉。

那是楚昭华。

夏国名义上的天子，楚氏皇族现任皇帝，十八岁，瘦削的肩膀裹在华贵的绛紫色丝绸被面里，像一只蜷缩在巢穴中的雏鸟。

高德海轻手轻脚地走到床前，弯腰凑近楚昭华的耳边。

"陛下。"他的声音又尖又细，像一根绣花针刺进绸缎。

楚昭华猛地惊醒。

他一骨碌坐起来，瞪大了眼睛。琉璃灯昏黄的光照在高德海那张苍老的脸上，皱纹像刀刻出来的沟壑，深处藏着一辈子宫廷里积攒下来的阴冷和算计。楚昭华下意识地张了张嘴，想喊"来人"。

但声音卡在了喉咙里。

因为他看到了高德海身后的人影。

叶素理站在纱帐外面，一只手随意地插在袖中，另一只手的指间把玩着一把匕首。匕首的刀身极窄，薄得像一片秋天的蝉翼，在琉璃灯的微光下泛着幽蓝的冷光。叶素理的翡翠色瞳孔在暗处格外明亮，像是两颗被抛光的宝石。

"别急着喊。"叶素理轻声说，嘴角微微翘起，"喊了也没用。你外面那些侍卫，半个时辰前就已经被高公公换成自己人了。"

楚素华的十根手指在锦被上攥出了深深的褶皱，指节发白。他下意识地朝床角缩了缩，绛紫色的丝绸被面从他肩头滑落，露出单薄的丝绸中衣。

叶素理把匕首在指间转了一圈，缓步走到床前，居高临下地看着这位夏国的小皇帝。

"楚昭华，"叶素理说，声音很轻，轻得像是两个人之间的私语，"你的死期到了。"

他微微偏了偏头，目光越过楚昭华，落在寝殿深处那扇紧闭的窗户上。仿佛透过那扇窗户，他能看到更深处——地下三百米，那扇正在被打开的黑铁巨门。

"通天宫下面的世界树主根节点，"叶素理的声音变得更轻了，每一个字都咬得很清楚，"归我们中山国了。"

楚昭华终于找回了自己的声音。

"来人——！来人——！"他扯着嗓子尖叫，声音尖利得几乎刺穿了纱帐，赤着脚从龙床上跳下来，丝绸中衣的衣摆绊在床沿上，他一个踉跄摔在金砖地面上，膝盖磕得生疼。

但寝殿外面什么动静也没有。

没有靴子踩在石阶上的声响，没有金吾卫拔刀的金属碰撞，没有值夜太监慌张的询问。月光透过窗棂的缝隙照进走廊，在金砖地面上投下一格一格的银色光影。光影里空无一人。

"我说过了。"叶素理的声音从身后传来，依然是那种平淡而从容的语调，"喊了也没用。"

楚昭华跪在地上，肩膀剧烈地起伏着。他不敢回头，但他听到了脚步声——叶素理踩着软底靴子，一步一步地朝他走来，不急不缓，仿佛在丈量这间寝殿的尺寸。

叶素理在他身后停下来。

一只手按上了他的肩膀。

楚昭华整个人僵住了，像是被人往脊梁骨里灌了一瓢冰水。

"站起来。"叶素理说。

楚昭华没有动。

叶素理的手稍稍加力，把楚昭华从地上提了起来。十八岁的小皇帝瘦得像一根竹竿，在叶素理手里几乎没有分量。叶素理把他按在床沿上坐好，然后从袖中取出一卷黄色的绢帛，在他面前展开。

那是一份密令。

绢帛上盖着楚昭华的私印——一方只有天子才能使用的蟠龙朱印。印泥是上好的朱砂，颜色至今鲜艳。密令上的字迹是楚昭华自己的——他认得自己那手清秀却怯懦的楷书，连最后那个习惯性的顿笔都一模一样。

内容也很简单：着内侍监总管高德海，即日起削弱监国公爵楚舜华麾下北方军团兵权，收其虎符，调其主力离京畿，另行整编。事成之后，赏高德海黄金千两，荫其子入太学。

落款处还附了一行蝇头小字——"此事须密，勿令皇兄知悉。"

"这……这是我……"楚昭华的眼珠子几乎要从眼眶里凸出来。

"三个月前你亲笔写给高公公的密令。"叶素理把绢帛在楚昭华眼前晃了晃，然后收进袖中，笑容变得更深了，"可惜，高公公收到密令之后，没有交给楚舜华。"

叶素理偏过头，看了高德海一眼。

高德海佝偻着背站在角落里，垂着头，双手缩在袖中，枯瘦的身影像一截被遗忘在墙角的枯木。

"他把这份密令，"叶素理收回目光，重新落在楚昭华脸上，"交给了我。"

楚昭华的目光猛地转向高德海。

"高德海！你——你这条老狗！"他的声音因为愤怒和恐惧变得嘶哑，像是一根快要崩断的琴弦，"我待你不薄！你吃我楚家的饭，穿我楚家的衣，你竟然——"

"陛下，"高德海低声道，"老奴的干儿子们，都在叶大人手中。"

一句话把所有的话都堵了回去。

楚昭华张了张嘴，最终什么都没有说出来。他的眼神像是一面碎裂的镜子，映出支离破碎的倒影。

叶素理蹲下身来，和楚昭华平视。

两个人之间的距离不过一尺。叶素理能闻到楚昭华身上那股属于少年的、尚未完全褪去奶腥气的体味。翡翠色的瞳孔在琉璃灯的橘红色光芒中变成了一种奇异的琥珀绿，像是深山老林中毒蛇的眼睛。

"楚昭华，"叶素理轻声说，"你这个昏君。"

他的声音不急不缓，像在陈述一个与己无关的事实。

"楚舜华为夏国立下了多少汗马功劳？北击蛮族，南平百越，东征瀛洲——你算算，这些年夏国的仗，哪一场不是他打的？你呢？你这个皇帝在深宫里养尊处优，不理朝政，连早朝都三天打鱼两天晒网。你唯一上心的事，就是怎么害死你的亲哥哥。"

他的声音渐渐变冷，像冬天的河水在石头底下结冰。

"今天，"叶素理一字一顿地说，"我就替天行道。"

楚昭华的身体剧烈地颤抖起来。

他从床沿上滑下去，扑通一声跪在叶素理面前。绛紫色丝绸中衣的衣摆拖在金砖地面上，沾满了灰尘。他的额头触地，双手撑在冰冷的地砖上，指甲在砖缝里抠出了血丝。

"叶大人！叶大人饶命！"他抬起头，满脸都是泪水和鼻涕，嘴唇哆嗦得几乎说不出完整的句子，"我给你钱！我给你权！中山国想要什么我都给！封地！官职！商路！通通都给你！只要——只要你不杀我！"

叶素理低头看着跪在地上的小皇帝。

他的表情没有变化。翡翠色的瞳孔里甚至闪过一丝极淡的、近乎悲哀的东西——不是对楚昭华的悲悯，而是一种更深的、像是站在高处俯瞰棋盘时才会有的苍凉。

"你知不知道，"叶素理轻声说，"中山国想要的东西，你给不了？"

楚昭华愣住了。

"我……"他张着嘴，喉咙里发出含混的声响。

"世界树主根节点下面藏着的东西，比你这整座通天宫加起来都值钱。"叶素理站起身，低头俯视着楚昭华，"中山国要的不是你的钱，不是你的权。"

他微微一顿。

"中山国要的是整个天下。"

他手中那把匕首缓缓举了起来。

匕首的刀刃在琉璃灯的光芒中划出一道银色的弧线，像一弯冰冷的月牙。叶素理右臂的肌肉在黑色夜行衣下绷成一条流畅的线，匕首的尖端对准了楚昭华的后颈——那里是大椎穴的位置，一刀下去，不必太深，就能切断延髓。

楚昭华感觉到了身后那股冰冷的杀意。他的身体僵硬得像一块石头，泪水无声地流下来，滴在金砖地面上。

叶素理的手腕翻转，匕首落了下来——

轰——！

寝殿的门被从外面一脚踢开。

巨大的力量让两扇红木门板同时向内飞去，撞在墙壁上发出震耳欲聋的巨响。门板碎裂的木屑在空气中纷纷扬扬地飘落，琉璃灯的火焰被气浪冲击得剧烈摇晃，差点熄灭。一扇门板飞出去时砸翻了床头的紫檀木小几，上面的茶盏和铜镜摔在地上，发出清脆的碎裂声。

一个银色的人影站在被踢开的门口。

月光从那人身后照进来，在金砖地面上投下一道长长的影子。影子越过倒塌的门板，越过碎裂的茶盏，落在楚昭华面前，像一道冰冷的刀痕。

楚昭华猛地抬起头。

门口站着的人穿着一身银色的甲胄。

那副甲胄和西方教会骑士团的制式完全不同——线条修长，棱角分明，每一片甲叶上都雕刻着繁复的云雷纹路，仿佛是某种古老神兽的鳞片层层叠压。甲胄的胸口处嵌着一颗淡蓝色的核心，核心发出稳定的、脉搏一般的微光。甲胄的双肩处伸展出两片锋利的肩刃，刃口在月光下闪着冷厉的银光，像两柄出鞘的短剑。

鬼武者初型。

夏国初代机动甲胄，通体银甲，以西域玄铁与昆仑寒玉混合锻造，关节处嵌有精密的硬金齿轮，能让穿戴者获得远超常人的力量与速度。首批一百具已经列装夏国金吾卫，是楚舜华手中最锋利的一把刀。

此刻，这把刀的刀柄握在楚舜华手中。

他的面容隐藏在甲胄的面罩后面，只露出一双漆黑的眼睛。那双眼睛里没有怒火，没有焦灼，只有一种极致的冷静——像是深冬的冰湖，表面光滑如镜，底下却藏着足以吞噬一切的暗流。

他的目光从楚昭华身上扫过，落在叶素理身上。

然后落在叶素理手中那把还悬在半空的匕首上。

"大哥——！"楚昭华发出一声撕心裂肺的喊叫，声音都变了调，泪水和鼻涕糊了满脸。

叶素理的匕首停在了半空。

他缓缓转过身来，看着门口那个银色的人影。翡翠色的瞳孔在月光的照射下泛出一种冷冷的绿，像是深山老林中毒蛇的眼睛，瞳孔缩成了一条极细的竖线。

"楚舜华。"叶素理叫出了那个名字，语气依然平稳，甚至带着一丝笑意，"你来得比我预想的快。"

楚舜华没有回答。

他抬起右手，按在腰间佩剑的剑柄上。

那柄长剑的剑鞘是黑色鲨鱼皮的，镶着银边，剑格处雕着一只展翅的夔龙。楚舜华的手指扣住剑格，缓缓地，一寸一寸地，将长剑从鞘中抽了出来。

剑身出鞘的声音极轻，像是一声叹息。

但当那柄剑完全出鞘时，月光照在剑身上，映出一种奇异的琥珀色。剑刃极薄，薄得几乎透明，但刃口处却泛着一种让人心悸的寒光——那不是金属的光泽，而是某种更加古老、更加危险的东西。

那是夔龙马的角。

夏国传说中，夔龙马是上古神兽夔牛的后裔，生于雷泽，食铁饮泉，骨角能辟邪断金。楚舜华胯下的那匹赤红色夔龙马"朱砂"，其额前独角在二十年前一次战役中折断，断角被宫中巧匠打磨成这柄长剑。剑身保留了角质的天然纹理，纹路如凝固的闪电，握在手中微微发热，仿佛仍有血液在其中流淌。

楚舜华把剑尖指向叶素理。

银色甲胄与琥珀色长剑同时映着月光，像两片不同色泽的寒冰，在寝殿的空气中碰撞出无声的杀意。

"叶素理。"楚舜华的声音从面罩后面传出来，被金属滤过之后变得低沉而冷硬。

他顿了顿。

剑尖在月光中纹丝不动。

"你敢动我弟弟一根头发——"

他的声音很平静，平静得像是深冬的雪落在冰封的湖面上，没有一丝波澜。

"我就让你死无葬身之地。"

【English】
Chapter 222 — The Revolt at Coelestia (I)

The black iron doors behind him were still shuddering.

Each blow fell at the same interval, slow, patient, the cadence of something immense drawing breath somewhere far below. The shock ran up through three hundred feet of stone, ran the length of the gallery wall, and trembled faintly in the bones of his jaw.

Ezzelino did not look back.

The men he'd left at the gates were sufficient — twenty of them, divided between the two leaves, working in tandem with pry-bar and prepared charges, on the plan he had worked out two weeks before over a basin of cold water and a stick of charcoal. Two incense-sticks of time, he had calculated, and the first ward would be torn open. What he was after tonight lay above. In the High Palace. In the bed of an eighteen-year-old boy who called himself emperor.

"Move," he said, very quietly.

He climbed. The stairs were slick with mineral water; the soles of his boots were wrapped in felt, and his footfalls made almost no sound at all. Behind him, in single file, a dozen figures in black followed — short blades at the hip, longer steel stowed in shoulder scabbards. They were the product of twenty years of patient investment by the court of Montcœur; professional in the arts of slipping a knife between ribs in a dark stair, of setting a charge, of being somewhere else before the echo had died. They had done harder work than this, in the dunes east of the Bosphorus, in the years before the present war.

One incense-stick's worth of stair. Three hundred feet. And then the last slab of dressed stone was pushed aside, and a crack opened in the artificial mountain at the heart of the High Palace's rear garden. The autumn wind off the northern heights came in cold and smelt of pine resin. Ezzelino narrowed his eyes. In the moonlight the green of his pupils went the colour of uncut jade.

An old man in the grey smock of the palace eunuchry was waiting for him in the gap between two ornamental boulders.

He was bent nearly double. The three white hairs at his chin trembled in the draught. At a glance he might have been any one of a thousand aged, half-forgotten menials who haunted the lower corridors of the imperial household. Ezzelino knew better. The creature before him had sat at the centre of the spider's web for forty years. He had served the boy's father; he served the boy now. Through those liver-spotted hands had passed, in their time, every private dispatch, every whispered appeal, every pillow-confession of every woman the imperial bed had ever held.

"Sir Ezzelino," the old man murmured, and bowed.

"Eunuch Godfrey," said Ezzelino, and inclined his head a degree.

"The young lord is abed. The guard on the sleeping-chamber door was changed half an hour ago, as you instructed. They are my own men, drawn from the Aurelian."

"And the regent?"

"The Duke keeps his watch in the front palace tonight, on the matter of the northern army's pay-chests. His personal guard is bivouacked on the parade ground north of the wall. From anywhere in the rear palace, no courier could reach him in time to bring up a single man."

Ezzelino nodded.

He turned his head and looked, over the rim of the artificial rock, at the building beyond.

The imperial sleeping-chamber had been built at the very crown of the palace, set on a shelf of living stone. Its eaves lifted at the corners like the wings of a roosting bird; the tiles were the black of lacquered beetles, and in the moonlight the glazed crests picked up a faint, almost mineral blue. A thin scatter of leaves lay on the apron of steps before the door. They would have crunched underfoot — but Eunuch Godfrey had already had them swept, and the stone dressed with a fine layer of sand. The wind tonight was also, by a small providence, in the north. Whatever sounds were made inside would be carried south, over the garden, into the cold belly of the ornamental lake. No one would hear.

"Open it," said Ezzelino.

Godfrey hesitated.

A small ripple passed over the old man's face — like a stone dropped into a still pond — and was gone. He bent, and drew from his sleeve a brass key. The wards were worn to brightness. The key looked, in the cage of his long yellow fingers, like a twig snapped from a dead tree.

"Sir Ezzelino," he said, in a voice like paper tearing, "when this is done — "

"Montcœur will remember what you have done," said Ezzelino, as if he were settling the price of a bale of silk. "Your three adopted sons, the ones you keep outside the wall. Not one of them will be touched. After the change, we shall settle them in the southern trade. Clean business. Well away from this city."

Godfrey said no more.

He turned and led the way along the colonnade to the side door of the sleeping-chamber, his bent back like a shrimp drying on a hook. Ezzelino followed. The twelve in black had already broken into three parties; four men slid to each of the other two doors and pressed themselves flat against the wall. Godfrey fitted the key to the lock. There was a soft click. The hinges, which he had taken care to oil, made no sound at all.

The chamber inside was dark.

A single small lamp of blown glass was burning on the bedside table. Through three veils of gauze its flame reached the floor as a wash of blurred amber. The air smelt of aloeswood and the faintly animal warmth of new silk — that particular, almost too-precise smell that belongs to the rooms in which emperors sleep. Through the gauze a shape could be seen, curled on its side under a quilt of imperial crimson, breathing with the slow regularity of the very young and the very tired.

Lucian Chu, eighteenth of his name, Emperor of Hesperia in name, lay in a nest of imperial linen and looked, in the ember-light, like a fledgling that had fallen from the eaves.

Godfrey went to the bedside and bent close to the boy's ear.

"Sire," he said, in that thin and needle-fine voice of his.

Lucian woke as if he had been struck.

He sat up, blinking. The amber light caught the deep lines of the old eunuch's face — they were the lines a life of waiting had cut, and behind them, in the shadows, lay forty years of court calculation. The boy's mouth opened. He was going to call for the guard.

The word stuck in his throat.

He had seen the figure behind the eunuch.

Ezzelino stood outside the gauze, one hand in the sleeve of his coat, the other turning a thin-bladed knife between his fingers. The blade was narrow as a cicada's wing in autumn. In the dying lamp-light it gave back a sliver of blue, like a crack in ice. Ezzelino's eyes, set in the moon-shadow, were the colour of a green stone that has been polished too long.

"No need to shout," he said, mildly. "And no use, if you do. The men on the doors have been Eunuch Godfrey's for half an hour."

Lucian's ten fingers closed on the quilt. The silk went white at the seams of his knuckles. He drew back, on the bed, towards the bolster, and the crimson quilt slid from one thin shoulder, and the silk of his nightshirt showed through.

Ezzelino turned the knife in his fingers once more, walked to the bedside, and stood looking down.

"Lucian," he said, almost privately, "your hour has come."

He tilted his head, as if his gaze could pass through the stone wall of the chamber and through another three hundred feet of rock, and find, far below, the black iron door that his men were prying open.

"The root-node of the World-Tree, beneath this palace," he said, in a voice so soft that every syllable was distinct, "belongs now to Montcœur."

Lucian found his voice.

"Help!" he cried. "Help me — !"

The sound was high enough to cut the gauze. He flung himself from the bed, one bare foot catching the hem of his nightshirt, and went down hard on the gilded tiles of the floor, the bones of his knees taking the blow. There was no answering cry from the corridor. No boot on the stone. No blade drawn from a scabbard. No sleepy question from a eunuch on watch. The moonlight through the lattice fell in silver bars on the floor, and the bars were empty.

"I did tell you," said Ezzelino, from behind him, in the same unhurried tone, "there is no one to hear."

Lucian stayed where he had fallen, his shoulders rising and falling. He could not turn his head; he could hear, behind him, the soft steps of a man in felt boots, pacing him, taking the measure of the room.

The steps stopped.

A hand came down on his shoulder.

The boy's spine went rigid, as if a cup of ice-water had been poured along it.

"On your feet," said Ezzelino.

Lucian did not move.

The hand tightened, a little, and lifted him as if he were made of paper. The eighteen-year-old emperor weighed nothing. Ezzelino set him on the edge of the bed and took from his sleeve a roll of yellow silk, and held it open before the boy's face.

It was a decree.

The seal at the foot was Lucian's own — the coiled dragon in cinnabar paste that only the reigning emperor was permitted to use. The colour was still good, still wet-looking after three months. The handwriting was his. He knew his own careful, somewhat frightened calligraphy, even down to the small, habitual tick of the brush at the end of each line.

The wording was plain. Eunuch Godfrey, Superintendent of the Inner Palace, was hereby empowered to begin the reduction of the northern army, then under the command of the Duke Regent; the army's tally of command was to be called in; its main strength to be drawn out of the capital district; the whole to be reformed under new officers. For his services, Eunuch Godfrey was to receive a thousand gold imperials, and a place at the Imperial Academy for one of his sons.

At the foot, in a small cramped hand, was added — This must be secret from my brother.

"That — " said Lucian. "That is — "

"The private order you wrote to Eunuch Godfrey three months ago," said Ezzelino, and waved the silk once, in front of the boy's face, before rolling it away and tucking it into his sleeve. "Pity Godfrey, when he received it, did not pass it on to the Duke."

He glanced, briefly, at the eunuch.

Godfrey stood in the corner, very straight for once, his hands hidden in his sleeves, his shadow a small broken thing against the wainscot.

"He passed it," said Ezzelino, looking back to Lucian, "to me."

Lucian's eyes snapped to the old man.

"Godfrey — you — you old dog — !" The boy's voice had broken in two, and what came out was a kind of dry, animal sound, like a string wound past its limit. "I treated you — I gave you — you have eaten at our table, you have worn our livery, and you — "

"Sire," said Godfrey, in his smallest voice, "my sons are in Sir Ezzelino's keeping."

The words closed the door on whatever Lucian had been about to say.

The boy opened his mouth, and then closed it again. His face was the face of a mirror that has just been struck.

Ezzelino knelt, so that his eyes were level with the boy's.

A foot of space between them. He could smell the lad — that half-sweet, not-yet-soured animal scent of an eighteen-year-old who has not yet learned to be a man. The green of his eyes, under the amber of the lamp, had gone the colour of an old wasps' nest.

"Lucian," he said, "you wretched little emperor."

His voice was level, and a little tired, as if he were reciting a thing that did not concern him.

"What has the Duke done for Hesperia? The northern barbarians broken on his sword, the southern kingdoms brought under his heel, the eastern isles carried by his fleet — count them up, the wars of these last ten years, every one of them his work. And you? You have sat in this room, and let the morning court go by, and let the petitions pile, and your one interest — your one industry — has been how best to bring your own brother down."

His voice cooled as he spoke, the way a river cools under stones in winter.

"Tonight," said Ezzelino, and the words came out one by one, "I do what you could not."

Lucian began to shake.

He slid off the edge of the bed and onto his knees on the gilded tiles. The crimson silk of his nightshirt pooled in the dust. He pressed his forehead to the cold floor. His nails scratched at the seams between the bricks until the skin broke.

"Sir Ezzelino — Sir Ezzelino, have mercy — !" He looked up. The tears and the mucus had made a single mask of his face. His lips would not stay still enough to finish a sentence. "Money — I will give you money — rank — I will give you rank — what Montcœur wants, I will give it — land — a marquisate — a road of trade — all of it, all of it — only — only — "

Ezzelino looked down at the boy on the floor.

His face did not change. Something moved, very briefly, in the green of his eyes — not pity, not for Lucian, but a kind of older, drier thing, the way a man looks down on a chessboard when the game is already lost.

"Do you know," he said, almost gently, "that what Montcœur wants is something you cannot give?"

Lucian stared.

"I — "

"What lies under the root-node of the World-Tree," said Ezzelino, and rose, so that he stood over the boy, "is worth more than this whole palace, and everything in it. Montcœur does not want your money, Lucian. Montcœur does not want your title."

He paused.

"Montcœur wants the world."

The knife came up in his hand.

The blade drew a thin silver curve through the lamp-light, the curve of a cold new moon. Ezzelino's right arm, under the black of his coat, was one taut line. The point of the knife rested, very lightly, at the top of the boy's spine — the great vertebra, the one that joins the neck to the shoulders; a single careful thrust, and the marrow of the spine would be parted, and the boy would never finish the scream he had not yet begun.

Lucian felt the cold of the blade on the back of his neck. His body locked, all of it, every joint. The tears ran, soundless, and fell on the gilt tiles.

Ezzelino's wrist turned.

The knife came down —

Boom.

The doors of the chamber were kicked in from the outside.

The force of the blow took both leaves at once and hurled them inwards, and they struck the wall with a noise like a falling tree, and the air was full of a fine rain of wood-splinters, and the flame of the bedside lamp leapt and nearly died, and a side table of red sandalwood went over, and a brass mirror and a teacup hit the floor and shattered with a clean bright sound.

A figure in silver stood in the broken doorway.

The moonlight was at his back, and his shadow ran in across the floor of the chamber — over the fallen leaves, over the smashed teacup, over the boy on his knees — and stopped, sharp-edged, like the cut of a blade, at Lucian's feet.

Lucian looked up.

The figure in the doorway was wearing a suit of silver armour.

It was not the long fluted plate of the western military orders. The lines were slim and angular; every leaf was chased with a dense pattern of cloud and thunder, as if the scales of some ancient beast had been layered, one on top of another, by a careful and patient hand. A small core of pale blue was set in the breastplate, and it pulsed with its own slow, regular heartbeat. From each shoulder a short, sharp blade projected, the edges of which caught the moonlight in a long cold flash, like the wink of a drawn sword.

A Wraith-Knight, First Pattern.

The first of the new mobile armours of Hesperia, hammered from a black sand-iron of the western deserts and a strange cold jade from the heights of the Kunlun. The joints were of fine red-brass gears, and the man inside could move with a speed and a force that no unarmoured body had ever managed. The first hundred had been issued to the Aurelian Guard. They were the sharpest blade in the hand of the Duke.

That blade's hilt was in the hand of Cyrus Chu.

His face was hidden by the visor of the helm. Only his eyes were visible, and they were black, and there was nothing in them — no anger, no haste, only an absolute, glacial calm, the calm of a frozen lake whose surface is glass and whose depths are cold enough to swallow you whole.

His gaze moved, once, from Lucian on the floor, to Ezzelino, to the knife in Ezzelino's hand, still raised.

"Brother — !" cried Lucian, and the word was so cracked it was almost unrecognisable.

Ezzelino's knife stopped in the air.

He turned, slowly, and looked at the figure in the doorway. In the moonlight the green of his eyes went the colour of a snake's, and the pupils drew down to a single very thin line.

"Cyrus," he said, and the name was level, and there was even, in it, the smallest edge of a smile. "You are earlier than I had allowed for."

Cyrus did not answer.

He raised his right hand to the hilt of the sword at his hip.

The scabbard was black, of ray-skin, bound in silver. The guard was a chi-dragon, wings spread. Cyrus's fingers closed on the guard, and he drew the blade — slowly, a hand's-breadth at a time — out of the scabbard.

The sword made almost no sound coming out, as if it were a long breath let out.

When it was clear of the sheath, the moonlight ran along the blade, and the steel was the colour of a strange dark honey. The edge was so thin it was almost not there, and yet the light that came off it was not the light of any metal. It was the light of something older, and more dangerous.

It was the horn of a unicorn.

The destrier that Cyrus had ridden for twenty years, the red unicorn Cinnabar, had lost the single horn at his brow in a battle, two decades ago. The broken horn had been taken back to the imperial workshops, and a sword had been made of it. The natural grain of the horn was still in the blade — the grain of a thing that had grown, like a tree, in lightning. When Cyrus held it, the metal was warm, as if a slow blood were still moving somewhere in it.

Cyrus pointed the point of the sword at Ezzelino.

The silver armour and the dark-honey blade stood, in the moonlight, like two different shades of the same cold thing, and the air of the chamber had gone sharp with a kind of soundless killing.

"Ezzelino," said Cyrus, from behind the visor, and his voice, sifted through the metal, was low and hard.

He paused.

The point of the sword did not move.

"If you touch one hair on my brother's head," he said, and his voice was very calm, the way snow falling on a frozen lake is calm, and the way a thing is calm in the moment before it kills, "I will leave no piece of you that the dogs will recognise."

第223章 通天宫的叛乱（中）

【中文】
第223章 通天宫的叛乱（中）

夔龙角剑出鞘的刹那，寝殿里的空气像是被抽走了。

叶素理没有看楚舜华手中的剑，他的目光越过那柄琥珀色的利刃，落在银色鬼武者甲胄的胸口——那里嵌着一枚暗金色的六芒纹章，是夏国初代皇帝亲铸的"龙雀"印，只有监国公爵才能佩戴。

"大夏龙雀亲临，"叶素理缓缓松开扼住楚昭华咽喉的手，匕首垂落在身侧，"真是好大的排场。"

楚昭华像一只被踩断脊椎的老鼠，软倒在地，浑身剧烈地抖着，牙关上下打战，咬得咯咯作响。涎水顺着嘴角流下来，和眼泪鼻涕混在一起，糊了半张脸。

"大夏龙雀？"楚舜华的声音从面罩后传来，带着金属的嗡鸣，"叶素理，你带三十个人闯进通天宫，就为了这四个字？"

"不敢。"叶素理微微躬身，姿态优雅得仿佛他此刻不是身处夏帝寝殿，而是中山国使节馆的宴席上，"下官只是来给陛下送一份大礼。"

他没有解释那份大礼是什么。

楚舜华也没问。

他只是抬起了左手。

寝殿外，通天宫的回廊上响起了密集的脚步声——不是一个人，是很多人，几十双靴子踩在金砖地面上的声音整齐划一，仿佛一台精密的蒸汽机正在运转。

那是金吾卫的军靴。

叶素理的瞳孔微微变化了一下。

他是个聪明人，聪明人能从脚步声里听出对方的兵力部署。那不是一个分队，也不是两个分队，至少有四个分队的人从回廊的四个方向同时压过来，把整个寝殿围成了铁桶。

"好快。"叶素理轻声说。

"你以为我在洛阳城外跟楚国使者喝茶？"楚舜华说。

他的夔龙角剑在月光中划出一道弧线——极轻，极薄，划过去的时候连空气都没有被撕裂的声音，只有一缕极细的白色霜雾从剑刃两侧散开，仿佛剑身周围的温度在一瞬间被抽空了。

那一剑没有指向叶素理。

它指向了叶素理身后那三个中山国死士。

第一个死士还没来得及举刀，剑光已经到了他面前。夔龙角剑的剑刃贴着他手中的长刀刀身滑过去，那柄用精钢打造的长刀像是纸糊的一样被削成了两截，断口处平滑如镜，没有一丝毛刺。断刃的惯性带着死士的手腕猛地一偏，下一息，夔龙角剑已经从他的脖颈左侧切入，从右侧贯出。

没有血喷出来。

因为伤口两侧的皮肤和肌肉在剑刃经过的瞬间就被极寒冻住了，像是两片被霜打过的薄冰。死士的身体僵在原地，眼睛还睁着，嘴里还在吐气，但已经死了。

"好剑。"叶素理说。

他的语气依然平稳，仿佛在评价一壶新酿的桂花酒。

楚舜华没有理他。

夔龙角剑横移，划向第二个死士。那个死士是个老手，知道自己手中的精钢长刀挡不住夔龙角剑，干脆扔了刀，双手各持一支短戟扑上来。短戟的尖端淬了毒，泛着幽蓝色的光。

楚舜华没有闪避。

银色鬼武者甲胄的左臂抬起来，硬生生地接下了两支短戟的攒刺。短戟的尖端刺在甲胄小臂的影金属护板上，迸出两团火星，戟尖被弹开了——影金属的硬度远超精钢，那两支短戟连在甲胄表面留下一个白印都做不到。

而夔龙角剑已经到了第二个死士的胸口。

穿心而过。

和第一个人一样，伤口两侧的肌肉瞬间冻结，死士张大了嘴，口中呼出的白气在月光下凝成一团雾气。

第三个死士转身就跑。

他不是朝门口跑，而是朝窗户跑——和叶素理一样，他也看出了今夜的局面已经不可挽回。但他的反应比叶素理慢了半拍。

他刚跑出两步，楚舜华的夔龙角剑已经从身后掷了出去。

不是投掷，是甩。楚舜华握剑的手腕猛地一抖，夔龙角剑脱手的瞬间发出一声低沉的嗡鸣，仿佛剑身里封着的夔龙角活了过来，在发出一声愤怒的咆哮。长剑化作一道琥珀色的闪电，准确地贯穿了第三个死士的后背，从胸口穿出，钉在了前方三步远的一根红漆柱子上。

剑身没入红漆柱子足有两寸深，尾端还在微微震颤。

死士被长剑的惯性带着向前扑倒，整个人挂在了柱子上，脚尖离地，慢慢地，不再动了。

三个中山国死士，从出剑到全部倒下，不到十息。

叶素理没有看那三具尸体。

他一直在看楚舜华。

"你的剑比传闻里更快。"叶素理说。

"你也比传闻里更蠢。"楚舜华说。

"哦？"

"三十个人就想控制通天宫？你把金吾卫当成了摆设，还是把楚舜华当成了死人？"

叶素理没有回答。

他的身体忽然向后倒去。

不是倒，是跳——他的后背猛地撞开了身后那扇雕花木窗，整个人从窗口翻了出去。碎木和窗纸在空中飞散，月光照亮了他在空中的姿态：左手已经从腰间解下了一根细索，甩向对面飞檐的檐角。

细索的前端是一个三爪铁锚，锚爪准确地钩住了飞檐的边缘。叶素理借着铁锚的拉力在半空中荡了一个弧度，像一只巨大的灰色蝙蝠，从寝殿二层的窗口飞向对面三层高的藏书楼。

"追！"一个金吾卫军官从门口冲进来，拔刀就要跳窗。

"不必。"楚舜华说。

军官停下了脚步，回过头来看着楚舜华。

"他跑不了。"楚舜华说，"他跑得越远，对我们越有利。"

军官愣了一下，旋即明白了楚舜华的意思。叶素理是中山国的外交大臣，私自潜入夏帝寝殿行刺，无论成功与否都是死罪——他只要还在洛阳城外的官道上逃窜，夏国就有充足的理由向中山国宣战。

"可是大人，如果中山国不认账呢？"

"他会认的。"楚舜华说，"不认账，中山国主第一个杀他。"

楚舜华弯腰，从红漆柱子上拔出了夔龙角剑。剑身上的血迹已经冻成了薄薄的冰霜，在月光下闪着暗红色的光。他用袖子擦了擦剑身，将它重新归鞘。

寝殿里忽然安静了下来。

那三个死士倒在地上，伤口处的冰霜正在慢慢融化，开始有暗红色的血水渗出来，汇成细细的溪流，沿着金砖地面的缝隙蜿蜒。

楚昭华还缩在龙榻的角落里，两只手抱着膝盖，整个人蜷成了一团，肩膀一抽一抽的，像是在无声地哭泣。

楚舜华朝他走过去。

鬼武者甲胄的靴子踩在金砖上，发出沉重的声响。每一步都让楚昭华的身体抖得更厉害一些。

"昭华。"楚舜华站在他面前，低头看着他。

楚昭华没有抬头。他不敢看楚舜华的脸，不敢看那身银色甲胄，也不敢看地上那三具尸体。

"哥……"他终于挤出了一个字，声音像是从喉咙深处挖出来的，带着浓重的鼻音和哭腔。

"你知不知道你今晚做了什么？"楚舜华说。

楚昭华猛地抬起头来，泪痕未干的脸上写满了惊恐和茫然："我……我没有……我不知道他要……"

"你不知道？"

楚舜华蹲下来，摘下了鬼武者甲胄的头盔。

月光照在他的脸上。那是一张和楚昭华有五分相似的脸，但线条更加硬朗，颧骨更高，下颌更方，眉骨处的皮肤被多年的战场风霜磨出了细密的纹路。眼窝比弟弟深，眼睛里没有泪水，只有一种让人脊背发凉的沉静。

"他带着三十个人从你寝殿的密道进来，密道的钥匙只有你和高德海有。"楚舜华说，"他用匕首指着你的脖子，你吓得尿了裤子——你知道这意味着什么吗？"

楚昭华的身体又剧烈地抖了一下。

"意味着中山国已经买通了通天宫里所有该买通的人，只差最后一步就能把整个夏国卖给西方。"楚舜华说，"而那最后一步，就是你。"

"我没有……"楚昭华的眼泪又涌了出来，"我只是想……"

"你只是想保住你的皇位。"楚舜华说，"叶素理告诉你，只要配合他演一出戏，西方就会支持你继续坐在龙椅上。我说得对不对？"

楚昭华不说话了。

他张着嘴，瞪着楚舜华，脸上的肌肉一抽一抽的，像是有什么东西在他体内撕裂。

"哥……你……你要废了我？"

"那要看你接下来怎么做。"楚舜华说。

他站了起来，把头盔重新扣在甲胄上，转身朝门外走去。

走到门口时，他停了一下，没有回头。

"昭华。"

"……"

"明天开始，你搬出乾清宫，住到西苑去。没有我的命令，不许踏出西苑一步。"

楚昭华的脸一下子变成了死灰色。

"哥！你不能这样对我！我是皇帝！我是大夏的皇帝！"他挣扎着从龙榻上滚下来，爬向楚舜华的方向，"你不能——你答应过父皇的！你答应过母后的！"

楚舜华没有停下脚步。

他的身影消失在寝殿的门口。银色的甲胄在月光中闪了一下，然后被走廊里的黑暗吞没了。

"哥！哥！！"楚昭华的哭喊声在空旷的寝殿里回荡，越来越远，越来越弱，最后被夜风吹散了。

"陛下。"一个金吾卫军官走到他面前，弯腰把他扶起来，"请您回龙榻上休息。"

楚昭华抬起头，茫然地看着那张年轻的脸。他张了张嘴，想要说什么，但嘴唇只是无声地翕动了几下，然后，他的眼睛翻了上去，整个人软倒在金吾卫军官的怀里，昏了过去。

军官叹了口气，把他抱起来放回龙榻上。

这时，另一个金吾卫军官从侧门快步走来，附在第一个军官耳边低声说了几句话。

"什么？"第一个军官脸色变了。

他立刻转身追了出去。

"大人！"他在走廊上喊住了楚舜华，"高德海已经被拿下了，在他的寝宫里搜出了——"

他顿了一下，似乎在斟酌措辞。

"搜出了什么？"

"三箱黄金，二十箱白银，还有……"军官从怀里取出一卷黄绢，双手呈上，"一份名单。"

楚舜华接过黄绢，展开。

月光下，黄绢上写满了密密麻麻的人名。每一个名字后面都跟着一行小字，注明了官职、收买金额和日期。

楚舜华的目光从第一个名字看到最后一个名字。

他的脸色一点一点地沉了下去，沉到了一种让人不敢直视的程度。

"李崇恩，兵部侍郎，三万两。"他念出了第一个名字。

"周成栋，户部郎中，两万两。"

"赵彦之，禁军都指挥使同知，五万两。"

他的声音越来越低，越来越冷，每一个名字从嘴里吐出来都像是一块冰。

"还有这个。"军官指向名单最后一行，"大理寺少卿，刘……刘明远，十万两。"

刘明远。

楚舜华闭上了眼睛。

刘明远是先帝钦点的探花郎，是楚舜华少年时在太学的同窗，是他亲手提拔进大理寺的年轻干将，也是他一直以为最忠诚的人之一。

"大人？"军官试探着问。

楚舜华没有回答。

他只是把那卷黄绢慢慢卷起来，卷得很紧，很紧，仿佛要把所有名字都勒死在黄绢里。

"高德海在哪里？"

"已经押在金吾卫的值房里了，大人。"

"把他关进诏狱。"楚舜华说，"告诉狱里的人，明天之前我要他供出这份名单上每一个人的下落。"

"是。"

"还有。"楚舜华顿了顿，"派人去追叶素理。"

"大人刚才不是说——"

"不是去抓他。"楚舜华说，"是去看着他。看他往哪里跑，看他见什么人。"

"是。"

军官转身要走，又被楚舜华叫住了。

"风林。"

"属下在。"一个声音从走廊的阴影里传来。风林从暗处走出来，还是那身东方黑色长袍，莲花圣徽别在胸口，倒置五芒星的刺绣在月光下泛着暗金色的光。

"你去一趟翡冷翠。"楚舜华说。

风林抬起头，眼中闪过一丝意外。

"现在？"

"现在。"楚舜华说，"告诉西泽尔，通天宫出事了。叶素理已经动手，虽然没有成功，但他掌握的那部分夏国情报——关于世界树残枝的——现在都在他手里。"

风林沉默了一瞬。

"属下明白了。"他说，"属下明日一早就出发。"

"不。"楚舜华说，"今晚就走。"

风林愣了一下。

"大人，通天宫今夜刚刚平叛，各处城门必定——"

"所以你不能走城门。"楚舜华从怀里取出一块令牌，递给风林，"拿着这个去金吾卫的马厩，挑一匹最快的马，从北门出城。我会让人把北门的守卫撤掉。"

风林接过令牌，沉默了几息。

"大人。"他低声说，"您是要请西泽尔来洛阳？"

楚舜华没有立刻回答。

他转身朝走廊尽头走去，银色甲胄的关节在行走中发出轻微的咔哒声，像是一台精密的钟表在走动。

"西泽尔·博尔吉亚。"他低声说，像是在念一个只有他自己才能听懂的名字。

走到走廊尽头时，他停下了脚步。

通天宫的最高处就在那里——一座八角形的观星台，檐角挂着的铜铃在夜风中发出清脆的响声。从这里望出去，能看到整座洛阳城的轮廓，万家灯火星星点点，像是撒在黑色天鹅绒上的碎金。

再远一些，是西方的天际线。

那个方向，翡冷翠在等着。

"西泽尔。"楚舜华望着西方，声音很轻。

风林站在他身后，听不太清他在说什么，但隐约听到了几个字。

"现在……只有我们两个了。"

"你一定要来。"

【English】
Chapter 223 — The Revolt at Tongtian Palace: Part Two

The air left the chamber when the Kui Dragon Horn Sword left the scabbard.

Ye Suli did not look at the blade in Chu Shunhua's hand. He looked past the amber edge, past the thin white mist curling off the fuller, and fixed his gaze on the chest of the silver armor — there, set into the breastplate at the sternum, a six-pointed seal worked in dull gold. The Dragon-Sparrow. Cast in the founding year of the dynasty by the first Xia Emperor. Worn by one man, and one only: the Regent Duke.

"The Dragon-Sparrow of Great Xia, in person," Ye Suli said. He eased his grip on the Emperor's throat. He let his hand fall. The knife hung loose at his side. "What an honor."

The young Emperor of Great Xia collapsed to the floorboards like a rat whose spine had been trodden on. He shook. His teeth chattered so loud they seemed to crack in his own jaw. Snot and tears and saliva ran together across the lower half of his face and dripped onto the gilt brick.

"The Dragon-Sparrow," said Chu Shunhua. His voice came from behind the visor of the Ghost Warrior helm, and it carried that hum of metal underneath, the way a bell carries its note long after the clapper has stopped. "Ye Suli. You brought thirty men into Tongtian Palace. For this. For four words."

"Hardly four, Your Grace." Ye Suli gave a small bow. A court bow. The kind one gave in the reception hall of the Zhongshan embassy over sweet wine, in a different season, in a different life. As if he stood anywhere but the bedchamber of the Xia Emperor, in the small hours of the morning, with a dead man already at his feet. "I came to bring His Majesty a gift."

He did not say what the gift was.

Chu Shunhua did not ask.

He raised his left hand.

From the corridor outside the chamber came the sound of boots. Not one pair, not two, but many — a great organized thunder of them, each stride landing on the gilt brick in the same beat, the same weight, the same rhythm, as if a great engine somewhere beneath the palace had begun to turn. Jinwu Guards. Moving in formation.

Ye Suli's pupils narrowed by a fraction.

He was a clever man, and clever men could read an army by the sound it made against stone. That was not one squad. Not two. Four squads at least, coming from four directions at once, sealing the chamber in a ring of steel and shadow.

"Fast," Ye Suli murmured.

"You thought I was drinking tea with the Chu envoys outside Luoyang," Chu Shunhua said.

The Kui Dragon Horn Sword moved.

It was a small movement. A single arc through the moonlight slanting in through the broken window. The blade was thin, almost weightless, and it made no sound as it cut — no hiss, no whistle — only a faint white vapor that bloomed off either edge of the steel, as if the air along the sword's path had been drained of every degree of warmth in a single instant.

The cut was not aimed at Ye Suli.

It was aimed at the three Zhongshan deadmen standing behind him.

The first of them never got his long knife up. The amber edge slid along the flat of his blade, and the blade — good Chu steel, a weapon of some price — came apart at the kiss of the sword as if it had been cut from paper. The break was clean as a mirror. The deadman staggered as the off-weighted half of his own weapon carried his wrist sideways, and the Kui Dragon Horn Sword passed on through the left side of his neck and out the right.

No blood came out.

The wound had frozen shut in the instant the blade crossed it — both sides of the gash sealed in a thin white rime, like two slices of frost-touched glass laid against one another. The deadman stood where he was. His eyes were still open. He was still breathing out, the last of his air leaving him in a slow white plume. Then he was dead, and the plume thinned, and he was still.

"A fine sword," Ye Suli said.

His tone was that of a man tasting a new vintage.

Chu Shunhua did not acknowledge him.

The Kui Dragon Horn Sword swung sideways, level and unhurried, into the second deadman. This one was older, and knew his craft. He let his long knife fall, abandoned it, and came in low with two short halberds, one in each hand — the points ground in something that caught the moonlight with a faint blue bloom. Venom.

Chu Shunhua did not step back.

The left arm of the Ghost Warrior armor came up and took both halberd points against the vambrace of shadow-metal. Sparks spat. The blue-tinged tips skidded off the plate as if they had struck the side of a cliff, and the deadman had time to feel, in the small part of him that was still surprised, that the surface of the armor had not even been marked — not a scratch, not a chalk-line.

The Kui Dragon Horn Sword was already in his chest.

Through the heart and out the back, in a single line, as if the man had been a candle and the sword a needle pushed straight through the wax. The wound froze shut the same way. The deadman opened his mouth. What came out was breath, and a white cloud of it, and nothing more.

The third deadman ran.

Not for the door. For the window — the same calculation Ye Suli had made a heartbeat earlier. He had seen the shape of the night, and understood that the night was lost. But he had understood it half a beat too late.

He had covered two strides when the Kui Dragon Horn Sword left Chu Shunhua's hand.

Not thrown. Flung. The Regent Duke's wrist turned, and the sword left his grip with a low, hollow moan — as if the kui-dragon horn that gave the weapon its name had woken in the metal and was letting out one long note of rage. The amber blade crossed the chamber in a flat line, took the running man square between the shoulder blades, punched through his chest, and pinned him, arms spread, to a red-lacquered pillar three paces the other side.

The blade sank a good two inches into the wood. The hilt quivered. The deadman hung there, his toes an inch from the floor, and after a moment he hung still.

Three Zhongshan deadmen. From draw to silence, less than ten breaths.

Ye Suli did not look at the bodies.

He had not stopped looking at Chu Shunhua.

"Your sword is faster than the stories say," he said.

"And you are stupider than the stories say," Chu Shunhua replied.

"Oh?"

"Thirty men to take Tongtian Palace. Do you take the Jinwu Guard for furniture, or do you take me for a dead man?"

Ye Suli did not answer.

His body fell backward.

Not fell. Jumped. His shoulders struck the carved lattice of the window behind him, and the wood and paper came apart in a single breath, splinters and pale scraps whirling into the moonlight. He was already turning in the air. From his belt his left hand had drawn a length of thin cord, and the end of that cord was a small three-pronged iron grapnel, and the grapnel flew true and caught the upturned eave of the archive tower across the courtyard.

He swung on the cord the way a great gray bat might have swung, in another age, on the rigging of a merchantman. One long pendulum out of the second-story window, up over the courtyard stones, and in through a high casement of the three-story tower on the far side.

"After him," said a Jinwu officer, bursting through the door, knife half-drawn and already moving toward the broken window.

"No," said Chu Shunhua.

The officer stopped. Turned.

"He will not escape," Chu Shunhua said. "The farther he runs, the better for us."

The officer thought it through. A beat. Two. Then his face cleared. Ye Suli was the foreign minister of the Kingdom of Zhongshan. The foreign minister of a foreign kingdom, caught in the Xia Emperor's bedchamber in the small hours of the morning, with three of his own deadmen on the floor and a knife that had not been put down. Whether the attempt had succeeded or not was almost beside the point. The man was a walking declaration of war, and the longer he ran through the dark, the longer the Xia Dynasty's righteous fury had a face to chase.

"But Your Grace," the officer said, "if Zhongshan refuses to acknowledge him —"

"They will acknowledge him." Chu Shunhua crossed the chamber, took the hilt of the Kui Dragon Horn Sword in one gauntleted hand, and wrenched the blade free of the pillar. A small shower of red lacquer fell to the floor. The blood that had begun to thaw on the steel came away in a thin red slush. He cleaned the blade on his sleeve, and slid it home into the scabbard at his hip. "If they do not, the King of Zhongshan will be the first man to put a knife in him."

The chamber went quiet.

The three bodies lay where they had fallen. The frost along their wounds was already beginning to melt, and a slow dark water was gathering in the seams of the gilt brick, winding away in thin red threads across the floor.

In the corner of the room, against the foot of the dragon bed, Chu Zhaohua was curled into a ball. Knees drawn up. Arms wrapped around them. His shoulders hitched, hitched, hitched, in the small convulsions of a man who could not get sound out of his own throat.

Chu Shunhua walked toward him.

The Ghost Warrior boots were heavy. Each step landed on the gilt brick with a small, deliberate weight, and the sound of it moved across the chamber and reached the Emperor, and the Emperor shook harder.

"Zhaohua," Chu Shunhua said. He stood over his brother. He did not sit.

The Emperor did not look up. He did not want to see the armor, the visor, the bodies on the floor.

"Ge," he said at last. The word came out scraped, as if he had dug it out of the bottom of his throat with his fingernails. "Ge."

"Do you know what you did tonight?"

The Emperor's head snapped up. His face was streaked and swollen. His eyes moved without meaning, between his brother's visor and the three corpses and the red water on the floor. "I — I didn't — I didn't know he was going to —"

"You did not know?"

Chu Shunhua crouched. The armor's joints gave a low, oiled sound. He reached up and lifted the helm off his head, and set it, very carefully, on the floorboards beside his knee.

The moonlight found his face.

It was a face with five parts of the Emperor in it, and the other five parts were something else. The bones were harder. The cheekbones cut higher. The jaw was squarer, weathered, mapped with the fine tight lines that the wind of a hundred northern campaigns writes into a man's skin. The eye sockets were deeper, and the eyes that sat in them were dry, and very still, and of a kind that made a man think of a long corridor with no doors at the far end.

"He came into your chamber by the secret passage," Chu Shunhua said, speaking slowly, as if to a child who had not yet learned the shapes of the words. "He brought thirty men with him. The key to that passage is held by two men in the whole of Tongtian Palace. You. And Gao Dehai. He held a knife to your throat, and you — you lost control of yourself. Do you understand what that means?"

Chu Zhaohua's whole body flinched.

"It means Zhongshan has bought every man in this palace worth buying. It means there is only one step left between the Kingdom of Zhongshan and the entire Xia throne. And that step was you."

"I didn't —" Chu Zhaohua's voice cracked, and the tears began again, sliding through the grime on his face. "I only —"

"You only wanted to keep your throne. Ye Suli told you that if you played along — if you played a part in a small piece of theater — the West would see you sit on the Dragon Throne for another twenty years. That is what he told you. Am I wrong?"

Chu Zhaohua did not answer.

His mouth was open. The muscles of his face were jumping in small irregular spasms, as if something inside him were trying to tear its way out.

"Ge," he whispered. "Ge. You — you're going to depose me?"

"That depends," Chu Shunhua said, "on what you do next."

He stood. He picked up the helm. He set it back on the armor's neck-peg and locked the catch with a small click that carried, in the silence, like the click of a clock.

Then he turned, and walked toward the door.

At the threshold he stopped. He did not look back.

"Zhaohua."

Nothing.

"Tomorrow, you will leave the Qianqing Palace. You will move to the Western Garden. Until I say otherwise, you will not cross its wall."

The color went out of Chu Zhaohua's face, all at once, as if a candle had been blown out behind his skin.

"Ge! You cannot — I am the Emperor! I am the Emperor of Great Xia!" He slid off the dragon bed and onto his hands and knees on the gilt bricks and crawled toward the door, toward the retreating shape of his brother. "You cannot do this — you promised Father — you promised Mother —"

The Ghost Warrior armor passed under the lintel.

The moonlight caught the silver plating once. Then the corridor took him, and the dark took the silver, and there was nothing left in the doorway but the faint smell of cold steel and the sound of his footsteps, growing smaller, growing farther, until they were not a sound at all.

"Ge," Chu Zhaohua whispered. "Ge."

The word went on for a long time in the empty chamber. It thinned. It went out. The night wind through the broken window took the rest of it.

"Your Majesty." A Jinwu officer had come in from the side. He bent, took the Emperor gently by the arm, and tried to draw him to his feet. "Please, let me help you back to bed."

The Emperor looked up at the young face above him. His mouth worked. The lips moved. No sound came out. Then his eyes rolled back into his head, and he went limp, and the officer caught him under the arms and carried him back to the dragon bed and laid him down.

The officer straightened and let out a long breath.

Another officer came in through the side door, moving quickly. He leaned in to the first man's ear and spoke a string of low words.

"What?" The first officer's face changed. He turned on his heel and went out of the chamber at a pace just short of running.

"Your Grace!"

Chu Shunhua was halfway down the long outer corridor, the Ghost Warrior armor picking up a slow, regular chime of its own weight at every step. The officer's boots rang behind him on the stone.

"Your Grace — Gao Dehai has been taken. We searched his apartments. We found —"

He hesitated, as if reaching for the right shape of the sentence.

"We found what?"

"Three chests of gold. Twenty of silver. And —" The officer reached into his tunic and produced, with both hands, a roll of yellow silk tied with a cord. "A list."

Chu Shunhua took the silk. He untied the cord. He unrolled the silk.

The moonlight from the high corridor windows fell across the silk, and the names stood out, written in small, careful characters, row after row after row. Beside each name, three short lines: the office, the amount paid, the date.

Chu Shunhua read.

He read from the top of the roll to the bottom of the roll without moving his head, only his eyes. As he read, the color of his face went out — not in a rush, but slowly, degree by degree, as if the warmth were being drawn out of him by some long, patient hand.

"Li Chong'en," he read. "Vice Minister of War. Thirty thousand taels."

"Zhou Chengdong," he read. "Bureau Director, Ministry of Revenue. Twenty thousand taels."

"Zhao Yanzhi," he read. "Vice Commander, Imperial Guard. Fifty thousand taels."

His voice had dropped. It had also thinned. Each name, as it left his lips, fell into the corridor like a piece of ice dropped onto stone.

"And this one." The officer pointed to the last line of the roll, in a different ink, in a different, larger hand, as if the writer of the list had wanted to be sure this name was read. "Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review. Liu Mingyuan. One hundred thousand taels."

Liu Mingyuan.

Chu Shunhua closed his eyes.

The years came back. The long stone benches of the Imperial Academy, in the autumn, when the leaves of the old scholar-tree by the well came down. A young man with a scholar's cap set wrong on his head, laughing at something one of the other students had said. A young man who had taken third place in the Palace Examination under the late Emperor's own eye. A young man Chu Shunhua had drawn into his own service with his own two hands. A young man he had been certain, all the years since, was one of the few he did not have to watch.

"Your Grace?"

Chu Shunhua did not answer.

He rolled the silk up. He rolled it very tight. The motion was slow and precise, the motion of a man winding a cord around something that must not, no matter what, be allowed to come undone.

"Where is Gao Dehai now?"

"In the Jinwu Guard house, Your Grace."

"Take him to the imperial prison. Tell the wardens — by tomorrow morning, I want the name of every man on this list and the place where he can be found."

"Yes, Your Grace."

"And." Chu Shunhua paused. "Send men after Ye Suli."

"But, Your Grace, you said —"

"I did not say to take him. I said to watch him. To see where he runs. To see who he meets."

"Yes, Your Grace."

The officer turned to go, and Chu Shunhua's voice came once more, very quiet, very low.

"Feng Lin."

"Here, Your Grace."

A voice out of the shadows of the corridor. A shape unfolded from the place it had been standing, very still, against the wall. The Eastern black robe. The holy lotus badge at the throat, the inverted pentagram worked into it in a dark gold thread that drank the moonlight rather than catching it.

"You will go to Florence."

Feng Lin's head came up by a fraction. The eyes beneath the cowl were steady, but something in them moved.

"Now?"

"Now. Tell Cesare — Tongtian Palace has fallen into revolt. Ye Suli made his move tonight. He failed, but the part of the Xia intelligence he was carrying with him is still in his hands. The part that concerns the branch of the World Tree."

Feng Lin was quiet for a moment.

"I understand, Your Grace. I will leave at first light."

"No." Chu Shunhua said. "Tonight."

Feng Lin hesitated. "Your Grace, the palace has only just been secured. The city gates will be —"

"Which is why you will not go through the gates." Chu Shunhua reached into the breastplate of the Ghost Warrior armor, beside the Dragon-Sparrow seal, and drew out a small black token, struck through with the sigil of the Regent Duke's own seal. He held it out. "Take this to the Jinwu stables. Take the fastest horse there is. Ride out through the north gate. I will have the guard on that gate pulled back before you reach it."

Feng Lin took the token. He held it in his palm and looked at it for some time.

"Your Grace." He said it at last, very low. "You mean to bring Cesare to Luoyang?"

Chu Shunhua did not answer at once.

He had turned, in the last few paces, toward the end of the corridor. The corridor ended in a small octagonal platform, open to the sky, and from the eaves of the platform hung a number of small copper bells that the night wind was just stirring into a thin, irregular chime. From this height, the whole of Luoyang lay out beneath him, a long dark bowl pricked with a great scatter of small warm lights, as if someone had spilled a tin of fine gold leaf across a sheet of black velvet.

Farther out, on the western horizon, the lights stopped. Past the stop, past the edge of the Xia, was the West.

Chu Shunhua stood at the parapet and looked west.

"Cesare," he said, very softly, to no one in the corridor. To no one on the parapet. To the air, or the wind, or the figure he had already half-seen standing on a balcony in Florence, on the other side of the same night. "Cesare Borgia."

Feng Lin stood three paces behind. He could not quite make out the words his master was saying. But he caught the end of them, in the wind, as clearly as if they had been written in the air.

"Now, there is only the two of us."

"You have to come."

第224章 通天宫的叛乱（下）
