【中文】
第226章 维苏威火山的召唤（中）

改装蒸汽汽车在碎石山道上狂奔，蒸汽机的轰鸣被夜风撕碎，抛在车后的尘埃像一条灰黄色的尾巴。瓦莲京娜把油门踩到了底，金色的长发被风扯成一面白色的旗帜，但她双手稳得像焊在方向盘上。

警报声仍然在远处回荡。

"嗚——嗚——嗚——"

三声长鸣之后是两秒沉默，沉默之后又是三声。声音从东方的天际线传来，穿透夜风和引擎的噪音，像一根冰冷的铁钉楔入每个人的耳膜。那是神圣灾难警报——整个教皇国最高级别的紧急警报，触发条件只有一个：S级危险等级的欧米茄级能量信号。

唐璜把手搭在腰间蔷薇之鬼的备用短铳上，指节发白。他的嘴难得地闭上了，没有贫嘴。

佛朗哥教授坐在副驾驶的位置上——那个位置本该是西泽尔的，但佛朗哥坚持说"我需要看到路况"，语气不容反驳——他透过老花镜紧盯着前方，脸上的皱纹像是被刀刻出来的深谷。

"停。"他说。

瓦莲京娜没停，但松开了油门。

"我说停！"佛朗哥猛地拍了一下仪表板。

改装蒸汽汽车在碎石路上滑了十几米才停下来，蒸汽机发出一声嘶鸣，像一头被勒住脖子的野兽。车轮碾过碎石的尖锐声响在山谷里回荡了好几遍才渐渐消失。

前方的路面上，有什么东西在移动。

不是一辆车，不是一头野兽。是一个金色的影子。

它从路边的灌木丛后面探出头来，距离蒸汽汽车不到五十米。它的高度超过五米，全身覆盖着暗金色的装甲板，每一片甲板都在微弱地反光，像是有人把月亮碾碎了熔进金属里。它的头部呈流线型，面罩下露出两点翡翠色的冷光。

眼睛。

翡翠色的眼睛。

和马斯顿教堂里那台被铁棺封存的欧米茄一模一样——同样的暗金色装甲，同样的翡翠瞳孔，同样让人灵魂发颤的低频嗡鸣。八十二章的记忆像一道闪电劈进西泽尔的脑海：黑铁冰封棺被打开的瞬间，翡翠色的眼睛从黑暗中亮起，龙德施泰特将圣剑碎片嵌入它胸腔时它起身的恐怖画面。

此刻那个画面和眼前的影子完全重合。

"开车。"西泽尔说。

瓦莲京娜没踩油门。她盯着前方的影子，翡翠色的光也正在盯着她。

"动不了了。"瓦莲京娜说，声音很平，"它在看我们。"

那台欧米茄原型体没有动。它只是站在路中央，歪着头，像一头猎食者在打量猎物。它的关节发出极低频的嗡鸣，那种声音不是金属摩擦的，而是某种更深层的震动，像是地壳底下有东西在呼吸。

"教授。"阿方索从后排探过身来，声音压得很低。

佛朗哥教授的脸色变了。

不是苍白，而是一种灰败的、像是被抽走了所有血色的灰败。他的嘴唇动了动，老花镜后面的眼睛骤然放大了。

"不可能……"他喃喃道，手指攥紧了膝盖上的皮包，"这是欧米茄原型体。封存了四十年的欧米茄原型体。原罪机关到底做了什么？它们应该在维苏威火山深处……"

"教授。"西泽尔打断了他，"是几台？"

佛朗哥数了数影子。不是一台。

路两边的高坡上，低矮的灌木丛后面，山道的拐角处，到处都有暗金色的影子在闪动。它们像从地底冒出来的幽灵，沉默地站着，翡翠色的光点散布在整条山道的两侧，像是有人在山脊上撒了一把碧绿的萤火虫。

"七台。"佛朗哥的声音干涩，"不对……九台。还有更多在后面，我看不见。"

"通讯。"阿方索突然说了一声。

他伸出右手的机械臂，腕表上的微型机械蜘蛛探测天线旋转了一圈，发出一连串的电子嘀嘀声。然后他抬起手腕看了一眼，脸色沉了下来。

"整个翡冷翠的通讯系统都瘫痪了。军用频段、民用频段、密涅瓦专用频段，全是死信号。"他顿了顿，"有人在用宽频干扰幕覆盖了整片区域。"

"原罪机关？"唐璜问。

"不是原罪机关。"佛朗哥摇着头，"原罪机关没有能力同时瘫痪翡冷翠的通讯。这是欧米茄原型体群——它们就是移动的信号干扰源。那种S级能量信号在空气中弥漫，能直接烧穿所有电子设备的接收回路。"

他转过头来看着西泽尔，眼镜后面的目光里第一次出现了真正的恐惧。

"这是先遣部队。"他说，"真正的欧米茄原型体群，还在后面。"

西泽尔没有说话。他的手仍然扣在座椅边缘，指节发白，但他的脸上没有表情。

就在这时，前方那台欧米茄原型体动了。

它没有沿着大路走来，而是忽然从路边的灌木丛后面跃起——那个动作不像是一台五米高的重型机械，倒像是一头蹲伏已久的猎豹。暗金色的身影在月光下划出一道弧线，轰然落在改装蒸汽汽车前方不到十米的位置，碎石被它落地的冲击力震得四散飞溅。

"操！"唐璜猛地往后一缩。

那台欧米茄原型体落地之后没有停顿，直接抬起了一只手臂。

那只手足有蒸汽汽车的引擎盖那么大，暗金色的五根手指张开，像是五道铁闸。它朝着改装蒸汽汽车的引擎盖抓下来，速度快得几乎看不清动作，只有指节切开空气时带起的风压在挡风玻璃上刮出了一声尖锐的嘶响。

"昆提良！"阿方索吼道。

昆提良已经在动了。

他从后座探出半个身子，手里不知什么时候多了一柄枪。那是一把精钢和硬金铸成的手铳，枪管短粗如蜜蜂的腹部，管壁上密布着散热孔，在月光下泛着暗沉的金属光泽。蜂巢式手铳——密涅瓦机关为甲胄骑士配备的近身备用武器，射程不到三十米，但火力密集，一扣扳机就能把十几发硬金弹头倾泻到敌人脸上。

"砰！砰！砰！"

昆提良扣死了扳机。十几发硬金弹头带着灼热的尾焰砸在欧米茄原型体的面罩和胸甲上，发出密集的金属碰撞声，像是有人用铁锤猛敲铜钟。火花四溅，几颗弹头被弹飞出去，砸在路边的岩石上崩出了几道白痕。

但没有一颗弹头穿透那层暗金色的甲板。

那些硬金弹头打在欧米茄原型体的装甲上，就像是把石子丢进铁板——连凹痕都没留下。它们被甲板表面的硬度和光滑度直接弹开，叮叮当当地散落在碎石路面上，有的还在冒烟。

"打不穿！"昆提良的牙关咬得咯咯响。

欧米茄原型体根本不在乎那些子弹。

它甚至没有看昆提良一眼。那只巨手继续往下压，暗金色的指尖已经碰到了引擎盖的铁皮，金属与金属摩擦发出让人牙酸的尖啸。

"打它的手！"阿方索吼。

昆提良调整枪口，把剩下的弹匣朝着欧米茄原型体的手腕关节倾泻过去。弹头密集地砸在关节的缝隙处，溅出一连串的火花——但那层暗金色的甲板下面，仿佛有某种活着的东西在蠕动，那些被弹头撞击出的微小凹痕在几秒钟之内就自动修复了。

自愈神经纤维。

"没有用！它的甲会自己长回来！"昆提良的声音第一次带上了一丝慌急。

欧米茄原型体的手猛地往下压。

指尖碰到了车窗框的边缘，整辆改装蒸汽汽车被那股巨力压得猛地一震，底盘撞上了路面的碎石。车篷的帆布在压力下发出撕裂的声音，几根支撑用的铁管直接弯折了。

昆提良半个身子还探在车外。那只暗金色的巨手从他头顶不到半米的位置压下来，五根手指张开后的阴影已经把他整个人罩住了。指尖带起的风压把他的头发都压平了，衣领被那股气浪掀起来，拍在他脸上啪啪作响。

他能看到那只手的每一个细节——暗金色甲板上细密的纹路，指节处微微闪动的翡翠色光芒，还有掌心深处某个缝隙里透出的、像是心脏跳动般的低频脉动。

"昆提良！缩回来！"唐璜一把抓住他的后领往回拽。

但来不及了。

欧米茄原型体的五指开始合拢。

那不是人类抓握的动作，而是某种精密机械的闭合——五根暗金色的手指以不同的速度向内收拢，关节处的微型齿轮在月光下飞速旋转，像是一台运转中的精密车床。指尖距离昆提良的头顶不到二十厘米，金属表面散发的热量已经烫得他额前的头发都卷曲了。

然后方向盘动了。

不是瓦莲京娜踩刹车——她踩的是油门。

改装蒸汽汽车猛地蹿了出去，但不是朝前，而是朝右。瓦莲京娜把方向盘往右打死了，轮胎在碎石上发出一声尖锐的嘶叫，整辆车在惯性中侧倾了将近三十度，左侧的两个轮子离地，车身几乎是贴着碎石路面的斜面滑行过去的。

昆提良被甩回了车厢里，后脑勺撞在唐璜的胸口上，唐璜闷哼一声，两个人滚成了一团。

欧米茄原型体那只巨手从车顶上方半米的位置扫过，五根暗金色的指尖在月光下划过一道弧线，差一寸就要合拢。指节带起的风压把车篷残余的帆布碎片全部掀飞了，铁制的支撑管像面条一样被折弯，整辆车篷塌下去一半。

但改装蒸汽汽车没有停。

瓦莲京娜在车身回正的瞬间把方向盘打回正前方，油门踩到底，蒸汽机发出一声近乎破裂的嘶吼。改装蒸汽汽车像一头被鞭子抽醒的野马，轮胎碾着碎石疯狂旋转，朝前方那段空出来的路面直冲过去。

欧米茄原型体没有追上来。

它站在原地，歪着头，翡翠色的眼睛盯着远去的改装蒸汽汽车。它似乎并不着急。它只是抬起那只抓空了的手，看了看自己的指节——指尖的缝隙里还夹着几片帆布碎片和一截弯曲的铁管。

它把那些碎片弹掉了。

然后它转过身，暗金色的身影慢慢融入了路边的黑暗中，像是一头吃饱了的猎豹，懒洋洋地走回了自己的领地。

唐璜从昆提良身上爬起来，摸了一把自己的脸，手心全是冷汗。

"它……它为什么不追？"他问，声音有点发飘。

"因为它不需要追。"佛朗哥教授说，声音沙哑得像砂纸刮过木板，"先遣部队的任务不是消灭目标，是标记目标。它已经记住了我们的信号特征。"

"什么意思？"昆提良揉着后脑勺坐直了身子。

佛朗哥转过身来看着他们，老花镜后面的眼睛里倒映着车窗外不断闪过的暗金色光点。那些光点散布在道路两侧的高坡上，像是一群无声的猎犬在等待猎物精疲力竭。

"意思是，"他说，"真正的欧米茄原型体群会循着这个信号追过来。不是一台两台，是——"

他没说下去。

车里安静了三秒。

"必须尽快找到薇若兰。"西泽尔说。

他的声音仍然平静，像是翡冷翠秋天的风一样没有温度。但他的手已经从座椅边缘松开了，转而握成了拳头，放在膝盖上。指节收得很紧，关节处的皮肤泛着白。

"拿到世界树残枝样本，阻止原罪机关主人。"

没有人反驳。

改装蒸汽汽车继续在山道上狂奔。没有了车篷的遮挡，夜风毫无遮拦地灌进车厢，把每个人的头发都吹得乱七八糟。引擎的嘶鸣声和风声混在一起，像是某种野兽临死前的哀嚎。佛朗哥教授从皮包里摸出那张折叠的纸——维苏威火山内部结构勘测第三版图纸——在颠簸中展开，手指沿着图纸上的等高线滑动。

"从这里到维苏威火山还有十七公里。"他说，"按照现在的速度，至少需要二十分钟。"

"二十分钟后那些东西就会追上来。"阿方索看了一眼腕表上的通讯界面，全是灰白色的死信号。

"不会追上来。"佛朗哥摇头，"它们不会进入维苏威火山的核心区域。"

"为什么？"

"因为那里是世界树残枝的所在地。"佛朗哥说，手指点了点图纸上那个用红色圆圈标注的位置，"欧米茄原型体是它结出的果实，果实不会攻击母体。"

车里又安静了。

"有多少了？"阿方索低声问，目光扫向车窗外的山坡。

唐璜从塌掉一半的车篷缝隙里探出头去数了数。他的眼睛在月光下眯成一条线，盯着远处那些不断浮现的暗金色光点。

"二十……三十……我数不清了，"他缩回脑袋，喉结动了一下，"后面整片山都在发光。"

瓦莲京娜握着方向盘，指节发白。她的目光盯着前方的路，但视线似乎穿过了路面、穿过了山体，落在了某个更远的地方。风吹动她金色的长发，忍冬的香气和蒸汽的味道混在一起飘进车厢。

然后她开口了。

"我知道一条小路。"

所有人都看向她。

"可以更快到达维苏威火山。"她说，声音很稳，"我母亲当年带我来翡冷翠的时候走的那条路。"

唐璜张了张嘴。

"你母亲？"

"我母亲是锡兰人。"瓦莲京娜说，"她带着我逃出锡兰的时候，走的就是这条难民路线。沿着山脊往东，穿过那片废弃的采石场，从侧面绕到维苏威火山的北麓。路很窄，但那些东西追不上来。"

她顿了顿。

"因为那条路是给难民走的。难民不会走大路。"

阿方索已经在看地图了。他的机械臂在腕表上投射出一片全息地形图，佛朗哥的维苏威火山图纸和他记忆中的翡冷翠周边地形重叠在一起，很快标出了一条蜿蜒的细线，从他们当前的位置绕过维苏威火山的南侧，穿过一片标注为"废弃采石场"的灰色区域，最后从北麓接入一条通往火山口的窄路。

"有这条路。"阿方索说，"但地图上标注的是'季节性便道，雨季不可通行'。"

"现在是旱季。"瓦莲京娜说。

她没有说更多。但车里没有人追问。一个叶尼塞公主的母亲带着女儿从锡兰逃出来，走的不是大路，不是官道，而是刻在骨头里的难民小径——这里面藏着什么样的故事，在场每个人都猜得到，但没有人会在这个时候问出来。

"走。"西泽尔说。

改装蒸汽汽车猛地右转，冲出了碎石山路，驶入了一条几乎被灌木完全覆盖的野径。瓦莲京娜对这条路的熟悉程度超出了所有人的预期——每一个弯道、每一处坑洼、每一段需要减速的碎石坡她都了然于胸。蒸汽汽车在暗夜的野径上像一条灵活的黑鱼，钻过灌木丛的缝隙，越过干涸的溪床，沿着山脊的走向一路向东。

车窗外，那些暗金色的光点渐渐被抛在了后面。它们似乎不愿意离开大路太远，翡翠色的眼睛在山脊的边缘闪烁了一阵，然后一个一个地熄灭了，像是被风吹灭的烛火。

"它们不追了。"唐璜说。

"不是不追。"佛朗哥说，"是它们还没接到命令。先遣部队的标记信号需要时间传回主群。等真正的欧米茄原型体群收到信号——"

他没说下去，但意思已经很清楚了。

改装蒸汽汽车在野径上又行驶了大约十分钟。路越来越窄，坡度越来越大，两侧的山壁向内合拢，像是在挤压这条最后的通道。蒸汽机的嘶鸣在岩壁间来回反射，变成一种沉闷的、像是从地底传来的轰鸣。

然后瓦莲京娜踩下了刹车。

改装蒸汽汽车在山脊的最高点停了下来。蒸汽机喘息着，白色的蒸汽从车底的排气管里喷出来，消散在夜风中。没有了车篷的车身在山风中微微晃动，金属框架发出细碎的咯吱声。

前方，维苏威火山的轮廓在夜色中浮现。

它比翡冷翠的任何建筑都要庞大，像是一头蛰伏了千年的巨兽，山体的轮廓在星光下呈现出一种沉甸甸的黑色。火山口的边缘像是被什么巨力撕开了一样，参差不齐的岩壁在月光下投下深深的阴影。

但那不是让人屏住呼吸的原因。

维苏威火山的山顶——那个本该是岩浆翻涌的火山口——正在发出金色的光。

那不是火光。不是岩浆的光。

那是某种更冷、更锐利、更古老的光。金色的光从火山口里涌出来，沿着山体的裂缝向四面八方流淌，像是有人把融化的黄金倒进了大山的血管里。光线的强度在不断变化，时而微弱像是残烛，时而又猛地暴涨，把整座火山的轮廓都照得清清楚楚。山体上每一道裂缝、每一块突出的岩石、每一片剥落的火山灰都在那道光里投下了清晰的影子。

在那些光线的照耀下，可以看到维苏威火山的周围有无数暗金色的身影在移动。它们从火山口里涌出来，像莲花的花瓣从花心里一片一片地展开，沿着山坡向下蔓延，铺满了整座火山的山体。

不是几十台。

不是几百台。

是——数不清。

暗金色的光点从山顶一直铺到山脚，像是有人在维苏威火山的身上披了一件由活体金属铸成的铠甲。每一台欧米茄原型体都在缓慢地移动，翡翠色的眼睛在金光的照耀下闪烁着冰冷的光芒。它们的低频嗡鸣汇聚在一起，变成了一种持续的、像是地壳在呻吟的震颤，连脚下的岩石都在微微发抖。

唐璜张了张嘴，又合上了。他罕见地没有说出任何俏皮话。

佛朗哥教授摘下老花镜，用衣角擦了擦镜片，又戴了回去。他的手在抖。

"世界树残枝……"他喃喃道，"它苏醒了。三百年的封印，被撕开了。"

西泽尔盯着维苏威火山山顶那道金色的光，拳头攥得死紧。后颈的黄金套管在发烫，热度沿着脊椎向上蔓延，一直烧到了后脑勺，像是有什么东西在他的神经通路里猛烈地跳动。

他知道那是什么。

那是世界树残枝。

那是被封存了三百年的、足以改写整个世界命运的东西。

在所有人之前，它先醒了。

瓦莲京娜转过头来看着他，金色的长发垂在肩头，忍冬香气和蒸汽的味道混在一起，在夜风中飘散。她的目光平静，但平静的底下压着某种滚烫的东西。

"准备好了吗？"她问。

西泽尔没有回答。

他推开了车门。

【English】
Chapter 226 — The Summons of Vesuvius (II)

The modified steam-car slewed around a bend in the gravel road and the boiler answered with a shriek like a soul being dragged out by the roots. Valentina had the throttle buried in the floorboards. Her hair — that impossible pale gold — was streaming back from her face in a single white sheet, but her hands on the wheel did not move. They had been welded there, it seemed, at the foundry.

The night tore the engine's noise to pieces and threw it behind them in a yellow-grey ribbon of dust.

And through the dust, that sound.

Uuu — uuu — uuu —

Three long notes, two seconds of silence, three long notes again. It came off the eastern skyline, cut through the wind and the boiler's clatter, slid into each ear like a cold iron nail being driven home.

The Sacred Disaster Alarm. The highest emergency the Papal States could declare. There was exactly one trigger for it: an S-class Omega energy signature.

Don Juan's hand had found the grip of his spare pistol, the Phantom Rose, before the first note had finished sounding. His knuckles were the colour of cut bone. For once, he was not talking. That alone said everything that needed to be said about how afraid he was.

Professor Franco sat in the passenger seat — Cesare's seat, but Franco had insisted on it with the particular gentle immovability of a man who has outlived most of the things that kill younger men, and said he needed to see the road. He was squinting forward through his reading-glasses, the deep channels of his face caught in the headlights of the steam-car, and the deeper channels inside those.

"Stop," he said.

Valentina did not stop. She eased her foot off the throttle.

"I said stop."

Franco slapped the dashboard with the flat of his hand.

The steam-car slid on the loose stone for a dozen metres before it came to rest, the boiler releasing a hiss like a beast with a rope around its throat. The grit of the tyres rang in the valley, and was answered, faintly, by something else. Something below. Something ahead.

It was not a vehicle. It was not an animal. It was a shape of gold.

It stepped out from behind a low tangle of scrub no more than fifty paces ahead of them, and it stood in the road. Five metres of it. Plates of darkened gold sheathed it from crown to heel, and each plate caught a little of the moonlight and gave it back, so that the thing seemed to have been made by melting down the moon and pouring it into a mould. Its head was streamlined, featureless save for a faceplate, and in the dark of that faceplate two points of jade-green light.

Eyes.

Jade eyes.

The same eyes.

The memory hit Cesare like a black iron door flung open in his chest. Marston. Eighty-two chapters ago, although he had not known at the time it was a chapter at all. The black iron sarcophagus under the church. The seal broken. The jade gaze opening out of nothing. Rohnstedt slotting the relic-blade of the Holy Lance into its chest, and the thing rising — a god-awful slow-motion unfolding of metal and intent.

That memory and the shape before him were a perfect overlay. The same dark gold. The same jade. The same low hum beneath hearing, beneath sound, that made the marrow of his teeth itch.

"Drive," Cesare said.

Valentina did not press the throttle. She was staring at the shape, and the shape was staring back at her.

"It won't let me," she said, very calmly. "It's watching us."

The prototype did not advance. It stood in the middle of the road and tilted its head, the way a predator tilts its head when the prey has done something unexpected. From its joints came that sub-audible hum, but it was not the hum of metal on metal; it was deeper, slower, as if somewhere under the road the earth's crust had begun to breathe.

"Professor," Alfonso said from the back, leaning forward between the seats, his voice low. "Professor."

The colour went out of Franco's face. Not the pallor of fear. Something worse — the grey of a man who has just seen a thing he had been quietly certain he would never see. His lips moved. Behind his glasses his eyes went wide.

"Impossible," he said. His fingers closed on the leather briefcase in his lap and would not let it go. "That's the Omega prototype. The sealed one. Forty years sealed. What has the Bureau of Original Sin done — they should still be in the deep of Vesuvius, they should be—"

"Professor." Cesare cut him off. "How many?"

Franco began to count. Not this one. The others.

The hills on both sides of the road were low and scrubby, but the scrub was no longer empty. Out of it, on the high ground, at the bends of the road, behind the stones, shapes of darkened gold were standing in the dark, perfectly still. Their jade eyes were lit. From this angle, this distance, they looked like someone had walked along the ridge and scattered a fistful of cold green fireflies into the long grass.

"Seven," Franco said, and his voice was sand on wood. "No — nine. There are more behind. I cannot count them all."

"Comms," Alfonso said.

He lifted his right arm. The mechanical one. The miniature mechanical spider at the cuff spun its antenna in a quick circle and delivered a long unhappy chatter of bleeps. He read the result on the dial and his face closed.

"Florence is dark," he said. "Military band, civilian band, Minerva's private bands — every channel is dead. Someone has thrown a wide-band interference curtain over the whole region."

"The Bureau of Original Sin?" Don Juan asked.

"No." Franco shook his head. "The Bureau cannot do that. Not on this scale. These prototypes are the interference. The S-class energy in the air is cooking every receiver in range. Their very presence is the jamming."

He turned in his seat to look at Cesare, and the thing Cesare saw in his eyes, in the flicker of the headlights off his glasses, was not the look of a man who was afraid of being killed. It was the look of a man who had just understood the shape of the disaster he was in.

"This is the advance guard," he said. "The true swarm is still behind us."

Cesare said nothing. His hand was still on the edge of his seat, and his knuckles were still white, and his face was still a mask. He held it that way. He held it the way his mother had taught him to hold it, in a different life, before the world of gears and blood.

Then the prototype at the centre of the road moved.

It did not walk towards them. It leapt.

From a crouch behind a thicket, the entire five metres of it uncoiled like the body of a cat that has been waiting a long time, and the next second it was in the air. It came down no more than ten paces in front of the steam-car, and the gravel went out from under it in a fan of white stones, struck flat by the impact. The percussion rolled back through the chassis and into Cesare's teeth.

"Christ—" Don Juan threw himself backwards in his seat.

The prototype did not pause. It raised one arm.

The hand at the end of the arm was the size of the bonnet of the steam-car. Five fingers of dark gold spread like five iron gates. It came down towards them so fast the eye could not quite track it; what reached Cesare first was the wind of it, the displaced air screaming across the windscreen in a high thin whistle.

"Quintilian!" Alfonso shouted.

Quintilian was already moving.

He had half-risen out of his seat in the back, and there was a pistol in his hand that had not been there a moment ago. A stubby thing, the barrel not much longer than a man's thumb, the metal dark and heavy, the wall of it pitted with cooling holes. A hive-pattern sidearm — the Minerva Bureau's last-ditch answer for an armoured knight caught at close quarters. Thirty paces of useful range, but at this range it was a hose. He pulled the trigger and held it.

Bam bam bam bam bam.

A dozen rounds of hardened gold spat out in a single stammering burst, the muzzle-flash washing the inside of the car with orange light. The slugs hit the prototype's faceplate and chest in a rising hammer of impacts, sparks spraying sideways off the dark gold as if someone had taken a hammer to a cathedral bell. Two of the rounds went ricocheting off into the rocks at the roadside and left white scars in the stone.

Not one round went through.

The bullets were bouncing off that plating the way a child throws pebbles at an iron door — they left no mark, no dimple, nothing. They tinkled to the gravel at the prototype's feet, some of them still smoking.

"Can't pierce it!" Quintilian said through his teeth.

The prototype did not look at him. It was not interested in the pistol. The hand kept coming down.

"Aim for the joints!" Alfonso was shouting. "The joints!"

Quintilian hauled the muzzle down and emptied what was left of the magazine into the wrist. The bullets cracked into the seams of the plating and threw up a chain of sparks, and for a moment Cesare thought he saw the plating give — a hairline dimple, no more — and then the dimple closed. The metal flowed back into itself like water finding its level. The faintest jade pulse moved through the joint and was gone.

Self-healing nerve-fibre. The Bureau of Original Sin had written about it in the file Cesare had memorised when he was fourteen. The Bureau had called it a rumour then.

"Nothing's getting through," Quintilian said, and his voice had gone up half a register. "It heals as fast as I dent it—"

The prototype's hand slammed down.

The fingertips hit the edge of the windscreen frame. The whole car lurched sideways, the chassis struck the gravel with a sound like a breaking rib, and the canvas roof took the next of it. The canvas screamed. One of the iron staves that held it up bent like wet cane. Then another.

Quintilian was still half out of the car. The hand was above him. The dark-gold fingers, spread, made a shadow the size of a chapel floor. The wind of them had pressed his hair flat against his skull. His collar was flapping in the air of the descent and slapping his face.

He could see every detail of the hand, that close. The fine grain of the dark-gold plate. The faint green pulse moving through the knuckles. The slow steady throb in the palm — a heartbeat, a mechanical heartbeat, a thing that should not have had a heart.

"Quintilian — get back!" Don Juan caught him by the scruff of the coat and hauled.

The fingers began to close.

It was not a human closing of the hand. It was the closing of a machine — five fingers of dark gold folding inward at five different speeds, the little gears in the knuckles turning fast enough to throw moonlight off them, the whole apparatus functioning with the oily precision of a watchmaker's bench. The fingertips were twenty centimetres above Quintilian's crown. The heat of the metal was curling the hair at his temples.

Then the wheel moved.

Not Valentina's foot on the brake. Her foot was on the throttle.

The steam-car went sideways. The wheel came hard over to the right and stayed there, the tyres screaming in the gravel, and the whole machine tilted onto its left side until it was running on two wheels and the edge of the chassis, sliding along the road at a steep angle, the underbody grinding a furrow in the loose stone. Quintilian was thrown back into the cabin and the back of his head cracked into Don Juan's chest, and the two of them ended in a single heap on the floor.

Above them, the hand.

The dark-gold fingers swept over the roof of the car a hand's breadth clear, drawing a half-moon of empty air as the steam-car passed beneath. The canvas that was left of the roof was lifted clean off, and the bent staves folded over like tinfoil in a forge.

But the steam-car did not stop.

Valentina got the wheel back to centre as the chassis came down, slammed the throttle to the boards, and the boiler answered with a noise that was not a noise — it was the sound a kettle makes when it has decided to die. The car lunged forward through the gap the prototype had left in the road, gravel spitting out behind it, and was gone.

The prototype did not follow.

It stood in the road where it had stood, and it tilted its head, and it watched the red sparks of the steam-car's exhaust dwindle down the pass. It lifted the hand that had missed. There was a flap of torn canvas between two of the fingers. There was the bent half of an iron stave. It considered these, the way a man considers a fish that got off the hook.

It flicked the debris away.

Then it turned, unhurried, and walked back into the dark at the side of the road the way a fed leopard walks back into its own country.

Don Juan pulled himself up off Quintilian and put a hand to his own face. It came away wet. He looked at his palm in the dark. Cold sweat.

"Why—" his voice was a thread. "Why didn't it follow?"

"Because it does not need to." Franco's voice was the voice of a man who has not slept in two days. "The advance guard is not for killing. It is for marking. It has recorded our energy signature."

"What does that mean?" Quintilian sat up, rubbing the back of his skull.

Franco turned in his seat to look at them. The light from outside was moving now — a slow drift of dark-gold glow along the high ground on either side of the road, the jade eyes of prototypes pacing them, low and patient, like hounds that knew exactly where the deer was.

"It means," he said, "the true swarm will follow this signature back to us. Not one. Not two."

He did not finish the sentence.

The car was quiet for three full seconds.

"Then we find Violante," Cesare said.

His voice was level. It had the temperature of the Florentine autumn — no temperature at all. But his hand had left the edge of the seat. It was in his lap now, and it was a fist, and the knuckles of it were pressed so hard into the fabric that the cloth had gone the colour of bone.

"We get the Yggdrasil Remnant. We stop the master of the Bureau of Original Sin."

No one contradicted him.

The steam-car kept climbing. Without the canvas roof the night came into the cabin unmixed, and the wind tore at every loose thing in it. Hair, scarves, the corners of the map Franco had spread on his knees. The boiler's shriek and the wind together made a single long wail, the sound an animal makes when it knows it is being hunted.

Franco took the folded paper out of his briefcase — the third-edition survey of Vesuvius's interior — and worked it open on his lap. The car jolted. The paper tried to fold itself again. He weighted the corners with his thumbs and rode it out, his eyes following the contour lines.

"Seventeen kilometres from here to the mouth of Vesuvius," he said. "At this speed, twenty minutes."

"The swarm will be on us in twenty minutes," Alfonso said, without looking up from the dead dial of his wrist.

"No," said Franco. "They will not come into the deep of Vesuvius."

"Why not?"

"Because that is where the Remnant is." Franco put his finger on the red circle drawn on the map. "The prototypes are its fruit. Fruit does not attack the tree."

The car was quiet again.

"How many now?" Alfonso asked. He was looking past Don Juan, out at the hillside.

Don Juan put his head up through the gap where the canvas used to be. The night came at him cold and the wind flattened his eyes. Down the road, on both sides, the dark-gold shapes were moving with them, parallel, keeping their distance, the jade points of them shining in the long grass like a second, lower constellation.

"Twenty," he said. "Thirty. I can't—" He swallowed. "The whole back of the hill is lit up."

Valentina's hands on the wheel were white at the knuckles. She was looking at the road, but Cesare had the sense that she was looking through the road, through the rock under the road, at something further off. The wind moved her pale hair across her shoulder. The smell of honeysuckle that was always somewhere on her, and the smell of hot steam, came into the cabin in a single breath.

Then she spoke.

"I know a shorter way."

They all looked at her.

"A way to reach Vesuvius faster." Her voice was very steady. "The road my mother took when she brought me out of Ceylon."

Don Juan opened his mouth.

"Your mother?"

"My mother was a Ceylonese." Valentina did not look at him. "When she brought me out, we did not take the imperial road. We took the refugee road. Along the ridge to the east, through the abandoned quarries, and round to the north flank of Vesuvius. It is narrow. They will not be able to follow us there."

She paused.

"Refugees do not take the main road."

Alfonso was already working. He raised his mechanical arm and the wristpiece threw a small blue ghost of terrain against the roofless cabin — a holographic map, layered over the memory of the countryside he had been raised in. Franco's survey of Vesuvius slid into it. A thin white line appeared, winding east, climbing, then south-east, dropping into a wedge of land marked in grey, then climbing again, and finally meeting the red circle of the crater from the north.

"The path is here," Alfonso said. "But the map labels it 'seasonal track, impassable in rains.'"

"It is the dry season," Valentina said.

She did not say anything else. No one asked her to. The story of a Yenisei princess's mother, fleeing Ceylon with a small girl on her back, taking neither road nor imperial highway but the path that only the desperate know — they could each of them feel the shape of it without being told, and none of them were the kind of man who would pry it open at the gallop.

"Go," Cesare said.

The steam-car slewed right, off the gravel and into a track so narrow that the scrub tore at both flanks. Valentina drove it as if she had driven it before. She had not, but her hands knew it — every bend, every pothole, every patch of loose scree that needed a breath off the throttle, came to her the way a familiar song comes. The car plunged into the dark of the track like a black fish into a deeper current, threading between the bushes, fording a dry streambed, climbing the spine of the ridge towards the east.

Behind them, on the proper road, the dark-gold lights hesitated. They drew up at the edge of the track, jade eyes blinking in the scrub, and one by one, as if on a quiet order, they went out. Like a row of candles being snuffed.

"They have stopped," Don Juan said, after he had watched this for a long minute.

"They have not stopped," Franco said. "They have not yet been given the order. The mark the advance guard has left on us must travel back to the swarm. When the swarm receives it—"

He did not finish. He did not need to.

The car went on. Ten minutes more. The track narrowed and the slopes on either side rose up, leaning in on them, and the wind that funnelled between them made the boiler's voice a long, low, organ-like moan, as if the mountain itself were singing under its breath.

Then Valentina put her foot on the brake.

The steam-car stopped on the spine of the ridge. The boiler coughed out its white breath into the dark. The bare metal frame of the cabin, where the canvas was gone, creaked in the wind. The whole car rocked on its springs like a small boat in a slow swell.

Below them, Vesuvius.

It was larger than any building in Florence, larger than the cathedral, larger than the domes and the towers and the walls put together. It lay along the southern horizon the way a sleeping animal lies, and the outline of it was the outline of something that had been there for a very long time and was not yet done. The lip of the crater was ragged, torn, the rock of it dark and uneven, the shadows inside the lip deep enough to lose a man in.

That was not the reason Cesare stopped breathing.

The crater was lit.

The light that came out of it was gold, but it was not the gold of fire. It was not the gold of any forge or any furnace. It was a colder, thinner, older gold, the kind of gold you see in old icons when the gilt has cracked and the light comes through the cracks in long, slow, deliberate lines. The light was pouring up out of the crater, and as Cesare watched, it began to run down the slopes. It traced every fault in the rock. It found every crack. It lit every loose flake of volcanic ash on the side of the mountain and threw its shadow outward, so that the whole bulk of Vesuvius seemed to be drawn in lines of gold and lines of black, an etching of itself, a diagram.

And in that gold light, shapes were moving.

They were coming up out of the crater as if the crater were a flower opening, the dark-gold petals of them unfolding one by one from the centre, spreading outward, down the slope, on every side. Not in ranks. Not in any order a man could read. They were simply emerging, and once emerged, they began to move, slowly, with the unhurried patience of a thing that knows it has all the time there is.

Not dozens.

Not hundreds.

Cesare could not count them.

The dark-gold bodies covered the mountain from crown to foot. They gave the mountain a second skin, a moving skin, each of them with its two jade points of light glowing steadily through the gold haze. The low hum of them all — every one of those sub-audible heartbeats — had climbed out of the range of any single ear and become a single sustained vibration in the ground under Cesare's boots, the kind of vibration you feel in your sternum when a cathedral organ is played in a small room.

Don Juan opened his mouth. Closed it. He did not say a word.

Franco took off his reading-glasses. He cleaned them on the tail of his coat. He put them on again. His hand, Cesare noticed, was shaking.

"The Remnant," Franco said, almost to himself. "It has woken. The seal of three hundred years. It has been broken."

Cesare did not answer. He was looking at the gold light on the mountain. The heat he had felt in his collar all evening was climbing again — out of the gold conduit set into the back of his neck, down the channel that the Bureau of Original Sin had cut into his spine when he was a boy, up into the base of his skull, where it settled and beat. He knew what it was. He had always known what it was.

The Remnant was calling him.

It had woken before any of them.

Valentina turned in her seat. The wind had laid her pale hair across one shoulder. The honeysuckle and the steam came off her together. Her face was very still, and under the stillness there was something else — something that ran hot, the way steel runs hot just before it remembers it is steel.

"Are you ready?" she said.

Cesare did not answer.

He opened the door.

第227章 维苏威火山的召唤（下）

【中文】
第227章 维苏威火山的召唤（下）

夜风从山顶灌下来，带着一股烧焦矿石的呛味。

西泽尔站在改装蒸汽汽车的车门前，望着维苏威火山的轮廓。整座山在呼吸，金色的光从火山口涌出来，沿着山脊向四面流淌，像是大地裂开了一道口子，底下是滚烫的太阳。山坡上密布着暗金色的光点，欧米茄原型体仍在缓慢移动，但它们并没有向山脚涌来，只是围成一圈又一圈，像是花瓣簇拥着花心。

"不走正面。"佛朗哥教授在车里说，"从北麓的旧矿道进去。那是三百年前密涅瓦机关修建的备用通道，只有初代总工程师知道路线。"

瓦莲京娜转动方向盘，礼车掉头，沿着山脊的碎石小路向西北方向疾驰。碎石打在车底板上噼啪作响，车身剧烈颠簸，金色的忍冬花瓣在颠簸中从瓦莲京娜的发间掉落。唐璜伸手接住了一片，凑到鼻尖闻了闻，没说话，又放回了瓦莲京娜的肩头。

山路越来越窄，两侧的岩石越来越黑，像是被什么烧焦过。瓦莲京娜把车灯关掉，改用甲胄的夜视模式，红外光把前方的路照成一片惨白。

"这里。"佛朗哥教授忽然说。

瓦莲京娜踩下刹车。

前方是一面看似普通的岩壁，高约八米，宽约十二米，灰黑色的火山岩和周围的岩石没有区别。但西泽尔注意到了一个细节：岩壁的正中央，嵌着一枚拳头大小的铜质徽记。六只翅膀的猫头鹰，每只翅膀上布满了细密的齿轮纹路。六翼猫头鹰——密涅瓦机关的徽记。

徽记下方，还有一枚更小的徽记，几乎被铜锈覆盖：齿轮中心嵌着一颗五芒星，五芒星的五个角末端各连接着更小的一圈齿轮。

两个徽记，一上一下，刻在同一块岩石上。

"那不是密涅瓦的标志。"阿方索走近岩壁，眉头皱起，"第二个徽记——齿轮嵌五芒星——我见过这个图案，在密涅瓦最深的档案库里。但从来没有记录说这个图案和密涅瓦有什么关系。"

"因为它不该和密涅瓦有关系。"佛朗哥教授说，"那是蒸汽机械神教的教徽。三百年前密涅瓦初创时期，初代总工程师同时也是机械神教的核心成员。密涅瓦机关和机械神教从一开始就是一体两面。"

西泽尔走上前，伸手触碰那枚六翼猫头鹰徽记。金属冰凉，表面布满铜绿色的锈斑，但触碰到的一瞬间，后颈的黄金套管猛地一烫。

他收回手，注视着徽记下方的一行小字。字迹被风化得模糊了，但借助车灯的微光仍能辨认——那是拉丁文，刻得很深：

"QUI SCRUTATUR ABYSsum ABYSSUM INVENIT."

谁窥探深渊，深渊便来迎他。

"有密码盘。"唐璜蹲下身，在徽记左侧的岩石缝隙里发现了一个凹陷的圆盘。圆盘边缘刻着二十六个拉丁字母，可以旋转。

佛朗哥教授走过来，沉默了片刻，说："初代总工程师的名字。"

"达·芬奇·波吉亚。"西泽尔说。

他蹲下身，手指按住圆盘，一个字母一个字母地旋转。D-A-V-I-N-C-I-B-O-R-G-I-A。

最后一个字母归位的瞬间，整个岩壁发出一声低沉的轰鸣。

那不是机械的声音，更像是大地深处某根琴弦被拨动了。岩壁正中央的徽记开始发光，不是红水银的冷光，而是一种暗金色的、温暖的脉动，像是心跳。光芒从徽记向四周蔓延，沿着岩壁上那些肉眼几乎看不见的细纹流淌，最终勾勒出一个巨大的圆。

圆内的岩石无声地向两侧裂开，露出了一条黑漆漆的通道。

"进去之后把入口重新关上。"佛朗哥教授说，"从里面关。"

西泽尔点了点头，率先走了进去。瓦莲京娜跟在他身后，礼车开不进去，她把车停在了通道口外面，拔下车钥匙揣进口袋。唐璜犹豫了一下，拍了拍引擎盖："好车。等我们出来。"

昆提良和阿方索殿后。在昆提良的脚踏进通道的那一瞬间，身后沉重的岩壁缓缓合拢，黑暗吞没了一切。

"灯。"西泽尔说。

瓦莲京娜打开甲胄的近距照明，一束惨白的光劈开黑暗。通道很窄，仅容两人并肩通过，墙壁粗糙，到处是开凿时留下的工具痕迹。空气干燥，带着一股陈年的铁锈味和隐约的机油气味。

走了大约五十米，通道向左拐了一个弯。

弯道过后，墙壁忽然变了。

不再是粗糙的火山岩，而是一面平整的、被打磨过的黑色玄武岩。玄武岩上刻满了东西。

"天哪。"唐璜低声说。

那是壁画。

不是一幅两幅，而是从脚底一直延伸到目光所不能及的远方。整条通道的墙壁都是画布，黑色玄武岩上用暗金色和银白色的矿物颜料描绘着连绵不断的画面。

最靠近入口的一幅，画的是一棵树。

不是普通的树。那是一棵巨大的、遮天蔽日的金属树，树干是暗金色合金，树冠展开如伞盖，树枝的末梢挂着一颗颗散发着微光的圆形果实——红水银核心。树叶是一片片大小不一的金色齿轮，所有的齿轮都在缓慢转动，发出极轻的嗡鸣。

画面的底部刻着两个词。

WORLD TREE.

世界树。

"继续看。"佛朗哥教授的声音从背后传来，带着一丝难以抑制的颤抖。

第二幅画紧挨着第一幅。画的是一座城市，但那不是翡冷翠，不是君士坦丁堡，也不是任何一座人类已知的城市。城市里没有街道，没有房屋，没有教堂。取而代之的是无数条金属管道和齿轮机械，它们从世界树的根部延伸出来，盘旋交错，形成了一个巨大而精密的网络。网络的核心是世界树，树冠展开处有一个圆形的金色光晕，光晕中隐约可见一个站立的人影。

画面的底部刻着：MACHINA DEI.

机械神国。

西泽尔的脚步停了一拍。

第三幅画。

圆形的中心不再是城市或建筑，而是一个人的背影。那人站在世界树前，双手按在树干上，从他的肩膀和脊背延伸出无数条金色的线，连接着周围所有的齿轮和管道。他的眼睛是紫色的，瞳孔中心有一道金色的纹路。

画的底部刻着一行拉丁文，字体比前两幅都大：

"PERFECTUS NUNTIUS."

完美神使。

西泽尔站在那幅画前，一动不动。

画中人的背影和西泽尔几乎一样。身高，肩宽，甚至头发的长度和垂落的弧度都如出一辙。唯一不同的是那双眼睛——画中人的眼睛是紫色的，瞳孔里有金色的纹路在闪烁。

"老板。"阿方索轻声说。

西泽尔没有回答。他继续向前走。

第四幅画，第五幅画，第六幅画——壁画的内容越来越复杂，描绘着机械神国的建造过程、欧米茄原型体的诞生、欧洲各国的朝圣者在世界树前跪拜。但每一幅画的中心，那个完美神使的身影从未改变。他站在世界树前，紫色的眼睛注视着前方。

"它一直在这里等着。"佛朗哥教授说，"三百年前达·芬奇·波吉亚把这些壁画刻在通道里，就是为了告诉后来的人——世界树在等它的主人。"

西泽尔没有说话。

他注意到壁画上的颜料并没有因为三百年的时间而褪色。那些暗金色和银白色的线条依然鲜明，矿物颜料嵌在岩石的缝隙里，保存得比任何人类文明的遗迹都完整。世界树残枝的封印哪怕只是松动一丝，也足以让这些壁画保持原样。

通道越来越深，坡度越来越陡。空气变得潮湿，夹杂着一股硫磺味和隐约的金属腥味。墙壁上开始出现蒸汽管道，铜质管壁上凝结着水珠，管道的走向都指向同一个方向——通道的最深处。

"停一下。"阿方索忽然说。

他从手腕上解下那块改装过的蜘蛛巢腕表，按下了侧面的一个按钮。表盖弹开，六只微型机械蜘蛛依次爬出，沿着墙壁和天花板向通道深处飞快地跑去。蜘蛛的腹部嵌着红水银微晶，在黑暗中发出淡红色的微光。

"我需要确认前面的情况。"阿方索盯着表盘上的小型显示屏，"前方三百米内没有生命信号，但有——"

他的声音忽然断了。

表盘上，六只蜘蛛中的一只传回了异常数据。显示屏上跳出一个不断攀升的能量读数曲线，颜色的标识从绿色变成黄色，又从黄色跳到了刺目的红色。

"S级。"阿方索抬起头，脸色变了，"前方大约四百米，有红水银反应。不是普通浓度，是——浓缩态的。纯度比我见过的任何红水银核心都高。"

"世界树残枝样本。"佛朗哥教授说，"就在前面。"

阿方索调整了蜘蛛的信号频率，将扫描范围扩大到最大。六只蜘蛛在通道里散开，像一张看不见的网，将前方的地形和能量分布一点一点地勾勒出来。

"通道在大约四百米处终止。"阿方索看着显示屏，"终止点是一个巨大的圆形空间。蜘蛛探测到那里的温度异常——至少三百摄氏度。那里就是……"

"熔岩之心。"佛朗哥教授说。

"样本信号就在那个圆形空间里。"阿方索说，"距我们四百米。"

西泽尔点了点头："走。"

他们加快了脚步。壁画的密度渐渐降低，最后几幅画已经变得模糊不清，大概是通道末端没有经过精细的打磨。最后一幅画只剩下一个轮廓——世界树的根，扎在地面以下无数条细密的根须，每一条根须的末端都写着密密麻麻的文字。

梵文。

"锡兰文。"佛朗哥教授辨认着那些文字，"不，不完全是锡兰文。比锡兰文更古老。这是……史前梵文。"

通道在前方忽然开阔了。

那是一个椭圆形的空间，比通道宽了三倍不止。穹顶极高，嵌着几盏已经不再发光的铜灯。地面铺着一层薄薄的火山灰，踩上去发出细碎的沙沙声。空气灼热，每一次呼吸都带着硫磺的呛味。

空间的正中央，有一个人坐在地上。

她背靠着墙壁，双腿伸直，脑袋微微垂着，像是在打盹。银色的短发乱糟糟地贴在额头上，军服的左袖被烧掉了一半，露出里面包着绷带的小臂。绷带已经发黄了，上面洇着淡褐色的血渍。

她的右手搭在膝盖上，手指尖夹着一本硬壳日记和几张泛黄的老照片。

薇若兰。

"薇若兰！"唐璜第一个冲过去，蹲在她面前，伸手探她的鼻息。

"别……别碰那里。"薇若兰睁开眼睛，抬手挡开了唐璜的手。她的声音嘶哑得像是被砂纸磨过，但嘴角还是弯了弯，"绷带下面有伤，你手不干净。"

"你活着。"唐璜说。

"废话。"薇若兰撑着墙壁慢慢坐直。她的脸色苍白到近乎透明，嘴唇干裂，但眼睛还是亮的——那种密涅瓦副总长特有的、像是永远在计算着什么的精明目光。

她的目光越过唐璜的肩膀，落在西泽尔身上。

"你来了。"她说。

然后她笑了。

笑容很淡，牵动了干裂的嘴唇，有一丝血珠渗出来。笑意只到了眼睛的一半就停住了，另外一半沉在眼底，是她一贯的疲倦和此刻新添的某种柔软。她看起来确实很虚弱，但那种虚弱反而让她的轮廓变得柔和了一些，像是密涅瓦机关的副总长这个头衔暂时被卸掉了，只剩下一个二十多岁的、受了伤的年轻女人。

"你看起来糟透了。"西泽尔走到她面前，蹲下身。

"你也是。"薇若兰说，"比上次在密涅瓦见面的时候瘦了一圈。不过你的眼睛更亮了。"

"日记。"西泽尔伸出手。

薇若兰低头看了看自己手里的硬壳日记本和那几张老照片。日记本已经很旧了，硬壳封面上刻着机械神教的齿轮徽记，边角被磨得发白。那几张照片更旧，照片的边缘泛着黄，上面的人物面孔已经有些模糊了。

"先回答我几个问题。"西泽尔说。

薇若兰的手指微微收紧。

"日记最后几页到底写了什么？"西泽尔看着她，"你为什么故意删掉录音的最后一段？"

薇若兰的笑容慢慢消失了。

她没有立刻回答，而是低下头，拇指摩挲着日记本的封皮。指甲刮过齿轮徽记的凸起纹路，发出极轻的沙沙声。空气灼热而沉闷，只有这个声音在椭圆形空间里回响。

"这个空间里说话不太方便。"薇若兰说，"后面跟来的那帮人，脚步声很重，他们至少有一半不是我们的人。"

西泽尔转头看了一眼身后。佛朗哥教授、瓦莲京娜、阿方索、昆提良——只有这四个人跟上来了。通道入口的岩壁已经关死，从外面打不开。

"这里只有我们。"西泽尔说。

"我知道。"薇若兰说，"但日记最后几页的内容……不是三言两语能说清楚的。"

她抬起头，紫色的眼睛——不，薇若兰的眼睛不是紫色的，是深褐色的，但在熔岩之心的暗红色光线里，看起来像是某种更深的、更不可测的颜色。

"等我们拿到世界树残枝样本。"她说，"样本就在前面那扇门后面。拿到样本、活着出去之后，我再告诉你。"

"你现在就可以告诉我。"西泽尔说。

"不。"薇若兰说。

她的声音很轻，但语气里有一种西泽尔很少在她身上听到的固执。

"有些事情必须在合适的时候说。"薇若兰把日记本和照片一起递到西泽尔手里，"日记你拿着。最后几页我撕掉了，但前面的内容足够你了解到达·芬奇·波吉亚这个人。照片上是他和家人的合影。"

西泽尔接过日记本和照片。他翻到最后一页——果然，最后几页被整齐地撕掉了，撕口的边缘很平，用的是裁纸刀。

"我撕掉它不是要隐瞒什么。"薇若兰说，"是怕你看了之后会冲动。你现在不能冲动。"

"我不能冲动什么？"西泽尔问。

薇若兰张了张嘴，又合上了。她垂下眼睛，看着自己手臂上的绷带，过了好一会儿才说："等我们拿到世界树残枝样本，我再告诉你。这是命令。"

"你什么时候开始对我下命令了？"西泽尔说。

"从你成为密涅瓦的人开始。"薇若兰说，"密涅瓦的规矩是副总长管日常，总长管技术，总长的老师管老师的老师。佛朗哥老师在这里，所以我听佛朗哥老师的。佛朗哥老师说了，一切行动听副总长安排。"

佛朗哥教授咳嗽了一声，没说话。

"而且——"薇若兰的嘴角又弯了弯，那个弯度比刚才大了一些，但笑意仍然没有抵达眼底，"你现在不也在听我的吗？"

西泽尔看着她。

他忽然觉得薇若兰此刻的表情和他在密涅瓦机关里第一次见到她时很像。那时候她也是这样笑着，笑容里藏着一把刀，把最要紧的事情用最漫不经心的语气说出来，好像那不过是明天食堂加不加餐的小事。

他没有再追问。

他把日记本揣进军服的内袋，照片夹在日记本的封底里。泛黄的照片边角从封底的缝隙里露出来，他低头看了一眼——照片上是一群穿着三百年款式服饰的人站在一株巨大的树前面，树的根须盘绕在地面上，每一条根须的末端都刻着细密的纹路。人群的最前方站着一个男人，五官清俊，下巴微微扬起，眼神里有一种西泽尔很熟悉的骄傲和悲悯。

达·芬奇·波吉亚。

照片上的世界树很小，远没有壁画上画得那么巨大。但西泽尔注意到，世界树的根须末端，刻着和通道墙壁上最后一幅画完全相同的史前梵文。

"走吧。"西泽尔说，"世界树残枝样本就在前面。"

薇若兰撑着墙壁站了起来。唐璜伸手想扶她，被她瞪了一眼，缩回了手。她站稳之后，从腰间拔出了那把改装过的雷霆牙连射铳，检查了一下弹匣。

"还有多少子弹？"阿方索问。

"七发。"薇若兰说，"但我不需要用枪。枪留着给真正需要的人。"

她没有解释"真正需要的人"是谁。

椭圆形空间的尽头是一扇铁门。铁门不大，刚好容一个人侧身通过，门板上布满了铆钉和锈迹。铁门的一侧有一个拳头大小的圆形凹槽，凹槽的形状很奇特——是一朵半开的莲花，花瓣的中央嵌着一个齿轮。

瓦莲京娜盯着那个凹槽，忽然从领口内侧取出了什么东西。

一枚拇指盖大小的银饰。

银饰的断面刻着半朵莲花，背面有微型齿轮纹路。

"这是我妈留给我的。"瓦莲京娜说，"她说如果有一天我找到了和我一样的人，就把这个拿出来。"

她把银饰按进了凹槽里。

银饰的莲花图案和凹槽中的莲花图案严丝合缝。齿轮咬合的那一瞬间，铁门发出一声沉闷的咔嚓声，门板向内裂开了一条缝。

缝隙里透出了光。

不是红水银的暗红色，也不是火光的橙黄色。是一种——金色的。温暖的，脉动的，像是阳光被碾碎后洒在水面上的光。

铁门完全打开了。

门后是一条向下延伸的阶梯，阶梯的尽头是无尽的黑暗，但那黑暗中有一个光源。光源的中心是一棵树。

真的树。

和壁画上画的一模一样。

树干是暗金色合金，树冠在头顶展开，树枝的末梢挂着一颗颗散发着脉动光芒的圆形果实——红水银核心。树叶是一片片大小不一的金色齿轮，所有的齿轮都在缓慢转动，发出极轻的、像是摇篮曲一样的嗡鸣。

世界树残枝。

它就在那里。

"它在等我们。"佛朗哥教授摘下老花镜，手在抖。

西泽尔迈出了第一步。他的脚刚踏上阶梯的第三级台阶，后颈的黄金套管猛地一烫，热度从脊椎蹿到后脑勺，像是被一根烧红的铁丝贯穿。眼前的世界忽然变得极其清晰——他能看到世界树每一片齿轮的纹路，每一颗红水银果实内部能量的流动，甚至能看到树枝上附着的那些极细的、像神经纤维一样的金色丝线在轻轻颤动。

那些丝线全部指向他。

山顶传来一声沉闷的轰鸣，整座火山都在颤抖。阶梯两侧的岩壁开始剥落，火山灰簌簌地往下掉。

"快走！"阿方索大喊，"山体在崩！"

瓦莲京娜一把抓住西泽尔的手腕，把他往阶梯下拽。西泽尔没有抗拒，任由她拽着，跟在薇若兰身后向下跑去。

世界树残枝的金色光芒越来越亮，亮到刺眼。那光芒像是活物一样在追着他们，在他们身后翻滚涌动，把整个阶梯都染成了金色。

薇若兰跑在最前面，银色的短发在金光中像是一簇跳跃的火焰。她一边跑一边回头看西泽尔，嘴唇翕动了一下，似乎想说什么，但轰鸣声太大了，什么都听不见。

她的眼睛在金光中变成了某种说不清的颜色。

西泽尔忽然意识到——

薇若兰刚才撕掉日记最后几页的时候，她的手在抖。

而她没有让任何人注意到。

山体又剧烈地晃动了一下，一块人头大小的岩石从穹顶砸落，擦着西泽尔的肩膀砸在阶梯上，碎成一片粉末。

阶梯的尽头，那棵暗金色的世界树残枝，近在咫尺。

薇若兰停下了脚步。

【English】
Chapter 227 — The Summons of Vesuvius (II)

The night wind came down off the summit with a throatful of scorched ore.

Cesare stood at the door of the modified steam car, watching the outline of Vesuvius. The whole mountain was breathing. A gold light rose from the crater and spilled along the ridgeline in both directions, as if the earth had been cracked open and the molten sun beneath was leaking through. The slope was freckled with that same dim-gold radiance where the Omega proto-bodies still crept in their slow orbit around the peak — not pouring down toward the foothills but circling, one ring inside the other, like petals closing around a heart.

"Not the front," Professor Franco said from the back seat. "Take the old mining road on the north flank. A service passage built three hundred years ago by the Minerva Bureau. Only the founding chief engineer knew the route."

Valentina turned the wheel. The car swung about and tore along the loose stone of the ridge toward the northwest, every impact on the gravel drumming up through the floorboards. The car pitched hard, and a spray of golden honeysuckle petals fell from somewhere in Valentina's hair. Don Juan caught one petal in the air, lifted it to his nose, said nothing, and set it carefully back on her shoulder.

The road narrowed. The rock on either side grew black, as if something had burned it. Valentina cut the headlamps and switched the armor's night-vision mode. The road ahead turned the sickly white of an old bone under infrared.

"Here," Professor Franco said abruptly.

Valentina stamped the brake.

What stood before them was an unremarkable face of rock — eight meters high, perhaps twelve across, the same grey-black volcanic stone as everything else. Cesare saw it first because he was looking. Set dead center in the wall, no higher than his chest, was a bronze medallion the size of a fist: an owl with six wings, and on every one of those wings a fine pattern of gear teeth. The six-winged owl — the mark of the Minerva Bureau.

Below it, half-covered in verdigris, a smaller mark: a gear at the center, and a five-pointed star set into the gear, and at each of the five points a yet smaller ring of teeth.

Two marks, one above the other, cut into the same stone.

"That isn't Minerva's sigil," Alfonso said, stepping closer. His brow furrowed. "The second one — the gear-and-pentagram — I've seen that pattern. In the deepest archive of the Bureau. But no record connects it to Minerva."

"Because it was never meant to," Professor Franco said. "That is the emblem of the Cult of the Machine God. In Minerva's first years, the founding chief engineer was also one of the Cult's inner circle. Minerva and the Machine God were always two faces of the same body."

Cesare stepped up to the wall and laid his hand against the six-winged owl. The bronze was cold, crusted with the green of long oxidation, but the instant he touched it, the golden cannula set into the back of his neck flared hot.

He drew his hand back. Beneath the medallion he could see a line of small letters, wind-softened but still legible by the car lamp's reflected glow. Latin, cut deep.

QUI SCRUTATUR ABYSSUM ABYSSUM INVENIT.

Whoso scans the abyss, the abyss will come to meet him.

"Password," Don Juan said, crouching. In a seam of rock to the left of the medallion, his fingers had found a sunken disc, a thumb's width thick, its rim lettered with the twenty-six shapes of the Latin alphabet. It could be turned.

Professor Franco came forward. He was quiet for a long moment.

"The name of the founding chief engineer," he said at last.

"Da Vinci Borgia," Cesare said.

He went down on one knee. His fingers found the disc. D-A-V-I-N-C-I-B-O-R-G-I-A. The final letter seated itself with a soft click, and the wall answered.

It was not the sound of any mechanism he knew. It was lower than that, rounder, as though some vast string had been plucked far down in the body of the mountain. The bronze owl began to glow. Not the cold radiance of red mercury, but a dim gold, and the gold pulsed — slowly, the way a heart does when it is very old and very patient. The light ran out from the medallion along hairlines in the stone that he had not seen before, and where the lines met they formed a circle the size of a cathedral door.

The rock inside the circle split, soundless, and fell open to either side, and a black passage exhaled at them.

"Seal the entrance behind us," Professor Franco said. "From the inside."

Cesare nodded. He stepped through first. Valentina followed, then parked the car in the mouth of the passage — it would not fit further — and pocketed the ignition key. Don Juan hesitated, laid a palm flat on the bonnet.

"Good car," he said. "Wait for us."

Quintilian and Alfonso came last. The moment Quintilian's boot cleared the threshold, the rock began to grind shut behind them. The dark closed over them whole.

"Light," Cesare said.

Valentina brought up the armor's close-illumination. A single beam of white struck the dark and broke it. The passage was narrow — two men abreast at most, the walls rough, scarred with the chisel marks of the men who had cut it three centuries before. The air was dry and tasted of old iron and a thin thread of machine oil.

Fifty paces in, the passage bent to the left.

Beyond the bend, the wall changed.

The rough volcanic stone was gone. In its place stood a face of polished black basalt, smooth as a looking-glass, and the basalt was covered in marks.

"God above," Don Juan said quietly.

They were paintings. Not one and not two. From the floor at their feet, the painted surface ran on into the dark ahead, further than the eye could follow. The whole length of the passage was a canvas, and the artist had worked in two mineral pigments only — a dim gold and a silver-white — and had used them as though they were daylight and moonshine.

The first painting was closest to the entrance. A tree.

Not any tree that had ever grown. A metal tree, vast as a cathedral, the trunk of a dark-gold alloy, the canopy spreading above like an opened umbrella, and at the ends of the branches, glowing with a faint internal light, hung round fruits — red mercury cores. The leaves were gears of every size, all of them turning, very slowly, with a thin harmonic hum.

At the base of the painting, two words cut into the stone:

WORLD TREE.

"Keep going," Professor Franco said, and his voice had a tremor in it that Cesare had never heard there.

The second painting butted against the first. A city, but no city in the catalogue of human memory. Not Florence. Not Constantinople. No streets here, no houses, no spires. Instead, a web of metal pipes and gears that ran from the roots of the World Tree outward in slow spirals, locking into one another in a pattern that was at the same time precise and terrible. The center of the web was the Tree. Where its canopy spread there was a disc of gold light, and in the disc, dimly, the outline of a man standing.

At the base of the painting:

MACHINA DEI.

The Kingdom of the Machine.

Cesare's foot halted, half a beat, and resumed.

The third painting.

The center of the round was no city. It was a man's back. He stood before the World Tree with his hands laid flat against the trunk. From his shoulders and along his spine there ran a fan of gold lines, and each line threaded outward into the surrounding gears and pipes. His eyes — turned, somehow, so that the painter had given them to the viewer — were violet, and there was a line of gold in each pupil that pulsed faintly with the same rhythm as the medallion at the entrance.

At the base of the painting, in letters larger than the others:

PERFECTUS NUNTIUS.

The Perfect Messenger.

Cesare stood in front of it and did not move.

The man in the painting had his back. The same height, the same breadth of shoulder, even the same length of hair and the way it fell. The only thing different was the eyes. Violet eyes, with a moving filament of gold.

"Chief," Alfonso said softly.

Cesare did not answer. He walked on.

The fourth painting, the fifth, the sixth. They grew more intricate. The building of the Kingdom of the Machine. The birth of the Omega proto-bodies. The pilgrims of the nations of Europe kneeling before the World Tree. Through every one of them, at the center, the same Perfect Messenger stood in the same posture, with the same violet eyes, watching the painter, watching them.

"It has been waiting here," Professor Franco said. "Three hundred years, da Vinci Borgia carved these into the passage, so that whoever came after would know. The World Tree has been waiting for its master."

Cesare said nothing.

He had noticed that the pigments had not faded. The dim gold and the silver-white were as fresh in the stone as though the painter had laid them down the week before. The red mercury in the World Tree's seal, even cracked a hair's breadth, was enough to keep them perfect.

The passage deepened. The floor began to slope. The air grew wet, and in the wetness there was the smell of sulfur and the deeper, fainter smell of hot metal. Copper pipes began to run along the walls, sweating beads of condensation, and every pipe ran the same way — inward, deeper, toward the heart of the mountain.

"Hold," Alfonso said.

He unstrapped the modified Spider Nest wristpiece and pressed the side stud. The lid popped, and six mechanical spiders marched out one by one, scuttling up the wall and along the ceiling into the dark, their bellies lit with the faint red of micro-crystallized mercury.

"I need to see what is ahead." He watched the tiny screen on the dial. "Nothing alive in the first three hundred meters. But there is —"

He stopped.

One of the six had sent back an anomaly. On the screen a curve was climbing, climbing — green, then yellow, then a red so sharp it seemed to burn the glass.

"Class S." Alfonso looked up. His face had changed. "At roughly four hundred meters. Mercury response. Not ambient. Concentrated. Purer than any core I have ever read."

"A sample of the World Tree," Professor Franco said.

Alfonso widened the scan. The six spiders fanned out into a net and began to map the geometry of what lay ahead. "The passage ends at approximately four hundred meters. A circular chamber. Temperature in the chamber is anomalous — at least three hundred degrees. That must be the —"

"Heart of the Lava," Professor Franco said.

"The sample's signal is in the chamber. Four hundred meters." Alfonso looked at Cesare. "Straight in."

They walked faster. The paintings thinned. The last of them was little more than an outline — the roots of the World Tree plunged down through the floor, and each rootlet was lined with a dense, cramped script.

"Sanskrit," Professor Franco said, bending close. "No. Not quite. Older than Sanskrit. Pre-Vedic. The script of — the script of before."

The passage opened.

The chamber was oval, three times the width of the passage, the ceiling lost above them. A few dead copper lamps were set into the rock. The floor was dusted with a thin skin of grey ash that whispered under their boots. The air was hot. Each breath came in with sulfur and a metallic taste that sat on the back of the tongue.

In the middle of the chamber, against the far wall, a person sat on the ground.

She was leaning back against the stone. Her legs were stretched out before her. Her head was tipped forward as though she had been dozing. Silver hair, short, stuck to her forehead in wet clumps. The left sleeve of her uniform had been burned away to the shoulder; the arm inside was bandaged, the bandage yellowed, a brown bloom of old blood seeping through at the elbow. Her right hand rested on her knee, and between her fingers were a hardbound journal and a few yellowed photographs.

Violante.

"Violante!" Don Juan was the first to her, dropping to his knees. His hand went to her face.

"Don't — not there." Violante opened her eyes and lifted a hand to push his away. Her voice had been raked over by something coarser than gravel, but the corner of her mouth lifted. "The wound is under the bandage. Your hands are filthy."

"You're alive," Don Juan said.

"Evidently." Violante braced a hand against the wall and levered herself slowly upright. Her face was bloodless, the lips cracked, but the eyes were still the eyes of the deputy director of Minerva — the eyes of a woman who was always, at every moment, calculating two moves ahead.

Her gaze passed over Don Juan's shoulder and found Cesare.

"You came," she said.

Then she smiled.

It was a small smile. It split the cracked skin of her lip, and a bead of blood welled at the corner. The smile reached only halfway to her eyes. The other half lay under the surface — her usual exhaustion, and a thing newly added to it, something softer. She looked, for the first time since Cesare had known her, not like the deputy director of anything. She looked like a young woman in her twenties who was hurt.

"You look dreadful," Cesare said, going down on one knee before her.

"So do you." Violante studied his face. "You've lost weight since Minerva. But your eyes are brighter."

"The journal," Cesare said, and held out his hand.

Violante glanced down at the hardbound volume and the photographs in her own hand. The journal was old; the Machine God's gear was stamped on the cover, the corners rubbed to the colour of tallow. The photographs were older still; their edges were the deep yellow of age, and the faces of the figures in them had gone soft with the years.

"Answer me a few things first," Cesare said.

Violante's fingers tightened, almost imperceptibly.

"What do the last pages say? Why did you cut the last stretch of the recording?"

The smile thinned and went.

She did not answer at once. She looked down at the journal in her lap, and her thumb moved across the cover, back and forth across the raised teeth of the gear, and the only sound in the oval chamber was that faint dry rasp.

"It isn't a good place to talk in here," she said. "The people behind us — their boots are heavy. Half of them are not ours."

Cesare looked back into the passage. Franco. Valentina. Alfonso. Quintilian. The four of them. The rock had sealed behind them. There was no one else.

"We're alone," he said.

"I know." Violante said. "But the last pages — they're not something I can say in two sentences."

She looked up. Her eyes were dark brown. In the dull red light of the Heart of the Lava they looked almost a different colour — a deep and unaccountable violet, but that was only the light, only the light.

"When we have the sample. The sample is through the door at the back. When we have it, and we are out, alive — then I will tell you."

"Tell me now," Cesare said.

"No." Her voice was soft, but in it there was a kind of stubbornness Cesare had seldom heard from her. "Some things have to be said at the right time." She held out the journal and the photographs together. "Take the journal. I tore the last pages out. What's left is enough to know the man that da Vinci Borgia was. The photographs are of him with his family."

Cesare took the journal. He opened it to the back. The last pages had been cut out cleanly, a single razor slice, the edge of the paper clean as a knife wound.

"I didn't cut them to hide anything." Violante said. "I cut them because if you read them you will do something rash. You cannot do something rash right now."

"What will I do that is rash?" Cesare said.

Violante opened her mouth, and closed it again. She looked at the bandage on her own arm. A long moment passed.

"When we have the sample. I will tell you then. That is an order."

"Since when do you give me orders?"

"Since you became Minerva's." Violante said. "The Bureau's rules: the deputy director runs the day, the director runs the tech, the director's teacher runs the director. Franco is here, so I listen to Franco. Franco has said that, for this operation, all arrangements are at the deputy director's discretion."

Professor Franco coughed once, and said nothing.

"And —" The corner of Violante's mouth lifted again. The lift was larger this time, but the smile still did not quite reach her eyes. "You're listening to me, aren't you?"

Cesare looked at her.

He thought, suddenly, of the first time he had met her in the Bureau. She had smiled at him then, too, in just this way, a smile that carried a small knife in it. The most important thing, said in the most offhand voice, as though it were a question about tomorrow's menu.

He did not press her.

He slipped the journal into the inside pocket of his uniform. The photographs he tucked into the back cover. The yellowed edge of one photograph poked out from the seam, and he looked down at it. A group of figures in three-hundred-year-old dress stood in front of a tree, its roots coiled across the ground, every rootlet lined with the same pre-Vedic script they had seen at the end of the passage. At the front of the group, a man. Fine features. Chin lifted. The eyes held a pride and a sorrow Cesare knew.

Da Vinci Borgia.

The tree in the photograph was small. Nothing like the painted World Tree. But Cesare saw, at the tip of every root, the same pre-Vedic script.

"Move," Cesare said. "The sample is through the next door."

Violante braced against the wall and stood. Don Juan reached for her. She shot him a look and he withdrew his hand. Once she was steady, she drew the modified Thunder-Tooth repeater from her belt and checked the magazine.

"How many rounds?" Alfonso asked.

"Seven." Violante holstered the weapon. "I don't need the gun. The gun is for whoever does."

She did not say who that was.

At the back of the oval chamber was a door. Small. Barely wide enough for a man to edge through sideways. Rivets and rust across the iron. On one side of the door, a circular depression the size of a fist, and in the depression the shape of a half-opened lotus flower, and at the heart of the lotus a small gear.

Valentina stared at the depression. Without a word she reached up into the collar of her dress and took out something she wore on a cord against her skin.

A silver ornament, no bigger than a thumbnail.

Cut into its face, half a lotus. On the back, a micro-pattern of gear teeth.

"My mother left it to me." Valentina said. "She told me that if I ever found someone like me, I should show it."

She pressed the silver ornament into the depression.

The lotus on the ornament met the lotus in the iron. The gear on the back met the gear in the iron. There was a single, deep click. The door cracked inward along its seam.

Light came through the crack.

Not the dim red of mercury. Not the orange of any common fire. A gold. A warm gold. A gold that pulsed. The colour of sunlight crushed and poured out across water.

The door opened.

Behind it, a flight of stairs going down. At the bottom of the stairs, a darkness. And in the darkness, one light. And at the center of the light, a tree.

A real tree.

Exactly as the painting had shown it. The trunk of a dark-gold alloy. The canopy above, spread. At the end of every branch, a round fruit of red mercury, each one pulsing with its own slow rhythm. The leaves were gears, every size, all of them turning at their own pace, the thin collective hum of them a sound like a lullaby sung very far away.

A branch of the World Tree.

It stood before them, as it had stood in the painting for three hundred years.

"It has been waiting for us," Professor Franco said, and he took off his spectacles because his hand was shaking too much to see through them.

Cesare took the first step. The second. On the third step, the golden cannula at the back of his neck flared — a heat that ran from his spine to the back of his skull, as though a red wire had been drawn through him from end to end. The world sharpened. He could see the pattern of every gear on the Tree, the slow current of energy in every mercury fruit, the thin gold filaments — like nerve fibres — that clung to the bark, trembling in the heat.

Every filament pointed at him.

The mountain answered. A deep, grinding boom, the kind that does not come from stone or steam. The rock around them shuddered. Pebbles and ash rained from the ceiling.

"Move," Alfonso shouted, "the whole flank is giving."

Valentina seized Cesare's wrist and hauled him down the stairs. He did not resist. He let himself be pulled, running now, behind Violante, down toward the Tree.

The gold of the Tree was brightening. Brighter. Bright as the sun at noon. The light moved, almost alive, lapping at their backs as though it were chasing them, pouring down the stair and turning the stone to gold.

Violante ran first. Her silver hair was a small flame in the gold light. She half turned, once, and her mouth moved — something she was trying to say — but the booming was too loud; he could not hear her.

Her eyes, in the gold light, were a colour he could not have named.

Cesare understood, then, in a single, clean stroke, what he had not understood before.

When Violante had torn the last pages from the journal, her hand had been shaking.

And she had not let anyone see.

The flank of the mountain heaved again. A rock the size of a man's head broke loose from the ceiling and fell past Cesare's shoulder and burst on the stair in a cloud of powder.

The Tree, dark gold, its canopy of turning gears, was at the foot of the stair.

Violante stopped.
