【中文】
第231章 高加索山脉的伏击（下）

暗河水面不再颤动。
那块巨石上的六翼猫头鹰浮雕在薇若兰的青铜镜触碰下缓缓亮起微弱的金色光芒,浮雕与镜面之间的细如发丝的白光向两侧延伸,勾勒出一道刚好容一人侧身通过的暗门轮廓。
"开。"薇若兰说。
浮雕旋转半圈,暗门无声地向内滑开。暗门后是一条倾斜向上的隧道,石壁上刻着和浮雕相同的机械神教齿轮纹路,只是那些齿轮全都静止不动,像死去三百年的眼睛。
"走。"瓦莲京娜说。
蒸汽小艇无法驶入倾斜隧道,所有人弃船上岸。唐璜第一个跳上石阶,昆提良殿后,薇若兰和阿方索护着西泽尔走在中间。
西泽尔的紫瞳已经退回了常态。
他抬起头看向隧道顶,顶部的石块间渗出冰冷的水滴,像一层薄薄的汗。后颈的黄金套管安静下来,但他知道那种安静是"待机"而非"关闭"——就像把剑放在手边,握不握是另一回事。
瓦莲京娜在隧道口停下脚步。
"我留下。"她说。
所有人回头看她。
"我穿神怒Ⅲ型。"她伸手从背上的金属长匣里取出折叠整齐的暗银色装甲板,动作利落得像在展开一把折扇,"从这里到隧道出口,大概四百米。如果欧米茄原型体的信号能穿透岩层,我们的位置已经暴露了。普罗米修斯侦察型甲胄不需要过隧道——它们会直接等在出口。"
"你一个人?"唐璜皱眉。
"神怒Ⅲ型不是摆设。"瓦莲京娜已经开始在狭窄的隧道里展开甲胄,她的动作极快,金属卡扣咬合的声音在石壁间回荡,"再说,不是一个人。"
她回头看了一眼西泽尔。
"红龙在,我就在。"
西泽尔没有说话。
他只是微微点头。
那已经是他能给出的最重的承诺。

瓦莲京娜的改装神怒Ⅲ型是在这座隧道里第一次完整展开的。
它比密涅瓦的任何炽天使试制版都要高大——三米二,暗银色装甲板,每一片都嵌着冰原寒玉的微粒,在隧道里散发出微弱的冷蓝光晕。胸腔是叶尼塞王妃遗物改造的红水银晶块核心,比普通核心小一圈却亮得多,像一颗被压缩的蓝白色恒星。
它的右手是破甲锤——锤头是硬金铸成,表面刻满叶尼塞忍冬花纹,重量超过一百五十公斤;左手是战斧,斧刃经过冰原寒玉粉末研磨,能在撞击瞬间释放零下四十度的低温,让金属装甲变脆。
背部是蒸汽喷射推进器,两组共四个喷射口,可以让这台三米高的重型甲胄短时间飞行。
瓦莲京娜把胸甲扣合,金属合拢的沉闷声响在隧道里滚了好几圈。
她低头看着自己甲胄上反射出来的冷光,自言自语:"妈妈,我穿着它了。"

阿方索坐在隧道中段一块平坦的岩石上,膝上摊开小艇上拆下来的无线电组件。
这套设备是叶尼塞专列上的备用件,被普罗米修斯侦察型甲胈击落时摔坏了天线,但收发电路还完整。他用随身工具箱里的细铜丝、焊锡和从自己机械臂关节里拆下的一小段电缆做了根临时天线。
"没有加密频道。"阿方索一边焊一边说,"我只能用明码。"
"明码会被截获。"薇若兰皱眉。
"我知道。"阿方索的手很稳,焊锡在铜丝上凝成银色小球,"但楚舜华的密探在玉门关外等候,如果他们一直在用这个频段监听,我发出去的明码他们三秒内就能收到。"
"发给谁?"
"发给任何听到的、骑着夔龙马、说着东方话的人。"阿方索吹了吹焊点,"我赌楚舜华的密探已经在这一带活动了。"
薇若兰没再反对。

西泽尔靠在隧道壁上,闭着眼。
他没有睡。
他在"听"。
不朽之王系统接入后,他的感知范围比常人宽得多——不是超自然的预知,而是神经接驳系统激活后,周围所有金属物体的微弱电磁场都像潮水一样涌入他的意识。他能感觉到薇若兰手中青铜镜的振动频率,能感觉到瓦莲京娜甲胄里红水银晶块核心稳定而有力的脉动。
也能感觉到隧道外,正在靠近的东西。
三台普罗米修斯侦察型甲胄。
它们没有进隧道——瓦莲京娜说对了。
它们等在出口。
西泽尔能感觉到其中一台正在启动六管转轮机枪的供弹机构,齿轮咬合的声音像蟋蟀在远处鸣叫。
"三台。"他睁开眼睛,"隧道出口外三百米,呈品字形散开。中间那台探照灯已经亮了。"
"它会照进隧道。"唐璜瞬间进入战斗状态。
"挡住。"西泽尔说,"挡住光,我们出其不意。"
唐璜会意,解下外套挂在隧道口。外套的布料被探照灯照成半透明,光线的方向暴露了普罗米修斯的位置。
"等瓦莲京娜从侧翼。"西泽尔说。
瓦莲京娜没有回答。
她的甲胄已经走出了隧道,她是从另一条更窄的裂缝出去的——那条裂缝只够神怒Ⅲ型侧身通过,出去后是一片乱石坡,可以俯瞰隧道出口外的开阔地。

瓦莲京娜在半山腰停下。
她看见了三台普罗米修斯侦察型甲胄,正如西泽尔所说,品字形散开,探照灯把隧道出口照得雪亮。六管转轮机枪的供弹链垂在枪身一侧,像蛇的鳞片。
她的手指在破甲锤的握柄上收紧。
破甲锤的锤头在寒玉微粒的作用下泛着冷光,她能感觉到那重量——一百五十公斤,以前她能举着它连续挥击三十次,现在她想举着它砸穿一台普罗米修斯的脑袋。
她启动了蒸汽喷射推进器。
两组四个喷射口同时喷出高压蒸汽,甲胄在三秒内从半山腰升起,越过乱石坡的顶端,越过普罗米修斯的探照灯,出现在它们的头顶。
三台普罗米修斯几乎同时抬头。
六管转轮机枪仰射,弹道在空中划出交叉的赤红弧线。
瓦莲京娜侧身,一枚弹头擦着她的右肩关节飞过,在装甲板上犁出一道浅沟。她没有还击,她把所有的蒸汽压力都灌进了推进器,让自己的速度再快一截。
她锁定了中间那台。
破甲锤从上方砸下,锤头带着一百五十公斤的重量和叶尼塞忍冬花纹的冷光,像一柄从天而降的死神之锤。
锤头砸在普罗米修斯的骑士舱顶盖上。
硬金撞硬金。
金属碰撞的声音像丧钟。
顶盖塌陷,碎裂,向内凹陷了半米。瓦莲京娜紧接着第二锤,这一次她把锤头从凹陷处砸了进去,直接把骑士舱砸成了废铁。
普罗米修斯侦察型甲胄的躯干在她脚下摇晃,最终轰然倒下,激起一圈灰尘。
瓦莲京娜落地,蒸汽喷射器喷出的余热在空气中凝成白雾。
她拉开骑士舱的残骸,准备查看里面的骑士是否还有救——
空的。
没有骑士。
没有人。
只有青铜。
整个骑士舱内部全是青铜铸造的机械结构,关节、传动轴、齿轮,全都刻着世界树神经祈祷文。那些关节自己在动——即使甲胄已经倒下,那些青铜关节还在以极慢的速度收缩和伸展,像一只死去的手还在抽搐。
"它是活的。"瓦莲京娜低声说。
剩余两台普罗米修斯同时开火,六管转轮机枪的弹道把瓦莲京娜的视野切成碎片。她侧身闪避,破甲锤横扫,锤头带着千钧之力砸在其中一台的腿部关节,青铜关节在暴力下崩裂,暗红金色的液体从裂口中喷涌而出——那是欧米茄的体液。
那台普罗米修斯单膝跪地,但它的上半身还在动,六管转轮机枪还在射击。它没有痛觉,没有恐惧,只有命令。
"西泽尔!"瓦莲京娜高喊。
西泽尔从隧道中冲出。
他的紫瞳没有完全激活——瞳孔依旧是紫色,但没有金色纹路的延伸。他做的是另一件事:他把不朽之王系统的预热状态维持在临界点,让系统以最低功率向外释放神经电流。
那些神经电流对人类无害,但对青铜关节里刻着世界树祈祷文的欧米茄原型体来说,那是"母体的呼唤"——世界树残枝的共鸣频率。
两台普罗米修斯的青铜关节同时出现了短暂的痉挛。
它们没有倒下,但动作明显慢了一拍,六管转轮机枪的射速骤降。
瓦莲京娜抓住了这一拍的时间。
她的破甲锤再次挥出,这一次是从侧面,直接砸在普罗米修斯的腰部关节——那是它全身最薄弱的连接处,所有青铜结构的枢纽。
关节崩碎。
第二台普罗米修斯轰然倒下。
最后一台普罗米修斯试图后撤,六管转轮机枪调转方向——
黑暗中响起了密集的射击声。
不是重机枪,是小口径连射铳,声音短促而密集,像暴雨打在铁皮屋顶上。
那是来自高加索山脉另一侧山脊的火力。
楚舜华的密探到了。
密探们骑着夔龙马,马匹的毛色是暗红色,在夜色中几乎隐形。马背上的密探身着轻便皮甲,手持小型连射铳,枪口喷出的火焰在黑暗中像一串串红色的萤火虫。
他们的射击极准——不是打普罗米修斯的装甲,而是打它的探照灯。
探照灯被打碎,普罗米修斯的视野瞬间陷入黑暗。
瓦莲京娜在黑暗中冲了上去。
她的破甲锤带着寒玉的冷光划出一道弧线,砸在最后一台普罗米修斯的头部。
头部碎裂。
甲胄轰然倒下,扬起漫天灰尘。
战场安静下来。
密探们没有下马,他们保持着一个整齐的半圆形阵列,把西泽尔一行人围在中间。领头的是个四十岁上下的东方男人,脸上有刀疤,眼神像鹰,他在马背上抱拳,说的是标准但带着口音的拉丁语:"楚监国麾下斥候营副尉吴铁,奉命在此接应西方贵客。"
"你们怎么知道我们在哪?"阿方索问。
"无线电。"吴铁说,"半个时辰前,有人用叶尼塞专列的备用频段发了明码求救。我们在这一带搜寻了三天,频段一开就收到了。"
阿方索微微点头,没有再解释。
吴铁从马背上跳下来,走到倒下的普罗米修斯残骸前,蹲下,用刀挑开骑士舱的碎片。
他看见了那些青铜关节。
他的眉头猛地一皱。
"这是……活的?"他用东方话说,声音很轻。
"欧米茄原型体。"薇若兰走过来,蹲在他身边,手指触上青铜关节的表面。关节在她指尖下微微颤动,像有呼吸,"世界树残枝结出的果实。机械神国的士兵。"
吴铁看了她一眼,眼神里有警惕,也有震惊。
"贵客是……"
"我们的身份,等见到楚监国再说。"薇若兰打断他,"先让我们离开这里。这些欧米茄原型体是先锋,后面还有大部队。"
吴铁点头,转身对密探们做了一个手势。密探们从马背上取下备用的鞍具——那不是普通的马鞍,而是带有蒸汽辅助动力的双座鞍具,专门用来在马背上搭载无法自己骑行的伤员或装备。
"夔龙马日行三百里,夜行一百五十里。"吴铁说,"从这里到玉门关,正常行军需要五天,骑夔龙马只需要两天。"
"走。"西泽尔说。
他没有回头看那些倒在地上的普罗米修斯残骸。
他已经感觉到了——那些残骸里,青铜关节还在动,还在试图修复,还在向某个方向发送信号。
欧米茄原型体不会死,只会等待。
它们在等母体的命令。

楚舜华在洛阳通天宫的密室里收到了吴铁的密报。
密报是用信鸽送来的——无线电明码容易被截获,信鸽是最后的安全通道。密报写在一条杏黄色的绢帛上,字迹端正,用的是楚舜华规定的密文格式。
楚舜华展开绢帛。
"西方贵客紫瞳有金纹,神怒Ⅲ型击败自动普罗米修斯,空舱有青铜机械关节——贵客果然是监国要找的人。"
他盯着"紫瞳有金纹"四个字看了很久。
星见血脉。
金纹。
他放下绢帛,伸手从案上拿起一枚夔龙角剑的玉坠——那是他母亲的遗物,玉坠里嵌着一块发黄的锡兰纸莲花残片,是他母亲从锡兰逃出时唯一带出来的东西。
"母亲,"他低声说,"他来了。"
烛火在案上跳动。
密室的阴影里,世界树残枝东方主根节点的位置地图被他用红水银墨水画在一面墙上,密密麻麻的线条和符号像一张巨大的蛛网。
其中一根线,刚刚被点亮了。

【English】
Chapter 231 — Ambush in the Caucasus (II)

The dark water had stopped trembling.

That was the first thing Cesare registered when the lamps steadied. The subterranean river that had carried them out of the Vitruvian pits beneath the Roman Pale lay flat and black, a held breath. The launch rocked once against the cut-stone ledge, then stilled, and in the silence the only sound left was the faint ticking of cooling brass.

Beside the river, half-buried in the clay of the bank, squatted a great block of granite. A six-winged owl carved into its face. Wings spread, talons closed around a gear, the whole thing rendered in a style that belonged to the Mechanicum's older, stranger centuries — the kind of icon the Chapter of the Cogwheel had not made for three hundred years.

Violante stepped forward, her bronze mirror held before her like a small, polished moon. She did not touch the stone with her hand. She let the glass touch the relief.

A thin filament of white light bloomed where glass met granite.

The light spread, tracing the outline of a door. A door tall enough for a man to pass through, but only sideways.

"Open," Violante said.

The owl relief rotated half a circle. The door slid inward without sound.

Beyond it, a tunnel slanted up into the mountain. The stone walls were carved with the same gearwork as the relief, but every wheel was frozen. Static. Dead. Like three centuries of eyes watching nothing.

"Move," said Valentina.

They could not take the steam-launch up the slope. The hull scraped stone and the bow jammed against the first rise. One by one they climbed out onto the slick rock, Don Juan leaping to the first step without waiting for help, Quintilian coming last, his wounded leg dragging a little at the knee. Violante and Alfonso flanked Cesare in the middle of the line.

Cesare's violet eyes had returned to their normal shade. He tilted his head back to look at the ceiling. Between the fitted stones, droplets of cold water gathered, broke, fell. A thin sweat on the inside of a tomb. The gold collar at the back of his neck was quiet. Not off. The Undying King system never truly went off. It stood at standby the way a drawn sword stands in its scabbard — present, awake, ready.

Valentina stopped at the tunnel mouth.

"I stay," she said.

The others turned.

"I am wearing Fury III." She was already reaching behind her, fingers finding the buckles of the long metal case strapped across her back. "From here to the far end of the tunnel, four hundred metres. If the Omega prototype's signal penetrates the rock, our position is already known. The Prometheus scouts will not need to come inside. They will wait at the exit."

"Alone?" Don Juan asked.

"Fury III is not a decoration." She unfolded the first plate of dark silver armour, and the joint of her elbow made the sound of a fan being spread. The next plate. The next. Metal latches bit into metal with a small, savage precision that ran in quick echo along the stone walls. "And I am not alone."

She looked at Cesare.

"The Red Dragon is here. So am I."

He did not answer. He gave her the smallest inclination of the head.

That was the heaviest promise he had left to give.

Valentina's modified Fury III had not been built for tunnels. It had been built for the open steppe of Yenesia, for the long white roads where the air could carry the thunder of a war-hammer without being lost. To bring it into the mountain was to make a cathedral kneel in a chapel. But she made it kneel.

It unfolded around her the way a second skeleton unfolds around a first.

Three point two metres at the shoulder. Dark silver plates, every one of them flecked with the crushed pearl of glacial jade, so that the whole suit threw a faint cold blue into the dark. The breast was a block of crystallised red mercury, smaller than the standard core by a hand's width and brighter by a sun's worth — a piece of the late Yenesian Tsarina's heart, reforged, beating blue-white at the centre of the harness.

Right hand: a war-hammer. Head of hard-gold, chased all over with the Yenesian honeysuckle pattern, weight a hundred and fifty kilograms. The kind of weight that could crack a clocktower bell.

Left hand: a war-axe, the edge ground against powdered glacial jade so that on the moment of strike it would vent a cold of forty below zero into whatever it touched, and make metal turn brittle as old ice.

Back: two banks of four steam-jets. Not for the long flight. For the single leap.

Valentina closed the breastplate. The clang of it rolled three times down the tunnel and came back to her as a low, patient echo.

She looked down at herself, at the cold light running along her arms.

"Mother," she said, very quietly, to no one, "I am wearing it."

A few hundred metres deeper into the slope, Alfonso sat on a flat stone with the launch's radio-set spread across his knees. The set had come out of a Yenesian state-carriage. When the Prometheus scouts had shot the carriage down, the antenna had shattered, but the receive-and-send circuits were still good.

He had a tool-roll. From it he took fine copper wire, solder, a length of cable stripped from his own mechanical arm at the wrist. He twisted. He tinned. He made himself an antenna.

"There is no cipher channel," he said, working as he spoke. "I will have to send in the clear."

"In the clear, the transmission will be intercepted," said Violante.

"I know." Alfonso's hand was steady. The solder ran onto the copper in a small silver bead. "But Chu Shunhua's scouts have been waiting beyond Yumen Pass. If they have been monitoring this frequency, my call in the clear will reach them in three seconds."

"Call to whom?"

"To any ear that hears it, on the back of a Kui-long horse, speaking an Eastern tongue." He blew on the joint. "I am betting Chu Shunhua's scouts are already operating in these hills."

Violante did not object again.

Further up the tunnel, Cesare leaned against the wall. He did not close his eyes.

He listened.

When the Undying King was coupled to his nerves, the world became a different, more crowded country. Not prophecy. Not the second sight of the holy. Something mechanical, almost humble: the perception of the small magnetic fields that every piece of worked metal gives off, all the time, the way a candle gives off heat. Brass and steel and iron whispered to him in their own slow frequencies. The bronze of Violante's mirror pulsed like a second heart. The red mercury core in Valentina's breastplate beat like the first.

And outside, in the mountain, three other hearts beat.

Three. Lighter than the Prometheus war-shells he had known. Faster. In a triangle, three hundred metres beyond the upper mouth of the tunnel, just as he had been told they would be. The middle one was warming its six-barrel rotary. He could feel the feed-rack rolling over the first cartridge, the way a man feels a clock in the next room.

He opened his eyes.

"Three," he said. "Three hundred metres beyond the upper exit. Triangular spread. The centre one has lit its lamp."

"The lamp will shine into the tunnel," said Don Juan. He was already on his feet.

"Then cover the light." Cesare looked at the tunnel mouth. "Cover the light, and we take them in the dark."

Don Juan took off his coat and hung it across the mouth of the tunnel, the way a man hangs a curtain across a doorway. The fabric went half-translucent in the beam, and the angle of the brightness told Cesare everything else he needed to know.

"Wait for Valentina on the flank," he said.

Valentina did not answer.

Her suit had already taken the side-crack. The crack ran off the main tunnel halfway up, narrower than a man's shoulders, narrow enough that a war-hammer had to be carried at full extension. She went through it sideways. The dark silver scraped the stone on both sides. She did not stop. The cold blue light of her plates lit the rock for a moment, then was gone.

She came out on a slope of broken stone above the exit. From there she could see the whole.

Three Prometheus scouts, spread in a triangle on the open ground before the tunnel mouth, search-lamp in the centre washing the rock white. The six-barrel rotaries hung on their right arms, feed-belts hanging like snakes' bellies in the light.

She closed her fingers around the haft of the hammer.

The hammer-head shone, in the light of the lamp, with the cold of the Yenesian honeysuckle. She felt the weight of it as though the weight were a thing she had been waiting to feel again for a long time. A hundred and fifty kilograms. She had been able to swing it thirty times running. Now she wanted to swing it once, and crack a Prometheus open like an egg.

She lit the steam-jets.

Four nozzles at once. A hissing, and a column of white vapour, and three tonnes of dark silver lifted off the broken stone and went up over the rim of the slope, over the heads of the three Prometheus scouts, and hung there in the dark.

The three scouts looked up.

Six barrels came up to meet her, and the air above the open ground was cut into red arcs of tracer.

Valentina twisted. A round took the joint of her right shoulder and walked across the plate, gouging a shallow furrow. She did not fire back. She put all the steam she had into the jets and let herself fall.

She had chosen the middle one.

The hammer came down from above. Hard-gold on hard-gold. A sound like a bell being struck in a pit. The crown of the cockpit caved inward, half a metre of metal, and Valentina put the second blow into the hollow she had made. The cockpit became scrap.

The Prometheus scout rocked, then fell, and the fall raised a ring of dust that went rolling out across the open ground.

Valentina landed. The steam bled off in a long white plume around her.

She pulled the wreckage of the cockpit aside. She wanted to see if there was a rider still alive to pull out.

The cockpit was empty.

No rider. No man. Only bronze.

The whole of the inside was cast bronze. Joints, drive-shafts, gears, every surface inscribed with the neural prayer-text of the World Tree. The joints moved. Even with the body of the thing on its side, even with the cockpit caved in, the bronze moved — slow, slow, slow, opening and closing, the way a dead hand will sometimes open and close in the cold.

"It is alive," she said, very quietly.

The other two scouts opened fire together. Six barrels each. The air in front of her was cut into shreds of red.

Valentina threw herself sideways. The hammer swept around, and the head came down on the leg-joint of the second scout. Bronze cracked. Out of the crack came a dark red-gold liquid, slow, almost ceremonial.

The second Prometheus went down on one knee. Its upper half was still working. The six barrels were still firing. There was no pain in it. There was no fear. There was only the order.

"Cesare!" she shouted.

Cesare came out of the tunnel at a run.

His eyes were not fully lit. The violet was there, but the gold tracery had not run out of the iris. What he was doing was smaller, and stranger. He held the Undying King at the very edge of its warm-up, a single hair's breadth above zero, and let the system bleed out the smallest possible pulse of neural current into the air around him.

The current would have done nothing to a man.

To a body whose every bronze joint was inscribed with the prayer-text of the World Tree, it was the call of the mother.

The two scouts' joints seized. Briefly. The bronze inside them clashed and trembled. They did not fall, but they slowed — the rotary on the right arm of the nearer one dropped its rate by half, the second by more.

Valentina took the second.

The hammer came from the side this time. She put it into the waist-joint, which is the weakest hinge of any armoured frame, the one place where every load meets. The hinge blew. Out of the broken bronze came the dark red-gold again, and the second Prometheus went down in its own dust.

The last one tried to back away. The six-barrel came around—

A different sound answered it. Small. Quick. A rapid hammering of small arms on tin. The other side of the ridge.

Kui-long horse, dark red coats nearly invisible in the night, riders in light leather with small rapid-fire hand-guns, the muzzles throwing little orange flames into the dark like a string of fireflies.

They were not shooting the Prometheus.

They were shooting the lamp.

The glass went. The eye of the middle scout went black, and the open ground fell into darkness.

Valentina went in.

The hammer came around in an arc of cold blue, and the head of it came down on the head of the last Prometheus, and the head of the Prometheus broke.

The body went over. Dust went up. After a moment the dust began to settle.

The riders did not dismount. They came in on a wide half-circle, fifty of them perhaps, and held the line, and the cold blue of Valentina's plates and the small orange of their pistols' last shots were the only lights left in the valley.

The leader swung down from his horse. He was an Easterner of perhaps forty, a thin scar running down his left cheek to the corner of his mouth, the look of a hawk that has decided what it wants. He put his fist in his palm and bowed from the waist, in a way the chapter's teachers had not used for three centuries.

"Wu Tie," he said, in a Latin that was correct and slightly accented. "Vice-commander of the Scout Battalion under the Protector Chu. Sent to receive the Western guests."

"How did you know where to find us?" asked Alfonso.

"The radio." Wu Tie nodded. "Half an hour ago, on a frequency that belongs to the Yenesian state-carriage, someone called in the clear. We have been hunting for three days in these hills. The moment the frequency opened, we heard it."

Alfonso inclined his head, and did not explain.

Wu Tie walked over to the wreck of the first scout and knelt by it. He took a long knife from his belt and lifted away a flap of the broken cockpit.

He saw the bronze inside.

His scar went pale.

"It is…" he said, in his own tongue, very softly. "It is alive?"

"An Omega prototype," said Violante, who had come up beside him. She knelt, and put the tips of her fingers on the bronze. The joint under them trembled, faintly, the way a sleeping man's wrist will sometimes tremble. "The fruit of the World Tree's severed branch. A soldier of the Mechanicum."

Wu Tie looked at her. There was caution in his eyes, and there was also something else.

"The guests, then—"

"Our names," said Violante, "we will give to the Protector Chu, when we see him. First let us get out of this valley. These prototypes are the advance. The main body will follow."

Wu Tie nodded. He turned to his men and made a small gesture. The riders brought forward the spare saddlery from the packs of the Kui-long horses — not ordinary saddles, but double-rig frames with steam-assist, the kind that had been built to carry a wounded officer or a heavy piece of equipment in a fast retreat.

"The Kui-long horse can do three hundred leagues by day and a hundred and fifty by night," said Wu Tie. "From here to Yumen Pass, on foot, five days. On the Kui-long, two."

"Go," said Cesare.

He did not look back at the wreckage.

He did not need to. The Undying King was still listening. In the fallen brass of all three scouts, the bronze joints were still moving. Slowly. Carefully. Trying to put themselves back together. Trying, even through the rock, to send a small steady signal south, and east, and down.

The Omega prototype does not die. It waits.

It waits for the order of the mother.

---

In the sealed chamber of the Tongtian Palace at Luoyang, Chu Shunhua read the courier-pigeon's message.

The pigeon was the last safe channel. The radio in the clear was being watched by every enemy in the Empire, but a pigeon with a yellow silk slip tied to its leg was, for a few hours longer, a private road. The silk slip was apricot-yellow. The characters on it were in the cipher Chu Shunhua had set down with his own hand, eight years before.

He unrolled the silk.

"The Western guests have violet eyes with gold tracery. A suit of Fury III has destroyed three unmanned Prometheus scouts. The cockpits are empty. The interiors are of cast bronze, with inscribed prayer-text of the World Tree. The guests are, beyond doubt, the ones the Protector is seeking."

He read the line about the eyes three times.

Violet with gold tracery.

The bloodline of the star-seers.

The line of the See-and-Be-Seen.

He set the silk down. On the desk beside him lay a small jade pendant, cut in the shape of a Kui-long horn, and inside the pendant, folded, a yellowed scrap of paper lotus from Ceylon. The only thing his mother had carried out of Ceylon, the year she walked out of it barefoot, with a child on her hip, and never came back.

"Mother," he said, in a voice that no one in the chamber would have recognised as his, "he has come."

A candle on the desk leaned and recovered in a small draught.

On the wall behind him hung a map. The map was of the eastern root-system of the World Tree, its main nodes drawn in red mercury ink, in lines and sigils so dense that the whole wall looked like the inside of a spider's web.

One of the lines had just begun, very faintly, to glow.

第232章 沙漠绿洲的夜谈

【中文】
第232章 沙漠绿洲的夜谈

夔龙马跑起来像一团团暗红色的风。

从高加索暗河出口到东方的第一个绿洲，整整跑了八个小时。西泽尔在马背上把阿方索的蜘蛛巢腕表调成了导航模式，蛛形机械体表投射出的淡蓝色光路在沙丘上方弯弯曲曲地延伸，像一根从大地深处抽出的神经。楚舜华的密探们骑术精湛，夔龙马与密探之间几乎不需要口令，马蹄踏在砾石上发出闷响，偶尔有流星从头顶划过，拖着白色的尾迹坠入东方的天际。

绿洲在子夜前出现了。

那是一片胡杨林围出的浅水洼，周围散落着几座被风沙磨圆了棱角的驿站废墟，残墙上还残留着褪色的壁画，依稀能辨认出商队和骆驼的轮廓。密探们在水洼边支起帐篷，夔龙马被牵到胡杨树下饮水，它们低着通红的头，鼻息喷出白色的雾气。

篝火燃起来的时候，西泽尔才觉得自己还活着。

高加索的寒气、矿道的霉味、欧米茄原型体残骸里渗出的金属腥味——所有这些都暂时被胡杨木燃烧的焦香替代了。火光跳动，把每个人的影子拉得又长又瘦，像六根插在沙地上的黑色长矛。

"老板，你要是再不坐下来歇歇，我就要去跟夔龙马借个鞍子把你绑起来了。"昆提良把一壶烧热的马奶酒递给西泽尔，自己则盘腿坐在火堆旁，那件被青铜甲胄关节划破的军服露出一截结实的胸膛，上面横七竖八地贴着纱布。

"你的伤。"西泽尔接过酒壶。

"皮肉伤。"昆提良大咧咧地摆手，"我在南边岛上当兵的时候，有一次被椰子蟹夹了三个手指头，比这疼多了。"

"椰子蟹能夹断骨头么？"唐璜凑过来，手里拎着半只烤得焦黄的沙鸡。

"夹不断，但它能夹得你怀疑人生。"昆提良一本正经。

唐璜把沙鸡递给薇若兰，薇若兰接过去，没吃，只是盯着火光出神。她的膝盖上摊着达·芬奇·博尔吉亚的日记，纸页被翻得起了毛边——她在高加索暗河里就开始读了。

阿方索坐在最远的那棵胡杨树下，背靠树干，膝盖上摆着一块黄铜碎片。

那是他在高加索暗河里从一台被击倒的普罗米修斯侦察型甲胄关节处掰下来的——欧米茄原型体的微型红水银引擎碎片，只有拇指甲盖大小，表面布满了比芝麻粒还细的齿轮。他用一只放大镜对着篝火的光反复端详，手指偶尔动一下，在随身的皮面笔记本上画几笔。

篝火噼啪作响，远处有夜枭在胡杨树冠上叫。

瓦莲京娜从水洼边走过来，白靴上溅了些泥点，金色长发用一根皮绳松松地束在脑后。她手里握着一样东西，走到西泽尔身边坐下，把那样东西搁在两人之间的沙地上。

是一枚戒指。

纯银质地，戒面宽而厚，正中铸着叶尼塞双头鹰的浮雕，鹰爪下交叉着两柄战斧；翻过来，戒面内侧嵌着一枚更小的博尔吉亚狼头徽记，狼的眼睛是两颗极细的红宝石。

"我母亲留下的。"瓦莲京娜说。

西泽尔低头看着那枚戒指，篝火把红宝石映成两点微弱的火星。

"婚约信物。"瓦莲京娜的语气平淡，像在陈述一件与己无关的事，"我出生那年，我母亲跟你的母亲交换过信物。博尔吉亚的狼，叶尼塞的鹰。她说，等我们长大了，这两样东西合在一起，就是我们两个人的婚约。"

她顿了顿，目光落在西泽尔颈间露出的那根银链上——项链坠被军服领口遮住，只露出一小截链子。

"你母亲给你留了什么？"

西泽尔沉默了几秒。

他伸手从领口里拉出那枚项链坠。银莲花造型，花瓣薄得能透光，正面雕着博尔吉亚家的狼头纹章——琳琅夫人当年送给他的，外人看了只会觉得是博尔吉亚家的女眷饰品。

但他翻过项链坠，让瓦莲京娜看背面。

莲花底座上刻着一行极细的铭文，不是拉丁文，不是希腊文，而是某种古老的、像蛇一样弯弯绕绕的符号。西泽尔到现在也没能完全辨认它们，只能勉强认出其中两个——"莲花"和"根"。

"我母亲没有告诉我这行字是什么意思。"西泽尔说，"她只说，等我找到能读懂它的人，就知道答案了。"

瓦莲京娜盯着那行铭文看了很久。

"这不是波吉亚家的文字。"她低声说。

"不是。"

"我见过类似的笔法。"瓦莲京娜抬眼看他，"在我母亲的旧书里。叶尼塞皇宫的藏书阁最深处，有一批从东方收来的古卷，上面就是这种文字。我母亲说，那是'星见的文字'。"

篝火"啪"地炸开一朵火星，落在沙地上熄灭了。

西泽尔把项链坠重新塞回领口。

"你为什么来？"他忽然问。

瓦莲京娜没有立刻回答。她拿起那枚纯银戒指，在指间转了一圈，双头鹰的浮雕在火光中明明灭灭。

"你问我为什么来翡冷翠？"

"不。"西泽尔看着她，"我问你为什么来维苏威火山。为什么跟着我进暗河。为什么把自己的甲胄拿去跟三台活着的欧米茄原型体硬拼。"

"因为那是叶尼塞的目标。"瓦莲京娜说，"也是我的目标。"

她把戒指放回沙地上，直视着西泽尔。

"叶尼塞皇室三十年前就在北方冻土层里挖到过类似的东西。一片残枝。不是世界树，是世界树的一部分——像被什么东西从主树上撕下来的一截树枝，埋在永冻冰里。我母亲临终前把那片残枝的投影给我看过，她说那东西跟翡冷翠的某些秘密有关。她让我长大后去西方找到答案。"

她的声音没有起伏，像在背诵一份作战命令。

"我不是为了婚约才来的，西泽尔。婚约只是我母亲留给我的一把钥匙，用来打开西方的大门。如果我只是个来相亲的公主，根本进不了密涅瓦机关的档案室。"

西泽尔没有说话。

"阿瓦隆残片。"瓦莲京娜说出了那四个字，"你母亲项链上的文字，我母亲冻土里的残枝，阿瓦隆的冰原——这些全连在一起。东方有东方的那一半，西方有西方的那一半。分开了三百年，现在有人想把它们重新合到一起。"

"如果合到一起呢？"西泽尔问。

"我母亲没有告诉我。"瓦莲京娜说，"但她说过一句话——'如果两半合一，叶尼塞的冬天将永远结束，翡冷翠的秋天将永远不再回来'。"

"什么意思？"

"我不知道。"瓦莲京娜站起身，拍了拍白靴上的沙，"但我打算在它发生之前弄明白。"

她往火堆旁走了两步，又停下来，回头看着西泽尔。

"你呢？你到底在追什么？"

西泽尔盯着篝火。

他的影子被火光投在身后的沙丘上，瘦长，肩膀很窄，像一柄还没出鞘的刀。

"我不知道算不算追。"他说，"我只是想……把该保护的人保住。"

"哪些人？"

"阿黛尔。碧儿。阿方索。昆提良。唐璜。还有——"他顿了顿，"我母亲生前没能保护的那些人。"

瓦莲京娜看了他一会儿，没再说什么，转身走回火堆旁。

"公主殿下，尝尝这个！"昆提良把另一只烤好的沙鸡递过去，瓦莲京娜接过来咬了一口，眉头微微皱起——显然不合叶尼塞公主的口味。

"盐放多了。"她把沙鸡塞回昆提良手里。

"凑合吃吧公主殿下，咱们现在在沙漠里，不是在叶尼塞皇宫。"唐璜一边啃着鸡腿一边含含糊糊地说。

"沙漠里也要有尊严。"瓦莲京娜说。

昆提良和唐璜对视一眼，同时笑了。

篝火映着六个人的脸。薇若兰始终没说话，她的目光从日记上抬起来，看了西泽尔一眼，又看了瓦莲京娜一眼，最后落回日记的某一页上。阿方索在远处胡杨树下的剪影像一尊铜像，只有放大镜的微光偶尔闪一下。

过了一会儿，昆提良从贴身的内衣口袋里掏出一样东西。

是一封信。羊皮纸已经发黄了，边角磨得起了毛，折痕处几乎要断开。他小心翼翼地展开，凑到篝火旁给大家看。信纸上是工整的旧式拉丁文，末尾有一个火焰十字的印章——炽天骑士团的军徽。

"我父亲写的。"昆提良说。

"你父亲？"唐璜凑过来看。

"他是炽天骑士团的人。三十二年前退役的。"昆提良的声音忽然低了下去，"他活着的时候跟我说，他这辈子最后悔的事，就是没有亲手杀过一头欧米茄。他说欧米茄那种东西根本不是人，是'会走路的绞肉机'，他见过一个战友被欧米茄的关节缠住，整个人的骨头被拧成了麻花。"

他用粗糙的指尖抚过信纸上的军徽。

"他退役之后就再也没有摸过甲胄。但他把所有的军功章、退役证、还有这封信，全都藏在床底下的箱子里。他死之前拉着我的手说，'儿子，如果有一天炽天骑士团重新征召你，你就去。但记住——能跑就跑，活下来比当英雄重要'。"

篝火的光在他脸上跳了跳。

"所以我从来不对别人说我是炽天骑士团的人。"昆提良把信折好塞回内衣口袋，"我怕我爹地下知道了爬起来骂我。"

唐璜沉默了一会儿。

然后他从自己的靴筒里摸出一个油布小包，打开来，里头是一枚铜质徽章。徽章上铸着十字架和火焰的图案，跟昆提良那封信上的军徽一模一样，只是小得多，铜绿斑驳。

"炽天骑士团见习骑士徽章。"唐璜说。

"你什么时候——"昆提良瞪大了眼。

"训练营结业那天发的。"唐璜把徽章在衣角上擦了擦，"马斯顿那帮朋友都不在了，就剩这一枚。"

他把徽章在火光下翻了一面，背面刻着一行小字：唐璜·洛佩兹，星历166年，见习。

"我以前偷东西的时候，习惯在身上藏各种不值钱的小玩意当纪念品。值钱的当天就脱手了，不值钱的反而能留一辈子。"他笑了笑，把徽章收好，"这枚徽章大概是我偷过最不值钱的东西了，但也是唯一没卖掉的。"

篝火旁的空气安静了几秒。

远处有风穿过胡杨林，发出呜咽一样的声响。

阿方索那边忽然传来一声极轻的金属碰撞声。

所有人都扭头看过去。阿方索从胡杨树下的阴影里站起身，手里还举着那块欧米茄原型体的微型引擎碎片，但他的另一只手正按在左腕的蜘蛛巢腕表上——腕表的表盖不知什么时候弹开了，里面那只拇指大小的显示屏幕上正在快速滚动着文字。

"阿方索？"西泽尔站起来。

"别过来。"阿方索的声音压得很低，但语速比平时快了一倍，"这块碎片里残留的微量红水银跟我的蜘蛛巢的微晶发生了共振——是双向的。碎片里有记忆。"

他用放大镜凑近屏幕，屏幕上的文字滚动得越来越慢，最后定格在几行断断续续的古旧字符上。

"机械……神国。"阿方索念出第一个词，声音有点发紧。

然后是第二个名字。

"达·芬奇·波·吉亚。"

第三个地名。

"王屋山。"

西泽尔的脚步顿住了。

王屋山在东方的洛阳。楚舜华的脚下。

"这不是我父亲的无封面书册上的插图结构——"阿方索忽然抬起头，目光扫过所有人，最后落在薇若兰身上，"薇若兰教授，您父亲那本没有封面的书……您带来了么？"

薇若兰合上达·芬奇日记，从随身的挎包里抽出一本薄薄的手抄本，纸页泛黄，没有封面也没有书脊。她递给阿方索。

阿方索接过手抄本，翻到其中一页——那一页上画着一幅精密的齿轮结构图。他把欧米茄碎片的放大镜图像和书上的插图并排放在一起。

齿轮的排列咬合方式、中心轴的粗细、辐条的角度——完全一致。

"这是我父亲从B-07档案库最底层抄出来的。"薇若兰低声说，"他说这幅图是三百年前密涅瓦初代总长画的。"

阿方索没有说话。他把碎片和书并排放在沙地上，用随身的炭笔飞快地在笔记本上画着什么，眉头拧成了一团。

这时候，一匹快马从绿洲北侧的沙丘后冲了出来。

马上的骑手穿着东方样式的黑色短打，外罩一件半旧的皮甲，腰间挂着信筒。他翻身下马，踩着沙子一路小跑到篝火旁，单膝跪地，双手呈上一封用杏黄绢帛封好的信。

"监国大人急件。"骑手说，"命小的务必在贵客抵达玉门关之前送到。"

西泽尔接过绢帛。封口处是楚舜华私印的火漆，一枚夔龙纹的圆形凸起。

他拆开火漆，展开绢帛。

楚舜华的字迹端正有力，墨色浓黑，像是蘸了满斗的墨一气呵成——

"贵客不必伪装。洛阳城已备好迎接仪式，王屋山等你揭开真相。"

绢帛的左下角还有一行小字，是另一支笔补上去的，笔锋更细更急：

"令尊曾托我照看一人，其名与贵客相同。我等了十七年。"

西泽尔盯着最后一行字看了很久。

"令尊曾托我照看一人"——令尊，是说他的父亲隆·博尔吉亚。

"我等了十七年"——十七年前，西泽尔七岁，刚刚被带离克里特岛送往翡冷翠。

那一年，发生了什么事？

他还没来得及细想，远处传来了蒸汽机车的汽笛声。

不是一列，是一整列。

一长串通体漆黑的车厢从沙丘后驶出，车头铸着夏国金吾卫的夔龙纹徽记，蒸汽管道从车底密密麻麻地排出来，像一头多足巨兽缓缓爬过沙漠。每节车厢都是全机械密封的，连窗户都没有，只有车顶开了几个巴掌大的通气孔。

楚舜华的密探们吹响集合哨。

"请贵客们上车。"带队的吴铁说，"这是监国大人专门为贵客准备的密封车厢——沙漠里风沙大，普通的客车会灌沙子。而且这列车厢的蒸汽管道全部在车体内部循环，不会向外散逸任何气味。"

他看了西泽尔一眼，意味深长。

"监国大人说，有些东西，还是不让人闻到的好。"

红水银的气味。紫瞳的气息。

全机械密封的车厢，是为了保护西泽尔——保护他身上那些不能被任何第三方察觉的信号特征。

西泽尔把楚舜华的绢帛折好，揣进军服内袋。

篝火被沙土掩灭。一行人收拾行装，走向那列漆黑的车厢。薇若兰抱着达·芬奇日记走在最前面，阿方索把那本没有封面的手抄本和欧米茄碎片一起塞进挎包，昆提良扶着艾莲——她是被临时从密探的马背上扶下来的，走路还有点不稳。唐璜最后走，他弯腰把沙地上吃剩的鸡骨头踢进沙坑里。

就在他转身的那一瞬间，他余光瞥见了什么东西。

阿方索左腕上的蜘蛛巢腕表。

表盖还弹着。屏幕——

屏幕变黑了。

阿方索低头看了一眼，没有在意，正要合上表盖。

忽然，一根极细的青铜色节肢从屏幕的右下角慢慢探了出来。

那节肢比头发丝还细，却带着一种不属于这个世界的精密。它在屏幕边缘摸索了两秒，然后是第二根、第三根。接着，一只拇指甲盖大小的青铜蜘蛛从屏幕的黑色里爬了出来，沿着阿方索的指节缓缓上行。

它没有眼睛——或者说，它全身就是一只眼睛。

它爬到阿方索中指的第二关节时停了下来，抬起了头。

两点微弱的绿色光芒，从它头部中央的凹槽里亮起来，直直地映在阿方索的眼睛上。

那不是光。

是目光。

青铜蜘蛛发出一声极轻的、金属齿轮咬合的"咔哒"声。

像是叩门。

阿方索的手指僵在了半空。

【English】
Chapter 232 — Night Talk at the Desert Oasis

The Kui-long horses ran like clots of dark red wind.

Eight hours from the Caucasus underground river's eastern mouth to the first oasis. Eight hours of grit between the teeth, sweat drying to a fine white salt on the upper lip, the slow tilt of the stars wheeling overhead from west to east. Cesare had set Alfonso's spider-nest watch to navigation mode in the first hour of the ride. The spider-mech's body threw out a thin blue light-path that curved and forked across the dunes, like a nerve drawn up out of the earth. Chu Shunhua's scouts needed almost no word from him; the horses and the men moved as if they had been built for each other. Hooves thudded soft on the gravel, and now and again a meteor would slide down the eastern sky with its long white tail, falling into some unseen trough of darkness ahead of them.

The oasis came just before midnight.

A ring of poplars closed around a shallow pool. Around the pool sat the bones of what had once been a caravanserai — walls worn to rounded edges by the wind, faded murals on the plaster showing, just barely, the shapes of a merchant caravan and its camels. The scouts put up tents at the water's edge. The Kui-longs were led to the poplars to drink, their great red heads lowered, breath steaming white in the cold.

It was not until the campfire caught that Cesare realized he was still alive.

The Caucasus cold, the mineral smell of the deep tunnels, the metallic tang of the Omega prototype's leaking corpse — all of it gave way, for a moment, to the dry sweet char of burning poplar. The firelight jumped and threw their shadows out long and thin behind them, six dark lances planted in the sand.

"Captain, if you do not sit down, I am going to borrow a saddle off one of the Kui-longs and strap you into it."

Quintilian passed Cesare a flask of fermented mare's milk, warm from the coals, then settled cross-legged by the fire himself. His tunic had been torn at the joints by his bronze carapace, and the gap showed a stretch of hard chest across which bandages had been slapped on with cheerful disorder.

"Your wounds," Cesare said, taking the flask.

"Surface." Quintilian waved a big hand. "When I was a soldier down on the southern islands, a coconut crab took three of my fingers once. That hurt worse."

"Can a coconut crab break bone?" Don Juan was suddenly there, holding half a sand-grouse roasted to a turn.

"No. But it makes you doubt the goodness of God."

Don Juan handed the bird across the fire to Violante. She took it without eating. Her eyes were fixed on the flames, and on her knees lay Leonardo da Vinci Borgia's journal, its pages already curling at the edges — she had been reading it since the underground river.

Alfonso sat at the far poplar, back to the trunk, a piece of brass balanced on his knee.

He had wrenched it from the joint of a downed Prometheus scout in the Caucasus tunnels: a sliver of the Omega prototype's micro red-mercury engine, no bigger than a thumbnail, its surface crowded with gears smaller than sesame seeds. He held a lens up to the firelight and studied it in silence, his pencil moving now and then over a leather-bound notebook in his lap.

The fire cracked. An owl complained somewhere up in the poplar canopy.

Valentina came up from the pool's edge. Her white boots were speckled with mud. Her gold hair was tied at the nape of her neck with a leather cord, loose. She carried something in her hand. She sat down beside Cesare and set it on the sand between them.

A ring.

Sterling silver, broad and heavy of face. On its top, the Yenisei double-headed eagle in relief, two crossed war-axes under its claws. Turn it over, and on the inner face, a smaller Borgia wolf's head was inset, its eyes two minute rubies.

"My mother's," Valentina said.

Cesare looked down at it. The fire put two faint sparks into the rubies.

"It is a betrothal token," Valentina said, as flat as a parade-ground report. "The year I was born, my mother and yours exchanged tokens. The Borgia wolf. The Yenisei eagle. She said, when the children are grown, these two pieces together will be the contract of their marriage."

She paused, eyes on the silver chain that showed at Cesare's collar — the pendant lost in the opening of his coat, just a few links of it visible.

"What did your mother leave you?"

Cesare was quiet for a few seconds.

He reached into his shirt and drew out the pendant. A silver lotus, the petals so thin they almost let the firelight through. On the obverse, the Borgia wolf's crest — Donna Linlang's gift, the kind of thing a stranger would take for a piece of women's jewelry from the family.

He turned it.

On the back, around the base of the lotus, a line of tiny inscription. Not Latin. Not Greek. Some older script, snake-coiled, dense as ivy. Cesare had never been able to read it fully. He could make out two of the words, with effort: *lotus*, and *root*.

"My mother never told me what the line meant," Cesare said. "She told me that, when I found the person who could read it, I would have my answer."

Valentina studied the inscription a long while.

"That is not a Borgia script."

"No."

"I have seen its hand, though." She looked up at him. "In my mother's old books. In the deepest room of the imperial library at Yenisei there is a stack of old scrolls brought back from the East, and that is the script on them. My mother called it the writing of the *star-seers*."

A knot of resin popped in the fire and spat a spark onto the sand, where it died.

Cesare slid the pendant back under his collar.

"Why did you come?" he said, suddenly.

Valentina did not answer at once. She picked up the silver ring and turned it slowly between her fingers; the eagle on its face rose and vanished, rose and vanished, in the moving light.

"You are asking why I came to Florence?"

"No." He looked at her. "I am asking why you came to Vesuvius. Why you followed me into the underground river. Why you put your own armor against three live Omega prototypes and held."

"Because it is the Yenisei objective," Valentina said. "And my objective."

She set the ring back down in the sand, and looked at him.

"Thirty years ago the Yenisei royal house dug something out of the northern permafrost. A branch — not the World-Tree, but a piece of it, like a length of bough torn from the main trunk and buried in eternal ice. On her deathbed my mother showed me the projection of the branch. She said it was connected to certain secrets of Florence. She told me to go west when I was grown, and find the answer."

Her voice was level, as if she were reciting a field order.

"I did not come for the betrothal, Cesare. The betrothal is a key my mother left me to open the West's door. If I had been no more than a princess sent to be matched, I would never have made it past the archives of the Minerva Bureau."

Cesare said nothing.

"Fragments of Avalon," Valentina said. "The words on your mother's pendant. My mother's branch in the permafrost. The ice-plain of Avalon. All of it is the same web. The East has the half that belongs to the East. The West has the half that belongs to the West. They were separated three hundred years ago. Now someone is trying to fit them back together."

"And if they are fit together?"

"My mother did not tell me." Valentina stood, brushed the sand from her white boots. "But she said this: *If the two halves are joined, the winter of Yenisei will end forever, and the autumn of Florence will never come again.*"

"What does that mean?"

"I do not know." She took a step toward the fire, then stopped, half-turned. "But I intend to find out before it happens."

"What about you," she said. "What are you really chasing?"

Cesare looked into the fire.

His shadow lay long on the dune at his back, narrow in the shoulders, like a blade still sheathed.

"I do not know if *chase* is the right word," he said. "I only want to keep safe the people I ought to have kept safe."

"Who?"

"Adele. Bielle. Alfonso. Quintilian. Don Juan. And —" he paused — "the people my mother could not protect while she lived."

Valentina looked at him for a long moment. Then she turned and walked back to the fire.

"Your Highness, try this!" Quintilian, with ceremony, pressed a second roasted sand-grouse into her hand. Valentina took a bite. Her brow drew in — it was, evidently, not the way a Yenisei princess had been raised to eat.

"Too much salt." She thrust the bird back at him.

"Make do, Your Highness. We are in the desert, not in the palace of Yenisei." Don Juan spoke around a mouthful of thigh.

"One keeps one's standards even in the desert," Valentina said.

Quintilian and Don Juan looked at each other. They both grinned.

The firelight was on the six of them. Violante had not spoken. Her eyes lifted from the journal once, touched Cesare, touched Valentina, and went back to a single page. Alfonso, at the far poplar, was a brass-coloured silhouette; only the small glint of his lens moved.

After a while, Quintilian drew something out of his inner breast pocket.

A letter. Sheepskin, yellowed, the corners rubbed to a fluff, the fold almost parting. He unfolded it with care and held it close to the fire for the rest of them to see. Old-fashioned Latin, neatly lettered; at the foot, the wax seal of the Burning Cross — the insignia of the Order of the Seraphim.

"My father wrote it," Quintilian said.

"Your father?" Don Juan leaned in.

"He was a man of the Seraphim. Discharged thirty-two years ago." Quintilian's voice dropped, almost without his noticing. "When he was alive he told me the one thing he most regretted in his life was never having killed an Omega with his own hand. He said an Omega was not a man, it was a *walking meat-grinder*. He had seen a brother-in-arms caught in an Omega's joints. He said the man's bones were wrung out like wet rope."

He ran the pad of a rough thumb over the wax seal.

"After he left the Order he never touched a suit of armor again. He kept his medals, his discharge, this letter, all in a box under the bed. Before he died he took my hand. *Son*, he said, *if the Order of the Seraphim ever calls you up again, you go. But remember — when you can run, run. A live man is worth more than a dead hero.*"

The firelight shifted on his face.

"So I have never told anyone I am of the Seraphim," Quintilian said, folding the letter and slipping it away. "I am afraid my old man will crawl up out of his grave to curse me for it."

Don Juan was quiet a moment.

Then he drew a small oilcloth packet from his boot. Inside, a copper badge. A cross and a flame. The same insignia as Quintilian's seal, only smaller, and gone green with verdigris.

"Apprentice-knight badge of the Order of the Seraphim," Don Juan said.

"You —" Quintilian's eyes went wide.

"It was issued the day I left the training camp. The lads from Marston are all dead. This is the only one I have left."

He turned the badge in the firelight. On the reverse, a small line of letters: *Don Juan Lopez, 166 of the Star Era, Apprentice.*

"When I used to steal," he said, with a small smile, "I carried all kinds of worthless things on me, for keepsakes. The valuable ones I fenced the same day. The worthless ones I never got rid of. This is probably the most worthless thing I have ever stolen. It is also the only one I never sold."

The air by the fire was still for a few seconds.

Wind came through the poplars somewhere, a low, grieving sound.

A tiny chime of metal came from Alfonso's tree.

They all looked. Alfonso had risen from the shadow, the Omega sliver still in one hand. His other hand was on the spider-nest watch at his left wrist — its cover had flipped open, and on the thumbnail-sized display, text was scrolling fast.

"Alfonso?" Cesare stood.

"Stay where you are." Alfonso's voice was low, but twice its usual speed. "The trace of red mercury in the fragment has entered a resonance with my spider-nest's micro-crystal. It is two-way. The fragment has *memory* in it."

He held the lens to the screen. The text slowed, broke into segments, and settled on a few lines of old, broken characters.

"Mechanical… Divine Kingdom." Alfonso read the first phrase. His voice tightened.

Then the second name.

"Leonardo *da Vinci Borgia*."

The third was a place.

"Mount Wangwu."

Cesare's foot stopped mid-step.

Mount Wangwu was east of Luoyang. Under Chu Shunhua's hand.

"This is not the figure-structure from my father's unbound book —" Alfonso looked up, swept them all, and landed on Violante. "Professor Violante — your father's book, the one with no cover. Did you bring it?"

Violante closed the da Vinci journal. From the satchel at her hip she drew a thin handwritten volume, the pages yellow, no cover, no spine. She passed it to him.

Alfonso opened the book to one page. On that page was a precise drawing of a gear-arrangement. He laid the magnified image of the Omega sliver beside the page.

The tooth-count of the gears, the thickness of the central axle, the angle of the spokes — the same.

"My father copied this from the lowest level of the B-07 Archive," Violante said, low. "He said the drawing was made three hundred years ago, by the first Director-General of Minerva."

Alfonso said nothing. He put the sliver and the book down on the sand side by side, and began to draw, very quickly, in his notebook with his charcoal stick. His brow was a knot.

Then a fast horse came around the northern dune of the oasis.

The rider was in the short black coat of the East, with a half-worn leather cuirass over it and a message-tube at his hip. He slid off the saddle, half-jogged across the sand to the fire, dropped to one knee, and held up a letter sealed in apricot silk.

"From the Lord-Regent. Urgent. I was told it must reach the honoured guests before Yumen Pass."

Cesare took the silk. The seal was Chu Shunhua's private stamp, a circular boss with a Kui-long device in the wax.

He broke the seal. He unfolded.

Chu Shunhua's hand was upright and strong, the ink black as if dipped from a full well in one long breath —

*Honoured guests need not dissemble. Luoyang has prepared the welcome. Mount Wangwu awaits the truth you shall lift.*

At the lower left of the silk, a second hand had added a line in a finer, more hurried nib:

*Your late father once asked me to look after a person. That person bears your name. I have waited seventeen years.*

Cesare stared at the last line for a long while.

*Your late father* — that was his father, Lorenzo Borgia.

*I have waited seventeen years* — seventeen years ago, Cesare was seven. He had just been taken from Crete and sent to Florence.

What had happened, that year?

He had no time to think. The whistle of a steam-engine came in from somewhere.

Not one whistle. A whole train of them.

A long string of black carriages came out from behind the dune. The locomotive at the head was cast with the Kui-long device of the Summer Country's Golden Guard, steam-pipes fanning thick from its belly like the legs of a many-footed beast crawling slowly across the sand. Every carriage was fully sealed in metal. No windows. Only a few palm-sized vents in the roof.

Chu Shunhua's scouts blew the rally-whistle.

"If the honoured guests would board." The captain of the riders, a man named Wu Tie, came forward. "The Lord-Regent had these sealed carriages prepared specially for the guests — the desert wind carries sand into an open coach. And all of this train's steam-pipes cycle inside the body of the car. They release no scent outside."

He looked at Cesare. There was something knowing in his look.

"The Lord-Regent says, some things are better not smelled out."

The smell of red mercury. The breath of the violet-eyed.

The sealed carriages were to protect Cesare — to protect the world's noticing him the signal in his own blood.

Cesare folded Chu Shunhua's silk and slipped it inside his coat.

The fire was kicked into sand. The company broke camp and moved toward the black train. Violante walked at the head of them, the da Vinci journal in her arms. Alfonso stowed the sliver and the unbound book together into his satchel. Quintilian half-carried Aileen — she had been lifted onto a scout's horse for the ride and was still unsteady on her feet. Don Juan brought up the rear, stooping to kick the picked-clean bones of the sand-grouse into a small pit in the sand.

As he turned, his eye caught something.

Alfonso's spider-nest watch, at his left wrist.

The cover was still up. The screen —

The screen was black.

Alfonso glanced down, unbothered, and reached to snap the cover shut.

A thread of bronze, finer than a hair, slid slowly out of the lower-right corner of the screen.

It was a limb. A jointed limb. And it carried with it a precision that did not belong to any workshop of this world. It felt its way along the edge of the screen for two seconds. A second limb followed. A third.

Then a bronze spider, no bigger than a thumbnail, climbed out of the black of the screen and began to move up the length of Alfonso's finger.

It had no eyes. Or rather — its whole body *was* an eye.

It stopped at the second knuckle of Alfonso's middle finger. It raised its head.

Two points of faint green light came on, in the hollow at the centre of its head. They fell, perfectly, into the pupils of Alfonso's eyes.

That was not light.

That was *gaze*.

The bronze spider made a small sound — a soft, mechanical *click*, gear against gear, tooth against tooth.

It sounded, exactly, like a knuckle rapping on a door.

Alfonso's hand froze in the air.

第233章 叩门者的铜铃

【中文】
第233章 叩门者的铜铃

阿方索的手指没有落下来。

他整个人像是被什么东西从身体内部掐住了后颈，两只眼睛定定地盯着那两点绿光，瞳孔缓缓放大，像两口无底的井。

然后他开口了。

不是他自己的声音。那声音从阿方索的胸腔里升起来，低沉、空旷，带着一种回声似的金属颤音，像是从一口很深很深的井底传上来的。

"……莲花指引迷途之人……齿轮度量星辰轨迹……吾辈仰望天机，窃取未来……"

每个字都咬得极准，可那不是拉丁文，不是希腊文，也不是任何西泽尔听过的语言。古老的蛇形笔画在阿方索的舌尖上翻滚，像是某种被封存了几百年的祷词终于找到了出口。

唐璜的刀已经握在手里了，可他不敢动。昆提良一只胳膊护着艾莲退后两步，另一只手在摸战斧。薇若兰最先反应过来，她没有拔枪，而是把怀里那本达·芬奇日记往地上一摔，三步并作两步冲过来，左手扣住阿方索的下颌，右手按住他的额头，硬生生把那张脸别向了另一边，迫使他与那两点绿光脱离接触。

"别看它！"薇若兰厉声道。

可那声音没有停。阿方索的嘴唇还在动，眼睛却已经失焦了，像是有人在替他说，又像是一个沉睡了很久的人终于被叫醒，正在努力拼凑自己是谁。

青铜蜘蛛仍然停在阿方索中指的第二关节上，纹丝不动。那两点绿光在薇若兰的动作下微微一颤，仿佛在审视这个打断仪式的人。

西泽尔伸手。

他本不该伸手的。他比任何人都清楚那种感觉——世界树残枝共鸣时那种被拽入深海的窒息感。可他还是伸出了手，用食指和拇指轻轻捏住了那具拇指甲盖大小的青铜造物，把它从阿方索的手指上取了下来。

青铜蜘蛛没有反抗。

它落在西泽尔的掌心里，八条节肢微微收拢，发出一声极轻的"咔哒"，这次不是叩门。

是铜铃。

那声音清脆得像小时候克里特岛教堂里早祷的钟声，从西泽尔的掌心传上来，顺着骨骼一路攀升，震得他后颈的黄金套管都在发烫。

阿方索像被抽走了脊梁骨一样软了下去，薇若兰一把捞住他，把他放平在地上，探了探鼻息才松了口气。

"活着，"薇若兰皱眉，"但脑电波全乱了。"

她抬头看西泽尔，目光落在他掌心那团青铜色上。

"那是机械神教的东西。"

不是问句，是判断。

西泽尔点了点头。

他知道。刚才阿方索念出的那些蛇形文字，和琳琅夫人那本锡兰星见预言书里的祷词是同一套系统——机械神教留下的语言，世人早已遗忘的三百年。

西泽尔把蜘蛛暂时放在地上，从领口拽出那枚项链坠。

母亲留下的锡兰星见坠子，银质，莲花底座，背面刻着几个已经模糊的蛇形符号。他一直没能完全辨认，只依稀读出"莲花"和"根"两个字。

他把坠子翻过来，凑近那只青铜蜘蛛。

蜘蛛动了。

它从西泽尔的掌心爬起来，沿着他的指节爬到手背，然后掉头，沿着无名指再爬回来，绕着西泽尔摊开的掌心跳了一圈。

一圈。

两圈。

三圈。

每经过那枚坠子时，它头部凹槽里的绿光就会亮一下，像是在校准某种信号。

第三圈走完，青铜蜘蛛停在了坠子正上方。

它仰起头，八条节肢慢慢舒展开来，像一朵正在绽放的金属花。

然后它塌了。

不是碎裂，而是从内部开始瓦解。青铜色的金属外壳一层层剥落，化作一缕极淡的青烟，从西泽尔的指缝间无声无息地消散了。

空气里留下了一丝极淡的气味。

像旧铜，也像新雪。

唐璜蹲下来，用刀尖拨了拨那缕青烟消散后留在地面上的东西——一张薄如蝉翼的铜片，上面用细如发丝的蚀刻线条画着一张地图。

"……等等，"唐璜把铜片翻过来，"这是洛阳城。"

他用指腹擦去表面的浮灰，那张地图渐渐清晰了。洛阳城的轮廓在铜片上铺展开来，城墙、街道、坊市标注得极为详尽，底部有一条弯弯曲曲的虚线，从城南的洛水渡口一直延伸到城东的一片坊区，虚线尽头画着一个倒置的莲花符号。

"这是地下通道，"唐璜抬头看西泽尔，"从洛水底下进城，通到城东的黑市。"

昆提良凑过来看了一眼："中山国人在洛阳城地下挖了密道？"

"不止密道，"唐璜指着虚线沿途那些细小的齿轮标记，"这是机械神教三百年前留下的旧路。这条虚线穿过了至少三个标注着'齿轮'的位置——那是世界树残枝的根须节点。"

西泽尔把坠子收回领口。

"这张图先收好。"他说。

唐璜把铜片折好塞进贴身的内袋，拍了拍。

"老板，青铜蜘蛛不是来找我的。"阿方索被薇若兰扶着坐起来，脸色发白，声音发涩，"它是在扫描你——"

他抬起左手。

腕表旁边的皮肤上多了一个东西。

一个极小的齿轮纹身，只有米粒大小，线条精密得不像是刺上去的，倒像是从皮肤内部生长出来的。铜色，嵌着一颗比芝麻还小的绿点。

"……那玩意留了标记在我身上。"阿方索的声音有一丝不安，"我感觉到了，有东西在通过这个齿轮读我。"

薇若兰翻开他的眼皮看了看，又从随身的医疗包里摸出一支细长的银针，刺入他耳后的一处穴位。

"你跟着我念。"薇若兰的声音忽然变了，冷静得近乎冰冷，"'机械归于寂静，齿轮停止咬合。'"

她念的是机械神教的祷文。

"机械归于寂静，齿轮停止咬合。"阿方索跟着念了一遍。

腕表旁的齿轮纹身闪了一下，然后熄灭了。

"暂时封住了，"薇若兰收回银针，"但这不是长久之计。这个标记是活的，等它适应了你体内的频率，还会重新激活。我需要密涅瓦的精神诊断椅才能彻底分析它的结构。"

"回去之后第一件事。"西泽尔说。

薇若兰点头。

吴铁在远处一直等着，没有催促。等西泽尔一行人收拾妥当，他才抬手一挥，密探们重新上马，在前方的沙丘上拉成一条散兵线。

全密封的车厢在月色下泛着暗哑的黑色光泽。

西泽尔第一个上了车。车厢内部比外面看起来要宽敞得多，靠窗一排软座，对面是固定的折叠行军床，蒸汽管道全部嵌在车壁里，车顶还装了一台小型冷凝机，把灌进来的热气压下去。角落里堆着几只密封的军用补给箱，贴着密涅瓦机关的六翼猫头鹰徽记——那是薇若兰从翡冷翠出发前就托人送来的。

车厢门从内侧锁死。

"从现在起，车厢是全封闭的，"吴铁隔着车窗说，"气味、信号、声音都不会外泄。"

他顿了一下。

"沿途会有四拨暗哨，都是监国大人的人。"

马鞭一响，列车启动。

蒸汽机的低鸣从车底传上来，细密而稳定，像是某种巨兽的心跳。车窗外是漆黑的大漠，星星低得仿佛伸手就能摘到。

车厢里安静了很久。

昆提良和艾莲坐在最里面的行军床上，艾莲已经靠在他肩上睡着了。薇若兰靠着车窗翻那本达·芬奇日记，一页一页极其缓慢地看。阿方索抱着那只挎包蹲在角落里，时不时低头看自己手腕上那个熄灭的齿轮纹身，眼神里有一种说不清的情绪。

唐璜凑到西泽尔身边，压低了声音。

"老板，那张图上标了三个齿轮节点。其中一个——"他用指尖在膝盖上比划，"——在洛阳城东的黑市底下，另一个在城北的邙山，还有一个在城南龙门石窟的奉先寺。"

他停了一下。

"龙门石窟奉先寺的卢舍那大佛是武则天捐了两万贯脂粉钱修的，佛像肚子里是中空的，这事儿只有少数人知道。那条虚线穿过佛像底座的时候画了个齿轮的符号——"

"你想说什么。"西泽尔说。

"我想说，那张图上标注的'齿轮'不是普通节点，"唐璜的声音更低了，"那是世界树残枝的根须在地面上的出口。那东西的根须从维苏威火山一路往东延伸，穿过整个中亚，进了夏国地界。"

他看着西泽尔。

"叶素理是中山国的外交大臣。中山国就在洛阳和长安之间。"

西泽尔没有接话。

车窗外的星星在缓缓移动。车厢的振动在脚下持续着，像一条沉入地底的河流正在载着他们穿过大半个大陆。

他闭上眼睛。

后颈的黄金套管还残留着刚才被铜铃声震过的那种微微发烫的感觉，像是某种信号还没有完全消退，正在他的神经通路里慢慢沉淀。

——三天后。洛阳。

列车在黎明前抵达了洛阳城外的驿站。

天还没亮透，东方的天际线压着一层灰蓝色的光。洛阳城墙在远处横亘着，巨大而沉默，像一头沉睡的巨兽。

西泽尔下车时第一眼看到的是城墙上的两堆篝火。

左边一堆，火焰上方悬挂着一面大旗——黑色底，鎏金丝绣着一只展翅的朱雀，振翅欲飞。

大夏龙雀旗。

右边一堆，火焰上方悬挂着另一面旗——白色底，黑色齿轮层层叠叠嵌成同心圆，中心是一颗倒置的五芒星。

齿轮旗。

两堆篝火相距不过三十步，火焰在黎明前的冷风里交织着，把那两面旗帜照得忽明忽暗。一面是夏国军政的最高权力，一面是三百年前从西方消失的机械神教遗物。

西泽尔盯着那面齿轮旗看了三秒。

旗帜是新的。布料没有褪色，齿轮的漆面反着光。它不是从什么地方翻出来的老古董，而是最近才被制作出来，挂在洛阳城墙上的。

"监国大人在这边。"吴铁说。

驿站门口站着一匹马。

通体红如朱砂，比寻常的蒙古马高出一个头，肩宽臀圆，肌肉在晨光中泛着缎子一样的光泽。马的额头上有一个圆圆的弹洞疤痕，鬃毛被仔细地梳理过，用红绸带扎成了一把。

朱砂。

楚舜华的坐骑。

马背上没有人。马被缰绳系在驿站门柱上，安静地打着响鼻，偶尔用前蹄刨一刨地面。

一个人从驿站里面走了出来。

他穿着全身漆黑的重型甲胄，每一片甲叶上都刻着细密的夔龙纹，胸前浮雕着一只张牙舞爪的鎏金夔龙。甲胄的造型和西泽尔见过的任何西方甲胄都不同——线条更流畅，重心更低，肩甲和护臂的弧度是按照东方人的身体比例设计的，把穿着者的力量感推到了极致。

鬼武者Ⅱ型。

夏国最新一代的机动甲胄，通体漆黑，力量压倒性强大，各项性能均达到甚至超过设计指标。

穿甲的人戴着一张银色面具——不是西泽尔在翡冷翠见过的任何样式。面具的造型是一张鬼面，獠牙外翻，双目深凹，眉骨处嵌着两片微小的红水银晶片，在黎明的光线里闪着暗红色的微光。

他和朱砂一样安静地站在那里，披风在晨风里缓缓翻卷。

西泽尔下了马车。

两个人隔着十步的距离对视。

就在目光相接的那一瞬间，西泽尔后颈的黄金套管猛地烫了一下。不是之前那种隐隐的温热，而是被烧红的铁块烙上去一样的剧痛。

他的瞳孔骤然变色。

紫色被金色的纹路贯穿，像是被熔岩灌入的裂纹，在他的虹膜里迅速蔓延开来。视野里的一切都变得异常清晰——他甚至能看到那张银色面具上每一道划痕，每一颗铆钉的纹路。

而对面那张银色鬼面之下，那双被深凹的眼窝藏住的眼睛里，同样亮起了紫金色的光芒。

西泽尔感觉自己的身体像是被一只无形的巨手攥住了。不是从外面，而是从里面——从他的脊椎，从他后颈的黄金套管，从他血液最深处的某个正在苏醒的角落。

他的紫瞳在共鸣。

不只是和世界树残枝。

是在和另一个人共鸣。

那个穿鬼武者Ⅱ型甲胄的人也在同时经历同样的事情。他伸出一只手，缓缓摘下了自己的银色鬼面。

面具下面是一张年轻的脸。眉骨高而锋利，颧骨略宽，下颌线条硬朗得像是用刀刻出来的。皮肤带着常年在风沙里行军的人才有的粗糙纹理，颜色比翡冷翠人深了两个色号。

眼睛。

那双眼睛在西泽尔见过的所有眼睛里都找不到对应的词。

不是紫，不是金，是两种颜色在他瞳孔深处旋转、融合，最终凝结成一种灼热的紫金色——和西泽尔此刻眼中的纹路一模一样。

那双眼睛看着西泽尔。

西泽尔看着那双眼睛。

两人之间像是有一道无形的桥梁正在被搭建，每一秒都在变得更粗、更紧、更不容切断。从他的脊椎到对方的身体里，从他的黄金套管到对方的血液中，某种三百年前被分割的东西正在发出悲鸣。

对方开口了。

声音不大，却清晰得像刀刃划在磨石上。

"欢迎来到洛阳。"

那双紫金色的眼睛在黎明的光线里微微弯起。

"锡兰星见之子。"

车马在驿站外嘶鸣。城墙上的两堆篝火渐渐熄灭，大夏龙雀旗和机械神教齿轮旗在晨风里一起翻卷着。

西泽尔握紧了拳头。

他后颈的黄金套管已经烫到了极限，可他一动不动地站在原地，等那股灵魂深处的震动慢慢平息下来。

"楚舜华。"他叫出了对面那个人的名字。

那不是问句。

对方点了点头。

"是我。"

——

（未完待续）

【English】
Chapter 233 — The Bell of the Door-Knocker

Alfonso's hand did not fall.

He stood as though something had seized him by the nape from inside his own body. Both eyes fixed on the two green points of light, the pupils dilating slowly, the way the mouth of a well opens when you look down into it.

Then he began to speak.

It was not his own voice. The sound rose out of Alfonso's chest, low and hollow, with a metallic tremor in it, the way sound carries up from the bottom of a well that is very deep.

"...The lotus guides the wayfarer lost... the gear measures the track of stars... we, who look up at the secret of the heavens, who steal the future..."

Every word bitten off cleanly, but the tongue was not Latin, nor Greek, nor any speech Cesare had ever heard. The ancient serpentine strokes rolled off Alfonso's lips as if some prayer sealed away for three centuries had finally found its mouth.

Don Juan had his knife in his hand, but he did not move. Quintilian put one arm around Elaine and stepped back two paces, the other hand finding his war-axe. Verolan was the first to recover; she did not draw a pistol, but hurled the Leonardo diary she had been carrying onto the floor, and came in three quick strides, her left hand gripping Alfonso by the jaw, her right palm pressed flat to his forehead, wrenching his face away, forcing his gaze off those two green pinpricks.

"Don't look at it," Verolan said, sharp as a slap.

The voice did not stop. Alfonso's lips kept moving, but his eyes had gone out of focus, as if someone else were speaking through him — or as if a sleeper long buried were waking and trying to remember who he was.

The bronze spider still sat on the second joint of Alfonso's middle finger, motionless. The two green lights quivered faintly at Verolan's grip, as if the thing were studying the woman who had interrupted it.

Cesare reached out.

He should not have. Of anyone alive he knew the feeling — the drowning pull of the World-Tree branch resonating, that sensation of being hauled under. He reached out anyway, pinched the small bronze thing between thumb and forefinger — it was no larger than a thumbnail — and lifted it from Alfonso's hand.

The spider did not resist.

It settled in Cesare's palm, its eight jointed legs folding in with a faint click. This time the click was not a door-knocker. It was a bell.

The sound was clear and sweet, like the morning bell of a Cretan church from his childhood. It rose from his palm, climbed the bones of his wrist, and set the gold tubing at the back of his neck burning.

Alfonso folded as though his spine had been pulled out of him. Verolan caught him, lowered him flat, put two fingers to his nose, and let out a breath.

"He's alive," she said, frowning. "But his brainwaves are all over the place."

She looked up at Cesare. Her gaze fell to the small bronze thing in his hand.

"That's from the Mechanist Church."

Not a question. A judgment.

Cesare nodded.

He knew. The serpentine words Alfonso had spoken came from the same system as the prayers in Lady Linlang's Ceylon star-seer book — the language the Mechanist Church had left behind, the tongue the world had forgotten for three hundred years.

Cesare set the spider on the ground for the moment and pulled the chain from beneath his collar.

The pendant his mother had left him. Silver. A lotus for its base. On the back, a few blurred serpentine characters. He had never been able to read them all. He had made out only "lotus" and "root."

He turned the pendant over and held it close to the bronze spider.

The spider moved.

It crawled out of his palm, climbed the knuckle of his index finger, went around to the back of his hand, turned at the wrist, came back up the ring finger, and made a circuit of his open palm.

One circuit. Two. Three.

Each time it passed the pendant, the green slot in its head brightened, as though it were calibrating a signal.

After the third circuit, the bronze spider stopped directly above the pendant.

It lifted its head. The eight legs spread slowly, like a metal flower opening.

Then it came apart.

Not shattered — dissolved. From the inside out, the bronze skin flaked away in layers, thinned to a wisp of pale blue smoke, and slipped soundlessly through the gaps between his fingers.

A faint smell lingered in the air. Old copper, and new snow.

Don Juan crouched down and used the tip of his knife to poke at what the smoke had left on the ground — a copper sheet, thin as a cicada's wing, on which a map was etched in lines no thicker than a hair.

"Wait," Don Juan said, and turned the sheet over. "This is Luoyang."

He rubbed the dust away with the ball of his thumb, and the map came clear. The outline of Luoyang spread across the copper sheet. The walls, the streets, the market wards marked in careful detail. At the bottom, a dotted line wound from the river crossing at Luo Shui in the south of the city all the way to a market ward in the east, and at the end of the dotted line, an inverted lotus.

"It's a passage under the earth," Don Juan said, looking up at Cesare. "In from under the Luo, out at the black market in the east of the city."

Quintilian leaned in. "The Zhongshan folk dug tunnels under Luoyang?"

"Not only tunnels." Don Juan pointed to the small gear-marks along the dotted line. "This is an old route the Mechanist Church laid down three hundred years ago. The dotted line passes through at least three places marked 'gear.' Those are the root-nodes of the World-Tree branch."

Cesare tucked the pendant back beneath his collar.

"Hide that map well," he said.

Don Juan folded the sheet, slipped it into the inner pocket of his coat, and patted it once.

"Captain, the bronze spider was not looking for me." Alfonso was sitting up, propped against Verolan's arm, his face the color of tallow, his voice dry. "It was scanning you—"

He raised his left hand.

Beside his wristwatch, the skin bore something new. A tiny gear-tattoo, the size of a grain of rice, the lines so fine they did not look pricked in but grown out from under the skin. Copper-colored, with a green dot in its center no larger than a sesame seed.

"...That thing left a mark on me." There was an edge of unease in Alfonso's voice. "I can feel it. Something is reading me through that gear."

Verolan lifted one of his eyelids, looked, then took a long thin silver needle from the medical case at her hip and pressed it into a point behind his ear.

"Say it after me." Her voice had changed, suddenly cold as a poured glass of water. "Machinery returns to silence. Gears cease to mesh."

It was a Mechanist prayer.

"Machinery returns to silence. Gears cease to mesh," Alfonso repeated.

The gear-tattoo at his wrist flickered once, and went dark.

"Sealed for now." Verolan withdrew the needle. "But it won't hold. The mark is alive. Once it has tuned itself to the frequencies in your body, it will wake again. I will need Minerva's diagnostic chair to take it apart properly."

"The moment we are back," Cesare said.

Verolan nodded.

Wu Tie waited at a distance, patient, in no hurry. When Cesare's company was ready, he raised a hand. The agents of the secret service mounted up, and spread themselves along the crest of the dunes ahead in a loose skirmish line.

The sealed carriage stood in the moonlight, the dull black of its lacquered panels drinking the light.

Cesare climbed in first. Inside, the carriage was far roomier than it looked from without — a bench seat along the windows, a folding campaign cot fixed to the opposite wall, the steam-piping tucked into the paneling, and a small condensation unit set in the ceiling that pressed the heat of the incoming air back down. In one corner, a stack of sealed military supply crates, each stamped with the six-winged owl of the Minerva Bureau — Verolan had arranged for them to be sent on from Florence before she left.

The carriage door was locked from the inside.

"From this moment on, the carriage is fully sealed," Wu Tie said through the window. "No scent, no signal, no sound will pass out."

He paused.

"There will be four sets of hidden sentries along the road. All of them the Regent's men."

The driver's whip cracked. The carriage began to move.

The low hum of the steam-engine came up through the floor, fine and steady, the heartbeat of some great sleeping beast. Outside the windows, the desert was a black sheet. The stars hung so low it felt one could have reached up and taken one down.

The carriage was quiet a long while.

Quintilian and Elaine sat together on the cot at the far end; Elaine had fallen asleep against his shoulder. Verolan leaned against the window, turning the pages of the Leonardo diary one by one, very slowly. Alfonso sat in a corner with his satchel in his lap, looking down at the dead gear-tattoo at his wrist, an unreadable thing moving behind his eyes.

Don Juan moved close to Cesare, and lowered his voice.

"Captain, there are three gear-nodes on that map. One of them—" he drew it with his fingertip on his knee, "—lies under the black market in the east of the city. The second is at Mangshan, in the north. The third is at the Fengxian Temple in the Longmen Grottoes, south of the city."

He paused.

"The Vairocana Buddha in the Fengxian Temple was paid for by Empress Wu with twenty thousand strings of cosmetics money. You can count on one hand the people who know that the statue is hollow inside. When the dotted line passes the base of the Buddha, there is a gear marked—"

"What are you trying to say," Cesare said.

"I'm trying to say that the 'gears' on that map are not ordinary nodes." Don Juan's voice dropped further. "They are the exits of the World-Tree branch's roots above the ground. Its root system runs east from Vesuvius, through all of Central Asia, and on into Xia territory."

He looked at Cesare.

"Ye Suli is the Foreign Minister of Zhongshan. Zhongshan lies between Luoyang and Chang'an."

Cesare said nothing.

The stars drifted slowly past the carriage window. The vibration of the wheels went on and on beneath his feet, the way a river that has gone underground runs with you across a continent.

He closed his eyes.

The gold tubing at the back of his neck still held a faint warmth from the bell's stroke, as though some signal had not yet finished pouring itself into his nerve-paths and was settling there, grain by grain.

— Three days later. Luoyang.

The train reached the relay station outside Luoyang's walls before dawn.

The sky had not yet lightened. The eastern horizon was pressed under a layer of blue-grey. Luoyang's city wall lay ahead, vast and silent, the body of some great beast in its sleep.

The first thing Cesare saw when he stepped down from the carriage was the two bonfires on the wall.

The one to the left, above its flame, hung a great banner — black ground, gold thread, a vermilion bird with outspread wings, on the point of taking flight.

The flag of the Great Xia Dragon-Sparrow.

The one to the right, above its flame, hung another — white ground, a black gear built up in concentric rings, and at its heart an inverted five-pointed star.

The Gear flag.

The two bonfires stood less than thirty paces apart. Their flames crossed in the pre-dawn wind, and lit the two banners, now bright, now dim. One was the highest secular-military authority of Xia. The other was a relic of the Mechanist Church, which had vanished from the West three hundred years ago.

Cesare looked at the Gear flag for three seconds.

The flag was new. The cloth had not faded. The lacquer on the gear caught the light. It was not an old curio dragged out of some storeroom. It had been made recently, and hung on the wall of Luoyang.

"The Regent is this way," Wu Tie said.

At the door of the relay station stood a horse.

Red as cinnabar from the tips of its ears to the feathering of its hooves. A full head taller than an ordinary Mongol horse. Broad across the shoulder, deep through the hindquarters, the muscles under its coat shining in the early light like rolled silk. On its forehead, a round bullet-scar. Its mane had been carefully combed and tied with a crimson cord into a single tassel.

Cinnabar.

Chu Shunhua's mount.

There was no one on the horse. It was tied to the post by the door of the relay station, snorting quietly, pawing the ground every now and then with a forefoot.

A man came out of the relay station.

He was wearing full heavy armor the color of black lacquer. On every plate, a fine kui-dragon pattern had been etched. Across his chest, in raised gilt, a kui dragon bared its teeth. The lines of the armor were like nothing Cesare had seen in the West — they flowed more easily, the center of gravity was lower, and the curve of the shoulder-plate and the vambrace had been cut to the proportions of an Eastern body. The sense of power in the suit had been pushed to its last degree.

Ghost Warrior, Type II.

The newest generation of powered armor in Xia, lacquered black, overwhelming in strength, every metric at or above design specification.

The man inside the armor wore a silver mask — not any style Cesare had seen in Florence. The shape was a demon's face, fangs thrust outward, eyes sunken deep, and in the brow, two small cinnabar-mercury lenses that threw back a dull red glint in the dawn light.

He stood as still as his horse, the cloak at his shoulders lifting and falling in the morning wind.

Cesare stepped down from the carriage.

The two of them faced each other across ten paces.

The moment their eyes met, the gold tubing at the back of Cesare's neck flared. Not the dim warmth of before, but a savage pain, as though a brand fresh from the fire had been pressed to the skin.

His pupils changed.

The violet was cut through with veins of gold, like cracks in a rock into which molten ore has been poured, and the cracks spread fast across the iris. Everything in his field of vision went unnaturally sharp — he could see every scratch on the silver mask, every rivet, the pattern of the steel grain beneath.

And inside the eye-sockets of that silver demon face, the eyes themselves were answering. A purple-gold light rose in them.

Cesare felt his body taken in the grip of a hand he could not see. Not from outside. From inside — from the spine, from the gold tubing at the back of his neck, from somewhere deep in the blood that was only just waking.

His purple irises were resonating.

Not only with the World-Tree branch.

With another person.

The man in the Ghost Warrior was going through the same thing at the same moment. He lifted one hand, and slowly drew the silver demon mask away from his face.

The face underneath was young. The brow-bone was high and sharp, the cheekbones a little wide, the line of the jaw cut as if it had been done with a knife. The skin carried the rough grain a man gets from years of campaigning in windblown sand, two shades darker than a Florentine's.

His eyes.

There was no word in any catalogue of eyes Cesare had ever read that could have covered them.

They were neither violet nor gold. The two colours turned and melted into each other somewhere deep in the pupils, and at last came together into a kind of burning purple-gold — exactly the pattern that was, at this same moment, spreading through Cesare's own iris.

Those eyes looked at Cesare.

Cesare looked back at them.

Between the two of them an invisible bridge was being built, and every second it thickened, tightened, grew harder to cut. From his spine to the other's body. From the gold tubing at his neck to the blood in the other's veins. Something that had been split apart three hundred years before was crying out.

The other man spoke.

His voice was not loud, but it was clear, the way a blade is clear against the stone it is being sharpened on.

"Welcome to Luoyang."

The purple-gold eyes, in the dawn light, narrowed a little, as if in the beginning of a smile.

"Son of the Ceylon star-seer."

The horses stamped and blew at the bit outside the relay station. The two bonfires on the city wall were going out, and the Great Xia Dragon-Sparrow flag and the Mechanist Gear flag turned together in the morning wind.

Cesare closed his hand into a fist.

The gold tubing at the back of his neck was at the limit of what he could bear, but he did not move. He stood where he was, and waited for the tremor in the deep place of his soul to quiet.

"Chu Shunhua," he said, naming the man opposite.

It was not a question.

The other man inclined his head.

"It is."

— end of chapter

第234章 洛阳城的欢迎
