【中文】
第234章 洛阳城的欢迎

夔龙马踏在洛阳的青石板路上，声音像沉闷的鼓点。

这种马比翡冷翠的安达卢西亚马高了整整一个头，肩胛处的肌肉隆起如铁块，通体红如朱砂，每一匹的眼底都泛着野性的光。西泽尔骑在马背上，能感觉到那种力量隔着马鞍传过来——不是翡冷翠马匹那种训练有素的温顺，而是一种蓄势待发的杀意，仿佛骑手一声令下它就会冲向敌人，哪怕前面是刀山火海。

楚舜华在最前面，银色鬼面已经重新戴回去了，只露出一双紫金色的眼睛。他没有穿甲胄，而是一身素白长袍，腰间系着那条刻满夔龙纹的玉带，朱砂马在他身下格外驯服，马蹄轻快如踩着鼓点。

他们身后跟着十几名金吾卫，再后面是西泽尔一行人——阿方索、唐璜、昆提良、瓦莲京娜、薇若兰。

洛阳的秋天和翡冷翠完全不同。

翡冷翠的秋是金红色的，从高处往低处看，枫叶像火焰一样层层叠叠地烧。洛阳的秋是金黄色的，银杏叶铺满了整条街道，被风一吹就沙沙作响，像下了一场碎金子的雨。空气里有一股淡淡的桂花香，混着路边食摊传来的面饼和烤肉的焦香。

街道两旁是鳞次栉比的木楼，飞檐翘角，漆成朱红和墨黑，檐下挂着成串的红灯笼。行人穿着东方样式的衣裳，男人束发戴冠，女人长裙曳地，小孩子穿着虎头鞋在人群里钻来钻去，追逐着一种木头削出来的风车。

然后西泽尔看见了那些小贩。

他们蹲在路边，面前铺着红布，红布上摆着成排的小玩意儿——木制的、铁打的、镀了金漆的，全是同一种东西。

机动甲胄。

"鬼武者初型！夏国第一甲！五文钱一个！"

"鬼武者Ⅱ型模型！纯铜打造！能走能动能挥剑！十文钱！"

小贩们扯着嗓子叫卖，孩子们围成一圈，举着铜板争抢那些只有巴掌大小的甲胄模型。西泽尔勒住缰绳，仔细看了一眼——那些模型的做工意外地精细，头部雕刻着夔龙首，胸甲浮雕着皇族夔龙纹，右臂的小型蒸汽连铳甚至能扣动扳机，左臂的精钢重盾可以开合。

"这是你们的制式装备？"西泽尔偏头问楚舜华。

楚舜华回头看了一眼，银色鬼面下的嘴角微微扬起："夏国男儿，人手一具。"

他的语气里有一种毫不掩饰的骄傲。不是炫耀，而是理所当然——就像翡冷翠人理所当然地使用蒸汽机械一样，夏国人也理所当然地把鬼武者甲胄当成日常。

"十年前这种东西还是机密，只有金吾卫和北境军团装备。"楚舜华继续说，"三年前我下令向民间开放图纸，鼓励匠人仿制。现在你看到的这些玩具，有些做得比军方的还精细。"

唐璜骑在马上，伸手从路边小贩那里买了一个鬼武者Ⅱ型模型，在手里翻来覆去地看："做工不错，关节用的是……"他皱了皱眉，凑近看了看模型胸口的齿轮结构，"用的是青铜齿轮？"

"夏国不产红水银，青铜是最容易获取的金属。"楚舜华说，"所以我们走了一条和西方完全不同的路。"

瓦莲京娜骑在他旁边，目光一直在扫视街道两侧的建筑。那双冰雪般浅灰的眼睛里带着审视，也带着某种她自己都没意识到的怀念。她的母亲是锡兰人，当年在翡冷翠住过，后来带着她从锡兰逃出走的就是难民小路。

"这条路……"她忽然低声说。

"嗯。"楚舜华听见了，"三十年前，王妃从这里走过。我母亲送她出的城。"

瓦莲京娜沉默了一会儿，没有再说话。

他们穿过三道城门，拐入一条更宽阔的街道。街道尽头是一座巨大的圆形穹顶建筑，穹顶涂着金漆，在阳光下像一颗燃烧的太阳。

"东方机械博览会。"楚舜华翻身下马，"每年秋天举办一次，各国使团都会来参观。我让人给你们安排了专场。"

博览会的大厅比西泽尔想象的大得多。穹顶挑高至少有三十米，巨大的蒸汽吊灯悬在半空，地面铺着青砖，两侧是高达五米的展示台。展示台上陈列着各种东方机械的样品——蒸汽机车、蒸汽纺织机、蒸汽印刷机、蒸汽抽水机，还有十几具真人大小的鬼武者甲胄模型。

"那是鬼武者Ⅱ型的原型。"楚舜华指着最中央的展示台。

那具模型和街头卖的玩具完全不是一个级别。通体漆黑如墨，头部的夔龙首钢盔比人头还大，龙睛镶嵌着拇指盖大小的红水银晶片，在灯光下闪着妖异的红光。胸甲浮雕鎏金夔龙纹，每一道纹路都精致得像是用金丝一笔一笔勾出来的。右臂的小型蒸汽连铳连射速度极快，左臂的精钢重盾厚度惊人。

"单台能单手举起千斤重的镇国鼎。"楚舜华淡淡地说。

阿方索站在原型甲胄前，目光却不在那具模型的威武外表上。他盯着模型胸甲内部暴露的齿轮结构——那是一组极其精密的联动齿轮，由青铜打造，每一颗齿轮的齿牙都打磨得如同镜面。

"这个齿轮组……"阿方索蹲下身，从腰间的工具袋里摸出一枚东西。

是他从那台被击败的普罗米修斯侦察型甲胄关节上拆下的微型红水银引擎碎片。

他把碎片贴近模型的齿轮组。

咔。

两者的齿牙竟然完全吻合。引擎碎片上的微型红水银纹路和齿轮表面的润滑纹路严丝合缝，仿佛是同一张图纸制造出来的。

阿方索僵住了。

"怎么了？"唐璜凑过来。

阿方索没回答，他的眼睛瞪得极大，盯着那枚碎片和齿轮组的结合处。他做了二十年机械师，看过世界上几乎所有型号的齿轮，从翡冷翠的精密仪器到叶尼塞的重型甲胄，从没见过两种完全不同的文明产物能有如此精确的匹配度。

除非……它们有同一个源头。

他没有说出声。他只是把碎片收回去，站起身时腿微微发软。

博览会大厅的二楼回廊上，有两个人正在往下看。

叶素理穿着一身中山国样式的黑色长袍，腰间挂着一枚蛇形玉佩。他的脸保养得极好，五十多岁的人看起来只有四十出头，目光如鹰隼般锐利。

纯公主站在他旁边，十八岁的少女穿着一身鹅黄色的襦裙，长发用一支白玉簪绾起。她手里捏着一条青丝古剑的剑穗，正漫不经心地把玩。

"那就是西泽尔·博尔吉亚？"纯公主低声问。

"是。"叶素理点头。

"长得很瘦。"

"瘦的人往往最危险。"叶素理的目光穿过人群，落在西泽尔身边的楚舜华身上，"你看楚舜华亲自出城迎接他，用的规格是迎接国宾的规格。这个西方人，能让大夏龙雀亲自出马，分量不轻。"

纯公主瞥了西泽尔一眼："他来做什么？"

"通婚。"叶素理说，"和亲。教皇国想要和夏国结盟，把东方公主嫁给西方贵族，换取军事支持。"

"所以父王才派我来？"

"不只是这个。"叶素理微微侧过身，压低声音，"贵客果然是能改变世界的人。你看他们一行人——那个金发的是叶尼塞公主，瓦莲京娜·罗曼诺夫，神怒骑士团副团长；那个红衣女人是密涅瓦机关的副总长，教皇国的核心技术人员；其他几个都是西泽尔的旧部，每一个都上过战场杀过人。"

"这样的队伍能改变什么？"

"这样的队伍能改变的东西，"叶素理的目光沉了下去，"比我们中山国倾尽全国之力能改变的还要多。"

纯公主沉默了一会儿。

"那我们中山国怎么办？"

"抓住这次机会。"叶素理低声说，"楚舜华和楚昭华的矛盾已经公开了，教皇国想要利用这个矛盾，中山国也可以。我们不需要打败任何一方，我们只需要在正确的时机站在正确的一边。"

"哪一边是正确的？"

叶素理没有回答。他的目光穿过博览会大厅，落在西泽尔的背影上。那个穿着黑色军服的少年正站在鬼武者Ⅱ型原型甲胄前，和楚舜华并肩而立，阳光从穹顶的玻璃窗洒下来，在他们身上镀了一层金边。

"现在还不知道。"叶素理说，"所以我们要继续观察。"

"大夏龙雀馆"在洛阳使馆区的最深处。

这是夏国专门接待最高规格国宾的馆驿，平日里空着，只有最重要的客人来才会启用。整座馆驿按照东方传统建筑风格修建，主楼是三层木结构，飞檐斗拱，漆成朱红色，门前立着两座石狮子。

但真正让西泽尔停下脚步的是门厅里的壁画。

那是一幅横贯整面墙的巨型壁画，用矿物颜料绘制，色彩历经岁月依然鲜亮。壁画的内容是一个女人——她穿着东方的白色长袍，长发披散，眼睛是深紫色的。女人的双手捧着一颗巨大的金色齿轮，齿轮中心嵌着一朵倒置的白色莲花。

女人的背后是一棵巨大的树。

树枝伸展开来覆盖整面墙壁，树叶全是大小不一的齿轮，每一颗都在缓慢地转动，发出细微的嗡鸣声。

西泽尔的后颈烫了一下。

"这是什么？"他问。

"东方的星见。"楚舜华站在他身边，声音平静，"一千年前夏国就有观星测命的传统，观星的人被称为星见，星见中的领袖被称为大星见，负责守护夏国国运。"

"一千年前？"

"比你们锡兰星见的历史还要早三百年。"楚舜华转头看着西泽尔，银色鬼面下的紫金双瞳闪着微光，"你以为只有西方才有世界树的传说？"

西泽尔没有说话。他只是盯着壁画上那个紫瞳女人的眼睛。

那双眼睛画得太真了，仿佛正在看着他。

"我母亲就是星见出身。"楚舜华说，"她从锡兰逃到东方，在夏国王宫里住了三十年，教我观星，告诉我世界树的秘密。她说世界树是东西方共同的根，东西方的星见血脉同源。"

他伸手触碰壁画上那棵世界树的树干，指尖在金色的颜料上停留了一瞬。

"她等了三十年，等一个能听懂这个秘密的人从西方来。"

唐璜没有听那段对话。

他一进入大夏龙雀馆就开始四处打量，目光像一把尺子，丈量着每一面墙壁、每一处转角、每一扇窗户的位置。这是他的老本行——作为一个在翡冷翠上流社会混迹多年从未失手的盗贼，他对建筑结构的敏感度比任何人都强。

"这面墙后面是空的。"

唐璜站在二楼西侧一间客房里，手指按在墙壁的某块木板上。

昆提良走过来，用指节敲了敲："空的？"

"空的。"唐璜又敲了敲，耳朵贴近墙面听了一会儿，"后面有空间，大概两米深、五米长。"

"你怎么知道？"

"干这行的基本功。"唐璜耸耸肩，从腰间摸出一把细长的撬棍，沿着木板的缝隙轻轻一撬。

木板无声地弹开了。

后面是一条狭窄的暗道，宽度仅容一人通过，向下倾斜，尽头看不见光。暗道的两侧墙壁上每隔十米嵌着一盏小油灯，灯芯已经干枯，但没有燃起。

"进去看看？"昆提良问。

"当然。"唐璜迈步走进了暗道。

暗道不长，向下走了约三十级台阶就到底了。尽头是一扇半掩的铁门，铁门后面是一间不大的石室。

石室中央摆着一张石桌，桌上放着一个圆形的青铜器物。器物约有脸盆大小，表面刻满了细密的纹路——齿轮、莲花、五芒星，全都交织在一起。

唐璜走近一看，愣住了。

那是机械神教的徽记。

齿轮中心嵌着一颗五芒星，五芒星的五个角末端各连接一圈更小的齿轮——和翡冷翠密涅瓦机关使用的徽记一模一样。

但石桌上的徽记是三百年前的风格。

唐璜蹲下身，仔细观察徽记底座。底座上刻着一行极小的字，他凑近才能辨认——

"吾妹艾琳娜，赠予东方友人。永志不忘。"

唐璜的呼吸停了一瞬。

他回头看了一眼昆提良。

昆提良也看到了那行字，他的脸色变了："艾琳娜·博尔吉亚？"

"密涅瓦机关的初代工程师之一。"唐璜压低声音，"三百年前被教廷火刑处死的那个。"

他们对视了一眼。

"这说明什么？"

"说明三百年前就有人把密涅瓦的东西带到了东方。"唐璜说，"而且是艾琳娜亲自带来的。"

薇若兰是在大夏龙雀馆三楼东侧找到那台占卜仪的。

她本来在整理西泽尔一行人的行李，偶然推开一扇落满灰尘的隔板门，发现里面是一间封闭的小屋。小屋里空荡荡的，只有正中央摆着一台机器。

那是一台占卜仪。

通体用青铜和黄铜打造，底座是一个八角形的星盘，星盘上刻满了东方特有的卦象符号。星盘上方悬浮着三枚赤金色的圆钱——正面是人面蛇身男神，背面是人面蛇身女神，和东方的伏羲金钱一模一样。

"老式翻译器……"薇若兰喃喃道。

她认出了这台机器的底座和密涅瓦机关B-07档案库里的老式翻译器是同一种风格，齿轮嵌五芒星的机械神教徽记赫然在目。不同之处在于，这台机器的上半部分被改装成了占卜仪。

占卜仪的中央有一块圆形的青铜屏幕，屏幕表面覆盖着一层极薄的红水银。

薇若兰伸手触碰了占卜仪的底座。

嗡的一声，机器启动了。屏幕上的红水银开始缓缓流动，像液态的水银在自组织，凝结成文字。

第一行字是古锡兰文。

薇若兰认识那种文字——她在B-07档案库里见过。

"龙战于野，其血玄黄。"

第二行字浮现出来。

"见群龙无首，吉。"

第三行字是用东方篆书写的。

"东西方握手。"

薇若兰的手停在了半空中。

她盯着那三行字看了很久。

红水银屏幕上的字迹持续了大约三十秒，然后缓缓消散，屏幕恢复了平静。机器底座上有一行小字——

"东方星见·楚氏家族·守护"

薇若兰退出小屋时，脚步比来时重了许多。

黄昏时分，一名太监手持明黄色的圣旨到了大夏龙雀馆。

那太监穿着蟒袍，头顶三山帽，手持拂尘，尖声细气地宣读圣旨——

"奉天承运皇帝诏曰：闻西方贵客远道而来，朕心甚慰。今晚于通天宫设宴款待，着楚舜华陪宴，钦此。"

太监宣读完，恭敬地将圣旨双手递向楚舜华。

楚舜华没有接。

"贵客一路劳顿，"他平静地说，"今晚不便赴宴。"

太监愣住了："监国大人，这是圣旨……"

"我知道了。"楚舜华从太监手中取过圣旨，随手折了两折，塞进了袖子里，"回去告诉皇帝陛——"

他顿了一下。

"贵客不必见皇帝。"

他的声音不大，但每个字都清晰得像刀刻在石头上。

"今晚去通天宫见真正的大夏。"

太监的脸涨得通红，嘴唇哆嗦着想说什么，最终什么都没说出来，躬身退了出去。

大夏龙雀馆的院子里安静了片刻。

"你把圣旨压下了。"西泽尔说。

"嗯。"

"那是你弟弟。"

"是。"楚舜华摘下了银色鬼面，紫金色的眼睛在暮色中闪烁，"但他不是夏国真正的主人。"

他转身朝馆外走去。

"跟我来。"

通天宫在洛阳城的正中央。

整座宫殿建在一座人工堆筑的高台上，层层叠叠的宫殿沿中轴线展开，飞檐斗拱层层递进，仿佛要一直延伸到天上去。暮色中，最后一抹阳光照在最高处的金顶上，反射出万道金光。

楚舜华带着西泽尔走的是中轴线正中央的石阶。

石阶很宽，每一级都用整块汉白玉雕成，两侧的石栏杆上雕刻着夔龙纹和莲花纹。越往上走风越大，吹得楚舜华的白袍猎猎作响。

"这整座通天宫，"楚舜华一边走一边说，"都是建在世界树残枝的根系之上的。"

西泽尔的脚步顿了一下。

"你脚下的每一块石板下面，都有世界树的根须。"楚舜华继续说，"洛阳城不是随便建在这里的，这里是世界树东方主根的正上方。"

他们走到了最顶层。

面前是一座巨大的明堂。

明堂的大门是纯铜铸造的，门上雕刻着九排九列共八十一颗金钉，每颗金钉都有拳头大小，在暮色中闪着暗金色的光。门两侧各立着一只石雕的夔龙，夔龙的眼睛是红水银镶嵌的，在黑暗中发出妖异的红光。

"明堂的门只有两个人能打开。"楚舜华站在门前，"一个是我，另一个——"

他转身看着西泽尔。

"是你。"

西泽尔走到门前。他没有伸手去推门，他只是站在那里，抬起眼睛看着门上那些金钉。

后颈的黄金套管开始发烫。

不是以前那种被动的热，而是一种从内向外的、主动的、像心脏跳动一样的温热。门上的金钉开始发出微光，每一颗金钉都从内向外亮起来，光芒由暗金变成亮金，再变成刺目的白金色。

咔。

门开了。

明堂内部没有点灯。

但不需要灯。

整座明堂的穹顶镶嵌着数以万计的微型齿轮，每一颗齿轮都在缓缓转动，发出极其轻微的嗡鸣声。齿轮的转动带动了穹顶上的某种光学装置，将天空中的星光折射下来，洒满了整座明堂。

地面是纯黑色的汉白玉铺就，每一块汉白玉上都刻着极其细密的梵文。

楚舜华走到明堂正中央，那里摆着一张石桌，桌上放着一个青铜香炉。香炉的造型是一棵微型的世界树——树干是暗金色合金，树枝末梢挂着红水银核心当成果实，树叶是大小不一的金色齿轮。

楚舜华从袖中取出三炷香。

那香和普通的香不同，颜色是暗金色的，隐约能闻到一股奇异的香气——不是檀香也不是沉香，而是一种让人心绪宁静、仿佛置身于莲花池畔的清冷香味。

"这是世界树香料。"楚舜华说，"用世界树残枝的落叶研成粉末制成，整个夏国只有三份。"

他点燃了第一炷香。

暗金色的烟气缓缓升起，在明堂的穹顶下盘旋。

"第一炷，敬世界树。"

他点燃了第二炷香。

烟气和第一炷香的烟气交织在一起，在空中凝聚成了一个隐约的形状——

一只巨大的朱红色大鸟，双翼展开，尾羽如火焰般翻卷。

龙雀。

"第二炷，敬大夏三百年基业。"

他点燃了第三炷香，然后把三炷香一起插进了香炉里。

三股烟气在明堂中央盘旋、融合。

龙雀的形状旁边，渐渐浮现出另一个形状——

一条红色的龙，鳞片如火焰，双角如弯月，金色的瞳孔里燃烧着灼热的光。

红龙。

"第三炷——"

楚舜华转向西泽尔。

他伸出右手。

"敬东西方共同的根。"

西泽尔看着那只伸出的手。

那是楚舜华的手。指节粗大，掌心有常年握剑磨出的老茧，皮肤上有一道很浅的旧伤疤——那是十几年前在战场上留下的。

西泽尔伸出了自己的右手。

两只手握在一起。

那一刻，明堂穹顶上的所有齿轮同时发出了一声清越的鸣响，三股烟气骤然膨胀，红龙和龙雀的形状在穹顶下交汇、旋转、融为一体，最后化作一道金红色的光柱直冲而上。

光柱散去时，明堂里恢复了平静。

楚舜华松开了手。

"我们结盟了。"

"嗯。"西泽尔说。

两人都没有再多说什么。

烟气渐渐稀薄，龙雀和红龙的形状慢慢消散，明堂里重新变得昏暗。

就在这时，西泽尔注意到明堂的地面发生了变化。

正中央的石桌下方，原本严丝合缝的汉白玉地砖正在无声地分开。沉重的石头相互摩擦，发出低沉的轰响，一道暗门从地面升起。

暗门是纯黑色的，高约三米，宽两米。

门面上刻着四个徽记。

最上面是一颗巨大的齿轮，齿轮中心嵌着一朵倒置的白色莲花——

机械神教徽记。

齿轮的下方是一只展翅的六翼猫头鹰，翅膀上布满了细密的齿轮纹路——

密涅瓦机关徽记。

猫头鹰的右侧是一面大夏龙雀旗，金色的龙雀在朱红色的旗面上振翅欲飞。

龙雀旗的左侧是一面锡兰莲花旗，白色的莲花在深紫色的旗面上盛开。

四个徽记围绕着一把钥匙孔。

楚舜华站在暗门前，紫金色的眼睛在暗中闪着微光。

"我母亲临终前告诉我，"他的声音很轻，"通天宫的地下，才是真正的大夏。"

他退后一步，让出了暗门前的位置。

"她让我等那个人来。"

他看着西泽尔。

"我等了十七年。"

【English】
Chapter 234 — Welcome in Luoyang

The kui-dragons struck the blue stone of Luoyang like muffled drums.

They stood a full head taller than the Andalusian mounts of Florence, those horses — great slabs of iron muscle across the shoulder, coats the colour of cinnabar rubbed to powder, and a feral light at the bottom of every eye that any horseman knew to read. Cesare felt the power come up through the saddle. It was not the trained gentleness of a Florentine destrier, all collected breath and bent neck. It was restrained violence. A word and the beast would charge whatever was in front of it, even a wall of pikes, even a line of burning waggons.

Chu Shunhua rode at the head of the column. He had put the silver mask back on — the half-mask that hid everything but the eyes — and those eyes, a pale bruised purple-gold, watched the city as if it were a patient. He wore no armour. A plain robe of unbleached linen, the jade belt at his waist carved end to end with coiling kui-dragon motifs, and the kui-dragon beneath him, otherwise so savage, went softly as a cat in slippers, hooves falling in time with some interior music only it could hear.

Behind him, a dozen men of the Golden Guard in dark lacquered cuirasses. Behind them, Cesare's own people — Alfonso, Don Juan, Quintilian, Valentina, Veronika.

Autumn in Luoyang was nothing like autumn in Florence.

In Florence the season was a slow fire climbing down the hills. The maples went first, then the sweet chestnuts, and by November the Val d'Arno was one long russet wound from San Miniato to Fiesole. Luoyang's autumn was a different idea. It was gold. The ginkgo trees lining every avenue had come into full yellow, and at the least breath of wind they let go of their little fans, and the fans fell through the still air in slow continuous drifts, whispering against the stones, a rustle like a purse of small coins tipped out on a merchant's table. Under the gingko smell there was something sweeter — a thread of osmanthus, almost lost — and under that the smoke and oil of the cook-stalls at the corners, the warm animal smell of grilling flatbread and the long, drawn-out scent of mutton fat burning on a brazier.

The buildings pressed in close on either side. Wooden. Three storeys and four, jutting over the street at the eaves, painted in the two colours of the dynasty — red as fresh blood, black as old lacquer — and from every rafter hung strings of red paper lanterns not yet lit for the festival. People in Eastern dress moved along the flagstones. The men with their hair bound up under black gauze caps; the women in long trailing skirts that hissed against the stone as they walked; children in tiger-head shoes threading the crowd with the easy malice of puppies, chasing small whirring windmills carved from pale wood.

Then Cesare saw the stalls.

They crouched on the kerb at the foot of every other cross-street, and in front of each squatting vendor a square of red cloth had been spread, and on every red cloth the same wares in their dozens — wood, iron, brass, a few even touched with gilding. All of one subject.

Mecha-armour.

"First-pattern Oni Warrior! The first armour of the Xia! Five cash!"

"Second-pattern Oni Warrior, scale model, solid bronze, walks, strikes, swings its sword! Ten cash!"

The vendors shouted till their throats went raw. The children came running, copper coins held out in grubby fists, jostling for the palm-sized figures. Cesare pulled the rein and looked.

The models were finer than he had expected. The little heads had been carved into kui-dragon snouts, complete with the curling horn above each temple. The breastplates bore a relief of the imperial dragon, every scale picked out. The right arm carried a miniature steam repeater, and a child could cock it; the left arm was a tiny steel shield that hinged open and shut.

"This is your standard kit?" he asked Chu Shunhua, without turning his head.

Chu Shunhua glanced back. Behind the silver mask the corner of his mouth moved a fraction of an inch. "Every Xia lad has one."

He said it without boasting. The way a Florentine would say that every household has a clock. The way it rained in winter.

"Ten years ago," he went on, as the column moved forward, "this was a state secret. The Golden Guard only. The Northern Army only. Three years ago I signed the order opening the drawings to the workshops, and I paid the workshops to copy them. Some of the toys you see on the kerb are more finely made than what the regiments are wearing."

Don Juan had produced a coin from somewhere — Don Juan always had a coin — and a Second-Pattern model from the nearest stall. He turned it over in his fingers, frowning.

"The joint-work is interesting," he said, and held it up to the light. "Bronze gearing, here, in the chest — and the pivot pins are the same shape as the ones they put in the Florentine commercial revolvers. They are using your screw, you know. The tapered one. They must have got it from somewhere."

"They did not get it from us," Chu Shunhua said. "The Xia has no crimson mercury of its own. We do not have your metal. Bronze is what we have. So we walked a different road."

Valentina was riding at his stirrup, her pale grey eyes moving the way grey eyes move — never quite still, never quite warm. She was looking not at the stalls but at the buildings. The timber and the paint and the rows of identical narrow doors. The scrutiny was a habit with her — daughter of a Ceylonese mother who had fled by the refugee road — but the thing in her face as she looked was not quite scrutiny. It was the half-remembered feeling of a place one had seen in childhood and could not quite place.

"This road," she said, low, after a while.

"Yes," said Chu Shunhua. He had heard. "Thirty years ago the Princess Consort walked this way. My mother saw her out of the city."

Valentina said nothing more. The column moved on.

They passed through three gates, each older and taller than the last, and came at last into a broader avenue that ran straight to a single building. A drum of a building, thatched over with a great dome the colour of hammered gold, the kind of building that, in any city of the West, would have been the cathedral. In the lower light of the afternoon sun the dome was a small private sun of its own.

"The Eastern Mechanical Exhibition," Chu Shunhua said, and dismounted.

The hall inside was larger than Cesare had prepared himself for. The dome climbed at least thirty metres above the floor. Steam-chandeliers of a size he had never seen hung from the apex on chains the thickness of a man's wrist; the floor was set with green-grey brick; the display platforms on either side rose to a man's height and were crowded with samples of every kind — steam road-engines, steam looms, steam presses, steam pumps, and, at the centre of the centre platform, a full-sized Oni Warrior in its black lacquer, three metres tall and silent as a sentry.

"That," said Chu Shunhua, "is the prototype of the Second Pattern."

It was nothing like the kerb-stall toys. The helmet, shaped into a kui-dragon's head, was larger than a man's skull, and where the eyes should have been two thumb-sized crimson mercury crystals had been set, which caught the gaslight and gave back a sick, beautiful red. The breastplate was chased and fire-gilt in the imperial dragon pattern, every line of the relief a single hair's-breadth deep. The steam repeater on the right arm was built for a true rate of fire, not a toy rate. The shield on the left was a slab of fine steel thicker than a man's spread hand.

"One machine," Chu Shunhua said, "can lift the State Cauldron single-handed. A thousand catties. No man needed."

Alfonso was not looking at the armour. He was looking into it.

He had crouched, and his head was nearly between the breastplates of the open display piece, and his eyes were on the gear-train inside the chest — a stack of bronze wheels, each tooth polished to a mirror, every wheel meshed to its neighbour with a precision that made his mouth go dry. Twenty years he had spent at the bench. He had taken apart Florentine clocks, and Yeniseian heavy armour, and machines the Promethean corps had sworn could not be taken apart. He had never in his life seen two artefacts from two different civilisations fit the way these gears were about to fit.

He drew from his tool-roll a thing wrapped in oiled cloth. A fragment — no larger than his thumb — of a micro-engine he had cut from the knee of a fallen Promethean scout-pattern armour on the road into Luoyang. The micro-engine's gears were crimson mercury. They gleamed faintly even in shadow.

He held the fragment against the bronze gear-train.

Click.

Tooth against tooth. Tooth into tooth. The faint crimson striations of the engine aligned with the polish-lines of the bronze wheels as if the two had been cut on the same wheel, by the same hand, from the same drawing.

Alfonso did not move for a long moment. He was thinking that he had just been given, in the middle of a foreign exhibition hall, evidence that two machines built by two empires that had never heard of each other had been conceived by a single mind. The thought made his legs go light under him. He stood. He put the fragment back in its cloth. He did not speak.

"What's the matter with you?" Don Juan said, at his shoulder.

"Nothing," Alfonso said. "Dust in my eye."

Above them, on the second-storey gallery of the exhibition hall, two people were looking down.

Ye Suli was dressed in the long black scholar's robe of the Kingdom of Zhongshan, and at his waist hung a small jade piece carved into a coiled serpent. He was past fifty, but the years had agreed with him; he had the look of a man of forty, and the look of an eagle. The eyes were the worst of it. The eyes did not blink often enough.

Beside him stood the Princess Chun. She was eighteen. She wore a willow-yellow silk tunic and trailing skirt, a single white jade pin holding up her hair; in her right hand she turned, almost without thought, the tassel of a long sword wrapped in green silk cord.

"Is that Cesare Borgia?" she asked, quietly.

"Yes."

"He is thin."

"Thin men are often the most dangerous," Ye Suli said. "Look at the man who has come out of the city to meet him. That is Chu Shunhua himself. The Great Xia Dragon Sparrow. He has used the protocol reserved for a state guest. The Westerner is heavy enough to be worth that."

"What has he come for?"

"Marriage. Alliance. The Holy See wishes to bind itself to the Xia with a princess. An Eastern bride for a Western lord, in exchange for military support."

"So that is why my father sent me."

"It is one of the reasons." Ye Suli turned half a step towards her, and lowered his voice. "Look at the rest of them. The fair one in the white cloak is the Princess of Yenisei — Valentina Romanov, deputy-commander of the Wrath-of-God Order. The red-haired woman in the leather coat is the deputy-director of the Minerva Institute — the brain-trust of the Holy See. The others are his old soldiers, every one of them a veteran of open battle. A column like that can shift more than the whole Kingdom of Zhongshan has ever shifted, even with its last breath behind it."

The princess was quiet for a moment.

"What are we to do?"

"We seize this chance." Ye Suli's voice went very low. "The split between Chu Shunhua and the Emperor is public. The Holy See intends to use it. Zhongshan can use it too. We do not have to beat anybody. We only have to stand in the right place at the right moment."

"And which moment is the right one?"

Ye Suli did not answer. His gaze, after a long time, drifted down to the floor of the hall and settled on Cesare's back. The young man in the dark uniform was standing with Chu Shunhua under the dome, the two of them side by side, the light coming through the glass above and gilding them in a thin line of gold.

"We do not know that yet," he said. "So we watch."

The Great Xia Dragon Sparrow Inn stood at the deep end of the Luoyang legation quarter, in a cul-de-sac walled off by a low brick parapet. It was the inn the Xia kept for guests of the first rank, and the inn was kept empty almost always. Only the most important visitor in a generation was brought here.

It was built in the old Eastern style: a three-storey timber hall, flying eaves, dougong brackets in rows, lacquered red as a fresh wound. Two stone lions flanked the gate. Cesare, who had been too long in the saddle to feel much, stopped when he saw the wall of the entrance hall.

The mural ran the full width of the wall. It had been painted in mineral pigment, and the pigment, after so many years, was still unbearably bright. A woman filled the centre of it. She wore the white robe of the East, her hair loose, her eyes a deep purple. In her cupped hands she held a great gear of gold, and in the centre of the gear a white lotus, inverted.

Behind the woman a tree.

The tree covered the whole wall. Its branches spread and spread and spread, and the leaves of the tree were gears of every size, and every one of them turned, very slowly, with a small collective hum, like a hive heard through a wall.

Cesare felt his neck heat.

"What is this?" he asked.

"The Eastern star-seers," said Chu Shunhua, at his side. "A thousand years ago, the Xia already had a tradition of reading the heavens. The readers were called the Seers. The chief Seer was called the Great Seer, and it was her office to keep the destiny of the Xia."

"A thousand years ago."

"Three centuries before your Ceylonese Seers had a name for themselves." Chu Shunhua turned his head, and the purple-gold of his eyes caught a flake of the gaslight. "Did you think the West was the only one with a World Tree in its stories?"

Cesare did not answer. He was looking at the woman's eyes in the mural. They had been painted too well. They were looking at him.

"My mother was a Seer," Chu Shunhua said, after a while. "She came from Ceylon to the Xia when she was young. She lived in the palace for thirty years. She taught me to read the stars. She told me the World Tree is a root common to East and West, and the blood of the Seers in both lands is one blood."

He reached out and laid a fingertip on the trunk of the painted tree, on the curve of a branch, on a single golden leaf. He held it there.

"She waited thirty years," he said, "for a Westerner who could understand the secret."

Don Juan had not been listening.

He had been inside the inn for less than a minute, and his eyes were already doing what Don Juan's eyes did in any new building — measuring. He was a man who had lived for years by slipping into rooms that did not want him slipped into, and his gift was a kind of architectural hearing. He could feel load-bearing walls the way other men could feel a draft.

"The wall at the back of this room is hollow," he said, from a guest chamber on the second floor. Quintilian came over. He rapped his knuckles against the panel.

"Hollow," Don Juan said, and put his ear to it. "Two metres deep, about five wide."

"How do you know that?"

"It is the job." He shrugged, and produced a thin pry from his belt, and eased it into the seam of a panel. The wood came away cleanly. Behind it, a narrow passage. The passage would take one man abreast, no more. It went downward at a gentle pitch. The walls were fitted at ten-metre intervals with little oil-lamps whose wicks had dried to nothing.

"Go in?" Quintilian asked.

"Of course."

The passage went down, thirty steps. The steps were of dressed stone. At the bottom, a half-open iron door.

The room behind the door was small. There was a stone table in the middle of it, and on the table, a round bronze object the size of a washbasin. Its surface was covered with a dense pattern: gears, lotuses, five-pointed stars, all of them woven into each other.

Don Juan stopped.

The pattern at the centre of the object was the emblem of the Mechanist Church. A gear with a five-pointed star at its hub, the points of the star each tied off into a ring of smaller gears. It was the exact emblem used in Florence by the Minerva Institute, in this year's engraving.

But the style of the work was three hundred years old.

He crouched. The base of the object was engraved with a line of very small letters. He bent close.

*To my sister Elena, in friendship to the East. May it not be forgotten.*

He stopped breathing for a second. He looked at Quintilian. Quintilian had read it too. His face had changed.

"Elena Borgia?" Quintilian said.

"One of the first engineers of the Minerva Institute," Don Juan said, very low. "Burned at the stake by the Curia three hundred years ago."

They looked at each other.

"What does this mean?"

"It means that three hundred years ago," Don Juan said, "somebody brought Minerva's work to the East. And it was Elena herself who brought it."

Veronika found the divining engine on the third floor, in a small locked chamber behind a panel of dusty wood.

The engine was built of bronze and yellow brass. Its base was an eight-pointed star disc, the disc engraved with the trigrams and hexagrams of the Eastern I Ching. Above the disc, three coins of a dark red-gold hovered, unsupported — heads a man-serpent god, tails a woman-serpent god, the ancient Xia fortune-coins of Fuxi.

"Old-style translator," Veronika said, half under her breath.

She recognised the base at once. The same school of work as the early translators filed away in the B-07 archive at the Minerva Institute. The same Mechanist emblem — a gear, a five-pointed star. The upper half of the engine, though, had been re-purposed into something else. A diviner. A question-answerer.

At the centre of the engine was a circular bronze screen, and across the face of the screen there had been laid a film of crimson mercury, a skin no thicker than paper.

She laid her hand on the base.

A low note came out of the engine. The screen woke. The crimson mercury stirred, the way quicksilver stirs in a hand that is not quite shaking, and began to gather itself, of its own accord, into letters.

The first line, in the old Ceylonese script.

*The dragon wars upon the plain, his blood is black and yellow.*

The second line.

*A multitude of dragons without a head: fortunate.*

The third line, in the seal-script of the Xia.

*The East and the West clasp hands.*

Veronika's hand stopped, an inch above the screen. She read the three lines again, and again, and after a long time she drew her hand back and stepped away from the engine. Her shoes were heavier on the boards than they had been when she came in.

The letters held for about thirty seconds. They broke. The mercury was mercury again.

At the foot of the engine, in small engraved letters, a line:

*Xia Seer, House of Chu, Guardian.*

In the failing light of the afternoon, a eunuch of the Imperial Household came to the Dragon Sparrow Inn carrying a vermilion-yellow edict.

He wore the python robe and the three-peaked cap and carried the horse-tail duster, and he read the edict in a high, sharp voice:

"By the grace of Heaven, the Emperor commands: Hearing that honoured guests from the West have arrived after long travel, Our heart is greatly comforted. This evening a feast is to be set in the Tongtian Palace. Chu Shunhua shall attend as host. So it is commanded."

He read it through. He held the vermilion scroll out to Chu Shunhua with both hands, in the prescribed form.

Chu Shunhua did not take it.

"Our guest is tired from the road," he said. "Tonight he does not attend a feast."

The eunuch's face went the colour of a sunset. "Lord Regent, this is an imperial edict — "

"I have heard it," Chu Shunhua said. He took the scroll from the eunuch's hands, folded it once, then again, and pushed it into the wide sleeve of his robe. "Go back to His Majesty and tell him — "

He stopped.

"The guest is not required to see the Emperor."

He said it without raising his voice. He said it the way a man says the time of day, and each word landed on the stones of the courtyard like a chisel on a slab of marble.

"Tonight he goes to the Tongtian Palace, to see the true Xia."

The eunuch's mouth worked. He bowed, lower than etiquette required, and went backwards out of the gate.

The courtyard of the Dragon Sparrow Inn was quiet for a moment.

"You declined an edict," Cesare said.

"I did."

"The edict was from your brother."

"It was." Chu Shunhua lifted the silver mask off his face. The purple-gold of his eyes, in the dusk, was almost the colour of the last of the light. "My brother is not the true master of the Xia."

He turned towards the gate.

"Come with me."

The Tongtian Palace stood at the centre of Luoyang.

The whole of it had been raised on a man-made platform, and the platform climbed. Layer upon layer of hall, eaves upon eaves, dougong bracket upon dougong bracket, the central axis running straight as an arrow to the highest roof of all, and the golden finial at the top of the highest roof catching the very last of the setting sun, and giving it back ten thousand times. Chu Shunhua took Cesare by the central stair. The stair was wide; each step was a single slab of white marble; the balustrades on either side were carved in the kui-dragon and the lotus. The wind rose as they climbed, and the wind took Chu Shunhua's white robe at the hem and laid it flat against his back.

"The whole of the Tongtian Palace," Chu Shunhua said, climbing, "is built upon the root of the World Tree. The eastern taproot. Every flagstone under our feet has a rootlet of it under the stone. Luoyang is not here by accident. It is directly above the eastern taproot of the World Tree."

At the top of the stair, the Bright Hall.

The doors of the Bright Hall were of solid bronze. They were studded with nine rows of nine, eighty-one great gold nails, each nail the size of a fist, each nail giving back the dusk in a dark gold. On either side of the door stood a stone kui-dragon. The eyes of the stone kui-dragons were of crimson mercury, and in the dark they gave back a strange red light of their own.

"There are two men who can open the door of the Bright Hall," Chu Shunhua said. He stood before it. "One is me. The other — "

He turned his head towards Cesare.

" — is you."

Cesare went to the door. He did not put out his hand. He stood, and he lifted his eyes, and he looked at the gold nails.

The gold sleeve at the back of his neck began to heat.

Not in the old way. Not the slow soak of warmth that came when the sleeve was pleased, or that came when something on the other side of a wall was reaching out. This was different. This heat moved outward from somewhere inside him, in time with his heart, as if it had a pulse.

The gold nails on the door began to give back their light. One by one, row by row, inwards to outwards — dark gold, bright gold, white gold, a pale fire.

Click.

The door swung open.

The Bright Hall was not lit. It did not need to be.

The whole of the inner dome had been set, like a pavement of constellations, with thousands of tiny gears, and the gears turned, very slowly, all of them, in one continuous whisper of a hum. The turning of the gears turned some optical engine in the dome, and the optical engine took the light of the first stars of evening and broke it, and let it fall on the floor of the hall in a fine silver rain.

The floor was a pavement of black-and-white marble, and on every slab, in letters so small that the eye could not take them in at any distance, the Sanskrit of the very old astronomers.

Chu Shunhua walked to the middle of the hall. There was a stone table there, and on the table a bronze burner. The burner was cast in the shape of a miniature World Tree: the trunk of a dark gold alloy; the fruit, hanging at the ends of the branches, globes of crimson mercury; the leaves, gears of gold of every size.

Chu Shunhua drew from his sleeve three sticks of incense.

They were not like any incense Cesare had seen. They were the colour of old gold, and they gave off, as Chu Shunhua struck the light, a strange cold scent — not sandalwood, not aloes — something that fell on the lungs like the air of a lotus pool at the first hour of a winter morning.

"This is the incense of the World Tree," Chu Shunhua said. "It is made from the fallen leaves of the World Tree, ground to powder. There are only three measures of it in the Xia."

He lit the first stick. The dark-gold smoke rose, slowly, and began to turn in on itself in the still air of the hall.

"The first stick, in honour of the World Tree."

He lit the second. The smoke of the first stick and the smoke of the second wove into each other, and out of the weaving there took shape, very faintly, a great bird. It was the colour of cinnabar. Its wings were spread. The feathers of its tail were a row of small flames.

The Dragon Sparrow.

"The second stick, in honour of three hundred years of the Xia."

He lit the third. He set the three sticks together in the burner, and the three smokes rose as one. Beside the shape of the sparrow there began, slowly, to take shape a second shape: a dragon, red as a forge-coal, the scales of it like flames, the horns of it like a new moon, the gold of its eyes burning in the gloom.

The red dragon.

"The third — "

Chu Shunhua turned to Cesare. He put out his right hand.

" — in honour of the root common to East and West."

Cesare looked at the hand. It was a soldier's hand. The knuckles were squared off; the palm was a map of callus from years of sword-work; on the back of the wrist, almost lost in the skin, a long pale scar, the relic of a wound taken in the field when he was a younger man.

Cesare put out his own right hand.

The two hands met.

The dome of the Bright Hall rang. Every gear, all at once, gave out a single clear note, and the three smokes blew wide, and the shape of the sparrow and the shape of the dragon turned about each other under the dome, faster and faster, and were one shape, and the one shape became a column of gold-red light that went up through the dome and was gone.

The light was gone. The hall was quiet again.

Chu Shunhua let go.

"We have made our alliance," he said.

"Yes," said Cesare.

Neither of them said anything more.

The smoke thinned. The shape of the sparrow and the shape of the dragon came apart, and were smoke, and were gone. The hall was dark again, and the small rain of starlight fell on the black-and-white marble.

It was then that Cesare saw the floor was moving.

Under the stone table, the marble slabs were drawing apart, one from another, with the slow grinding sound of great weights on great weights, and out of the floor a door was rising. The door was of a single black stone. It was three metres high. It was two metres wide.

On the face of the door, four emblems.

At the top, a great gear, and at the heart of the gear, an inverted white lotus — the emblem of the Mechanist Church.

Below the gear, a six-winged owl with its wings spread, every feather of the wings picked out as a tiny gear — the emblem of the Minerva Institute.

To the right of the owl, a Dragon Sparrow banner, the sparrow of beaten gold on a field of cinnabar, wings half-spread as if to lift from the silk.

To the left of the owl, a Ceylonese lotus banner, the white lotus open on a field of deep violet.

The four emblems ringed a keyhole.

Chu Shunhua stood before the door. The purple-gold of his eyes was the only light on his face.

"My mother, on the last night of her life, told me," he said, very low, "that the true Xia is not above the floor of the Tongtian Palace. It is below it."

He stepped back, and left the place before the door free.

"She told me to wait for the man who would come to open it."

He looked at Cesare.

"I have waited seventeen years."

【中文】
第235章 通天宫的鬼武者

暗门缓缓打开。

不是机械铰链的转动，而是整面黑铁向两侧滑开时，石头相互摩擦的低沉轰响。门后的空气涌出来，干燥、温热，带着一种金属与檀木混合的气味，像是一头沉睡了很久的巨兽刚刚张开嘴。

西泽尔看着门后。

那是一条向下的石阶，汉白玉砌成，每一级都打磨得极为平整，但边缘被无数靴底磨出了浅浅的弧度。两侧岩壁上每隔五米嵌着一盏铜灯，灯芯燃烧的不是油脂，而是一种淡金色的火焰，安静地悬浮在铜盏上方，像是被固定住的萤火虫。

楚舜华走在前面，没有回头，只说了一句："跟我来。"

他的脚步很稳。

西泽尔跟上。

台阶很长。

一级，两级，三十级，五十级。越往下走，空气越温暖，那种金属与檀木的混合气味越发浓烈，隐约还混进了蒸汽管道泄漏的嘶嘶声和金属碰撞的叮当声。

第一百零八级台阶走完，眼前豁然开朗。

西泽尔停住了脚步。

他面前是一个巨大的地下穹顶空间，纵深至少两百米，宽度超过百米。穹顶最高处离地面有将近十五米，由粗大的青铜柱支撑，每根柱子上都刻满了东方星见特有的星图——那些星图的绘制方式与西方完全不同，线条更流畅、弧度更大，像是把天穹直接压印在了青铜上。

而穹顶之下，是整齐排列的甲胄。

黑色的。

全是黑色的。

西泽尔数了数，最近的这一排就有十二台，再往深处看，还有更多的排，每排之间留着足够宽的过道供运输车通过。每一台甲胄的头部都雕刻着夔龙首，额前的龙角向后弯曲，鳞片刻画得纤毫毕现，胸甲上浮雕着鎏金的夔龙纹，纹路在铜灯的淡金色火焰下微微泛光。

鬼武者Ⅱ型。

数量之多，远超西泽尔的预料。

"一百台。"楚舜华站在他身旁，声音平淡，"这只是已经完成组装的。备件库在东面，还堆着三百台的核心零件，等着装配。"

西泽尔沉默地看着那些黑色甲胄。

每一台鬼武者Ⅱ型的高度都接近三米半，肩宽、臂长、腿粗，比例不像西方甲胄那样追求人形美学，而是带着一种兽性的压迫感，仿佛它们不是人造的武器，而是某种被驯服后披上铁甲的猛兽。

"跟我来。"楚舜华再次说。

他领着西泽尔穿过第一排甲胄之间的过道，走向穹顶空间的西侧。

那面墙上挂着东西。

不是武器，不是旗帜，而是一幅幅图纸。

西泽尔走近了，看清了第一张图纸的内容。那是一台机械的结构剖面图，用极细的朱砂笔绘制，线条精密到了变态的程度。图的中央是一颗拳头大小的核心，核心周围伸出数十根管道，每根管道都标注了名字和参数。

图纸的右下角，有一行用朱砂写的小字："星历三四七年，王屋山采录。"

西泽尔的目光在"王屋山"三个字上停了两秒。

"这些图纸，"楚舜华站在他身后，"是我母亲生前三十年的积累。她从星见家族的密档中抄录，结合自己观星所得，一笔一画绘出了东方星见对天机的理解。"

他走到下一张图纸前。

那是一张更大的图，描绘的不是一台机械，而是一棵树。

一棵从地面延伸到天穹的巨树。树根深入地底，树干粗壮到需要几十人才能合抱，树枝末梢悬挂着数十颗发光的球体。每一颗球体旁边都用蝇头小字标注着"果实"二字。

"世界树。"楚舜华说。

西泽尔看着那棵树。

他见过类似的图。

在密涅瓦机关的B-07档案库里，在达·芬奇·博尔吉亚的私人手稿中，在世界树残枝投射出的莲花通道两侧墙壁上。世界树的形象跨越了东西方，跨越了三百年，却始终保持着同样的基本结构——根、干、枝、果。

但这张图有一个细节是西泽尔从未在其他版本中见过的。

树干与树根的交界处，画着一个极小的人形。

那人形的头顶标注着一个符号——倒置的五芒星，五芒星的每个角末端各嵌着一颗微小的齿轮。

"星见。"西泽尔说。

"嗯。"楚舜华点头，"东方星见守护世界树的根，西方星见守护世界树的叶。三百年前，两边的星见分头行动，但血脉同源，职责相同——都是替世界树看守门户。"

他顿了顿。

"但两边的星见对世界树的理解不一样。"

楚舜华走到穹顶空间的最西端，那里有一扇铁门。他从腰间取出一枚黑铁钥匙，插进锁孔，转了两圈。

铁门打开。

门后是一个相对较小的房间，大约二十平方米，地面铺着厚厚的羊毛毯，四面墙上挂满了兽皮和丝绸，角落里燃着檀香，空气中弥漫着一股安静的、略带苦涩的气味。

房间中央摆着一台甲胄。

不是鬼武者Ⅱ型。

那台甲胄比旁边的Ⅱ型矮了将近一米，通体漆黑，没有任何装饰，头部不是夔龙首，而是一个光滑的椭圆面罩，面罩上只开了两条极窄的缝隙作为"视窗"。它的胸甲上没有浮雕纹路，只有一行用梵文书写的铭文，被岁月磨得几乎看不清。

但西泽尔看清了。

因为他的瞳孔在那一瞬间变了颜色。

紫瞳金纹。

他后颈的黄金套管猛烈发烫，烫到他几乎伸手去摸，那种热度从脊椎一直蔓延到脑干，让他脑海中瞬间涌入了一个不属于他的画面——

一棵树。

世界树。

不是图纸上描绘的、平面的世界树，而是一棵活生生的、正在呼吸的巨树。树根深入地底深处，穿过岩层、穿过地下暗河、穿过远古的地壳，一直延伸到某种西泽尔无法理解的深处。树根的末端不是静止的，而是在缓慢地、有节律地蠕动，像是无数条巨蟒在泥土中游动。

树根上附着着无数微小的光点。

那些光点闪烁的频率与西泽尔的心跳完全同步。

画面一闪即逝。

西泽尔回过神时，发现自己的额头已经渗出了一层细汗。

"你看到了。"楚舜华站在那台黑色甲胄旁边，紫金色的瞳孔直视着西泽尔，"世界树的根。"

"这是……"西泽尔的声音有些干涩。

"原型机。"楚舜华拍了拍那台甲胄的肩甲，"鬼武者的第一代。所有的Ⅱ型都是从它演化而来的。它的核心不是普通甲胄的蒸汽轮机，而是一个连接器。"

他走到甲胄的背部，掀起一块装甲板。

装甲板下面是一个凹槽，凹槽中嵌着一块拇指大小的暗金色金属。

"连接器插入骑士的脊椎后，不是读取骑士的神经信号，"楚舜华说，"而是将骑士的意识接入王屋山地下深处的一个节点。那个节点……是世界树东方主根意识的一个碎片。"

西泽尔盯着那块暗金色金属。

"世界树残根意识。"他说。

"对。"楚舜华点头，"母亲在王屋山发现了一块特殊的方柱——白色大理石质地，没有铭文，没有来源，被埋在地下三十米深的土层中。她花了十年时间才弄清楚那块方柱的本质：它不是石头，而是世界树残根的衍生物，内部封存着世界树残根的意识碎片。"

他合上了装甲板。

"鬼武者的核心技术，不是蒸汽压力，不是硬金骨架，不是神经接驳，"楚舜华说，"是世界树残根意识。骑士穿上鬼武者后，残根意识会与骑士的意识形成共鸣，残根意识能感知到极远处的危险信号，并将这些信号以本能反应的方式传递给骑士。"

"本能反应？"西泽尔皱眉。

"简单来说，"楚舜华走到房间角落的墙壁上，拉下一块兽皮，露出一块暗红色的投影石，"就是预知。"

投影石亮了。

画面中是一片荒野，背景是连绵的雪山和枯黄的草原。荒野上，一台鬼武者Ⅱ型甲胄正面对着三十台敌方的量产型机动甲胄。

敌方齐射。

数十发炮弹同时飞来，划出密集的弹道。

鬼武者Ⅱ型动了。

它没有闪避，没有举盾，而是以一种诡异的、不符合物理学的方式侧身——就在炮弹即将命中它前零点三秒，它的身体像是一条蛇那样扭动，炮弹从它的肩甲和胸甲之间不到两指宽的缝隙中擦过，轰在它身后的大地上。

然后它继续侧身。

第二发，第三发，第四发。

每一发炮弹都被它以毫厘之差闪过，甲胄表面甚至没有留下弹痕。

西泽尔看着那段录像，一言不发。

画面切换。另一段录像。

这次是近距离格斗。三名敌方骑士同时举刀斩向鬼武者Ⅱ型的颈部、胸部和腿部。三个方向，三个角度，三把刀同时落下。

鬼武者Ⅱ型后退一步。

仅仅一步。

但这一步让三把刀全部落空——不是靠速度闪避，而是靠某种预判，仿佛它在敌人出刀之前就知道刀会落在哪里。

"这就是残根意识的力量。"楚舜华说，"它不是让骑士变得更快或更强，而是让骑士提前知道危险在哪里。残根意识与世界树残枝同源，能感知到以自身为圆心、数百米范围内所有移动物体的轨迹。"

投影石暗了下去。

楚舜华从墙边取下一把钥匙，走向房间另一侧。

那边停着一辆马车。

不是普通的马车，而是一辆装甲运输车，车厢上印着大夏龙雀旗。楚舜华打开车厢门，车厢里铺着干草，干草上躺着一匹马的残骸。

那是一匹夔龙马。

皮毛还是红的，朱砂一样的红，但已经失去了生命的光泽，肌肉干瘪了下去，像是被抽干了水分。它的胸腔被剖开，露出内部的结构。

西泽尔走近了。

夔龙马的胸腔内，在心脏的位置，不是生物心脏，而是一个拇指大小的金属容器。容器外壳是暗金色的，与鬼武者原型机背部的连接器材质相同。容器内部透出微弱的红光。

"微型红水银引擎。"楚舜华说，"每一匹夔龙马的心脏位置都植入了这个。它的能量来源不是红水银矿脉，而是王屋山地下残根意识通过某种我们还不完全理解的方式传递过来的能量。"

他看着那具马的残骸。

"夔龙马在战场上不知疲倦、不惧伤痛，能在炮火中保持高速冲锋，靠的不是兴奋剂，是残根意识。残根意识将马也纳入了自己的感知范围，夔龙马能像鬼武者骑士一样提前感知到危险。"

他转向西泽尔。

"我父亲是夏皇，我母亲是星见。"楚舜华的声音平静得不像是在说自己的身世，"我出生前，父亲需要一样东西来对抗西方的机械。一个能够承载东西方两种力量的存在。"

"你。"西泽尔说。

"我。"楚舜华点头，"皇帝与星见的儿子。拥有皇族的政治血统和星见的血脉共鸣能力。三十年前那个还在位的楚氏皇帝与我母亲合作，制造了我这个……工具。"

他说"工具"两个字时，语气没有任何波澜。

"我自幼接受最严苛的训练。五岁开始学习星见祷文，七岁穿上第一代鬼武者，十二岁第一次在实战中穿上Ⅱ型。残根意识接受了我，但接受的方式很奇怪。"

楚舜华伸出右手。

他的右臂从肘部以下布满了紫金色的纹路，那些纹路像是树根的须根，从前臂一直延伸到手背，在指尖处汇聚成五个极小的圆点。

"它没有让我变成预知者，而是让我的身体本身成为了残根意识的延伸。普通人穿上鬼武者只能获得危险感知能力，但我穿上鬼武者后，残根意识会直接驱动我的身体。"

他握了握拳，指尖的圆点亮了一下。

"也就是说，我不只是骑士，我是残根意识的一个……载体。和西方那些被枢机会选中的紫瞳孩子一样，我也是一个被制造出来的容器。只不过枢机会的容器里装的是炽天使，而我的容器里装的是世界树残根。"

西泽尔看着楚舜华右臂上的纹路。

那些纹路的走向和西泽尔后颈黄金套管附近偶尔浮现的金红色纹路惊人地相似。

"你想让我连接原型机。"西泽尔说。

"不是想。"楚舜华摇头，"是残根意识想。它在三千公里外感知到了你的到来，就在刚才，你看到世界树根的那一瞬间，残根意识从王屋山传来了一道信号。"

"什么信号？"

"它说——"楚舜华顿了顿，"'那个人来了。'"

房间安静了几秒。

然后楚舜华走到那台原型机前，掀开了胸甲的装甲板，露出内部那个拇指大小的暗金色连接器。

"试试。"他说，"不连接神经，只让残根意识感知你。"

西泽尔走到原型机前。

他没有犹豫。

他伸出右手，将手掌按在了那个连接器上。

金属冰凉，但接触到他皮肤的那一刻，连接器猛然变得滚烫。一股远比之前更强烈的力量从掌心涌入，顺着骨骼、神经、血液，直冲脑干。

西泽尔的瞳孔在一瞬间变成了灼热的亮紫色，金色纹路从瞳孔中央炸开，像闪电一样向四周蔓延。

与此同时，楚舜华的瞳孔也亮了。

紫金色，从瞳孔中心爆开。

两人的眼睛同时发出微弱的光芒。

然后西泽尔听到了。

不是声音，是感觉。一种来自地底深处的、无法用语言描述的震颤，像是整片大地都在呼吸。那个震颤穿过岩层、穿过混凝土、穿过三百年的人工建筑，直达他的意识核心。

世界树残根。

活的。

在等。

画面在两人脑海中同时展开。

一棵巨树，根须如蟒，从地底深处一直延伸到视野的尽头。根须的末端散发出淡金色的光芒，每一条根须都像是一条活的血管，在缓慢地、有节律地搏动。

而树根的中央，有一片空地。

空地上站着一个人影。

那人影模糊不清，但轮廓与西泽尔完全一致。

人影的脚下刻着四个徽记——齿轮、六翼猫头鹰、大夏龙雀旗、锡兰莲花旗。

那人影在等西泽尔。

画面碎裂。

西泽尔猛地抽回手，后退了两步。

他的胸口剧烈起伏，额头的汗水沿着下颌滴落。楚舜华也后退了一步，右臂上的紫金色纹路正在慢慢消退。

"你看到了。"楚舜华说。

"它……"西泽尔的声音沙哑，"它知道我要来。"

"不是知道。"楚舜华摇头，"是它一直在等。它是三百年前被种下的。"

就在这时，原型机动了。

没有任何人操控，那台黑色甲胄的关节忽然发出了"咔嗒"一声脆响。紧接着是第二声、第三声——膝关节、髋关节、腰椎、颈椎依次解锁，整台甲胄的骨架从完全静止的状态变成了一种微微摇晃的、活物般的姿态。

西泽尔和楚舜华同时看向那台原型机。

原型机的头部缓慢地转向西泽尔。

椭圆面罩上那两条极窄的缝隙中，透出了微弱的淡金色光芒。

然后它跪下了。

单膝跪地。

左膝着地，右腿支撑，上身微微前倾，右拳抵在地面上。

那是东方甲胄骑士向君王行效忠礼的标准姿势。

这台已经在地下封存了不知多少年的原型机，在见到西泽尔的第一面，自行启动，自行判定，自行行礼。

楚舜华看着那台跪下的甲胄，沉默了几秒。

"鬼武者选择了你。"他说。

西泽尔盯着那台甲胄。

"我是西方人。"

"你不是西方人，也不是东方人。"楚舜华说，"你是东西方的桥梁。你身上同时流淌着锡兰星见的血液和博尔吉亚家族的机械适配基因。你是唯一能同时连接世界树残根和炽天使残枝的人。"

他走到西泽尔面前。

"我母亲临终前说过一句话——'当那个人来的时候，世界树的根会震动，鬼武者会自行下跪，东西方会重新连为一体。'她等了三十年，我等了十七年。"

他伸出右手。

"而你来了。"

西泽尔看着那只手。

他没有立刻握上去。

他还在消化刚才涌入脑海中的那些画面——世界树的根、等待他的人影、那四个徽记。太多的信息在短时间内砸下来，让他需要几秒钟来整理。

但就在他犹豫的时候，他的口袋里忽然传出一阵尖锐的震动。

那是一个巴掌大小的黄铜圆盘，圆盘表面嵌着六翼猫头鹰徽记——密涅瓦机关的远程通信器，是临行前薇若兰交给他的。

西泽尔取出通信器，按下了接收键。

通信器的微型扬声器里传出了薇若兰的声音。

她的声音没有平时的慵懒和从容，取而代之的是一种极度克制的、几乎听不出情绪波动的平静。

"西泽尔。"

"在。"

"佛朗哥教授的病情恶化了。"薇若兰说，"脑白质切除手术的排异反应比预期严重，昨夜开始持续高烧，意识已经模糊。今天凌晨他醒了一次，只说了一句话就又昏过去了。"

西泽尔的手指无声地收紧了通信器的边缘。

"他说什么？"

"他说——'让西泽尔来见我最后一面。我有东西要交给他。'"

通信器里沉默了两秒。

"我会安排最快的路。"薇若兰说，"但你自己决定要不要回来。"

通信结束。

西泽尔握着那枚黄铜圆盘，站在原地，沉默了很长时间。

楚舜华没有催他。

"我必须回去。"西泽尔最终说。

"嗯。"楚舜华点头，"我派最快的马送你到玉门关，你在那边换专列直回翡冷翠。路上需要多久？"

"四天。"

"来不及。"楚舜华说。

西泽尔看向他。

"从洛阳到翡冷翠，坐叶尼塞的专列最少四天半。"楚舜华说，"你那个教授能撑四天半吗？"

西泽尔没有回答。

他不需要回答。

楚舜华看了一眼跪在地上的原型机，转向西泽尔："今天的事你先消化。佛朗哥教授的事，我们一起想办法。现在——"

他的话没有说完。

头顶忽然传来一声沉闷的撞击声，像是什么重物砸在了地面上。

紧接着是第二声、第三声。

楚舜华的脸色微变。

"这不是工厂的声音。"他快步走向门口，掀开兽皮帘子，侧耳听了几秒。

脚步声。

不是一个人的脚步，是很多双靴子在石阶上快速移动的声音。

而那些脚步的方向——不是从上面下来的，是从工厂东面备件库方向传来的。

就在这时，西泽尔口袋里的通信器又震动了。

这次不是薇若兰的频道。

是唐璜的加密短波。

唐璜的声音从通信器中传出，压得很低，但每个字都咬得很清楚：

"老板。我在大夏龙雀馆外面。有人跟踪我们。"

西泽尔按下回复键："几个人？"

"一个。"

"抓住他。"

"已经在抓了。这小子滑得像条泥鳅。"唐璜的声音里带着一丝咬牙切齿的味道，"但我抓到了。"

"问他是谁。"

"他不说。"

短暂的沉默。

"他手臂上有东西。"唐璜的声音忽然变了调，"老板……他的右手臂不是肉。是青铜的。关节是齿轮结构。"

西泽尔的手指停住了。

"什么？"

"青铜的！"唐璜提高了声音，"就像……就像他身体里装着机械！和您那位神出鬼没的'米迦勒大人'一模一样的机械结构！"

西泽尔猛地转身看向楚舜华。

楚舜华的脸色已经沉了下来。

"能控制住吗？"西泽尔对着通信器问。

"绑住了。"唐璜说，"但他不太对劲。他在笑。"

"笑什么？"

"笑我们抓错了人。"

话音未落，通信器中传来一声短促的、像是牙齿咬碎什么东西的脆响。

然后是一声极轻的"噗"。

像是水汽被加热后消散的声音。

"老板！"唐璜的声音尖锐了，"他嘴里有毒囊！他咬碎了！他的身体在——在化！变成烟了！"

西泽尔握着通信器，一动不动。

楚舜华看着他。

两人对视。

谁都没有说话。

明堂外的风穿过石阶的缝隙，带起一阵低沉的呜咽。

那台跪在地上的原型机，椭圆面罩缝隙中的淡金色光芒，缓缓熄灭了。

【English】
Chapter 235 — Ghost Warriors of the Tongtian

The hidden door did not swing on mechanical hinges. It slid, the two halves of black iron parting with a grinding whisper, and from the seam came a breath of air so dry it tasted of heated brass and sandalwood — the exhalation of something that had been sealed a long time.

Cesare stood on the threshold and looked down.

A staircase of white marble dropped away from him, each step so finely dressed the stone caught the light like still water. But the edges of the steps were worn — not cracked, only rounded, as if ten thousand boots had climbed down here and never climbed back. Every five meters along the rough-cut rock walls, a copper lamp was set, and in each lamp burned a small flame that was not fire. It did not flicker. It did not smoke. It hung above the bronze cup like a moth pinned to velvet, and it gave off a light the color of old gold.

Chu Shunhua went first.

He did not look back. He said only, "Follow me," and his voice was level, the voice of a man who had been down these stairs more times than he could count.

Cesare followed.

The steps were many.

He counted. Twenty, forty, sixty. The air grew warmer as he descended, and the smell of brass and sandalwood deepened, and somewhere below he began to hear other sounds: the thin hiss of steam leaking from a valve, the small ringing of metal against metal, as if a workshop full of patient men were still at work in the dark.

One hundred and eight steps. The number meant something. Chu Shunhua would not have cut it into the bones of the place for nothing.

At the bottom, the staircase ended in a low arch, and Cesare stepped through, and stopped.

The chamber was a vault cut from living rock and roofed with a ribbed dome of bronze and copper alloy. The dome's apex sat nearly fifteen meters above the floor, held aloft by a thicket of dark bronze columns. Each column was engraved, not with figures or with scripture, but with a sky. Stars. Whole constellations laid out in flowing lines that curved in ways no Western celestial chart had ever used. It was as if someone had pressed the night sky of another continent flat against the metal, like a leaf in a book.

And beneath the dome, in long ordered ranks, stood the armor.

Black.

All of it black.

The nearest row held twelve suits. Cesare counted them without meaning to. The rows behind stretched back into the vault's dim reach, each separated by a service road wide enough for a wagon. Each suit stood nearly three and a half meters tall, the proportions deliberate and unhuman: shoulders too wide, arms too long, the heavy low-slung haunches of something bred for the charge rather than the parade. The head of each suit was carved into the face of a Kui-long — a one-legged dragon of the old Eastern bestiaries — its horn curving back over a skull ridged with scales so fine the work had to have been done under a loupe. Across the chest plate ran a relief of the same dragon picked out in dull gold, and in the still golden light of the lamps, the lines of those reliefs seemed faintly to move, as if the metal itself were breathing.

Ghost Warriors. Mark II.

Cesare had not expected this many.

"A hundred," Chu Shunhua said from beside him. His voice did not change. "These are the ones fully assembled. The parts stores to the east hold the cores of three hundred more, waiting to be built."

Cesare said nothing. He was still looking at the suits — at the way the shadows gathered under their visors, at the way the dragon faces regarded the empty air with a patience that had nothing to do with metal.

"This way," Chu Shunhua said again, and led him between the ranks toward the western wall.

There were things pinned there. Not weapons, not banners. Drawings.

Cesare approached the first. It was a sectional diagram, drawn in cinnabar ink so fine the lines looked like threads of blood. The drawing showed a single mechanism, its heart a core the size of a fist, ringed by a dozen pipes, each pipe labeled in a script Cesare could not read but could almost feel. In the lower right corner, in the same red ink, a careful hand had written: Copied in the thirty-seventh year of the Star Reckoning, at Wangwu Mountain.

Cesare's eyes rested on the three characters for Wangwu.

"These drawings," Chu Shunhua said, behind him, "are my mother's life. Thirty years of it. She copied them out of the sealed archives of the Stargazer clans and added her own observations, line by line, until she had pieced together the Eastern understanding of the mechanism of heaven."

He moved to the next drawing.

It was larger. It was not a machine at all.

It was a tree.

A single tree, drawn as if seen from outside the world, its roots plunging down past the floor of the drawing and its trunk so vast it had to be measured in embraces — a dozen men could not have ringed it with their arms. From the branches, dozens of luminous globes hung like fruit, each one annotated in a small, careful hand with the single word Fruit.

The World Tree.

Cesare knew the image. He had seen versions of it before — in the B-07 stacks of the Minerva Bureau, in a private folio of da Vinci Borgia, in the lotus-lit corridor of a passage that had opened for him once on the broken bough of the Tree itself. Three hundred years, two continents, and the shape had not changed. Root. Trunk. Branch. Fruit.

But there was one detail he had never seen in any other version.

At the meeting of the trunk and the roots, a tiny human figure was drawn. And above its head, a symbol: an inverted five-pointed star, each of its points studded with a minute gear.

"The Stargazers," Cesare said.

"Yes," Chu Shunhua said. "The Eastern Stargazers keep the Tree's roots. The Western Stargazers keep its leaves. Three centuries ago the two orders went their separate ways. Same blood. Same task. Both are doorkeepers of the World Tree."

He paused.

"But the two halves of the order do not see the Tree the same way."

He led Cesare to the far western wall of the vault, where an iron door was set into the rock. From his belt he took a black iron key, slid it into the lock, and turned it twice. The bolt fell with the sound of a hammer on an anvil.

The room behind was small — perhaps twenty feet across. The floor was covered in thick wool. The walls were hung with animal hides and silk, and in one corner a stick of sandalwood smoldered in a bronze dish, throwing off a slow, faintly bitter smoke. The room had the feel of a place someone had lived in, for a long time, alone.

In the center of the room stood a suit of armor.

It was not a Ghost Warrior Mark II.

It stood nearly a meter shorter than the suits outside. It was finished, if it was finished at all, in the deepest black Cesare had ever seen — a black that seemed to drink the light around it. The head was not a dragon's skull but a smooth oval visor, the face of a man who has agreed to forget his own features, with only two narrow slits for eyes. The chest plate was unmarked except for one line of inscription — a script Cesare did not at first recognize, worn down by time to a shadow. The script was Sanskrit. Or near enough to it.

Cesare read it.

And as he read, his pupils changed.

The brown of his irises bled out at the edges. What replaced it was a hot, mineral purple, and in the purple, threads of gold. The metal collar at the back of his neck — the gold socket fitted there in a room he did not like to remember — flared with a heat that ran down the ridge of his spine and into the base of his skull.

A picture came.

Not a picture. A presence.

A tree.

The World Tree, but not the diagram, not the folio engraving. A living tree, breathing, its roots plunging down through layer after layer of stone, through underground rivers, through the old bones of the earth's crust, down and down to a depth the mind could not hold. The tips of the roots were not still. They were moving. They were undulating, slowly, with the patience of enormous serpents, in a rhythm that Cesare's body recognized before his mind did. The rhythm was the rhythm of his own heart.

And on the roots, all along their length, points of light pulsed. They pulsed in time with his heart. They pulsed as if they had been waiting for him to come close enough to count.

The picture went out.

Cesare came back to himself standing where he had been, with sweat running down into his collar.

"You saw it," Chu Shunhua said. He stood beside the black armor, his own eyes the same hot purple, the same gold threads running through them. "The roots of the Tree."

"This is—"

"The original," Chu Shunhua said. He put his hand on the suit's shoulder plate. "The first Ghost Warrior. Every Mark II is a child of it. Its core is not a steam engine. It is a connector."

He walked around the suit and lifted a panel on the back.

Beneath the panel was a small socket. In the socket sat a piece of metal the size of a man's thumb, dark gold, faintly warm.

"The connector does not read the knight's nerve signals," Chu Shunhua said. "It opens the knight's mind to a node beneath Wangwu Mountain. That node is a fragment of the World Tree's Eastern root-consciousness. A splinter of awareness the Tree lost three hundred years ago, when the bough broke."

Cesare did not look away from the dark gold.

"The Tree's root-fragment," he said.

"Yes. My mother found it on Wangwu. A white marble block, no inscription, no known origin, buried thirty feet under the hill. It took her ten years to understand what she had found. It was not stone. It was a derivative of the Tree's root, and inside it, preserved, was a piece of the Tree's own mind."

He closed the panel.

"That is the heart of the Ghost Warrior. Not steam pressure, not the hard-gold skeleton, not the nerve-coupling. The root-consciousness. When a knight puts on a Ghost Warrior, the root-consciousness and the knight's mind begin to resonate. The root-consciousness can feel threats at a great distance. It feeds those threats to the knight, not as thoughts, but as instinct."

"Instinct," Cesare said.

"To put it simply," Chu Shunhua said, "prescience."

He crossed the small room and pulled down a hide that covered the far wall. Behind it was a slab of deep red projection-stone. He touched it, and it woke.

The first image was open country. A line of pale mountains in the distance, brown grass under a low sky. In the middle of the field, a single Ghost Warrior Mark II.

Facing it, thirty enemy armored suits of the production pattern.

A volley. The air filled with the bright lines of shells.

The Ghost Warrior did not duck. It did not raise a shield.

It leaned.

In the fraction of a second before the first shell reached it, its body bent sideways in a way no machine should have been able to bend, and the shell passed through the gap between its shoulder and its chest, close enough to scrape the paint, and buried itself in the ground behind. It leaned again. The second shell missed. The third. The fourth. The lines of fire came in a thick interlocking pattern, and the Ghost Warrior passed through them the way a fish passes through a net — not faster than the shells, but earlier. Always earlier, by a finger's width.

Then the picture changed. Close work, this time. Three enemy knights, blades raised, striking together at the Ghost Warrior's neck, chest, leg. Three directions. Three angles. Three swords falling as one.

The Ghost Warrior took one step back. One step. And the three blades cut only air.

"You see," Chu Shunhua said. "The root-consciousness does not make the knight faster or stronger. It tells him, before the blow is thrown, where the blow will fall. The root-consciousness is a splinter of the same mind that the Tree used to feel the wind in its branches. It can feel every moving object within a few hundred meters of the knight, the way a spider feels a fly on its web."

The stone went dark.

Chu Shunhua took a key from the wall and walked to the other side of the room. A wagon stood there — a closed armored transport, the Great Xia dragon-sparrow banner painted on its flank. He opened the rear door.

Inside the wagon, on a bed of straw, lay the carcass of a horse.

The hide was still red, the red of cinnabar, but the sheen of life was gone. The muscles had collapsed inward, as if the animal had been drained of every drop of moisture. The chest had been opened. The ribcage stood apart.

Cesare moved closer.

Where the heart should have been, there was no heart. There was a metal capsule, the size of a man's thumb, set into a cage of dark gold. The capsule was the same dark gold as the connector in the back of the prototype armor. Inside the capsule, a faint red light pulsed, weakly, as if it were a coal that had been long cold.

"A micro red-mercury engine," Chu Shunhua said. "Every Kui-long horse carries one in the chest. It does not run on red mercury from a mine. It runs on energy transmitted up from the root-consciousness beneath Wangwu, by a method we do not yet fully understand."

He looked at the carcass.

"That is why a Kui-long does not tire. That is why a Kui-long does not flinch under fire. The root-consciousness folds the horse into its own web of awareness, the same way it folds a knight. The horse knows what is coming before it comes."

He turned back to Cesare.

"My father is the Xia Emperor. My mother was a Stargazer." His voice did not change. "Before I was born, my father needed something to face the machines of the West. Something that could carry both of our halves of the world in the same body."

"You," Cesare said.

"Me. The son of an Emperor and a Stargazer. Imperial blood for politics. Stargazer blood for the resonance. Thirty years ago, the reigning Emperor of the Chu line and my mother made me for that purpose."

He said the word tool the way a man says the name of a country he no longer lives in. Without emphasis. Without bitterness.

"I was raised for the suit. I learned the Stargazer prayers at five. I wore the first Ghost Warrior at seven. I fought in a Mark II for the first time at twelve. The root-consciousness accepted me. The way it did was strange."

He held out his right arm.

From the elbow down, the skin of his arm was traced with purple-gold lines, as fine as the hairlines on a printed map, branching and rebranching the way the smallest roots of a tree branch in the earth. The lines ran down to the back of his hand and gathered at the fingertips in five tiny points, like grains of pollen.

"It did not make me prescient. It made me an extension of itself. A common knight wears the Ghost Warrior and gains a sense of danger. When I wear the Ghost Warrior, the root-consciousness drives my body directly."

He closed his hand. The five points at his fingertips pulsed once, faintly, and went out.

"I am not only a knight. I am a vessel of the root-consciousness. The Conclave in the West picks its purple-eyed children and puts the Seraph inside them. The Xia did the same thing to me, except that what they put inside me was a splinter of the World Tree."

Cesare looked at the lines on Chu Shunhua's arm. The pattern of them, the way they branched, was uncomfortably close to the pattern of the faint red-gold lines that sometimes surfaced along the socket at the back of his own neck.

"You want me to use the original," Cesare said.

"No," Chu Shunhua said. "The root-consciousness wants you to. It felt you arrive from three thousand miles away. The moment you saw the roots just now, it sent a signal up from Wangwu."

"What signal?"

"It said, 'He has come.'"

The room was quiet for a few seconds.

Then Chu Shunhua stepped to the prototype armor and lifted the chest panel, exposing the dark gold connector in its socket.

"Try it," he said. "Do not couple the nerve-line. Let the root-consciousness feel you. That is all."

Cesare walked to the suit.

He did not hesitate. He put his right hand flat against the connector.

The metal was cold. The instant it touched his skin, it was not cold.

A force came up through his palm that was nothing like steam, nothing like the shock of a galvanic line. It ran inward through the bones of his hand, up the radius and the ulna, into the shoulder, down the spine, and struck the base of his skull like a fist wrapped in cloth. His pupils blew out into a hot, incandescent purple, and from the centers of the irises threads of gold shot outward across the whites of his eyes like cracks in a furnace wall.

Chu Shunhua's eyes did the same.

Both men were lit from within, faintly, by a light no lamp in the room had kindled.

Then Cesare heard it.

Not with his ears. With the inside of his chest. A tremor, vast and slow, rising up from under the stone of the floor, through the rock of the hill, through three hundred years of dead masonry, into his awareness. As if the whole earth were drawing a long breath and holding it.

The World Tree's root.

Alive.

Waiting.

The picture opened in both their minds at the same time.

A tree, so vast that the eye could not follow it to its top. Roots like the bodies of great serpents running out of sight into the deep. At the tips of the roots, a soft gold luminescence, each root pulsing in its own time, like a vein.

And at the center of the root system, a clearing.

In the clearing, a figure.

The figure was not clear, but its outline was Cesare's outline, down to the cut of the coat across the shoulders.

Under the figure's feet, four emblems had been cut into the earth: a gear, a six-winged owl, the dragon-sparrow of Great Xia, the lotus banner of Ceylon.

The figure was waiting for him.

The picture broke.

Cesare wrenched his hand back. He took two steps away from the suit. His chest was moving. Sweat ran off the line of his jaw and fell to the wool carpet. Chu Shunhua, on the other side of the room, had also stepped back, the purple-gold lines on his arm fading slowly into his skin.

"You saw it," Chu Shunhua said.

"It—" Cesare's voice was rough. "It knew I was coming."

"No," Chu Shunhua said. "It has been waiting. It was planted in this earth three hundred years ago."

At that moment, the prototype armor moved.

No one had touched it. No one had spoken a word of command. Inside the suit, the joints made a small, dry sound — the sound of a key turning in a lock that had not been turned for a long time. Then a second sound, from the knee. A third, from the hip. A fourth, the lumbar. A fifth, the cervical. The whole frame, locked since before Chu Shunhua was born, came out of its long stillness into a faint, living sway, the sway of a thing that has just opened its eyes.

Cesare and Chu Shunhua both looked at the suit.

The head of the suit turned, slowly, until the oval visor faced Cesare.

In the two narrow slits of the visor, a faint gold light appeared.

The armor dropped to one knee.

Left knee to the ground. Right leg braced. The torso inclined, a little, in front of the bracing leg. The right fist settled on the stone, knuckles down, the way a knight of the old Xia court lowered himself before a sovereign.

The prototype, sealed in the dark under the hill for a length of time no one present could name, had woken on its own, had judged on its own, and had bowed on its own.

Chu Shunhua looked at the kneeling suit for a long moment. He did not speak.

Then he said, "The Ghost Warrior has chosen you."

Cesare looked down at the suit.

"I am a Westerner."

"You are not a Westerner," Chu Shunhua said. "You are not an Easterner. You are the bridge between the two. In your veins runs the blood of the Ceylon Stargazers, and in your bones runs the mechanical-apparatus gene of the Borgias. You are the only living person who can couple with the Tree's root and with the Seraph's remnant at the same time."

He stepped closer to Cesare.

"My mother, on her deathbed, said a single thing. She said: when that one comes, the roots of the Tree will shake. The Ghost Warriors will kneel of their own accord. And the East and the West will be made one body again. She waited thirty years for it. I have waited seventeen."

He held out his right hand.

"And you have come."

Cesare looked at the hand.

He did not take it. Not yet. The pictures were still moving through him — the roots, the waiting figure, the four emblems cut into the ground. Too much, too fast. He needed a few seconds to put it in order.

While he was still standing there, the brass disc in his coat pocket began to buzz.

It was the size of a small palm, and on its face was set the six-winged owl of the Minerva Bureau. A long-range resonator, handed to him by Violante on the morning he had left Florence.

Cesare took the disc out and pressed the receiver.

Violante's voice came through the small speaker. There was none of her usual languor. There was none of her usual mockery. There was a calm so tightly held that it barely covered anything at all.

"Cesare."

"I am here."

"Professor Franco is failing." She said it without softening. "The rejection from the leucotomy is worse than we hoped. He has been running a fever since last night. His mind is going. At dawn he woke once, said one sentence, and went under again."

Cesare's thumb pressed into the edge of the disc.

"What did he say."

"He said, 'Send Cesare to me before the end. There is something I have to put into his hands.'"

A pause on the line.

"I will arrange the fastest route I can. Whether you take it is your own decision."

The line went dead.

Cesare stood holding the disc for a long time.

Chu Shunhua did not press him.

"I have to go back," Cesare said at last.

"Yes." Chu Shunhua nodded. "I will put the fastest horse I have on the road to Yumenguan. From there you can take a direct rail to Florence. How long?"

"Four days."

"You will not make it," Chu Shunhua said. "Even on Yenisei's private line, Luoyang to Florence is four and a half days. Can your professor last four and a half days?"

Cesare did not answer.

He did not need to.

Chu Shunhua looked once at the kneeling armor, then back to Cesare.

"Take the night to think. The Franco problem, we will work on together. For the moment—"

He did not finish.

A sound came from above. A heavy, flat sound, as if something large had been dropped onto solid ground from a height. Then a second. Then a third.

Chu Shunhua's face changed.

"That is not the sound of the workshop." He walked to the door, pulled the hide curtain aside, and stood for a few seconds with his head tilted.

Footsteps.

Not one pair. Many. The hard, regular tread of boots moving fast down the stone steps from above — not from the way they had come in, but from the east, from the direction of the parts stores.

At the same moment, the disc in Cesare's pocket buzzed again.

This was not Violante's channel. This was Don Juan's encrypted shortwave.

Don Juan's voice came through the speaker, pitched low, with each word bitten off cleanly.

"Chief. I am outside the Great Xia dragon-sparrow tavern. Someone has been following us."

Cesare thumbed the reply. "How many."

"One."

"Take him."

"Already have. The little bastard is slippery as an eel. But I have him."

"Find out who he is."

"He is not saying."

A short silence on the line.

"There is something on his arm, Chief." Don Juan's voice had changed. "His right arm is not flesh. It is bronze. The joints are gear work."

Cesare's thumb stopped on the edge of the disc.

"What."

"Bronze," Don Juan said, raising his voice. "Gears in the wrist. As if there is machinery built into him, the same as that Lord Michael of yours who comes and goes when he pleases."

Cesare turned to Chu Shunhua.

Chu Shunhua's face had gone still.

"Can you hold him," Cesare said into the disc.

"Bound," Don Juan said. "But he is not right. He is smiling."

"Smiling at what."

"At us. At having caught the wrong man."

Before the last word was off the line, a small, sharp sound came through the disc — the sound of teeth closing on something brittle.

Then a soft, short pop, like steam escaping from a kettle.

"Chief!" Don Juan's voice rose. "He had a poison sac in his mouth! He bit through it! His body is — it is coming apart — he is turning into smoke!"

Cesare stood very still, the disc in his hand, the small speaker going dead against his thumb.

Chu Shunhua looked at him.

The two men looked at each other.

Neither of them spoke.

The wind from the upper levels of the Tongtian Palace pressed down through the seams of the staircase, and from somewhere far above came a long, low sound, the way the wind will sometimes speak through a crack in a wall at night.

On the floor of the small room, the prototype armor stayed where it had knelt.

Slowly, the faint gold in the two narrow slits of its visor thinned.

Thinned.

Went out.

第236章 翡冷翠的黄昏
