【中文】
第236章 翡冷翠的黄昏

密涅瓦机关医务室的白炽灯管在头顶嗡嗡作响，光线惨白，像融化的锡液。

佛朗哥教授躺在床上，消瘦得几乎脱了形。

三个月前他还能在鹰巢的车间里连续工作十四小时，校准新型红龙甲胄的神经耦合参数，那时候他骂阿方索焊缝粗糙的嗓门能让整个走廊都听见。如今那副嗓子只剩下沙沙的气声，像风穿过干裂的芦苇管。

薇若兰站在床边。

她没有哭。她只是把教授枯瘦的手指一根根地掰开，替他换上一块新的散热贴。贴片是温的，覆在老人的手背上，像一只小动物。

"……还有多久？"薇若兰的声音很平。

身旁的塔拉夏看了看神经电流读出器的曲线，低声说："三十分钟。也许更短。"

薇若兰点了点头。

佛朗哥教授的眼睛忽然睁开了。

不是那种弥留之际的回光返照，而是恢复了清澈的、属于密涅瓦初代总长后裔的、拥有三百年传承记忆的深褐色瞳仁。他看着薇若兰，嘴角微微动了动。

"若兰。"他说，"关门。"

薇若兰一怔。塔拉夏已经在拉医务室的隔音铁门了，沉重的门扇在导轨上滑过，发出一声低沉的闷响。

"只留你一个人。"佛朗哥说。

塔拉夏停下了动作，看了薇若兰一眼。薇若兰朝他点了点头，塔拉夏退出铁门，门在身后合拢。

医务室里只剩下灯管的电流声。

佛朗哥教授撑着床沿想要坐起来。薇若兰伸手去扶，老人摇了摇头，自己坐了起来。他的动作缓慢，但每一步都在控制之中——这是机械师的习惯，哪怕濒死也要测量自己的肌肉还能输出多少牛顿的力。

"听好。"佛朗哥说，"我接下来的话，你必须记住每一个字。"

他伸出那只贴着散热贴的手，按下了床头的一个隐藏机关。

床架内部发出一声细微的咔嗒，金属面板滑开，露出一只嵌入式暗格。暗格里有三样东西：一个巴掌大的六翼猫头鹰黄铜徽章——密涅瓦机关总长权限芯片；一卷缠在黄铜轴上的红水银墨水绘制的技术图纸；以及一只拇指大小的全息投影仪。

"芯片是密涅瓦机关的最高控制权。"佛朗哥把徽章放在薇若兰的掌心，"从现在起，密涅瓦的一切——鹰巢、叹息之墙、熔岩之心、骷髅地的每一条通道、每一架甲胄、每一个神经网络——都听你的。"

薇若兰的手指收拢，那枚徽章冰凉，沉甸甸的。

"图纸是'梵天陨落'反物质炸弹的完整设计图。"佛朗哥把黄铜轴递过来，"初代总长留下的最后底牌。三百年没有人碰过它，因为它的引爆条件太苛刻了——需要一台欧米茄原型体的核心作为启动介质，而世界上只有一棵世界树能结出那种果实。"

他的声音顿了一下，喉头滚了滚，咽下一口带血丝的唾液。

"但它的引爆器不在图纸里。"佛朗哥说，"也不在密涅瓦的任何档案库中。"

薇若兰抬起了眼睛。

"引爆器刻在一条项链坠的背面。"佛朗哥的目光变得很安静，那种属于老人的、见过太多生死的安静，"琳琅夫人的项链。莲花纹银坠。背面刻着一段极细的铭文——你用放大镜才能看见。那段铭文就是'梵天陨落'的启动密钥。"

"西泽尔的母亲……"薇若兰的声音微微发紧。

"她是锡兰星见的后裔，持有星见家族代代相传的紫瞳圣物。"佛朗哥说，"而初代总长把'梵天陨落'的引爆密钥，刻在了那条项链上。三百年前就刻好了。等待着有一天，项链会回到它该去的地方。"

他停了停，喘了两口气。

"那条项链现在在谁手里，我不确定。但西泽尔一定会找到它。他母亲留给他的每一样东西，他都留着。"

佛朗哥拿起了那只拇指大的全息投影仪。

"这是最后一样。"他把投影仪放在自己的胸口，"里面录了一段全息留言，发送对象设定为西泽尔·博尔吉亚的神经电流特征。只要他还在这个世界上，全息投影仪就会自动追踪他的信号，把这段话送到他眼前。"

他看着薇若兰。

"若兰。我本来应该亲口告诉他这些话的。但我没有时间了。"

"教授——"

"让他听这段全息。"佛朗哥打断了她，"不要由你转述。我需要他看见我的脸。"

他按下了全息投影仪的录制键。

一个巴掌大的光幕在床头亮起来，光幕上是佛朗哥教授的脸——比现在年轻一些，比现在胖一些，背景是密涅瓦机关的总长办公室。他穿着那件永远沾着机油的深灰色工装外套，眼镜歪在鼻梁上，像刚从车间里走出来。

这是三个多月前录制的。

画面里的佛朗哥开口了：

"西泽尔。如果你在看这段话，说明我已经死了。别难过，我活够了——密涅瓦初代总长的寿命本来就有上限，我们家的人心脏都不太好，这是遗传病。"

他笑了一下，笑容在光幕中有些失真。

"我接下来说的话，关系到你和整个世界的命运。"

"你一直在找的敌人——原罪机关的主人——不是别人。他是达·芬奇·博尔吉亚的直系后裔。也是我的老师的老师。"

薇若兰的手指无声地收紧了床沿。

"三百年前，达·芬奇·博尔吉亚用初代总工程师的身份建立了密涅瓦机关，把世界树残枝封印在维苏威火山最深处。但同时，他用教皇的身份秘密建立了原罪机关，用来打破那层封印。他一个人分裂成两个角色，互相博弈了三百年。"

"三百年来，原罪机关的真正主人从来没有暴露过真名。他用十三个替身——十三具改造了八成以上的机械人偶——轮流出面。对外活动的'米迦勒'，从来不是同一个人。"

"现在坐在原罪机关主人位置上的那个，是达·芬奇家族最后一代直系后裔。他继承了达·芬奇的全部知识、全部疯狂，以及那个从未完成的目标——重启机械神国。"

画面里的佛朗哥摘下眼镜，揉了揉眼睛。

"西泽尔，密涅瓦机关存在的意义，从来不是为教皇国制造武器。它的真正使命是阻止机械神国重启。三百年来，每一任总长都在守护这同一个秘密。"

"现在我把密涅瓦交给了薇若兰。但密涅瓦最终要交给你。"

"你是唯一一个能够同时连接世界树东西两支残枝的人。达·芬奇三百年前就预见了你的存在。他称你为'Rex Immortalis'——不死之王。"

"去打碎枷锁，西泽尔。给人类一个未来。"

"密涅瓦初代总长，达·芬奇·博尔吉亚的第十一代传人，佛朗哥·波吉亚，绝笔。"

光幕熄灭了。

佛朗哥教授把投影仪从胸口拿下来，放在薇若兰的手中。

"让他看。"老人说。

"我会的。"薇若兰的声音很低。

佛朗哥教授点了点头，慢慢躺回了枕头上。他的眼睛看着天花板上那盏嗡嗡作响的白炽灯管，目光里有一种奇异的轻松——像是交完了一份积压了三百年的作业。

"若兰。"他说。

"在。"

"给西泽尔说……那台圣乔治甲胄……莲生已经修好了……我把第四颗心脏也换上了……"

"我知道了。"

"达·芬奇日记里……最后那几页……撕掉的那几页……"佛朗哥的声音越来越轻，像蒸汽在铜管里最后一缕消散的尾音，"别让他看……别让他知道……"

"教授？"

佛朗哥没有回答。

神经电流读出器的曲线，缓慢地、不可逆转地，走向了一条直线。

塔拉夏推门进来时，薇若兰还站在床边，手里攥着那枚六翼猫头鹰徽章和那台全息投影仪。教授的散热贴还温着。

"副总长……"塔拉夏的声音哑了。

"我知道。"薇若兰把徽章别在了自己的胸口，六翼猫头鹰的翅膀张开，齿轮纹路在白炽灯下闪着冷光，"通知鹰巢全体技术员，半小时后我在中央圣所召开紧急会议。"

她停顿了一下。

"以及，给西泽尔发一封加密短波。"

"内容？"

"教授走了。"

——

与此同时。翡冷翠，教皇厅。

史宾赛厅长从地下密道钻出来的时候，闻到了一股甜腥的味道。

那是血的甜腥。

他停在了密道尽头的铁门后面。门外是教皇厅私人礼拜堂的侧廊，这个时间本该是空的——晚祷刚刚结束，侍从们都去后厨用晚餐了。

但侧廊里站着人。

不，不是站着。

是立着。

十二具。

金属骨架支撑着半人高的体型，胸腔是敞开的，齿轮与红水银管路暴露在外，关节处嵌着微型梵文。没有面孔，只有两个铜质凹槽，发出两点暗绿色的微光。每一具的右手都握着一柄蒸汽连射铳，铳口还在冒着残余的青烟。

史宾赛的目光越过那些机械人偶，落在了侧廊的尽头。

枢机会保守派的三位老枢机卿并排跪在地上，双手被反绑，身后各站着一具同样的机械人偶。博尔吉亚家族核心家长团的几位长老被按在礼拜堂的长椅上，手腕被红水银焊死的铁环锁在扶手上，脸上的表情是那种"刚刚意识到自己已经死了"的茫然。

鲜血从三位老枢机卿的脖颈流下来，在大理石地面上汇成缓慢流淌的暗红色细流。

史宾赛在密道口站了整整三秒。

他今年五十三岁，担任教皇厅厅长二十年，亲手签署过上千份处决令，见过足够多的死亡。但此刻他的手指在微微发麻——不是因为恐惧，而是因为他终于意识到了一件事：

教皇厅的权力结构，在今天傍晚，被人从根部连根拔起了。

不是枢机会。不是教皇。也不是他自己。

是那些站在血泊中的、没有面孔的机械人偶背后的那个人。

一个一直在暗处操控着所有人的、原罪机关真正的主人。

史宾赛缓缓地退回密道。他没有拔枪——他知道自己的随身武器对那些机械人偶毫无意义。他转身，踩着密道里冰凉的石阶，朝来路快步返回。

他需要找到教皇。真正的教皇。博尔吉亚三世。

无论那位老人还剩下多少力气，他必须知道——翡冷翠的天，已经塌了。

——

教皇的私人寝室在教皇厅的第三层，白色大理石墙，窗框是深红色翡冷翠大理石雕的。史宾赛赶到时，门没有锁。

博尔吉亚三世坐在窗前的躺椅上。

他穿着一件旧式的睡袍，领口敞着，露出枯瘦的胸膛。他面前的小桌上放着一只白瓷药瓶——那种他每天傍晚都要吃的绿色药片。

但老人没有在吃药。

他在咳血。

帕子捂在嘴上，白色的麻布上洇开了一朵一朵暗红色的花。他的肩膀在抖，每一声咳嗽都像是要把整个胸腔撕裂。

"陛下。"史宾赛快步走到他身边，扶住他的肩膀。

博尔吉亚三世摆了摆手，示意他不要紧。但他的眼睛已经红了，虹膜里布满了细密的血丝，那是连续咳血导致的毛细血管破裂。

"水……"老人的声音嘶哑。

史宾赛倒了一杯温水递过去。博尔吉亚三世就着他的手喝了一口，又开始咳。咳到最后，他用帕子擦嘴时，忽然停住了。

他盯着帕子看了两秒。

然后他伸手拿起了小桌上那只白瓷药瓶，拧开瓶盖，把里面的绿色药片倒了几粒在掌心。药片是圆的，翠绿色，表面有一层糖衣。

他用指甲把一颗药片掰开。

药片的核心不是粉末。

是一颗米粒大小的、暗红色的金属颗粒。

红水银。

史宾赛的脸色瞬间变了。

"陛下……"

博尔吉亚三世把那颗药片放在桌上，双手在发抖，但他的声音却出奇地平静："史宾赛。我吃了这种药……多久了？"

"您……您从马斯顿回来之后就开始吃这种药了。是枢机会保健处的处方……"

"多久了？"

"……七个多月。"

老人闭上眼睛。

"七个多月。每日两片。每片含零点三克红水银微粒。"他的声音像在念一份死亡通知书，"四百二十克。足以把一个成年人的神经系统和脑白质彻底摧毁。"

他睁开眼，那双浑浊的老眼里忽然透出了一种可怕的清醒。

"我本来以为我的咳血是'那种病'。"

那种病。弥赛亚圣教历任教皇的遗传病——从博尔吉亚一世开始，每一任教皇都在六十岁前后出现咳血的症状，三百年来无一人幸免。教廷内部称之为"圣座的代价"。

但博尔吉亚三世今年才五十七岁。

"这不是遗传病。"老人把药瓶攥在手里，瓶子在他指间嘎吱作响，"有人要我死。"

他忽然笑了。

那是一种极其古怪的笑——像是释然，又像是愤怒，又像是某种更深层的、已经超越了愤怒的绝望。

"史宾赛。"

"在。"

"给我纸。"

史宾赛从桌上取来一张空白的羊皮纸和一支钢笔。博尔吉亚三世接过笔，笔尖在纸面上悬了几秒，然后开始写。

他写得很快，字迹潦草而有力，墨水在纸面上划出深深的凹痕：

"西泽尔。"

"对不起。"

"我利用了你。我从一开始就知道达·芬奇·博尔吉亚的疯狂计划——三百年来每一任博尔吉亚教皇都知道——而我选择用你作为诱饵，把原罪机关的注意力从教皇厅转移到密涅瓦机关。我需要时间。我需要你成为他们的眼中钉，从而忽略真正的危险。"

"但我也希望你能拯救世界。"

"因为你是Rex Immortalis。三百年来唯一一个能连接世界树东西两支残枝的人。"

"如果你能读到这封信，说明我已经被杀了。"

"不要为我复仇，西泽尔。去做你该做的事。"

"教皇，博尔吉亚三世，绝笔。"

老人把笔放下。

他把羊皮纸对折，再对折，折成一个小小的方块，递给史宾赛。

"如果我死了，"博尔吉亚三世说，"把这封信交给西泽尔。"

"陛下——"

"还有一件事。"老人抬起眼睛看着史宾赛，"下令疏散翡冷翠的所有市民。"

"什么？"

"疏散。立刻。"博尔吉亚三世的目光里，那种可怕的清醒正在消退，取而代之的是一种近乎疯狂的执念，"告诉所有人——维苏威火山要喷发了。"

史宾赛愣住了。

维苏威火山。密涅瓦机关所在的那座活火山。维苏威火山一旦喷发——

"不是普通的喷发。"博尔吉亚三世闭上了眼睛，"是机械的喷发。"

他抬手指向窗户。窗外是翡冷翠的黄昏，夕阳正从阿尔诺河的方向沉下去，把整座城市染成了血红色。

"快走。"

——

维苏威火山。熔岩之心。底层。

黑铁巨门完全打开了。

那扇十二尺高的巨门，重量相当于三辆斯泰因重机，此刻像两片被风吹开的巨大黑色翅膀，静静地敞向两侧。门后是无尽的黑暗——不是普通的黑暗，而是一种连光线都能吞噬的、属于世界树残枝最深处的绝对漆黑。

原罪机关主人站在巨门前。

他摘下了那副白银面具。

面具下不是一张人脸。

是一具金属骨架支撑着的、近乎人类轮廓的躯体。头颅的左半边是精密咬合的齿轮组，颅骨表面刻着密密麻麻的微型梵文；右半边覆盖着一层仿生皮肤，皮肤下面是红水银管路纵横交错的机械肌肉。颈椎是分段式的金属关节，每转动一节都发出低沉的咔嗒声。右眼眶里嵌着一颗暗红色的红水银晶片当瞳孔，左眼眶是空的，里面嵌着一只微型齿轮组，会在黑暗中发出两点微弱的绿光。

他的身体超过八成是机械。

那是三百年的改造——用初代教皇留下的技术，把一个凡人一点一点地替换成了一台活着的、会思考的机械。

"米迦勒。"他开口了。

声音不是从喉咙里发出的，而是从胸腔里那台精密齿轮组咬合的震动中产生的，带着一种金属与金属摩擦的冷硬质感。

"属下在。"身后一具戴着银色猫头鹰面具的替身应声。

"启动维苏威火山的欧米茄原型体群。"原罪机关主人说，"让人类感受神的愤怒。"

替身沉默了一秒。

"主人，"替身问，"全部？"

"全部。"

黑铁巨门后的黑暗开始震动了。

起初是一种低沉的嗡鸣，像千万只蜜蜂同时振翅。然后那嗡鸣变成了节律——一种类似于心跳的、越来越快的节律。黑暗深处亮起了无数暗红色的光点。

那不是灯。

那是欧米茄原型体胸腔中红水银核心被唤醒时发出的光。

一架。两架。十架。更多。

它们从黑暗深处走出来，踏着整齐的、莲花花瓣般的无声步伐。每一架都超过五米高，暗金色装甲板在它们行走时发出细密的金属摩擦声，胸前镶嵌的红水银核心像心脏一样跳动。它们的关节刻着世界树神经祈祷文，那些铭文在它们启动时发出金色的微光。

世界树残枝在它们身后，散发着温热的光芒——那棵由暗金色合金构成的巨树，正在苏醒。

原罪机关主人抬起了那只由精密机械构成的手臂，张开五指。

树上的齿轮开始转动。

嗡鸣声穿透了整座维苏威火山。

——

翡冷翠的摩斯密码箱在十一秒内同时触发了神圣灾难警报。

那是一种三声长鸣、间隔两秒、重复三次的刺耳信号。它从教皇厅的每一台接收器中爆发出来，从圣堂装甲师每个分队的随身信标中爆发出来，从密涅瓦机关鹰巢的每一台监控屏上爆发出来。

整个翡冷翠的每一名军人都停下了脚步。

他们看向天空。

夕阳已经完全沉下去了。阿尔诺河的方向，第一架暗金色的欧米茄原型体正穿过暮色，向北飞去。

它的飞行轨迹笔直，指向马斯顿。

与此同时，第二架正飞向君士坦丁堡。

第三架飞向伦敦。

第四架飞向梵蒂冈。

数百架。数千架。

世界树的果实，正在离开母体。

【English】
Chapter 236 — Twilight Over Florence

The tubes above the Minerva sickroom buzzed in their housings, a thin electric whine that never quite let you forget it was there. The light they gave off had the color of melted tin.

Professor Franco lay on the bed beneath them, and the bed seemed too wide for him. Three months earlier he had been a man of certain girth, a man who could stand for fourteen straight hours in the Eyrie's workshops recalibrating the neural coupling of a fresh Red Dragon armor and still find breath, at the end of it, to shout down a corridor that Alfonso's weld seams looked like they had been laid by a drunk spider. The shouting was gone now. What came out of him was a dry whisper, the kind of sound wind makes in a cracked reed.

Violante stood at the bedside. She did not cry. She bent to the work of prying his wasted fingers open one by one, peeling away the spent thermal patch from the back of his hand and laying a fresh one in its place. The new patch was warm. It sat there over the blue vein-snakes of his old man's hand like a small animal that had decided to trust him.

"How long," she said. Her voice was level.

Tarascia, at the foot of the bed, read the curve on the neural-current scope. "Half an hour. Perhaps less."

Violante nodded.

Franco's eyes opened.

Not the way a dying man's eyes open. There was no last flare, no film of glazing recognition. The brown irises that looked back at her were the same clear brown they had been when he was a young man striding the corridors of Minerva, and they carried, somewhere behind the color, three hundred years of inherited memory that no one in the room except him could have named. The first Director's line. The long unbroken chain of keepers.

"Violante," he said. "Close the door."

She blinked. Tarascia had already turned toward the iron soundproofing leaf and was hauling it along its track. It gave one low, weighty groan, then seated itself with a thud that left only the hum of the lights.

"Leave us," Franco said.

Tarascia stopped. He looked at Violante. She nodded once, and the younger woman slipped through the closing gap, and the door sealed behind her.

The room was the lights, and Franco's breathing, and the smell of the iron-cored beds and the red-mercury coolant that had been pumped through his blood for the last six weeks.

Franco braced his hand on the bedrail and began to lever himself upright. Violante reached to help him. He shook his head. Slowly, with the deliberate care of a man measuring each newton his muscles could still deliver, he sat up on his own. Even now, the engineer's habit. Even now, calibration.

"Listen to me," he said. "What I am about to say, you will remember. Every word."

He reached to the head of the bed and pressed, with one thumbnail, a place on the rail where no press was meant to fall. A small click. A panel of brushed steel slid aside, revealing a recess cut into the frame. Inside, three things lay on a pad of dark felt. A badge no larger than a child's palm, cast in brass, in the shape of a six-winged owl — the Minerva command cipher. A scroll of technical drawing, wound around a brass roller, its ink the dull, unmistakable red of red mercury. And a holo-projector the size of a man's thumb.

Franco placed the owl in her palm.

"From this moment, Minerva answers to you. The Eyrie. The Wall of Sighs. The Heart of Lava. Every corridor in Golgotha. Every suit of armor. Every nerve-net we have ever laced through the bones of this mountain. All of it."

The badge was cold. It weighed more than it looked as if it ought to.

Franco set the scroll across her hand as well. "These are the complete schematics for the Brahmastra Fall. The antimatter bomb. The last card the First Director ever played. In three hundred years no one has touched it, because its trigger condition is obscene — it needs the core of an Omega prototype as its activation medium, and there is only one tree in the world that grows that kind of fruit."

He paused. Swallowed. The swallow came back tasting of copper.

"But the detonator," he said, "is not on the schematic. It is not in any archive of Minerva."

Violante's eyes came up from the scroll.

"It is engraved on the back of a pendant," Franco said. His voice had gone very quiet, the quiet of a man who has seen too much death to perform it any longer. "A silver pendant. Lotus pattern. The inscription is so fine you need a loupe to read it. That inscription is the Brahmastra's ignition key."

"Lady Linara's pendant," Violante said. The name came out tighter than she had meant it to.

"She was a daughter of the Ceylonese Star-Readers," Franco said. "The violet-eye relic passed down their line. The First Director set the ignition key into the pendant three centuries ago, and he set it there because he knew — knew as certainly as a man can know anything — that one day the chain would bring the pendant back to where it needed to be."

He stopped. Two breaths, ragged at the edges.

"I do not know who holds the pendant now. But Cesare will find it. He has kept every single thing his mother ever left him. Not one piece lost. You may count on that."

He picked up the thumb-sized holo-projector. He set it against his chest for a moment, the way a man sets a hand against a wound, then held it out to her.

"This last. It is keyed to Cesare Borgia's neural signature. Anywhere on the earth that he is alive, the projector will find him and play the message into his eyes."

He looked at her.

"I should have told him all of this in person. I do not have that left."

"Professor —"

"Play it for him, Violante. Do not retell it. I need him to see my face."

He pressed Record. Then Play.

A palm of light rose from the projector and hung in the air above the bed, and in the light was Franco's face. A Franco three months younger and a stone heavier, the grease-dark work coat he always wore, his spectacles sitting crooked on a nose that had been broken twice in the workshops. Behind him, the Director's office. The shelves of brass weights. The standing clock with the Minerva owl carved into its pendulum.

He had recorded this standing up, then. He had not known he was about to spend the rest of his short life in this room.

The image began to speak.

"Cesare. If you are watching this, I am dead. Do not be sorry for me. I have had my full count — the First Director's line has always run short on hearts; it is the family inheritance, and I will not be the last to pay it."

The recorded Franco smiled, and the smile broke up a little at the edges of the projection.

"What I am about to tell you will decide your life and the shape of the world.

The enemy you have spent these years hunting — the master of the Original Sin agency — is no stranger to you in blood. He is a direct descendant of Leonardo da Vinci. He was, in life, my teacher's teacher.

Three hundred years ago, da Vinci built Minerva in the open, as the chief engineer of the Holy See, and he sealed the World Tree's severed branch in the deepest chamber of Vesuvius. At the same moment, in his other name, he built the Original Sin agency in secret, to one day break that seal. Two roles. One man. They have played against each other across three centuries.

In all that time, the true master of the Original Sin agency has never shown his face. He has spoken to the world through thirteen surrogates — thirteen mechanical puppets, each of them eighty percent rebuilt. The Michael you have heard named, the Michael you have fought, the Michael you have feared — never the same man twice.

The one who sits in that chair now is the last of da Vinci's line. He carries every fragment of the old man's knowledge, every fragment of the old man's madness, and the one project the old man never finished — the restoration of the Machine-God's kingdom."

The image removed its spectacles and rubbed at the corners of its eyes. The eyes, even through the projection, looked tired.

"Cesare. Minerva was never built to make weapons for the Pope. Its true purpose is to prevent the Machine-God from waking. Every Director for three hundred years has been the keeper of that one secret.

I have given Minerva to Violante. But Minerva, in the end, belongs to you.

You are the only living human being who can connect the eastern and western branches of the severed World Tree. Da Vinci foresaw you three centuries before you were born. He called you Rex Immortalis — the immortal king.

Go break the chains, Cesare. Give humankind a future.

First Director of Minerva, eleventh inheritor of Leonardo da Vinci, Franco Borgia, end of message."

The light went out.

The real Franco, on the bed, took the projector from his chest and laid it in Violante's hand. His fingers were cold.

"Play it for him," he said again.

"I will."

He nodded. Slowly, with the same measured care he had used to sit up, he let himself back down onto the pillow. He lay there looking up at the buzzing tube light above his head, and the expression on his face was one Violante had never seen on him before — a kind of lightness, the look of a man who has at last set down a piece of work that has been on his desk for three hundred years.

"Violante," he said.

"I am here."

"Tell Cesare — the Saint George armor. Lotus-Born has finished the rebuild. I put in the fourth heart for him. He will need it."

"I will tell him."

"The last pages of the da Vinci journal," Franco said. His voice was thinning, the way steam thins at the end of its run through a copper pipe. "The ones that were torn out. Do not let him see them. Do not let him know."

"Professor?"

Franco did not answer.

The trace on the neural-current scope slid, slow and patient and quite without malice, toward the flatline.

When Tarascia came through the door, Violante was still standing where she had been. In her right hand she held the six-winged owl. In her left, the projector. The thermal patch on the old man's hand was still warm.

"Deputy Director," Tarascia said. Her voice caught.

"I know." Violante pinned the owl to the breast of her coat. The brass wings spread, the gearwork inside them catching the white light and throwing it back cold. "Tell the Eyrie. Full muster of every technician. I want a crisis council in the central sanctum in thirty minutes."

She paused.

"And send a coded shortwave to Cesare Borgia."

"What shall I say?"

"The Professor is dead."

—

Florence. The Papal Palace.

Spencer, the palace chamberlain, climbed out of the underground passage and smelled blood.

The sweet, metallic kind. The kind that has been out of the body long enough to start thinking about itself.

He stopped at the iron door that led from the passage into the side aisle of the private chapel. At this hour the aisle should have been empty. Vespers had ended a quarter of an hour ago. The attendants were all in the back kitchens, eating.

The aisle was not empty.

Twelve of them stood along the wall. Metal skeletons the height of a child's waist, chests open to the air, gear trains and red-mercury tubing visible inside, joints inlaid with microscopic梵文. No faces. Two dim green points in copper sockets where eyes would have been, in each one. In the right hand of each, a steam repeater. The barrels still trailed the last wisps of blue cordite.

Spencer's gaze went past them, to the end of the aisle.

The three conservative cardinals of the College knelt in a row, hands bound behind their backs, a puppet standing behind each of them. The senior elders of the Borgia family council were pinned to the chapel pews, wrists welded into iron cuffs by red mercury that had set fast to the wood. The expressions on their faces were the particular blankness of men who have only just understood that the world they lived in no longer exists.

A slow dark river of blood was finding its way across the white marble floor from beneath the cardinals' chins.

Spencer stood in the mouth of the passage for a long three seconds.

He was fifty-three years old. He had been chamberlain for twenty of them. He had signed more death warrants than he could count, and he had seen the dead and the soon-to-be-dead in numbers that should have blunted the sight of it. His fingers were tingling now. Not with fear. With the much colder recognition that the power structure of the Papal Palace had just been pulled out of the ground by the roots. Not by the College. Not by the Pope. Not by him. By the thing standing at the end of that blood trail, behind those twelve faceless brass skeletons.

The master of the Original Sin agency. The one who had been in the dark for three hundred years.

Spencer stepped backward into the passage. He did not draw his sidearm. He knew what a hand-weapon would do against those things. He turned and went down the cold stone stairs, taking them two at a time, and he did not slow down until he was back under the street.

He had to find the Pope. The real Pope. Borgia the Third. Whatever the old man still had left in him, he had to know — the sky over Florence had come down.

—

The Pope's private chambers were on the third floor of the Papal Palace, white marble walls, window frames cut from the deep red marble of Florence itself. The door was not locked.

Borgia the Third was sitting in a reclining chair by the window, in an old-fashioned nightgown with the collar open to the sternum. On the small table in front of him, a white porcelain apothecary bottle. The kind of bottle that held the little green tablets he took every evening.

He was not taking one.

He was coughing blood into a square of linen. The cloth came away from his mouth each time with a fresh dark flower opened on it. His shoulders shook with each cough, and each cough sounded as if it were trying to tear the entire chest open from the inside.

"Your Holiness," Spencer said, and crossed the room in four strides and took the old man's shoulder.

Borgia waved him off, the way a man waves off a fly, and reached for the water. Spencer poured, steadied the glass against the Pope's shaking hand. The old man drank, and coughed again, and looked down at the linen in his hand as if he had not seen it before.

Then he reached for the porcelain bottle. Unscrewed it. Tipped three green tablets into his palm. Sugar-coated, perfectly round, the color of young leaves.

He broke one open with his thumbnail.

The core of the tablet was not powder.

It was a grain of dark red metal, the size of a rice seed, with a faint unnatural sheen.

Red mercury.

Spencer's face changed.

"Your Holiness —"

"How long," Borgia said. His voice was a torn whisper. He had not asked it as a question. He had asked it the way a man reads a number off a headstone.

"You — you began taking this after Marston, Your Holiness. The College's medical office prescribed it."

"How long."

"Seven months, Your Holiness."

The old man closed his eyes. When he opened them, the cloudiness was gone from them. What was left was something worse: a terrible, clinical wakefulness.

"Seven months. Two tablets a day. Point three grams of red mercury per tablet." He spoke the arithmetic as if he were reading a death warrant on someone else. "Four hundred and twenty grams. Enough to take the brain and the nerve trunks of a grown man and pulp them to nothing."

He looked at Spencer.

"I had thought it was the sickness."

The sickness. The inherited wasting of the Popes of the Messianic See — Borgia the First, Borgia the Second, every one of them coughing blood around their sixtieth year. The curial name for it was the Price of the Throne.

Borgia the Third was fifty-seven.

"This is not the sickness," the old man said. He closed his hand around the porcelain bottle, and the glass ground against the bones of his fingers. "Someone wants me dead."

He laughed.

It was a very strange laugh. The laugh of a man who has been made free, and does not yet know what use to make of the freedom.

"Spencer."

"Your Holiness."

"Paper. Pen."

Spencer put a sheet of vellum on the table and laid a steel-nibbed pen across it. Borgia lifted the pen. The nib hovered above the surface for a few seconds, and then he began to write, the script fast and slanted and pressed hard enough to dent the sheet.

Cesare.

Forgive me.

I used you. I have known of Leonardo da Vinci's madness from the beginning — every Borgia Pope for three centuries has known — and I chose to make of you a decoy, to draw the Original Sin agency's eye away from the Papal Palace and onto Minerva. I needed time. I needed you to be the thorn in their side, while the real danger passed unnoticed.

But I also wanted you to save the world.

Because you are Rex Immortalis. Because you are the only living human being who can join the severed branches of the World Tree.

If you are reading this letter, then I have been killed.

Do not avenge me, Cesare. Do what must be done.

Pope Borgia the Third, end of letter.

He set the pen down. He folded the vellum in quarters, and again in quarters, until it was a small square that fit in a man's fist, and he held it out to Spencer.

"If I die," he said, "give this letter to Cesare Borgia."

"Your Holiness —"

"One more thing." The old man lifted his eyes to Spencer. The terrible clarity in them was fading now, and what was coming up under it was something that looked almost like a fever, almost like rapture. "Order the evacuation of the city of Florence."

Spencer stopped.

"Evacuation. At once. Tell everyone that Vesuvius is about to erupt."

"Your Holiness, Vesuvius —"

"Not a normal eruption." Borgia closed his eyes. "A mechanical one."

He raised one hand toward the window. Outside, the sun was going down over the Arno. The whole city was the color of blood, and the long shadows of the buildings were black as iron.

"Go."

—

Vesuvius. The Heart of Lava. The lowest level.

The black iron gates stood open.

Twelve feet of forged metal, three Stein heavies in weight, and they stood like two black wings drawn back by the wind. Beyond them was not the dark of a closed room. It was the dark of a throat. The dark that swallows light as it falls.

The master of the Original Sin agency stood before the gates.

He lifted the silver mask from his face.

What was under it was not a face. It was the rough draft of one, sketched in brass and steel. The left hemisphere of the skull was a tightly meshed bank of gears, the bone etched over with micro-梵文. The right was sheathed in a layer of synthetic skin, under which a web of red-mercury tubes traced the shape of muscle. The cervical vertebrae were a stack of metal segments; they clicked, one by one, as he turned his head. The right eye-socket held a chip of red mercury for a pupil. The left was empty, save for a small clockwork assembly that turned slowly, throwing two faint green points into the dark.

More than eighty percent of the body that called itself master of the Original Sin agency was machine.

Three centuries of slow replacement. The last living scrap of a man, rebuilt one piece at a time, by the techniques the first Pope had left behind in his black books, into something that thought, and remembered, and wanted.

"Michael," he said. The voice did not come from a throat. It came from the precise mesh of gears inside his chest, and it had the cold, dry scrape of metal on metal.

"My lord." A surrogate in a silver owl mask answered from the dark behind him.

"Activate the Omega prototypes. All of them. Let mankind feel what the anger of a god feels like."

The surrogate was silent for a heartbeat.

"All of them, my lord?"

"All of them."

The dark behind the gates began to tremble.

It began as a low hum, the way ten thousand bees might sound from a great distance. Then the hum took on a rhythm, the rhythm of a heart, a rhythm that was quickening. And in the dark, points of dim red began to appear. Not lamps. The cores of red mercury, lighting up in the chests of machines as they woke.

One. Two. Ten. More. More.

They walked out of the dark in formation, five meters tall, the color of dull gold. As they moved, the plates of their armor gave off the fine, dry whisper of metal on metal. The red-mercury cores at their breasts pulsed like hearts. Along the joints, the world-tree prayer script caught its own light and threw it back as a thin gold glow.

Behind them, the World Tree was waking. The immense dark-gold alloy trunk gave off a slow heat, the way a sleeping animal gives off heat.

The master lifted his right hand, the hand that was all mechanism, and opened it. The fingers spread. The gears in the wrist began to turn.

On the tree behind him, somewhere far up in the dark, a single great gear engaged with the next. The sound that came down the trunk was a low, sustained, enormous hum. It passed through the floor of the Heart of Lava. It passed through the mountain. It went out into the world.

—

In Florence, the Morse cabinets of every church, every barracks, every guard-post, every signal-tower in the Curial network went off in the same eleven seconds.

The Holy Disaster alarm. Three long blasts, two seconds of silence, three more blasts. The sound the See had not sounded in a hundred and fifty years.

Every soldier in Florence stopped where he stood.

They looked up.

The sun was down. Over the Arno, in the last of the dusk, a single dark-gold shape was moving through the sky, on a straight course. North. Toward Marston.

A second shape rose from behind the cathedral roofline. East. Toward Constantinople.

A third. A fourth. A fifth. More. A steady procession, climbing out of the dark over the volcano and fanning out across the sky in clean, purposeful lines.

One of them flew west. Toward London. One of them flew south. Toward the Vatican.

Hundreds of them. Thousands.

The fruits of the World Tree were leaving the mother.

第237章 马斯顿的再临

【中文】
第237章 马斯顿的再临

暮色像一盆冰水从马斯顿王立机械学院的穹顶上浇下来。

圣母光婴堂的钟塔敲了八下，最后一声铜鸣还没散尽，北方的天际线上就亮起了一团暗金色的光。那光不是月亮，也不是星星——月亮在东边，星星还没有这种能把云层烧穿的亮法。

那团光以不符合任何物理常识的速度坠向学院。

操场上还有学生在散步。仲夏夜庆典的彩灯没有拆，五颜六色的玻璃灯笼在晚风里轻轻摇晃，几对年轻男女挽着手经过喷泉池，水面倒映着他们黑色的校服和金色的袖扣。

那团光落在操场正中央。

没有声音。或者说，声音来得太迟了，迟到了所有人的耳朵还来不及做出反应。暗金色的冲击波从落点向四面八方扩散，草坪像被一只无形的巨手从地底掀起，连根带泥翻卷出去。喷泉池里的水瞬间汽化，白色的水雾腾起三米多高，周围的彩灯全部炸裂，玻璃碎片像彩色的雨。

然后才是声音。

一声沉闷到几乎超出人耳接收范围的轰鸣从地底涌上来，大地在震颤，教堂的彩色玻璃窗发出细碎的龟裂声。钟塔顶上那只铸铁圣婴像被震得歪了头。

暗金色的尘埃散去之后，操场上站着的东西让所有还活着的人同时停止了思考。

它超过五米高。

暗金色装甲板在夕阳余晖中反射出冷硬的光，每一片甲板都雕刻着繁复到令人眩晕的花纹——齿轮、莲花、还有无数看不懂的铭文。它的胸腔中央嵌着一颗跳动的东西，拳头大小，暗红色，像一颗正在呼吸的心脏。

那就是红水银核心。

它的关节处刻着一种特殊的铭文，那些铭文在它启动的时候开始发出金色的微光，像被点亮的血管。它的头部没有面孔，只有一个光滑的、椭圆形的面甲，面甲正中央裂开一道竖缝，竖缝后面是一片深不见底的暗金色。

操场边缘，喷泉池的废墟旁，一个一年级学生停下脚步。

他很好奇。

他摘下帽子，仰起头，直直地看向那架东西的面甲。

竖缝后面那片暗金色忽然亮了一下。

不是反射光。是那道竖缝本身亮了，像一只眼睛在黑暗中猛地睁开，暗金色的光柱从竖缝中射出，笔直地打在那名学生的脸上。

学生没有发出任何声音。

他只是站在那里，帽子上冒出了细小的白烟。

然后他的眼睛着了。

两团金色的火焰从他的眼眶里窜出来，舔过他的额头，烧焦了他的头发。他的身体还直立着，嘴巴张得很大，像是想尖叫，但火焰比声音更快，吞掉了他的舌头、牙齿和颅骨。

三秒钟后，他变成了一根燃烧的火炬。

周围的人这才反应过来。尖叫声从四面八方爆发，有人跌倒在地，有人拔腿狂奔，有人被自己绊倒后又被后面的人踩过去。操场变成了一片混乱的漩涡。

那架东西没有追任何人。

它只是站在那里，一动不动，像一尊刚从地底被挖出来的神像。

——

圣母光婴堂的地下室里，庞加莱正用手掌堵住通风口。

他的动作很镇定，但掌心在发抖。

地下室原本是存放教堂祭祀用品的储藏室，积了几十年的灰尘，蛛网从拱顶上垂下来，空气里弥漫着蜡烛油和霉斑的味道。铁架上堆满了落满灰尘的圣杯、烛台和经书匣子，角落里立着几尊等身大的圣徒木雕，漆面斑驳，眼珠用廉价的玻璃珠代替，在烛光中忽明忽暗。

四个人蹲在铁架后面。

米内蹲在最里面，缩成了一团，双手抱着膝盖。他不再是当年那个意气风发的年轻贵族少爷了，下城区的风霜在他脸上刻出了过早的纹路，但那双眼睛还亮着——是那种见过太多死亡之后反而更加清醒的亮。

拜伦半蹲半跪在一尊圣徒木雕旁边，手指按在那柄家传骑士剑的剑柄上。那把剑的剑鞘是深蓝色的，镶嵌银线狮鹫纹章，是新罗马帝国军事贵族的制式装备。他的指节发白，但他没有拔剑。他知道拔剑没有用。甲胄格斗的剑术是用来对付甲胄的，不是用来对付那种东西的。

上校背靠墙壁，用那条独臂的肘部抵在砖面上，另一只手里攥着一块暗银色的金属碎片——炽天铁骑Ⅳ型的胸甲残片，上校从地下斗兽场的废料堆里捡出来的，一直当镇纸用。

现在那不是镇纸了。

"你们都看见外面那东西了。"庞加莱的声音很轻，但每个字都像钉子一样钉进空气里。

"看见了。"上校说。

"知道那是什么吗？"

"不知道。"上校说，"但我知道它每秒钟能杀死一百个人。"

"不只一百个。"庞加莱的掌心还堵着通风口，"直视它面甲的人会被金色火焰烧死。安妮就是这么死的。"

地下室里沉默了一瞬。

米内的喉头动了动。

"我认识安妮。"他低声说，"她帮我写过论文。"

"我知道。"庞加莱说，"所以我不能让她白死。"

他从风衣内袋里掏出一个东西。

那是一个信封。

黑色信封，边角已经泛黄，但封口的火漆印记还是完好的。火漆上压着一只展翅的黑天使——异端审判局的徽记。

米内认出了那个徽记。他的脸白了一度。

"这是……"拜伦压低声音。

"十二年前我刚来马斯顿任职的时候收到的。"庞加莱说，"我以为是哪个疯子的恶作剧。"

他用拇指按住了火漆。

信封自动打开了。

火漆印记从中间裂开，像一只眼睛在眨动，裂开的缝隙里吐出一张折叠得整整齐齐的薄纸。纸张的质地很特殊，摸上去像蝉翼，带着一股陈旧的防腐药剂气味。

庞加莱把纸展开。

上面只有一行字。

"马斯顿王立机械学院是圣战之路的起点，也是世界树残枝的一个节点。"

字迹是印刷体，标准的教廷公文体，每一个字母都方方正正。

"世界树残枝。"上校重复了一遍这个名词，嗓音像生锈的铰链，"那是什么？"

"我不知道。"庞加莱说，"但我知道一件事——异端审判局从不会用黑天使加急信封来寄玩笑。"

他把那张纸折好，塞回信封，收进风衣内袋。

"现在我们需要一个计划。"他说。

"什么计划？"拜伦问，"用一把剑去砍那个东西？"

"我们需要武器。"庞加莱转向拜伦，"你有剑。"

拜伦犹豫了一秒，然后拔出了那柄家传骑士剑。剑身出鞘时发出一声清脆的金属鸣响，窄长的剑身在烛光中闪过一道冷光。剑格上铸着狮鹫展翅的浮雕，剑刃上还保留着新罗马帝国军械库出厂时的油光——他从来没有用过这把剑杀人。

"米内。"庞加莱又转向米内。

米内没有说话。

他从铁架后面拖出一个布包。布包很旧，帆布的边角都磨毛了，沾着铁锈和油渍。他解开系带，里面是一套折叠得整整齐齐的软甲。

钢丝软甲。

每一片钢丝都被打磨得像丝绸一样薄，编织成鱼鳞状，叠了三层，衬着黑色的皮革内衬。这不是给学生防身用的普通货色——这是当年学院教堂祭坛下面藏的旧物，庞加莱在一次翻修教堂地基时偶然发现的，一直假装不知道。

米内从软甲下面又抽出一把猎刀。刀柄是鹿角制的，刀刃有七寸，磨得雪亮。

"我以为你在下城区混日子。"上校看着那把猎刀，声音里多了一丝复杂的东西。

"下城区教会了我怎么活。"米内说。

"上校。"庞加莱最后转向独臂男人。

上校扬了扬手里那块暗银色的金属碎片。

"炽天铁骑Ⅳ型胸甲残片。"他说，"蒸汽管道还在，核心没有完全报废。"

"能改造成什么？"

"小型蒸汽炮。"上校说，"给我四十分钟。"

"你有三十分钟。"庞加莱说。

上校没有回答，他已经把那块残片放在地上，从靴筒里抽出一把多功能工具刀开始拆解。

——

地面上，混乱还在持续。

那架暗金色的东西仍然站在操场中央，一动不动，像一座等待了太久终于等到的纪念碑。

它不攻击任何人。但它散发出的那种气息让方圆两百米内所有活着的东西都无法思考——不是恐惧，是一种更深层的、来自生物本能底部的敬畏，仿佛站在它面前的不是一个人形机械，而是一个从古老壁画中走下来的神。

教堂地下室里，上校的手飞速地工作着。

他用工具刀把那块炽天铁骑Ⅳ型胸甲残片拆成了三块：蒸汽管道、阀门和一小段残存的红水银导管。然后他把蒸汽管道和阀门用铁丝绑在一起，做成了一个简易的蒸汽发射管。没有炮架，他把发射管绑在一根从铁架上拆下来的铁管上，铁管另一头抵在墙壁的砖缝里。

"只能开一炮。"上校说，"蒸汽管道的老化程度比我想的还严重。"

"一炮够了。"庞加莱说。

"瞄准哪？"

"胸口。"

上校的手停了一秒。

"红水银核心。"他低声说，"你疯了吗？那东西的核心暴露在外就是诱饵。"

"我宁愿轰掉一座山，也不愿看它站在操场上当雕像。"庞加莱说。

上校看了他一眼。

然后他把发射管的角度调整了五度。

"我出去。"他说，"你们从侧门走。"

"不行。"米内说，"太危险。"

"我在地下斗兽场开了十年场子。"上校用独臂把发射管扛上肩，那管子比他的胳膊还粗，重量压得他身体微微一沉，"我赌过比这更大的注。"

"这次不是赌。"拜伦说。

"所有的事都是赌。"上校说。

他拉开了地下室通往地面的石板门。

暮色和那股令人窒息的暗金色气息同时涌进来。

——

上校从教堂侧门绕到操场边缘。

那架东西就站在那里，比他记忆中任何一台炽天铁骑都要高大，暗金色装甲板在最后一缕夕阳中反射出冷硬的光。它的面甲上那道竖缝仍然紧闭着，像一只闭着眼睛的神。

他趴在一堵断墙后面，把发射管架在墙头，瞄准了那颗跳动的暗红色核心。

风停了。

操场上一片死寂，连那些尖叫和奔跑的声音都消失了，仿佛所有人都已经逃进了建筑里，或者已经死了。

上校屏住半口气。

扣下了扳机。

蒸汽管道发出一声刺耳的尖啸，压缩蒸汽推动着一枚用断剑剑尖临时改制的破甲弹头射出。弹头在空气中划出一道白线，直奔那架东西的胸口核心而去。

击中。

弹头撞上暗金色装甲板的瞬间，溅出一串火花，然后弹头被弹开了——不是被装甲弹开，是被弹开后又被吸了回去。

弹头嵌进了胸口装甲的凹痕里。

三秒钟后，凹痕消失了。

弹头被那颗红水银核心吞噬了，连渣都没有剩下。

那架东西的竖缝裂开了一条极细的缝。

暗金色的光从缝隙里透出来，像一只正在醒来的眼睛。

上校扔掉发射管，转身就跑。

他跑过断墙，跑过教堂侧门，跑过倒塌的彩灯架，跑进教堂正门的时候，他听到身后传来一种声音——

不是脚步声。

是莲花花瓣落地的声音。

无声的，整齐的，越来越近的。

——

"走！"上校冲进地下室的时候，声音已经变了调，"往下面走！"

"什么下面？"拜伦一把扶住他。

"地下斗兽场。"上校喘着粗气，"从教堂后殿的暗门下去，穿过旧矿道，能通到城北。"

"你早说！"米内已经一把掀开了储藏室角落里那块看上去和其他石砖一模一样的石板。石板下面是黑洞洞的台阶，一股潮湿的、发霉的风从下面涌上来。

四个人鱼贯钻进了地道。

庞加莱最后一个下去，他在入口处犹豫了一秒，回头看了一眼储藏室。铁架上的圣徒木雕们仍然在烛光中安静地站立着，玻璃珠眼珠在忽明忽暗。

他没有点蜡烛。

地道很窄，两侧是粗糙的岩壁，渗着水。台阶向下延伸了大约二十米，然后变成了一条平直的矿道。矿道的高度不到三米，上校不得不弯着腰走。

"这些矿道是什么时候挖的？"米内问。

"一百多年前。"上校说，"挖地下斗兽场的时候顺便挖的。学院建校之前，这里是采石场。"

他顿了一下。

"但这条矿道不是我们自己挖的。"

"什么意思？"

上校停下脚步，从怀里摸出火折子，点燃了。

火光在矿道里跳动着，照亮了两侧岩壁。

岩壁上刻着东西。

不是普通的凿痕，是精心雕刻的徽记。左边的岩壁上是一只六翼猫头鹰，翅膀上布满细密的齿轮纹路，铜绿斑驳，但线条仍然清晰可辨。右边的岩壁上是一枚更古老的徽记——齿轮中心嵌着一颗五芒星，五芒星的五个角末端各连接一圈更小的齿轮。

米内的手电筒光束扫过那些徽记，照亮了猫头鹰的眼睛。

"这是……"米内的声音发紧。

"密涅瓦机关。"上校说。

"还有这个。"庞加莱指向右边，"机械神教的徽记。达·芬奇·博尔吉亚的版本。"

"达·芬奇·博尔吉亚？"拜伦皱眉。

"密涅瓦机关的初代总工程师。"庞加莱说，"传说中设计了维苏威火山整个地下结构的人。"

"传说他三百年前就死了。"

"传说。"庞加莱重复了这个词。

他们继续往前走。矿道越来越宽，层高也在增加。空气中的金属腥味越来越浓，仿佛这条矿道通往某个巨大的金属矿脉。

大约走了十分钟后，矿道尽头出现了一扇铁门。

门上贴着一张泛黄的纸条，纸条上是潦草的机械神教祷文，墨迹已经褪得几乎看不清。

上校用工具刀撬开了门锁。

门后面是一个更大的空间。

这里显然是旧矿道的交汇点，天花板高得看不到顶，岩壁上的六翼猫头鹰和齿轮徽记反复出现，像某种古老的路标。地面上散落着采矿用的旧工具、生锈的铁轨和被遗弃的矿车。角落里有一台报废的蒸汽抽水机，铜管已经氧化成青绿色。

四个人钻进了这个空间。

上校刚把铁门关上，就听到了一个声音。

滴答。滴答。滴答。

那不是钟表的声音。

那是一种更清脆的、带着金属回音的节拍，像什么东西在敲击金属表面。

米内最先注意到声音的来源。

矿道深处，黑暗的最远端，有什么东西在发光。

"那是什么？"拜伦压低声音。

"别动。"庞加莱说。

光点越来越近。

那是一只机械蜘蛛。

拇指盖大小，通体青铜结构，八只腿在矿道地面上发出细碎的叩击声。它的头部有两个凹槽，凹槽里发出两点绿色的微光，像两盏小小的灯笼。

它径直朝他们爬过来。

滴答。滴答。滴答。

像叩门声。

上校的喉结动了一下。

"都别动。"他的声音压到了极低，"那东西能标记人。被它咬一口，你的信号就暴露了。"

米内的手按在了猎刀上。

"那怎么办？"

"等它过去。"上校说，"它只是在找信号最强的那个。"

机械蜘蛛在距离他们三米远的地方停了一下。

它抬起了头，绿色的两点光芒在黑暗中转动，像在扫描。

然后它继续向前爬去。

爬进了矿道更深处的黑暗中。

滴答声渐渐远去，最终消失在无尽的黑暗里。

四个人又等了整整三十秒。

庞加莱才从怀里摸出一样东西。

那是一个摩斯密码箱。巴掌大小，黄铜外壳，边角磨得发亮。这是马斯顿王立机械学院每间教室里都有的标配设备，用于接收校长室的紧急通知。

密码箱的屏幕正在闪烁。

一串绿色的字在屏幕上跳动。

"西泽尔·博尔吉亚正在前往王屋山，准备摧毁欧米茄原型体群。"

字跳动了两遍，然后消失了。

屏幕恢复成一片漆黑。

地下室里死一般寂静。

"西泽尔·博尔吉亚。"拜伦念出了这个名字，嗓音发紧，"那个……马斯顿出去的？"

"他两年前从马斯顿离开的。"庞加莱说，"他走的时候，我送他到校门口。"

"他要去摧毁那个东西？"米内指了指头顶的方向。

庞加莱没有回答。

他看着密码箱的黑色屏幕，看着自己映在屏幕上的模糊倒影。

倒影里有一张苍老的、布满皱纹的脸。

"我们该做什么？"拜伦问。

庞加莱把密码箱收进风衣内袋。

"我们该活下去。"他说。

矿道深处，黑暗中传来了一声极轻的铜铃响。

叮——

极清脆。极遥远。

像某种古老的召唤。

四个人同时转头看向声音的来源。

黑暗中什么都没有。

但所有人都知道，有什么东西正在朝他们走来。

【English】
Chapter 237 — The Return of Maseton

Dusk fell on the domes of the Maseton Royal College of Mechanical Arts like ice water poured from a great height.

The bell tower of the Church of the Holy Infant of Light struck eight. The last bronze note had not finished ringing when, on the northern horizon, a knot of dark gold light unfurled. It was neither moon nor star — the moon stood over the eastern quarter, and the stars, for all their varieties, had never learned to burn clean through cloud.

The light fell.

It came down at a speed that answered to no physics Poincaré had ever trusted. Across the quad, students still walked in the long cool of the evening. The Midsummer lanterns had not yet been taken down; coloured glass swung in the slow wind, and a few couples drifted past the fountain, their black uniforms doubled in the still water, the gold of their cuff-links catching the last light.

The dark gold light struck the centre of the quad.

There was no sound. Or rather, the sound arrived too late for any ear to do anything with it. A shockwave of dark gold spread from the impact in every direction at once. The lawn lifted as though an enormous hand had been thrust up beneath it, roots and all, and rolled outward in a single slow sheet. The fountain vanished into a white column of vapour three metres high. Every coloured lantern in range detonated, and the glass drifted down in confetti.

Then came the sound.

A low, near-subsonic detonation rolled up through the ground. The chapel's stained glass ticked and cracked along its leading. The cast-iron Christ Child at the top of the bell tower tipped his head, as though listening.

When the dark gold dust thinned, what stood at the centre of the quad was enough to stop the mind of every living soul that could still see.

It was more than five metres tall.

Dark gold armour plating, hard-edged and immaculate, caught the last of the sunset and gave it back as something colder. Every plate had been engraved — gear and lotus, and a script of dense curling characters no one in the quad could read. Set into the centre of its chest, a thing pulsed. The size of a fist. Dark red. A heart that knew it was being watched.

The red mercury core.

Where the joints met the plating, the script was different again — thinner, sharper — and as the construct settled, those characters began, one by one, to light up with a thread of gold, as though someone had been igniting veins.

The head bore no face. There was only a smooth oval visor, and down the centre of the visor, a single vertical seam. Behind the seam, dark gold, and nothing more.

At the edge of the quad, beside the broken lip of the fountain, a first-year stopped walking.

He was curious.

He took off his cap. He tilted his head back. He looked straight into the visor.

The dark gold behind the seam lit up.

It was not reflected light. The seam itself went incandescent — a long, slow blink — and a column of dark gold light passed out of it, struck the student's face, and held.

The student made no sound.

He stood very still. A thin white thread of smoke began to rise from the crown of his cap.

Then his eyes took fire.

Two small gold flames climbed out of his eye-sockets, licked across his brow, charred his hair to a black powder. His body stayed upright. His mouth was open as wide as a mouth could go, the shape of a scream that had not yet been paid out, and the fire moved faster than the scream, took the tongue, the teeth, the plates of the skull.

Three seconds, and he was a burning post.

The quad remembered what it was for. Sound rushed in from every side. People were down. People were running. One man tripped over another and was then stepped on by a third. The quad became a single slow whirlpool of panic.

The construct did not chase anyone.

It stood. It did not move. It had the look of a monument that had been waiting a long time for the right holiday to come back around.

---

In the cellar beneath the chapel, Poincaré was using the flat of his hand to seal a vent.

His movements were calm. His palm was shaking.

The cellar had been a vestry once, a place to store the things a chapel used and forgot. Decades of dust. Spiders had built a ceiling of their own, and the air tasted of tallow and old damp. Iron racks held chalices and candlesticks gone grey, and a row of saint statues the height of a man stood in the corner, their paint flaking, their eyes of cheap glass catching the candlelight and giving it back as a slow untrustworthy wink.

Four people crouched behind the racks.

Minet was at the back, folded in on himself, his arms around his knees. He was no longer the bright young nobleman of anyone's memory. The lower city had carved lines into his face well before their time. But the eyes were the same — the kind that only come from having watched too many people die.

Byron was on one knee beside a saint, his hand on the hilt of the family sword. The scabbard was deep blue, inlaid with silver gryphons — the regulation pattern of a New Roman military house. The knuckles of his hand were the colour of old candle wax. He did not draw. He knew there was no point. Sword work against armoured plate was one thing. Sword work against that, on the grass above his head, was something else.

The Colonel sat with his back against the wall, his single elbow wedged into the brick, the other hand holding a sliver of dark silver metal — a piece of Seraphim Type IV chest plate, picked out of a scrap heap under the old arena, kept ever since as a paperweight.

It was no longer a paperweight.

"You saw it," Poincaré said. His voice was very low. Each word was a tack being driven into the room.

"We saw it," the Colonel said.

"Do you know what it is?"

"No." The Colonel considered the sliver in his hand. "I know it can kill a hundred people a second."

"Not a hundred." Poincaré's palm was still on the vent. "Whoever looks into the visor dies. Annie died like that."

A silence opened in the cellar.

Minet swallowed.

"I knew Annie," he said, after a while. "She used to help me with my essays."

"I know," Poincaré said. "Which is why I will not let her be the end of it."

He reached into the inside pocket of his coat.

What he took out was an envelope.

Black. The corners were foxed, but the seal was intact. The seal bore a black angel, wings outspread, struck in wax — the device of the Office of Heretical Judgment.

Minet recognised it. He went the colour of the dust on the chalices.

"This —" Byron's voice fell.

"It came to me twelve years ago," Poincaré said, "the year I took the post. I thought some madman had taken a fancy to me."

He set his thumb against the seal.

The envelope opened itself.

The wax cracked neatly down the middle, like an eye deciding to blink, and a sheet of paper slid out of the crack, folded and refolded to a small neat square. The paper was strange under the fingers — light as a cicada's wing, faintly medicinal, the smell of an old preservative.

Poincaré unfolded it.

One line of print.

"Maseton Royal College of Mechanical Arts is the starting point of the Holy War, and one of the nodes of the bough of the World Tree."

The type was the House Roman of the papal chancery. Every letter of every word had been set square and true.

"The bough of the World Tree," the Colonel said, the way a man might say the name of a disease. "What is that?"

"I don't know." Poincaré folded the paper. He put it back. He put the envelope back inside his coat. "What I do know is that the Office of Heretical Judgment has never, in living memory, used a black-angel courier for a joke."

"We need a plan," he said.

"What plan?" Byron asked. "Sword against that thing?"

"We need a weapon." Poincaré turned to him. "You have the sword."

Byron hesitated. Then he drew.

The sword came out of the scabbard with a single clear note of metal, and lay across his palm — narrow, cold, the gryphon on the guard lifting its wings. The edge still held the oil of the New Roman armoury, the way a thing holds the look of the day it was made. He had never killed a man with it.

"Minet," Poincaré said.

Minet did not answer.

He dragged a canvas bag out from behind the rack. The bag was old. The corners had gone to hair, and the cloth was stained with rust and grease. He untied the thong and folded the flap back. Inside, folded flat, was a soft armour — a soft armour of woven steel. Each link had been filed as thin as silk, and the links were laid in fish-scale, three deep, over a black leather lining. This was not the cheap protection sold to students. This was old. Poincaré had found it once under the altar stone of the chapel, during a refit of the foundations, and had chosen, for reasons he had never quite put into words, not to know it was there.

Under the armour, Minet took out a hunting knife. The handle was antler. The blade was seven inches long, and had been recently ground to a fine bright edge.

"I thought you had gone soft in the lower city," the Colonel said, looking at the knife. There was something complicated in his voice.

"The lower city taught me how to stay alive," Minet said.

"Colonel," Poincaré said.

The Colonel held up the sliver of dark silver.

"Seraphim Type IV," he said. "Steam channel still in it. The core didn't die all the way down."

"What can you make of it?"

"A small steam gun." The Colonel considered. "Give me forty minutes."

"You have thirty."

The Colonel did not answer. He set the sliver on the floor, drew a multi-tool out of his boot, and began to take the world apart.

---

Up on the grass, the panic had not stopped, but it had thinned.

The construct stood where it had stood, in the dead centre of the quad, a column of dark gold. It did not move. It did not need to. Within two hundred metres, nothing with a pulse could manage thought. The pressure was not fear. It was something older, something that lived underneath fear, in the cellar of the blood — the recognition, before the brain has time to dress it in language, that what is standing over there is not a machine.

In the cellar, the Colonel's single hand worked like a watchmaker who had been told he had less time than the watch would take.

He split the sliver of chest plate into three pieces with the multi-tool: the steam channel, the valve, and a short surviving length of red mercury conduit. He wired the channel to the valve with iron wire, and bound the assembly to a length of pipe torn from one of the racks. The far end of the pipe he wedged into a gap in the brickwork.

"It will fire once," he said, without looking up. "The channel is older than I thought."

"Once is enough," Poincaré said.

"Aim where?"

"The chest."

The Colonel's hand stopped, for a single beat, on the wire.

"The red mercury core," he said softly. "You are out of your mind. They leave the core open as bait."

"I would rather blow a mountain down than have that thing stand on the grass a moment longer."

The Colonel looked at him.

Then he tilted the pipe up by five degrees.

"I'll go out," he said. "The rest of you take the side door."

"No," Minet said. "It's too dangerous."

"I have run fights in the old arena for ten years." The Colonel lifted the pipe to his shoulder with his one good arm. The barrel was thicker than his arm. It dipped him a finger's width. "I have bet on worse."

"This isn't a bet," Byron said.

"Everything is a bet," the Colonel said.

He lifted the flagstone over the passage to the chapel above.

Dusk and the dark gold pressure of the construct came in together.

---

The Colonel took the long way around, through the chapel side door, and crouched behind a low wall at the edge of the quad.

It was there.

The thing.

Taller than any Seraphim he had ever seen in the arena. The dark gold plating took the last of the sunset and gave it back in a way that made the eye water. The seam of the visor was still closed. The whole head had the look of a god that had, for reasons of its own, decided to sleep standing up.

He laid the pipe along the wall. He sighted along it and found the dark red fist in the centre of the chest, pulsing against its housing as though it knew he was there.

The wind dropped.

The quad went quiet. Even the screams and the running seemed to have been told to stop, and had listened. He had the feeling, which he could not put down, that everyone above ground had either already run inside or had stopped being people.

He took half a breath.

He pulled the release.

The steam channel screamed. A single improvised shot — a sword tip turned into a penetrator, lashed to the rod — punched along the barrel, drew a white line in the air, and struck the construct square in the chest.

Sparks. A spatter of bright shards.

The shot bounced — and then, before it could finish bouncing, it was pulled back in.

The penetrator bit into a shallow crater in the plate and stayed there. Three seconds later the crater was no longer a crater. The dark red core had closed over the shot the way a mouth closes, and there was nothing left of the steel that had been a sword an hour ago.

The seam in the visor cracked open. A single thin line of dark gold.

The Colonel threw the pipe away and ran.

He went over the wall, through the chapel side door, through a stand of broken lantern poles, and into the main door of the church. As he crossed the threshold he heard, behind him, a sound he could not for a moment place.

It was not the sound of footsteps.

It was the sound of lotus petals falling on stone. One. Then another. Then more, in a slow, even, deliberate rhythm, drawing closer.

---

"Go!" The Colonel's voice, as he came down into the cellar, had lost its arrangement. "Below. Below us."

"Below what?" Byron had him by the arm.

"The old arena. Through the back of the chapel, into the old mine, and out under the north wall of the city."

"You should have said so earlier." Minet was already on his knees at the back of the room, prying at a flagstone that looked — to any reasonable eye — exactly like every other flagstone in the cellar. It came up. A square of black opened under it, and a breath of damp, ancient, faintly rotten air rose out of the dark.

They went down in single file, Poincaré last. He paused a single second at the lip of the hole and looked back at the vestry. The saint statues in their corner stood as they had stood for a hundred years, glass eyes giving back the last of the candlelight in their slow, unreliable way.

He did not light a candle for them.

The passage was narrow, the walls of rough-cut stone weeping a thin clear water. The steps went down for what felt like twenty metres, and then levelled out into a mine tunnel. The ceiling was lower than a man could stand under; the Colonel walked with his back bent.

"When were these cut?" Minet asked, the question half-eaten by the dark.

"More than a hundred years ago," the Colonel said. "When they built the arena. The college was a quarry before the college."

He stopped.

"But this stretch of tunnel is not ours."

"What do you mean?"

The Colonel felt into his coat and brought out a tinder strip. He struck it. The little flame jumped and steadied, and the two walls of the tunnel came into view.

The walls were carved.

Not the rough pick-marks of a working mine. The marks were deliberate, careful, and old. On the left wall, a six-winged owl, every feather a fine mesh of gear-teeth, the whole thing gone over with a green verdigris, but the lines still readable. On the right wall, an older device — a wheel of gears with a five-pointed star in the centre, and the points of the star each joined to a smaller ring of gears.

Minet's light — he had fished a small hand-lamp out of his coat — moved across the carvings and lit the owl's eyes.

"This —" Minet said, the word not quite making it to the end.

"The Minerva Mechanism," the Colonel said.

"And this," Poincaré said, on the right wall. "The arms of the Mechanical Theocracy. The Leonardo Borgia version."

"Leonardo Borgia?" Byron's mouth pulled.

"The first chief engineer of the Minerva Mechanism," Poincaré said. "The man who, by all the surviving legend, drew up the entire subterranean plan of Vesuvius."

"By all the surviving legend he died three hundred years ago."

"By all the surviving legend," Poincaré said.

They moved on. The tunnel widened. The ceiling rose. The smell of metal thickened, the way air thickens in the mouth of a forge — as though the rock had, somewhere ahead, opened onto a vein of something that should not be in the earth.

Ten minutes more, and there was a door at the end of the passage.

An iron door, with a yellowed slip of paper pasted to it. The paper was covered in a slanted cursive — a Mechanical Theocracy prayer, in a hand so faded it was almost a memory.

The Colonel worked the lock open with the multi-tool.

The room on the other side was larger than the door had suggested. It was a junction of the old workings, the ceiling lost somewhere in the dark, the walls going on with their slow repetition of the six-winged owl and the star-and-gear. The floor was a graveyard of the working mine — picks, rusted rails, an ore-cart left with its back broken. In a corner, a steam pump had been abandoned to the damp, its copper pipework eaten down to a handsome verdigris.

The four of them filed in. The Colonel swung the door shut behind them.

That was when he heard it.

Tick. Tick. Tick.

Not the tick of a clock. A cleaner tick, with a metal ring at the back of it, the way a thing sounds when it strikes metal.

Minet was the first to find the source.

Far down the passage they had not taken, something was moving, and the thing that was moving was giving off light.

"What is that?" Byron, very low.

"Don't move," Poincaré said.

The light came closer.

It was a mechanical spider.

A thing the size of a thumb, all bronze, its eight feet tapping out a polite little rhythm on the stone floor. On its head, two hollows gave out two points of green light, the colour of two very small lamps held up to see by.

It came straight at them.

Tick. Tick. Tick.

As though it were knocking.

The Colonel's throat worked.

"None of you move," he said, under his breath. "It can mark. One bite and your signal is in the open."

Minet's hand closed on the antler handle of the knife.

"What do we do?"

"Wait for it to pass." The Colonel's eyes had not left the green lamps. "It is just looking for the strongest signal in the room."

The spider stopped.

It was three metres away. It lifted its head, and the two green lights rotated in their hollows, the way a head rotates when it is looking carefully at something it is not sure of.

Then it went on.

It crossed the floor in front of them, paying them no more attention than a beetle pays a stone, and went on down the dark of the other passage, tick tick ticking, until the ticking had gone, and then a long time after the ticking had gone.

They gave it thirty seconds more.

Then Poincaré reached into the inner pocket of his coat and brought out the thing he had carried down.

A Morse box.

The size of a palm, brass-cased, the corners worn to a bright shine. Every classroom at the Maseton Royal College carried one — the standard rig for taking the headmaster's emergency traffic.

The screen was blinking.

A string of green letters was making its way, one at a time, across the glass.

CESARE BORGIA EN ROUTE TO MOUNT WANGWU. INTENDS DESTRUCTION OF THE OMEGA PROTOTYPE GROUP.

The letters ran the line twice, and then the screen went black.

In the cellar that was no longer a cellar, the silence had a temperature.

"Cesare Borgia," Byron said. The name did not sit well in his mouth. "The one who —"

"Who was at Maseton," Poincaré said. "Who left two years ago. I walked him to the gate when he went."

"He is going to destroy that thing?" Minet pointed up, with the flat of the knife, at the rock above their heads, where the dark gold was standing.

Poincaré did not answer.

He was looking at the black glass of the screen, and at the shape that looked back out of it — the shape of an old man, lined, tired, very far from home.

"What do we do?" Byron asked.

Poincaré put the box back into his coat.

"We live," he said.

Somewhere far down the dark of the other passage, a small copper bell rang.

Ding.

A single clear note. Distant. Long.

The way an old summons sounds, when the thing it summons is not in a hurry, because it knows you are not going to be.

All four of them turned, very slowly, toward the sound.

There was nothing to see.

But the four of them, in four different ways, knew that there was something coming.

第238章 王屋山的召唤
==================================================

【中文】
第238章 王屋山的召唤

雨停了。

洛阳城外的秋夜，帐外还挂着湿润的桂花香。帆布上的水珠偶尔被风吹落，砸在泥地上发出细碎的响。马厩里夔龙马在打低沉的响鼻，偶有马蹄铁碰在青石上，溅出一星碎火星。

营帐角落，一张折叠凳。

西泽尔坐在那里，左手搁在膝盖上，右手握着一枚巴掌大的黄铜徽章。徽章是六翼猫头鹰，翅膀上布满细密的齿轮纹路，边缘磨得发亮。

密涅瓦机关总长的信物。

三天前，这枚徽章和远程通信器一起由薇若兰从翡冷翠寄出，辗转三千多里，此刻终于到了他手边。

怀中的通信器忽然震动了三下。

短促，沉重，像心脏被人隔着胸腔捏了一下。

这是密涅瓦机关最高级别的通讯加密信号。知道这个频率的人不超过三个。佛朗哥知道。薇若兰知道。现在第三个在他手里。

西泽尔按下接收键。

杂音里挤出来一个女声。嗓音沙哑，背景里有金属咬合的嗡鸣，她应该是在移动中。

"西泽尔。"

薇若兰。

"佛朗哥教授……走了。"

西泽尔的手指在徽章上收紧。齿轮纹路硌进掌心，印出深红的痕。

"什么时候？"

"四个小时前。"薇若兰说，"他撑到了最后。所有该交代的事都交代完了。"

她停了一下。

"他给你留了一段全息留言，我现在转给你。"

西泽尔从腰间取出一枚圆盘形的小型投影仪，搁在面前的弹药箱上。

空气里浮现出一个苍老的身影。

佛朗哥坐在一张堆满图纸的工作台后面，穿着洗得发白的旧毛衣，肩膀瘦削得像一张纸。眼窝深陷，但那双眼睛依然锐利如刀——刀子用了太久，最后总是磨成这个形状，又薄又亮。

"西泽尔。"

投影里的老人开口。声音沙哑，但平稳。

"如果你收到这段话，说明我大概已经不在了。"

营帐里安静得只剩投影仪运转的轻微嗡鸣。

"密涅瓦机关的控制权，我已经交给薇若兰了。她会告诉你接下来该怎么做。"

佛朗哥抬起手，骨节突出的手指指着镜头。

"梵天陨落的设计图，在薇若兰手里。她会在合适的时机转交给你。"

他停顿了一下。

"原罪机关背后的人……不是米迦勒。"

他的声音压低了。

"米迦勒只是一个面具。一个用了三百年的面具。真正的幕后之人，是一个活了三百多年的存在，体内流着和达·芬奇·博尔吉亚一样的血。他要用世界树残枝，重启机械神国。"

"密涅瓦存在的意义，就是阻止这一切。三百年前，达·芬奇建立密涅瓦机关，不是为了制造武器……而是为了封印。"

他看着镜头。

"现在，这个使命落在你身上了，西泽尔。"

投影里的佛朗哥忽然沉默了。

他抬起手，按了按眉心。

"我本来想说很多话。"他说，"但时间不多了。"

他看着镜头，眼神忽然柔和了下来。那种柔和是不属于他的——佛朗哥永远是锋利的、尖锐的、像一把被磨了无数遍的刻刀。

"你是个很好的孩子。"

他顿了顿。

"……照顾好自己。"

投影熄灭。

营帐里重新陷入黑暗。

西泽尔坐在原地，没有动。

很静。

静得能听见自己的心跳。

帐帘被掀开，楚舜华走了进来。

他看了一眼西泽尔，刚要开口，动作停住了。

月光透过帐篷的缝隙照在西泽尔的侧脸上。在颧骨的位置，有一道极细的、反射着微光的水痕。

不是汗。

楚舜华没有说话。他转过身，背对着西泽尔，假装在检查挂在帐柱上的夔龙角剑。

"慢慢来。"楚舜华说。

西泽尔没有回答。

他用左手手背极快极轻地擦了一下脸，然后重新握紧了那枚徽章。

怀中的通信器再次震动。

"西泽尔。"薇若兰的声音再次传来，"我补充一件事。"

"密涅瓦机关核心团队已经整编完毕。三支甲胄小队，十二名工程师，我和阿方索的几个助手都在名单里。我们明天凌晨从翡冷翠乘坐专列出发，预计三天后到达王屋山。"

她停了一下。

"梵天陨落的核心零件已经全部备齐。一号原型体核心、欧米茄自愈神经纤维的绝缘层、还有黄铜引爆器。一旦到达，我们可以立刻开始组装。"

"你在王屋山等我。"

西泽尔沉默了一秒。

"我会到。"

……

第二天清晨，天还没亮透，雾气从东方的山脉里漫过来。

楚舜华骑在最前面，胯下是那匹通体红如朱砂的夔龙马。朱砂额前有一个弹洞，是当年战场上留下来的，丝毫不影响它的凶猛和耐力。马蹄踏在青石板上，嵌在心脏位置的暗金色微型引擎发出低沉的嗡鸣，像一台永远不知疲倦的蒸汽机。

西泽尔骑着一匹稍矮的夔龙马紧随其后。瓦莲京娜在他左侧，金色长发用粉色发带扎成马尾，在晨风里飘来飘去。阿方索、唐璜、昆提良在后面压阵。

王屋山还有半日的路。

"看天上。"

瓦莲京娜忽然说。

她抬起下巴，指向东方刚刚泛白的天际线。

西泽尔抬起头。

天际线上，一排黑点正在快速移动。

不是鸟。不是云。

是欧米茄原型体。

一架，两架，五架，十架——密密麻麻，从东方的地平线涌出，像一股暗金色的洪流，飞向西方的天际。高度在云层之上，在晨光中闪着冷硬的金属光泽。每一架都有五米多高，胸腔里的红水银核心在远处看像一颗颗暗红色的星。

"这么多……"昆提良低声说，嗓音发紧。

楚提华抬手示意队伍停下。

所有人勒马站在山脊上，看着那股暗金色的洪流从头顶掠过。

数不清有多少架。三十架，五十架，也许更多。它们飞得高，速度快，方向一致——全部朝着西方，朝着翡冷翠的方向。

"它们在分散。"楚舜华的声音冷了下去。

西泽尔盯着那些暗金色的身影，手无意识地按在了腰间那把残缺的断剑上——龙牙剑和圣剑碎片拼接成的Excalibur残刃。

"一旦全部散开，就再也追不回来了。"楚舜华说。

"我不去追。"西泽尔说。

楚舜华看向他。

"它们的母体在王屋山。"西泽尔说，"我去那里等它们。"

楚舜华沉默了一秒。

"走。"

队伍转向东方，沿着山脊向下，进入王屋山的范围。

王屋山的雾和别处不同。不是水汽凝结成的白雾，而是一种带着淡淡金色的薄纱，像是什么东西在雾的深处缓慢地燃烧。

山路越来越窄，两侧的树木越来越古老。

松树。都是松树。树皮银白，树干扭曲如虬龙，枝桠上挂满了青苔。树龄至少几百年，有些要两人合抱才能围住。

雾越来越浓，能见度降到不足十米。

然后西泽尔看到了别的东西。

路边。

第一块石碑。

灰白色，高约三尺，上面没有文字，只刻着一个倒置的五芒星，五芒星的五个角末端各嵌着一枚小齿轮。

第二块。第三块。第四块。

越往深处走，石碑越密。它们安静地立在雾里，有些倾斜，有些已经被青苔吞没大半。每一块上都是同样的倒置五芒星，同样的齿轮。

墓碑。

"这些是……"阿方索推了推眼镜，声音压得很低。

"东方星见。"楚舜华说，"三百年来，守护世界树东支的星见都葬在这里。"

他顿了顿。

"我母亲是最后一个。她葬在山顶。"

队伍沉默地穿过这片墓地。夔龙马的蹄子踏在青石上，声音被雾吞掉大半，像是隔了一层棉。

唐璜忽然勒住了马。

他的脸色变了。

他的手按在腰间的剑柄上，眼睛死死盯着前方十步开外。

"别动。"

他的声音压到了极低，像是从牙缝里挤出来的。

"前面有东西。"

所有人停下。

雾在前方凝成了一团。比周围的雾更浓，更黑，像是一团没有重量的浓墨悬浮在山路中央。

那团黑雾在缓缓移动。

不是风吹的。是自行的。

楚舜华没有拔剑。他只是把手按在了夔龙角剑的剑格上。

"谁？"他问。

黑雾渐渐散开。

一个人形的身影站在山路中央。

那是一个没有重量感的身影，轮廓像是在雾中凝结而成的虚影。五官模糊，但身形高大，穿着一套巨大的、由无数齿轮和金属片拼合而成的甲胄。甲胄的胸腔里嵌着一颗暗金色的核心，跳动的频率极慢，像是一颗行将熄灭的心脏。

西泽尔认出了那个轮廓。

屠龙者圣乔治。

那个在密涅瓦机关的旧照片里出现过三次、在达·芬奇日记的角落里被反复提及、据说是初代总长留在熔岩之心最深处的百年前顶级炽天使原型甲胄的轮廓。

那个身影看着他们。

然后它开口。

声音像是从极深的地方传来，带着齿轮咬合的金属质感——嗒，嗒，嗒，每个音节之间都有一个微小的间隙，像是发声的结构是机械的。

"英雄会拯救世界。"

它说。

"但也会牺牲自己。"

它的目光——如果那模糊的面甲后面能算作"目光"的话——锁定了西泽尔。

"你准备好了吗？"

西泽尔策马向前走了两步。

他没有回答那个问题。

他只是开口：

"我是西泽尔·博尔吉亚。"

他的声音平静，没有颤抖。

"锡兰末代星见的直系血裔。"

他抬起手，慢慢拉开了衣领。

后颈的黄金套管在晨光中发出微弱的嗡鸣。

然后他的瞳孔开始变化——

从边缘开始，紫色亮了起来，虹膜像是被点燃了，透出灼热的光。然后金色纹路从瞳孔的边缘浮现，像是龙鳞一样一片一片地展开，沿着虹膜的边缘缓慢旋转。紫瞳金纹。

后颈的黄金套管同时发烫。

不是高温，是一种温热的、像血液流动的温热。

瓦莲京娜按住了剑柄。阿方索推了推眼镜。唐璜的嘴唇动了一下没出声。昆提良握紧了战斧的把手。

那个虚影看着西泽尔的眼睛，沉默了几秒。

"……果然。"它说，"你就是他说的那个人。"

它没有阻拦。

它让开了路。

但当队伍从它身边经过时，它又跟了上来，保持着十步左右的距离，不远不近。

山路尽头是一片空地。

空地中央立着一根方柱。

方柱通体白色大理石，没有任何装饰，高约两米，截面边长约半米。在晨雾中看起来像一根被遗忘的界碑。

但方柱的基座——周围一米范围内的地面——刻满了图案。

世界树。

树干从基座中心向上延伸，树枝末梢雕刻成齿轮状，树叶是一片片大小不一的齿轮。树根从基座向四面八方蔓延，根须末端刻着细如发丝的梵文，有几条根须甚至延伸到了墓地那边。

"这根……"楚舜华低声说。

他下马，走到方柱前。

"我父母合葬墓里的那根方柱……"西泽尔低声说。

"是分支。"楚舜华说，"这根是母体。"

他抬起手，掌心按在方柱的侧面。

咔嗒。

方柱的一侧无声地滑开了一道缝。

不是机械的声音。是石头和石头摩擦的声音。

缝隙里透出淡绿色的光。

"跟紧我。"楚舜华说。

他首先走下石阶。

石阶潮湿，两侧岩壁上有水珠。空气逐渐变暖，一股淡淡的花香从深处飘上来。

金色莲花。

和西泽尔在密涅瓦机关深处闻到的味道一模一样。

石阶尽头是一个圆形石室。

石室中央——

一团暗金色的根须，盘根错节，像一颗巨大的心脏，缓慢地、有节奏地跳动着。

每一次跳动，都有一圈淡绿色的光从根须的深处透出来，照亮整个石室。

世界树主根节点。

西泽尔站在石室入口，没有动。

那团暗金色的根须开始颤动。

淡绿色的光变亮了。从深处涌出的光芒越来越强，像是一颗沉睡了几百年的心脏突然苏醒。

嗡——

低沉的嗡鸣声在石室里回荡。

然后西泽尔听见了。

不是耳朵听见的。是通过后颈的套管，通过皮肤下的血管，通过紫瞳金纹的共鸣，听见的。

一个声音。

非常古老。非常遥远。像是从世界树的核心深处传出来的。

"……来……了……"

西泽尔向前走了一步。

他伸出手。

指尖触碰到了一根最粗的暗金色根须。

温热。

像触碰到活着的皮肤。

记忆碎片开始涌入他的脑海——三百年前锡兰圣女塔的黄昏，达·芬奇·博尔吉亚在齿轮隧道里测绘蓝图，一个白色长发的年轻人在王屋山下埋下种子，欧米茄原型体第一次启动时发出的低沉咆哮……

但他没有倒下。

他站在原地，手指按在根须上，紫瞳金纹的光在黑暗中跳动着。

那个屠龙者圣乔治轮廓的虚影，不知何时已经跟到了石室入口。

它看着西泽尔与世界树主根节点接触的样子，沉默了很久。

然后它说：

"三百年前，达·芬奇走到了同样的位置。"

它的声音还是那种齿轮咬合的金属质感。

"但他选择了另一条路。"

它看着西泽尔。

"你是第二个走到这里的人。"

"你会做出不同的选择。"

虚影开始消散。

不是慢慢消失，而是像烟一样，从边缘向中心散开。

在它消散的地方，地面上有什么东西反射着绿光。

西泽尔走过去，蹲下来。

一把剑。

剑身弯曲如蛇，窄而长，表面覆盖着一层淡绿色的铜锈。剑柄是青铜色，缠着已经褪色发白的绿绢。剑格处刻着两个细小的梵文。

"这不是普通的剑。"阿方索推了推眼镜，蹲下来端详。

他从腰间取出便携式神经电流读出器，扫描了一下剑身。读出器上的数值跳了一下。

"材质……和屠龙者圣乔治的武器库里那批武器是同源的。"

"它叫'青蛇'。"楚舜华说。

所有人都看向他。

"我母亲告诉过我。达·芬奇在初代原型机备件库里藏了七把剑。每一把都有名字。青蛇是其中之一。"

他看向西泽尔。

"这是达·芬奇留给继承者的礼物。"

西泽尔伸出手，握住了剑柄。

剑柄刚好合适。像是为他的手量身定做的一样。剑身在掌心里微微发热。

就在他握住剑的瞬间——

石室深处传来一声低沉的金属撞击声。

轰。

整个石室都震了一下。暗金色的根须剧烈地颤动，淡绿色的光芒闪烁不定。

像是有什么东西，正在从最深处醒来。

【English】
Chapter 238 — The Summons of Wangwu Mountain

The rain had stopped.

Outside the camp at Luoyang, an autumn night still smelt of wet osmanthus. Droplets clung to the canvas and fell, when the wind shook them, in small precise strikes on the trampled earth. In the line of stables a kui-long stamped and blew through its nose; a horseshoe rang against blue stone and a single spark jumped and died.

At the corner of a tent, a folding stool.

Cesare sat there, his left hand on his knee, his right closed around a brass badge the size of a palm. The badge was a six-winged owl, its pinions incised with a pattern of fine gears, the edges worn to brightness by years of handling.

The seal of the Chief of the Minerva Bureau.

Three days before, the badge and a long-range communicator had been despatched by Veronika out of Florence — three thousand li and more — and at last had come to hand.

The communicator at his hip pulsed. Three times. Short. Heavy. As if a fist had closed on his heart through the meat of his chest.

It was the Bureau's highest-grade encryption, a frequency known to no more than three living souls. Francesco had known. Veronika knew. And now the third, in his own pocket.

He thumbed the receiver.

Static. Then a woman's voice, hoarse, with the whine of meshing metal in the background — she was moving, in some engine-room or other.

"Cesare."

Veronika.

"Professor Francesco is gone."

His fingers tightened on the badge. The gear-ridges bit into his palm and left a red weal.

"When?"

"Four hours ago. He held on to the end. Everything that needed saying, he said."

A pause.

"He left you a holographic message. I'm relaying it now."

He took the small disc-shaped projector from his belt and set it on the ammunition crate before him.

An old man's shape took form in the air.

Francesco sat at a workbench buried in drawings, wearing a sweater washed to the colour of old bone, his shoulders thin as paper. The hollows of his eyes were deep, but the eyes themselves were still sharp as a blade — and a blade that has been sharpened too many times is always like that, in the end: thin, and bright, and almost transparent.

"Cesare."

The projection spoke. The voice was hoarse but level.

"If you are receiving this, I am most likely no longer present in the world."

The tent was silent except for the small working hum of the projector.

"Control of the Minerva Bureau I have transferred to Veronika. She will tell you what comes next."

Francesco lifted a hand, the knuckles sharp as knotted rope, and pointed at the lens.

"The blueprints for Brahma's Fall are in Veronika's keeping. She will pass them to you at the right hour."

A pause.

"The one behind the Original Sin Bureau is not Michael."

He lowered his voice.

"Michael is only a mask. A mask worn for three hundred years. The true hand is something that has lived for more than three centuries, and the blood in his veins is the same blood that runs in da Vinci Borgia. He means to use the remnant branch of the World Tree to reboot the Mechanical Kingdom of God."

"The reason the Minerva Bureau exists is to prevent exactly that. Three hundred years ago, when da Vinci founded the Bureau, it was not to make weapons. It was to set a seal."

He looked into the lens.

"Now that task falls to you, Cesare."

The projection fell silent.

The old man lifted a hand and pressed his brow.

"I had meant to say many things," he said. "But there is no more time."

He looked at the lens, and something in his gaze softened. That softening did not belong to him — Francesco had always been sharp, always keen, like a burin ground down to a sliver on a thousand attempts.

"You are a good child," he said.

He hesitated.

"…Look after yourself."

The projection went out.

The tent returned to darkness.

Cesare did not move.

It was very quiet.

Quiet enough to hear his own pulse.

The tent-flap stirred. Cassian came in.

He glanced at Cesare, opened his mouth to speak, and stopped.

Moonlight, through a seam in the canvas, fell on the side of Cesare's face. Across the cheekbone, a single line — very fine — caught a small cold glint.

It was not sweat.

Cassian said nothing. He turned his back, pretending to inspect the kui-long horn-sword buckled to the tent-pole.

"Take your time," he said.

Cesare did not answer.

He drew the back of his left hand, very quickly, very lightly, across his face, and closed his fist on the badge again.

The communicator at his hip pulsed.

"Cesare," Veronika's voice came again. "One more thing."

"The core team of the Minerva Bureau is already stood up. Three squads of armour, twelve engineers. I am on the list. So are several of Alfonso's assistants. We are leaving Florence on the special train before dawn. Three days to Wangwu Mountain."

A pause.

"The core components of Brahma's Fall are all ready. The Number One prototype's core, the insulating sheath for the Omega self-healing nerve-fibres, and the brass detonator. Once we arrive, we can begin assembly at once."

"Wait for me at Wangwu Mountain."

Cesare was silent a second.

"I'll be there."

…

Next morning, before the sky was fully lit, fog came boiling out of the eastern ranges.

Cassian rode at the head, mounted on a kui-long the colour of cinnabar. A bullet-hole marked the beast's forehead, souvenir of an old campaign, but it did nothing to dim its savagery or its stamina. Its hooves struck blue stone, and the little dark-gold engine set into its heart gave out its low working hum, like a steam-engine that never wearied.

Cesare rode a shorter kui-long at his shoulder. Valentina at his left, her golden hair tied off with a pale pink ribbon, the tail of it swinging in the morning wind. Alfonso, Don Juan, and Quintilian brought up the rear.

Wangwu Mountain was still half a day away.

"Look at the sky," Valentina said.

She tipped her chin up, toward the whitening line of the eastern horizon.

Cesare raised his head.

A row of black dots was moving fast along the ridgeline.

Not birds. Not clouds.

Omega prototypes.

One. Two. Five. Ten — they came pouring up out of the eastern horizon, a dark-gold flood pouring westward, riding above the cloud-line, each one catching the early light along the hard planes of its plating. They were each better than five metres tall, and the red mercury cores set in their chests showed, at that distance, like a sprinkle of dim red stars.

"So many…" Quintilian said. His voice had gone thin.

Cassian raised a hand. The column halted.

All of them reined in on the ridge and watched the dark-gold river pass overhead.

There was no counting them. Thirty. Fifty. Perhaps more. They flew high, fast, in one direction — all of them west, all of them toward Florence.

"They are scattering," Cassian said. His voice had gone cold.

Cesare watched the dark shapes. His hand, without his willing it, closed on the broken blade at his hip — the remnant Excalibur, spliced together from the Dragon Fang sword and a fragment of the Holy Blade.

"Once they have all dispersed, we will never catch them again," Cassian said.

"I'm not chasing them," Cesare said.

Cassian looked at him.

"Their mother-body is on Wangwu Mountain," Cesare said. "I'll wait for them there."

Cassian was silent a second.

"Ride."

The column swung east, descended the ridge, and entered the bounds of Wangwu Mountain.

The fog of Wangwu Mountain was not the same fog as elsewhere. It was not the white of condensed water-vapour, but a thin veil of pale gold, as though something inside the fog were burning, very slowly.

The road grew narrow. The trees on either side grew old.

Pines. All pines. Their bark silver-white, their trunks twisted like sleeping dragons, their branches bearded in moss. Some of them were centuries old; some of them a man could not put his arms around.

The fog thickened. Visibility dropped below ten metres.

Then Cesare saw other things.

At the roadside.

The first stele.

Grey-white, about three feet tall, with no inscription on it — only an inverted five-pointed star carved into the face, and at each of the five points a small gear let into the stone.

A second. A third. A fourth.

The deeper they went, the thicker the steles stood. They stood quietly in the fog, some of them leaning, some of them half-eaten by moss. Each one bore the same inverted star, the same gears.

Grave-stones.

"Those are — " Alfonso pushed his glasses up, lowering his voice.

"Eastern Star-Readers," Cassian said. "For three hundred years, those who guarded the eastern branch of the World Tree have been buried here."

A pause.

"My mother was the last of them. She is buried at the summit."

The column passed through the cemetery in silence. The hooves of the kui-long rang on the blue stone, but the fog ate most of the sound, as if it were passing through a thickness of cotton.

Don Juan suddenly reined in.

His face had changed colour.

His hand fell to the hilt at his hip, and his eyes fixed on something ten paces ahead.

"Don't move," he said.

His voice was barely louder than his breath, as if it had been squeezed out from between his teeth.

"There's something ahead."

All of them stopped.

The fog ahead of them had gathered into a single mass. Denser than the rest. Blacker. Like a ball of liquid ink with no weight to it, hanging in the middle of the road.

The black fog was moving of its own accord.

Not blown by the wind. Moving on its own.

Cassian did not draw his sword. He simply laid his hand on the cross-guard of the kui-long horn-blade.

"Who is there?" he asked.

The black mist thinned.

A figure stood in the middle of the road.

A figure that seemed to have no weight. Its outline looked as if it had congealed out of the fog — features blurred, but the form tall, and clad in a vast suit of armour pieced together out of countless gears and metal plates. A dim-gold core was set into the chest of the armour, beating at a very slow pulse, like a heart that was about to go out.

Cesare recognised the outline.

Saint George the Dragonslayer.

The outline that had appeared three times in the Bureau's old photographs, that had been mentioned again and again in the margins of da Vinci's diaries — the silhouette, supposedly, of the first-generation Chief's hundred-year-old top-of-the-line Seraphim prototype, left at the deepest level of the Molten Heart.

The figure looked at them.

Then it spoke.

The voice came from a great depth, and carried the metallic clink of meshing gears — click, click, click, a small interval between each syllable, as if the mechanism that produced the sound were mechanical.

"The hero saves the world," it said.

"But the hero also sacrifices himself."

Its gaze — if the blurred visor-face could be said to have a gaze — fixed on Cesare.

"Are you ready?"

Cesare urged his mount two paces forward.

He did not answer the question.

He only said:

"I am Cesare Borgia."

His voice was level, and did not shake.

"Direct blood-descendant of the last Star-Reader of Ceylon."

He raised a hand, and slowly drew aside his collar.

The golden collar-set at the back of his neck gave out a faint low hum in the morning light.

Then the colour of his pupils began to change —

Beginning at the rim, a violet light came on, the iris as if it had been lit from within, and threw out a hot bright glow. Then, from the edge of the pupil, gold markings began to surface, scale by scale, like dragon-scales unfolding, rotating slowly around the rim of the iris. Violet pupil. Gold veins.

At the same moment the golden collar-set grew warm.

Not the warmth of heat. A warmth like blood moving.

Valentina's hand went to her sword-hilt. Alfonso pushed his glasses up. Don Juan's lips moved but made no sound. Quintilian tightened his grip on the haft of his war-axe.

The blurred figure looked at Cesare's eyes, and was silent for several seconds.

"…As I was told," it said. "You are the one he spoke of."

It did not bar the way.

It stepped aside.

But as the column passed, it fell in behind them, keeping a distance of about ten paces — neither nearer nor further.

At the end of the road was a clearing.

In the centre of the clearing stood a square pillar.

The pillar was plain white marble, without any ornament, about two metres tall, with a cross-section of half a metre a side. In the morning fog it looked like a boundary-stone that had been forgotten.

But the base of the pillar — for a metre around it on every side — was carved with patterns.

The World Tree.

From the centre of the base, the trunk rose up; the ends of the branches were cut into the shape of gears; the leaves were a constellation of gears of different sizes. The roots ran out from the base in all directions, the fine tips of them incised with Sanskrit finer than a hair, and several of the roots had even run all the way over to the cemetery.

"This pillar — " Cassian said, low.

He dismounted and walked to it.

"The pillar in my parents' joint tomb — " Cesare said, also low.

"Is a branch," Cassian said. "This is the mother-body."

He raised his hand and laid the flat of his palm against the side of the pillar.

Click.

A seam slid silently open on one side of the pillar.

Not the sound of any machine. The sound of stone against stone.

Through the seam a faint green light came.

"Stay close to me," Cassian said.

He went first down the steps.

The steps were damp, with beads of moisture on the rock walls. The air grew warmer as they went down, and a faint scent of flowers rose from below.

Golden lotus.

The same scent Cesare had caught in the depths of the Minerva Bureau.

At the foot of the steps, a round stone chamber.

At the centre of the chamber —

A ball of dark-gold roots, knot upon knot, like a vast heart, beating slowly, with rhythm.

With every beat, a ring of faint green light welled up out of the depths of the roots and lit the whole chamber.

The main root-node of the World Tree.

Cesare stood at the entrance, and did not move.

The dark-gold mass of roots began to tremble.

The green light grew brighter. The light pouring up from the depths grew stronger, as if a heart that had slept for several hundred years had suddenly wakened.

Hummm —

A low drone filled the chamber.

Then Cesare heard it.

Not with his ears. Through the collar-set at the back of his neck, through the vessels under the skin, through the resonance of the violet pupil and the gold veins.

A voice.

Very old. Very far away. As if it had come up out of the core of the World Tree itself.

"…Come…"

Cesare took one step forward.

He held out his hand.

His fingertips touched the thickest of the dark-gold roots.

Warm.

Like the warmth of living skin.

Fragments of memory began to pour into his mind — the dusk over the Saintess Tower of Ceylon three hundred years ago, da Vinci Borgia surveying blueprints in the gear-tunnel, a young man of white hair burying a seed at the foot of Wangwu Mountain, the low roar of an Omega prototype at its first start —

But he did not fall.

He stood where he was, his fingers on the root, the violet-and-gold light pulsing in the dark of the chamber.

The blurred figure of Saint George the Dragonslayer, without anyone noticing when, had followed them to the entrance of the chamber.

It looked at Cesare where he stood in contact with the main root-node, and was silent a long while.

Then it said:

"Three hundred years ago, da Vinci Borgia stood in the same place."

The metallic click of its voice was unchanged.

"But he chose a different path."

It looked at Cesare.

"You are the second to stand here."

"You will make a different choice."

The blurred figure began to disperse.

Not slowly. Like smoke, the edges dissolving inward toward the centre.

Where it had been, something on the floor caught the green light.

Cesare went over. He crouched.

A sword.

The blade curved like a snake, narrow and long, its surface crusted over with a thin patina of pale green. The grip was the colour of old bronze, wrapped in silk that had faded to the colour of dead bone. Two small Sanskrit characters were cut into the cross-guard.

"This is no ordinary sword," Alfonso said, pushing his glasses up and crouching to look.

He took the portable nerve-current reader from his belt and ran it over the blade. The reading jumped.

"The material… is the same as the weapons in Saint George's own arsenal."

"It is called the Green Serpent," Cassian said.

All of them looked at him.

"My mother told me of it. In the first-generation prototype's reserve, da Vinci hid seven swords. Each of them has a name. The Green Serpent is one of them."

He looked at Cesare.

"It is a gift from da Vinci to his heir."

Cesare reached out and closed his hand on the grip.

The grip fitted his hand as if it had been made for it. The blade grew faintly warm in his palm.

The moment his hand closed on it —

From the deep of the chamber came a low metallic concussion.

Boom.

The whole chamber shook. The dark-gold roots trembled violently. The pale green light flickered, in and out.

As if something, in the deepest place of all, were waking up.

第239章 世界树的根
