【中文】
第239章 世界树的根

轰。

又一声低沉的金属撞击从石室最深处传来。暗金色的根须剧烈颤动，淡绿色光芒明灭不定，墙壁上的梵文随之一亮一暗地闪烁，像是整座王屋山都在共鸣中震颤。

西泽尔握紧青蛇剑。

剑身在他掌心里越来越热，淡绿色的铜锈下面浮现出细如蛛丝的光纹。那些光纹不是反射，是自内而外地亮起来，像是沉睡了三百年的血液重新开始流动。

与此同时，他后颈的黄金套管烫得像一块烧红的烙铁。锁骨下方的皮肤传来针刺般的灼烧感，肋骨间有什么东西在跳动。

不是心脏。

比心脏更深的地方。

他低下头。

胸前那枚母亲留下的银莲花项链坠正在震颤。坠面上泛起淡金色的光，光沿着一条条细如发丝的纹路蔓延开去——那是星见文字，是母亲项链坠背面他一直看不太清的铭文。

文字亮了起来。

不是全部，只有其中三行。

第一行：达·芬奇·博尔吉亚。

第二行：新神使载体。

第三行：梵天陨落。

三个名字在坠面上浮现了约莫十秒钟，然后缓缓隐入金属深处，只剩坠子还在微微发烫。

青蛇剑与银莲花坠在同一个频率上震动着。两件器物之间仿佛存在一根看不见的引线，嗡鸣声低沉得像是有人在他胸腔里敲钟。

"这是……"阿方索推了推眼镜，手里的便携式神经电流读出器在剧烈跳动，数字翻了一倍又一倍，"两份器物在共振。频率完全吻合。材料同源。"

他顿了顿，又补充了一句。

"和屠龙者圣乔治武器库里那批武器是同一种金属。"

楚舜华一直站在暗金色根须的旁边，静静地看着西泽尔胸前那枚坠子。他的表情没有变化，但眉心拧了一下。

很轻。

像是在克制什么。

"你母亲留给你的东西，从来都不只是纪念品。"他说。

他没有解释更多。他只是转过身，伸出右手，掌心按上了一根最粗的暗金色根须。

根须亮了。

不是淡绿色，而是一种更为古老的、带着金属质感的暗金色光芒。那光芒沿着根须蔓延，向上、向下、向四面八方扩散，在石室中央汇聚成一个缓慢旋转的全息投影。

投影里出现了一棵树。

不是普通的树。

树干是暗金色的合金，表面的纹路像是某种极其精密的电路图。树枝末梢悬挂着数以千计的红色核心，每一颗核心都像是一颗跳动的心脏，表面有微弱的电流在闪。树叶是大小不一的金色齿轮，所有齿轮以不同的速度缓缓转动，发出一种低沉的、像是远古合唱般的嗡鸣。

整棵树的根部深深扎入地面以下，根须向四面八方延伸，穿过岩层、穿过地壳、穿过海洋——投影的边界被刻意拉高拉远，让他们能看见根须末端消失在视野尽头。

"这就是世界树。"楚舜华说。

他的声音在石室中回荡，被根须的嗡鸣衬得格外清晰。

"不是弥赛亚圣教经文里那棵伊甸园中的卡巴拉之树。也不是大夏巫教供奉的神树。"

"它是史前文明的遗产。"

"一台量子计算机的核心。"

"一千年前，它还完整地生长在东西方交界的阿瓦隆冰原上。那时候没有教皇国，没有大夏，没有锡兰，没有查理曼，没有叶尼塞。整个世界的人类都生活在它结出的红水银果实所驱动的机械神国之中。"

"没有瘟疫。没有饥荒。没有战争。"

"……至少，最初的一千年是这样。"

投影里的画面切换。

无数精密的机械建筑高耸入云，建筑外壁覆盖着缓缓转动的金色齿轮，齿轮之间用红水银管道连接，红水银在管道里流动时发出柔和的光。天空中飞翔着齿轮驱动的飞艇，地面行走着各种形态的机械造物，有机械鸟、机械狗、还有漂浮在半空中的圆盘。人们穿着统一的银白色长袍，面上带着平静而满足的神情。

那是一座真正意义上的机械之城。

"然后分歧出现了。"

投影里的城市开始坍塌。

机械建筑一座接一座倒下，齿轮从天空中坠落，红色核心的碎裂像是血一样从天空洒落。人们四散奔逃，银白色长袍被火焰染黑。

"两个最强大的家族为了争夺世界树的控制权而开战。世界树被劈成两半。"

"东半归楚氏守护。"

"西半归锡兰星见守护。"

"弥赛亚圣教，是西方残枝的守护组织。"

"大夏巫教，是东方主根的守护组织。"

"所有的宗教、所有的神话、所有的战争、所有的文明——都是为了保护这两半残枝而存在。"

"都是为了防止世界树再次合一。"

石室里的温度似乎在下降。

"三百年前，"楚舜华的声音顿了顿，"一个疯狂的人从阿瓦隆冰原的西半残枝中切下了一根枝条，秘密带回了翡冷翠。"

"他用那根枝条，培育出了第一批欧米茄原型体。"

投影再次切换。

一个身披教皇法衣的人影站在一棵较小的金色树木前。枝条末端的红色核心已经变成了暗金色，像是熟透了的果实。数十架暗金色甲胄从枝条中"生长"出来，以莲花状排列在他周围。每架甲胄的胸腔都嵌着一颗巨大的红水银核心，核心的跳动频率与那棵金色小树完全同步。

"他以为他可以控制世界树。他以为他可以重启那个没有瘟疫、没有饥荒、没有战争的机械神国。"

"但他错了。"

"机械神国的重启需要一个条件。"

楚舜华的声音停了一拍，目光从投影上移开，落在西泽尔的紫瞳上。

"需要一个完美适配者。"

"一个同时拥有锡兰星见血脉和博尔吉亚家族机械适配基因的人。"

"能够连接世界树的东西两半残枝，让它们重新合为一体。"

"同时保留完整的人性。"

他看着西泽尔。

"也就是你。"

投影消失了。石室重新陷入黑暗，只剩下根须上残余的暗金色光芒和青蛇剑剑身上那一线淡绿。

"原罪机关的主人，"楚舜华的声音很轻，但每个字都像是钉子一样钉在空气里，"他花了三百年时间寻找这个完美适配者。"

"他知道只有通过你，才能让西方残枝和东方主根同时苏醒。"

"才能把世界树重新合为一体。"

"999架欧米茄原型体，是他三百年培育出的全部军队。"

"它们不是天使。"

"不是弥赛亚圣教经文里描述的神造之物。"

"它们是世界树结出的果实。是史前机械神国最后的一批守护者。"

"被初代教皇用暴力封印在维苏威火山的熔岩之心深处，沉睡了四十年。"

"他想释放它们，作为他的军队。然后利用世界树核心控制全人类，重建那个没有瘟疫、没有饥荒、没有战争的机械神国。"

"但那个神国里没有自由。"

"没有不同的声音。"

"只有一个人说了算。"

楚舜华说完这句话后停了下来。暗金色的根须在他身后微微颤动，像是在呼吸。

石室里很安静。

根须的暗金色光芒在每个人脸上投下摇曳的影子，把石室映得像是一座被遗忘在地底的教堂。

"可是，"唐璜忽然开口，声音里带着他一贯的吊儿郎当，但眼神却异常认真，"有阻止的办法对吧？"

楚舜华看着他。

"有。"

"什么办法？"

楚舜华没有立刻回答。他从腰间取出一卷黄绢，缓缓展开。黄绢上是一幅精细的机械图纸，密密麻麻的标注和计算公式铺满了整幅绢面。图纸的右下角有一个签名，墨迹已经有些褪色，但笔锋仍然锋利。

"梵天陨落反物质炸弹。"

他将黄绢举到西泽尔面前。

"用红水银核心制造反物质爆炸，摧毁世界树的西方残枝和所有欧米茄原型体。"

"原罪机关主人的军队会在爆炸中灰飞烟灭。"

"但是——"

他没有说下去。

"但是什么？"昆提良握紧了拳头。

楚舜华的声音没有波动，像是在陈述一个与他无关的事实。

"西方残枝被摧毁时产生的能量冲击波，会沿着世界树的东西方根须网络传导。"

"东方主根节点——也就是我们现在所在的位置——会被同时摧毁。"

"王屋山会被夷为平地。"

"爆炸的能量会以王屋山为中心向外扩散数百公里。"

"半个夏国……会从地图上消失。"

石室里的空气仿佛被抽干了。

"你知道这个结果。"西泽尔说。

不是疑问。

是陈述。

"我知道。"楚舜华平静地回答。

"从三十年前我母亲临终时告诉我这个秘密的那一刻起，我就知道。"

"她说，等一个锡兰星见的直系血裔从西方来。等他走到世界树的主根节点。"

"她说，那个人会做出不同的选择。"

楚舜华看着西泽尔手中的青蛇剑。

"三百年前，达·芬奇走到了同样的位置。但他没有引爆梵天陨落。"

"因为代价太大了。"

"他不想牺牲他自己。"

"他选择了另一条路——封印世界树，让它沉睡。"

"他成功了。但封印不是永远的。"

"四十年后，原罪机关找到了沉睡中的残枝。"

"它开始重新苏醒。"

"又一个四十年后，你来到了这里。"

楚舜华向前走了一步，站在西泽尔面前。两个人的身高差不多，但楚舜华身上那种沉稳如山岳的气场让这个距离显得很短。

"梵天陨落反物质炸弹的引爆器——"

他的目光落在西泽尔胸前的银莲花坠上。

"不仅需要秘文。"

"还需要完美适配者的血。"

"也就是你的血。"

石室里又是一阵沉默。

根须的暗金色光芒在每个人脸上投下摇曳的影子。

"我愿意。"

第一个说话的是瓦莲京娜。

她从改装神怒Ⅲ型甲胄的胸腔前走出来——她一直站在那里，金色的长发在根须的光芒中像是燃烧的火焰。

"西泽尔的目标就是我的目标。"她说，声音冷峻而坚定，"从我母亲临终时让我去西方探寻秘密的那一刻起，我就知道会有这一天。"

"叶尼塞人不是懦夫。"

"我跟你们一起。"

"我也去。"唐璜收起了所有的玩笑表情，紫色的眼睛里映着暗金色的光，"老板救过我的命。我唐璜这条命早就是他的了。"

"我欠他的情分，十辈子都还不清。"

"算我一个。"昆提良把艾莲留给他的那块画纸纸条塞进了胸口的内袋里，"我答应过她，要活着回去。"

"但我也答应过西泽尔。"

"我欠他两条命。一条是我的，另一条是艾莲的。"

"我也去。"阿方索推了推眼镜，声音平稳，"我在高加索山脉已经死过一次了。再死一次也没什么。"

"而且，"他顿了一下，"我是机械师。炸弹组装需要我。"

楚舜华看着他们，没有说话。

但他的嘴角动了一下。

很轻。

像是在克制什么。

西泽尔也没有说话。

他只是看着这些人——他的旧部，他的未婚妻，他的盟友。看着他们站在暗金色的光芒中，脸上的影子被根须的颤动切得忽明忽暗。

他的手指收紧了青蛇剑的剑柄。

剑身在他掌心里发出低沉的嗡鸣。

就在这时——

嗡。

他腕上的蜘蛛巢腕表震了一下。

不是普通的消息提示。是密涅瓦机关最高级别的加密通讯频率，全世界知道这个频率的人不超过三个。

西泽尔抬起手腕。

表盘上浮现出一行红字。

"西泽尔。"

薇若兰的声音从表盘的微型扬声器中传来，带着急促的呼吸声和山风呼啸的背景音。

"我们已经到达王屋山脚下。"

"梵天陨落反物质炸弹的核心零件全部就位。"

"但是……组装需要时间。"

她停顿了一下。

"至少三天。"

"三天之内，你们必须守住主根节点。"

"不能让原罪机关的人靠近。"

"一旦他们启动残枝，梵天陨落就失效了。"

通讯中断。

表盘上的红字消失了。

石室重新安静下来。

只剩下根须的嗡鸣声，像是世界树自己的心跳。

西泽尔垂下手腕。

"三天。"他说。

"三天。"

楚舜华点了点头。

"我们守住这里。"

他转过身，面对着那棵最粗的暗金色根须。

"三天。"

石室深处的金属撞击声又响了一下。

比之前更重。

比之前更近。

像是有什么东西，正在从世界树的最深处，一步一步地朝他们走来。

然后——

嵌在石室角落墙壁上的一个黄铜齿轮，忽然开始缓缓转动。

那个齿轮原本毫无异样。它和其他嵌在墙壁里的齿轮一样，安静地待在那里，表面覆盖着三百年的灰尘。

但现在它在转。

而且它的表面浮现出了暗金色的光芒。

那光芒向外扩展，在石室中央投射出了另一个全息投影。

投影里站着一个人。

一个戴着银色猫头鹰面具的人。

面具下露出的是一只湛蓝色的眼睛——

不，不是眼睛。

是光学镜头。冰冷的、精密的、带着机械反光的光学镜头。

"完美适配者终于来了。"

声音从四面八方传来，带着精密齿轮咬合的质感，没有一丝人类声带的温度。

面具的嘴角微微上扬。

不是笑。

是一种计算过的、精确到毫米的表情。

"新的弥赛亚……将诞生。"

【English】
Chapter 239 — The Roots of the World Tree

Boom.

Another low metallic impact rolled out of the deepest part of the stone chamber. The dark-gold roots shuddered, their pale green glow flickering like a candle in a draft, and the Sanskrit inscriptions carved into the walls pulsed in sympathy—bright, dim, bright again—as if the whole of Mount Wangwu were vibrating in answer.

Cesare tightened his grip on the Green Snake sword.

The blade grew warmer in his palm. Beneath the patina of pale verdigris, hair-fine lines of light began to surface—rising from inside the metal, not reflected from without—as though some blood that had been sleeping for three hundred years had begun to move again through it.

At the same moment the gold collar set into the back of his neck burned like a brand fresh from the forge. Below his collarbones his skin prickled with needles of heat. Something in the cage of his ribs was beating.

Not his heart.

Something deeper than his heart.

He looked down.

The silver lotus pendant his mother had left him was trembling. Across its face a faint gold light was spreading, following lines as fine as hair—the star-seer characters engraved on the back of the pendant that he had never quite been able to read.

Three lines lit up.

Only three.

The first: *Leonardo Borgia.*
The second: *New God-bearer vessel.*
The third: *The Fall of Brahma.*

The names held the light for perhaps ten seconds, then sank back into the metal of their own accord. The pendant was still warm against his breastbone.

The Green Snake sword and the silver lotus pendant trembled at the same frequency. Between them, somewhere in the air, a thread of resonance pulled taut. The hum of it sat low in his chest, like a bell being struck inside a cathedral.

"This is—" Alfonso pushed his spectacles up his nose. The portable neural current reader in his hand was jumping, its numerals doubling, doubling again. "Two artifacts in resonance. Frequency a perfect match. Same source material."

He paused. Then, quieter:

"Same alloy as the weapons in Saint George's armory in Florence. The dragon-slayer's stock."

Chu Shunhua had been standing beside the thickest of the dark-gold roots. He had not moved. His expression had not changed. But the muscle between his brows tightened, just once.

A small thing.

The kind of small thing a man does when he is holding something back.

"What your mother left you," he said, "was never a keepsake."

He did not explain. He turned instead and laid his open palm against the broadest of the dark-gold roots.

The root lit up.

Not the pale green of before. A far older light, dark gold, metallic, the color of something that had been buried so long it had forgotten the sun. That light ran along the root—up, down, out, in every direction—and gathered in the center of the chamber, where it slowly turned itself into a hologram.

A tree appeared in the air.

Not a tree.

The trunk was dark-gold alloy, its surface veined with patterns that resembled, at very close inspection, an extraordinarily precise circuit diagram. From the branches hung thousands of red cores, each one pulsing like a small heart, faint current flickering across their skins. The leaves were gears of varying sizes, all of gold, each turning at its own pace. Together they produced a low, choral hum—the sound of a thing that had been running for a very long time.

The roots of the tree plunged through the floor. They ran through stone, through the earth's crust, through oceans—the projection was pulled up and back, high and far, so that the four of them could see the root-tips disappear into the horizon.

"This," said Chu Shunhua, "is the World Tree."

His voice carried oddly in the chamber, lifted by the roots' hum and held there.

"It is not the Kabbalistic tree of Eden described in the Messiah's scripture. It is not the god-tree worshipped by the Xia witches."

"It is a relic of a civilization that came before us."

"The core of a quantum computer."

"A thousand years ago it grew whole, on the Avalon Ice Plains, where east and west had not yet learned to call themselves different names. There was no Pope, no Xia, no Ceylan, no Charlemagne, no Yenisei. All the people of the earth lived in a machine-theocracy driven by the red-mercury fruit the tree bore."

"No plague. No famine. No war."

"—at least, not for the first thousand years."

The projection shifted.

Cities of precise machinery rose into a sky without smoke. Their walls were sheathed in slow-turning gold gears, gears joined by pipes of red mercury that glowed softly as the liquid ran. Gearships drifted in the air. Mechanical dogs padded along the avenues. Floating discs hung at every height. People moved through it all in identical silver-white robes, their faces marked by a calm that looked, from a distance, like contentment.

A real city. A real theocracy of metal.

"Then came the schism."

The cities came down.

One by one the buildings folded. Gears fell out of the sky. The red cores broke apart over the streets like a rain of small, dark hearts. The silver-white robes caught fire and turned black at the hems. People ran.

"The two most powerful houses went to war over control of the tree. The World Tree was split in two."

"The eastern half passed to the guardianship of the Chu."

"The western half to the guardianship of the Ceylan star-seers."

"The Holy Church of the Messiah is the protective order of the western branch."

"The Xia witches' cult is the protective order of the eastern root."

"Every religion. Every myth. Every war. Every civilization. They were all built to guard these two broken halves."

"All built to keep the World Tree from ever joining back together."

The temperature in the chamber seemed to drop.

"Three hundred years ago," Chu Shunhua said, and his voice faltered for the first time, "a madman cut a branch from the western half of the tree on the Avalon Ice Plains and brought it secretly back to Florence."

"From that branch he grew the first Omega prototypes."

The projection shifted again.

A figure in papal vestments stood before a smaller gold tree. The red cores at the branch-tips had darkened to a deep, ripe gold. Dozens of dark-gold armors grew out of the branches in the shape of opening lotus flowers. At the chest of each armor a great red-mercury core pulsed in time with the tree.

"He thought he could master the World Tree. He thought he could restart the machine-theocracy. The one without plague, without famine, without war."

"He was wrong."

"To restart the theocracy, one condition had to be met."

Chu Shunhua paused. He looked away from the projection and into Cesare's violet eyes.

"A perfect adapter."

"A person who carried the Ceylan star-seer bloodline and the Borgia mechanical-adaptation gene in the same body."

"A person who could connect the eastern main root to the western broken branch and make them one again."

"And remain fully human while doing it."

He looked at Cesare.

"That is you."

The projection died. The chamber went dark. There was nothing left but the dim gold glow on the roots and the thin green line of the Green Snake sword.

"The master of the Original Sin Bureau," Chu Shunhua said, very quietly. Every word landed in the air like a nail being driven home. "He has spent three hundred years looking for this perfect adapter."

"He knows that only through you can the western branch and the eastern root be woken together."

"Only through you can the World Tree be made whole again."

"Nine hundred and ninety-nine Omega prototypes. The entire army he has cultivated in three hundred years."

"They are not angels."

"They are not the divine creations the Messiah's scripture describes."

"They are fruit of the World Tree. The last guardians of the old machine-theocracy."

"Sealed by the first Pope in the molten heart of Mount Vesuvius. Sleeping for forty years."

"He means to wake them. To make them his army. And through the core of the World Tree to bind all humanity. To rebuild a theocracy without plague, without famine, without war."

"But a theocracy in which there is no freedom."

"No dissent."

"Only one voice, in one throat, deciding for everyone."

Chu Shunhua stopped speaking. Behind him the dark-gold roots trembled faintly, as if breathing.

The chamber was quiet.

The light of the roots threw moving shadows across every face in the room, and for a moment the chamber looked less like a tomb than like a forgotten church buried under a mountain.

"But," said Don Juan, "there is a way to stop it. Right?"

He had not lost the lift at the corner of his mouth. But his eyes were not joking.

"Yes," said Chu Shunhua.

"Tell us."

Chu Shunhua did not answer at once. He drew a yellowed silk scroll from his belt and unrolled it slowly. The scroll was a mechanical drawing, dense with annotation, with calculation, with small precise symbols that marched across the silk in ordered rows. In the lower right corner there was a signature. The ink had faded, but the strokes were still sharp.

"The Fall of Brahma antimatter bomb."

He held the scroll out in front of Cesare.

"Built around a red-mercury core, it destroys the western branch of the World Tree and every Omega prototype with it."

"The master of the Original Sin Bureau and his army will be turned to ash."

"But—"

He did not finish.

"But what?" said Quintilian. His fist had closed.

Chu Shunhua's voice did not change. He was speaking, Cesare realized, the way a man speaks about something that has nothing to do with him.

"When the western branch is destroyed, the shockwave of released energy will travel along the eastern root network of the World Tree."

"The eastern main-root node—where we are standing now—will be destroyed at the same moment."

"Wangwu Mountain will be flattened."

"The energy of the explosion will spread outward from the mountain for hundreds of kilometers."

"Half of Xia—"

He did not finish that sentence either. He did not need to.

The air in the chamber seemed to leave.

"You knew this," Cesare said.

It was not a question.

"I knew it," said Chu Shunhua, calmly. "I have known it from the night my mother told me the secret, thirty years ago, on her deathbed."

"She told me: wait. Wait until a direct descendant of the Ceylan star-seers arrives from the west. Wait until he reaches the main root of the World Tree."

"She said: that man will choose differently."

He looked at the Green Snake sword in Cesare's hand.

"Three hundred years ago, Leonardo Borgia stood in the same place. He did not detonate the Fall of Brahma."

"The price was too high."

"He would not pay it himself."

"So he chose another road. He sealed the World Tree. He put it to sleep."

"He succeeded. But seals are not forever."

"Forty years later the Original Sin Bureau found the sleeping branch."

"It began to wake."

"Another forty years, and you walked in."

Chu Shunhua stepped forward. They were almost the same height. The stillness of him made the small distance between them feel very small.

"The detonator of the Fall of Brahma antimatter bomb—"

His gaze dropped to the silver lotus pendant at Cesare's chest.

"—requires the secret text."

"It also requires the blood of the perfect adapter."

"That is, your blood."

The chamber was quiet again. The roots' light moved over their faces in slow, broken patterns.

"I will do it."

The first voice was Valentina's.

She stepped out from behind the chest plate of her modified Wrath-of-God Mark III armor, where she had been standing all along, her gold hair burning in the roots' light like a slow flame.

"Whatever Cesare has set himself to do, I have set myself to do." Her voice was cool, and it did not waver. "From the night my mother, dying, told me to go west and find the secret, I knew it would come to this."

"A Yenisei does not flinch."

"I am with you."

"I'm in." Don Juan had put away every trace of his usual levity. The violet of his eyes was full of the roots' dark gold. "The boss saved my life once. My life stopped being mine a long time ago."

"I owe him a debt I will not pay off in ten lifetimes."

"Count me in." Quintilian pushed the folded slip of paper Elen had given him into the breast pocket of his coat. "I promised her I would come back alive."

"But I made Cesare a promise first."

"I owe him two lives. Mine, and Elen's."

"I'm going too." Alfonso adjusted his spectacles. His voice was steady. "I have already died once in the Caucasus mountains. It is not a particular inconvenience to die again."

"Also," he added, "I am a mechanic. You will need me to assemble the device."

Chu Shunhua looked at them. He said nothing.

But the corner of his mouth moved.

Just once.

The way a man's mouth moves when he is holding something back.

Cesare also said nothing.

He looked at the people around him. His old subordinates. His betrothed. His allies. He looked at them standing in the dark-gold light, their faces cut by the roots' slow trembling into strips of brightness and shadow.

His fingers tightened on the hilt of the Green Snake sword.

The blade hummed, low, in his palm.

And then—

Hum.

The spider-nest wristwatch on his wrist gave a single pulse. Not the usual message-buzz. The most heavily encrypted frequency of the Minerva Bureau. There were no more than three people in the world who knew that frequency.

Cesare raised his wrist.

A line of red text appeared on the dial.

*Cesare.*

Violaine's voice came through the dial's tiny speaker. There was the sound of quick breathing, and the wind of a high mountain behind her.

"We have reached the foot of Wangwu Mountain."

"All the core components of the Fall of Brahma antimatter bomb are in place."

"But the assembly will take time."

A pause.

"Three days, at least."

"Within three days, you must hold this root node."

"You must not let the people of the Original Sin Bureau get close."

"If they start the branch waking, the Fall of Brahma will not work."

The connection broke.

The red text vanished.

The chamber went quiet.

There was only the hum of the roots. The sound of the World Tree's own heartbeat.

Cesare lowered his wrist.

"Three days," he said.

"Three days," said Chu Shunhua.

He nodded.

"We hold this place."

He turned to face the thickest of the dark-gold roots.

"Three days."

The metallic impact from the deepest part of the chamber sounded again.

Louder this time.

Closer.

As if something was walking up out of the lowest roots of the World Tree, toward them, one step at a time.

And then—

A brass gear set into the wall of the chamber, in a corner where the eye had not gone, began to turn.

The gear had been still, like every other gear set into the wall. Three hundred years of dust on its surface.

Now it was moving.

And dark-gold light was spreading across its face.

That light reached out and threw a second hologram into the center of the chamber.

A figure stood in the air.

A figure in a silver owl mask.

Below the mask, where a mouth should have been—

No, that was not a mouth.

It was a lens. Cold, precise, throwing back the mechanical gleam of polished metal.

"The perfect adapter," said the voice, "has finally come."

The voice came from every direction at once. It had the quality of well-fitted gears, of a clockwork mechanism running true. There was no human warmth in it, not anywhere.

The corner of the mask, where a mouth would be, lifted.

It was not a smile.

It was a calculation, made to the millimeter.

"The new Messiah," the voice said, "is about to be born."

第240章 龙雀与红莲的约定
==================================================

【中文】
第240章 龙雀与红莲的约定

投影碎裂的光点最后消失在根须之间。

猫头鹰面具的轮廓像被擦去的炭笔痕迹，只在石壁上留下一道转瞬即逝的暗红色余烬。

"三天。"

合成嗓音的尾音还在根须的缝隙里游荡，像一根细丝被慢慢抽走。

然后什么都没有了。

石室重新被根须的嗡鸣填满。那声音低沉、稳定、从不间断，仿佛世界树有自己的脉搏。根须上的黄铜齿轮在暗中缓缓转动，每个齿轮的齿尖都刻着细如发丝的梵文，金属与金属咬合时发出极轻的咔哒声。

"新弥赛亚将诞生"——这句话悬在空气里，像一枚还没有落地的硬币。

楚舜华最先动了。

他把夔龙角剑收回剑鞘，动作很慢，剑身与鞘口摩擦的声响在石室中格外清晰。

"三百年前的人想造神，三百年后还是想造神。"他说，"人性倒是一点儿没变。"

"他不是想造神。"西泽尔说。

楚舜华转过头来看他。

"他只是想造一个听话的神。"西泽尔垂下眼睫，目光落在手腕上那块密涅瓦总长徽章的反光上，"但他错了。神不会听话。"

"那他想造的是什么？"

"一个容器。"

楚舜华沉默了几秒。

"我母亲临终前说——'等他来'。"楚舜华说。

"等谁？"

"她没说。"

西泽尔抬起头来。

两人的目光在半空中相触。

"你等了十七年。"西泽尔说。

"你也是。"楚舜华说。

石室的暗金色光线把他们的脸切成了明暗两半。

"楚监国。"西泽尔说。

"西泽尔少校。"楚舜华说。

两个正式到近乎疏远的称呼落在根须的嗡鸣里。

然后西泽尔向石室深处走去。

"我母亲也在等。"他没有回头，"她埋在翡冷翠，墓碑上只有两个字——'异端'。是教皇派人刻的。"

"但她从来没去看过那座墓。"

"我也没有。"

楚舜华跟了上去。

"她等的人是谁？"楚舜华问。

"我不知道。"西泽尔说，"但她临终前对碧儿说了一句话——'等那个孩子从东方来'。"

楚舜华的脚步停了一拍。

"从东方来。"他重复了一遍。

"嗯。"

他们沿着根须之间的缝隙向石室最深处走去。暗金色的金属根须在头顶交错，缝隙间漏下的光在他们的肩甲上投下细密的纹路。脚下的地砖刻着梵文和倒置五芒星，每走一步都能感觉到脚底传来微弱的震动——那是世界树根须脉动的回响。

墓地在石室尽头一块被根须环绕的开阔地。

七座墓碑。

每一座都刻着带齿轮的倒置五芒星圣徽。碑面被根须分泌的暗金色液体浸润了不知多少年，金属与石头的边界已经模糊不清，像是被时间本身慢慢消化。

最高处那座墓碑前立着一根白色大理石方柱。

无字。

无名。

表面被打磨得光可鉴人，映出根须间漏下的暗金色光。

楚舜华在那根方柱前停下。

"这是我父母的合葬碑。"他说，"父亲没有姓氏，母亲是最后一位东方星见。碑上不刻字——我们家族的传统，守护者的名字不能留在石头上。"

"石头记得就够了。"

他伸出手，掌心贴在方柱冰凉的表面上。

"她走的时候我才十一岁。"楚舜华说，"她最后拉着我的手说——'他会来的'。"

"谁？"

"她没说名字。"楚舜华从袖中取出一只小小的银盒，盒面雕着一朵五瓣白莲花，"她只留了这个。"

盒盖打开。

里面是一枚铜色护身符，刻着星见家族的倒置五芒星和齿轮纹路，背面密密麻麻地刻着细如发丝的星见古文。

"我戴了十七年。"楚舜华把护身符放在西泽尔摊开的掌心里，"她说——它能保护持有者不被世界树的意识过度侵蚀。"

护身符触碰西泽尔掌心的瞬间，他后颈的黄金套管猛地发烫。不是普通金属被握紧后的体温——是某种共鸣，从护身符内部透出，沿着掌心的纹路向上游走，钻入腕骨，经过肘部，直抵肩胛。

西泽尔的瞳孔变了。

紫色从虹膜深处浮上来，被金色的纹路贯穿，像被点燃的回路。

而楚舜华的瞳孔也在同一时刻改变——紫金色，深邃的、带着金属光泽的紫金色，瞳孔中央有一道竖直的金线，仿佛某种古老的印记。

"我母亲去世时，我才四岁。"西泽尔说，"我不记得她抱过我。"

"但你来了。"楚舜华说。

"嗯。"

"我也等了十七年。"

西泽尔伸出右手。

骑士握手礼。

指尖相触。

后颈的黄金套管同时发烫——不只是西泽尔的，楚舜华颈后某个看不见的位置也似乎有什么东西在共鸣，热度隔着皮肤都能感觉到。

然后——

石室亮了。

不是暗金色。

是绿色。

一种深邃的、仿佛千年古木年轮深处才会透出的翠绿光芒，从他们脚下那根最粗的暗金色根须中涌出。

不是爆发。

是渗透。

像春水渗入干裂的河床，光芒沿着根须的纹理向四面八方扩散，每一寸暗金色的金属表面都被染上了一层透明的翠绿。根须上的黄铜齿轮开始加快转动，墙壁上的齿轮跟着转动，整座石室仿佛是一台沉睡了三百年的机器，正在被某种力量唤醒。

"世界树在——"阿方索后退一步，手腕上的蜘蛛巢腕表在绿光中闪烁着暗红色的光点。

"不是回应。"唐璜屏住了呼吸，"是共振。"

两双相握的手上汇聚了整间石室最亮的光芒。

不是金色。

不是紫色。

是两种颜色交融后产生的第三种颜色——青金色，像被月光浸透的铜。

"两支残枝的东西方持有者……第一次……"瓦莲京娜低声说，翡翠色的眼睛里映着绿光，"在同一时刻相认。"

光柱从他们的掌心升起，细如发丝，穿过根须交错的天花板，消失在看不见的深处。

持续了整整十秒。

然后慢慢消退。

石室重新沉入暗金色的阴影之中。

楚舜华松开了手。

他的掌心有一道浅浅的烫痕——青金色的，像被烙印。

西泽尔的掌心也有一道。

"从现在起——"楚舜华说。

"东西方同盟。"西泽尔说。

他们同时向后退了一步。

"作战计划。"西泽尔说，"三天。我们需要三天。"

"说。"

"第一——"西泽尔看向手腕上的密涅瓦总长徽章，"梵天陨落反物质炸弹需要组装。薇若兰已经带着核心零件抵达王屋山脚下。但组装至少需要三天。"

"三天之内，不能有任何原罪机关的人接近这间石室。"

"第二——"西泽尔转向瓦莲京娜，"我需要一支能挡住欧米茄原型体群的军队。"

瓦莲京娜站在唐璜身侧，金色长发在暗金色的光线中泛着冷光。

"我昨晚已经用叶尼塞军用频段联系了父皇。"她说，"沙皇同意派遣神怒骑士团全机械化师团支援。"

"多少人？"

"八千台改装神怒Ⅲ型甲胄。四十台巨型蒸汽投石机。"她停顿了一下，"以及——沙皇口谕。"

"什么？"

"'告诉西泽尔·博尔吉亚，他欠我叶尼塞一个外孙。'"

石室安静了两秒。

"……"唐璜张了张嘴，又闭上了。

"复议。"昆提良低声说。

"第三——"楚舜华接过话头，"在炸弹组装完成后，需要完美适配者的血来引爆。"

他看向西泽尔。

"引爆密钥在你母亲的项链坠背面。"

西泽尔点头。

"我知道。"

"你知道代价吗？"

"知道。"

"半个夏国从地图上消失。"

"知道。"

"那就这么定了。"

楚舜华抬起手，从腰间的剑鞘中抽出两把剑。

一把是夔龙角剑。

另一把——蛇形。

剑身弯曲如蛇，窄而长，覆淡绿色铜锈，剑柄缠着褪色绿绢。

"这把蛇形剑是我让铁匠按照鬼武者Ⅱ型的设计理念特制的。"楚舜华把蛇形剑递向西泽尔，"和屠龙者圣乔治武器库中达·芬奇留下的青蛇剑——是一对。"

西泽尔接过来。

左手青蛇，右手鬼武者蛇形剑。

两把剑在他手中同时发出细微的嗡鸣，一把低沉，一把清越，仿佛某种古老的呼应。

"谢了。"西泽尔说。

"礼尚往来。"楚舜华说。

西泽尔从怀中取出一枚碎片。

银白色，枪尖形状，断面刻着拉丁文和古梵文交织的铭文，中心嵌着一点淡紫色的光。

朗基努斯圣枪碎片。

炽天骑士团团长专属。

"这是我父亲留给我的。"西泽尔把碎片递向楚舜华，"他临终前说——'这件东西，将来会有用'。"

楚舜华接过碎片的瞬间——

他的紫金色瞳孔猛地一跳。

碎片上那点淡紫色的光，与他瞳孔中央那道金线产生了某种共鸣，光芒从碎片中央沿着他掌心的纹路向手腕蔓延，在他的脉搏处停了一拍，又退回碎片中。

"……"楚舜华低头看着掌心的碎片，沉默了三秒。

"这东西——"他抬起头，紫金色的瞳孔里多了一道细微的金色纹路，"我好像在梦里见过。"

"也许不是梦。"西泽尔说。

楚舜华把碎片收入袖中。

"我会把它交给东方星见的传人保管。"

"随你。"

他们再次对视。

然后同时点头。

就在这时——

石室外忽然传来一阵脚步声。

不是普通的脚步。

是靴声。

金属靴声。

整整齐齐的金属靴声。

一个穿着太监服饰的老人从根须的缝隙中走进来。他穿着深红色的太监袍服，头戴黑色便帽，面容枯槁，双手捧着一卷明黄色的绢帛。

"圣旨到——"老人高声唱道。

楚舜华转过身。

"楚舜华接旨。"

老人展开绢帛。

"奉天承运皇帝诏曰："

"监国公爵楚舜华，受先帝重恩，辅政多年，本应鞠躬尽瘁以报皇恩。"

"然近日风闻，楚舜华私通西夷，意图颠覆社稷，罪不容诛。"

"着即革去楚舜华一切官职爵位，贬为庶人。"

"凡我大夏军民人等，有能擒获楚舜华者，赏金万两，封侯拜爵。"

"钦此。"

老人的声音在石室中回荡。

楚舜华听完，脸上没有任何表情。

"念完了？"

"回……回楚庶人，念完了。"

"知道了。"

老人把绢帛双手呈上。

楚舜华没有接。

"拿回去。"他说。

"是……是。"

"告诉楚昭华——"楚舜华说，"十七年前母后去世时，他来过。"

老人的身体微微抖了一下。

"她说——'等你皇兄回来'。"

"他没听懂。"

"我也没听懂。"

"现在我听懂了。"

老人抱着绢帛退出石室，脚步声匆匆，像在逃命。

楚舜华转回身来。

仿佛什么都没发生。

"第三件事。"他说。

话音未落，石室外又传来一阵急促的脚步声。

一个穿着鬼武者甲胄的年轻军官快步走进来。

他单膝跪地。

"监国——"

"我不是监国了。"楚舜华说，"刚下的圣旨。"

"……"军官抬起头。

"有事说事。"

"是。"军官从怀中取出一封密信和一只银盒，"叶素理在通天宫发动叛乱，陛下已经下旨拆散风林山军团，命卑职前来传达。"

"风林山军团副团长白元朗听令——"楚舜华接过密信扫了一眼，"密令。"

"卑职在。"

"传令全军：拆散风林山军团的圣旨是矫诏。楚昭华已经被叶素理软禁。"

"是！"

"立刻南下洛阳，救出陛下。"

"是！"白元朗起身，又停住脚步，"可是——欧米茄原型体群正向王屋山方向移动。"

"挡住它们。"楚舜华说，"三天。"

"三天之内，我会让风林山军团的每一台鬼武者都站在这里。"

"卑职遵命！"

白元朗转身快步离去。

楚舜华把那只银盒打开。

里面是一张折叠成莲花形状的纸，纸面泛着淡淡的金光，边缘嵌着一圈极细的齿轮纹路。

"这是我母亲的另一件遗物。"楚舜华把纸莲花递给西泽尔，"她说——'等他来时，把这个也给他'。"

西泽尔接过纸莲花。

它在他手中微微发热，像一颗小小的、正在跳动的心脏。

"里面有三十七句祷词。"楚舜华说，"每一句都能降低世界树残枝意识对神经系统的侵蚀。"

"……谢了。"西泽尔说。

他想说点别的，但最终只说出了这两个字。

楚舜华伸手按了按他的肩。

"别死。"

"不会。"

就在这时——

阿方索手腕上的蜘蛛巢腕表忽然发出一声尖锐的蜂鸣。

所有人都转过头来。

表盘上原本显示着"通讯中断"的红字，此刻正在疯狂闪烁。

然后——

红字变成了一行新的文字。

"机械神教叩门者全体集合，前往王屋山保护新神使载体。"

"……"

阿方索抬起头。

"老板。"他说，"有东西在联系我。"

"什么东西？"

"我也不知道。"阿方索看着表盘上不断跳动的齿轮标记，"它说——'青铜蜘蛛'。"

石室角落的阴影里传来一阵轻微的金属摩擦声。

众人循声望去。

一个高大的身影正从根须的缝隙中走出来。

不是人类。

是一件甲胄。

屠龙者圣乔治。

但不是之前那个仿佛要撕裂一切的战争机器。

它的四肢折叠起来，肩甲上的羽翼收拢在背后，暗金色的装甲表面覆盖着一层薄薄的灰尘。每走一步，脚底都会在石砖上留下一个浅浅的印痕——三百年的重量。

它在西泽尔和楚舜华面前停下。

然后——

它单膝跪地。

这是百年来从未有过的姿态。

"完美适配者。"一个苍老的声音从甲胄内部传出来，带着精密齿轮咬合的质感，但又有某种古老的人性，"我等你很久了。"

"你是谁？"西泽尔问。

"我是机械神教的创始人之一。"

"也是达·芬奇·博尔吉亚的学生。"

"三百年前，我把一部分意识留在了这副甲胄里，等着完美神使的出现。"

"现在你来了。"

"我将协助你——"

它缓缓抬起头。面甲下没有面孔，只有两团淡青色的光。

"——关闭黑铁巨门。"

"——摧毁世界树。"

"——终结三百年的疯狂。"

石室中所有人都屏住了呼吸。

"你有名字吗？"西泽尔问。

"有过。"苍老的声音说，"但名字是会消失的东西。"

"你只需要知道——我是达·芬奇的学生。"

"也是艾琳娜的兄长。"

"三百年前，我们三人共同创立了机械神教，想要用机械的力量拯救人类。"

"但教皇疯了。"

"他也疯了。"

"三百年的疯狂，该结束了。"

它缓缓起身。

"让我们开始吧。"

就在这时——

石室外传来一阵密密麻麻的金属摩擦声。

不是一台。

是无数台。

众人冲到石室入口，向外望去。

王屋山的山道上，从山脚到山腰，从山腰到山顶——

密密麻麻的青铜色机械造物正在快速移动。

蜘蛛。

拇指盖大小的蜘蛛。

成千上万只。

它们的腹部嵌着红水银微晶，腿部的青铜关节在暗金色的光线下闪着冷光。它们沿着山路向上攀爬，沿着根须的缝隙钻入石室，沿着墙壁的齿轮缝隙钻入山体深处。

每一只蜘蛛的头部凹槽都发出两点绿色光芒。

"机械神教叩门者全体集合——"

"——保护新神使载体。"

声音不是从某一只蜘蛛中传出的。

是从每一只蜘蛛中同时传出的。

仿佛它们是同一个意识的不同分身。

西泽尔看着那漫山遍野的青铜蜘蛛，看着它们沿着山道向上攀爬，看着它们涌入石室的每一个角落。

"叩门者——"他低声念出这三个字。

"三百年前，达·芬奇把'它们'留在了机械神教里。"屠龙者圣乔治说，"每一只蜘蛛都是一扇门。"

"叩门者——是连接每一扇门的钥匙。"

"现在——"它转向西泽尔，"所有的门都将为你打开。"

石室角落里的黄铜齿轮开始以此前三倍的速度转动。

石室外的山道上，更多的青铜蜘蛛正从裂缝中钻出。

而王屋山的天空——

正在被一层暗金色的薄雾笼罩。

【English】
Chapter 240 — The Pact of the Dragonbird and the Red Lotus

The last motes of the projection drifted down through the tangle of roots and were swallowed.

The owl-mask, sketched in pale cinder-light a moment before, had been rubbed out of the air. Only a faint ember-red afterimage lingered against the stone wall, like a thumbprint of heat, and that too was gone.

"Three days."

The synthesized voice was already at the bottom of its breath. The last syllable thinned into a filament, and the filament drew itself out of the chamber through the root, and then there was nothing.

The hum of the roots returned. It had been there all along, of course — that low, unhurried pulse, the heartbeat of something that had outlived every dynasty and would outlive the next. The brass cogs set into the roots turned, slow and sweet, their teeth etched with Sanskrit so fine it looked like a rash of frost. When metal met metal, the chamber said, *click*. When a thousand cogs said it together, the chamber said, *hum*.

Chu Shunhua was the first to move.

He slid the Kuílóng-horn sword back into its scabbard. The motion was unhurried; the sound of steel against lacquer filled the chamber with an unlikely softness.

"Three hundred years ago, men wanted to build a god," he said. "Three hundred years later, men still want to build a god. Human nature, it seems, has not changed at all."

"He did not want to build a god," Cesare said.

Chu Shunhua turned his head.

"He wanted to build a god that obeyed him," Cesare said. He had not lifted his gaze. He was watching the Minerva chief's badge at his wrist catch the dim light. "He was wrong. Gods do not obey."

"Then what was he building?"

"A vessel."

Chu Shunhua was quiet for the length of a held breath.

"My mother," he said, "on the night she died, said — *wait for him to come*."

"Wait for whom?"

"She did not say."

Cesare looked up.

Their eyes met in the dark.

"You have been waiting," Cesare said, "for seventeen years."

"So have you," Chu Shunhua said.

The chamber's dim-gold light cut both their faces in two. The bright half; the half the roots hid.

"Lord Regent Chu," Cesare said.

"Major Cesare," Chu Shunhua said.

Two titles, so formal they were almost cruel, dropped into the hum of the roots.

Then Cesare turned and walked toward the back of the chamber.

"My mother waited also," he said, without turning. "She is buried in Florence. Two words on the headstone — *heretic*. The Pope had it carved."

"She never went to see the grave."

"Neither did I."

Chu Shunhua followed.

"Who was she waiting for?" he asked.

"I do not know," Cesare said. "But on the night she died, she said to Bielle — *wait for the child who comes from the East*."

Chu's step missed a beat.

"From the East," he repeated.

"Yes."

They picked their way between the roots. The dark-gold metal struts crossed overhead like a vault whose architect had died before he could finish his own name. Light fell through the gaps in narrow blades across their pauldrons. The floor tiles were incised with Sanskrit and, everywhere, with the inverted five-pointed star; under each step the stone shivered with the slow pulse of the World Tree.

The cemetery was a clearing at the back of the chamber, ringed with roots.

Seven headstones.

Each was carved with the inverted five-pointed star and the gear. The faces of the stones had been wet for a long time with the dark-gold liquid the roots wept, and where the metal ended and the marble began you could no longer tell. The years had been eating the boundary.

Before the tallest of the headstones stood a square pillar of white marble.

No words.

No name.

Polished to a dark mirror; the dim-gold of the roots stared back out of it.

Chu Shunhua stopped before the pillar.

"This is where my parents are," he said. "My father had no surname. My mother was the last of the Eastern Star-seers. The stone is blank — by our tradition, the name of a guardian must not be left in stone."

"Stone remembers anyway."

He laid his palm against the cool surface of the pillar.

"She was leaving me when I was eleven," he said. "The last thing she said, with my hand in hers — *he will come*."

"Who?"

"She did not say a name." Chu Shunhua drew from his sleeve a small silver box, the lid of which was chased with a five-petalled white lotus. "She left me only this."

He opened the lid.

Inside, on a bed of black silk, lay a copper talisman. The face of it was engraved with the inverted five-pointed star and the gear of his mother's house. The back was a thicket of Star-seer script, each character no wider than a hair.

"I have worn it seventeen years," Chu Shunhua said, and laid it in Cesare's open palm.

The moment the talisman touched his skin, the gold-tubing at the back of Cesare's neck went hot.

Not the warmth of a metal that had been held. A sympathy. It came up out of the talisman, traced the lines of his palm, climbed into the bones of his wrist, ran the length of his arm, and lodged in his shoulder-blade.

Cesare's pupils changed.

Violet rose from the bottom of his iris, threaded through with gold, like a circuit lit. The light in his eyes was not a light. It was a fact.

Chu Shunhua's eyes were changing in the same breath. A deep purple-gold, with a vertical bar of gold through the centre of each pupil, as if some old seal had been pressed into them from behind.

"When my mother died, I was four years old," Cesare said. "I do not remember her ever holding me."

"But you came," Chu said.

"I did."

"I, too, have waited seventeen years."

Cesare held out his right hand.

The knight's clasp.

Fingertip to fingertip.

The gold tubing at the back of his neck went hot again, and at the same time something behind Chu's neck — some unseen point, a place where the body remembers what the mind does not — answered it. The heat was on the inside of the skin.

And then —

The chamber lit.

Not with the dim gold it had lived in.

With green.

A deep green. The green that lives at the heart of an old tree-ring. It came up out of the thickest of the dark-gold roots under their feet, not as a flare, not as an explosion, but as a soaking, as springwater soaks a cracked riverbed. The green crept along the grain of the metal, into every face of every strut, every cog, every rib. The brass began to turn three times as fast, then five, and the walls themselves began to turn, and the whole chamber sounded, suddenly, like a machine that had been sleeping for three hundred years and had been, at last, woken.

"The Tree is —" Alfonso stepped back. The spider-nest chronometer at his wrist threw a rash of red sparks into the green.

"It is not answering," Don Juan said, his breath held. "It is in sympathy."

Where the two hands clasped, the chamber's brightest light gathered.

Not gold.

Not violet.

A third colour. A blue-gold, the colour of copper under moonlight.

"Eastern and Western holders of the broken branches," Valentina said softly, and her emerald eyes held the green, "recognising each other, for the first time."

A pillar of light — fine as a hair — rose from between their palms, threaded up through the crossing roots, and was lost in the dark above.

It lasted ten full seconds.

Then it withdrew.

The chamber settled back into its dim gold.

Chu Shunhua let go.

Across the centre of his palm was a brand, fresh, blue-gold.

Cesare's palm carried the same.

"From this moment —" Chu said.

"East and West, an alliance," Cesare said.

They stepped back, together.

"The plan," Cesare said. "Three days. We have three days."

"Speak."

"First." Cesare touched the Minerva badge at his wrist. "The Brahma-Fall antimatter device must be assembled. Verolan has brought the core components to the foot of Wangwu Mountain. Assembly is three days at the minimum."

"For three days, no one of the Original Sin Bureau is to come within a league of this chamber."

"Second." Cesare turned to Valentina. "I will need a force that can hold the Omega Prototypes in the open."

Valentina stood at Don Juan's shoulder. Her long fair hair caught the dim gold and gave it back as cold light.

"Last night I put a call through on the Yenisei military band to my father the Tsar," she said. "He consents to send the Divine-Wrath Knightly Order — a fully mechanised division — in support."

"How many?"

"Eight thousand modified Divine-Wrath Mark III exoskeletons. Forty great steam-trebuchets." She paused. "And an oral message from the Tsar."

"Which is?"

"*Tell Cesare Borgia that he owes me a grandchild from the banks of the Yenisei.*"

The chamber was quiet for two seconds.

"…" Don Juan opened his mouth, then closed it.

"Objection noted," Quintilian murmured.

"Third." Chu Shunhua took the floor. "Once the device is assembled, the blood of the perfect adapter will be required to detonate it."

He looked at Cesare.

"The trigger is in the back of your mother's pendant."

Cesare nodded.

"I know."

"Do you know the cost?"

"I know."

"Half the Xia will vanish from the map."

"I know."

"Then it is decided."

Chu Shunhua drew two swords from the scabbard at his hip.

One was the Kuílóng-horn.

The other — a serpent.

The blade curved like a snake, narrow and long, washed in a pale green rust; the grip was bound in a faded green silk.

"This serpent-blade," Chu said, "I had my smith forge to the design philosophy of the Wraith-Knight Mark II. It is the matched piece of Leonardo's Green Serpent, kept in the Saint George armouries."

He held it out.

Cesare took it.

Left hand: the Green Serpent. Right hand: the Wraith serpent-blade.

In his grip the two swords sang — one low, one clear — as if two old voices, parted for centuries, were answering each other across a room.

"Thank you," Cesare said.

"Quid pro quo," Chu said.

Cesare drew from inside his coat a fragment.

Silver-white. The shape of a spearhead. The broken face was incised with Latin and Old Sanskrit, layered through each other. At the centre, a single point of pale violet light.

A fragment of the Holy Lance of Longinus.

The badge of office of the Captain of the Seraph Knights.

"This is what my father left me," Cesare said, and laid it in Chu's palm. "On the night he died he said — *this will be of use, one day*."

The instant Chu's hand closed on the fragment —

His purple-gold pupils jumped.

The pale violet at the heart of the spearhead spoke to the gold bar at the centre of his iris, and the light of the fragment went running up the lines of his palm to the wrist, halted for one beat at the pulse, and ran back into the metal.

"…" Chu looked down at the fragment in his hand. He was quiet for three seconds.

"This thing —" he said, "I think I have seen it in a dream."

"Perhaps not a dream," Cesare said.

Chu tucked the fragment into his sleeve.

"I will see that it is kept by the heir of the Eastern Star-seers."

"As you wish."

They looked at each other.

Then, at the same time, they nodded.

It was at this moment that a sound reached the chamber.

Not a footfall.

A bootfall.

A metal bootfall.

Many metal bootfalls, in order, in step.

An old man in the dress of a court eunuch stepped out from between the roots. He wore a deep red eunuch's robe and a black cap; his face was a handful of dry lines. In both hands he bore, as if it were heavier than he was, a bolt of imperial-yellow silk, unrolled.

"Imperial edict —" he sang out.

Chu Shunhua turned.

"Chu Shunhua receives the edict."

The old man unrolled the silk.

"By the Grace of Heaven, the Emperor decrees —

"Regent Duke Chu Shunhua, who for many years bore the late Emperor's trust and served as the empire's guide, ought by rights to have given his life in dutiful return.

"However, of late, word has reached the throne that Chu Shunhua has trafficked in secret with the Western barbarians, intending the overthrow of the realm. The crime admits of no pardon.

"Let Chu Shunhua be stripped, this day, of every office and title, and reduced to a commoner.

"Let any subject of Great Xia, soldier or civilian, who takes him, be rewarded with ten thousand taels of gold, and raised to a marquisate.

"Thus by Imperial command."

The old man's voice went on reverberating in the chamber.

When it was done, Chu Shunhua's face had not moved.

"Is that the end of it?" he asked.

"Y-yes, Commoner Chu."

"Good."

The old man held the silk forward with both hands.

Chu did not take it.

"Take it back," he said.

"Yes, sir, yes."

"Tell Chu Zhaohua —" Chu said, "that when our mother died, seventeen years ago, he came to her."

The old man's body trembled, very slightly.

"She said to him — *wait for your elder brother to come home*."

"He did not understand."

"I did not understand."

"Now I understand."

The old man gathered the silk to his chest and walked backwards out of the chamber, his steps quick, as a man walks away from a thing that might still bite him.

Chu Shunhua turned back.

As if nothing had happened.

"The third matter," he said.

Before the words were out of his mouth, another set of footsteps — quick, hard, military — came running down the passage. A young officer in the lacquered plate of the Wraith-Knights ducked through the last of the roots and dropped to one knee.

"My lord Regent —"

"I am no longer the Regent," Chu said. "The edict has just been read."

"…" The officer looked up.

"Speak your business."

"Yes, sir." The officer drew from his breast a sealed letter and a small silver box. "Ye Suli has raised a rebellion at the Tongtian Palace. His Majesty has been confined. The order has gone out to disband the Wind-Forest Mountain corps. I was sent to bring you the word."

"Wind-Forest Mountain, deputy commander Bai Yuanlang, hearing," Chu said, taking the letter. "Confidential order."

"Sir."

"Carry this to the whole corps: the edict disbanding us is a forged one. Chu Zhaohua is being held prisoner by Ye Suli."

"Sir!"

"March south, by the quickest road, to Luoyang. Free the Emperor."

"Sir!" Bai got to his feet, then stopped. "But — the Omega Prototypes are moving on Wangwu."

"Hold them," Chu said. "Three days."

"Within three days I will put every Wraith-Knight of the Wind-Forest Mountain corps on this spot."

"Understood, sir."

Bai turned and went out, fast.

Chu Shunhua opened the silver box.

Inside lay a single sheet of paper folded in the shape of a lotus. The paper was faintly luminous, as if a thin gold had been laid into it; the edge was inlaid with a ring of gear-work so fine it could only have been made for looking at.

"This is my mother's other relic," Chu said, and held the paper lotus out to Cesare. "She said to me — *when he comes, give him this as well*."

Cesare took it.

It was warm in his hand. Warm, and faintly pulsing, as a small heart pulses.

"It holds thirty-seven prayers," Chu said. "Each one of them will blunt, by some measurable degree, the way the consciousness of the broken branch of the World Tree eats at the nervous system." He paused, faintly. "The first of them, I am told, is the one your mother used to read to you as a child — *we are hard pressed on every side, yet not crushed*."

Cesare was quiet.

He would have said something else. He did not.

Chu Shunhua set a hand on his shoulder.

"Do not die."

"I will not."

It was at this moment that the spider-nest chronometer on Alfonso's wrist gave a high, thin whine.

Every head in the chamber turned.

The dial, which a moment ago had been showing *communications lost* in a slow red flicker, was throwing letters at the air.

*Mechanical-Cult Knocker corps, full muster. Move to Wangwu. Protect the new Divine-Envoy vessel.*

Alfonso looked up.

"Boss," he said. "There is something trying to speak to me."

"What is it?"

"I do not know," Alfonso said, watching the gear-marks in the dial keep ticking over. "It calls itself the Bronze Spider."

A small, dry sound of metal against metal drifted out of the dark at the corner of the chamber.

They looked.

A tall figure was stepping out of the tangle of roots.

It was not a man.

It was an armour.

Saint George the Dragon-slayer.

But not the war-engine they had fought beside, the one that had looked as if it would tear the world in two.

Its limbs were folded. The wings on its pauldrons were closed against its back. A thin dust lay on the dark-gold plate. With each step, the foot left a shallow print in the stone, as if the armour carried the weight of three hundred years.

It stopped, before Cesare and Chu Shunhua.

And it —

— went down on one knee.

A posture it had not taken once in a hundred years.

"Perfect adapter," said a voice from inside the armour. The voice had the clean, meshing sound of small gears running true; but under that, somewhere far back, an old humanity.

"I have waited for you a long time."

"Who are you?" Cesare asked.

"One of the founders of the Mechanical Cult."

"A pupil of Leonardo Borgia."

"Three hundred years ago I left a part of my mind in this harness, to wait for the perfect Divine-Envoy."

"Now you are here."

"I will assist you —"

The helmet lifted, slowly. There was no face under it. There were two faint blue-green lights.

"— to close the Black-Iron Gate."

"— to bring down the World Tree."

"— to end three hundred years of madness."

Every person in the chamber had stopped breathing.

"Do you have a name?" Cesare asked.

"I did, once," said the old voice. "But names are the kind of thing that vanishes."

"You need only know — I was a pupil of Leonardo."

"And the elder brother of Elena."

"Three hundred years ago the three of us founded the Mechanical Cult, meaning to save mankind with the force of mechanism."

"But the Pope went mad."

"And he went mad with him."

"Three hundred years of madness. It is time it was ended."

The armour rose, slowly.

"Let us begin."

It was at this moment that the chamber was filled with the sound of metal on metal.

Not one sound.

A thousand.

A hundred thousand.

They ran to the mouth of the chamber and looked out, down the long slope of the mountain.

From the foot of Wangwu to its waist, from its waist to its crown —

The slope was alive with brass.

Spiders.

Spiders the size of a thumb's nail, by the tens of thousands, pouring out of the cracks in the rock, scuttling up the path, sliding through the gaps in the roots, climbing into the chamber by every gap and seam in the wall. Each carried a small quicksilver-thermic chip set in the belly. Each had, in the hollow of its head, two green points of light.

*Mechanical-Cult Knocker corps, full muster —*

*— protect the new Divine-Envoy vessel.*

The voice was not coming from any one of them.

It was coming from all of them at once.

As if they were the limbs of a single mind.

Cesare stood in the light of the green points and watched the swarm come up the mountain. He watched it pour over the path, pour into the chamber, pour down the dark between the gears of the wall.

"Knockers," he said, under his breath.

"Three hundred years ago," Saint George said, "Leonardo left *them* inside the Mechanical Cult. Every spider is a door."

"The Knocker is the key to every door."

"Now —" it turned its head to Cesare, "— every door will open for you."

The brass cogs at the corners of the chamber began to turn, three times as fast as they had been turning.

Down the slope, more spiders were coming up out of the cracks.

And above Wangwu —

A thin dark-gold mist was drawing itself across the sky.

第241章 鬼武者的防线

【中文】
第241章 鬼武者的防线

西泽尔站在石室入口，秋风裹着暗金色的薄雾从山口灌进来。那些青铜蜘蛛仍在往山上爬，从王屋山的每一条裂缝中涌出，密集得像是地底流淌出一条金属的河。远处山道上传来整齐的马蹄声和蒸汽阀门开启的嗤嗤声，那不是欧米茄的脚步声。

是人。

楚舜华大步走出石室，夔龙角剑悬在腰侧，他抬眼望向山脚的方向，薄雾中隐约可见一列列黑色的旗帜在移动。

"风林山军团到了。"他说。

山脚下的缓坡上，一百台漆黑的重型机动甲胄排成了三道横列。它们的体型不如炽天使那般夸张，但每一台都厚实沉稳，头部雕刻成夔龙首的形状，龙睛处镶嵌的红水银晶片在雾气中发出暗红色的微光。右臂加装小型蒸汽连铳，左臂是精钢重盾，胸甲浮雕着鎏金夔龙纹，仿佛一头头蛰伏的铁兽。

这就是鬼武者Ⅱ型。

它们是楚舜华用三年时间打造的成果，每一台都能单手举起千斤重的镇国鼎。首批一百台已经完成第一轮实战测试，今天是它们第一次真正意义上面对成群的敌人。

在甲胄队列的后方，风林山军团的夔龙马骑兵排成两翼。那些马匹通体红如朱砂，额前断角打磨过的夔龙马在雾气中喷着白气，马背上的骑士身着玄色轻甲，佩戴着夏国制式的长刀和短铳。

再往后，三十门小型蒸汽炮架在山道的弯折处，炮口朝下，正对着从东方平原延伸上来的官道。炮管由精钢铸成，蒸汽锅炉在炮组后面冒着浓烟，炮手们正在用铁楔固定炮架。

楚舜华沿着山道往下走，脚步沉稳，石阶上的露水被他踩得粉碎。他没有穿甲，鬼武者原型机的面甲夹在臂弯里，但从他走上山道的那一刻起，山道两侧的碎石开始轻轻震动，仿佛连地底都感知到了他的存在。

世界树残根意识正在与他共鸣。

"停。"楚舜华抬起手。

百台鬼武者Ⅱ型同时停步，蒸汽阀门关闭的嗤嗤声连成一片。

"第一道防线，由鬼武者Ⅱ型正面承压，夔龙马骑兵两翼包抄，蒸汽炮组远程覆盖。"楚舜华站在半山腰，声音不高，但每一个字都清晰地传到山下，"所有人不准越过山脚那道石坎。没有我的命令，任何人不得擅自出击。"

他转身望向西泽尔："我守前面三天。三天之内，一只欧米茄也不能从山道上踏过去。"

西泽尔点了点头，没有说多余的话。

石室内部，薇若兰已经展开了那张从翡冷翠带来的梵天陨落反物质炸弹设计图。图纸在地面上铺开，几乎占满了半个石室，黄铜零件的编号密密麻麻地排列在每一行说明文字旁边。碧儿从旁边递过一只锡封匣，匣子打开后，数十枚精密的红水银雷管整齐地排列在棉垫上。

"零件下午到。"薇若兰抬起头，"我已经联系了密涅瓦机关运输机，它们会从翡冷翠空投核心组件。"

"三天够吗？"西泽尔问。

"必须够。"薇若兰说，"炸弹的引爆密钥在……"

她停了一下，看向西泽尔的胸口。

琳琅夫人的银莲花项链坠，就挂在那里。

西泽尔伸手按住项链坠，金属冰凉。

"我知道。"他说。

石室深处的屠龙者圣乔治缓缓起身，金属关节发出沉重的摩擦声。它走到石室入口处，残存的意识通过青铜机械蜘蛛的网络向整座王屋山扩散。

"我们守侧翼。"它说。

第一波欧米茄原型体群在正午时分到达王屋山脚下。

它们从东方平原的方向涌来，远远望去像是一条暗金色的河流在地面上蔓延。近了才能看清每一架的细节——高度超过五米，全身覆盖暗金色装甲板，胸腔内嵌着一颗跳动的红水银核心，面甲的竖缝里透出灼热的金色光。它们的关节是青铜结构，关节表面刻满了世界树神经祈祷文的细密铭文，每动一下，铭文就闪一下暗金色的光。

超过一百架。

它们整齐地排列在山脚下的平原上，没有立刻发起冲锋。

"先遣侦察型。"西泽尔站在半山腰说，"它们在标记我们的信号。"

话音未落，领头的三架欧米茄原型体同时抬起了面甲，竖缝中射出三道暗金色的光柱，笔直地扫过山脚防线。光柱扫过之处，地面的青石被烧出焦黑的痕迹，蒸汽炮组的一门火炮被光柱切过，整个炮管从中间熔断，断裂处还在滴着橘红色的铁水。

"开火。"楚舜华的声音很平静。

三十门小型蒸汽炮同时发射，炮弹在弧线最高点划出三十道灰白色的烟迹，然后密集地砸在欧米茄原型体群中。爆炸的火光在平原上此起彼伏，泥土和石块被掀到半空，暗金色的装甲板在爆炸中出现了凹痕——但几秒钟之后，凹痕消失了，神经纤维在装甲板下流动，自动修复了每一处损伤。

"自愈神经纤维。"阿方索在石室入口处低声说，"常规武器伤不了它们。"

楚舜华没有回应，他举起了夔龙角剑。

山脚下的百台鬼武者Ⅱ型同时启动了蒸汽核心。一百股青蓝色的蒸汽从背部排气口喷出，在秋日的阳光下像是给山脚铺上了一层薄雾。它们开始向前推进，步伐整齐，每一步都在地面上留下深深的足印。

楚舜华走在最前面。

他没有穿甲，他不需要。

当鬼武者Ⅱ型推进到山脚石坎处时，欧米茄原型体群也动了。

一百多架暗金色的巨人同时迈步，它们的速度远比想象中快，关节的青铜结构在高速运动中发出刺耳的摩擦声。它们不是杂乱地冲锋，而是以莲花状的阵型包围过来，每三架为一组，互相掩护着侧翼。

楚舜华闭上了眼睛。

世界树残根意识在他的神经通路中涌动着，王屋山地下数百米范围内的每一丝震动都清晰地传入他的感知。他能"看见"每一架欧米茄原型体的移动轨迹——不是通过视觉，而是通过地层深处传来的震动。

他睁开眼睛。

"第一组，左前方十二步，三架。"

鬼武者Ⅱ型第一排的二十台甲胄同时举起精钢重盾。

三架欧米茄原型体从左前方的雾气中冲出，它们的右臂化为了巨大的金属刃——那是欧米茄原型体独有的变形能力，暗金色的装甲板在战斗形态下重组为各种武器。

刃落下。

二十面精钢重盾同时承接。

"轰——"

整座山都在震动。重盾表面的鎏金夔龙纹在冲击下扭曲变形，但二十面盾没有一面被切开。鬼武者Ⅱ型的设计初衷就是承受重击，盾牌的内部结构采用五层交错锻造，外两层是影金属，中间三层是硬金，最内层还嵌着一层极薄的冰原寒玉碎料。

"反击。"楚舜华说。

后排的鬼武者Ⅱ型蒸汽连铳齐射，密集的弹雨倾泻在三架欧米茄原型体的胸口。弹头撞击在暗金色装甲上，火花四溅，但自愈神经纤维迅速修复了每一处弹坑。

不过楚舜华要的并不是弹头。

他要的是一瞬间的停顿。

在这三架欧米茄原型体被弹雨压制的两秒钟里，楚舜华动了。

他像一头猎豹那样从石坎上跃下，夔龙角剑出鞘，剑身保留着夔龙角天然纹路如凝固闪电。落地的瞬间，世界树残根意识向他传来了一个清晰的画面——右侧那架欧米茄原型体的右臂关节处，是装甲板拼接的缝隙，神经纤维在缝隙下流淌。

楚舜华的身体先于意识做出了反应。

夔龙角剑刺出。

剑尖从暗金色装甲板的缝隙中钻入，贯穿了神经纤维密集的关节腔。

"嗤——"

一股金红色的高温液体从伤口喷出，那是欧米茄原型体的体液。右臂连同变形后的金属刃从空中脱落，在地上砸出一个坑。

楚舜华没有停。

他旋身，夔龙角剑在空中划出一道闪电般的弧线，第二剑从另一架原型体的颈部装甲缝隙切入。

两剑。

两架欧米茄原型体失去了右臂。

第三架试图后退，但鬼武者Ⅱ型的蒸汽连铳已经再次齐射，弹雨封锁了它的退路。楚舜华从它的正面掠过，夔龙角剑斜劈而下，从肩关节一直切到胸腔侧面。

红水银核心在胸腔内剧烈跳动了一下。

然后——

"轰！"

那架原型体从胸腔处断裂为两半，红水银核心在地面上滚动，滚出十几米远才停下。暗金色的光从核心中泄出，核心表面的纹路闪烁了几下，然后彻底暗了下去。

楚舜华站在三架残骸之间，夔龙角剑的剑尖还滴着金红色的液体。

他抬眼望向山道下方——更多的欧米茄原型体正在向山脚涌来。

"换剑。"石室入口处，西泽尔把青蛇剑抛下山道。

楚舜华单手接住。

青蛇剑窄而长，剑身覆着淡绿色的铜锈，剑柄缠着褪色的绿绢。它和夔龙角剑刚好配对——一长一短，一古一新，一弯一直。

楚舜华将两柄剑分别握在双手中。

夔龙角剑在右，青蛇剑在左。

"双龙斩。"他低声说。

就在这时，东方的天际线上出现了一个新的声音——不是欧米茄的金属摩擦声，而是蒸汽轮机的轰鸣。

巨大的暗银色飞艇从云层中钻出，飞艇的气囊上铸着叶尼塞忍冬花徽记。飞艇的腹部悬挂着数十台改装神怒Ⅲ型甲胄，甲胄在风中摇晃着，但每一个甲胄骑士都牢牢地握住了固定索。

飞艇后面是叶尼塞神怒骑士团全机械化师团。

神怒Ⅲ型甲胄排成整齐的方阵，暗银色装甲在阳光下闪耀着冷光。每一台高三米二，胸腔都嵌着叶尼塞王妃遗物改造的红水银晶块核心。重型蒸汽坦克在两翼展开，履带碾过平原上的碎石，炮塔转动着寻找目标。

瓦莲京娜的改装神怒Ⅲ型走在师团最前方，她的甲胄右臂上嵌着一门比普通型号更大的炮管。

龙吼炮。

瓦莲京娜抬起右臂，龙吼炮的炮口对准了山脚平原上最密集的欧米茄原型体群。

"全师团听令。"她的声音通过密涅瓦最高级别加密通讯传遍了王屋山。

"第一波欧米茄群——"

"歼灭。"

龙吼炮开火。

炮口的火焰像是从地狱深处喷出的岩浆，暗红色的光柱笔直地贯穿了五架欧米茄原型体。光柱所过之处，装甲板不是被击穿，而是直接汽化。五架原型体在光柱中化为了飞散的金属颗粒，红水银核心还没来得及从胸腔中弹出就一起被高温熔毁了。

神怒Ⅲ型方阵同时开火。

破甲锤和叶尼塞战斧在阳光下闪着寒光，重型蒸汽坦克的炮塔齐射，炮弹在欧米茄原型体群中炸开。神怒飞艇从空中投下了密集的燃烧弹，燃烧弹在地面上炸出一片火海。

五架。

十架。

二十架。

第一波欧米茄原型体群在东西方联军的火力下急剧减少，残存的原型体试图向后退却。

就在它们后退的瞬间——

"现在。"屠龙者圣乔治说。

成千上万只青铜蜘蛛从山道两侧的岩壁缝隙中涌出，它们不是向前冲锋，而是沿着地面向后退的欧米茄原型体群爬去。每一只蜘蛛的腹部红水银微晶都开始剧烈闪烁，它们张开腿部的青铜关节，关节内部发出一种低沉的嗡鸣声。

嗡鸣声汇合在一起，形成了一道宽频电磁脉冲。

这不是阿方索电子蛛巢那种针对电子设备的干扰波——这是针对神经接驳系统的干扰波。

青铜蜘蛛们的嗡鸣声直击每一架欧米茄原型体的核心，那些暗金色的巨人突然停下了脚步。它们的自愈神经纤维剧烈抽搐，装甲板下的流动中断了，胸腔中的红水银核心跳动的频率也开始紊乱。

欧米茄原型体群——暂时瘫痪了。

"三分钟。"屠龙者圣乔治说，"只有三分钟。"

楚舜华没有浪费一秒钟。

他带着夔龙角剑和青蛇剑冲入了瘫痪的原型体群中，双剑交替挥出。右剑的夔龙角纹路如凝固闪电，左剑的青蛇剑身弯曲如蛇，每一剑都精准地切入装甲板缝隙——

一台。

两台。

三台。

每一台的红水银核心都被他或劈或刺地击穿，暗金色的光从破碎的胸腔中泄出。

瓦莲京娜的龙吼炮再次开火，又是五架原型体在光柱中汽化。

神怒Ⅲ型方阵趁乱冲入残存的原型体群中，叶尼塞战斧和破甲锤在暗金色的装甲上留下了密集的伤痕。重型蒸汽坦克从两翼包抄，履带碾过倒下原型体的残骸，炮塔对天上的欧米茄飞艇型原型体开火。

三分钟后。

青铜蜘蛛的嗡鸣声停止了，它们的红水银微晶全部耗尽，数千只蜘蛛同时瘫软在地，再也无法动弹。

但欧米茄原型体群已经所剩无几了。

楚舜华站在满地的残骸之间，双剑垂在身侧，剑刃上滴着金红色的液体。他的玄色长袍被烧出了几个洞，露出里面影金属丝线编织的防火内衬。

"第一波——"他转身望向山道上方，"清理完毕。"

西泽尔站在半山腰，看着山下那片焦黑的战场。

他什么都没说。

但他按在银莲花项链坠上的手指收紧了一下。

石室内，薇若兰正在用精密的校准仪校准梵天陨落炸弹的第一个红水银雷管。阿方索在帮她接线，唐璜负责搬运零件，昆提良在最外围站岗，手中的强化版奥古斯都秘银重盾在阳光下反射着冷光。碧儿跪在图纸旁，用极细的笔在零件清单上做标记。

密涅瓦机关的运输机刚刚飞过王屋山的上空，第一批核心组件从机舱中被空投下来。橙色的降落伞在暗金色的薄雾中缓缓飘落。

三天。

他们有三天。

就在这时——

阿方索抬起头，他的蜘蛛巢腕表突然发出了刺耳的警报声。

"又有欧米茄信号。"他说，"数量——"

他的声音停顿了。

"多少？"薇若兰问。

阿方索看着腕表上疯狂跳动的数字，脸色第一次变了。

"超过一千架。"

西泽尔从半山腰向下望去。

东方平原的尽头，第二波暗金色的河流正在向王屋山涌来。那条河流比第一波宽了十倍，暗金色的光在雾气中连成一片，像是地平线上燃起了一场金属的野火。

而在第二波的最前方——

一台特殊的原型体走在所有原型体的最前面。

那台原型体的胸腔内嵌着的不是普通的红水银核心，而是一颗硕大的暗金色晶块，晶块表面刻满了世界树神经祈祷文。晶块上方悬浮着一个全息投影。

投影中，一个人戴着银色猫头鹰面具，露出的下颌和右手都是精密的机械假肢。

他看着王屋山的方向。

"新弥赛亚——"投影中传出冰冷而机械的声音。

"——我来了。"

【English】
Chapter 241 — The Wraith-Knight Line

Cesare stood at the mouth of the stone chamber while autumn wind carried a thin gold-tinged mist down from the pass. The bronze spiders were still climbing. They poured from every fissure in Mount Wangwu, shoulder to shoulder, so many that the rock itself seemed to be running upward in a river of metal. Farther down the mountain path, beyond the curtain of fog, came the orderly percussion of hooves and the thin hissing of steam valves opening — not, this time, the footfalls of Omegas.

Men.

Chu Shunhua strode out of the chamber past him, the Kuilong-horn sword riding easy at his hip. He lifted his chin toward the foot of the mountain. Through the mist, banners moved in black, regular as a pulse.

"The Fenglin Mountain Legion has come," he said.

Below them, on the gentler slope at the mountain's foot, a hundred heavy mobile armors were drawn up in three ranks across the trail. They were not as large as a Seraph, and not built to swagger. Each was thick and planted, head carved in the likeness of a Kuilong dragon, the eyes set with small chips of red mercury that glowed a sullen crimson through the fog. A light steam repeater rode the right arm. A heavy shield of fine steel, the left. Across the breastplates, gilt Kuilong reliefs had been tooled into the metal, so that the machines, motionless, looked less like war engines than iron beasts dozing on a chain.

Ghost Warrior Mark II.

Three years in the making. Each one capable of lifting a single-handed the thousand-catty Ding of the Empire. The first hundred had cleared their first round of field testing. Today was the first day any of them would face an enemy in earnest.

Behind the armor line, the Kuilong-horse cavalry of the Fenglin Mountain Legion fanned into two wings. The horses were the color of cinnabar, every one, and the broken horn of the breed had been polished smooth at the forehead. Steam huffed from their nostrils in the mist. Their riders wore matte-black light armor and carried the long blade and short pistol of the Summer Country pattern.

Further back, thirty small steam cannon had been wheeled into the bend of the mountain path, muzzles pointed downhill toward the official road that climbed out of the eastern plain. The barrels were fine cast steel. The boilers behind them belched thick smoke. The crews were driving iron wedges under the trails to seat them into the stone.

Chu Shunhua began the descent. His steps were unhurried, the dew on the steps crushed to nothing underfoot. He was not wearing armor. The faceplate of a Ghost Warrior prototype was tucked under one arm. But from the moment he came out onto the path, the loose scree at either side began to tremble, a low almost-not-there shudder, as if the bones of the mountain had decided to take note of him.

The remnant consciousness of the World Tree was resonating with him.

"Halt," Chu Shunhua said, lifting one hand.

A hundred Ghost Warriors stopped as one. The hiss of closing steam valves ran down the line like a single drawn breath.

"First line. The Mark IIs will absorb the frontal pressure. The Kuilong horse on both wings, sweep. The steam batteries will provide overhead fire." He stood at the mid-slope. His voice was not raised, and yet every word reached the foot of the mountain without effort. "No man crosses the stone kerb below us. No one sallies without my word."

He turned to look at Cesare.

"I hold the front for three days. In three days, not a single Omega sets foot on the path."

Cesare nodded. He had nothing to add.

Inside the chamber, Violaine had already spread out the design drawings for the Brahma's Fall antimatter bomb they had brought out of Florence. The plans covered nearly half the stone floor, brass-part callouts crowded in long ranks beside every line of explanatory text. Bielle passed her a tin-sealed case, and when the lid came off dozens of precision red-mercury detonators lay neat in the cotton padding, row on row.

"Parts arrive this afternoon," Violaine said without looking up. "I've already spoken with the Minerva corps transport. They'll drop the core assemblies over Mount Wangwu from the air."

"Will three days be enough?" Cesare asked.

"It has to be." She paused. Her gaze went to his chest.

The silver-lotus pendant of the Madam of Linlang hung there, against his breastbone.

Cesare's hand rose to the pendant. The metal was cold under his fingers.

"I know," he said.

From the far end of the chamber, the Dragonslayer Saint George rose. The sound of its metal joints grinding under the strain ran through the stone floor and up into the bones of everyone present. It walked, slowly, to the mouth of the chamber. What remained of its awareness fanned outward through the network of bronze mechanical spiders, and spread down through the whole of Mount Wangwu.

"We hold the flank," it said.

The first wave of Omega prototypes came up to the foot of Mount Wangwu at noon.

They boiled out of the eastern plain. From the slope, they looked at first like a river of dim gold running across the land. It was only when they were closer that you could see what the river was made of. Each one stood over five meters. Every inch of them was plated in dark-gold armor. A red-mercury core throbbed in the chest cavity of each. The vertical slit of the face mask glowed with a hot, almost-white light. The joints were bronze, and the bronze was covered in fine engraved lines — the prayer-texts of the World Tree's neural network, dense and minute, each one flashing a dim gold whenever the joint moved.

Over a hundred of them.

They drew up at the foot of the mountain in good order. They did not charge.

"Forward reconnaissance types," Cesare said, watching from the mid-slope. "They're marking our signal."

As he spoke, the lead three prototypes lifted their faceplates as one. From the vertical slits, three columns of dark-gold light lanced out, perfectly level, sweeping the defense line at the foot of the mountain. Where the beams passed, the bluestone of the path went black and smoking. One of the steam cannon took the edge of a beam cleanly through the barrel. The tube sheared in the middle, and the broken end was dripping a sluggish orange iron.

"Fire," Chu Shunhua said. His voice was calm.

Thirty small steam cannon fired at once. The shells drew thirty pale grey arcs against the sky, hung at the peak, then came down together into the body of the Omega line. Explosions broke across the plain in sequence, throwing dirt and rock into the air. Dimples appeared in the dark-gold armor of a dozen prototypes. Within seconds, the dimples were gone, the neural fibers under the plate flowing like water to mend the wound.

"Self-healing neural fiber," Alfonso murmured from the chamber mouth. "Conventional munitions won't do it."

Chu Shunhua did not answer. He lifted the Kuilong-horn sword.

Down at the foot of the mountain, a hundred Ghost Warriors Mark II came on line. A hundred plumes of pale blue steam blew from the vents on their backs, and in the autumn sun it looked for a moment as if a thin fog had been laid across the mountain's foot. They began to advance, in step, each footfall a heavy print in the dirt.

Chu Shunhua walked at their head.

He wore no armor. He did not need to.

When the Mark IIs came down to the stone kerb, the Omega prototypes moved.

Over a hundred dim-gold giants began to walk forward, all at once, far faster than anyone had prepared for. The bronze of their joints screamed at the speed. They were not charging in a mob. They came on in a lotus formation, each triplet covering the others' flanks, and the shape of the formation closed around the defense like a cupped hand.

Chu Shunhua closed his eyes.

The remnant consciousness of the World Tree surged up through his neural pathways. Every tremor in the rock for several hundred meters under and around the mountain entered his sense at once. He could see, not by sight, the path each prototype was taking — a picture built of nothing but the small earthquakes they made as they moved.

He opened his eyes.

"First section. Twelve paces forward and to the left. Three of them."

The first rank of twenty Ghost Warriors raised their heavy fine-steel shields as one.

Three prototypes broke from the fog on the front-left, and the arms of the lead machine were already no longer arms. The dark-gold armor had flowed and re-knit. Where its right arm had been, there was now a single enormous blade.

The blade came down.

Twenty fine-steel shields took the blow.

The mountain rang. The gilt Kuilong reliefs on the shield faces twisted under the impact, buckled, but none of the twenty shields was cut. The Mark II had been built to take hits. The internal structure of each shield was five layers interleaved — shadow-metal outer, hard-gold middle, and innermost a thin stratum of broken iceplain jade.

"Counter," Chu Shunhua said.

The rear rank of the Mark IIs fired their steam repeaters. The storm of lead walked across the chest of the three prototypes, hammering into the dim-gold plate, throwing bright sparks from every impact. Each pit was healed almost as fast as the bullet made it.

That was not what Chu Shunhua wanted.

He wanted the moment of hesitation.

For the two seconds the three prototypes were pinned by the barrage, Chu Shunhua moved.

He dropped off the kerb like a hunting cat, the Kuilong-horn sword clearing its scabbard in a single motion, the natural grain of the horn still running along the blade like frozen lightning. The World Tree's remnant consciousness sent him, in the same instant, a clean picture: the second prototype in the right flank, the seam in its armor where the plates met at the right shoulder, the dense weave of neural fibers running just under the seam.

His body answered the picture before thought did.

The Kuilong-horn sword went in along the seam, through the gap, and into the joint cavity where the fibers were thickest.

A hiss. A gout of gold-red liquid — the prototype's working fluid — blew from the wound. The right arm, blade and all, came away from the body in the air and struck the ground so hard it left a pit.

Chu Shunhua did not pause.

He turned, and the Kuilong-horn sword drew a second arc through the air, lightning-quick, and bit in through the seam of another prototype's neck plate.

Two strokes. Two prototypes down an arm.

The third tried to back away. The Mark II steam repeaters fired again, and the wall of lead closed the door behind it. Chu Shunhua went through its front in a single stride. The Kuilong-horn sword came down at an angle, from the shoulder joint all the way through the side of the chest cavity.

The red-mercury core inside throbbed once, hard.

Then —

The prototype split in two at the chest, and the core came loose and rolled across the ground, fifteen meters, twenty, before it stopped. A dim-gold light bled from it. The light on the core's surface flickered a few times. Then the core was dark.

Chu Shunhua stood among the three hulks. The point of the Kuilong-horn sword was still dripping the gold-red of the prototype's fluid.

He looked down the mountain. More prototypes were coming up the path.

"Change swords," Cesare said from the chamber mouth, and threw the Green Snake down the slope.

Chu Shunhua caught it one-handed.

The Green Snake was a narrow long blade, older than the Kuilong-horn, the body of it under a faint patina of green copper, the grip wound in a length of faded green silk. It sat against the Kuilong-horn the way a key sits against its lock — one long, one short; one ancient, one new; one straight, one curved.

Chu Shunhua took a sword in each hand.

Kuilong-horn in the right. Green Snake in the left.

"Double-Dragon Cut," he said, low.

A new sound came then, off to the east, on the far side of the plain — not the scream of Omega metal, but the deep rolling thunder of steam turbines. A vast dim-silver airship broke through the cloud layer. The envelope of the ship was cast with the ridged-flower device of the house of Yenisei. Hanging from the keel of the ship, swaying a little in the wind, were dozens of refitted Divine-Wrath Mark III armors. Every rider had a hand on a fixed cable.

Behind the airship came the full mechanized division of the Yenisei Divine-Wrath Order.

The Divine-Wrath Mark IIIs were drawn up in a clean square formation. Their dim-silver plate ran cold under the sun. Each was three meters and a change. The chest of each was set with a red-mercury crystalline core cut from a relic of the Yenisei Queen-Mother. Heavy steam tanks unlimbered at the wings, treads chewing the scree of the plain, turrets swinging as they hunted for targets.

Valentina's refitted Mark III walked at the head of the division. A gun barrel larger than the standard issue was set into the right arm.

The Dragon Roar.

Valentina raised her right arm. The muzzle of the Dragon Roar came to bear on the densest knot of Omega prototypes at the foot of the mountain.

"All division," she said, her voice going out from the topmost cipher of the Minerva network to every corner of Mount Wangwu. "On the first Omega wave —"

"Annihilate."

The Dragon Roar fired.

The flame at the muzzle looked as if it had been drawn up from the lowest pit of the underworld. A column of dim-red light ran straight through five prototypes and out the other side. Where the column passed, the armor did not pierce. It vaporized. The five machines came apart in the column as a scatter of metal grains. Their red-mercury cores had not even had time to leap from the chest cavity. They were gone with the rest of the machine.

The Mark III square fired as one.

Armor-piercing hammers and Yenisei war-axes ran cold and bright in the sun. The heavy steam tanks fired their turrets in unison, the shells bursting in among the prototypes. The Yenisei airship began to drop its incendiaries from above. The bombs hit the plain and made a sea of fire.

Five. Ten. Twenty.

The first Omega wave shrank visibly under the combined fire of the eastern and western armies. The remnants began to back away.

The moment they began to retreat —

"Now," the Dragonslayer Saint George said.

Tens of thousands of bronze mechanical spiders boiled out of the seams in the rock on both sides of the path. They did not charge forward. They went to ground, scuttling on their bellies along the rock toward the retreating prototypes. On the underside of every spider, the tiny red-mercury crystals began to throb and flash. The spiders opened the bronze joints of their legs, and a deep humming rose from inside the joint, building, building, as thousands of the small machines sang in the same key.

The hums met. They locked into a single broadband pulse.

This was not the kind of pulse Alfonso's spider-hive wristwatch put out — a pulse that scrambled electronics. This one was aimed at neural interface systems.

The hum bit into the cores of every Omega prototype in range. The dim-gold giants stopped, all at once. Their self-healing fibers twitched. The flow under the plate stuttered. The red-mercury cores in their chests began to lose their rhythm.

The Omega wave — for the moment — was paralyzed.

"Three minutes," the Dragonslayer Saint George said. "Three minutes only."

Chu Shunhua did not waste a second of them.

He took the Kuilong-horn and the Green Snake and went into the paralyzed line. The two swords worked in alternation, one to the right, one to the left. The grain of the right blade was frozen lightning; the curve of the left blade was a snake through the air. Every stroke found a seam.

One. Two. Three.

The red-mercury core of every machine he reached was broken, hammered or stabbed through. Dim-gold light bled from the open chest cavities of the fallen.

Valentina's Dragon Roar fired a second time. Five more prototypes came apart in the column.

The Mark III square waded into the survivors. The war-axes and armor-piercing hammers left a dense mat of cuts on the dim-gold plating. The heavy steam tanks came in at the wings, treads grinding over the wreckage of the fallen, turrets lifting to find the Omega flyer-types in the air above.

Three minutes later, the hum of the bronze spiders stopped. Every red-mercury crystal in every spider was spent. Thousands of them sagged at once onto the stone, dead and still.

By then, the first wave was nearly gone.

Chu Shunhua stood in the middle of the field of wreckage, both swords hanging at his side, the blades still dripping the gold-red of the prototype's fluid. The dim black robe he wore had been burned through in three places. Underneath, you could see the inner lining — fireproof thread woven of shadow-metal filament.

"First wave —" He turned to look up the slope toward the chamber. "Cleared."

Cesare, at the mid-slope, said nothing.

But the fingers of the hand he had laid on the silver-lotus pendant tightened, just a little.

Inside the chamber, Violaine was using a precision caliper to seat the first red-mercury detonator of the Brahma's Fall device. Alfonso was running leads for her. Don Juan was hauling parts from the piles. Quintilian stood on the outside of the work, guarding, the reinforced Augustan secret-silver shield on his arm throwing back a cold sliver of the daylight that crept in from the mouth of the chamber. Bielle knelt at the corner of the plan, marking off items in the parts list with a fine brush, in small and careful letters.

The Minerva transport had just passed over Mount Wangwu. The first of the core assemblies fell from the bay. Orange parachutes drifted down through the dim-gold mist, slow.

Three days. They had three days.

And then —

Alfonso looked up. The spider-hive on his wrist screamed.

"Another Omega signal," he said. "Number —"

He stopped.

"How many?" Violaine asked, not looking up from the detonator.

Alfonso stared at the numbers jumping and jumping on the dial of the wristwatch. For the first time since Cesare had known him, the color went out of his face.

"Over a thousand."

Cesare looked down the slope.

At the far edge of the eastern plain, a second river of dim gold was moving toward Mount Wangwu. The river was ten times the breadth of the first. The dim-gold light ran together in the mist until it looked as if a metal wildfire had broken out along the horizon.

And at the head of this second wave, in front of every other machine —

A single prototype, set apart from the rest.

The chest of this one did not hold a common red-mercury core. Inside the chest cavity, a great dim-gold crystal was suspended, and the surface of the crystal was covered in the prayer-texts of the World Tree's neural network. Above the crystal, a holo-projection hung in the air.

In the projection, a man. He wore a silver owl mask. The jaw and the right hand that showed beneath the mask were both fine mechanical prostheses.

He was looking toward Mount Wangwu.

"New Messiah," the projection said, in a voice that was cold and machined clean of any human grain. "I am here."

第242章 梵天陨落的零件
