【中文】
第245章 梵天陨落的倒计时

血滴在银莲花项链坠背面的古锡兰文铭文上。

铭文亮了。

不是烛火般摇曳的光，是从石头深处涌出的金红色岩浆般炽烈的光。铭文上每一道古锡兰文的笔画都像被点燃的引信，暗金色的纹路顺着项链坠向外蔓延，流过薇若兰的指尖，流过那个直径一米的球形外壳。

梵天陨落反物质炸弹醒了。

低沉的嗡鸣从球体内部传出，像一头沉睡了三百年的巨兽终于睁开了眼。球体表面刻满的梵文逐一亮起，红水银的能量在金属壳下奔涌，发出暗金色的脉动。球体侧面的凹槽里，一圈古老的红水银刻度正缓缓亮起，像水面涟漪从底层向上攀升。

一圈。两圈。三圈。

薇若兰盯着那刻度，嘴唇无声地动了动。

十分钟。

她抬起头，看着西泽尔。他站在那里，没有穿甲胄，紫瞳中的金龙已经停止旋转但没有完全黯淡。手腕上的血还在一滴一滴地落，每一滴都带着淡淡的金色纹路，滴在暗金色的球面上，发出极其轻微的嗤声，像水滴落在滚烫的铁板上。

"开始了。"薇若兰说。

"嗯。"西泽尔说。

石室的入口处传来沉重的脚步声。

阿方索先走进来，机械手上满是灼烧的痕迹，欧米茄体液正从指缝间缓缓滴落。他身后是昆提良，奥古斯都的重盾只剩下半块，肩甲完全断裂，秘银碎片扎在肌肉里，每走一步都有暗红色的血顺着碎片往外渗。唐璜走最后，蔷薇之鬼的曲刃镰断了半截，左臂软软地垂着，整条袖子被鲜血浸透。

三个人走进石室，看见西泽尔，看见那个发出低沉嗡鸣的暗金色球体，看见球体侧面正在亮起的红水银刻度。

"那就是……"昆提良低声说。

"梵天陨落。"西泽尔说。

沉默了几秒钟。

然后唐璜笑了。他靠在石壁上，断掉的蔷薇之鬼被随手丢在地上，发出清脆的金属碰撞声。

"老板，"唐璜说，"我跟你多少年了？"

"七年。"西泽尔说。

"七年啊。"唐璜说，"七年前我在翡冷翠的画廊里偷一幅画，被你当场抓住。你本来可以把我扭送骑警，但你没有。你说'你的手很稳，跟我走'。"

他抬起那只还能动的右手，看了看。

"我这双手，偷过金币，偷过宝石，偷过贵族少女的心。"唐璜说，"但最好的一次，是偷了一个愿意用我当刺客的老板。"

"来生还要做你的刺客。"他说。

西泽尔看着他，沉默片刻。

"来生我还用你。"西泽尔说。

昆提良重重地哼了一声，把那半块秘银重盾往地上一顿，金属撞击石板的声音在空旷的石室里回响。

"我呢？"昆提良粗声粗气地说，"老板，我跟你的时候，你还是个毛头小子，连甲胄都穿不稳。我教你握枪，教你挡刀，教你怎么用胸膛去接敌人的剑——当然，后来你比我能打了。"

他咧开嘴，露出满嘴沾着血的白牙。

"我这辈子就守过一个人的后背。"昆提良说，"来生还要守。"

西泽尔伸出手，按在昆提良的肩上。肩甲断裂处冰冷的金属触感透过手套传来。

"来生你还守。"西泽尔说。

阿方索一直站在最后，没有说话。他摘下蜘蛛巢腕表，看了看表盘上已经彻底瘫软的八只微型机械蜘蛛残骸，又把它戴回去，扣上表扣的声音很轻。

"老板。"阿方索说。

"嗯。"

"我这辈子修过很多甲胄。"阿方索说，"从翡冷翠贫民区的街边修理铺，到密涅瓦的最高级实验室。但我修得最好的一台，是你的红龙。"

他抬起头，那双总是冷静的灰蓝色眼睛里有一种西泽尔从未见过的东西。

"来生还要做你的机械师。"阿方索说。

西泽尔看着他们三个，看了很久。

"你们都活着出去。"西泽尔说。

"老板——"唐璜想说什么。

"这是命令。"西泽尔说。

沉默。

石室的深处传来另一个人的脚步声。

楚舜华走进石室。

他的鬼武者原型机已经不见了，身上只穿着一件单薄的夏国丝绸内衬，左胸的位置有一块深色的血渍，还在缓慢地扩大。紫瞳金纹几乎完全黯淡了，只有最深处还有一点微弱的金光在挣扎着闪烁。

但他走得很稳，每一步都踩在石室地板的同一个位置，仿佛脚下有一条看不见的直线。

"西泽尔。"楚舜华说。

"舅舅。"西泽尔说。

楚舜华走到他面前停下，从怀里摸出一枚铜色护身符。护身符上刻着带齿轮的倒置五芒星，边缘已经磨得发亮。

"戴上它。"楚舜华说。

西泽尔接过护身符。铜色金属贴上皮肤的瞬间，一股淡淡的暖意从指尖传入血管，像是握住了一只温热的手。

"它会保护你。"楚舜华说，"完美适配者不会轻易死亡。"

他停了一下。

"我母亲……等了你三十年。"楚舜华说，"我等了十七年。她把这枚护身符留给我，让我交给能打开王屋山秘密的人。现在我把它交给你。"

西泽尔把护身符挂在脖子上，铜色金属贴着锁骨，微微发热。

"舅舅。"西泽尔说。

"嗯？"

"新秩序建立之后——"西泽尔停了一下，"您想要什么样的夏国？"

楚舜华看着他。

沉默了很久。

"不要再让夏国被皇帝和星见控制。"楚舜华说，"让人人平等。"

他的声音很轻，但在空旷的石室里，每一个字都清清楚楚。

"我母亲用一生守护王屋山的秘密，她不是要任何人当皇帝，她要的是这块土地上的人都能活得像个人。"楚舜华说，"我继承她的遗志。我希望我的子子孙孙，不要再跪在任何人脚下。"

他伸出手，按在西泽尔的肩膀上。

"我看不到那一天了。"楚舜华说，"你替我看。"

西泽尔没有说话。他只是点了点头。

楚舜华的手从他肩上滑落，转身往石室入口走去。他的脚步依然很稳，紫瞳中最后一点金光在他转身的瞬间熄灭了。

石室的另一侧传来轻柔的脚步声。

瓦莲京娜·罗曼诺夫走进来。

改装神怒Ⅲ型甲胄已经卸下了，她只穿着一件暗银色的轻甲内衬，金色长发散落在肩上，发间那股清冷的忍冬香气在满是红水银金属味的石室里显得格外突兀。

她走到西泽尔面前，停下。

"西泽尔。"瓦莲京娜说。

"瓦莲京娜。"西泽尔说。

"我来跟你告别的。"瓦莲京娜说。

西泽尔看着她。

"你会活着出去的。"瓦莲京娜说，"我相信。"

她的声音平静，没有颤抖，没有哭腔，像叶尼塞冰原上落下的雪。

"我会在叶尼塞等你。"瓦莲京娜说，"叶尼塞的冬天很长，但春天总会来。"

她伸出手，握住了西泽尔的手。

那枚冰原寒玉银戒指隔着西泽尔的手套，传来一丝极淡的凉意。

"来生还要做你的未婚妻。"瓦莲京娜说。

西泽尔没有说话。他反手握住了她的手，握得比平时更紧。

"来生我去找你。"西泽尔说。

瓦莲京娜松开了手。她退后一步，转身，走了出去。脚步声在石室的通道里渐渐消失。

薇若兰走过来。

她手里拿着一个黑色的金属圆筒，圆筒侧面嵌着一个拇指大小的拨轮，拨轮上刻着精密的齿轮纹路。

"梵天陨落有一个隐藏开关。"薇若兰说，"达·芬奇三百年前预留的。"

她蹲下身，把圆筒贴上梵天陨落球体侧面一个不起眼的凹槽。圆筒和球体咬合的瞬间，齿轮纹路严丝合缝。

"这个开关可以把爆炸范围从五十公里缩小到五百米。"薇若兰说，"只摧毁世界树残枝和这一层的欧米茄原型体，不会波及到地面上的人。"

西泽尔看着她。

"代价呢？"

薇若兰的手在拨轮上停了一秒。

"开关需要完美适配者的神经系统作为锚点。"薇若兰说，"否则反物质湮灭的能量会无序扩散，五百米会变成五千米，五千公里，整个中原。"

她抬起头。

"所以你必须把神经系统接入这个圆筒。"薇若兰说，"用你的意识去引导那股能量，让它精确地只摧毁目标。"

"接入之后呢？"西泽尔问。

薇若兰没有回答。

"接入之后呢？"西泽尔又问了一遍。

"我不知道。"薇若兰说，"达·芬奇日记的最后几页写了这个代价。佛朗哥临死前让我不要让你看到。我撕掉了。"

石室里安静了几秒钟。

"我来接。"西泽尔说。

"你——"

"我来接。"西泽尔说，"不需要别人。"

薇若兰看了他一眼，没有再说话。她把圆筒递过去。

西泽尔接过圆筒，把那根黑色的金属接驳线贴在后颈的黄金套管接口上。金属接触皮肤的那一刻，一股冰凉的感觉从后颈蔓延向全身，沿着脊椎一路向下，像是有人在他的神经通路里灌入了一杯冰水。

圆筒侧面的拨轮开始缓缓转动。

就在这个瞬间，梵天陨落球体内部那枚蓝鲟的二代普罗米修斯残骸核心突然发出强烈的蓝色光芒。

那光芒从球体的缝隙中透出来，冰冷，明亮，像是沉在深海底的一颗心脏突然重新跳动。蓝色的光柱冲上天花板，照亮了整个石室，也照亮了西泽尔的紫瞳。

他的瞳孔中，被金色纹路贯穿的灼热亮紫与那蓝色的光交织在一起，瞳孔深处有什么东西正在苏醒。

石室的入口处传来沉重的金属脚步声。

那脚步声比之前所有的脚步都要沉重，每一步都带着让地面颤抖的重量。

莱昂纳多·波尔吉亚走进石室。

他的第三代普罗米修斯·古洛诺斯左臂已经断裂，半个身体被青铜蜘蛛的自毁脉冲烧得焦黑。但他站得很稳，机械结构的眼睛里重新亮起了暗金色的光。电磁脉冲的干扰已经过去，他的神经接驳系统正在重新校准。

"西泽尔·波尔吉亚。"莱昂纳多说，"你跑不掉了。"

他的声音是精密齿轮咬合的质感，没有一丝人类的温度。

"我花了三百年。"莱昂纳多说，"三百年，从达·芬奇先生留下这个计划的那一天开始。培育完美适配者，建造世界树残枝的母体，编写梵天陨落反物质炸弹的引爆程序。每一步都不能错。"

古洛诺斯残破的巨刃缓缓举起。

"你以为你赢了？你只是走到了我设计好的最后一步。"莱昂纳多说，"把血滴在密钥上，把神经系统接入开关——你做的每一件事都是我要你做的。"

唐璜上前一步。

他没有捡起断掉的蔷薇之鬼，他只是用那只还能动的右手从腰间拔出了蜂巢式手铳。

"老板。"唐璜说。

"退后。"西泽尔说。

"不退。"唐璜说，"来生还要做你的刺客。"

他冲向莱昂纳多。

蔷薇之鬼的驾驶者没有甲胄，只有一具血肉之躯。但他跑得很快，比穿着全套炽天使甲胄时还快，仿佛这一刻他的身体终于卸下了所有钢铁的重量，变回了七年前那个在翡冷翠画廊里偷画的年轻人。

莱昂纳多的巨刃劈下。

唐璜没有躲。他张开双臂，用自己的身体挡住了那柄六米长的巨型反曲锯齿巨刃。

锯齿切入肩膀，切入胸膛，切入肋骨。鲜血喷涌而出，溅在巨刃的暗金色刃面上，又顺着锯齿往下滴。

唐璜的身体挂在巨刃上，回头看了西泽尔一眼。

他笑了。

"老板，"唐璜说，"七年前你说我的手很稳。"

"现在也是。"

薇若兰一把抓住阿方索和昆提良的胳膊，往石室入口拖。

"走！"薇若兰厉声说。

昆提良想挣回去，薇若兰死死扣住他的手腕。

"你回去就是送死！"薇若兰说，"他让你们活着出去！"

阿方索没有说话。他拉着昆提良往后退了一步，又一步。

楚舜华已经在石室入口处等着。他看见薇若兰拖着三个人出来，紫瞳中已经完全没有金纹，但他的脚步依然很稳。

"撤。"楚舜华说，"密涅瓦的运输车在地表。"

薇若兰最后回头看了一眼石室内部。

她看见西泽尔站在梵天陨落反物质炸弹旁边，紫瞳中金纹与蓝光交织，后颈的黄金套管连着黑色的接驳线，铜色护身符贴在锁骨上。Excalibur残刃握在手中，刃口上暗金色的光正在一点一点地变亮。

球体侧面的红水银刻度已经亮到了最后几圈。

六十秒。

西泽尔低下头。

"我答应过阿黛尔，会给她留一个家。"他说，"我答应过我父亲，会保护母亲和她。我答应过瓦莲京娜，会把叶尼塞的冬天还给她。"

他抬起手。

手腕内侧那道浅浅的伤疤又裂开了，暗红色的血带着淡金色的纹路涌出来。

"我还答应过我自己。"他说，"要守护人类最强大的武器。"

他用 Excalibur 残刃的刃尖再次划开了手腕。

血珠涌出来，比上一次更多。

血滴在梵天陨落反物质炸弹的核心上，滴在那枚正在发出蓝色光芒的蓝鲟残骸上。蓝色的光与暗金色的血融合在一起，整个球体开始震颤。

三十秒。

球体表面的梵文全部亮起，暗金色的光芒从每一条刻痕中涌出，把整个石室照得如同白昼。

二十秒。

西泽尔的后颈传来剧烈的灼烧感，黄金套管与圆筒之间的神经接驳线已经烫得发红。他能感觉到自己的意识正在被拽入一个无底的深渊，深渊里有一棵树，树干是暗金色的，树枝末梢挂着红水银核心当成果实，树叶是大小不一的金色齿轮。

十五秒。

他听见了树的声音。那声音不是人类的语言，而是一种古老的、来自血脉深处的低语。

十秒。

球体的光芒已经从暗金色变成了纯白色。

九。

八。

七。

西泽尔闭上了眼睛。

六。

五。

四。

三。

二。

一。

梵天陨落反物质炸弹发出强烈的白色光芒。

【English】
Chapter 245 — The Countdown to Brahma's Fall

Blood fell onto the ancient Sinhala inscription on the back of the anemone pendant.

The inscription lit.

Not the wavering light of a candle, but gold and red, fierce and molten, as though a vein of magma had cracked open inside the stone. Each stroke of the old script flared like a fuse. Dark gold tracery ran outward from the pendant, over Verolan's fingertips, across the curved surface of the sphere that hung a metre wide in the centre of the chamber.

Brahma's Fall woke.

A low drone rose from within the shell, the sound of a great beast at last opening an eye after three centuries of sleep. The Sanskrit carved across its surface kindled letter by letter, the red mercury racing beneath the metal in dark gold pulses. On the sphere's flank, in a recessed channel, a ring of ancient red-mercury markings began to brighten, slowly, like ripples climbing a well from below.

One ring. Two. Three.

Verolan watched the markings. Her lips moved without sound.

Ten minutes.

She looked up at Cesare. He stood without his Seraph harness, and the gold dragon in his violet eyes had ceased to turn but had not gone dark. Blood was still falling, one drop at a time, from his wrist. Each drop carried faint gold tracery, and where each drop struck the dark gold of the sphere's flank it hissed faintly, like water on a red-hot iron.

"It has begun," Verolan said.

"Yes," Cesare said.

From the entrance of the chamber came the sound of heavy footsteps.

Alfonso came in first. His mechanical hand was scored with burns, Omega ichor dripping slowly between his fingers. Behind him, Quintilian: of Augustus's tower-shield only half remained, the shoulder plate was broken clean through, and slivers of mithril were embedded in the muscle, each step pushing a thin dark line of blood along the edge of the metal. Don Juan came last. The Rose Ghost's recurved scythe had been broken short, his left arm hung loose, and the entire sleeve was soaked to a wet black.

The three of them entered the chamber and saw Cesare, and the dark gold sphere that hummed low, and the red-mercury markings climbing the sphere's flank in lit rings.

"That —" Quintilian said quietly.

"Brahma's Fall," Cesare said.

A silence of a few seconds.

Don Juan laughed. He leaned against the wall, set the broken Rose Ghost down at his feet, and the clatter of metal on stone was very small in the wide chamber.

"Chief," Don Juan said. "How long have I been with you?"

"Seven years," Cesare said.

"Seven years," Don Juan said. "Seven years ago I was lifting a painting out of a gallery in Florence, and you caught me in the act. You could have handed me to the mounted police. You didn't. You said, 'Your hand is steady. Come with me.'"

He lifted the right hand that still moved, and looked at it.

"These hands," he said, "have stolen coin, have stolen jewels, have stolen the hearts of noble girls. But the best thing they ever stole was a chief who would make me an assassin."

"In the next life, too," he said, "I want to be your assassin."

Cesare looked at him. A silence.

"In the next life," Cesare said, "I will still use you."

Quintilian gave a rough grunt and drove the half of his mithril tower-shield down onto the stone. The clang echoed a long time in the chamber.

"What about me?" Quintilian said, in his rough, loud voice. "When I came to you, you were still a whelp — couldn't even keep a harness on straight. I taught you to hold a gun. I taught you to block a blade. I taught you how to take an enemy's sword into the chest with your teeth — though I'll grant, in the end, you could beat me."

He bared his teeth, a wide grin, all of them white with blood at the roots.

"In this life I have only ever watched one man's back," he said. "In the next life, I want to watch it still."

Cesare reached out and set his hand on Quintilian's shoulder. The cold of the broken plate came through the glove.

"In the next life," Cesare said, "you will still watch it."

Alfonso had been standing the furthest back, saying nothing. He unclasped his Spider Nest wristwatch, looked at the dial where the eight tiny mechanical spiders were now nothing but a smear of slack metal, and clipped it back on. The sound of the clasp was very small.

"Chief," Alfonso said.

"Yes."

"In my life I have repaired many harnesses," he said. "From the back-street workshops in the Florence slums to the highest laboratory in Minerva. But the best one I ever repaired was your Red Dragon."

He looked up. In those cool, pale grey-blue eyes there was something Cesare had never seen in them before.

"In the next life, too," Alfonso said, "I want to be your engineer."

Cesare looked at the three of them for a long time.

"You will all walk out of here alive," Cesare said.

"Chief —" Don Juan began.

"That is an order," Cesare said.

Silence.

From the depths of the chamber came another pair of footsteps.

Chu Shunhua entered the room.

His Oni-Warrior prototype was gone. He wore only a thin inner tunic of Cathayan silk, and on the left side of his chest a dark stain was still slowly widening. The gold tracery in his violet eyes had almost gone out; only at the very bottom of the iris did a faint gold light still struggle to keep itself alight.

But he walked steadily. Each step fell on the same place on the chamber's stone floor, as if there were an invisible line drawn there for his feet.

"Cesare," Chu Shunhua said.

"Uncle," Cesare said.

Chu Shunhua stopped in front of him, and reached into his tunic and brought out a copper talisman. The talisman was engraved with an inverted five-pointed star wrapped in gearwork, the edges worn to a bright polish.

"Put it on," Chu Shunhua said.

Cesare took the talisman. The moment the copper touched his skin, a faint warmth ran from his fingertips into the vessels of his hand, as though he had taken hold of a warm human hand.

"It will protect you," Chu Shunhua said. "A perfect adaptor does not die easily."

A pause.

"My mother," he said, "waited thirty years for you. I waited seventeen. She left me this talisman, and told me to give it to the one who would open the secret of Mount Wangwu. Now I give it to you."

Cesare hung the talisman on a cord around his neck. The copper lay against his collarbone, and a small heat went on there.

"Uncle," Cesare said.

"Yes?"

"After the new order is built —" Cesare said, and stopped. "What kind of Cathay would you want?"

Chu Shunhua looked at him.

A long silence.

"No more Cathay ruled by an Emperor and a Star-Reader," Chu Shunhua said. "Let every man be the equal of every other."

His voice was very quiet, but in the wide chamber each word came through clear.

"My mother spent her whole life guarding the secret of Mount Wangwu. She did not want anyone to be Emperor. She wanted the people of this land to be allowed to live like human beings. I take up what she could not finish. I want my children's children never to kneel at anyone's feet."

He reached out and set his hand on Cesare's shoulder.

"I will not live to see that day," he said. "See it for me."

Cesare said nothing. He only nodded.

Chu Shunhua's hand slipped from his shoulder, and he turned and walked back toward the entrance. His steps were still steady. The last faint gold in his violet eyes went out, somewhere, in the moment of the turn.

From the far side of the chamber came the sound of soft footsteps.

Valentina Romanov entered.

Her modified Wrath-of-God Mark III harness had been removed. She wore only the dark silver inner lining, and her long gold hair hung loose over her shoulders, and through the reek of red mercury and hot metal in the chamber there was the strange, clear, cold scent of honeysuckle.

She walked up to Cesare and stopped.

"Cesare," she said.

"Valentina," he said.

"I have come to say goodbye to you," she said.

Cesare looked at her.

"You will walk out of here alive," she said. "I believe it."

Her voice was level. It did not shake. There was no sob in it. It fell like snow on the Yenisei plain.

"I will wait for you on the Yenisei," she said. "The Yenisei winter is long, but spring always comes."

She held out her hand and took Cesare's.

The Yenisei Ice Jade silver ring, through the glove, gave a faint coolness into his palm.

"In the next life," she said, "I want to be your betrothed."

Cesare did not speak. He turned his hand over and held hers back, and held her tighter than he had ever done.

"In the next life," he said, "I will come and find you."

Valentina let go. She stepped back one pace, turned, and went out. The sound of her steps faded down the corridor of the chamber.

Verolan came forward.

In her hand was a black metal cylinder, and on its side a dial no bigger than a thumb, cut with the fine teeth of gearwork.

"Brahma's Fall has a hidden switch," she said. "Da Vinci left it three hundred years ago."

She crouched, and fitted the cylinder into an unobtrusive socket on the sphere's flank. The moment cylinder and sphere engaged, the teeth of the dial met the teeth of the socket as if they had been cut for each other.

"This switch can reduce the blast from fifty kilometres to five hundred metres," she said. "It will destroy only the World Tree bough and the Omega prototype on this level. It will not reach the surface."

Cesare looked at her.

"What is the cost?"

Verolan's hand stopped on the dial for a second.

"The switch must be anchored on the perfect adaptor's nervous system," she said. "Otherwise the antimatter's energy will disperse without order, and the five hundred metres will become five kilometres, and five thousand, and the whole of Cathay."

She looked up.

"So you will have to plug your nervous system into this cylinder. Use your mind to guide the energy, to make it strike only at its target."

"And after I am plugged in?" Cesare asked.

Verolan did not answer.

"And after I am plugged in?" he asked again.

"I do not know," she said. "The last few pages of da Vinci's journal set out the cost. Franco, before he died, told me not to let you read them. I tore them out."

The chamber was quiet for a few seconds.

"I will take it," Cesare said.

"You —"

"I will take it," he said. "No one else."

Verolan looked at him for a moment, and said nothing more. She held the cylinder out.

Cesare took it, and pressed the black metal coupling-line to the gold socket at the back of his neck. The moment the metal touched the skin, a cold went from the back of his neck down through his whole body, down the spine, as if someone had poured a cup of iced water into the channels of his nerves.

The dial on the side of the cylinder began to turn, slowly, of its own.

At that exact moment, the remains of the Blue Sturgeon Mark II Prometheus core inside the sphere threw out a strong blue light.

The light came through the seams of the shell, cold and bright, like the heart of something at the bottom of a deep sea deciding to beat again. A blue column of it went up and struck the ceiling, and lit the whole chamber, and lit Cesare's violet eyes.

In his pupils, the hot bright violet cut through with gold tracery twined with the blue light, and somewhere in the depths of the iris something was beginning to stir.

The chamber entrance gave up the sound of a heavy metal tread.

It was heavier than any of the footsteps that had come before. With every step the floor trembled.

Leonardo Borgia came into the chamber.

The third-generation Prometheus, Chronos, had lost its left arm. Half his body was charred black by the self-destruct pulse of the bronze spider. But he stood steady, and the dark gold light had come back on in the mechanical eyes. The EMP interference had passed, and his neural link was recalibrating.

"Cesare Borgia," Leonardo said. "You have nowhere to run."

His voice had the precise, gear-on-gear quality of a clockwork mouth, with not the least trace of human warmth in it.

"I spent three hundred years," he said. "Three hundred years, from the day Master da Vinci set this plan in motion. To breed the perfect adaptor. To build the mother of the World Tree bough. To write the firing programme for Brahma's Fall. Every step was exact."

The broken great-blade of Chronos rose.

"You think you have won? You have only walked into the last step I designed for you. To let the blood fall on the key. To plug the nervous system into the switch. Everything you have done is what I required you to do."

Don Juan stepped forward.

He did not pick up the broken Rose Ghost. He drew the revolver out of his belt with the one hand that still worked.

"Chief," Don Juan said.

"Step back," Cesare said.

"I will not," Don Juan said. "In the next life, I want to be your assassin."

He ran at Leonardo.

The driver of the Rose Ghost wore no harness. He was only a man, of flesh and blood. But he ran faster than he had ever run in the suit of the Seraph, as if, in this one moment, his body had been set down of all its steel, and was again the body of the young man who had once stolen a painting from a gallery in Florence.

Leonardo's great-blade came down.

Don Juan did not dodge. He opened his arms, and his body took the six-metre recurved saw-toothed blade.

The saw-teeth went into the shoulder, and into the chest, and into the ribs. Blood came out in a great wash, and spattered the dark gold of the blade, and ran down along the teeth.

Don Juan's body hung on the blade, and he turned his head and looked back at Cesare.

He smiled.

"Chief," he said. "Seven years ago you said my hand was steady."

"It still is."

Verolan caught Alfonso and Quintilian by the arms and dragged them toward the entrance.

"Go!" she said, sharp.

Quintilian tried to twist back. Verolan's grip on his wrist did not give.

"If you go back, you are dead!" she said. "He ordered you to walk out of here alive!"

Alfonso said nothing. He took Quintilian by the arm and drew him back. One step. Another.

Chu Shunhua was already waiting at the chamber's entrance. He saw Verolan drag the two of them out, and the gold in his violet eyes was completely gone, but his feet were still steady.

"Retreat," he said. "The Minerva transport is on the surface."

Verolan looked back, one last time, into the chamber.

She saw Cesare standing beside Brahma's Fall, the gold in his eyes woven with the blue, the gold socket at the back of his neck joined to the black coupling-line, the copper talisman against his collarbone. The broken Excalibur in his hand, and on its edge the dark gold light was growing, slowly, brighter.

The red-mercury rings on the sphere's flank had climbed to the last few.

Sixty seconds.

Cesare lowered his head.

"I promised Adele I would leave her a home," he said. "I promised my father I would protect my mother and her. I promised Valentina I would give her back the Yenisei winter."

He raised his hand.

The pale scar on the inside of his wrist had opened again. Dark red blood, with the pale gold tracery, came welling out.

"I also promised myself," he said, "that I would protect humanity's most powerful weapon."

He laid the broken tip of Excalibur to his wrist, and opened it once more.

The blood welled, more than the last time.

It fell onto the core of Brahma's Fall, onto the remains of the Blue Sturgeon that were giving out the blue light. The blue light and the dark gold of the blood ran into each other, and the whole sphere began to shake.

Thirty seconds.

The Sanskrit on the surface of the sphere was all alight, and the dark gold light was pouring out of every cut, and the chamber was lit up like the middle of the day.

Twenty seconds.

The back of Cesare's neck was on fire. The gold socket and the cylinder's coupling-line had gone red with the heat. He could feel his consciousness being dragged down into a bottomless pit, and at the bottom of the pit there was a tree, and the trunk of the tree was dark gold, and at the ends of the branches red-mercury cores hung like fruit, and the leaves of the tree were gold gears of every size.

Fifteen seconds.

He heard the voice of the tree. It was not a human language. It was an old murmur, from the bottom of the blood.

Ten seconds.

The light of the sphere had gone from dark gold to pure white.

Nine.

Eight.

Seven.

Cesare closed his eyes.

Six.

Five.

Four.

Three.

Two.

One.

Brahma's Fall let out a great white light.

【中文】
第246章 新的黎明

白光。

不是光，是光的尽头。

当梵天陨落反物质炸弹到达临界的那一瞬，整个王屋山地下像是被一只无形的巨手从内部攥紧了。所有的黑暗、所有的齿轮声、所有的红水银蒸汽都在同一刹那被碾成了粉末，取而代之的是一种不属于这个世界的颜色——纯白，比雪更白，比骨更白，比人眼所能承受的极限更白。

光从世界树主根石室的核心向四面八方奔涌，速度快过声音，快过思维，快过恐惧。

紫瞳金纹的西泽尔站在球体前方，闭着眼睛。

光芒触及他胸口那枚铜色护身符的瞬间，护身符上刻着的倒置五芒星与齿轮纹路同时亮起，像是一层薄薄的金色光幕将他整个人包裹。同时，蓝鲟残骸的核心也在轰鸣，那颗暗金色的红水银核心在球体内猛烈跳动，释放出一股与白色光芒截然相反的暗金色能量场，像是一颗微型的恒星在炸弹内部坍缩又膨胀，以自身为代价构建了一个直径仅两米的保护气泡。

光芒从气泡边缘流过，没有穿透。

但西泽尔已经感觉不到了。

他的意识被拽入了世界树残枝的最后一瞬——那棵暗金色的巨树在白光中开始碎裂，树干上的齿轮叶片像秋天的枯叶般纷纷剥落，树枝末梢的红水银核心一颗接一颗地爆裂，发出连绵不绝的闷响。世界树在尖叫，那声音通过血脉直接灌入他的神经，让他清晰地感受到了三百年积攒的痛苦与不甘。

然后，一切归于寂静。

没有光。

没有声音。

没有树。

地面传来沉闷的震颤，像是一头巨兽在地底翻了个身。

王屋山脚下的联军阵地中，所有人都不由自主地趴在了地上。地震持续了整整十二秒，等震动停止的时候，人们抬起头，看见王屋山方向升起了一道冲天的白色光柱，光柱持续了三秒钟后骤然收缩，变成一个拳头大小的白色光球悬浮在半空中，又过了两秒，光球无声无息地炸开，化作无数细碎的光点如雪花般飘落。

光点落在盔甲上、刀刃上、人的肩膀和头发上，温热如春日的细雨。

"结束了。"有人说。

"什么结束了？"

"我不知道……但我觉得……结束了。"

阿方索是第一个爬起来的人。他的所罗门王甲胄在刚才的冲击波中被掀翻在地，左肩装甲板裂开了一条缝，露出里面的电缆和润滑液管道。他挣扎着站起来，抬起机械手臂护住面甲，眯着眼睛朝王屋山方向望去。

山还在。

但山顶的植被在以肉眼可见的速度枯萎，叶片从翠绿变成枯黄，从枯黄变成灰白，从灰白变成粉末。风一吹，整座山头像是一位老人在抖落身上的旧衣。

"阿方索！"瓦莲京娜的声音从通讯器里传来，带着电流的杂音和一丝几乎听不出来的颤抖，"你还能动吗？"

"能。"阿方索回答。

"去找老板。"瓦莲京娜说，"我去找其他人。"

阿方索没有再多问。他启动了所罗门王的辅助动力系统，踉跄着朝王屋山地下通道的入口跑去。蜘蛛巢腕表上六只微型机械蜘蛛自动弹射出去，腹部红水银微晶闪烁，像六只萤火虫在他前方探路。

通道入口已经被坍塌的碎石堵了大半。

阿方索举起所罗门王的重型机械臂，开始一块一块地搬开碎石。他的机械臂发出刺耳的金属摩擦声，液压杆在极限负载下发出咯吱咯吱的抗议，但他没有停。

"老板！"他一边搬一边喊，"西泽尔！"

没有人回答。

他把最后一根横梁挪开，钻进了通道里。通道壁上的灯柱有的还在亮，有的已经碎了，玻璃碎片在地面上反射出昏暗的光。空气中弥漫着一种奇怪的味道，像是烧焦的金属和枯萎的花瓣混合在一起。

他跑了大约三百米，在接近世界树主根石室的岔路口处，看见了倒在地上的唐璜。

蔷薇之鬼的超轻型甲胄已经严重变形，胸甲凹陷，左臂从肩关节处断裂，只靠几根电缆连接着，耷拉在地上。唐璜本人被甩出了骑士舱，半跪在碎石堆里，一只手撑着地面，另一只手捂着胸口。他的脸被鲜血糊住了大半，嘴角还挂着一丝笑意。

"哟，阿方索。"唐璜抬起头，声音沙哑得像砂纸，"你来得真快。"

"你还能笑？"阿方索蹲下来检查他的伤势。

"瓦莲京娜把我拽出来的，"唐璜咳了一声，吐出一口带血丝的唾沫，"最后一秒。一只手把我从驾驶舱里揪出来，就像揪一只小猫。改装神怒Ⅲ型的力气真他妈大。"

阿方索松了口气。他的蜘蛛已经探到了石室内部，正在将画面传回面甲上的微型显示屏。

画面很模糊，到处都是扬起的灰尘和残余的红水银蒸汽。但蜘蛛的绿光在黑暗中找到了目标——

石室中央，梵天陨落反物质炸弹的球体已经消失了，只留下一个浅浅的凹痕。凹痕中央，西泽尔面朝下倒在地上，一动不动。

铜色护身符贴在他的锁骨上，已经碎裂成两半，但金属表面仍残留着微弱的金色光泽。在他身下，蓝鲟残骸的红水银核心嵌在碎石之间，已经完全黯淡，但核心的外壳完整无损，像是一只用尽了全部力气的拳头，在最后一刻握紧了自己的主人。

"他还活着。"阿方索说。

唐璜愣了一下，然后笑了，这次是真的笑，露出一口被血染红的牙齿。

"那个混账。"

阿方索站起来，拍了拍唐璜的肩膀，朝石室跑去。他的脚步在空旷的通道里回响，像是一面鼓，敲打着这座刚刚经历了浩劫的古老山脉。

走到石室门口时，他停住了。

有人在里面。

不是西泽尔。

一个人形的轮廓站在石室最深处的断壁残垣之间，身上覆盖着厚厚的灰尘和碎石粉末，金属质感的银灰色双眼在昏暗中发出微弱的光。那不是活人的眼睛，也不是死人能发出的光，而是精密齿轮与红水银晶片组合成的机械造物，在主人最后的意识消散前，自动进入了休眠模式。

原罪机关的真正主人。

莱昂纳多·波吉亚。

他站在那里，姿态像是一尊被时间凝固的雕像。第三代普罗米修斯·古洛诺斯座机已经在爆炸中被彻底摧毁，巨大的残骸散落在他周围，暗金色的装甲板扭曲成各种不可能的形状，暴龙级动力核心暴露在外，管道和电缆像是被扯断的血管一样垂挂着。

但莱昂纳多本人没有倒下。

他的身体超过八成是机械结构，这些机械在白光抵达的前一刻全部自动切换到了防御模式，层层叠叠的合金装甲板从四肢和躯干中弹出，像是一只铁甲的刺猬将自己裹了起来。白光穿透了这层防御，灼烧了外层的装甲和电缆，但核心结构——那个承载着他三百年意志的机械大脑——还完整地保留着。

他还活着。

或者说，他的意识还没有完全熄灭。

阿方索举起了所罗门王的臂载连射铳，瞄准了莱昂纳多的头部。

"不必了。"莱昂纳多说。

他的声音已经不是人类的声音了，金属质感的声带发出的每个音节都带着精密齿轮咬合的杂音，像是钟表内部被搅碎的声音。但那句话的语气，仍然属于一个活了一千多年的老人。

"我输了。"

阿方索没有放下枪。

莱昂纳多没有看他，而是转过头去，看着石室中央那个倒下的年轻人。银灰色的机械双眼最后一次聚焦在那个方向，残存的瞳孔对焦系统自动调整了焦距，将西泽尔模糊的身影拉到清晰。

"三百年前，"莱昂纳多说，"我的祖先在阿瓦隆冰原找到了世界树残枝。他以为自己是在拯救人类。他以为机械神国可以消灭瘟疫、饥荒和战争。他错了。"

他的声音越来越低，机械声带开始出现故障，每个词之间都有不自然的停顿。

"瘟疫来自人性，饥荒来自人性，战争……也来自人性。把人类的命运交给一台机器，不是因为机器比人更好，而是因为……创造机器的人不敢面对自己。"

他的右臂——那条精密的机械假肢——缓缓抬起，指向西泽尔的方向。机械手指上的微型红水银晶片已经碎裂了大半，只剩几颗还在发出最后的光。

"他做到了我祖先没有做到的事，"莱昂纳多说，"他没有成为神。他只是一个……人。"

他的手臂垂落。

"我错了。"

银灰色的双眼闪了最后一下。

"人性……才是……最强大的……武器。"

光芒熄灭。

莱昂纳多·波吉亚的身体保持着站立的姿态，银灰色的双眼变成了两个黑洞。他的意识在三百年布局的最后一刻彻底消散，机械结构在失去意志的驱动后停止了所有运转。

阿方索站在原地，看着那具一动不动的机械躯壳，许久没有说话。

然后他收起连射铳，转身走向西泽尔。

他蹲下来，伸出机械手，探了探西泽尔的颈动脉。

脉搏很微弱，但稳定。

西泽尔的脸贴着冰冷的碎石，呼吸浅得几乎看不出来。紫瞳中的金纹已经黯淡，只剩下一层极淡的底色，像是燃尽之后的余烬。后颈的黄金套管完好无损，铜色护身符碎成两半但仍然紧贴着他的锁骨。

"老板，"阿方索轻声说，"我背你出去。"

他没有等到回答。

他将西泽尔从地上翻过来，机械手臂从腋下穿过，稳稳地托起了那具轻得不像话的身体。一百一十斤。这是阿方索在炽天骑士团训练营时就知道的体重。三年过去，还是这个数字。

他一步一步地朝通道外面走去。

走到唐璜身边时，唐璜已经自己站起来了，用断裂的蔷薇之鬼左臂当拐杖，一瘸一拐地跟在后面。

"他怎么样？"唐璜问。

"活着。"

"那就好。"

他们走出通道口的时候，天已经快亮了。

王屋山东面的天际线呈现出一种极淡的灰蓝色，像是绸缎被浸过水。最东边的那一条线上，有一丝极细极亮的金红色光芒正在慢慢扩散，像是谁在天地之间拉开了一道口子，露出了缝隙后面燃烧的黎明。

楚舜华的鬼武者原型机半跪在阵地前沿，夔龙首钢盔上的龙睛已经碎了，鎏金夔龙纹的胸甲上布满了裂纹和灼烧的痕迹。楚舜华本人被瓦莲京娜从驾驶舱里拉出来，靠在一块石头上，闭着眼睛，呼吸平缓。他腰间的夔龙角剑还在，微微发热，像是握着一截凝固的闪电。

瓦莲京娜站在他身边，裙摆沾满了灰尘和血渍，金色的长发散乱地披在肩上。她的改装神怒Ⅲ型甲胄也受损不轻，右肩装甲板翘起了一角，蒸汽管道破裂处正往外冒着白汽。

她看见阿方索背着西泽尔从通道里走出来，愣了一下。

然后她跑了过去。

白靴踩在碎石上发出咯吱咯吱的声响，忍冬香气被晨风吹散，混进了山野间泥土和硝烟的气味里。她跑到阿方索面前，伸出手，碰了碰西泽尔的脸。

西泽尔没有反应。

"他活着，"阿方索说，"只是晕过去了。"

瓦莲京娜没有说话。她从腰间解下那条绣着叶尼塞国徽忍冬花的白手帕，轻轻盖在西泽尔的额头上。手帕上还残留着她发间的香气，被晨风一吹，清冷而悠远。

"昆提良呢？"阿方索问。

"在后面，"瓦莲京娜说，"奥古斯都的左臂断了，但人没事。他正在帮薇若兰清理通道里的碎石。"

"莲生呢？"

"不知道。"

阿方索没有再问。他把西泽尔放在一块平坦的石头上，然后靠着旁边的一棵枯树坐了下来。枯树的叶子在刚才的爆炸中全部掉光了，光秃秃的枝干指向天空，像是一把把沉默的剑。

瓦莲京娜在他身边蹲下来。

"莱昂纳多？"她问。

"死了。"阿方索说，"或者说他那台机器死了。身体还在，但已经没有意识了。"

瓦莲京娜点了点头。

"欧米茄呢？"

"全灭了。"阿方索指了指王屋山方向，"我的蜘蛛在爆炸结束后扫描了方圆五公里的范围，没有任何欧米茄原型体的信号源。"

"世界树呢？"

"也灭了。"

两个人沉默了一会儿。

晨光继续从东方的天际线扩散，灰蓝色渐渐被金红色取代。风从山谷里吹来，带着枯叶和尘土的气味。远处传来士兵们零星的呼喊声，有人在清点伤亡，有人在搜索幸存者，有人在试图重新启动被震坏的通讯设备。

唐璜一瘸一拐地走过来，在西泽尔身边坐下，把那条断裂的蔷薇之鬼左臂扔在地上，掏出一块被血浸透的手绢擦了擦脸。

"老板以前说，"唐璜忽然开口，"他想和一个贤惠的女孩过平凡的生活。有一栋带斜窗的房子，养一只猫，院子里种点花。"

阿方索看了他一眼。

"现在看来，这个愿望大概要推迟很长一段时间了。"唐璜咧嘴笑了笑，笑容里有疲惫，有释然，也有一丝连他自己都说不清楚的东西。

瓦莲京娜没有接话。

她伸出手，将西泽尔额头上那条白手帕的边角掖了掖，挡住从东面吹来的晨风。

西泽尔仍然没有醒。

但他的脉搏比刚才强了一些。

昆提良从通道口跑出来的时候，晨光正好照到了他的脸上。他满身灰尘，眼眶发红，巨大的身躯在逆光中显得格外笨拙。奥古斯都甲胄的左臂从肩关节处完全断裂了，秘银重盾碎成了三大块，被他用仅存的右臂夹在肋下，闭眼狮头纹章的狮耳已经没了，狮眼被裂缝切成了两半。

他跑到西泽尔身边，蹲下来，什么都没说。

他只是伸出那只巨大的手，握住了西泽尔冰凉的手。

薇若兰最后走出来。

她的密涅瓦核心骑士制式军服沾满了泥土和灰尘，半块世界树残根守护符青铜镜挂在胸前，还在微微发烫。她的怀里抱着一个长条形的物体——达·芬奇·博尔吉亚的日记本，用她自己的外套裹着，封面被血迹和汗水浸得发皱。

她走到西泽尔身边，看了一眼他安静的脸，松了口气。

"碧儿和塔拉夏呢？"她回头问薇若兰。

"在翡冷翠。"薇若兰说，"密涅瓦的通讯恢复了，我已经发了加密电报过去，让她们待在坎特伯雷堡不要出来。"

"圣堂装甲师呢？"

"莱希特伯爵在枢机会撤销命令后已经撤走了。"薇若兰说，"格拉古大主教也被亚历山大·格里高利拦下了。现在翡冷翠的局势暂时稳定。"

她看了一眼王屋山的方向。

那座古老的山在晨光中沉默着，山顶的树木全部枯死，岩石表面覆盖着一层薄薄的白霜——那是红水银蒸发后凝结的残渣。但山还在，山脚的村庄还在，山下的田野还在。

"世界树残枝被摧毁了，"薇若兰说，"所有的欧米茄原型体也被摧毁了。梵天陨落反物质炸弹完成了它的使命。"

她低下头，看着西泽尔。

"缩小范围开关被激活了。爆炸范围从五十公里缩小到了五百米。"

阿方索抬头。

"西泽尔激活的？"

薇若兰点了点头。

阿方索沉默了很久。

"他还活着？"

"还活着。"薇若兰说，"护身符挡住了大部分湮灭能量，蓝鲟残骸的核心构建了最后的保护气泡。莲生说那枚核心里储存着蓝鲟最后的意识碎片，是蓝鲟在最后一刻自动启动了防御模式。"

"蓝鲟……"阿方索低声重复。

他想起来了。那个总是用冰冷声音说话的女人。那个临死前把自己核心塞进蓝鲟残骸里的骑士。她到死都在保护红龙。

"莲生呢？"阿方索问。

薇若兰没有回答。

她的目光移向了通道口的黑暗深处。那里站着一个人。

一个身形矮小的老人，身穿三百年前东方款式的灰色长袍，银白色的长发垂到腰际，面容枯槁却异常平静。他的右手握着一杆刻满梵文的骑枪，枪头雕刻的六翼天使浮雕已经碎了半边。

莲生。

他站在通道口，面朝王屋山方向，一动不动。

晨光打在他苍老的脸上，照亮了每一道皱纹、每一缕银发、每一寸历经三百年的疲惫。

"世界树……真的没了。"他的声音很轻，像是在自言自语。

然后他笑了。

那个笑容很淡，淡得像是黎明前最后一颗隐入天际的星。但那是真正的、发自心底的笑。他等了三百年，就是为了看见这一刻。

他转过身，朝西泽尔的方向慢慢走来。走到一半的时候，他的身体晃了晃，单膝跪在了地上。那杆梵文骑枪从手中滑落，枪杆触地发出一声清脆的金属声。

"莲生！"薇若兰快步走过去，扶住他的肩膀。

"我没事。"莲生说，"红水银秘药的效果到头了。"

他抬起头，看着薇若兰怀里那本被外套裹着的日记本。

"达·芬奇……他终于可以安息了。"

他闭上了眼睛。

三百年的等待，在这一刻画上了句号。

阿方索站起身，走到西泽尔身边。晨光已经完全铺开了，金红色的光芒从东方倾泻而下，将整座王屋山染成了一片暖色。枯树、碎石、散落的甲胄残骸、疲惫的人们，都被这层金色覆盖了。

他伸出机械手，轻轻拍了拍西泽尔的肩膀。

"老板，"他低声说，"该醒了。天亮了。"

西泽尔没有动。

但他的手指微微动了动。

阿方索愣了一下，然后看向瓦莲京娜。瓦莲京娜也看见了。她的手还握在西泽尔的手上，她感觉到了那根手指的微弱动作。

金红色的晨光继续铺展，像是一匹巨大的绸缎从天际线那头一直延伸到王屋山脚下。

风从山谷吹来，带走了最后一缕硝烟的气味。

远处，一架叶尼塞跨东西方直通专列的汽笛声隐约传来，像是在回应这新的一天。

【English】
Chapter 246 — A New Dawn

Whiteness.

Not light but its terminus.

In the instant Brahma's Fall reached critical mass, the hollow beneath Mount Wangwu seemed to be gripped from inside by an invisible hand. All the dark, all the clatter of gears, all the red mercury steam was crushed to powder in the same heartbeat, and what replaced it was a color that did not belong to this world—pure white, whiter than snow, whiter than bone, whiter than the human eye was built to bear.

The light poured outward from the heart of the World Tree's root-chamber, faster than sound, faster than thought, faster than fear.

Cesare stood before the sphere, his eyes closed, the violet of his irises banded with threads of gold.

The moment the brilliance touched the copper amulet at his breast, the inverted pentagram and the gear-work etched into its face lit at once, as though a thin golden screen had drawn itself around his whole body. At the same moment, deep inside the Blue Sturgeon wreckage, the dull-gold red-mercury core convulsed. It beat like a dying heart. It gave off a field of energy the precise opposite of the white that was eating the world—a small private star, collapsing and re-expanding inside the bomb's radius, spending itself to build a shell of safety exactly two meters across.

The white streamed past the bubble's edge and did not pass through.

Cesare felt none of it.

His awareness was dragged, instead, into the last moment of the World Tree's branch. The vast dark-gold tree began to break apart in the glare. The gear-shaped leaves fell from its trunk like dead leaves in autumn. The red mercury cores at the tips of its boughs burst one after another in a long, low, grudging percussion. The tree was screaming. The sound ran down his blood into his nerves, and he tasted three centuries of stored pain and refusal.

Then there was silence.

No light.

No sound.

No tree.

The ground gave a slow, deep shudder, like some buried beast turning in its sleep.

In the allied positions at the foot of Mount Wangwu, every man and woman was already on the ground. The tremor lasted twelve full seconds. When it stopped, they raised their heads and saw, rising from the direction of the mountain, a column of white that went up to the sky. It held for three seconds, then suddenly contracted into a fist-sized white orb hanging in the air, and two seconds after that the orb burst soundlessly into a rain of fine luminous specks that drifted down like snow.

The specks settled on armor, on blades, on shoulders and hair, warm as a spring drizzle.

"It is over," somebody said.

"What is over?"

"I don't know. But I think it is over."

Alfonso was the first man on his feet. The Solomon King had been knocked flat by the shockwave. A crack had opened in the left shoulder plating, exposing the cabling and the hydraulic line beneath. He dragged himself upright, raised his mechanical arm to shield his faceplate, and squinted toward the mountain.

The mountain was still there.

But the vegetation along its crown was dying as he watched—green to yellow, yellow to ash, ash to powder. The wind took it. The whole ridge shook off its old coat like an old man.

"Alfonso." Valentina's voice came through the comm, full of current-noise and a tremor so small only he would have heard it. "Can you move?"

"I can."

"Then find the boss. I'll round up the others."

He did not waste breath on questions. He brought the Solomon King's auxiliary drive online, staggered toward the entrance to the underground passage, and let the six micro-spiders on his wristwatch pop out one by one. Their abdomens flashed with red mercury crystal. Six little fireflies, scouting ahead.

The entrance was half-blocked by fallen stone.

Alfonso raised the Solomon King's heavy manipulator arm and began, piece by piece, to clear it. The limb screamed with metal-on-stone, the hydraulics complaining in a thin, strained whine. He did not stop.

"Boss!" he called between lifts. "Cesare!"

No answer.

He moved the last crossbeam, slipped through the gap, and went in. Some of the wall-lamps were still lit, some were broken, the glass on the floor throwing back dim, scattered reflections. The air held a strange smell—scorched metal and withered flowers, mixed in equal parts.

He ran perhaps three hundred meters. Near the fork that led down to the World Tree's main root-chamber, he found Don Juan on the ground.

The Rose Ghost's superlight frame was badly warped, the breastplate caved in, the left arm torn away at the shoulder joint and hanging by a few cables. Don Juan himself had been thrown clear of the cockpit and now knelt in the rubble, one hand pressed to the floor, the other to his chest. His face was mostly hidden by blood. At the corner of his mouth there still sat a smile.

"Hey, Alfonso," Don Juan said. His voice was dry as sandpaper. "You got here fast."

"How are you laughing?" Alfonso dropped to a crouch and began checking him over.

"Valentina pulled me out." Don Juan coughed, spat a red-tinged thread of saliva. "Last second. One hand, out of the cockpit, like a kitten. That girl hits hard for someone in a modified Wrath-of-God III."

Alfonso let out a breath. His spiders had reached the inner chamber. The picture coming back to the small display inside his faceplate was a wash of dust and residual red mercury steam.

The green optics of the lead spider found the target.

At the center of the chamber the sphere of Brahma's Fall was gone. In its place, a shallow depression in the floor. And in the middle of the depression, Cesare lay face-down, not moving.

The copper amulet rested against his collarbone. It had split into two halves. The metal still held a faint sheen of gold. Beneath him, the Blue Sturgeon's red mercury core was wedged in the rubble, fully dark, its casing intact—a fist that, having spent every drop of strength it had, had closed around its master at the last possible moment.

"He's alive," Alfonso said.

Don Juan blinked. Then he laughed, properly, showing teeth stained with blood.

"That bastard."

Alfonso got to his feet, clapped him on the shoulder, and went on at a run toward the chamber. His footfalls came back to him off the bare stone, a slow drumbeat through a mountain that had just survived the end of something.

He stopped in the doorway.

There was someone inside.

Not Cesare.

A man-shaped outline stood in the deep wreckage at the back of the chamber, coated in dust and powdered stone, the silver-gray mechanical eyes throwing back a dim, mechanical light. It was not the light a living man's eyes make. It was not the light a dead man's eyes make either. It was the light of a precision instrument—gears and red mercury wafers, locked into rest mode by the last flickers of a consciousness that had not quite let go.

The true master of the Original Sin bureau.

Leonardo Borgia.

He stood like a figure arrested in time. The third-generation Prometheus Gulo Nos had been torn apart by the blast. Its remains lay scattered around him in a forest of dark-gold plating twisted into shapes the metals had never been meant to hold. The Tyrannosaur-class power core was exposed to the air, its pipes and cables hanging loose like severed vessels.

But Leonardo had not fallen.

His body was more than eighty percent mechanical, and all of it had, in the last instant before the white arrived, thrown itself into defense. Layer after layer of alloy plate had slid from the limbs and torso, and the man had sealed himself inside, an iron hedgehog bracing for the end. The white had come through that shell and burned the outer skin of plating and cable to slag, but at the center—inside the housing that held three hundred years of unbroken will—the mechanical brain was still there, whole.

He was still alive.

Or rather, his mind had not entirely gone out.

Alfonso raised the Solomon King's arm-mounted rotary gun and trained it on the head.

"That will not be necessary," Leonardo said.

His voice was no longer a human voice. The metal vocal cords put a small clockwork rasp behind every syllable, the sound of a watch's works being shaken to pieces. But the cadence of the sentence still belonged to a man who had been alive for a thousand years.

"I have lost."

Alfonso did not lower the gun.

Leonardo did not look at him. He turned, instead, toward the young man lying in the center of the room. The silver-gray eyes made one last attempt to focus. The remains of a pupil-finding system shifted, the way a camera lens will, and pulled the blurred shape of Cesare into clarity.

"Three hundred years ago," Leonardo said, "my ancestor found the World Tree's branch on the Avalon Ice Plains. He believed he was saving humanity. He believed the Kingdom of the Machine could end plague, famine, and war. He was wrong."

The voice was dropping. The metal cords were failing. There was a tiny catch, a tiny silence, between every word.

"Plague comes from human nature. Famine comes from human nature. War… also comes from human nature. To put the fate of mankind in the hands of a machine is not because the machine is better. It is because the man who made it… could not face himself."

His right arm—the precise mechanical prosthesis—rose slowly, and pointed, with the last steadiness it had, in Cesare's direction. Most of the small red mercury wafers set in the fingers had shattered. A few still held a remnant of light.

"He did what my ancestor could not," Leonardo said. "He did not become a god. He was only… a man."

His arm fell.

"I was wrong."

The silver-gray eyes flickered, once.

"Human nature… is the most powerful… weapon… there is."

The light went out.

Leonardo Borgia kept his standing posture. The two circles of his eyes were now simply two holes. Three hundred years of design dissolved at the moment his will departed. Every mechanical subsystem stopped.

Alfonso stood for a long time, looking at the body that was no longer a body.

Then he holstered the gun, turned, and walked to Cesare.

He crouched. The mechanical hand reached out and found the carotid.

A pulse. Faint, but steady.

Cesare's face was pressed to the cold stone. His breathing was so shallow that it was almost easier to imagine it than to see it. The gold threads in his violet irises had gone out, leaving only the palest of base colors, the last of an ember after the fire has left it. The golden sheath at the back of his neck was undamaged. The copper amulet, broken in two, still lay against his collarbone.

"Boss," Alfonso said, quietly. "I'm going to carry you out."

He did not wait for an answer.

He rolled Cesare onto his back, slid the mechanical arm beneath the armpit, and lifted. A hundred and ten pounds. He had known the number since his days at the Seraph Knight training corps. Three years on, it was still the number.

He walked, step by step, toward the passage.

At Don Juan's side, Don Juan had hauled himself upright. He had taken the broken left arm of the Rose Ghost and was using it as a crutch, limping along behind.

"How is he?" Don Juan asked.

"Alive."

"Good."

They came out of the passage mouth and the sky was nearly light.

The eastern horizon over Mount Wangwu was a thin band of pale blue-gray, as though a length of silk had been dipped in water. Along the very edge of it, a single thread of gold-red was opening, the color of something burning behind a crack in the world.

Chu Shunhua's Ghost Warrior prototype knelt at the forward edge of the line. The eyes of the kui-dragon helm were broken. The gilt kui-dragon relief across the breastplate was laced with cracks and burns. Chu Shunhua himself had been hauled from the cockpit by Valentina, and sat now against a stone with his eyes closed, his breathing even. At his waist the kui-dragon horn-sword still hung, faintly warm, like a length of frozen lightning.

Valentina stood beside him. Her skirt was muddy and dark with blood. Her pale hair hung loose and unwashed over her shoulders. The modified Wrath-of-God III was also badly damaged; the right shoulder plate was buckled at one corner, and the busted steam pipe threw a thin plume of white into the cold air.

She saw Alfonso coming out of the passage with Cesare over his shoulder, and stopped.

Then she ran.

The white boots made a small, quick sound on the loose stone. The scent of honeysuckle was in her hair, thinned by the dawn wind into something colder and further away. She reached Alfonso, reached up, touched Cesare's face.

No response.

"He is alive," Alfonso said. "He has only fainted."

Valentina said nothing. She undid the white handkerchief at her waist—the one embroidered with the Yenisei national crest, the honeysuckle vine—and laid it, with great care, across Cesare's forehead. The cloth still carried the smell of her hair. The morning wind took the edge of it.

"Quintilian?" Alfonso asked.

"Behind us," Valentina said. "The Augustus's left arm is gone, but he is fine. He is helping Violante clear rubble from the lower passage."

"Liansheng?"

"I do not know."

Alfonso did not ask again. He set Cesare down on a flat stone and sat himself against a leafless tree nearby. The tree had lost every leaf to the shock of the explosion. Its bare branches pointed up into the sky like a sheaf of silent swords.

Valentina crouched beside him.

"Leonardo?" she asked.

"Dead." Alfonso said. "Or the machine is dead. The body is there, but there is no one left inside it."

Valentina nodded.

"Omega?"

"All of them." Alfonso pointed toward the mountain. "My spiders ran a five-kilometer sweep after the blast. No Omega signatures."

"The World Tree?"

"Gone, too."

They sat in silence for a while.

The dawn kept spreading. The blue-gray gave way, in long slow rolls, to gold and red. The wind came up out of the valley with the smell of dead leaves and dust. From somewhere in the distance came the ragged sounds of a camp coming back to life—officers calling headcounts, men searching for the living, someone trying to coax a smashed radio back to speech.

Don Juan limped up and lowered himself onto the stone beside Cesare. He tossed the broken left arm of the Rose Ghost to the ground, pulled a handkerchief out of his coat, and pressed it to his face. The cloth came away red.

"The boss once said," Don Juan said, after a while, "that he wanted to live a plain life with a good woman. A house with a slanted window. A cat. Flowers in the yard."

Alfonso glanced at him.

"I suppose that plan is going to have to wait a while," Don Juan said, and grinned. The grin was tired. The grin was relieved. The grin was something else that he himself could not quite have named.

Valentina did not reply.

She reached out and tucked the corner of the white handkerchief more firmly across Cesare's forehead, against the wind from the east.

Cesare still did not wake.

But his pulse was stronger than it had been a few minutes before.

Quintilian came out of the passage mouth at a run and the dawn caught him full in the face. He was covered in dust. The rims of his eyes were red. The enormous body of him looked, in the backlight, more awkward than usual. The left arm of the Augustus had come off at the shoulder, and he had the broken silver shield clamped under the remaining arm. The lion's-ear on the closed-eye lion crest was gone. The lion's-eye itself was split in two by a long crack.

He made his way to Cesare and crouched, and said nothing.

He only put out his enormous hand and held Cesare's cold one in it.

Violante was the last out.

Her Minerva-core uniform was thick with mud and grit. The bronze mirror that was the World Tree's branch-ward hung at her chest, still faintly warm. In her arms she carried a long bundle wrapped in her own coat—the journal of Leonardo da Vinci Borgia, the cover darkened with sweat and blood.

She came to where Cesare lay, looked down at his still face, and let out a breath she had not realized she was holding.

"Bier and Talasha?" she asked, looking to Violante.

"In Florence," Violante said. "Minerva's comms are back. I have sent ciphered orders to them to stay inside Canterbury Castle and not to come out."

"The Holy Chapel Armored Division?"

"Count Leicht withdrew his forces after the College of Cardinals countermanded the order. Archbishop Gracchus was intercepted by Alexander Grigori. The situation in Florence is, for the moment, stable."

She looked once at the mountain.

The old ridge stood silent in the dawn. The trees along its crown were dead. A thin rime of white had settled on the rock, a residue of vaporized red mercury, and the wind moved it slowly along. The mountain was still there. The villages at its foot were still there. The fields below them were still there.

"The branch of the World Tree has been destroyed," Violante said. "Every Omega prototype has been destroyed. Brahma's Fall has fulfilled its purpose."

She looked down at Cesare.

"The reduction switch was activated. The blast radius was reduced from fifty kilometers to five hundred meters."

Alfonso looked up.

"Cesare did it?"

Violante nodded.

Alfonso was quiet for a long time.

"He is alive?"

"He is alive. The amulet absorbed most of the annihilation energy. The Blue Sturgeon's core built the final protective bubble. Liansheng said the core was carrying the last fragments of the Blue Sturgeon's consciousness. It was the Blue Sturgeon herself who, in the last moment, triggered the defense."

"The Blue Sturgeon," Alfonso said, very quietly.

He remembered her. The woman whose voice was always cold. The knight who, at the end, had put her own core into the wreckage of the Blue Sturgeon to keep the Red Dragon safe.

"Liansheng?" Alfonso asked.

Violante did not answer.

Her eyes moved, instead, to the dark of the passage mouth. Someone was standing there.

A small, slight old man, in the gray robe of a style no one in the West had worn for three hundred years. Long silver hair to his waist. A face that was withered but very calm. In his right hand he held a lance inscribed with Sanskrit; the relief of the six-winged angel at its head had been broken on one side.

Liansheng.

He stood at the threshold of the passage, facing Mount Wangwu, and did not move.

The dawn light fell on his old face and laid out, in gold, every wrinkle, every silver hair, every inch of three hundred years of waiting.

"The World Tree," he said, very softly, as if to himself. "It really is gone."

Then he smiled.

It was a very slight smile, slight as the last star going down just before the dawn. But it was a real smile. It came from somewhere underneath the withering. He had waited three hundred years to see this single moment.

He turned, and began to walk, slowly, toward where Cesare lay. Halfway there, his body swayed, and he went down on one knee. The Sanskrit lance slipped from his fingers. The shaft rang against the stone with a clean metallic note.

"Liansheng!" Violante stepped quickly to him and caught his shoulder.

"I am all right," he said. "The red mercury elixir has run out."

He looked up, and his gaze fell on the journal bundled in Violante's coat.

"Da Vinci," he said. "At last he can rest."

He closed his eyes.

Three hundred years of waiting, ended with a single sentence.

Alfonso stood. He went to Cesare. The dawn was fully laid down now, gold and red pouring out of the east and washing the whole flank of Mount Wangwu in a warm wash of color. The leafless trees, the rubble, the scattered pieces of armor, the tired people—all of it was under that same gold.

He put out his mechanical hand and laid it, very gently, on Cesare's shoulder.

"Boss," he said, low. "It is time. The sun is up."

Cesare did not move.

But his finger moved, a little, against the stone.

Alfonso stared. Then he looked up at Valentina. She had seen it too. Her hand was still wrapped around Cesare's, and she had felt the small answering motion.

The gold-red light kept spreading, a long silk laid down from the far edge of the world to the foot of the mountain.

The wind came up out of the valley and took the last of the cordite with it.

Somewhere, far off, a Yenisei transcontinental express let out the long note of its whistle, as if to greet the new day.


==================================================
第247章 黎明前的翡冷翠
==================================================

【中文】
第247章 黎明前的翡冷翠

台伯河的水面漆黑如墨，驳船的蒸汽锅炉压到最低，引擎声被河水声吞没。船头那只探照灯被黑布罩着，只漏出指甲盖大小的一线光，刚好能照清前方三尺的水面。

西泽尔蹲在船头，拇指无意识地摩挲着锁骨下方那枚合金项链坠。坠子是银莲花形状的，背面刻着他至今未能完全辨认的星见文字——隐约能看出"莲花"和"根"两个字符的轮廓。金属贴着皮肤，微微发烫，血管里有一缕极淡的金红色纹路正从锁骨向颈侧蔓延，像某种被唤醒的古老脉络。

他没去压制它。

"前方两百米就是废弃码头。"阿方索的声音从船尾传来，压得极低，"上校的人三天前已经把那段河岸清理过，码头边的巡逻被他们用一辆抛锚的蒸汽货车堵住了，至少能给我们争取十分钟。"

西泽尔点了点头，没有说话。驳船无声地滑过最后一段弯道，岸边废弃的吊臂剪影从黑暗中浮现出来，像一具巨大的骨架。

瓦莲京娜先跳上了岸，靴跟在湿漉漉的石板上磕出一声脆响。她回身伸出手，金色长发在夜风中掠过苍白的面颊，冷绿色的眼睛在黑暗中亮得像两块冰。她没有说话，只是用眼神示意——快。

唐璜第二个登岸，落地时顺势一个翻滚卸力。他摘下帽子，露出那张玩世不恭的脸，刚要张嘴说点什么，看见瓦莲京娜的眼神又把话咽了回去。

昆提良最后一个上岸，甲胄和背包压得他闷哼一声。他放下背上的行李箱，抬头看了一眼翡冷翠方向——远处城墙上的探照灯正在缓慢扫过夜空，像一只硕大无朋的独眼。

"进去。"西泽尔低声道。

他转身最后看了一眼驳船，阿方索正把船底凿穿一个洞，黑水迅速涌入船舱。十分钟后这艘船就会沉到河底，连一块木板都不会留下。

一行人沿着废弃码头的石阶鱼贯而上，消失在城墙的阴影里。

二

翡冷翠的夜和以前不一样了。

从城墙根到中央广场，每隔两百米就停着一辆圣堂装甲师的巡逻车。军用级蒸汽履带底盘上架着旋转灯塔，青白色的强光每隔三十秒就会扫过一条街道。天空更低的地方，至少三艘小型巡逻飞艇正以缓慢的巡航速度绕着城市内环飞行，探照灯的光柱从云层缝隙间漏下来，像细长的银针刺在石板路面上。

他们从一条几乎被遗忘的排水渠进入旧城区。渠道里弥漫着陈年积水和铁锈的气味，脚下满是碎砖和青苔。西泽尔走在最前面，右手按在腰间的指挥剑柄上，那是父亲临别时交给他的东西。

唐璜用袖口掩着鼻子，压低声音："真他妈把这儿当铁十字堡了。"

没人接话。

从排水渠出口钻出来的时候，昆提良先看见了那张告示。

那是一张足有半面墙大的异端通缉令，用厚实的牛皮纸印成，黑底白字，印着西泽尔的侧脸素描像——画得相当精准，连下颌线的弧度都没走样。告示顶端是黑色天使展翼的徽记，底部用红墨水写着罪名和悬赏金额。

西泽尔·博尔吉亚，代号红龙，密涅瓦机关逃犯。

参与颠覆教廷、谋杀枢机卿、私藏S级危险武器、勾结异端。

悬赏：十万金币。死活不论。

"老板的画比本人好看。"唐璜凑上去看了一眼，咂了咂嘴，"就是没画出你的神韵，你这双眼睛画师得照着真紫瞳去临摹才能画出来。"

西泽尔没理他。通缉令下方还贴着一排小一号的告示，是阿方索、昆提良和唐璜的——他们三个的悬赏金额加起来才五千金币，显然被认为只是小角色。

瓦莲京娜的名字没出现在任何一张告示上。叶尼塞公主的外交豁免权还在起作用，至少目前是这样。

"走。"西泽尔把帽檐拉低，转身钻进了窄巷。

三

上校把他在马斯顿的地下斗兽场整套搬了回来。

旧址位于翡冷翠城南一座废弃的圣玛格丽特教堂地下三层。教堂在三十年前就已经被教会除名，只剩一具空壳。上校买下它的地契，用旧矿道的图纸重新挖通了一条通往城外的通风竖井，又在地下三层浇筑了新的承重柱和铁栅门。

西泽尔一行人从教堂背后的墓园入口进去，沿着墓碑之间的小径走到最深处——一块刻着"安息"字样的白色大理石碑。唐璜伸手按住石碑底部的凸起，用力一推，整块石碑向右滑开，露出一条向下的石阶。

台阶尽头是一扇厚重的铁门，门后站着两个戴着黑铁面具的守卫。面具上刻着上校斗兽场的标志——一只张嘴咆哮的金属狗头。

守卫看见西泽尔，什么都没说，直接拉开了门。

门后是一片出乎意料的宽阔空间。这原本是教堂的地下墓穴，上校把它改造成了一个兼具居住、维修和仓储功能的多层据点。空气里弥漫着机油味和金属切割留下的焦味，头顶的煤油灯被换成了一排排白炽灯管，灯光白得发青。

阿方索一进门就直奔工作台。他的工作台在最靠墙的角落，上面铺着各种零件和图纸，蜘蛛巢腕表搁在固定架上，旁边是一只被拆得只剩框架的雷霆牙改型。阿方索边走边脱外套，外套还没挂上椅子，他的手已经按在了那堆图纸上。

薇若兰比他到得更早。

她在据点正中央那张被拼凑起来的长桌前坐着，面前摊着一张翡冷翠的地下管网图。烛光从她脸侧照过来，把那张疲倦却依然锋利的脸切成明暗两半。乌黑的长发被随意束在脑后，几缕碎发垂在耳际。

看见西泽尔进来，她只是抬了抬眼皮。

"密涅瓦机关叹息之墙已经被圣堂装甲师接管了。"她没起身，声音沙哑，"总长权限被枢机会冻结，我进不去武器库。"

"我知道。"西泽尔在她对面坐下。

薇若兰把一张薄薄的纸片推过来。纸片上是一个六翼猫头鹰的徽记——密涅瓦机关总长徽章的图样。

"佛朗哥老师留了一手。"她说，"真正的总长徽章在他失踪前就交给了我。密涅瓦机关的全部资产和权限，包括叹息之墙内侧所有装备的解锁权，都在这枚徽章里。但我现在不能公开拿出来用——只要我亮出这枚徽章，枢机会就会知道我还活着，我的潜伏就没有意义了。"

"所以你需要一个能代替你进武器库的人。"西泽尔说。

薇若兰看着他，没有否认。

西泽尔低头看了一眼那张管网图。叹息之墙后方是密涅瓦的核心区——武器库、维修车间、骑士起降平台，以及最深处那间存放着历代炽天使残骸的圣所。他当年在那里待过整整三年，熟悉那条走廊的每一个转角。

"我进去。"他说。

"你进去就出不来了。"薇若兰说，"叹息之墙现在由圣堂装甲师三班倒值守，莱希特伯爵亲自坐镇。你刚被通缉，进门那一刻就会被识破。"

"我不会从正门进。"

薇若兰沉默了几秒。"备份通道。"

"佛朗哥教授告诉我过那条路。"西泽尔说，"在密涅瓦机关建造初期，初代总长在叹息之墙外围开凿了一条备用通道，紧急撤离用的。四十年没被启用过，图纸上标注的位置在城北铁路桥下方的排水暗渠。"

"那条路我能走。"薇若兰说，"但是太窄。只能容一个人通过，无法携带大型装备。"

"不需要大型装备。"西泽尔说，"我需要你列一份清单——武器库里哪些东西是受控的、必须用总长权限才能解锁的。你把清单给我，我去解锁带出来。"

薇若兰拿起炭笔，在管网图的空白处写下第一行字。

两人正低声交谈，走廊尽头传来铁栅门沉重的开启声。脚步声由远及近，沉稳而有力，每一步踩下去都带着军人特有的节奏感。

李锡尼从阴影中走出来。

他今天没穿那身标志性的猩红十字黑袍，而是换了一身普通的灰色长风衣，胸口和袖口没有任何徽记。左肩略微下垂——那是三年前旧伤的后遗症，抬臂过肩会引发不可控的痉挛。但他的眼睛依然像两把冰冷的手术刀。

他身后跟着四个人。

第一个人是塔拉夏，密涅瓦机关的年轻机械师，薇若兰的助手。她今天穿着一身深色工装，怀里抱着一只金属箱子，箱子里传来蒸汽管路轻微的嘶嘶声。

后面三个人西泽尔没见过。都是中年人，穿着密涅瓦机关的制式工程师服，胸口绣着蒸汽机械神教的齿轮徽记。他们面色苍白，嘴唇紧抿——显然知道今晚的会面意味着什么。

李锡尼走到长桌前，没有坐下。他从风衣内袋里取出一封信，信封上盖着佛朗哥教授的私人火漆印——密涅瓦机关只有最高级别的技术机密才会使用这种印。

"佛朗哥教授在失踪前三天给我写了这封信。"李锡尼的声音冷硬如铁，"信里写明：如果他出了事，就用这封信作为密令，召集他指定的三十七名核心技术人员。这些人散布在翡冷翠各个角落，每个人都不知道其他人的存在。"

他把信递给薇若兰。

"今晚到齐了四个人。"他说，"剩下的三十三个，我已经派人去通知了，明晚之前会陆续抵达。"

薇若兰接过信，拆开火漆。她快速扫了一眼内容，眉头皱紧又松开。

"老师留了后手。"她轻声说。

"他一辈子都在留后手。"李锡尼冷冷地说。

四

长桌四周的灯全打开了。

西泽尔把据点里的所有人聚拢在桌前，铺开那张翡冷翠地下管网图。薇若兰用炭笔在图上标注了叹息之墙的三个出入口——正门、备份通道和位于城东的一座废弃通风井。阿方索同时把两张图纸摊开：一张是雷霆牙暴力增强型的改装设计图，另一张是新型红龙试制版的维修手册。

"先说装备。"阿方索从金属箱里取出零件，摆在桌面上，"我在据点的库房里找到了三台还能用的雷霆牙基础型，加上我从马斯顿带回来的那台暴力增强原型——总共有四台。"

他指着改装图上的核心区域："暴力增强型雷霆牙在原来的基础上加入了红水银填充弹头。薇若兰副总长之前改造过一台原型机，但炸药量不够。这次我重新设计了弹头结构——把红水银的注入量提高到原来的三倍，但用一个微型蒸汽阀来控制引爆时机，骑士可以在扣下扳机的瞬间选择击发还是延时。"

"延时多久？"唐璜问。

"最长五秒。"阿方索说，"五秒之内骑士可以把它当成普通连射铳使用，五秒之后弹头里的红水银会被点燃，铳身会在三秒内解体爆炸——炸药量足够把一辆重型机车掀翻。"

"这玩意儿是一次性的。"昆提良插嘴。

"对。"阿方索点头，"所以我把它当作最后的保命手段来设计——当你已经被敌人逼到绝路、跑不掉也打不赢的时候，可以假装投降，扣下扳机，把铳口对准自己。敌人会以为你在自杀，会有一瞬间的犹豫。"

他停顿了一下。

"五秒之后，他们会发现自己错了。"

桌旁安静了两秒。

"另一张图。"阿方索把新型红龙维修手册翻到标注页，"新型红龙试制版在马斯顿一战后龙吼炮能量管出现裂纹，必须更换。所罗门王的右臂微型轴承在矿道里被欧米茄的碎片击伤过，精度下降了百分之十五。我在库房找到了备件，今晚连夜修。"

"我的呢？"昆提良敲了敲自己的奥古斯都维护手册。

"秘银重盾上次的裂纹还没完全修好。"阿方索瞥了他一眼，"你扛得住普罗米修斯一记斧劈，但要再来第二次，盾面会断。"

昆提良咧了咧嘴，没说话。

"机械蜘蛛我重新换了微型轴承。"阿方索继续说，"新批次每只可以维持十二分钟的有效活动窗口，比原来多四分钟。信号干扰模式的有效距离也从八十米扩展到一百二十米。但——"

他顿了顿。

"如果对方是欧米茄原型体级别的对手，蜘蛛会在接触装甲的瞬间被自愈神经纤维烧穿。"

"所以蜘蛛只能用来对付普通敌人。"西泽尔说。

"对。"阿方索点头，"用来对付欧米茄的是另一套东西——机械神教叩门者的青铜蜘蛛集群。我从那批小家伙身上学到了一件事：它们自毁时释放的电磁脉冲，对欧米茄自愈神经纤维有奇效。"

他看了西泽尔一眼。

"问题是青铜蜘蛛已经全部用完了。要想补充，得先找到薇若兰副总长从翡冷翠带回来的那批备件。"

薇若兰从工装口袋里摸出一只小皮袋，解开袋口倒在桌面上。十几只拇指盖大小的青铜蜘蛛滚了出来，每一只头部凹槽里都还亮着两点暗绿色的微光。

"还有这么多。"她说。

"够了。"阿方索把它们一颗颗拾起来放回皮袋，"我今晚给它们重新校准一下共振频率。"

五

装备问题说完，长桌上安静了片刻。塔拉夏默默地把金属箱打开，里面是一套神经电流读出器的备件。三个工程师开始低头检查各自带来的工具和文档。

西泽尔等他们各自忙开，才转向薇若兰。

"战术。"他说。

薇若兰把地下管网图上用红笔圈出的几个位置指给他看。

"我们的目标分三层。"她说，"第一层是碧儿·丹缇和塔拉夏之前被困的坎特伯雷堡方向——那里被圣堂装甲师第二分队接管，戒备森严，但具体关押位置我还没有确认。"

"第二层是密涅瓦机关武器库。叹息之墙现在由莱希特伯爵和格拉古大主教联合控制，必须拿到总长权限才能解锁受控装备。"

"第三层——"她顿了一下，"原罪机关。他们手里还有大约一半的欧米茄原型体和全部第三代普罗米修斯试制机。一号在马斯顿被引爆了红水银核心，二号古洛诺斯也报废了，但零号还在。"

"零号才是最难对付的那个。"西泽尔说。

"对。"薇若兰点头，"所以我们不能分散太多力量。"

西泽尔低头看着管网图，手指无意识地敲着桌面。节奏很慢，每一下间隔三秒——那是他在思考时的习惯。

"分兵。"他说，"但不是三路，是四路。"

所有人都看向他。

"第一路。"他指向坎特伯雷堡方向，"唐璜。你的甲胄最快、最轻、最适合侦察。我需要你摸清楚圣堂装甲师第二分队在坎特伯雷堡周围的部署、换岗时间和通讯频段。碧儿和塔拉夏还困在那里——我要知道她们具体被关在哪里、有多少人看守、什么时候换防。"

"你不能去救她们。"薇若兰提醒。

"今晚不救。"西泽尔说，"今晚只看。"

唐璜难得地没有开玩笑，只是点了点头。

"第二路。"西泽尔指向城北铁路桥方向，"昆提良。你的伤还没好利索，奥古斯都的秘银重盾也还没修完。你不适合正面作战，但铁十字堡那边还有一批退役的炽天铁骑——老戈特、赫尔曼、还有几个我没记住名字的。他们当年在马斯顿帮过李锡尼副局长，欠他人情。"

他看向李锡尼。

李锡尼微微颔首："我写几封信。昆提良带过去。"

"第三路。"西泽尔看向薇若兰，"你带塔拉夏和那三个工程师走备份通道进密涅瓦武器库。我需要你解锁的东西——"

他把薇若兰之前写的那张清单推到她面前。

"清单上一共七件。"西泽尔说，"其中三件是常规装备：备用神经接驳缓冲剂、紧急医疗包、便携式蒸汽动力焊枪。另外四件是受控的——两份佛朗哥教授留下来的研究备份、一套完整的炽天使神经接驳系统图纸、一枚密涅瓦初代总长留下的特殊金属焊料。"

"焊料？"薇若兰抬眼。

"佛朗哥教授说它在关键时刻有用。"西泽尔说，"我信他。"

薇若兰沉默了几秒，把清单折好放进工装内袋。

"第四路。"西泽尔转向瓦莲京娜，"殿下。"

瓦莲京娜靠在墙边，双臂抱在胸前。她从进门开始就没有说话，金色长发垂在肩上，在灯光下泛着冷光。

"我需要你联络叶尼塞使团。"西泽尔说。

瓦莲京娜挑了挑眉。

"制造外交骚乱。"西泽尔说，"翡冷翠现在是圣域，叶尼塞使团享有外交豁免权。如果叶尼塞特使以'圣域条款侵犯盟约'为由向枢机会提出正式抗议，枢机会就必须分出人手来应付外交纠纷。"

"你要我分他们的心。"瓦莲京娜说。

"对。"西泽尔说，"枢机会现在把全部注意力放在追捕我身上。圣堂装甲师、异端审判局、圣域内所有机动力量——他们以为我还在马斯顿。我要让他们在翡冷翠也睡不好觉。"

瓦莲京娜看了他很久。

"这是你求人办事的态度？"她轻声问。

"我付得起代价。"西泽尔说。

"什么代价？"

西泽尔沉默了两秒。锁骨下方的项链坠微微发烫，紫瞳的边缘有一缕极细的金红色纹路闪过。

"等这一切结束之后。"他说，"我会亲口回答你一个问题。任何一个。"

瓦莲京娜盯着他的眼睛。

"成交。"她说。

六

战术会议持续了将近两个小时。工程师们在角落里低声讨论维修方案，薇若兰和塔拉夏反复核对备份通道的入口坐标，阿方索把青铜蜘蛛的共振频率校准到与密涅瓦制式设备同步。

西泽尔一直坐在长桌前，没有起身。他的紫瞳偶尔会闪过金红色的光——频率不高，大概每二十分钟一次，每次持续不到一秒。瓦莲京娜注意到了，但她没问。

凌晨四点，会议结束。

薇若兰带着塔拉夏和三名工程师从教堂墓园的东侧出口离开，消失在排水渠的方向。瓦莲京娜在临走前从墙边取下自己的大衣，回身看了西泽尔一眼。

"等这一切结束。"她说，"别忘了你答应我的。"

她没等他回答就转身走了。金色长发在大衣领口处微微摆动，消失在门口。

昆提良已经回维修间休息——阿方索坚持让他躺下，说重盾裂纹的修复必须等他睡醒之后进行。维苏威矿道里那一战耗尽了他的体力，他再扛下去会影响明天的状态。

据点里最后只剩下三个人。

西泽尔，阿方索，唐璜。

阿方索在工作台前沉默地校准着青铜蜘蛛，工具在他手指间翻飞，发出细碎的金属碰撞声。

唐璜坐在桌角，一条腿盘在椅子上，另一条腿晃来晃去。他的蔷薇之鬼轻型甲胄已经预热完毕，关节处泄出淡淡的蒸汽。

"我走了。"他说。

西泽尔抬头看了他一眼。

"小心。"

"老板，你今天说的字加起来都没超过三百个。"唐璜站起来，把帽子重新扣上，"照顾好自己。别在我回来之前死掉。"

他没等西泽尔回话就转身走向了铁栅门。脚步声在地下墓穴里回荡，越来越轻，最后消失在通风竖井的方向。

阿方索没抬头，只是说了句："蜘蛛的共振频率我调到第三档了。对付普通装甲有效，对付欧米茄有奇效。你自己掂量着用。"

西泽尔点了一下头。

他靠回椅背，闭上眼睛。锁骨下方的项链坠依然微微发烫。

七

唐璜从通风竖井爬出来的时候，天还是黑的。

他蹲在教堂墓园的墓碑后面，让眼睛适应了一会儿夜色的灰度。翡冷翠的天空被巡逻飞艇的探照灯染成一种不健康的青白色，远处的城墙轮廓在灯光下像一道黑色的铁幕。

他沿着墓碑之间的小径快步往城南走，蔷薇之鬼的甲胄被收在一只特制的狭长背包里，背包的肩带勒得他肩膀生疼。这套装甲加上他的工具包，总重超过一百二十斤——但对前炽天骑士团见习骑士来说，这点重量只够热身。

城南的方向是坎特伯雷堡。

他没走大路。从墓园出来之后他就钻进了一片废弃的工人宿舍区，绕过三个巡逻岗哨，沿着一条他两年前踩过点的暗巷来到了城南区的主干道边缘。

主干道上很热闹——凌晨四点的翡冷翠城南依然有零星的蒸汽货车在跑。但让唐璜放慢脚步的不是货车。

是一队人。

一队大约十二人的士兵正沿着城南的青石板路快步前行，方向是坎特伯雷堡。士兵们穿着圣堂装甲师的制式深灰色军服，胸口绣着银色双翼徽记，腰间挎着制式短铳。

走在最前面的是一个让唐璜几乎要骂出声的人。

法比奥。

假面骑士兄弟会的前任会长。

他今天没穿学生制服——而是一身圣堂装甲师中尉的正式军服，肩章和袖口都用金线绣着花边。他那张原本还算英俊的脸在路灯下显得格外苍白，嘴角挂着一丝唐璜熟悉到骨子里的假笑。

他的胸口别着一枚徽记。

不是圣堂装甲师的银色双翼——而是那枚唐璜永远认不出来的、刻着撕裂面具和交叉长剑的假面骑士兄弟会徽记。徽记被擦得锃亮，在路灯下反射出一道冷光。

唐璜把身子缩进了暗巷的阴影里，一动不动。

法比奥从他藏身的位置三步远的地方走过。士兵们的靴子踩在青石板上的声音整齐划一，没有人说话。

唐璜数了数——十二个。都是熟面孔。都是假面骑士兄弟会的老成员。

他看见法比奥转过头，对身边一个士兵说了句什么。士兵点了点头。

然后他听见了法比奥的声音，被夜风送进巷子：

"——老师交代过，今晚要把那个叫碧儿的女人转移到叹息之墙去。格拉古大主教亲自下的命令。"

脚步声渐渐远去，消失在城南的方向。

唐璜蹲在阴影里，手指无声地扣紧了巷壁的砖缝。

他等了整整五分钟才从暗巷里直起身来。

然后他转身，朝教堂墓园的方向飞奔而去。

【English】
Chapter 247 — Florence Before Dawn

The Tiber ran black as ink, its surface catching only the faintest smudge of starlight. The barge's steam boiler had been throttled to its lowest register, the engine's complaint swallowed by the river's long slow whisper. A single lamp was lashed to the bow, its hooded lens tipped with a black rag that allowed no more than a thumbnail's breadth of yellow to escape—just enough to read the three feet of water sliding past the prow.

Cesare crouched there, thumb working the small medallion beneath his collarbone out of habit. The pendant was shaped like a silver anemone, its reverse incised with two characters of the old stargazer's script he had never quite been able to read in full: a flower, and beneath it, something that meant *root*. The metal lay against his skin warm, warmer than the night should have allowed, and a thread of pale gold-red was threading itself from his collarbone up the side of his neck, a vein reawakening along an ancient map.

He did not try to suppress it.

"Two hundred meters to the abandoned quay." Alfonso's voice came from the stern, almost inaudible. "The Colonel's people cleared that stretch of bank three days ago. They've blocked the riverside patrol with a broken-down steam lorry. It should buy us ten minutes."

Cesare nodded without turning. The barge slid around the last bend, and the silhouette of a disused loading crane rose out of the dark ahead, a ribcage of rust and riveted iron.

Valentina stepped onto the quay first. The heel of her boot cracked once against the wet stone, a small clean report in the silence. She turned and extended a hand, her pale face cut by the wind, and the cold green of her eyes caught what little light there was and held it, two chips of ice in the dark. She said nothing. She did not need to.

Don Juan came next, landing in a roll that ate the impact. He stripped off his cap, the roguish mouth already beginning to open, caught Valentina's look, and closed it again.

Quintilian was last, and the weight of his armor and pack brought a grunt out of him when his boots found the stone. He set down the battered case on his back and looked once toward Florence, where the watchlights of the city wall were slowly sweeping the sky like a single enormous, unblinking eye.

"In," Cesare said, low.

He turned for one last look at the barge. Alfonso was already punching a hole in the hull below the waterline; black water was rushing in, hissing faintly against the iron. In ten minutes there would be nothing left to find.

They went up the broken steps of the quay in single file, and the wall of the city took them.

II

Florence at night was a different animal than it had been a month ago.

Every two hundred meters from the river wall to the central piazza now stood a Holy See armored patrol: tracked steam chassis, a rotating lantern turret atop each, the cold blue-white of the searchlight bleaching the stones at thirty-second intervals. Higher up, three small patrol dirigibles were working the inner ring at a slow cruising pace, their beams leaking down through gaps in the cloud cover and pinning thin silver needles onto the streets below.

They had entered the old quarter through a stormwater conduit the city had half-forgotten. The channel smelled of standing water and old rust. The floor was broken brick and a slick of moss, and Cesare led them with his right hand on the hilt of the command sabre his father had pressed into his hands at parting.

Don Juan, muffling his nose with one sleeve: "They've turned the bloody place into Iron Cross Fortress."

No one answered him.

When they came out of the conduit, Quintilian saw the broadside first.

It was a heresy notice the size of a wall, printed on heavy calfskin paper, black ink on a black ground, with a profile portrait in white line that had caught Cesare's jaw exactly—every angle of the chin faithfully drawn. The seal at the top was the black-winged angel of the Inquisition. Across the foot, in red, ran the charges and the bounty.

CESARE BORGIA. ALIAS: THE RED DRAGON. FUGITIVE OF THE MINERVA BUREAU.

Conspiracy against the Holy See. Murder of a Cardinal. Possession of an S-class proscribed weapon. Communion with heretics.

Bounty: One hundred thousand gold crowns. Alive or dead.

"Painter made you prettier than the original," Don Juan murmured, leaning in. "He didn't get the eyes, though. He'd have had to copy a real purple iris to do that."

Cesare did not answer. Below the great poster, in smaller type, were three more—Alfonso, Quintilian, Don Juan—their bounties adding up to a paltry five thousand. The world apparently thought them small change.

Valentina's name was not on any of them. The diplomatic immunity of the Yenisei mission was still holding. For now.

"Move," Cesare said, and pulled the brim of his cap low, and turned into the narrow street.

III

The Colonel had brought his Marston operation home in pieces.

The new site sat three floors below a disused church of St. Margaret, the building deconsecrated thirty years ago and now only a husk. He had bought the ground deed, run a ventilation shaft along the line of an old mining tunnel, and poured new load-bearing pillars and iron gates on the third underground level.

They came up through the graveyard behind the church, threading the path between tombstones, and stopped at the far end of it before a slab of white marble inscribed with the single word *Requiescat*. Don Juan pressed the small boss at the foot of the slab, and the whole stone slid sideways, revealing a flight of steps going down.

At the foot of the steps was a heavy iron door. Two guards flanked it, their faces hidden behind black iron masks stamped with the metal dog's head of the Colonel's old arena.

They saw Cesare. They said nothing. They opened the door.

The space behind it was larger than anyone had a right to expect. The Colonel had taken the old crypt and rebuilt it into a working settlement: quarters above, repair bays and storage below, the whole lit by a long row of incandescent tubes so white the air around them looked bruised.

Alfonso was at his bench before his coat was off. The bench stood in the far corner, a nest of drawings and parts; the Spider Nest wristwatch was clamped in its stand, and beside it lay a Thunder Fang in pieces, reduced to a bare frame. He had his hands on the drawings before the coat had finished settling on the back of his chair.

Violaine had got there before him.

She sat at the long improvised table in the middle of the chamber, the underground pipe map of Florence spread in front of her. The candle at her shoulder halved her face into a sliver of light and a half of dark, and her features, tired and very sharp, gave back nothing. The black of her hair was tied loosely at the nape; two long strands had escaped and hung by her ears.

When she looked up and saw Cesare, she did not rise.

"The Wall of Sighs has been taken over by the Holy See Armored Division," she said, her voice hoarse. "The Chief's authority has been frozen by the Cardinal Conclave. I can't get into the arsenal."

"I know." He sat down across from her.

Violaine pushed a thin slip of paper across the table. On it was drawn the sigil of a six-winged owl—the chief's seal of the Minerva Bureau.

"Professor Frango left a contingency." She said it carefully. "The real seal was given to me before his disappearance. Full access to all Minerva assets and authorities—the unlocking rights to everything behind the Wall of Sighs—is in this seal. But I can't produce it openly. The moment I do, the Conclave will know I am alive, and my cover is finished."

"So you need a pair of hands you can send in instead of your own," Cesare said.

She did not contradict him.

He looked at the pipe map. The territory behind the Wall of Sighs was the heart of Minerva—the arsenal, the maintenance halls, the takeoff platforms for the armored knights, and, in the deepest chamber, the reliquary that held the broken remains of the Seraphs of past generations. He had spent three years of his life in those corridors. He knew every turn.

"I'll go in," he said.

"If you go in, you will not come out." Violaine said. "The Wall is on a three-watch rotation, with Count Reichert himself in command. You have been posted as a fugitive. The moment you cross the threshold they will know you."

"I'm not crossing the threshold."

A short silence. "The backup passage."

"Professor Frango told me about it once. In the early days of Minerva the first chief cut a service tunnel outside the Wall, an emergency evacuation route. It hasn't been opened in forty years. On the old plans its mouth is in a storm drain under the railway bridge in the north of the city."

"I can manage that route." Violaine said. "But it is narrow. It will only take one person, and no large equipment."

"I won't be bringing any."

"Then give me a list. Mark what is in the arsenal that is sealed, that needs a chief's seal to open. I will write it down, you will bring it out."

She picked up the charcoal and began to write.

They were still bent low over the map, speaking in undertones, when the iron gate at the end of the corridor groaned open. Footsteps, measured and heavy, came down the long passage with the rhythm of a man who had worn a uniform for longer than he cared to remember.

Licinius stepped out of the shadow.

He was not in his customary scarlet-crossed black coat today. He wore a plain grey greatcoat, the collar turned up, the breast and cuffs empty of insignia. His left shoulder sat a little lower than the right—the relic of a wound three winters old, one that spasmed past the horizontal if he tried to lift the arm. His eyes were the same: two cold surgical instruments.

Four people came out of the dark behind him.

The first was Talaxia, the young mechanic of Minerva, Violaine's assistant. She was in dark work clothes, a metal case in her arms, the soft hiss of steam lines from inside it. Behind her came three men Cesare did not know, all in their middle years, all in the standard Minerva engineering smocks with the brass gear of the Steam-Mech Church stitched on the breast. They were pale. They were holding their mouths very tight. They knew what this meeting meant.

Licinius came to the long table and did not sit. He drew a letter from the inside of his coat. The envelope was sealed with Professor Frango's private wax—a mark used only for the highest-grade technical secrets of Minerva.

"Professor Frango wrote this to me three days before he disappeared." Licinius's voice was iron. "The letter is to be treated as a sealed order. By its terms I am to assemble the thirty-seven core technical staff he names. These people are scattered across Florence. None of them knows the others exist."

He handed the letter to Violaine.

"Four have arrived tonight. The other thirty-three I have sent word to. They will be here by tomorrow night."

Violaine broke the seal. She read it quickly. Her brow tightened, then eased.

"The professor left himself a key," she said, quietly.

"He always left himself a key," Licinius said, without affection.

IV

The lamps at the long table were all turned up.

Cesare drew everyone in the chamber around the table and unfolded the underground map of Florence. Violaine marked in charcoal the three entries to the Wall of Sighs: the main gate, the backup passage, and a disused ventilation shaft in the east of the city. Alfonso spread two drawings beside it: the modified design of the Thunder Fang Overload, and the maintenance manual for the Red Dragon Mark II.

"Equipment first." Alfonso was already laying parts out of the metal case. "In the stores here we have three functional Thunder Fangs in base configuration, plus the Overload prototype I brought back from Marston. Four machines in total."

He tapped the core section of the diagram. "The Overload variant takes the existing frame and adds a red mercury–filled warhead. Violaine built a prototype once, but the charge was too small. I've redesigned the warhead structure—three times the red mercury, but with a micro steam valve controlling the ignition. The rider can choose, on the trigger pull, between firing it as a gun and a delayed detonation."

"Delayed how long?" Don Juan asked.

"Five seconds maximum. In that window the rider can use it as an ordinary repeater. After five seconds the mercury ignites, the gun body comes apart in three seconds, and the yield is enough to flip a heavy armored car."

"It's a one-shot," Quintilian said.

"It is. I built it as a last-resort weapon. The moment you're cornered, can't run, can't win—you can drop the rifle, raise your hands, and let the enemy think you're surrendering. They hesitate for a second. They will be wrong."

Two seconds of quiet in the chamber.

"Other drawing." Alfonso turned the manual to its tabbed page. "The Red Dragon Mark II took a crack in the energy pipe of the Dragon Roar after Marston, and the right micro-bearing of Solomon's Right Arm was chipped by an Omega fragment in the mine. Precision is down fifteen percent. I've found the spares. I'll have it done tonight."

Quintilian knocked on his own maintenance book. "Me?"

"Your mithril shield's crack from last time isn't fully set. The shield will take one Prometheus axe-blow. Two will split it."

Quintilian showed his teeth, said nothing.

"Mechanical spiders, I've replaced the micro-bearings on the new batch. Each unit holds an active window of twelve minutes, up from eight. Jamming range is up to a hundred and twenty meters from eighty. But—" He paused. "—against an Omega-grade prototype, the spider's casing will be burned through on contact by the self-healing nerve fibers."

"So spiders are for ordinary soldiers," Cesare said.

"They are. Against Omegas, I want to use something else. I learned it from a small thing: the bronze spider swarm of the Knocker sect, of the Steam-Mech Church. When they self-destruct, they throw an electromagnetic pulse that does strange things to an Omega's nerve fibers."

He looked at Cesare.

"The problem is, the bronze spiders are spent. If we want more, we have to find the spares Violaine brought back from Florence."

Violaine reached into a pocket of her work coat, untied a small leather bag, and tipped a dozen thumb-sized bronze spiders onto the table. Each had two dim green points of light in the eye-socket of its head.

"Plenty left," she said.

"Enough." Alfonso gathered them carefully and put them back. "I'll recalibrate the resonance tonight."

V

When the equipment business was done, the table went quiet for a moment. Talaxia opened the metal case and laid out the spare parts of a neural current reader. The three engineers bent to the work of checking their instruments and documents.

Cesare waited until they had all found their own corners.

"Tactics," he said.

Violaine turned the map so he could see, and pointed out the positions she had circled in red.

"Three layers of target," she said. "The first is Canterbury Keep, where Bir and Talaxia were being held. It is under the Second Squadron of the Holy See Armored Division. Heavily guarded. I have not yet confirmed the exact cell."

"Second layer is the Minerva arsenal. The Wall of Sighs is under joint command of Count Reichert and Archbishop Glagus. The chief's seal is required to open the sealed stores."

"Third—" She hesitated. "—is the Original Sin Bureau. They still hold roughly half of the Omega prototypes and all of the third-generation Prometheus test units. Mark One detonated its red mercury core at Marston. Mark Two, Gronostay, is also scrap. But Mark Zero is still out there."

"Mark Zero is the hard one," Cesare said.

"It is. So we cannot spread our force too thin."

He looked down at the map. His finger, without his noticing, was tapping the table in a slow rhythm—three seconds between each tap, the way he always counted when he was thinking.

"We split. Not three ways. Four."

Every face at the table turned to him.

"First prong." He indicated Canterbury Keep. "Don Juan. Your armor is the fastest and lightest in the room. You are the recon. I want the Second Squadron's deployment around the Keep, the watch rotation, the comms frequencies. Bir and Talaxia are in there. I want to know where, how many guards, and when the shift changes."

"You cannot rescue them tonight," Violaine reminded him.

"Tonight we look."

Don Juan, for once, did not jest. He nodded.

"Second prong." He pointed toward the railway bridge in the north. "Quintilian. Your injuries are not yet set, and the Augustus's mithril shield is not yet repaired. You are no good in a frontal fight. But Iron Cross Fortress still has a company of retired Seraph Knights—old Goth, Hermann, and a few whose names I never caught. They helped Deputy Licinius in Marston. They owe him."

He looked at Licinius.

Licinius inclined his head. "I will write the letters. Quintilian will carry them."

"Third prong." Cesare looked at Violaine. "You will take Talaxia and the three engineers through the backup passage into the Minerva arsenal. I need you to unlock—"

He pushed the slip she had written on across to her.

"Seven items on the list," he said. "Three of them are routine: reserve neural interface buffer, emergency medical kit, portable steam welder. The other four are sealed: two sets of research backups the professor left behind, a complete schematic of the Seraph neural interface system, and a special metal solder left by the first chief of Minerva."

"Solder?" Violaine looked up.

"Professor Frango said it would be useful at a crucial moment. I trust him."

She folded the slip and put it into the breast of her coat.

"Fourth prong." Cesare turned to Valentina. "Your Highness."

She had been leaning against the wall all the while, arms folded, her long pale hair catching the light at the shoulder.

"I need you to reach the Yenisei mission," he said.

Her eyebrow moved a fraction.

"Stir up a diplomatic incident. Florence is the Holy Domain. The Yenisei mission holds full diplomatic immunity. If the Yenisei envoy lodges a formal protest with the Cardinal Conclave under the charge that the Holy Domain has violated the Covenant, the Conclave will be forced to spare some of its attention for the diplomatic mess."

"You want to distract them," Valentina said.

"I want them to stop sleeping."

She studied his face for a long moment.

"Is that how you ask a favor?" she said, very quietly.

"I can pay for it," Cesare said.

"With what?"

He was quiet for two seconds. The pendant at his collarbone pulsed warm, and along the rim of his iris, for the smallest instant, a thread of gold-red ran.

"When this is over," he said, "I will answer any one question you put to me. Of your choosing."

Valentina did not look away.

"Done," she said.

VI

The tactical session ran nearly two hours. The engineers spoke in low voices in their corner about maintenance. Violaine and Talaxia went over the backup passage's coordinates twice, then a third time. Alfonso recalibrated the bronze spiders' resonance to the standard Minerva frequency.

Cesare sat at the head of the table the whole time, and never rose. Every twenty minutes or so the purple of his eyes threw a single thin flash of gold-red, gone almost before it began. Valentina noticed. She did not ask.

At four in the morning, the meeting broke.

Violaine took Talaxia and the three engineers out through the eastern crypt gate, and they were swallowed by the storm channel. At the doorway Valentina stopped for her coat, then turned.

"When this is over," she said, "do not forget what you promised."

She did not wait for his answer. Her hair stirred once at the collar of the coat, and she was gone.

Quintilian had already gone back to the repair bay. Alfonso had insisted he lie down. The repair of the shield's crack could not be undertaken until he had slept; the Vesuvius mine fight had emptied him out, and another day of strain would cost him tomorrow.

There were three of them left in the chamber.

Cesare. Alfonso. Don Juan.

Alfonso sat at the bench, calibrating the bronze spiders in silence, his tools moving in his fingers with a faint, bright clatter.

Don Juan perched on the corner of the table, one leg folded under him, the other swinging. His Ghost of Roses light armor had been preheated, and the joints let off a thin whisper of steam.

"I'm off," he said.

Cesare looked up.

"Be careful."

"Boss, you've said fewer than three hundred words tonight in total." Don Juan stood, set the cap on his head again. "Look after yourself. Don't die before I get back."

He did not wait for an answer. His footsteps went down the corridor, light at first, then swallowed by the ventilation shaft.

Alfonso, still not looking up: "I've set the spiders' resonance to the third band. Good against standard armor. Better than good against Omega. Use your own judgment."

Cesare nodded, once.

He leaned back in the chair and closed his eyes. The pendant at his collarbone was still warm.

VII

When Don Juan came out of the ventilation shaft, the sky was still black.

He crouched behind a tombstone in the graveyard and let his eyes find their footing in the dark. The patrol dirigibles overhead had stained the sky of Florence a sickly blue-white, and the wall of the city stood against the lights like a curtain of black iron.

He made his way south between the gravestones, the Ghost of Roses armor stowed in a long, narrow pack on his back. The shoulder-straps bit into him. The whole rig—the armor, his tool roll—ran over a hundred and twenty pounds. For a former Seraph Knight, that was barely a warm-up.

South lay Canterbury Keep.

He avoided the main roads. From the graveyard he cut through an abandoned workers' quarter, skirted three patrol posts, and worked his way along a back alley he had mapped two years before, until he came to the edge of the main thoroughfare of the southern city.

The southern road was busy. Even at four in the morning there were the occasional steam wagons running along it. But it was not the wagons that slowed Don Juan's step.

It was a column of men.

Twelve soldiers moving at a fast march along the blue-grey paving stones of the south road, in the direction of Canterbury Keep. They wore the Holy See Armored Division's standard dark grey, the silver double-wing pinned to the breast, the regulation short-rifle at the hip.

The man at the head of the column was the one who nearly made Don Juan curse aloud.

Fabio.

Former President of the Masked Knight Brotherhood.

He was not in a student's uniform tonight. He was in the formal grey of a Holy See Armored Division lieutenant, the shoulder boards and cuffs picked out in gold. His face, which had been passably handsome in a schoolroom, looked bloodless under the streetlamps, and the corner of his mouth was turned up in the same false smile Don Juan remembered to his marrow.

Pinned to his breast was a badge.

Not the silver double-wing of the Division. The other one. The Masked Knight Brotherhood's sigil of the torn mask and the crossed swords, polished to a high cold shine.

Don Juan pressed himself into the shadow of the alley and did not move.

Fabio passed within three paces of where he stood. The boots of the twelve went by on the paving in clean unison, no one speaking.

Don Juan counted them. Twelve. Every face familiar. Every face a veteran of the Brotherhood.

He saw Fabio turn his head and say something to the man beside him. The man nodded.

Then Fabio's voice, carried to the alley on a breath of night air:

"—orders from the teacher. Tonight we move the woman called Bir to the Wall of Sighs. Direct order from Archbishop Glagus."

The footsteps went on. The column thinned and vanished into the south of the city.

Don Juan stayed in the shadow, his fingers pressed into the brick of the wall, and did not move for five full minutes.

Then he turned and ran, hard, for the graveyard.

第248章 假面下的陷阱
