阿黛尔在唱锡兰圣歌。

那首能——

莱昂纳多的暗红镜头猛地转向阿黛尔，他的金属身体第一次有了明显的反应——金属脊柱僵硬地转动，金属手指在按钮上捏紧，捏得指节发出了咯吱声。

"停下！"他厉声说，"停下那首歌！"

阿黛尔没有停。

她的嘴唇还在动，歌声还在继续。

那首西泽尔听不懂的锡兰圣歌，像一缕细细的清泉，正在这个充斥着红水银蒸汽、金属齿轮和欧米茄原型体心跳的圆形石室里，缓缓地、缓缓地蔓延开来。

"砰"的一声闷响。

圆形平台上方，废弃矿道的入口处，红水银蒸汽还未散尽，碧儿·丹缇的咳嗽声被金属碰撞声打断。

李锡尼扶着碧儿，抬头看着天空。

那些暗金色的光柱——几十道、几百道——从维苏威火山的山体里升起，从翡冷翠的方向飞来，从更远的西方飞来，像无数道金色的闪电，把清晨的天幕撕得粉碎。

"那是什么……"碧儿的声音在发抖。

"欧米茄原型体群。"李锡尼的声音沙哑，"全部启动了。"

他扶着碧儿，招呼塔拉夏，三个人背靠背地站在圆形平台上，看着那些金色的光柱越来越近。

矿道外面，山的另一侧，传来了马蹄声。

不是普通的马蹄声，是蒸汽机械骑兵特有的、蒸汽引擎轰鸣和金属蹄铁踏地的混响。

一匹红色蒸汽骏马从山坡后冲出来，骑在马上的金发少女在晨光中勒住缰绳，忍冬香气在金属蒸汽的辛辣中依然清冽。

瓦莲京娜·罗曼诺夫。

她身后是叶尼塞使团的二十骑蒸汽机械骑兵，机械马通体暗银色，鬃毛是用红水银微晶驱动的金属丝，随风飘动像流动的水银。骑兵们穿着叶尼塞特有的忍冬花纹胸甲，手持改装马其顿阵蒸汽弩机。

"公主殿下。"李锡尼沙哑地喊。

瓦莲京娜翻身下马，长靴踏在碎石上，忍冬香气的风里她走到李锡尼面前。

"人在哪里？"她问。

"在最深处。"李锡尼说，"西泽尔少爷、阿方索、唐璜、昆提良、薇若兰小姐——都进去了。"

瓦莲京娜看了一眼脚下深不见底的矿道，再看了一眼天空上那些越来越近的暗金色光柱。

"封住井口。"她对骑兵们说，"不能放任何一架欧米茄原型体下去。"

她抽出腰间的叶尼塞战斧，斧刃在晨光中闪着冰原寒玉特有的冷光。

"他们在下面战斗，"她低声说，"我们就在上面守住。"

金属的暗金色光柱越来越近。

圆形石室里，阿黛尔的歌声还在继续。

【English】
Chapter 254 — The Master of the Original Sin Engine

The first step rang like a small bell struck at the bottom of a well.

Cesare felt it through the sole of his boot before he heard it — a faint, answering warmth in the metal, as if something underfoot had woken to meet him. The floor was not floor. It was a planting of forged blossoms, dark-gold six-petaled lotuses cast in some alloy heavier than brass and quieter than bronze, every petal polished until it caught the lamplight and held it the way still water holds a moon. Along the edges ran a fine, continuous tracework of teeth, infinitesimally small, so that when he shifted his weight the petals kissed one another with a clean, metallic sound, and from the seams rose a thread of heat — not the dead heat of a fired hearth but the slow, deliberate heat of red mercury coursing through channels bored into the metal.

Violante, two paces behind him, had stopped breathing.

"This is the passage," she said, in a voice she was plainly trying to keep level and failing. "The one in the Leonardo uncle's manuscripts. The extension of the World Tree's root. I thought—" She stopped. "I thought it was a metaphor."

It was not a metaphor. The walls on either side confirmed it. Tiny gears, no larger than thumbnails, turned in slow, deliberate unison along ribs of yellow copper that ran the corridor's length like the veins of some patient giant. Each tooth was incised with a character — not Latin, not Greek, something older and more angular, Devanagari hands in cipher — and as the wheels revolved the characters seemed to slide forward, to flow along the wall like a procession of small dark animals.

The air was thick with the smell of the lotus. Not the watery floral of a garden; something heavier, almost narcotic, the perfume of metal heated from within.

Thirty steps. He counted them. At the thirtieth the corridor gave way.

The chamber opened like the inside of an astrolabe.

It was round. The dome above was high and dark, and set into it — packed in concentric rings, the way scales overlap on a fish — were tens of thousands of minute gears, each one turning so slowly that the eye perceived motion only as a faint shimmer, an illusion of a metal sky turning above them. The light they threw was a low, unwavering gold, the color of a coin held over a candle.

At the center of the room stood the machine.

Cesare's first thought was that it was a cathedral collapsed into mechanism. A black-iron skeleton rose from the floor and embraced a single vertical column of polished steel; yellow-copper gearing crusted the joints like moss on a stone wall; dark-gold tubing ran in from all sides, the walls and the dome and even, he realized after a moment, the floor, and converged on the column with a slow, deliberate hunger. The tubing pulsed. He could feel it through the soles of his boots — a faint, even heartbeat, deep in the rock, as though the volcano itself had been taught a rhythm.

To the column a person was bound.

"Belle—" Alfonso began, and then Belle was already running.

It was Adele.

She hung from the column by a pair of brass cuffs at the wrists, her arms pulled high above her head, her chin dropped, her pale hair fallen across half her face. The position looked designed less for cruelty than for display — the body of a small, slack puppet arranged for an audience. Pinned to the hollow of her throat was a plate of metal the size of a spread hand, and on the plate, picked out in red-gold inlay against black iron, was a sigil: a five-pointed star nested in a ring of gear-teeth, the star itself cogged at each point. The plate was glowing. The glow was a thin, steady red, the color of a wound seen through a closed eyelid.

"Adele!" Belle's voice cracked in the middle.

The figure on the column moved. A head lifted. Hair slid back from a face that Cesare knew better than his own — the straight nose, the set of the mouth, the way the left eyelid always sat a little lower than the right. Adele's eyes opened. They were clear. They found him.

She tried to speak. What came out was a dry whisper, as of a hinge rusted shut for a long time.

"Brother—" she said. "Don't — don't come closer."

Cesare did not stop because she told him to stop.

He stopped because of the man behind the machine.

The figure stood in the shadow of the black-iron skeleton, half-shrouded by the dark-gold tubing. He was tall, and the robe he wore was the deep, arterial red of old wine, falling in a long unbroken fall to the floor, where the hem lay across the stone in a small pooled crescent. Embroidered on the breast of the robe, in silver thread that caught the dome's gold and gave it back, was a device Cesare did not recognize. It was not the Kabbalistic Tree of the Messianic Church, nor the six-winged owl of the Minerva Order. It was a five-pointed star nested in a ring of gears, the star's five points each tipped with a small concentric ring of its own, like a wheel within a wheel. A machine-religion sigil. The Leonardo version of it, the one that had been lost from every printed catechism for three centuries.

And over the man's face was a mask of plain white silver, no ornament on it but the two eye-holes, and out of those holes, instead of eyes, came a low, dull amber glow.

"Welcome to the deepest heart of the lava, Red Dragon," the figure said.

The voice was strange. It had the clean articulation of well-cut gears finding one another; it had no inflection, no human warmth, no breath behind it. A clock, if a clock could speak, would have spoken in that voice.

Cesare said nothing.

"Three hundred years," the figure went on. "To be precise, three hundred and seventeen. I have been waiting for you for three hundred and seventeen years."

He raised his right hand. The motion made a small dry sound, leather on metal. His fingers closed around the edge of the silver mask and lifted it away.

What was underneath was not a face.

It was a face the way a ruin is a house. The right side, in a thin strip running from temple to chin, was still human — but the humanity of a body long exposed to weather, the skin gone the color of old tallow, drawn tight against the metal of the jaw beneath, the corner of the mouth a strip of dried tissue adhering to an iron plate. Set into the right eye-socket, where the eye had been, was a lens of dark ruby, and at the center of the lens a point of red light pulsed, slowly, patiently, like a mechanical heart.

The left half of the face was metal. It was covered in fine incised script, the same angular characters as on the corridor walls, and at the hinge of the jaw the gearwork was visible, teeth and spring exposed, so that every small movement of the mouth produced a faint, domestic click.

He turned, slowly. The robe moved with him but the body underneath did not. The body underneath clicked. The chest was a plate of dark metal; between the seams leaked a steady red luminescence, the same red as the plate on Adele's throat. The arms from the shoulder down were articulated dark-gold — bone after bone after bone, each joint a small Sanskrit-inscribed hinge, the fingers jointed in brass segments like a cathedral organ's pipes. Where the robe's hem should have concealed the legs, it only half-concealed them: two columns of hydraulic metal ending in the suggestion of feet, steam venting from a small brass valve at each knee with a soft, tired sigh.

"Are you surprised?" The dried skin at the corner of the mouth drew back a little, an arithmetic of a smile. "Three hundred and seventeen years of mechanical replacement. Every year a little more of me is taken out and put back in metal, driven by a red-mercury core. It is not pain. It is evolution."

He lifted the right hand — the fully metal one — and rapped the knuckles of it twice against the air. The sound was very clear, like a small hammer on an anvil, and the air in the chamber rang with it.

"I am Leonardo Borgia," he said. "Direct descendant, in the unbroken line, of Pope Borgia the First."

He paused. The ruby eye turned in its socket with a tiny oiled sound, and the metal finger pointed at his own chest, at the red-lit seams.

"Three hundred and seventeen years ago, my great-grandfather came down from the Avalon ice plain with a branch of the World Tree. He came back with a branch of the World Tree, and he came back with a truth.

"The world," he said, "was never made by God."

The ruby eye, turning on its axis, swept the faces in the room — Cesare's, Alfonso's, Don Juan's, Quintilian's, Violante's — as if it were reading them one by one.

"It was made by a Maker. The Maker left a tree. The tree is the heart of the mechanical civilization; the tree makes red mercury, and red mercury moves the mobile armor and the steam-engines and the Prometheuses and the Seraphim. Everything the Messianic Church has ever told you about the Creation is a lie. The Kabbalistic Tree they show you in the cathedrals is one of the smallest root-hairs of the real one, picked up by a clever priest and dressed up in a sermon."

He lowered his hand. The metal finger went out, past Adele's column, and pointed to a thing Cesare had not properly seen — a device on the back of the machine, set into a plate of black iron, the size of a clenched fist. It was a button. The button was red.

"That device is the heart of the Western branch of the World Tree. Beyond it, nine hundred and ninety-nine Omega prototypes wait for my order. All I have to do is press this." He tapped the red button once with the steel nail of his index finger; the sound was the smallest possible sound, a soft percussive tick, but every gear in the dome above seemed to hold its breath at it. "And Florence, and the Papal States, and every Western capital, will be returned, in a single night, to the embrace of God.

"The new Kingdom of God."

He turned the ruby eye back to Cesare. It did not blink. It could not blink.

"I have been cultivating you for three hundred years. From your great-grandmother on your mother's side. From the last direct blood-heir of the Ceylan line of Star-Readers. I have been waiting, all this time, for the two bloods that run in you. The violet-eyed blood of the Ceylans, and the machine-adapted blood of the Borgias.

"There is no other vessel like you in the world. There is no other perfect divine vessel."

The dried corner of the mouth did its arithmetic again.

"I did not bring you here to kill you. I brought you here so that you would help me open the last seal behind the Black Iron Gate. Only your blood can open it.

"Your sister—" The metal finger swung lazily to Adele. "—is the guarantee that you will help me."

"Help me, Red Dragon. Help me restart the machine-kingdom. I will make you the second ruler of the new Kingdom. We will rule the world together."

He let the offer hang in the dome for a moment. The gears above turned, slow, slow.

"If not—"

His metal finger came down.

The button made a sound like a single bone breaking.

" — I will use the nine hundred and ninety-nine Omega prototypes to erase Florence from the face of the earth."

The floor of the chamber shuddered.

It was not a mechanical shudder. It came up through the rock from far below, a long, rolling, percussive wave, like a giant's pulse transmitted through the bones of the world. The dome of gears stuttered, all of them at once, stopped dead for the length of a held breath, and then spun up — ten times, twenty times the speed they had been turning — into a shrieking, golden cyclone, a vortex of small bright teeth.

And then Cesare felt it.

It was in the floor, and in the walls, and in the column at Adele's back, and in the tubing, and in the air. Thousands of red-mercury cores, from the deepest galleries of the mine to the uppermost reaches of the volcano's body, were waking in the same instant, the way a field of coals is woken by a wind. He felt it as a heat at the back of his neck, and as a low singing in the fillings of his teeth, and as a pressure on the drums of his ears.

Outside, the sky changed.

The dome of the chamber was not a real sky; it was a question of stone and gear. But above Vesuvius, above Florence, the real sky was answering. Pillars of dark-gold light were punching up out of the volcano's flanks, out of the earth under the city, out of the buried machinery of three centuries — hundreds of them, then thousands, each one the energy-pulse of an Omega prototype opening its eyes. Across Florence the spires of the cathedrals were touched with the same dark gold, then the domes of the noble houses, then the parade-grounds of the Sacred Armor Companies, one by one, block by block, the whole city lighting up from underneath like a body remembering it has a heart.

Nine hundred and ninety-nine of them.

Waking.

Alfonso's wrist-piece — the Spider's Nest — was vibrating so hard the leather strap chafed. He looked down. The little dial was swinging against the pegs. His face, when he raised it, had lost a decade.

"Boss," he said, and his voice had gone flat in the way that men's voices go flat when they are not yet afraid and are already past surprise. "Omega prototype signatures. From the surface to a hundred kilometers down. All of them. They are moving. They are moving toward us."

In Don Juan's earpiece, the small clear voice of the Rose Ghost, Violante, cut in. "Cesare — Omega prototypes at the outer rim of the volcano. Concentrating on the crater from the north flank, the east flank, the west flank at once. They are converging on the entrance."

Quintilian's hand closed on the haft of his spare battle-axe. The veins on the back of it stood out like cords.

Cesare did not answer any of them.

He was watching the metal hand that was still resting on the red button.

Then, very slowly, he drew Excalibur from his side.

What came out of the sheath was not a sword. It was a memory of one — the broken tooth of the holy blade married to the broken tooth of the Dragonfang, the two halves bound together in a forge he did not remember entering, the join visible as a thin dark line across the steel like a scar. The metal was dark gold, and along the flat of the blade the Sanskrit characters were turning, turning, a slow procession of small bright animals, and the whole weapon gave off a dry, sustained heat, the heat of something that had been waiting to be drawn.

"My sister," Cesare said.

His voice was very quiet. It did not fill the dome. It did not need to.

"Release her."

It was not a question. The way he said it made the air of the dome not quite a question.

Leonardo's ruby eye did not move. The metal fingers, still on the red button, drummed once — a small deliberate tattoo of knuckles on iron.

"Kill me," he said, "and she dies. The moment my heart stops, the machine releases red mercury into her chest. She burns to ash in three seconds."

Cesare's eyes narrowed.

The violet in them was not the violet they had been. A tracery of gold and red had come up into the irises from underneath, like veins of ore surfacing in a cut stone, and the gold collar at the back of his neck was hot enough that he could feel the shape of it on his skin, a phantom brand pressed against the spine. What was moving in his blood was not blood. It was older than blood, and it had been waiting, the way the red button had been waiting, for someone to press the thing that would set it free.

"You think you are the only one who can use a bloodline," Cesare said, very low.

He raised the broken blade. He leveled it at the thing behind the machine.

The Sanskrit on the flat of the metal woke.

He took a step forward—

A sound came from the entrance of the chamber.

It was a single, heavy, percussive note, the sound of a great weight striking a stone floor from a great height — a door giving, a wall shifting, a thing of iron and old gold arriving in a place where it had been told to arrive.

Belle made a small, involuntary sound. Every head in the room turned.

The entrance to the circular chamber was a tall, narrow door of black iron set into the corridor they had walked through. Its frame bore the Kabbalistic Tree of the Messianic Church. The Tree was doing something it was not meant to do: it was flashing, on and off, on and off, the carved branches running with a dark-gold light as if the metal had been heated to the point of weeping. And from the gap between the door and the frame, light was pouring in — not in pillars, not in beams, but in a tide, a slow heaving flood of dark-gold motes, the way sunlight pours through a stained window on a windy day, only heavier, and moving, and full of intent.

The first Omega prototype came through the door the way a man comes through a door that is too small for him. It was five meters tall. Its body was a dark-gold skeleton, broad at the shoulder, long in the arm, the chest a flat ribbed plate through which the red mercury pulsed, the helmet a long, severe wedge with a single vertical slit in the faceplate, and from that slit it threw a column of dark-gold light, perfectly straight, that swung once around the dome, then down the walls, then across the machine that held Adele, then off.

It did not attack.

It stopped. It stood in the entrance like a sentry posted exactly where it had been told to stand, and the red mercury in its chest beat, beat, beat, with the patient regularity of a clock.

The second came behind it. Then the third. Then the fourth.

They came in without haste, each one the same, each one five meters of dark-gold, each one with the same slit of light in the face, each one with the same red beating at its core. They arranged themselves in a half-circle, in a fan, shoulder to shoulder, until the entrance of the chamber was a wall of metal taller than the doorframe. The red pulses of their cores were synchronized. The chamber had a heartbeat now, and the heartbeat was theirs.

The advance guard of nine hundred and ninety-nine.

"You see," said Leonardo's voice, from behind the machine, and the voice was almost gentle. "You have only the one choice, in the end. Obedience, or death."

Cesare did not answer him.

He was looking at the half-circle of dark-gold giants, at the synchronized pulse of their red cores, at the way the light from the face-slits threw a moving ladder of dark gold across the floor —

He heard a sound.

It was small.

It was thin.

It was the sound a small voice makes when it begins, with no accompaniment, in a stone room. The sound a single reed makes before the wind reaches it.

Adele had lifted her head.

She was not looking at Cesare. She was not looking at Leonardo. She was not looking at the half-circle of Omega prototypes with their red hearts and their slit-eyed faces. She was looking up, past all of them, at the dome — at the tens of thousands of small gears turning in their concentric rings, at the metal sky of the chamber.

She began to sing.

The song was in no language Cesare knew. The melody was very simple — four notes, then four notes, then four notes, in a repeating figure that made the ear expect the next phrase and find it already there. It had no force to it. It was the kind of singing one does to a child at bedtime, in a kitchen, in a quiet house, with a hand on the child's head. It was small, and thin, and it was being swallowed at every moment by the synchronized heartbeat of the Omega prototypes' cores and by the rising whine of the gears in the dome.

And yet he heard it.

He heard it because of what was underneath it. The repeating four notes, when he listened past the notes themselves, were the four notes of the lullaby Lady Linara used to hum in the long gallery at the Ceylan house in winter, when the light was failing and the brass fittings of the room caught the fire and Adele was small and would not go to sleep.

It was a Ceylan hymn.

Adele was singing a Ceylan hymn.

The hymn that—

Leonardo's ruby eye snapped to her.

It was the first time the body behind the machine had moved quickly. The metal spine turned on its axis with a tight, hard click; the metal hand clenched on the red button, the brass knuckles creaking; the left shoulder, the gear-shoulder, ground forward in its housing an inch, the way a dog brings its weight forward on its forelegs.

"Stop," he said, and the voice had lost its clockwork. "Stop that song."

Adele did not stop.

Her mouth moved. The four notes kept coming. Four, and four, and four. The thin sound of it pushed at the dome, and at the air, and at the synchronized hearts of the Omega prototypes in the entrance, and the dome-gears, which had been turning in their golden cyclone, faltered, for a moment, all together, in their turning.

The hymn was very small, and very old, and it was moving through the chamber, slowly, the way a single lit match moves through a dark room.

—

A hundred meters above, on the broken platform of stone outside the abandoned mine-shaft, Licinius was holding Belle upright, and the sky was wrong.

Red-mercury steam still leaked from the shaft, white and acrid, and Belle was coughing into her sleeve. The first light of morning had not yet come. The light that was coming was a different light: pillars of dark gold rising out of the body of Vesuvius, out of the fields to the south, out of the direction of Florence, dozens of them, then hundreds, each one a slow column of luminescence, climbing, climbing, until they were lost in the low cloud.

"What is that," Belle said, and her voice was not steady.

"Omega prototype array," Licinius said. His voice was hoarse and very level. "All of them. They are waking up."

He got Belle standing. He called Taras over. The three of them stood back to back to back on the cracked platform, looking out, the way men do in the last minutes of a siege when the noise from beyond the wall has changed and no one has yet named what the change means.

From the far side of the mountain, beyond the rim of the crater, came the sound of hooves.

It was not the sound of horses. It was the sound horses make when they are not horses: a deeper note underneath, the rhythmic bark of a small steam-engine, and over it the regular bright clatter of metal shoes on stone.

A red mechanical horse came over the edge of the rise and down the slope in a long, controlled stride. Its hide was lacquered crimson, the joints of it articulated brass, the mane a fall of mercury-thread that rippled in the morning wind as though it were a real mane, only heavier. The rider, in a single practiced motion, hauled the rein and brought the horse to a halt on the loose scree.

Valentina Romanov dismounted.

Her hair was the color of new wheat, and the wind pushed it across her face. She was wearing the Yenisei field-armor, the honeysuckle-stamped breastplate over a coat of boiled leather, and at her hip was a long-handled war-axe with a blade of polar jade that threw back the gold light of the pillars without warming to it. Behind her, in two lines of ten, came the rest of the Yenisei embassy horse — twenty mechanical riders, twenty mechanical horses, their breath white jets of steam in the cold air.

"Princess," Licinius said, and his voice broke on it and then steadied.

Valentina came across the scree to him. The smell of her came with her, the clean cold scent of winter honeysuckle, sharp against the bitter mercury-steam.

"Where are they," she said.

"The lowest level," Licinius said. "The young master, and Alfonso, and Don Juan, and Quintilian, and the lady Violante. They went in."

Valentina looked down. The shaft dropped into the dark of the mountain, the lamps at its head still flickering, the rope they had used to descend coiled and wet at the lip. Then she looked up. The dark-gold pillars in the sky were not slowing. They were closer now, and there were more of them.

"Seal the shaft," she said to the riders, without turning. "Nothing comes up out of that hole, and nothing goes down into it. Not one of those machines."

She drew the war-axe from her hip and rested the butt of it on the stone. The jade of the blade did not warm.

"They are fighting in there," she said, more quietly, to no one in particular. "We hold the door, up here."

The pillars came closer.

A hundred meters below, in the chamber of the original sin engine, Adele's voice went on, four notes, and four notes, and four, and the gears of the dome hesitated in their golden turning, and the synchronized heartbeats of the Omega prototypes at the entrance faltered, one beat out of step, then another, then another, as if somewhere in the machine of them, very far down, something small and very old had begun to listen.

第255章 莲花之歌

【中文】
第255章 莲花之歌

阿黛尔的歌声没有停。

那个被锁链缚在黑铁王座上的女孩，苍白的面孔上泪痕未干，嘴唇微微张开，吐出的是西泽尔从未听过的旋律。不是翡冷翠的弥撒，不是马斯顿的童谣，也不是博尔吉亚家族晚宴上那种华丽的歌剧唱段。

那声音极轻极细，像莲花花瓣从水面上浮起来时推开的第一圈涟漪。

"满池莲花在淤泥中根脉相连——"

阿黛尔的声音开始变大，旋律从细弱变得清晰，每一个音节都带着一种古老的、仿佛从地底深处渗出来的共鸣。

"我们是同一棵树上的花朵——"

那不是人类世界的语言。

西泽尔听不懂歌词的含义，但他的后颈忽然传来灼烫的温度，像有什么东西在皮肤下面被点燃了。那股热顺着脊椎往上蔓延，抵达后脑时忽然炸开——不是疼痛，而是一种铺天盖地的、被记忆淹没的错觉。他看到了锡兰，看到了圣女塔的尖顶在夕阳下投出长长的影子，看到了满池白莲在微风中摇曳。

那是世界树灌入他神经通路里的记忆碎片。

可现在那些碎片没有被强行灌入，它们随着阿黛尔的歌声自行涌出来，像潮水退去后沙滩上留下的贝壳，一枚一枚，安静地摆在他面前。

"根在深处，叶在高处——"

阿黛尔的歌声越来越大。

整个圆形石室都在回荡着她的声音。那些暗金色的黄铜齿轮开始加速旋转，嗡鸣声从低沉的蜂鸣变成尖锐的金属嘶叫，仿佛有千万条弦同时被拨动。穹顶上镶嵌的数以万计的微型齿轮一个接一个亮起来，发出暗金色的光，像一片倒悬的星空骤然苏醒。

莱昂纳多·博尔吉亚脸上的表情变了。

"让她闭嘴！"他低声说，声音里没有方才那种从容的优雅，而是一种被突然打断的焦躁。

数十架红色眼睛的欧米茄原型体应声而动，向黑铁王座扑去。

可阿黛尔的歌声没有中断。

"三千世界，同根同源——"

那些向王座冲去的欧米茄原型体忽然停住了。

不是全部，是其中一部分。

西泽尔看见了——在那群冲在最前方的暗金色巨人中间，有几架的瞳孔颜色正在变化。从暗金色，到赤铜色，到翠绿色，像被阿黛尔的歌声一层一层地洗刷。金色纹路从它们的面甲上褪去，取而代之的是一种更古老、更安静的纹路，那些纹路的形状像是莲花的花瓣。

"莲花开时，根须知道——"

七架。

八架。

十二架。

越来越多的欧米茄原型体停下了脚步，它们的瞳孔从暗金色变成了翠绿色，面甲上浮现出锡兰古梵文的纹路，仿佛世界树残枝在它们的装甲上重新刻下了自己的名字。

莱昂纳多的右臂抬起来了。那条由精密齿轮和红水银微晶构成的机械臂顶端伸出一个控制装置，六边形的黑色金属盒子，表面刻满了机械神教齿轮纹章的微型铭文。他将装置对准那些绿色眼睛的欧米茄原型体，手指按下了中央的暗金色按键。

一声尖锐的高频脉冲从装置中释放出来。

圆形石室的空气仿佛被一根无形的针刺穿。

那些绿色眼睛的欧米茄原型体同时颤抖了一下，它们的装甲板上的莲花纹路在高频脉冲的冲击下闪烁不定，像风中的烛火。

可它们没有服从。

十二架绿色眼睛的欧米茄原型体同时转身，暗金色的巨刃和蒸汽连铳对准了身后那些仍然保持着红色眼睛的同类。

第一架绿色眼睛的欧米茄原型体动了。

它的动作快得不像是一台巨型机动傀儡，而是像一头被激怒的犀牛。它横冲直撞地撞进了红色眼睛的欧米茄原型体群中，暗金色巨刃横扫，一刀将一架红色眼睛的同类从腰部斩成两截。切口处喷涌出金红色的粘稠液体——不是鲜血，是欧米茄原型体的体液，那种带着金属光泽的暗红金色。

圆形石室瞬间变成了战场。

绿色眼睛的欧米茄原型体群与红色眼睛的欧米茄原型体群扭打在一起，暗金色巨刃交错，蒸汽喷发的嘶叫声和金属碰撞的巨响混成一片。穹顶上那些刚刚苏醒的齿轮被冲击波震得脱落下坠，砸在地上碎成一堆冒烟的废铜烂铁。

莱昂纳多再次按下控制装置的按键，频率比上一次更高。

脉冲。

可绿色眼睛的欧米茄原型体群只是停顿了不到一秒钟，然后更加猛烈地扑向红色眼睛的同类。

"不可能……"莱昂纳多的声音第一次出现了裂痕。

他看向黑铁王座上的阿黛尔，女孩的歌声仍在继续，翠绿色的眼睛里倒映着穹顶上齿轮转动的暗金色光芒，泪水从她的眼角滑落，可嘴唇上那个古老的旋律没有中断。

那首歌不是普通的歌。

那首歌是三百年前锡兰末代星见留给后代的钥匙，是世界树残枝与其造物之间最后的血脉纽带。琳琅夫人把这首歌教给阿黛尔，不是作为摇篮曲，而是作为一道封印——当世界树残枝的造物失控时，这首歌可以唤醒它们体内被埋藏的星见记忆，让它们想起自己本来的面目。

不是兵器。

是花朵。

"阿方索！"西泽尔在混乱中高喊。

阿方索已经动了。

他蹲在碎石后面，新款蜘蛛巢腕表上八只微型机械蜘蛛全部释放出去，那些拇指盖大小的青铜造物以极快的速度穿越战场，避开正面交战的欧米茄原型体，从侧面迂回到黑铁王座附近。机械蜘蛛钻入锁链的关节缝隙，齿轮咬合的细微声在金属碰撞的巨响中几乎听不见。

"密码是七位……"阿方索的手指在腕表上飞速跳动，读取着锁链控制装置反馈回来的信号特征，"不对……六位……也不对……五位机械编码加两位锡兰校验码……"他的额头渗出了细密的汗珠，"唐璜！帮我挡三十秒！"

蔷薇之鬼已经冲到了他身前，超轻型的刺客甲胄在战场上灵活得像一条游鱼，梵天骑枪的枪尖接连刺穿两架试图靠近的红色眼睛欧米茄原型体的关节部位，金红色的体液从穿刺口喷涌而出。

黑铁王座上，阿黛尔终于唱完了最后一句。

"——根须相连，永不分离。"

旋律在圆形石室中缓缓消散，像一池涟漪终于归于平静。

可那些绿色眼睛的欧米茄原型体没有停止战斗。

西泽尔不再等了。

他从碎石后面冲出来，新型红龙试制版甲胄的蒸汽核心轰然全开，超重武装的动力系统将他的速度推到了极限。他的目标只有一个——莱昂纳多·博尔吉亚，那个站在石室中央、浑身超过八成都是机械结构的男人。

原罪机关真正的主人。

初代教皇的直系后裔。

三百年来在暗处操控着一切的幕后黑手。

莱昂纳多看见了他。

"红龙。"莱昂纳多低声说，那双和西泽尔极为相似的眼睛里没有恐惧，只有一种古怪的、像是在欣赏一件自己亲手雕刻的艺术品的平静，"你终于来了。"

他抬起右手，机械臂的控制装置对准了西泽尔。

高频脉冲再次释放。

新型红龙甲胄表面的电子系统在脉冲的冲击下剧烈闪烁，不朽之王系统芯片传来一阵灼热的警告信号，可西泽尔没有减速。他咬着牙把蒸汽压推到了三倍——超荷，甲胄的关节发出金属过载的尖锐嘶叫。

Excalibur残刃在他手中亮起来。

那把由龙牙剑断茬和圣剑碎片拼成的残缺圣剑，散发着只有欧米茄原型体才能感知的特殊频率，那种频率像一根烧红的铁针刺进了红色眼睛欧米茄原型体的神经接驳系统，让它们产生了短暂的混乱。

西泽尔从混乱中穿过。

距离莱昂纳多还有三十米。

二十米。

十米——

一架红色眼睛的欧米茄原型体挡在了他面前，暗金色巨刃从上方近乎笔直地劈下来。那一刀的速度极快，力道极重，劈下的瞬间空气都被压缩出一声闷响。

西泽尔侧身闪避，Excalibur残刃在闪避的同时横切，刀锋上那层焚烧欧米茄自愈神经纤维的特殊频率在切口处留下一道焦黑的痕迹。红色眼睛的欧米茄原型体的左臂被齐根切断，金红色的体液从断面喷出，像一堵滚烫的瀑布。

他没有停顿，从断臂的间隙中穿过，继续向前冲。

莱昂纳多终于后退了一步。

只是一步，却是这位原罪机关真正的主人在这场战斗中第一次后退。

而此刻，在维苏威火山更深处的密涅瓦机关旧基地中，薇若兰正站在武器库的最后一道铁门前。

她的手里握着密涅瓦机关总长六翼猫头鹰黄铜徽章，徽章的芯片嵌入了铁门旁的识别槽中，齿轮咬合的细微声响过后，铁门缓缓打开。

武器库里很暗，空气中弥漫着红水银特有的金属腥味。

她点燃了一根火柴。

火光摇曳，照亮了武器库中央的展示台。台面上放着一只金色的机械鸟。

那鸟和西泽尔八岁在克里特岛手工制作的那只一模一样。

一样的黄铜翅膀，一样的红水银微晶眼睛，一样的弹簧发条结构。鸟的胸口刻着一行极小的字——

"Rex Immortalis."

佛朗哥教授留下的梵天陨落炸弹启动装置。

【English】
Chapter 255 — The Lotus Song

Adele's voice did not stop.

The girl chained to the black-iron throne had stopped weeping some minutes ago, but the tracks of the tears were still on her pale face, catching the dim light of the brass gears turning in the wall. Her lips were barely parted, and what came out was a melody Cesare had never heard in his life. Not a Florentine Mass. Not a Marston lullaby. Not one of the ornamented operatic arias the Borgia liked to pour into their banquets.

The voice was very fine, very thin, like the first ring a lotus petal makes when it lifts off the water.

"Full pools of lotus, roots entwined in the mud—"

The voice began to swell. The melody clarified. Each syllable carried an old resonance, as if it had been rising out of the earth for a long, long while.

"We are flowers on the same tree—"

It was not a language of the human world.

Cesare could not parse the words. But at the nape of his neck something caught — a heat under the skin, as if a wire were being drawn through his spine toward the back of his skull. He gritted his teeth, expecting pain. What came instead was a kind of drowning. He saw Ceylon. The pointed roofs of the Saintess Tower, throwing long shadows at sunset. A pond of white lotus, the petals moving in a thin wind. The smell of iron in rain.

These were the memory-fragments the World-Tree had pushed down his nerve-channels. He had felt them before, and they had felt like a thing being forced in.

Not this time. This time they came of their own accord, rising with Adele's voice, and lay down in front of him like shells left by a retreating tide.

"Root in the deep, leaf in the high—"

Her voice grew.

The whole circular stone chamber rang with it. The dark-gold brass gears set into the walls began to turn faster. Their drone climbed from the low hum of bees into the metallic whine of ten thousand strings plucked at once. High on the dome, the thousands of pinhead gears woke one by one — a dark-gold inverted sky opening its eyes.

The cold-stern mask on Leonardo Borgia's face cracked.

"Make her stop," he said, very quietly. The cultivated ease was gone from his voice. What was left was a man interrupted.

Dozens of the red-eyed Omega prototypes surged toward the throne.

Adele did not stop singing.

"Three thousand worlds, one root, one source—"

And the prototypes at the front of the charge faltered.

Not all. Some of them. The fastest of the dark-gold giants slowed, and the color of their pupils began to change. From dark-gold to copper, from copper to emerald, as if her voice were washing them in successive coats. The filigree on their faceplates was fading; in its place older, quieter lines were surfacing — lines shaped like lotus petals, as if a piece of the World-Tree were carving its name back into their armor.

"Lotus opens, and the root knows—"

Seven.

Eight.

Twelve.

More and more of the prototypes stopped their advance. Their pupils settled into green. The faceplates showed Sinhalese glyphs older than the cathedrals of Constantinople. They had remembered, Cesare realized, what they had been made from before the Borgia had made them into weapons.

Not weapons.

Flowers.

Cesare had not known he was holding his breath until it came out of him in a sharp line. He looked over his shoulder at the cover of broken stone where Alfonso was crouched.

"Alfonso."

Alfonso was already moving.

He thumbed the release on the new-style Spider-Nest wristwatch. Eight micro-spiders, no bigger than a thumbprint, brass-bodied and quick as cockroaches, spilled out and broke into a wide arc around the battle. They were not built for fighting. They were built for working their way into the joints of things that should not be opened, and they did it now, slipping between the feet of the fighting Omegas, threading sideways toward the black-iron throne, climbing the chains.

"Password's seven digits," Alfonso murmured, his eyes half-closed, reading the signal-pattern the chain-locks were broadcasting back to his watch. "No — six. No — five mechanical, two Ceylon check-digits. Sweat crawled at his temples. "Don Juan! Thirty seconds!"

The Rose-Ghost was already there.

The assassin's light-frame armor moved through the chaos like a fish moving through reeds, the Brahma lance punching through the knee-joints of two red-eyed prototypes that had got too close. Gold-red fluid — not blood, the Omegas' own kind of ichor, dark and metallic, hot — gouted from the punctures and hissed on the stone.

On the black-iron throne, Adele sang the last line.

"— Roots entwined, never to part."

The melody faded. A circle of ripples went out across the air of the chamber and was gone.

The green-eyed prototypes did not stop fighting.

Cesare came out of cover.

The new Red Dragon prototype's steam-core caught and roared, the over-weight rig taking him at the limit of what it had been designed to do. He aimed himself at the figure in the center of the chamber — the man whose body was more than eight parts in ten mechanism, who had stood quite still while the world around him tore itself to pieces.

The true master of the Original Sin Bureau.
Direct descendant of the first Pope.
The hand behind three hundred years of hidden history.

Leonardo saw him coming.

"Red Dragon," Leonardo said softly. His eyes, so like Cesare's own, held no fear. There was only a strange calm in them — the way a man watches a sculpture he carved years ago finally come to life. "You came at last."

He raised his right arm. The control-device at the end of the mechanical limb — a hexagonal black box, etched over its surface with the toothed cogs of the Mechanist creed — turned toward Cesare. His finger found the dark-gold button at its center.

A high-frequency pulse screamed out of the device.

It was the sound of a needle pushed through the air of the chamber. The Red Dragon's electronics flickered. The Immortal-King system chip behind Cesare's eyes flashed a hot warning into his skull. He gritted his teeth, shoved the steam-pressure to three times rated — over-load — and the joints of the suit began to scream with the pitch of metal being asked to do what it was not built to do.

The Excalibur shard in his hand lit up.

The broken thing — a length of dragon-fang blade married to a fragment of the holy sword, more holy relic than weapon now — gave off a frequency only an Omega could feel, a frequency like a red-hot needle driven into the healing nerve-fibers of the red-eyed machines, jamming them for half a heartbeat, just enough.

Cesare went through the jam.

Thirty meters to Leonardo.

Twenty.

Ten —

A red-eyed Omega stepped into his path. The dark-gold cleaver came down nearly vertical. The wind of its fall made a flat thud in the air. Cesare twisted. The Excalibur shard came across at the same time; its burning frequency left a blackened scorch where it cut. The Omega's arm came off at the root. Gold-red fluid fountained out, a hot wall of it, and the severed hand kept its grip on the cleaver as it hit the ground.

Cesare did not slow. He went through the gap where the arm had been, and kept going.

Leonardo Borgia took a step back.

One step. Only one. But it was the first step backward the master of the Original Sin Bureau had taken in this whole fight, and the sound of it was louder than the rest.

—

Far below Vesuvius, in the older chambers of the Minerva Bureau, the air was colder than it should have been.

Violante stood in front of the last iron door of the armory. The six-winged owl badge in her hand was a heavy piece of brass, dull with age. She pressed the chip in its center into the slot beside the door. A small sound of gears taking hold, a click, and the door rolled open on its old tracks.

The armory was dark.

The air tasted of red mercury — that particular metallic tang at the back of the throat that no ventilation could ever quite clear, the smell of the Bureau's oldest weapons, the smell of things not meant to be used and so kept here in the dark.

She struck a match.

The flame wavered, steadied. In the middle of the room, on a single display stand, there was a mechanical bird.

It was the same bird.

The one Cesare had built by hand on Crete when he was eight, with borrowed tools and a piece of red mercury he had stolen from his tutor's desk. The same brass wings, with the same carefully filed feathers. The same red-mercury micro-crystal eyes, which caught the match-light and threw it back red. The same spring-wound works, the same tiny escapement. Etched into the breast, in letters so small you had to lean in close to read them —

Rex Immortalis.

Professor Franco's ignition device for the Prometheus Fall.

Violante held the match steady and did not move for a long time.

【中文】
第256章 红莲刺穿心脏

五米。

西泽尔的视野收窄成一条隧道。隧道尽头只有一个目标。

Excalibur残刃在他手中脉动，那种只有欧米茄原型体才能感知的特殊频率像一根烧红的铁针刺进它们混乱的神经接驳系统，让红色眼睛的欧米茄原型体群陷入了短暂的痉挛。他从痉挛的机体之间穿过，龙牙剑断茬和圣剑碎片拼成的残刃所过之处，自愈神经纤维被焚烧出焦黑的痕迹，金红色的体液像瀑布一样从断口喷涌。

三米。

一架红色眼睛的欧米茄原型体挡在他面前，比之前那些都要高大，胸前红水银核心跳动得明亮而稳定——这是四十年封存中保持着最佳状态的一架。它的暗金色巨刃从上方近乎垂直劈下，速度极快，力道极重，仿佛一柄死神的铡刀从天而降。

西泽尔侧身闪避，残刃在闪避的同时横切。刀锋上那层焚烧频率在切口处留下一道焦黑的灼痕，欧米茄原型体的左臂从肩关节处被齐根切断，金红色的体液喷了他半身。他没有停顿，从断臂的间隙中穿过，踩着倒下机体的肩膀借力前跃。

一米——

然后他到了莱昂纳多面前。

原罪机关真正的主人站在圆形大厅正中央，背后是那棵粗壮到需要数十人才能合抱的世界树主干。暗金色的树干上密布着黄铜微型齿轮，每一个都在缓缓转动，发出低沉绵长的嗡鸣。树枝末梢悬挂的红水银核心像一颗颗暗红色的果实，在穹顶投下血一样的微光。地面从树根基座向外刻满梵文同心圆纹路，每一道纹路都在发光。

莱昂纳多的银色猫头鹰面具反射着红光，金属质感的下颌和右手在灯光下泛着冷辉。

"红龙。"他开口，声音是精密齿轮咬合的质感，冰冷，不带一丝人类的温度，"你走了这么远——就为了她？"

大厅深处，莲花通道的方向，阿黛尔的声音远远传来。锡兰莲花之歌的旋律在大厅里回荡，每一个音符都像一滴滴进钢铁森林的清水，甜而哀伤，像是母亲在深夜哼给孩子听的摇篮曲。

西泽尔没有回答。

他只是收紧了握着残刃的手指。

不朽之王系统的安全阈值是三分钟。芯片过载后他将彻底失去对英雄人格的控制权。他不知道自己已经战斗了多久——两分钟？三分钟？系统的金色光芒正在从他的视野边缘消退，取而代之的是越来越沉重的四肢和越来越尖锐的耳鸣。

够了。他只需要一次机会。

他冲了出去。

莱昂纳多的金属下颌咔嗒一声，似乎是笑。

"你母亲也是这样，"他说，"明知道是死，还是往前冲。"

他没有拔刀。他的右臂从肘关节处裂开，露出内部层层叠叠的机械结构——活塞、电缆、红水银导管。手指分成了五片，每一片都变成一柄窄刃刀，五刃合拢时如同一只张开的钢铁手掌，向西泽尔的颈部横扫而来。

速度快得不可思议。

三百年的时光让这副机械身体被调试到了人类永远无法企及的极限，每一寸金属都经过了上万次精密校准，每一次动作都精确到毫秒。

西泽尔低头。

五柄刀刃从他头盔上方掠过，刮掉了一层红色涂装，露出下方银灰色的精金骨架。他没有后退，新红龙甲胄右臂内置的龙牙剑弹出——一把长而弯曲的暗金色大剑，刃口泛着冷光——自下而上撩向莱昂纳多的右肘关节。

龙牙剑切入关节缝隙。

金属发出尖锐的嘶叫，像人临死前的惨叫。一截机械前臂从肘部断裂，带着火花和红水银飞溅的液体砸在地上，手指还在无意识地一张一合。

但莱昂纳多的左手已经动了。

左肩甲片翻开，一门口径不大的红水银短管炮从肩槽中伸出，炮口亮起灼目的白光。

西泽尔侧扑。

炮弹出膛。红水银等离子束擦过他的右肩甲，在地面打出一个拳头大小的熔洞，洞口的金石还在冒着红烟。

"三百年，"莱昂纳多平静地说，仿佛那截断裂的手臂不是他的，"我把血肉的弱点全部剔除了。我不会再衰老，不会再疲倦，不会再恐惧。"他抬起左手，五指并拢成刀，向西泽尔的胸口直刺，"这就是完美的代价。"

西泽尔用龙牙剑格挡。

两柄金属刃口撞在一起，溅出一蓬火星。莱昂纳多的手指刀在龙牙剑刃上刮出刺耳的声响，然后——那五片刀刃忽然散开，像张开的爪子绕过剑身，抓向西泽尔的面甲。

西泽尔后仰。

指尖从面甲前方三厘米处掠过。他抬脚踹向莱昂纳多的膝关节，靴底的弹簧驱动装置迸发出一吨的推力。金属膝盖凹陷下去一寸，莱昂纳多后退了半步。

新红龙甲胄的龙牙剑顺势劈下，斩向莱昂纳多左肩的炮槽。

莱昂纳多用左臂去挡。

左前臂从肘部被整齐地切断，断面整齐得像是用尺子量过，红水银和润滑液混合的液体喷涌而出。那截带着炮槽的前臂飞出去，撞在一架倒伏的欧米茄原型体上，滚了两圈才停下来。

莱昂纳多低头看了看自己两截断裂的手臂。

圆形大厅里安静了一瞬。头顶的世界树齿轮还在转动，红水银果实还在散发着血光，远处阿黛尔的声音还在唱。

"你有一双和她一样的眼睛。"莱昂纳多抬起头，面具下露出的湛蓝眼睛第一次有了某种人类的表情——不是愤怒，不是恐惧，而是一种古老的、疲惫的怀念，"你的母亲。琳琅。"

西泽尔没有说话。龙牙剑从莱昂纳多的残臂中拔出，金属摩擦的嘶叫在空旷的大厅里回荡。

他挥剑。

Excalibur残刃从另一只手同时斩出，刃口上那层焚烧频率在空气中划出一道灼目的弧光。但那弧光在接触莱昂纳多胸甲的瞬间便熄灭了——特殊频率只对欧米茄原型体的自愈神经纤维有效，对人类改造的机械结构毫无作用。残刃在胸甲上只留下一道浅浅的白印。

莱昂纳多低低地笑了一声。齿轮咬合的笑声。

"你以为Excalibur能杀我？"他说，"我是Excalibur创造者的直系后裔。我是机械神国真正的继承者。"他残存的左臂肩膀处又伸出一截机械触手，触手的末端是一柄锯齿短刃，"你的母亲明白。她明白人性才是设计中最致命的缺陷。"

西泽尔收住攻势。

身后阿黛尔的声音又近了一些，莲花之歌的旋律变得清晰可辨。歌声明明是温柔的，却让圆形大厅里所有幸存的欧米茄原型体都停下了动作——那些被歌声策反的、拥有绿色眼睛的十余架机体安静地站在原地，胸前红水银核心的光芒从金红变成了柔和的翠绿，像是睡着的孩子。

而那些红色眼睛的欧米茄原型体仍在骚动，但没有一架再向前。

西泽尔低下头。

他看着自己胸甲正中央——Excalibur碎片嵌在那里，像一颗跳动的白色星辰。碎片是莲花作战后从残存的圣剑中取回的核心残片，嵌入红龙胸甲后引发了他后颈黄金套管的紫瞳金纹共鸣，是唤醒不朽之王模式的关键钥匙。

如果要取出来——

他抬起左手。

指尖找到了胸甲的接缝，找到碎片底座卡扣的位置。那是三道磁力锁扣，将碎片牢牢固定在胸甲的动力回路中。

如果取出来，不朽之王系统将失去供能核心。芯片会在数秒内过载烧毁，英雄人格将彻底反噬他的神经系统。他的四肢会失去控制，他可能会死。

但如果取不出来，他就杀不掉莱昂纳多。

他扣住了卡扣。

第一道锁扣崩断。胸甲内传出短路的噼啪声。

第二道锁扣崩断。不朽之王系统开始发出尖锐的过载警报。

第三道——

他猛地一扯。

碎片从胸甲中脱出的瞬间，一道白光从他的胸腔爆射而出，刺得整个大厅都为之一亮。白光中夹杂着金色的纹路，像是某种古老文字在他的皮肤下燃烧。后颈的黄金套管剧烈发烫，烫得他几乎失去知觉，但那种痛楚很快就被另一种更深层的撕裂感取代——

英雄人格在系统崩溃的瞬间挣扎着想要挣脱束缚。

西泽尔咬紧牙关，把那股狂暴的力量压回神经通路最底层。鲜血从他的鼻孔和耳道同时渗出，面甲内侧的视野染上了一层红色。

但他手中多了一枚碎片。

纯粹的、未经拼合的、完整的Excalibur碎片。它在他掌心中脉动着白金色光芒，那种光芒比残刃上的频率更纯粹、更暴烈，像是一团被压缩到极致的恒星。

莱昂纳多的湛蓝眼睛终于变了。

那不是恐惧。是三百年来第一次真正的不确定。

"你——"他的声音第一次失去了齿轮咬合的稳定，"你不能——"

西泽尔没有给他说完的机会。

新红龙甲胄的双腿弹簧驱动同时弹射，他整个人像一颗暗红色的炮弹射向莱昂纳多。莱昂纳多残存的机械触手挥锯齿短刃迎面劈来，西泽尔没有躲。

锯齿切入他的左肩甲，金属与金属的碰撞溅出一蓬火花。但他的右手已经贴上了莱昂纳多的胸甲。

掌心下，金属冰冷，传来沉重的、有节奏的震动。

机械心脏还在跳。

西泽尔把Excalibur碎片抵在莱昂纳多胸甲正中央。

然后——

刺了进去。

碎片切入精金和影金属层叠的胸甲，像热刀切入牛油。白金色的光芒从切口处喷涌而出，照亮了莱昂纳多面具下方那张由齿轮和金属丝构成的脸。他能看见那具机械心脏——拳头大小的暗金色球体，悬浮在由红水银导管和金属肋骨编织的笼架中，正在以每分钟三百次的速度疯狂跳动。

碎片没入机械心脏。

白光在球体内部炸开。

红水银在高温中沸腾，齿轮在白光中一个接一个停转，金属肋骨一片片崩断向外弹射。莱昂纳多的身体剧烈痉挛，残存的所有机械触手同时失控——有的在空中胡乱挥舞，有的蜷缩成一团，有的朝着西泽尔的身体猛刺过来。

西泽尔没有松手。

他把碎片往里推了一寸。

机械心脏的跳动骤然变慢。

三百次。

两百次。

一百次。

五十次。

"你……"莱昂纳多的声音从齿轮咬合变成了气流穿过碎裂金属管的嘶嘶声，"你应该……成为……新的……神使……新的……载体……"

十次。

"你母亲……的……记忆……就在……"

机械心脏停了。

最后一次跳动像是被什么东西猛地掐断，连一个完整的搏动都没有完成。暗金色的球体在笼架中缓缓黯淡下去，红水银从沸腾变成死寂，齿轮一片片停转。

莱昂纳多金属眼睛里的红光熄灭了。

不是突然熄灭，而是像一盏油尽的灯，挣扎着明灭了两次，最终沉入黑暗。

银色猫头鹰面具从脸上滑落，摔在地上，裂成两半。面具下没有脸——只有更多的金属、更多的齿轮、更多的电缆。但那些金属上布满了岁月的痕迹，每一道划痕、每一处磨损都是三百年时光的证据。

而那对金属眼睛中最后一缕光芒消失之前，在面部的金属表层上，浮现出了某种类似于人类表情的纹路。

不是愤怒。

不是怨恨。

是悔恨。

"我错了……"

声音几乎听不见，只是一股微弱的气流从碎裂的声带机械中挤出，但大厅里安静得连针落地都清晰可闻。

"人性……才是……最强大的……武器……"

光芒彻底熄灭。

西泽尔从莱昂纳多的胸口抽出碎片。白金色的光芒已经黯淡下去，碎片表面的纹路出现了细密的裂纹。机械心脏的位置只剩下一个黑乎乎的空洞，里面还冒着红水银蒸发的青烟。

他把碎片攥在手中，退后一步。

圆形大厅里忽然安静得可怕。

头顶世界树的齿轮还在转，但转速明显慢了下来，像是一台运转了太久的机器终于开始疲惫。树枝上红水银核心的光芒一明一暗地闪烁，像是心跳。远处阿黛尔的声音渐渐弱下去，莲花之歌的最后一个尾音在大厅穹顶回荡了很久，才终于消散。

那些拥有绿色眼睛的欧米茄原型体停下了所有动作。

十余架曾经被策反的机体安静地站在大厅各处，胸前红水银核心的翠绿光芒缓缓暗淡，最终变成了一种柔和的、近乎透明的浅金色。它们不再攻击，不再移动，甚至不再发出运转的嗡鸣声，像是一群终于被允许入睡的孩子。

红水银核心的跳动变得极慢、极轻，几乎感受不到。

幸存者们抬起头，看着这一切。

唐璜站在大厅边缘，蔷薇之鬼甲胄的剑尖还指着地面。他的面甲下传来一声极轻的、像是叹息的气流。

昆提良的奥古斯都缓缓放下秘银重盾。闭眼狮头纹章在红光中显得格外沉默。

阿方索的所罗门王甲胄垂下了狙击枪管，枪口还在冒着冷却后的青烟。

瓦莲京娜站在大厅入口的高台上，改装神怒Ⅲ型甲胄的暗银色装甲上满是战斗的痕迹，冰原寒玉在胸口微微发光。

阿黛尔坐在黑铁王座上，双手放在膝头，歌声停止后她的脸色苍白得近乎透明，额头上细密的汗珠顺着脸颊滑落。但她的眼睛是亮的，亮得像两颗星星。

碧儿跪在王座旁边，双手抓着阿黛尔的手，无声地哭。

西泽尔站在莱昂纳多的尸体旁边。英雄人格的反噬正在他体内翻涌，四肢末端已经开始失去知觉，视网膜上的红点越来越多。

然后他听见了一个声音。

很小。很轻。

咔。

像是某种精密的机械装置被触发了开关。

他低下头。

莱昂纳多胸口的空洞旁边，残存的机械肋骨之间，嵌着一个他之前没注意到的装置——比拳头略小，暗金色金属外壳，上面有一颗红色按钮。

按钮正在亮起来。

红光脉动。一次。两次。三次。

然后不再闪烁，保持着恒定的、稳定的红色。

一种高频的嗡鸣声从装置中传出，向四面八方扩散。圆形大厅地面的梵文纹路突然全部亮起，金光如潮水般从同心圆中心向外扩散，穿过大厅的每一道缝隙，穿过岩壁，穿过矿道，传向维苏威火山更深处。

西泽尔后颈的黄金套管再次剧烈发烫。

他感受到了——通过神经接驳系统，通过红水银的共鸣，他感受到了维苏威火山内外的欧米茄原型体群正在发生的变化。

那些在火山内各层矿道中待命的红色眼睛的机体——数以百计的——正在启动。它们的红水银核心从休眠状态中被唤醒，开始加速跳动。它们的四肢开始活动。它们的飞行机构开始展开。

它们在上升。

向着地表。向着天空。

向着东方。

西泽尔通过神经接驳系统读到了那些机体的目标坐标。

东方。

王屋山。

世界树主根节点。

莱昂纳多临死前为自己设下的最后一个指令——当生命体征消失时，将所有可调动的欧米茄原型体送往东方，摧毁世界树残枝的另一半。

不是重启机械神国。

是毁掉它。

让所有人都得不到。

而更可怕的是——西泽尔能感觉到那些正在升空的欧米茄原型体的红水银核心正在进入一种特殊的运转模式。核心温度在持续升高。内部压力在持续增大。

自毁程序。

每一个飞向东方的欧米茄原型体，都是一颗正在倒计时的红水银炸弹。

西泽尔单膝跪在莱昂纳多的尸体旁边，Excalibur碎片从他失去知觉的手指间滑落，叮当一声掉在地上。英雄人格的反噬让他的视野变成了一片模糊的血红，但他的意识比任何时候都清醒。

他听见身后传来碧儿惊恐的声音："少爷——！"

他听见瓦莲京娜在远处低声说了一个数字。

"十五分钟。"

十五分钟。

数百架欧米茄原型体将飞抵王屋山。届时它们会像数百颗流星一样坠落在世界树主根节点上，将那里的一切——楚舜华、鬼武者军团、世界树残根——全部化为灰烬。

他必须阻止这一切。

而他手中，最后的底牌，刚刚被佛朗哥教授藏在这座火山深处某处的反物质炸弹。

西泽尔抬起头，望向圆形大厅穹顶那片被红光照亮的天空。血一样的光在他紫瞳中跳动，金色纹路在瞳孔深处明灭不定。

他感觉到自己的心跳正在放缓。

不是因为恐惧。是因为他已经做出了决定。

【English】
Chapter 256 — The Red Lotus Pierces the Heart

Five meters.

Cesare's field of vision had narrowed itself to a tunnel. At the far end of that tunnel there was only one thing that mattered.

The broken edge of Excalibur pulsed in his hand, and that frequency — a frequency only an Omega prototype body could read — burned through the scrambled neural-link of the red-eyed units like a red-hot needle slipped between the wires. For half a heartbeat every Omega prototype in the hall seized at once, a cascade of seizing limbs and twisting shoulders, and he went through them. The remnant blade — Dragonfang shank spliced to the saint-sword's tooth — opened a path. Where it passed, the self-healing nerve fibres blackened and smoked, and the gold-red ichor that stood these machines in for blood came out in fans, in sheets, in sheets of it, as though he were walking through a field of cut saplings.

Three meters.

One of the red-eyed prototypes stood in his way. Bigger than the others, taller by a head, its chest-core bright and steady with the calm pulse of a thing that had slept forty years in perfect vacuum. The dark-gold cleaver came down from above, almost vertical, the speed and weight of a headsman's blade if the headsman were the grave.

Cesare stepped off the line. The remnant blade came across in the same motion. The cut left a charred seam at the joint. The Omega's left arm came away at the shoulder, ichor fountaining half across his cuirass, and he did not pause. He went through the gap where the arm had been, set a boot on the falling shoulder, and launched himself forward.

One meter.

And then he was at Leonardo.

The true master of Original Sin stood in the centre of the round hall, his back to the world-tree trunk — a column of dark wood so wide it would have taken twenty men with linked hands to ring it. The trunk was studded with thousands of tiny brass gears, each turning at its own slow rate, and the low hum they made together was the sound of a clock that had been running since before the world had a name for clock. Hanging at the ends of the branches, dark-red fruits of cinnabar-mercury glowed in their cradles and threw a blood-coloured light down over the polished stone of the floor. Concentric rings of Sanskrit-script had been incised into that floor outwards from the tree's base, every line of them glowing.

Leonardo's silver owl-mask caught the red light. The metal jaw and the metal right hand both had that cold, workmanlike sheen.

"Red Dragon." His voice had the precision of meshed gears. Cold. Not a shred of human temperature in it. "You have come all this way — for her?"

From the lotus-vault, far back in the depths of the hall, Adele's voice. The Ceylon Lotus Song moving through the stone. Every note fell into the iron forest of the chamber like a drop of clear water, sweet and grieving, the kind of thing a mother hums to a child she has not been allowed to keep.

Cesare did not answer.

He only tightened his grip on the remnant blade.

The safety-threshold of the Immortal King system was three minutes. When the chip overloaded he would lose the Hero-persona entirely and not get it back. He did not know how long he had already spent in this hall — two minutes, three? The system's gold was retreating at the edges of his sight, and in its place the slow lead of his limbs, the whine in his ears, the red dots gathering on the dark of his visor.

He only needed one opening.

He went.

Leonardo's metal jaw clicked. Almost a laugh.

"Your mother was the same," he said. "She knew it was death, and she went forward anyway."

He did not draw a weapon. His right arm split at the elbow, layer after layer of mechanism revealed — pistons, cabling, the bright wet tubing of the cinnabar-mercury line. The five fingers each became a narrow blade, and as they closed together they made the shape of a steel hand spread wide, and that hand came for Cesare's neck.

The speed of it was not human. Three hundred years of tuning had pushed the body past anything flesh could ever approach. Every joint calibrated ten thousand times. Every motion accurate to the millisecond.

Cesare dropped his head.

The five blades passed a finger's width over his helm, shearing a curl of red paint from the crest and exposing the bright adamantine skeleton beneath. He did not retreat. The Dragonfang built into the right arm of the new Red Dragon cuirass came out — a long, curved dark-gold sword, the edge cold in the light — and he lifted it, underhand, into the joint of Leonardo's right elbow.

The Dragonfang bit into the gap between plates.

The sound the metal made was the kind of sound a man makes when he is dying. A section of the mechanical forearm broke away at the elbow and went tumbling to the floor trailing sparks and a fine spray of mercury-oil, and the fingers at its end still opened and closed, opening and closing, as if they had not yet been told their master was hurt.

But Leonardo's left arm had already moved.

A panel in the left pauldron slid back. From the slot a small-bore cinnabar-mercury cannon emerged, and the mouth of it came up white.

Cesare threw himself sideways.

The shot went off. The plasma bolt licked across his right shoulder-plate, and where it passed through the floor it cut a hole the size of a fist in the stone, the lip of which was still smoking red.

"Three hundred years," Leonardo said, as if the missing arm were not his. "I have cut every weakness of the flesh out of me. I will not age again. I will not tire. I will not be afraid." He lifted the left hand, the fingers pressed together into a blade, and thrust it straight for Cesare's chest. "This is the price of perfection."

Cesare caught it on the Dragonfang.

The two metal edges met, and a shower of sparks went up. Leonardo's finger-blade screamed along the Dragonfang's edge, and then — the five blades fanned open like a hand, like a claw, and went around the sword and for Cesare's visor.

Cesare threw his head back.

The fingertips passed three centimetres in front of the face-plate. He stamped up into the inside of Leonardo's knee, and the spring-driver in the boot struck a ton of force into the metal. The knee caved a finger's width. Leonardo took a half-step back.

The Dragonfang came down through that half-step, aimed for the cannon-slot in the left shoulder.

Leonardo put up the left arm to block it.

The left forearm came away at the elbow as cleanly as though it had been measured, and the stump vented a mingled red and silver mist. The severed limb — cannon and all — flew off across the hall, hit a fallen Omega prototype, rolled twice, and lay still.

Leonardo looked down at the two stumps of himself.

For a moment the round hall was absolutely quiet. Above, the world-tree's gears were still turning. The cinnabar-mercury fruit were still giving off their blood-coloured light. Far off, Adele was still singing.

"You have her eyes," Leonardo said. He raised his head, and the blue of the eyes that showed under the mask had, for the first time, a thing in them that was human. Not anger. Not fear. Something old, something tired, something that remembered. "Your mother. Linglong."

Cesare said nothing. He drew the Dragonfang up out of the ruined shoulder, and the shriek of metal on metal went on echoing through the empty hall for a long time.

He swung.

The Excalibur remnant came in from the other hand at the same moment, the burning frequency along its edge drawing a bright arc in the air. The arc died the moment it touched Leonardo's breastplate — that frequency worked only on the self-healing nerve-fibre of an Omega body; on a man-made mechanical architecture it was useless. The blade left only a shallow white nick in the adamantine-and-shadow-metal plate.

Leonardo laughed, low, the laugh of meshing gears.

"You think Excalibur will kill me?" he said. "I am the direct descendant of the one who forged it. I am the true inheritor of the Machine Kingdom." A new mechanical tentacle pushed out of the stump of his left shoulder, the end of it a short serrated blade. "Your mother understood. She understood that the human element is the most fatal flaw in the design."

Cesare held his stroke.

Behind him, Adele's voice was nearer now, the melody of the Lotus Song coming into focus. The song was gentle, but the effect of it on the hall was strange: every surviving Omega prototype that had been turned by it, the dozen or so with green eyes, had gone still, and the cinnabar-mercury cores in their chests had shifted from the hot gold-red of war to the soft emerald of a sleeping child.

The red-eyed ones still seethed. None of them came forward.

Cesare looked down.

He looked at the centre of his own breastplate. The Excalibur shard was set there, like a small white star. It had been recovered after the Lotus Operation from the wreckage of the saint-sword, and slotted into the Red Dragon plate; it had woken the gold-traced resonance in the violet pupils of the gold casing at the back of his neck, and that resonance was the key that had called up the Immortal King mode at all.

If he took it out —

He raised his left hand.

The fingertips found the seam in the plate, found the catches at the base of the shard's mount. Three magnetic locks holding the shard fast in the plate's power-circuit.

If he took it out, the Immortal King system would lose its power-core. In a few seconds the chip would overload and burn out, and the Hero-persona would feed back through his own nerves. He would lose his limbs. He would die.

And if he did not take it out, he could not kill Leonardo.

He caught the first catch.

It broke. A shorting crackle came out of the plate.

He caught the second.

The Immortal King system began to scream its overload warning.

The third —

He wrenched it open.

The shard came out of the plate, and a white light blew out of his chest and made the whole of the round hall flinch. In the white there were gold tracings, like an old script burning under his skin. The gold casing at the back of his neck went so hot he nearly lost the feel of his own body, and then the heat was replaced by a deeper tearing, as if something vast and very angry were trying to claw its way out of him from the inside.

The Hero-persona, at the moment of the system's collapse, had lunged for freedom.

Cesare set his teeth and shoved the thing back down into the deepest channel of his nerve-bus, and held it there. Blood came out of his nose. Blood came out of his ears. The inside of the visor went red.

But in his right hand he was holding a shard.

A clean, unjoined, complete Excalibur shard. It pulsed in his palm with a white-gold light that was purer, wilder, more violent than the frequency on the broken blade — the light of a star that had been folded down to the size of a man's hand.

Leonardo's blue eyes changed.

It was not fear. For the first time in three hundred years it was genuine uncertainty.

"You —" his voice lost, for the first time, the steady mesh of the gear, "you cannot —"

Cesare did not let him finish.

Both leg-spring drivers of the new Red Dragon cuirass fired together, and he went at Leonardo like a dark-red bolt. Leonardo's remaining tentacle came up, the serrated short-blade chopping down to meet him; Cesare did not dodge.

The serrations took him across the left shoulder-plate, metal on metal, a shower of sparks. But his right hand was already flat against Leonardo's breastplate.

Under his palm, the metal was cold, and there was a heavy, regular throb coming up through it.

The mechanical heart was still beating.

Cesare set the Excalibur shard against the centre of the breastplate.

And pressed.

The shard bit into the layered adamantine and shadow-metal as easily as a hot knife into tallow. White-gold light poured out of the cut, and the light fell on the thing that had been Leonardo's face, where it showed under the broken edge of the owl-mask: a face of gears and metal wires, nothing more. Cesare could see the heart — a fist-sized dark-gold globe held in a cage of mercury-tube and metal rib — and it was beating at three hundred a minute, the rhythm gone ragged with fear.

The shard went into the heart.

The white light went off inside the globe.

The cinnabar-mercury boiled. The gears stopped, one by one, in the white. The metal ribs broke outwards and spat themselves across the floor of the hall. Leonardo's body went into a hard spasm; every remaining mechanical limb came loose at once — some of them waving wildly in the air, some of them curling in on themselves, some of them stabbing blindly into Cesare's body.

Cesare did not let go.

He pushed the shard a finger's width deeper.

The mechanical heart slowed.

Three hundred.

Two hundred.

A hundred.

Fifty.

"You —" The voice had gone from gears to air leaking through a cracked metal pipe, "you were — meant to be — the new — the new god's vessel — the new —"

Ten.

"Your mother's — memories — are —"

The mechanical heart stopped.

The last beat had been cut off in the middle. The dark-gold globe dimmed in its cage, the mercury cooled, the gears finished coming to rest. The red glow in Leonardo's metal eyes faded — not all at once, but as a lamp with the oil out, flickering, flickering, and then gone.

The silver owl-mask slipped from his face and hit the floor and cracked in two. Under the mask there was no face — only more metal, more gears, more cabling. But every surface of it was scored with the marks of years, the small wear of three centuries of use, the kind of marks that only time can put on a thing.

Before the last light went out of the metal eyes, a kind of expression had surfaced in the lines of the metal face.

Not anger.

Not hatred.

Regret.

"I was wrong —"

The voice was almost inaudible. A thread of air out of a broken voice-box. But the hall was so quiet that a needle would have been too loud.

"Humanity — is the — strongest — weapon —"

The light went out.

Cesare drew the shard out of the chest. The white-gold was dim now, and the tracings on the shard's surface had begun to craze with hairline fractures. Where the heart had been there was nothing but a blackened cavity, still trailing the thin blue smoke of boiled mercury.

He held the shard in his fist and stepped back.

The round hall went quiet in a way that was almost unendurable.

Above, the world-tree's gears were still turning, but the rate of them had fallen off, as though the great machine of the place had finally begun to feel its age. The cinnabar-mercury fruit on the branches pulsed with a slower light, the light of a thing almost asleep. Adele's voice, far off, had begun to fade. The last long note of the Lotus Song went on sounding under the dome of the hall for a long time before it finally let go.

The green-eyed prototypes had stopped moving.

The dozen or so units that had been turned by the song stood in their places about the hall, the emerald in their chest-cores going slowly, slowly down, down to a pale, almost transparent gold. They were not attacking, not moving, not even humming. They looked, in the red light, like a roomful of children who had at last been given permission to sleep.

The survivors looked up at this.

Don Juan stood at the edge of the hall, the blade of the Ghost Rose still pointed at the floor. From under the visor a very soft sound came out — a sigh, perhaps, or the shape a sigh would have if it were made of metal.

Augustus of Quintilian lowered the mithril heavy shield. The closed-eyed lion of the device said nothing in the red light.

Alfonso let the barrel of the Solomon's-sniper drop, the muzzle still giving off the thin blue smoke of cooling.

Valentina stood on the high platform at the hall's entrance, the dark-silver plate of her modified Wrath-of-God III cuirass scored from end to end with the marks of the fighting, and the Arctic Jade at her breast pulsed faintly with its own cold blue.

Adele sat on the black iron throne, her hands in her lap. The colour had gone out of her face almost entirely; the sweat on her temples was running down into the line of her jaw. But her eyes were bright. The eyes were the bright thing in the hall.

Belle knelt beside the throne with both her hands wrapped around Adele's, crying without making any sound at all.

Cesare stood beside Leonardo's body. The backwash of the Hero-persona was boiling through his nerves, and the feeling had begun to leave his fingers and his toes. The red in his visor was thickening. There were more dots on the dark of it now, and they were not going away.

And then he heard a sound.

Very small. Very faint.

Click.

The sound of a precision mechanism finding its catch.

He looked down.

In the cage of metal ribs beside the empty socket of the mechanical heart there was a small thing he had not noticed. A little larger than a fist, dark-gold case, a single red button set into the top of it.

The button was lighting up.

It pulsed. Once. Twice. Three times. Then stopped flickering and held a steady, constant red.

A high thin hum went out of the device in every direction at once. Every line of the Sanskrit-circle on the floor woke at the same moment, and a tide of gold went out from the centre, through the seams of the hall, through the rock, through the mine-tunnels, down into the deeper parts of Vesuvius.

The gold casing at the back of Cesare's neck went hot again.

He felt it — through the nerve-link, through the resonance of the cinnabar-mercury — he felt what was happening to the Omega prototypes in the chambers above and below the hall, in every corridor and gallery of the volcano.

The red-eyed units, the ones in reserve, the hundreds of them, were waking from their dormant state. The cinnabar-mercury cores in their chests were accelerating. Their limbs were beginning to move. Their flight-rigs were unfolding.

They were going up.

Toward the surface. Toward the sky.

Toward the east.

Through the nerve-link Cesare read the destination they had been given.

The east.

Wangwu Mountain.

The main root-node of the world-tree.

The last instruction Leonardo had set for himself. The instruction that was to be carried out the moment his own life-signs went. Send every Omega prototype he could still reach to the east. Destroy the other half of the world-tree's remaining branch.

Not to rebuild the Machine Kingdom.

To make sure no one else ever had it.

And there was something worse.

Cesare could feel, in the cores of the units as they rose, a new pattern of running. The temperature in the cores was climbing, steadily, and the pressure inside them was climbing with it. A pattern he had seen only in weapon data-sheets.

A self-destruct routine.

Every one of the units now lifting into the air above Vesuvius was a cinnabar-mercury bomb with a timer on it.

Cesare knelt on the floor beside Leonardo's body. The shard of Excalibur slid out of his fingers, and the small clear sound of it hitting the stone was the only sound in the hall. The backwash of the Hero-persona was turning his sight into a smeared red field, but his mind had never been clearer.

Behind him, Belle's voice, very small: "Young master —"

From the high platform, Valentina spoke a single number.

"Fifteen minutes."

Fifteen minutes. In fifteen minutes the first of the bombs would be over Wangwu Mountain. In fifteen minutes the main root-node, Chu Shunhua, the army of ghost-warriors, every living thing still standing in the shadow of the great tree, would be brought down in a rain of mercury-white fire.

He had to stop it.

And the only card left in his hand was the one Professor Franco had hidden somewhere in the deep of this volcano. The anti-matter charge. The one piece of ordnance the Borgia of Florence had not wanted anyone to know he had built.

Cesare lifted his head. He looked up through the dome of the round hall, through the red light, up at the slice of the sky the dome gave back to him. The light of the place pulsed in his violet eyes. The gold in the pupils of those eyes was there one moment and gone the next.

He could feel his own heart slowing.

It was not fear that was slowing it.

It was the fact that the decision had already been made.

第257章 梵天陨落倒计时
